System DesignMasterclass

Build L5/L6 and staff-level system design judgment through foundations, deliberate practice, complete case studies, and specialist architecture tracks.

Explore the course Start designing 01 / Find your baselineDiagnose your gapsChoose the next skill to practice with evidence. 02 / Test an assumptionOpen the capacity labSee how traffic, storage, and headroom change a design. 03 / Make it deliberateRun a timed attemptFrame, design, and defend. docs.title: Choose your track
docs.text:
ENGINEERING From Mechanisms to Evidence Machine and distributed foundations, performance science, contract lifecycles, operations, and safe evolution. Follow one system through scale, incident, migration, and retirement. 11 chapters, 8 executable fault labs, 1 evolving capstone

01 Foundations Frame ambiguity, estimate scale, model data and indexes, and reason about consistency, reliability, and regions. 17 modules →

02 Patterns Build a reusable vocabulary for hot paths, contention, workflows, search, streams, coordination, and approximation. 13 modules →

03 Networks (L5/L6) Trace packet paths, quantify protocol limits, debug with evidence, and design secure global traffic behavior. 16 chapters + 16 labs + 3 scenarios →

04 Applied AI Systems (L5/L6) Design bounded AI decisions across data, models, retrieval, agents, evaluation, security, reliability, and platform governance. 18 chapters + 12 labs + 3 scenarios ->

05 Practice Lab Diagnose gaps, run progressive drills, break and recover designs, and complete three interview scenario packs. 39 practice pages →

06 Java Concurrency (LLD) Design thread-safe Java 21 components by making shared state, invariants, liveness, cancellation, and test strategy explicit. 13 modules →

07 Case Studies Practice complete designs across commerce, social, media, infrastructure, data, AI, and gaming. 65 designs →

08 Staff Architecture Lead evolution, isolation, control-plane, operability, evidence, privacy, organization, and economics decisions. 9 modules →

09 Specialist Electives Extend generalist design into AI, GPU, local-first, edge, governance, evidence, and formal-method domains. 9 modules →

10 Learning Tools Turn assumptions into capacity consequences and run timed, locally stored practice attempts. 2 interactive tools →

docs.title: L5 · Own the design
docs.text:
Clarify scope, quantify load, produce a coherent end-to-end architecture, and defend its core correctness and scaling decisions.

L5 practice guidance →

docs.title: L6 · Shape the system
docs.text:
Surface hidden invariants, control-plane boundaries, migration paths, failure isolation, policy, cost, and organizational consequences.

L6 practice guidance →

docs.title: The practice loop
docs.text:
1. Frame: clarify users, scope, invariants, SLOs, and exclusions.
  2. Quantify: estimate peak traffic, data volume, skew, and fan-out.
  3. Design: start with the smallest correct system and evolve it under pressure.
  4. Defend: explain consistency, overload, failure recovery, and alternatives.
  5. Compress: deliver the complete answer again in five minutes.

Do not read case studies passively

Open a blank page first. Spend 35–45 minutes on your own design, then use the chapter to find missing decisions: not to memorize boxes and arrows.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text: This course teaches a repeatable way to make and defend system design decisions. It progresses from concepts to evidence: foundations explain the forces, patterns provide reusable moves, Networks develops packet-to-global-path depth, Applied AI Systems develops production AI judgment, the Practice Lab measures and repairs skill gaps, case studies test integrated judgment, and staff and specialist tracks extend the design into evolution, operations, economics, and domain-specific constraints. Java concurrency develops the same discipline at low-level design scope.

docs.title: Recommended learning sequence
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Assess current evidence] --> B[Frame and quantify]
    B --> C[Model contracts and state]
    C --> D[Choose mechanisms and patterns]
    D --> E[Build and trace a baseline]
    E --> F[Break, recover, and migrate]
    F --> G[Defend operations and economics]
    G --> H[Specialize and lead evolution]

docs.title: 1. Establish the fundamentals
docs.text:
Start with the delivery framework, then work through estimation, API and data modeling, and consistency. These four modules shape every interview answer. Use database indexing and relational databases when the design depends on query plans, transactions, replicas, or an evidence-based path beyond one database.

Continue through caching, partitioning, messaging, reliability, and multi-region architecture. After each module, explain when its technique would be unnecessary or harmful.

For the mechanisms underneath those contracts, use Engineering Foundations and Practice: eleven chapters in three waves, eight offline Python fault fixtures, an evolving six-stage capstone, and a scoped concept registry. It deepens machine/runtime behavior, theory and clocks, performance, storage recovery/query execution, temporal data, API lifecycle, authorization/privacy, operations, decisions, and migrations without replacing the canonical foundations. Follow the engineering study routes and keep assessment evidence, not just reading progress.

docs.title: 2. Build a pattern vocabulary
docs.text:
Patterns are decision templates, not canned architectures. Group them by pressure:

Pressure Start with Add when needed Read volume and fan-out Scaling Reads Feed Generation, Search Write volume and hot keys Scaling Writes Handling Contention, Streaming Aggregation Asynchrony and orchestration Long-Running Tasks Multi-Step Workflows, Realtime Updates Specialized access Proximity Search Large Blob Storage Compact state and control planes Probabilistic Data Structures Distributed Coordination

docs.title: 3. Convert knowledge into evidence
docs.text:
Begin the Practice Lab with the entry diagnostic, record observed evidence in the learner scorecard, and route weak competencies to progressive drills. Then alternate integrated scenario packs with failure labs and migration labs. Use the Capacity Lab when estimates are not yet changing decisions and the Practice Console for timed attempts and local progress history.

For network depth, take the dedicated Networks (L5/L6) track: 16 chapters, 16 evidence labs, a calculations workbook, failure cards, a level rubric, and three 10-page scenarios. Use the four-week L5 or six-week L6 route instead of reading it as an undirected reference.

For production AI depth, take Applied AI Systems (L5/L6): 18 chapters organized across five planes, 12 evidence labs, a calculations workbook, failure cards, a level rubric, and three 10-page scenarios. Follow the six-week L5 or eight-week L6 route to connect probabilistic behavior to deterministic authority, evaluation, operations, and safe evolution.

docs.title: 4. Practice JVM concurrency as low-level design
docs.text: Use the Java Concurrency (LLD) track to design correct in-process Java 21 components. This route focuses on threads, shared memory, synchronization, executors, virtual threads, linearization points, liveness, cancellation, shutdown, and deterministic tests. It complements distributed system design, but does not replace it: JVM concurrency coordinates work inside one process, while distributed systems must also handle networks, partial failure, replication, and independently failing nodes.

docs.title: 5. Practice by domain
docs.text: CommerceMoney movement, reservations, contention, and workflows SocialFan-out, timelines, offline tracking, presence, messaging, and collaboration ContentMedia, crawling, indexing, ranking, and geospatial access InfrastructureControl planes, coordination, scheduling, and observability Data & financeLedgers, streams, fraud, ads, recommendations, and markets AI & specializedModel serving, streaming output, games, and discovery

docs.title: 6. Choose an advanced route
docs.text: Use Staff Architecture when the design must survive migration, correlated failure, tenant isolation, policy propagation, organizational boundaries, and cost constraints. Choose a Specialist Elective when AI lifecycle, agent security, accelerators, offline replicas, edge fleets, governance, regulated evidence, or formal verification changes the correctness model. These routes follow a strong generalist baseline rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Learning routes
docs.text: Starting evidence Route Exit evidence New to system design Readiness → foundations → patterns → guided case studies A coherent L5 baseline with justified scale and failure choices Interview approaching Diagnostic → targeted drills → three scenario packs → timed mocks Repeated scorecard evidence at the target level Strong senior engineer Case-study gap scan → failure/migration labs → Staff Architecture Migration, rollback, operability, ownership, and economics artifacts Domain specialist Generalist baseline → relevant elective → domain case adaptation Domain invariants, control plane, capacity limit, and launch evidence Java LLD candidate Delivery framework → Java concurrency track → timed implementations Explicit safety, liveness, cancellation, shutdown, and test decisions Network depth needed Network foundation → 16-chapter network route → labs and scenarios Packet-path, capacity, failure, security, and global-routing evidence at L5/L6 depth Applied AI depth needed Generalist baseline -> 18-chapter Applied AI route -> labs and scenarios Bounded decision, data/model, grounding, action, and governance evidence at L5/L6 depth

docs.title: The L5 bar
docs.text:
An L5 answer should independently:

  • turn ambiguous requirements into a bounded problem;
  • use estimates to justify storage, partitioning, and capacity decisions;
  • connect APIs, state, and data flow in one coherent design;
  • identify primary bottlenecks, consistency needs, and failure paths;
  • make tradeoffs explicit instead of listing technologies.

Practice target: finish a credible baseline in 20 minutes, then spend the remaining time on the two highest-risk deep dives.

docs.title: The L6 bar
docs.text:
An L6 answer includes the L5 bar and also:

  • finds hidden invariants and second-order product consequences;
  • separates control planes, data planes, and ownership boundaries;
  • reasons about overload, isolation, regional failure, and safe degradation;
  • plans migrations, reconciliation, observability, and operational recovery;
  • connects architecture to policy, security, cost, team topology, and evolution.

Practice target: actively shape the question. Explain not only how the design works now, but how it can change safely while serving traffic.

docs.title: How to use each case study
docs.text:
1. Read only the title and define three core requirements.
  2. State invariants and SLOs before drawing components.
  3. Estimate peak, not merely average, load and identify skew.
  4. Produce a smallest-correct baseline from API to durable state.
  5. Stress one correctness path, one scaling path, and one failure path.
  6. Compare against the chapter and record missed decisions.
  7. Score the attempt with the interview scorecard.
  8. Re-deliver the answer in five minutes the next day.

Progress is decision quality

Track whether your assumptions, invariants, and tradeoffs improve. Diagram complexity and technology count are poor proxies for interview readiness.

docs.title: Study Plans
docs.text: Choose the shortest plan that leaves time for repeated timed practice. Reading every chapter once is less valuable than designing a smaller set twice.

docs.title: Assessment-driven route
docs.text:
Use this route when elapsed time matters less than closing demonstrated gaps.

  1. Read the competency model and take the entry diagnostic under its time limit.
  2. Record only observable evidence in the learner scorecard; do not average away a correctness-critical miss.
  3. Assign the two weakest competencies to progressive drills, then run one matching failure lab or migration lab.
  4. Complete one scenario pack from its prompt before opening hints, rubric, exemplars, or design review.
  5. Retry after a spaced interval. Advance when two attempts independently meet the target-level evidence, not when every chapter has been read.

docs.title: Two-week interview sprint
docs.text:
If a diagnostic exposes mechanism-level gaps, substitute the relevant engineering assessment and fixture for a reading block below; do not try to compress the entire engineering track into this sprint.

Best when the interview is close and fundamentals are already familiar.

Days Focus Output 1–2 Delivery framework, estimation, API/data modeling One 15-minute framing drill each day 3–4 Consistency, caching, partitioning, reliability Failure and correctness notes for two systems 5–6 Scaling reads/writes, contention, workflows Pattern selection matrix 7–10 One commerce, social, content, and infrastructure design Four timed 45-minute attempts 11–12 Weak-domain case studies Two targeted retries 13 Full mock and scorecard Evidence-backed gap list 14 Five-minute summaries; light review Interview-ready narratives

Suggested anchor cases: Payment System, Facebook News Feed, YouTube, and Distributed Job Scheduler.

docs.title: Four-week core plan
docs.text:
Best for most L5 candidates and L6 candidates refreshing breadth.

The canonical foundation plan remains unchanged. Use the engineering route below as a deeper extension, not as an implicit increase in this plan's weekly reading requirement.

docs.title: Week 1: Foundations
docs.text:
Complete all foundation modules. For each one, write:

  • the problem it solves;
  • the invariant or SLO that activates it;
  • its most important cost;
  • one case where you would not use it.

docs.title: Week 2: Patterns
docs.text: Complete the pattern track. Redesign one familiar product using different traffic or correctness assumptions and observe which patterns change.

docs.title: Week 3: Domain breadth
docs.text: Do five blank-page designs: commerce, social, content, infrastructure, and data/financial. Alternate between a 45-minute full design and a 15-minute focused deep dive.

docs.title: Week 4: Interview execution
docs.text: Run three mocks. Use the scorecard, retry the weakest design, and rehearse five-minute summaries. L6 candidates should add migration, control-plane, cost, and organizational-boundary passes.

docs.title: Engineering foundations routes
docs.text: Use Engineering Foundations and Practice alongside the canonical chapters. Each week must produce a worked artifact, a counterexample, a tested or manually reproduced correction, and an explicit evidence limitation. Run Python fixtures offline; they do not require production access.

docs.title: Six-week L5 engineering path
docs.text: Week Focus Evidence gate 1 Machine/runtime and storage; capstone stage 1 Memory/CPU budget, four crash cuts, durable-counter fixture, A1/A4 2 Distributed theory and clocks; stage 2 Quorum and clock history, sink-installed fencing, outbox/inbox fixtures, A2 3 Performance and temporal data; stage 3 Queueing sensitivity, benchmark contract, cache/temporal fixtures, A3/A5 4 API lifecycle and authorization Old/new compatibility matrix, revocation fixture and deletion runbook, A6/A7 5 Operations and correctness; stage 4 Bounded-scheduling fixture, incident timeline, independent-oracle review, A8/A10 6 Decisions, migration, retirement; stages 5-6 Shard-movement fixture, cutover/reverse path, ADR, final defense, A9

docs.title: Eight-week L6 engineering path
docs.text:
Complete weeks 1-6 above with the L6 answer checks. In week 7, rerun the capstone under a changed assumption: policy authority outage, an old-unrepresentable schema state, or a much shorter restore objective. Produce a revised decision record, cross-team authority map, consumer census, and quantified cost/recovery tradeoff.

In week 8, have a reviewer choose three adversarial pivots. Add one boundary regression to a fixture, identify the strongest unsupported claim, and specify the approved real-world experiment needed to support it. Retire the old capstone path with explicit data, credential, billing, and restore obligations. Advance on evidence gates, not a summed score that hides a safety failure.

Use the coverage registry to locate prerequisites and declared lab gaps. Existing eight-week mastery and staff routes below can substitute these artifacts for corresponding failure, migration, and operating-model exercises; they do not need a second complete reading pass.

docs.title: Four-week Java concurrency LLD plan
docs.text:
Best for Java engineers who can write ordinary object-oriented code and want a practical Java 21 concurrency interview route.

Week Focus Practical output 1 Interview method, threads and task lifecycle, thread safety and the memory model Annotate shared state and invariants for two designs; write one lifecycle state machine and one visibility test 2 Synchronization, locks, and conditions, coordination primitives, atomics and concurrent collections Implement one blocking component and one atomic or concurrent-collection variant; identify each linearization point 3 Executors and backpressure, async, parallel, and virtual threads, liveness, debugging, and testing Build a bounded execution pipeline with cancellation and shutdown; test overload, interruption, deadlock risk, and task failure 4 Concurrency patterns, classic problems, LLD problems Complete three timed designs; implement one; defend safety, liveness, backpressure, cancellation, shutdown, and test choices

For each exercise, begin with the track interview method. Do not choose a lock, executor, atomic, or virtual thread until the shared state, invariant, ownership boundary, and blocking behavior are clear.

docs.title: Network engineering routes
docs.text: Both routes use the Networks (L5/L6) track. Complete each lab from evidence first, then use the rubric to score the related scenario artifact.

docs.title: Four-week L5 network path
docs.text: Week Focus Required output 1 Chapters 01-04; Labs 01-03 Request trace, CIDR and route proof, transport capacity calculation, and MTU budget 2 Chapters 05-08; Labs 04-06 DNS cache timeline, HTTP contract, protocol choice, and TLS identity diagnosis 3 Chapters 09-12; Labs 07-10 and 14 Load-balancer lifecycle, bounded retry/pool model, RPC contract, and reconnect analysis 4 Chapters 13-16; Labs 11-13 and 15-16; one scenario pack Cloud/global path, failure evidence, recovery plan, and an L5-scored design

docs.title: Six-week L6 network path
docs.text: Week Focus Required output 1 Chapters 01-04; Labs 01-03 Bidirectional path proof with state, queues, bounds, and falsifiable evidence 2 Chapters 05-08; Labs 04-06 Naming, protocol, trust, and rotation decisions with control/data-plane boundaries 3 Chapters 09-12; Labs 07-10 and 14 Overload model, deadline ledger, connection lifecycle, and realtime failure containment 4 Chapters 13-16; Labs 11-13 and 15-16 Tuple and failover capacity, route risk, mesh migration, and incident decision tree 5 Calculations workbook, failure cards, checkout and certificate scenarios Quantified design reviews, rollback gates, ownership, and remediation evidence 6 Global realtime scenario and L5/L6 rubric Timed L6 defense covering blast radius, migration, economics, and recovery proof

docs.title: Applied AI systems routes
docs.text: Both routes use the Applied AI Systems (L5/L6) track. Run labs from prediction to recovery, keep calculations with units, and attempt scenario prompts blind before opening hints or answer-bearing pages.

docs.title: Six-week L5 Applied AI path
docs.text: Week Focus Required output 1 Chapters 01-03; Labs 01-02 Product decision and error contract, workload classification, version bundle, token budget, and gateway ledger 2 Chapters 04-06; Lab 03 Batch publication plan, online serving path, capacity envelope, and exact-versus-approximate retrieval evidence 3 Chapters 07-09; Labs 04-06 Hybrid ranking trace, RAG stage metrics, citation and abstention policy, and provenance-safe ingestion manifest 4 Chapters 10-12; Labs 07-09 Workflow-versus-agent decision, typed capability contract, unknown-outcome reconciliation, and durable replay proof 5 Chapters 13-16; Labs 10-12 Confidence-aware release gate, threat controls, version-correlated telemetry, and overload containment plan 6 Chapters 17-18; workbook, failure cards, rubric; one scenario Adaptation decision, platform boundary, four checked calculations, incident diagnosis, and an L5-scored blind design

docs.title: Eight-week L6 Applied AI path
docs.text: Week Focus Required output 1 Chapters 01-03; Labs 01-02 Risk-partitioned product contract, workload isolation, lineage model, compatibility bundle, and policy-before-route proof 2 Chapters 04-06; Lab 03 Multi-class execution plan with publication, admission, failure reserve, vector migration, and measured recall tradeoff 3 Chapters 07-09; Labs 04-06 Tenant-safe knowledge pipeline with stage evaluation, provenance, deletion, corpus activation, and parser migration 4 Chapters 10-12; Labs 07-09 Authority-class model, durable state machine, capability policy, approval digest, replay, reconciliation, and regional recovery 5 Chapters 13-16; Labs 10-12 Governed evaluation sets, calibrated gates, adversarial tests, evidence retention, capacity economics, and degraded modes 6 Chapters 17-18; calculations workbook and failure cards Adaptation portfolio, shared-platform contracts, fleet policy, cost attribution, feedback governance, and falsifiable review evidence 7 Enterprise knowledge and support-resolution scenarios Two blind designs plus migration and failure-lab artifacts covering data, authority, rollback, and ownership 8 Incident-response scenario and L5/L6 rubric Timed L6 defense covering correlated failure, provider/region strategy, exceptions, economics, retirement, and recovery proof

docs.title: Eight-week mastery plan
docs.text:
Best when moving toward staff-level scope or rebuilding fundamentals deeply.

Weeks Workstream 1–2 Foundations with quantitative exercises and failure scenarios 3–4 Patterns, paired comparisons, and implementation tradeoffs 5–6 Eight domain-diverse case studies from blank pages 7 L6 overlays: migrations, multi-region, policy, cost, and ownership 8 Four mocks, targeted retries, and compressed delivery

docs.title: Staff architecture route
docs.text:
Best for senior engineers preparing for L6/staff interviews or taking ownership of cross-team evolution. First demonstrate the L5 bar on one timed case; then use the Staff Architecture curriculum as an eight-session sequence.

Sessions Focus Required artifact 1-2 Evolutionary architecture and multi-tenant isolation Mixed-state migration diagram, rollback boundary, and blast-radius model 3-4 Control planes and operational readiness Stale-control behavior, overload tiers, SLOs, alert, and operator action 5-6 Distributed-systems testing and privacy lifecycle Evidence plan, fault experiment, lineage map, and deletion proof 7-8 Organizational architecture and capacity economics Ownership boundaries, dependency contract, failure headroom, and cost decision

Apply every artifact to one scenario pack or existing production-shaped design. Finish with a 60-minute review in which the interviewer changes traffic, regional availability, compliance, and budget assumptions; revise the migration and operating model rather than merely adding components.

docs.title: Weekly practice cadence
docs.text:
60 minutes30 minutes15 minutes
  • 5 min: scope and assumptions
  • 8 min: estimates and invariants
  • 12 min: API and data model
  • 15 min: baseline architecture
  • 15 min: scaling, correctness, and failure deep dives
  • 5 min: summary and self-score
  • 5 min: frame the problem
  • 10 min: baseline design
  • 10 min: one chosen deep dive
  • 5 min: tradeoffs and summary

Pick one skill only: estimation, data modeling, a failure path, a migration, or a five-minute delivery. Do not attempt a compressed full interview every time.

docs.title: Level-specific emphasis
docs.text:
Area L5 emphasis L6 emphasis Scope Resolve ambiguity Challenge framing and expose policy Architecture Coherent end-to-end design Evolvable boundaries and control planes Scale Main bottlenecks and skew Overload isolation, cost, and capacity strategy Correctness Invariants, consistency, idempotency Reconciliation, migration, and cross-boundary semantics Operations Failures, metrics, recovery Safe rollout, regional strategy, and ownership

A plan is working when

Your second attempt is materially clearer than your first: fewer unjustified components, earlier invariants, sharper tradeoffs, and a more credible failure story.

docs.title: Applied AI Systems (L5/L6)
docs.text:
Design AI products as production systems: bounded decisions built from versioned data, model execution, deterministic controls, measurable evidence, and reversible releases. This track develops the judgment needed to design, review, operate, and evolve those systems at L5 and L6 depth.

The complete track contains 18 chapters, 12 executable evidence labs, a 44-problem calculations workbook, incident failure cards, an L5/L6 rubric, and three 10-page scenario packs. Start with the method, produce evidence while reading, then complete a scenario blind before opening its answer-bearing material.

docs.title: The five planes
docs.text:
The planes are reasoning boundaries, not a requirement for five services. A component can participate in several planes, but its authority and state should remain explicit.

Plane Question Core state and mechanisms Chapters Decision and workload What user decision is being improved, under which error, latency, privacy, and authority contract? product contract, answerability, workload class, invariants, budgets 01-02 Data, model, and execution How are data and artifacts produced, and how is inference admitted, isolated, published, and changed? pipelines, snapshots, lineage, batch jobs, model gateways, online serving, adaptation 03-05, 17 Knowledge and grounding Which evidence may influence an answer, and how are retrieval quality, provenance, ACLs, deletion, and citations preserved? embeddings, lexical and vector candidates, reranking, corpus manifests, multimodal ingestion 06-09 Orchestration and action How does probabilistic reasoning interact with deterministic workflow state, tools, approvals, and side effects? bounded plans, typed tools, capabilities, idempotency, replay, human review 10-12 Evidence, governance, and operations How is quality established, risk contained, behavior observed, capacity funded, and fleet evolution governed? evaluation gates, guardrails, traces, SLOs, capacity, cost, platform policy, feedback 13-16, 18

Every production request should make four runtime concerns visible inside these planes: a data plane executes against one compatibility bundle; an evidence plane records versions, attempts, and outcomes; an evaluation plane decides whether quality and safety remain acceptable; and a control plane approves, deploys, limits, and retires versions.

docs.title: Plane 1: Decision and workload
docs.text:
• 1. Applied AI System Design Method - frame the product decision, error contract, invariants, version bundle, and evidence loop before selecting infrastructure.
  • 2. AI Workload Taxonomy - separate online, batch, embedding, training, streaming, and durable-agent workloads by deadline, resources, state, and recovery semantics.

docs.title: Plane 2: Data, model, and execution
docs.text:
• 3. ML and AI Pipelines - build reproducible artifact pipelines with lineage, checkpoints, release state, and failure recovery.
  • 4. Batch and Bulk Inference - design partitioned, restartable inference and atomic result publication.
  • 5. Online Model Serving - design gateways, admission, batching, compatibility, fairness, rollout, and fallback.
  • 17. Model Adaptation - choose prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, preference optimization, or distillation through evidence rather than fashion.

docs.title: Plane 3: Knowledge and grounding
docs.text:
• 6. Embeddings and Vector Retrieval - reason about vector spaces, approximate search, filters, recall, memory, and index migration.
  • 7. Hybrid Search and Reranking - combine lexical and semantic candidates, fuse ranks, rerank, and evaluate each stage.
  • 8. Production RAG Systems - preserve authorization, provenance, freshness, citations, abstention, deletion, and atomic corpus activation.
  • 9. Multimodal Document Pipelines - ingest complex documents while retaining structure, coordinates, lineage, and bounded processing.

docs.title: Plane 4: Orchestration and action
docs.text:
• 10. Workflows and Bounded Agents - choose deterministic workflows first and bound planning by steps, time, tokens, tools, and spend.
  • 11. Typed Tool Calling and MCP - treat model output as a proposal behind typed schemas, principal-bound capabilities, policy, and audit.
  • 12. Durable Agents, Memory, and Human-in-the-Loop - make workflow state replayable, side effects reconcilable, memory governed, and approvals exact.

docs.title: Plane 5: Evidence, governance, and operations
docs.text:
• 13. Evaluation Engineering - build representative sets, stage metrics, slices, confidence-aware gates, canaries, and rollback evidence.
  • 14. AI Security and Guardrails - define trust boundaries, capability controls, data handling, adversarial tests, and incident containment.
  • 15. AI Observability - correlate versions and stages while controlling cardinality, privacy, retention, and delayed outcomes.
  • 16. AI Reliability, Capacity, and Cost - connect token and memory demand to queues, admission, degraded modes, resilience, and economics.
  • 18. AI Platforms and Data Flywheels - establish shared contracts, golden paths, governed feedback, tenant isolation, and fleet ownership.

docs.title: Evidence labs
docs.text:
The lab guide defines a predict-run-break-recover method. Every fixture uses Python 3 and the standard library, so results can be reproduced without model weights, API keys, network access, Docker, or paid services.

Lab Evidence produced 01. Token and context budget context fit, KV-cache, GPU, and cost budget 02. Model gateway deterministic policy, route, fallback, and accounting ledger 03. Vector index tradeoffs exact-versus-approximate recall and distance-work comparison; memory is a production measurement task 04. Hybrid search and reranking RRF ranking and retrieval metrics 05. RAG evaluation retrieval, citation, support, and abstention scores 06. Document ingestion chunk manifest, provenance, and tombstone proof 07. Workflow versus agent reliability and budget comparison 08. Tool idempotency one in-memory effect across repeated attempts, not a durability proof 09. Durable agent replay retained in-memory ledger and simulated resume without repeated effects 10. Evaluation release gate confidence bound and explicit release decision 11. Prompt-injection defense allow/deny trace and an encoded-secret filter bypass, not general exfiltration resistance 12. AI capacity incident token/GPU envelope and overload response

docs.title: Workbooks, cards, and scoring
docs.text:
• Calculations Workbook - 44 solved exercises covering context, throughput, GPU memory, retrieval, reliability, queues, evaluation, and cost. Values are explicit fixtures, not vendor claims.
  • Failure Cards - symptom, discriminator, containment, recovery, and prevention prompts for design reviews and incidents.
  • L5/L6 Rubric - a 100-point evidence rubric with level gates and hard safety/correctness caps. It scores reasoning, not product names.

docs.title: Scenario packs
docs.text: Each scenario is a complete 10-page blind-first practice system: overview, prompt, workbook, hints, rubric, interviewer packet, exemplars, failure lab, migration, and adversarial design review. Open only the prompt and workbook on the first attempt.

docs.title: Enterprise Knowledge Assistant
docs.text:
Design permission-aware RAG with tenant isolation, evidence quality, deletion, freshness, regional control, operations, and safe index evolution.

Pack overview | Start blind

docs.title: Incident Response Copilot
docs.text:
Design an evidence-first copilot that correlates operational signals without silently acquiring production authority.

Pack overview | Start blind

docs.title: Support Resolution Agent
docs.text:
Design a durable support workflow that combines probabilistic proposals with deterministic policy, bounded refunds, approvals, reconciliation, and escalation.

Pack overview | Start blind

docs.title: Recommended sequence
docs.text:
1. Read Chapters 01-02 and write one product decision contract before drawing architecture.
  2. Follow the relevant plane through Chapters 03-12; run its matching lab immediately after the chapter.
  3. Complete Chapters 13-16 so evaluation, security, observability, capacity, and cost constrain the design rather than decorate it.
  4. Use Chapter 17 to make an adaptation decision and Chapter 18 to lift one product design into a governed platform.
  5. Work the calculations workbook and use failure cards to challenge the design.
  6. Complete one scenario blind, score it with the rubric, then inspect hints, exemplars, the failure lab, migration, and design review.
  7. Retry the same scenario before moving to the next pack.

For a scheduled route, use the six-week L5 and eight-week L6 Applied AI plans.

docs.title: L5: own one production design
docs.text: An L5 candidate should produce a coherent request and data path, explicit authority boundaries, correct calculations, bounded queues and retries, stage-specific evaluation, safe release and rollback, provenance, deletion, and recovery evidence. Use one lab per major plane and complete at least one scenario at the rubric's L5 bar.

docs.title: L6: shape the platform and its evolution
docs.text: An L6 candidate should also govern compatibility and migration across model, prompt, index, tool, policy, and ledger versions; quantify correlated provider or regional failure; define fleet economics and exceptions; and assign evidence, decision, and rollback ownership. Complete all three scenarios, including their migration and design-review pages, and meet every L6 gate without relying on interviewer repair.

docs.title: Relationship to canonical course material
docs.text:
This track extends the repository's canonical distributed-systems material; it does not replace it.

  • Use Search and Indexing for inverted indexes, shards, segments, ANN basics, and zero-downtime reindexing. Applied AI adds embedding compatibility, hybrid retrieval, grounding, and evaluation.
  • Use Multi-Step Workflows for durable state, idempotency, unknown outcomes, compensation, and migration. Applied AI adds bounded model planning, typed tool proposals, memory, and human approval.
  • Use GPU Inference Platforms for deep runtime mechanics; Chapters 05 and 16 connect those mechanics to the product path and capacity contract.
  • Use Production AI Lifecycle for a compact advanced treatment of model and evidence state; this track expands it into pipelines, evaluation, operations, adaptation, and platform governance.
  • Use RAG and Agent Security for a compact security elective; Chapters 08 and 10-14 develop the full knowledge, action, evaluation, and guardrail path.
  • Use the ChatGPT-Like Assistant and Recommendation System as integrated reference designs after learning the mechanisms here.
  • Reuse the general foundations for estimation, storage, consistency, messaging, reliability, multi-region design, security, and cost whenever the mechanism is not AI-specific.

docs.title: Primary-source standard
docs.text:
The track follows the repository Source and Evidence Standard. Prefer primary papers, standards, official specifications, and versioned product documentation. Place sources beside consequential claims, label assumptions and derived calculations, include dates for version-sensitive behavior, and preserve uncertainty. A paper's measured result supports its reported setup; it does not establish a universal production invariant. Scenario fixtures and workbook prices are explicit exercises, not external performance claims.

Start Chapter 01 | Open the labs | Read the rubric

docs.title: Applied AI System Design Method
docs.text:
Applied AI design starts with a product decision, not a model. The system must turn uncertain model behavior into a bounded, measurable, reversible service. This chapter gives a repeatable L5/L6 method for doing that without hiding ordinary distributed-systems concerns behind AI terminology.

Use the Applied AI L5/L6 rubric to score a completed design. Use this chapter to construct one.

docs.title: 1. Frame the decision before the architecture
docs.text:
Write a one-paragraph problem contract:

  1. Actor: who requests or receives the result?
  2. Decision: what prediction, ranking, generation, or action occurs?
  3. Evidence: what data may influence it, and how fresh must that data be?
  4. Consequence: what happens when the result is wrong, late, unavailable, or refused?
  5. Authority: may the system advise, decide, or execute?
  6. Feedback: when does ground truth arrive, and can it be trusted?

Principle: A model score or generated answer is evidence inside a product decision. It is not, by itself, the decision policy or authority to act.

docs.title: Decide whether AI is justified
docs.text:
Compare the AI proposal with a deterministic baseline. Rules, search, templates, or an ordinary workflow are often cheaper to test and easier to reverse.

Question Deterministic baseline favored Statistical model favored Generative model favored Output contract exact rule or lookup score, class, or rank open-ended synthesis Error definition fully specifiable measurable from labeled examples partly judgment-based Required evidence structured state patterns across features language, images, or mixed context Reversibility usually direct depends on downstream action generated text may already influence users Evaluation assertions labeled metrics and calibration task, grounding, safety, and human judgment

Do not proceed until the team can state why the baseline fails and which measurable outcome the AI path should improve.

docs.title: 2. Define scope, requirements, and invariants
docs.text:
For a customer-support answer assistant, a useful contract might be:

  • return a cited draft within 3 seconds at p95;
  • answer only from documents authorized for the requesting agent;
  • abstain when evidence is missing or conflicting;
  • never send a reply or mutate an account;
  • retain a replayable decision record for 30 days;
  • support an immediate return to keyword search and templates.

Important exclusions might include autonomous refunds, unrestricted web access, foundation-model training, and legal advice.

Write invariants as conditions that remain true during retries, failover, migration, and overload:

  • policy and tenant checks happen before any provider route;
  • a logical request has one immutable input envelope and may have several attempts;
  • every result records model, prompt, policy, data, and index versions;
  • output and spend reserves cannot be silently consumed by retrieved context;
  • side effects use deterministic authorization and idempotency outside the model;
  • shadow output cannot affect users or learning labels;
  • deletion propagates to source, projection, cache, ledger, and future datasets under a stated policy.

For write-capable systems, apply the stricter controls in RAG and Agent Security. For model lineage and delayed labels, use Production AI Lifecycle.

docs.title: 3. Turn quality into an error contract
docs.text:
"High quality" is not a requirement. Enumerate observable error classes and assign each a response.

Error Example Detection evidence Product behavior false positive safe payment blocked mature outcome label review, appeal, policy cap false negative fraud approved delayed loss signal defense in depth, monitoring unsupported answer claim lacks evidence citation judgment abstain or label uncertainty stale answer superseded policy cited source/index version suppress stale generation unsafe content disallowed instruction safety suite and report block, transform, escalate latency miss answer after usefulness window stage spans degrade or time out unavailable dependency feature or model endpoint down health and attempt ledger tested fallback unknown side effect tool timed out after submit idempotency/status lookup reconcile before retry

Define the cost of each error by user, slice, and action reversibility. Accuracy can be the wrong objective when classes are imbalanced, review capacity is constrained, or errors have unequal cost. Ranking requires top-K and downstream outcome measures. Generation requires task success, support, refusal, safety, latency, and cost.

docs.title: 4. Quantify workload and uncertainty
docs.text:
Separate request traffic from model work:

input tokens/s  = requests/s * mean input tokens/request
output tokens/s = requests/s * mean generated tokens/request
concurrency     = arrival rate/s * mean service time/s
usage cost/day  = sum over attempts in the day and unit types (units/attempt * currency/unit)
capacity cost/day = reserved compute-hours/day * currency/compute-hour
daily cost      = usage cost/day + capacity cost/day + storage cost/day
                  + network cost/day + other resource cost/day

Use distributions, not only means. Record p50, p95, and maximum prompt size; expected output caps; retrieval fan-out; feature fan-out; class mix; burst factor; retry rate; and deadline.

Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): An answer service receives 120 requests/s at peak. Mean input is 3,200 tokens, p95 input is 9,000 tokens, mean output is 350 tokens, 5% of requests use a shadow model, and the permitted attempt rate is 1.03.

Primary demand is 120 * 3,200 = 384,000 input tokens/s and 120 * 350 = 42,000 output tokens/s. Including shadows and attempts, the planning multiplier is 1.05 * 1.03 = 1.0815, giving about 415,296 input tokens/s and 45,423 output tokens/s. Capacity must still be tested against the p95 length mix because a mean-only model hides queue and memory pressure.

Keep units and assumptions visible. The calculations workbook provides solved token, GPU, queue, reliability, retrieval, and cost exercises without prescribing vendor performance.

The 1.05 * 1.03 estimate assumes shadow requests have the same mean token demand as primary requests and that 1.03 attempts applies to both streams. If either differs, sum arrival_rate * route_fraction * mean_attempts * mean_tokens_per_attempt by route and class. Avoid multiplying by retries again when measured token usage already includes all attempts. Provider usage charges and self-hosted capacity cost must cover disjoint resources rather than charging the same accelerator twice.

docs.title: 5. Draw the decision and evidence loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[User or producer] --> G[Policy and admission]
    G --> O[Orchestrator]
    O --> D[Data and retrieval]
    O --> M[Model route]
    D --> M
    M --> V[Validation and decision policy]
    V --> R[Result or bounded action]
    G --> L[(Decision ledger)]
    D --> L
    M --> L
    V --> L
    R --> F[Outcome and feedback]
    F --> E[Evaluation and monitoring]
    E --> C[Release control plane]
    C --> G
    C --> O

This diagram separates four concerns:

  • the data plane serves requests under a fixed version bundle;
  • the evidence plane records what happened and joins later outcomes;
  • the evaluation plane determines whether quality and safety remain acceptable;
  • the control plane approves, deploys, limits, and retires versions.

A request must never observe an accidental mixture such as prompt B with parser A, query embedding B with index A, or model B with feature schema A. Publish a compatibility bundle and bind each request to one generation.

docs.title: 6. Define interfaces and durable state
docs.text:
Keep a provider-neutral logical interface. Provider attempts are internal details.

POST /v1/decisions
Idempotency-Key: 5f54...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "task": "support.answer.v3",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-17",
  "subject": {"ticket_id": "t-902"},
  "input": {"question": "..."},
  "constraints": {
    "deadline_ms": 3000,
    "max_output_tokens": 500,
    "data_class": "internal"
  }
}

{
  "request_id": "req-481",
  "status": "succeeded",
  "result": {"text": "...", "citations": ["chunk-31"]},
  "completion_reason": "stop",
  "version_bundle": "support-prod-2026-09-14.2"
}

Core records:

VersionBundle(id, model, tokenizer, prompt, policy, feature_view, index, evaluator)
LogicalRequest(id, principal, tenant, task, input_digest, budget, deadline, bundle, state)
Attempt(id, request_id, route, provider_request_id, start, end, usage, outcome)
Evidence(id, request_id, source_versions, chunk_spans, feature_versions, digests)
Decision(id, request_id, raw_output_digest, validated_result, action, reason)
Outcome(decision_id, label, observed_at, maturity, source, correction_version)

Store sensitive payloads only when purpose, retention, access control, and deletion behavior are explicit. Metrics should use redacted dimensions; replay payloads belong in a narrower encrypted store.

docs.title: 7. Allocate latency, capacity, and failure budgets
docs.text:
Start from the end-to-end SLO and assign internal deadline allocations:

Stage Illustrative deadline allocation Timeout behavior edge, auth, admission 80 ms reject before paid work data and retrieval 350 ms return bounded partial evidence or fail queue 300 ms shed by class model 1,800 ms cancel attempt validation and rendering 170 ms use validated fallback network reserve 300 ms preserve for variance total 3,000 ms product deadline

These allocations sum to the product deadline; they are not independently measured p95 values. Percentiles of dependent stage latencies are not additive. Validate the caller-visible p95 from joint per-request traces under representative load, and use stage distributions to identify which allocation is burning the deadline.

Principle: A timeout is a statement that the caller stopped waiting. It does not prove that the dependency stopped work or that a side effect did not occur.

Retries must fit the original deadline and spend budget. Retry only errors that are transient and safe. Hedge only where duplicate work is acceptable, cancellation is effective, and the added load is part of capacity planning. Admission should consider tokens, accelerator memory, queue age, tenant quota, data class, model availability, and spend rather than request count alone.

docs.title: 8. Design evaluation before rollout
docs.text:
Create a versioned evaluation contract with:

  • representative tasks and traffic slices;
  • difficult, adversarial, and unanswerable cases;
  • expected evidence or labels and judgment instructions;
  • stage metrics for retrieval, model output, policy, and end-to-end behavior;
  • operational gates for latency, error, fallback, and cost;
  • confidence intervals or paired tests where statistical comparison matters;
  • contamination controls and a renewal owner;
  • explicit release, rollback, and exception criteria.

Offline evidence does not establish production safety by itself. Use replay, shadowing, stable-entity canaries, bounded exposure, and mature outcome checkpoints. For detailed lifecycle mechanics, link to Production AI Lifecycle rather than duplicating its registry and delayed-label design.

Benchmark (measurement requirement, 2026-09): Before launch, benchmark the exact model, tokenizer, prompt, hardware or provider class, input/output length distribution, concurrency, warm-up, duration, and success definition. Record p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, errors, quality gates, and cost. A catalog limit or another team's result is not this workload's benchmark.

docs.title: 9. Make degradation explicit
docs.text:
Define a fallback matrix before incidents:

Failure Safe degradation Must not happen primary model saturated smaller approved model for eligible classes route restricted data to an unapproved region retrieval stale cited search or abstention answer against mismatched source/index epochs feature service unavailable compatible reduced feature view silently default safety-critical features evaluator unavailable freeze releases approve without evidence ledger unavailable reject high-risk decisions execute unaudited irreversible action cost budget exhausted reduce optional context or queue batch reset budget on every retry

The failure cards contain incident discriminators and containment patterns. Use Reliability, Deadlines, Retries, and Pools, and Operational Readiness for the general distributed-systems mechanisms.

docs.title: 10. Threat model data and authority
docs.text:
Classify data before choosing a route. Define allowed regions, providers, retention, training use, logging, and human access for each class. Authenticate producers, authorize subjects and purpose, validate schemas, encrypt storage and transport, and log administrative changes.

Treat prompts, documents, model output, and tool output as untrusted. The model never receives standing credentials. Side effects require a typed command, caller-bound authorization, current-state validation, idempotency, and reconciliation. High-impact actions need approval bound to exact arguments.

Deletion is a workflow across source objects, feature stores, embeddings, caches, replay ledgers, snapshots, and future training filters. Define lawful exceptions for immutable audit evidence and prevent broad replay access from becoming a second data lake. See Privacy and Data Lifecycle.

docs.title: 11. Compare alternatives and evolution paths
docs.text:
State why the selected design wins under current evidence:

Choice Prefer when Cost or risk managed model API variable demand, small platform team, approved data route provider limits, dependency, unit economics self-hosted model steady scale, specialized runtime, residency/control need accelerator capacity and serving expertise one model simple policy and evaluation correlated failure and capability ceiling routed model fleet distinct tasks, cost tiers, residency needs policy, compatibility, and evaluation complexity synchronous request result is immediately needed and bounded tail latency and client coupling asynchronous job large input, long runtime, resumable output state machine and delayed UX

Use reversible phases: deterministic baseline, offline evaluation, shadow, small canary, staged expansion, and retirement. Keep the old compatible bundle warm through the rollback window. A model, prompt, index, feature, parser, threshold, or policy change is a release when it can change behavior.

Vendor (Kubernetes documentation, accessed 2026-09-06): Kubernetes exposes vendor device plugins as schedulable extended resources, but its documentation does not define model-level batching, KV-cache admission, or AI quality gates. Schedule GPUs

Decision: Use cluster scheduling for allocatable devices and build or adopt a separate model-serving control plane for model compatibility, warm capacity, request admission, and quality-bearing releases.

Production report (Uber, published 2017-09-05): Uber described Michelangelo as an internal platform spanning data management, training, evaluation, deployment, prediction, and monitoring. This is evidence that lifecycle integration mattered in Uber's environment, not proof that every organization needs the same platform boundary. Introducing Michelangelo

docs.title: 12. Interview exercise
docs.text:
Prompt: Design an AI assistant that summarizes insurance claims, identifies missing documents, and recommends whether a claim should enter manual investigation. It processes 4 million claims/month. The recommendation must arrive within 10 seconds, documents contain sensitive data, investigation outcomes mature over 90 days, and the assistant may not deny a claim.

Clarify:

  • claim types, document sizes and languages, arrival bursts, and retention;
  • whether summarization and investigation recommendation use the same evidence;
  • false-positive review cost versus false-negative loss;
  • citation and explanation obligations;
  • reviewer capacity and queue-age SLO;
  • regional and provider restrictions;
  • label maturity, corrections, and feedback-loop risk;
  • availability, cost, and fallback expectations.

docs.title: Worked design outline
docs.text:
Use immutable document versions and a manifest per claim. Parse and classify asynchronously, quarantine failures, and retain offsets and parser versions. Build a point-in-time feature view for the recommendation and tenant-scoped retrieval for cited summaries. The synchronous decision request binds a compatible model, prompt, index, feature, and policy bundle. A deterministic policy prevents denial and routes only bounded recommendations to the review queue.

Record the evidence bundle, raw score, recommendation, policy reason, citations, and later reviewer/outcome versions. Gate releases on parser coverage, retrieval support, summary factuality, calibrated ranking at review capacity, critical slices, 10-second latency, fallback, and cost. Shadow first; canary by stable claim hash; retain an exploration/control slice until 90-day labels mature. Degrade to deterministic completeness checks and document search. Never silently substitute a provider that violates the claim's data class.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Converts the product request into users, decisions, errors, SLOs, authority, and exclusions.
  • Quantifies tokens, concurrency, storage, retries, and spend with labeled assumptions.
  • Defines versioned interfaces, evidence, evaluation, fallback, and rollback.
  • Separates model output from deterministic policy and authorization.
  • Handles overload, privacy, deletion, and delayed outcomes coherently.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Partitions risk and degradability across products, tenants, regions, and action classes.
  • Establishes compatibility bundles, release governance, exception ownership, and retirement evidence.
  • Models provider and capacity concentration, evacuation, fairness, and portfolio economics.
  • Designs cross-team provenance, deletion, evaluation-set stewardship, and incident accountability.
  • Names which assumptions must be retired by benchmark or production evidence and who owns that work.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• The decision, evidence, consequence, authority, and feedback are explicit.
  • A deterministic baseline and important exclusions are documented.
  • Quality is an error contract with slices and product responses.
  • Workload estimates use distributions and separate input, output, memory, and attempts.
  • One immutable compatibility bundle binds every request.
  • Logical requests, attempts, evidence, decisions, and outcomes are distinguishable.
  • Deadlines, admission, retries, fallback, and unknown outcomes are bounded.
  • Offline, shadow, canary, mature-outcome, and rollback gates are defined.
  • Data-class routing, least privilege, retention, and deletion are enforced.
  • Operational metrics identify the causal stage, version, tenant, and route.
  • Alternatives and evolution triggers are tied to evidence.
  • The five-minute summary explains correctness, capacity, recovery, and governance.

docs.text:
