Next: AI Workload Taxonomy

docs.title: AI Workload Taxonomy
docs.text: AI systems fail when unlike work shares one queue, one SLO, or one scaling signal. Classify work by execution shape, resource demand, state, quality risk, and deadline before choosing infrastructure.

docs.title: 1. Classification dimensions
docs.text:
Do not classify only by model family. A transformer can power a two-second interactive request, an hour-long batch job, an embedding backfill, or a tool-using workflow. Those workloads need different contracts.

Dimension Questions Architecture consequence arrival steady, bursty, scheduled, or event-driven? reserve, queue, or elastic batch deadline milliseconds, seconds, minutes, or none? synchronous path versus durable job unit of work row, document, image, sequence, token, or episode? partition and admission key resource vector CPU, RAM, accelerator compute, accelerator memory, I/O, network? placement and isolation variability bounded or long-tailed input/output? queue policy and straggler handling state stateless, cached context, online features, or workflow checkpoint? affinity and recovery result semantics score, rank, text, artifact, or side effect? validation and idempotency quality evidence immediate label, delayed label, rubric, or no ground truth? release and monitoring plan data class public, internal, confidential, regulated? route, region, retention, isolation reversibility advisory, user-visible, financial, or physical action? approval and audit

Principle: Schedule and admit AI work by its constrained resources and deadline, not by request count or model name.

docs.title: Online discriminative inference
docs.text:
Examples include fraud scores, ranking, classification, forecasting, and anomaly scores. Inputs are commonly structured features; outputs are small and bounded. The critical path often includes online feature reads, preprocessing, model execution, and decision policy. Tail latency, feature freshness, calibration, and fallback dominate.

Read Online Model Serving and the Fraud Detection case study.

docs.title: Online generative inference
docs.text: Input and output length vary. Streaming exposes time to first token and inter-token latency separately. The scheduler must budget prompt processing, generated tokens, KV-cache memory, cancellation, and tenant fairness. See GPU Inference Platforms for runtime depth.

docs.title: Batch inference
docs.text: Millions of independent or weakly dependent records are scored against a pinned model and snapshot. Throughput, restartability, deterministic output identity, stragglers, and publication matter more than per-row latency. See Batch and Bulk Inference.

docs.title: Embedding and indexing
docs.text: Documents or entities are transformed into vectors, then written into a compatible index generation. It is a dual-write migration problem: a new embedding model defines a new coordinate space and cannot safely query an old index. See Embeddings and Vector Retrieval.

docs.title: Training, tuning, and evaluation
docs.text: These are long-running, artifact-producing jobs over versioned data. They require reproducibility, checkpointing, lineage, fair accelerator scheduling, and signed evaluation. Training completion is not release approval. See ML and AI Pipelines and Production AI Lifecycle.

docs.title: Durable AI workflow or agent
docs.text: A run may retrieve, call tools, wait for approval, and resume. Step count and cost vary, and tool outcomes can be unknown after timeout. The source of truth is durable workflow state, not model conversation text. Prefer deterministic workflows whenever the path is known. Use RAG and Agent Security for authority and containment.

docs.title: Streaming feature and prediction workloads
docs.text: Events update windows, features, indexes, or decisions continuously. Correctness depends on event time, watermarking, duplicates, late data, and replay. The online path reads a materialized projection; it should not reconstruct an unbounded stream window synchronously. See Streaming Aggregation and Messaging and Streams.

docs.title: 2A. Model behavior and selection
docs.text: Workload shape tells the platform how to execute. Model behavior tells the product what can fail and what evidence is required. Select a model only after defining the task, answerability boundary, quality/safety errors, context distribution, latency, data class, authority, and cost ceiling.

docs.title: Base and instruction-tuned models
docs.text:
A base model is trained primarily to continue its input distribution. An instruction-tuned model receives additional adaptation to follow instructions, conversation formats, preferences, or safety behavior. The distinction is about the artifact and training history, not a guarantee of capability or safety.

Use an instruction-tuned model for general assistants and typed interaction unless evaluation demonstrates a reason not to. A base model can be appropriate for controlled completion, research, domain adaptation, or a pipeline that supplies its own training. Do not expose a base model as an assistant merely by adding a system prompt.

Selection evidence must include:

  • exact model and tokenizer revision;
  • expected chat or completion template;
  • stop and structured-output behavior;
  • task and critical-slice evaluation;
  • prompt-injection and refusal behavior for the intended authority;
  • serving latency, memory, throughput, and cost under the real length distribution.

docs.title: Dense and mixture-of-experts models
docs.text:
A dense model activates its model path broadly for each token. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model routes token representations through a subset of expert components. Parameter count, active compute, memory footprint, and communication cost therefore answer different questions.

flowchart LR
    A[Token representation] --> B{Architecture}
    B -- dense --> C[Shared dense blocks]
    B -- MoE --> D[Router]
    D --> E[Expert 1]
    D --> F[Expert 2]
    D --> G[Other experts]
    E --> H[Combined output]
    F --> H
    G --> H
    C --> H

Do not infer serving cost from total parameters alone. For MoE, measure active parameters, weight residency, expert balance, interconnect traffic, batch behavior, and tail effects. Routing imbalance can create hot experts even when average accelerator utilization looks healthy. Dense models are not automatically cheaper; model size, precision, runtime, batching, and output length still dominate.

The diagram depicts alternative selected experts, not a requirement to execute every branch per token. Switch Transformers, verified 2026-09-08, uses sparse routing; its reported training speedups are not serving-throughput guarantees. A model's context limit similarly does not establish evidence-use quality: Lost in the Middle reports position sensitivity on its evaluated tasks and models, motivating local position/length tests rather than a universal defect claim.

docs.title: Context windows and effective context
docs.text:
The advertised context window is a hard compatibility limit, not proof that every position is equally useful for every task. Define:

context_budget
= system_and_policy_tokens
 + tool_schema_tokens
 + conversation_tokens
 + retrieved_context_tokens
 + reserved_output_tokens
 + safety_margin_tokens

For a 32,768-token limit with 1,200 system/policy, 2,000 tool schema, 6,000 conversation, 12,000 retrieval, 4,000 reserved output, and 10% safety margin on the hard limit:

used_before_margin = 25,200
safety_margin      = 3,277
remaining          = 32,768 - 25,200 - 3,277 = 4,291 tokens

Specify truncation by semantic priority, never by accidental string order. Preserve system policy and exact tool schemas. Summarize or retrieve older conversation with provenance. Drop low-value candidates before required evidence. Re-run evaluation across length and evidence-position slices because long-context behavior can degrade before the hard limit.

Context cost also changes admission and cache pressure. Two requests with the same QPS can have radically different prefill work and KV-cache demand.

docs.title: Reasoning-oriented models
docs.text:
Some model products expose behavior optimized for multi-step reasoning or additional internal inference work. Treat that as a different workload class when it changes latency, output accounting, cancellation, observability, or cost.

Use reasoning-oriented models when task-level paired evaluation shows enough gain to justify their tail latency and spend. Bound total deliberation and output. Do not expose hidden reasoning as an audit explanation; preserve task evidence, citations, tool records, policy decisions, and concise user-facing reasons instead.

Route simple classification, extraction, and deterministic transformations to smaller specialized paths when they meet the error contract. A routing model adds its own false-route error and needs evaluation by task and slice.

docs.title: Multimodal models
docs.text:
Multimodal input changes ingestion and threat boundaries. Images, audio, video, and documents need media validation, decoding limits, malware handling, OCR or transcription provenance, temporal/positional references, and modality-specific evaluation.

Represent work as a modality-aware resource vector:

multimodal_demand = {
  text_tokens,
  image_patch_or_provider_units,
  audio_seconds,
  video_frames_or_seconds
}

Provider units are not interchangeable and must not be added directly. Benchmark the exact media size, resolution, frame sampling, and preprocessing. Convert components to a scalar only through an explicit provider-specific pricing function or a measured service-time/compute model. Evaluate text-only, modality-only, conflicting-modality, low-quality, accessibility, language, and injection slices. A caption generated upstream is a derived artifact with a version and error surface, not the original image.

docs.title: Hosted, open-weight, and specialized choices
docs.text:
Hosted model API: the provider operates weights and runtime. It can reduce time to first production use, but introduces provider policy, quota, retention, region, version, telemetry, and concentration dependencies.

Open-weight deployment: the operator can inspect and host released weights under their license. It increases control over routing, isolation, adaptation, and lifecycle, while transferring runtime, security, evaluation, capacity, and patch responsibility to the operator. Open weights do not imply open training data, open source, or unrestricted use.

Specialized model or deterministic system: a smaller classifier, reranker, embedding model, OCR engine, speech model, rules engine, or domain model can outperform a general generator on a bounded task's latency, cost, determinism, or evaluation burden.

Use a model-selection ADR rather than a leaderboard screenshot:

ModelSelectionADR(
  task_contract, candidates, baseline,
  model_and_tokenizer_versions,
  data_and_license_constraints,
  quality_and_safety_evidence,
  context_and_modality_limits,
  latency_capacity_and_cost_curves,
  provider_region_and_retention,
  portability_and_exit_plan,
  decision, owner, review_trigger, date
)

flowchart TD
    A[Task and error contract] --> B{Deterministic or specialized path passes?}
    B -- yes --> C[Choose simpler path]
    B -- no --> D{Data may leave controlled boundary?}
    D -- no --> E[Evaluate approved self-hosted weights]
    D -- yes --> F[Evaluate hosted and self-hosted candidates]
    E --> G[Paired quality safety and operations gate]
    F --> G
    G --> H{Meets SLO and cost with reserve?}
    H -- no --> I[Adapt task prompt retrieval or capacity]
    H -- yes --> J[Record ADR and fallback]

Minimum ADR alternatives:

Question Hosted Open-weight/self-hosted Specialized quality task evidence for exact provider revision task evidence for exact artifact/runtime direct bounded-task evidence data retention, training-use, region, subprocessors operator controls plus infrastructure exposure depends on deployment operations quota, rate limits, version changes accelerator, runtime, patches, scaling often simpler but task-limited cost token/media/tool pricing and retry effects utilization, idle reserve, labor, energy task unit economics exit compatible provider route and export limits artifact/runtime portability compose with broader fallback

Review the ADR when the task changes, critical slices regress, provider terms or regions change, a model is deprecated, utilization crosses the safe envelope, or a simpler candidate meets the contract. The approved route is a versioned portfolio, not a permanent vendor preference.

docs.title: 3. Workload decision tree
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Need a result] --> B{User waits now?}
    B -- yes --> C{Bounded execution?}
    C -- yes --> D[Online serving]
    C -- no --> E[Accept job and stream status]
    B -- no --> F{Many independent items?}
    F -- yes --> G[Batch or bulk inference]
    F -- no --> H{Known step graph?}
    H -- yes --> I[Durable deterministic workflow]
    H -- no --> J[Bounded planner with tools]
    D --> K{Needs fresh features?}
    K -- yes --> L[Online feature projection]
    K -- no --> M[Request-contained input]
    G --> N{Creates new vector space?}
    N -- yes --> O[Versioned embedding and index build]

The decision tree chooses execution semantics, not a product. A single user feature may traverse several families: asynchronous document ingestion, batch embedding, online retrieval, generative serving, and delayed evaluation.

docs.title: 4. Sync, async, streaming, and deferred contracts
docs.text:
Contract Return Best fit Failure semantics synchronous unary final result bounded score or short generation timeout and safe retry server stream partial output plus final status token generation partial prefix, cancellation, resume policy asynchronous job accepted job ID bulk and long-running work durable state and polling/callback event-driven acknowledged event projection and enrichment replay, dedupe, watermark human-deferred pending decision high-impact ambiguous action approval expiry and reassessment

A synchronous HTTP timeout must not erase work that should be durable. Conversely, wrapping a 100 ms score in a job API adds state and operational surface with little value.

docs.title: 5. Resource vectors and interference
docs.text:
Represent each class as a vector rather than one utilization number:

Demand = {
  input_tokens,
  output_tokens,
  cpu_ms,
  gpu_ms,
  gpu_memory_bytes,
  feature_reads,
  index_candidates,
  network_bytes,
  deadline,
  spend
}

Common interference patterns:

  • large prefills delay decode iterations;
  • batch embedding fills accelerator queues needed by interactive generation;
  • feature backfills overload the same database used by online prediction;
  • one tenant's long contexts consume shared KV memory;
  • vector compaction or graph builds compete with search replicas;
  • shadow traffic consumes real capacity while appearing absent from product QPS;
  • tool retries amplify downstream writes and cost.

Use separate pools when deadline, security boundary, failure domain, or resource shape differs materially. Use shared pools when utilization gain exceeds isolation and scheduling complexity.

docs.title: 6. Capacity example
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): One regional fleet receives 80 interactive requests/s with 2,500 input and 300 output tokens on average. A nightly batch adds 60 million documents of 500 input tokens over a six-hour window. Interactive target utilization is 60%; batch may use only residual capacity.

Interactive demand:

input  = 80 * 2,500 = 200,000 input tokens/s
output = 80 * 300   = 24,000 output tokens/s

Batch input demand to finish in six hours:

60,000,000 * 500 / (6 * 3,600)
= 1,388,889 input tokens/s

The batch is roughly seven times the interactive input-token rate. Request QPS obscures that difference. Run batch in a preemptible class with a completion forecast, and reserve measured interactive capacity. If shared workers cannot preempt safely or batch destroys cache locality, use separate pools.

Little's Law still applies to stable queues. If interactive arrival is 80/s and mean end-to-end time is 2.5 seconds, mean concurrency is 80 * 2.5 = 200. This is not a safe concurrency limit: p95 length, bursts, and failure reserve require a distribution-aware benchmark.

docs.title: 7. Admission and scheduling matrix
docs.text:
Workload Admission unit Queue discipline Shed or preempt first Recovery unit online score request plus feature fan-out deadline with tenant quota optional features/shadows request generation prompt/output tokens plus KV bytes weighted deadline/fair queue batch, long optional output sequence batch score partition bytes and estimated compute weighted fair-share low-priority job partition training accelerator-hours and topology quota/reservation experiments checkpoint embedding build records, tokens, output bytes throughput/fair-share stale rebuild partition/generation workflow steps, tool calls, wall time, spend per-run plus tool pools optional branches durable step stream feature partitions and event lag lag-aware noncritical projection source offset

Benchmark (measurement requirement, 2026-09): Build service curves per workload class by sweeping concurrency and realistic size distributions. Record queue time, service time, throughput, memory, errors, quality, and cost. The safe envelope ends before latency becomes unstable, not at the highest observed throughput point.

docs.title: 8. Data, APIs, and state
docs.text:
Expose the execution contract explicitly:

WorkRequest(id, tenant, class, input_ref, version_bundle, budget, deadline, priority)
WorkAttempt(id, request_id, worker, start, lease, checkpoint, resource_usage, outcome)
Artifact(id, request_id, type, uri, digest, schema, created_at)
Publication(id, artifact_ids, manifest_digest, state, activated_at)

For asynchronous work:

POST /v1/inference-jobs
Idempotency-Key: job-key-31

GET /v1/inference-jobs/{job_id}
POST /v1/inference-jobs/{job_id}:cancel

POST returns the same job for a repeated idempotency key and equivalent normalized request. Status distinguishes QUEUED, RUNNING, CANCELLING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, and CANCELLED. Cancellation is cooperative and the response states whether publication already happened.

For online work, return explicit completion reasons such as stop, length, policy_block, budget, deadline, and dependency_failure. A partial stream is not a successful final result until its terminal record is durable.

docs.title: Interactive
docs.text: Bound queues and reject early. Propagate deadlines. Keep retries within the original budget. Separate fallback eligibility by data class and task. Preserve capacity for health and recovery traffic.

docs.title: Batch and training
docs.text: Lease partitions, checkpoint progress, make output identity deterministic, and commit manifests atomically. A worker loss should replay one partition, not the entire dataset. Detect poison records separately from transient infrastructure errors.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: Coordinate source positions, operator state, and sink recovery at the checkpoint boundary. A transactional sink may prepare output before checkpoint completion and publish it afterward under the recovery protocol; an idempotent sink may publish earlier and safely repeat writes. Persisting offsets alone is not an exactly-once guarantee. Expect duplicates and late events, track event-time lag and replay boundaries, and keep schema and feature versions in output keys.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
Persist the state transition before acknowledging it. Reconcile unknown external outcomes before retry. Compensation is a domain action, not database rollback. Pin tool schema and policy versions for replay.

The failure cards map common symptoms to discriminating evidence.

docs.title: 10. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Every metric should identify workload class, tenant tier, version bundle, route, and outcome without exposing sensitive payloads.

Measure:

  • arrivals, admissions, queue age, service time, and deadline misses;
  • input/output units, size distributions, concurrency, memory, and accelerator utilization;
  • feature and retrieval fan-out, freshness, empty results, and cache behavior;
  • attempts per logical request, cancellations, wasted work, and fallback reasons;
  • quality and safety by stage and slice;
  • job progress, stragglers, retries, poison records, and publication lag;
  • cost per successful result and reserved-but-idle capacity.

Test each family differently: deterministic contract fixtures for APIs; load curves for online service; kill/restart and duplicate delivery for jobs; exact-neighbor comparison for ANN; replay and point-in-time tests for features; prompt injection and authorization tests for tool systems.

docs.title: 11. Product and vendor boundaries
docs.text:
Managed services can implement endpoints, queues, training jobs, or indexes, but product names do not remove workload semantics.

Vendor (KServe 0.20.0, released 2026-08-06): KServe documents InferenceService resources for predictive and generative model serving on Kubernetes, including deployment modes and autoscaling integrations. These capabilities do not define an application's label maturity, fallback safety, or release evidence. KServe 0.20.0 source and documentation

Production report (Netflix, published 2019-12-03): Netflix introduced Metaflow as a framework developed for its data-science workflows, emphasizing versioned code/data, execution, and scaling. The report describes Netflix's context; it does not imply that interactive serving and workflow orchestration should share one scheduler. Open-Sourcing Metaflow

docs.title: 12. Tradeoffs and evolution triggers
docs.text: Current choice Revisit when Likely evolution shared online/batch fleet preemption misses SLO or cache interference rises reserved interactive plus elastic batch pools synchronous generation clients disconnect or work exceeds bounded deadline durable job with stream/poll status one regional endpoint residency or correlated provider failure matters policy-aware regional/provider routes full recompute corpus growth breaks completion window snapshot plus incremental delta one queue tenant or length skew causes starvation hierarchical class and tenant fairness generic autoscaling queue delay rises before utilization demand-aware scaling with warm reserve

docs.title: 13. Interview exercise
docs.text:
Prompt: Design one platform for a retailer with product embeddings, interactive recommendations, nightly demand forecasts, a customer chat assistant, and an internal agent that may draft inventory transfers.

An L5 answer should refuse the premise that "one platform" means one runtime. Define shared control-plane capabilities - identity, registry, version bundles, evaluation, cost attribution, and policy - while assigning separate execution contracts and pools. Quantify each unit of work, choose synchronous or durable interfaces, isolate interactive capacity, and define workload-specific recovery.

An L6 answer should also define organization-wide workload classes, exception policy, capacity reservations, region/provider concentration, artifact lineage, common telemetry dimensions, and when teams may bypass shared infrastructure. The agent remains draft-only until exact action authorization, approval, and idempotency exist.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Classifies by deadline, resource vector, variability, state, and result semantics.
  • Separates online, batch, stream, training, embedding, and workflow contracts.
  • Uses the correct admission and recovery unit for each class.
  • Quantifies demand in tokens, records, bytes, memory, and attempts.
  • Defines workload-specific failure, observability, and evaluation.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Designs shared policy without forcing unlike workloads onto one data plane.
  • Governs reservations, fairness, preemption, evacuation, and exception paths.
  • Accounts for fleet-wide shadows, backfills, retries, and idle reserve.
  • Establishes common lineage and telemetry across independently evolving runtimes.
  • Connects workload taxonomy to team ownership and capacity economics.

docs.title: Final summary
docs.text: Name the workload before naming the product. Choose an interface from the deadline and durability requirement. Admit against the real resource vector. Isolate classes whose SLO, security, or interference profile differs. Recover at a deterministic unit, record versions and evidence, and evaluate the result using a contract appropriate to its error modes.

docs.title: ML and AI Pipelines
docs.text: An ML pipeline converts versioned data and code into evidence-bearing artifacts. Its correctness property is not merely "the DAG completed." The resulting dataset, model, evaluation, and publication must be reproducible, compatible, authorized, and safe to activate.

docs.title: 1. Scope and requirements
docs.text:
Design a platform that trains and releases ranking models for several product teams. It supports scheduled and event-triggered runs, offline and online features, backfills, human approval, and regional serving.

Core requirements:

  • reproduce a released artifact from immutable inputs or explain every irreproducible dependency;
  • prevent future data and mutable dimensions from leaking into historical examples;
  • separate artifact creation, evaluation, approval, and serving activation;
  • retry work without duplicating published artifacts or corrupting lineage;
  • backfill without starving production reads or mixing feature definitions;
  • support deletion, retention, access, and regional policy across snapshots and artifacts;
  • roll model, feature, parser, schema, and policy versions forward or back as compatible bundles.

Out of scope are optimizer internals and a universal notebook environment. The platform provides execution and evidence; teams remain responsible for task-specific labels, metrics, and risk decisions.

Principle: A successful task exit proves process completion. It does not prove point-in-time correctness, reproducibility, model quality, authorization, or release readiness.

docs.title: 2. Architecture: creation is not activation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Versioned sources] --> C[Snapshot catalog]
    C --> V[Validation and contracts]
    V --> F[Feature materialization]
    F --> T[Training]
    T --> A[(Artifact registry)]
    A --> E[Evaluation]
    E --> G[Release gate]
    G --> P[Publication controller]
    P --> O[Online serving bundle]
    P --> B[Batch scoring bundle]
    O --> L[(Prediction ledger)]
    B --> L
    Y[Outcomes and corrections] --> L
    L --> M[Quality and drift]
    M --> G
    R[Run orchestrator] --> V
    R --> F
    R --> T
    R --> E

The orchestrator manages durable execution. The catalog and registries are sources of truth for identity and lineage. Feature tables, online stores, indexes, and serving caches are rebuildable projections. The publication controller atomically changes a small active pointer only after every referenced artifact is present and compatible.

docs.title: 3. Run and artifact model
docs.text:
PipelineDefinition(id, version, owner, task_graph, parameter_schema)
Run(id, definition_version, trigger, parameters, principal, state, started_at)
TaskAttempt(id, run_id, task, attempt, input_manifest, lease, output_manifest, state)
DatasetSnapshot(id, source_versions, cutoff, query_digest, schema, partitions, digest)
FeatureView(id, definition_digest, entity_keys, event_time, created_time, ttl, schema)
ModelArtifact(id, training_run, bytes_digest, signature, interface, environment_digest)
Evaluation(id, model_id, dataset_id, suite_version, slices, metrics, uncertainty, decision)
ReleaseBundle(id, model, feature_view, tokenizer, prompt, policy, schema, status)
Publication(id, target, bundle_id, generation, approver, activated_at)

Use content-addressed immutable artifacts. Human-readable aliases may move, but a run records digests, not only aliases such as latest. Sign high-impact model and evaluation artifacts. A registry state transition should be auditable and authorization-controlled.

Suggested run states:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> QUEUED
    QUEUED --> RUNNING
    RUNNING --> SUCCEEDED
    RUNNING --> FAILED
    RUNNING --> CANCELLING
    CANCELLING --> CANCELLED
    FAILED --> RUNNING: retry eligible task
    SUCCEEDED --> PUBLISHED: separate gate
    SUCCEEDED --> REJECTED: evidence fails
    PUBLISHED --> RETIRED

SUCCEEDED means outputs are durable and verified. It does not imply PUBLISHED.

docs.title: 4. Pipeline and control interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/pipeline-runs
Idempotency-Key: ranker-train-2026-09-06

{
  "pipeline": "search-ranker",
  "definition_version": "sha256:...",
  "parameters": {
    "snapshot_id": "snapshot-842",
    "cutoff": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"
  }
}

POST /v1/releases/{bundle_id}:approve
If-Match: "candidate-generation-7"

POST /v1/targets/search-us:activate
Idempotency-Key: activate-bundle-482
If-Match: "active-generation-91"

Activation uses compare-and-swap so two approvers or automation paths cannot silently overwrite one another. The target reports desired and observed generation. Rollback activates a previous compatible immutable bundle; it does not mutate model bytes in place.

docs.title: 5. Orchestration semantics
docs.text: Tasks should be deterministic functions of declared inputs where practical. When they read time, randomness, remote mutable state, or external libraries, capture those dependencies explicitly.

docs.title: Leases and retries
docs.text:
An orchestrator grants a renewable lease. A worker writes outputs to an attempt-scoped location, calculates checksums, and commits an output manifest conditionally. If the lease expires, another worker may rerun the task. Only one manifest becomes canonical; abandoned bytes are garbage-collected later.

Exactly-once task execution is not required. Idempotent or fenced publication is.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Reuse output only when the cache key covers code digest, normalized parameters, input manifest digests, schema, environment, and relevant nondeterminism. Do not reuse an artifact merely because task names match. Security and deletion policy may invalidate otherwise identical cache entries.

docs.title: Dynamic DAGs
docs.text: Permit bounded fan-out derived from a committed manifest. Record the expanded graph. Avoid a task that discovers unlimited work while running because cancellation, cost prediction, and audit become unclear.

docs.title: 6. Point-in-time data correctness
docs.text:
For a training example representing a decision at time t, every feature must have both an eligible domain event time and an availability time no later than t, subject to the production system's actual availability semantics. A naive join against the latest customer row leaks future state.

Maintain event time and creation or ingestion time:

FeatureValue(entity_id, feature, value, event_time, created_time, source_version)
Label(entity_id, value, event_time, created_time, correction_version)

An as-of join must select a feature with event_time <= t and created_time <= t, where created_time is the first time the production decision path could observe that version. The pipeline's later simulation cutoff may limit which historical records the replay process can read, but it must never make a late arrival or correction appear available to the original decision. This bitemporal distinction exposes late arrival and correction.

[Vendor boundary, verified 2026-09-08] Feast's current point-in-time documentation says default historical joins constrain event time; a created timestamp otherwise selects the newest duplicate, which can leak later corrections. Its documented filter_by_created_timestamp=True adds availability-time filtering, excludes NULL creation timestamps, and is not supported by every offline store. Pin the installed Feast/store version and test the generated join. The flag cannot repair a timestamp that records file creation rather than actual online availability.

Test point-in-time logic with adversarial fixtures:

  • a feature changes after the label event;
  • a late event has old event time but new creation time;
  • an entity ID is reused or merged;
  • a source correction arrives after training;
  • a daylight-saving or timezone boundary occurs;
  • a deletion request removes an entity from future dataset construction.

docs.title: 7. Feature definitions and serving parity
docs.text:
A feature view declares entity keys, transformation, source, schema, freshness, default or missing semantics, and online/offline materialization behavior. Share definitions where possible, but do not claim perfect parity when execution engines differ. Compare values on sampled entity/timestamp fixtures and preserve missingness explicitly.

Online publication pattern:

  1. compute immutable offline partitions;
  2. validate schema, ranges, nulls, freshness, and cardinality;
  3. write online values with feature-view version and source watermark;
  4. reconcile counts and sampled values;
  5. advance the readable generation;
  6. retain the prior generation for rollback.

A missing value is not automatically zero. The model input should include a missingness indicator or use a documented model-compatible default. Safety-critical features may require fail-closed behavior.

docs.title: 8. Backfills and incremental processing
docs.text:
Backfills are production migrations. They can overload sources, create duplicate outputs, expose old code paths, and publish inconsistent windows.

Use a backfill contract:

Backfill(id, definition_version, input_range, snapshot, priority, max_parallelism,
         output_namespace, validation_policy, publication_policy, owner, state)

Controls:

  • read from snapshots or bounded source ranges rather than unrestricted live scans;
  • use separate quotas and pools from freshness-critical work;
  • partition by deterministic keys and record completion bitmaps;
  • quarantine poison partitions after bounded retries;
  • write to a new namespace or generation;
  • compare cardinality, checksums, distributions, and sampled records;
  • publish only after the full manifest passes;
  • throttle or pause automatically when online source SLOs burn.

Incremental processing starts from a snapshot watermark and applies ordered changes after it. Reconciliation checks both missing and extra keys. Replaying a feature transformation under new code must produce a new version, not overwrite history.

docs.title: 9. Capacity and cost
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): A daily pipeline reads 12 TB compressed, emits 2 TB of features, trains for 2,400 accelerator-hours, and must finish within 8 hours. Average source throughput may use at most 600 MB/s to protect shared storage. A task worker sustains 80 MB/s on the representative transform.

The source cap is stricter than worker count:

minimum source read time = 12,000,000 MB / 600 MB/s
                         = 20,000 s
                         = 5.56 h

workers to reach source cap = 600 / 80 = 7.5, so 8 workers

More transform workers do not reduce the source-bound stage below 5.56 hours. The training requirement needs average 2,400 / 8 = 300 accelerators if perfectly parallel, before topology constraints, checkpoints, failures, and queue time. If only 200 accelerators are available, the nominal training floor is 12 hours and the eight-hour requirement is infeasible without changing work, capacity, or deadline.

The 300-accelerator number is only a training-stage lower bound if training can use the entire eight-hour window. If training waits for the full scan/materialization, at most 8 - 20,000/3,600 = 2.4444 hours remain: even with perfect scaling, ceil(2,400/2.4444) = 982 accelerators are needed before validation and publication time. Sum sequential stage durations along the critical path; use a maximum only for stages whose overlap is actually supported. Extra accelerators cannot shorten a source-bound dependency.

Cost attribution includes source scans, intermediate storage, egress, failed attempts, idle reservations, feature publication, evaluation, and retained rollback artifacts. Charge by run and owner, but preserve shared-platform costs separately so team optimization does not hide fleet waste.

Benchmark (measurement requirement, 2026-09): Benchmark each material stage with representative schema, compression, partition size, skew, engine version, worker shape, storage path, and concurrency. Record input/output bytes, rows/s, accelerator utilization, shuffle/spill, p50/p99 partition time, failure rate, and cost. Extrapolate only after identifying the limiting resource.

docs.title: 10. Validation and release gates
docs.text:
Validation layers should identify the causal stage:

Layer Examples source contract schema compatibility, required columns, ownership, freshness dataset row count, uniqueness, ranges, nulls, slice coverage, leakage probes transformation golden fixtures, determinism, online/offline comparison training finite loss, checkpoint integrity, reproducibility tolerance model interface schema, tokenizer, feature order, runtime compatibility quality task metric, calibration, slices, confidence, baseline comparison safety abuse, privacy, fairness, prohibited behavior, high-impact slices operations latency, memory, throughput, fallback, cost, artifact loading

Evaluation sets are versioned products with owners and contamination controls. A generic model judge can support evaluation, but its prompt/version, repeatability, agreement with qualified humans, and slice biases must be measured. Do not let a single aggregate judge score approve a release.

docs.title: 11. Failure, recovery, and observability
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Recovery partial partition write missing/invalid output manifest discard attempt prefix and replay partition stale lease commits late fencing generation mismatch reject commit schema drifts mid-run source versions differ across manifest fail run and pin snapshot skewed hot partition p99 partition time and spill split key/range or isolate heavy entities poison record deterministic repeat at same record quarantine under policy; do not retry forever online publication partial desired/observed generation mismatch keep old readable pointer and repair model loads but feature order differs golden interface fixture fails block release deletion misses snapshot lineage query shows affected artifact restrict, rebuild, or expire by policy orchestrator unavailable workers retain bounded leases recover from durable run state

Monitor run and task state age, lease expiry, attempts, queue delay, stage throughput, bytes and rows, skew, source pressure, artifact verification, lineage completeness, data-quality failures, feature freshness, online/offline mismatch, release-gate outcomes, exception approvals, publication convergence, cost, and deletion workflow age.

docs.title: 12. Security and governance
docs.text:
Pipeline identity is workload identity, not a shared user credential. Authorize source reads, artifact writes, decryption, and release transitions separately. Isolate untrusted training code from credential and control-plane access. Scan dependencies and containers, pin environments, verify artifact digests at load time, and log administrative actions.

Training data can carry personal, licensed, confidential, or poisoned content. Record purpose and policy in snapshot construction. Keep secrets out of feature values and logs. Apply retention and deletion to intermediate tables, cached task output, checkpoints, registries, evaluation examples, and replay data.

Separation of duties matters for high-impact releases: the training principal produces a candidate; an evaluation service produces evidence; an authorized approver changes state; the deployment controller activates exactly the approved digest.

docs.title: 13. Alternatives and tradeoffs
docs.text:
Choice Advantage Cost or risk general workflow engine mature retries, schedules, observability ML lineage and gates remain application work ML-specific platform integrated artifacts, experiments, deployment platform coupling and governance assumptions shared feature definitions less training-serving skew engine parity and broad blast radius duplicate offline/online transforms optimized execution explicit parity testing and version coordination full snapshots simple reproducibility scan cost and freshness incremental deltas lower work and latency watermark, replay, and reconciliation complexity automatic retraining fast candidate creation feedback loops if activation is also automatic

Vendor (MLflow 3.16.0, released 2026-09-04): MLflow documents model lineage, versions, aliases, and tags in its Model Registry. Registry capabilities do not determine an application's approval policy, point-in-time dataset correctness, or serving compatibility bundle. MLflow 3.16.0 Model Registry

Production report (Google, published 2017-08): The TFX paper describes a production ML platform with data analysis, transformation, training, validation, and serving components, informed by Google's deployment experience. It demonstrates one integrated approach; teams must still adapt contracts and ownership to their environment. TFX paper

docs.title: 14. Rollout and migration
docs.text:
Start with immutable snapshots, artifact digests, a prediction ledger, and manual release gates. Add task caching only after cache identity is correct. Add shared features after point-in-time and parity tests exist. Add automatic candidate creation after evaluation and rollback are reliable; never let scheduling success self-approve a high-impact model.

For a feature or model migration:

  1. define compatibility and rollback bundles;
  2. build new offline and online generations from a pinned snapshot;
  3. catch up ordered deltas from the snapshot watermark;
  4. reconcile keys, values, freshness, and checksums;
  5. replay and shadow with the complete new bundle;
  6. canary by stable entity;
  7. expand through predefined gates;
  8. retain the old bundle until the rollback and audit windows close;
  9. retire data under retention and deletion policy.

docs.title: 15. Interview exercise
docs.text:
Prompt: Design pipelines for a delivery-time model trained daily from orders, courier locations, weather, and map data. Predictions serve at 20,000 requests/s. Weather corrections arrive late, map versions change weekly, and the company needs a 180-day historical replay.

An L5 answer pins order, weather, and map versions in dataset manifests; uses event and creation time; builds versioned feature views; separates training success from release; gates quality, slices, latency, and fallback; and rolls model plus features as one compatible bundle. It quantifies snapshot scans, training completion, online publication, and ledger storage.

An L6 answer adds source contracts across owning teams, correction semantics, backfill quotas, cross-region publication, deletion and retention, evaluation-set renewal, exception authority, and capacity governance. It explains how a historical replay handles information that arrived late without pretending it was known at prediction time.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Uses immutable manifests and content digests rather than mutable queries and tags.
  • Defines leases, retry-safe output, checkpoints, and atomic publication.
  • Handles point-in-time joins, late data, online/offline parity, and backfills.
  • Separates candidate creation, evaluation, approval, and activation.
  • Defines stage-level validation, recovery, lineage, and cost.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes cross-team data contracts, release policy, exceptions, and artifact retirement.
  • Governs shared source capacity, accelerator quotas, and backfill interference.
  • Plans bundle migrations, regional convergence, correction replay, and legal deletion.
  • Treats evaluation datasets, feature definitions, and lineage schemas as owned products.
  • Makes organizational and security boundaries visible in the control plane.

docs.title: Final summary
docs.text: A trustworthy pipeline is an evidence graph with durable execution. Pin source versions and time semantics. Commit attempt outputs through manifests. Treat features, models, evaluations, and release bundles as immutable artifacts. Validate every stage, publish atomically, preserve rollback, and make backfills respect production capacity and policy.

docs.title: Batch and Bulk Inference
docs.text: Batch inference applies a pinned model bundle to a finite dataset and publishes a verifiable output generation. Its main design problems are deterministic identity, restartability, throughput, source protection, stragglers, and safe publication - not request/response latency.

docs.title: 1. Problem framing and boundaries
docs.text:
Design a multi-tenant service that scores hundreds of millions of records for recommendations, risk review, and document enrichment. Jobs range from minute-scale deltas to full-corpus backfills.

Requirements:

  • accept a dataset manifest, model bundle, output contract, deadline, and priority;
  • partition work deterministically and retry without duplicate logical output;
  • isolate batch load from online databases and interactive inference;
  • expose progress, estimated completion, cancellation, and partial-failure evidence;
  • validate and atomically publish a complete output generation;
  • preserve lineage from each output to input snapshot, code, model, and attempt;
  • support incremental runs, backfills, corrections, deletion, and rollback.

Important exclusions: continuous online prediction, foundation-model training, and unbounded autonomous workflows. Use Online Model Serving for low-latency requests and ML and AI Pipelines for training and release governance.

Principle: Batch completion is a manifest transition. Individual output files are not visible as a complete dataset until validation succeeds and one generation is atomically published.

docs.title: 2. Job architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Client or scheduler] --> A[Job API and admission]
    A --> J[(Job metadata)]
    A --> P[Planner]
    P --> Q[Partition queues]
    Q --> W[Inference workers]
    S[(Input snapshots)] --> W
    R[(Model registry)] --> W
    W --> T[(Attempt output)]
    W --> J
    T --> V[Validation and reconciliation]
    V --> M[Manifest commit]
    M --> O[(Published generation)]
    D[Desired-state controller] --> Q
    D --> V
    J --> D

The control plane owns job state, quotas, version policy, and publication. The data plane leases partitions and creates immutable outputs. Workers do not advance the published dataset pointer directly.

docs.title: 3. API and state machine
docs.text:
POST /v1/batch-inference-jobs
Idempotency-Key: catalog-embed-2026-09-06

{
  "input_manifest": "s3://snapshots/catalog/epoch-410/manifest.json",
  "bundle_id": "embedding-bundle-29",
  "output": {
    "uri": "s3://derived/catalog-embeddings/",
    "schema": "catalog-embedding.v4"
  },
  "priority": "standard",
  "deadline": "2026-09-07T06:00:00Z",
  "failure_policy": {"max_bad_records": 100, "max_bad_fraction": 0.000001}
}

The service normalizes the request and returns the existing job when the same idempotency key and digest repeat. Reusing a key with different content returns a conflict.

Job(id, tenant, request_digest, input_manifest, bundle, output_schema,
    deadline, priority, quota, state, desired_state, published_generation)
Partition(id, job_id, key_range, input_digest, estimated_work, state, generation)
Attempt(id, partition_id, number, lease_generation, worker, start, output_uri,
        row_count, output_digest, usage, outcome)
BadRecord(job_id, partition_id, input_identity, reason_code, payload_ref)
OutputManifest(id, job_id, partition_outputs, row_count, schema, digest, state)

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> VALIDATING
    VALIDATING --> QUEUED
    VALIDATING --> REJECTED
    QUEUED --> RUNNING
    QUEUED --> CANCELLING
    RUNNING --> VALIDATING_OUTPUT
    RUNNING --> CANCELLING
    RUNNING --> FAILED
    CANCELLING --> CANCELLED
    VALIDATING_OUTPUT --> SUCCEEDED
    VALIDATING_OUTPUT --> CANCELLING
    VALIDATING_OUTPUT --> FAILED
    SUCCEEDED --> PUBLISHED
    SUCCEEDED --> CANCELLING: cancellation wins activation CAS
    PUBLISHED --> RETIRED

Cancellation stops new leases and asks active workers to checkpoint or finish their current partition. The final status states whether any output generation was already published.

Cancellation must also race safely with validation and publication, not only RUNNING. Persist a cancellation generation and condition the final active-pointer transaction on that generation still permitting publication. If activation wins first, report already published and use a separately authorized rollback; if cancellation wins, late validator/worker commits cannot activate the output. A queue message or cancellation flag checked only by workers cannot serialize this race.

docs.title: 4. Deterministic partition and output identity
docs.text:
Partition by stable input identity: manifest file and row group, key range, or (source_partition, offset_range). Avoid worker-count-dependent partitioning because changing fleet size then changes output identity and replay scope.

An output key can be:

output_key = hash(job_definition_digest, input_partition_digest, record_primary_key)

The inference result also includes the model bundle and schema version. Attempts write to unique temporary prefixes. Commit accepts one fenced attempt per partition. Retried attempts may produce the same logical output even when floating-point execution is not byte-identical; define whether validation compares exact digests, stable quantized values, or task-level tolerances.

Exactly-once execution across workers and object storage is unnecessary. At-least-once attempts plus deterministic identity, fenced partition commit, and idempotent publication provide the required observable semantics.

docs.title: Full snapshot
docs.text: Read one immutable source manifest, score every eligible key, validate completeness, and publish generation G. Full snapshots simplify reconciliation but can miss the deadline or overload sources at large scale.

docs.title: Incremental delta
docs.text: Start from a full snapshot watermark, then process ordered create/update/delete events. Keep output sequence or source version per key so late attempts cannot overwrite newer results. Periodic full reconciliation detects dropped events and drift.

docs.title: Corrections
docs.text: A corrected source record creates a new input version and output version. Do not edit the historical run. Publish a correction generation or delta with provenance. Downstream consumers define whether they need latest state, as-scored history, or both.

docs.title: Deletion
docs.text: Emit tombstones to active serving projections immediately when required, then remove output data, caches, retained inputs, and future dataset eligibility according to policy. Immutable audit exceptions need narrow access and expiration; "object storage is immutable" is not a deletion design.

docs.title: 6. Throughput and completion planning
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): A job scores 600 million records in a four-hour window. Mean serialized input is 4 KiB, mean output is 1 KiB, one worker sustains 220 records/s at the quality and error target, and usable target utilization is 70%.

Work rate and workers:

required records/s = 600,000,000 / (4 * 3,600)
                   = 41,667 records/s

usable worker rate = 220 * 0.70
                   = 154 records/s

workers = ceil(41,667 / 154)
        = 271

Storage traffic before replication and retries:

input  = 41,667 * 4 KiB = 162.8 MiB/s
output = 41,667 * 1 KiB = 40.7 MiB/s

This estimate is insufficient until the design checks model load time, request batch size, partition skew, source read caps, output commit rate, accelerator topology, failures, and a completion reserve. If 10% of partitions consume three times normal work, average worker throughput over uniform fixtures overstates capacity.

Use a completion forecast:

remaining_work_units / effective_recent_throughput

Break it down by stage and partition class. Alert before the deadline becomes mathematically unreachable.

Benchmark (measurement requirement, 2026-09): Measure worker throughput on the exact model/runtime/hardware tuple using production-shaped input sizes, batching, storage path, warm-up, concurrency, and skew. Report records/s, input and output units/s, p50/p99 partition duration, memory, errors, retries, and cost. Do not use peak accelerator utilization as a completion benchmark.

The calculations workbook contains additional batch throughput, retry, and storage exercises.

docs.title: 7. Batching and model execution
docs.text:
Batch records by compatible shape, token length, model, and deadline. Larger execution batches improve device utilization but increase buffering, padding, memory, and replay loss after failure. Cap batch wait time and total tokens or bytes, not only record count.

For generative bulk inference, output length is unknown. Reserve generated-token budget, checkpoint at record boundaries, and classify length-capped output explicitly. One long sequence should not hold an entire static batch; length buckets or continuous batching can reduce waste. Interactive and batch generation may share a runtime only when preemption, fairness, and recovery have been measured. See GPU Inference Platforms.

Load and verify the model bundle once per worker where possible. The bundle pins weights, tokenizer, preprocessing, runtime, prompt, and output schema. A worker reports readiness only after artifact digest checks and golden interface probes pass.

docs.title: 8. Stragglers, skew, and poison records
docs.text:
Partition duration has a tail. Diagnose before speculating:

  • size skew: partition contains more records or tokens;
  • compute skew: unusual inputs take longer;
  • placement: slower hardware or topology;
  • I/O: storage throttling or remote locality;
  • runtime: memory pressure, compilation, or leak;
  • poison data: deterministic parser/model failure.

Split large planned partitions before execution using manifest statistics. Allow a running worker to checkpoint subranges if the format supports deterministic boundaries. Speculative duplicate execution can reduce tail time for pure tasks, but it adds cost and source load; accept only one fenced output.

Retry transient infrastructure failures with backoff and an attempt cap. Quarantine deterministic bad records with reason codes only when the product contract allows partial completion. A failure threshold should include both count and fraction, because a fixed count behaves badly across job sizes. Never silently skip records.

docs.title: 9. Multi-tenancy, fairness, and overload
docs.text:
Use hierarchical scheduling:

  1. reserve recovery and system capacity;
  2. enforce tenant concurrency, accelerator-hour, source-bandwidth, and spend quotas;
  3. assign service by priority and weighted fair share;
  4. age waiting jobs to prevent starvation;
  5. permit controlled borrowing of idle quota;
  6. revoke borrowed capacity at safe partition boundaries.

Protect shared sources with global and per-source token buckets. Backfills use lower-priority pools and pause when source latency, replica lag, or online error budgets cross thresholds. Admission rejects a deadline the available capacity cannot plausibly meet rather than accepting an impossible job.

docs.title: 10. Validation and publication
docs.text:
Before publication, verify:

  • every expected partition has exactly one accepted output;
  • input and output manifests reference the intended digests;
  • row count, unique-key count, schema, nulls, ranges, and bad-record thresholds pass;
  • sampled records reproduce within declared tolerance;
  • deletion and eligibility filters were applied;
  • output size and distribution changes are explained;
  • serving replicas can load the generation;
  • downstream contract checks pass.

Write a complete immutable output manifest, then atomically advance the active pointer. Consumers read by generation or receive an activation event containing the manifest digest. Keep the old generation until consumers confirm readiness and the rollback window closes.

If activation events drive consumers, record the event in an outbox in the same transaction as the pointer change, then publish it with retry. Otherwise a crash after activation but before notification can strand consumers on the old generation. After an activation timeout, read the authoritative pointer and operation record before retrying; a missing response does not prove no change.

docs.title: 11. Failure and recovery table
docs.text: Failure Required evidence Recovery worker dies after upload lease and uncommitted attempt prefix replay partition; garbage-collect loser stale worker commits lease generation mismatch reject fenced commit model artifact unavailable bundle load failure by digest stop admission or route only to approved replica pool source snapshot missing part manifest verification failure reject before expensive work output store throttles write latency and retry queue reduce workers; preserve local bounded buffer control plane unavailable durable leases and desired state workers finish bounded leases; recover state incomplete generation before activation active pointer still old repair generation and revalidate activation response lost pointer and operation record identify committed generation return recorded outcome or retry the same conditional activation duplicate activation event generation/idempotency key consumer treats activation idempotently region lost mid-job committed partition manifest resume remaining partitions elsewhere if policy permits

docs.title: 12. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track admitted, queued, running, blocked, and completed jobs; queue age; estimated completion; partitions by state; attempt distribution; straggler ratio; records/tokens/bytes per second; model load time; accelerator/CPU/memory/I/O; source throttling; bad-record reasons; reconciliation gaps; publication lag; cancellation waste; cost per successful million records; and fairness by tenant.

Test:

  • worker death before and after output upload;
  • lease expiry and late commit;
  • duplicate queue delivery;
  • source throttling and output-store outage;
  • one partition 100 times larger than median;
  • deterministic poison records;
  • cancellation during validation and publication;
  • region recovery from the committed manifest;
  • model and schema incompatibility;
  • deletion during a long-running job.

docs.title: 13. Security and data governance
docs.text:
Authorize job submission separately from source access, model use, output destination, and activation. Bind workload identity to exact resources. Validate output URIs to prevent arbitrary writes. Keep secrets out of input rows and logs; use short-lived storage and registry credentials.

Data classification constrains worker region, provider, encryption key, retention, logging, and whether temporary local storage is permitted. Record who launched and approved a job, but do not expose raw sensitive rows in progress APIs. Quarantine storage requires tighter access and retention than successful aggregate output.

docs.title: 14. Vendor and production evidence
docs.text:
Vendor (Apache Spark 3.5.6 documentation, accessed 2026-09-06): Spark documents speculative execution settings that relaunch slow tasks. This mechanism may reduce some stragglers, but duplicate model work and source reads must fit the job's cost and load envelope. Spark configuration

Production report (Meta, published 2016-05-09): Meta described its FBLearner Flow platform as supporting reusable ML workflows, experiments, and large-scale training and prediction. The report shows the value of shared workflow abstractions in Meta's environment; it does not establish universal throughput or consistency guarantees. Introducing FBLearner Flow

docs.title: 15. Tradeoffs and evolution
docs.text:
Choice Benefit Cost small partitions fine recovery and balancing scheduler and manifest overhead large partitions efficient sequential work stragglers and expensive replay full snapshot simple completeness source and compute cost incremental delta fresh and efficient ordering, tombstones, reconciliation shared interactive fleet utilization SLO interference and limited preemption isolated batch fleet predictable deadline and failure domain idle capacity partial output allowed availability for tolerant tasks explicit missingness and repair contract all-or-nothing publication coherent generation waits for tail and repair

Evolve from scheduled full snapshots to snapshot-plus-delta when completion or freshness breaks. Introduce a mutable delta index only with deterministic merge and compaction semantics. Add cross-region continuation after manifests, artifact availability, residency policy, and output ownership are explicit.

docs.title: 16. Interview exercise
docs.text:
Prompt: Re-embed 2 billion marketplace listings within 36 hours while 5 million listing updates/day continue. Outputs feed semantic search. The old model must remain available, and deletion requests must take effect within 15 minutes.

An L5 design builds embedding/index generation B from a pinned listing snapshot, partitions by stable listing ranges, benchmarks tokens and records per worker, and catches up ordered changes after the snapshot watermark. It writes attempt-scoped output, reconciles cardinality and digests, benchmarks retrieval against exact neighbors, then shadow/canaries model B with index B as one bundle. A deletion tombstone blocks serving immediately in both generations while physical cleanup proceeds.

An L6 design adds source-read protection, tenant/category skew, global and regional capacity, impossible-deadline admission, correction ordering, dual-generation cost, rollback duration, deletion audit, publication ownership, and organizational coordination between catalog, search, privacy, and ML platform teams.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Defines immutable inputs, model bundle, deterministic partitions, attempts, and output manifest.
  • Uses fenced commit and idempotent publication rather than claiming exactly-once execution.
  • Quantifies throughput, bytes, retries, skew, and completion reserve.
  • Handles stragglers, poison records, cancellation, and partial failure.
  • Protects online sources and validates before atomic activation.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Governs tenant fairness, backfill priority, source budgets, and deadline admission.
  • Designs snapshot-plus-delta migration, regional recovery, deletion, and correction semantics.
  • Separates platform, source-owner, model-owner, and consumer responsibilities.
  • Models dual-generation economics and retirement evidence.
  • Defines policy for partial results, exceptions, and cross-product compatibility.

docs.title: Final summary
docs.text: Treat a batch run as a durable state machine over immutable manifests. Partition by stable identity, retry eligible attempts within deadline and cost bounds, fence commits, and publish only a validated generation. Plan from records, tokens, bytes, skew, and source limits. Make incremental updates, deletion, cancellation, fairness, and regional recovery explicit.

docs.text:
