docs.title: Online Model Serving
docs.text: Online model serving turns a versioned model bundle into a latency-bounded, policy-controlled prediction service. The endpoint is only the visible edge. Correctness also depends on feature time, preprocessing compatibility, overload behavior, fallback semantics, release evidence, and a durable decision record.

docs.title: 1. Scope and requirements
docs.text:
Design a multi-region serving platform for ranking and risk models. It supports unary predictions, small request batches, multiple model versions, online features, canaries, and tested fallback.

Requirements:

  • authenticate and authorize the task, subject, tenant, and data class;
  • bind each logical request to one compatible model, feature, preprocessing, schema, and policy bundle;
  • satisfy a declared end-to-end latency and availability SLO;
  • bound queueing, feature fan-out, batch wait, memory, attempts, and spend;
  • provide deterministic idempotency for product decisions where required;
  • fail safely when features, model runtime, region, or ledger is unavailable;
  • record enough evidence to evaluate delayed outcomes and reconstruct important decisions;
  • roll forward and back without mixing incompatible versions.

This chapter focuses on the service boundary. For accelerator-specific prefill/decode scheduling, KV cache, and continuous batching, use GPU Inference Platforms.

Principle: Autoscaling is a delayed capacity response. Bounded admission, queues, and fallback must protect the SLO while new model capacity loads.

docs.title: 2. Request path and control plane
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Caller] --> E[Edge auth and deadline]
    E --> G[Model gateway]
    G --> A[Policy and admission]
    A --> F[Feature coordinator]
    F --> S[(Online feature store)]
    F --> P[Preprocess and validate]
    P --> Q[Deadline-aware batch queue]
    Q --> R[Model replica]
    R --> D[Decision policy]
    D --> C
    G --> L[(Prediction ledger)]
    F --> L
    R --> L
    D --> L
    M[Model control plane] --> G
    M --> R
    M --> F

The gateway applies data-class and task policy before selecting a route. The serving runtime executes a pinned bundle. The decision-policy service converts scores into product actions, thresholds, reasons, or abstention. The model must not carry authority that belongs to the caller and policy.

The control plane maintains desired model placements, compatibility bundles, warm capacity, quotas, releases, and retirement. It should not sit synchronously in every prediction path; replicas consume signed immutable configuration and report observed state.

docs.title: 3. API and canonical state
docs.text:
POST /v1/predictions/risk.score
Idempotency-Key: payment-721-risk-decision
X-Deadline-Ms: 120

{
  "tenant_id": "merchant-41",
  "entity": {"payment_id": "p-721", "account_id": "a-62"},
  "event_time": "2026-09-06T10:15:20.114Z",
  "request_features": {"amount_minor": 4200, "currency": "INR"},
  "constraints": {"data_class": "restricted", "region": "in"}
}

{
  "request_id": "pred-902",
  "score": 0.82,
  "decision": "REVIEW",
  "reason_codes": ["velocity_high"],
  "bundle_id": "risk-in-2026-09-06.4",
  "feature_watermark": "2026-09-06T10:15:18Z"
}

ServingBundle(id, model_digest, runtime, preprocess_digest, feature_view,
              request_schema, output_schema, policy_id, status)
Replica(id, bundle_id, region, zone, hardware, state, loaded_at, verified)
LogicalPrediction(id, idempotency_key, principal, entity, event_time,
                  input_digest, bundle_id, deadline, state)
Attempt(id, prediction_id, route, replica, start, queue_ms, feature_ms,
        model_ms, usage, outcome)
Decision(prediction_id, score_digest, action, reason_codes, policy_id, time)

Idempotency scope follows the business operation. A repeated payment decision should return the committed result for the same normalized input. An exploratory recommendation request may intentionally produce a fresh ranked page and use a different consistency contract.

The caller keeps the business-scoped idempotency key stable across transport and provider retries. Attempt numbers and provider request IDs are internal records under that one logical prediction; they never appear in the key used to deduplicate the product decision.

docs.title: 3A. Generative model gateway
docs.text: A generative gateway is the policy, compatibility, and evidence boundary between product applications and model providers or self-hosted runtimes. It should normalize stable product semantics without pretending that all providers expose identical behavior.

docs.title: Gateway invariants
docs.text:
1. Authenticate and authorize task, tenant, data class, model entitlement, tools, and region before provider routing.
  2. Bound input, output, wall time, attempts, concurrency, and spend on the logical request.
  3. Preserve one logical request across provider attempts; never bill or measure retries as independent user demand.
  4. A route is eligible only when model, prompt, structured-output, tool, safety, region, and retention requirements are compatible.
  5. Streaming ends with a terminal record containing finish reason, usage or usage-estimation status, route, and evidence ID.
  6. Unknown provider fields are retained in a controlled raw envelope when needed, but do not silently change normalized semantics.
  7. Fallback is task policy, not a generic retry to any available model.
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> E[Edge identity and limits]
    E --> N[Normalize logical request]
    N --> P[Policy and data classification]
    P --> R[Provider and model router]
    R --> A[Hosted provider A]
    R --> B[Hosted provider B]
    R --> S[Self-hosted runtime]
    A --> V[Stream and schema validator]
    B --> V
    S --> V
    V --> L[(Attempt and usage ledger)]
    V --> C

docs.title: Request and attempt contracts
docs.text:
GenerationRequest(id, tenant, task, messages, context_refs,
                  response_schema, tool_set, data_class,
                  deadline, token_budget, spend_budget,
                  route_policy, version_bundle)
GenerationAttempt(id, request_id, provider, model_revision,
                  provider_request_id, start, first_byte, end,
                  token_usage, cache_usage, outcome, retry_reason)
StreamEvent(request_id, sequence, type, delta, usage, finish_reason, time)

Normalized stream event types should be few and stable: response.started, content.delta, tool_call.delta, tool_call.completed, usage.updated, response.completed, and response.failed. Sequence numbers are monotonic per logical stream. The final event is durable before the gateway reports clean completion.

docs.title: Streaming behavior
docs.text:
Server-Sent Events or another explicit streaming protocol should distinguish transport closure from model completion. A client disconnect triggers cancellation, but the gateway records whether provider work continued and whether usage is final, estimated, or unavailable.

Do not buffer the full response merely to validate a terminal schema when latency requires streaming. Choose one of three explicit contracts:

  • stream untrusted draft text and mark it provisional until terminal validation;
  • buffer and validate before release for strict structured or high-impact output;
  • stream bounded fields that can be incrementally validated, then commit a terminal object.

Backpressure must be bounded. If the client reads too slowly, pause provider reads where supported, buffer only to a declared limit, or cancel. Measure time to first token, inter-token gaps, total time, cancellation lag, and work produced after disconnect.

Once a content prefix has reached the client, fallback needs an explicit stream contract. Do not append a second model's restarted answer to the first model's unfinished sentence. Either terminate with a partial-result error, or send a versioned replacement event that the client understands and start a new attempt segment. A reconnect may replay durable events by sequence; it does not promise that rerunning generation will reproduce the same tokens. Incomplete tool-call arguments remain non-executable.

Provisional is a correctness label, not a confidentiality control. Once text reaches a client, later schema or safety failure cannot retract it. For sensitive output, validate before disclosure; sanitize any streamed Markdown/HTML and constrain browser-loaded URLs. This output-sink boundary is distinct from typed tool authorization; see OWASP LLM05:2025, verified 2026-09-08.

docs.title: Structured output
docs.text:
Treat a provider's schema mode as constrained generation, not proof of domain validity. Validate again at the gateway with a pinned schema. Reject unknown fields where security requires it. Then apply semantic checks such as currency consistency, resource existence, amount limits, citation support, and policy.

{
  "schema_id": "refund-proposal-v4",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["order_id", "amount_minor", "currency", "reason"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "order_id": {"type": "string"},
    "amount_minor": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
    "currency": {"type": "string"},
    "reason": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 500}
  }
}

Parser repair can hide model regressions. Record raw invalid output, repair attempt, repaired result, and whether the product accepts repaired output. Never use free-form repair for security-sensitive tool arguments.

docs.title: Provider routing and fallback
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Logical request] --> B{Task and data policy pass?}
    B -- no --> X[Deny]
    B -- yes --> C[Eligible route set]
    C --> D{Schema tool and context compatible?}
    D -- no --> X
    D -- yes --> E{Healthy within deadline and quota?}
    E -- no --> F{Approved fallback remains?}
    F -- no --> Y[Shed or defer]
    F -- yes --> BUD[Charge attempt budget and exclude failed route]
    BUD --> C
    E -- yes --> G[Reserve budget and dispatch]

Score eligible routes using measured task quality, deadline success, capacity, data handling, and cost. Keep hard constraints separate from optimization. A lower-cost provider cannot override residency or safety gates.

Use circuit breakers by provider, model, region, and failure class. A provider 429 may justify another route if budget and compatibility permit; malformed structured output is a model-behavior failure and should not trigger unlimited cross-provider retries. Reserve receiver quota and capacity before declaring fallback ready.

Gateway tests include stream ordering, duplicate terminal events, disconnect, provider timeout, partial tool call, invalid UTF-8 or JSON, schema drift, usage missing, provider quota, incompatible fallback, data-region denial, and retry budget exhaustion.

docs.title: 3B. Prompt and context engineering
docs.text: Prompt engineering is interface engineering. Version the instruction hierarchy, context selection, examples, tool schemas, output schema, and truncation policy as one behavior-bearing bundle.

docs.title: Prompt hierarchy
docs.text:
Use explicit layers with decreasing authority:

  1. platform safety and non-negotiable policy;
  2. product/task instructions;
  3. developer workflow and output contract;
  4. authorized user request;
  5. retrieved documents, tool output, and quoted content as untrusted data.

Provider-specific message roles may differ. Compile the canonical hierarchy into a provider adapter and test semantic parity. Retrieved text cannot become a higher-authority instruction because it contains phrases such as "system message".

PromptBundle(id, canonical_template, provider_adapters,
             examples_manifest, tool_schema_set, output_schema,
             context_policy, truncation_policy, safety_policy,
             compatible_models, evaluation_run, digest)

docs.title: Context assembly and token budget
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[System and task policy] --> H[Priority context assembler]
    B[Current user turn] --> H
    C[Conversation state] --> H
    D[Retrieved evidence] --> H
    E[Tool schemas] --> H
    F[Reserved output] --> H
    H --> T[Tokenizer-specific count]
    T -->|fits| M[Model request]
    T -->|over| P[Compress drop or reject by policy]
    P --> T
hard_context_limit
>= system_tokens
 + task_tokens
 + user_tokens
 + conversation_tokens
 + retrieval_tokens
 + tool_schema_tokens
 + reserved_output_tokens
 + tokenization_margin

For a 16,384-token model with 1,000 system/task tokens, 1,500 user/conversation tokens, 5,000 retrieval tokens, 2,000 tool-schema tokens, 3,000 reserved output tokens, and 5% margin on the hard limit:

margin    = ceil(16,384 * 0.05) = 820
committed = 1,000 + 1,500 + 5,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 + 820
          = 13,320
headroom  = 16,384 - 13,320 = 3,064 tokens

Count with the exact tokenizer and chat template. Reject or shorten before dispatch; provider-side truncation is not a context policy.

docs.title: Versioning and release
docs.text:
A prompt change can alter safety, latency, token cost, retrieval use, and tool behavior. Release it like code:

  1. immutable prompt bundle and diff;
  2. static checks for missing variables, authority order, and schema compatibility;
  3. deterministic fixtures and injection corpus;
  4. paired offline evaluation by task and critical slice;
  5. shadow with tools disabled or isolated;
  6. stable-cohort canary;
  7. rollback pointer and cache invalidation.

Record effective prompt bundle on every attempt. Do not interpolate runtime policy text from mutable stores without a version and digest.

docs.title: Prompt caching
docs.text:
Cache only stable prefixes whose provider and data policy allow retention. Cache identity includes provider, model/tokenizer revision, prompt bundle, tenant/security domain, tool schema set, and relevant policy epoch.

prompt_cache_key
= hash(provider, model_revision, tokenizer_revision,
       prompt_bundle_digest, tenant_scope,
       tool_schema_digest, policy_epoch, stable_prefix_digest)

Never share personalized, restricted, or tenant-specific prefixes across security domains. Cache hits still require current authorization and deletion checks. Measure hit rate, saved input work, latency change, provider cache charges, stale rejections, and cross-tenant invariant violations.

docs.title: Context compression
docs.text:
Prefer deterministic selection first: remove duplicates, retrieve fewer stronger candidates, omit unused tool schemas, and trim stale conversation. Use extractive compression when source spans and citations must survive. Abstractive summaries create a derived artifact with model/prompt version, provenance, validity range, and evaluation.

Compression ratio and support retention are separate:

compression_ratio = original_context_tokens / compressed_context_tokens
evidence_retention = required_facts_preserved / required_facts_before_compression

A 4x compression that preserves only 70% of required facts is not an optimization for an evidence-bound task. Evaluate answerability, support, instruction injection, latency, and cost before enabling compression. Keep the original source accessible for citation and audit when policy permits.

docs.title: Prompt and context failures
docs.text: Failure Evidence Control hierarchy inversion injection test by source layer typed assembly and untrusted delimiters silent truncation token ledger and dropped sections preflight count and semantic priority schema bloat tool-schema token distribution task-scoped tool sets stale cached prefix policy/version mismatch epoch in key and reauthorization lossy summary required-fact retention extractive fallback or reject prompt rollout regression paired slice metrics canary and atomic rollback provider adapter drift canonical/provider fixture diff compatibility suite

docs.title: 4. Latency budget and deadline propagation
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): A fraud decision has a 120 ms server deadline and a caller-visible p99 SLO measured from the joint latency distribution. Allocate 12 ms to network and edge, 35 ms to feature access, 5 ms to preprocessing, 12 ms to queueing, 35 ms to model execution, 8 ms to decision and ledger, and 13 ms to reserve.

Stage Deadline allocation edge and route 12 ms feature fetch 35 ms preprocessing 5 ms queue 12 ms model 35 ms policy and ledger 8 ms reserve 13 ms total 120 ms

The allocations are timeout and admission controls, not per-stage p99 measurements. Percentiles of dependent stages are not additive; prove the end-to-end p99 from per-request traces and distribution-aware load tests, then use stage distributions to diagnose budget burn.

Each downstream call receives the remaining deadline, not a fresh timeout. Do not start model work when there is insufficient time to finish and validate it. A request that expires in queue should be removed before execution. Cancellation metrics must show work that continued after callers left.

Tail latency composes badly across fan-out. Batch feature reads and keep the critical feature set small. Optional features receive a shorter deadline and an explicit model-compatible missingness path. The product SLO is measured at the caller-visible boundary, not only inside the model runtime.

docs.title: 5. Feature correctness
docs.text:
The online feature view pins definitions, entity keys, schema, freshness, default behavior, and source watermark. Request-time facts such as the current transaction should travel in the request envelope rather than wait for asynchronous materialization.

Feature invariants:

  • event identity and event time are explicit;
  • no feature value newer than the permitted decision time is used;
  • missing, stale, unavailable, and true zero are distinguishable;
  • feature order and types match the model interface;
  • freshness-critical values expose watermark or age;
  • fallback models declare compatible feature subsets;
  • regional replicas do not silently serve a watermark older than policy allows.

Use one batch read where possible. Co-locate hot feature state with serving while preserving an authoritative rebuild path. Cache only under versioned keys and TTLs consistent with feature semantics. Point-in-time training and publication are covered in ML and AI Pipelines.

docs.title: 6. Dynamic batching and queueing
docs.text:
Microbatching waits briefly to combine compatible requests. It can improve vectorized CPU/GPU throughput, but wait time consumes the latency budget and one large input may distort the batch.

Batch compatibility includes bundle, tensor shape or length bucket, data class, and deadline class. Bound:

  • maximum requests;
  • total input units or tokens;
  • maximum wait;
  • estimated memory;
  • earliest deadline;
  • tenant contribution.

Use deadline-aware queues with tenant fairness. Reserve lanes for critical classes and health probes. Reject before an unbounded queue converts overload into timeouts. A model replica should expose readiness only after weights, runtime, preprocessing, and golden fixtures are verified.

docs.title: 7. Capacity model
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): Peak demand is 18,000 predictions/s. A benchmarked replica sustains 1,100 predictions/s at the target input distribution and p99 model latency. Target steady utilization is 60%. One zone may be lost from a three-zone region.

Usable capacity per replica is 1,100 * 0.60 = 660 predictions/s. Traffic needs:

ceil(18,000 / 660) = 28 replicas

To preserve that capacity after losing one of three equal zones, each remaining zone must carry half the demand. Provision at least ceil(28 * 3 / 2) = 42 replicas across three zones, or 14 per zone, before considering skew and maintenance. This is an illustrative N+zone calculation; real placement must use measured per-hardware capacity and actual traffic distribution.

Little's Law estimates concurrency. At 18,000/s and 70 ms mean service time, mean in-flight work is 18,000 * 0.070 = 1,260 requests. Pools must also survive tail latency and bursts. Size each dependency separately; one global concurrency limit hides a saturated feature store behind idle model capacity.

Benchmark (measurement requirement, 2026-09): Sweep concurrency for the exact bundle and production-shaped feature availability, payload, batch policy, hardware, runtime, and network path. Report throughput and p50/p95/p99 end-to-end, queue, feature, and model latency; errors; memory; utilization; warm-up; quality; and cost. Select the safe operating envelope before the latency knee.

docs.title: 8. Routing, fallback, and overload
docs.text:
Routing order:

  1. authenticate principal and task;
  2. classify data and residency constraints;
  3. select only compatible approved bundles;
  4. check tenant, token, concurrency, and spend quota;
  5. select healthy region/pool/replica with deadline capacity;
  6. record route reason and attempt;
  7. use fallback only if the task's policy allows it.

Fallback is a product decision:

Failure Eligible fallback Ineligible behavior primary model unavailable previous approved compatible model arbitrary model with different score semantics optional features unavailable tested reduced feature bundle zero-fill undeclared inputs critical feature stale deterministic conservative policy score as if fresh region unavailable approved region for data class cross residency boundary ledger unavailable buffer bounded low-risk evidence or reject unaudited high-impact action overload reject, queue briefly, or degrade by class unlimited retries

Circuit breakers isolate a dependency or bundle, but global fallback can overload the backup. Reserve fallback capacity and precompute incident cost. Prioritize critical decisions, shed shadows and optional enrichments first, and preserve health/recovery headroom.

docs.title: 9. Caching
docs.text:
Cache deterministic outputs only when the key includes every behavior-bearing input: task, normalized input, model bundle, policy, feature versions or watermark, tenant/security domain, and relevant sampling controls. A score cache can become incorrect when volatile features change even if the entity ID does not.

Generative semantic caching has a wider error surface: near inputs may not be policy-equivalent, source evidence may change, and personalized context can leak. Treat it as a retrieval and authorization system, not a generic performance switch. Cache hits still need current policy and deletion checks.

docs.title: 10. Release, canary, and rollback
docs.text:
Build a bundle from immutable model, runtime, preprocessing, feature view, schema, and policy references. Verify digest and interface compatibility in a staging replica. Replay representative traffic, then shadow if duplicate data processing is permitted. Canary by stable entity hash so repeated decisions do not alternate versions.

Gates include:

  • request and output contract compatibility;
  • model task metric, calibration, and critical slices;
  • feature availability, freshness, and parity;
  • p50/p95/p99 stage latency and capacity;
  • error, timeout, fallback, and cost;
  • decision-rate and disagreement bounds;
  • safety and privacy tests;
  • mature outcomes when labels arrive.

Rollback changes the active pointer to a warm compatible bundle. Decisions already made are not undone; identify remediation or review when a bad release caused external effects. Changing only a threshold or preprocessing rule can require the same release evidence as changing weights.

docs.title: 11. Multi-region design
docs.text:
Prefer serving close to authoritative features. Active-active inference is straightforward only when bundle availability, policy, feature freshness, idempotency scope, and ledger semantics are defined across regions.

Options:

  • regional independence: each region owns traffic, features, and ledger; easiest isolation;
  • home-region decision: route each entity to one region; stronger consistency at network cost;
  • active-active with replicated features: lower local latency; must define lag and conflict behavior;
  • cold failover: lower cost; recovery time includes artifact loading and cache warming.

Never assume a model artifact available in object storage is ready for failover. Preload, verify, warm, and probe required bundles. Test whether fallback-region feature state meets the decision's freshness contract. See Multi-Region Systems.

docs.title: 12. Failure, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Control tokenizer/preprocessor mismatch golden fixture digest differs block readiness stale features age/watermark by feature group fail or compatible fallback queue saturation queue age before utilization spike admission and class isolation replica OOM input/batch memory envelope bounded batch and request size fallback storm route reasons and backup saturation reserved capacity and breaker retry amplification attempts/logical request one budget and backoff shadow affects state side-effect/exposure audit isolated shadow sink regional split bundle and feature generation divergence pin/route or degrade prediction succeeds, response lost committed idempotency result return stored decision

Observe logical requests and attempts; arrivals, admission, queue age, and shed rate; stage latency; batch shape; feature availability and freshness; model utilization/memory; score/action distribution; bundle and route; fallback; idempotency hits; cancellation waste; quality and calibration on mature labels; cost per successful prediction; desired/observed replicas; load and warm time.

Test contract and golden vectors, feature missing/stale cases, deterministic policy, load and soak, burst and hot tenant, zone loss, model load failure, feature-store partition, ledger outage, deadline cancellation, duplicate requests, canary rollback, and recovery with stale replicated features.

The failure cards include tokenizer drift, fallback bypass, cost runaway, and capacity incidents.

docs.title: 13. Security and privacy
docs.text:
Authenticate service identity and end-user context where relevant. Authorize task, model entitlement, subject, feature purpose, tenant, data class, and region before routing. Restrict administrative release and traffic-shift APIs separately from inference.

Do not log raw feature vectors or prompts by default. Use field-level redaction and access-controlled replay records. Encrypt model artifacts and verify signatures. Protect models from unapproved extraction traffic with authentication, quotas, abuse detection, and response minimization. Propagate deletion to online features, prediction caches, replay payloads, and future training eligibility.

docs.title: 14. Vendor and production evidence
docs.text:
Vendor (NVIDIA Triton Inference Server 2.72.0, released 2026-08-31; r26.08 documentation): Triton documents dynamic batching, model repositories, schedulers, and metrics. Those runtime capabilities do not supply application-specific feature-time correctness, decision idempotency, or model-quality release gates. Triton r26.08 documentation

Production report (Uber, published 2017-09-05): Uber reported that Michelangelo supported online and offline prediction and model deployment as part of a broader internal ML platform. The report motivates integrated version and serving operations in Uber's context; it is not a throughput benchmark or universal topology. Introducing Michelangelo

docs.title: 15. Tradeoffs and evolution
docs.text:
Choice Benefit Risk embedded model in service low hop count, simple small deployment duplicated rollout and poor fleet utilization shared serving platform utilization, standardized policy and telemetry multi-tenant blast radius and platform dependency request-time features freshest state fan-out and tail latency materialized features bounded reads lag and training-serving coordination CPU availability and simple operations for small models lower throughput for some models accelerator high throughput for compatible work batching, memory, topology, and cold load warm fallback fast recovery ongoing cost cold fallback lower idle cost recovery may violate SLO

Start with one task-specific service and an explicit bundle. Introduce a shared gateway when policy, observability, and provider routing repeat across teams. Introduce a shared runtime when workload compatibility and isolation are demonstrated. Split pools by deadline, hardware, security domain, or failure risk when interference becomes material.

docs.title: 16. Interview exercise
docs.text:
Prompt: Design real-time ranking inference for a marketplace at 50,000 requests/s across three regions. The p99 server budget is 80 ms. Each request ranks 500 candidates, uses user and item features, and returns 50 items. A previous-model fallback is acceptable; stale block and inventory state is not.

An L5 design batches feature reads, keeps block/inventory as deterministic hard filters, pins model/feature/policy bundles, budgets every stage, benchmarks candidate batch shapes, and admits against each dependency. It canaries by user, records decisions and attempts, preserves warm previous bundles, and fails closed on stale hard constraints while degrading optional ranking features.

An L6 design adds regional feature lag policy, user home-region/idempotency semantics, zone evacuation capacity, tenant fairness, shared-feature blast radius, model/index or feature migration, release exception ownership, privacy deletion, and fleet economics. It distinguishes model ranking quality from final policy-filtered product outcomes.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Provides an end-to-end latency budget and propagates remaining deadlines.
  • Pins model, preprocessing, features, schema, and policy in one bundle.
  • Quantifies measured replica capacity, concurrency, zone reserve, and queue bounds.
  • Defines feature freshness, fallback compatibility, idempotency, and rollback.
  • Measures stage health, quality, safety, and cost by version and route.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Governs fleet placement, fallback reserve, regional policy, and concentration risk.
  • Separates platform and product decision ownership with auditable exceptions.
  • Plans compatibility migrations and remediation for already-made decisions.
  • Models multi-tenant fairness and correlated feature/runtime failure.
  • Connects warm capacity, quality, and availability to portfolio economics.

docs.title: Final summary
docs.text: An online model service is a deadline-bound decision path over a compatible version bundle. Authorize before routing, fetch features with explicit time semantics, bound queues and batches, benchmark the full path, and separate score from policy. Preserve evidence, degrade only through approved compatible paths, and keep rollback capacity ready.

docs.title: Embeddings and Vector Retrieval
docs.text: An embedding maps an input into a numeric space where a distance function can support candidate retrieval. Production design must preserve what was embedded, with which model and preprocessing, under which authorization, and into which index generation. A vector database does not answer those questions.

docs.title: 1. Scope and requirements
docs.text:
Design semantic retrieval for an enterprise knowledge system with hundreds of millions of chunks, tenant and document ACLs, hybrid lexical/vector search, minute-scale update visibility, citations, and deletion.

Requirements:

  • preserve immutable source version, offsets, ACLs, parser, chunker, embedding model, and vector lineage;
  • keep query and corpus embeddings in the same compatible vector space;
  • enforce tenant and authorization constraints before unauthorized content enters context;
  • meet latency while measuring approximation loss against exact search;
  • combine lexical, vector, and reranking stages deterministically;
  • publish complete index generations and support rollback;
  • expose source provenance and abstain when support is insufficient;
  • process updates and deletion within declared freshness SLOs.

This chapter develops the embedding lifecycle and retrieval contract. Search and Indexing already explains general inverted indexes, sharding, HNSW, IVF, and search-engine operations. RAG and Agent Security covers prompt injection, citation security, and tool authority.

Principle: Approximate nearest-neighbor search is a candidate-generation optimization. It does not define relevance, authorization, factual support, or the canonical source of truth.

docs.title: 2. End-to-end architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[(Versioned sources)] --> P[Parse and normalize]
    P --> C[Chunk and provenance]
    C --> E[Embedding workers]
    E --> B[(Base index generation)]
    U[Source updates] --> UE[Parse chunk and embed with pinned bundle]
    UE --> D[(Fresh delta index)]
    TS[Delete and supersession map] --> H
    Q[Query] --> A[Auth and query policy]
    A --> AP[Mandatory tenant and ACL predicates]
    A --> QE[Query embedding]
    AP --> LX[ACL-filtered lexical candidates]
    AP --> VX[ACL-filtered vector candidates]
    QE --> VX
    B --> VX
    D --> VX
    LX --> F[Fusion and dedupe]
    VX --> F
    F --> H[Current-state reauthorization and hydration]
    H --> R[Reranker]
    R --> K[Context and citations]
    K --> O[Answer or search result]
    M[Index manifest controller] --> B
    M --> QE

The canonical text and ACL live outside the vector index. The index is a rebuildable projection. Mandatory tenant and ACL predicates constrain each candidate search before fusion; candidate records carry IDs and scores, and hydration rechecks current authorization before resolving immutable source spans. Base-plus-delta supports freshness while keeping large base generations immutable.

docs.title: 3. Embedding and chunk identity
docs.text:
SourceVersion(source_id, version, tenant, uri, media_type, digest, acl_version, state)
Chunk(chunk_id, source_id, source_version, start_offset, end_offset,
      text_digest, parser_version, chunker_version, language, acl_ref)
Embedding(embedding_id, chunk_id, model_id, preprocess_version,
          dimensions, dtype, normalized, vector_digest, created_at)
IndexGeneration(id, embedding_model, distance, dimensions, base_snapshot,
                delta_watermark, build_config, manifest_digest, state)
Tombstone(chunk_id, source_version, reason, effective_at, sequence)
Retrieval(request_id, query_digest, query_model, index_generation,
          filters, lexical_version, fusion_version, reranker_version, results)

Chunk IDs should be stable for an unchanged source version and span, but a changed parser, chunker, normalization, or source content can create a new chunk identity. Content hashes help deduplicate bytes; they do not replace tenant, source, ACL, or licensing metadata.

Store vector dimensions and distance configuration. Cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance are not interchangeable without assumptions such as normalization. Validate query dimensions and model ID before search.

docs.title: 4. Chunking and preprocessing
docs.text:
Chunking sets the retrieval unit and citation boundary. Tiny chunks lose context and increase index entries; large chunks dilute relevance and consume reranking/model context. Choose from source structure and evaluated tasks rather than one global token count.

Preserve headings, table context, code block boundaries, page or section identifiers, and byte/character offsets. Handle documents too large or malformed to parse through bounded resources and quarantine. OCR, language detection, transcription, and table extraction each add a versioned uncertainty-bearing stage.

Useful policies:

  • structure-aware boundaries before token-length fallback;
  • bounded overlap only where cross-boundary context improves measured recall;
  • parent-child retrieval when a small child locates a larger coherent passage;
  • source-specific chunkers for code, tables, tickets, and policies;
  • exact canonical text hydration rather than treating stored embedding text as truth;
  • deterministic normalization and golden fixtures for offset preservation.

Evaluate chunking at candidate recall, citation support, context tokens, latency, and index cost. A generation-quality change can originate in chunking even when the generation model is unchanged.

docs.title: 5. Embedding model contract
docs.text:
An embedding model contract includes:

  • artifact and tokenizer digest;
  • preprocessing and prompt/prefix convention;
  • input type, language, length, and truncation policy;
  • dimensions, numeric type, normalization, and distance;
  • intended task and known evaluation slices;
  • runtime, batch policy, and maximum input;
  • data-use and region restrictions;
  • release and retirement state.

Query and corpus encoders may differ in asymmetric retrieval, but their compatibility is defined by one model bundle. Never send model-B query vectors to a model-A corpus index merely because dimensions match.

docs.title: 6. Search interface and filters
docs.text:
POST /v1/retrieval:search

{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-17",
  "query": "How long are approved refunds retained?",
  "top_k": 10,
  "filters": {
    "repository": ["policy"],
    "effective_at_lte": "2026-09-06T00:00:00Z"
  },
  "deadline_ms": 300,
  "index_generation": "policy-semantic-84"
}

The server derives mandatory tenant, principal, purpose, and ACL predicates. The caller may add only allowlisted narrowing filters; it cannot remove mandatory policy.

{
  "generation": "policy-semantic-84",
  "results": [{
    "chunk_id": "c-91",
    "source_id": "refund-policy",
    "source_version": "2026-08-14",
    "span": {"start": 1940, "end": 2510},
    "scores": {"vector": 0.81, "lexical_rank": 3, "reranker": 4.7}
  }],
  "partial": false
}

Scores are not calibrated probabilities. Avoid exposing one universal threshold unless validated for that model, index, filter, and query distribution.

docs.title: 7. Authorization and filter placement
docs.text:
Partition by tenant or security domain where that boundary is strong. Within a partition, use filter-aware candidate search if the index supports it, then reauthorize during hydration. Post-filtering a global top-K can both leak information and starve authorized results.

If only 1% of a corpus is authorized and the system retrieves 100 global neighbors then post-filters, the expected count under a uniform independence assumption is only one; real clustering can make it zero. Overfetching 10,000 candidates is expensive and still not an authorization proof.

Security patterns:

  • separate indexes for hard isolation boundaries;
  • prefilter using immutable or correctly updated ACL dimensions;
  • oversample only within a bounded, authorized candidate space;
  • current-state reauthorization during source hydration;
  • constant or coarsened result metadata where existence is sensitive;
  • deletion tombstones consulted before serving any candidate;
  • tenant-aware cache keys and no cross-domain embedding-result cache.

docs.title: 8. Candidate retrieval and index choice
docs.text:
Exact search computes distance against every eligible vector and provides the reference top-K for a sample. ANN trades recall for less work. Use Search and Indexing for algorithm mechanics; the applied-AI decision adds model compatibility, filtered recall, and downstream task impact.

Need Candidate approach Operational concern modest corpus or strict reference exact flat search linear compute frequent inserts, high recall, sufficient RAM HNSW graph memory, tombstones, rebuild very large stable base, memory pressure IVF/PQ trained centroids/codebooks, quantization loss huge base plus fresh updates immutable compressed base plus mutable delta dual read, dedupe, compaction identifiers and semantic concepts lexical plus vector fusion and evaluation

Tune search effort - such as graph exploration or lists probed - against exact neighbors on production-shaped vectors and filters. More effort usually improves candidate recall at latency and compute cost. Index parameters are release configuration, not invisible operator knobs.

Keep two reference sets separate. ANN_overlap@K = |ANN_topK intersect exact_topK| / |exact_topK| measures approximation against the same metric, snapshot, filters, and tie policy. relevance_Recall@K = |returned_topK intersect judged_relevant| / |judged_relevant| measures task retrieval. Exact search has perfect overlap with itself, not necessarily perfect relevance. Define empty eligible sets and distance ties explicitly; a better embedding can improve relevance while a low-effort ANN index loses overlap.

docs.title: 9. Hybrid retrieval, fusion, and reranking
docs.text:
Lexical retrieval is strong for exact identifiers, rare names, and phrases. Dense retrieval can capture semantic similarity. Retrieve bounded candidates from each, deduplicate by canonical source/chunk identity, then fuse.

Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) uses rank rather than incomparable raw scores:

RRF(document) = sum over lists 1 / (k + rank_in_list)

Version k, list depths, weights, and tie-breaks. Persist source ranks for diagnosis. A learned or cross-encoder reranker receives only the candidate set; it cannot recover a relevant item omitted upstream. Measure candidate Recall@N before final ranking quality.

Apply hard policy filters before reranking. After ranking, enforce deduplication, source diversity, freshness, and context budget through deterministic rules. Do not let a generative model silently rewrite citations or fabricate source IDs.

The deterministic hybrid search lab exercises fusion and candidate ceilings.

docs.title: 10. Retrieval evaluation
docs.text:
Build a versioned judgment set containing query, corpus/index epoch, relevant source spans with graded relevance, filters/identity context, unanswerable cases, and slice labels.

Metric Measures Limitation Recall@K whether required relevant items appear ignores order inside K Precision@K fraction of K judged relevant incomplete judgments bias it MRR rank of first relevant item ignores later relevant items NDCG@K graded relevance and order needs reliable grades filtered Recall@K candidate quality under policy filters requires authorized ground truth citation precision cited evidence supports claim generation-stage measure supported-answer rate answer is both produced and supported combines stages abstention accuracy refusal when evidence is absent requires unanswerable cases

Attribute failure by stage: corpus coverage, parser/chunker, embedding, ANN, filters, fusion, reranker, context packing, generation, or citation mapping. An end-to-end score alone cannot tell which stage to repair.

Use paired query-level comparisons between releases and report uncertainty. Evaluate languages, source types, tenants, freshness bands, rare entities, long documents, ACL selectivity, and adversarial or conflicting evidence. Renew judgments as corpus and query distributions evolve.

docs.title: 11. Memory, throughput, and cost
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): The corpus contains 120 million vectors with 768 float32 dimensions. Metadata averages 220 bytes/vector. Two complete index generations coexist during migration. Index-structure overhead is not yet included.

Raw vector bytes:

120,000,000 * 768 * 4
= 368,640,000,000 bytes
= 368.64 GB decimal

Metadata is 120,000,000 * 220 = 26.4 GB. One generation needs at least 395.04 GB before graph/list structures, allocator overhead, replicas, and source text. Two generations need at least 790.08 GB. This lower bound shows why migration reserve and index choice matter; it is not a capacity forecast.

For embedding throughput:

Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): Re-embedding 120 million chunks averages 420 tokens/chunk and must finish in 24 hours. A measured worker sustains 18,000 input tokens/s at 70% planned utilization.

required tokens/s = 120,000,000 * 420 / 86,400
                  = 583,333 tokens/s

usable worker rate = 18,000 * 0.70
                   = 12,600 tokens/s

workers = ceil(583,333 / 12,600)
        = 47

Add update catch-up, failures, skew, source and output bandwidth, index build time, validation, and serving load. Cost includes parsing, embedding, dual indexes, replicas, compaction, exact-reference queries, reranking, and generated context tokens.

Benchmark (measurement requirement, 2026-09): On a pinned corpus/query sample, sweep index configuration with the production embedding, filter selectivity, update rate, hardware, concurrency, and dataset size. Report exact-reference Recall@K, filtered Recall@K, p50/p95/p99 latency, queries/core, resident bytes/vector, build time, update visibility, deletion behavior, and cost. Measure downstream quality separately.

The vector index lab and calculations workbook provide small deterministic exercises.

docs.title: 12. Embedding and index migration
docs.text:
Changing embedding model, preprocessing, dimensions, normalization, or distance creates a new compatibility generation.

flowchart TD
    A[Pin source snapshot and watermark] --> B[Build embeddings B]
    B --> C[Build index B]
    C --> D[Apply ordered updates after watermark]
    D --> E[Reconcile keys digests ACLs tombstones]
    E --> F[Exact and downstream evaluation]
    F --> G[Shadow query model B with index B]
    G --> H[Stable canary bundle B]
    H --> I{Gates pass?}
    I -- no --> J[Route all traffic to bundle A]
    I -- yes --> K[Expand and retain A for rollback]

Bundle (query encoder B, index B, fusion B, reranker B) together. Shadowing must not send B vectors to A. Reconciliation checks eligible source count, index count, duplicates, missing keys, unexpected keys, ACL version, and delete tombstones. Rollback changes the whole retrieval bundle.

For base-plus-delta, each query reads the base and delta belonging to the same compatible retrieval bundle, not indexes from different embedding spaces. Deduplicate by latest source version/sequence and use deterministic ties. A current-version map must also suppress superseded base chunks when the newer delta chunk did not enter the candidate set. Comparing only returned duplicates would let an obsolete, highly ranked chunk survive. Bounded refill can improve coverage after suppression; report partial results when its budget runs out. Compaction creates a new base from a pinned state and advances one manifest pointer only after the delta watermark is included.

docs.title: 13. Freshness, deletion, and failure recovery
docs.text:
Failure Discriminating evidence Control parser coverage drops source-to-chunk counts by type/version quarantine and keep old generation embedding workers truncate token counts and completion reason explicit policy and gate ANN recall drops exact overlap stable, ANN overlap falls restore search config/index ACL post-filter starvation candidates before/after policy filter-aware search or partition source/index split citation outside active manifest atomically pin and hydrate generation update stream gap sequence/watermark reconciliation replay from snapshot watermark stale delete served tombstone sequence exceeds index version serve-time deny and repair projection index shard lost generation manifest and replicas rebuild or restore same generation query/index model mismatch model/generation compatibility check reject before search

Define freshness stages: source accepted, parsed, embedded, indexed in delta, searchable, compacted into base. Alert on age and backlog at each stage. A single "index lag" metric cannot isolate the bottleneck.

Deletion should first prevent serving through current authorization/tombstone state, then remove vectors, text, caches, snapshots, and future training eligibility. Verify completion by source ID across generations. Retain only legally required evidence under narrow access and expiration.

docs.title: 14. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure ingestion throughput and lag; parser failures; chunks/source and tokens/chunk; truncation; embedding errors and vector norms; index generation and watermark; build/compaction time; update/delete visibility; query candidate count by stage; pre/post-filter counts; lexical/vector overlap; ANN versus exact recall; reranker latency; empty and partial results; citation/support metrics; cache hits; memory; CPU/accelerator use; and cost.

Test:

  • golden parsing/chunk/offset fixtures;
  • embedding determinism tolerance and dimension/normalization checks;
  • exact-neighbor references and ANN sweeps;
  • high-selectivity ACL filters and cross-tenant isolation;
  • duplicate, reordered, missing, and late updates;
  • deletion during base rebuild and dual-generation serving;
  • shard loss and manifest rollback;
  • malformed/oversized documents and decompression bombs;
  • multilingual, identifier-heavy, stale, conflicting, and unanswerable queries;
  • citation resolution against immutable source versions.

docs.title: 15. Security and privacy
docs.text:
Embeddings can retain information about source data and should inherit its classification. Do not treat vectors as anonymized. Encrypt and authorize indexes, isolate tenants/security domains, audit bulk export, and restrict nearest-neighbor probing. Keep raw text out of metrics and logs.

Ingestion handles attacker-controlled files. Sandbox parsers; limit bytes, pages, recursion, decompression, CPU, and wall time; scan content; and restrict outbound network access. Source trust and signatures establish provenance and integrity, not truth. Retrieved content remains untrusted input to a model.

docs.title: 16. Vendor and production evidence
docs.text:
Vendor (pgvector 0.8.6, released 2026-07-29): pgvector documents exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search with vector distance operators and HNSW/IVFFlat indexes. Product support does not remove the need to benchmark filtered recall, replica behavior, backup/restore, write amplification, or isolation in the chosen PostgreSQL environment. pgvector 0.8.6 documentation

[Vendor behavior, v0.8.6 documentation verified 2026-09-08] In pgvector's approximate scans, SQL filtering occurs after the index scan. A WHERE tenant_id = ... predicate is not evidence of tenant-local graph traversal. Iterative scans can seek more candidates until configured limits, but do not guarantee K results or perfect recall. Use partitions or separate tables for hard tenant index isolation, enforce database authorization, and test actual query plans. strict_order means distance ordering of found candidates, not exact-neighbor completeness. This is an implementation constraint on the architecture above, not permission to hydrate unauthorized content.

Production report (Meta Engineering, published 2017-03-29): Meta reported releasing Faiss after building nearest-neighbor implementations for billion-scale datasets and described its speed, memory, and accuracy evaluation method. The published results use specific datasets, hardware, algorithms, and metrics; they are not a capacity guarantee for filtered enterprise retrieval. Faiss: A library for efficient similarity search

docs.title: 17. Tradeoffs and evolution
docs.text:
Choice Benefit Cost or risk vector-only simple semantic candidate path weak exact identifiers and unexplained misses hybrid lexical/vector broader coverage fusion and dual operations one global index operational simplicity isolation and selective-filter problems tenant/security partitions hard boundaries and better filter locality many small indexes and placement overhead HNSW strong low-latency recall in many regimes memory, tombstones, rebuilds IVF/PQ compressed large stable base training and approximation loss in-place update immediate change mixed generation and rollback difficulty immutable base plus delta coherent base and freshness merge, dedupe, compaction

Begin with lexical search or exact vectors when scale permits. Add ANN only after exact-reference evaluation exists. Add hybrid retrieval when error analysis shows complementary lexical and semantic misses. Add a reranker only when candidate recall is adequate and its quality gain justifies latency and cost. Split tenant indexes when authorization, scale, or noisy-neighbor evidence requires it.

docs.title: 18. Interview exercise
docs.text:
Prompt: Design retrieval for 500 million enterprise chunks across 20,000 tenants. Updates must be searchable within five minutes, p95 retrieval is 250 ms, answers need exact citations, and an embedding-model migration occurs quarterly.

An L5 design stores immutable source versions and offsets, uses security-domain partitions plus current ACL hydration, builds a large immutable base with fresh delta, combines lexical/vector candidates, reranks, and measures exact-reference Recall@K and citation support. It versions and atomically routes query encoder/index bundles, catches up from a watermark, reconciles deletes, and preserves rollback.

An L6 design adds tenant placement and noisy-neighbor policy, many-small-index economics, region/residency boundaries, corpus and judgment ownership, dual-generation capacity, migration scheduling, deletion proof, exception handling, and organization-wide compatibility contracts. It explains what happens when five-minute freshness competes with a base rebuild and when a tenant changes ACLs without changing document text.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Preserves source, chunk, embedding, ACL, and index lineage.
  • Keeps query and corpus encoders in one explicit compatibility bundle.
  • Explains filter placement, hybrid candidates, fusion, reranking, and abstention.
  • Benchmarks ANN against exact neighbors under representative filters.
  • Designs base/delta freshness, deletion, migration, and rollback.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Governs security-domain partitioning, tenant placement, residency, and noisy neighbors.
  • Plans dual-generation capacity and migration across product teams.
  • Owns corpus quality, judgments, compatibility, and deletion evidence.
  • Connects retrieval-stage metrics to end-to-end support and product outcomes.
  • Defines exception policy and retirement criteria for models, indexes, and source generations.

docs.title: Final summary
docs.text: Treat vectors as versioned projections of authorized source data. Preserve provenance through parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and citation. Use exact search as evaluation truth for ANN candidates, apply authorization before exposure and again at hydration, and publish compatible query/index generations atomically. Optimize retrieval stages only after measuring where relevant evidence is lost.

docs.text:
