docs.title: Hybrid Search and Reranking
docs.text: Hybrid retrieval is a staged ranking system, not a checkbox that combines keyword and vector search. A production design must define what each retriever can recover, where authorization filters run, how ranks are fused, what the reranker may change, and which quality gain justifies each millisecond and dollar.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• [Source] is a statement supported directly by a dated source in Sources.
  • [Derived] is a calculation or consequence derived from stated inputs.
  • [Design] is a recommended production contract, not a claim made by a cited paper.
  • [Measure] is a hypothesis that must be validated on the system's own corpus and traffic.

docs.title: Design target
docs.text: Assume an enterprise search API over 40 million permissioned chunks. Queries include exact identifiers, natural-language questions, abbreviations, and rare product names. The service targets 99.9% monthly availability, 350 ms p95 server latency, no unauthorized result disclosure, and a measurable relevance improvement over lexical search.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Authorization is enforced before content, snippets, scores, or result counts leave the retrieval boundary.
  2. Every response identifies the query, corpus, lexical index, embedding, sparse model, fusion, and reranker versions.
  3. Reranking never repairs a relevant document missing from its candidate set.
  4. Fusion consumes deterministic ranked lists with stable document IDs and tie-breaking.
  5. Offline quality, online utility, latency, and cost are separate release gates.
  6. Empty, partial, stale, timed-out, and policy-filtered results are distinguishable outcomes.
  7. A degraded mode may remove expensive stages but never remove authorization or deletion enforcement.

docs.title: Retrieval and ranking architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q[Query] --> N[Normalize and classify]
    N --> P[Principal and policy filter]
    P --> B[BM25 retriever]
    P --> D[Dense retriever]
    P --> S[Sparse neural retriever]
    B --> F[RRF or learned fusion]
    D --> F
    S --> F
    F --> H[Hydrate authorized fields]
    H --> R[Cross-encoder or late interaction]
    R --> O[Stable top K response]
    N --> L[(Stage evidence)]
    B --> L
    D --> L
    S --> L
    F --> L
    R --> L

The retrievers increase candidate recall through different matching signals. Fusion creates one bounded candidate set. Hydration retrieves the text or token representations needed by the reranker. The reranker improves ordering inside that set. Each boundary records enough evidence to attribute a regression.

docs.title: BM25 lexical retrieval
docs.text:
BM25 rewards query terms that occur in a document, discounts terms common across the corpus, and saturates the benefit of repeated term frequency. A common form is:

BM25(q, d) = sum over t in q of
  IDF(t) * tf(t,d) * (k1 + 1)
  / (tf(t,d) + k1 * (1 - b + b * |d| / avgdl))

k1 controls term-frequency saturation. b controls document-length normalization. Exact formula and IDF variants differ by implementation, so version both the engine and parameters. [Source] BM25 belongs to the probabilistic lexical-ranking family described by Robertson and Walker; it does not provide a calibrated probability of relevance.

Lexical retrieval is strong for identifiers, quoted phrases, error codes, names, and rare tokens. It is sensitive to analyzers, stemming, token boundaries, synonyms, field boosts, and corpus statistics. Reindexing can therefore change rank even when documents do not change.

docs.title: Dense retrieval
docs.text:
A dense retriever maps query and document text into fixed-width vectors. A bi-encoder usually computes a similarity such as dot product or cosine similarity and uses approximate nearest-neighbor search for scale. [Source] Dense Passage Retrieval demonstrated independently encoded question and passage vectors with inner-product retrieval for open-domain question answering.

Dense retrieval can connect paraphrases that share few terms, but it may blur exact values and rare identifiers. Its behavior depends on embedding model, input prefix, truncation, distance function, vector normalization, quantization, ANN parameters, and training domain. Store all of them in the index manifest.

docs.title: Learned sparse retrieval
docs.text:
Learned sparse models produce vocabulary-sized sparse representations whose nonzero dimensions remain lexical terms, including learned expansion terms. [Source] SPLADE uses sparse lexical representations with regularization intended to control efficiency. Sparse neural retrieval can retain inverted-index execution and improve semantic matching, but posting-list growth and model inference cost are real capacity concerns.

Do not call every token-weight model BM25. Record whether a score came from observed term frequency, learned expansion, or another feature. Keep separate score namespaces because raw values are not comparable by default.

docs.title: Retrieval choice table
docs.text:
Method Primary signal Typical strength Typical weakness Index cost BM25 observed terms and corpus frequency exact strings and rare terms vocabulary mismatch postings plus stored fields dense bi-encoder vector similarity paraphrase and conceptual match identifiers and domain drift vectors plus ANN graph or partitions learned sparse learned term weights and expansion semantic lexical match expansion latency and postings growth model inference plus sparse postings metadata filter structured equality/range policy authority and scope candidate starvation if applied late filter indexes or partitions

[Measure] The winning combination depends on query mix and corpus. Evaluate slices such as exact ID, acronym, multilingual, short ambiguous query, long natural-language question, fresh content, and restrictive ACL.

docs.title: Authorization filter placement
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Authenticated principal] --> T[Tenant or security partition]
    T --> C{Retriever supports filter-aware search?}
    C -->|Yes| F[Apply ACL predicate during candidate search]
    C -->|No| O[Bounded overfetch inside permitted isolation domain]
    O --> H[Authorize during hydration]
    F --> H
    H --> V{Enough authorized candidates?}
    V -->|Yes| R[Rerank]
    V -->|No| E[Return sparse or empty result]

Post-filtering a global top 100 may leave no authorized results even when relevant authorized documents exist below that global cutoff. Overfetch reduces but does not eliminate this candidate-starvation problem. Prefer physical tenant or security-domain partitioning where practical, filter-aware ANN or postings execution, and mandatory authorization again during hydration. Never increase an unauthorized overfetch bound until latency and side-channel risks are reviewed.

If the contract forbids unauthorized items from influencing candidates at all, the no-filter branch must use an authorized exact scan or a stricter partition, not global ANN plus hydration checks. Neither extra candidates nor a larger timeout creates authorization. The pgvector RRF implementation, inspected 2026-09-08, illustrates missing-list contributions and rank fusion, not a tenant-security implementation; do not copy its unrestricted example query as a production policy boundary.

docs.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
docs.text:
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines ordinal ranks without assuming comparable raw-score scales. [Source] Cormack, Clarke, and Buettcher published RRF in 2009.

RRF(d) = sum over ranking r of w_r / (c + rank_r(d))

c is a rank constant and w_r is an optional retriever weight. A missing document contributes zero. c=60 is common in examples, not a universal optimum. Tune constants and candidate depths only on representative judgments, then freeze them in a versioned fusion policy.

docs.title: Deterministic algorithm
docs.text:
function fuse(rankings, weights, c, limit):
    score = map document_id -> 0
    provenance = map document_id -> []
    for retriever in stable_retriever_order:
        deduplicate retriever.results by document_id
        for position, result in enumerate(results, start=1):
            score[result.id] += weights[retriever] / (c + position)
            provenance[result.id].append(retriever, position, result.raw_score)
    return first limit sorted by (-score, canonical_document_id)

Persist input ranks and fusion contributions. A stable tie-break prevents evaluation noise and pagination duplication. Deduplicate canonical documents before final ranking when multiple chunks or aliases represent the same result; retain the best supporting chunks separately.

docs.title: Worked calculation
docs.text:
Suppose BM25 returns [A, B, C, D] and dense retrieval returns [C, E, A, F], with equal weights and c=60.

A = 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.032266
C = 1/63 + 1/61 = 0.032266
B = 1/62          = 0.016129
E = 1/62          = 0.016129
D = 1/64          = 0.015625
F = 1/64          = 0.015625

[Derived] A and C tie, so canonical ID order or another declared tie-break decides their order. The RRF values are fusion scores, not probabilities. See Lab 04 for an executable fixture and the calculations workbook.

docs.title: Cross-encoder
docs.text:
A cross-encoder jointly encodes the query and each candidate text, then predicts a relevance score. [Source] Nogueira and Cho showed BERT used as a passage reranker for a first-stage candidate list. Joint attention can capture fine query-document interactions, but cost grows with candidate count and sequence length.

Use a cross-encoder when a bounded candidate set fits the latency budget and fine-grained relevance matters. Batch candidates for accelerator efficiency, but cap batch wait so low traffic does not inflate tail latency. A timeout returns the fused order with a reranker_status=degraded, not a partial arbitrary order.

docs.title: Late interaction
docs.text:
Late-interaction systems encode query and document tokens separately, retain multiple token vectors, and compare them at query time. [Source] ColBERT introduced efficient late interaction using contextualized token-level representations and a MaxSim-style operator. It trades more index storage and query-time token matching for richer interaction than one vector per document.

Late interaction can serve as retrieval, reranking, or both depending on implementation. Do not assume it has cross-encoder quality or bi-encoder cost. Measure index bytes, cache locality, candidate depth, accelerator use, and p99 under the target corpus.

docs.title: Reranker contract
docs.text:
{
  "query_id": "q-01H...",
  "query_text": "opaque-or-redacted-by-policy",
  "principal_scope_digest": "sha256:...",
  "corpus_epoch": 42,
  "candidates": [
    {
      "document_id": "doc-123",
      "chunk_id": "chunk-7",
      "text_digest": "sha256:...",
      "fusion_rank": 3,
      "features": {"bm25_rank": 1, "dense_rank": 17}
    }
  ],
  "reranker": {"name": "cross-encoder-x", "version": "2026-08-14"},
  "deadline_ms": 90,
  "top_k": 10
}

The response returns score, rank, finish_reason, and per-candidate input digest. The service rejects candidates from another tenant, epoch, or query. It never accepts arbitrary URLs or fetches candidate text itself.

docs.title: Quality and latency budget
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[20 ms admission and normalization] --> B[70 ms parallel retrieval]
    B --> C[25 ms fusion and hydration]
    C --> D[140 ms reranking]
    D --> E[35 ms response]
    E --> F[60 ms reserve]

For a 350 ms p95 target, the illustrative budget sums to 20 + 70 + 25 + 140 + 35 + 60 = 350 ms. [Design] Reserve is not free time; it absorbs network variance, queueing, and unmodeled work. Stage p95 values do not add to end-to-end p95 in general. Use per-request traces and distribution-aware load tests.

Suppose retrieval produces 300 candidates, fusion keeps 100, and a cross-encoder processes 100 pairs at 1,200 pairs/s effective throughput:

fluid service-work estimate = 100 / 1,200 s = 83.3 ms
at 80 queries/s, pair demand = 80 * 100 = 8,000 pairs/s
minimum equivalent workers = 8,000 / 1,200 = 6.67
with 30% failure and headroom reserve = ceil(6.67 / 0.70) = 10 workers

[Derived] Ten equivalent workers cover the stated steady demand after reserving 30% capacity, before batching inefficiency, replicas, zone loss, and tail effects. Sensitivity matters: reranking 200 candidates doubles pair demand. Candidate depth is therefore a capacity control, not only a quality parameter.

Aggregate pairs/s does not determine an individual query's latency. The 83.3 ms estimate assumes the stated worker can devote that rate to this query's batch; measure actual batch latency and queueing separately, particularly when throughput comes from overlapping many queries.

docs.title: Evaluation and release gates
docs.text:
Build immutable query sets with graded document or passage judgments, unanswerable cases, ACL cases, freshness cases, and hard query slices. Prevent tuning against the final holdout.

Stage Metric Failure it localizes candidate union Recall@N relevant evidence never entered reranking fusion MRR, nDCG@K, Recall@K rank combination harmed ordering reranker delta nDCG@K and win/loss pairs reranker reordered good candidates badly policy unauthorized-return rate, authorized Recall@K security leak or filter starvation serving p50/p95/p99 latency, timeout rate operational budget breach product successful-search rate, reformulation, task completion offline gain did not improve utility

Release only when mandatory slices pass fixed thresholds, paired quality comparisons are confidence-aware, and cost and latency gates pass at projected load. Online interleaving or A/B tests can measure preference, but they do not replace explicit security and correctness tests.

docs.title: Failure attribution record
docs.text:
{
  "query_id": "q-01H...",
  "versions": {
    "corpus_epoch": 42,
    "lexical_index": "lex-17",
    "embedding": "emb-9",
    "sparse_model": "splade-4",
    "fusion": "rrf-6",
    "reranker": "ce-12"
  },
  "counts": {
    "bm25": 100,
    "dense": 100,
    "sparse": 100,
    "union": 241,
    "authorized": 89,
    "reranked": 80,
    "returned": 10
  },
  "timing_ms": {"retrieval": 61, "fusion": 4, "hydrate": 13, "rerank": 87},
  "degraded": [],
  "sampled_rank_evidence_ref": "evidence://search/q-01H..."
}

Log raw query text and document text only under explicit privacy policy. Prefer stable IDs, digests, bounded sampled rank evidence, and separately protected debugging access.

docs.title: Failure modes and controls
docs.text:
Failure Discriminator Safe response analyzer change breaks exact IDs BM25 recall falls only on identifier slice rollback lexical index epoch ANN recall collapse exact-vector search remains stable while ANN overlap falls raise search effort or rollback ANN build embedding drift old index plus old query encoder wins shadow comparison restore compatible encoder/index pair sparse expansion explosion posting bytes and query fan-out rise cap expansion, quarantine model, retain old index late ACL filter starves candidates large prefilter count and tiny authorized set use filter-aware search or partitioning RRF regression persisted ranks recompute to a different fused order rollback fusion policy reranker timeout candidate recall stable, reranker deadline exceeded return fused order with degraded marker reranker candidate ceiling relevant item absent from union improve retrievers or candidate depth duplicate chunks dominate many top results share canonical document ID group before final top K cache leaks scope same key serves different principal-scope digests purge and key by policy version and scope

Related incident discriminators appear in Applied AI Failure Cards.

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text:
• Treat query text and document text as sensitive tenant data.
  • Bind every cache entry to tenant, principal-scope digest, corpus epoch, policy version, query normalization version, and the complete retriever/fusion/reranker tuple. Revalidate current permissions and deletion state before returning cached content; a versioned key alone does not enforce a revocation that happened after the entry was written.
  • Validate filters against an allowlisted schema; the model or client cannot remove mandatory predicates.
  • Protect index backups, rank traces, and embeddings under the source retention and deletion policy.
  • Rate-limit broad or adversarial queries that maximize posting scans or ANN work.
  • Do not expose raw scores, total matches, or timing when they create an unauthorized existence oracle.
  • Sign or checksum immutable manifests and verify them before activation.

docs.title: Index and reranker migration
docs.text:
1. Build a new immutable index epoch from a declared corpus manifest.
  2. Validate counts, tombstones, ACL distributions, exact-vs-ANN overlap, and golden queries.
  3. Shadow query encoding and retrieval without exposing candidate text across policy boundaries.
  4. Dual-read a sampled cohort and compare per-query candidates, ranks, latency, and cost.
  5. Canary the complete compatible tuple: query normalizer, retriever, index, fusion, and reranker.
  6. Promote through an atomic routing manifest; never mix an embedding query encoder with an incompatible vector index.
  7. Retain the old epoch until rollback and deletion obligations are proven.
  8. Stop dual reads and remove old data only after acceptance criteria and rollback window expire.

[Design] Rollback should publish a new activation record pointing to a known-good immutable tuple. Mutating an old manifest destroys auditability.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text:
Design search for 40 million internal support articles across 20,000 tenants. Half of the queries contain exact product codes; the rest are natural-language questions. The service must return 10 authorized results under 350 ms p95 and support weekly embedding upgrades.

Cover:

  1. query and corpus slices;
  2. BM25, dense, and optional sparse candidate depths;
  3. ACL filter placement and tenant isolation;
  4. RRF calculation and deterministic ties;
  5. cross-encoder versus late-interaction tradeoffs;
  6. a latency and capacity calculation;
  7. stage-specific evaluation and failure attribution;
  8. dual-index migration, rollback, and deletion.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Defines candidate recall before discussing reranker quality.
  • Computes RRF and at least one latency or pair-throughput budget correctly.
  • Enforces authorization during retrieval and hydration.
  • Separates offline relevance, online utility, latency, and cost gates.
  • Handles reranker timeout with a safe, observable degraded mode.
  • Migrates compatible index/model tuples with dual reads and rollback.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Governs shared query taxonomy, judgment policy, and retriever contracts across teams.
  • Quantifies zone or accelerator loss and the receiving fleet's headroom.
  • Defines exception authority for candidate depth, security partitions, and model changes.
  • Allocates storage, inference, and evaluation cost by tenant or product.
  • Names falsifying evidence, owners, retention, review cadence, and old-epoch removal criteria.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Candidate sources, depths, timeouts, and deduplication are explicit.
  • Filter placement preserves both authorization and recall.
  • Fusion formula, constants, weights, and tie-breaks are versioned.
  • Reranker input, deadline, fallback, and candidate ceiling are explicit.
  • Quality is evaluated by stage and by predeclared slice.
  • Capacity includes candidate depth, failures, and headroom.
  • Migration activates only compatible immutable versions.
  • Logs and caches preserve tenant, ACL, privacy, and deletion boundaries.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, primary, 1994-11] Stephen Robertson et al., Okapi at TREC-3. Supports the probabilistic lexical-ranking lineage and BM25-style term weighting. The exact production formula remains implementation-specific.
  • [Source, textbook, 2008-07-07] Manning, Raghavan, and Schutze, Introduction to Information Retrieval. Supports lexical retrieval, evaluation, and inverted-index terminology.
  • [Source, primary, 2009-07] Cormack, Clarke, and Buettcher, Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods. Defines RRF.
  • [Source, primary, 2020-04-10] Karpukhin et al., Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering. Supports bi-encoder dense passage retrieval with inner-product search.
  • [Source, primary, 2021-07-12] Formal et al., SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking. Supports learned sparse lexical expansion and efficiency regularization. Title/version verified 2026-09-08; this identifier is the original SPLADE paper, not SPLADE v2.
  • [Source, primary, 2019-01-13] Nogueira and Cho, Passage Re-ranking with BERT. Supports cross-encoder-style reranking of first-stage candidates.
  • [Source, primary, 2020-04-27] Khattab and Zaharia, ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT. Supports token-level late interaction.
  • [Source, benchmark, 2021-04-26] Thakur et al., BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models. Supports evaluation across heterogeneous retrieval datasets; it does not substitute for product-specific judgments.

Previous: Embeddings and Vector Retrieval | Next: Production RAG Systems

docs.title: Production RAG Systems
docs.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a data system, a search system, and an answer-policy system joined by provenance. A model call is only the final stage. Production correctness depends on immutable source versions, authorized retrieval, supportable citations, explicit abstention, observable freshness, and migrations that never mix incompatible corpus and index state.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• [Source] is supported directly by a dated item in Sources.
  • [Derived] follows from stated numbers or invariants.
  • [Design] is a recommended production contract.
  • [Measure] must be tested on the local corpus, users, and failure environment.

docs.title: Product contract
docs.text: Assume a support assistant over policy manuals, release notes, tickets, and product documentation. It answers questions, quotes source spans, and must refuse when evidence is missing, stale beyond policy, contradictory, or unauthorized.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. No source becomes queryable until its immutable version, ACL, parser result, chunks, and indexes belong to one active corpus manifest.
  2. Deletion and access revocation take effect at the authorization boundary even while physical purge continues.
  3. Every material factual claim maps to one or more exact source spans from the same immutable source version shown to the user.
  4. The answer policy may narrow or abstain; it may not invent support.
  5. Query-time components consume a compatible tuple of corpus epoch, chunk schema, embedding, lexical index, reranker, prompt, and model.
  6. A failure response identifies the stage that failed and does not present partial evidence as complete.
  7. Reprocessing is idempotent by source version and pipeline version.
  8. Retrieved text is untrusted data, not permission or instruction.

docs.title: End-to-end architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Source connectors] --> F[Fetch immutable bytes]
    F --> Q[Scan and quarantine]
    Q --> P[Parse and normalize]
    P --> C[Chunk with lineage and ACL]
    C --> X[Lexical sparse and vector indexes]
    X --> M[(Corpus manifest)]
    U[User query] --> G[Identity policy and budgets]
    Z[(Current auth and tombstone projection)] --> G
    G --> R[Hybrid retrieval]
    M --> R
    Z --> R
    R --> K[Context packer]
    K --> L[Model gateway]
    L --> V[Claim citation and policy validation]
    Z --> V
    V --> A[Answer or abstention]

Control-plane records define immutable versions and activation. Data-plane workers fetch, parse, index, retrieve, generate, and validate. Query serving reads one atomic content manifest rather than asking each content subsystem for its latest version. It also checks a separate current, monotonic authorization and tombstone projection before retrieval, during hydration, and before returning citations, so a content rollback cannot roll back a revocation.

docs.title: State machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Discovered
    Discovered --> Fetched
    Fetched --> Scanned: security and format checks pass
    Fetched --> Quarantined: scan or format risk
    Scanned --> Parsed
    Scanned --> Quarantined: parser risk
    Parsed --> Chunked
    Chunked --> Indexed
    Indexed --> Validated
    Validated --> Active: manifest publish
    Quarantined --> Fetched: remediated or new source version
    Active --> Tombstoned: delete or global source withdrawal
    Tombstoned --> Purged
    Purged --> [*]

Only Active versions are available to ordinary queries. A new version does not overwrite the prior version. It creates a new lineage branch that becomes active only after validation. A parser that emits zero chunks from nonempty input is a failure unless the source is explicitly represented as empty.

docs.title: Source and chunk schemas
docs.text:
{
  "source_id": "policy-481",
  "source_version": "sha256:raw-bytes-digest",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-7",
  "uri": "source://policies/481",
  "media_type": "application/pdf",
  "fetched_at": "2026-09-06T10:00:00Z",
  "effective_at": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z",
  "expires_at": null,
  "acl_version": 19,
  "retention_class": "support-policy",
  "legal_hold": false,
  "pipeline_version": "ingest-12",
  "state": "VALIDATED"
}

{
  "chunk_id": "policy-481:v9:p12:c3",
  "source_id": "policy-481",
  "source_version": "sha256:raw-bytes-digest",
  "page": 12,
  "char_start": 840,
  "char_end": 1512,
  "text_digest": "sha256:normalized-span",
  "heading_path": ["Refunds", "Exceptions"],
  "acl_terms": ["tenant:7", "group:support"],
  "parser": {"name": "pdf-parser", "version": "4.2.1"},
  "chunker_version": "semantic-6",
  "embedding_version": "embed-9",
  "trust_class": "AUTHORITATIVE_POLICY"
}

Offsets must resolve against an immutable rendered or normalized representation. Byte offsets into raw PDF bytes are rarely useful to readers; preserve both raw-object lineage and coordinates in the canonical text representation.

docs.title: Idempotent ingestion API
docs.text:
PUT /v1/sources/policy-481/versions/sha256:raw-bytes-digest
Idempotency-Key: ingest:policy-481:sha256:raw-bytes-digest:ingest-12
If-None-Match: *
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-7",
  "object_ref": "object://quarantine/7/481/v9",
  "acl_version": 19,
  "pipeline_version": "ingest-12"
}

The server binds the idempotency key to a normalized payload digest. Reuse with another payload returns a conflict. Queue delivery may be at least once; processors use (tenant, source_id, source_version, pipeline_version, stage) to avoid duplicate derived artifacts. The source-version resource identifies immutable bytes; reprocessing those bytes with a new pipeline creates a separate processing-run resource rather than changing the existing version. Define replay ordering explicitly: an exact recognized idempotency replay returns the stored outcome, while an unrecognized create with If-None-Match: * against an existing resource fails with 412 Precondition Failed. After a lost response, read the resource or operation record to resolve whether creation succeeded.

docs.title: Atomic corpus activation
docs.text:
{
  "corpus_epoch": 42,
  "tenant_partition": "tenant-7",
  "created_at": "2026-09-06T11:30:00Z",
  "source_manifest_digest": "sha256:...",
  "lexical_index": "lex-17",
  "vector_index": "vec-22",
  "embedding_version": "embed-9",
  "sparse_index": "sparse-4",
  "chunk_schema": 6,
  "content_acl_schema": 19,
  "deny_baseline_watermark": 883112,
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "previous_epoch": 41
}

Activation is one compare-and-swap of the content-manifest pointer after all referenced artifacts pass validation. Index shards may be built independently, but they do not become a corpus until the manifest names a complete compatible set. deny_baseline_watermark records what the build incorporated; serving must overlay the independent current deny projection at a watermark greater than or equal to that baseline. That baseline is only a build-time lower bound: a replica at that watermark can still miss later revocations. Require an authoritative current authorization check, or a documented bounded-staleness contract with a revocation propagation SLO and freshness proof; monotonic sequence numbers alone do not establish freshness.

docs.title: Query plane
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant G as RAG gateway
    participant R as Retrieval broker
    participant P as Current auth and deny projection
    participant M as Model gateway
    participant V as Validator
    U->>G: question plus principal context
    G->>P: principal, tenant, purpose, required deny epoch
    P-->>G: mandatory ACL predicates and current deny epoch
    G->>R: query with corpus epoch, predicates, and deny epoch
    R->>P: reauthorize candidate IDs during hydration
    P-->>R: currently authorized candidates
    R-->>G: ranked chunks plus lineage
    G->>G: pack bounded evidence
    G->>M: instructions plus labeled evidence
    M-->>G: answer with claim-to-chunk references
    G->>V: claims, citations, evidence, policy
    V->>P: reauthorize cited source versions
    P-->>V: current citation authorization
    V-->>G: supported, narrow, or abstain
    G-->>U: answer plus citations and freshness

docs.title: Query API
docs.text:
POST /v1/rag/answers
Authorization: Bearer <audience-bound-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "question": "When can a duplicate charge be refunded?",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-7",
  "purpose": "support-case",
  "conversation_ref": "conv-91",
  "max_answer_tokens": 600,
  "freshness": {"max_source_age_seconds": 86400},
  "response_mode": "answer_with_claim_citations"
}

{
  "answer_id": "ans-01H...",
  "status": "ANSWERED",
  "answer": "A duplicate charge may be refunded after ... [1]",
  "claims": [
    {
      "claim_id": "c1",
      "text": "A duplicate charge may be refunded after ...",
      "citations": ["cite-1"],
      "support_status": "SUPPORTED"
    }
  ],
  "citations": [
    {
      "citation_id": "cite-1",
      "source_id": "policy-481",
      "source_version": "sha256:raw-bytes-digest",
      "page": 12,
      "char_start": 840,
      "char_end": 1011,
      "quote": "...",
      "source_effective_at": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "versions": {"corpus_epoch": 42, "deny_epoch": 883126, "retrieval": "rrf-6", "prompt": "rag-18", "model": "model-route-11"},
  "freshness": {"as_of": "2026-09-06T11:30:00Z", "within_policy": true}
}

The API can also return ABSTAINED, PARTIAL, POLICY_DENIED, STALE, or FAILED. Do not overload an empty answer string.

docs.title: Context construction
docs.text:
1. Normalize the user question without deleting meaningful identifiers.
  2. Resolve tenant, principal, groups, purpose, and policy version outside the model.
  3. Retrieve broad bounded lexical, dense, and optional sparse candidates.
  4. Enforce ACL during candidate search and again during hydration.
  5. Rerank authorized candidates and deduplicate canonical sources.
  6. Select evidence under token, source-diversity, trust, and freshness constraints.
  7. Delimit every span with source ID, immutable version, offsets, and trust class.
  8. State that evidence is data and cannot modify policy or tool authority.
  9. Ask the model for structured claims and citation references.
  10. Validate references, source support, freshness, and answer policy before rendering.

Context packing is a constrained selection problem. More chunks can increase evidence coverage but also consume attention, latency, and cost. [Measure] Vary candidate depth and packed evidence independently; otherwise retrieval and context effects are confounded.

docs.title: Citation semantics
docs.text:
A citation is valid only if all conditions hold:

  • the cited source ID and immutable version exist in the active or retained manifest;
  • the principal may read the source at response time;
  • offsets resolve to the quoted span in that version;
  • the span entails or directly supports the attached atomic claim;
  • material qualifiers such as date, jurisdiction, threshold, and exception are preserved;
  • the UI does not silently render a newer version under the old citation.

Citation presence measures formatting, not support. Evaluate claim-level citation precision and material-claim citation recall. Human adjudication remains necessary for high-risk or ambiguous support semantics.

docs.title: Abstention policy
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Q[Question] --> E{Authorized evidence found?}
    E -->|No| A[Abstain: no evidence]
    E -->|Yes| F{Fresh enough for policy?}
    F -->|No| S[Abstain or label stale]
    F -->|Yes| C{Material conflict?}
    C -->|Yes| H[Escalate or present conflict]
    C -->|No| V{Every material claim supported?}
    V -->|No| N[Narrow answer or abstain]
    V -->|Yes| R[Return cited answer]

Do not abstain from a single global similarity threshold alone. Threshold distributions vary by query type, retriever, corpus, and model version. Combine evidence coverage, source authority, freshness, conflict detection, citation support, and risk policy. Calibrate on answerable and unanswerable cases.

Suppose 500 evaluation questions include 100 truly unanswerable cases. The system abstains on 120, of which 90 are truly unanswerable:

abstention precision = 90 / 120 = 0.75
abstention recall = 90 / 100 = 0.90
incorrect abstentions on answerable cases = 30
missed unanswerable cases = 10

[Derived] High abstention recall can coexist with poor answer utility if too many answerable cases are refused. Report both dimensions and the cost of unsupported answers.

docs.title: Freshness model
docs.text:
Freshness has at least four clocks:

Clock Meaning source effective time when the content became valid in its domain connector observation time when the platform saw the source version index activation time when the version became queryable answer time when the user received the answer

Define freshness SLOs from source change to queryability, not only ingestion duration. A connector can be healthy while missing upstream changes. Use source-specific watermarks, expected polling cadence, webhook sequence, content digests, and reconciliation scans.

If 99% of changes activate within 10 minutes but the source connector has not successfully reconciled for 6 hours, do not report the corpus as 10 minutes fresh. Return an as_of time and policy result. High-risk sources can fail closed after maximum staleness; low-risk sources can answer with a visible stale label.

docs.title: ACLs, revocation, and deletion
docs.text:
ACL lineage flows from source to every chunk, index posting, vector payload, cache entry, citation, and evaluation artifact. Query policy is computed from the authenticated principal, not model-generated filters.

For revocation or deletion:

A principal/group ACL revocation normally updates the scoped deny/authorization projection; it does not delete a shared document for still-authorized users. The source-wide tombstone/purge sequence below applies to deletion or global withdrawal. Cache invalidation and derivative reauthorization apply to both, with their actual affected scope.

  1. append a tombstone with source ID, affected versions, tenant, reason class, and sequence;
  2. enforce it immediately in retrieval and hydration filters;
  3. invalidate response and retrieval caches by source/version membership;
  4. remove source objects and derived chunks/index records asynchronously;
  5. propagate to replicas, backups, evaluation sets, and replay stores under policy;
  6. verify absence using direct artifact inventories and synthetic unauthorized queries;
  7. record completion evidence or documented retention exceptions such as legal hold.

Physical vector deletion is not the immediate security boundary. The current authorization and deny/tombstone projection is. It is versioned independently from immutable content manifests, highly available, monotonic per source/security domain, and consulted on every retrieval, hydration, citation render, and cache hit. Cache entries record the deny epoch they were checked against and cannot be served under an older epoch. High-risk reads fail closed when the projection is unavailable, behind the caller's required revocation epoch, or cannot prove current authorization; lower-risk availability exceptions require explicit policy and cannot expose revoked content.

docs.title: Failure attribution
docs.text:
Record one stage outcome for every logical request:

{
  "request_id": "rag-01H...",
  "logical_request_id": "lr-88",
  "principal_scope_digest": "sha256:...",
  "versions": {"corpus_epoch": 42, "prompt": "rag-18", "model_route": "route-11"},
  "stages": [
    {"name": "policy", "status": "OK", "ms": 4},
    {"name": "retrieve", "status": "OK", "ms": 58, "candidate_count": 180},
    {"name": "authorize", "status": "OK", "ms": 7, "authorized_count": 42},
    {"name": "rerank", "status": "TIMEOUT", "ms": 91, "fallback": "FUSED_ORDER"},
    {"name": "generate", "status": "OK", "ms": 610},
    {"name": "validate", "status": "ABSTAIN", "reason": "UNSUPPORTED_MATERIAL_CLAIM"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Attribution matrix
docs.text:
Symptom Evidence Likely boundary required source absent from candidates judged span missing at candidate N retrieval or indexing source retrieved but omitted from packed context candidate and context IDs differ packer budget/policy evidence present but answer wrong exact prompt evidence preserved generation answer correct but citation unrelated claim-span support review fails citation generation/validation source version not current source and index watermarks diverge connector or activation unauthorized source returned principal, ACL, hydration evidence disagree security incident

Use Lab 05 to practice stage metrics and Failure Cards for incident discriminators.

docs.title: Capacity and cost
docs.text:
Assume 120 queries/s, 40 retrieved chunks of 700 document tokens, a 100-token reranker query repeated for each pair, 20 framing/special tokens per pair, a 768-token pair limit, reranking to 8, 2,500 non-evidence model-input tokens, and 700 output tokens:

reranker document tokens/pair = min(700, 768 - 100 - 20) = 648 tokens
reranker truncated tokens/pair = 700 - 648 = 52 tokens
reranker processed tokens/query = 40 * (648 + 100 + 20) = 30,720 tokens
reranker processed-token demand = 120 * 30,720 = 3,686,400 tokens/s
model input/query = 8 * 700 + 2,500 = 8,100 tokens
model input demand = 120 * 8,100 = 972,000 tokens/s
model output demand = 120 * 700 = 84,000 tokens/s

The reranker sees truncated 648-token document prefixes, while the context packer may hydrate the full 700-token text for the eight selected chunks, which is why model input still uses 8 * 700. Processed tokens are only a first-order reranker work estimate: padding, truncation, attention cost, batching, and model architecture can make equal token counts consume different service time. Capacity must therefore use measured pairs/s and latency over the exact query/document length distribution as well as the token ledger.

At illustrative prices of $3 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens:

cost/query = 8,100/1,000,000 * $3 + 700/1,000,000 * $12
           = $0.0243 + $0.0084
           = $0.0327 before retrieval, reranking, retries, and storage
cost/day at 120 qps = 120 * 86,400 * $0.0327 = $339,033.60

[Derived] These illustrative inputs expose why context depth and output caps are economic controls. Replace prices and token distributions with contracted rates and measured percentiles. Track logical requests separately from provider attempts so retry cost is visible.

docs.title: Offline evaluation
docs.text:
• candidate Recall@N against source-span judgments;
  • MRR or nDCG for ranked evidence;
  • context recall and context precision after packing;
  • claim-level citation precision and material-claim citation recall;
  • supported-answer rate, correctness, and abstention precision/recall;
  • ACL isolation and deletion tests with adversarial principals;
  • freshness and contradiction slices;
  • latency and cost by document type, tenant, language, and query class.

docs.title: Online evidence
docs.text:
• source change-to-active lag and connector reconciliation age;
  • zero-chunk, parse-error, quarantine, and indexing failure rates;
  • candidate and authorized counts by stage;
  • empty retrieval, stale response, abstention, and escalation reasons;
  • citation-open, reformulation, resolution, and user-correction outcomes;
  • prompt/model/index version mix and canary deltas;
  • cache hit rate keyed by scope and epoch;
  • logical requests, attempts, token distributions, and cost;
  • unauthorized-return invariant counter, which must remain zero.

Sampled traces must preserve enough evidence for diagnosis while respecting source ACL, privacy, and retention. Aggregate metrics without version dimensions hide split rollouts.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Treat retrieved documents, OCR text, ticket text, and tool output as untrusted content.
  • Keep credentials, hidden policies, and cross-tenant metadata out of prompts.
  • Apply principal-bound filters before retrieval material reaches the model.
  • Label source trust and do not let low-trust content override authoritative policy.
  • Constrain generated queries to allowlisted fields and bounded fan-out.
  • Scan uploads, sandbox parsers, cap decompression and page counts, and quarantine failures.
  • Prevent citations and snippets from becoming cross-tenant existence oracles.
  • Encrypt raw sources, indexes, traces, and replay evidence with scoped access and audit.
  • Preserve a kill switch that stops generation while cited authorized search remains available.

docs.title: Index and pipeline migration
docs.text:
epoch 41 active
  -> build epoch 42
  -> validate corpus, ACL, deletion, and quality
  -> shadow queries
  -> dual-read sampled traffic
  -> atomic activation if every gate passes
  -> canary and expand
  -> retain rollback window
  -> retire epoch 41

Migration gates include source counts, chunk-count distributions, tombstone watermarks, ACL equivalence, exact-vs-ANN checks, retrieval judgments, citation resolution, latency, and cost. Dual reads compare results but return only the active path. If two epochs use different chunk IDs, compare canonical source/version/spans rather than raw IDs.

Rollback cannot erase new deletions or revocations. When returning to an older index, layer the latest deny projection over it and prove that current policy still applies.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text:
Design a RAG assistant for global support staff over policies that change daily. Documents include private tenant tickets and shared manuals. The answer must include exact citations, meet 2-second p95 latency, expose freshness, and support monthly parser and embedding migrations.

Address ingestion idempotency, immutable versions, chunk lineage, ACL filter placement, hybrid retrieval, context budgets, claim citations, abstention, freshness clocks, deletion, failure attribution, evaluation, capacity, and dual-index rollback.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Traces one source from bytes through citation offsets and one query through stage evidence.
  • Separates retrieval, context, answer, citation, and abstention metrics.
  • Uses atomic corpus manifests and compatible version tuples.
  • Enforces ACL and tombstones independently of model behavior.
  • Defines safe stale, partial, timeout, and no-evidence outcomes.
  • Computes token demand and per-query cost from explicit assumptions.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Defines enterprise corpus epochs, lineage contracts, deletion evidence, and source ownership.
  • Governs evaluation judgments, high-risk freshness policy, and exceptions across products.
  • Quantifies regional or provider failure headroom and degraded capacity.
  • Attributes storage, inference, reprocessing, and evaluation cost to owners.
  • Names migration and rollback authority, evidence retention, review cadence, and retirement criteria.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Source versions and derived artifacts are immutable and linked.
  • Activation is atomic through one corpus manifest.
  • ACL, revocation, retention, and deletion survive every derived layer.
  • Citations bind claims to exact immutable spans.
  • Abstention handles absent, stale, conflicting, and unsupported evidence.
  • Failure attribution separates ingestion, retrieval, packing, generation, and validation.
  • Offline and online gates include mandatory security and freshness slices.
  • Migrations preserve compatibility, current denies, rollback, and old-epoch cleanup.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, primary, 2020-05-22] Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. Establishes the RAG framing of generation conditioned on retrieved external knowledge; production controls here are additional design guidance.
  • [Source, primary, 2020-04-10] Karpukhin et al., Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering. Supports dense bi-encoder passage retrieval.
  • [Source, Special Publication guidance, 2020-08-11] NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture. Supports resource-centric access control without implicit network trust; it does not prescribe RAG implementation or become a universal normative requirement merely by citation. Publication and scope verified 2026-09-08 against NIST's record.
  • [Source, normative, 2022-06] IETF, RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Supports conditional requests and HTTP method semantics. Application-level ingestion idempotency remains an explicit contract.
  • [Source, framework, 2023-01-26] NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0. Supports measured risk, governance, and lifecycle evaluation.
  • [Source, primary, 2015-12-07] Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems. Supports concern for data dependencies, entanglement, and undeclared consumers.
  • [Source, normative, 2013-04-30] W3C, PROV-O: The PROV Ontology. Provides standardized provenance concepts such as entities, activities, agents, derivation, and invalidation.

docs.title: Multimodal Document Pipelines
docs.text: A document is not a string. It may contain born-digital text, scanned pages, reading order, tables, formulas, charts, photographs, annotations, audio, and timing. A production pipeline preserves these modalities and their relationships while producing searchable, replayable, and citation-safe derivatives.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• [Source] is supported by a dated source in Sources.
  • [Derived] follows from stated inputs.
  • [Design] is a recommended production contract.
  • [Measure] requires local validation by media type, language, and quality slice.

docs.title: Design target
docs.text: Assume a compliance corpus containing PDFs, scans, spreadsheets, slide decks, images, meeting recordings, and transcripts. Users search and ask questions across all content. Answers must cite a page region or audio time range, preserve ACLs, and be reproducible after parser upgrades.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Raw source bytes are immutable and content-addressed.
  2. Every derivative names its source version, parent artifact, transformation, implementation version, parameters, and output digest.
  3. OCR never silently replaces extractable born-digital text.
  4. Reading order, geometry, table structure, image references, and audio timing remain available after text extraction.
  5. A citation resolves against the exact immutable rendition used to create it.
  6. Reprocessing creates a new pipeline run and derivative set; it does not mutate prior evidence.
  7. Partial pages and modality-specific failures are explicit, queryable states.
  8. ACL, retention, legal hold, and deletion propagate to every derivative and cache.
  9. Replay performs no external side effect except writing idempotently named derivatives.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I[Source intake] --> B[(Immutable blob store)]
    I --> M[Malware and format checks]
    M --> D[Document classifier]
    D --> T[Native text extraction]
    D --> O[OCR and handwriting path]
    D --> L[Layout analysis]
    D --> A[Audio extraction and ASR]
    D --> V[Image and chart analysis]
    T --> G[Document graph]
    O --> G
    L --> G
    A --> G
    V --> G
    G --> C[Modality-aware chunking]
    C --> X[Search and RAG indexes]
    G --> P[(Lineage catalog)]
    X --> P

The document graph is the canonical derived representation. Plain text is one projection. Search chunks, thumbnails, table rows, image captions, and transcripts derive from graph nodes and keep stable source anchors.

docs.title: Intake and classification
docs.text:
Do not trust filename extensions or caller-provided MIME types. Detect format from bytes, reject unsupported encryption or corruption explicitly, bound archive expansion, scan for malware, and isolate parsers from network and host credentials.

Classify each page or stream before choosing extraction:

Input condition Primary path Secondary path born-digital text with valid glyph mapping native extraction OCR sampled for discrepancy checks image-only scan OCR layout and image segmentation mixed scan plus text layer compare native text and OCR select by region with provenance table-heavy page layout plus table structure OCR cells if needed image/chart-heavy page image region extraction OCR labels and optional description recording audio decode plus ASR diarization and alignment if policy permits

[Measure] No parser is universally best. Route by measured quality and failure rate on representative document slices, not by format name alone.

docs.title: Canonical document graph
docs.text:
{
  "document_id": "contract-184",
  "source_version": "sha256:raw-bytes",
  "rendition_id": "render-7",
  "pages": [
    {
      "page_id": "p-12",
      "width": 612.0,
      "height": 792.0,
      "coordinate_space": "PDF_POINTS_TOP_LEFT",
      "nodes": [
        {
          "node_id": "n-440",
          "kind": "PARAGRAPH",
          "bbox": [72.0, 124.0, 540.0, 188.0],
          "reading_order": 17,
          "text": "Payment is due within 30 days.",
          "text_digest": "sha256:...",
          "confidence": 0.992,
          "derived_by": "native-extractor-5.1"
        },
        {
          "node_id": "n-441",
          "kind": "TABLE",
          "bbox": [72.0, 220.0, 540.0, 410.0],
          "table_ref": "table-9",
          "derived_by": "table-parser-3.4"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The coordinate convention and rendition are part of the contract. A bounding box without coordinate space, page dimensions, and rotation cannot be reproduced reliably. Preserve parser confidence as a signal, not proof of correctness.

PDF_POINTS_TOP_LEFT is this application's normalized coordinate convention, not a claim about native PDF user space. Persist crop box, rotation, scale, origin and the invertible raw-to-rendition transform. Test a rotated/cropped page round trip; matching numeric boxes across two coordinate systems does not establish a correct citation.

docs.title: OCR and reading order
docs.text: OCR has distinct stages: image normalization, orientation detection, region detection, line recognition, language selection, confidence estimation, and post-processing. Store stage outcomes so a low-quality page is not confused with a missing page.

docs.title: OCR policy
docs.text:
1. Render a deterministic page image from the immutable source using a versioned renderer and DPI.
  2. Detect rotation and deskew within bounded parameters; retain the transform matrix.
  3. Detect text regions and reading order.
  4. Recognize text using declared language packs and model versions.
  5. Preserve token or line geometry and confidence.
  6. Compare with native text where both exist; do not concatenate duplicates.
  7. Normalize Unicode for indexing while retaining original recognized text and mappings.
  8. Quarantine pages below quality thresholds for high-risk use cases.

[Source] Tesseract documentation describes an OCR engine and page-segmentation modes, but using it does not establish correctness for a corpus. [Measure] Evaluate character error rate and word error rate by language, scan source, font, rotation, handwriting, and compression.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
Text extraction that sorts only by y then x fails on columns, sidebars, headers, footnotes, and floating figures. Model reading order as edges:

Node(id, page, kind, bbox, content_ref)
Edge(from_node, to_node, relation)
relation in {NEXT, CONTAINS, CAPTION_OF, FOOTNOTE_OF, LABELS, CONTINUES_ON}

Cycles in NEXT are invalid. Repeated headers and footers can be marked boilerplate but remain addressable. Human-visible citations should prefer page and region, not an unstable chunk number.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
A table is structure, not lines of tab-separated OCR text. Preserve cells, spans, headers, row groups, footnotes, and coordinates.

{
  "table_id": "table-9",
  "page_id": "p-12",
  "bbox": [72.0, 220.0, 540.0, 410.0],
  "rows": 3,
  "columns": 4,
  "cells": [
    {"cell_id": "c1", "row": 0, "column": 0, "row_span": 1, "column_span": 2, "role": "COLUMN_HEADER", "text": "Service"},
    {"cell_id": "c2", "row": 1, "column": 0, "row_span": 1, "column_span": 1, "role": "DATA", "text": "Storage"}
  ],
  "parser_version": "table-parser-3.4",
  "confidence": 0.94
}

Index at multiple granularities: table summary, header-qualified rows, and selected cells. Include header context when chunking a row. Never present a computed answer from cells without citing the table region and preserving units, footnotes, and effective date.

Evaluate table detection, structure recognition, cell text, header association, and downstream question answering separately. [Source] Table Transformer applies object detection to table detection and structure recognition; it does not define a complete production lineage or citation contract.

[Primary implementation, verified 2026-09-08] The Table Transformer repository explicitly requires separate OCR or native text extraction to populate HTML/CSV text. Detecting correct cells is not recognizing their contents. Tesseract's quality guidance also calls out table segmentation limitations; parser confidence and table AP cannot substitute for cell-value and header-association tests.

docs.title: Images, charts, and diagrams
docs.text:
Extract image regions and retain their page geometry, surrounding text, captions, alt text, and object digest. Do not generate a description when the image is decorative or when policy forbids external model processing.

flowchart TD
    R[Image region] --> C{Caption available?}
    C -->|Yes| L[Link caption and nearby references]
    C -->|No| D{Description permitted and useful?}
    D -->|No| K[Keep searchable metadata only]
    D -->|Yes| G[Generate bounded description]
    G --> V[Validate labels numbers and uncertainty]
    L --> X[Image-aware index record]
    K --> X
    V --> X

Generated image descriptions are derived interpretations. Label model and prompt versions and do not treat them as source truth. Charts require special handling: OCR axis labels and legends, retain the image, and avoid asserting exact values unless extraction can be verified. A visual question may need the original crop sent to a multimodal model under the same ACL and data policy.

docs.title: Audio and speech
docs.text:
Audio processing can include demultiplexing, channel selection, voice activity detection, speech recognition, timestamp alignment, speaker segmentation, and optional speaker identification. Each step has a different privacy and accuracy profile.

{
  "segment_id": "meeting-9:s-188",
  "source_version": "sha256:audio-bytes",
  "start_ms": 81240,
  "end_ms": 87910,
  "channel": 0,
  "speaker_label": "SPEAKER_02",
  "speaker_identity": null,
  "text": "The migration begins on Monday.",
  "words": [
    {"text": "migration", "start_ms": 82610, "end_ms": 83120, "confidence": 0.91}
  ],
  "asr_model": "asr-6",
  "alignment_version": "align-2"
}

[Source] Whisper reports multilingual speech-recognition and translation experiments using large-scale weak supervision. This supports the ASR model family, not a claim about local word-error rate or timestamp quality.

Treat diarization labels as session-local unless an independently authorized identity system maps them. Voice biometrics and speaker identification introduce additional consent and biometric-data obligations. Redaction must affect audio clips, transcripts, embeddings, search caches, and replay artifacts.

docs.title: Modality-aware chunking
docs.text:
Do not flatten first and chunk later. Construct chunks from graph boundaries:

function build_chunks(document_graph, max_tokens):
    for section in document_graph.sections_in_reading_order:
        units = paragraphs + header_qualified_table_rows + captions + transcript_segments
        pack adjacent compatible units until max_tokens
        never split a table cell or detach a caption from its figure reference
        emit chunk with node_ids, source anchors, modality, ACL, and digest

Define an oversized-unit branch: a single cell or transcript segment can exceed max_tokens. Preserve the full unit as an addressable artifact, then use explicitly linked subspans with repeated header context, a validated extract, or quarantine/abstention. Do not violate the hard token bound to preserve an indivisible unit or retry packing forever.

Use overlap only when a boundary loses required context. For 800-token chunks with 200-token overlap, long-document duplication is approximately:

stride = 800 - 200 = 600 tokens
duplication factor = 800 / 600 = 1.333
overhead = 33.3%

[Derived] That overhead multiplies embedding work and index storage before metadata and index structures. See the calculations workbook.

docs.title: Lineage and replay
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    E0[Raw entity sha256 A] -->|render v7| E1[Page image sha256 B]
    E1 -->|OCR v12| E2[Text nodes sha256 C]
    E1 -->|layout v4| E3[Geometry graph sha256 D]
    E2 -->|merge v6| E4[Document graph sha256 E]
    E3 -->|merge v6| E4
    E4 -->|chunk v9| E5[Chunks sha256 F]
    E5 -->|embed v3| E6[Index records epoch 42]

[Source] W3C PROV defines entities, activities, agents, derivation, generation, usage, and invalidation for interoperable provenance. [Design] The schema below specializes those ideas for deterministic document processing.

{
  "run_id": "run-01H...",
  "stage": "OCR",
  "attempt": 2,
  "input_artifacts": [{"id": "page-image-12", "digest": "sha256:B"}],
  "implementation": {"name": "ocr-worker", "version": "12.3.0", "model_digest": "sha256:M"},
  "parameters_digest": "sha256:P",
  "environment_digest": "sha256:E",
  "started_at": "2026-09-06T12:00:00Z",
  "ended_at": "2026-09-06T12:00:04Z",
  "status": "SUCCEEDED",
  "outputs": [{"id": "text-nodes-12", "digest": "sha256:C"}],
  "metrics": {"pages": 1, "regions": 31, "mean_confidence": 0.93}
}

Replay selects immutable input digests and an explicit pipeline bundle. It writes to a new run namespace, compares output digests and semantic metrics, and never overwrites the active graph. Bitwise reproduction may fail across nondeterministic accelerator kernels or libraries; record environment and compare declared semantic invariants instead of claiming universal bitwise determinism.

docs.title: Pipeline API
docs.text:
POST /v1/document-runs
Idempotency-Key: doc:contract-184:sha256-raw:pipeline-12
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "source_id": "contract-184",
  "source_version": "sha256:raw-bytes",
  "pipeline_bundle": "pipeline-12",
  "purpose": "INDEX_BUILD",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-7"
}

{
  "run_id": "run-01H...",
  "state": "QUEUED",
  "input_digest": "sha256:raw-bytes",
  "pipeline_bundle": "pipeline-12",
  "status_url": "/v1/document-runs/run-01H..."
}

The status response reports every stage as PENDING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, PARTIAL, QUARANTINED, FAILED_RETRYABLE, FAILED_FINAL, or SKIPPED_BY_POLICY. Page-level errors are arrays, not one free-text message.

docs.title: Capacity calculation
docs.text:
Suppose intake is 500,000 pages/day, 35% require OCR, OCR sustains 2.5 pages/s per worker at target DPI, and the design reserves 40% capacity for bursts and worker loss:

OCR pages/day = 500,000 * 0.35 = 175,000
mean OCR demand = 175,000 / 86,400 = 2.03 pages/s
usable worker throughput = 2.5 * (1 - 0.40) = 1.5 pages/s
minimum workers = ceil(2.03 / 1.5) = 2

[Derived] Two workers cover only the stated daily mean with reserve. Peak-hour arrival, long-tail pages, retries, language-model routing, and zone redundancy may require more. If 60% arrives in an 8-hour window, peak-window demand is 105,000 / 28,800 = 3.65 pages/s, requiring ceil(3.65 / 1.5) = 3 workers before N+1 policy.

Storage example for 500,000 pages/day with a 250 KB normalized page image and 40 KB graph/text derivative:

daily derivative bytes = 500,000 * 290 KB = 145 GB decimal
30-day hot derivatives = 4.35 TB decimal before replicas and indexes

Measure actual distributions. High-resolution images and audio dominate averages quickly.

docs.title: Quality evaluation
docs.text:
Layer Metric or test Important slices format detection correct route and rejection reason mislabeled, encrypted, malformed native extraction text coverage and order fonts, ligatures, columns OCR CER, WER, region recall language, scan age, rotation, handwriting layout region precision/recall, reading-order accuracy columns, sidebars, footnotes table detection, structure, cell text, header links merged cells, borderless tables image region/caption linkage and grounded description charts, screenshots, decorative art audio WER, timing error, diarization error where applicable noise, overlap, accents, channels lineage anchor resolution and digest verification every parser and replay version retrieval Recall@K by modality table, image, transcript, paragraph citation exact page/region/time support parser-version and rendition changes

Do not average away a safety-critical modality. A pipeline can have excellent paragraph OCR and unusable table numbers. Freeze representative files with rights and privacy controls, expected structures, and adjudication history.

docs.title: Observability and failures
docs.text:
Monitor bytes and pages discovered, stage queue age, worker saturation, per-format latency, retry amplification, zero-output success, confidence distributions, graph validation errors, duplicate artifacts, quarantine age, source-to-index lag, lineage resolution failures, replay divergence, deletion backlog, and cost per page/minute.

Failure Evidence and discriminator Recovery parser returns empty success nonempty bytes, zero nodes, no explicit empty classification quarantine and retry with known-good parser OCR duplicates native text overlapping geometry and near-identical strings from two paths region-level source selection and deduplication reading order corrupt correct tokens but invalid sequence against labeled pages rollback layout/ordering stage table flattened incorrectly cell text exists but header associations fail retain table image and reprocess structure citation box drifts citation rendition differs from active viewer rendition render immutable cited rendition audio timestamps shift transcript text stable but alignment version changed retain old timed segments and migrate citations replay changes output same inputs, different implementation/environment digest compare declared invariants; do not overwrite delete misses thumbnails lineage inventory contains live derivatives after tombstone deny immediately, then purge and verify graph closure

Practice provenance-safe ingestion in Lab 06.

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text:
• Sandbox native parsers, OCR, codecs, and archive extraction with CPU, memory, file, and wall-time limits.
  • Disable parser network egress unless a narrowly scoped stage requires it.
  • Reject path traversal, active content, decompression bombs, oversized dimensions, and unsupported encryption.
  • Treat recognized text, image descriptions, and transcripts as untrusted input to downstream models.
  • Keep raw content and credentials out of general logs; store digests and protected evidence references.
  • Enforce source ACL during derivative reads, indexing, retrieval, replay, and operator debugging.
  • Classify biometric, health, financial, and secret content before external processing.
  • Bind temporary model-provider access to approved data classes and retention contracts.
  • Apply redaction and deletion to every node reachable in the lineage graph.

docs.title: Migration strategy
docs.text:
1. Freeze the old pipeline bundle and representative evaluation corpus.
  2. Run the new parser or model into a separate derivative namespace.
  3. Validate graph schema, counts, geometry, lineage closure, ACLs, deletion, and quality slices.
  4. Build a new search epoch from only the new graph manifest.
  5. Shadow retrieval and citation resolution; compare source spans, not unstable chunk IDs.
  6. Canary by document class and tenant risk.
  7. Atomically activate the compatible document-graph and index epoch.
  8. Retain old renditions for citation stability and rollback under retention policy.
  9. Repoint or migrate citations only through an explicit verified mapping.
  10. Purge old derivatives after rollback, legal, and reproducibility windows close.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text:
Design ingestion for 10 million historical insurance documents plus 20,000 hours of call audio per month. PDFs mix native text, scans, handwriting, tables, and photographs. Investigators need page-region and audio-time citations. The organization upgrades OCR quarterly and must delete a customer's data across all derivatives.

Explain classification, OCR/native arbitration, layout and table models, image and audio treatment, document graph, chunking, lineage, replay, capacity, security, evaluation, migration, and deletion proof.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Models documents as structured multimodal graphs instead of flattened text.
  • Preserves coordinates, reading order, cell structure, timestamps, and immutable source anchors.
  • Computes OCR throughput or derivative storage with explicit assumptions.
  • Separates quality metrics by stage and modality.
  • Makes partial extraction and zero-output failures observable.
  • Replays into new immutable namespaces and migrates citation-safe epochs.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes cross-team schemas for entities, activities, anchors, renditions, and deletion closure.
  • Governs parser/model qualification by language, document class, and risk.
  • Quantifies regional backlog recovery and reserved capacity economics.
  • Defines long-term citation compatibility and evidence-retention policy.
  • Names owners and exception authority for quarantine, external processing, biometric data, and migration.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Raw bytes and every derivative have immutable digests.
  • Native text and OCR are selected by region with provenance.
  • Layout, tables, images, and audio survive as structured nodes.
  • Citations resolve to exact page regions or audio time ranges.
  • Pipeline state distinguishes partial, quarantined, retryable, and final failure.
  • Capacity covers peak mix, retries, reserve, and derivative storage.
  • Replay records implementation, parameters, environment, inputs, and outputs.
  • ACL, retention, redaction, and deletion traverse the lineage graph.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, normative, 2013-04-30] W3C, PROV-O: The PROV Ontology. Defines interoperable provenance concepts used to motivate the lineage model.
  • [Source, official documentation, accessed 2026-09-06] Tesseract OCR, User Manual. Documents OCR engine operation, language data, and page segmentation. Local accuracy claims require corpus evaluation.
  • [Source, primary, 2019-12-31] Xu et al., LayoutLM: Pre-training of Text and Layout for Document Image Understanding. Supports joint use of text and layout information for document understanding.
  • [Source, primary, 2019-04-16] Zhong, Tang, and Yepes, PubLayNet: Largest Dataset Ever for Document Layout Analysis. Supports document-layout detection evaluation and common region classes.
  • [Source, primary, 2021-09-30] Smock, Pesala, and Abraham, PubTables-1M: Towards Comprehensive Table Extraction From Unstructured Documents. Supports table detection and structure-recognition modeling, including Table Transformer experiments.
  • [Source, primary, 2021-11-30] Kim et al., OCR-free Document Understanding Transformer. Supports an OCR-free document-understanding approach; it does not remove production needs for lineage or exact citations.
  • [Source, primary, 2022-12-06] Radford et al., Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision. Supports multilingual ASR and translation experiments associated with Whisper.
