docs.title: Workflows and Bounded Agents
docs.text: Use deterministic code when the path, policy, and success condition are known. Add model-controlled choice only where it creates measured value. An agent is not a reliability mechanism: it expands the set of possible paths, costs, and failures. Production autonomy must therefore be explicit, least-privileged, durable, observable, and bounded.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• [Source] is supported directly by a dated source in Sources.
  • [Derived] follows from stated assumptions.
  • [Design] is a recommended production contract.
  • [Measure] must be tested on representative tasks and failures.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
• A deterministic workflow chooses transitions in code from typed state and declared conditions.
  • A model-assisted workflow has fixed topology but uses a model inside bounded steps such as classify, extract, draft, or evaluate.
  • An agent lets a model choose some next actions or tools based on state and observations.
  • Autonomy is the authority to select or execute actions without another decision maker. It is a vector, not a boolean.

[Source] Anthropic's 2024 guidance distinguishes workflows with predefined code paths from agents whose model dynamically directs process and tool use. This chapter uses that useful distinction but adds its own production contracts.

docs.title: Start with the authority map
docs.text:
Before choosing a pattern, classify every operation:

Class Examples Model role Required control A0: pure computation summarize local text, rank options may execute schema and budget A1: reversible read search docs, read ticket may propose/call principal-bound scope and audit A2: reversible write create draft, add label may propose; limited execution idempotency, validation, undo A3: consequential write refund, publish, change access proposal only by default exact approval, policy, compensation A4: irreversible/high impact delete evidence, wire funds no autonomous execution established human workflow and separation of duties

This is a [Design] taxonomy, not an industry standard. Organizations should map classes to their own legal and operational policy.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Identity, authorization, data policy, spend policy, tool validation, and approval are deterministic controls outside the model.
  2. Every run has maximum steps, model calls, tool calls, input/output tokens, wall time, spend, and parallel fan-out.
  3. A tool call is a proposal until the tool gateway authorizes and executes it.
  4. Unknown tool outcomes are reconciled by stable operation key before retry.
  5. Repeated actions without new evidence consume a progress budget and trigger stopping.
  6. Partial and degraded outcomes are explicit; exhaustion is not reported as success.
  7. Side effects have duplicate-prevention or explicit unknown-outcome controls independently of replay; compensation is a separate authorized recovery action, not a substitute for deduplication.
  8. The runtime can remove write capabilities without disabling safe reads.

docs.title: Pattern selection
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Task] --> B{Path and rules known?}
    B -->|Yes| W[Deterministic workflow]
    B -->|No| C{Can bounded classification choose a path?}
    C -->|Yes| R[Router plus fixed workflows]
    C -->|No| D{Subtasks known and independent?}
    D -->|Yes| P[Parallel workflow]
    D -->|No| E{Success can be evaluated incrementally?}
    E -->|No| H[Human-led process]
    E -->|Yes| F{Actions reversible and low risk?}
    F -->|No| G[Agent plans; workflow approves and executes]
    F -->|Yes| I[Bounded agent]

Prefer the least dynamic pattern that passes quality gates. A single call with retrieval may outperform a complex loop after latency, cost, and failures are counted.

docs.title: Deterministic workflow
docs.text:
Use a state machine for known business processes, mandatory approvals, deadlines, and compensation. A model can classify or draft inside a step, but code owns transitions.

RECEIVED -> VALIDATED -> ENRICHED -> DRAFTED -> REVIEWED -> COMMITTED

Best fit: regulated writes, stable forms, fixed integrations, and high-volume repeatable tasks.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
A router maps an input to a bounded set of specialist paths. Routing can be rules, a classifier, or an LLM with a strict enum output. Add an UNKNOWN route and confidence policy. Never let a route label grant authority; downstream policy evaluates the original principal and request.

{
  "route": "REFUND_QUESTION",
  "confidence": 0.91,
  "alternatives": ["ORDER_STATUS"],
  "reason_codes": ["MENTIONS_DUPLICATE_CHARGE"],
  "router_version": "router-8"
}

Evaluate route confusion by class, business impact, language, and adversarial input. A cheap router that sends hard cases to the wrong specialist can cost more than a single capable model.

docs.title: Prompt chain
docs.text: Chaining decomposes a task into fixed steps such as extract -> validate -> draft. Each step has a typed contract and gate. Serial chains improve focus but multiply latency and failure opportunities. Persist intermediate values only when needed for recovery, audit, or evaluation.

docs.title: Parallelization
docs.text:
Use sectioning when independent subtasks can run concurrently and a deterministic aggregator can combine them. Use voting when independent attempts provide useful diversity and a declared decision rule exists. Correlated model errors limit the benefit of voting.

flowchart LR
    I[Input] --> A[Worker: facts]
    I --> B[Worker: policy]
    I --> C[Worker: safety]
    A --> J[Typed join]
    B --> J
    C --> J
    J --> V[Deterministic validation]

Bound fan-out. If one request starts 20 workers and each retries twice, the worst-case 60 attempts can overload shared inference and tools.

docs.title: Orchestrator-worker
docs.text: The orchestrator chooses subtasks dynamically; workers execute narrow bounded jobs. This fits tasks where decomposition depends on the input, such as investigating several unknown systems. The orchestrator does not inherit every worker capability. Give each worker the minimum read or write scope and cap spawned tasks, depth, and aggregate budget.

docs.title: Evaluator-optimizer
docs.text:
One component produces an artifact; another evaluates it against a rubric and returns structured defects. Iterate only while the score or defect set demonstrates progress.

stop when any condition holds:
  all mandatory checks pass
  maximum iterations reached
  marginal score gain < epsilon for two iterations
  same normalized defect set repeats
  deadline, token, or spend budget exhausted
  evaluator confidence is below review threshold

Do not let an evaluator convert subjective confidence into permission for a consequential action. The business policy remains deterministic.

docs.title: ReAct-style agent loop
docs.text:
[Source] ReAct interleaves reasoning-oriented model outputs with actions and observations. In production, store a concise decision record and typed actions rather than depending on hidden free-form reasoning.

flowchart TD
    S[Load durable state] --> O[Observe bounded context]
    O --> M[Model proposes action]
    M --> P{Policy and schema allow?}
    P -->|No| D[Record denial]
    P -->|Yes| T[Execute tool with operation key]
    T --> R[Record result]
    D --> G{Stop condition?}
    R --> G
    G -->|Continue| S
    G -->|Complete| C[Validate completion]
    G -->|Exhausted| E[Partial or abstain]

docs.title: Bounded autonomy contract
docs.text:
{
  "run_id": "run-01H...",
  "principal": "user-71",
  "purpose": "support-resolution",
  "authority_class": "A2",
  "capabilities": ["ticket.read", "draft.create", "label.add"],
  "budgets": {
    "max_steps": 12,
    "max_model_calls": 8,
    "max_tool_calls": 10,
    "max_parallelism": 3,
    "max_input_tokens": 60000,
    "max_output_tokens": 8000,
    "max_spend_usd": 0.50,
    "deadline_at": "2026-09-06T13:01:00Z"
  },
  "stopping": {
    "repeat_action_limit": 2,
    "no_progress_limit": 3,
    "require_completion_validator": true
  },
  "versions": {"workflow": "wf-9", "prompt": "agent-14", "model_route": "route-11", "policy": "policy-21"}
}

Budgets are cumulative across retries and resumes. A retry does not create fresh spend or authority. Child-worker budgets are carved from the parent's remaining budget, not added to it. Reserve the maximum allowed attempt cost atomically before dispatch, then settle measured usage; checking a balance without reserving it lets concurrent workers overspend. Provider-enforced output limits and deadline controls bound each reservation.

docs.title: Step transition algorithm
docs.text:
function advance(run):
    lease = acquire_fenced_lease(run)
    if not lease: return RETRY_LATER
    state = load_and_fold(run.events)
    if terminal(state): return state.result
    if state.pending_operation:
        return reconcile_without_replanning(state.pending_operation, lease)
    if any_budget_exhausted(state): return terminate(EXHAUSTED)

    reservation = reserve_attempt_budget_fenced(state, lease)
    if not reservation: return terminate(EXHAUSTED)
    observation = build_bounded_observation(state)
    proposal = model.propose(observation, allowed_action_schemas)
    append_fenced(ActionProposed(proposal, versions, budget_snapshot), lease.fencing_epoch)

    decision = policy.authorize(principal, purpose, proposal, state)
    append_fenced(PolicyDecided(decision), lease.fencing_epoch)
    if denied(decision): return schedule_next_or_stop(state)

    intent = persist_intent_once(run.id, state.logical_effect_slot,
                                 proposal, decision, lease.fencing_epoch)
    key = intent.operation_key
    prior = tool.lookup(key)
    if terminal(prior): return record_and_advance(prior, intent, lease)
    if not safe_to_dispatch_or_retry(prior, intent, tool.contract):
        return persist_unknown_and_schedule_reconciliation(intent, lease)
    reauthorize_and_check_preconditions(intent)
    append_fenced(ToolDispatchStarted(key), lease.fencing_epoch)
    result = tool.execute(key, intent.canonical_args)
    append_fenced(ToolResultRecorded(key, digest(result), redacted_result), lease.fencing_epoch)
    return schedule_next_or_stop(state)

Budget exhaustion stops new work but does not erase an unresolved side effect. Transfer it to a bounded recovery queue with its own operational budget, retaining UNKNOWN until status lookup or human reconciliation resolves it; recovery must not replan or automatically redispatch a non-idempotent effect. A terminal user-facing run may still have a separately visible pending recovery record.

The lease plus fencing on durable commits excludes stale planners; lease expiry alone does not stop their processes. Release leases on every exit or let a bounded lease expire. These controls do not create exactly-once external effects. The tool's idempotency record and reconciliation contract protect the side effect, including a crash after dispatch but before result persistence.

The orchestrator assigns a durable logical-effect slot, persists its operation key and canonical payload before dispatch, and reuses them across physical attempts and resumes. Argument and resource-version digests bind approval/preconditions; a changed version cannot silently mint a new financial identity for an unresolved effect. A genuinely new effect needs an explicit new authorized intent. Model-provided IDs are correlation only. Reusing a key with a different canonical payload is a conflict.

docs.title: Stopping and progress
docs.text:
An agent must prove progress using task-specific state rather than claiming it in prose. Examples:

  • unresolved required fields decrease;
  • failing deterministic checks decrease;
  • uncovered source set decreases;
  • test failures decrease without increasing higher-severity failures;
  • plan frontier gains a new nonduplicate observation.

Normalize action identity as (tool, canonical_args_digest, relevant_resource_version). Repeating it with the same observation is nonprogress unless the tool contract says polling is required and bounded. Backoff polling does not reset the limit.

Terminal reasons should include:

SUCCEEDED
PARTIAL_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED
PARTIAL_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
ABSTAINED_INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE
BLOCKED_POLICY
BLOCKED_APPROVAL
FAILED_TOOL
FAILED_VALIDATION
CANCELLED_USER
CANCELLED_KILL_SWITCH

docs.title: Reliability and cost calculations
docs.text:
Suppose a fixed four-step workflow has independent success probabilities 0.999, 0.995, 0.998, and 0.999:

all-step success = 0.999 * 0.995 * 0.998 * 0.999 = 0.991025

Suppose an agent requires 10 successful steps, each with an illustrative independent success of 0.98:

all-step success = 0.98^10 = 0.817073

[Derived] Added mandatory steps can reduce completion reliability. Dependence invalidates the product of marginal success probabilities but does not determine the direction of error: common failures can increase joint success relative to independent fixed marginals, while changed outage exposure can worsen the marginals themselves. These products illustrate sensitivity; they are not availability forecasts. See the explicit counterexamples and primary reliability reference in Lab 07.

For a router followed by three parallel workers and a join:

router p95 = 80 ms
worker p95 values = 300, 420, 250 ms
join and validation = 60 ms
naive critical-path budget = 80 + max(300,420,250) + 60 = 560 ms

Actual end-to-end p95 is not generally the sum of stage p95s. Measure joint traces under load, including queueing.

If 50 requests/s spawn 3 workers and 5% of workers retry once:

base worker attempts/s = 50 * 3 = 150
retry attempts/s = 150 * 0.05 = 7.5
total worker attempts/s = 157.5
attempt amplification = 157.5 / 150 = 1.05

docs.title: Failures and recovery
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Safe behavior router misclassification confusion slice and downstream correction disagree route to safe general path or human chain schema drift producer output fails consumer version compatibility adapter or rollback parallel fan-out overload child attempts rise faster than parent requests admission and aggregate child budget worker contradiction typed results disagree on same fact/version preserve conflict and escalate evaluator loop repeated defects or negligible score gain stop with partial artifact agent nonprogress repeated normalized action and observation terminate; do not reset budget timeout after commit no response but operation-key lookup finds effect record reconciled result; no duplicate write model provider outage model stage unavailable deterministic queue, safe read-only fallback, or fail prompt injection proposes action untrusted content correlates with denied proposal preserve denial evidence; remove unsafe capability kill switch activated policy version removes write tools complete reads or stop at safe boundary

See Failure Cards and RAG and Agent Security.

docs.title: Security and side effects
docs.text:
• Keep credentials inside the tool gateway; the model sees tool names and bounded schemas, not secrets.
  • Bind capabilities to principal, tenant, purpose, action, resource, expiry, and policy version.
  • Treat user, retrieved, web, email, image, and tool-result text as untrusted.
  • Reauthorize every call. A prior model decision or approval is not authorization.
  • Use strict input and output schemas, business preconditions, destination controls, and response-size limits.
  • Require approval over exact normalized arguments for high-impact actions.
  • Use stable operation keys, payload digests, status lookup, and explicit unknown-outcome states.
  • Compensate only through domain-approved actions; do not pretend compensation erases history.
  • Log redacted evidence and retain a per-tool kill switch.

docs.title: Offline suite
docs.text:
• route accuracy and cost-weighted confusion;
  • per-step schema validity and deterministic gate pass rate;
  • end-to-end task success, partial utility, and false-success rate;
  • tool selection and argument correctness;
  • unknown-outcome reconciliation and duplicate-effect tests;
  • stopping precision: unnecessary stop versus harmful continuation;
  • prompt-injection and capability-escalation suites;
  • latency, attempts, tokens, and spend distributions;
  • human override and approval-quality review.

docs.title: Production telemetry
docs.text:
Record logical run, parent/child relationship, state transition, model/prompt/tool/policy versions, proposed action, authorization result, operation key, redacted result digest, budgets before and after, stop reason, and final validation. High-cardinality traces need sampling and protected access, but invariant counters are unsampled.

Monitor:

  • success, partial, abstention, and false-success audits;
  • steps and repeated actions per run;
  • child fan-out and depth;
  • logical runs versus model and tool attempts;
  • token, latency, queue age, and spend percentiles;
  • policy denials and approval age;
  • unknown outcomes, reconciliations, and duplicate suppression;
  • tool error by version;
  • kill-switch activations and writes attempted after removal, which must be zero.

docs.title: Migration and rollout
docs.text:
1. Begin with a deterministic baseline and representative task set.
  2. Add one model-assisted step in shadow mode; preserve baseline outputs.
  3. Compare task quality, route errors, latency, cost, and safety slices.
  4. Introduce read-only tools with narrow capabilities.
  5. Shadow model-proposed writes without execution.
  6. Enable low-risk reversible writes behind exact approval and low limits.
  7. Canary prompt, model, workflow, tool schema, and policy changes as compatible bundles.
  8. Keep event readers tolerant of old versions and tool adapters available through the replay window.
  9. Roll back by activating a known-good bundle and removing capabilities; do not rewrite run history.
  10. Retire old schemas only after active, paused, and replayable runs no longer require them.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text:
Design an operations assistant that investigates incidents, queries metrics and logs, drafts mitigations, and may restart one low-risk service after approval. Inputs can contain untrusted log text. The system must finish within five minutes and remain safe during tool timeouts and model outages.

Choose among router, chain, parallel workers, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer, and a bounded ReAct loop. Define authority classes, budgets, typed state, progress, stopping, idempotency, approval, evaluation, telemetry, and migration.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Uses deterministic workflows for known controls and model choice only where justified.
  • Defines cumulative step, tool, token, time, fan-out, and spend budgets.
  • Treats actions as typed proposals and reconciles timeout-after-commit.
  • Gives concrete progress and stopping rules.
  • Quantifies serial reliability, critical path, or fan-out attempts.
  • Evaluates route, step, tool, safety, and end-to-end outcomes separately.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes organization-wide authority classes, capability policy, and exception governance.
  • Quantifies correlated provider/tool/region failure and receiver capacity.
  • Defines compatible workflow, event, prompt, model, policy, and tool migrations for paused runs.
  • Allocates autonomy cost and incident risk to owning products.
  • Names falsifying evidence, retention, review cadence, and rollback authority.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• The simplest sufficient pattern was evaluated first.
  • Deterministic controls own identity, policy, spend, validation, and approval.
  • Every run and child run consumes bounded cumulative budgets.
  • Progress and every terminal reason are machine-checkable.
  • Unknown side-effect outcomes reconcile before retry.
  • Evaluation includes false success, safety, latency, and cost.
  • Write capabilities can be removed independently.
  • Migration supports active, paused, and replayed runs.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, official guidance, 2024-12-19] Anthropic, Building Effective Agents. Defines workflows versus agents and describes routing, prompt chaining, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer, and bounded agent loops. It is implementation guidance, not a normative standard.
  • [Source, primary, 2022-10-06] Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models. Supports interleaving reasoning-oriented outputs, actions, and observations.
  • [Source, framework, 2023-01-26] NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0. Supports lifecycle risk management, measurement, governance, and human oversight.
  • [Source, normative, 2022-06] IETF, RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Defines HTTP idempotent-method semantics; application operation keys and exactly-once side effects are outside its guarantee.
  • [Source, primary, SIGMOD 1987] Garcia-Molina and Salem, Sagas. Introduces long-lived transactions composed from transactions and compensating transactions. Publisher-deposited metadata identifies the May 27-29 conference, not a December publication claim.

docs.title: Typed Tool Calling and MCP
docs.text:
Tool calling turns model output into a request to software that can read or change the world. JSON shape alone does not make that safe. Production systems need typed contracts, protocol capability declaration, principal-bound authorization, credential isolation, explicit side-effect semantics, idempotency, approval, and lifecycle-aware recovery.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes host-client-server communication for context and capabilities. It does not replace business authorization, transaction semantics, or safe tool implementation.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• [Normative] reflects requirements in the dated MCP or IETF specification cited in Sources.
  • [Source] is supported by a dated primary or official source but is not restated as a protocol requirement.
  • [Derived] follows from stated assumptions.
  • [Design] is a recommended production control beyond the protocol.
  • [Measure] requires local evaluation.

docs.title: Typed tool contract
docs.text:
A useful tool is narrow, explicit, and hard to misuse. Separate read, prepare, commit, reconcile, and compensate operations instead of hiding them behind a broad do_anything tool.

The example is a local registry record enriched with contract_version and authority_class, not an exact wire Tool definition. Those two fields are application-owned metadata; serialize only supported MCP fields or a declared metadata extension on the wire. The host enforces its governed registry, not a server's self-reported authority label.

{
  "name": "refund.prepare",
  "description": "Validate and prepare a refund. Does not move money.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "required": ["payment_id", "amount_minor", "currency", "reason_code"],
    "properties": {
      "payment_id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^pay_[A-Za-z0-9]+$"},
      "amount_minor": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100000},
      "currency": {"type": "string", "enum": ["USD", "EUR"]},
      "reason_code": {"type": "string", "enum": ["DUPLICATE", "SERVICE_FAILURE"]}
    }
  },
  "annotations": {
    "readOnlyHint": false,
    "destructiveHint": false,
    "idempotentHint": true,
    "openWorldHint": false
  },
  "contract_version": "2.1.0",
  "authority_class": "PREPARE_ONLY"
}

[Normative] MCP tool annotations are hints and must not be trusted when received from an untrusted server. [Design] Enforce authority from a separately governed registry keyed by trusted server identity, tool name, and contract version.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. The model never receives long-lived operational credentials.
  2. The caller's authenticated principal and policy determine capabilities; model text does not.
  3. Every tool input and output is validated against a versioned schema.
  4. Side-effecting calls carry a stable operation key bound to normalized arguments.
  5. Timeout or disconnect after dispatch produces UNKNOWN, not automatic FAILED.
  6. Approval binds the exact action, arguments, principal, resource versions, policy version, and expiry.
  7. Tool results are untrusted data when returned to a model.
  8. MCP capability declaration or legacy negotiation indicates protocol support, not user authorization.
  9. Application retry or explicitly selected legacy resumption never implies exactly-once business effects.

docs.title: MCP architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[User] --> H[MCP host]
    H --> C1[MCP client A]
    H --> C2[MCP client B]
    C1 --> S1[MCP server: documents]
    C2 --> S2[MCP server: operations]
    H --> P[Identity policy and consent]
    P --> C1
    P --> C2
    S2 --> G[Tool policy gateway]
    G --> D[Downstream API]
    G --> K[Credential broker]
    H --> L[(Audit and run ledger)]
    G --> L

[Normative] In MCP terminology, the host is the LLM application, clients are connectors created by the host, and servers provide context and capabilities. MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over transport bindings. In the current 2026-07-28 revision, requests are independently versioned and can be served statelessly; older revisions may establish connection- or session-scoped state.

The host is the user-trust boundary. It decides what servers may see, what capabilities are exposed to the model, what consent UI appears, and whether a proposal reaches a tool server. A remote MCP server is not automatically trusted because it speaks the protocol.

docs.title: Versioning and capability declaration
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as MCP client
    participant S as MCP server
    C->>S: optional server/discover
    S-->>C: supported protocol versions
    C->>S: tools/list with per-request version, identity, capabilities
    alt version and capabilities supported
    S-->>C: typed result
    else unsupported version or missing capability
    S-->>C: typed protocol error
    end

For the current 2026-07-28 specification:

  • [Normative] there is no initialization negotiation handshake;
  • every request declares protocol version and client capabilities in _meta; clientInfo is optional and SHOULD be included unless configured otherwise;
  • server/discover is mandatory for servers and optional for clients;
  • an unsupported version returns UnsupportedProtocolVersionError with supported versions, after which the client may retry with a mutually supported version;
  • required client capabilities are validated per request;
  • optional extensions are declared under the capabilities extensions map; an unsupported extension requires core fallback or rejection, and extensions SHOULD document that behavior;
  • dual-era implementations detect and explicitly fall back to initialization-based legacy behavior rather than silently mixing eras.
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "tools/list",
  "params": {
    "_meta": {
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": {"name": "support-host", "version": "3.8.0"},
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {"roots": {}}
    }
  }
}

Pin and test protocol versions. Do not silently reinterpret unknown fields or methods. Persist the effective era, request version, and capability digest with each run so a replay can explain what was available.

[Normative, base fields verified 2026-09-08] The pinned base specification makes clientInfo self-reported, not authenticated identity. It also requires supported result types (complete or input_required in core), rejects unrecognized types, and treats absent resultType as complete for legacy compatibility. Schema validators MUST NOT automatically dereference network $ref URLs; unresolved schemas must not silently become permissive. These requirements prevent conformance checks from rejecting valid metadata omissions or turning tool schemas into SSRF requests.

docs.title: Legacy initialization-based revisions
docs.text: MCP 2025-11-25 and earlier use an initialize request, server-selected version, notifications/initialized, and session-scoped capability negotiation. A modern client that supports both eras probes as required by the current transport compatibility rules and falls back only when the response identifies a legacy server. Legacy semantics remain valid for a connection that explicitly selected that era; they are not current defaults.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Resources expose data identified by URIs. The client can list and read resources when the server advertises the capability. Resources can represent files, schemas, records, or generated views. Resource templates describe parameterized URIs.

[Design] A resource URI is an identifier, not authorization. The server reauthorizes each read and returns only fields allowed for the principal and purpose. Bind cache entries to identity scope, policy version, and resource version.

{
  "uri": "support://tickets/tkt-481",
  "name": "Ticket 481",
  "mimeType": "application/json",
  "annotations": {"audience": ["assistant"], "priority": 0.8}
}

Treat resource content as untrusted when inserted into a model context. Preserve origin, server identity, URI, version, digest, and trust class.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
Prompts are server-provided templates intended for user-controlled selection and argument filling. They are not hidden policy. A prompt returned by a server can contain malicious instructions and must not receive authority over tools, credentials, or host controls.

Version approved prompts in the host. Show the user which server supplied a prompt when trust matters. Validate arguments and cap expanded content.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tools are callable functions exposed by servers. Listing a tool tells the client that a method is available; it does not grant the model permission to invoke it. The host should filter the list by principal, purpose, environment, risk, and run budget before showing schemas to the model.

Tool results can contain structured content, text, images, audio, embedded resources, or error indicators depending on protocol version and implementation. Validate result size, type, schema, and trust before it enters model context.

docs.title: Roots
docs.text:
Roots let a client expose URI or filesystem boundaries within which a server may operate. They are coordination hints, not a sandbox. A server can still attempt arbitrary filesystem or network access unless the operating-system and network boundary prevent it.

[Design] Canonicalize paths, reject traversal and symlink escapes, mount only approved roots, use a restricted process identity, and deny network egress by default for local filesystem servers.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
Sampling allows a server to request model generations through the client. It keeps model access and provider credentials under host control, but creates a recursive control path: server -> client -> model -> possible action.

[Normative] Sampling is deprecated as of MCP 2026-07-28. New implementations should not adopt it, and existing implementations should migrate to direct LLM-provider integration. For compatibility, sampling is delivered as an input request inside an MRTR InputRequiredResult, not as an independent server-initiated JSON-RPC request. The specification recommends human ability to deny requests and review prompts and results. [Design] While legacy sampling remains, apply separate budgets, recursion depth, data-loss prevention, model policy, and consent. A server cannot use sampling to gain capabilities not granted to its direct requests.

docs.title: stdio
docs.text:
In stdio, the client launches the server as a child process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC on standard input and output. [Normative] Standard output contains only valid MCP messages; logs go to standard error. The current stdio binding carries modern per-request metadata and defines explicit probing for compatibility with initialization-based servers.

Unlike HTTP request-scoped SSE, cancelling one stdio operation uses notifications/cancelled with its request ID; closing the shared process would disrupt unrelated calls. The pinned stdio binding, verified 2026-09-08, carries server input requests inside MRTR results rather than independent server JSON-RPC requests. Restart/resend still requires application-side reconciliation for writes.

Security boundary:

  • pin executable path and artifact digest;
  • pass a minimal environment;
  • do not place reusable secrets in command-line arguments;
  • restrict filesystem, process, device, and network access;
  • capture bounded stderr without secrets;
  • close stdin, then use bounded graceful and forced termination.

docs.title: Streamable HTTP
docs.text:
The 2026-07-28 specification defines Streamable HTTP with one MCP endpoint that accepts POST. Each JSON-RPC request is a separate POST, and the response is either one JSON object or a request-scoped Server-Sent Events stream. [Normative] Clients must support both response types. Every POST carries matching protocol metadata in the body and MCP-Protocol-Version header, plus required Mcp-Method and, where applicable, Mcp-Name headers.

[Normative] Servers must validate a present Origin and reject an invalid origin with HTTP 403, local servers should bind to localhost rather than all interfaces, and servers should authenticate connections. Current Streamable HTTP has no protocol-level session ID, GET stream, or DELETE session endpoint.

[Normative, verified 2026-09-08 against the pinned transport source] HTTP clients also support tool parameters annotated with x-mcp-header: mirror valid primitive fields into Mcp-Param-*, apply the specified Base64 sentinel encoding when required, and exclude invalid annotated tool definitions. Body-processing servers validate decoded header/body agreement and reject mismatches with HTTP 400 and HeaderMismatch (-32020). [Design] Do not annotate secrets or sensitive query text for mirroring: headers often enter proxy logs outside payload-retention controls. Redact Mcp-Name too when it carries a sensitive resource URI. Header routing is not principal authorization.

flowchart TD
    R[HTTP request] --> O{Origin absent or allowed?}
    O -->|No| X[Reject]
    O -->|Yes| T{TLS and token valid?}
    T -->|No| X
    T -->|Yes| A{Audience and scope valid?}
    A -->|No| X
    A -->|Yes| V{Protocol metadata valid?}
    V -->|No| X
    V -->|Yes| P[Method policy and schema]
    P --> B[Bounded execution]

Current SSE responses are scoped to the originating request and are not resumable with Last-Event-ID. Closing the stream signals cancellation of that request; it does not undo a downstream effect already committed. The server stops work as soon as practical, while the application retains an unresolved operation for reconciliation. Server-to-client interactions such as elicitation, roots, and legacy sampling use Multi Round-Trip Requests: the server returns InputRequiredResult, and the client retries the original operation with matching input responses. Long-lived change notifications use the response stream of subscriptions/listen.

MCP revisions from 2025-03-26 through 2025-11-25 allowed optional sessions, GET streams, independent server requests, and Last-Event-ID resumption. Implement these only after explicitly selecting a compatible legacy revision. Neither old redelivery nor a new application retry proves whether a business effect occurred; reconcile by operation key.

docs.title: Authorization and credentials
docs.text:
For HTTP authorization in MCP 2026-07-28:

  • [Normative] authorization is optional at the MCP implementation level; when used with HTTP, implementations should conform to the MCP authorization specification;
  • protected MCP servers act as OAuth resource servers and MCP clients act as OAuth clients;
  • MCP servers implement RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata and clients use it to discover authorization servers;
  • authorization servers expose RFC 8414 or OpenID Connect discovery metadata, and clients support both discovery mechanisms;
  • before authorization, clients obtain a client ID through Client ID Metadata Documents, preregistration, or legacy Dynamic Client Registration in the specified priority order;
  • clients use PKCE, record the expected issuer, and validate a returned iss according to RFC 9207 before exchanging an authorization code;
  • clients include the RFC 8707 resource parameter in authorization and token requests;
  • access tokens travel in the Authorization header, not URI query strings;
  • servers validate that a token was issued for that MCP server;
  • clients request least-privilege scopes and handle bounded WWW-Authenticate scope challenges through step-up authorization;
  • token passthrough to downstream APIs is forbidden by the MCP authorization security guidance.

The MCP server obtains separate downstream credentials for its own upstream API call. Prefer workload identity or a credential broker that mints short-lived, audience-bound credentials after policy approval.

inbound token audience: https://mcp.example.com/mcp
downstream token audience: https://payments.example.com
these are different tokens with different scopes and lifetimes

Store refresh tokens and client secrets in a dedicated secret store. Redact authorization headers, tool arguments containing secrets, and downstream responses. Rotation must not require prompt changes.

docs.title: Side-effect protocol
docs.text:
Use prepare/commit/reconcile for consequential tools:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant H as Host
    participant G as Tool gateway
    participant A as Approver
    participant S as System of record
    H->>G: prepare typed action
    G->>S: validate current resource and policy
    S-->>G: prepared intent plus versions
    G-->>A: exact action and argument digest
    A-->>G: approve digest with expiry
    H->>G: commit intent plus operation key
    G->>G: reauthorize and revalidate
    G->>S: commit with same operation key
    S-->>G: terminal result
    G-->>H: effect ID and status

docs.title: Operation record
docs.text:
{
  "operation_key": "run-91:refund:1",
  "tool": "refund.commit",
  "contract_version": "2.1.0",
  "normalized_args_digest": "sha256:...",
  "principal": "user-71",
  "prepared_intent": "intent-481",
  "approval_digest": "sha256:...",
  "policy_version": "policy-21",
  "state": "COMMITTED",
  "effect_id": "refund-992",
  "created_at": "2026-09-06T14:00:00Z",
  "terminal_at": "2026-09-06T14:00:01Z"
}

The system of record atomically binds operation key to payload digest and terminal effect when possible. Same key plus same payload returns the prior result. Same key plus different payload returns conflict. A timeout after dispatch is UNKNOWN; call refund.status(operation_key) before retrying with the same key. A NOT_FOUND response is not proof that an earlier attempt cannot still commit. Redispatch requires a downstream contract that deduplicates concurrent attempts with the same key, or proof that the old attempt has been fenced and cannot take effect. Keep the deduplication record for the entire allowed retry and replay window; after its expiry, require reconciliation rather than treating the key as new.

Compensation is a new authorized action, such as refund.reverse, with its own operation key and audit trail. It is not rollback in the database sense and may be impossible after settlement.

docs.title: Capacity calculation
docs.text:
Suppose 200 active clients each read a resource every 10 seconds, 20 tool calls/s arrive, and 5% of tool calls require one MRTR input request:

resource reads/s = 200 / 10 = 20
tool requests/s = 20
MRTR input requests/s = 20 * 0.05 = 1
base logical application operations/s = 20 + 20 = 40
additional MRTR continuation POSTs/s = 20 * 0.05 = 1
client-to-server POST attempts/s = 40 + 1 = 41

If callers retry 30% of 1,000 in-flight application requests after disconnects:

retried requests = 1,000 * 0.30 = 300
transport attempt amplification = 1,300 / 1,000 = 1.3

[Derived] Under successful deduplication, duplicate effects per logical write remain zero and total effects per successfully committed logical write remain one. These are different denominators from transport amplification. The MRTR estimate assumes one continuation per affected call and excludes input collection, discovery, subscriptions, authentication, and ordinary retries. Load tests must include retries, cancelled streams, lost acknowledgements, slow consumers, MRTR retries, and explicitly supported legacy-session expiry.

docs.title: Failures and security controls
docs.text:
Failure or attack Discriminator Control schema-valid but unsafe amount schema passes, business limit fails deterministic policy and current-state validation tool-name spoofing untrusted server claims privileged name registry binds server identity plus tool contract tool-description injection description asks host to reveal data descriptions have no authority; consent and policy outside model malicious resource retrieved text proposes secret exfiltration trust labels, no model-visible secrets, egress policy root traversal canonical path exits allowed mount OS sandbox plus canonical path validation deprecated sampling recursion nested requests exceed depth migrate to direct provider integration; budget remaining legacy use token passthrough downstream sees inbound MCP token reject architecture; exchange for downstream credential DNS rebinding hostile Origin reaches local HTTP server Origin validation and localhost binding timeout after commit status lookup finds effect return reconciled result, no new key modern stream disconnect request outcome is unknown reconcile writes before an application retry explicitly selected legacy session loss HTTP 404 for session ID initialize a new legacy session; reconcile writes oversized tool result bytes exceed declared limit truncate safely or store protected resource reference capability changes mid-run list-change digest differs policy review; do not auto-enable new tools

See Lab 08, Lab 11, and RAG and Agent Security.

docs.title: Contract tests
docs.text:
• valid, invalid, boundary, unknown, and extra input fields;
  • output schema and size bounds;
  • operation-key same-payload deduplication and different-payload conflict;
  • lost acknowledgement after commit;
  • cancellation before and after effect boundary;
  • principal, tenant, purpose, scope, expiry, and resource-version policy;
  • approval digest mismatch and expiry;
  • root traversal, symlink escape, redirect, DNS, and egress tests;
  • MCP modern/legacy era, version, and capability matrix;
  • stdio contamination, Streamable HTTP cancellation, MRTR, subscriptions, and legacy resumption compatibility;
  • deprecated sampling migration, recursion, and budget exhaustion.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Record host, client, trusted server identity, protocol era and version, transport, legacy session reference when applicable, capability digest, method, tool contract, principal-scope digest, policy decision, operation key, attempt, duration, redacted result digest, and terminal status.

Monitor logical operations versus attempts, validation failures, policy denials, approvals, unknown outcomes, reconciliation latency, deduplicated attempts, payload conflicts, capability-list changes, MRTR rounds, subscription churn, legacy session churn, deprecated sampling depth, bytes, timeouts, and downstream effects. Never place tokens or unrestricted resource contents in telemetry.

docs.title: MCP and tool migration
docs.text:
1. Inventory hosts, clients, servers, transports, protocol versions, tool schemas, and active/paused runs.
  2. Add a new tool contract version alongside the old one; avoid changing meaning in place.
  3. Make consumers tolerant of additive output fields while rejecting unknown authority-bearing values.
  4. Shadow calls or compare prepare results without executing duplicate effects.
  5. Canary by host version, server identity, principal class, and tool risk.
  6. For transport or protocol-era migration, reconcile every in-flight side effect before retrying or reconnecting.
  7. Persist protocol and contract version in durable run state.
  8. Remove old contracts only after replay, paused-run, and rollback windows expire.

For legacy initialization-based MCP or HTTP+SSE migration, follow the current dual-era and transport compatibility guidance rather than assuming endpoint equivalence. Test modern, dual-era, and legacy peers explicitly.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text:
Design an MCP integration that lets a support assistant read orders, prepare refunds, and commit refunds after approval. Some servers run locally over stdio; others are remote over Streamable HTTP. The design must survive disconnect after commit, server capability changes, and indirect prompt injection from order notes.

Explain per-request versioning and capabilities, legacy initialization, resources, prompts, tools, roots, MRTR, sampling deprecation, transports, OAuth discovery and audience binding, credential exchange, schema validation, consent, approvals, operation records, reconciliation, telemetry, and migration.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Separates protocol capability from user authorization and business authority.
  • Gives the model typed proposals but no operational credentials.
  • Describes modern per-request metadata, legacy initialization, MRTR, and both standard transports accurately.
  • Handles timeout-after-commit with same-key reconciliation.
  • Treats roots as hints plus sandboxing and tool output as untrusted.
  • Tests protocol versions, schemas, reconnects, and security boundaries.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes a governed registry for server identity, tool contracts, authority classes, and exceptions.
  • Defines fleet compatibility across protocol, transport, schema, and paused-run versions.
  • Quantifies reconnect storms, correlated server loss, and receiving capacity.
  • Governs credentials, consent evidence, retention, and cross-product audit.
  • Assigns cost, risk, rollback authority, and retirement evidence to owners.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Every tool has narrow typed inputs, outputs, errors, and side-effect semantics.
  • MCP era, request version, and capabilities are declared, validated, and recorded.
  • Resources, prompts, tool results, and annotations are treated according to trust.
  • Roots are enforced by an actual sandbox.
  • New systems avoid deprecated sampling; retained legacy use has user control and separate budgets.
  • HTTP tokens are audience-bound and never passed through downstream.
  • Unknown outcomes reconcile before retry with the same operation key.
  • Transport and schema migrations account for active and paused runs.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Normative, protocol version 2026-07-28] Model Context Protocol, Specification. Defines current per-request metadata, message patterns, capabilities, and protocol security principles.
  • [Normative, protocol version 2026-07-28] Model Context Protocol, Versioning and Compatibility. Defines per-request version selection, server/discover, protocol errors, extensions, and dual-era fallback.
  • [Normative, protocol version 2026-07-28] Model Context Protocol, Transports. Defines stdio and current POST-only Streamable HTTP bindings.
  • [Normative, protocol version 2026-07-28] Model Context Protocol, Streamable HTTP. Defines request-scoped SSE, MRTR, subscriptions, cancellation, required headers, Origin validation, and legacy compatibility.
  • [Normative, protocol version 2026-07-28] Model Context Protocol, Authorization. Defines the HTTP OAuth profile, discovery, client registration, issuer validation, scope challenges, resource indicators, token use, audience validation, and prohibition on token passthrough.
  • [Normative, deprecated in protocol version 2026-07-28] Model Context Protocol, Sampling. Defines legacy-compatible sampling over MRTR and directs new implementations not to adopt it.
  • [Legacy normative, protocol version 2025-06-18] Model Context Protocol, Lifecycle and Transports. Define initialization, sessions, GET streams, and resumption for that explicitly selected revision only.
  • [Normative, 2010-03-26] JSON-RPC Working Group, JSON-RPC 2.0 Specification. Defines request, response, notification, and error message structure used by MCP.
  • [Normative, 2025-04] IETF, RFC 9728: OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata. Defines protected-resource metadata used in MCP authorization discovery.
  • [Normative, 2020-02] IETF, RFC 8707: Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0. Defines the OAuth resource parameter used for audience restriction.
  • [Normative, 2022-06] IETF, RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Defines HTTP semantics; it does not guarantee exactly-once application effects.

docs.title: Durable Agents, Memory, and Human-in-the-Loop
docs.text: Long-running agents need two different kinds of persistence: memory that helps future decisions and durable state that proves what already happened. Conflating them creates unsafe replay, stale beliefs, duplicate effects, and unauditable approvals. Durable execution records authoritative events; memory remains a governed, fallible input.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• [Source] is supported by a dated source in Sources.
  • [Derived] follows from stated assumptions.
  • [Design] is a recommended production contract.
  • [Measure] must be evaluated on local tasks, users, and failure modes.

docs.title: Memory taxonomy
docs.text:
Memory type Purpose Example Authority working bounded state for the current step or run current plan, retrieved evidence, remaining budget temporary input, never policy episodic records of prior experiences a resolved incident trace or past customer interaction historical evidence with provenance semantic consolidated facts or concepts product glossary, learned user preference fallible assertion requiring freshness and scope procedural instructions for how to perform tasks approved runbook, tool-use procedure executable only through current policy and tools

[Source] CoALA presents an agent-memory framework influenced by cognitive memory categories and separates working from long-term memory forms. The exact production schema here is [Design], not a standard taxonomy.

docs.title: Durable state is not memory
docs.text:
Durable truth:
  PaymentCommitted(operation_key, payment_id, amount, effect_id)

Memory:
  "The customer usually prefers account credit."

The first is an authoritative event from a system boundary. The second is a scoped, revisable assertion that may be stale or wrong. Never decide whether to repeat a side effect by asking semantic memory. Fold the durable operation ledger or query the system of record.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. A run is reconstructed from ordered immutable events plus versioned snapshots; current mutable rows are projections.
  2. Every external effect has a stable operation key and durable terminal or unknown outcome.
  3. Replay reuses recorded nondeterministic decisions and tool results unless explicitly running a forked simulation.
  4. Pause releases compute but preserves event position, budgets, capabilities, deadlines, and waiting condition.
  5. Resume reauthorizes principal, capability, policy, approval, and business preconditions.
  6. Approval binds exact normalized intent and expires; editing the intent invalidates approval.
  7. Memory carries tenant, subject, provenance, confidence, validity interval, retention, and deletion metadata.
  8. Retrieved memory and tool output are untrusted inputs, not instructions or authorization.
  9. Compensation is a new forward action with its own failure modes and audit trail.
  10. Concurrent workers cannot advance the same run without fencing.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[User or trigger] --> G[Run gateway]
    G --> O[Durable orchestrator]
    O --> E[(Append-only event store)]
    E --> P[State projector]
    P --> S[(Run snapshots)]
    O --> W[Workers]
    W --> T[Typed tool gateway]
    T --> X[Systems of record]
    O --> M[Memory service]
    M --> V[(Vector and structured memory indexes)]
    O --> H[Approval service]
    H --> A[Human reviewer]
    O --> Q[Timers and signal queue]

The orchestrator owns transitions, not business credentials. Workers may disappear after any instruction. Events and independently idempotent tools make recovery safe. Memory service failures can degrade personalization or recall; they must not corrupt the event ledger.

docs.title: Event-sourced run state
docs.text:
{
  "event_id": "evt-000184",
  "run_id": "run-01H...",
  "sequence": 184,
  "event_type": "TOOL_RESULT_RECORDED",
  "event_version": 2,
  "occurred_at": "2026-09-06T15:00:01Z",
  "causation_id": "cmd-91",
  "correlation_id": "case-481",
  "actor": {"type": "WORKER", "id": "worker-7"},
  "payload": {
    "operation_key": "run-01H:refund:1",
    "tool_contract": "refund.commit@2.1",
    "status": "COMMITTED",
    "effect_id": "refund-992",
    "result_digest": "sha256:..."
  },
  "policy_version": "policy-21",
  "payload_digest": "sha256:..."
}

Recommended event families:

RunCreated
BudgetReserved
ModelDecisionRecorded
ActionProposed
PolicyDecided
ToolDispatchStarted
ToolResultRecorded
ToolOutcomeUnknown
MemoryReadRecorded
MemoryWriteProposed
MemoryWriteAccepted
ApprovalRequested
ApprovalGranted
ApprovalRejected
TimerScheduled
SignalReceived
RunPaused
RunResumed
CompensationStarted
CompensationCompleted
RunCompleted
RunFailed
RunCancelled

Events describe facts that occurred. Do not store commands such as CommitRefund as if they proved the effect. ToolDispatchStarted followed by no result is evidence of uncertainty, not failure.

docs.title: Fold algorithm
docs.text:
function rebuild(run_id):
    snapshot = load_latest_valid_snapshot(run_id)
    state = snapshot.state if snapshot exists else initial_state()
    last_sequence = snapshot.last_sequence if snapshot exists else 0
    expected = last_sequence + 1
    for event in read_events(run_id, after=last_sequence):
        assert event.sequence == expected
        assert verify_digest(event)
        state = apply_versioned_reducer(state, event)
        expected += 1
    return state

Use optimistic append with expected sequence or a fenced single-writer lease. A snapshot accelerates folding but never replaces retained events required by policy. Verify snapshot hash and event position before use.

docs.title: Durable execution and replay
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant E as Event store
    participant W as Worker
    participant T as Tool
    O->>E: append ToolDispatchStarted with operation key
    O->>W: execute activity
    W->>T: call with operation key
    T-->>W: committed effect
    Note over W,O: worker crashes before reply
    O->>E: append ToolOutcomeUnknown after timeout
    O->>T: reconcile same operation key
    T-->>O: committed effect and result
    O->>E: append ToolResultRecorded

Replay has two modes:

  • Recovery replay folds history and reuses recorded decisions/results. It may continue only from the first incomplete command after reconciliation.
  • Simulation fork copies an authorized, redacted input state into a new run ID and may invoke new model or tool simulations. It cannot write to production systems.

Record nondeterministic values such as model output, tool result, random choice, external query response, selected clock instant, and human signal. During recovery, code reads those events instead of calling the dependency again.

Workflow code must remain compatible with open histories. Version reducers and commands. A new deployment should pass replay tests over representative historical event streams before activation.

docs.title: Pause and resume
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> Running
    state Waiting {
        WaitingApproval
        WaitingTimer
        WaitingSignal
    }
    Running --> WaitingApproval
    Running --> WaitingTimer
    Running --> WaitingSignal
    Running --> OutcomeUnknown
    WaitingApproval --> Running: approval revalidated
    WaitingApproval --> Failed: approval deadline expired
    WaitingTimer --> Running: durable timer
    WaitingSignal --> Running: signal deduplicated
    OutcomeUnknown --> Running: effect reconciled
    Waiting --> Cancelled: cancellation accepted
    Running --> Completed
    Running --> Failed
    Running --> Cancelled

The Waiting container groups the three resumable wait states; it is not an additional stored status. Its cancellation edge applies to each enclosed state. An unknown external effect must first be reconciled.

A pause event stores:

{
  "run_id": "run-01H...",
  "wait_type": "APPROVAL",
  "wait_key": "approval-481",
  "last_sequence": 184,
  "resume_not_before": null,
  "expires_at": "2026-09-07T15:00:00Z",
  "remaining_budget": {"steps": 4, "tool_calls": 2, "spend_usd": 0.12},
  "required_capability": "refund.commit",
  "intent_digest": "sha256:..."
}

Resume performs compare-and-append against last_sequence. Duplicate signals carry stable signal IDs and return their prior acceptance result. Late approval after expiry records a rejected signal; it does not wake the run. Cancellation races are resolved by event order and fencing. Durable cancellation must also wake waiting runs so they do not remain parked forever. A run with an unknown external effect can stop new work, but keeps an owned reconciliation record until the effect is resolved; cancellation cannot assert that the effect did not happen.

docs.title: Human approval
docs.text:
An approval UI must show what the human is authorizing, not merely an agent summary:

  • principal and acting service;
  • action and target;
  • normalized arguments, amount, currency, destination, and environment;
  • evidence and source versions;
  • current resource version and material preconditions;
  • policy decision and exceptions;
  • expected effect, reversibility, and compensation limits;
  • expiry and separation-of-duties requirements.
{
  "approval_id": "approval-481",
  "run_id": "run-01H...",
  "intent_id": "intent-992",
  "intent_digest": "sha256:normalized-exact-action",
  "resource_versions": {"payment": "v17", "case": "v9"},
  "policy_version": "policy-21",
  "required_roles": ["REFUND_APPROVER"],
  "quorum": 1,
  "requested_at": "2026-09-06T15:00:00Z",
  "expires_at": "2026-09-07T15:00:00Z",
  "status": "PENDING"
}

At commit time, verify approval signature, intent digest, role, quorum, expiry, current principal authority, resource versions, policy, and limits. If anything material changed, prepare and approve a new intent.

This new-intent rule applies before an effect has been dispatched. After dispatch, reconcile the existing operation first; changed policy, expiry, or resource version cannot justify issuing another payment while the original is unresolved. Preserve required capability names across a pause, not reusable credentials or an assumption that old authority remains valid. Temporal's workflow execution documentation, verified 2026-09-08, describes command/history replay; it does not turn a retried external Activity into an exactly-once business effect.

Track approval queue age, abandonment, rejection, modification, override, and downstream incident outcomes. Optimizing approval rate alone encourages rubber-stamping.

docs.title: Compensation and sagas
docs.text:
[Source] The Sagas paper describes long-lived transactions as sequences of transactions with compensating transactions. Compensation semantically counteracts prior work; it does not make history disappear.

flowchart LR
    A[Reserve inventory] --> B[Charge payment]
    B --> C[Create shipment]
    C -->|authoritative rejection| D[Void or refund payment]
    C -->|unknown outcome| U[Reconcile shipment before compensation]
    U -->|proved not shipped| D
    D --> E[Release inventory]
    E --> F[Record compensated outcome]

For each forward step define:

Field Meaning commit evidence authoritative proof the step occurred operation key deduplication and reconciliation identity compensation domain action that counteracts the effect compensation deadline last time reversal is allowed preconditions resource versions and states required failure owner team responsible for manual resolution

Compensations can fail and require their own retries, idempotency, alerts, and approval. Some actions have no valid compensation. Keep those outside autonomous authority or require human confirmation before the irreversible boundary.

An unknown shipment is not a proved failure: refunding and releasing inventory while it is actually shipping can compound the incident. Conflicting or still-pending shipment evidence remains in reconciliation or an owned manual queue; it does not flow automatically to compensated success.

docs.title: Memory records
docs.text:
{
  "memory_id": "mem-01H...",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-7",
  "subject_id": "user-71",
  "kind": "SEMANTIC",
  "assertion": "Prefers account credit when permitted",
  "structured_value": {"refund_preference": "ACCOUNT_CREDIT"},
  "provenance": [
    {"source_type": "USER_STATEMENT", "source_id": "conv-91", "source_version": "v4", "span": [188, 231]}
  ],
  "confidence": 0.82,
  "valid_from": "2026-08-01T00:00:00Z",
  "valid_until": "2026-11-01T00:00:00Z",
  "acl": ["subject:user-71", "service:support-assistant"],
  "retention_class": "user-preference",
  "created_by": {"extractor": "memory-5", "model": "route-11"},
  "supersedes": null,
  "status": "ACTIVE"
}

docs.title: Working memory
docs.text: Working memory is a bounded projection of current run state: goal, current plan, verified observations, unresolved requirements, recent tool results, and remaining budgets. Keep authoritative events outside the model context. Summaries can reduce tokens, but retain links to the events they summarize and validate critical values directly.

docs.title: Episodic memory
docs.text: Episodic memory stores prior interactions or run episodes. Retrieve it by tenant, subject, purpose, time, and similarity. Before reuse, check outcome quality, policy compatibility, source availability, and whether the episode was later corrected. A successful past action is an example, not permission to repeat it.

docs.title: Semantic memory
docs.text: Semantic memory stores consolidated assertions. Consolidation should preserve supporting and contradicting evidence, confidence, validity, and last verification. Use deterministic sources of record for account status, balances, permissions, and other operational facts.

docs.title: Procedural memory
docs.text: Procedural memory stores methods such as runbooks or approved playbooks. Version and sign authoritative procedures. A model-generated procedure remains a proposal until reviewed. Current tool schemas and policy override stale procedure text.

docs.title: Memory write policy
docs.text:
function consider_memory(candidate):
    reject if source is missing or unauthorized
    reject secrets and prohibited sensitive classes
    reject operational facts owned by a system of record
    reject low-confidence or contradicted assertions for automatic promotion
    normalize subject, tenant, kind, validity, and provenance
    deduplicate against active memories
    require review for procedural or high-impact semantic memory
    append accepted version; never silently mutate prior record

Memory poisoning can come from users, retrieved documents, tool results, or a compromised server. Separate observation from consolidation. A memory writer has less authority than the original system of record and cannot broaden ACLs.

docs.title: Memory retrieval and forgetting
docs.text:
Filter before semantic search by tenant, subject, purpose, ACL, status, and validity interval. Then rank by relevance, recency, confidence, source authority, and contradiction state. Include provenance in the model-visible memory envelope.

Forgetting includes:

  • natural expiry;
  • supersession by a newer assertion;
  • user correction;
  • retention expiry;
  • consent withdrawal;
  • legal deletion;
  • source invalidation;
  • policy-driven deactivation.

Deletion tombstones memory immediately at read time, then removes text, embeddings, caches, snapshots, and exports according to retention and legal-hold rules. Put sensitive event payloads behind encrypted references so their keys and payload objects can be destroyed without rewriting the append-only event ledger; retain only non-sensitive event facts, tombstones, and minimum deletion proof allowed by policy. If an authorized replay no longer has a deleted payload, it must produce an explicit redacted-input outcome rather than inventing the old value. Cryptographic erasure and reference deletion do not prove removal from an already trained model.

docs.title: Event storage
docs.text:
Assume 2 million runs/day, 24 events/run, 1.2 KB/event after encoding, 30-day hot retention, and three stored copies:

events/day = 2,000,000 * 24 = 48,000,000
logical bytes/day = 48,000,000 * 1.2 KB = 57.6 GB decimal
30-day replicated hot storage = 57.6 * 30 * 3 = 5.184 TB decimal

[Derived] This excludes indexes, snapshots, encryption overhead, transaction logs, and object-store history. Large model/tool payloads should live in separately protected content-addressed storage with bounded event references.

docs.title: Approval capacity
docs.text:
If 4% of 120,000 daily runs require approval, reviewers handle 20 approvals/hour, and demand arrives uniformly over an 8-hour staffed window:

approvals/day = 120,000 * 0.04 = 4,800
required reviewer-hours/day = 4,800 / 20 = 240
mean concurrent reviewers over 8 hours = 240 / 8 = 30

With 25% absence and surge reserve:

scheduled reviewers = ceil(30 / 0.75) = 40

[Derived] Forty reviewers cover the stated mean under the simplistic assumptions. Arrival bursts, case complexity, second approvals, and service-level targets require queueing analysis.

docs.title: Replay recovery
docs.text:
If 600,000 paused runs average 30 unsnapshotted events and one worker folds 3,000 events/s:

events to fold = 600,000 * 30 = 18,000,000
one-worker time = 18,000,000 / 3,000 = 6,000 s = 100 minutes
50-worker ideal time = 100 / 50 = 2 minutes

Actual recovery includes storage bandwidth, hot partitions, downstream reconciliation, and admission control. Do not resume every run at once after an outage.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Containment and recovery replay repeats side effect effect exists but terminal event is missing reconcile operation key, append result, then continue duplicate run advancement two workers append from same sequence expected-sequence reject and fenced lease poison semantic memory assertion traces to untrusted or later-retracted input deactivate descendants and re-evaluate affected runs stale procedure tool or policy version newer than runbook block execution and require compatible procedure summary loses qualifier summary digest maps to events containing omitted constraint rebuild working projection from source events approval after mutation current intent digest differs reject approval and prepare new intent compensation fails compensation operation remains unknown or failed reconcile, retry within policy, then manual queue resume storm timers and signals release large paused cohort partitioned admission, jitter, and priority queues event schema break new reducer cannot fold old fixture stop rollout and restore compatible reader deletion misses snapshot active projection hides item but snapshot still contains it deny reads, rebuild/purge snapshots, verify closure

See Lab 09, Failure Cards, and Typed Tool Calling and MCP.

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text:
• Encrypt events, snapshots, memory, approvals, and payload objects with tenant-aware access control.
  • Keep credentials out of events and model-visible state; store opaque secret references only.
  • Separate audit-reader, replay-operator, approver, policy-admin, and deletion roles.
  • Treat memory search as a cross-session data disclosure boundary.
  • Apply purpose limitation and prevent one product from reusing another product's memory by default.
  • Redact free text from ordinary telemetry and cap event payload size.
  • Sign approvals or preserve tamper-evident identity, intent digest, and timestamp evidence.
  • Sandbox simulation forks and deny production write capabilities.
  • Test indirect prompt injection through episodic and procedural memories.
  • Maintain a kill switch that stops new actions while preserving audit and reconciliation access.

docs.title: Durable-execution tests
docs.text:
• crash before dispatch, after dispatch, after commit, and after result append;
  • duplicate delivery, out-of-order signal, stale worker, and lease expiry;
  • pause/resume across deployment and policy changes;
  • historical replay across event and reducer versions;
  • approval expiry, digest mismatch, role loss, and resource-version conflict;
  • compensation success, failure, timeout, and manual escalation;
  • regional event-store recovery and controlled resume rate.

docs.title: Memory evaluation
docs.text:
• retrieval precision/recall for useful memories;
  • unsupported-memory rate and provenance completeness;
  • stale, contradictory, cross-tenant, and wrong-subject retrieval rate;
  • impact on task success compared with no-memory baseline;
  • correction and deletion propagation latency;
  • procedural adherence and current-tool compatibility;
  • privacy red-team cases and membership-inference probes where applicable.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Monitor append latency and conflicts, event lag, snapshot age, fold duration, stuck wait states, timer lag, duplicate signals, unknown tool outcomes, reconciliation age, compensation backlog, approval queue age, expiry, reviewer overrides, memory reads/writes, contradiction rate, stale-memory use, deletion backlog, and resume admission.

Invariant counters are unsampled:

duplicate_external_effects = 0
unauthorized_memory_reads = 0
commit_with_invalid_approval = 0
production_writes_from_simulation = 0
events_with_sequence_gap = 0

docs.title: Event and workflow migration
docs.text:
1. Keep event envelopes stable and add versioned payload readers.
  2. Add new event types rather than changing the meaning of old facts.
  3. Run deterministic replay tests over sampled and adversarial historical streams.
  4. Deploy readers before writers for additive schema changes.
  5. Route new runs to the new workflow while old code remains available for paused histories.
  6. If migrating open runs, append an explicit migration event with source and target workflow versions.
  7. Canary resume and reconciliation before fleet expansion.
  8. Remove old reducers and activities only when no retained or open history requires them.

docs.title: Memory migration
docs.text: Build a new memory projection or embedding index from immutable accepted memory records. Dual-read under the same ACL and validity filters, compare retrieval by memory ID, and activate through an atomic manifest. Tombstones remain newer than either index and apply to both. Re-embedding does not create new authority or extend retention.

docs.title: Regional recovery
docs.text: Define one write authority for a run or use a consensus-backed event store. After regional failover, fence the old writer before resuming. Reconcile unknown side effects against systems of record, then release paused runs through rate-limited queues. Recovery-point and recovery-time objectives must include event payload objects, timers, signals, approvals, and keys, not only the event table.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text:
Design a durable claims agent that gathers documents, asks adjusters for missing information, proposes payouts, waits up to 14 days for approval, executes approved payments, and remembers claimant communication preferences. Deployments occur daily and a region can fail while a payment result is in flight.

Address memory taxonomy, authoritative state, event schema, fold and snapshot behavior, pause/resume, timers and signals, model nondeterminism, operation-key reconciliation, exact approvals, compensation, deletion, regional recovery, evaluation, capacity, and version migration.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Separates working/episodic/semantic/procedural memory from authoritative events.
  • Reconstructs runs from ordered events and handles crash-after-commit safely.
  • Persists budgets and capabilities across pause/resume.
  • Reauthorizes and revalidates exact approval at commit.
  • Treats compensation as a fallible forward action.
  • Computes event storage, approval staffing, or replay throughput.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Defines fleet event, memory, authority, approval, and deletion standards with owners.
  • Supports compatible replay across daily deployments and explicit open-run migrations.
  • Quantifies regional failure, fencing, reconciliation, and controlled resume capacity.
  • Governs memory purpose, retention, correction, provenance, and exceptions across products.
  • Connects operational and review economics to SLOs and capacity commitments.
  • Names evidence that can falsify exactly-once, replay, memory-quality, and HITL assumptions.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Durable events and fallible memory have separate contracts.
  • Every side effect has operation-key reconciliation and terminal evidence.
  • Replay reuses recorded nondeterminism; simulations cannot write production.
  • Pause/resume preserves budgets, versions, authority, and waiting condition.
  • Approvals bind exact intent and are revalidated at commit.
  • Compensation has idempotency, deadlines, failure ownership, and audit.
  • Memory preserves provenance, ACL, validity, correction, retention, and deletion.
  • Migrations retain readers and activities for open and replayable histories.
  • Regional recovery fences writers and rate-limits resume.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, primary, 2023-09-05] Sumers et al., Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents. Provides a conceptual framework for language-agent memory and action; production schemas and controls in this chapter are additional design guidance.
  • [Source, primary, 2023-04-07] Park et al., Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior. Supports an architecture using stored experiences, reflection, planning, and retrieval in simulated agents; it does not establish production safety.
  • [Source, primary, 2023-10-12] Packer et al., MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems. Supports tiered memory-management concepts for language-model agents.
  • [Source, primary, SIGMOD 1987] Garcia-Molina and Salem, Sagas. Introduces long-lived transactions and compensating transactions; publisher-deposited metadata verified 2026-09-08 identifies the May 27-29 conference.
  • [Source, normative, 2013-04-30] W3C, PROV-O: The PROV Ontology. Defines provenance concepts relevant to entities, activities, agents, derivation, generation, and invalidation.
  • [Source, official documentation, accessed 2026-09-06] Temporal, Workflow Execution. Documents durable workflow execution and event-history replay in one production implementation. It is implementation documentation, not a vendor-neutral standard.
  • [Source, framework, 2023-01-26] NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0. Supports governance, measurement, lifecycle risk management, and human oversight.
  • [Source, Special Publication guidance, 2025-09] NIST, SP 800-88 Rev. 2: Guidelines for Media Sanitization. Defines sanitization and cryptographic-erase concepts; application-level tombstones, replay behavior, and legal retention remain system-specific controls.
