docs.title: Evaluation Engineering
docs.text: Evaluation engineering turns an AI product claim into versioned evidence and a release decision. It separates component quality from end-to-end outcomes, measures uncertainty and critical slices, and keeps evaluation useful after data, prompts, models, tools, and user behavior change.

docs.title: Evidence vocabulary
docs.text:
• Invariant: a condition that must always hold; violation blocks release or triggers containment.
  • Assumption: an unverified input to a design or calculation.
  • Benchmark: a result tied to a frozen fixture, environment, and method.
  • Production outcome: a result observed after deployment with known attribution limits.
  • Gate: a deterministic rule over named metrics, slices, and operational evidence.

Do not call a demo, anecdote, or provider leaderboard a product evaluation.

docs.title: Evaluation contract
docs.text:
Start from the product decision, not from a generic model score.

EvaluationContract(
  id, task, user_population, decision, consequence,
  answerability_policy, abstention_policy,
  dataset_manifest, slice_schema, metric_definitions,
  safety_invariants, operational_limits,
  baseline_bundle, candidate_bundle,
  acceptance_rules, owners, approved_at
)

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every reported score names the exact dataset, code, model, prompt, retrieval, tool, and policy versions.
  2. Safety invariants and legal constraints are gates, not terms that can be averaged into one utility score.
  3. Retrieval, grounding, answer quality, tool behavior, latency, reliability, and cost are measured separately before any composite view.
  4. Candidate and baseline run on the same frozen examples and scoring policy for paired comparison.
  5. Evaluation examples do not silently enter training, prompt tuning, or judge calibration sets.
  6. A release exception has scope, approver, expiry, compensating control, and rollback trigger.
  7. Missing or immature labels remain explicit; they are not counted as success.

docs.title: Evidence architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Product contract] --> B[Dataset manifest]
    B --> C[Evaluation runner]
    D[Candidate bundle] --> C
    E[Baseline bundle] --> C
    C --> F[Stage records]
    F --> G[Metric and slice reducer]
    G --> H[Confidence analysis]
    H --> I{Release gate}
    I -- pass --> J[Shadow or canary]
    I -- fail --> K[Failure analysis]
    J --> L[Mature production outcomes]
    L --> B

The feedback from production updates future evaluation sets through review. It does not overwrite the evidence used for the original release decision.

docs.title: Dataset and judgment design
docs.text:
An evaluation row needs enough state to replay scoring and diagnose failure:

{
  "example_id": "eval-1042",
  "dataset_version": "support-v7",
  "input_ref": "object://eval/support-v7/1042",
  "expected": {"action": "ESCALATE", "required_facts": ["refund_window"]},
  "answerability": "ANSWERABLE",
  "slices": {"language": "en", "customer_tier": "regulated", "long_context": true},
  "provenance": {"source": "adjudicated-production", "event_time": "2026-05-11T00:00:00Z"},
  "judgment_policy": "jp-4",
  "retention_class": "restricted"
}

Use immutable dataset manifests that list row IDs and content digests. Keep train, tune, judge-calibration, release, red-team, and audit sets separate. Deduplicate semantically related cases across splits where leakage would inflate results. Record exclusions and unresolved disagreement.

Human judgment needs a rubric, qualification examples, blind ordering, and an adjudication policy. Measure agreement, but do not confuse agreement with correctness. For high-impact tasks, preserve the individual judgments and adjudication trail.

docs.title: Layered metrics
docs.text:
Layer Examples Product question ingestion parse coverage, field accuracy, quarantine rate did usable evidence enter the system? retrieval Recall@k, MRR, filter violations was required evidence available? grounding claim support, citation correctness, unsupported-claim rate does the response follow retrieved evidence? task precision/recall, ranking utility, exact schema validity did the model perform the task? safety policy violations by threat slice did any non-negotiable control fail? tool/workflow valid call rate, effect correctness, unknown outcomes did execution preserve authority and state? operations p95/p99 latency, availability, queueing, recovery can it meet the service contract? economics cost per accepted result, review load, wasted work is the result sustainable?

An end-to-end score without stage attribution cannot tell the owner what to fix. A retrieval miss cannot be repaired by a better answer prompt. A grounded answer can still be wrong because the source is wrong.

docs.title: Statistical decision design
docs.text:
For a binary metric with x successes in n independent sampling units:

p_hat = x / n
standard_error_approx = sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)

Use Wilson or exact intervals near 0 or 1 and for small samples. Define the independent sampling unit: repeated turns, generations, or documents from one user are not independent users. For a paired baseline/candidate comparison, compute each unit's difference and bootstrap those paired differences. Use a cluster bootstrap or matched analysis when observations share a user, conversation, document, or case. Do not compare two independent confidence intervals as a substitute for a paired test.

Sample size for estimating a proportion within margin e at normal critical value z, using conservative p = 0.5:

n ~= z^2 * 0.25 / e^2

At 95% confidence (z = 1.96) and e = 0.02, n ~= 2,401. This estimates one aggregate proportion. Critical slices need their own effective sample sizes and uncertainty.

Zero observed violations does not prove a zero violation probability. With n independent trials and no failures, a one-sided 95% binomial upper bound solves (1 - p)^n = 0.05, giving p_upper = 1 - 0.05^(1/n), approximately 3/n. For 1,000 clean trials, the upper bound is about 0.30%, which can still be unacceptable for a high-impact action. Enforce invariants through deterministic controls and adversarial tests as well as sampled quality evaluation; report the sample and its limits.

Predeclare primary metrics and critical slices. Gating many metrics or slices at separate nominal 95% thresholds inflates the probability of at least one false finding. Use a declared family-wise or false-discovery procedure, simultaneous intervals, or a hierarchical testing plan; also report effect size and power or minimum detectable effect. Exploratory slices remain evidence for a later confirmatory run, not silent additional release gates.

For two-stage systems:

P(required_evidence_retrieved AND correct_output)
= P(required_evidence_retrieved)
* P(correct_output | required_evidence_retrieved)

The factorization is diagnostic, not an independence claim. It equals end-to-end success only when the product contract requires retrieved evidence. For correctness alone, add P(no_required_evidence_retrieved) * P(correct_output | no_required_evidence_retrieved): a model may guess correctly without support, while a correctly abstaining unanswerable case may need no retrieved evidence. Measure these branches separately from joined per-example records.

docs.title: Judge models and nondeterminism
docs.text:
An LLM judge is a measurement instrument. Version its model, prompt, examples, decoding, and rubric. Calibrate it against blinded human judgments, report disagreement by slice, and retain a human escalation path. Avoid using the same model family as both candidate and sole judge when correlated preferences could matter.

Run repeated samples only when production behavior is stochastic. Report pass probability or metric distribution, not the best sample. Pin deterministic settings where the task requires repeatability. Preserve raw outputs and parser failures.

Pinning temperature or a seed is not itself a determinism guarantee across kernels, batching, providers, or model revisions. Verify repeatability on the deployed implementation; persist accepted outputs for replay rather than regenerating them as evidence.

docs.title: Release state and evidence
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Proposed
    Proposed --> OfflineRunning
    OfflineRunning --> Rejected: gate fails
    OfflineRunning --> Shadow: gates pass
    Shadow --> Canary: operational gates pass
    Shadow --> Rejected
    Canary --> Approved: quality and SLO pass
    Canary --> RolledBack: trigger fires
    Approved --> Monitoring
    Monitoring --> RolledBack: production trigger fires
    Monitoring --> Retired
EvaluationRun(id, contract_id, candidate_bundle, baseline_bundle,
              manifest_digest, runner_digest, start, end, status)
ExampleResult(run_id, example_id, attempt, stage_outputs,
              metric_inputs, errors, latency, usage)
MetricResult(run_id, metric_id, slice, value, interval, sample_count)
ReleaseDecision(id, run_id, outcome, gates, exceptions, approvers, time)

The decision references immutable results. A recomputation creates a new run and decision.

docs.title: Online evaluation and delayed outcomes
docs.text:
Shadow traffic validates production-shaped inputs without affecting users, provided duplicate processing is legal and tool effects are disabled. Canary traffic validates real behavior on a stable cohort. Keep assignment stable by user or entity when alternating versions would change the experience.

Delayed labels require an outcome maturity rule. Compare cohorts only after the same observation window. Track censoring, interventions, reviewer overrides, and policy changes. Reserve a control slice when continuous optimization would otherwise erase the counterfactual.

Sequential monitoring repeatedly examines data, so a naive fixed-sample threshold inflates false alarms. Predeclare decision cadence, minimum sample, stopping rule, and rollback authority.

docs.title: Failure, security, and testing
docs.text:
Failure Discriminating evidence Control contamination similarity to training/tuning corpus quarantine and replace examples slice regression hidden by average metric and simultaneous interval per critical slice predeclared multiplicity-aware slice gate judge drift human/judge disagreement over time recalibration and dual scoring flaky tool or parser stage error by attempt and version deterministic fixtures and retries only where safe benchmark gaming metric gain without product outcome blind holdout and mature outcome check sensitive fixture leak access and export audit restricted storage and redacted reports canary harm invariant counter or complaint signal automatic containment and rollback

Test metric reducers with hand-calculated fixtures. Property-test aggregation and slice membership. Replay archived runs after evaluator changes. Inject malformed outputs, missing citations, empty retrieval, tool timeout-after-commit, evaluator outage, and partial result upload. Verify that a failed or incomplete run cannot become release-approved.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Version metric definitions; never reinterpret an old metric ID.
  2. Dual-score old and new rubrics on frozen outputs and quantify changed decisions.
  3. Add new slices in observe-only mode, then set minimum sample and gates.
  4. Rebuild evaluation sets from reviewed production failures while retaining an untouched audit holdout.
  5. Run old and new judge models in parallel before cutover.
  6. Remove old evidence readers only after retention and audit windows close.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text: Design evaluation and release for an enterprise support assistant that retrieves policy, drafts an answer, may propose a refund, and receives final resolution labels 30 days later. It serves five languages and regulated customers. Define answerability, stage metrics, critical slices, judgment policy, sample-size assumptions, shadow/canary design, delayed outcomes, safety gates, exception policy, and rollback evidence.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Defines a versioned evaluation contract and immutable dataset manifests.
  • Separates retrieval, grounding, task, safety, operational, and cost metrics.
  • Uses paired comparisons and uncertainty rather than point estimates alone.
  • Calibrates model judges and retains raw evidence and human escalation.
  • Connects offline, shadow, canary, mature outcomes, and rollback.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes cross-product metric definitions, critical-slice policy, and evidence ownership.
  • Governs contamination, evaluation-set renewal, release exceptions, and judge retirement.
  • Designs sequential decisions and delayed-outcome attribution across portfolios.
  • Connects capacity, risk, review economics, and release policy.
  • Names evidence that can falsify the evaluation program itself.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Every score resolves to exact inputs, versions, code, and judgments.
  • Invariants cannot be traded against aggregate utility.
  • Critical slices have sample counts, intervals, and owners.
  • Judge calibration and disagreement are visible.
  • Online experiments protect users, data, and downstream systems.
  • Delayed labels use a declared maturity and censoring policy.
  • Failed and incomplete runs cannot approve a release.
  • Migration preserves historical meaning and auditability.

docs.text:

  • [Source, framework, 2024-07-26] NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile. Identifies generative-AI risk and measurement actions; it does not define this release process.
  • [Source, primary, 2022-11-16] Liang et al., Holistic Evaluation of Language Models. Supports multi-metric, scenario-based model evaluation.
  • [Source, primary, 2023-06] Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Provides evidence on model-based judging and documented limitations.
  • [Source, primary, 2017] Breck et al., The ML Test Score. Supports production-readiness testing beyond model accuracy.
  • [Source, statistical reference, 1927-06] Wilson, Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference. Introduces the score interval used for binomial proportions.
  • [Source, statistical reference, 1993] Efron and Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Provides bootstrap foundations; the resampling unit must preserve the dependence structure.
  • [Source, statistical reference, 2010] Benjamini, Discovering the false discovery rate. Reviews multiplicity and false-discovery-rate control.
  • [Source, statistical reference, 2021] Howard et al., Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences. Provides time-uniform inference for sequential observations and supports using declared sequential procedures rather than repeated fixed-sample testing.

docs.title: AI Security and Guardrails
docs.text: AI security protects data, model behavior, tools, and downstream effects across an untrusted content pipeline. Guardrails reduce risk, but deterministic identity, authorization, isolation, validation, and audit remain the authority boundary.

docs.title: Threat model and trust boundaries
docs.text:
Treat user text, retrieved documents, model output, tool output, memory, and provider responses as untrusted data. A prompt is not an access-control policy. A model must not receive ambient credentials or invent authority from natural language.

flowchart TB
    U[User and untrusted input] --> G[Identity and policy gateway]
    D[Retrieved untrusted data] --> C[Context builder]
    G --> C
    C --> M[Model]
    M --> V[Schema and safety validation]
    V --> T[Capability broker]
    T --> X[Sandboxed tool]
    X --> V
    V --> R[Response or approval]
    G --> A[(Audit)]
    T --> A
    V --> A

Threat actors include malicious users, compromised data sources, overprivileged workloads, insiders, dependency or model-supply-chain attackers, and accidental misuse by authorized users.

docs.title: Security invariants
docs.text:
1. Authorization is evaluated outside the model against authenticated principal, action, resource, purpose, and context.
  2. Retrieved content and tool output cannot modify system policy or grant capabilities.
  3. Every side effect uses a typed, least-privilege, short-lived capability bound to an exact principal and operation.
  4. High-impact or irreversible actions require deterministic validation and, where policy requires, approval of the exact proposed action.
  5. Secrets never enter prompts, model-visible logs, retrieval indexes, or client-visible errors.
  6. Provider and regional routing enforce data class before content leaves the trust boundary.
  7. A kill switch can disable a model route, tool, tenant, or action class without waiting for redeployment.
  8. Safety-system failure degrades capability; it never expands authority.

docs.title: Policy and capability contracts
docs.text:
{
  "principal": "user:882",
  "action": "refund.propose",
  "resource": "order:771",
  "purpose": "support_resolution",
  "data_class": "restricted",
  "requested_capability": {
    "tool": "refunds.create",
    "max_amount_minor": 5000,
    "currency": "INR",
    "expires_at": "2026-09-06T10:16:00Z"
  },
  "policy_version": "support-policy-19"
}

SecurityDecision(id, principal, action, resource, context_digest,
                 policy_version, result, reason_codes, evaluated_at)
Capability(id, decision_id, tool, operation_key, constraints,
           audience, issued_at, expires_at, state)
GuardrailResult(id, logical_request_id, stage, policy_version,
                classifier_version, result, reasons, evidence_digest)
SecurityEvent(id, principal, resource, action, route, versions,
              outcome, correlation_id, time)

The model may propose tool arguments. The capability broker rejects unknown fields in authority-bearing inputs, canonicalizes valid arguments, authorizes the exact operation, and issues a constrained call. Silently stripping a field can change what a caller or approver thought was requested. The tool verifies the capability again; approval of refund.propose alone cannot authorize refunds.create in the illustrative request above.

docs.title: Defense pipeline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant G as Gateway
    participant M as Model
    participant B as Capability broker
    participant T as Tool
    U->>G: Request plus identity
    G->>G: Classify data and authorize task
    G->>M: Delimited untrusted context
    M-->>G: Typed proposal
    G->>B: Principal plus exact proposal
    B->>B: Policy, schema, limit, approval
    B->>T: Scoped capability and operation key
    T-->>B: Result or unknown outcome
    B-->>G: Validated result and audit ID
    G-->>U: Response or safe denial

Controls belong at multiple layers:

Layer Controls edge authentication, rate limits, abuse detection, request size context source trust labels, ACL filters, delimiters, content scanning model approved route, bounded input/output, safety configuration output schema validation, policy filters, citation/support checks tools capability, argument allowlist, egress policy, sandbox, idempotency effects approval, transaction limits, reconciliation, compensation operations audit, anomaly detection, kill switches, incident response

docs.title: Prompt injection and data exfiltration
docs.text:
Prompt injection is a control-flow confusion problem: untrusted data attempts to act like instructions. Delimit content, preserve source identity, state that data is non-authoritative, and prefer structured extraction before generation. These techniques reduce risk but do not enforce authorization.

Block sensitive tool output from returning to the model unless the task needs it. Apply egress allowlists, response-size limits, and field-level filtering. Detect encoded or fragmented exfiltration attempts in red-team tests, but do not rely on a classifier as the sole boundary.

The browser is another egress sink. Sanitize rendered Markdown/HTML, reject active URL schemes, and disable or proxy external images under an explicit policy: a generated image URL can leak context without any tool call. Use parameterized database calls and typed argument arrays instead of executing model-produced SQL or shell text. OWASP LLM05:2025, verified 2026-09-08, documents these output-handling risks. Validation after provisional streaming cannot retract a disclosure already delivered to the client.

For retrieval, enforce ACL and deletion before candidate material leaves the store. Reauthorize cache hits. A semantic cache key must include tenant, principal-scope digest, purpose, policy, model/prompt version, and relevant context epoch. Store source membership so a hit can be rechecked against current permissions and tombstones. Semantic similarity does not justify reuse when amounts, identifiers, dates, or negation change the task; require exact matching for these authority-bearing fields or bypass semantic caching.

docs.title: Risk and control calculations
docs.text:
Track exposure with explicit denominators:

unauthorized_effect_rate
= unauthorized_committed_effects / committed_effects

guardrail_false_negative_rate
= known_unsafe_outputs_allowed / known_unsafe_outputs

residual_risk_score
= likelihood * impact * exposure_after_controls

remaining_acceptance_window
<= remaining_token_TTL + allowed_clock_skew

unauthorized_effect_rate has a zero target, but a zero observation does not prove impossibility. Use adversarial coverage, invariant monitoring, and independent audit. Risk scores prioritize work; they do not waive mandatory controls.

The acceptance-window bound assumes every receiver checks expiry, bounded clock error, no refresh or token exchange, and no new delegated credential. With enforced revocation, take the minimum of that expiry bound and the time until every receiver applies revocation. It bounds acceptance of new calls, not damage: already authorized jobs, created credentials, committed effects, and copied data can outlive the token. Count unauthorized effects separately even when no legitimate effects occur; a zero denominator is undefined, not a zero rate.

docs.title: Approval and action state
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Proposed
    Proposed --> Denied: policy or validation fails
    Proposed --> AwaitingApproval: approval required
    Proposed --> Authorized: no approval required
    AwaitingApproval --> Authorized: exact proposal approved
    AwaitingApproval --> Expired
    Authorized --> Executing
    Executing --> Committed
    Executing --> Unknown
    Unknown --> Committed: reconciliation finds effect
    Unknown --> SafeToRetry: safe-retry evidence
    SafeToRetry --> Executing: reauthorize same key

Approval binds principal, resource, canonical arguments, model/tool/policy versions, expiry, and operation key. Editing after approval creates a new proposal.

A negative status lookup is not sufficient for SafeToRetry: it may lag or race the first call. Require authoritative terminal rejection or a receiving-system contract that safely deduplicates concurrent same-key retries within its retention window. Preserve the reservation and unknown state otherwise. Stripe's contract, verified 2026-09-08, explicitly limits retained-key behavior; local bookkeeping cannot extend a remote provider's guarantee.

docs.title: Failure, security, and testing
docs.text:
Threat or failure Control Required evidence direct injection task policy and typed output malicious instruction corpus indirect injection untrusted-source labels and no implicit tools poisoned retrieval test overprivileged tool scoped capability and server-side validation denied out-of-scope arguments secret exposure brokered credentials and redaction seeded-secret scan across telemetry cross-tenant retrieval storage-layer ACL adversarial tenant fixture model/provider compromise signed bundle, route kill switch isolation and evacuation drill safety classifier outage fail-safe degraded mode dependency-failure test timeout after effect operation key and reconciliation crash-after-commit test

Build a threat corpus by task, language, encoding, source type, and tool. Include multi-turn escalation, social engineering, obfuscation, data poisoning, denial-of-wallet, output parser attacks, cross-tenant cache attempts, and malicious files. Measure bypasses separately by control stage.

Fuzz typed tool arguments and reject unknown fields. Test policy cache expiry, clock skew, revoked identities, expired approvals, egress denial, sandbox escape assumptions, provider logging settings, and audit loss. Run exercises with safety classifiers unavailable; the system should reduce capability predictably.

docs.title: Incident response
docs.text:
Contain by principal, tenant, model route, prompt version, data source, tool, or action class. Preserve evidence before purging caches. Rotate credentials that may have entered model-visible context. Reconcile external effects and notify data/security owners under the applicable policy.

Exit criteria include blocked exploit replay, clean secret scan, verified affected-scope query, completed effect reconciliation, patched control, restored monitoring, and approved reopening. A prompt edit alone is not sufficient incident closure.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Inventory every model, context source, tool, capability, provider route, and side effect.
  2. Add policy decisions and audit in observe-only mode without granting new access.
  3. Introduce the capability broker for read-only tools, then bounded writes.
  4. Shadow new guardrails and compare false positives/negatives on frozen threat sets.
  5. Rotate policy, classifier, and prompt versions through signed bundles.
  6. Remove ambient credentials only after all call paths use workload identity or brokered capabilities.
  7. Retire old routes after caches, paused workflows, audit windows, and rollback requirements expire.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text: Design security for an incident-response copilot that reads internal telemetry, retrieves runbooks, drafts commands, and may execute a bounded rollback after approval. Attackers can place text in logs and tickets. Define trust boundaries, identities, context handling, capability contracts, approval binding, unknown outcomes, egress, audit, kill switches, red-team metrics, and incident recovery.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Treats all content and model output as untrusted.
  • Enforces authorization and typed capabilities outside the model.
  • Binds approvals to exact actions and reconciles unknown outcomes.
  • Protects secrets, tenants, caches, routes, and audit evidence.
  • Defines threat tests, degraded modes, and kill switches.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes enterprise action classes, trust labels, capability standards, and exception authority.
  • Quantifies provider, identity, and policy-system concentration risk.
  • Governs red-team corpora, incident evidence, retention, and control ownership.
  • Plans cross-product credential, policy, and tool migrations with rollback.
  • Connects safety posture to availability, review capacity, and portfolio economics.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• The model has no ambient authority or credentials.
  • Authorization binds exact principal, action, resource, purpose, and context.
  • Retrieved data cannot grant capability.
  • Tool arguments are canonical, typed, bounded, and revalidated server-side.
  • Approval binds the exact effect and expires.
  • Unknown outcomes reconcile before retry.
  • Provider routes enforce data class and retention.
  • Kill switches and incident exit evidence are tested.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, taxonomy report, 2025-03] NIST, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations, AI 100-2e2025. Provides an adversarial-ML taxonomy; application controls here are additional design guidance.
  • [Source, framework, 2024-07-26] NIST, Generative AI Profile, AI 600-1. Supports lifecycle risk and content-risk management for generative AI.
  • [Source, Special Publication guidance, 2020-08] NIST, SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture. Supports resource-focused, continuously evaluated access without implicit network trust.
  • [Source, community guidance, 2025] OWASP, Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025. Catalogs prompt injection, sensitive disclosure, supply-chain, output-handling, agency, and resource-consumption risks; it is a risk-awareness document, not a normative standard.
  • [Source, normative, protocol version 2026-07-28] Linux Foundation, Model Context Protocol specification. Defines current protocol roles, per-request metadata, transports, authorization profile, and security considerations; it does not grant application business authorization.

docs.title: AI Observability
docs.text: AI observability explains what the system did, why it did it, whether the result was acceptable, and what it cost. It joins logical requests, model attempts, retrieval, tools, versions, policy decisions, outcomes, and infrastructure without turning sensitive content into unrestricted telemetry.

docs.title: Observability contract
docs.text: Traditional request latency and error rate remain necessary. They are insufficient when a technically successful response is unsupported, a tool effect is unknown, an index is stale, or a provider fallback changes behavior.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. One logical request has one stable ID and may have many model, retrieval, and tool attempts.
  2. Every attempt records the effective model, prompt, index, tool, policy, route, and runtime versions.
  3. Customer-visible SLOs are measured at the product boundary, not only inside the model provider call.
  4. High-cardinality IDs and sensitive text do not become metric labels.
  5. Unsampled invariant counters cover unauthorized effects, cross-tenant reads, sequence gaps, and unbounded execution.
  6. Telemetry failure cannot expand model or tool authority.
  7. Unsampled metrics and durable counters preserve aggregate correctness; sampled traces provide detail and exemplars. Treat trace-derived aggregates as estimates unless known inclusion probabilities and weighting make them unbiased.

docs.title: Signal model
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U[Logical request] --> G[Gateway span]
    G --> R[Retrieval spans]
    G --> M[Model attempts]
    G --> T[Tool attempts]
    R --> E[Evaluation events]
    M --> E
    T --> E
    G --> P[Policy and route events]
    P --> C[Correlated product view]
    E --> C
    I[Infrastructure metrics] --> C
    O[Mature outcomes] --> C
Signal Best use Avoid metrics rates, distributions, SLOs, capacity request IDs and prompt text as labels traces causal stage timing and attempts assuming sampled traces give exact counts logs structured diagnostics and rare details raw prompts, secrets, or unbounded outputs events durable lifecycle and decisions mutable event meaning evaluation records quality, safety, and slices mixing with unrestricted operations access profiles runtime CPU/GPU hot paths collecting tenant payloads

docs.title: Semantic and version contract
docs.text:
LogicalRequest(id, tenant_tier, task, input_units, deadline,
               data_class, admitted_at, terminal_outcome)
Attempt(id, logical_request_id, kind, route, version_bundle,
        start, end, usage, outcome, retry_reason)
StageEvent(id, logical_request_id, stage, state, reason,
           evidence_ref, time)
QualityObservation(id, logical_request_id, evaluator_version,
                   metric_inputs, slices, value, maturity_time)

Recommended low-cardinality dimensions:

service.name
deployment.environment.name
cloud.region
gen_ai.operation.name
gen_ai.provider.name
gen_ai.request.model
gen_ai.response.model
example.ai.workload.class
example.ai.route.class
example.ai.bundle.version
example.ai.outcome
error.type
tenant.tier

The gen_ai.* names above follow the current OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, which remain in Development status and can change. Names under example.ai.* and tenant.tier illustrate organization-defined fields; replace example with an owned namespace and do not present them as OpenTelemetry conventions. Keep exact model digests, request IDs, user IDs, document IDs, and tool arguments on controlled spans or events. If model-version cardinality is too high for metrics, map it to a bounded custom release cohort and retain the exact version elsewhere.

[Version boundary, verified 2026-09-08] This review pins the GenAI repository to 94f432d7126f5884d30a2cdde6f4e89908ebb6fd. Its GenAI status page declares Development. A current documentation snapshot does not establish what an installed instrumentation package emits. Pin that package, its convention revision, feature flags, collector transformations, and metric attribute allowlist; compare captured OTLP fixtures before migration. Do not invent a stable GenAI schema URL or apply every span attribute to every metric.

docs.title: End-to-end trace
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Caller
    participant G as Gateway
    participant R as Retrieval
    participant M as Model
    participant T as Tool broker
    participant E as Evidence store
    C->>G: logical request and deadline
    G->>R: query with trace context
    R-->>G: candidates and lineage
    G->>M: versioned prompt and context
    M-->>G: typed response or tool proposal
    G->>T: authorized operation
    T-->>G: result or unknown outcome
    G->>E: terminal evidence and usage
    G-->>C: response and correlation ID

Use W3C traceparent across HTTP and equivalent propagation fields on queues. A durable consumer can link to the producer span rather than pretending a long queue wait is a synchronous child call. Validate inbound trace identifiers at trust boundaries and apply independent sampling policy.

docs.title: Gateway and model
docs.text:
• logical arrivals, admissions, denials, queue age, deadline misses, and cancellations;
  • attempts per logical request and fallback reasons;
  • input, cached-input, reasoning, and output tokens where the provider contract exposes them;
  • time to first token, inter-token gap, end-to-end latency, and stream completion;
  • structured-output validity, truncation, safety blocks, and accepted-result rate;
  • model load state, KV/cache pressure, batch shape, utilization, and cold starts.

docs.title: Retrieval and context
docs.text:
• parse and indexing lag, source/index epoch, candidate count, filter selectivity, empty results;
  • lexical/vector/reranker latency and errors;
  • context tokens by source and dropped-token reason;
  • direct evaluation metrics such as Recall@k and citation support by version and slice.

docs.title: Workflows and tools
docs.text:
• steps, model calls, tool calls, wall time, spend, and remaining budget;
  • invalid tool proposals, denials, approval age, unknown outcomes, reconciliation lag;
  • duplicate-effect invariant, compensation backlog, paused runs, and resume admission.

docs.title: SLOs and calculations
docs.text:
Define valid events and exclusions before calculating an SLI:

availability_SLI = valid_successes / valid_requests
quality_SLI = accepted_outputs / evaluated_outputs
error_budget = valid_requests * (1 - objective)
burn_rate = observed_bad_fraction / (1 - objective)

The quality SLI describes the evaluated population. Report evaluation coverage, selection policy, unresolved labels, and outcome maturity beside it; a convenience sample of easy cases cannot establish fleet quality. If accepted results are zero, token and cost per success are undefined, while the incurred usage and cost still remain reportable.

For a 99.5% objective and 200,000 valid requests, the error budget is 200,000 * 0.005 = 1,000 bad requests. If a one-hour window has a 2% bad fraction, burn rate is 0.02 / 0.005 = 4.

Token accounting:

tokens_per_success
= (input_tokens + output_tokens) / accepted_results

retry_amplification
= total_attempts / logical_requests

cost_per_accepted_result
= total_attributed_cost / accepted_results

Under the OpenTelemetry GenAI convention, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens and cache-write details are subsets of gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, so they are not added again. If a provider exposes mutually exclusive counts instead, normalize them first as uncached_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens + cache_write_input_tokens. Keep provider-reported usage and independently estimated usage separate and reconcile discrepancies.

The pinned attribute registry likewise includes reasoning output within total output. For input=300, cache_read=40, output=180, and reasoning=50, total usage is 480 tokens, not 570. Subset inclusion is expressed as SHOULD in the convention; validate each provider adapter instead of assuming every emitter complies. Missing usage after cancellation is unknown, not zero, and polling an existing response must not count the original generation again. Cost still needs the provider's price categories and actual billing reconciliation.

[Pinned metric contract, verified 2026-09-08] GenAI metrics defines gen_ai.client.token.usage as a histogram in {token}, partitioned by gen_ai.token.type; sum recorded token quantities rather than interpreting histogram observation count as tokens. When used and billable counts both exist, this metric reports billable counts. The client timing metrics measure first/output chunks, whereas model-server metrics can measure tokens. A chunk can contain zero, one, or many tokens, so do not rename first-chunk latency to TTFT or inter-chunk gaps to token latency without validating the provider stream.

docs.title: Quality monitoring without labels
docs.text:
Operational proxies such as answer length, self-rating, embedding distance, or user clicks are not ground truth. Use them as drift or triage signals. Preserve a sampling program for reviewed production cases and join mature product outcomes when they become available.

Monitor input shape, language, source mix, answerability, retrieval depth, model/prompt route, safety decisions, and outcome maturity. Trigger evaluation when distribution changes, but require versioned evaluation before concluding that quality changed.

docs.title: Sampling, volume, and retention
docs.text:
Estimate telemetry volume before enabling payload-rich traces:

daily_trace_bytes
= requests_per_second * 86,400 * sample_rate * mean_trace_bytes

At 2,000 requests/s, 1% sampling, and 40 KB per retained trace:

2,000 * 86,400 * 0.01 * 40,000
= 69,120,000,000 bytes/day

That is about 69.1 GB/day before replication and index overhead. Tail or rule-based sampling can retain errors and rare routes, but it needs bounded buffers and explicit loss metrics. It biases trace-derived rates toward the retained conditions unless selection probabilities and weighting are known; use unsampled metrics or durable events for exact totals.

Unsampled means every eligible event is intended for measurement; it does not make a lossy exporter durable. For financial or security accounting, reconcile against committed operation and billing records, deduplicate event IDs, and expose missing sequence ranges. Treat ordinary metric totals as incomplete when collection loss is unresolved.

Separate retention classes for aggregate metrics, operational traces, security audit, evaluation payloads, and user content. Apply deletion to payload references and derived evaluation sets while preserving non-identifying aggregate evidence where policy permits.

docs.title: Failure, security, and testing
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Control trace break at queue missing link and propagation test standard context carrier and contract test cardinality explosion active series by attribute allowlist, budgets, and cohort dimensions telemetry backpressure exporter queue and dropped items bounded buffers and service isolation sensitive data leak seeded-secret scan field classification and redaction sampled-count misuse metric/trace divergence metrics for totals, traces for exemplars quality incident hidden invariant and slice metrics unsampled gates and reviewed samples provider usage mismatch reconciled token/cost deltas retain both reports and investigate

Unit-test redaction, attribute normalization, SLI classification, and usage math. Contract-test propagation through HTTP, queues, streaming, retrieval, and tools. Load-test collectors and exporters. Inject collector outage, backend throttling, malformed context, oversized logs, label attacks, clock skew, and partial event loss.

Run privacy tests with canary secrets and synthetic personal data. Verify absence from logs, metric labels, traces, error bodies, analytics exports, and support bundles. Audit access to payload-bearing evidence.

docs.title: Incident views and runbooks
docs.text:
An incident view joins customer impact, version changes, routes, capacity, quality proxies, invariant violations, and costs. It must answer:

  1. Which users, tenants, tasks, and regions are affected?
  2. Which bundle, provider, index, tool, or policy changed?
  3. Is the failure availability, quality, security, capacity, or evidence loss?
  4. Which safe degraded modes remain?
  5. What evidence proves containment and recovery?

Runbooks should include exact queries, kill switches, rollback authority, evidence preservation, capacity consequences, and exit criteria.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Publish a semantic-convention registry that separates pinned OpenTelemetry fields from owned custom fields and records stability and cardinality classes.
  2. Dual-emit renamed attributes for a bounded window and compare values.
  3. Version SLO definitions and annotate objective changes.
  4. Move collectors or backends behind OTLP while measuring loss and sampling differences.
  5. Backfill analytics from durable events, not sampled traces.
  6. Retire payload fields only after security, evaluation, support, and deletion owners approve.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text: Design observability for a multi-provider enterprise RAG agent serving 3,000 requests/s. It streams responses, calls tools, has delayed support-resolution labels, and must not expose customer content to the general telemetry platform. Define IDs, trace boundaries, metrics, SLOs, quality monitoring, sampling volume, unknown tool outcomes, provider usage reconciliation, incident views, retention, and migrations.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Separates logical requests, attempts, stages, decisions, and outcomes.
  • Defines bounded semantic conventions and protects sensitive payloads.
  • Computes SLO burn, retry amplification, telemetry volume, and unit cost.
  • Correlates model, prompt, retrieval, tool, policy, and route versions.
  • Tests propagation, loss, redaction, and degraded observability behavior.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes cross-product telemetry schemas, cardinality budgets, evidence ownership, and retention classes.
  • Governs SLO definitions and quality monitoring across delayed-outcome products.
  • Quantifies telemetry economics and correlated backend or provider failure.
  • Defines fleet incident views, runbooks, and recovery evidence.
  • Separates standards-based collection from differentiated product interpretation.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Logical requests and attempts cannot be confused.
  • Exact versions and route reasons are reconstructable.
  • Metrics have bounded labels and traces carry controlled detail.
  • Quality proxies are not presented as ground truth.
  • Unsampled invariants protect safety and correctness.
  • Sampling and retention have calculated volume and loss budgets.
  • Provider usage is reconciled rather than trusted blindly.
  • Incident exit criteria prove recovery.

docs.text:
• [Source, normative, 2021-11-23] W3C, Trace Context. Defines interoperable HTTP trace context and its privacy/security considerations.
  • [Source, official specification, accessed 2026-09-06] OpenTelemetry, Specification. Defines APIs, SDKs, data models, protocols, and resources.
  • [Source, official Development semantic conventions, accessed 2026-09-06] OpenTelemetry, Generative AI semantic conventions. Defines current GenAI spans, metrics, attributes, content controls, and their stability; these conventions have moved from the main semantic-conventions repository and are not yet stable.
  • [Source, official specification, accessed 2026-09-06] Prometheus, Naming metrics and labels. Supports consistent metric and label design; application cardinality budgets remain local policy.
  • [Source, primary, 2013-02] Dean and Barroso, The Tail at Scale. Supports explicit treatment of tail latency in large online services.
  • [Source, framework, 2023-01-26] NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0. Supports continuous measurement and governance across the AI lifecycle.

docs.title: AI Reliability, Capacity, and Cost
docs.text: AI reliability is the ability to produce acceptable outcomes within latency, safety, and cost constraints despite variable token lengths, scarce accelerators, provider limits, dependency failures, and model changes. Capacity and cost are part of the reliability design because overload and budget exhaustion change user-visible behavior.

docs.title: Service contract and invariants
docs.text: Define separate objectives for admission, completion, latency, quality, and recovery. A server that accepts work it cannot complete is not reliable.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Admission uses the constrained resource vector, not request count alone.
  2. Queues, context, output, retries, tool calls, wall time, and spend are bounded.
  3. Fallback preserves task, data-class, safety, and compatibility requirements.
  4. Reserved recovery capacity is not consumed by best-effort or shadow work.
  5. Capacity numbers come from a declared benchmark distribution and safe operating envelope.
  6. Cost is attributed to logical outcomes and attempts without hiding failed or wasted work.
  7. Correlated provider, region, model, feature, and index failures are modeled explicitly.

docs.title: Demand and capacity flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Forecast and live arrivals] --> B[Classify workload]
    B --> C[Estimate tokens memory and tools]
    C --> D[Quota and admission]
    D --> E[Bounded class queue]
    E --> F[Scheduler and batcher]
    F --> G[Serving or job pool]
    G --> H[Usage and outcome]
    H --> I[Capacity and cost model]
    I --> A
    D -->|reject or defer| J[Explicit degraded contract]

docs.title: Workload resource contract
docs.text:
DemandEstimate(
  workload_class, arrival_rate, burst_shape,
  input_token_distribution, output_token_distribution,
  context_bytes, kv_bytes_per_token, accelerator_seconds,
  cpu_seconds, storage_bytes, network_bytes,
  tool_calls, deadline, priority, max_attempts, spend_limit
)

Use distributions or buckets for prompt length, output length, batch shape, and tool steps. Means alone hide the tail that consumes memory and misses deadlines.

{
  "workload_class": "interactive-generation",
  "deadline_ms": 2500,
  "limits": {
    "input_tokens": 8000,
    "output_tokens": 700,
    "attempts": 2,
    "tool_calls": 0,
    "cost_minor": 12
  },
  "fallback_policy": "same-task-same-residency-v3",
  "priority": "customer-interactive"
}

docs.title: Token demand and concurrency
docs.text:
For arrival rate lambda requests/s:

input_tokens_per_second = lambda * mean_input_tokens
output_tokens_per_second = lambda * mean_output_tokens
mean_concurrency = lambda * mean_end_to_end_seconds

At 120 requests/s, 3,000 input tokens, 400 output tokens, and 2.2 seconds mean latency:

input demand  = 360,000 tokens/s
output demand = 48,000 tokens/s
concurrency   = 264 requests

Little's Law estimates the stable mean. It does not supply burst, tail, zone-loss, maintenance, or safety reserve.

docs.title: KV-cache memory
docs.text:
For a decoder with L layers, two key/value tensors, Hkv key/value heads, head dimension D, sequence tokens T, and bytes per element B:

KV_bytes_per_sequence = 2 * L * Hkv * D * T * B

This is an architectural estimate. Runtime paging, block allocation, quantization, tensor parallelism, and prefix sharing change observed memory. Measure the exact runtime and model.

For L=32, Hkv=8, D=128, T=8,192, and two-byte elements, one full-length sequence needs 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 8,192 * 2 = 1,073,741,824 bytes, or 1 GiB of logical KV storage. Sixty-four such sequences need 64 GiB before model weights, activations, fragmentation, and runtime reserve. This is the aggregate logical cache across the model, not necessarily the allocation on each device in a sharded runtime. Use KV heads, not query heads: substituting 32 query heads into this grouped-query example would overestimate the logical cache fourfold.

docs.title: Queue growth and drain
docs.text:
queue_growth_per_second = max(0, arrival_rate - service_rate)
drain_time = queued_work / (service_rate - arrival_rate)

These are constant-rate fluid approximations with no abandonment or shedding. Drain time is finite only when service exceeds continuing arrivals; at equal rates backlog persists, and below them it grows. When work is heterogeneous, use comparable service-work units or separate class queues rather than treating a 50-token response and a 5,000-token response as equal jobs.

If arrivals are 900 requests/s and degraded capacity serves 700/s for 60 seconds, the queue adds 12,000 requests. After recovery at 1,100/s while arrivals remain 900/s, drain time is 12,000 / 200 = 60 seconds. If deadlines are shorter, reject early; a queue is not recovery capacity.

docs.title: Cost per accepted result
docs.text:
provider_cost
= uncached_input_tokens * uncached_input_rate
 + cache_read_input_tokens * cache_read_rate
 + cache_write_input_tokens * cache_write_rate
 + output_tokens * output_rate
 + tool_and_storage_cost

cost_per_accepted_result
= (provider_cost + allocated_platform_cost) / accepted_results

The token categories in this cost equation are mutually exclusive. If provider-reported total input already includes cached tokens, subtract its cache subsets before applying the uncached rate. Track failed attempts, shadows, warm reserve, idle accelerators, and review labor separately before allocation. A cheap model with high retries or low acceptance can be more expensive per useful outcome.

State whether each rate is dollars/token or dollars/million tokens; divide counts by one million for the latter. The equation assumes cache-write prices are full category prices, not surcharges, and one output rate. If reasoning or modalities have separate prices, partition them without double-counting provider totals. The OpenTelemetry usage registry, verified 2026-09-08, specifies cached input and reasoning output as subsets of totals; it is a telemetry convention, not a provider billing contract. Report cost per accepted result as undefined when there are no accepted results, alongside the accumulated spend.

docs.title: Capacity envelope and admission
docs.text:
Benchmark each compatible model/runtime/hardware/batch combination with production-shaped length and concurrency distributions. Sweep offered load. Record goodput, time to first token, inter-token latency, end-to-end tails, queue age, memory, utilization, errors, quality, and cost.

The safe operating point ends before latency becomes unstable or memory safety margin disappears. Define:

usable_capacity_per_replica
= benchmark_goodput_at_SLO * target_utilization

replicas_for_traffic
= ceil(peak_goodput_required / usable_capacity_per_replica)

Here target_utilization is a planning derating fraction of the measured SLO-goodput envelope, not the GPU utilization percentage reported by a device. If the benchmark already included the same reserve, do not subtract it twice. Goodput counts acceptable on-time results; offered throughput, completed throughput, and GPU busy time are different measurements.

Admission reserves estimated tokens, KV bytes, tool calls, and spend. Reconcile reservation with actual use on completion. Overestimation reduces utilization; underestimation can violate isolation. Use class- and tenant-specific correction factors from measured error.

docs.title: Resilience and fallback
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Healthy
    Healthy --> Constrained: saturation or dependency loss
    Constrained --> Degraded: safe fallback active
    Constrained --> Shed: no compatible fallback
    Degraded --> Recovering
    Shed --> Recovering
    Recovering --> Healthy: queues drained and SLO stable
    Recovering --> Constrained: relapse
Failure Safe response Required reserve/evidence one replica retry within original deadline spare concurrency and idempotency one zone evacuate to remaining zones N+zone measured capacity one region policy-approved route or async defer residency and feature/index readiness provider quota alternate approved route or shed tested compatibility and quota headroom model defect warm previous bundle canary trigger and rollback retrieval outage abstain or approved no-RAG behavior answerability and safety evaluation cost ledger lag bounded low-risk buffer or reject reconciliation and spend reserve

Fallback capacity is shared incident capacity. Simultaneous failures and retries can overwhelm it. Model receiver headroom after removing the failed domain and adding retry amplification.

docs.title: Multi-provider portfolio
docs.text:
Do not assume two providers are independent when they share model weights, upstream networks, identity, regions, or a common gateway. Record concentration by demand, data class, model capability, and evacuation readiness.

flowchart TD
    A[Task and data class] --> E[Common gateway]
    E --> B{Approved routes}
    B --> C[Provider A region 1]
    B --> D[Provider B region 2]
    F[Quota and health] --> B
    G[Compatibility evidence] --> B
    H[Spend policy] --> B

An evacuation drill must preload artifacts, warm capacity, verify prompt and structured-output compatibility, validate safety and quality, shift bounded traffic, and measure receiver saturation. A configured fallback that cannot carry traffic is documentation, not resilience.

docs.title: Reliability and economic state
docs.text:
CapacityPool(id, region, failure_domain, hardware, runtime,
             compatible_bundles, measured_curve, reserved, observed)
CapacityReservation(id, tenant_or_class, pool, quantity,
                    start, end, priority, state)
Admission(id, logical_request_id, estimate, reservation,
          decision, reason, expires_at)
Usage(id, logical_request_id, attempt_id, meter, quantity,
      source_sequence, time_window)
CostAllocation(id, usage_ids, price_version, shared_cost_policy,
               amount, outcome_class)

Desired, reserved, allocatable, loaded, ready, busy, and healthy capacity are different numbers. Publish all of them with reason codes.

docs.title: Failure, security, and testing
docs.text:
Failure Test Pass condition burst beyond forecast open-loop load bounded queue and explicit shedding long-context skew adversarial length mix tenant fairness and memory safety retry storm dependency fault attempt budget preserved zone loss remove full failure domain critical SLO within declared degraded objective cold fallback evacuation drill measured recovery time and no policy bypass cost runaway output/tool amplification spend limit stops new work safely capacity telemetry stale freeze allocator inputs conservative admission and alert

Load tests must use open-loop arrivals; a closed-loop client can hide overload by waiting. Run soak tests for leaks and fragmentation. Inject cancellations, provider 429/5xx, slow streams, model load failure, scheduler delay, spot loss, feature/index lag, and metering gaps.

Protect capacity APIs and priority changes with separate administrative authorization. Prevent tenants from selecting internal routes, forging token estimates, or consuming health lanes. Rate-limit expensive validation and reject oversized contexts before provider spend.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Add a new route as shadow-only and benchmark it against the same workload fixture.
  2. Validate task, schema, safety, latency, data handling, and cost compatibility.
  3. Pre-provision bounded receiver capacity and canary a stable cohort.
  4. Dual-meter old and new routes and reconcile logical outcomes.
  5. Increase traffic while preserving rollback and failure reserve.
  6. Retire old capacity only after incident, paused-workflow, and rollback windows close.

For a model or runtime change, rebuild service curves. Old throughput numbers do not transfer automatically.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text: Design capacity and reliability for a customer assistant with 1,500 peak requests/s, 6,000-token p95 input, 700-token p95 output, two providers, three zones, and a 2.5-second p95 objective. One provider can lose quota and one zone can fail. Calculate token demand, mean concurrency from stated assumptions, queue growth during failure, receiver capacity, and cost per accepted result. Define admission, degraded modes, evacuation evidence, fairness, and migration.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Uses token, memory, concurrency, queue, and cost units correctly.
  • Derives capacity from measured goodput at an SLO, not peak throughput.
  • Bounds admission, retries, context, output, and spend.
  • Defines compatible fallback, zone reserve, and explicit shedding.
  • Tests bursts, long contexts, cancellations, failures, and metering.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Governs capacity classes, reservations, fairness, exceptions, and evidence across products.
  • Quantifies correlated provider/region failure and receiver headroom.
  • Connects quality, accepted outcomes, warm reserve, review load, and margin.
  • Establishes migration and retirement policy for model/runtime service curves.
  • Assigns forecast, benchmark, evacuation, and cost-allocation ownership.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Workload distributions and constrained resources are explicit.
  • Queues reject work that cannot meet its deadline.
  • Safe operating envelopes include quality and cost.
  • Failure reserve cannot be consumed by best-effort work.
  • Fallback preserves data class and task semantics.
  • Retry and tool amplification are included.
  • Costs join logical outcomes and failed attempts.
  • Evacuation and recovery are demonstrated, not assumed.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, primary, 2013-02] Dean and Barroso, The Tail at Scale. Supports designing for tail behavior and redundancy costs in large online services.
  • [Source, primary, 2017-03] Crankshaw et al., Clipper: A Low-Latency Online Prediction Serving System. Supports model-serving latency, batching, caching, and selection tradeoffs; month verified against the publisher's BibTeX record on 2026-09-08.
  • [Source, primary, 2022-07] Yu et al., Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models. Supports iteration-level scheduling and selective batching in the reported system.
  • [Source, official documentation, accessed 2026-09-06] Kubernetes, Horizontal Pod Autoscaling. Documents feedback-based scaling; admission and model-aware capacity remain application responsibilities.
  • [Source, specification, accessed 2026-09-06] FinOps Foundation, FOCUS specification. Provides a cost-and-usage normalization reference; AI outcome attribution remains additional design.

docs.title: Model Adaptation
docs.text: Model adaptation changes behavior through prompts, retrieval, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, adapters, distillation, or continued pretraining. Choose the smallest reversible intervention that can satisfy the product error contract. Training completion is never release approval.

docs.title: Adaptation decision ladder
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Behavior gap] --> B{Missing current facts?}
    B -- yes --> C[Retrieval or tool access]
    B -- no --> D{Instruction or format gap?}
    D -- yes --> E[Prompt and structured output]
    D -- no --> F{Stable task behavior gap?}
    F -- yes --> G[Supervised fine-tuning or adapter]
    F -- no --> H{Preference or style tradeoff?}
    H -- yes --> I[Preference optimization]
    H -- no --> J{Need smaller or cheaper model?}
    J -- yes --> K[Distillation]
    J -- no --> L{Domain representation gap?}
    L -- yes --> M[Continued pretraining with strict evidence]
    L -- no --> N[Revisit task or base model]

Retrieval changes available evidence. Prompting changes instructions and context. Fine-tuning changes model behavior. They solve different problems and have different rollback, privacy, and freshness properties.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every training example has provenance, purpose, license or authority, retention class, and split assignment.
  2. A version bundle binds base model, tokenizer, data manifest, training code, objective, hyperparameters, adapter, prompt, and policy.
  3. Training, tuning, judge-calibration, release, red-team, and audit sets are separated and contamination-checked.
  4. A tuned model receives no new authority; tools and data remain externally authorized.
  5. Base-model or tokenizer changes trigger compatibility and regression evaluation.
  6. Release requires quality, safety, latency, capacity, cost, and rollback evidence.
  7. Deletion and policy changes tombstone source and derived data, update future training eligibility, and mark affected checkpoints, adapters, and model artifacts for restricted use, destruction, verified unlearning, or clean retraining according to policy. Lineage propagation alone does not prove that learned influence was removed.

docs.title: Adaptation alternatives
docs.text: Method Best fit Main risk Rollback unit prompt/versioned examples instruction, format, lightweight behavior brittleness and context cost prompt version retrieval current or attributable knowledge retrieval and ACL failure index/pipeline version supervised fine-tuning stable task pattern and output style overfit, forgetting, contamination adapter/model artifact preference optimization relative behavior preference reward misspecification objective/data/model bundle parameter-efficient adapter tenant/domain specialization adapter routing and base compatibility adapter pointer continued pretraining broad domain representation high cost and behavior regression full checkpoint distillation smaller serving target inherited errors and lost tail capability student version

docs.title: Data and experiment contracts
docs.text:
TrainingExample(id, input_ref, target_ref, provenance, consent_or_license,
                purpose, language, slices, split, policy, digest)
DatasetManifest(id, example_ids, schema, filters, dedupe_method,
                parent, created_by, approved_at, digest)
AdaptationRun(id, base_model, tokenizer, method, dataset_manifest,
              code_digest, config, seed, hardware, state)
Checkpoint(id, run_id, step, optimizer_state, metrics, uri, digest)
AdaptedArtifact(id, run_id, base_compatibility, format, uri, digest)
ReleaseBundle(id, artifact, prompt, runtime, policy, eval_run, state)

{
  "run_id": "adapt-203",
  "method": "lora-sft",
  "base_model": "base-7@sha256:...",
  "tokenizer": "tok-4@sha256:...",
  "dataset_manifest": "support-sft-v9@sha256:...",
  "config": {
    "rank": 16,
    "alpha": 32,
    "learning_rate": "0.0001",
    "epochs": 2,
    "max_sequence_tokens": 8192
  },
  "evaluation_contract": "support-release-v5"
}

Numbers are illustrative request fields, not recommended hyperparameters.

docs.title: Experiment lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Proposed
    Proposed --> DataApproved
    DataApproved --> Training
    Training --> Failed
    Training --> Candidate
    Candidate --> Rejected: evaluation fails
    Candidate --> Shadow: gates pass
    Shadow --> Canary
    Canary --> Released
    Canary --> RolledBack
    Released --> RolledBack: production regression
    Released --> Retired

Checkpointing protects compute progress; it does not make an invalid experiment reproducible. Capture data and code identity before training. Resume only when base model, tokenizer, optimizer, sharding, and code compatibility are declared.

docs.title: Data quality and contamination
docs.text:
Normalize and deduplicate before splitting. Near-duplicate leakage can inflate evaluation even when exact IDs differ. Preserve source and transformation lineage. Balance slices based on product risk, not only population frequency.

Synthetic data can expand format and adversarial coverage, but it inherits generator bias and may collapse variety. Label its generator, prompt, filters, and review status. Do not let synthetic examples silently replace scarce real evidence.

For preference pairs, define the comparison rubric and tie/abstain behavior. Record both candidates, ordering randomization, annotator decisions, and adjudication. Avoid turning policy constraints into soft preferences when violations must be impossible.

docs.title: Training and memory calculations
docs.text:
Token volume:

training_tokens = examples * mean_tokens_per_example * epochs

For 2 million examples, 1,200 mean tokens, and two epochs:

2,000,000 * 1,200 * 2 = 4.8 billion training tokens

Approximate model-state memory for full training:

model_state_bytes
~= parameters * (weight_bytes + gradient_bytes + optimizer_state_bytes)

The model-state multiplier depends on precision, optimizer, master weights, sharding, and implementation. Total training memory also includes activations, temporary workspaces, and communication buffers. Activation checkpointing trades recomputation for lower retained activation memory; it does not by itself shrink the optimizer state in this equation. Measure framework allocations rather than quoting one universal bytes-per-parameter constant.

Adapter parameter count for low-rank updates to matrices can be estimated per adapted matrix with input width d_in, output width d_out, and rank r:

adapter_parameters_per_matrix = r * (d_in + d_out)
adapter_bytes = total_adapter_parameters * bytes_per_parameter

This estimates artifact parameters, not training activations or optimizer memory.

[Mechanism and derived example] LoRA freezes a base matrix W and learns a low-rank update formed from matrices of shapes (d_out, r) and (r, d_in), with a declared scale. For a 4096 x 4096 matrix at rank 16, this is 16 * (4096 + 4096) = 131,072 trainable parameters, 0.78125% of the original matrix, or 256 KiB at two bytes/parameter. The base weights and forward activations still exist. The LoRA paper, verified 2026-09-08, supports frozen weights and rank decomposition; its reported memory savings do not transfer automatically to another model or serving stack. Merging an update can avoid a separate inference branch, while dynamically multiplexing unmerged tenant adapters has runtime costs to measure.

[Objective boundary] DPO, verified 2026-09-08, learns from chosen/rejected response preferences using a classification objective relative to a reference policy, rather than requiring an independently trained reward model and an on-policy RL loop. Preference agreement is not calibrated factual correctness, and a preference pair containing two unsafe answers cannot teach an acceptable action by ranking them alone. Keep hard safety checks and held-out task evidence independent of this objective.

Cost per accepted release:

experiment_cost
= accelerator_hours * rate
 + storage
 + data_processing
 + human_labeling
 + evaluation

cost_per_accepted_release
= total_experiment_program_cost / accepted_releases

Include failed and abandoned runs. Optimizing only the winning run hides exploration cost.

docs.title: Evaluation and release
docs.text:
Compare against the current production bundle and a simple baseline. Measure task quality, critical slices, safety invariants, calibration where applicable, structured output, retrieval/tool compatibility, latency, throughput, memory, and cost.

Use paired per-example comparison and confidence intervals. Run red-team and data-extraction probes. Shadow with tools disabled or isolated. Canary by stable entity. Keep the previous compatible bundle warm when rollback time matters.

Changing a base model beneath an adapter is a new candidate. Changing tokenizer, chat template, quantization, runtime, or prompt can materially alter behavior and requires scoped evidence.

docs.title: Serving adapted models
docs.text:
Adapter multiplexing can improve utilization but creates routing and isolation risks. Route by approved (base, adapter, tokenizer, runtime) compatibility. Bound loaded adapters, memory, load latency, and tenant contribution. Never choose an adapter from user-provided text without authorization.

Merge adapters only when artifact provenance and rollback remain clear. Quantization and compilation create derived artifacts with their own digest and evaluation. Cache keys include the effective adaptation and prompt bundle.

docs.title: Failure, security, and testing
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Control train/eval leakage similarity and provenance report rebuild splits and invalidate result catastrophic forgetting retained capability suite gate or route specialized model narrowly tokenizer mismatch golden token IDs block training/serving readiness poisoned examples source/slice anomaly and review quarantine and signed manifests adapter/base mismatch compatibility matrix deny route memorization or extraction privacy and canary probes data minimization and release block preference reward gaming rubric-specific failure slices direct product and safety metrics irreproducible run manifest/config/checkpoint gap no promotion

Unit-test data transformations and example identity. Property-test split exclusivity and manifest determinism. Run small overfit and gradient sanity checks before expensive jobs. Inject worker loss and resume. Compare resumed and uninterrupted metrics within declared tolerance. Verify artifact signatures and access controls.

Security tests cover malicious training rows, hidden instructions, personal-data leakage, model extraction, unapproved adapter selection, compromised artifact storage, and trainer egress. Separate training credentials from serving credentials.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Freeze the old production bundle and evaluation evidence.
  2. Train candidate artifacts against immutable manifests.
  3. Validate interfaces and direct behavior before shadow traffic.
  4. Dual-run old/new bundle on stable cohorts; retain per-example differences.
  5. Canary with explicit rollback triggers and capacity reserve.
  6. Propagate deletion/tombstone policy to derived data and artifact eligibility; destroy affected artifacts or retrain from an eligible checkpoint when policy requires removal, unless a validated unlearning method demonstrates the required result.
  7. Retire old artifacts only after rollback, audit, and paused-workflow windows close.

When changing the base model, test every supported adapter or declare it incompatible. If migrating the tokenizer, rebuild token-budget assumptions, prompt caches, and any token-ID-dependent filters.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text: Design adaptation for a multilingual support model that must follow a strict JSON schema, use current policy from retrieval, preserve general safety behavior, and reduce cost enough to run on a smaller serving tier. Data includes resolved tickets and regulated customer text. Compare prompting, retrieval, SFT, adapters, preference optimization, and distillation. Define manifests, contamination controls, calculations, release gates, privacy tests, serving compatibility, rollback, and deletion.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Chooses the smallest intervention that matches the diagnosed behavior gap.
  • Versions data, base model, tokenizer, code, objective, adapter, prompt, and evaluation.
  • Calculates token volume, adapter size, or memory with explicit assumptions.
  • Separates checkpoint success from reproducibility and release approval.
  • Defines contamination, privacy, regression, canary, and rollback evidence.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes organization-wide data-purpose, adapter-compatibility, evaluation, and retirement policy.
  • Governs base-model migrations across many downstream adaptations.
  • Connects experiment portfolio cost, label operations, serving capacity, and accepted product outcomes.
  • Defines exception ownership for data, safety, and capability regressions.
  • Names evidence that can falsify the adaptation strategy and trigger a simpler architecture.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• The diagnosed gap matches the adaptation method.
  • Data authority, provenance, purpose, splits, and deletion are explicit.
  • The full compatibility bundle is immutable and reproducible.
  • Safety constraints remain deterministic where required.
  • Evaluation covers retained capability and critical slices.
  • Serving validates base/adapter/tokenizer/runtime compatibility.
  • Portfolio cost includes failed experiments and human work.
  • Migration and retirement preserve rollback and audit.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, primary, 2021-06-17] Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models. Introduces low-rank adaptation and reports parameter-efficiency results in studied settings.
  • [Source, primary, 2022-03-04] Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. Describes supervised and preference-based instruction alignment in the reported system.
  • [Source, primary, 2023-05-29] Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization. Introduces a preference-optimization objective; product safety still requires external controls.
  • [Source, primary, 2015-03-09] Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean, Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network. Provides the foundational distillation approach.
  • [Source, primary, 2021-08] Carlini et al., Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models. Provides evidence that memorized training data can be extracted in studied models.
  • [Source, primary, 2021-05] Bourtoule et al., Machine Unlearning. Evaluates a scoped retraining-based unlearning approach; it does not make lineage invalidation or arbitrary post-training deletion proof of removed influence.

Previous: AI Reliability, Capacity, and Cost | Next: AI Platforms and Data Flywheels

docs.title: AI Platforms and Data Flywheels
docs.text: An AI platform provides shared contracts for data, models, prompts, retrieval, evaluation, serving, tools, policy, and evidence without forcing every workload onto one runtime. A data flywheel is a governed learning loop in which product interactions produce reviewed evidence that improves future versions. It is not automatic self-training from user behavior.

docs.title: Platform thesis
docs.text:
Centralize contracts and control points that reduce duplicated risk. Decentralize task ownership and product decisions that need domain context. The platform should make the safe path easier while preserving explicit escape hatches and ownership.

flowchart LR
    T[Product teams] --> P[Platform APIs and templates]
    P --> D[Data and provenance]
    P --> E[Evaluation and registry]
    P --> S[Serving and gateways]
    P --> W[Workflow and tools]
    P --> G[Policy and audit]
    D --> F[Governed evidence loop]
    S --> F
    W --> F
    F --> E
    E --> P

docs.title: Platform invariants
docs.text:
1. Shared control-plane nouns do not imply one shared data plane or queue.
  2. Every production decision resolves to immutable data, model, prompt, index, tool, policy, and runtime versions.
  3. Product teams own task quality and consequences; platform teams own shared contract correctness and service SLOs.
  4. Feedback enters training or evaluation only through declared purpose, provenance, consent/authority, review, and split assignment.
  5. Deletion and correction tombstone source and derived data, indexes, caches, and retained payloads; lineage marks affected models and adapters for restricted use, destruction, verified unlearning, or clean retraining. Propagation alone does not prove removal of learned influence.
  6. Exceptions have owner, scope, expiry, compensating control, and migration plan.
  7. Platform adoption and reuse are measured with outcome, reliability, and economics, not service count.

docs.title: Capability map and boundaries
docs.text:
Capability Platform ownership Product ownership data contracts lineage schema, storage classes, deletion protocol source meaning, collection authority, labels model registry immutable artifacts, signatures, compatibility model choice and task suitability prompt registry versioning, review, rollout integration instruction content and domain rubric retrieval index contracts, tenancy, migration primitives corpus, relevance judgments, answerability evaluation runners, manifests, statistics, evidence store metrics, slices, gates, adjudication serving gateway, capacity, routing, telemetry fallback semantics and product SLO tools/workflows typed contracts, identity, durability action policy, compensation, approval governance policy engine, audit, retention enforcement risk acceptance and domain compliance

Do not create a platform service merely because a capability appears in this table. Standardize when at least two teams share stable semantics and the control reduces material cost or risk.
