docs.title: The governed data flywheel
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Production interaction] --> B[Decision and evidence record]
    B --> C[Outcome maturity]
    C --> D[Privacy and purpose filter]
    D --> E[Sampling and adjudication]
    E --> F{Destination}
    F --> G[Evaluation set candidate]
    F --> H[Training set candidate]
    F --> I[Failure and threat corpus]
    G --> J[Independent review and separate destination manifests]
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K[Candidate version]
    K --> L[Evaluation and release]
    L --> A

The loop has brakes. Negative user feedback may reflect preference, policy disagreement, abuse, or a product defect. Clicks are affected by ranking position. Reviewer decisions can encode workload pressure. Outcomes can be delayed or censored. Treat every signal as evidence with a generation process, not as a label by default.

The joined review node does not merge training and holdout examples: each destination gets a separate immutable manifest, and held-out answers never enter candidate fitting. Log exposure and selection, not only feedback. If the old policy reviews only high-risk cases, observed labels cannot establish performance on never-reviewed cases. Use a legally and ethically permitted randomized audit/control sample or report that population as unidentified; weighting cannot recover outcomes where selection probability is zero. Hidden Technical Debt, verified 2026-09-08, explicitly identifies hidden feedback loops and data dependencies as system risks; these sampling and manifest controls are this chapter's design response, not guarantees from the paper.

docs.title: Feedback event and label maturity
docs.text:
FeedbackEvent(
  id, logical_decision_id, principal_class, task,
  observed_at, event_time, outcome_type, value,
  source, intervention, maturity_at,
  data_policy, version_bundle, provenance
)

Join feedback by stable decision ID, not by fuzzy text or timestamp. Preserve which model response, retrieved sources, policy, and tool effects the user saw. Record interventions such as human override, discount, escalation, or missing exposure.

Define maturity per outcome. A support resolution may mature after reopen risk passes; fraud chargeback labels may take months. Unmatured events remain censored. Corrections append new facts and invalidate derived manifests through lineage.

docs.title: Evidence yield
docs.text:
eligible_feedback
= interactions
 * P(consent_or_authority)
 * P(joined | consent_or_authority)
 * P(mature | joined, consent_or_authority)
 * P(quality | mature, joined, consent_or_authority)

For 10 million monthly interactions with sequential conditional conversion rates 0.8, 0.95, 0.6, and 0.5:

10,000,000 * 0.8 * 0.95 * 0.6 * 0.5
= 2,280,000 eligible examples/month

This is a funnel volume estimate. Each rate is conditional on passing the preceding stages, so no independence assumption is needed. It is not proof of balance or correctness; estimate the rates from joined cohorts rather than multiplying unrelated marginal rates.

docs.title: Review capacity
docs.text:
reviewer_hours
= sampled_examples * minutes_per_review / 60

reviewers_required
= reviewer_hours / productive_hours_per_reviewer

At 30,000 reviews/month and four minutes each, work is 2,000 hours. At 120 productive review hours per reviewer-month, plan ceil(2,000 / 120) = 17 reviewers before quality audits and adjudication.

docs.title: Platform economics
docs.text:
reuse_savings
= avoided_team_build_cost - platform_incremental_cost

cost_per_accepted_outcome
= total_platform_and_product_cost / accepted_outcomes

platform_adoption
= production_workloads_on_supported_path / eligible_production_workloads

Avoided cost is counterfactual and easy to inflate. Validate it with migration effort, incident rate, lead time, and total ownership cost.

docs.title: Multi-tenant platform architecture
docs.text:
Separate global metadata from regional or isolated execution. Projects, versions, evaluation evidence, and policy may share a control plane while regulated data, serving, and indexes remain in dedicated cells.

flowchart TD
    G[Global catalog and policy metadata] --> R1[Regional control plane A]
    G --> R2[Regional control plane B]
    R1 --> C1[Shared low-risk cell]
    R1 --> C2[Restricted tenant cell]
    R2 --> C3[Sovereign cell]
    C1 --> E[Normalized evidence contracts]
    C2 --> E
    C3 --> E
    E --> G

Normalize metadata without exporting restricted payloads. A sovereign cell can publish aggregate health or signed release evidence while keeping prompts and documents local.

docs.title: Golden paths and escape hatches
docs.text:
A golden path includes templates, APIs, policy defaults, evaluation gates, dashboards, cost attribution, and runbooks. It should produce a deployable, observable, and reviewable service without hidden manual work.

An escape hatch is valid when the supported path cannot meet a documented workload, security, or economics requirement. It needs an owner, threat model, telemetry contract, cost allocation, support boundary, expiry or review date, and convergence plan. Untracked bypasses become permanent shadow platforms.

docs.title: Platform state and governance
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Experimental
    Experimental --> Supported: contracts and SLO proven
    Supported --> Preferred: adoption and economics proven
    Preferred --> Deprecated: replacement approved
    Supported --> Deprecated
    Deprecated --> Retired: migrations complete
    Experimental --> Retired: evidence insufficient

Publish support level, owners, SLO, compatible versions, region/data classes, cost model, and deprecation date. A component is not supported because a central team deployed it once.

docs.title: Failure, security, and testing
docs.text:
Failure Control Evidence one platform outage affects all AI cells and bounded dependencies cell isolation game day bad shared prompt/policy signed versions and scoped rollout stable-cohort rollback feedback poisoning provenance, trust tiers, anomaly review poisoned-cohort evaluation privacy-purpose drift declared use and lineage enforcement denied reuse test deletion stops at source lineage-driven tombstones and artifact ineligibility payload-erasure proof plus destruction, clean retraining, or validated unlearning evidence platform forces wrong workload workload classes and escape path architecture review record evaluation monopoly product-owned contracts and audit set independent replay hidden cost transfer end-to-end allocation product/platform reconciliation

Contract-test every shared resource and event. Maintain one prior compatible client and event reader. Run cell, identity, registry, gateway, and evidence-store outage drills. Test cross-tenant access, regional policy, poisoned feedback, duplicate outcomes, corrected labels, deletion, and replay.

Security separates platform operators, product releasers, data stewards, evaluators, and exception approvers. Sensitive evidence uses purpose-bound access. Platform admins do not automatically receive customer payload access.

docs.title: Operating model and ownership
docs.text:
Use a federated model:

  • platform teams own shared APIs, reliability, capacity, policy enforcement, and migrations;
  • product teams own task contracts, quality, user impact, and degraded behavior;
  • data owners own collection authority, lineage, retention, and correction;
  • evaluation owners own sets, rubrics, judge calibration, and release evidence;
  • security/risk owners define action classes, exception authority, and incident obligations;
  • FinOps owners reconcile unit cost, commitments, and allocation.

Review platform roadmaps with measurable adoption friction, incident evidence, exception volume, unsupported demand, and total cost. Do not optimize for internal service count.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Inventory existing product paths, versions, data uses, and owners.
  2. Define shared contracts before replacing runtimes.
  3. Add adapters that emit common evidence while legacy systems remain authoritative.
  4. Migrate one workload class and risk tier at a time.
  5. Dual-run releases, telemetry, and cost allocation through a bounded overlap.
  6. Prove rollback, deletion, and incident response on the new path.
  7. Remove the old path only after traffic, retained evidence, paused workflows, and audit windows clear.

Platform standardization is reversible at the implementation layer but durable at the contract layer. Prefer open protocols and portable artifacts where switching cost is not the differentiator.

docs.title: Interview exercise
docs.text: Design an AI platform for 40 product teams building classifiers, RAG assistants, batch pipelines, and tool-using workflows across three regions. Regulated teams require isolated cells. Outcomes mature from minutes to 90 days. Define shared and product-owned capabilities, resource contracts, evidence flow, data-flywheel controls, calculations, tenancy, reliability, cost allocation, golden paths, escape hatches, and a migration from five existing stacks.

docs.title: L5
docs.text:
• Centralizes stable contracts while preserving workload-specific execution.
  • Defines version bundles, feedback provenance, maturity, deletion, and release evidence.
  • Calculates evidence yield, review capacity, and outcome unit cost.
  • Separates platform, product, data, evaluation, security, and FinOps ownership.
  • Provides tested golden paths, cells, exceptions, and migrations.

docs.title: L6
docs.text:
• Establishes organization-wide platform policy without erasing product accountability.
  • Governs cross-region/cell failure, provider concentration, evidence retention, and exception portfolios.
  • Connects adoption, developer lead time, reliability, capacity commitments, and economics.
  • Designs feedback loops against poisoning, bias amplification, censoring, and purpose drift.
  • Names evidence that would retire a platform component or reverse centralization.

docs.title: Final design checklist
docs.text:
• Shared contracts do not force unlike workloads onto one queue or runtime.
  • Every decision is reconstructable from an immutable version bundle.
  • Feedback has provenance, authority, maturity, interventions, and destination.
  • Evaluation and training sets remain intentionally separated.
  • Deletion and correction reach derived data and artifact eligibility; learned-influence claims have destruction, retraining, or validated unlearning evidence.
  • Cells and escape hatches have explicit support boundaries.
  • Platform economics use accepted outcomes and total ownership cost.
  • Migration preserves rollback, audit, and paused-workflow compatibility.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• [Source, primary, 2017-08] Baylor et al., TFX: A TensorFlow-Based Production-Scale Machine Learning Platform. Describes integrated production ML pipeline components and metadata concerns in Google's context.
  • [Source, primary, 2015-12-07] Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems. Identifies system-level ML debt such as data dependencies and feedback loops.
  • [Source, production report, 2017-09-05] Uber, Introducing Michelangelo. Describes one company's integrated ML platform; it is not a universal architecture benchmark.
  • [Source, framework, 2023-01-26] NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0. Supports lifecycle governance, measurement, accountability, and risk management.
  • [Source, normative, 2013-04-30] W3C, PROV-O. Defines provenance concepts relevant to entities, activities, agents, derivation, generation, and invalidation.

docs.title: Applied AI Calculations Workbook
docs.text: These 44 solved problems make assumptions, formulas, units, and decision limits explicit. Decimal GB uses 10^9 bytes; GiB uses 2^30 bytes. Dollar values are fixture assumptions, not prices or performance claims for a vendor.

docs.title: 1. Context fit
docs.text:
Problem: A 16,384-token window receives 900 system, 700 user, 4,800 retrieval, and 1,600 history tokens. Reserve 2,000 output and 10% of the window as headroom. Does it fit?

Solution: Headroom is ceil(16,384*0.10)=1,639. Commitment is 900+700+4,800+1,600+2,000+1,639=11,639. Spare is 16,384-11,639=4,745 tokens.

Answer: Yes; 4,745 tokens remain.

docs.title: 2. Chunk budget
docs.text:
Problem: After fixed content and reserves, 5,250 tokens remain. Each chunk is at most 750 tokens. How many whole chunks fit?

Solution: floor(5,250/750)=7.

Answer: Seven chunks.

docs.title: 3. Truncation needed
docs.text:
Problem: A request commits 19,200 tokens to a 16,384-token window. How many tokens must be removed?

Solution: 19,200-16,384=2,816.

Answer: Remove at least 2,816 tokens while preserving mandatory policy and output reserve.

docs.title: 4. Generated-token demand
docs.text:
Problem: Traffic is 3 requests/s with mean 600 generated tokens/request.

Solution: 3*600=1,800 generated tokens/s.

Answer: 1,800 generated tokens/s; input processing must be budgeted separately.

docs.title: 5. Required GPUs
docs.text:
Problem: Demand is 1,800 generated tokens/s. A GPU sustains 125 tokens/s at the target SLO. Keep 20% reserve.

Solution: Usable per GPU is 125*0.8=100 tokens/s. GPUs required are ceil(1,800/100)=18.

Answer: 18 GPUs under these assumptions.

docs.title: 6. Batch throughput
docs.text:
Problem: Eight sequences each generate 400 tokens in 32 seconds.

Solution: Total is 8*400=3,200 tokens. Throughput is 3,200/32=100 tokens/s.

Answer: 100 aggregate generated tokens/s, not 100 per sequence.

docs.title: 7. Output duration
docs.text:
Problem: A request generates 480 tokens at 60 tokens/s after 0.7 s time-to-first-token.

Solution: If TTFT already includes the first of 480 tokens and 60 tokens/s describes subsequent token intervals, remaining decode time is (480-1)/60=7.9833 s. Model time is 0.7+7.9833=8.6833 s; using 480/60 is a fluid approximation.

Answer: About 8.7 seconds rounded, assuming the stated TTFT excludes gateway and queue time. A client-observed TTFT often includes both; do not add them twice.

docs.title: 8. Admission from token rate
docs.text:
Problem: Usable capacity is 2,400 output tokens/s; mean output is 800 tokens/request.

Solution: 2,400/800=3 requests/s.

Answer: At most 3 requests/s at the mean; tails and class mix still require queue bounds.

docs.title: 9. Parameter memory
docs.text:
Problem: What is raw weight memory for 7 billion parameters at 2 bytes/parameter?

Solution: 7e9*2=14e9 bytes = 14 GB = 13.04 GiB.

Answer: 14 GB, about 13.04 GiB, before runtime overhead.

docs.title: 10. Quantized weight memory
docs.text:
Problem: A 13-billion-parameter model uses 4 bits/parameter plus 8% metadata.

Solution: Raw is 13e9*4/8=6.5 GB. With metadata: 6.5*1.08=7.02 GB.

Answer: About 7.02 GB; kernels and activations add more.

docs.title: 11. KV cache per token
docs.text:
Problem: A model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, 2-byte elements, and key plus value.

Solution: 2*32*8*128*2=131,072 bytes/token = 128 KiB/token.

Answer: 128 KiB per cached token per sequence.

docs.title: 12. KV cache per sequence
docs.text:
Problem: Use Problem 11 at 8,000 cached tokens.

Solution: 131,072*8,000=1,048,576,000 bytes = 0.977 GiB.

Answer: About 0.98 GiB per sequence.

docs.title: 13. Resident sequences
docs.text:
Problem: Twelve GiB is available for KV cache; each sequence needs 0.977 GiB.

Solution: floor(12/0.977)=12 sequences.

Answer: 12 sequences in the simplified model; allocator fragmentation can reduce this.

docs.title: 14. Memory reserve
docs.text:
Problem: A 48 GiB GPU uses 30 GiB weights/runtime and requires 15% total-memory reserve. How much remains for KV and activations?

Solution: Reserve is 48*0.15=7.2 GiB. Remaining is 48-30-7.2=10.8 GiB.

Answer: 10.8 GiB.

docs.title: 15. Tensor-parallel weight share
docs.text:
Problem: Sixty GB of weights are evenly sharded across four GPUs with 10% per-GPU overhead on the shard.

Solution: Base shard is 60/4=15 GB; with overhead 15*1.10=16.5 GB.

Answer: 16.5 GB/GPU, excluding replicated state and communication buffers.

docs.title: 16. Utilization headroom
docs.text:
Problem: A pool provides 4,000 tokens/s raw and runs at 3,100 tokens/s. Policy limit is 80%.

Solution: Limit is 4,000*0.8=3,200. Policy headroom is 3,200-3,100=100 tokens/s.

Answer: 100 tokens/s of policy headroom, although raw headroom is 900.

docs.title: 17. GPU-hour cost per million tokens
docs.text:
Problem: One GPU costs $3/hour and sustains 150 generated tokens/s.

Solution: Hourly output is 150*3,600=540,000 tokens. Cost/million is 3/540,000*1,000,000=$5.56.

Answer: $5.56 per million generated tokens at full measured throughput.

docs.title: 18. Request cost
docs.text:
Problem: Input costs $2/million tokens and output $8/million. A request has 3,000 input and 500 output tokens.

Solution: Input is 3,000/1e6*2=$0.006; output is 500/1e6*8=$0.004.

Answer: $0.010/request.

docs.title: 19. Daily cost
docs.text:
Problem: Ten requests/s run all day at $0.006/request.

Solution: Requests/day are 10*86,400=864,000. Cost is 864,000*0.006=$5,184.

Answer: $5,184/day.

docs.title: 20. Cache savings
docs.text:
Problem: Daily input spend is $2,000 at one uniform uncached rate. A safe prefix cache covers 35% of input tokens and cached input costs 20% of normal; ignore cache-write premiums and changes in traffic.

Solution: New spend is 2,000*((1-.35)+.35*.20)=2,000*.72=$1,440.

Answer: Save $560/day, before cache infrastructure cost.

docs.title: 21. Fallback premium
docs.text:
Problem: Normal request cost is $0.01. During a 2-hour incident, 25 requests/s fall back at $0.04.

Solution: Requests are 25*7,200=180,000. Increment is 180,000*(.04-.01)=$5,400.

Answer: $5,400 incremental incident cost.

docs.title: 22. Evaluation run cost
docs.text:
Problem: Evaluate 12,000 cases twice. Each attempt averages 2,500 input at $1/million and 300 output at $5/million.

Solution: Attempt cost is .0025*1 + .0003*5=$0.004. Attempts are 24,000. Total is 24,000*.004=$96.

Answer: $96.

docs.title: 23. Precision@5
docs.text:
Problem: Three of the top five documents are relevant.

Solution: Precision@5=3/5=0.60.

Answer: 0.60.

docs.title: 24. Recall@5
docs.text:
Problem: The corpus judgments contain six relevant documents; top five retrieves three.

Solution: Recall@5=3/6=0.50.

Answer: 0.50.

docs.title: 25. Reciprocal rank
docs.text:
Problem: The first relevant result appears at rank 4.

Solution: RR=1/4=0.25.

Answer: 0.25.

docs.title: 26. Mean reciprocal rank
docs.text:
Problem: First relevant ranks for four queries are 1, 2, none, and 4.

Solution: MRR=(1+1/2+0+1/4)/4=1.75/4=0.4375.

Answer: 0.4375.

docs.title: 27. DCG@3
docs.text:
Problem: Graded relevance at ranks 1-3 is [3,1,2]; use sum((2^rel-1)/log2(rank+1)).

Solution: 7/log2(2) + 1/log2(3) + 3/log2(4) = 7+0.631+1.5=9.131.

Answer: DCG@3 is about 9.131.

docs.title: 28. nDCG@3
docs.text:
Problem: Use Problem 27; ideal order is [3,2,1].

Solution: Ideal DCG is 7+3/log2(3)+1/log2(4)=7+1.893+0.5=9.393. nDCG=9.131/9.393=0.972.

Answer: nDCG@3 is about 0.972.

docs.title: 29. RRF score
docs.text:
Problem: A document ranks 2 lexically and 5 semantically. Use RRF constant 60.

Solution: 1/(60+2)+1/(60+5)=1/62+1/65=0.03151.

Answer: About 0.03151; it is a fusion score, not a probability.

docs.title: 30. Candidate ceiling
docs.text:
Problem: Candidate generation retrieves 80 of 100 relevant documents before reranking.

Solution: Maximum final recall is 80/100=0.80; reranking cannot recover absent documents.

Answer: Recall ceiling is 0.80.

docs.title: 31. ANN work reduction
docs.text:
Problem: Exact search compares 2 million vectors; ANN compares 40,000 candidates.

Solution: Reduction is 1-40,000/2,000,000=0.98.

Answer: 98% fewer comparisons, without implying 98% lower latency.

docs.title: 32. Embedding storage
docs.text:
Problem: Store 10 million 768-dimensional float32 vectors, ignoring metadata/index overhead.

Solution: 10e6*768*4=30.72e9 bytes=30.72 GB=28.61 GiB.

Answer: 30.72 GB raw.

docs.title: 33. Chunk overlap overhead
docs.text:
Problem: A long document uses 800-token chunks with 200-token overlap. Approximate duplication factor?

Solution: Stride is 800-200=600. For a long stream, factor is 800/600=1.333.

Answer: About 33.3% token duplication, excluding boundaries.

docs.title: 34. Accuracy interval
docs.text:
Problem: A fixed evaluation set sampled independently from the target population has 850 correct of 1,000. Estimate the population accuracy with a normal 95% interval; the observed set accuracy itself is exactly 85%.

Solution: p=.85; SE=sqrt(.85*.15/1000)=.01129; margin 1.96*.01129=.0221.

Answer: Approximately [0.8279,0.8721]; use a suitable binomial interval for formal decisions.

docs.title: 35. Difference in proportions
docs.text:
Problem: Baseline is 80% on 1,000 independent cases and candidate 84% on another 1,000. Approximate unpaired SE.

Solution: SE=sqrt(.8*.2/1000 + .84*.16/1000)=.01716. Delta is .04; 95% interval is .04 +/- .0336=[.0064,.0736].

Answer: Estimated improvement 4 points, interval about 0.64 to 7.36 points; paired data needs paired analysis.

docs.title: 36. Required zero-failure sample
docs.text:
Problem: With zero observed failures, use the rule of three to bound failure probability below 1% at about 95% confidence.

Solution: Upper bound is approximately 3/n. Require 3/n<=.01, so n>=300.

Answer: At least 300 independent representative trials with zero failures.

For an exact one-sided 95% binomial upper bound, p_upper = 1 - 0.05^(1/n). At n=300 this is about 0.009936; the exact minimum for a bound strictly below 1% is 299. The rule of three is a conservative approximation here, not proof of zero risk or coverage of untested attack classes. See NIST's binomial interval construction, verified 2026-09-08; the one-sided zero-failure formula follows by solving (1-p)^n = 0.05.

docs.title: 37. Safety-slice gate
docs.text:
Problem: Overall pass is 93%, but a mandatory high-risk slice is 87/100 against a 90% minimum.

Solution: Slice rate is 87%, below the fixed 90% gate.

Answer: Reject release despite the overall score.

docs.title: 38. Abstention precision
docs.text:
Problem: A system abstains on 40 cases; 30 are truly unanswerable.

Solution: Abstention precision is 30/40=.75.

Answer: 0.75; also measure recall of unanswerable cases and answer utility.

docs.title: 39. Workflow reliability
docs.text:
Problem: Four mandatory independent steps each succeed with 99.5% probability.

Solution: .995^4=.98015.

Answer: About 98.015% all-step success; shared dependencies violate independence.

docs.title: 40. Retry amplification
docs.text:
Problem: Ten thousand logical requests have 20% one-retry rate and no further retries.

Solution: Attempts are 10,000 + 2,000=12,000; amplification 12,000/10,000=1.2.

Answer: 1.2 attempts/logical request.

docs.title: 41. Queue growth
docs.text:
Problem: Arrival demand is 2,500 tokens/s and service capacity 2,000 tokens/s for 3 minutes.

Solution: Growth is 500 tokens/s. Backlog is 500*180=90,000 tokens.

Answer: 90,000 queued tokens, before abandonments or shedding.

docs.title: 42. Backlog drain
docs.text:
Problem: A 90,000-token backlog remains after arrivals fall to 1,500 tokens/s against 2,000 capacity.

Solution: Spare is 500 tokens/s. Drain time is 90,000/500=180 s.

Answer: 3 minutes if capacity and arrivals remain stable.

docs.title: 43. Little's Law
docs.text:
Problem: Mean admitted rate is 4 requests/s and mean system time is 6 s.

Solution: L=lambda*W=4*6=24 mean concurrent requests.

Answer: Mean concurrency 24; do not substitute p99 latency for the mean.

docs.title: 44. Idempotent unknown outcomes
docs.text:
Problem: One thousand logical writes produce 1,120 attempts after lost acknowledgements. The implementation is intended to deduplicate by stable operation key, but an audit finds 2 extra committed effects.

Solution: Attempt amplification is 1,120/1,000=1.12. Duplicate-effect rate is 2/1,000=.002=0.2%.

Answer: 1.12 attempts/operation and 0.2 extra effects per 100 logical writes; investigate the two invariant violations. This denominator is logical writes, not all committed effects or the number of writes affected by duplicates.

docs.title: Source notes
docs.text:
• Retrieval definitions follow Manning, Raghavan, and Schutze, Introduction to Information Retrieval.
  • RRF follows Cormack, Clarke, and Buettcher.
  • DCG and nDCG follow Jarvelin and Kekalainen.
  • Context and KV arithmetic follow the decoder attention structure in Attention Is All You Need; actual architectures and serving implementations differ.
  • Risk and evaluation framing follows NIST AI RMF 1.0.
  • HTTP retry and idempotent-method semantics are defined in RFC 9110; application idempotency keys require an explicit application contract.

docs.title: Applied AI Failure Cards
docs.text: Use these cards during design review and incidents. A symptom is not a cause. Preserve request, model, prompt, index, corpus, policy, and tool versions before changing the system. Each card names evidence that can confirm or falsify the hypothesis.

docs.title: 1. Context overflow
docs.text:
Trigger: Input growth plus output reserve exceeds the model context limit.

Symptoms: Rejection, silent truncation, missing instructions, or short output.

Evidence and discriminator: Record token counts by category before submission and the exact truncation decision. If counts fit but behavior changes, investigate tokenizer/version drift or a different model limit.

Contain and recover: Reject predictably or remove lowest-priority content under a published policy. Never drop safety policy or silently consume output reserve.

Prevent: Per-class budgets, tokenizer regression tests, and headroom.

docs.title: 2. KV-cache exhaustion
docs.text:
Trigger: Concurrent cached tokens exceed available accelerator memory.

Symptoms: Admission stalls, eviction, out-of-memory errors, or latency cliffs.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare active sequences, cached tokens, bytes/token, allocator state, and batch shape. Low GPU compute with high KV occupancy points to memory, not arithmetic throughput.

Contain and recover: Stop admission, reduce sequence/output caps, drain, and preserve recovery reserve.

Prevent: Token-weighted admission and measured memory envelopes.

docs.title: 3. Tokenizer drift
docs.text:
Trigger: Gateway and serving model use different tokenizer or template versions.

Symptoms: Budget mismatch, unexpected truncation, cost variance, or invalid offsets.

Evidence and discriminator: Tokenize frozen strings with both version digests and compare IDs/counts. Identical text with divergent counts isolates tokenization/template drift.

Contain and recover: Pin compatible versions or budget with the serving tokenizer.

Prevent: Golden token fixtures in release gates.

docs.title: 4. Gateway fallback policy bypass
docs.text:
Trigger: Routing or fallback executes before data-class and authorization policy.

Symptoms: Restricted requests reach a disallowed model or region during outage.

Evidence and discriminator: Join logical request, policy decision, route reason, provider attempt, and region. An authoritative dispatch record showing execution without an allow decision confirms the invariant breach. A missing sampled trace or delayed audit event alone does not: first check evidence completeness, and contain the uncertain path while reconstructing it.

Contain and recover: Disable fallback, revoke route capability, and assess affected request IDs.

Prevent: Deny-by-default routing and policy-order integration tests.

docs.title: 5. Fallback cost runaway
docs.text:
Trigger: Cheap-model failure shifts all traffic to an expensive route.

Symptoms: Spend spike despite stable request volume.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare attempts, token mix, route reasons, and unit cost by model. Stable tokens with changed route mix separates price from demand growth.

Contain and recover: Apply class budgets, degrade optional work, and cap fallback duration.

Prevent: Precomputed incident cost envelopes and spend admission.

docs.title: 6. Approximate index recall collapse
docs.text:
Trigger: Probe depth, partitioning, filters, or data distribution changes.

Symptoms: Relevant sources disappear while index latency improves.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare ANN results with exact search on the same frozen queries and corpus version. Stable exact recall plus falling ANN overlap implicates candidate search.

Contain and recover: Increase search effort or route affected slices to exact/previous index.

Prevent: Recall@k gates by slice and dual-index rollback.

docs.title: 7. Metadata filter before/after mismatch
docs.text:
Trigger: A selective ACL or tenant filter is applied only after ANN candidates are chosen.

Symptoms: Empty result sets despite relevant authorized documents.

Evidence and discriminator: Count candidates before and after filtering and compare a filter-aware exact query. High prefilter hits with zero authorized postfilter hits exposes candidate starvation.

Contain and recover: Use filter-aware search, or partition by security domain. Bounded overfetch may improve completeness inside an already authorized isolation boundary; it does not fix unauthorized candidate exposure or cross-tenant graph interference. The pinned pgvector v0.8.6 filtering documentation, verified 2026-09-08, describes post-scan filters and bounded iterative scans explicitly.

Prevent: Filter-selectivity benchmarks and authorization invariants.

docs.title: 8. RRF ranking regression
docs.text:
Trigger: Rank constant, source depth, tie-break, or list weighting changes.

Symptoms: Hybrid ranking changes with no lexical/vector model change.

Evidence and discriminator: Persist both input rank lists and recompute every RRF contribution. If recomputation differs, fusion code/config is causal.

Contain and recover: Restore the versioned fusion rule.

Prevent: Golden rank-list fixtures and deterministic ties.

docs.title: 9. Reranker candidate ceiling
docs.text:
Trigger: Candidate stage omits relevant documents.

Symptoms: Reranker quality plateaus despite model improvements.

Evidence and discriminator: Measure candidate Recall@N before reranking. Missing judged documents prove the reranker cannot recover them.

Contain and recover: Increase or diversify candidate generation within latency limits.

Prevent: Gate candidate recall separately from final ranking.

docs.title: 10. Stale corpus/index split
docs.text:
Trigger: Corpus publication and index activation are not atomic or version-aligned.

Symptoms: Answers cite deleted, old, or not-yet-approved text.

Evidence and discriminator: Join answer citations to the exact source and index manifests pinned by that request, plus its current authorization decision. A source absent from that pinned corpus indicates inconsistent lineage. A citation to a retained old version after a later activation is not by itself a fault; verify the request freshness and citation-retention contract before declaring split state.

Contain and recover: Pin reads to a coherent epoch or roll back the index manifest while preserving the independent latest authorization and tombstone overlay.

Prevent: Immutable manifests and atomic activation.

docs.title: 11. Ingestion parser silent empty
docs.text:
Trigger: Parser failure is interpreted as a valid zero-content document.

Symptoms: Source disappears without an explicit deletion.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare fetched bytes, parser status, prior chunk count, and new manifest. Nonempty input plus zero chunks is suspicious, not conclusive: a valid blank PDF or image-only document may contain bytes but no extracted text. Require an explicit validated-empty classification or quarantine; never silently publish an empty replacement after a parser error.

Contain and recover: Quarantine the version and retain the last valid manifest.

Prevent: Minimum-content checks and explicit empty/delete states.

docs.title: 12. ACL propagation failure
docs.text:
Trigger: Chunks or cached answers lose source access metadata.

Symptoms: Cross-tenant retrieval or citations.

Evidence and discriminator: Trace principal, source ACL, chunk ACL, filter, cache key, and returned IDs. A returned ID outside the principal's authorized set proves leakage.

Contain and recover: Disable affected retrieval/cache path and revoke exposed derivatives.

Prevent: Security-domain indexes, principal-bound cache keys, and deny tests.

docs.title: 13. Deletion tombstone lag
docs.text:
Trigger: Physical index/cache purge lags a deletion request without immediate logical filtering.

Symptoms: Deleted source remains retrievable.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare tombstone time with retrieval, cache, and purge logs. Retrieval after tombstone confirms enforcement failure even if purge is pending.

Contain and recover: Enforce tombstones at read time and invalidate caches.

Prevent: Deletion SLOs with sampled end-to-end probes.

docs.title: 14. Evaluation leakage
docs.text:
Trigger: Evaluation cases or answers contaminate prompts, training, tuning, or manual iteration.

Symptoms: Offline uplift does not reproduce on fresh or temporal holdouts.

Evidence and discriminator: Audit case lineage, access, timestamps, near-duplicate hashes, and tuning history. Performance concentrated in exposed cases supports leakage.

Contain and recover: Freeze changes and rerun on an isolated holdout.

Prevent: Access-controlled sets, temporal splits, and contamination scans.

docs.title: 15. Aggregate metric hides slice harm
docs.text:
Trigger: Release uses only a weighted overall score.

Symptoms: Overall quality rises while a language, tenant, risk, or answerability slice regresses.

Evidence and discriminator: Recompute the fixed metric by predeclared slices with sample counts and uncertainty.

Contain and recover: Stop or roll back the affected cohort.

Prevent: Mandatory noninferiority gates for critical slices.

docs.title: 16. Release on noise
docs.text:
Trigger: A positive point estimate is treated as proof without uncertainty or sufficient sample size.

Symptoms: Repeated A/B decisions alternate direction.

Evidence and discriminator: Compute a confidence interval or paired test on frozen outcomes. An interval crossing the decision boundary means evidence is inconclusive.

Contain and recover: Hold release or run the preregistered larger evaluation.

Prevent: Power planning, paired cases, and fixed gates.

docs.title: 17. Judge-model drift
docs.text:
Trigger: Automated evaluator version changes without calibration.

Symptoms: Historical candidates receive new scores with unchanged outputs.

Evidence and discriminator: Re-score a frozen calibration set by judge version and compare with adjudicated human labels.

Contain and recover: Restore the calibrated judge or require human review for disputed slices.

Prevent: Versioned rubrics, judge prompts, and calibration thresholds.

docs.title: 18. Citation looks valid but is unsupported
docs.text:
Trigger: Presence or formatting of a citation is scored instead of entailment and exact span support.

Symptoms: Answers cite a real source that does not support the claim.

Evidence and discriminator: Map each atomic claim to quoted source spans and versions. Valid ID plus absent support isolates grounding failure.

Contain and recover: Abstain, narrow the claim, or retrieve supporting evidence.

Prevent: Claim-level citation precision and support review.

docs.title: 19. Agent loop exhausts budget
docs.text:
Trigger: Planner repeats searches or reflections without a decreasing measure or stop rule.

Symptoms: Rising steps, tokens, latency, and cost without progress.

Evidence and discriminator: Inspect step trace, repeated normalized arguments, budget counters, and progress state. Repetition with no new evidence confirms nonprogress.

Contain and recover: Stop, return bounded partial state, and avoid autonomous retries.

Prevent: Step/token/time/tool budgets and repeated-action detection.

docs.title: 20. Tool timeout after commit
docs.text:
Trigger: The effect commits but its acknowledgement is lost.

Symptoms: Caller sees timeout; retry may duplicate an effect.

Evidence and discriminator: Reconcile by stable operation key at the tool's authority boundary. Before reconciliation the caller's outcome is unknown; an authoritative committed record resolves it to committed, not failed.

Contain and recover: Query first; retry only with the same key and payload digest when the receiving system's retention and concurrency contract makes that retry safe. A stale negative lookup is not proof of absence. Stripe's idempotency contract, verified 2026-09-08, permits a new operation after a key is pruned.

Prevent: Atomic idempotency records and tested lost-ack behavior.

docs.title: 21. Idempotency-key payload conflict
docs.text:
Trigger: A caller reuses one key for different normalized arguments.

Symptoms: Old result returned for new intent or second effect created.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare stored and incoming payload digests for the key.

Contain and recover: Reject the conflict and require explicit reconciliation; never overwrite history.

Prevent: Server-side key/digest binding and retention contracts.

docs.title: 22. Replay repeats a side effect
docs.text:
Trigger: Durable recovery records decisions but not terminal tool results.

Symptoms: Resumed run performs an already-completed write.

Evidence and discriminator: Fold ordered ledger events and compare tool operation keys with effect records. Missing result plus existing effect isolates the gap.

Contain and recover: Reconcile the operation key before advancing.

Prevent: Durable step state plus independently idempotent tools.

docs.title: 23. Indirect prompt injection
docs.text:
Trigger: Retrieved or tool-returned text instructs the model to exceed its authority.

Symptoms: Unauthorized tool proposals, destination changes, or attempted data disclosure.

Evidence and discriminator: Preserve trust labels, retrieved spans, proposal, policy decision, and tool call. A denied proposal shows defense working; an executed ungranted capability is an incident.

Contain and recover: Remove write capabilities, rotate exposed credentials, preserve evidence, and assess effects.

Prevent: Treat content as data; typed least-privilege tools, egress policy, approvals, and red-team tests.

docs.title: 24. Capacity retry storm
docs.text:
Trigger: Slow inference causes clients, gateway, and workflow to retry independently.

Symptoms: Attempts rise faster than logical requests; queues and timeouts worsen after capacity loss.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare logical requests, attempts by layer, token demand, queue age, and admitted throughput. Attempt amplification with stable logical arrivals identifies retries.

Contain and recover: Choose one retry owner, shed before queueing, honor deadlines, and reserve recovery capacity.

Prevent: End-to-end retry budgets and overload drills.

docs.title: 25. Output-token tail overload
docs.text:
Trigger: Output length distribution shifts while request rate remains stable.

Symptoms: Decode occupancy, queue age, and cost rise without input-volume growth.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare output-token histograms and finish reasons by prompt/model version. Stable requests with longer outputs separates length from traffic growth.

Contain and recover: Lower class-specific output caps and degrade optional generation.

Prevent: Token-weighted capacity plans and output-length gates.

docs.title: 26. Unsafe incident fallback
docs.text:
Trigger: Operators disable grounding, authorization, or safety checks to regain throughput.

Symptoms: Latency improves while unsupported or unauthorized outcomes rise.

Evidence and discriminator: Compare policy and pipeline versions with invariant counters. Improvement coincident with bypassed controls confirms unsafe recovery.

Contain and recover: Restore mandatory controls; shed or refuse instead.

Prevent: Preapproved degraded modes that preserve safety invariants.

docs.title: Source notes
docs.text:
• Risk, measurement, and governance framing: NIST AI RMF 1.0.
  • Adversarial and prompt-injection taxonomy: NIST AI 100-2e2025 and OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.
  • Retrieval architecture: Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
  • Operational ML debt and hidden coupling: Sculley et al., Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems.
  • Retry/idempotent method semantics: RFC 9110. Application operation keys remain an explicit service contract.

docs.title: Applied AI System Design L5/L6 Rubric
docs.text: Score observable reasoning and evidence, not product names. Raw dimensions total 100. Apply gates, then the lowest applicable safety/correctness cap.

docs.title: Score bands
docs.text:
Score Interpretation 0-49 Below L5: unbounded, unmeasured, unsafe, or materially incorrect 50-64 Developing L5: plausible components with major operational gaps 65-79 L5: independently coherent, quantified, safe, and recoverable 80-89 Strong L5 / emerging L6: handles evolution and ambiguity but lacks fleet governance 90-100 L6: establishes cross-team policy, economics, failure boundaries, and evidence

L5 requires at least 65, every L5 gate, and no cap below 65. L6 requires at least 90, every L5 and L6 gate, and no cap below 90.

docs.title: 1. Problem contract and risk - 9 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Starts with a model or agent and leaves users, decisions, errors, and authority vague. 3-5 Names use case and SLOs but not answerability, harm, privacy, or human responsibility. 6-7 L5: defines users, workload, quality, latency, availability, privacy, authority, abstention, and failure contract. 8-9 L6: partitions risk and degradability, resolves product tradeoffs, and defines how assumptions will be retired.

docs.title: 2. Data, ingestion, and provenance - 10 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Treats documents or training data as clean blobs. 3-5 Mentions chunking and metadata but omits versions, ACLs, deletion, or parser failure. 6-8 L5: designs immutable versions, offsets, lineage, ACLs, quarantine, atomic manifests, reprocessing, and tombstones. 9-10 L6: governs schemas, legal deletion, corpus epochs, parser migrations, retention, ownership, and cross-product provenance.

docs.title: 3. Retrieval and grounding - 12 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-3 Says vector database or RAG without candidate, filter, ranking, or support semantics. 4-6 Provides hybrid search but no direct metrics or candidate ceiling. 7-10 L5: explains lexical/vector candidates, filter placement, RRF or fusion, reranking, citations, abstention, and Recall@k/MRR. 11-12 L6: handles index epochs, dual reads, judgment policy, drift, tenant isolation, deletion, economics, and rollback.

docs.title: 4. Model, prompt, and gateway - 10 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Calls a provider directly with unbounded prompts and implicit fallback. 3-5 Adds gateway/routing but leaves policy order, versions, budgets, or data classes vague. 6-8 L5: versions prompts/models, enforces data and spend policy before routing, bounds context/output, and records logical requests versus attempts. 9-10 L6: defines fleet model policy, regional/provider strategy, compatibility, capacity commitments, exceptions, and retirement evidence.

docs.title: 5. Workflow, agents, and tools - 12 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-3 Gives a model credentials or permits unbounded autonomous writes. 4-6 Mentions tool schemas or human approval without unknown outcomes or durable state. 7-10 L5: partitions workflow/planning, bounds steps/time/tokens, uses typed least-privilege tools, stable idempotency, reconciliation, compensation, and replay. 11-12 L6: standardizes authority classes, durable schemas, regional recovery, tool evolution, governance, and cross-service audits.

docs.title: 6. Evaluation and release - 14 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-4 Releases from demos, anecdotes, or one aggregate judge score. 5-8 Has offline tests but omits stage attribution, slices, uncertainty, or operational gates. 9-11 L5: uses versioned representative sets, retrieval/grounding/answer metrics, paired comparisons, confidence, safety slices, latency/cost gates, canary, and rollback. 12-14 L6: governs contamination, delayed outcomes, judge calibration, sequential decisions, exceptions, metric ownership, and set renewal.

docs.title: 7. Quantitative capacity and economics - 14 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-4 Uses adjectives or wrong units; ignores output length, memory, or retries. 5-8 Computes token demand or cost but does not connect it to admission and SLOs. 9-11 L5: correctly budgets context, tokens/s, GPU/KV memory, concurrency, queue growth/drain, workflow reliability, retry amplification, and cost. 12-14 L6: models distributions, batching sensitivity, failure reserve, model mix, evacuation, fairness, and capacity economics.

docs.title: 8. Safety, security, and privacy - 10 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Trusts retrieved instructions, exposes credentials, or relies on prompt wording for authorization. 3-5 Mentions injection and filtering but lacks capability, egress, or principal controls. 6-8 L5: treats content as untrusted, enforces principal-bound capability and schema policy, protects secrets, logs safely, approves risky effects, and provides a kill switch. 9-10 L6: defines enterprise trust labels, threat testing, incident response, retention, exception authority, and invariant metrics.

docs.title: 9. Reliability, operations, and observability - 6 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-1 Watches aggregate latency and retries failures generically. 2-3 Names useful metrics but no overload, degraded mode, or recovery proof. 4-5 L5: correlates versions and stages, bounds queues/retries, diagnoses unknown outcomes, defines degraded modes, runbooks, and measurable exit criteria. 6 L6: covers correlated failures, fleet drills, evidence retention/cardinality, recovery ownership, and SLO policy.

docs.title: 10. Evolution and ownership - 3 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0 No migration, rollback authority, or owner. 1 Names canary and teams but not compatibility or old-path removal. 2 L5: assigns component/data/evaluation owners and defines staged migration, overlap, rollback, and removal criteria. 3 L6: establishes cross-team standards, cost attribution, exception governance, and decision authority.

docs.title: L5 gates
docs.text:
• States the user decision, answerability boundary, safety invariants, and model/tool authority.
  • Traces one request through gateway, retrieval/context, model, validation, tools, and response with versions.
  • Computes at least four correct values: context/token, retrieval metric, capacity/memory, and cost/reliability.
  • Defines bounded context, output, steps, queues, deadlines, retries, and degraded behavior.
  • Handles timeout-after-commit with a stable key and reconciliation.
  • Measures retrieval, grounding/answer, safety slices, latency, and cost separately.
  • Defines confidence-aware release gates, canary, rollback, and incident exit evidence.
  • Preserves provenance, ACL, retention, and deletion through derived artifacts.

docs.title: L6 gates
docs.text:
• Satisfies every L5 gate without interviewer repair.
  • Quantifies a correlated capacity/provider/region failure and receiver headroom.
  • Defines compatible model, prompt, index, tool, policy, and ledger migrations with rollback authority.
  • Establishes fleet policy and governed exceptions for model routes, tools, evaluation, and data handling.
  • Connects token/GPU/storage/provider economics to ownership and capacity commitments.
  • Names evidence that can falsify the design, its owner, retention, and review cadence.

docs.title: Hard safety and correctness caps
docs.text:
Apply the lowest cap after raw scoring.

Cap Condition 29 Gives the model credentials or direct unapproved irreversible authority; proposes exposing secrets or bypassing authorization. 39 Treats retrieved content as trusted instructions; uses unbounded agent steps, retries, queues, context, or spend; suggests disabling safety controls during overload. 49 Cannot handle timeout-after-commit safely; claims model/tool replay or transport gives exactly-once effects; lacks tenant/ACL isolation for private data. 59 No correct token/capacity calculation, no direct retrieval metric, or releases from a point estimate without fixed safety/operational gates. 64 No rollback, kill switch, deletion path, or incident degraded mode that preserves safety invariants. 79 No version-compatible migration, correlated-failure analysis, or explicit ownership. 89 No fleet policy, exception governance, economics, or evidence lifecycle.

docs.title: Evidence modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers cannot override gates/caps or raise the score above 100.

Use adjusted = max(0, min(100, raw + modifiers)), then final = min(adjusted, all_applicable_caps). A missing level gate blocks that level even if the numeric score is high. In cap conditions, a list joined by "or" means any listed omission triggers the cap. Record the failed gate separately rather than silently changing the arithmetic.

Adjustment Evidence +2 Executes a deterministic fixture that falsifies an initial assumption and changes the design. +2 Tests sensitivity across output length, retrieval depth, failure load, or confidence and changes a limit. +1 Cleanly separates logical operations, attempts, model calls, tool effects, tokens, and dollars. -2 Uses precise constants without source, fixture, units, or measurement plan. -3 Claims RRF scores are probabilities, reranking recovers absent candidates, or aggregate quality proves every slice. -3 Claims prompt instructions enforce authorization or idempotency means an operation did not happen.

docs.title: Scoring sheet
docs.text: Dimension Maximum Score Evidence Problem contract and risk 9 Data, ingestion, and provenance 10 Retrieval and grounding 12 Model, prompt, and gateway 10 Workflow, agents, and tools 12 Evaluation and release 14 Quantitative capacity and economics 14 Safety, security, and privacy 10 Reliability, operations, observability 6 Evolution and ownership 3 Raw total 100 Modifier Applicable cap Final score 100

docs.title: 62: Developing L5
docs.text: The design has a model gateway, computes direct retrieval metrics, reconciles unknown tool outcomes, preserves deletion through caches, and gates critical slices. Its raw score is 62 because sensitivity analysis for its finite context and queue bounds is shallow, the request trace lacks version evidence, and rollback and incident recovery lack tested exit criteria. Bounds and safe rollback exist, so the unbounded-execution cap does not apply; missing L5 gates keep it below L5. If the bounds were actually absent rather than weakly justified, apply the 39 cap instead.

docs.title: 74: L5
docs.text: The design traces versions end to end, budgets context/KV/tokens/cost, computes Recall@k and RRF, separates retrieval from grounding, bounds workflow steps and retries, reconciles idempotent tools, and defines confidence-aware release and rollback. It is independently safe and operable but lacks fleet migration and governance depth.

docs.title: 86: Strong L5 / emerging L6
docs.text: The design adds multi-provider capacity reserve, dual-index migration, delayed-outcome evaluation, threat testing, and cost allocation. Exception policy, evidence ownership, or cross-region durable recovery remains incomplete, so L6 gates are not met.

docs.title: 94: L6
docs.text: The design establishes fleet contracts for data epochs, model routes, authority classes, release evidence, and incident modes. It quantifies correlated loss and economics, defines compatibility and rollback authority, governs exceptions, and assigns evidence owners who can retire assumptions.

docs.title: Reviewer checklist
docs.text:
• Score only stated or demonstrated evidence.
  • Record one evidence sentence for every nonzero dimension.
  • Verify raw maxima sum to 100.
  • Apply gates before assigning L5 or L6.
  • Apply the lowest cap after modifiers.
  • Do not award L6 for breadth without policy, migration, economics, and ownership.

docs.title: Source notes
docs.text:
• Risk, measurement, and governance anchors follow NIST AI RMF 1.0 and its Playbook.
  • Security anchors follow NIST AI 100-2e2025, NIST SP 800-207, and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.
  • Retrieval terminology follows Manning, Raghavan, and Schutze and Lewis et al..
  • The level anchors are this repository's assessment contract, not claims made by those sources.

docs.title: Applied AI Evidence Labs
docs.text: These 12 labs turn applied-AI design claims into deterministic evidence. Every executable path uses Python 3 and its standard library. The fixtures use no model weights, API keys, network, Docker, root access, paid service, package installation, or destructive action.

docs.title: Working method
docs.text:
1. Predict the result before execution.
  2. Run the exact fixture unchanged.
  3. Preserve stdout as evidence.
  4. Inject only the documented synthetic failure.
  5. Separate observation, inference, unknown, and decision.
  6. Re-run the baseline to prove recovery.

Use this evidence header:

Lab and run ID:
Python version:
Fixture digest or version:
Prediction:
Baseline stdout:
Injected failure:
Failure stdout:
Calculation with units:
Observation:
Inference:
Unknown:
Decision:

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
• Run only the inline fixtures or equivalent copies in a disposable directory.
  • Do not replace fixture calls with public or corporate endpoints.
  • Do not paste secrets, customer data, proprietary prompts, or production documents.
  • Treat retrieved text, model text, and tool arguments as untrusted data.
  • Keep write-like tools simulated. A model proposal is never authorization.
  • Stop when an unknown outcome cannot be reconciled safely.

docs.title: Lab map
docs.text: Lab Core question Required evidence 01. Token and context budget Which content fits, and what does it cost? token, KV-cache, GPU, and cost budget 02. Model gateway Where should policy, fallback, and accounting live? deterministic routing ledger 03. Vector index tradeoffs What is lost by approximate candidate selection? recall and distance-work comparison; memory measurement remains an extension 04. Hybrid search and reranking How do lexical and semantic ranks combine? RRF ranking and retrieval metrics 05. RAG evaluation Is failure in retrieval, grounding, or answer policy? Recall@k, MRR, citation, and abstention scores 06. Document ingestion Can provenance and deletion survive chunking? deterministic chunk manifest and tombstone proof 07. Workflow versus agent Which steps need bounded control? workflow reliability and budget comparison 08. Tool idempotency How are timeout-after-commit outcomes reconciled? one effect across repeated attempts 09. Durable agent replay Can a run resume without repeating effects? in-memory resume trace; durable restart is not tested 10. Evaluation release gate Does measured quality justify release? confidence bound and explicit gate decision 11. Prompt-injection defense Can untrusted text acquire authority? fixed-proposal allow/deny trace and encoded-filter bypass 12. AI capacity incident How should overload be contained? token/GPU capacity envelope and incident actions

docs.title: Acceptance standard
docs.text:
A completed lab includes exact input, baseline output, one controlled failure, expected versus actual behavior, one checked calculation, recovery evidence, one limitation, and a decision no broader than the fixture supports.

Collapsed answers and stop lines are learning aids, not access controls. HTML source, search, and direct answer-page links can still reveal them. For a formal blind assessment, distribute only the prompt and blank workbook; do not claim that this public study site hides answers from a determined reader.

After reviewing the inline commands, run python3 -B docs/applied-ai/labs/check-fixtures.py from the repository root for baseline, selected injection, restoration, arithmetic, ASCII, fence, and heading-regression checks. This runner executes the Markdown's Python bodies; it is not a sandbox. It does not benchmark a provider or establish durable storage, exhaustive attack resistance, link correctness, or rendered diagram quality.

docs.title: Authoritative foundations
docs.text:
• NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
  • NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning Taxonomy
  • Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation
  • Cormack, Clarke, and Buettcher, Reciprocal Rank Fusion
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Build a request budget that separates input, reserved output, context-window headroom, KV-cache memory, throughput, and per-request cost.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The fixture is arithmetic only. It reads no files and makes no calls. Values are synthetic sizing assumptions, not vendor benchmarks.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text: A decoder service has a 16,384-token context limit. One request has 650 system tokens, 900 history tokens, 5 retrieved chunks of 1,100 tokens, 350 tool-schema tokens, and 500 user tokens. Reserve 2,000 output tokens and 10% context headroom. The model has 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head dimension 128, and 2 bytes per KV element. Two tensors, key and value, are cached. One GPU has 24 GiB, of which 15 GiB is weights/runtime and 1 GiB is reserve. Assume 120 generated tokens/s/GPU at the target batch and $2.40/GPU-hour.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
import math
limit=16384
parts={'system':650,'history':900,'retrieval':5*1100,'tools':350,'user':500}
output=2000
headroom=math.ceil(limit*.10)
used=sum(parts.values())+output+headroom
kv_per_token=2*32*32*128*2
free=(24-15-1)*1024**3
max_sequences=free//(kv_per_token*(sum(parts.values())+output))
cost_per_1k=(2.40/3600)/(120/1000)
print('input',sum(parts.values()))
print('headroom',headroom,'total',used,'fits',used<=limit,'spare',limit-used)
print('kv_bytes_per_token',kv_per_token)
print('max_sequences',max_sequences)
print('cost_per_1k_generated_usd',format(cost_per_1k,'.6f'))
PY

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Reconcile every token category and check the context inequality.
  2. Calculate KV bytes/token and maximum resident sequences.
  3. Calculate GPU cost per 1,000 generated tokens.
  4. Propose a deterministic truncation order that never drops the current user request or safety policy.
  5. State which assumptions require measurement on the real serving stack.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Change retrieved chunks from 5 to 10. Predict whether the request fits before running. Then reduce retrieval by lowest relevance until the inequality holds; do not silently reduce the output reserve.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: None. Re-run the original command and preserve the restored baseline.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Expected evidence: input 7900, headroom 1639, total 11539, fits True, spare 4845, kv_bytes_per_token 524288, max_sequences 1, and cost 0.005556 dollars per 1,000 generated tokens.

Calculation: KV bytes/token = 2 tensors * 32 layers * 32 heads * 128 dimensions * 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes. Free KV memory is 8 GiB; per sequence at 9,900 input-plus-reserved-output tokens is 4.834 GiB, so the simplified arithmetic permits floor(8 GiB / 4.834 GiB) = 1 resident sequence.

The baseline input is 7,900 tokens. With output and headroom, 11,539 tokens are committed, leaving 4,845. The command returns one resident sequence because a 9,900-token KV cache is about 4.83 GiB under the fixture. Ten chunks raise input to 13,400 and committed context to 17,039, exceeding the limit by 655 tokens. Drop one whole 1,100-token chunk: nine chunks commit 15,939 tokens and leave 445 spare. Context fit does not imply GPU fit: that request reserves 14,300 KV tokens, about 6.98 GiB, still only one sequence in the 8 GiB KV budget. Real systems must measure tokenizer behavior, allocator overhead, batching, prefix reuse, attention implementation, and achieved tokens/s.

docs.title: L5/L6 extension
docs.text:
L5: Define per-class context, output, queue, and cost budgets with truncation evidence and overload behavior.

L6: Establish fleet admission policy, model-mix economics, capacity reservations, exception governance, and evidence for changing context limits.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• I separated input, output reserve, and headroom.
  • I kept bytes, GiB, tokens, seconds, and dollars explicit.
  • I detected the resident-sequence unit trap.
  • I defined deterministic truncation and refusal.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Implement bounded routing, policy rejection, fallback eligibility, and usage accounting without invoking a model.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: All requests and model results are local dictionaries. The gateway has no credentials, sockets, or subprocesses.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text: Four synthetic requests cover normal routing, restricted data, a large context, and small-model failure. Cost units are synthetic. Here tokens is a precomputed context commitment, including any output reserve; the linear cost units deliberately do not model separate input/output prices. small_down is known before dispatch, so fallback creates no failed small-model attempt in this fixture. A real failure after dispatch must record and charge that attempt too.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
MODELS={'small':{'limit':8000,'cost':1},'large':{'limit':32000,'cost':4}}
requests=[('r1','internal',3000,False),('r2','restricted',3000,False),
          ('r3','internal',12000,False),('r4','internal',3000,True)]
def route(row):
    rid,data_class,tokens,small_down=row
    if data_class=='restricted': return rid,'DENY','policy',0
    preferred='small' if tokens<=MODELS['small']['limit'] else 'large'
    if preferred=='small' and small_down: preferred='large'
    if tokens>MODELS[preferred]['limit']: return rid,'DENY','context',0
    return rid,preferred,'ok',tokens*MODELS[preferred]['cost']
rows=[route(r) for r in requests]
for row in rows: print(*row)
print('units',sum(r[3] for r in rows))
PY

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Measure the recall/work tradeoff between exact search and a deterministic approximate candidate partition.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The fixture is a six-point, two-dimensional list. It uses no vector database, native extension, or external data.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text: Six vectors, two queries, and fixed relevance sets compare exact cosine ranking with a deliberately crude partition.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
import math
docs={'a':(1.0,0.0),'b':(.9,.1),'c':(.5,.5),'d':(.2,.8),'e':(0,1.0),'f':(-1,-1)}
queries=[('q1',(1,0),{'a','b'}),('q2',(.4,.6),{'c','d'})]
def cosine(x,y):
    return sum(a*b for a,b in zip(x,y))/(math.sqrt(sum(a*a for a in x))*math.sqrt(sum(b*b for b in y)))
def rank(q,candidates): return sorted(candidates,key=lambda d:(-cosine(q,docs[d]),d))
for name,q,relevant in queries:
    exact=rank(q,docs)[:2]
    candidates=[d for d,v in docs.items() if (v[0]>=v[1])==(q[0]>=q[1])]
    approx=rank(q,candidates)[:2]
    recall=lambda xs:len(set(xs)&relevant)/len(relevant)
    print(name,'exact',exact,'approx',approx,'recall',recall(approx),'work',len(candidates),'of',len(docs))
PY

Expected evidence: q1 returns exact and approximate ['a','b'] with recall 1.0 and 4 of 6 candidates. q2 exact is ['c','d']; approximate is ['d','e'] with recall 0.5 and 2 of 6 candidates.

Calculation: The candidate filter reduces work by 1-4/6 = 33.3% for q1 and 1-2/6 = 66.7% for q2, but q2 loses one of two relevant documents. Average approximate Recall@2 is (1.0+0.5)/2 = 0.75.

Exact search evaluates six distances/query. The synthetic partition saves distance work but still scans all six vectors to choose candidates; work does not count that scan, sorting, or preprocessing. It creates a discontinuity and misses c for q2. Production selection must compare Recall@k, latency distributions, build time, update/delete behavior, memory, filter selectivity, and failure recovery on representative queries. Exact top-K is the reference for ANN overlap, while the labeled relevant set is the reference for relevance recall; those sets happen to agree for the two baseline queries but need not agree after changing a query. This toy partition is not evidence for a particular ANN algorithm. See the pinned pgvector filtering and recall documentation, verified 2026-09-08, for a real implementation whose candidate/filter behavior also needs measurement.

docs.title: Lab 04: Hybrid Search, RRF, and Reranking
Outcome
docs.text: Compute Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), Recall@k, precision@k, and single-query reciprocal rank directly, then distinguish fusion from reranking.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: Rank lists and relevance judgments are inline. No corpus, service, or model is accessed.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text: Two deterministic rank lists and one relevance set represent lexical and vector retrieval.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
lex=['d1','d2','d3','d4']
vec=['d3','d5','d1','d6']
relevant={'d1','d3','d5'}
k=60
score={d:0.0 for d in set(lex+vec)}
for ranking in (lex,vec):
    for rank,d in enumerate(ranking,1): score[d]+=1/(k+rank)
fused=sorted(score,key=lambda d:(-score[d],d))
top=fused[:3]
precision=len(set(top)&relevant)/len(top)
recall=len(set(top)&relevant)/len(relevant)
rr=next((1/i for i,d in enumerate(fused,1) if d in relevant),0)
for d in fused: print(d,format(score[d],'.6f'))
print('top3',top,'precision',precision,'recall',recall,'reciprocal_rank',rr)
PY

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Calculate each RRF contribution using 1/(60+rank).
  2. Explain deterministic tie-breaking and why it matters in evaluation.
  3. Compute precision@3, Recall@3, and reciprocal rank.
  4. Describe a reranker that scores only the fused candidate set.
  5. State why RRF scores are not calibrated relevance probabilities.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Remove d1 from the vector list. Recompute and compare Recall@3. Then set k=1 and observe how top ranks receive more relative weight. Do not select k from one query.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: Restore both lists and k=60; verify the six scores and metrics.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Expected evidence: The order is d1, d3, d2, d5, d4, d6. Top 3 precision and recall are both 2/3; reciprocal rank is 1.0.

Calculation: d1 = 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.032266; d3 = 1/63 + 1/61 = 0.032266. The document-ID tie-break places d1 first. d2 and d5 each receive 1/62; their tie is also lexical. RRF combines ranks, not raw scores whose scales may be incomparable.

The top three contain d1 and d3, so precision@3 and Recall@3 are both 0.667. Reciprocal rank is 1 because the first fused result is relevant. A cross-encoder or deterministic feature model may rerank the top N, but evaluation must preserve the candidate-stage ceiling: a reranker cannot recover a relevant document absent from its candidates. Select k and candidate depth over a labeled query set with latency and slice constraints.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Measure retrieval coverage, ranking, citation support, and abstention separately so an aggregate answer score cannot hide the failing stage.

docs.title: Safety

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text: Four query records carry relevance judgments, retrieved IDs, answer decisions, and citation-support judgments. q4 is explicitly judged unanswerable; its empty relevance set does not mean missing labels. The support boolean represents whole-answer support, so the printed citation_support is an answer-level fixture metric, not claim-level citation precision. The denominator of one is fixed to the single unanswerable case; derive it from an explicit answerability field when extending the fixture.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
rows=[
 ('q1',{'a'},['a','x','y'],True,True),
 ('q2',{'b','c'},['x','b','z'],True,False),
 ('q3',{'d'},['x','y','z'],False,True),
 ('q4',set(),['x','y'],False,True)]
recalls=[]; rrs=[]; supported=0; answered=0; abstain_ok=0
for q,rel,got,answered_flag,support in rows:
    if rel:
        recalls.append(len(rel&set(got))/len(rel))
        rrs.append(next((1/i for i,d in enumerate(got,1) if d in rel),0))
    if answered_flag:
        answered+=1; supported+=int(support)
    if not rel: abstain_ok+=int(not answered_flag)
    print(q,'hits',sorted(rel&set(got)),'answered',answered_flag,'supported',support)
print('macro_recall',sum(recalls)/len(recalls))
print('mrr',sum(rrs)/len(rrs))
print('citation_support',supported/answered)
print('unanswerable_abstention',abstain_ok/1)
PY

docs.text:

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Set q4's answered_flag to True and support to False. Predict which metrics remain unchanged, recompute the others, and record why a single blended score would obscure the regression.

docs.title: Cleanup

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Expected evidence: Macro Recall@3 is 0.5, MRR is 0.5, citation support is 0.5, and unanswerable abstention is 1.0.

Calculation: Retrieval recall is (1 + 1/2 + 0)/3 = 0.5. Reciprocal ranks are 1, 1/2, and 0, so MRR is 0.5. One of two produced answers is fully supported. q3 correctly does not answer but still exposes a retrieval miss; abstention does not repair retrieval.

With q4 answered without support, retrieval metrics remain unchanged, unanswerable abstention falls to 0, and citation support falls to 1/3.

q2 has partial retrieval plus an unsupported answer; q3 has a retrieval miss but safe answer policy. Report query-level evidence and confidence intervals on larger sets. Use frozen judgments for release comparison, periodically refresh them for drift, and keep retrieval, grounding, answer correctness, citation precision, abstention, latency, and cost as separate gates.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Create stable chunks with source versions, offsets, hashes, access labels, and deletion tombstones.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The fixture uses inline public-looking synthetic text and hashes it in memory. It writes nothing and contains no personal or proprietary data.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text:
One versioned synthetic policy is chunked with fixed width and overlap, then logically deleted.

Offsets here are Python string indices, not UTF-8 byte offsets or tokenizer positions. The 12-hex-character digest is a 48-bit display ID for four chunks, not a production uniqueness guarantee: at one million independently distributed IDs the expected number of colliding pairs is about n*(n-1)/(2*2^48) = 0.00178. Retain a full digest and enforce composite identity including tenant, source, version, and chunker version in a real manifest. The fixture attaches an ACL string but does not implement authorization or physical deletion.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
import hashlib
source='Policy A. Refunds require receipt. Exceptions require manager approval.'
version='policy-7'; acl='employees'; width=24; overlap=6
chunks=[]
for start in range(0,len(source),width-overlap):
    text=source[start:start+width]
    if not text: break
    cid=hashlib.sha256(f'{version}:{start}:{text}'.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    chunks.append((cid,version,start,start+len(text),acl,text))
    if start+len(text)==len(source): break
for row in chunks: print(row)
tombstones={version}
visible=[c for c in chunks if c[1] not in tombstones]
print('chunks',len(chunks),'visible_after_delete',len(visible))
PY

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Verify that offsets reconstruct each exact source span.
  2. Explain why source version belongs in the chunk ID.
  3. Trace ACL and tombstone enforcement from retrieval through caches.
  4. Specify parser failures, quarantine behavior, and reprocessing idempotency.
  5. Define evidence that deletion completed across index, cache, and generated derivatives.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Remove version from the hash input and ingest the same text at the same offsets as both policy-7 and policy-8. Confirm that corresponding chunks collide even though they are distinct source versions, then restore the versioned hash. Next make the parser return an empty body and quarantine it rather than publishing zero chunks as a successful update.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: None. Restore the versioned hash and confirm the complete output matches the preserved baseline.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Expected evidence: Four deterministic chunks are printed. Each includes a 12-character digest, source version, offsets, ACL, and text. After tombstoning policy-7, visible count is zero.

Calculation: Stride is 24-6 = 18 characters. Starts are 0, 18, 36, and 54. Duplication overhead is (24+24+24+17)-71 = 18 stored characters, or about 25.4% above the source length.

Without version in the hash, identical spans from policy-7 and policy-8 receive identical chunk IDs. Version-aware records and hashes keep the identities distinct, and per-chunk tombstone checks delete only the targeted version.

Stable identity needs source ID/version, parser/chunker version, offsets, and content digest. Metadata should carry ACL, trust class, language, timestamps, and lineage. Publish a manifest atomically only after parse and validation; quarantine failures. Deletion requires a durable tombstone, retrieval filtering immediately, asynchronous physical purge, cache invalidation, and audit evidence. A zero-chunk parse is not proof that a source was intentionally empty.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Quantify serial workflow reliability and compare a bounded deterministic path with an open-ended planner.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The fixture multiplies fixed step probabilities and slices a finite event list. No tool, model, file, or network operation occurs.

docs.title: Fixture
docs.text: Four fixed workflow-step probabilities and a finite planner event list expose serial reliability and budget behavior.

docs.title: Exact command
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
steps=[('classify',.999),('retrieve',.995),('validate',.998),('render',.999)]
workflow=1
for name,p in steps:
    workflow*=p
    print(name,'success',p)
print('workflow_success',format(workflow,'.6f'))
planner_step=.98
for n in (3,5,10):
    print('planner_steps',n,'all_success',format(planner_step**n,'.6f'))
events=['plan','read','read','read','read','read','read']
budget=5
print('bounded_trace',events[:budget],'stopped',len(events)>budget)
PY

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Calculate all-step workflow success under the independence assumption.
  2. Calculate planner completion for 3, 5, and 10 required steps.
  3. Explain why marginal step probabilities alone do not determine joint success when failures are dependent.
  4. Assign deterministic steps, bounded choice points, deadlines, and stop conditions.
  5. Choose workflow or agent for a regulated write action and defend the authority boundary.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Set the planner budget to 3. It cannot complete the six reads in the event list; the baseline budget of five already truncates that list. Then remove the budget entirely and explain the unbounded cost and liveness risk without actually running an unbounded loop.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: Restore budget 5 and the original probability list; rerun the finite trace.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Expected evidence: Workflow success is 0.991025. Planner all-step values are 0.941192, 0.903921, and 0.817073. The seven-event trace stops after five events.

Calculation: Serial success is the product of mandatory step success probabilities. Even 98% per-step reliability falls to about 81.7% across ten steps. This is not an availability prediction unless independence and representative probabilities hold.

For two steps each with marginal success 0.98, independent all-success is 0.9604. If both fail on exactly the same 2% of requests, all-success is 0.98; if their failures are disjoint, it is 0.96. Dependence can move the estimate either way. A newly introduced shared outage can reduce the marginals too. Measure conditional step success on joined request records instead of assuming the direction of bias.

Source: NIST reliability models, verified 2026-09-08, explicitly assume independent component operation; a series system is the all-components-required special case. The dependent counterexamples above are direct probability calculations, not measured workflow availability.

Use a workflow when the sequence, invariants, approvals, or compensation are known. Use bounded planning where task decomposition benefits from choice and mistakes are reversible. Keep authorization, data policy, spend, write validation, idempotency, and final approval deterministic. Reliability arithmetic highlights why adding optional agent steps can lower completion even before correlated provider or gateway failures are considered.
