Property-test recurrence against standards corpora across leap years, month ends, gaps, folds, exclusions, and series splits. Model-test organizer updates racing attendee responses and deletion racing reminders. Test cursor snapshots, retries, duplicate/out-of-order events, ACL revocation, and resource overlap. Chaos-test queue and region failures. Shadow every tzdb/library upgrade and compare occurrence sets over a multi-year horizon.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Storing only UTC simplifies indexes but destroys recurring wall-clock intent; local intent plus derived UTC wins. Eager infinite expansion is impossible; bounded windows add read fallback and rebuild complexity. Embedding attendee responses in one event document simplifies reads but creates lost updates and large fanout; independent rows win. Active-active calendar writes reduce latency but complicate splits, ACLs, and sync order; home ownership is usually preferable. Exactly-once reminder delivery is unattainable across external providers; idempotent intents and user-visible deduplication target the actual effect.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Apps --> Regional[Regional API and query cells]
    Regional --> Owner[Calendar home owner]
    Owner --> Canon[(Series, overrides, attendees, ACL, changes, outbox)]
    Canon --> Stream[(At-least-once event stream)]
    Stream --> Materialize[Versioned recurrence expansion]
    Materialize --> Index[(Occurrence and free/busy indexes)]
    Stream --> Workflow[Invitation workflows]
    Stream --> Schedule[Reminder scheduler]
    Workflow --> Delivery[Email and push adapters]
    Schedule --> Delivery
    Regional --> Index
    Regional --> Canon
    Control[Signed tzdb and policy control plane] --> Materialize

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is occurrence identity not its UTC start time?
  2. How does editing this-and-future split a recurring series?
  3. What happens to a 9:00 meeting across daylight-saving changes?
  4. How can an attendee respond while the organizer edits the title?
  5. How do you prevent a stale cancellation email or reminder?
  6. How do room bookings differ from human calendar events?
  7. How would you roll out a new timezone database safely?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should model series and overrides, preserve timezone intent, paginate ranges, separate attendee responses, make invitations/reminders idempotent, and address materialization and failures. An L6 answer should define occurrence identity, future-series splitting, DST gap/fold policy, tzdb migration, resource exclusion, projection repair, regional fencing, privacy, overload tiers, and organizational ownership of standards and notification policy.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: A calendar stores civil-time intent in a series, not just UTC rows. Persist local start/end, IANA zone, tzdb version, recurrence rule, stable occurrence identity, overrides, independent attendee responses, ACLs, a calendar change sequence, and outbox atomically. Expand only bounded windows into versioned UTC occurrence indexes, and merge canonical exceptions at read time. A single edit writes an override; a future edit splits the rule at a deterministic boundary. Internal invitations are idempotent cross-calendar workflows, while email and push are retryable delivery. Reminder workers claim time buckets and recheck current source version before sending. Partition by calendar, keep one fenced home-region writer, rebuild projections from snapshots plus changes, and treat ACL deletion as higher priority than cache freshness. Test DST gaps, folds, leap dates, retries, concurrent responses, and timezone-library migrations as core correctness, not edge cases.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a conversational AI product that accepts multimodal prompts, maintains conversation context, streams model output, uses tools and retrieval, enforces safety, and controls expensive GPU capacity. Clarify model scope, latency, privacy, tenant isolation, and whether training is included. Begin with one model and stateless inference, then add durable conversations, batching, routing, tool execution, retrieval, quotas, evaluation, and regional governance.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Users create conversations, send messages, receive streamed answers, stop or regenerate, upload files, and optionally invoke approved tools. Organizations configure retention, model access, data residency, and tool policy. Operators deploy model versions and safety rules. Training the foundation model is out of scope; model serving, feedback, and safe rollout are in scope.

Target API acceptance below 300 ms p99, time to first token below 2 seconds p95 for the standard tier, steady generation above 20 tokens/s, 99.9% successful request completion excluding client cancellation, and explicit overload responses rather than unbounded queues. Conversations are durable; token streams are resumable only from persisted checkpoints and may be regenerated. Safety and authorization cannot be bypassed when optional ranking or retrieval fails.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A client idempotency key creates one user message and at most one active generation lineage.
  • Conversation branches are immutable parent-linked messages; regenerate creates a sibling, not an overwrite.
  • Tokens are exposed only after input policy and authorization pass, and tool results are treated as untrusted input.
  • A tool with side effects requires explicit policy, stable invocation ID, and idempotent or confirmed execution.
  • Billing is derived from metered accepted input and generated output with auditable model/tokenizer versions.
  • Tenant data, caches, retrieval indexes, and encryption keys never cross authorization boundaries.
  • Model output is probabilistic; infrastructure guarantees concern lifecycle and provenance, not factual correctness.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 100 million daily users and 20 million prompts/hour at peak, or 5,556 prompt starts/s. Average input is 2,000 tokens and output 500 tokens: approximately 11.11 million input tokens/s and 2.78 million output tokens/s. Their sum is 13.89 million tokens/s, but prefill and autoregressive decode have different costs and cannot be sized as interchangeable output tokens. If one model replica sustains 1,000 output tokens/s under the measured context-length, batching, and latency constraints, decode alone needs about 2,778 replica equivalents before headroom. Prefill compute and KV-cache memory impose additional constraints; tensor parallelism may make one replica span several GPUs. At 4 KB/message metadata, one billion messages/day add 4 TB/day before attachments; 40 messages/conversation imply 25 million conversations/day. KV-cache sizing must specify layers, KV heads, head dimension, precision, and retained tokens rather than relying on a universal bytes-per-sequence constant.

docs.title: Entities and interfaces
docs.text:
Conversation(conversation_id, tenant_id, owner_id, policy, home_region, version)
Message(message_id, conversation_id, parent_id, role, content_uri, state, created_at)
Generation(generation_id, user_message_id, model_version, tokenizer_version,
           parameters_hash, state, input_tokens, output_tokens, finish_reason)
TokenChunk(generation_id, sequence, text_or_token_ids, checksum)
ToolInvocation(invocation_id, generation_id, tool_version, arguments_hash, state, result_uri)
UsageRecord(record_id, tenant_id, generation_id, meter_type, quantity, pricing_version)

POST /v1/conversations
POST /v1/conversations/{id}/messages   Idempotency-Key: ...
GET  /v1/generations/{id}/stream?after_sequence=42
POST /v1/generations/{id}:cancel
POST /v1/messages/{id}:regenerate
DELETE /v1/conversations/{id}

Streaming uses SSE for simple server-to-client delivery or WebSocket for bidirectional real-time voice. The initial response returns generation ID and queue state. Each chunk has a monotonic sequence. A final event contains finish reason, usage, safety metadata, and model version.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Clients] --> E[Edge auth and quota]
 E --> O[Conversation orchestrator]
 O --> D[(Conversation DB and outbox)]
 O --> P[Input policy]
 O --> X[Context builder]
 X --> R[Retrieval service]
 X --> F[File service]
 O --> S[Inference scheduler]
 S --> G[GPU model pools]
 G --> Y[Output policy]
 Y --> T[Stream gateway]
 O <--> W[Tool sandbox]
 D --> U[Usage and audit pipeline]

docs.title: Message acceptance and context construction
docs.text:
The API authenticates tenant/user, checks model entitlement and coarse quota, validates bounded content references, then transactionally inserts the immutable user message, generation row, and outbox. Repeated keys with the same request hash return the existing generation; a different hash conflicts. The orchestrator runs input policy and builds context from the selected parent chain.

Context has a strict token budget. Reserve space for system policy and output, include recent turns, then select older turns or summaries by relevance and recency. Summaries are derived data with source message IDs and summarizer version; they never replace canonical messages. Retrieval chunks include tenant, document ACL, source, version, and relevance score. Recheck ACL at query time and before including content. Prompt assembly is reproducible only with a recorded builder version plus the exact retrieved chunks, authorization decisions, summaries, tokenizer and ordering inputs; the builder version alone cannot recreate mutable retrieval results.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant O as Orchestrator
 participant D as Conversation DB
 participant P as Policy/context
 participant S as Scheduler
 participant G as Model worker
 participant T as Stream gateway
 C->>O: message plus idempotency key
 O->>D: commit message, generation, outbox
 D-->>C: generation ID
 O->>P: authorize, moderate, assemble context
 P->>S: tokenized request and deadline
 S->>G: admitted batch slot
  G->>T: token chunks through output-policy holdback
 T-->>C: SSE chunks
 G->>D: terminal state and usage

docs.title: Inference scheduling and continuous batching
docs.text:
Prefill processes all input tokens and is compute-heavy; decode produces one token per sequence and is memory-bandwidth-heavy. Separate pools or scheduling classes when workload warrants. The scheduler groups requests by compatible model, adapter, precision, and maximum sequence shape. Continuous batching admits new sequences between decode iterations, improving GPU utilization without waiting for an entire batch to finish.

Use weighted fair queuing across tenants and service tiers, with token-cost estimates rather than request counts. Admission checks available KV-cache blocks, queued token-seconds, deadline, and regional reserve. Reserve capacity for short interactive requests; long contexts cannot monopolize every batch. Under overload, reject low-tier requests with retry hints, cap output, route to a smaller model when policy permits, or degrade retrieval. Never queue beyond the point where the latency SLO is already impossible.

KV cache uses paged blocks to reduce fragmentation. Prefix caching can reuse common system prompts only when model, tokenizer, exact tokens, policy version, and tenant-sharing classification match. Tenant-private prompt prefixes never enter a global cache. Eviction favors cancelled, over-deadline, and low-priority sequences. Preemption saves block mappings where feasible; recomputation trades compute for memory.

docs.title: Streaming lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> ACCEPTED
 ACCEPTED --> POLICY_REJECTED
 ACCEPTED --> QUEUED
 ACCEPTED --> CANCELLED
 QUEUED --> RUNNING
 QUEUED --> CANCELLED
 RUNNING --> TOOL_WAIT
 TOOL_WAIT --> QUEUED
 TOOL_WAIT --> CANCELLED
 TOOL_WAIT --> FAILED
 RUNNING --> COMPLETED
 RUNNING --> CANCELLED
 RUNNING --> FAILED
 FAILED --> RETRYABLE
 RETRYABLE --> QUEUED

Workers emit sequence-numbered chunks into a bounded stream buffer. The gateway acknowledges consumption internally and persists periodic chunks or the completed answer depending on product guarantees. A disconnected client reconnects after sequence N if chunks remain; otherwise it receives the durable partial/final text or an explicit non-resumable result. Slow clients cannot block GPU decode: buffer to a limit, then detach the stream while generation continues or cancel according to request policy.

Cancellation is a versioned flag delivered to scheduler and worker; races may produce a few extra tokens that are metered according to documented policy but not streamed after terminal cancellation. Worker death before a checkpoint can restart the generation, which may produce different text. Expose restarted provenance and a new attempt/stream epoch with explicit replacement or branch semantics. Clients must never concatenate newly sampled text onto an old partial answer or treat reused sequence numbers as the same chunk. The output gateway fences the old attempt before accepting the new epoch.

docs.title: Tool execution
docs.text:
The model proposes a typed tool call; the orchestrator validates schema, tenant allowlist, user authorization, argument policy, and budget. Read-only tools execute in network-isolated sandboxes with egress allowlists and time/output limits. Side-effecting tools require confirmation unless preauthorized, receive stable invocation IDs, and should expose idempotency. Persist the invocation ID, canonical argument hash, authorized scope and durable dispatch intent before making the external call; store the result and provenance afterward. An after-the-call audit record cannot recover an ambiguous effect safely. Tool output is escaped and labeled as untrusted to resist prompt injection.

flowchart TD
 M[Model proposes tool call] --> V[Schema and policy validation]
 V --> A{Side effect?}
 A -->|yes| C[User confirmation or prior grant]
 A -->|no| X[Sandbox execution]
 C --> X
 X --> R[Result size and content filter]
 R --> P[Append tool message with provenance]
 P --> Q[Resume inference]
 V -->|deny| D[Safe error to model]

Loops are bounded by invocation count, wall time, and spend. A tool timeout is not assumed failed if an external side effect may have occurred; reconcile by invocation ID or ask the user before retry. Tool credentials are scoped, short-lived, and unavailable to the model text.

docs.title: Retrieval and files
docs.text: Uploads are malware-scanned, parsed asynchronously, chunked with document/version/ACL metadata, embedded, and written to a tenant-scoped vector index. Hybrid lexical/vector retrieval improves identifiers and names. Retrieve a broad bounded set, enforce ACL, rerank, and include citations. Index freshness is eventual and visible. Deletion tombstones content immediately in ACL filtering, then removes chunks, embeddings, caches, and source objects asynchronously with completion audit.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and regions
docs.text:
Partition conversation metadata by tenant and conversation ID in its home region. Object storage holds large content. Stream gateways shard by generation ID and are stateless beyond bounded buffers. GPU pools partition by model/version, hardware, region, and trust class. The scheduler has hierarchical queues: global model capacity, tenant fairness, then request priority. Very large tenants receive reserved pools or quotas to limit noisy-neighbor effects.

Keep inference near users where model availability and residency allow, but fetch canonical conversation context from the home region or replicate encrypted read views. Enterprise residency may prohibit cross-region routing even during shortage; consumer traffic may opt into fallback. Control-plane model artifacts are signed, staged, and immutable. Rollout uses shadow evaluation, one-region canary, small traffic cohorts, then promotion. Old versions drain existing generations; conversation turns may explicitly cross model versions.

Regional failure reroutes only eligible tenants. Durable message/outbox state replicates to a paired region with a recovery point objective. A failover epoch fences orchestrators, output gateways and tool dispatch. Generation uniqueness prevents two active lineages only if acknowledged lineage, invocation and idempotency state survived; otherwise pause side effects and reconcile the missing prefix before restart. GPU work in the failed region is lost and may restart non-deterministically; billing reconciliation removes duplicated metering.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Messages, generation lineage, tool confirmation, and terminal usage records need transactional consistency. Search indexes, summaries, analytics, and feedback are eventual projections. Outbox solves DB/event publication. Consumers deduplicate event IDs. Token streaming is at least once by sequence, so clients replace/ignore duplicate sequence numbers. Side effects depend on tool idempotency, never a platform claim of exactly once.

Model-worker OOM quarantines the batch, reduces sequence limits, and retries individually only within deadline. GPU loss restarts or fails based on persisted progress. Scheduler partition prevents new admission and leases expire by epoch. Safety-service failure fails closed for disallowed risk classes and may use an approved local classifier for ordinary traffic. Retrieval failure returns an answer labeled without retrieval if product policy permits. Usage pipeline lag does not block bounded prepaid quotas because online reservations reconcile later.

Reconciliation scans nonterminal generations past lease expiry, completed text without terminal usage, usage without generation, orphaned tool invocations, and deletion tombstones. Replay is scoped by tenant/model/time and cannot silently re-execute side-effecting tools. Disaster recovery tests include artifact registry, tokenizer/config parity, keys, conversation DB, and billing offsets.

docs.title: L6 GPU capacity model
docs.text:
Capacity starts from a concrete model profile rather than a generic GPU replica. For P parameters at b bytes per weight, raw weights consume P*b; add quantization scales, runtime workspaces, graph buffers, and 10% to 20% allocator reserve. Tensor parallelism shards tensor operations within layers across GPUs; pipeline parallelism assigns different layer ranges to stages, and data parallelism replicates the serving unit for throughput. The smallest valid serving unit must fit weights plus peak KV cache plus workspace on every rank; losing one rank loses that unit.

For example, a 70B-parameter model at BF16 needs about 140 GB of weights. On 80 GB GPUs, two-way tensor parallelism nominally leaves 10 GB per GPU after 70 GB of weights, which is too tight for KV and workspace; four-way tensor parallelism leaves about 45 GB per GPU before reserve and is plausible. At INT8 the weights are about 70 GB, so two-way tensor parallelism leaves roughly 45 GB per GPU, but quality and kernel throughput must pass evaluation. Using the 2.78 million output tokens/s demand above and an alternative measured 800 output tokens/s per four-GPU replica, decode needs ceil((20M / 3,600) * 500 / 800) = 3,473 replicas, or 13,892 GPUs before reserve. A 70% utilization target and an additional 10% capacity margin require ceil(3,473 / 0.70 * 1.10) = 5,458 replicas, or 21,832 GPUs. This 10% additive margin is not the same as surviving loss of 10% of installed capacity. Prefill is sized separately: disaggregated pools add their GPU requirements, while a shared pool must pass a joint prefill/decode workload test, not merely take the maximum of two isolated benchmarks.

KV sizing comes from architecture, not a fixed per-request guess. Without grouped-query attention, bytes per sequence are approximately 2 * layers * hidden_size * bytes_per_element * cached_tokens; with grouped-query attention replace hidden size by KV-head width. A 32-layer model with KV width 1,024 and BF16 uses 2 * 32 * 1,024 * 2 = 128 KiB per cached token. An 8,000-token sequence therefore consumes about 1 GiB; 32 such sequences need 32 GiB before fragmentation. With 16-token, 2 MiB pages and a 40 GiB KV budget, only 20,480 blocks fit, and admission reserves blocks for the promised output rather than hoping decode memory appears later.

FLOPs bound prefill and decode feasibility. A useful lower-bound estimate is roughly 2 * parameters * tokens per forward pass, excluding attention and communication. A 70B model generating 800 tokens/s requires at least 112 TFLOP/s of useful model work per replica for decode; measured kernels, memory bandwidth, all-reduce, attention growth, and batching determine the real sustainable rate. Capacity tests therefore publish a versioned profile by model, precision, GPU SKU, tensor/pipeline degree, input bucket, output bucket, and latency target. Planning uses p10 measured throughput, not vendor peak FLOPs, and reserves whole serving units because fractional stranded ranks cannot serve the model.

flowchart TD
  D[Prompt and output demand forecast] --> T[Token and sequence buckets]
  M[Model parameters precision and architecture] --> W[Weight workspace and KV model]
  H[GPU memory FLOPs bandwidth and fabric] --> W
  T --> C[Prefill and decode capacity calculation]
  W --> C
  C --> U[Serving unit topology]
  U --> R[Replica count plus zonal reserve]
  R --> L[Load and failure qualification]
  L -->|pass| P[Production capacity profile]
  L -->|fail| C

docs.title: Token-second admission and KV block scheduling
docs.text:
Each request declares input tokens, maximum output, deadline, tier, model, and residency. The profiler predicts prefill milliseconds and decode tokens/s for its buckets. Use consistent work units: replica_seconds = prefill_replica_seconds + expected_output_tokens / profiled_replica_output_tokens_per_second; multiply each stage by its GPUs/replica when converting to GPU-seconds. This is compute-time accounting, not KV token-seconds, which integrate retained tokens over residence time. Reserve expected work for queueing and quota, but reserve KV blocks for input plus the allowed output cap. Request counts are insufficient because one 100,000-token prompt can cost more than hundreds of short turns.

Suppose a pool has 100 replicas, each delivering 800 output tokens/s at target latency: raw decode capacity is 80,000 tokens/s. At a 70% utilization target, admit 56,000 tokens/s. If accepted traffic already reserves 48,000 tokens/s, the next scheduling horizon has 8,000 tokens/s left. A request expected to emit 400 tokens over 20 seconds reserves 20 tokens/s of decode rate plus its profiled prefill burst; 400 such requests fill the decode remainder. A queue holding 1.2 million predicted output tokens contains about 1,500 replica-seconds of decode work at 800 tokens/s. With only ten replica-equivalents of spare capacity, it takes about 150 seconds to drain, so a request with a 30-second start deadline is rejected immediately instead of aging in queue.

The scheduler maintains hierarchical deficit counters for tier, tenant, then request and reconciles measured replica-seconds or GPU-seconds against its work estimates, separately tracking KV token-seconds. Prefill is chunked so a long prompt cannot block decode iterations. A KV allocator reserves logical pages, maps physical blocks only as tokens materialize, applies copy-on-write for shared prefixes, and records (model_version, tenant_scope, block_table_epoch). Decode selects sequences whose next-token step fits compute and available blocks; cancelled and deadline-expired sequences release pages first. Preemption order is over-deadline, best-effort, then largest recomputation-to-progress tradeoff. Interactive capacity and an emergency KV reserve are not borrowable by batch jobs.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant A as Admission
  participant Q as Fair queue
  participant S as Batch scheduler
  participant K as KV block manager
  participant G as GPU serving unit
  A->>A: estimate prefill decode and KV
  A->>K: reserve maximum logical blocks
  K-->>A: reservation or capacity denial
  A->>Q: enqueue replica-second work estimate and deadline
  Q->>S: eligible request by deficit
  S->>K: materialize input blocks
  S->>G: chunked prefill
  loop Each decode iteration
    S->>K: allocate next-token pages
    S->>G: continuous batch step
    G-->>S: tokens and actual cost
  end
  S->>K: release or retain prefix pages
  S-->>A: reconcile reservation and usage

Failure operations are explicit. A block leak detector compares scheduler ownership with allocator epochs and fences a suspect worker before reclaim. Fragmentation above a threshold triggers draining, not risky live compaction. Repeated OOM for one shape quarantines that profile and lowers admission while preserving small-request capacity. Alert on predicted-versus-actual token cost, reserved/used KV, block allocation latency, preemption loss, per-tier deficit, deadline rejection, prefilling starvation, decode batch occupancy, and stranded tensor-parallel ranks.

docs.title: Serving cells and model rollout guardrails
docs.text:
A serving cell is the blast-radius unit: zonal ingress, admission shard, fair queues, stream gateways, model-serving units, KV managers, local safety classifiers, artifact cache, and telemetry collector. A regional router selects only cells matching model, residency, trust class, and adapter, using signed capacity advertisements with epoch and expiry. Cells do not share live KV state; failover restarts from durable conversation/generation state and is marked non-deterministic. The regional control plane distributes signed artifacts and policy, but a control-plane outage does not mutate an already loaded cell. Separate cells for premium interactive, standard, and batch traffic prevent batch saturation or one tenant adapter from exhausting all regional KV.

flowchart TD
  R[Regional router] --> C1[Serving cell A]
  R --> C2[Serving cell B]
  CP[Regional control plane] -. signed artifacts and policy .-> C1
  CP -. signed artifacts and policy .-> C2
  C1 --> A1[Admission and fair queues]
  A1 --> G1[GPU serving units and KV blocks]
  G1 --> S1[Safety and stream gateways]
  C2 --> A2[Admission and fair queues]
  A2 --> G2[GPU serving units and KV blocks]
  G2 --> S2[Safety and stream gateways]
  D[(Durable conversation state)] --> C1
  D --> C2

If a region needs 10,000 serving replicas across five cells, place 2,000 per cell and keep one cell-equivalent of regional failover headroom distributed across zones. Losing a cell then raises surviving utilization from 67% to about 84% when normal load used 6,700 replicas, leaving a narrow but viable degraded mode. Router advertisements expire in seconds; withdrawal stops new sessions, while existing streams drain unless worker safety requires termination. Cell evacuation caps concurrent context rebuilds and prefill traffic so failover does not create a GPU and network retry storm.

Model rollout promotes an immutable bundle containing weights, tokenizer, chat template, kernels, quantization, safety model, tool schema compatibility, and capacity profile. Stages are offline golden/adversarial evaluation, shadow traffic with outputs discarded, one-cell canary, small sticky user cohort, regional ramp, then global default. Hard gates include artifact signature and checksum, tokenizer parity, deterministic smoke prompts, output schema/tool-call validity, memory headroom, and rollback compatibility. Statistical guardrails compare task quality and safety severity by locale plus p95 first-token latency, inter-token gaps, OOM, tokens/GPU-second, refusal rate, tool errors, user stops, and cost. A severe safety regression, cross-tenant leak signal, or artifact mismatch stops immediately; noisy quality metrics require minimum sample sizes and confidence intervals.

Rollback changes routing to the previous complete bundle and drains the candidate; it never overwrites loaded weights in place. Conversations record model bundle per generation, so rollback does not rewrite history. New tokenizer or context semantics require compatibility handling at context construction, not mixed ranks in one serving unit. Operators retain enough old capacity until candidate traffic and long generations drain, and rehearse rollback under full load. If the new model needs 25% more KV per token, rollout capacity includes that tax before any traffic shift rather than discovering it through canary OOMs.

docs.title: Streaming safety mechanics
docs.text:
Input policy runs before GPU admission. During generation, output is accumulated into small sentence- or token-window buffers and checked by a low-latency local classifier; high-risk domains use a larger holdback window or non-streamed completion. Only approved spans receive monotonically sequenced stream events. The client treats final, blocked, cancelled, and replaced as terminal and discards any later event. A final whole-answer classifier can replace or truncate previously buffered but not yet released text; already emitted text cannot be recalled, so holdback length is a product risk decision rather than a perfect guarantee.

For example, at 25 tokens/s a 20-token holdback adds about 800 ms before the first releasable span but gives the classifier more context. Standard benign traffic might use a 5-token rolling buffer after initial clearance, while self-harm, sexual, financial, or tool-action contexts use sentence-level buffering or wait for a complete safe response. Classifier timeout fails closed for high-risk traffic; ordinary traffic may fall back to a versioned in-cell model only if policy explicitly permits. If unsafe continuation is detected, stop decode, release KV, emit a terminal blocked event with safe replacement text generated through a separately approved path, persist the hidden unsafe span in restricted audit storage only when retention policy allows, and do not send it through analytics logs.

Safety versions are pinned for a generation so a mid-stream policy deployment cannot produce contradictory decisions. Emergency deny rules may terminate active generations through a higher policy epoch, with the terminal event recording both versions. Slow safety service backpressure reduces admission before unreviewed buffers grow without bound. Operations monitor classifier latency/timeouts, held-token depth, blocked-after-partial rate, unsafe-token exposure estimate, fallback usage, appeals, locale skew, and policy-version divergence. Chaos tests kill the streaming classifier, reorder token events, disconnect clients before a block, and roll policy epochs during generation; release tests verify that no chunk follows a terminal safety event.

docs.title: Security, safety, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Encrypt data, isolate tenant keys and indexes, use short-lived service identities, verify model artifacts, sandbox parsers/tools, prevent SSRF, redact logs, and audit privileged access. Defend against prompt injection, data exfiltration, account abuse, automated scraping, denial through huge contexts, unsafe file formats, tool escalation, and feedback poisoning. Layer input/output classifiers, model alignment, tool policy, rate limits, user reporting, and human escalation. Safety decisions are versioned and appealable where policy requires.

Observe acceptance, time to first token, inter-token latency, completion latency, tokens/s, prefill/decode utilization, batch occupancy, KV-cache use/fragmentation, queue token-seconds, admission rejection, cancellation waste, stream reconnects, model errors, safety outcomes, retrieval latency/groundedness, tool success/ambiguity, token accounting drift, cost per completion, and fairness by tier. Do not place prompt content in ordinary traces.

Property-test lineage, idempotency, stream sequencing, ACL precedence, quota reservations, and cancellation races. Golden and adversarial sets evaluate usefulness, safety, hallucination, citation support, bias, and regression by locale. Load-test mixed context lengths and slow clients. Chaos-test GPU death, scheduler failover, artifact corruption, retrieval lag, tool timeout, region loss, and metering duplication. Red-team prompt/tool boundaries. Canary model and policy versions with automated operational and quality guardrails.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
One large model simplifies quality but wastes cost and capacity; policy-aware routing across models improves economics at consistency cost. Larger batches improve throughput but hurt first-token latency. Persisting every token improves resume but adds write amplification; periodic checkpoints plus final text are usually sufficient. Longer context seems accurate but increases latency/cost and can dilute relevance; retrieval and source-aware summaries win. Global prompt caches save GPU work but create privacy risk; cache only explicitly shareable exact prefixes.

flowchart TD
 I[Idempotent user message] --> P[Authorization and input policy]
 P --> C[Versioned context and retrieval]
 C --> A[Token-cost admission and fair queue]
 A --> B[Continuous-batched model pool]
 B --> O[Output policy and sequenced stream]
 B --> T[Governed tool loop]
 T --> C
 O --> D[(Immutable conversation lineage)]
 D --> U[Metering, evaluation, audit]

The final design separates durable conversation lifecycle from expensive, replaceable inference. A policy/context orchestrator prepares authorized prompts; a cost-aware scheduler admits them to versioned GPU pools using continuous batching and paged KV cache. Sequenced gateways stream bounded output. Retrieval and tools are governed subsystems with provenance, ACL, and side-effect controls. Usage, safety, and model changes remain auditable.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. Why schedule by token cost instead of request count?
  2. How does continuous batching affect latency and fairness?
  3. What happens to a stream when a GPU dies?
  4. How can a model safely call a payment or email tool?
  5. Which data can participate in prefix caching?
  6. How do conversation deletion and retrieval indexes interact?
  7. How would you roll out a model whose quality cannot be captured by one metric?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should model immutable conversations and generations, estimate token/GPU load, explain context limits, streaming, batching, quotas, tool isolation, retrieval, failures, and idempotency. They should distinguish probabilistic model quality from infrastructure guarantees.

An L6 candidate should define safety and side-effect invariants, token-economic admission, model/control-plane rollout, residency, fairness, deletion proof, metering reconciliation, non-deterministic recovery, and degradation policy. They should connect GPU utilization, latency tiers, privacy, evaluation, and organizational governance.

Use the Applied AI Systems track to practice the serving, retrieval, agent, evaluation, security, capacity, and platform mechanisms behind this integrated design.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Transactionally accept an idempotent user message into immutable conversation lineage, then authorize, moderate, and assemble a versioned token-bounded context from recent turns, summaries, files, and ACL-checked retrieval. Admit by estimated token-seconds and KV capacity through tenant-fair queues; continuously batch compatible requests on signed model pools. Stream sequence-numbered chunks through bounded gateways and explicitly handle disconnect, cancellation, checkpoint loss, and non-deterministic restart. Validate model-proposed tools, confirm side effects, pass stable invocation IDs, sandbox execution, and treat results as untrusted. Partition conversations by tenant/home region and GPUs by model/trust class. Degrade or reject before queues violate SLOs. Reconcile generations, usage, and tools; measure first-token latency, token rate, queue cost, KV use, safety, groundedness, fairness, and spend. Never promise factual truth or exactly-once external effects.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify whether checkout owns cart, inventory, pricing, payment, and order creation. Define the invariants, estimate peak order rate, then present the smallest correct saga: one order record coordinates reservations and side effects. Trace happy path and retries before adding queues, regional cells, or workflow engines. Reserve time for price snapshots, inventory races, payment ambiguity, and reconciliation.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Checkout converts a mutable cart into a durable order. It validates products and addresses, freezes the commercial terms, reserves stock, authorizes or captures payment, and initiates fulfillment. The system must explain partial failure to customers without double charging or silently overselling.

Assume physical goods, one currency per order, multiple warehouses, cards and wallets, and guest or registered shoppers. Catalog browsing, recommendation, warehouse picking, and returns are adjacent but out of scope.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements

  • Preview totals, shipping options, taxes, promotions, and stock.
  • Submit checkout once and retrieve its status after disconnects.
  • Reserve inventory, pay, create an order, and start fulfillment.
  • Cancel safely before fulfillment and release inventory or refund payment.

Non-functional requirements

  • Never create two orders or charges for one submitted checkout key.
  • A confirmed order has immutable line, price, tax, and address snapshots.
  • Target 99.95% submit availability and p99 under three seconds excluding step-up authentication.
  • Isolate slow providers, apply backpressure, and recover every intermediate state.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. One shopper-scoped idempotency key maps to one checkout and request hash.
  2. An order is confirmed only after required stock is reserved and payment policy succeeds.
  3. Reserved plus available inventory never exceeds physical sellable stock for a SKU-location.
  4. The amount sent to payment equals the server-generated order total and currency.
  5. Every intended external effect has a durable identity before dispatch; unknown outcomes remain discoverable and are reconciled. Failed orders retain owned compensation work until resolved or explicitly escalated, since compensation is not guaranteed to succeed immediately or be fully reversible.
  6. Cart, quote caches, and event projections are not canonical order state.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100 million monthly active shoppers, 20 million orders per day, an average of three lines, and a ten-times peak. Orders average 230 QPS and peak near 2,500 QPS; preview traffic may peak at 25,000 QPS. At about 5 KB for order snapshots and workflow history, a year is roughly 36 TB before indexes and replicas. Events add similar magnitude. Payment and tax calls dominate latency; the write volume fits sharded relational storage comfortably.

Popular SKUs create contention far above average. If one promotion drives 5,000 reservation attempts per second to one SKU-location, that key needs atomic counters, admission limits, or preallocated inventory buckets rather than indiscriminate database scaling.

docs.title: Core Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Checkout(checkout_id, shopper_id, cart_version, request_hash, status,
         idempotency_key, quote_id, order_id, expires_at, version)
Quote(quote_id, currency, subtotal, discounts, tax, shipping, total, expires_at)
QuoteLine(quote_id, sku_id, quantity, unit_price, adjustments_json)
Order(order_id, shopper_id, status, amount, currency, address_snapshot,
      quote_snapshot, created_at, version)
OrderLine(order_id, sku_id, seller_id, quantity, fulfillment_status)
InventoryReservation(reservation_id, order_id, sku_id, location_id,
                     quantity, status, expires_at)
PaymentAttempt(attempt_id, order_id, provider, provider_ref, amount, status)
WorkflowStep(order_id, step, status, attempt, last_error)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

Unique constraints cover (shopper_id, idempotency_key), provider references, and one active reservation per order-line allocation. The order stores snapshots rather than foreign keys to mutable prices or addresses. A relational database is the initial source of truth; inventory may be a separate service with its own transactional store.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/checkouts/preview
{"cart_id":"c1","cart_version":7,"shipping_address_id":"a2"}

POST /v1/checkouts
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"cart_id":"c1","cart_version":7,"quote_id":"q9",
 "payment_method_token":"pm4","shipping_option_id":"standard"}

GET /v1/checkouts/{checkoutId}
POST /v1/orders/{orderId}/cancellations
Idempotency-Key: 01J...

Preview returns a signed, expiring quote and stock warnings, not a reservation. Submit returns 201 CONFIRMED, 202 PROCESSING with a polling URL, or a stable business error. Reusing a key with a different body returns 422. Authentication challenges carry a resumable checkout token rather than requiring a fresh order.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Client --> Gateway[API gateway]
    Gateway --> Checkout[Checkout orchestrator]
    Checkout --> Orders[(Order SQL)]
    Checkout --> Pricing[Pricing and promotion]
    Checkout --> Tax[Tax provider]
    Checkout --> Inventory[Inventory service]
    Checkout --> Payment[Payment service]
    Orders --> Relay[Outbox relay]
    Relay --> Bus[(Event stream)]
    Bus --> Fulfillment[Fulfillment]
    Bus --> Notify[Notifications]
    Bus --> Analytics[Projections]
    Recon[Reconciler] --> Orders
    Recon --> Payment
    Recon --> Inventory

Start with the orchestrator and order tables in one database. Direct synchronous calls are acceptable at modest scale if every intent is persisted and bounded. Move long-running retries to durable workers when provider latency or operational complexity justifies it.

docs.title: Preview Checkout
docs.text: The service reads a specific cart version, batches catalog and pricing lookups, computes promotions, requests tax and shipping estimates, and returns a quote with a short expiry. The quote captures inputs and computed totals. Cache product and tax metadata, but reject checkout if the signed quote expired or regulated price changed. Preview can degrade by hiding unavailable shipping options; it must not invent totals.

docs.title: Submit Checkout
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant D as Order SQL
    participant I as Inventory
    participant P as Payment
    C->>O: Submit(quote, key)
    O->>D: Create CHECKOUT_STARTED once
    O->>I: Reserve(order, lines)
    I-->>O: reservation IDs
    O->>P: Authorize(order ID, amount)
    alt authorized
        O->>I: Idempotently confirm still-owned reservations against expiry
        O->>D: Confirm order plus outbox
        O-->>C: CONFIRMED
    else declined
        O->>I: Release reservations
        O->>D: Mark PAYMENT_FAILED
        O-->>C: stable decline
    else timeout
        O->>D: Mark PAYMENT_UNKNOWN
        O-->>C: 202 PROCESSING
    end

The orchestrator re-enters from durable state after crashes. Each step checks whether its effect already completed before retrying. Authorize-first is an alternative when stock is abundant; reserving first avoids charging for unavailable items. Capture can occur at confirmation or fulfillment depending on payment rules and shipping duration.

Before order confirmation, inventory must turn each live reservation into a non-expiring fulfillment allocation or an explicitly renewed guarantee under its own authority. A remembered reservation ID is not proof that stock survived a long payment challenge. If expiry already won, void/refund the resolved payment and fail the checkout. Persist progress for each inventory confirmation so a crash between that step and order commit resumes or compensates rather than releasing a confirmed order's stock.

docs.title: Cancel and Fulfill
docs.text: Cancellation conditionally transitions the order only if fulfillment has not crossed its cutoff. It then voids authorization or refunds capture and releases unconsumed reservations. These effects may finish asynchronously, so the customer sees CANCELLATION_PENDING. Fulfillment consumes reservations idempotently by order-line ID and emits shipment events. Split shipments do not mutate the original commercial snapshot.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Saga Boundaries
docs.text:
Two-phase commit across inventory, payment, and fulfillment is unavailable and undesirable. The order database stores the saga state and next action. A worker leases due workflows, invokes one dependency with a stable operation ID, records the response, and advances state. Lease expiry permits another worker to continue. Compensation is business logic, not rollback: release stock, void or refund money, and explain any delay.

Ordering matters. Reserve then authorize minimizes refunds but temporarily locks inventory while payment challenges run. Authorize then reserve improves stock utilization but creates voids and customer confusion. A practical flow reserves for a short period, authorizes, confirms, and releases on decline. For scarce items, serialize or limit admissions upstream.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Inventory Reservation
docs.text:
Inventory owns (sku_id, location_id) counters: on_hand, reserved, safety_stock, and version. A transaction checks on_hand - reserved - safety_stock >= quantity, increments reserved, and inserts reservation rows. Reservation expiry is logically evaluated during allocation; a sweeper performs cleanup. Warehouse selection considers stock, delivery promise, split cost, and capacity, but persist the chosen allocation so retries do not rerun a changing optimizer.

For hot SKUs, partitioning by SKU cannot divide one key. Preallocate bounded stock tokens to regional or channel buckets. Each bucket sells only its allocation; a rebalancer moves unused capacity conservatively. This may show sold out while global stock remains, but it prevents oversell without global consensus on every purchase.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Payment Ambiguity
docs.text:
The dangerous result is timeout, not decline. The provider may have authorized the card while the caller lost the response. Never issue a second provider operation with a new key. Mark the attempt UNKNOWN, query by merchant order ID, consume signed webhooks idempotently, and reconcile until terminal. Provider-reference uniqueness deduplicates one provider resource; it does not stop two different references from charging the same order. A conditional order-level payment winner and stable provider-operation identity prevent local double acceptance, while reconciliation detects any extra external charge. If duplicate captures occur despite controls, automatically refund the extra and alert.

Step-up authentication pauses the saga. Store a short-lived continuation linked to the existing attempt. The browser callback cannot assert payment success; the backend verifies provider state before advancing.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Price and Promotion Correctness
docs.text: Catalog price is mutable, but an order total is immutable. The quote includes line prices, promotion rule versions, tax basis, currency, and expiry. At submit, verify its signature, ownership, cart version, and policy freshness. Server-side arithmetic uses integer minor units and explicit rounding by jurisdiction. Promotion usage is reserved transactionally when globally limited; otherwise eventual counters can exceed a campaign cap. The product owner must choose which guarantee applies.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition orders by shopper_id or order_id; choose shopper if order history is dominant and mitigate celebrity-account hot keys. Keep workflow and payment attempts colocated with order. Inventory partitions by SKU hash and optionally location. Queries by provider reference use a global lookup index containing only the owning shard. Analytics consumes events rather than scanning transactional shards.

Apply bounded concurrency separately to tax, inventory, and payment. Shed previews before submits, serve cached catalog data within freshness policy, and stop admitting new checkouts if durable workflow backlog breaches the reservation window. Autoscaling cannot rescue an exhausted database or provider quota; load shedding must occur at the gateway.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Order transitions, quote acceptance, and each inventory counter update are strongly consistent within their owners. Search, shipment views, email, and analytics are eventual. The checkout key is stored before external calls. Every downstream command uses (order_id, operation, logical_step_id) as a stable key. Repeated refunds, split allocations, and shipments have distinct durable step identities; retries preserve the identity of the original step. Outbox events are atomic with order changes and delivered at least once; consumers keep inbox records or make naturally idempotent upserts.

Optimistic versions reject competing cancellation and fulfillment transitions. Reconciliation joins canonical local intent with provider APIs and inventory reservations. It detects paid orders not confirmed, confirmed orders lacking reservations, expired workflows, and orphaned reservations. Operators repair by replaying named transitions, never editing totals ad hoc.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> STARTED
    STARTED --> STOCK_RESERVED
    STOCK_RESERVED --> PAYMENT_PENDING
    PAYMENT_PENDING --> ALLOCATION_CONFIRMING: authorized
    PAYMENT_PENDING --> PAYMENT_UNKNOWN: timeout
    PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> ALLOCATION_CONFIRMING: reconciled success
    ALLOCATION_CONFIRMING --> CONFIRMED: all inventory allocations durable
    ALLOCATION_CONFIRMING --> COMPENSATING: stock no longer owned
    COMPENSATING --> FAILED: release and verified void/refund
    PAYMENT_PENDING --> FAILED: declined
    PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> FAILED: reconciled failure
    STOCK_RESERVED --> FAILED: reservation expires
    CONFIRMED --> CANCEL_PENDING: cancellation accepted
    CANCEL_PENDING --> CANCELLED: release and void/refund

An orchestrator crash is harmless because state precedes effects. Database unavailability rejects new submits rather than accepting memory-only orders. Inventory timeout leaves the step retryable. Payment outage holds a bounded workflow queue and reservation lifetime; beyond policy, cancel safely. Event-stream outage accumulates outbox rows while confirmed orders remain correct. Poison events move to a quarantine queue with alerts and replay tooling.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text: Deploy regional checkout cells near shoppers, but assign an order to one home cell. Its database is synchronously replicated across zones and asynchronously to a disaster-recovery region. Inventory may be globally allocated into regional buckets; payment routing follows regulatory and provider constraints. Failover fences the prior writer with a database epoch before accepting workflow commands. In-flight orders resume only from a verified recovery prefix that preserves operation identities and reservations. If asynchronous replication lost acknowledged steps, hold affected orders for authoritative reconciliation instead of inventing new effect keys. Strong global stock without buckets would require consensus and adds latency, so reserve it for genuinely scarce goods.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Use hosted fields or provider tokens so checkout does not receive raw card data. Encrypt addresses, minimize log fields, and separate PCI and general workloads. Authenticate webhooks with signatures and replay windows. Validate all price and amount inputs server-side. Rate limit by account, device, IP, address, and payment instrument; detect card testing, promotion farming, inventory hoarding, and address manipulation. Admin cancellation and manual repair require least privilege, dual approval for high-value cases, and immutable audit records.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure conversion by step, preview and submit latency, inventory conflict, reservation age, payment declines versus unknowns, saga age, compensation failures, outbox lag, dependency saturation, and confirmed-to-fulfillment delay. Trace by checkout, order, and provider reference while redacting personal and payment data. Alert on invariant symptoms such as paid-unconfirmed age rather than only HTTP errors.

Use state-machine property tests, contract tests with provider simulators, and concurrency tests against hot inventory keys. Inject duplicate callbacks, reordered events, crashes before and after each durable write, long authentication, expired quotes, and region fencing. Shadow price calculations during rule migrations and compare totals. Periodically restore backups and rebuild projections from snapshots plus events.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Orchestration centralizes workflow visibility but can become a coupling hub; choreography reduces central knowledge but obscures state and compensation. SQL costs more per write than an append-only workflow log but gives simple constraints and operator queries at this scale. Reserving before payment protects customer experience but can be abused to hoard inventory. Regional inventory buckets trade utilization for availability and bounded oversell risk. Synchronous fulfillment would reduce apparent lag but places warehouse availability on checkout's critical path.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Edge[Global edge] --> Cell[Regional checkout cell]
    Cell --> Orch[Durable orchestrator]
    subgraph State[Order state and disaster recovery]
        DB[(Orders, steps, outbox)] -. fenced async DR .-> DR[(Recovery region)]
    end
    Orch --> DB
    Orch --> Inv[Inventory shards and regional buckets]
    Orch --> Pay[PCI payment service]
    Orch --> Quote[Pricing, tax, shipping]
    subgraph Events[Asynchronous order events]
        Stream[(Event stream)] --> Fulfill[Fulfillment]
        Stream --> Read[Order read models]
        Stream --> Notice[Notifications]
    end
    DB --> Stream
    Recon[Reconciliation workers] --> DB
    Recon --> Inv
    Recon --> Pay

The final system is a durable, idempotent saga whose order database records truth. It adds partitioned inventory, queues, and regional cells only where contention, latency, and provider behavior require them.

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. Would you reserve stock before or after payment authorization, and why?
  2. How do you recover when the provider times out after charging?
  3. How are globally limited promotions enforced?
  4. How do you prevent a hot SKU from overloading one partition?
  5. What changes for marketplace orders with multiple sellers?
  6. How do you migrate orchestration logic while workflows are active?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer produces immutable order snapshots, a clear saga, inventory conditional writes, payment idempotency, and concrete failure handling. An L6 answer additionally sets product policy for ambiguity and compensation, isolates provider and regional failures, handles hot inventory through bounded allocations, designs migration and repair tooling, and reasons about conversion, fraud, compliance, and operating cost.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Checkout turns a cart into an immutable order through a recoverable saga. Start with one multi-AZ relational order database and persist checkout identity and workflow state before calling anything external. Validate a signed, expiring quote; reserve inventory atomically; authorize payment with the order ID as idempotency key; then confirm the order and write an outbox event in one transaction. Timeouts become PROCESSING, not blind retries. Compensation releases stock and voids or refunds payment. Inventory owns canonical counters and uses regional buckets only for hot or globally distributed stock. Partition orders independently from inventory, isolate each dependency with bounded concurrency, and keep one home region per order. Reconciliation resolves payment ambiguity and orphaned reservations. Security centers on tokenized payment, server-generated totals, webhook verification, and defenses against card testing and inventory hoarding. Test every crash boundary, duplicate event, stale quote, and hot-key race.

docs.title: Flash Sale System
docs.text:
This chapter develops an end-to-end design for selling a tiny amount of inventory under extreme, synchronized demand. It is structured as both a detailed study guide and a 45-60 minute system design interview walkthrough.

Imagine that 10,000 pairs of a limited-edition shoe go on sale at exactly noon while tens of millions of users attempt to buy them. The system must remain available, allocate inventory fairly, let winners complete payment, and never sell more units than physically exist.

The hard part is not the product page. It is coordinating scarce inventory across concurrent requests and an unreliable, multi-second payment workflow without holding a database transaction open.

docs.title: 1. Interview Roadmap
docs.text:
Phase Time Goal Requirements 5 minutes Define sale rules, correctness, scale, and fairness Entities and APIs 5 minutes Establish reservation and order boundaries High-level design 15 minutes Build view, reserve, and purchase paths Deep dives 15-20 minutes Contention, expiry, burst handling, and fairness Wrap-up 5 minutes Payment races, failures, tradeoffs, and final design

A strong interview answer should surface the reservation requirement without prompting:

View item -> Reserve one unit -> Pay before reservation expires -> Confirm purchase

Payment takes seconds and involves an external provider. Holding an inventory row lock or database transaction during payment would destroy throughput and reliability. A reservation removes inventory from circulation immediately and gives payment a bounded time window.

docs.title: 2. Understanding the Problem
docs.text:
A flash sale differs from ordinary e-commerce in several ways:

  • Demand arrives at a known instant instead of gradually.
  • Demand may exceed supply by thousands of times.
  • One SKU or a handful of variants become extreme hot keys.
  • Users care about fairness and visible progress, not only raw latency.
  • Bots and duplicate attempts can consume scarce capacity.
  • Payment is slower and less reliable than inventory allocation.
  • Overselling is a correctness failure, not a tolerable stale-read issue.

The system should absorb excess demand before it reaches inventory or payment systems.

docs.title: Core requirements
docs.text:
1. Users can view a flash-sale item and sale status.
  2. During an active sale, an eligible user can reserve one available unit for a limited time.
  3. A user with an active reservation can complete payment and purchase the unit.

docs.title: Clarifications
docs.text:
• The example sale contains 10,000 units across size or color variants.
  • A reservation lasts five minutes by default.
  • A user can hold at most one reservation for the sale.
  • A unit cannot belong to two active reservations or completed orders.
  • An expired or cancelled reservation returns its unit to inventory.
  • A sold-out response may be eventual for display, but allocation must be exact.
  • Clients may retry every mutation; APIs must be idempotent.
  • Users arriving before the start join a randomized waiting room; arrivals after the start join behind them.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• General catalog browsing and search.
  • Shipping, fulfillment, returns, and order history.
  • Sale creation and merchant administration.
  • Product recommendations.
  • Complex tax and fraud implementation details.
  • Multi-item carts spanning ordinary and flash-sale products.

docs.title: 3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Target Reasoning Inventory correctness Never oversell Physical inventory cannot be manufactured by retrying Reservation durability No acknowledged reservation loss Winners must not lose valid claims silently Product-page availability 99.99%+ Tens of millions may load it simultaneously Reservation availability Graceful admission, not overload collapse Excess demand should wait or receive a definitive response Product-page latency p95 below 200 ms Static and highly cacheable Reservation decision Normally below 1 second after admission Queueing happens before inventory service Fairness Explainable and bot-resistant Trust matters for scarce allocations Payment workflow Idempotent and recoverable PSP callbacks and client retries are unavoidable Auditability Reconstruct every unit transition Required for disputes and incident recovery

docs.title: 3.3 Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
State these explicitly. They drive the design.

  1. available + reserved + sold = configured inventory for each inventory pool.
  2. A physical or logical inventory unit is in exactly one state.
  3. A user has at most one live reservation per sale.
  4. A reservation can create at most one successful order.
  5. A payment attempt can affect an order at most once.
  6. Releasing a reservation is idempotent.
  7. A sold unit never returns to available inventory without an explicit refund/cancellation workflow.

docs.title: 3.4 Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume:

  • 50M users open the event page around noon.
  • 10M users attempt to reserve within the first 10 seconds.
  • 10,000 total units.
  • 5-minute reservation TTL.
  • 80% of reservations attempt payment.
  • 70% of payment attempts succeed.
  • Product page response is 20 KB before media.
  • A sale has 10 product variants.

Uncontrolled burst:

Reservation attempts = 10M / 10 seconds = 1M requests/second
Inventory units       = 10,000
Demand-to-supply      = 1,000:1

There is no reason to send 1M reservation requests per second into the authoritative database. At least 99.9% cannot win.

If the waiting room admits 5,000 users per second:

Maximum inventory pressure = 5,000 reserve requests/second
First allocation round      = at least 2 seconds if 5,000 claims/s all succeed
Expected first-round sales   = 10,000 * 0.80 * 0.70 = 5,600
Remaining first-round units  = 4,400 to resolve or recycle

The 2-second floor describes allocation, not paid completion. Five-minute holds, unknown payments, variant skew, and later rounds determine sell-through time.

Page traffic at 50M views and 20 KB is roughly 1 TB before images. A CDN must serve nearly all of it.

The architecture should scale with request attempts while the authoritative allocation path scales roughly with inventory plus a bounded amount of contention.

docs.title: 4. Core Entities
docs.text:
erDiagram
    PRODUCT ||--o{ SKU : has
    FLASH_SALE ||--o{ SALE_ITEM : contains
    SKU ||--o{ SALE_ITEM : offered_as
    SALE_ITEM ||--o{ INVENTORY_UNIT : owns
    USER ||--o{ QUEUE_ENTRY : joins
    FLASH_SALE ||--o{ QUEUE_ENTRY : controls
    USER ||--o{ RESERVATION : creates
    SALE_ITEM ||--o{ RESERVATION : reserves

    FLASH_SALE {
        uuid sale_id PK

    SALE_ITEM {

    INVENTORY_UNIT {
        uuid unit_id PK

    QUEUE_ENTRY {

    }

    RESERVATION {
        uuid reservation_id PK

    ORDER {
        uuid order_id PK

docs.title: Counted versus unit-level inventory
docs.text:
Two valid models exist:

  • Counted inventory: atomically decrement available_quantity when it is greater than zero.
  • Unit tokens: pre-create exactly 10,000 logical inventory units and atomically claim one.

Counted inventory is simple but concentrates all writes on one hot row per SKU. Unit tokens spread lock contention and make the no-oversell invariant intuitive. This design uses unit tokens as the allocation primitive while retaining aggregate counters as derived, quickly readable state.

The token can represent a logical sale unit, not necessarily a serialized physical shoe.

docs.title: 5.1 Sale state
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SCHEDULED
    SCHEDULED --> WAITING_ROOM_OPEN
    WAITING_ROOM_OPEN --> ACTIVE
    ACTIVE --> SOLD_OUT: all units sold, not merely held
    ACTIVE --> ENDED
    SOLD_OUT --> ENDED
    SCHEDULED --> CANCELLED
    WAITING_ROOM_OPEN --> CANCELLED
    ACTIVE --> CANCELLED

docs.title: 5.2 Inventory unit state
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AVAILABLE
    AVAILABLE --> RESERVED: atomic allocation
    RESERVED --> SOLD: successful checkout
    RESERVED --> AVAILABLE: expiry or cancellation
    SOLD --> [*]

docs.title: 5.3 Reservation state
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ACTIVE
    ACTIVE --> PAYMENT_PROCESSING: checkout starts before expiry
    ACTIVE --> EXPIRED: expiry wins race
    ACTIVE --> CANCELLED: user or operator cancels
    PAYMENT_PROCESSING --> CONFIRMED: authorization verified and inventory committed
    PAYMENT_PROCESSING --> ACTIVE: payment fails with time remaining
    PAYMENT_PROCESSING --> EXPIRED: payment deadline passes
    CONFIRMED --> [*]
    EXPIRED --> [*]
    CANCELLED --> [*]

Only conditional transitions are permitted. A generic UPDATE reservation SET state = ... without checking the previous state would create double releases and payment races.

docs.title: 6.1 View the sale item
docs.text:
GET /v1/flash-sales/{sale_id}/items/{sale_item_id}

Response:

{
  "saleId": "sale_2026_shoe",
  "saleItemId": "item_size_9",
  "name": "Limited Edition Shoe",
  "variant": "Size 9",
  "price": { "amount": "199.00", "currency": "USD" },
  "saleState": "ACTIVE",
  "startsAt": "2026-09-05T12:00:00Z",
  "availability": "IN_STOCK",
  "media": ["https://cdn.example.com/products/shoe/hero.webp"]
}

Do not promise an exact live inventory number to millions of viewers. Return a coarse state such as COMING_SOON, IN_STOCK, LOW_STOCK, or SOLD_OUT. The reservation response is authoritative.

docs.title: 6.2 Join the waiting room
docs.text:
POST /v1/flash-sales/{sale_id}/queue
Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
Authorization: Bearer <token>

Response:

{
  "queueEntryId": "qe_83b",
  "state": "WAITING",
  "statusToken": "signed-opaque-token",
  "nextPollAfterMs": 5000
}

docs.title: 6.3 Get queue status
docs.text:
GET /v1/flash-sales/{sale_id}/queue/me
Authorization: Bearer <token>

When admitted, return a short-lived admission token bound to the sale, user, device/session, and expiry.

{
  "state": "ADMITTED",
  "admissionToken": "signed-single-purpose-token",
  "admittedUntil": "2026-09-05T12:01:30Z"
}

docs.title: 6.4 Reserve inventory
docs.text:
POST /v1/flash-sales/{sale_id}/reservations
Authorization: Bearer <token>
X-Admission-Token: <signed-token>
Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "saleItemId": "item_size_9"
}

Response:

{
  "reservationId": "res_91c",
  "state": "ACTIVE",
  "expiresAt": "2026-09-05T12:06:00Z",
  "checkoutToken": "signed-checkout-token"
}

Return 409 SOLD_OUT only for committed exhaustion, not merely an empty SKIP LOCKED scan; contention receives a retryable response. A timeout is ambiguous, so the client must retry with the same idempotency key or query its reservation.

docs.title: 6.5 Start checkout
docs.text:
POST /v1/reservations/{reservation_id}/checkout
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: <uuid>

The response contains an order ID and payment-provider client secret or redirect URL. The reservation must still be active when checkout begins.

docs.title: 6.6 Get order status
docs.text:
GET /v1/orders/{order_id}
Authorization: Bearer <token>

docs.title: 6.7 Payment webhook
docs.text:
POST /v1/payments/webhooks/{provider}
Provider-Signature: <signature>

Webhooks are authenticated, deduplicated by provider event ID, and processed idempotently. Client-reported success is not authoritative.

docs.title: 7. High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    User[Web and Mobile Clients] --> Edge[CDN / WAF / Bot Defense]
    Edge --> Gateway[API Gateway]

    Gateway --> Product[Product Service]
    Product --> ProductCache[(Product Cache)]
    ProductCache --> ProductDB[(Catalog DB)]

    Gateway --> Waiting[Virtual Waiting Room]
    Waiting --> QueueStore[(Queue State Store)]
    Waiting --> Admission[Admission Controller]

    Gateway --> Reservation[Reservation Service]
    Admission --> Reservation
    Reservation --> InventoryDB[(Authoritative Inventory DB)]
    Reservation --> Idempotency[(Idempotency Store)]
    Reservation --> Outbox[(Transactional Outbox)]

    Gateway --> Order[Order Service]
    Order --> OrderDB[(Order DB)]
    Order --> Payment[Payment Orchestrator]
    Payment --> PSP[External Payment Provider]

    Outbox --> Relay[Outbox Relay]
    Relay --> Kafka[Kafka]
    Kafka --> Expiry[Reservation Expiry Workers]
    Kafka --> Projection[Availability Projection]
    Kafka --> Audit[Immutable Audit Log]

    Expiry --> InventoryDB
    Projection --> ProductCache
    subgraph CatalogLane[Catalog reads]
      Product
      ProductCache
      ProductDB
      Projection
    end
    subgraph AdmitLane[Admission]
      Waiting
      QueueStore
      Admission
    end
    subgraph ReserveLane[Reservation authority]
      Reservation

    end

    end

docs.title: Responsibility boundaries
docs.text: Component Responsibility CDN and WAF Product assets, cached sale state, DDoS and bot filtering Waiting room Absorbs excess arrivals and creates a fair admission order Admission controller Releases only bounded traffic to reservation services Reservation service Sole authority for available, reserved, and sold transitions Inventory database Durable source of truth for unit ownership Order service Owns order lifecycle and checkout records Payment orchestrator Integrates with PSP and coordinates payment saga Expiry workers Reclaim timed-out reservations using conditional transitions Availability projection Publishes coarse, eventually consistent UI availability Audit log Reconstructs allocation, payment, expiry, and operator actions

docs.title: 8. Requirement 1: View the Flash Sale Item
docs.text:
The product page is public, identical for most users, and changes infrequently. It should never reach the inventory database.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant CDN as CDN Edge
    participant P as Product Service
    participant R as Redis
    participant DB as Catalog DB

    C->>CDN: GET sale page or product API
    alt Edge cache hit
        CDN-->>C: Cached product and coarse sale state
    else Edge cache miss
        CDN->>P: Product request
        P->>R: Read product projection
        alt Cache hit
            R-->>P: Product projection
        else Cache miss
            P->>DB: Read product and sale metadata
            DB-->>P: Product record
            P->>R: Cache projection
        end
        P-->>CDN: Cacheable response
        CDN-->>C: Product response
    end

docs.title: Caching policy
docs.text:
• Product name, description, price, and media can have long TTLs with versioned URLs.
  • Sale state can use a short TTL, for example 1-5 seconds near the event.
  • Publish scheduled state transitions proactively to edge caches.
  • Use stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error.
  • Keep reservation APIs uncacheable and separate from public product APIs.

docs.title: Why coarse availability?
docs.text: An exact count changes too frequently and would turn every page refresh into a synchronized read against the hottest state. It can also mislead users because visible availability may be claimed before they reserve. Coarse availability is a projection; only an allocation transaction answers whether the user won.

docs.title: 9.1 Reservation sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Admitted Client
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant R as Reservation Service
    participant I as Idempotency Store
    participant DB as Inventory DB
    participant O as Outbox
    Note over I,O: Idempotency and outbox are tables in the inventory transaction

    C->>G: POST reservation + admission token + idempotency key
    G->>G: Verify auth, admission token, rate limit
    G->>R: Validated request
    R->>I: Find prior result
    alt Existing result
        I-->>R: Canonical response
        R-->>C: Same response
    else New request
        R->>DB: Begin transaction
        R->>DB: Check one-live-reservation invariant
        R->>DB: Atomically claim one AVAILABLE unit
        alt Unit claimed
            R->>DB: Insert ACTIVE reservation
            R->>O: Insert ReservationCreated event
            R->>I: Store response in the same transaction
            R->>DB: Commit
            R-->>C: Reservation and expiry
        else No unlocked unit
            R->>DB: Roll back
            R-->>C: retryable contention unless committed exhaustion proven
        end
    end

docs.title: 9.2 Authoritative SQL transaction
docs.text:
One unit-token implementation uses row locking:

BEGIN;

SELECT unit_id
FROM inventory_units
WHERE sale_item_id = :sale_item_id
  AND state = 'AVAILABLE'
ORDER BY allocation_bucket, unit_id
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;

UPDATE inventory_units
SET state = 'RESERVED', version = version + 1
WHERE unit_id = :unit_id
  AND state = 'AVAILABLE';

INSERT INTO reservations (
  reservation_id, sale_id, sale_item_id, unit_id,
  user_id, state, expires_at, version
) VALUES (
  :reservation_id, :sale_id, :sale_item_id, :unit_id,
  :user_id, 'ACTIVE', :expires_at, 1
);

INSERT INTO outbox_events (...);
-- Persist the scoped key, request hash, and result in this transaction.
INSERT INTO idempotency_results (...);

COMMIT;

Important database constraints:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_live_reservation_per_user_sale
ON reservations (sale_id, user_id)
WHERE state IN ('ACTIVE', 'PAYMENT_PROCESSING', 'CONFIRMED');

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_reservation_per_unit
ON reservations (unit_id)
WHERE state IN ('ACTIVE', 'PAYMENT_PROCESSING', 'CONFIRMED');

Including CONFIRMED makes this a one-purchase-per-user-sale policy as well as one-live-hold policy. A failed-capture cancellation must transition ownership and release the unit atomically under the documented repurchase policy. The ER diagram shows historical reservations; the partial unique index limits current ownership. The exact partial-index syntax depends on the database. If unsupported, enforce the invariant through a dedicated ownership table whose key is (sale_id, user_id).

docs.title: 9.3 Why SKIP LOCKED?
docs.text:
Without it, many workers may wait behind the first available row. SKIP LOCKED lets each transaction claim a different unlocked unit. Preassign units to allocation buckets and vary the starting bucket to reduce index-page contention.

An empty SKIP LOCKED result means no matching unlocked row was found, not proof of sold out: another transaction may still roll back its claim. Return a bounded retry/admission outcome unless canonical committed inventory proves exhaustion. The application must also abort the transaction if the select returns no unit or the conditional update affects zero rows; never insert a reservation using an unset or stale unit_id. The count-based alternative below must commit the counter change, reservation, idempotency result, and outbox together, rolling back the decrement on a uniqueness conflict. Test two concurrent requests from one user and a locked last unit whose owner rolls back.

docs.title: 9.4 Count-based alternative
docs.text:
A minimal approach is:

UPDATE sale_inventory
SET available = available - 1,
    reserved = reserved + 1,
    version = version + 1
WHERE sale_item_id = :sale_item_id
  AND available > 0;

If one row is updated, the reservation won. This is correct and often sufficient after the waiting room limits admission. Its bottleneck is serialization on one hot row. Mention it first in an interview, then evolve to buckets or unit tokens only if required by measured throughput.

docs.title: 9.5 Bucketed inventory
docs.text:
Split a SKU's units across a bounded number of inventory buckets:

item:size9:bucket0 -> 25 units
item:size9:bucket1 -> 25 units
...
item:size9:bucket39 -> 25 units

For an even illustrative split across ten variants, size 9 has 1,000 units across these forty buckets; the full sale has 10,000.

Route an admitted user to a bucket using a hash, then probe another bucket if necessary. Each bucket is a single-writer or atomically updated partition. The sum of configured bucket quotas equals physical inventory, so buckets cannot collectively oversell.

Do not create more buckets than necessary. Excessive partitioning complicates utilization and rebalancing.

docs.title: 10.1 Why payment is a saga
docs.text: The inventory database and payment provider cannot participate in one atomic transaction. Failures can occur after either side commits. The workflow needs explicit state, idempotency, retries, compensation, and reconciliation.

docs.title: 10.2 Recommended checkout flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant O as Order Service
    participant R as Reservation Service
    participant P as Payment Orchestrator
    participant PSP as Payment Provider
    participant DB as Order and Inventory Stores

    C->>O: Start checkout for reservation
    O->>R: Begin payment processing
    R->>DB: CAS ACTIVE -> PAYMENT_PROCESSING
    DB-->>R: Processing deadline established
    R-->>O: Reservation protected briefly
    O->>DB: Create PENDING_PAYMENT order
    O->>P: Create payment attempt
    P->>PSP: Create/authorize payment with idempotency key
    PSP-->>C: Hosted payment or client flow
    PSP-->>P: Signed success webhook
    P->>O: PaymentAuthorized
    O->>R: Confirm reservation
    R->>DB: Transactionally mark unit SOLD and reservation CONFIRMED
    R-->>O: Inventory committed
    O->>DB: Mark order CAPTURE_PENDING
    O->>P: Capture payment if authorization/capture is separate
    P-->>O: verified capture or already-captured evidence
    O->>DB: Mark order CONFIRMED
    O-->>C: Order confirmed

Persist a unique order identity per reservation, not only per checkout request key. Retry or reconciliation reuses that order if a crash occurs after inventory enters processing but before order creation finishes; the bounded processing expiry repairs abandoned starts.

Prefer payment authorization followed by capture when the provider supports it:

  1. Authorize the amount without final settlement.
  2. Commit the inventory reservation to sold.
  3. Capture the authorization.
  4. Void the authorization if inventory confirmation unexpectedly fails.

If the provider captures immediately, a successful charge followed by failed local confirmation requires an automatic refund saga.

Capture timeout retains CAPTURE_PENDING and allocated inventory while the existing provider operation is resolved. A definitive capture failure starts an idempotent order-cancellation and inventory-release workflow before any fulfillment. Authorization alone does not prove capture, and a lost capture response is not failure.

docs.title: 10.3 Starting payment near expiry
docs.text:
When checkout starts before expires_at, conditionally transition:

ACTIVE -> PAYMENT_PROCESSING
