Set a short payment-processing deadline. Expiry workers no longer release ordinary ACTIVE TTL, but a separate timeout eventually releases abandoned PAYMENT_PROCESSING reservations.

This makes the boundary explicit: merely opening a checkout page should not extend inventory indefinitely, while a legitimate payment attempt gets a bounded grace period.

Processing expiry terminates the allocation, not an unknown provider operation. Fence that reservation from future confirmation before releasing its unit. Later authorization is voided and later capture refunded through the original payment identity; a delayed callback must never sell a unit reassigned to someone else.

docs.title: 10.4 Webhook and client race
docs.text:
Both the client and webhook may report success. Only signed provider status is authoritative. Process provider events with a uniqueness constraint:

UNIQUE (payment_provider, provider_event_id)

Every state transition checks the current order/payment version. Duplicate callbacks return success without repeating inventory or financial effects.

docs.title: 10.5 Order status
docs.text: The initial checkout response may be asynchronous. If the client times out, it polls GET /orders/{id} or receives a push notification. Never ask the user to pay again solely because the client did not receive the success response.

docs.title: 11. Deep Dive: Consistency Under Extreme Contention
11.1 The naive read-then-write bug
docs.text:
This is unsafe:

available = SELECT available FROM inventory
if available > 0:
    UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1

Thousands of requests can all read available = 1 before any update commits. The check and mutation must be one atomic conditional operation or transaction.

docs.title: 11.2 Correct approaches
docs.text: Approach Correctness Throughput Complexity Atomic conditional SQL decrement Strong Moderate per hot SKU Low Pessimistic row lock Strong Serialized Low Optimistic CAS with version Strong with retries Poor under extreme contention Medium Unit rows with SKIP LOCKED Strong Higher parallelism Medium Bucketed inventory ownership Strong if quotas are fixed High Medium-high Single-writer stream per inventory shard Strong ordered decisions High and predictable High Redis atomic script only Atomic in Redis, durability depends on setup Very high Hidden recovery risk

docs.title: 11.3 Recommended evolution
docs.text:
1. Start with an atomic SQL decrement and a waiting room.
  2. If one row cannot meet admitted throughput, split inventory into fixed buckets or unit tokens.
  3. If many simultaneous sales require predictable throughput, assign each inventory shard a single-writer command processor backed by a durable log.

The waiting room is not a correctness mechanism. It protects the correctness mechanism from unnecessary concurrency.

docs.title: 11.4 Single-writer allocation model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Admit[Admitted Requests] --> Commands[Durable Reservation Commands]
    Commands --> P0[Inventory Processor 0]
    Commands --> P1[Inventory Processor 1]
    Commands --> PN[Inventory Processor N]
    P0 --> S0[(Inventory Shard 0)]
    P1 --> S1[(Inventory Shard 1)]
    PN --> SN[(Inventory Shard N)]
    P0 --> Results[Reservation Results]
    P1 --> Results
    PN --> Results

Partition commands by inventory bucket so one processor owns transitions for that bucket. There is no concurrent writer inside a partition. The tradeoff is asynchronous response handling and careful failover so two processors never own the same partition simultaneously.

docs.title: 11.5 Redis in front of the database
docs.text:
A Redis Lua script can atomically decrement a hot counter, but treating Redis as the only inventory authority creates hard questions:

  • What happens after failover before asynchronous replication completes?
  • Can acknowledged reservations disappear?
  • How are database and Redis reconciled without overselling?
  • Can cache eviction or restore introduce stale inventory?

Use Redis for admission counters, rate limits, status projections, and locks only when their failure semantics are understood. If Redis allocates inventory, it must be configured and operated as a durable authority with a recovery design, not described casually as a cache.

docs.title: 12.1 Why not one timer per reservation?
docs.text: In-process timers disappear on restart, cannot coordinate across replicas, and are difficult to rebalance. Expiry must be recoverable from durable state.

docs.title: 12.2 Expiry index plus authoritative CAS
docs.text:
Use a time-ordered expiry index, such as a Redis sorted set or database index:

score  = expires_at epoch milliseconds
member = reservation_id

Workers claim due IDs in batches, but the inventory database decides whether expiry is still legal.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Z as Expiry Index
    participant W as Expiry Worker
    participant DB as Inventory DB
    participant K as Kafka

    W->>Z: Fetch reservation IDs due before now
    Z-->>W: Batch of IDs
    loop Each reservation
        W->>DB: CAS ACTIVE -> EXPIRED if expires_at <= now
        alt Transition won
            DB->>DB: RESERVED unit -> AVAILABLE in same transaction
            DB->>DB: Insert ReservationExpired outbox event
        else Already processing/confirmed/expired
            DB-->>W: No-op
        end
    end
    DB-->>K: Relay expiry events

The sorted set is an optimization and scheduling hint. If it loses data, a database sweeper repairs the gap:

SELECT reservation_id
FROM reservations
WHERE state = 'ACTIVE'
  AND expires_at <= now()
ORDER BY expires_at
LIMIT :batch_size
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Index (state, expires_at) and process bounded batches.

docs.title: 12.3 Delayed queues
docs.text: A delayed-message queue can schedule one expiry command per reservation. It simplifies normal processing but still needs an authoritative conditional state transition and periodic sweeper because messages may be duplicated, delayed, or lost beyond retention.

docs.title: 12.4 Payment versus expiry race
docs.text:
At the boundary, payment and expiry may execute concurrently:

  • Payment attempts ACTIVE -> PAYMENT_PROCESSING.
  • Expirer attempts ACTIVE -> EXPIRED.

Use a row lock or versioned compare-and-set. Exactly one transition wins. If expiry wins, checkout returns reservation expired. If payment processing wins, the normal expiry worker does not release the unit until the processing deadline.

docs.title: 12.5 Releasing inventory exactly once
docs.text: Release the inventory unit in the same transaction that transitions the reservation to EXPIRED or CANCELLED. A retry sees that the reservation is no longer active and performs no second increment.

docs.title: 13. Deep Dive: Millions of Simultaneous Arrivals
docs.text: The system cannot autoscale quickly enough at noon if it is cold at 11:59. Capacity and admission must be prepared before the event.

docs.title: 13.1 Virtual waiting room
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Users[Millions of Users] --> Edge[CDN / WAF / Bot Checks]
    Edge --> Queue[Virtual Waiting Room]
    Queue --> Status[(Distributed Queue State)]
    Controller[Admission Controller] --> Queue
    Metrics[Inventory and Service Health] --> Controller
    Queue -->|bounded admitted traffic| Reserve[Reservation API]
    Reserve --> Inventory[(Inventory Authority)]

The waiting room provides:

  • A stable place for excess users.
  • Bounded downstream concurrency.
  • A fairness policy.
  • Bot challenges and identity binding.
  • Estimated progress without hammering core services.

docs.title: 13.2 Admission rate
docs.text:
Admission should react to:

  • Remaining available inventory.
  • Active reservations and expected expiry rate.
  • Reservation-service p95/p99 latency.
  • Database lock wait and CPU.
  • Payment-provider health.
  • Error and timeout rates.

Use a conservative initial rate, then increase while SLOs remain healthy. Stop admitting when all units are sold and no meaningful reservation expiries remain.

docs.title: 13.3 Queue status delivery
docs.text:
Options:

  • Poll every 5-15 seconds with jitter.
  • Server-Sent Events for admitted state.
  • Edge-issued signed tokens containing coarse queue epochs.

Polling is operationally simple but can itself produce millions of QPS. Cache coarse queue-position bands at the edge and return Retry-After or nextPollAfterMs to control frequency.

Do not promise an exact position if batching, bot removal, or randomization can change it. Display a range or progress estimate.

docs.title: 13.4 Protecting downstream systems
docs.text:
• Pre-scale all critical services before the event.
  • Prewarm connections, caches, and database query plans.
  • Separate product-view capacity from reservation capacity.
  • Use bounded queues and reject excess work rather than allowing memory growth.
  • Apply per-user and per-device request limits.
  • Set short timeouts and circuit breakers around dependencies.
  • Degrade analytics, recommendations, and nonessential logging first.
  • Use load tests that reproduce a synchronized step function, not only gradual ramps.

docs.title: 13.5 Backpressure
docs.text: If the inventory database slows, reduce admissions immediately. Allowing the reservation-service queue to grow only turns a controlled slowdown into stale requests, timeouts, retries, and collapse.

docs.title: 14. Deep Dive: Fair Access to Limited Inventory
docs.text: "First come, first served" sounds fair but network distance, device speed, clock skew, and bots make it unequal.

docs.title: 14.1 Recommended policy
docs.text:
1. Open the waiting room before the sale.
  2. Collect eligible entrants during a published pre-sale window.
  3. At sale start, cryptographically randomize those entrants.
  4. Admit them in randomized order at a controlled rate.
  5. Append post-start arrivals in FIFO order or later randomized waves.
  6. Bind each queue entry and admission token to one account and device/session.

This is closer to a lottery among users who arrived on time and avoids rewarding millisecond-level races.

docs.title: 14.2 Fairness properties
docs.text:
• Document the policy before the event.
  • Use an auditable random seed committed before shuffling and revealed afterward when appropriate.
  • Ensure retries do not create new queue positions.
  • Preserve order across waiting-room failover.
  • Expire admission tokens quickly and make them single-purpose.
  • Do not allow queue tokens to be transferred between accounts.

docs.title: 14.3 Bot mitigation
docs.text:
• Require authenticated, verified accounts for reservation.
  • Apply CAPTCHA or proof-of-work selectively before queue admission.
  • Use device, IP, ASN, behavioral, and account-age signals.
  • Rate-limit account creation and payment instruments.
  • Enforce one live queue entry and reservation per account.
  • Detect token sharing and scripted checkout velocity.
  • Run suspicious winners through a fast fraud check without blocking every user equally.

Bot detection should reject or deprioritize with explainable policy. False positives during a scarce sale are costly.

docs.title: 14.4 Avoiding hidden unfairness
docs.text:
• Route all regions into the same logical policy rather than giving one region earlier sale activation.
  • Use server time, never client time.
  • Publish the sale start through one authoritative control plane.
  • Make admission independent of repeated refresh frequency.
  • Do not let internal retries consume a user's one opportunity.

docs.title: 15. Idempotency and Retry Semantics
docs.text:
Every mutation needs a stable idempotency key:

Operation Idempotency scope Stored result Join waiting room (sale_id, user_id) Queue entry and status token Reserve (user_id, idempotency_key) Reservation or terminal sold-out response Start checkout (reservation_id, idempotency_key) Order and PSP session PSP request Provider merchant key Provider payment reference Webhook Provider event ID Processing outcome Expire reservation Reservation state/version Conditional no-op or expiry result

In the selected design, reservation idempotency and the business mutation commit atomically in the inventory database. A separate response cache is only a projection. Financial retry safety additionally depends on the provider's documented idempotency horizon, not only a stable local key.

Responses should distinguish:

  • Definitive success.
  • Definitive sold out or expired.
  • Retryable overload.
  • Unknown outcome requiring status lookup.

Blind retries with new keys can create duplicate payments or consume additional capacity.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Partition by (sale_id, sale_item_id, allocation_bucket). Keep all transitions for a bucket on one database shard or single-writer partition.

Inventory units and their active reservations must be colocated in the same transactional shard. Diagrams show them as separate logical stores for ownership clarity, but claiming, confirming, expiring, or cancelling a reservation must update both sets of tables in one local transaction.

The baseline keeps all buckets for one sale in the same database uniqueness domain, including (sale_id,user_id) and idempotency records. Splitting buckets across independent databases would make a per-shard unique index insufficient for the one-reservation-per-sale rule. That evolution needs a durable sale/user claim protocol or a product restriction to one stable allocation shard per user; do not assume SQL uniqueness becomes global.

docs.title: Reservations
docs.text:
Primary reads occur by reservation ID, user and sale, and expiry time. Maintain:

  • Primary key on reservation_id.
  • Unique ownership key on (sale_id, user_id) for live claims.
  • Expiry index on (state, expires_at).
  • Inventory ownership key on unit_id.

docs.title: Orders and payments
docs.text: Partition by user or order ID, but retain direct indexes by reservation and provider reference. Keep financial state in a dedicated store with immutable ledger entries.

docs.title: Queue entries
docs.text:
Partitioning depends on fairness policy. A globally ordered per-sale queue is a hot logical stream. Store it as append-only segments with a sequence allocator or assign randomized ranks deterministically and partition by rank range.

The queue need not support arbitrary sorting on every status request. Store the user's assigned rank and a global admitted watermark.

approximate users ahead = max(0, user_rank - admitted_watermark)

docs.title: 17. Availability and Consistency Choices
docs.text:
Path or data Choice Reasoning Product page Highly available, eventually consistent Stale description or coarse availability is acceptable Queue status Highly available, slightly stale Exact position is not a correctness invariant Admission token Strong validation Prevent replay and bypass Inventory allocation Strong consistency Overselling is forbidden Reservation status Strong for transitions Payment and expiry races require one winner Availability counters Eventual projection Display does not allocate inventory Payment ledger Durable and strongly auditable Financial side effects must reconcile Analytics At-least-once, eventually aggregated Must not block purchases

During a network partition, the inventory authority should reject or pause allocations if it cannot guarantee exclusive ownership. This is a CP choice for the scarce-resource mutation, while public reads remain AP-style through caches.

docs.title: 18.1 Separate global reads from authoritative writes
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    DNS[Geo DNS / Anycast] --> US[US Edge and Waiting Room]
    DNS --> EU[EU Edge and Waiting Room]
    DNS --> AP[APAC Edge and Waiting Room]

    US --> GlobalAdmission[Global Sale Admission Policy]
    EU --> GlobalAdmission
    AP --> GlobalAdmission

    GlobalAdmission --> Home[Inventory Home Region]
    Home --> Primary[(Inventory Primary)]
    Primary --> Standby[(Synchronous AZ Standby)]

    Primary --> Events[Global Event Stream]
    Events --> USCache[(US Availability Cache)]
    Events --> EUCache[(EU Availability Cache)]
    Events --> APCache[(APAC Availability Cache)]

Product reads and waiting-room status are regional. Inventory for one sale or bucket has one active home region to prevent split-brain allocation. The home region spans availability zones with synchronous replication.

docs.title: 18.2 Regional fairness
docs.text:
A single global ordering may disadvantage users with longer network paths. The waiting room can admit regional quotas proportional to eligible entrants, while inventory buckets reserve corresponding quotas. Unused regional quotas can return to a global pool after a published interval.

This improves geographic fairness but adds policy and capacity complexity. For an interview, first choose one global waiting room and home-region allocator, then discuss regional quotas as an extension.

docs.title: 18.3 Failover
docs.text:
Inventory failover must use fencing:

  • A lease epoch identifies the active allocator.
  • Every write includes the current epoch.
  • The database rejects stale-epoch writers.
  • Promotion waits until the new primary has all committed state.

Availability is secondary to preventing two regions from allocating the same units.

docs.title: 19. Transactional Outbox and Events
docs.text:
Inventory transitions should commit an event in the same database transaction:

ReservationCreated
ReservationPaymentStarted
ReservationExpired
ReservationCancelled
ReservationConfirmed
InventoryBecameAvailable
SaleSoldOut
OrderCreated
PaymentAuthorized
PaymentCaptured
PaymentFailed
RefundRequested

flowchart LR
    Service[Reservation or Order Service] --> DB[(Business Tables + Outbox)]
    DB --> Relay[Outbox Relay]
    Relay --> Kafka[Kafka]
    Kafka --> Projection[Availability Projection]
    Kafka --> Notification[Notification Service]
    Kafka --> Analytics[Analytics]
    Kafka --> Audit[Audit Store]
    Kafka --> Reconcile[Reconciliation Workers]

At-least-once delivery is expected. Include event ID, entity ID, entity version, sale ID, trace ID, and schema version. Consumers ignore duplicates and stale entity versions.

Do not use eventual events to enforce immediate inventory ownership. Events propagate results after the authoritative transaction.

docs.title: CDN or product cache failure
docs.text:
• Fall back through regional caches to the catalog database.
  • Serve a static sale page with minimal dynamic state.
  • Protect the catalog database with rate limits and stale responses.

docs.title: Waiting room failure
docs.text:
• Stop new admissions rather than route everyone to inventory.
  • Continue honoring already issued, valid admission tokens.
  • Recover queue state and admitted watermark from durable storage.
  • Extend admission-token validity cautiously if the outage consumed users' windows.

docs.title: Reservation service failure after commit
docs.text: The client may see a timeout even though the reservation succeeded. A retry with the same idempotency key returns the committed result. The user can also query their active reservation.

docs.title: Inventory database failure
docs.text:
• Stop allocations until a fenced primary is available.
  • Continue product views and queue waiting.
  • Do not fail open or use a stale replica for allocations.

docs.title: Expiry worker failure
docs.text:
• Reservations remain unavailable longer but are not oversold.
  • Replacement workers resume from the expiry index.
  • A database sweeper catches missed expirations.
  • Alert on oldest overdue active reservation.

docs.title: Payment provider outage
docs.text:
• Stop or slow admission if winners cannot pay.
  • Allow existing reservations a bounded extension according to published policy.
  • Use circuit breakers and provider failover only if payment intent portability is understood.
  • Never silently submit the same charge to two providers.

docs.title: Payment succeeds but callback is lost
docs.text:
• Poll provider status for unresolved payment attempts.
  • Consume provider webhooks with retries.
  • Run periodic ledger reconciliation.
  • Keep the reservation in PAYMENT_PROCESSING until its processing deadline.

docs.title: Payment captured but inventory confirmation fails
docs.text:
• Retry the idempotent confirmation if the reservation still owns the unit.
  • If confirmation is impossible, create an automatic refund and notify the user.
  • Record both financial entries in an immutable ledger.

docs.title: Kafka unavailable
docs.text:
• Authoritative transactions continue with outbox rows.
  • Availability UI and analytics become stale.
  • Relay events after recovery.
  • Alert on oldest unrelayed outbox record.

docs.title: 21. Reconciliation and Audit
docs.text: Asynchronous and external systems require continuous repair.

docs.title: Inventory reconciliation
docs.text:
For each sale item, verify:

configured units
  = AVAILABLE unit rows
  + units owned by ACTIVE reservations
  + units owned by PAYMENT_PROCESSING reservations
  + SOLD units

Compare unit rows, reservation ownership, aggregate counters, and confirmed orders. Never repair by blindly increasing availability; determine the authoritative owner first.

docs.title: Payment reconciliation
docs.text:
• Compare provider settlement reports with local payment attempts.
  • Find authorized but uncaptured payments.
  • Find captures without confirmed orders.
  • Find refunds requested but not completed.
  • Produce an operator queue for ambiguous cases.

docs.title: Fairness audit
docs.text:
Retain:

  • Queue-entry time and assigned randomized rank.
  • Randomization algorithm version and committed seed reference.
  • Admission time and token identity.
  • Bot or eligibility decision reason.
  • Reservation decision and inventory bucket.

Avoid retaining more device or identity data than policy requires.

docs.title: 22. Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text:
• Sign queue, admission, and checkout tokens with key rotation.
  • Bind admission tokens to user, sale, expiry, and intended action.
  • Mark tokens as used atomically or make their effect idempotent.
  • Authenticate every reservation and checkout mutation.
  • Apply WAF, DDoS controls, and per-identity rate limits at the edge.
  • Protect sale configuration changes with strict authorization and audit.
  • Verify payment webhook signatures and timestamps.
  • Never store raw card data unless operating within the required compliance scope.
  • Encrypt personal and financial data.
  • Redact secrets from logs and traces.
  • Detect queue token marketplaces and account/payment-instrument reuse.

Rate limits should not punish normal retries caused by the system itself. Make clients obey server-provided retry intervals.

docs.title: User-facing SLIs
docs.text:
• Product-page p50/p95/p99 latency and edge hit rate.
  • Queue join and status availability.
  • Admission-to-reservation latency.
  • Reservation success, sold-out, conflict, and unknown-outcome rates.
  • Checkout conversion and payment latency.
  • Duplicate-charge and refund rates.

docs.title: Correctness metrics
docs.text:
• Invariant violations by sale item.
  • Units without a valid owner.
  • Multiple live reservations per user or unit.
  • Confirmed orders without sold inventory.
  • Captured payments without confirmed orders.
  • Double-release attempts.

Any nonzero oversell or duplicate-charge metric should page immediately.

docs.title: Contention and capacity
docs.text:
• Database lock-wait time and transaction aborts.
  • Allocation throughput by inventory bucket.
  • Reservation-service queue depth.
  • Admission rate and admitted watermark.
  • Waiting-room population and estimated drain time.
  • Idempotency hit rate and client retry volume.
  • Expiry lag and oldest overdue reservation.

docs.title: End-to-end tracing
docs.text: Propagate one trace ID across queue admission, reservation, order, PSP request, webhook, and confirmation events. Sample ordinary failures and retain all ambiguous financial outcomes.

docs.title: Correctness tests
docs.text:
• Run thousands of concurrent claims against one remaining unit and assert exactly one winner.
  • Race payment start against expiry repeatedly.
  • Deliver every webhook and event multiple times.
  • Crash services after each transaction boundary.
  • Retry timed-out reservations with the same and different idempotency keys.
  • Verify that cancellation and expiry cannot release the same unit twice.

docs.title: Load tests
docs.text:
• Model a vertical traffic step at the sale start, not a gradual ramp.
  • Include synchronized client retries and queue-status polling.
  • Test one hot SKU and skewed size preferences.
  • Run at least the expected breaking point, not only target load.
  • Include cache misses, cold connections, and dependency latency.

docs.title: Failure tests
docs.text:
• Kill the active allocator and validate fencing during failover.
  • Pause Kafka and expiry workers.
  • Fail Redis and the waiting-room state replica.
  • Delay or duplicate PSP callbacks.
  • Return ambiguous PSP timeouts after successful authorization.
  • Test database failover while reservations are committing.

docs.title: Shadow and rehearsal
docs.text: Run a full production-like rehearsal with synthetic inventory and traffic. Verify dashboards, paging, rollback controls, queue messaging, and operator runbooks before the public event.

docs.title: Database transactions versus distributed locks
docs.text: Prefer database conditional writes or row locks when inventory lives in that database. A separate distributed lock adds another failure mode and does not make the subsequent database mutation atomic by itself.

docs.title: Counted inventory versus unit tokens
docs.text: Counted inventory is the smallest correct design and may be enough after admission control. Unit tokens or buckets improve parallelism and auditability but add rows and allocation logic. Evolve only when the hot-row limit is real.

docs.title: Synchronous reservation versus queued command
docs.text: Synchronous reservation gives immediate decisions after admission. A durable single-writer command stream provides predictable ordering and throughput but turns the API asynchronous. Both can work; the waiting room already provides user-visible queueing, so synchronous database allocation is simpler initially.

docs.title: Short versus long reservation TTL
docs.text: A short TTL recycles inventory quickly but punishes slow payment methods and accessibility needs. A long TTL improves checkout completion but lets abandoned reservations hide inventory. Choose from measured payment latency and publish the timer clearly.

docs.title: Strict FIFO versus randomized admission
docs.text: Strict FIFO rewards low network latency and bots at the exact start time. Randomizing users present before the sale is usually more equitable, while FIFO can govern later arrivals. Fairness is a product requirement, not only a data-structure choice.

docs.title: Availability versus inventory correctness
docs.text: For product reads, serve stale data. For allocation, stop when exclusive ownership is uncertain. It is better to delay a purchase than sell the same unit twice.

docs.title: 26. Final Design
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Request[1. Admit and allocate]
      Clients[Clients] --> Edge[CDN and WAF]
      Edge --> Waiting[Virtual waiting room]
      Health[Inventory and service health] --> Admission[Bounded admission controller]
      Admission --> Waiting
      Waiting --> Queue[(Durable queue state)]
      Waiting -->|signed admission| Gateway[API gateway]
      Gateway --> Reservation[Reservation service]
      Reservation --> State[(Inventory, reservations, idempotency and outbox records)]
      Gateway --> Order[Order service]
      Order --> Reservation
      Order --> Ledger[(Orders and payment ledger)]
      Order --> Pay[Payment orchestrator]
      Pay <--> PSP[External PSP]
    end
    subgraph Events[2. Publish committed changes]
      Outbox[(Same committed outbox)] --> Relay[Outbox relay]
      Relay --> Kafka[Kafka]
      Kafka --> Projection[Availability projection]
      Projection --> Cache[(Regional product caches)]
      Cache --> CDN[CDN sale page]
      Kafka --> Audit[Immutable audit and notifications]
      Kafka --> Timer[Expiry workers]
    end
    subgraph Recovery[3. Repair and reconcile]
      Expiry[Expiry workers and DB sweeper] --> Conditional[Conditional expiry transition]
      Conditional --> Authority[(Same inventory and reservation records)]
      Reconcile[Inventory and payment reconciliation] --> Authority
      Reconcile --> PaymentState[(Same orders and payment ledger)]
    end

Read these as three views of the same system. Boxes labeled “same” repeat the existing stores, not additional databases. The first view groups reservation-owned records for readability; the transactional boundaries and uniqueness rules are defined above. Expiry workers in the event view feed the conditional recovery path.

docs.title: End-to-end behavior
docs.text:
1. The CDN serves the product page and media without touching core databases.
  2. The edge waiting room authenticates entrants, mitigates bots, establishes fair order, and absorbs millions of excess requests.
  3. The admission controller releases traffic according to remaining inventory and service health.
  4. The reservation service atomically claims a counted, bucketed, or unit-token inventory record and creates a time-bounded reservation.
  5. Database uniqueness constraints enforce one live reservation per user and one owner per unit.
  6. Checkout transitions the reservation into a bounded payment-processing state instead of holding a database transaction open.
  7. The payment orchestrator uses provider idempotency, signed webhooks, and preferably authorization before capture.
  8. Inventory confirmation atomically marks the reservation confirmed and unit sold; financial compensation handles rare cross-system failures.
  9. Expiry workers use a time index for efficiency and a conditional database transition for correctness; a sweeper repairs missed timers.
  10. Outbox events update coarse availability, notifications, analytics, and audit stores without participating in the allocation transaction.
  11. Reconciliation continuously checks inventory equations and external payment settlement.

docs.title: Why is a reservation necessary?
docs.text: Payment takes seconds and happens in an external system. Holding a lock throughout payment would serialize users and fail during PSP latency. A durable reservation removes one unit immediately and gives checkout a bounded window.

docs.title: How do you guarantee no overselling?
docs.text: Make one strongly consistent store authoritative and claim inventory through an atomic conditional write, locked unit row, or exclusively owned inventory bucket. Every retry is idempotent, and no cache is trusted for allocation.

docs.title: Is an atomic SQL decrement enough?
docs.text: Often yes, especially when a waiting room limits admitted concurrency. It is the smallest correct solution. If the single row becomes a measured bottleneck, evolve to fixed buckets or unit tokens.

docs.title: How do expired reservations return inventory?
docs.text: An expiry index schedules candidates, but a conditional database transition decides whether expiry wins. The reservation becomes expired and the unit available in one transaction. A database sweeper handles missed scheduled work.

docs.title: What if payment succeeds exactly as the reservation expires?
docs.text: Payment start and expiry compete through a versioned state transition. If payment moves ACTIVE to PAYMENT_PROCESSING first, it gets a short protected deadline. If expiry moves it to EXPIRED first, checkout cannot proceed. Only one transition wins.

docs.title: How do you absorb ten million requests in ten seconds?
docs.text: Serve public content from the CDN, put users into a virtual waiting room at the edge, issue status updates at controlled intervals, and admit only a bounded rate based on inventory and database health.

docs.title: How is the sale fair?
docs.text: Randomize authenticated entrants present during a published pre-sale window, then admit them at a controlled rate. Bind rank and admission tokens to identity, make retries position-preserving, mitigate bots, and audit the randomization.

docs.title: Why not use Redis to decrement inventory?
docs.text: Redis scripts are fast and atomic, but using Redis as authority requires a durability, failover, fencing, and reconciliation design. It is safer to use Redis for admission and projections while a transactional database owns scarce inventory, unless Redis is explicitly engineered as the durable authority.

docs.title: What if the reservation response times out after committing?
docs.text: The client retries with the same idempotency key or queries its active reservation. The service returns the previously committed result rather than allocating a second unit.

docs.title: What if the PSP charges the user but the order remains pending?
docs.text: Webhooks and reconciliation discover the successful charge. Retry idempotent local confirmation if inventory is still owned; otherwise trigger an automatic refund and alert on the ambiguous workflow.

docs.title: L5 Expectations: Core
docs.text:
• Identifies the need for time-bounded reservations.
  • Defines product, inventory, reservation, order, and payment entities.
  • Uses an atomic database operation to prevent overselling.
  • Uses caching for product reads and idempotency for retries.
  • Explains basic reservation expiry and payment flow.

docs.title: L5 Expectations: Strong Signals
docs.text:
• Quantifies the synchronized burst and introduces a virtual waiting room.
  • Handles payment/expiry races with explicit state transitions.
  • Designs efficient expiry with a scheduling index and authoritative CAS.
  • Discusses hot-row evolution, outbox events, reconciliation, and degradation.
  • Defines an auditable fairness and bot-mitigation policy.

docs.title: L6 Expectations
docs.text:
• Separates edge admission, authoritative commerce, and asynchronous recovery planes.
  • Connects admission rate to service health and inventory state.
  • Designs fenced multi-region ownership, disaster recovery, and financial compensation.
  • Distinguishes correctness data from approximate projections and analytics.
  • Drives policy tradeoffs around fairness, accessibility, TTL, geographic allocation, and failure behavior.

docs.title: 29. Five-Minute Interview Summary
docs.text:
A flash sale has extreme synchronized demand for a tiny inventory pool. I would serve the product page and coarse availability through a CDN, while a virtual waiting room absorbs reservation attempts and establishes an auditable order. An admission controller releases only bounded traffic based on remaining inventory and database health, so millions of impossible requests never reach the authoritative path.

The reservation service is the sole inventory authority. It uses an atomic conditional decrement initially, or fixed inventory buckets/unit tokens if one hot row becomes a bottleneck. In one transaction it claims inventory, creates a five-minute reservation, and writes an outbox event. Database uniqueness constraints enforce one live reservation per user and one owner per unit. Idempotency keys make timeout retries safe.

Checkout is a saga because the payment provider and inventory database cannot share a transaction. Starting payment conditionally moves the reservation into a short PAYMENT_PROCESSING state, preventing an expiry race. Prefer payment authorization, then atomically convert reserved inventory to sold, then capture. Duplicate client callbacks and provider webhooks are idempotent, and reconciliation handles ambiguous outcomes or refunds.

Reservation expiries are scheduled through a time index, but the database performs the authoritative conditional transition and inventory release in one transaction. A periodic sweeper catches missed timers. The design favors highly available stale reads but stops allocations whenever exclusive inventory ownership is uncertain, because no overselling is the primary invariant.

docs.title: 30. Final Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Introduce a reservation between viewing and paying; never hold inventory locks during external payment.
  2. State no-oversell and ownership invariants before choosing technology.
  3. Use a CDN for public reads and a waiting room for synchronized demand.
  4. Let admission control reduce contention; do not confuse it with correctness.
  5. Start with the smallest correct atomic inventory mutation and evolve only when measured throughput requires buckets or unit tokens.
  6. Make every mutation and asynchronous consumer idempotent.
  7. Resolve payment, expiry, cancellation, and confirmation races with conditional state transitions.
  8. Schedule expiry efficiently, but let durable state decide whether release is legal.
  9. Treat payment as a saga with authorization, capture, compensation, and reconciliation.
  10. Keep exact inventory authority separate from cached availability projections.
  11. Define fairness explicitly through waiting-room policy, identity binding, bot defense, and auditability.
  12. Prefer stale availability over failure for reads, but pause allocation rather than risk split-brain overselling.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Scope the marketplace: restaurant discovery, menu and quote, order placement, restaurant acceptance, courier dispatch, and live tracking. State the order and assignment invariants, estimate meal-time peaks, and begin with one regional transactional order service plus simple radius matching. Then evolve dispatch, ETA, location ingestion, and regional cells only when their distinct workloads demand it.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Customers choose food, restaurants prepare it, and couriers deliver it. The system coordinates three independently failing actors under time pressure. Discovery tolerates stale data; price, payment, order transitions, and courier assignment do not. Human behavior means every estimate is probabilistic, so operators need safe manual controls.

Out of scope are restaurant settlement, recommendation models, route-navigation internals, and workforce employment policy.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Search open restaurants, read menus, and obtain a priced delivery quote.
  • Place and pay for an order; restaurant accepts or rejects it.
  • Assign one courier, coordinate pickup/drop-off, and show live status and ETA.
  • Cancel and refund according to the current stage.
  • Target 99.95% order-write availability, p99 placement under three seconds, and tracking freshness under ten seconds.
  • Isolate restaurant, neighborhood, provider, and regional overload.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. One checkout idempotency key creates at most one order and intended charge.
  2. An accepted order uses an immutable menu, fee, tax, address, and currency snapshot.
  3. An active courier has at most one incompatible active assignment; one delivery has at most one active courier.
  4. Order transitions follow a legal state machine and terminal states do not reopen.
  5. Payment success is eventually paired with fulfillment or policy-correct refund.
  6. Search, courier locations, ETAs, and maps are projections, not order authority.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 10 million orders/day, 20-times meal peaks, and 500,000 simultaneously online couriers. Orders average 115 QPS and peak around 2,500 QPS. Discovery peaks at 50,000 QPS. If couriers publish location every five seconds, ingestion reaches 100,000 updates/s. Order records and events at 10 KB/order add about 100 GB/day. Location history at 100 bytes/update, if that peak persists all day, would add 864 GB/day; actual daily volume scales with average online couriers, so retain high-resolution points briefly and downsample aggressively.

Traffic is geographically skewed. A rainstorm can double demand while reducing couriers in a small cell. Partition and overload policy must follow geography, not only user IDs.

docs.title: Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Restaurant(restaurant_id, region_id, status, hours, service_area, version)
MenuItem(item_id, restaurant_id, version, price, availability)
Quote(quote_id, customer_id, menu_version, lines, fees, tax, total, expires_at)
Order(order_id, customer_id, restaurant_id, quote_snapshot, address_snapshot,
      status, payment_status, idempotency_key, version, created_at)
Delivery(delivery_id, order_id, pickup, dropoff, status, courier_id, version)
Courier(courier_id, region_id, capability, availability_status, version)
Assignment(assignment_id, delivery_id, courier_id, lease_expires_at, status)
Location(courier_id, source_epoch, sequence, observed_at, geocell, coordinates)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

Orders and deliveries use relational storage and optimistic versions. Menus have immutable versions for quotes. Latest locations live in a geospatial in-memory store; compressed history goes to a time-series or object store. An assignment uniqueness constraint covers active delivery and courier.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
GET /v1/restaurants?lat=&lng=&query=&cursor=
GET /v1/restaurants/{id}/menu
POST /v1/quotes
POST /v1/orders
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"quote_id":"q1","payment_method_token":"pm1","address_id":"a1"}
POST /v1/restaurant-orders/{id}/accept
POST /v1/couriers/{id}/locations
{"source_epoch":7,"sequence":481,"observed_at":"...","lat":12.9,"lng":77.6}
GET /v1/orders/{id}/tracking

Quote expiry and menu version are explicit. Restaurant and courier mutations carry expected versions. Location batches carry a server-issued source epoch and increasing sequence within that epoch. A new authenticated device session advances the epoch before sequence restarts; delayed packets from prior epochs cannot replace the latest point. Historical points may be retained for analysis separately. Tracking supports snapshot plus a resumable event cursor.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Apps[Customer, restaurant, courier apps] --> Edge[Regional gateway]
    Edge --> Discovery[Discovery and menu]
    Discovery --> Search[(Geo search index)]
    Edge --> Orders[Order orchestrator]
    Orders --> ODB[(Order SQL)]
    Orders --> Payment[Payment service]
    ODB --> Stream[(Outbox and event stream)]
    Stream --> Dispatch[Dispatch service]
    Dispatch --> Geo[(Courier geo index)]
    Apps --> Location[Location ingestion]
    Location --> Geo
    Dispatch --> ODB
    Stream --> Tracking[Tracking projection]
    Tracking --> Apps

The baseline manually or greedily assigns the nearest eligible courier from one region. Only add a global optimizer once volume and batching improve outcomes enough to justify complexity.

docs.title: Discover and Quote
docs.text: Search filters restaurant documents by delivery polygon, opening schedule, cuisine, and approximate availability. Menu reads use versioned cache entries. Quote creation fetches canonical item availability, applies fees and tax, predicts delivery duration, and signs the result with an expiry. Search can show a restaurant that just closed; quote or order provides the authoritative rejection.

docs.title: Place and Accept Order
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Customer
    participant O as Orders
    participant D as SQL
    participant P as Payment
    participant R as Restaurant
    C->>O: Place(quote, key)
    O->>D: Persist order and payment intent
    O->>P: Authorize(order ID)
    P-->>O: verified authorization
    Note over O,P: UNKNOWN stays pending and does not enter the restaurant-offer branch
    O->>R: Offer order
    alt accepted before timeout
        R->>O: Accept(expected version)
        O->>D: ACCEPTED plus durable capture intent and outbox
        O->>P: Capture with stable operation identity
    else rejected or timeout
        O->>D: CANCEL_PENDING
        O->>P: Void/refund
    end

The payment/restaurant ordering is policy. Authorization before offer proves ability to pay but creates voids. Restaurant acceptance first risks wasted preparation if payment fails. The shown flow authorizes, offers for a bounded interval, and starts capture at acceptance. Persist capture outcome separately from restaurant state: unknown capture retains its reservation and is reconciled; a definitive decline follows a recorded stop-preparation or merchant-credit/compensation policy. Ambiguous payment returns processing and is reconciled, never blindly repeated.

docs.title: Dispatch and Delivery
docs.text:
Dispatch begins around restaurant acceptance, using predicted preparation time to avoid courier waiting. It queries eligible couriers in expanding geocells, scores candidates, and offers to a small batch. Acceptance performs a conditional transaction that verifies delivery unassigned and courier available, then creates an assignment lease. The winning courier receives route details; losing offers expire.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED
    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> RESTAURANT_ACCEPTED
    RESTAURANT_ACCEPTED --> PREPARING
    PREPARING --> COURIER_ASSIGNED
    COURIER_ASSIGNED --> PICKED_UP
    PICKED_UP --> DELIVERED
    CREATED --> CANCELLED
    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> CANCEL_PENDING
    RESTAURANT_ACCEPTED --> CANCEL_PENDING
    CANCEL_PENDING --> CANCELLED

This diagram is the combined happy-path overview. Store restaurant preparation, delivery assignment, and payment as separate state dimensions because preparation and courier assignment can overlap; a courier accepting early must not falsely mark food ready. Pickup and drop-off use short codes or signed proofs. Status commands are idempotent and validate actor, assignment, and prior state.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Dispatch
docs.text:
Start with nearest eligible courier plus simple penalties for distance and workload. At higher scale, score pickup ETA, food-ready estimate, drop-off direction, courier capacity, batching compatibility, and fairness. Matching is a lease, not a permanent fact: offers expire, courier disconnects trigger reassignment before pickup, and post-pickup failures go to human operations.

Batch every few seconds within a small zone to improve global choices, but cap wait because optimization can harm customer latency. Use shadow scoring and compare assignment acceptance, pickup lateness, miles, and courier earnings before changing policy. Keep the final conditional assignment in SQL even if candidate ranking runs in memory.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Location and Tracking
docs.text:
Courier devices publish (courier, source_epoch, sequence, observed_at, coordinates, accuracy). Ingestion authenticates the current device session, rejects impossible jumps, maps the point to a geocell, and conditionally replaces latest state only for a newer sequence in the authorized epoch. Epoch issuance and latest-state checks prevent a delayed prior session from overwriting a new session; clients cannot choose an arbitrarily high epoch. It emits a throttled stream for tracking and dispatch. Backpressure asks clients to reduce frequency; order writes take priority.

Customer tracking uses a privacy-reduced projection, not raw telemetry. Push updates are sampled and resumable. If location is stale, show last update and widen ETA rather than inventing motion. Delete precise history after the operational and safety retention window.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: ETA and Supply-Demand Imbalance
docs.text:
ETA combines preparation, courier-to-restaurant, waiting, route, parking, and handoff distributions. Return a range and update it on state changes. Features and model version are recorded for later explanation. Model outage falls back to conservative regional percentiles.

During imbalance, cap restaurant delivery radius, lengthen quoted ETA, pause overloaded restaurants, meter orders, and expose truthful availability. Surge fees may shape demand but require policy and fairness review. Unbounded dispatch queues merely convert overload into cancellations.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Cancellations
docs.text: Cancellation cost depends on stage. Before acceptance, void payment. During preparation, customer refund and restaurant compensation follow policy. After pickup, dispatch operations decide whether to return, dispose, or complete. Persist the policy version and reason. Compensation is asynchronous but visible. Concurrent restaurant accept, courier pickup, and customer cancel commands use versions so exactly one transition wins.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Create regional cells and partition active orders by delivery geography so restaurant, courier, and dispatch data are local. Keep all writes for an order in its home cell even if the customer travels. Geo-index couriers by hierarchical cells and update membership atomically enough for candidate discovery; final assignment remains canonical SQL. Large restaurant chains need per-location IDs to avoid hot keys.

Partition history by order ID and month, and analytics from events. Bound fan-out when querying adjacent geocells. Separate location ingestion capacity from command APIs so telemetry storms cannot block order transitions.

docs.title: Consistency, Idempotency, and Failures
docs.text:
Order transitions, payment intent, and assignments are strongly consistent. Search, ETA, location display, and notifications are eventual. Client keys and request hashes deduplicate order creation; every downstream operation derives a stable key from order and step. Outbox delivery is at least once and consumers upsert by event ID or version.

Restaurant app outage leaves offers pending only to a deadline. Payment outage preserves durable intents and limits new orders. Dispatch outage does not corrupt accepted orders; queue age triggers radius reduction and operator fallback. Location-store outage uses last known positions and stops broad admission if assignments become unsafe. Reconciliation scans paid-unfulfilled orders, duplicate active assignments, expired offers, and delivered orders not captured.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text: Markets are naturally cellular. One region owns a city's active orders with synchronous multi-zone storage; neighboring regions serve discovery replicas. Asynchronous disaster recovery requires both an enforced old-writer fence and an explicit acknowledged-state recovery policy. Recover or reconcile missing order, assignment, and payment identities before reissuing work; location updates from devices cannot reconstruct an authoritative lost payment or acceptance. In-flight delivery location is reconstructed from devices after failover; order state is replicated. Cross-border orders are generally disallowed, reducing global transaction needs. Central services distribute menu, model, fraud, and policy versions but regional data planes continue with last known safe versions.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Tokenize payment, encrypt addresses and phone numbers, proxy communications, and reveal exact addresses only to assigned couriers near the proper stage. Enforce actor-specific authorization for every transition. Detect fake GPS, courier/customer collusion, promotion abuse, account takeover, restaurant fraud, and denial-of-service. Pickup codes prevent casual theft; support access is audited and time-bound. Safety features and legal requests require separate privileged workflows.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Track order funnel, restaurant response, payment unknown age, dispatch queue time, offer acceptance, reassignment, preparation and pickup lateness, location freshness, ETA error, cancellation by stage, and regional saturation. Slice by city, restaurant, courier cohort, and app version. Alert on paid orders stuck without progress and active deliveries without fresh courier data.

Property-test order transitions and assignment uniqueness. Simulate duplicate commands, delayed callbacks, GPS reordering, restaurant disconnects, courier churn, rain-driven peaks, and zone failure. Replay historical city workloads against dispatch changes. Contract-test payment and push integrations. Run restore, regional fencing, and manual-operations drills.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Greedy dispatch is explainable and fast but less efficient than batching. Regional cells limit blast radius but may strand supply near boundaries. Fresher GPS improves matching while increasing battery, cost, and privacy exposure. Authorizing before restaurant acceptance increases voids but avoids unpaid preparation. Strong consistency belongs on order and assignment, not on every map point.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Global[Global discovery edge] --> Catalog[Menu and geo search]
    Global --> Cell[City home cell]
    Cell --> Order[Order state machine]
    Order --> SQL[(Orders, assignments, outbox)]
    Order --> Pay[Payment adapter]
    SQL --> Events[(Regional stream)]
    Events --> Dispatch[Bounded dispatch optimizer]
    Courier[Courier devices] --> Loc[High-volume location plane]
    Loc --> Geo[(Latest courier geo index)]
    Geo --> Dispatch
    Events --> Track[Customer tracking projection]
    Events --> Ops[Reconciliation and operations]
    SQL -. fenced DR .-> DR[(Recovery cell)]
    subgraph StateLane[Order authority and recovery]
      SQL
      DR
    end
    subgraph EventLane[Regional event consumers]
      Events
      Dispatch
      Track
      Ops
    end

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. When should payment be authorized and captured relative to restaurant acceptance?
  2. How do two couriers racing to accept one delivery resolve?
  3. How does dispatch work when courier locations are stale?
  4. Which overload controls help during a city-wide demand spike?
  5. How would order batching alter assignment invariants?
  6. How do you migrate a city between cells with active deliveries?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer models the order state machine, immutable quote, idempotent payment, unique courier assignment, geospatial search, and major failures. An L6 answer separates telemetry and command planes, defines marketplace overload policy, evaluates dispatch and ETA changes safely, handles cell migration and operations, and connects privacy, courier fairness, restaurant economics, and cost to design choices.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Food delivery coordinates customer, restaurant, and courier through one durable regional order state machine. Start with SQL, immutable quotes, idempotent payment, restaurant offer deadlines, and a simple nearest-courier matcher. Candidate discovery may be approximate, but a conditional transaction enforces one active courier per delivery and compatible assignment per courier. Keep high-volume location ingestion and geo indexing separate from order commands; stale tracking must never mutate canonical workflow. Outbox events drive dispatch, customer projections, and notifications with idempotent consumers. Partition by city, meter overload truthfully, and fence one active regional writer. Reconcile paid-but-stuck orders and expired assignments. Protect exact location and addresses, test state races and telemetry disorder, and add batch optimization only after measuring its effect on pickup latency, customer ETA, and courier outcomes.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify whether inventory represents exact rooms or room-type capacity, and whether the platform is merchant-of-record. This design searches hotels, prices date ranges, temporarily holds room-type inventory, confirms payment, and manages cancellation. State the per-night no-oversell invariant, estimate search-to-book skew, show a single SQL database first, then discuss date partitions, channel-manager races, and regional ownership.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Travelers search by destination and dates, compare properties, select a room and rate plan, and book. Hotels distribute the same rooms through direct and external channels, so inventory updates can be delayed. Search favors availability and speed; final booking must revalidate price, policy, and every night.

Assume one property and room type per reservation, though multiple rooms are allowed. Flights, loyalty accounting, reviews, and hotel property-management software are out of scope.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Search properties by destination, date range, guests, amenities, and price.
  • Return room offers with taxes, cancellation policy, and expiry.
  • Hold all requested room-nights, pay or guarantee, and confirm a reservation.
  • Modify or cancel according to policy; synchronize hotel/channel inventory.
  • Never exceed configured sellable capacity for any property, room type, and night.
  • Search p99 under 800 ms; booking p99 under three seconds excluding customer challenge.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. For every inventory key, confirmed plus active held plus non-overlapping external-reserved quantity never exceeds sellable capacity plus an explicit overbooking allowance. External reservations already represented in confirmed counts must not be counted twice.
  2. An accepted complete hold or confirmed reservation owns all required nights and rooms. Any explicitly modeled chunked preparation is incomplete, cannot be sold as a complete hold, and has durable cleanup for partial allocations.
  3. One guest-scoped idempotency key creates at most one reservation and intended charge.
  4. Confirmed price, taxes, currency, occupancy, and cancellation terms are immutable snapshots.
  5. Cancellation releases only inventory owned by that reservation and cannot refund beyond paid amount.
  6. Search and availability indexes are projections; booking inventory is canonical.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 5 million properties, 100 room types each, two years of sellable nights, 100 million searches/day, and 2 million bookings/day. Search averages 1,150 QPS and peaks around 15,000 QPS; booking peaks near 1,000 QPS. Materializing every room-type-night produces 365 billion rows, too many for sparse properties, so generate a rolling horizon only for active inventory and compress default availability ranges. A reservation averages four nights and roughly 5 KB including snapshots, about 10 GB/day.

Search fan-out and destination skew dominate. A holiday query for Paris touches thousands of properties, while booking contention concentrates on one room type and night.

docs.title: Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Property(property_id, owner_id, region_id, timezone, status, attributes)
RoomType(room_type_id, property_id, occupancy, amenities, default_capacity)
RatePlan(rate_plan_id, room_type_id, policy_version, pricing_rules)
NightInventory(property_id, room_type_id, local_date, sellable,
               held, confirmed, external_reserved, version)
Offer(offer_id, property_id, room_type_id, rate_plan_id, stay_dates,
      nightly_prices, taxes, policy_snapshot, total, expires_at)
Hold(hold_id, reservation_id, quantity, start_date, end_date, expires_at, status)
Reservation(reservation_id, guest_id, property_id, offer_snapshot,
            status, payment_status, idempotency_key, version)
InventoryMutation(mutation_id, source, source_ref, inventory_key, delta, created_at)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

NightInventory has primary key (property_id, room_type_id, local_date). Hotel-local dates are explicit; UTC conversion must not shift nights around daylight-saving changes. Mutation source references are unique to deduplicate channel updates.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
GET /v1/hotels/search?destination_id=&check_in=2027-06-01&check_out=2027-06-05&guests=2&cursor=
GET /v1/hotels/{id}/offers?check_in=&check_out=&rooms=1&guests=2
POST /v1/reservations
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"offer_id":"of1","rooms":1,"guest_id":"g1","payment_method_token":"pm1"}
GET /v1/reservations/{id}
POST /v1/reservations/{id}/cancellations
POST /v1/channel-inventory-events

Offers are signed, owned, and expiring. Booking may return 409 OFFER_CHANGED with a replacement offer, 202 PROCESSING, or a confirmed reservation. Search pagination uses a stable query snapshot or cursor containing ranking version and last sort tuple, not offsets.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Traveler --> Edge[CDN and API gateway]
    Edge --> Search[Hotel search]
    Search --> Index[(Property and availability index)]
    Edge --> Offer[Offer and pricing service]
    Offer --> Inventory[Inventory service]
    Edge --> Booking[Reservation orchestrator]
    Booking --> Inventory
    Booking --> DB[(Reservation SQL)]
    Booking --> Payment[Payment service]
    DB --> Stream[(Outbox and event stream)]
    Inventory --> Stream
    Stream --> Index
    Channel[Hotel and OTA channels] --> Sync[Channel manager]
    Sync --> Inventory
    subgraph SearchLane[Discovery]
      Search
      Index
    end
    subgraph ReserveLane[Reservation]
      Booking
      DB
      Payment
    end
    subgraph InventoryLane[Supply and pricing]
      Offer
      Inventory
      Channel
      Sync
    end

Initially inventory and reservations share one SQL database, allowing room-night hold and reservation creation in one transaction. Separation comes later if ownership or throughput requires a saga.

docs.title: Search and Offer
docs.text:
Search queries a geospatial/text property index and a coarse availability projection such as minimum capacity over date buckets. It ranks candidates, then fans out in bounded batches to offer service for accurate prices on the top set. Slow properties are omitted or marked unavailable rather than delaying the page. The response carries as_of; final offer creation reads newer inventory and pricing.

Offer service evaluates occupancy, nightly rate rules, promotions, taxes, fees, and cancellation policy in property local time. It returns a snapshot but does not hold inventory. Caching keys include property, room type, dates, occupancy, currency, and rule versions to avoid price leakage between contexts.

docs.title: Book a Stay
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T as Traveler
    participant B as Booking
    participant D as SQL
    participant P as Payment
    T->>B: Reserve(offer, rooms, key)
    B->>D: Lock each night in date order
    B->>D: Check capacity and create hold and reservation
    B->>D: COMMIT hold, reservation, idempotency and outbox then release locks
    B->>P: Authorize/reserve payment(order ID)
    alt payment succeeds
        B->>D: Convert held to confirmed plus outbox
        B-->>T: CONFIRMED
    else decline
        B->>D: Release hold and mark failed
        B-->>T: payment failed
    else timeout
        B->>D: Mark PAYMENT_UNKNOWN
        B-->>T: 202 processing
    end

Lock nights in ascending date order to avoid deadlocks. Check confirmed + held + external_reserved + rooms <= sellable + allowance for every night. One transaction holds all nights or none. Payment ambiguity is reconciled using the same provider operation; expiration is logically enforced even if the sweeper is delayed.

docs.title: Cancel or Modify
docs.text: Cancellation reads the stored policy snapshot and current time in property timezone, computes penalty, conditionally changes state, releases confirmed inventory, and starts refund or collection. A modification is safer as an atomic inventory exchange: hold new dates, calculate difference, adjust payment, then release old dates. If cross-partition atomicity is unavailable, create the new reservation first and expose MODIFICATION_PENDING until compensation completes.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Date-Range Inventory
docs.text:
A booking touches every night in [check_in, check_out). Per-night rows make the invariant explicit and support variable capacity, stop-sell flags, and maintenance. For long stays, transaction size grows; cap stay length or reserve in chunks under one coordinator while withholding confirmation until all succeed. A range representation saves rows but makes overlapping updates and constraints much harder.

Availability projection can store the minimum remaining rooms for common windows or use per-night bitmaps/counts. It may produce false positives that booking rejects, but should avoid false negatives where practical. Search index updates coalesce many inventory mutations to prevent a popular property from flooding the stream.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> PENDING_PAYMENT
    PENDING_PAYMENT --> CONFIRMED: payment verified and all holds still owned
    PENDING_PAYMENT --> PAYMENT_UNKNOWN
    PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> CONFIRMED: payment resolved and all holds still owned
    PAYMENT_UNKNOWN --> FAILED
    PENDING_PAYMENT --> FAILED
    CONFIRMED --> MODIFYING
    MODIFYING --> CONFIRMED
    CONFIRMED --> CANCEL_PENDING
    CANCEL_PENDING --> CANCELLED
    CONFIRMED --> CHECKED_IN
    CHECKED_IN --> COMPLETED

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: External Channels
docs.text:
Hotels may sell through several OTAs and send delayed absolute counts or deltas. Assign each source event a unique ID and version. Prefer reservations and allocations over blind count replacement. A hotel can allocate bounded inventory pools per channel, reducing oversell risk at the cost of stranded capacity. A central channel manager can rebalance pools and publish stop-sell when remaining capacity is low.

When external truth conflicts, never silently delete a confirmed guest. Flag overbooking, stop further sales, and invoke property operations to relocate or honor based on policy. Reconciliation compares platform reservations, hotel acknowledgments, and channel reports per room-night.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Pricing and Policy Snapshots
docs.text:
Rates vary by night, occupancy, refundable status, meal plan, taxes, and promotions. Use integer minor units, explicit tax inclusion, and deterministic rounding. The offer records every nightly component and rule version. At booking, verify expiry and optionally tolerate only customer-favorable changes. A later policy edit cannot alter an existing reservation's cancellation charge.

For hotel-collected payment, the platform stores a guarantee token and commission claim rather than pretending capture occurred. Data and state names must distinguish platform-paid, hotel-paid, and pay-at-property flows.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Hold Expiry and Overbooking
docs.text:
Logical expiry lets a new transaction reclaim a hold at expires_at <= database_time by atomically changing its status and releasing its held counters before reusing that capacity. Sweepers release rows in batches and emit projection updates. Payment challenges may extend holds up to a strict cap. Attackers who repeatedly hold rooms face per-account, device, and payment-instrument limits.

Confirmation must conditionally consume the still-owned hold for every night under the same locks as expiry. If expiry wins, retain the external payment as unknown until resolved; late success triggers void/refund rather than confirming a stay against reallocated rooms. A modification reserves only the incremental per-night quantity beyond its existing allocation, so unchanged nights do not require double capacity. Never hold the room-night SQL transaction open during the payment call.

Overbooking is an explicit property-controlled allowance derived from expected cancellation/no-show rates, never an accidental race. Store the allowance and policy version per night, cap it operationally, and display exposure to hotels.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition inventory by property ID so all nights and room types for one property remain local. Partition reservations by property when property operations dominate, or by reservation ID with a lookup if guest history dominates. A giant chain is not one property key. Search indexes partition by geography and replicate popular destinations.

For destination bursts, cache property documents and fan out only to ranked candidates with a strict budget. Inventory shard backpressure rejects expensive broad offer requests before booking writes. Repartition properties between shards by snapshot, change log, verification, and a routing epoch; avoid moving during peak booking windows.

docs.title: Consistency, Idempotency, and Failures
docs.text:
Room-night counters, holds, reservation state, and policy snapshots are strongly consistent. Search, price sorting, notifications, and hotel dashboards are eventual. Idempotency records include request hash. Payment, inventory, channel, and refund commands use stable business references. Outbox events are delivered at least once and projections apply only newer aggregate versions.

Database failure rejects new bookings but cached search continues with an availability warning. Search outage falls back to curated destinations or no results without affecting reservations. Payment timeout creates processing state. Channel outage queues bounded updates and lowers or stops channel allocation before stale inventory becomes unsafe. Reconciliation finds paid-unconfirmed reservations, expired holds, counter mismatches, and unacknowledged hotel bookings.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text: Assign each property a home region close to its inventory owner and legal requirements. Global search and offer reads use replicated projections; booking routes to the property home. Synchronous multi-zone writes provide normal resilience. Disaster recovery uses asynchronous replication and requires fencing the old region and advancing a property routing epoch before sale resumes. The promoted inventory must also include the required acknowledged reservation and mutation prefix; an epoch cannot recover bookings lost under asynchronous RPO. Reconcile or recover missing evidence before reallocating potentially sold nights. If fencing is uncertain, pause that property's booking rather than risk oversell. Control-plane policy can be global, but signed last-known versions let regional booking continue safely.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Tokenize payment cards and restrict guarantee-token access. Encrypt guest identity, addresses, and stay details; those records create physical-safety risk. Authenticate hotels and sign channel callbacks. Rate limit scraping, credential stuffing, fake reservations, hold hoarding, promotion abuse, and card testing. Property content requires malware and fraud checks. Support access is purpose-bound and audited; privacy deletion pseudonymizes guest profiles while retaining required reservation and tax evidence.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Track search freshness, offer fan-out and timeout, price-change rate, booking conflict, lock wait, hold age, payment unknowns, channel lag, room-night reconciliation variance, overbooking exposure, and reservation acknowledgment. Slice by destination, property, room type, arrival date, channel, and shard. Alert on value and guest impact, especially arrivals soon.

Property-test date boundaries, capacity conservation, modifications, time zones, and cancellation calculations. Concurrency-test overlapping stays and lock ordering. Inject duplicate channel events, payment callbacks, stale projection, delayed sweeper, DST transitions, shard failover, and region fencing. Replay pricing changes in shadow mode and restore inventory from reservations plus mutation history.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Per-night rows consume storage but make overlap correctness tractable. Channel pools prevent oversell while stranding inventory. Global search improves discovery but final revalidation causes some disappointment. Property-home writes add cross-region latency but avoid global room-night consensus. Holds improve checkout completion but reduce availability and invite hoarding. Overbooking improves utilization only when explicitly governed.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Edge[Global search edge] --> Index[(Geo property and availability projections)]
    Edge --> Home[Property home region]
    Home --> Offer[Versioned offer service]
    Home --> Book[Reservation state machine]
    Book --> SQL[(Property-owned inventory and reservations)]
    Book --> Pay[Payment adapter]
    SQL --> Events[(Outbox and stream)]
    Events --> Index
    Events --> Notify[Guest and hotel notifications]
    Channels[Channel and hotel systems] --> Sync[Versioned channel sync]
    Sync --> SQL
    Recon[Room-night reconciliation] --> SQL
    SQL -. fenced DR .-> DR[(Recovery region)]

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. How do you atomically reserve a fourteen-night stay?
  2. What happens when a channel update conflicts with a confirmed reservation?
  3. Should inventory partition by property, room type, or date?
  4. How do property-local dates affect storage and expiry?
  5. How would multi-room or multi-property itineraries change the saga?
  6. Which overbooking policy belongs in product versus infrastructure?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer models per-night capacity, atomic range holds, immutable offers, idempotent payment, search staleness, and common failures. An L6 answer also handles channel disagreement, explicit overbooking policy, property routing and migration, modification sagas, legal/payment variants, reconciliation operations, and the cost and guest-experience effects of stale global discovery.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Hotel booking is date-range inventory allocation. Keep canonical property + room type + local date counters in SQL and atomically lock all requested nights in date order. Search and coarse availability are scalable projections and may be stale; a signed expiring offer snapshots nightly prices, taxes, occupancy, and cancellation policy, and booking revalidates it. Create a bounded hold, invoke payment idempotently, then convert every held night to confirmed. Expiry is logical, with sweepers only cleaning up. Partition by property and assign each property one fenced home region. External channels use deduplicated versioned updates or bounded allocations; disagreements trigger stop-sell and reconciliation, not deletion of confirmed guests. Monitor upcoming-arrival exposure, test overlapping stays and timezone edges, and treat overbooking as explicit governed product policy.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify physical versus sellable stock, locations, reservations, transfers, and audit needs. State conservation invariants, estimate SKU-location cardinality and update rate, and begin with a relational stock ledger plus transactional balances. Trace reserve, receive, and transfer. Scale by SKU-location partitioning and regional allocation only after addressing hot SKUs, external warehouse events, reconciliation, and negative adjustments.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
The service answers how much of each SKU is available at each location and accepts stock movements from purchasing, warehouses, checkout, returns, and corrections. It reserves stock for orders, consumes it when shipped, and exposes projections for commerce channels. Physical reality can differ from software due to damage, theft, scanning mistakes, and delayed integrations, so audit and reconciliation are first-class.

Out of scope are warehouse route planning, catalog authoring, demand forecasting models, and accounting valuation beyond recording unit-cost references.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Receive, adjust, quarantine, transfer, and count stock by SKU and location.
  • Reserve, extend, release, and consume inventory for orders.
  • Query on-hand, reserved, unavailable, and available-to-promise quantities.
  • Publish channel availability and support cycle-count reconciliation.
  • Prevent unintended oversell under a configured safety-stock and oversell policy.
  • Sustain high-volume warehouse scans and checkout reservations with auditable history.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every quantity change is represented by an immutable, uniquely identified stock movement.
  2. Serving balances equal prior checkpoint plus accepted movements; corrections append rather than rewrite history.
  3. available_to_promise = on_hand - reserved - quarantined - safety_stock + allowed_oversell under one versioned policy.
  4. A reservation cannot be consumed or released for more than its remaining quantity.
  5. A transfer decreases available source stock before increasing destination stock; in-transit stock is explicit.
  6. One source operation ID has one logical effect despite retries and duplicate delivery.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100 million SKUs, 10,000 locations, but only 2 billion active SKU-location pairs. At 150 bytes per current balance plus indexes, the serving set is several hundred GB before replicas. Process 500 million movements/day, about 5,800 average and 60,000 peak writes/s. Reads from product pages may exceed one million QPS and must use regional availability projections. Warehouse devices can reconnect and upload large duplicate batches. A promoted SKU can receive tens of thousands of reservations per second on one logical balance.

The ledger adds roughly 100 GB/day at 200 bytes per movement and should move from hot partitions to compressed immutable storage by age while retaining checkpoints.

docs.title: Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
StockBalance(sku_id, location_id, on_hand, reserved, quarantined,
             in_transit_in, safety_stock, allowed_oversell, version)
StockMovement(movement_id, sku_id, location_id, type, quantity,
              source_type, source_id, movement_kind, line_id,
              occurred_at, accepted_at, metadata)
Reservation(reservation_id, order_id, sku_id, location_id, requested,
            remaining, status, expires_at, version)
Transfer(transfer_id, source_location, destination_location, status, version)
TransferLine(transfer_id, sku_id, shipped, received, damaged)
CountSession(count_id, location_id, scope, status, snapshot_version)
AllocationPool(pool_id, sku_id, region_or_channel, allocated, consumed, version)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

StockMovement has unique (source_type, source_id, movement_kind, line_id). StockBalance is a transactionally maintained projection for low-latency checks. Database constraints reject negative quantities where policy disallows them. Define quarantined as on-hand units excluded from the sellable pool and avoid counting a unit as both sellably reserved and quarantined. Damage to already reserved stock triggers an explicit shortage/reallocation workflow; rejecting the physical adjustment would hide reality.

docs.title: APIs and Interfaces
docs.text:
GET /v1/inventory/{skuId}?location_id=&region_id=
POST /v1/reservations
Idempotency-Key: order-91-line-2
{"order_id":"o91","sku_id":"s7","quantity":3,"candidate_locations":["l1","l2"]}
POST /v1/reservations/{id}/consume
POST /v1/reservations/{id}/release
POST /v1/transfers
POST /v1/movements:batch
{"source":"wms-l1","batch_id":"b88","movements":[...]}

Mutation responses return accepted movement IDs, resulting version, and rejected lines. Batch ingestion is atomic per movement, not necessarily all-or-nothing, and supports a result cursor.
