Reads expose as_of, policy, and whether quantity is canonical or projected. Never promise availability from an unqualified aggregate count.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Checkout --> Inventory[Inventory command service]
    WMS[Warehouse systems] --> Ingest[Movement ingestion]
    Supplier --> Ingest
    Ingest --> Inventory
    Inventory --> DB[(Balance and movement SQL shards)]
    DB --> Relay[Outbox relay]
    Relay --> Stream[(Inventory event stream)]
    Stream --> ATP[Regional ATP projections]
    ATP --> Storefront[Storefront reads]
    Stream --> Lake[Immutable archive]
    Recon[Count and reconciliation] --> Inventory

The smallest correct design stores movement, balance update, reservation, and outbox in one SQL transaction. The ledger and serving balance split only when volume requires separate retention or processing.

docs.title: Reserve and Consume
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Order service
    participant I as Inventory
    participant D as SQL shard
    O->>I: Reserve(order line, quantity, key)
    I->>D: Lock candidate balance
    I->>D: Check ATP and expiry policy
    alt enough ATP
        I->>D: Increment reserved and insert reservation, movement, outbox
        I-->>O: RESERVED
    else insufficient
        I-->>O: OUT_OF_STOCK
    end
    O->>I: Consume(reservation, shipped quantity)
    I->>D: Decrease on_hand and reserved, then append SHIP movement
    I-->>O: remaining quantity

Location selection considers delivery promise and split cost but persists the choice before reply. For multiple lines, either reserve each and compensate prior successes, or colocate a bounded fulfillment group; pretending arbitrary SKU shards share a transaction is unsafe.

docs.title: Receive and Adjust
docs.text: Warehouse scans identify SKU, location, container, quantity, source event, and device sequence. Ingestion validates schema and authorization, then appends a movement and updates balance atomically. Offline device retries deduplicate by source identity. Adjustments require reason codes; large or negative corrections may need approval. Event occurrence time is retained, but accepted order determines ledger sequence.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> RESERVED_AT_SOURCE
    RESERVED_AT_SOURCE --> IN_TRANSIT: ship
    IN_TRANSIT --> PARTIALLY_RECEIVED
    PARTIALLY_RECEIVED --> RECEIVED
    IN_TRANSIT --> RECEIVED
    IN_TRANSIT --> EXCEPTION
    PARTIALLY_RECEIVED --> EXCEPTION
    CREATED --> CANCELLED
    RESERVED_AT_SOURCE --> CANCELLED

Shipping a reserved transfer atomically decreases both source on-hand and source reserved quantity, then records shipped/in-transit quantity. Decreasing only reserved would make the departed stock available again. Destination receipt increases destination on-hand once per transfer-line receipt ID. Across shards, the matched in-transit projection clears asynchronously and exposes its watermark; do not claim a single atomic global in-transit decrement with that remote receipt. Partial receipt, loss, and damage are normal states.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Ledger and Balance
docs.text:
An immutable movement ledger provides provenance; a current balance serves checks. Each command locks one balance row, validates policy, appends movement, updates balance and version, and writes outbox in one transaction. A checkpoint plus ordered movements can reconstruct state. Nightly and continuous verification recompute sampled or changed keys and compares every component.

Backdated events do not reorder accepted ledger history. They carry occurred_at for analytics and append a correction now. Otherwise historical rewrites could invalidate reservations already promised. Financial valuation can maintain a separate versioned projection.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Hot SKU
docs.text:
Hashing SKU-location pairs distributes ordinary traffic but cannot split one popular key. The safest baseline serializes conditional counter updates and meters callers. At larger scale, allocate bounded tokens from a global balance to regional, channel, or checkout-worker pools. Each pool reserves locally and cannot exceed its grant. A rebalancer leases and transfers unused tokens with epochs; expired leases return only after proving the old holder fenced.

Pools trade utilization for throughput and regional availability. Product pages may show a conservative aggregate, while checkout confirms against one pool. For extreme launches, admission control is still required because token buckets move contention rather than eliminate demand.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Reservation Expiry
docs.text: Reservations block ATP until consumed, released, or expired. At expires_at <= database_time, a conditional transition may reclaim the remaining reservation quantity. It must atomically mark that reservation released, decrement reserved, append its unique release movement, and update the balance before another allocation spends the freed stock. Merely ignoring the timestamp while leaving counters unchanged is not reclamation. Consume, extend, and expiry serialize on that same state; none can revive or consume an expired grant. A batched indexed sweeper appends release movements and emits events. Extension is idempotent, capped, and allowed only while the order remains eligible. Repeated holding is limited by customer, order, device, and channel.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Cycle Counts and Reconciliation
docs.text:
A cycle count captures a scope and logical starting version, records observed physical quantities, and computes expected stock adjusted for movements during counting. Freeze a small bin when operationally possible; do not freeze a warehouse. Differences create proposed adjustment movements with evidence and approval policy. Track shrinkage separately from damage and process errors.

Reconciliation also compares supplier receipts, transfer manifests, carrier scans, warehouse shipment confirmations, reservations, and order fulfillment. Operators see lineage from discrepancy to source events and repair through commands, not SQL edits.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition canonical balance and movement data by hash of (sku_id, location_id). This aligns reservation and warehouse updates for one key. Maintain secondary lookup projections for all locations carrying a SKU and all inventory within a location. Those indexes may lag and only propose candidates; the chosen canonical shard rechecks ATP.

Keep recent movements in partitioned SQL and archive immutable segments to object storage by date and shard with checksums. Consumer lag applies backpressure: if regional ATP is too stale, storefront becomes conservative. Separate warehouse bulk ingestion quotas from checkout reservations so a reconnecting device cannot starve sales.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Balance transitions, reservations, and movement insertion are strongly consistent per SKU-location. Regional availability, search, analytics, and replenishment are eventual. Commands store source ID and request hash; duplicates return original movement versions. Outbox and stream delivery are at least once. Consumers use movement ID and balance version and detect gaps before applying newer state.

Cross-SKU orders use a saga with releases on failure. Cross-location transfers use explicit in-transit state. There is no claim of exactly-once messaging: business deduplication and invariant checks supply the guarantee that matters.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
Database loss rejects inventory promises; conservative cached reads can continue for browsing. Stream outage accumulates outbox and makes channels progressively conservative. Warehouse integration outage buffers durable batches with per-source quotas. A worker crash after commit receives the committed response through idempotency lookup. Sweeper failure raises held quantity but does not permit oversell; logical expiry allows reclaim.

Poison movements enter quarantine without blocking unrelated partitions. If a balance and replay disagree, fence writes for that key, rebuild from checkpoint and ledger, compare, then resume at a higher key epoch. Reconciliation monitors reservations without orders, shipments without consumption, negative components, stale transfer lines, and version gaps.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text:
Physical stock naturally belongs to a location home region. Write warehouse movements there with multi-zone storage. For global ecommerce, allocate bounded sellable pools to regional checkout cells rather than running multi-primary updates to one stock counter. Pool grants and returns require leases and fencing; a disconnected region can sell only its remaining allocation. Asynchronous replicas and movement archives provide disaster recovery. If a home region fails without safe fencing, stop reallocating its stock and continue from other pools.

The control plane manages location topology, policy, schema, and pool sizes. Regional data planes retain signed last-known policy and cannot increase allowance while disconnected.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Authenticate service and warehouse devices with scoped identities. Authorize movement types by role and location. Encrypt supplier and operational data, sign batch files, validate sequence and replay windows, and maintain immutable audit trails. Require dual approval for large adjustments, safety-stock changes, oversell allowance, and pool grants. Detect reservation hoarding, fake receipts, insider shrinkage patterns, device cloning, batch replay, and inventory scraping. Retain only necessary order/customer references in inventory records.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure reservation success, ATP conflict, hot-key lock time, movement ingestion lag, duplicate rate, outbox and projection lag, expired-reservation age, pool utilization and stranded stock, transfer age, negative-balance rejection, and reconciliation quantity/value. Slice by SKU, location, source, channel, shard, and region. Alert on invariant violations and stale high-value inventory, not only API latency.

Property-test conservation across arbitrary receive, reserve, consume, release, transfer, damage, and correction sequences. Run concurrent hot-key tests, duplicate and reordered warehouse batches, sweeper delay, stream gaps, pool lease expiry, region fencing, and partial transfer receipt. Replay ledger segments to verify checkpoints and restore archived history regularly. Shadow policy changes and compare ATP before rollout.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Transactional balances plus immutable movements duplicate data but combine fast checks with audit. Granular SKU-location keys simplify invariants while creating many rows. Regional pools sacrifice global utilization for local availability and throughput. Conservative projections lose sales but bound oversell during lag. Cross-SKU sagas expose partial reservation briefly but avoid distributed transactions. Backdated correction preserves operational history at the cost of a less intuitive event timeline.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Sources[Checkout, WMS, suppliers, returns] --> Gateway[Scoped command gateway]
    Gateway --> Owner[SKU-location owner]
    Owner --> Shard[(Balance, reservation, movement, outbox)]
    Shard --> Stream[(Partitioned movement stream)]
    Stream --> ATP[Regional and channel ATP]
    Stream --> Archive[Checksummed ledger archive]
    Pools[Leased regional allocation pools] --> Owner
    Control[Policy and allocation control plane] --> Pools
    Counts[Cycle counts and external evidence] --> Recon[Reconciliation]
    Recon --> Owner
    Shard -. fenced replica .-> DR[(Recovery region)]

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. Why keep both a movement ledger and current balance?
  2. How do you reserve a cart whose lines span shards?
  3. How can a hot SKU sell in several regions without oversell?
  4. What does transfer state look like after a partial damaged receipt?
  5. How do you apply an offline warehouse event that occurred yesterday?
  6. How would you prove and repair a corrupted balance?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer defines stock components, atomic reservation, immutable movements, idempotency, hot-key handling, and reconciliation. An L6 answer also designs allocation leases and fencing, distinguishes control and data planes, explains cross-shard sagas and ledger rebuild, sets adjustment governance and degraded policy, and connects utilization, loss prevention, warehouse operations, cost, and organizational ownership.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Inventory is an auditable stock ledger with fast transactional balances. Begin with SQL: every command locks one SKU-location balance, validates available-to-promise, appends a uniquely identified movement, updates balance, and writes an outbox event atomically. Reservations are bounded and logically expire; sweepers clean up but are not correctness-critical. Consumption and release cannot exceed remaining reservation. Transfers avoid distributed transactions by making in-transit stock explicit. Product-page availability is an eventual conservative projection; checkout rechecks canonical stock. Partition by SKU-location, isolate warehouse bulk traffic, and address a hot SKU with metering first and bounded regional or channel pools only when necessary. Pools use leases and fencing and may strand capacity. Reconcile physical counts and external evidence against checkpoints plus movements, repair through append-only adjustments, secure high-risk controls, and test conservation under duplicates, disorder, crashes, and regional partitions.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Fix the auction format first: ascending-price, proxy bidding, one item, scheduled close, and optional reserve price. State bid ordering and close invariants. Estimate normal and final-second load, present a single SQL writer per auction, and trace proxy bidding. Scale only after explaining hot auctions, clock authority, anti-sniping policy, and payment after close.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Sellers list unique items with start and end times. Buyers submit maximum willingness-to-pay; the system displays the current price and leading bidder without exposing private maxima. At close, one winner is selected deterministically and receives an order. Browse and notifications may lag, but accepted bids and closure cannot disagree.

Out of scope are multi-unit auctions, real-time video, shipping execution, and full payment processing. A payment service is invoked after winner selection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Create and moderate listings; search and watch auctions.
  • Accept proxy bids, return acceptance and resulting public price.
  • Close at a defined deadline and determine winner and clearing price.
  • Notify participants and create a winner order; handle non-payment policy.
  • No accepted on-time bid may disappear; no late bid may win.
  • Bid submission p99 under 300 ms when admitted, with deterministic results.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. Each accepted bid has a unique monotonically ordered sequence within its auction.
  2. Eligibility uses the authority-time check after acquiring the auction serialization lock and the current owner epoch, never client time or an earlier edge receipt.
  3. Closure and bid acceptance serialize: a bid is either before close and considered, or rejected.
  4. The leader and public price are a deterministic function of accepted maximum bids, increment rules, reserve, and tie policy.
  5. A bidder is never charged above its submitted maximum.
  6. Search, watch counts, and notifications are projections, not bidding authority.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text: Assume 20 million active listings, 200 million searches daily, and 10 million bids daily. Average bidding is 115 QPS, but a celebrity auction can receive 20,000 bids per second near close. Each listing averages 2 KB and each immutable bid 300 bytes, so bids add about 3 GB/day before indexes and replicas. Search traffic peaks near 20,000 QPS and is cacheable. The single-auction hot key, not aggregate storage, is the primary constraint.

docs.title: Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Auction(auction_id, seller_id, item_snapshot, starts_at, ends_at, status,
        start_price, reserve_price, increment_rule_id, leader_id,
        public_price, highest_max, highest_sequence, owner_epoch,
        deadline_generation, effective_end, version)
Bid(bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, max_amount, received_at, sequence,
    idempotency_key, status)
BidderMaximum(auction_id, bidder_id, max_amount, earliest_sequence)
Watch(auction_id, user_id, created_at)
AuctionResult(auction_id, winner_id, clearing_price, closed_at, rule_version)
WinnerOrder(order_id, auction_id, winner_id, amount, status)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

Partition keys begin with auction_id. Bid rows are immutable. Auction is the materialized authoritative aggregate and uses a version or row lock. Unique (auction_id, bidder_id, idempotency_key) returns the previous result. Rule versions make replay deterministic.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/auctions
POST /v1/auctions/{auctionId}/bids
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"maximum_amount":12500,"currency":"USD","expected_owner_epoch":4}

GET /v1/auctions/{auctionId}
GET /v1/auctions/{auctionId}/bids?cursor=&limit=50
GET /v1/auctions/{auctionId}/events       Accept: text/event-stream
Last-Event-ID: <auction-version>
POST /v1/auctions/{auctionId}/watch

The bid response includes accepted sequence, public price, leadership status, authoritative receipt time, owner epoch, deadline generation, and auction version. Public history omits private maxima. Cursor pagination uses (sequence, bid_id). 409 covers a stale owner epoch or closed auction; 429 preserves the same idempotency key for retry.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Buyer --> Edge[CDN and gateway]
    Edge --> Browse[Browse service]
    Browse --> Search[(Search index)]
    Edge --> Bid[Bid command service]
    Bid --> Router[Auction owner router]
    Router --> Writer[Single auction writer]
    Writer --> DB[(Auction SQL partitions)]
    DB --> Relay[Outbox relay]
    Relay --> Stream[(Event stream)]
    Stream --> Search
    Stream --> Notify[Watch notifications]
    Stream --> Order[Winner order service]
    Closer[Deadline scheduler] --> Writer

Initially, the writer is a normal stateless service using one SQL transaction and row lock. At hot-auction scale, route commands for an auction to one leased actor or partition consumer. SQL remains durable authority and the lease epoch fences stale writers.

docs.title: Browse and Watch
docs.text:
Listing changes enter an outbox and asynchronously update the search index and CDN pages. Detail reads combine immutable listing data with a recent auction projection carrying as_of. Near close, clients poll or subscribe to a push gateway, but every displayed price is advisory until a bid response confirms sequence. Watch writes are independently partitioned and do not touch the auction row.

This design chooses a snapshot-plus-SSE path for live auction state. SSE is sufficient because bids already use authenticated HTTP commands and the live channel is server-to-client. Each public AuctionChanged event has id: auction_version, event: price, and data containing public price, pseudonymous leader, effective end time, owner epoch, deadline generation, status, and server time. Private maxima never enter this log.

On a fresh connection, the SSE service first subscribes to the public-event partition at a captured cursor C and buffers later events. It then reads an authoritative aggregate snapshot at version V, emits event: snapshot with id: V, replays durable or buffered events greater than V in version order, and tails the already-attached subscription. On reconnect with Last-Event-ID: K, it attaches and replays events greater than K before tailing. The client drops versions at or below its current version and applies only the next contiguous version. A gap freezes countdown-derived actions and reconnects; the bid command response remains authoritative even if SSE is stale.

Retain the replay log for 15 minutes beyond auction close. If K predates retention, belongs to another ownership history, or cannot be found, emit event: resync and close; the client reconnects without an ID to receive a new snapshot. Heartbeats every 20 seconds keep intermediaries from silently expiring the stream. Every aggregate version emits a public event, even when price is unchanged, so clients can enforce contiguity without exposing maxima. Attaching and buffering before the snapshot read closes the race: a commit concurrent with the read is either represented by snapshot V or present in the buffered/replay suffix.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant G as SSE gateway
    participant A as Auction store
    participant E as Public event log
    C->>G: Connect with optional Last-Event-ID K
    G->>E: Subscribe and buffer from cursor C
    alt K is retained
        G->>E: Replay versions greater than K
    else Fresh connection without an ID
        G->>A: Read snapshot at version V
        A-->>G: Public state and V
        G-->>C: snapshot id V
        G->>E: Replay versions greater than V
        G->>G: Merge replay and buffer above V
    end
    G->>G: Deduplicate and order by auction version
    E-->>G: Tail from attached subscription
    G-->>C: SSE events with version IDs

One million simultaneous viewers at one 25-byte heartbeat every 20 seconds produce about 50,000 heartbeat writes/s and 1.25 MB/s of payload before framing and TLS. Gateways therefore batch timer work, cap per-connection buffers, and use regional fanout relays so one auction event is consumed once per relay and copied locally. Slow viewers receive resync and disconnect instead of retaining an unbounded queue.

docs.title: Submit Proxy Bid
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Bidder
    participant S as Bid service
    participant W as Auction writer
    participant D as SQL
    B->>S: Bid(max, key, owner epoch)
    S->>W: Ordered command
    W->>D: BEGIN and lock auction
    W->>D: Check status and DB receipt time
    W->>D: Insert bid and recompute leader and price
    W->>D: Update aggregate plus outbox, then COMMIT
    W-->>B: sequence, price, leadership

For two maxima, the highest maximum leads and public price is the lesser of its maximum and second-highest maximum plus the configured increment, bounded by starting price. Equal maxima favor the earliest accepted sequence. A bidder raising its own maximum retains its original tie precedence only if policy says so; encode and test the exact rule.

Reserve price is a separate award condition: if the highest eligible maximum is below reserve, close with RESERVE_NOT_MET and no winner order. Once met, use min(highest_max, max(start_price, reserve_price, second_max + increment)) under the versioned increment policy; with one bidder omit the second-max term. Reject maxima below the starting minimum and compare maxima of distinct bidders, not two bids by the same bidder.

docs.title: Close Auction
docs.text:
The scheduler submits Close(auction_id, deadline_generation, expected_end) after the deadline. That command enters the same serialization path as bids. The writer closes only if the generation and expected end still match the aggregate and database time has reached effective_end; a stale timer schedules or confirms the current generation instead. It then writes AuctionResult, status, and outbox atomically. Duplicate close commands for the current generation return the existing result. The winner-order consumer creates one order keyed by auction ID. owner_epoch fences writers and is checked independently on command admission; timer freshness never changes ownership.

The winner order has a payment deadline and stable collection identity. A timeout is reconciled rather than called non-payment. Definitive non-payment follows the recorded seller policy: cancel/relist or offer a separately authorized second-chance purchase. Do not rewrite the original auction result or charge the runner-up without acceptance.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Ordering and Time
docs.text:
RECEIVED and ACCEPTED are different promises. RECEIVED semantics would make a bid eligible when a trusted edge durably records it before the deadline; the close path must then wait for or deterministically drain every admitted ingress record, preserve signed ingress order, and handle cross-region queue delay. This is friendlier during owner overload but adds a distributed durable admission system and makes the close latency bound part of correctness.

This design chooses writer-acceptance semantics: eligibility is decided at a serialized authority-time check before the effective deadline, and that decision becomes valid only if its transaction commits. The acknowledgement can arrive after the deadline; database fsync completion is not predictable from a pre-commit clock check. Check time after acquiring the auction lock, not a stale transaction-start timestamp. Bids and close commands share this ordering boundary. An edge receipt is transport only; the API returns durable ACCEPTED or a definitive rejection, not 202 RECEIVED. A request sent early but delayed can be rejected under this published policy.

Serialize the deadline check and state update in one owner, and define the authority clock uncertainty budget. Failover must not move observed auction time backward; excessive clock uncertainty pauses deadline-sensitive acceptance rather than extending a hard close implicitly. NTP monitoring alone is not this guarantee. A monotonically increasing sequence provides total order independent of timestamp ties.

Close policy is immutable and versioned after the first bid. HARD_CLOSE keeps scheduled_end fixed. SOFT_CLOSE(window,extension,max_end) moves effective_end when an accepted bid lands inside the window, for example extending by two minutes but never beyond a 30-minute cap. That update occurs in the bid transaction, increments deadline_generation, and emits the new effective deadline. Scheduled close commands carry deadline_generation and expected_end; stale commands refresh instead of closing. owner_epoch changes only when write ownership moves or is fenced, so frequent anti-sniping extensions do not masquerade as failovers. Operational overload must never extend an auction implicitly. A pause or moderation extension is a separate audited administrative state transition with customer-visible reason, not anti-sniping behavior.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Proxy-Bid Algorithm
docs.text:
Do not scan all bids per request. Maintain each bidder's highest maximum and the top two eligible maxima in the auction aggregate. Updating an existing bidder may change either. For a modest number of bidders, a transactional indexed query for top two is simplest. For a hot auction, the leased writer maintains a heap in memory but snapshots enough state and appends every accepted bid before acknowledging; on recovery it loads a snapshot and replays later sequences.

The maximum is sensitive data. Public events include current price and pseudonymous leader only. Internal access is restricted and audited because leaked maxima enable shill bidding.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Hot Auctions and Backpressure
docs.text:
Hash partitioning cannot split one auction while preserving simple ordering. Give it one owner with a bounded mailbox. Gateways route by auction ID and require a current lease epoch. When the mailbox approaches the latency budget, return 429 before the deadline with clear retry guidance; accepting unbounded queues would turn on-time requests into late rejections. For exceptional events, an admission queue can issue short-lived bid permits. Capacity tests establish maximum sustainable commands per owner.

If one owner cannot meet required throughput, batch commands into a short deterministic window and order by trusted ingress sequence. This changes semantics and latency and should be a product decision, not an invisible optimization.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Abuse and Market Integrity
docs.text: Shill bidding, bid shielding, account farms, seller collusion, scraping, and denial of service are domain risks. Build risk features from account age, device and payment links, seller-bidder relationships, bid retractions, velocity, and unusual maxima. High-risk bids may require verified payment credentials or a deposit before acceptance. Moderation can cancel an auction under an audited state transition; it must not secretly rewrite bid history.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition command data by auction ID and colocate aggregate, bids, and result. Listings and search use independent document partitions. Watches partition by user for "my watches" and maintain an auction-to-watchers fan-out index. Notifications fan out asynchronously with per-auction rate caps.

Move an inactive or long-running auction by snapshotting through sequence N and copying later bids while the old owner remains authoritative. Then fence its mutations, capture the final committed sequence F, prove the target has the complete prefix through F, and grant its higher owner epoch before switching routing. Avoid moves in the final minutes. Archive closed bid logs by close month while retaining a compact legal record and result.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Bid acceptance, price, and close are strongly consistent within one auction. Browse, push updates, counts, and notification are eventual. Bid idempotency stores key and request hash with accepted sequence. Outbox events are at least once, and consumers upsert by event or auction version. An SSE connection subscribes and buffers first, then obtains the current aggregate snapshot and replays the suffix, closing the snapshot-stream race.

Recovery replays immutable bids under the recorded rule version and compares the computed result with stored aggregate. A periodic invariant checker catches price above leader maximum, winner mismatch, duplicate sequences, and close before deadline.

docs.title: Reliability and Multi-Region
docs.text:
Use multi-zone storage and lease owners within an auction's home region. If an owner dies, a new owner acquires a higher epoch, reconstructs state, and resumes. During uncertainty, pause bids rather than run two writers. A disaster-recovery region receives asynchronous logs. Promotion requires fencing the home region and recovering every acknowledged accepted bid through the required committed prefix. If asynchronous replication lost accepted bids, pause and recover or invoke an explicit auction-abort policy; silently closing the shortened history would choose an invalid winner. Promotion may reject bids during RTO; cross-region active-active would need consensus per auction and usually harms deadline latency.

Globally distributed edges serve browse and forward bid commands to the home region. For geographically significant auctions, choose home based on seller regulation and expected bidders. Search can continue stale during command-plane failure. Notification failure never blocks bidding. Order-service failure leaves a durable WinnerSelected event and retry backlog.

docs.title: Security and Privacy
docs.text: Require authenticated bidders, signed session tokens, TLS, server-side amount validation, and step-up verification for high values. Encrypt private maxima and seller identity evidence, redact logs, and enforce role-separated moderator access. Rate limit by account, device, network, auction, and payment instrument. Protect listing creation against malware and prohibited goods. Retention and deletion policies preserve legally required bid evidence while pseudonymizing profiles.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure accepted and rejected bids by reason, owner mailbox depth, commit and routing latency, owner-epoch conflicts, stale deadline generations, bids near deadline, close lag, projection lag, notification backlog, and suspicious bidder graphs. Per-auction dashboards matter because fleet averages conceal a hot failure. Alert if any open auction lacks an owner or any close remains overdue.

Property-test proxy pricing across ties, self-raises, reserve prices, and increments. Run concurrent bid-versus-close tests using database time for both hard and capped soft closes. Inject duplicate commands, stale owner epochs, stale deadline generations, owner crashes before and after commit, delayed outbox, clock drift, and region isolation. For SSE, connect across the snapshot-tail race, reconnect from every retained version, expire replay, duplicate events, drop a version, and stall consumers; clients must converge or perform explicit resync. Load-test final-second admission separately under RECEIVED and chosen ACCEPTED semantics so dashboards and product copy cannot confuse transport receipt with eligibility. Replay production-like anonymized bid streams through new rule versions and compare every sequence and result before migration.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: A row lock is simpler than an actor and adequate until one auction saturates it. A single owner gives deterministic ordering but caps throughput. Acceptance-at-writer is easy to audit and close deterministically but disappoints bidders with slow networks; durable edge-receipt eligibility is fairer to admitted requests but requires ordered ingress draining. Soft close improves price discovery but removes fixed-end certainty, while hard close is predictable but rewards timing strategies. Snapshot-plus-SSE gives resumable one-way updates with ordinary HTTP infrastructure, but retention is bounded and slow clients must resync. Active-passive regions sacrifice availability to prevent conflicting winners. Exposing approximate live price improves scale while requiring clients to tolerate correction.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Users[Global users] --> Edge[Browse CDN and bid gateway]
    Edge --> Index[(Search and auction projections)]
    Edge --> Route[Auction routing map]
    Route --> Owner[Leased owner with epoch]
    Owner --> Part[(Auction-owned SQL partition)]
    Scheduler[Durable deadline scheduler] --> Owner
    Part --> Events[(Outbox and replicated log)]
    Events --> Index
    Events --> Push[Push and watcher fan-out]
    Events --> Orders[Winner orders and payment]
    Part -. fenced DR .-> DR[(Recovery region)]
    Audit[Replay and invariant checker] --> Part

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. What exactly determines whether a deadline bid is accepted?
  2. How does proxy pricing behave with equal maxima?
  3. Can one hot auction scale beyond a single writer without changing semantics?
  4. How do reconnecting clients avoid missing price events?
  5. What happens when a winner does not pay?
  6. How would multi-unit or sealed-bid auctions alter the model?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer gives deterministic bid ordering, transactional bid-and-price updates, a serialized close, hot-key recognition, and retry semantics. An L6 answer also defines fairness policy, owner fencing and migration, anti-sniping semantics, replay validation, degraded modes, market-integrity controls, and the business consequences of throughput and regional choices.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: An auction is an ordered state machine, not a generic write service. Begin with one SQL transaction per bid: lock the auction, use authoritative receipt time, allocate the next sequence, update bidder maximum and top-two-derived public price, and commit an outbox event. The close command goes through the same serialization path, making a bid either accepted before closure or rejected. Search, live views, watches, and notifications are projections. When a hot auction exceeds row-lock capacity, route it to one leased owner with a bounded mailbox and epoch fencing; do not pretend hashing removes a single hot key. Keep one home region unless willing to pay consensus latency. Record rule versions, replay immutable bids, protect private maxima, resist shill bidding, and test bid-close races, ties, stale owners, and final-second overload.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify rails, money movement, and whether the platform holds balances. This design accepts merchant payment intents, routes card or bank payments, records an immutable double-entry ledger, sends webhooks, and supports refunds. State money invariants before availability goals. Draw a single-region synchronous write path, trace an ambiguous provider timeout, then scale through account-owned partitions, reconciliation, and region fencing.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Merchants create a payment intent, collect a tokenized instrument, authorize it, optionally capture it later, and may cancel before capture or refund after capture. Providers respond synchronously, asynchronously, or ambiguously. The platform must expose a stable business state despite those differences and retain an auditable financial history.

Assume multiple currencies but no conversion within a payment. Settlement to merchant banks, disputes, and risk decisions are represented as downstream workflows; building card networks or a general bank is out of scope.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Create, confirm, query, cancel, and refund payment intents.
  • Support automatic capture and separate authorization/capture, including partial capture and authorization expiry.
  • Route to providers, process signed callbacks, and retry safe operations.
  • Maintain merchant payable balances and immutable accounting entries.
  • Deliver ordered-enough, retryable webhooks and reconciliation reports.
  • Never lose or invent money; target 99.99% query and 99.95% confirmation availability.
  • Return confirmation decisions in under two seconds at p99 when the rail responds.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every posted ledger transaction balances: sum of debits equals sum of credits per currency.
  2. A merchant idempotency key plus operation creates one logical effect.
  3. A provider operation ID is stable across retries, and one provider event is applied once logically.
  4. Payment state can advance only through permitted transitions; ledger entries are appended, never edited.
  5. Captures cannot exceed authorized amount, and successful refunds plus pending refund reservations cannot exceed captured amount.
  6. A client or webhook never proves money moved; verified provider state and ledger posting do.
  7. Cancel, capture, refund, callback, and timeout resolution serialize against the same intent version so mutually exclusive effects cannot both win.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Design for at least 10,000 peak payment operations/s. At 50 million payments/day the average is 580/s; a 17x event peak is about 10K/s. Status polling and dashboards can generate 50,000 peak read QPS. At 2 KB per intent, attempts, indexes, and metadata, transactional records add about 100 GB/day. Four ledger lines per payment at 250 bytes add 50 GB/day. Keep seven years in immutable archive while hot operational tables retain recent months.

One customer operation is not one backend operation. At 10K confirms/s, assume one intent write, one attempt write, one provider call, four ledger-entry writes, two outbox events, and three projection or webhook jobs: roughly 10K * 12 = 120K internal operations/s before retries. If 5% of provider calls time out and each causes two status queries, that adds 10K * 0.05 * 2 = 1K provider requests/s. A one-hour webhook outage at two events per payment accumulates 10K * 2 * 3,600 = 72M deliveries; draining it in two hours while live traffic continues requires an extra 10K deliveries/s of safe capacity. Size databases, provider quotas, stream partitions, and delivery storage from these amplified rates, not only API TPS.

Provider and merchant skew matter. A large merchant can create 20% of traffic, and a provider incident can cause retry amplification. Per-tenant and per-provider queues, quotas, and circuit breakers are therefore part of correctness under overload.

docs.title: Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Merchant(merchant_id, legal_entity_id, status, risk_tier, home_region)
MerchantCredential(credential_id, merchant_id, key_hash, scopes, status,
                   not_before, expires_at, rotated_from)
PaymentIntent(intent_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, currency, status,
              capture_method, amount_authorized, amount_captured,
              authorization_expires_at, idempotency_key, request_hash,
              version, created_at)
PaymentAttempt(attempt_id, intent_id, provider, operation_id, status,
               provider_ref, response_code, next_retry_at)
Refund(refund_id, intent_id, amount_minor, status, idempotency_key)
LedgerTransaction(txn_id, reference_type, reference_id, currency, posted_at)
LedgerEntry(txn_id, account_id, direction, amount_minor, sequence)
Account(account_id, owner_id, currency, type, partition_id)
ProviderEvent(provider, event_id, payload_hash, applied_at)
WebhookEndpoint(endpoint_id, merchant_id, https_url, subscribed_types,
                signing_key_version, status)
WebhookDelivery(delivery_id, endpoint_id, event_id, status, attempt,
                next_attempt_at, response_code)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

Unique indexes enforce merchant idempotency and provider event identity. Ledger entries use integer minor units and a transaction-level balance constraint. Balances are projections computed from entries or updated atomically with posting; entries remain canonical.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/payment-intents
Idempotency-Key: order-781-pay
{"amount":1299,"currency":"USD","capture_method":"manual","merchant_order_id":"781"}

POST /v1/payment-intents/{id}/confirm
Idempotency-Key: order-781-confirm
{"payment_method_token":"pm_x","return_url":"https://merchant/callback"}

POST /v1/payment-intents/{id}/capture
Idempotency-Key: order-781-capture-1
{"amount":1000,"final_capture":true}

POST /v1/payment-intents/{id}/cancel
Idempotency-Key: order-781-cancel

GET /v1/payment-intents/{id}
POST /v1/payment-intents/{id}/refunds
Idempotency-Key: order-781-refund-1
{"amount":500}

capture_method=automatic asks confirm to authorize and capture as one logical operation. manual makes successful confirmation produce REQUIRES_CAPTURE with an authorized amount and expiry. Capture may be partial only if the rail and merchant contract permit it; each request atomically reserves capture capacity. A successful non-final partial capture produces PARTIALLY_CAPTURED, while final_capture=true or exhaustion of the authorization produces SUCCEEDED and releases any unused remainder. A capture after expiry or above the remaining authorization returns 409 without calling the provider.

Cancel succeeds only while amount_captured=0. It cancels an unconfirmed intent locally or voids an untouched authorization in REQUIRES_CAPTURE through a stable provider operation. A cancel racing with the first capture uses optimistic intent versioning: one reserves the transition and the loser receives the resulting canonical state. An ambiguous void remains CANCEL_PROCESSING, not CANCELED, until callback, query, or reconciliation proves the result. Once any partial or final capture succeeds, cancel returns 409; the merchant must refund captured funds, while an unused authorization remainder is released only by a final capture, expiry, or an explicit provider operation modeled separately from intent cancellation.

202 means processing or customer action required and includes a client secret or polling URL. 201 or 200 returns the canonical resource; 409 represents an invalid state transition or idempotency payload conflict, not an unknown provider result. A retry returns the original response. Cursor pagination uses immutable creation ID and time. Merchant webhook consumers receive event IDs and must deduplicate.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Merchant --> Edge[API gateway]
    Edge --> Payments[Payment service]
    Payments --> DB[(Shared payment, ledger, and outbox SQL)]
    Payments --> Risk[Risk engine]
    Payments --> Router[Provider router]
    Router --> RailA[Provider A]
    Router --> RailB[Provider B]
    DB --> Outbox[Outbox relay]
    Outbox --> Stream[(Event stream)]
    Stream --> Webhooks[Webhook delivery]
    Stream --> Settlement[Settlement and reports]
    Recon[Reconciliation] --> Router
    Recon --> Compare[Match persisted outcomes]
    Compare --> DB
    subgraph ReconLane[Reconciliation]
      Recon
      Compare
    end
    subgraph PayLane[Payment decision]
      Payments
      Risk
    end
    subgraph RailLane[External payment rails]
      Router
      RailA
      RailB
    end
    subgraph EvidenceLane[Durable state and delivery]
      DB
      Outbox
      Stream
      Webhooks
      Settlement
    end

The baseline has one write component and one relational transaction boundary: payment state, balanced ledger rows, and the outbox event are colocated in Shared payment, ledger, and outbox SQL. The relay runs only after commit. There is no synchronous "record payment, then call ledger" gap in this baseline. Separate the ledger service and partitions only after throughput or organizational boundaries justify it; that later design commits verified capture plus a durable posting command and state CAPTURED_PENDING_LEDGER in payment SQL, then advances to SUCCEEDED only after the ledger acknowledges its idempotent posting reference.

docs.title: Confirm Payment
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant M as Merchant
    participant P as Payments
    participant D as Shared payment, ledger, outbox SQL
    participant R as Provider
    M->>P: Confirm(intent, key)
    P->>D: Persist attempt and operation ID
    P->>D: COMMIT attempt before external call
    P->>R: Authorize or authorize-and-capture(operation ID)
    alt success
        R-->>P: provider reference
        P->>D: BEGIN and lock intent version
        alt Capture verified
            P->>D: Update payment plus insert balanced ledger rows plus outbox
        else Authorization only
            P->>D: Update REQUIRES_CAPTURE plus outbox
        end
        P->>D: COMMIT atomically
        P-->>M: SUCCEEDED or REQUIRES_CAPTURE
    else challenge
        P->>D: ACTION_REQUIRED
        P-->>M: 202 challenge
    else timeout
        P->>D: UNKNOWN
        P-->>M: 202 processing
    end

The attempt and stable operation ID commit before the provider call. Risk evaluates a versioned decision input. Routing is sticky for the operation; retrying through another acquirer could double-authorize. A timeout transitions to UNKNOWN, and a resolver queries by operation ID or waits for a callback. Once capture success is verified, the baseline's second database transaction atomically changes payment state, inserts the balanced ledger transaction, and inserts its outbox event; no observer can see SUCCEEDED without the corresponding posting.

docs.title: Refund
docs.text: Within a transaction, reserve refundable capacity so concurrent refunds cannot exceed capture. Persist a provider refund operation, invoke it idempotently, and post reverse ledger entries only when provider success is verified. A definitive provider failure with no possible late success releases the reservation; ambiguity remains pending. Refund completion and merchant notification may be asynchronous.

docs.title: Authorization, Capture, and Cancel
docs.text: Authorization proves the provider has reserved up to an amount until an explicit expiry; it is not merchant revenue and does not credit merchant payable. Capture consumes all or part of that reservation and posts the financial ledger transaction only after verified provider success. Cancel before authorization is a local terminal transition; cancel after authorization requests a provider void. Expired unused authorizations transition through provider evidence or a scheduled resolver, not merely the application clock.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
An outbox event creates one delivery per subscribed merchant endpoint. Workers sign timestamp, event ID, and body; retry with exponential backoff and jitter for days. Ordering is guaranteed only per payment intent when required, not globally. A poison endpoint cannot block others because queues and concurrency are tenant-scoped. Merchants can list events and replay deliveries.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Outbox relay
    participant Q as Endpoint queue
    participant W as Webhook worker
    participant M as Merchant endpoint
    O->>Q: Persist delivery(event, endpoint)
    Q->>W: Lease due delivery
    W->>M: POST body with event ID, timestamp, signature, key version
    alt 2xx response
        M-->>W: Accepted
        W->>Q: Mark delivered
    else Timeout, 429, or 5xx
        W->>Q: Schedule exponential backoff with jitter
    else Permanent 4xx or retry horizon exceeded
        W->>Q: Disable or mark exhausted and alert merchant
    end
    Note over Q,M: Merchant can fetch event and request replay

Reuse the same immutable event ID and body across automatic attempts, but give each HTTP attempt a delivery-attempt ID. This lets merchants deduplicate business events while both sides diagnose individual retries. A merchant-requested replay creates a new delivery referencing the original event and is rate-limited and audited.

docs.title: Hosted Tokenization and Trust Boundary
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Customer browser
    participant H as Hosted payment fields
    participant V as Isolated token vault
    participant M as Merchant backend
    participant P as Payment API
    B->>H: Enter PAN and CVV in provider-owned origin
    H->>V: TLS submit card data
    V->>V: Encrypt PAN and create scoped token
    V-->>B: Single-use payment method token
    B->>M: Return opaque token only
    M->>P: Confirm intent with token and client secret
    P->>V: Resolve token inside PCI boundary
    V-->>P: Provider-specific credential reference

The merchant page, analytics scripts, logs, and general payment services never receive PAN or CVV. Browser isolation requires a distinct hosted origin, restrictive CSP and frame-ancestors, integrity-controlled scripts, and no postMessage payload containing card data. Tokens are scoped to merchant, environment, purpose, and lifetime; possession by another merchant is useless. The vault-to-provider adapter boundary is tightly authenticated, audited, and segmented from public API fleets.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Double-Entry Ledger
docs.text:
For a $10 capture with a $0.30 fee, debit a provider receivable account $10, credit merchant payable $9.70, and credit fee revenue $0.30. Settlement later debits merchant payable and credits bank cash. Refunds create new reversing entries rather than changing capture history. Each posting has a unique business reference, balanced entries, currency, effective time, and append sequence.

Do not use a cached balance to decide whether money exists unless it is transactionally maintained with entries. Periodically recompute balance from checkpoints plus entries and compare with the serving projection. Corrections use explicit adjustment transactions under audited permissions.

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION
    REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION --> PROCESSING: confirm
    REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION --> CANCELED: cancel
    PROCESSING --> ACTION_REQUIRED
    ACTION_REQUIRED --> PROCESSING: customer completed
    PROCESSING --> REQUIRES_CAPTURE: authorized manual
    PROCESSING --> SUCCEEDED: authorized and captured
    PROCESSING --> FAILED
    PROCESSING --> UNKNOWN
    REQUIRES_CAPTURE --> CAPTURE_PROCESSING: first capture
    REQUIRES_CAPTURE --> CANCEL_PROCESSING: cancel or void
    PARTIALLY_CAPTURED --> CAPTURE_PROCESSING: additional capture
    CAPTURE_PROCESSING --> PARTIALLY_CAPTURED: non-final partial capture
    CAPTURE_PROCESSING --> SUCCEEDED: final capture
    CAPTURE_PROCESSING --> UNKNOWN
    CANCEL_PROCESSING --> CANCELED
    CANCEL_PROCESSING --> UNKNOWN
    UNKNOWN --> REQUIRES_CAPTURE: resolved authorized
    UNKNOWN --> PARTIALLY_CAPTURED: resolved partial capture
    UNKNOWN --> SUCCEEDED: resolved captured
    UNKNOWN --> CANCELED: resolved voided
    UNKNOWN --> FAILED
    SUCCEEDED --> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED
    PARTIALLY_REFUNDED --> REFUNDED
    SUCCEEDED --> REFUNDED

Refund is also an independent resource: a partially captured intent may be refunded without erasing its remaining capture/authorization state. The refund arrows above summarize the fully captured case; retain captured, reserved-refund, refunded, and authorization amounts separately instead of forcing every combination into one status. A definitive failed capture or void returns to the applicable prior payment state; UNKNOWN remains tied to its specific operation until resolved.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Idempotency and Ambiguity
docs.text:
Store (merchant, operation, key, request_hash, resource_id, response) before side effects. Same key and hash returns the stored result; a different hash is rejected. Provider callbacks deduplicate by verified provider event ID and additionally guard state transitions, because some providers produce distinct events for the same fact.

Separate the platform's financial-record retention from the provider's idempotency window. Persist the provider key, request hash, first-submission time, documented retry deadline, and provider resource reference. A stable string is not permanent deduplication: Stripe's idempotency contract allows pruning after at least 24 hours and treats reuse after pruning as a new request (accessed 2026-09-08). Beyond the adapter's verified horizon, resolve the existing operation by resource reference or reconciliation rather than blindly resubmitting, even with the same key. A negative eventually consistent lookup alone does not prove the first request had no effect.

Exactly-once delivery is not assumed. Within the proven provider idempotency and reconciliation contract, durable intent, stable provider IDs, idempotent posting references, inbox/outbox records, and reconciliation combine to provide once-only business effects. If neither callback nor query can resolve an old unknown, quarantine it for operations instead of guessing failure.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Routing and Retries
docs.text: Routing considers instrument support, geography, cost, success rate, latency, merchant policy, and provider health. Use slowly changing health signals; routing every request away from a brief error can overload a healthy provider. Once an operation reaches a provider, keep retries there unless the rail proves no financial effect occurred. Hedging payment writes is unsafe. Retry only documented transient failures with a retry budget; decline codes are terminal.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Reconciliation
docs.text: Provider settlement files and APIs are independent evidence. Ingest raw files immutably, validate totals and signatures, normalize records, and match by provider reference, operation ID, amount, currency, and time. Classify missing-local, missing-provider, amount mismatch, and duplicate-provider cases. Automatic repair is limited to deterministic transitions; money adjustments require policy and audit. Reconciliation lag is a financial SLI, not a back-office afterthought.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition payment intents by merchant plus hash of intent to spread large tenants; maintain a narrow global lookup from intent ID to shard. Ledger partitions must keep accounts touched by one transaction together. A platform can use clearing accounts between partitions: each local transaction balances against a clearing account, and paired transfers reconcile globally. This complexity is justified only beyond a single database's write capacity.

Archive terminal attempts and webhook payloads by month. Read replicas serve dashboards, never confirmation decisions. Per-provider queues impose concurrency and rate limits. Backpressure rejects low-priority retries before new customer confirmations, but never drops persisted workflow work.

docs.title: Consistency and Reliability
docs.text:
Payment state and ledger posting require strong consistency within their transaction boundary. Dashboards, webhooks, reports, and settlement views may lag with visible as_of times. Outbox and inbox patterns bridge asynchronous boundaries. Optimistic versions serialize callback, poller, refund, and cancel races.

If the database is unavailable, reject new financial writes. If a provider is slow, open a circuit and return processing only after intent is durable. If the stream fails, outbox backlog grows while money state remains intact. If ledger posting is separated and unavailable, cap pending captures and prevent settlement until repaired. Every service restart resumes leased work from persisted state.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text: Assign each merchant or payment intent a home region with synchronous multi-zone storage. Keep financial writes in that region and replicate asynchronously for disaster recovery. Failover requires fencing the old writer through a monotonically increasing region epoch enforced by claim and posting authorities. Before new financial work, prove that the recovered prefix contains all relevant acknowledged intents, provider-operation identities, reservations, and postings. A nonzero asynchronous RPO can violate that requirement; hold affected work until authoritative recovery/reconciliation rather than recreating operations under fresh keys. Recovery may temporarily stop confirms rather than risk duplicate money movement. Globally active reads use replicas; local collection services may forward tokenized details to the home region. Data residency can create separate legal ledgers connected through explicit intercompany clearing, not hidden cross-region writes.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text:
Minimize PCI scope with tokenization and hosted collection. Encrypt secrets using managed keys, rotate webhook signing keys, and isolate provider credentials. Authenticate merchants with scoped credentials and optional mTLS; require strong controls and dual approval for refunds, routing changes, and ledger adjustments. Redact PAN, CVV, tokens, and personal data from logs. Risk controls detect card testing, refund abuse, replayed callbacks, account takeover, and velocity anomalies. Maintain immutable access and financial audit trails with retention policy.

Webhook endpoints are untrusted outbound destinations. Require HTTPS, reject URL credentials and fragments, resolve DNS through a controlled resolver, block loopback, link-local, private, metadata, and internal service ranges for every resolved address, and connect through an egress proxy that rechecks the destination after redirects. Pin the chosen public IP for the request while validating TLS hostname against the registered host; cap redirects, body bytes, response time, and concurrency. These controls limit SSRF, DNS rebinding, and endpoints that intentionally hold sockets open.

Use versioned webhook signing keys with an overlap window: sign new deliveries with the new key, publish both public verification keys or expose both secret versions to an authenticated merchant console, and accept operator rollback during a bounded period. Provider and merchant API credentials follow create, activate, drain, revoke, and delete stages; never replace a key in place. Record key ID, use, principal, and rotation lineage without logging secrets.

Callbacks and merchant requests carry a timestamp or nonce inside the authenticated payload. Reject timestamps outside a narrow window, verify the signature over the raw body before parsing, bind provider callbacks to endpoint and merchant context, and atomically insert (provider, event_id) before applying state. For APIs, idempotency prevents duplicate effects but does not replace authentication or nonce/rate controls. For webhooks, the receiver should verify signature and timestamp, store event_id, then acknowledge; a captured request replay cannot create a second business effect.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Monitor approval rate by normalized reason, unknown-state age, provider latency and circuit state, idempotency conflicts, ledger posting lag, unbalanced-posting rejection, webhook age, reconciliation breaks and value, and per-tenant queue depth. Alert on value at risk, not only counts. Trace by intent, attempt, operation, ledger transaction, and provider reference without sensitive payloads.

Test ledger conservation with property-based tests and replay all state transitions. Contract-test provider adapters using signed fixtures. Inject timeouts before and after provider acceptance, duplicate and reordered callbacks, database failover, stale region epochs, and corrupt settlement files. Run daily recomputation of balances and restore drills. A release that changes money logic shadows calculations and compares postings before activation.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: A synchronous monolithic transaction is simplest and safest but eventually limits independent scaling. Splitting ledger from payment improves isolation while introducing a visible pending state. Home-region writes add latency but avoid multi-primary financial conflicts. Provider routing improves success and cost but complicates ambiguity. Immutable entries consume storage but make audit and correction tractable. Availability must sometimes yield to financial integrity.

docs.title: Product-interface tradeoffs
docs.text:
Choice Simpler interface More capable interface Decision pressure Capture Confirm always captures Explicit manual capture and partial capture Hotels, marketplaces, and fulfillment need delayed capture, but merchants must handle expiry and races Cancel Generic cancel at any time Cancel before capture, refund after capture One button is friendly, but distinct resources and statuses make money semantics auditable Async state Hide pending behind a long request Return 202, status API, and webhooks Explicit processing handles rail latency and mobile retries without pretending a timeout is failure Card collection Merchant posts card data Hosted fields return scoped tokens Hosted collection reduces PCI and breach scope but constrains checkout customization Webhooks Fire-and-forget callbacks Signed events, retries, event retrieval, replay A richer contract costs storage and tooling but is operable under endpoint failures Errors Provider codes exposed directly Stable platform codes plus provider detail Stable codes preserve integrations when routing changes; detail still supports diagnosis

Start with automatic capture if the product serves immediate digital fulfillment. Add manual and partial capture only with explicit authorization-expiry UI, capture idempotency, and webhook states. Do not overload cancel to manufacture a refund after capture: preserving the distinction lets merchants, support teams, and ledgers explain whether funds were merely reserved or actually moved.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Edge[Regional edge and token vault] --> Home[Merchant home cell]
    Home --> Pay[Payment state machine]
    Pay --> PDB[(Intent, attempt, and posting-command shards)]
    Pay --> Route[Sticky provider routing]
    Route --> Rails[External rails]
    PDB --> Ledger[Balanced ledger poster]
    Ledger --> LDB[(Account-owned ledger partitions)]
    Ledger --> Ack[Durable posting acknowledgement]
    Ack --> Pay
    PDB --> Events[(Payment outbox and stream)]
    Events --> Hooks[Isolated webhook queues]
    Events --> Reports[Settlement projections]
    Files[Provider files and queries] --> Recon[Reconciliation]
    Recon --> Pay
    Recon --> Ledger
    PDB -. fenced DR .-> DR[(Recovery region)]

This final diagram is the later separated-ledger evolution, not the baseline above. A verified capture first commits CAPTURED_PENDING_LEDGER and an idempotent posting command in PDB; the balanced ledger poster consumes that command, commits to LDB, and emits an acknowledgement that lets the payment state machine advance to SUCCEEDED. Settlement excludes pending-ledger captures, and reconciliation repairs commands or acknowledgements without reposting the unique business reference.

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. How does capture differ from authorization in your state model?
  2. What prevents two concurrent refunds exceeding the capture?
  3. How do you partition a ledger transaction touching accounts on different shards?
  4. When is it safe to reroute a timed-out payment?
  5. How do you migrate provider adapters without changing financial behavior?
  6. Which reconciliation differences can be auto-repaired?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer defines idempotency, models payment states, handles provider timeout, uses balanced immutable entries, and separates canonical writes from asynchronous webhooks. An L6 answer additionally reasons about account partitioning, reconciliation value at risk, regional fencing, rail policy, operational repair, migrations, compliance boundaries, and why availability sometimes loses to integrity.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: The system exposes payment intents while hiding provider-specific workflows. Persist an intent and stable provider operation before any external call. A timeout becomes unknown and is resolved by callback, provider query, and reconciliation; it never triggers an unrelated charge. Successful captures post immutable, balanced double-entry transactions, while refunds reserve refundable capacity and add reversing entries. Idempotency records, conditional state transitions, inbox/outbox delivery, and unique posting references create once-only business effects over at-least-once transport. Start with payment and ledger in one multi-AZ SQL transaction; split by account only when throughput demands it. Assign each intent one fenced home region. Isolate providers and merchants with bounded queues, reconcile against independent provider evidence, tokenize card data, and monitor unknown money and reconciliation value rather than HTTP success alone.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify immediate rides, one rider and driver, pricing quote, matching, live trip, and payment. State assignment and fare invariants. Estimate GPS and request peaks, draw a city cell with separate location and trip planes, and trace request-to-match. Deep dive on geospatial indexing, dispatch races, surge, and safety before discussing regional recovery.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Riders request transportation from pickup to destination. Nearby available drivers receive offers, one accepts, both track approach and trip progress, and payment occurs after a server-computed fare. The workload combines high-rate disposable location data with low-rate, high-value state transitions.

Scheduled and pooled rides, navigation-map construction, driver onboarding, and payment-rail internals are out of scope.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Quote price range and pickup ETA; request and cancel a ride.
  • Match one eligible driver, support offer expiry and reassignment.
  • Track driver approach and trip; complete and charge final fare.
  • Provide receipts, ratings, support evidence, and safety escalation.
  • Trip commands target 99.99% availability; matching should usually finish in ten seconds.
  • Location shown during active trips should be less than five seconds stale at p95.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. A ride has at most one active driver assignment, and a driver has at most one incompatible active ride.
  2. Only authorized rider and assigned driver can advance a ride through legal transitions.
  3. One request idempotency key creates one ride; one completion creates one intended charge.
  4. Final fare uses trusted trip facts, a recorded pricing-policy version, integer money, and explicit adjustments.
  5. Location and ETA are advisory; trip and assignment records are canonical.
  6. A stale dispatch owner cannot assign after a higher region or lease epoch takes ownership.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text: Assume 20 million rides/day, 3 million online drivers at peak, and a five-second location interval. Ride requests average 230 QPS and peak near 5,000 QPS; location ingestion peaks at 600,000 updates/s. A ride plus events may consume 15 KB, or 300 GB/day. At 100 bytes/update, sustaining peak all day produces 5.184 TB; multiply by average/peak online-driver ratio for actual daily retention. Use short retention, compression, and downsampling. A stadium exit creates a pickup-zone hot spot even if city totals are normal.

docs.title: Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Ride(ride_id, rider_id, city_id, pickup, destination, quote_snapshot,
     status, driver_id, idempotency_key, pricing_version, version)
Driver(driver_id, city_id, status, vehicle_id, capability, version)
DriverLocation(driver_id, source_epoch, device_sequence, observed_at, geocell, point, accuracy)
Offer(offer_id, ride_id, driver_id, status, expires_at, dispatch_epoch)
Assignment(assignment_id, ride_id, driver_id, status, accepted_at)
TripEvent(event_id, ride_id, type, actor_id, observed_at, coordinates)
Fare(ride_id, base, distance, duration, tolls, adjustments, total, currency)
PaymentAttempt(attempt_id, ride_id, provider_ref, status)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

Ride, driver availability, offer acceptance, and assignment use transactional storage. Latest locations use an in-memory geo store with conditional sequence updates. Durable sampled trip points go to an append store for fare disputes and safety under a strict retention policy.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/ride-quotes
{"pickup":{"lat":..,"lng":..},"destination":{"lat":..,"lng":..},"class":"standard"}
POST /v1/rides
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"quote_id":"q1","payment_method_token":"pm1"}
POST /v1/drivers/{id}/locations
POST /v1/offers/{id}/accept
{"expected_dispatch_epoch":91}
POST /v1/rides/{id}/events
{"type":"TRIP_STARTED","expected_version":8}
GET /v1/rides/{id}/tracking?after_cursor=

Quotes expire and identify pricing and map versions. Location requests carry a server-issued source epoch and monotonically increasing sequence within that device session. On authenticated takeover or sequence reset, advance the authorized epoch first; reject old-session packets even if their sequence is larger. Tracking begins with a snapshot and resumes from a cursor. Mutation retries with the same key or event identity return the committed result.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Rider[Rider app] --> Edge[City gateway]
    Driver[Driver app] --> Location[Location ingestion]
    Location --> Geo[(Latest-driver geo index)]
    Edge --> Ride[Ride service]
    Ride --> DB[(Trip SQL)]
    DB --> Stream[(Outbox and event stream)]
    Stream --> Dispatch[Dispatch]
    Dispatch --> Geo
    Dispatch --> DB
    Stream --> Push[Realtime gateway]
    Stream --> Pricing[Fare calculation]
    Pricing --> Payment[Payment service]
    Safety[Safety and operations] --> DB

The smallest matcher queries nearby drivers and offers sequentially. Parallel offer waves and optimization are scaling choices, not baseline correctness requirements.

docs.title: Quote and Request
docs.text: Pricing reads map distance, estimated duration, vehicle class, city policy, and current supply-demand multiplier. It returns a signed quote range with expiry. Ride creation verifies rider eligibility and quote, stores SEARCHING plus outbox, and validates a payment method without charging. If dispatch is overloaded, the request is rejected or queued with truthful ETA rather than accepted indefinitely.

docs.title: Match a Driver
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Dispatch
    participant G as Geo index
    participant A as Driver app
    participant T as Trip SQL
    D->>G: Nearby eligible drivers
    D->>T: Persist offer wave and epoch
    D->>A: Offer(expires_at)
    A->>T: Accept(offer, epoch)
    T->>T: Check ride SEARCHING and driver AVAILABLE
    alt wins transaction
        T->>T: Create assignment and mark MATCHED and RESERVED
        T-->>A: accepted
    else conflict or expiry
        T-->>A: offer unavailable
    end

Candidate ranking may race and be stale; the database transaction resolves truth. Offer a small wave to reduce latency, cancel losers after one acceptance, and penalize excessive fan-out because it distracts drivers. A dispatch lease and epoch prevent two schedulers from issuing valid assignment decisions after failover.

docs.title: Start, Complete, and Pay
docs.text:
Driver arrival is inferred from location but confirmed by a driver command. A rider PIN can authorize trip start. During trip, sampled points and map matching estimate route distance; driver and rider commands record significant events. Completion freezes trusted duration, distance, tolls, pricing version, and adjustments, computes a fare, then invokes payment idempotently by ride ID. Payment failure does not reopen the trip; it creates collection workflow and may limit future rides.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SEARCHING
    SEARCHING --> MATCHED
    MATCHED --> DRIVER_ARRIVING
    DRIVER_ARRIVING --> DRIVER_WAITING
    DRIVER_WAITING --> IN_TRIP
    IN_TRIP --> COMPLETED
    SEARCHING --> CANCELLED
    MATCHED --> CANCELLED
    DRIVER_ARRIVING --> CANCELLED
    DRIVER_WAITING --> CANCELLED
    MATCHED --> SEARCHING: assignment revoked before trip
    DRIVER_ARRIVING --> SEARCHING: driver released before rematch
    COMPLETED --> PAYMENT_PENDING
    PAYMENT_PENDING --> PAID
    PAYMENT_PENDING --> COLLECTION_REQUIRED

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Geospatial Indexing
docs.text:
Map coordinates to hierarchical cells such as H3 or S2. Keep sets of available driver IDs by fine cell and expand rings until enough candidates appear. Dense downtown areas use smaller cells; sparse areas use larger rings. Location ingestion conditionally applies only newer sequences under the current authorized source epoch and updates old/new cell membership. Periodic repair rebuilds membership from latest records because a crash can leave stale set entries.

Geo results are candidates, not authority. Dispatch filters vehicle capability, driver status, recent rejection, location age, and policy. Final assignment reads canonical driver state. Hot airport cells can subdivide, sample candidates, and use venue queue policy rather than retrieving every driver.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Dispatch Optimization
docs.text:
Simple nearest-driver minimizes one pickup but may worsen overall supply. A batched bipartite matcher can minimize pickup ETA, cancellation risk, driver idle time, and zone imbalance across many rides. Batch windows improve choices but add rider delay. Establish hard constraints first, then weighted objectives and fairness bounds. Run new algorithms in shadow mode and evaluate match time, acceptance, cancellations, dead miles, earnings distribution, and neighborhood coverage.

Overload controls reduce candidate fan-out, lengthen batch windows modestly, meter low-confidence requests, and create pickup-zone queues. Never let an unbounded matcher backlog consume offers after riders have abandoned.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Pricing and Fare Disputes
docs.text:
The quote records model and multiplier versions and may guarantee a maximum unless route changes. Final fare uses trusted server times, map-matched sampled points, toll evidence, and explicit city rounding. GPS loss falls back to planned route plus event timestamps, with a flag for review. Adjustments append to the fare ledger; they do not overwrite original calculation.

Surge shapes supply and demand but can violate regulation or perceived fairness during emergencies. City policy caps multipliers and may disable them centrally. Regional data planes cache signed policy with expiry and fail to conservative pricing when stale.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Safety and Privacy
docs.text: Exact driver and rider positions are highly sensitive. Share only during the appropriate ride stage, use phone-number relay, restrict employee access, and retain precision only for safety and dispute windows. Detect impossible movement, rooted-device spoofing, route deviation, unexpected stops, and account sharing. An emergency workflow snapshots relevant evidence, alerts trained operations, and preserves access audit. Safety paths must not depend solely on the analytics stream.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition active rides and driver state by city or operating region. Within a large city, the geo index can shard independently, but a ride/driver pair still needs an atomic assignment boundary. Keep the pair in one assignment authority or use a real cross-shard transaction. A separately designed reservation saga may prepare a unique driver claim and a unique ride claim, but must expose MATCHED only after both are committed and fence/repair abandoned claims; sharding rides by ID alone does not preserve both uniqueness constraints. A ride remains in its home city even if route crosses a boundary; handoff of telemetry does not transfer command ownership. Location and push planes scale independently from SQL commands. Event history partitions by ride and date; analytics receives streams.

Hot venues use dedicated logical zones, bounded candidate sets, and queue policy. Drivers moving between city cells register in the destination only after the source removes availability or a higher mobility epoch fences it.

docs.title: Consistency, Idempotency, and Failures
docs.text:
Ride state, assignment, and final fare are strongly consistent in their owners. GPS, ETA, map display, and analytics are eventual. Idempotency keys cover ride creation and payment; unique event identities cover state commands. At-least-once streams use version-aware consumers. Snapshot plus cursor closes realtime subscription gaps.

If geo storage fails, stop or constrain new matching while active trips continue. If push fails, apps poll canonical state. If dispatch crashes, expired leases and persisted offer waves permit recovery. If payment is unavailable, complete rides and queue durable collection. If maps fail, use cached routes and conservative estimates. Reconciliation finds matched rides without valid assignments, stale reserved drivers, completed rides without fares, and charges without receipts.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text: Each city is a multi-zone cell, limiting blast radius and matching latency. A global control plane distributes maps, policy, experiments, and identity, but city data planes continue with last known safe versions. Asynchronous DR replicates ride state and important sampled locations. Failover fences the old city writer using region and dispatch epochs before matching resumes.
