Recover the acknowledged active-assignment prefix or quarantine uncertain drivers and rides; a newer epoch cannot reveal assignments missing from an asynchronous replica. During a network partition, preserve active-trip visibility locally but pause conflicting new assignments if ownership is uncertain.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Authenticate driver devices and bind sessions to approved vehicles. Tokenize payment, encrypt personal and location data, authorize every ride transition, and sign dispatch offers. Rate limit fake ride requests and detect GPS spoofing, collusion, promotion fraud, chargeback rings, account takeover, scraping, and denial-of-service. High-risk profile or payout changes require step-up authentication. Support tools use least privilege, purpose logging, and short-lived access.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure request-to-match, candidate count, location freshness, offer acceptance, driver reassignment, cancellation by stage, pickup ETA error, trip-state age, fare discrepancy, payment backlog, geocell saturation, and safety signal delivery. Slice by city, zone, vehicle class, app version, and algorithm version. Fleet averages hide airport or neighborhood starvation.

Property-test assignment uniqueness and state transitions. Inject duplicate accepts, stale dispatch epochs, reordered GPS, push loss, driver app death, map outage, database failover, and stadium bursts. Replay historical demand against matcher candidates and compare fairness and efficiency. Test policy expiry, backup restoration, and region fencing regularly.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Parallel offers reduce match time but annoy more drivers and increase races. Batched optimization improves fleet efficiency while delaying individual rides. City cells reduce latency and blast radius but complicate cross-boundary trips. Frequent GPS improves dispatch while consuming battery, bandwidth, and privacy budget. Completing trips during payment failure favors safety and availability over immediate collection.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Apps[Global rider and driver apps] --> Cell[City data-plane cell]
    Cell --> Trip[Trip state service]
    Trip --> SQL[(Ride, driver, assignment, outbox)]
    Driver[Driver telemetry] --> Ingest[Scalable location ingestion]
    Ingest --> Geo[(Hierarchical geo index)]
    SQL --> Events[(Regional stream)]
    Events --> Match[Leased dispatch partitions]
    Geo --> Match
    Match --> SQL
    Events --> Realtime[Tracking and push]
    Events --> Fare[Fare and payment]
    Control[Global policy and model control plane] --> Cell
    SQL -. fenced DR .-> DR[(Recovery cell)]
    subgraph StateLane[Trip authority and recovery]
      SQL
      DR
    end
    subgraph EventLane[Regional event consumers]
      Events
      Match
      Realtime
      Fare
    end

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. How do simultaneous driver accepts preserve both uniqueness constraints?
  2. What is canonical when the geo index says a driver is available but SQL disagrees?
  3. How do you evaluate a new matcher without risking production rides?
  4. What happens to an active cross-city ride during cell failure?
  5. How do surge caps and stale policy interact?
  6. Which GPS points can be deleted without weakening disputes and safety?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer separates location from trip state, enforces unique assignments, explains geospatial search, idempotent payment, and common failures. An L6 answer also treats matching as constrained optimization, defines overload and fairness policy, designs city-cell fencing and control-plane degradation, and balances safety, privacy, marketplace economics, regulation, and cost.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Ride hailing combines a high-volume approximate location plane with a strongly consistent trip state machine. Start with a city-local SQL store, a latest-driver geo index, and nearest-driver offers. Candidate data may be stale, so offer acceptance transactionally verifies ride still searching and driver available, then creates one assignment and changes both states. Store ride and pricing policy versions; complete the trip from trusted events and charge idempotently. Outbox events drive dispatch, realtime views, fare, and receipts. Partition by city, scale telemetry separately, and use bounded offer waves and venue controls for hot zones. Keep one fenced owner per city during failover. Protect exact location, build safety paths outside analytics, reconcile stuck rides and charges, and test duplicate accepts, GPS disorder, dispatcher crashes, and regional partitions.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Spend the first five minutes fixing scope: reserved-seat events, discovery, temporary holds, checkout, and electronic tickets. Then state the central invariant: a seat cannot belong to two paid orders. Estimate the onsale burst, draw the single-region design, trace hold and purchase, and use the remaining time for hot events, expiration, idempotency, and regional failure. Do not begin with Kafka or sharding; begin with one relational database whose conditional updates are correct.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Fans search events, inspect a venue map, hold exact seats for a short period, pay, and receive transferable barcodes. Organizers publish events and inventory. The difficult workload is not average traffic but a popular onsale where millions of people compete for tens of thousands of seats in minutes.

Out of scope are artist settlement, recommendation ranking, dynamic-pricing policy, and venue access-control hardware. General admission can be represented as counted inventory, but the primary design uses assigned seats.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements

  • Search events and view price tiers and approximate availability.
  • Hold selected seats for five minutes and purchase the hold.
  • Release expired holds and support cancellation or transfer after purchase.
  • Issue a ticket whose current owner and barcode can be validated at entry.

Non-functional requirements

  • No double sale, even under retries and process failure.
  • Hold and checkout writes should complete in under 500 ms at p99 when admitted.
  • Search may be seconds stale; authoritative seat status may not.
  • Survive instance and zone loss; degrade predictably during extreme demand.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. A seat has at most one active hold or completed allocation for an event.
  2. Only the owner of an unexpired hold can purchase it.
  3. One idempotency key creates at most one logical hold or order.
  4. A successful charge eventually yields either tickets or an automatic refund; reconciliation detects limbo.
  5. A barcode resolves to one current ticket version. Transfer invalidates the previous version.
  6. Availability caches and search indexes are projections, never sale authority.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100,000 active events, 50,000 seats at a stadium event, and 10 million daily searches. Search averages 115 QPS and peaks near 2,000 QPS. A major onsale may receive 1 million waiting users, 100,000 admitted users, and 20,000 hold attempts per second for one event. If each seat row and indexes consume roughly 500 bytes, five billion historical seat-event records require about 2.5 TB before replicas and history. Ticket images are generated artifacts in object storage, not database blobs.

The skew drives the design. Scaling average QPS is easy; one event partition and a few desirable sections become hot. The admission controller must cap contenders to a write rate that the inventory shard can sustain.

docs.title: Core Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Event(event_id, venue_id, starts_at, status, sales_version)
SeatInventory(event_id, seat_id, section_id, price_id, state,
              hold_id, hold_expires_at, order_id, version)
Hold(hold_id, user_id, event_id, status, expires_at, idempotency_key)
HoldSeat(hold_id, event_id, seat_id)
Order(order_id, user_id, hold_id, amount, status, idempotency_key)
PaymentAttempt(attempt_id, order_id, provider_ref, status)
Ticket(ticket_id, order_id, seat_id, owner_id, barcode_version, status)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, payload, published_at)

SeatInventory has primary key (event_id, seat_id). A transaction conditionally changes AVAILABLE to HELD, checking state and expiry. Hold.idempotency_key and Order.idempotency_key are unique per user. A unique active purchase claim on hold_id prevents a second order key from starting another payment for the same hold. The database is canonical; Redis stores short-lived maps and counters, and the search engine stores event documents.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
GET /v1/events?query=&city=&starts_after=&cursor=
GET /v1/events/{eventId}/availability?section=&cursor=
POST /v1/holds
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"event_id":"e1","seat_ids":["A-10","A-11"]}

POST /v1/orders
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{"hold_id":"h1","payment_method_token":"pm_7"}

POST /v1/tickets/{ticketId}/transfers
{"recipient_user_id":"u9"}
GET /v1/barcodes/{signedCode}/validation

The availability endpoint returns as_of, a signed map version, and next_cursor. It is advisory. 409 means a seat was lost; 429 includes a retry time or queue token. A repeated mutation returns the original resource and status.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Fan --> Edge[CDN and API gateway]
    Edge --> Search[Search service]
    Search --> Index[(Search index)]
    Edge --> Queue[Virtual waiting room]
    Queue --> Inventory[Inventory service]
    Inventory --> DB[(Inventory SQL shard)]
    Inventory --> Cache[(Availability cache)]
    Edge --> Order[Order service]
    Order --> DB
    Order --> PSP[Payment provider]
    DB --> Outbox[Outbox relay]
    Outbox --> Bus[(Event stream)]
    Bus --> Ticket[Ticket service]
    Bus --> Index

The smallest correct deployment uses stateless services and one multi-AZ SQL database. Add read replicas and search for reads, then split inventory by event only after measured lock or I/O pressure. The waiting room is required by burst shape, not fashion.

docs.title: Discover and View Availability
docs.text: Event publication writes SQL and emits an outbox event. An indexer builds search documents. Availability is a compact per-section bitmap or count in Redis, refreshed from inventory changes. A fan sees fast, slightly stale data and receives no promise until hold creation succeeds. Cache misses query a read replica with bounded concurrency; stale values are safer than allowing a cache outage to overload the primary.

docs.title: Hold Seats
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant F as Fan
    participant A as Admission
    participant I as Inventory
    participant D as SQL
    F->>A: Enter event queue
    A-->>F: Signed admission token
    F->>I: Create hold(token, seats, key)
    I->>D: BEGIN with conditional seat updates
    alt every seat available
        I->>D: Insert hold and outbox, then COMMIT
        I-->>F: HELD, expires_at
    else any conflict
        I->>D: ROLLBACK
        I-->>F: 409 unavailable
    end

Lock requested seat rows in sorted seat-ID order to avoid deadlocks. All seats succeed or none do. A database-time expiry avoids application clock disagreement. The admission token binds user, event, expiry, and queue position and is rate limited against replay.

docs.title: Purchase and Issue
docs.text: Order creation verifies the hold owner and changes the hold to CHECKOUT_PENDING. The payment provider call cannot share a database transaction. Persist an order and payment attempt first, call the provider with order_id as its idempotency key, then record the result. On success, one SQL transaction marks seats SOLD, hold PURCHASED, and order PAID, and adds TicketsRequested to the outbox. Ticket generation and email are retryable consumers. On an ambiguous timeout, return 202 PROCESSING; never start an unrelated charge.

docs.title: Transfer and Gate Validation
docs.text: A transfer transaction changes owner and increments barcode_version. Barcodes carry opaque ticket ID, version, and signature, not personal data. The GET validation API is read-only; a separate idempotent POST /v1/tickets/{id}/admissions atomically checks current version and records first entry. Strict one-entry semantics require all scanners to share that authority, including a venue-local server during WAN outage. Transfer and first-entry transitions must serialize against the same current ticket authority; moving authority to the venue fences cloud mutations or pauses transfers until a safe handback. Independent offline signed allow-lists verify authenticity but cannot prevent two disconnected gates accepting the same ticket or instantly learn a transfer. Offer them only as an explicitly weaker, reconciled fallback.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Seat Contention
docs.text:
Optimistic compare-and-set works when collisions are moderate:

UPDATE seat_inventory
SET state='HELD', hold_id=:h, hold_expires_at=:expiry, version=version+1
WHERE event_id=:e AND seat_id=:s
  AND (state='AVAILABLE' OR (state='HELD' AND hold_expires_at <= CURRENT_TIMESTAMP));

For a multi-seat request, execute these updates inside one transaction and validate distinct seat IDs and require the affected count to equal that distinct request size. Pessimistic locks can reduce repeated conflicts but increase queueing and deadlock risk. A distributed lock adds another failure mode and does not replace the database constraint. At extreme load, route one event to an inventory shard and serialize requests per section through a bounded command queue. This sacrifices latency for stable throughput, while SQL remains the durable authority.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Hold Expiration
docs.text:
Expiration has two meanings. Logically, an expired hold stops blocking a conditional update immediately. Physically, a sweeper later changes its rows to AVAILABLE. Correctness therefore does not depend on a timer firing exactly on time. Sweep by (state, hold_expires_at) index in small batches using SKIP LOCKED, publish availability changes, and tolerate duplicates. Checkout compares expiry using database time and may offer a grace period only if product policy reserves that capacity explicitly.

CHECKOUT_PENDING must also protect its seat rows under an explicit processing deadline, not only change the parent hold. Paid conversion verifies every row still has this hold ID and valid deadline. A sweeper releases only matching expired ownership; it cannot free a seat re-held by another customer. If late payment succeeds after ownership was lost, refund it rather than unconditionally setting those seats to SOLD.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Waiting Room and Fairness
docs.text: The edge assigns random positions within a short enrollment window rather than rewarding network proximity. It admits a controlled number per second based on inventory commit latency and conflict rate. Tokens are signed, short-lived, event-specific, and one-user scoped. Bots face account, device, IP, payment-instrument, and velocity controls. A queue outage fails closed for new admissions but allows already admitted users to finish. Operators can lower admission quickly; increasing it requires evidence that DB latency and lock waits are healthy.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition inventory, holds, and orders by event_id so a hold is local. Very large events may subpartition by section, but cross-section atomic holds then need a real distributed transaction protocol or co-location of the participating rows, otherwise they must be disallowed; a coordinator alone does not make independent commits atomic; the product tradeoff is preferable to distributed transactions. Search partitions by geography and time. Ticket history can partition by event month. Keep globally unique IDs independent of shard location to simplify moves.

Hot sections remain hot even after hashing. Admission, section-level queues, request limits, and cached maps address skew. Repartition an upcoming event offline by copying immutable layout, tailing changes, verifying counts, and switching routing before onsale. Never move an actively selling event casually.

docs.title: Consistency, Idempotency, and Recovery
docs.text: Inventory and order transitions require strong consistency. Search, maps, email, and analytics are eventual. Every command records a scoped idempotency key and request hash; key reuse with a different body is rejected. Outbox publication is at least once, so consumers deduplicate by outbox ID. Reconciliation compares paid provider transactions to order state and creates tickets or refunds. Rebuild projections by replaying outbox history plus a canonical snapshot.

docs.title: Reliability and Multi-Region
docs.text:
Run each event in one home region with multi-AZ synchronous storage. Route reads globally, but send hold and purchase writes to that home to avoid split-brain allocation. A second region receives asynchronous replicas and event logs. Promotion requires fencing the old writer, checking replication position, changing the epoch in routing tokens, and accepting a recovery interval; if fencing or completeness of acknowledged seat/order/payment identities is uncertain, pause sales. An asynchronous replica that has lost a paid allocation cannot safely sell that seat merely because it holds a newer epoch. Events near start time can use a region-local gate dataset independently of the commerce control plane.

Dependency failures have explicit behavior: stale search continues, cache loss sheds availability reads, payment outage preserves holds only up to a capped extension, stream outage grows the outbox backlog, and ticket email outage leaves tickets accessible in-app. Circuit breakers and bounded queues prevent a slow provider from consuming all threads.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Tokenize payment details through a PCI-scoped provider. Encrypt personal data, separate organizer administration, require MFA for high-risk actions, and audit price, inventory, refund, and transfer changes. Protect APIs with WAF rules, per-principal quotas, bot scoring, CAPTCHA only at suspicious thresholds, purchase limits, and payment-instrument velocity. Signed barcodes rotate after transfer and use short-lived presentation codes to reduce screenshots. Privacy deletion removes profiles while retaining legally required pseudonymous transaction records.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Track admitted users, hold success and conflict rates, DB lock wait, shard saturation, hold expiry lag, payment ambiguity, paid-without-ticket age, outbox lag, queue time, and gate rejection reasons. SLO alerts should be burn-rate based and split by event because fleet averages hide a broken onsale.

Test the seat state machine with model-based and concurrent property tests. Inject crashes after charge and before commit, duplicate every event, delay sweepers, skew application clocks, and fail a zone. Load tests must concentrate traffic on one event and one section. Periodic invariants scan for multiple allocations, sold seats without paid orders, and paid orders without active tickets.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: SQL conditional writes beat a distributed lock because the constraint and state change commit together. A waiting room loses immediate access but protects fairness and availability. Home-region writes add latency for distant buyers but avoid global consensus on every seat. Section sharding raises throughput but weakens easy atomic multi-section selection. Keeping expired rows logically reclaimable makes correctness independent of background jobs at the cost of more complex predicates.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Global[Global DNS and CDN] --> WR[Per-event waiting room]
    WR --> Home[Event home region]
    Home --> API[Inventory and order APIs]
    API --> Shard[(SQL shard: event-owned)]
    Shard --> Relay[Transactional outbox relay]
    Relay --> Stream[(Replicated stream)]
    Stream --> Proj[Search, maps, notifications]
    Stream --> Recon[Payment and ticket reconciler]
    Shard -. async replication .-> DR[(Fenced DR replica)]
    Stream --> Gate[Venue validation dataset]

The final design keeps one writer per event, SQL-enforced allocation, database-time expiry, idempotent payment orchestration, and asynchronous projections. The architecture scales by controlling offered load before adding shards.

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. How would you support general admission and assigned seating in one model?
  2. What happens if payment succeeds after the hold expires?
  3. How do you prove the old region cannot sell after failover?
  4. How would you make queue admission fair while resisting account farms?
  5. Which metrics tell you to split an event by section?
  6. How can venue entry continue through a regional internet outage?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer defines the no-double-sale invariant, uses transactional conditional writes, separates stale availability from authority, estimates the hot-event burst, and handles payment retries and expiry. An L6 answer also shapes demand, reasons about fairness and fencing, plans shard migration and reconciliation, defines degraded modes, and connects fraud, venue operations, policy, and cost to technical choices.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: This is a scarce-inventory system. Begin with a multi-AZ SQL database: seat rows are canonical, and a transaction conditionally changes all requested seats from available to held. Holds expire by database time; a sweeper is cleanup, not correctness. Checkout persists an order, calls payment idempotently, and atomically converts held seats to sold after payment success. An outbox drives ticket generation, maps, search, and notifications with deduplicating consumers. Cache and search results may be stale, so only hold creation promises inventory. A virtual waiting room caps and fairly meters a popular onsale. Partition by event and keep each event in one fenced home region; only split by section when measured load demands it. Reconcile payment, order, and ticket state continuously, and test concentrated contention, duplicate delivery, crash points, and regional fencing.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design query suggestions returned while a user types. Clarify sources, personalization, freshness, languages, safety, and latency. Build the smallest system from offline query counts and an in-memory prefix index, then add streaming updates, ranking, context, typo tolerance, hot-prefix protection, regional serving, and governance. The central tension is serving a safe ranked list in tens of milliseconds while popularity changes continuously.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
For a normalized prefix and context, return up to ten suggestions with display text and optional entity metadata. Sources include historical queries, catalog entities, editorial entries, and current trends. Results may vary by locale, market, device, and authenticated user. Administrators can block, pin, or expire phrases. We exclude full search and document retrieval; selection logs feed ranking asynchronously.

Target 50 ms p99 from edge, 99.99% availability, hourly baseline freshness, trend visibility within one minute, and policy removal within one minute globally. Empty-prefix discovery is a different product and is not served by this endpoint. Results can be eventually consistent across users, but policy filtering must meet its bounded staleness contract.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• Every returned suggestion begins with the normalized prefix unless explicitly labeled typo correction.
  • Policy-denied text is never intentionally published; emergency blocks override every score and cache.
  • A response contains unique canonical suggestion IDs and a deterministic order for the same captured index, model, policy, trend watermark, and request context. Index version alone does not freeze personalized or streaming inputs.
  • Offline snapshots are immutable, checksummed, and atomically activated.
  • Streaming deltas are monotonic by (partition, offset) and deduplicated by event ID.
  • User history is never exposed across identities or used outside consent and retention policy.
  • Ranking degradation may reduce relevance, not bypass safety.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 500 million daily search users, 20 searches/user/day, and six autocomplete requests/search: 60 billion requests/day, 700,000/s average and 5 million/s peak. A response around 1 KB yields 5 GB/s peak egress before protocol overhead. There are 500 million candidate strings across locales. Storing normalized text, ID, features, and top-prefix postings at 100 bytes is 50 GB raw, but replicated tries and postings may require hundreds of GB. Logs at 200 bytes/request produce 12 TB/day, so sample impressions while retaining selections and policy events fully.

docs.title: Data model and interface
docs.text:
Suggestion(id, normalized_text, display_text, locale, type, entity_ref, policy_tags)
Aggregate(id, window, market, impressions, selections, unique_users, last_seen)
PrefixPosting(prefix, locale, candidate_id, base_score, snapshot_version)
TrendDelta(prefix, candidate_id, score_delta, event_time, expires_at)
PolicyRule(rule_id, match_type, value, markets, action, version, expires_at)
UserSignal(user_id, candidate_id, last_selected, decayed_weight)

GET /v1/suggestions?q=iph&locale=en-US&limit=10&context=shopping
If-Index-Version: optional-debug-version

200 {"suggestions":[...], "index_version":"2026-09-05.12", "degraded":false}

The request normalizes Unicode according to locale, folds safe case variants, caps prefix length, and rejects control characters. Cursor pagination is unnecessary for ten results; an internal candidate API uses stable score/ID cursors for diagnostics.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
 C[Clients] --> E[Edge/API]
 E --> S[Suggestion servers]
 S --> Lookup[Prefix lookup]
 Lookup --> I[(Immutable prefix index)]
 S --> Recent[Trend lookup]
 Recent --> D[(Trend delta store)]
 S --> P[Policy filter]
 S --> R[Ranker]
 L[Query and selection log] --> B[Batch aggregation]
 L --> T[Streaming trends]
 B --> X[Index builder]
 X --> I
 T --> D
 G[Governance control plane] --> P
    subgraph Prefix[Prefix candidates]
      B
      X
      Lookup
      I
    end
    subgraph Trends[Trend candidates]
      Recent
      T
      D
    end
    subgraph Policy[Policy enforcement]
      G
      P
    end

docs.title: Normalization and candidate retrieval
docs.text:
Normalization applies locale-aware Unicode normalization, whitespace collapse, case handling, and script detection. Store the canonical form beside display variants; do not blindly strip accents because meaning changes in some languages. The prefix index maps each trie node to a bounded top-K candidate list. Lookup is O(length(prefix) + K), independent of corpus size. A compressed radix trie reduces pointers; a finite-state transducer compresses shared suffix/output structure further but complicates incremental changes.

Each node stores perhaps 100 candidates, larger than the returned ten, to leave room for filtering and reranking. For long-tail prefixes absent from the precomputed index, descend into a term dictionary and merge bounded postings. Single-character prefixes are extremely hot and broad, so they use dedicated replicated objects and aggressive edge caching.

docs.title: Ranking
docs.text:
Candidate score combines smoothed popularity, selection-through rate, recency, edit cost, locale match, entity quality, user affinity, and policy/editorial adjustment:

score = w1*log1p(decayed_frequency)
      + w2*bayesian_selection_rate
      + w3*freshness + w4*context_match + w5*personal_affinity
      - w6*edit_cost - policy_penalty

Use exponential decay weight = exp(-lambda * age) so old popularity fades. Bayesian smoothing prevents a phrase with one impression and one click outranking established results. The model reranks only a bounded candidate set and has a deterministic lexical/ID tie-break. If features or model are unavailable, fall back to snapshot base score and still run local policy filters.

docs.title: Build and publish
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant L as Event log
 participant A as Aggregator
 participant B as Index builder
 participant V as Validator
 participant C as Control plane
 participant S as Serving fleet
 L->>A: queries and selections
 A->>B: privacy-thresholded counts
 B->>B: normalize, score, top-K per prefix
 B->>V: immutable snapshot and manifest
 V->>V: safety, quality, checksum tests
 V->>C: approved version
 C->>S: staged activation
 S->>S: mmap then atomic pointer swap

Builders aggregate distinct-user counts and apply minimum support, bot filtering, privacy thresholds, and differential privacy where required. They generate immutable locale/market shards, manifests, checksums, model version, and source watermark. Servers download in the background, validate, warm key prefixes, then atomically switch pointers. Old snapshots remain for rollback and are deleted by retention policy.

docs.title: Trending deltas
docs.text:
A streaming job computes event-time windows and compares observed frequency with a seasonality baseline. A trend requires enough distinct trusted users, geographic dispersion, and selection evidence. Use burst score such as (observed - expected) / sqrt(expected + c), capped to prevent tiny baselines from exploding. Deltas have TTLs and merge with snapshot candidates at read time. The snapshot records the aggregate cutoff/watermark; an overlay adds only contributions not already represented, or supplies an explicitly defined replacement trend feature. On snapshot swap, reset/rebase the overlay atomically so the same events do not inflate both base and delta scores. Late events revise only open windows; replay deduplicates by event ID and partition offset.

flowchart TD
 Q[Prefix] --> N[Locale normalization]
 N --> C[Snapshot top candidates]
 N --> T[Fresh trend candidates]
 N --> U[Consented user history]
 C --> M[Deduplicate and feature join]
 T --> M
 U --> M
 M --> F[Hard policy filter]
 F --> R[Bounded reranker]
 R --> D[Diversity and deterministic top ten]

docs.title: Personalization, typo tolerance, and diversity
docs.text:
Personal history is a separate keyed store queried only for authenticated, consented users. Merge a few matching recent selections, never the raw history of another user. Cache personalized responses privately or not at all. Contextual models may consider country, app surface, and broad time bucket; sensitive attributes are prohibited.

For prefixes longer than two characters, retrieve bounded edit-distance-one candidates from a deletion index or trie traversal. Label corrections and demand a score margin before replacing literal-prefix results. Transliteration is locale-specific. Diversity constraints limit near-duplicates and ensure, where product requires, a mix of query and entity types. These post-ranking rules are versioned and tested against relevance sets.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and hot keys
docs.text:
Shard snapshots by locale/market and first normalized bytes, but replicate tiny hot-prefix tables everywhere. Serving nodes hold common shards in memory and memory-map colder shards. Consistent hashing assigns long-tail requests; replicas permit hedging only when the first request exceeds a percentile threshold, avoiding doubled normal load. Edge caches key by normalized prefix, locale, coarse context, policy generation, and index version. Personalized fragments do not enter shared caches.

The fanout from typing means client behavior matters: debounce 50-100 ms, cancel superseded requests, and reuse a request sequence so late responses are ignored. Under overload, shed typo correction and personalization, shorten candidate pools, serve stale verified snapshots, and return no result rather than unfiltered text. Token buckets protect tenants and abusive IPs. Backpressure pauses analytics sampling before affecting selection events or policy distribution.

Multi-region serving is active-active with complete local snapshots. Trend deltas replicate asynchronously and may differ briefly. The governance plane publishes signed policy generations through a high-priority channel; emergency deny rules are also pushed to edge processes. Snapshot activation is regionally staged, with a global minimum-safe policy version independent of content index version.

docs.title: Consistency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Index and model versions are eventually consistent, but each response is internally consistent because one request pins a snapshot pointer. Policy is bounded-staleness and fail-safe: servers refuse versions older than the emergency deadline. Selection ingestion is at least once; deterministic event IDs and aggregate upserts make effects idempotent. We do not promise exact counts.

Builder failure leaves the old snapshot active. Partial downloads never activate because manifests and checksums fail. A bad ranking release rolls back by pointer. Stream lag ages out deltas rather than making them permanent. Cache outage increases origin load, so admission control and local hot-prefix tables protect servers. Feature-store timeout uses defaults. A poison locale shard is quarantined while others publish. Region loss reroutes to another region with higher latency but no canonical write conflict.

Deletion removes user signals by subject key and ages raw logs; derived anonymous aggregates remain only if policy permits. A policy incident triggers rule publication, cache-key generation change, snapshot scan, and auditable proof of propagation. Rebuilds are reproducible from source watermarks and code/model artifacts.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Authenticate internal publishers, sign snapshots and rules, encrypt user history, isolate operator roles, and audit pins/blocks. Defend against suggestion poisoning, bots, offensive phrase amplification, celebrity harassment, election manipulation, Unicode confusables, scraping, and query leakage. Require distinct-user and reputation thresholds, rate-limit clients, cap editorial influence, and provide rapid kill switches. Never log raw sensitive prefixes indiscriminately.

Measure end-to-end and server latency, cache hit rate, candidates retrieved/filtered, empty rate, model fallback, index age, trend lag, policy generation lag, snapshot load failures, request cancellation, QPS by prefix entropy, hot-shard saturation, and selection metrics with guardrails for unsafe or low-diversity results. Track freshness and relevance by locale, not only globally.

Property-test normalization idempotence, prefix validity, uniqueness, deterministic ordering, and denied-term absence. Golden sets measure recall, mean reciprocal rank, and locale quality. Replay historical traffic against candidate/model changes. Fuzz Unicode and malformed context. Load-test one-character hot keys and synchronized trends. Chaos-test cache loss, stale policy, corrupt snapshots, stream duplication, and region evacuation. Canary versions by region and user bucket with automatic safety rollback.

docs.title: Important tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
A database query per keystroke is simple but cannot meet latency and hot-key scale. Precomputed top-K prefix lists trade storage for predictable reads. Tries are straightforward; FSTs compress better but are harder to update, so immutable batch FST plus a small delta store works well. Fully online ranking is freshest but fragile; bounded reranking over a verified snapshot gives a safe fallback. Global strong consistency for trends wastes latency, while strong emergency policy propagation is justified.

flowchart TD
 E[Debounced edge request] --> H[Versioned hot-prefix cache]
 H -->|hit| Gate[Check current edge policy freshness]
 Gate -->|valid| Response[Cached response]
 Gate -->|stale| Empty[Refuse stale policy response]
 H -->|miss| S[Regional serving node]
 S --> I[Immutable locale index]
 S --> T[TTL trend overlay]
 S --> U[Private user overlay]
 I --> F[Mandatory policy generation]
 T --> F
 U --> F
 F --> R[Bounded deterministic ranker]
  R -->|anonymous cohort only| H
  R -->|personalized| Private[Private uncached response]
 G[Signed governance control plane] --> F
 G --> Gate

The final architecture keeps immutable, validated prefix snapshots as the reliable base; a TTL streaming overlay supplies freshness. Regional in-memory servers merge bounded candidates, apply hard policy, then rerank and diversify. Edge and local caches absorb hot prefixes, while private overlays personalize safely. Batch and stream paths are replayable, versioned, independently degradable, and observable.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. How do you serve five million requests/s for one-character prefixes?
  2. How can trends become fresh without poisoning suggestions?
  3. What consistency does an emergency block require?
  4. How is a snapshot deployed and rolled back without mixed reads?
  5. How do typo suggestions preserve the prefix contract?
  6. Which signals can be sampled, and which must remain complete?
  7. How would you evaluate a ranking change before launch?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should estimate keystroke amplification, define normalization and top-K prefix lookup, separate offline build from serving, use caching and sharding, explain ranking, freshness, retries, and safe fallback. They should identify hot prefixes and eventual consistency.

An L6 candidate should define privacy and policy invariants, design snapshot migration and stream replay, quantify degradation stages, address multilingual ambiguity and poisoning, separate governance from serving, and connect model quality, logging cost, regional policy, and product constraints. They should propose measurable guardrails and incident recovery.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Build privacy-thresholded, immutable locale snapshots mapping normalized prefixes to generous top-K candidate lists. Validate and atomically activate them on regional in-memory servers. Stream trusted burst deltas with TTL for minute-level trends and merge a small consented user overlay. Apply emergency and normal policy before a bounded deterministic reranker; relevance fallback may simplify but never bypass safety. Cache versioned hot prefixes at edge, replicate tiny one-character tables, debounce clients, and ignore superseded responses. Shard colder data by locale and prefix, shed personalization and typo work under load, and serve an older verified snapshot during build failure. Observe index and policy age, hot-key saturation, candidate filtering, latency, empties, relevance, and abuse. Rebuild and rollback from signed manifests and source watermarks.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify Git protocol compatibility, repository size, branch protection, pull requests, forks, search, and CI integration. State immutable-object and ref-update invariants. Begin with Git smart HTTP/SSH, content-addressed object storage, and strongly serialized refs. Then add pack processing, replication, code review, mergeability, permissions, abuse controls, and disaster recovery.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
The platform hosts Git repositories and collaboration metadata. Developers clone, fetch, push, create branches and tags, open pull requests, review diffs, merge under policy, browse code, and receive webhooks. Git's content graph and mutable refs have different consistency needs: blobs, trees, and commits are immutable by object ID; branch names are mutable pointers.

Collaboration objects such as reviews and checks are not Git objects, yet branch protection can make them prerequisites for a ref transition. CI execution and package registries are out of scope; the platform emits authenticated events to them and consumes versioned check results.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Create, fork, archive, transfer, and delete repositories with private/public visibility.
  • Clone/fetch efficiently and accept validated, retryable pushes over SSH and HTTPS; byte-range push resume requires a separate negotiated extension, not ordinary Git receive-pack.
  • Update refs atomically under fast-forward and branch-protection rules.
  • Browse trees, files, commits, blame, and history with cursor pagination.
  • Open pull requests, compute diffs/mergeability, record reviews, and merge safely.
  • Support code search, webhooks, audit, quotas, large files, and regional recovery.
  • Target 99.99% read availability; never acknowledge an unreachable accepted ref.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. An object ID resolves to bytes whose canonical Git hash matches that ID; existing objects are never mutated.
  2. An acknowledged ref points to a complete reachable object graph durable under the repository's replication policy.
  3. A ref compare-and-swap either moves from the expected old ID to one new ID or has no effect.
  4. Protected refs change only through the policy version and principal recorded with the transition.
  5. A pull-request merge applies to the reviewed head and current base, or it is recomputed/rejected.
  6. Repository authorization and deletion epochs dominate caches, indexes, replicas, and stale signed URLs.
  7. Retries with one push or merge identity produce one logical ref transition and webhook event identity.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100 million repositories, 20 million active developers, 300 million fetches/day, 20 million pushes/day, and 10 million pull-request interactions/day. Average fetch traffic of 70 GB/s can peak far higher after releases; object egress dominates API QPS. Ten petabytes of unique packed Git data replicated three ways becomes 30 PB before forks, indexes, and backups.

Deduplication is naturally effective inside a repository object namespace; global cross-tenant dedup leaks object existence and complicates encryption and deletion. A monorepo may contain tens of millions of objects and multi-GB packs, while a popular public repository creates extreme read skew. Separate control-plane metadata capacity from object bytes, pack CPU, search, and diff workloads.

docs.title: Core Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Repository(repo_id, owner_id, visibility, object_namespace, default_ref,
           policy_version, deletion_epoch, home_region)
Object(object_id, type, size, storage_location, checksum, state)
Pack(pack_id, namespace, index_ref, generation, state)
Ref(repo_id, ref_name, object_id, version, updated_by, updated_at)
RefTransition(repo_id, ref_name, old_id, new_id, request_id, policy_version)
PullRequest(pr_id, repo_id, base_ref, base_id, head_repo, head_ref, head_id, state, version)
Review(pr_id, reviewer_id, reviewed_head_id, verdict, revision)
Check(pr_id, name, head_id, result, provider, revision)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, version, payload)

Git objects, refs, ref-transition history, repository policy, and review decisions are canonical. Pack layout, bitmap indexes, code search, rendered diffs, mergeability, activity feeds, and fork-network dedup maps are projections or physical optimizations.

docs.title: APIs and Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/git-upload-pack       # fetch/clone protocol
POST /v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/git-receive-pack      # push protocol
GET  /v1/repos/{id}/contents/{path}?ref=<oid-or-ref>
POST /v1/repos/{id}/refs                            {name, new_oid, expected_old_oid}
POST /v1/repos/{id}/pulls                           Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
POST /v1/repos/{id}/pulls/{pr}/reviews              {head_oid, verdict}
POST /v1/repos/{id}/pulls/{pr}/merge                {expected_head_oid, expected_base_oid}
GET  /v1/repos/{id}/commits?ref=...&cursor=...

Object-ID reads are immutable and highly cacheable. Ref reads return ref version. History cursors bind resolved starting object, traversal mode, and last visited object, preventing a moving branch from silently changing a page. Pushes carry protocol negotiation and stable server request identity.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Git[Git clients] --> Edge[SSH/HTTPS Git gateway]
    Web[Web/API clients] --> API[Repository and review API]
    Edge --> Receive[Receive-pack workers]
    Receive --> Stage[(Quarantine object store)]
    Receive --> Refs[(Ref metadata shards)]
    Stage --> Objects[(Durable object/pack store)]
    API --> Refs
    API --> Review[(Review metadata)]
    Refs --> Events[(Transactional outbox/log)]
    Events --> Index[Code/search indexes]
    Events --> Hooks[Webhook delivery]
    API --> Read[Browse/diff service]
    Read --> Objects
    subgraph ObjectLane[Git object path]
      Edge
      Receive
      Stage
      Objects
      Read
    end
    subgraph MetaLane[Metadata and events]
      Refs
      Events
      Index
      Hooks
      Review
    end

The ref database is the serialization point. Object bytes can scale independently in immutable storage. A push first proves object completeness in quarantine, then publishes objects and atomically changes refs plus outbox.

docs.title: Clone and Fetch
docs.text: The gateway authenticates, resolves advertised refs under current ACL, and negotiates wants/haves using Git protocol v2. Pack workers traverse reachability, use pack bitmaps and multi-pack indexes, reuse existing compressed deltas where possible, and stream a checksummed pack. CDN caches public packs keyed by immutable negotiation artifacts; private responses use short-lived scoped tokens. Partial clone filters can omit blobs from transfer; sparse checkout alone restricts the working tree, not the objects fetched. Receive-pack quarantine requires objects to leave quarantine before refs expose them (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Push
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Git client
    participant G as Receive-pack gateway
    participant Q as Quarantine
    participant R as Ref store
    participant O as Object store
    C->>G: commands(old,new,ref) + pack
    G->>Q: stream, hash, index, limit
    G->>G: connectivity, policy, hooks
    G->>O: make complete objects durable
    G->>R: CAS refs + transition + outbox
    alt expected old and policy pass
        R-->>C: accepted
    else conflict or rejection
        R-->>C: rejected, objects later garbage collected
    end

All ref commands in an atomic push either commit together or fail together where Git semantics request atomicity. Server-side hooks execute with deadlines and no unrestricted network access. A lost response is resolved through push request ID and ref transition history.

docs.title: Browse and History
docs.text: Browse resolves a ref once to an object ID, then traverses immutable commit/tree/blob objects. This gives snapshot-consistent pages while a branch moves. Large blobs return streaming signed URLs; archives are asynchronous and cacheable by commit ID. Commit history is a graph traversal, not a database offset, and cursors track traversal frontier under explicit first-parent or date ordering.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Git Object Storage and Packs
docs.text:
A blob stores file bytes, a tree maps names to modes and object IDs, a commit points to a root tree and parent commits, and an annotated tag points to another object. Object IDs include a type/length header in the hashed bytes. SHA-1 repositories require collision detection and may use a stronger internal checksum; migration to SHA-256 requires repository format negotiation rather than rewriting IDs opportunistically.

Small loose objects are inefficient. Ingest validates them in quarantine, then background repacking groups reachable objects, delta-compresses similar content, writes immutable packs and indexes, and atomically switches a pack-generation manifest. Readers pin a generation or retry if it disappears. Old packs remain through a grace period. Bitmaps accelerate reachability, while multi-pack indexes avoid repacking the entire repository for every increment.

Garbage collection starts from refs, recent reflogs, active push quarantines, open pull-request heads, and retention roots. Mark reachable object IDs, then sweep only objects older than grace. Refcount alone is unsafe under delayed events and shared packs. Ref publication pins newly reachable objects, including reused old objects, against the current GC generation until commit; a mark/sweep grace period alone cannot protect an old unreachable object that a concurrent push is about to reference. Fork object sharing stays within an explicit network/encryption scope; detaching a private fork copies reachable objects before revoking access.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Ref Transactions and Branch Protection
docs.text:
Refs are tiny but correctness-critical. A push command includes expected old object ID. The service locks or conditionally updates the repository's ref set, verifies new targets remain complete, checks fast-forward ancestry unless force push is permitted, evaluates signed policy, appends reflog/transition and outbox, then commits. A monotonically increasing ref version supports caches and replication.

Branch protection may require reviews, status checks, signed commits, linear history, path-owner approval, or a merge queue. Pin one immutable policy bundle for evaluation and compare its authoritative generation again in the ref-commit transaction. Concurrent policy changes, review withdrawal, or check invalidation force revalidation or fail the guarded commit; pinning stale inputs alone is not protection. Emergency revocations remain a separate current gate. External check results bind provider, repository, head object ID, and check run ID; a green result for an older head is irrelevant. Emergency bypass requires named capability, reason, and tamper-evident audit.

Concurrent pushes naturally conflict on expected old ID. Do not hide this with last-write-wins. Multi-ref transactions are local because repository refs share a shard. For huge ref namespaces, partition read indexes but retain a small transaction coordinator per repository.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Pull Requests and Code Review
docs.text:
A pull request identifies a base ref and a head ref/object, but discussion remains stable as the head advances. Each review binds reviewed_head_id; requested changes can become stale after new commits according to policy. Inline comments anchor to blob object IDs, path, side, and line context. When a patch shifts, a projection attempts remapping and labels uncertain comments outdated rather than changing canonical anchors.

Diff workers find a merge base, compare trees, detect renames under bounded CPU, and store rendered artifacts keyed by (base_id, head_id, algorithm_version). Large or generated diffs degrade to summaries/downloads. Mergeability is a cache, not truth. On merge, the server re-resolves base/head, verifies expected IDs, recomputes required checks and conflicts, creates the merge/squash commit, durably stores it, and CAS-updates base ref in one guarded workflow.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OPEN
    OPEN --> REVIEWABLE: diff ready
    REVIEWABLE --> CHANGES_REQUESTED
    CHANGES_REQUESTED --> REVIEWABLE: new head
    REVIEWABLE --> APPROVED
    APPROVED --> REVIEWABLE: protected head changes
    APPROVED --> QUEUED: policy passes
    QUEUED --> MERGED: base CAS succeeds
    QUEUED --> REVIEWABLE: base moved/conflict
    OPEN --> CLOSED
    REVIEWABLE --> CLOSED
    CHANGES_REQUESTED --> CLOSED
    APPROVED --> CLOSED
    QUEUED --> CLOSED: cancel queue membership

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Merge Queue and Derived Systems
docs.text:
Busy protected branches cannot test every PR against a moving base independently. A merge queue forms a speculative train: synthesize candidate merge commits in order, run required checks against those exact IDs, and advance the base ref by CAS. If one candidate fails, remove it and rebuild only affected descendants. Batch testing improves throughput but increases culprit isolation time.

Webhooks are signed, versioned events with stable IDs, sequence per repository where feasible, retries, exponential backoff, and dead-letter visibility. Consumers must deduplicate. Search and symbol indexes consume ref transitions, compare old/new trees, and index only changed blobs. Force pushes produce explicit deletion/update work; periodic reachability reconciliation repairs missed events.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition control metadata by repository ID, colocating refs, policy, and pull-request state where practical. Allocate giant repositories dedicated shards. Object namespaces shard by object-ID prefix but use repository/fork-network authorization scope. Separate CPU pools for receive validation, pack generation, diff, blame, archive, and search to prevent expensive reads from delaying pushes.

Popular public clones use precomputed packs, immutable CDN objects, protocol caching, and bandwidth quotas. Monorepos use bitmap indexes, partial clone, sparse checkout, changed-path indexes, and bounded diff algorithms. Reshard metadata through repository epochs and frozen ref boundary; objects need not move if addressing is independent.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Ref CAS, policy transitions, repository visibility, and merge commits require strong consistency per repository. Objects are immutable and become visible only after durability. Search, activity, diffs, blame, archive generation, mirrors, and webhooks are eventual. Every projection carries source ref version or object IDs.

Platform push and merge request IDs persist with request hashes and outcomes. Ordinary Git retries do not necessarily carry a stable cross-connection idempotency key; resolve ambiguous ref updates through expected old/new IDs and transition history, and document any extension. Outbox delivery is at least once. Deletion epochs must be enforced at the byte-serving boundary; already issued bearer URLs otherwise remain usable until expiry or storage-level revocation. Reflogs are recovery roots, not authorization escape hatches.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
An upload interrupted before ref commit leaves quarantined objects reclaimed later. A crash after ref commit returns prior outcome on retry. Object-store outage rejects ref publication. Ref-store outage allows immutable cached clone by object ID but not branch mutation. Pack worker overload serves less-compressed packs within egress budgets or queues cold clones; it never blocks policy removals.

Corrupt objects fail hash verification and repair from replicas. Missing reachable objects trigger an invariant alarm and fence affected refs. Search/webhook outages accumulate replayable lag. A bad repack keeps the old generation. Restore starts from ref/review snapshots, validates every advertised tip's reachability, then replays transition logs. Disaster drills clone sampled repositories and verify hashes, not merely storage byte counts.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text:
Give each repository a home region for ref writes with synchronous zonal replicas. Replicate immutable objects globally and route fetches nearby only after a replication manifest proves completeness. Public repositories can use asynchronous remote object availability; private disaster objectives dictate synchronous or acknowledged-region policy.

Failover promotes a fenced ref-store epoch. Ref updates carrying an old epoch fail. During uncertain fencing, serve object-ID reads and reject writes. Repository transfer or residency migration copies reachable objects, snapshots metadata at ref version V, catches up transitions, shadow-validates, and switches ownership. Global deletion and key revocation use a high-priority control path.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text:
Use SSH key and token rotation, MFA, SSO, workload identity, scoped app permissions, encrypted tenant scopes, secret scanning, signed commits where required, and immutable audit. Git parsing is hostile: bound object size/count/depth, zip-bomb-like delta chains, path length, hook CPU, archive expansion, and submodule/link behavior. Sandboxed renderers prevent XSS and command execution.

Defend against credential stuffing, repository scraping, malicious forks, webhook SSRF, dependency confusion links, spam, and cryptomining through CI integrations. Private object IDs confer no access. Deletion supports retention, legal hold, fork ownership, and cryptographic erasure. Branch bypass and repository export are high-risk audited actions.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure push/fetch latency and bytes, quarantine rejects, object verification, ref CAS conflicts, policy denials, pack reuse, delta depth, CDN hit rate, reachability failures, GC candidates, PR diff age, merge-queue throughput, check staleness, index/webhook lag, and cost by repository. Trace by repository and request ID without exposing code.

Use Git protocol compatibility suites, hash and pack corruption tests, randomized commit graphs, atomic multi-ref races, force-push/reflog cases, stale review/check tests, merge-base differentials, and path-parser fuzzing. Chaos-test object and ref stores, lost acknowledgements, regional fencing, and repack switches. Restore sampled private/public/fork networks and clone them byte-for-byte. Load-test one giant monorepo and one viral release separately.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Filesystem-per-repository is simple but difficult to elastically shard and replicate; immutable object storage plus metadata refs scales better at operational cost. Global dedup saves bytes but leaks existence and entangles deletion; scoped dedup wins. Strongly consistent global refs lower failover RPO but add push latency; home-region ownership fits developer workflows. Aggressive deltas reduce storage/egress but increase CPU and corruption blast radius. Cached mergeability improves UX but final CAS and revalidation remain mandatory.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Clients --> Gateways[Regional Git and API gateways]
    Gateways --> Home[Repository home control shard]
    Home --> Meta[(Refs, policy, reviews, transitions, outbox)]
    Gateways --> Quarantine[Validated quarantine]
    Quarantine --> Object[(Immutable scoped object and pack store)]
    Meta --> Stream[(Repository event stream)]
    Stream --> Collab[Diff, merge queue, webhooks]
    Stream --> Search[Code and history indexing]
    Object --> CDN[Authorized regional cache/CDN]
    CDN --> Clients
    Repack[Pack, bitmap, reachability and GC] --> Object
    Repack --> Meta

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. Why must objects become durable before a ref update?
  2. How does receive quarantine prevent repository corruption?
  3. How do reviews and checks remain valid as a PR head moves?
  4. Why is mergeability a projection rather than canonical truth?
  5. How do pack generations switch without breaking readers?
  6. How does a merge queue handle a failed speculative commit?
  7. How would you delete a private fork that shares objects?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should separate immutable objects from refs, describe fetch/push, ref CAS, pack storage, pull-request diffs, protection, caching, and failures. An L6 answer should formalize publication durability, policy pinning, merge queues, generation-safe repacking, reachability GC, scoped dedup, giant-repository isolation, regional fencing, migration, protocol evolution, security boundaries, and storage/egress economics.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: A code host stores immutable Git blobs, trees, commits, and tags separately from strongly serialized mutable refs. Push into quarantine, verify hashes, graph connectivity, limits, and policy, make all newly reachable objects durable, then atomically CAS refs and append transition/outbox records. Fetch resolves authorized refs and streams packs accelerated by bitmaps, partial clone, immutable caches, and scoped CDN. Repack into generation manifests; retain old packs through grace and garbage-collect only after reachability from refs, reflogs, pull requests, and quarantines. Reviews and checks bind exact head IDs. Merge revalidates current head/base and policy, creates a durable commit, and CAS-updates the base; busy branches use a speculative merge queue. Keep search, diffs, mergeability, and webhooks eventual and repairable. Own ref writes in one fenced region, replicate immutable objects near readers, and prove recovery by cloning and hashing repositories.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We design cross-device file sync, resumable chunk upload, folders, sharing, offline edits, conflicts, deletion, and change notification. The center is a transactional namespace plus immutable content-addressed blocks and a monotonic change log.

docs.title: 2. Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Users create/move/delete files and folders, sync offline devices, resume large uploads, share folders/links, recover versions, and receive near-real-time changes. Exclude collaborative character-level editing and office rendering. Targets: committed metadata never points to incomplete content; online changes notify devices within two seconds; acknowledged bytes survive zone failure; offline convergence is deterministic.

Invariants: each namespace entry has one parent/name identity at a committed revision; folder trees are acyclic; file revisions reference complete immutable block manifests; mutation idempotency returns one revision; clients never silently overwrite concurrent revisions; authorization is checked at metadata and block-token issuance; deletion tombstones outrank delayed updates.

docs.title: 3. Estimates
docs.text: Assume 100 million users, 10 million active/day, 100 file mutations and 2 GB sync traffic per active user/day: 1 billion mutations/day (11,600/s average) and 20 PB/day transfer. Deduplication/chunking and edge transfer dominate. Ten billion namespace entries at 500 bytes need 5 TB before indexes/replicas; retained blocks are exabytes at mature scale. A device cursor prevents full-tree scans.

docs.title: 4. APIs and model
docs.text:
POST /v1/uploads {size, blockDigests} -> missing blocks + uploadId
PUT /v1/blocks/{digest} (scoped token, checksum)
POST /v1/files:commit {parentId,name,baseRevision,manifest,idempotencyKey}
GET /v1/changes?namespaceId=...&cursor=...
POST /v1/entries/{id}:move {newParentId,newName,expectedRevision}
DELETE /v1/entries/{id}?expectedRevision=...

Entry(entry_id, namespace_id, parent_id, normalized_name, type, revision, state)
FileRevision(entry_id, revision, manifest_id, size, author_device, created_at)
Manifest(manifest_id, ordered[(digest,length)], file_digest)
Block(digest, length, storage_key, encryption_scope, reference_state)
Mutation(namespace_id, idempotency_key, request_hash, resulting_revision)
Change(namespace_id, sequence, entry_id, operation, revision)
Share(share_id, root_entry_id, principal, role, version)

docs.title: 5. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  D[Desktop/mobile client] --> E[Edge sync API]
  E --> M[Metadata service]
  M --> N[(Namespace DB)]
  M --> L[(Ordered change log)]
  E --> B[Block service]
  B --> O[(Object storage)]
  L --> P[Push notifier]
  P --> D
  L --> R[Search/share projections]
    subgraph MetaLane[Metadata and derived views]
      M
      N
      L
      P
      R
    end
    subgraph BlockLane[File content]
      B
      O
    end

docs.title: 6. Chunk upload and commit
docs.text:
Clients split files using content-defined chunking (rolling hash boundaries) so insertion near the front does not shift every block. Bound chunks, for example 1-8 MB, to control requests and dedup effectiveness. The client hashes blocks and asks which are absent in its encryption/dedup scope. It uploads missing blocks directly with checksums and scoped tokens, then commits an ordered manifest.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant A as Sync API
  participant O as Block store
  participant N as Namespace DB
  C->>A: begin(block digests)
  A-->>C: missing digests + tokens
  C->>O: parallel resumable blocks
  C->>A: commit(base revision, manifest, key)
  A->>O: verify durable blocks
  A->>N: transaction entry revision + change + idempotency
  N-->>A: revision and cursor
  A-->>C: committed

Upload blocks before metadata. Orphans are safe and reclaimed after a grace period; metadata referencing absent blocks is not. Global dedup leaks whether another user owns content and complicates cryptographic deletion. Dedup within an account/team encryption scope; convergent encryption is rejected for sensitive tenants. Refcounts are projections, not trusted alone for deletion: inventory traces reachable manifests before reclaim.

Existence verification must race safely with GC. Hold an upload/commit pin on every reused block until the manifest is committed; GC cannot delete a pinned or newly reachable block. An old unreferenced block can otherwise pass verification and be swept before the namespace commit, despite a long object-age grace period. Expired pins are reclaimed only after fencing the upload from later publication.

docs.title: 7. Sync and conflicts
docs.text:
Every namespace transaction allocates a monotonic sequence and appends a change in the same commit. Devices persist a cursor, long-poll/push only as a wake-up hint, then pull ordered pages. A compact snapshot plus subsequent log handles new devices and old cursors. Applying the same revision twice is harmless.

Clients commit against baseRevision. If current equals base, update in place. Otherwise preserve both: create a deterministic conflict copy containing device/time suffix, or for safe text formats perform a three-way merge from common base and still surface unresolved conflicts. Folder moves use expected revisions and ancestry checks; serialize changes in one namespace shard to prevent cycles.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> LOCAL_DIRTY
  LOCAL_DIRTY --> UPLOADING
  UPLOADING --> COMMITTED: base revision current
  UPLOADING --> CONFLICT: remote revision advanced
  CONFLICT --> COMMITTED: conflict copy or merge
  COMMITTED --> LOCAL_DIRTY: local edit
  COMMITTED --> TOMBSTONED: delete observed

Renames are entry-ID-preserving moves, not delete/create, so edits can follow identity. Case-insensitive clients require one server normalization/collision rule. Offline delete versus edit preserves the edited revision in recovery/conflict space instead of silently discarding data.

docs.title: 8. Sharing, deletion, and notifications
docs.text:
ACL inheritance is computed from a shared-root identity and cached with policy version. Block download tokens bind principal, entry revision, block set, operation, and short expiry; possession of a digest grants nothing. Public links use random secrets, optional password/expiry, quotas, and revocation epochs. A previously issued download capability remains usable until expiry unless every serving edge enforces the current revocation epoch. Publish that exposure bound and fail closed when the required revocation state is stale; neither an ACL commit nor deletion recalls already downloaded bytes.

Deletion atomically tombstones an entry/subtree root and emits change. Descendant cleanup can be asynchronous if authorization treats a tombstoned ancestor as inaccessible. Version history has retention; after grace/legal hold, reachability GC removes manifests and blocks. Late commits carrying old base revisions conflict and cannot resurrect tombstones.

Push may duplicate or disappear; it carries no canonical mutation, only "changes after cursor exist." Clients always pull. Webhooks use event IDs, signatures, retries, and consumer-side idempotency.

docs.title: 9. Partitioning, consistency, and regions
docs.text:
Partition by namespace/team so transactions, sequence, moves, and ACL roots are local. A giant enterprise namespace can split by stable subtree only with a namespace-wide serialization/transaction protocol that atomically validates ancestry and transfers both directory links; a coordinator that independently writes two shards is insufficient; avoid until measured. Blocks shard by digest and replicate independently. Hot shared downloads are CDN-cached under signed authorization; hot metadata is read-cached but writes retain one owner.

One home region owns namespace writes with synchronous zone replicas. Devices route mutations home; read-only block transfer uses nearest region. Immutable blocks replicate before a revision is advertised in a destination region. Failover promotes a fenced database epoch; clients retry idempotently. Eventual projections include search, quota, refcounts, and notifications; namespace revisions and ACL changes are strongly ordered.

Overload prioritizes commit/change pull over thumbnails/search, rate-limits abusive clients, bounds per-device outstanding block transfers, and applies fair queues by tenant. A change consumer lag cannot block namespace transactions if the durable log remains within capacity.

docs.title: 10. Reliability, security, and operations
docs.text:
Lost commit responses replay through mutation records. Block corruption is caught by digest and repaired from replicas. Missing referenced blocks trigger invariant alarms and disable publication. Expired cursors return a fresh snapshot boundary. Push outage degrades to polling. Partial regional failure keeps existing local files usable and queues edits; it must not invent server success.

Use TLS, encryption keys scoped by tenant, malware/ransomware detection, suspicious mass-delete rollback, device/session revocation, MFA, least-privilege sharing, audit logs, and download/upload quotas. Filenames and previews are hostile: normalize safely, escape UI, sandbox parsers, and scan archives with resource limits. Privacy deletion and legal hold are explicit retention states.

docs.title: Client protocol and local filesystem details
docs.text:
The desktop client keeps a journal mapping server entry IDs/revisions to local file identities. Filesystem watchers are hints: events can coalesce or disappear, so periodic scans reconcile inode/file IDs, names, size, modification time, and sampled hashes. The client writes downloads to a temporary file, verifies the manifest digest, fsyncs as required, then atomically renames; crashes cannot expose partial files. It avoids uploading its own downloaded change by recording the applied server revision.

Windows, macOS, and Linux differ in case sensitivity, reserved names, normalization, symlinks, permissions, and maximum paths. The server defines a portable normalized-name uniqueness rule and returns explicit materialization conflicts when a legal cloud name cannot exist locally. Symlinks are metadata or ordinary small files by policy, never followed during upload, preventing directory escape. Sparse files and executable bits require capability-versioned metadata rather than assumptions.

docs.title: Snapshots, recovery, and migration
docs.text:
A namespace snapshot records entries at sequence S; the change log retains all mutations after S. Snapshot construction uses database MVCC or incremental checkpoints, uploads a checksummed artifact, then publishes its pointer. A restoring client downloads the snapshot and replays from S + 1, avoiding a race between listing and live changes. If a cursor predates retention, this same path is mandatory.

For metadata resharding, assign namespace epochs. The old owner freezes briefly at a sequence boundary, copies and verifies state, transfers ownership through a fenced control record, and forwards retries carrying old routing metadata. Blocks do not move because their addressing is independent. Migration success is measured by sequence equality, manifest reachability, and shadow reads before old state is retired.

docs.title: 11. Observability
docs.text: Measure commit/change latency, cursor lag, conflicts, block reuse, bytes avoided, orphan/reclaim age, missing-block alarms, metadata lock contention, push delay, hot tenants, ACL denial, regional replication, restore success, and cost/stored versus transferred byte.

docs.title: 12. Testing
docs.text: Test rolling-boundary properties, manifest checksums, concurrent edit/delete/move, cycles, Unicode/case collisions, replay, snapshot-plus-log, and ACL inheritance. Chaos loses acknowledgments, reorders push, delays block replication, corrupts replicas, and fails over namespace ownership. Sync-model tests run randomized operations across offline devices and assert eventual convergence without silent loss.

docs.title: 13. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Whole-file upload is simple but expensive for large edits; fixed chunks fail under shifted bytes; content-defined chunks win despite client CPU and metadata. Last-write-wins converges but loses user data, unacceptable for files; explicit conflict revisions win. Active-active metadata writes reduce latency but make tree and revision invariants difficult; home-region ownership plus offline clients is simpler.

Final design stores immutable account-scoped chunks and manifests, then transactionally commits namespace revisions, idempotency outcomes, and ordered changes. Devices synchronize by cursor and optimistic base revision, preserving conflicts. Entry identity survives moves; tombstones prevent resurrection. Derived notifications, search, quota, and refcounts can lag, while authorization and namespace state cannot.

docs.title: 14. Interview questions and levels
docs.text:
• Why does content-defined chunking help insertions?
  • How do offline rename, edit, and delete converge?
  • Can a refcount safely decide block deletion?
  • How would you split a billion-entry enterprise namespace?
  • What does end-to-end encryption remove from server features?

L5 should design resumable chunking, metadata/blob separation, cursors, conflicts, sharing, partitioning, and retry safety. L6 should formalize tree transactions, dedup privacy, GC proofs, cross-region ownership, giant-tenant isolation, ransomware recovery, client protocol migration, and cost/retention policy.

docs.title: 15. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Dropbox is a transactional namespace over immutable blocks. Clients content-define chunks, hash them, upload only missing account-scoped blocks, and commit an ordered manifest against a base revision. The commit atomically updates entry state, records idempotency, and appends a monotonic namespace change. Devices use push only as a hint, pull ordered changes from cursors, and replay revisions safely.

Concurrent edits never silently overwrite: three-way merge safe text or preserve conflict copies. Moves retain entry identity; ancestry checks prevent cycles; tombstones defeat late offline updates. Partition by namespace with one home-region writer, transfer replicated blocks near users, and keep search/refcounts/notifications eventual. GC proves unreachable content after retention instead of trusting lagging counters. The decisive tradeoffs are chunk efficiency versus metadata, explicit conflicts versus convenient data loss, and simple regional ownership versus active-active write complexity.

docs.title: Google News: A Global News Aggregator
docs.text:
This chapter develops an end-to-end design for a Google News-like product. It is structured as both a detailed study guide and a 45-60 minute system design interview walkthrough.

The central challenge is scaling reads without sacrificing freshness. A news platform must continuously ingest articles from thousands of publishers, group duplicate coverage into stories, rank the result, and serve an effectively infinite feed in under 200 ms, including during unpredictable breaking-news spikes.

docs.title: 1. Interview Roadmap
docs.text:
Phase Time Goal Requirements 5 minutes Define feed behavior, freshness, and scale Entities and APIs 5 minutes Establish data ownership and client contracts High-level design 15 minutes Build ingestion and feed-serving paths Deep dives 15-20 minutes Pagination, caching, freshness, media, and spikes Extensions and wrap-up 5-10 minutes Categories, personalization, failures, tradeoffs

The interview should distinguish two independent paths early:

  1. The write or ingestion path discovers and processes publisher articles.
  2. The read or serving path returns ranked feed pages to users.

Decoupling these paths lets ingestion continue when serving is busy and lets cached feeds remain available when ingestion is delayed.

docs.title: 2. Understanding the Product
docs.text:
A news aggregator does not usually author the full article. It discovers content published elsewhere and presents a compact representation:

  • Headline and short snippet.
  • Publisher and publication time.
  • Thumbnail or media preview.
  • Topic or category.
  • A group of publishers covering the same underlying story.
  • A link to the publisher's website for the full article.

The feed is not merely a reverse-chronological table scan. It balances freshness, importance, source quality, topic diversity, geographic relevance, and duplicate suppression.

docs.title: Core requirements
docs.text:
1. Users can view an aggregated feed of news from thousands of publishers worldwide.
  2. Users can scroll through the feed effectively infinitely.
  3. Users can click an article and be redirected to the publisher's website.

docs.title: Clarifications
docs.text:
• The home feed is available to anonymous users.
  • Articles should normally appear within 30 minutes of publication.
  • Multiple articles about the same event should be grouped into one story cluster.
  • The feed may be slightly stale; availability is more important than strict consistency.
  • Deleted, retracted, or policy-violating articles should be removed promptly.
  • Feed pages should not repeat an item within a user's scrolling session.
  • The core design uses a globally or regionally ranked feed, not mandatory personalization.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Publisher registration and commercial agreements.
  • Full web-scale crawling of arbitrary sites.
  • User comments and social interactions.
  • Subscription payments and publisher paywall handling.
  • Full misinformation or editorial-policy systems.
  • Saved articles and social sharing.

docs.title: Bonus extensions
docs.text:
• Category feeds such as Sports, Politics, Business, and Technology.
  • Personalized feeds based on explicit interests and reading behavior.
  • Local and language-specific editions.

docs.title: 3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
