docs.text: Requirement Target Why it matters Feed latency p95 below 200 ms Scrolling is an interactive, high-frequency path Feed availability 99.99% Slightly old news is preferable to no feed Freshness 99% of eligible articles discoverable within 30 minutes News rapidly loses value Redirect latency p95 below 100 ms A click should feel immediate Durability Do not lose accepted article metadata Derived feeds can be rebuilt from canonical articles Consistency Eventual for feed ranking and counters Strong consistency is unnecessary for most reads Geographic reach Multi-region News readership and publishers are global Spike tolerance 10-50x for major events Breaking news creates correlated traffic

docs.title: 3.3 Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
• One accepted publisher item maps idempotently to one canonical article identity even when polling, push delivery, or event processing retries.
  • A published feed version references only fully written segments; readers never observe a partially activated snapshot.
  • A cursor remains bound to one immutable feed version and position, so pagination does not duplicate or skip items because a newer feed was published.
  • Retractions, policy blocks, and unsafe redirect destinations override ordinary ranking and cache freshness; tombstones prevent delayed events from republishing them.
  • Redirects resolve only to the validated URL stored for an accepted article and publisher, never to a caller-supplied destination.
  • Canonical articles and cluster state are durable sources of truth; feeds, caches, search indexes, and engagement counters are rebuildable projections.
  • At-least-once delivery may repeat work but cannot create duplicate canonical articles or apply the same entity version twice.

docs.title: 3.4 Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume:

  • 100M daily active users.
  • 20 feed page requests per user per day.
  • 20 cards per feed page.
  • 10M article clicks per day.
  • 100,000 active publishers.
  • 10M new article versions per day before filtering.
  • 2M accepted new articles per day.
  • 5 KB normalized metadata per article, excluding media.
  • 90-day hot article retention in the serving databases.

Traffic:

Feed page requests/day = 100M * 20 = 2B
Average feed QPS       = 2B / 86,400 ~= 23,000
Peak feed QPS          = 5 * average ~= 115,000
Breaking-news peak     = 10-50 * normal peak for hot objects

Clicks/day             = 10M
Average redirect QPS   ~= 116
Peak redirect QPS      ~= 1,000+

Accepted articles/day  = 2M
Average accepted rate  ~= 23 articles/second
Burst ingestion rate   = hundreds or thousands/second

Metadata storage:

Articles/year          = 2M * 365 = 730M
Raw metadata/year      = 730M * 5 KB ~= 3.65 TB
Indexes and replicas   ~= 10-20 TB/year

Feed card delivery dominates system traffic. This immediately suggests aggressive precomputation, caching, compact responses, and CDN or edge participation.

docs.title: Article versus story cluster
docs.text:
An article belongs to one publisher and has one destination URL. A story cluster represents an underlying event covered by one or more articles. The feed should primarily rank clusters, then select a representative article and expose alternative sources.

Without clustering, a major event may occupy every feed position with nearly identical headlines.

docs.title: 5.1 Get the home feed
docs.text:
GET /v1/feed?edition=en-US&limit=20&cursor=<opaque-token>

Response:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "storyId": "story_9f3",
      "headline": "Central bank announces new rate decision",
      "summary": "The central bank announced...",
      "publishedAt": "2026-09-05T12:34:00Z",
      "primaryArticle": {
        "articleId": "article_a72",
        "publisher": "Example News",
        "targetUrl": "https://news.example.com/article/abc"
      },
      "sourceCount": 42,
      "thumbnailUrl": "https://media.news.example/story_9f3/640x360.webp",
      "categories": ["Business", "Economy"]
    }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "eyJmZWVkVmVyc2lvbiI6...",
  "generatedAt": "2026-09-05T12:35:00Z"
}

The cursor should encode or reference:

  • Feed key or edition.
  • Feed snapshot version.
  • Last consumed position or ranking tuple.
  • Expiry time.
  • Optional user/session ID for deduplication.

Sign and encode the cursor so clients cannot alter internal pagination state.

docs.title: 5.2 Get a category feed
docs.text:
GET /v1/feed/categories/technology?edition=en-US&limit=20&cursor=...

This can use the same serving infrastructure with a different feed key: category:technology:en-US.

docs.title: 5.3 Get a story cluster
docs.text:
GET /v1/stories/{story_id}

Returns the representative story plus alternative publisher coverage. This endpoint is optional for the core problem but naturally follows from deduplication.

docs.title: 5.4 Redirect to the publisher
docs.text:
Option A: return the publisher URL in the feed and let the client navigate directly.

Option B: use a lightweight redirect endpoint for click analytics:

GET /v1/articles/{article_id}/redirect

Response:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://publisher.example/article/abc
Cache-Control: no-store

The analytics event must not block the redirect. Emit it asynchronously or log at the edge.

docs.title: Component responsibilities
docs.text: Component Responsibility Fetch scheduler Decides when each source should be fetched next Fetchers Download RSS, Atom, API, or page metadata safely Raw storage Preserves source payloads for replay and debugging Normalizer Extracts canonical fields and normalizes URLs/timestamps Deduplicator Detects duplicate URLs/articles and clusters related coverage Classifier Assigns language, geography, entities, and categories Policy filter Removes spam, unsafe content, blocked sources, and retractions Article store Canonical source of accepted article metadata Ranking pipeline Computes candidate and story scores Feed builder Materializes versioned global, regional, and category feeds Feed cache Serves hot feed segments with sub-millisecond lookups Feed API Performs cursor validation and returns compact feed cards Media pipeline Fetches allowed images, validates, transforms, and stores them

docs.title: 7. Requirement 1: Aggregate News from Thousands of Publishers
7.1 Ingestion sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Scheduler
    participant Q as Fetch Queue
    participant F as Fetcher
    participant P as Publisher
    participant K as Kafka
    participant N as Normalizer
    participant D as Deduplicator
    participant DB as Article Store
    participant B as Feed Builder

    S->>Q: Enqueue due source
    Q->>F: Lease fetch task
    F->>P: Conditional GET with ETag / Last-Modified
    P-->>F: 200 content or 304 unchanged
    F->>K: Raw items and fetch metadata
    K->>N: Parse and normalize
    N->>D: Canonical article candidate
    D->>DB: Commit article/cluster change and outbox
    DB->>K: Relay committed ArticleAccepted / ClusterUpdated
    K->>B: Eligible story update
    B->>B: Refresh affected feeds

docs.title: 7.2 Source discovery
docs.text:
Prefer explicit publisher integrations:

  • RSS or Atom feeds.
  • Publisher APIs.
  • News sitemaps.
  • WebSub or webhook pushes.
  • Controlled page fetching for approved sources without feeds.

Publisher pushes offer the lowest latency, but the system cannot require every publisher to support them. Polling remains necessary.

docs.title: 7.3 Adaptive scheduling
docs.text:
Polling every source at the same rate is wasteful. A national breaking-news publisher may update every minute, while a weekly local paper may update once a day.

Maintain a source state:

next_fetch_at
recent_publish_rate
last_success_at
consecutive_failures
etag
last_modified
publisher_priority

A simplified interval policy:

interval = clamp(
    3600 * target_updates_per_poll / max(expected_updates_per_hour, rate_floor),
    minimum_interval,
    maximum_interval
)

Then adjust it:

Here interval is seconds, target_updates_per_poll is a dimensionless desired batch size, and rate_floor is a positive updates/hour floor. Cap maximum_interval by the source's discovery-delay budget; a quiet source cannot silently escape a promised freshness tier.

  • Fetch sooner when recent requests found new content.
  • Back off when requests repeatedly return 304 Not Modified.
  • Exponentially back off on errors.
  • Temporarily accelerate trusted sources during breaking events.
  • Add jitter to prevent synchronized request bursts.
  • Respect Retry-After, robots rules, and publisher-specific quotas.

docs.title: 7.4 Safe and polite fetching
docs.text:
• Limit concurrency per publisher domain.
  • Use strict connection and response-size limits.
  • Reject private-network addresses to prevent SSRF.
  • Parse untrusted XML and HTML in sandboxed workers.
  • Disable dangerous XML external entities.
  • Identify the crawler and honor publisher agreements.
  • Avoid downloading full pages when feed metadata is sufficient.

docs.title: 7.5 Canonicalization and exact deduplication
docs.text:
The same article may appear through RSS, a sitemap, mobile URL, tracking URL, and syndication feed.

Normalize URLs by:

  • Lowercasing hostnames.
  • Removing fragments.
  • Removing known tracking parameters such as utm_*.
  • Resolving redirects and canonical-link metadata.
  • Applying publisher-specific URL rules.

Create a unique key such as:

SHA-256(publisher_id + canonical_url)

Also calculate a normalized-content hash. Storage-level uniqueness and idempotent upserts protect against retries and duplicate feed entries.

docs.title: 7.6 Near-duplicate detection and story clustering
docs.text:
Exact URL deduplication does not group different publishers covering the same event.

Use a staged pipeline:

  1. Extract title, entities, locations, keywords, and publication time.
  2. Generate a text embedding or MinHash signature.
  3. Retrieve candidate clusters from the same language and recent time window.
  4. Compare semantic similarity, entity overlap, and time proximity.
  5. Join the best matching cluster above a threshold; otherwise create a new cluster.

Example score:

cluster_similarity =
    0.55 * embedding_similarity
  + 0.20 * named_entity_overlap
  + 0.15 * title_token_similarity
  + 0.10 * time_proximity

Cluster updates are asynchronous and revisable. Two initial clusters can later merge as more evidence arrives. The feed references stable cluster IDs or receives a redirect from merged IDs. Freeze cluster identity for snapshot pagination, or resolve aliases against a pinned clustering version and deduplicate canonical cluster IDs in session state. Live merges can otherwise make two distinct snapshot IDs render as the same story; immutable positions alone do not prevent that semantic duplicate.

docs.title: 7.7 Classification and eligibility
docs.text:
Before entering feeds, derive:

  • Language and edition eligibility.
  • Topic categories.
  • Geographic relevance.
  • Named entities and event type.
  • Content safety and spam score.
  • Publisher quality and policy status.

The classifier emits versioned predictions. Reclassification should not overwrite audit history and should trigger feed updates when eligibility changes.

docs.title: 8.1 Fan-out on read, fan-out on write, or hybrid
docs.text:
Strategy Behavior Strength Weakness Rank on read Build each feed during the request Maximum freshness and flexibility High latency and repeated computation Precompute every user feed Materialize complete user feeds Fast reads Expensive writes and difficult invalidation Precompute shared feeds Materialize global, edition, and category feeds Excellent cache reuse Limited personalization Hybrid Shared candidates plus lightweight user reranking Good balance More serving complexity

For the core anonymous product, precompute shared feeds by edition and category. This is the most important read-scaling decision.

docs.title: 8.2 Candidate generation
docs.text:
Generate candidates from:

  • Recently created or updated story clusters.
  • Trusted-source breaking-news signals.
  • Region and language eligibility.
  • Category membership.
  • Trending click and engagement counters.

Candidate generation should retrieve hundreds or thousands of plausible stories, not scan every article.

docs.title: 8.3 Ranking signals
docs.text:
A deterministic initial score can combine:

score =
    w1 * freshness_decay
  + w2 * story_importance
  + w3 * source_quality
  + w4 * corroborating_source_count
  + w5 * regional_relevance
  + w6 * engagement_velocity
  + w7 * content_quality

Freshness may use exponential decay:

freshness_decay = exp(-ln(2) * age_hours / half_life_hours)

Different categories need different half-lives. Breaking politics may decay in hours, while an investigative feature may remain valuable for days.

docs.title: 8.4 Diversity and constraints
docs.text:
Pure score sorting often produces a poor feed. Apply post-ranking constraints:

  • Limit consecutive stories from one publisher.
  • Limit repeated topics and entities.
  • Mix local, national, and international coverage.
  • Guarantee a minimum number of categories.
  • Collapse near-duplicates into one cluster.
  • Avoid multiple stories using identical media.

This is a constrained reranking stage, not necessarily part of the base ranking model.

docs.title: 8.5 Versioned feed snapshots
docs.text:
Build immutable, ordered feed versions:

home:en-US:v1842
technology:en-US:v773
home:en-IN:v1261

Each version contains ordered cluster IDs and compact card metadata. Keep several recent versions so clients can continue paginating the version on which they started.

flowchart LR
    Updates[Article and Signal Updates] --> Candidates[Candidate Generator]
    Candidates --> Ranker[Ranker]
    Ranker --> Diversity[Diversity and Policy Rules]
    Diversity --> Snapshot[Immutable Feed Snapshot]
    Snapshot --> Store[(Feed Store)]
    Snapshot --> Redis[(Redis Segments)]
    Redis --> API[Feed API]

Publishing is a small control-plane transaction around immutable data, not a rename of partially written keys. A builder writes versioned segments and a manifest containing feed key, version, segment count, item count, ranker/policy versions, per-segment checksums, and build watermark. It then performs these steps:

  1. Seal the build so no segment can be changed in place.
  2. Read every segment through the serving decoder and validate checksum, contiguous positions, unique cluster IDs, expected edition/category, required card fields, and current block/retraction policy. Reject suspicious count or score-distribution changes against the active version.
  3. Write the checksum-verified manifest to durable storage with state GLOBALLY_VALIDATED. Every region may activate only this exact candidate checksum.
  4. In each required region, warm at least the first two segments. A region acknowledges the manifest checksum, not merely that a cache key exists. A lagging region continues serving its prior version.
  5. After one region is warm, compare-and-swap that region's active[region,feed_key] from the regional base observed before warming to the new manifest version. There is no global active pointer in this mode. If a concurrent build changed that regional pointer, the CAS loses and the candidate is not exposed there.
  6. Emit RegionalFeedActivated(region,feed_key,new_version,old_version,manifest_checksum). Regional pointers and CDN keys are versioned, so delayed invalidation cannot mix segments from two versions. A globally validated candidate may be active in some regions while others safely retain an older snapshot.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Feed builder
    participant D as Durable feed store
    participant V as Validator
    participant C as Regional cache
    participant P as Regional active pointer
    B->>D: Write immutable segments and manifest
    V->>D: Decode all segments and verify checksums
    V->>D: Mark manifest GLOBALLY_VALIDATED
    loop Each serving region
        V->>C: Warm leading segments by version
        C-->>V: Region acknowledgement with manifest checksum
        V->>P: CAS active region and feed key
        alt Regional CAS succeeds
            P-->>V: Candidate is active in region
        else Regional CAS loses
            P-->>V: Keep region's current version
        end
    end

Rollback is another fenced regional pointer update: compare-and-swap from the known bad version to that region's last checksum-verified version, then emit a regional activation event. Never overwrite segments or blindly set an older pointer, because a concurrent good build may already have replaced the bad version. Retain each region's prior version and warmed leading segments for at least the rollback window. If global validation, local warming, or regional CAS fails, readers in that region stay on the old version; if a post-activation quality alarm fires, rollback changes new sessions while existing snapshot cursors remain valid until normal expiry.

For example, a 2,000-card feed split into 100-card segments has 20 segments. At 1 KB per compact card it is about 2 MB per version. Across 200 feed keys, 12 retained versions, and three durable replicas, payload storage is roughly 2 MB * 200 * 12 * 3 = 14.4 GB, while warming only two segments per key per region limits each regional hot set to about 200 * 2 * 100 KB = 40 MB before cache overhead.

docs.title: 8.6 Feed refresh cadence
docs.text:
Use two complementary modes:

  • Periodic rebuild every few minutes for normal updates.
  • Event-driven partial refresh for major stories, retractions, and urgent policy changes.

Avoid rebuilding all editions for every article. Track affected language, region, and category feed keys.

docs.title: 9.1 Why offset pagination fails
docs.text: With OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20, the database or search engine may inspect and discard thousands of records. More importantly, newly inserted stories shift positions, causing duplicates or missed items across pages.

docs.title: 9.2 Snapshot-position cursor
docs.text:
For precomputed feeds, use:

cursor = signed(feed_key, feed_version, next_position, expiry)

Page 1 reads positions 0-19, and the returned cursor points to position 20 in the same immutable version.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Feed API
    participant R as Redis
    participant S as Feed Store

    C->>A: GET /feed without cursor
    A->>R: Read latest version and segment 0
    R-->>A: v1842, positions 0-19
    A-->>C: Items + cursor(v1842, 20)

    C->>A: GET /feed cursor(v1842, 20)
    A->>R: Read v1842 segment containing position 20
    alt Segment cached
        R-->>A: Positions 20-39
    else Cache miss
        A->>S: Read snapshot v1842 positions 20-39
        S-->>A: Feed entries
        A->>R: Cache segment
    end
    A-->>C: Items + cursor(v1842, 40)

This provides stable pagination even while version v1843 becomes current for new sessions.

Positions count scanned snapshot entries, not returned cards. Apply current eligibility to each candidate and backfill from later positions up to a scan budget; the next cursor points after the last scanned entry even when every candidate is retracted. Otherwise a page containing only removed stories can return the same cursor forever. The diagram's increments of 20 assume no filtering. Add a case where positions 20-39 are denied and 40-49 supply ten cards: the next position is 50, not 30 or 40. A snapshot pins order, never old permission to serve a withdrawn article.

docs.title: 9.3 Cursor expiry and old snapshots
docs.text:
Keep old snapshots for a bounded period, for example 30-60 minutes. If a client returns after expiry:

  • Return a cursor-expired response and restart from the latest feed.
  • Or map the position approximately into the new version while using session deduplication.

The first behavior is simpler and usually acceptable for a news feed.

docs.title: 9.4 Cursor alternatives
docs.text:
Cursor strategy Stable while new stories arrive Server state Best use Main cost or failure Signed snapshot version plus position Yes None beyond retained snapshots Precomputed home/category feeds Cursor expires when its immutable version is deleted Keyset (rank_key,cluster_id) Only if ordering keys do not change None Chronological archive or immutable score order Reranking can still skip or repeat items Stateful session cursor plus shown-ID set Yes across feed refreshes One bounded record per session Personalized sessions that intentionally advance versions Redis cost, expiry behavior, and regional routing Offset No None Static, small administrative lists Deep scans and position shifts under insertion

The chosen hot-feed cursor is snapshot plus position because ordering is precomputed and versions are already retained. The chronological archive switches to keyset pagination. A personalized feed may additionally carry a bounded shown-ID token, but that deduplication layer does not make offset pagination correct.

docs.title: 9.5 Session-level deduplication
docs.text:
Snapshots can still change if the product periodically advances users to a newer feed. Maintain a compact set or Bloom filter of recently shown story IDs:

  • Client can send a bounded list or opaque session token.
  • Server can keep a short-lived session set in Redis.
  • Filter duplicates and backfill from later positions.

Do not store unbounded feed history per anonymous user.

docs.title: 9.6 End of feed
docs.text:
"Infinite" means the client can continue requesting older pages, not that data is literally infinite. Feed storage may contain:

  • A ranked hot section for the last 24-48 hours.
  • A chronological archive partitioned by edition/category and time.

Once the ranked snapshot ends, continue through older eligible clusters using a keyset cursor such as (published_at, cluster_id). Pin an archive cutoff in the snapshot manifest and restrict the ranked section to stories at or after that cutoff and the archive to earlier stories. Without a disjoint boundary or an exact shown-ID set, ranked stories can repeat in the archive. Pin archive ordering timestamps too; corrections must not move a record across an active cursor.

docs.title: 10.1 Direct link versus redirect service
docs.text:
Direct links are simpler, faster, and avoid making the aggregator a dependency for navigation. A redirect service provides centralized analytics, abuse blocking, and URL changes.

A pragmatic approach:

  • Include the canonical publisher URL in the feed for resilient clients.
  • Use an edge-hosted redirect URL when click analytics is required.
  • Fall back to the canonical URL if the redirect service is unavailable.

docs.title: 10.2 Click path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant E as Edge Redirect
    participant K as Analytics Stream
    participant P as Publisher

    U->>E: GET /r/article_a72
    E-->>U: 302 publisher URL
    E--)K: Asynchronous click event
    U->>P: GET full article
    P-->>U: Publisher page

The redirect should not synchronously increment a database counter. During breaking news, one story can receive millions of clicks and create a hot row. Stream click events and aggregate them asynchronously.

docs.title: 10.3 URL safety
docs.text:
• Redirect only to URLs previously validated and stored for accepted publishers.
  • Never redirect to an arbitrary query parameter.
  • Block malicious, expired, retracted, or compromised destinations.
  • Use HTTPS where supported.
  • Keep a domain allowlist tied to publisher ownership.

docs.title: 11. Deep Dive: Achieving Feed Latency Below 200 ms
11.1 Latency budget
docs.text:
An illustrative server-side budget:

Stage Budget Edge and network 40 ms Gateway and authentication 10 ms Feed API execution 10 ms Redis/feed lookup 10 ms Metadata hydration 20 ms Serialization and compression 10 ms Safety margin 100 ms

Cross-region database calls or real-time ranking can easily consume the entire budget, so feed data should already be materialized in the serving region.

docs.title: 11.2 Cache hierarchy
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Client --> Edge[CDN / Edge Cache]
    Edge --> L1[L1 In-Process Cache]
    L1 --> L2[L2 Redis Cluster]
    L2 --> FeedStore[(Durable Feed Store)]
  • Edge cache public first pages by edition for a few seconds.
  • L1 caches the latest feed-version pointer and hottest segments.
  • Redis stores materialized feed segments.
  • Durable feed storage handles cache misses and snapshot retention.

First-page cache keys might be:

feed:{edition}:{category}:{version}:segment:{number}

Store complete display cards when practical. Fetching 20 IDs and then issuing 20 article reads creates a fan-out latency and availability problem.

docs.title: 11.3 Cache stampede protection
docs.text:
When a feed segment expires:

  • Use request coalescing or a per-key lease so one request refreshes it.
  • Serve stale data while revalidating.
  • Add randomized TTL jitter.
  • Prewarm the first segments of new feed versions before publishing the version pointer.

docs.title: 11.4 Compact responses
docs.text:
• Return only card fields needed for the viewport.
  • Use Brotli or gzip compression.
  • Use optimized thumbnail dimensions and formats.
  • Avoid embedding large publisher or taxonomy objects repeatedly.
  • Cache immutable media URLs aggressively.

docs.title: 12. Deep Dive: Meeting the 30-Minute Freshness Target
docs.text:
Freshness is an end-to-end SLO, not just a crawler interval.

publication
  -> source discovery
  -> fetch queue wait
  -> network fetch
  -> parse and normalize
  -> deduplicate and classify
  -> policy decision
  -> ranking and feed materialization
  -> regional cache visibility

Define stage budgets:

Stage Deadline allocation, not additive p99 Discover or poll source 15 minutes Fetch queue and download 3 minutes Normalize and deduplicate 3 minutes Classify and filter 3 minutes Rank and publish feeds 4 minutes Replicate and expose 2 minutes

These allocations sum to 30 minutes but do not prove a 30-minute p99: six component p99s can fail on different articles. Measure the complete publication-to-visible distribution, or apportion a joint tail-failure budget, including source discovery and backlog.

docs.title: Freshness mechanisms
docs.text:
• Prefer push integrations for high-value publishers.
  • Poll active sources every few minutes.
  • Prioritize sources with historically frequent updates.
  • Autoscale consumers based on queue lag.
  • Partition streams by publisher to preserve local ordering.
  • Trigger partial feed refreshes instead of waiting for a global rebuild.
  • Monitor feed_visible_at - publisher_published_at, segmented by source.

Publisher timestamps are not always trustworthy. Also track discovery and ingestion timestamps to distinguish publisher clock errors from system delay.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text:
If ingestion falls behind:

  1. Preserve raw events durably.
  2. Prioritize trusted and time-sensitive sources.
  3. Defer expensive enrichment that is not required for eligibility.
  4. Publish a minimally processed article, then enrich it later if policy allows.
  5. Shed duplicate refreshes before unique new articles.

docs.title: 13. Deep Dive: Media Content
docs.text:
News feeds are image-heavy, while media bytes dwarf metadata.

flowchart LR
    Article[Accepted Article] --> Extract[Media URL Extractor]
    Extract --> Fetch[Sandboxed Media Fetcher]
    Fetch --> Validate[Type, Size, Safety, Rights]
    Validate --> Original[(Object Storage)]
    Original --> Transform[Resize and Transcode]
    Transform --> Variants[(Image Variants)]
    Variants --> CDN[Global CDN]
    CDN --> Client[Clients]

docs.title: Media strategy
docs.text:
• Respect publisher rights and agreements before proxying media.
  • Validate MIME type from bytes, not only headers.
  • Enforce download, pixel-count, duration, and file-size limits.
  • Strip unsafe metadata where appropriate.
  • Generate fixed responsive sizes such as 320, 640, and 1280 pixels.
  • Prefer WebP or AVIF with JPEG fallback.
  • Use immutable content-hashed URLs and long CDN TTLs.
  • Lazy-load media below the viewport.

Videos should generally remain on the publisher platform. The aggregator can serve a thumbnail and metadata rather than ingest and transcode every full video.

docs.title: Failed media
docs.text: Feed cards must work without media. Use publisher logos or neutral placeholders and never delay feed publication waiting indefinitely for image processing.

docs.title: 14. Deep Dive: Breaking-News Traffic Spikes
docs.text:
Breaking news creates two simultaneous spikes:

  • Read spike: many users refresh the same feed and click the same story.
  • Write spike: many publishers release related updates and media.

docs.title: Read-side protection
docs.text:
• Cache anonymous first pages at the CDN by edition.
  • Use stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error.
  • Precompute shared feeds instead of ranking each request.
  • Keep feed services stateless and autoscalable.
  • Replicate feed caches regionally.
  • Use request coalescing for cache misses.
  • Degrade optional metadata before rejecting feed requests.
  • Rate-limit abusive refresh loops at the edge.

docs.title: Write-side protection
docs.text:
• Buffer fetch and processing work in Kafka or durable queues.
  • Autoscale workers from lag and oldest-message age.
  • Prioritize new canonical stories over repeated cluster updates.
  • Coalesce multiple updates to the same cluster within a short window.
  • Batch feed rebuilds.
  • Isolate media processing from article eligibility.

docs.title: Hot-key handling
docs.text:
Do not maintain one synchronous SQL counter for a viral story. Use sharded counters:

click_count:{story_id}:{shard_id}

Aggregate shards periodically for ranking. Approximate counters are acceptable for trend signals.

docs.title: Graceful degradation order
docs.text:
1. Serve a slightly stale cached feed.
  2. Omit expensive personalization or alternative-source lists.
  3. Use precomputed thumbnails and summaries only.
  4. Reduce page size.
  5. Fall back to a static emergency feed by edition.

docs.title: Publisher and source metadata
docs.text: Use a relational database because source ownership, status, schedules, and uniqueness have clear transactional relationships.

docs.title: Canonical articles
docs.text:
Use sharded SQL, a wide-column database, or a document store depending on scale and access patterns. Required operations are:

  • Idempotent upsert by canonical identity.
  • Lookup by article ID and canonical URL.
  • Recent articles by publisher and time.
  • Status and cluster updates.

Partition historical articles by publication month and hash publisher or article ID within each period. Time partitioning makes retention and archival manageable.

docs.title: Story clusters
docs.text: Store canonical cluster state in a durable database. Use a vector index or approximate nearest-neighbor service only for candidate retrieval; it should not become the sole source of truth.

docs.title: Feed snapshots
docs.text:
Options:

  • Redis sorted sets or lists for hot feed segments.
  • DynamoDB/Cassandra for durable regionally replicated feed entries.
  • Object storage for immutable large snapshots and archives.

A useful combination is Redis for hot segments, a distributed key-value store for recent versions, and object storage for rebuild artifacts.

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Search is not a core requirement here. If users need keyword search, project article and cluster metadata into OpenSearch rather than forcing the feed store to support text queries.

docs.title: 16. Consistency Model
docs.text:
Data Consistency Rationale Source configuration Strong Avoid duplicate or unauthorized fetching Article identity Strong uniqueness or idempotent effect Prevent duplicate canonical records Cluster assignment Eventual and revisable Semantic grouping improves as data arrives Feed membership and order Eventual Availability and latency are more important Feed pagination Stable within a snapshot Prevent duplicates and omissions while scrolling Click counters Eventual and approximate Used for ranking, not billing Retractions and blocks Fast event-driven invalidation Safety overrides ordinary cache staleness

The system should remain useful while components disagree briefly. Canonical data is durable; feeds and caches are rebuildable projections.

docs.title: 17. Event Model and Idempotency
docs.text:
Example events:

SourceFetchCompleted
ArticleDiscovered
ArticleNormalized
ArticleAccepted
ArticleRetracted
ClusterCreated
ClusterUpdated
ClusterMerged
ClassificationUpdated
FeedVersionPublished
ArticleClicked

Every event should contain:

  • Globally unique event ID.
  • Entity ID and entity version.
  • Event timestamp and producer timestamp.
  • Trace ID.
  • Schema version.
  • Minimal routing fields such as language, edition, and publisher.

Consumers should be idempotent. They can store processed event IDs, compare entity versions, or make writes naturally idempotent through upserts.

Use a schema registry and compatibility rules because ingestion and serving pipelines evolve independently.

docs.title: Publisher is unavailable
docs.text:
• Retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
  • Continue serving already ingested articles.
  • Alert only after source-specific thresholds to avoid noisy transient failures.
  • Do not let one domain occupy the fetch fleet.

docs.title: Parser or classifier is broken
docs.text:
• Preserve raw payloads for replay.
  • Route poison records to a dead-letter queue.
  • Roll back the model or parser version.
  • Publish minimally processed content only when safety rules permit.

docs.title: Kafka is delayed
docs.text:
• Existing feeds remain readable.
  • Freshness degrades while canonical input stays buffered.
  • Autoscale consumers and prioritize article eligibility stages.
  • Alert on oldest-event age, not just message count.

docs.title: Redis is unavailable
docs.text:
• Read recent feed snapshots from the durable feed store.
  • Use bounded process-local caches.
  • Serve stale edge responses.
  • Rate-limit requests to protect the fallback store.

docs.title: Feed builder fails
docs.text:
• Keep the previous successful version active.
  • Never publish a version pointer before all required segments exist.
  • Validate item count, policy status, duplicates, and schema before activation.

docs.title: Region is unavailable
docs.text:
• Geo-route clients to another healthy region.
  • Keep several feed versions replicated across regions.
  • Accept increased latency rather than losing the feed entirely.

docs.title: 19. Multi-Region Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Publishers[Global Publishers] --> Ingest[Regional Ingestion Edges]
    Ingest --> GlobalBus[Durable Global Event Backbone]
    GlobalBus --> Canonical[(Canonical Article and Cluster Stores)]
    Canonical --> Builder[Global and Regional Feed Builders]

    Builder --> US[(US Feed Store and Cache)]
    Builder --> EU[(EU Feed Store and Cache)]
    Builder --> AP[(APAC Feed Store and Cache)]

    DNS[Geo DNS / Anycast] --> USEdge[US Edge]
    DNS --> EUEdge[EU Edge]
    DNS --> APEdge[APAC Edge]
    USEdge --> US
    EUEdge --> EU
    APEdge --> AP
    subgraph IngestLane[Canonical ingestion]
      Publishers
      Ingest
      GlobalBus
      Canonical
      Builder
    end
    subgraph Regional[Regional serving]
      DNS
      USEdge
      US
      EUEdge
      EU
      APEdge
      AP
    end

The serving plane should be active-active across regions because reads dominate and feeds are immutable projections. Canonical article and cluster writes can use home-region ownership or a globally replicated database.

Feed-version activation occurs independently through active[region,feed_key], but every referenced version must first pass global full-manifest validation and then local checksum-bound warming. Include the generation time and active region in responses, monitor pointer skew and replication lag, and never let a global pointer direct an unwarmed region to a candidate.

docs.title: 20. Bonus: Category Feeds
docs.text: Category support is a natural extension of shared precomputed feeds.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
Assign each story zero or more categories with confidence scores:

Technology: 0.94
Business:   0.67
Sports:     0.01

Use publisher sections, text classification, entities, and taxonomy rules. Require thresholds and allow editorial or publisher overrides.

docs.title: Serving
docs.text:
Materialize feed keys such as:

category:technology:en-US
category:sports:en-GB
category:business:en-IN

The same versioned snapshot, cache, and cursor machinery works without a separate architecture.

docs.title: Category-specific ranking
docs.text: Signals and decay differ by category. Sports scores may emphasize live recency; long-form science reporting may use a longer half-life. Train or configure ranking by category rather than assuming one universal model.

docs.title: User profile
docs.text:
Derive a bounded profile from:

  • Explicitly selected topics and publishers.
  • Clicked, hidden, and followed stories.
  • Topic and entity affinity.
  • Language and region.
  • Recency-weighted reading history.

Apply privacy controls, retention limits, consent, and account deletion.

docs.title: Hybrid personalization architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Shared[Shared Edition and Category Candidates] --> Merge[Candidate Merger]
    Profile[(User Profile Store)] --> ReRank[Online Reranker]
    Trends[Regional Trends] --> Merge
    Following[Followed Topics and Publishers] --> Merge
    Merge --> ReRank
    ReRank --> Rules[Diversity, Safety, Deduplication]
    Rules --> User[Personalized Page]

Do not rank the entire corpus during a request. Retrieve a few hundred candidates from shared pools, then rerank them using a low-latency user profile.

docs.title: Cold start
docs.text:
• Anonymous users receive edition feeds.
  • New users choose optional interests.
  • Popular regional stories supply a baseline.
  • Exploration introduces unfamiliar categories without overwhelming the feed.

docs.title: Avoiding filter bubbles
docs.text: Personalization should include diversity constraints, source variety, and important public-interest stories. Product policy, not just click optimization, defines feed quality.

docs.title: 22. Retractions, Corrections, and Deletion
docs.text:
News changes after publication. Model article state explicitly:

DISCOVERED -> ELIGIBLE -> PUBLISHED
                       -> RETRACTED
                       -> BLOCKED
                       -> EXPIRED

Retraction flow:

  1. Detect a publisher removal, correction marker, or policy action.
  2. Update canonical article status.
  3. Emit a high-priority invalidation event.
  4. Remove or replace it in affected clusters.
  5. Build a new immutable feed version; old snapshots retain their bytes and are filtered by current retraction state.
  6. Purge Redis and CDN keys when necessary.
  7. Keep an audit trail and tombstone to prevent accidental reingestion.

Safety invalidations should bypass ordinary batch refresh windows. Define a removal bound, such as 60 seconds after the authoritative policy commit. Every serving layer, including edge cache hits, redirects, and known media URLs, checks a versioned denylist whose maximum permitted age fits that bound; if it cannot refresh, it withholds affected content or fails closed. Purge accelerates removal but does not establish the bound by itself. Snapshot rollback and stale-if-error never roll back this policy gate. Already downloaded cards, cached client redirects, and direct publisher links cannot be recalled by the aggregator; use no-store for redirects if repeat clicks must recheck policy.

docs.title: User-facing SLIs
docs.text:
• Feed API availability and p50/p95/p99 latency.
  • Empty-feed and cursor-error rates.
  • First-page cache hit rate by region and edition.
  • Duplicate cards per session.
  • Redirect success and latency.
  • Media error and layout-shift rates.

docs.title: Freshness SLIs
docs.text:
• Publication-to-discovery time.
  • Discovery-to-eligible time.
  • Eligible-to-feed-visible time.
  • End-to-end publication-to-feed-visible time.
  • Percentage meeting the 30-minute target by publisher and edition.

docs.title: Pipeline health
docs.text:
• Scheduler delay and fetch success rate.
  • Queue depth and oldest-task age.
  • Kafka lag and dead-letter volume.
  • Parser/classifier errors by version.
  • Feed build duration and activation failures.
  • Regional feed-version lag.

docs.title: Quality metrics
docs.text:
• Exact and near-duplicate rate.
  • Cluster merge/split correction rate.
  • Publisher and topic diversity.
  • Retraction-removal latency.
  • Click-through rate, dwell proxy, and rapid-return rate.

Propagate trace context for ingestion and feed requests; sample full traces with elevated sampling for errors and freshness violations. Carry trace IDs through event headers so a stale article can be followed from fetch to feed publication.

docs.title: Correctness and contract tests
docs.text:
• Replay identical poll, push, and Kafka inputs and assert one canonical article and idempotent downstream effects.
  • Publish feed segments concurrently with readers and assert that a version pointer never exposes an incomplete snapshot.
  • Corrupt one segment, omit a position, duplicate a cluster, return a false warm acknowledgement, and race two builders from the same base; validation or CAS must keep the old pointer active.
  • Roll back while a newer healthy build activates and assert that fenced CAS cannot overwrite the healthy pointer; old-version cursors must continue reading only their original segments.
  • Insert new feed versions while paginating and assert no duplicate or omitted cards within the cursor's snapshot.
  • Race retraction events against delayed ingestion, clustering, ranking, and cache fills; the retracted article must remain unavailable and unredirectable.
  • Validate canonicalization, redirect allowlists, event schema compatibility, and cursor tamper/expiry behavior.

docs.title: Quality and pipeline tests
docs.text:
• Maintain labeled corpora for exact deduplication, near-duplicate clustering, language, topic, geography, and policy classification; compare precision, recall, and cluster split/merge rates before rollout.
  • Run shadow feed builds and compare item eligibility, diversity constraints, freshness, and ranking movement against the active version.
  • Test raw-payload replay and full feed reconstruction from canonical state after parser, classifier, or schema changes.

docs.title: Load and failure tests
docs.text:
• Reproduce a breaking-news step spike with one viral story, publisher skew, synchronized refreshes, cold caches, and media fan-out.
  • Inject slow publishers, poison records, Kafka lag, Redis loss, failed feed builders, and regional failover while checking the documented degradation order.
  • Verify the 30-minute freshness budget stage by stage and confirm that backpressure prioritizes unique, eligible articles over duplicate enrichment work.

docs.title: 25. Security, Abuse, and Policy
docs.text:
• Authenticate publisher configuration changes.
  • Prevent SSRF and DNS rebinding in fetchers.
  • Sandbox parsers and media processors.
  • Validate redirect domains.
  • Rate-limit feed requests and click endpoints.
  • Detect publisher spam, copied content, malware, and coordinated manipulation.
  • Separate editorial/policy overrides from ranking code and audit every action.
  • Encrypt data in transit and at rest.
  • Minimize and expire user behavior data used for personalization.
  • Protect ranking signals against artificial click inflation.

Publisher quality is an input, not a permanent truth. Maintain explainable versioned signals and an appeal or review process.

docs.title: Precomputed feeds versus rank on read
docs.text: Precomputation wins for anonymous, highly shared feeds because it converts expensive ranking into cheap indexed reads. Online ranking is reserved for lightweight personalization or rare filters.

docs.title: Freshness versus stability
docs.text: Always switching users to the latest order improves freshness but causes duplicate and missing cards during scrolling. Versioned snapshots keep a session stable while new sessions receive the freshest version.

docs.title: Polling versus push
docs.text: Push gives excellent freshness but cannot cover every publisher. Adaptive polling is universal but consumes bandwidth and can miss a strict freshness target for slow schedules. Support both.

docs.title: Storing full articles versus metadata
docs.text: The core product redirects to publishers, so store only licensed or operationally necessary excerpts and metadata. Preserving raw fetch payloads for a limited replay window is different from republishing complete content.

docs.title: Exact versus approximate ranking signals
docs.text: Trending counters and engagement velocity can be approximate. Article identity, publisher ownership, retraction state, and redirect targets require correctness.

docs.title: Availability versus consistency
docs.text: Serve the previous feed version during pipeline or cache failures. A stale but safe feed is preferable to an error page, but retractions and policy blocks require priority invalidation.

docs.title: 27. Final Design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph SourcePlane[Publisher and Ingestion Plane]
        Sources[RSS / APIs / Sitemaps / Push] --> Scheduler[Adaptive Scheduler]
        Scheduler --> FetchQueue[Durable Fetch Queue]
        FetchQueue --> Fetchers[Sandboxed Fetchers]
        Fetchers --> Raw[(Raw Replay Storage)]
        Fetchers --> Kafka[Kafka]
        Kafka --> Normalize[Normalize and Canonicalize]
        Normalize --> Exact[Exact Deduplication]
        Exact --> Cluster[Near-Duplicate Story Clustering]
        Cluster --> Enrich[Language, Topic, Geo, Policy]
        Enrich --> Articles[(Canonical Article Store)]
        Enrich --> Clusters[(Story Cluster Store)]
    end

    subgraph RankingPlane[Ranking and Materialization Plane]
        Articles --> Candidate[Candidate Generation]
        Clusters --> Candidate
        Signals[(Trend and Quality Signals)] --> Ranker[Ranker]
        Candidate --> Ranker
        Ranker --> Constraints[Diversity and Safety Constraints]
        Constraints --> Builder[Versioned Feed Builder]
        Builder --> DurableFeeds[(Durable Feed Store)]
        Builder --> RegionalRedis[(Regional Redis)]
    end

    subgraph ServingPlane[Low-Latency Serving Plane]
        EdgePurge[Edge purge requests]
        User[Web and Mobile Clients] --> CDN[CDN / WAF / Edge]
        CDN --> Gateway[API Gateway]
        Gateway --> FeedAPI[Feed API]
        FeedAPI --> LocalCache[Process Cache]
        LocalCache --> RegionalRedis
        RegionalRedis --> DurableFeeds
        CDN --> Redirect[Edge Redirect Service]
        Redirect --> Publisher[Publisher Website]
    end

    subgraph MediaPlane[Media Plane]
        Enrich --> MediaRefs[Validated media references]
        MediaRefs --> MediaWorkers[Media Validation and Transform]
        MediaWorkers --> Blobs[(Object Storage)]
        Blobs --> CDN
    end

    Invalidation[Retraction and Policy Invalidation] --> Builder
    Invalidation --> RegionalRedis
    Invalidation --> EdgePurge
    EdgePurge --> CDN

docs.title: End-to-end behavior
docs.text:
1. The scheduler polls sources adaptively, while capable publishers push updates directly.
  2. Fetchers use conditional requests, preserve raw payloads, and publish durable ingestion events.
  3. Workers normalize URLs, deduplicate exact copies, cluster related articles, classify them, and enforce policy.
  4. Ranking jobs create immutable global, regional, and category feed snapshots.
  5. New snapshots are fully written and warmed before an atomic version-pointer switch.
  6. Feed APIs serve complete card segments from edge caches, local caches, or Redis, with durable snapshots as fallback.
  7. Snapshot-based cursors provide stable infinite scrolling while newer sessions receive fresher versions.
  8. Clicks redirect immediately to publishers and emit asynchronous analytics events.
  9. Media uses a separate validation, transformation, object-storage, and CDN path.
  10. Retractions use high-priority invalidation, while ordinary ranking changes remain eventually consistent.

docs.title: Why not query the latest articles table for each feed request?
docs.text: At 100,000+ peak QPS, repeatedly filtering, joining, ranking, deduplicating, and diversifying the same anonymous feed wastes compute and increases tail latency. Precompute shared feed snapshots and serve compact segments from cache.

docs.title: How does pagination remain stable when new articles arrive?
docs.text: The cursor references an immutable feed version and the next position. New articles appear in a newer version but do not shift the user's active snapshot.

docs.title: How do articles become visible within 30 minutes?
docs.text: Use publisher push where available, adaptive polling elsewhere, durable queues, bounded stage budgets, lag-based autoscaling, and event-driven partial feed refreshes.

docs.title: How do you prevent every headline about the same event from filling the feed?
docs.text: Perform exact URL/content deduplication followed by semantic story clustering using embeddings, entity overlap, title similarity, language, and time proximity. Rank clusters rather than raw articles.

docs.title: What happens if Redis fails?
docs.text: Serve stale edge or process-cache entries and fall back to the durable feed store. Apply load shedding to protect that store. Redis contains rebuildable projections, not canonical data.

docs.title: How do you handle a breaking-news spike?
docs.text: Exploit shared CDN and Redis cache keys, serve stale while revalidating, coalesce misses, precompute feeds, buffer ingestion in Kafka, batch cluster updates, and degrade optional hydration or personalization first.

docs.title: How do you update or retract an article already cached globally?
docs.text: Change canonical status, emit a priority invalidation, update the cluster and affected feed versions, and purge cache/CDN keys. Preserve a tombstone to prevent reingestion.

docs.title: Should click counting happen synchronously during redirect?
docs.text: No. Return the redirect immediately and emit an asynchronous event. Aggregate sharded or streamed counters later so viral stories cannot create hot-row contention.

docs.title: Where does strong consistency matter?
docs.text: Source ownership, article identity, redirect safety, and retraction state need strong or idempotent correctness. Feed ordering, clustering, ranking, and engagement counters can be eventual.

docs.title: L5 Expectations: Core
docs.text:
• Separates ingestion from feed serving.
  • Defines article, publisher, and feed entities.
  • Uses queues for asynchronous processing.
  • Uses Redis/CDN for read scaling and cursor pagination.
  • Redirects users to publisher URLs.

docs.title: L5 Expectations: Strong Signals
docs.text:
• Quantifies feed QPS and freshness requirements.
  • Designs adaptive polling, idempotent ingestion, deduplication, and story clustering.
  • Uses precomputed, versioned feed snapshots for low latency and stable pagination.
  • Handles media separately and explains failure degradation.
  • Addresses breaking-news spikes and cache stampedes.

docs.title: L6 Expectations
docs.text:
• Frames freshness as a measurable end-to-end SLO with stage budgets.
  • Separates canonical state from rebuildable projections.
  • Designs safe feed activation, replay, regional replication, and retraction invalidation.
  • Balances ranking quality, diversity, publisher policy, cost, and latency.
  • Presents category and personalization as evolutionary extensions rather than required initial complexity.

docs.title: 30. Five-Minute Interview Summary
docs.text:
I would split Google News into an ingestion plane and a feed-serving plane. An adaptive scheduler polls RSS, Atom, APIs, and sitemaps, while publishers that support push can send updates directly. Fetchers use conditional requests and publish raw items to Kafka. Downstream workers normalize URLs, perform exact deduplication, cluster semantically related coverage into stories, classify topics and geography, apply policy filters, and write canonical article and cluster records.

The read path must support over 100,000 peak feed requests per second below 200 ms, so I would not rank the corpus per request. Ranking jobs continuously build immutable feed snapshots by edition and category. They store complete display cards in versioned segments in regional Redis, with a durable feed store behind it and short-lived CDN caching for anonymous first pages. A cursor contains the feed version and next position, providing stable infinite scrolling even while newer versions are published.

Clicking an article redirects immediately to the validated publisher URL; analytics are emitted asynchronously. Media is validated and transformed in a separate pipeline and served from object storage through a CDN. During breaking news, shared cache keys, stale-while-revalidate, request coalescing, queue buffering, and partial feed refreshes absorb spikes. Existing feed versions remain available during ingestion failures, while retractions use priority invalidation across feed stores and caches.

docs.title: 31. Final Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Separate ingestion from read serving so each scales and fails independently.
  2. Treat canonical articles and story clusters as durable truth; feeds and caches are projections.
  3. Rank story clusters rather than raw articles to prevent duplicate coverage from dominating.
  4. Precompute shared feeds to turn expensive ranking into fast indexed reads.
  5. Use immutable feed versions and snapshot cursors for consistent infinite scrolling.
  6. Cache complete card segments instead of creating a per-item hydration fan-out.
  7. Measure freshness from publisher publication through regional feed visibility.
  8. Combine publisher push with adaptive, polite polling.
  9. Move media bytes to object storage and a CDN through a safe transformation pipeline.
  10. Design breaking-news behavior explicitly: stale serving, coalescing, buffering, batching, and graceful degradation.
  11. Make ingestion and event consumers idempotent because retries are unavoidable.
  12. Prioritize availability for ordinary feed updates but fast invalidation for retractions and safety actions.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We design map browsing, place search, route planning, turn-by-turn navigation, and live traffic. We separate slowly published geographic truth from fast traffic overlays, estimate tile and routing scale, and deep-dive into graph partitioning, shortest paths, map matching, ETA, offline behavior, failures, privacy, and operations.

docs.title: 2. Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Users pan/zoom maps, search places, request driving/walking routes with alternatives, start navigation, receive reroutes, and download offline regions. Producers ingest road geometry, restrictions, closures, places, and anonymized traffic observations. Exclude street imagery and transit scheduling.

Targets: cached tile p95 under 100 ms, route p95 under one second for regional trips, reroute under two seconds, traffic age under two minutes on major roads, and 99.99% navigation availability. Invariants: published map generations are internally compatible; routes obey hard access/turn/closure constraints; coordinates use declared versions/projections; stale traffic may worsen ETA but must not bypass closures; telemetry is bounded, consented, and de-identified.

docs.title: 3. Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100 million daily users, 50 tile requests/session and five route requests: 5 billion tiles/day (58,000/s average, 500,000/s peak) and 500 million routes/day. CDN hit above 95% is essential. A continental road graph might contain 500 million vertices/edges and hundreds of GB compressed per generation, replicated in RAM/SSD across routing clusters. Ten million active navigators reporting every five seconds produce 2 million observations/s; ingest must aggregate early and enforce privacy thresholds.

Routing capacity must be derived from measured CPU per query, not request count alone. If peak traffic is 60,000 route requests/s, 70% are regional routes costing 12 ms CPU, 25% are metro routes costing 35 ms, and 5% are long routes costing 120 ms, the weighted demand is 0.70 * 12 + 0.25 * 35 + 0.05 * 120 = 23.15 ms, or 1,389 CPU-seconds/s. At 60% target utilization and 32 usable cores/host, the steady-state fleet is 1,389 / (32 * 0.60) = 73 hosts. Provisioning 30% failover and rollout headroom gives 95 hosts, before replicas required for graph locality. Cache hit rate, K alternatives, vehicle constraints, and partition fanout must be included in the measured workload mix.

docs.title: 4. APIs and data model
docs.text:
GET /v1/tiles/{generation}/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt
GET /v1/places/search?q=coffee&near=lat,lng&cursor=...
POST /v1/routes {origin,destination,mode,departAt,avoid,alternatives}
POST /v1/navigation/{routeId}:update {location,bearing,speed,sequence}
GET /v1/offline-regions/{regionId}?generation=...

RoadEdge(edge_id, from, to, geometry, distance, mode_access, turn_rules,
         base_speed, road_class, map_generation)
Place(place_id, names, categories, point, address, popularity, version)
Traffic(edge_id, time_bucket, speed_distribution, confidence, observed_at)
Closure(edge_id, direction, starts_at, ends_at, severity, version)
Route(route_id, map_generation, traffic_epoch, ordered_edge_ids, maneuvers, expiry)

Road/place generations and closures are canonical inputs; tiles, spatial indexes, routing shortcuts, and traffic estimates are projections.

docs.title: 5. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  P[Map providers and edits] --> G[Geo validation pipeline]
  G --> V[(Versioned map store)]
  V --> T[Tile builders]
  T --> C[Tile CDN]
  V --> R[Routing graph builders]
  R --> Q[Routing clusters]
  U[Apps] --> C
  U --> A[Route API]
  A --> Q
  U -. probes .-> I[Traffic ingest]
  I --> F[Map match and aggregate]
  F --> Q

docs.title: 6. Map publication and tiles
docs.text:
Edits pass schema, topology, geometry, restriction, and referential checks in a staging generation. Builders create vector tiles and routing partitions against the same immutable map generation; a manifest lists checksums and compatibility. Regions can publish independently only where boundary contracts are versioned. Serving atomically switches manifests after replicas warm; old generations remain for active routes/offline clients.

Vector tiles contain clipped geometry and style attributes, allowing client rendering and language/style changes without new raster images. Key by generation/z/x/y, compress, and cache immutably at CDN. Low zoom tiles are globally hot; high zoom is long-tail. Delta packages update offline regions, but clients verify base/new generation and checksums.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant E as Edit pipeline
  participant B as Builders
  participant O as Artifact store
  participant M as Manifest controller
  participant S as Tile/router replicas
  E->>B: validated map generation
  B->>O: tiles, graph, indexes, checksums
  B->>M: compatible manifest
  M-->>S: warm generation
  S->>O: download and verify
  S->>S: atomic switch

docs.title: 7. Route computation
docs.text:
Model directed road segments as weighted edges, with turn restrictions represented in an edge-based graph. Baseline Dijkstra is correct but too slow. A* uses admissible straight-line/time lower bounds. At continental scale, contraction hierarchies or multi-level Dijkstra precompute shortcuts; customizable contraction hierarchies separate topology preprocessing from periodically changing weights. Partition graphs by geography with border nodes and overlay shortcuts.

The request snaps origin/destination candidates, filters by mode/vehicle restrictions, chooses a graph generation, applies closure and traffic weights, computes K diverse paths, validates hard constraints, generates maneuvers, and stores a short-lived route reference. Alternatives need overlap penalties, not simply second-shortest tiny deviations.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant A as Route API
  participant G as Graph shard coordinator
  participant T as Traffic/closure overlay
  C->>A: origin, destination, mode, departure time
  A->>T: snapshot epoch
  A->>G: endpoints, mode, epoch, deadline
  G->>G: snap + hierarchical search
  G->>T: edge weights/hard closures
  G-->>A: candidate edge paths
  A->>A: validate, diversify, maneuvers, ETA
  A-->>C: route + generations

docs.title: Contraction and customization preprocessing
docs.text:
A conventional contraction hierarchy orders vertices and inserts shortcuts using metric-dependent witness searches. When contracting v, add (u,w) if no witness path avoiding v is at most as cheap as (u,v,w); retain child edges for unpacking. Consequently conventional shortcut topology can depend on the weights used during preprocessing. The customizable variant below instead constructs a metric-independent elimination topology, then customizes its weights. Do not assume a traffic change preserves the correctness of an ordinary witness-pruned hierarchy.

Customizable contraction hierarchies first build nested-dissection separators and topology-only triangles. A customization pass assigns metric-specific shortcut weights bottom-up: driving, truck, bicycle, and avoid-toll metrics can share topology. Full customization follows a map or policy release; incremental customization marks shortcuts whose dependency triangles contain changed edges and propagates dirtiness upward. Minute-level traffic remains a query-time overlay or triggers regional partial customization. Every weight snapshot records (map_generation, metric_version, traffic_epoch), and a route is rejected if hard restrictions cannot be validated against that tuple.

flowchart LR
  G[Immutable edge graph] --> O[Separator and contraction order]
  O --> T[Topology-only shortcuts]
  M[Mode and policy metric] --> C[Bottom-up customization]
  T --> C
  C --> W[Versioned shortcut weights]
  D[Changed edge weights] --> I[Dirty triangle propagation]
  I --> C
  W --> Q[Bidirectional upward query]
  Q --> U[Unpack and validate original edges]

Worked preprocessing example. Suppose roads A-B-C cost 4 and 6 seconds, while the cheapest witness path from A to C avoiding B costs 15 seconds. Contracting B creates shortcut A-C with cost 10 and children A-B, B-C. A traffic customization changes B-C to 11, so in a customizable topology the dependent triangles are recomputed and the shortcut becomes 15. The original witness-pruned hierarchy cannot in general be updated by changing this one shortcut alone. A hard closure on B-C is not represented as a merely large traffic cost: the query either uses a closure-aware customized metric or validates and rejects the unpacked shortcut.

docs.title: Cross-partition route algorithm and bounds
docs.text:
Each balanced geographic partition owns interior vertices and exposes replicated boundary vertices. Offline preprocessing computes exact intra-partition boundary-to-boundary distances for the base metric and forms a much smaller overlay graph. A request runs local A from each endpoint to reachable boundaries, bidirectional Dijkstra/A over the overlay, then corridor refinement inside only the partitions touched by the selected overlay path. The coordinator pins one generation, sends bounded parallel RPCs, and carries the best complete route cost U; a shard can stop expanding when its queue lower bound is at least U.

For exact static weights, exact boundary matrices plus admissible local heuristics preserve optimality. A global multiplicative stretch bound additionally requires the overlay to represent every feasible boundary crossing on the true optimal route, each arc weight to upper-bound a realizable path by at most 1 + epsilon, and exact optimization over that overlay. Then substituting the optimal route's crossings proves cost_returned <= (1 + max epsilon) * optimal_cost. Bounds only along an already selected corridor do not prove global optimality: a better omitted corridor may exist. Dynamic traffic can invalidate the certificate; return an approximation flag unless current lower bounds prove a new guarantee. Hard closures disable affected arcs, trigger base-edge refinement, or fail safely.

flowchart LR
  S[Origin in partition A] --> LA[Local search to A boundaries]
  LA --> OA[Boundary overlay]
  T[Destination in partition D] --> LD[Reverse local search to D boundaries]
  LD --> OA
  OA --> K[Best overlay corridor A-B-D]
  K --> PA[Refine partition A]
  K --> PB[Refine partition B]
  K --> PD[Refine partition D]
  PA --> V[Unpack and validate]
  PB --> V
  PD --> V
  V --> R[Route with bound and epochs]

Worked cross-partition example. Exact endpoint connectors cost 7 and 8 seconds. The chosen crossing costs 72 seconds with a 2% certificate, so the candidate costs 87 seconds and the optimum within that crossing is at least 72 / 1.02 + 15 = 85.59 seconds. If every alternative corridor has been exhausted or has an admissible lower bound of at least 90, 85.59 is also a global lower bound and the candidate is within 87 / 85.59 = 1.0165, about 1.65%. One competing queue with bound 90 alone would not establish that all alternatives were covered.

docs.title: 8. Traffic, map matching, and ETA
docs.text:
Noisy GPS observations are batched, sequence-numbered, and assigned coarse ephemeral identifiers. A hidden Markov map matcher generates nearby edge candidates using distance/bearing and uses transition likelihood along the graph to avoid jumping between parallel roads. Aggregate speeds into time buckets only after minimum contributor thresholds, reject impossible motion, and weight by freshness/device quality. Raw traces have short retention.

Fuse live distributions with historical speed profiles, incidents, weather/event signals, and road priors. Low-confidence live data decays toward history. ETA sums edge travel-time distributions with correlation/calibration correction; machine-learned residuals account for intersections, time, road class, and route context. Continuously compare predicted arrival against actual, sliced by city/time/mode.

Closures are a high-priority strongly versioned overlay and fail closed when their required freshness cannot be established; traffic is a soft eventually consistent weight. Rebuilding all shortcuts per observation is impossible: use base/customized weights plus dynamic local overlays, labeling results approximate unless a current bound is proved, and validating routes.

docs.title: HMM map matching with Viterbi
docs.text:
For observation z_t, retrieve at most K directed-edge candidates within an accuracy-dependent radius. The emission log-probability combines perpendicular distance under a Gaussian noise model, heading agreement under a circular distribution, and optional road-access priors. For candidates i at t-1 and j at t, the transition log-probability penalizes the difference between shortest-path road distance and observed displacement, impossible speed, illegal turns, and reversal. Viterbi computes V_t(j) = emission_t(j) + max_i(V_{t-1}(i) + transition(i,j)) and stores the winning predecessor. A sliding window commits old states only after enough future evidence; beam pruning keeps the best B states, making work O(T * B * K) rather than unconstrained O(T * K^2) when transition candidates are bounded.

flowchart TD
  Z1[GPS z1] --> C1[Edge candidates at t1]
  Z2[GPS z2] --> C2[Edge candidates at t2]
  Z3[GPS z3] --> C3[Edge candidates at t3]
  C1 -->|road-distance transition| C2
  C2 -->|road-distance transition| C3
  C1 --> V[Viterbi scores and backpointers]
  C2 --> V
  C3 --> V
  V --> B[Best edge sequence]
  B --> A[Privacy-thresholded aggregates]

Worked map-match example. Three observations lie between a frontage road F and parallel highway H. At the middle sample, emissions favor H by 0.8 log units because it is closer. The previous and next samples match F; entering and leaving H would require 1.4 km of graph travel versus 220 m observed, adding a transition penalty of -6 twice. The Viterbi path remains F-F-F, while nearest-edge snapping incorrectly jumps to H.

docs.title: ETA model operations
docs.text:
The ETA service computes a deterministic baseline from calibrated edge or segment travel-time distributions, then applies a versioned residual model to features available at request time. Training labels derive from completed, map-matched traversals; examples are weighted to prevent dense-city and long-trip dominance. Training uses time-based splits and reports median absolute error, p90 absolute error, signed bias, and interval coverage by city, trip length, mode, road class, and incident state. A prediction includes model, feature, map, and traffic versions for replay.

Candidate models shadow production first. Promotion requires global improvement without violating slice guardrails, then geographic canaries ramp from 1% to 10% to 50%. Monitor feature nulls, drift, residual bias, calibration, late arrivals, and reroute churn. If a feature stream stalls, use bounded-stale values or a baseline-only model; if a model breaches bias or latency thresholds, atomically return to the previous artifact. Labels arrive after trips finish, so dashboards distinguish prediction-time cohorts from label-complete cohorts.

Worked ETA example. A 20-edge route has a baseline sum of 31 minutes. The residual model adds 2.5 minutes for six signalized turns and an event feature, producing 33.5 minutes with an 80% interval of 29-39. In a city canary, p90 error improves from 9.0 to 8.2 minutes, but trips under 3 km develop +1.8 minute bias against a +0.5 guardrail. Promotion stops even though aggregate error improved; the old model remains active while that slice is corrected.

docs.title: 9. Navigation and rerouting
docs.text:
Client map-matches locally for responsive maneuvers and sends bounded updates. Off-route detection uses distance, heading, confidence, and consecutive samples to avoid GPS-jitter reroutes. If confidently off route, request from current matched position; preserve destination and user avoids. Server pushes closure/major-delay hints by route corridor, but client periodically refreshes because push is lossy.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> ON_ROUTE
  ON_ROUTE --> UNCERTAIN: low match confidence
  UNCERTAIN --> ON_ROUTE: recovered
  UNCERTAIN --> OFF_ROUTE: repeated divergence
  ON_ROUTE --> REROUTE: closure or material delay
  OFF_ROUTE --> REROUTE
  REROUTE --> ON_ROUTE: new route accepted
  ON_ROUTE --> ARRIVED

Offline packs include tiles, compact graph, places, and signing metadata. Offline routing uses historical weights and cannot promise live closures; UI clearly marks freshness. Active route pins a compatible generation, while controlled migration remaps remaining edges or reroutes.

docs.title: 10. Partitioning, scaling, consistency, and regions
docs.text:
Tiles partition naturally by spatial cell/generation and CDN. Place search uses S2/H3 cells plus text index; dense cells subdivide, sparse cells combine. Routing graph shards use balanced geographic partitions, border overlays, and replicas; long routes query coarse overlays then detailed corridor partitions. Avoid latitude-longitude rectangles near poles and uneven cities.

Traffic streams partition by coarse cell then edge; metropolitan hotspots split by edge hash. Aggregate locally before global fusion. Route APIs run active-active with locally replicated immutable graph generations. Map publication is manifest-atomic, closures are rapidly replicated/versioned, and traffic is eventual with age/confidence. Idempotency keys cover route creation if billed; probe sequence IDs deduplicate bounded windows.

Under overload, protect active-navigation reroutes over browse alternatives, reduce K alternatives, use historical traffic, and shed low-priority probe processing. Deadline-aware routing returns a validated approximate route, never one violating hard constraints. If a graph partition is absent, route around only if correctness is provable; otherwise return degraded failure.

docs.title: 11. Reliability and security
docs.text:
Graph replica loss reroutes requests; old verified generations continue through control-plane outage only while a compatible closure overlay satisfies its freshness bound. Map rollback must retain current emergency restrictions, remapping them to the older graph or refusing affected routes. Traffic outage decays to historical estimates. Closure-feed conflicts choose safest effective restriction and alert operators. Bad map releases roll back manifest pointers; route IDs record generation for diagnosis. CDN loss uses another provider/origin shield with capacity controls. GPS loss keeps local dead reckoning briefly and announces degraded guidance.

Location is highly sensitive: explicit consent, minimization, transport/storage encryption, rotating identifiers, short raw retention, aggregation thresholds, access audit, and deletion controls are required. Never expose individual traces to traffic consumers. Prevent route API scraping/DoS with keys, quotas, cost-based limits, and bounded waypoint counts. Secure edit provenance and use anomaly/human review against malicious roads/closures and place spam. Signed offline packages prevent graph tampering.

docs.title: 12. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure tile latency/hit/bytes, route p50-p99, expanded nodes, partition fanout, no-route/timeout/approximation rates, graph-generation skew, closure propagation, traffic age/confidence/coverage, map-match accuracy, ETA error percentiles, reroute frequency, navigation completion, offline freshness, and cost/route. Slice by geography, mode, app generation, and road class; global averages hide dangerous regions.

Property-test geometry/projection and route constraint satisfaction. Golden routes cover turn bans, one-way roads, ferries, borders, time restrictions, and dateline/poles. Replay anonymized traces for map matching/ETA; simulate GPS noise and tunnels. Differential-test optimized paths against Dijkstra on sampled subgraphs. Chaos removes partitions, delays closures, publishes malformed candidates, and rolls generations. Canary map releases by region and automatically compare route/ETA regressions before expansion.

docs.title: Geocoding and place search deep dive
docs.text:
Forward geocoding combines a language-aware text index with spatial priors. Normalize abbreviations without discarding original language, retrieve name/address candidates, then rank by textual match, distance or viewport, administrative containment, category, and quality. Reverse geocoding searches containing polygons and nearby address points from finest to coarsest geography. Every result carries stable place ID and version; coordinates alone are not identity because entrances and road access points differ from centroids.

Place edits from businesses and users enter a provenance-weighted moderation pipeline. Conflicting sources do not overwrite canonical state directly. Merge candidates, retain evidence, detect duplicate places through spatial/name/category similarity, and support appeals. Popular queries can cache by language and coarse cell, but opening-hours and closures need shorter overlays. Pagination signs query, viewport, index generation, score, and place-ID tie-breaker.

docs.title: Route quality and safety controls
docs.text:
Fastest-path objective is not simply summed observed seconds. Edge costs include expected time plus configurable penalties for unsafe turns, unpaved roads, difficult intersections, tolls, and uncertainty; hard vehicle dimensions and legal access remain constraints. The system must prevent tiny ETA gains from causing unstable reroutes, so reroute only when improvement exceeds an absolute and relative threshold after maneuver disruption cost.

Route explanation records which constraints and major cost factors selected a path without exposing proprietary weights. Safety incidents trigger a versioned regional rule or closure, then retrospective replay finds affected routes. Launching a new weight model uses shadow computation on live requests, golden-route review, geographic canaries, and guardrails for illegal maneuvers, ETA error, route churn, and concentrated neighborhood traffic.

docs.title: 13. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Server routing has current global data but needs connectivity; on-device routing improves resilience/privacy but ships large stale graphs. Use both. Aggressive shortcut preprocessing improves latency but resists traffic updates; customizable hierarchy plus overlays balances them. Raw probes maximize model flexibility but create privacy risk; early aggregation and short retention win.

Final design publishes compatible immutable map/tiles/graph generations, distributes vector tiles through CDN, runs hierarchical routing on geographic replicas, and overlays strongly versioned closures plus confidence-weighted live traffic. HMM map matching feeds privacy-thresholded aggregation; clients combine local navigation/offline graph with server reroutes.

docs.title: 14. Interview questions and levels
docs.text:
• Why is A* alone insufficient for continental routing?
  • How can shortcuts coexist with minute-level traffic?
  • How do you prevent parallel-road GPS jumps?
  • What happens to an active route during map-generation rollout?
  • Which telemetry can produce traffic without retaining journeys?

L5 should cover tiles/CDN, graph model, shortest paths, traffic, GPS matching, partitioning, and failures. L6 should define generation compatibility, hard versus soft overlays, hierarchy customization, privacy budgets, regional release/rollback, metro skew, approximation bounds, multimodal evolution, and measurable route/ETA quality.

docs.title: 15. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Separate immutable geographic generations from dynamic overlays. Validate edits, build compatible vector tiles, place indexes, routing graphs, and checksummed manifests, then atomically warm/switch replicas. CDN serves generation-keyed tiles. Routing snaps endpoints and uses A* plus contraction/multi-level shortcuts across geographic partitions, applies hard closures and soft traffic weights, validates constraints, diversifies alternatives, and emits maneuvers.

Privacy-bounded GPS probes are HMM map-matched to edges, aggregated above contributor thresholds, fused with historical profiles, and decayed when stale. Active navigation handles jitter locally, rerouting only after confident divergence or meaningful closure/delay. Run active-active on replicated graphs, pin route generations, retain rollback, and degrade traffic to history rather than bypassing restrictions. Optimize not just latency but valid-route rate, ETA calibration, closure age, reroutes, geography slices, and location privacy.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text:
We design licensed-catalog ingest, entitlement-aware playback, adaptive delivery, profiles, progress, and regional availability. Unlike creator video, content arrives through trusted studio supply chains, is preprocessed before release, and is governed by territorial windows and DRM.
