This is a proposed architecture, not a reconstruction of Netflix's private control plane. Netflix Open Connect verifies ISP-embedded appliances, peering, content fill and appliance failover. The numerical workloads, account leases, DRM topology and ABR thresholds below are explicit design assumptions, not published Netflix guarantees (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 2. Requirements, SLOs, and invariants
docs.text:
Users browse a personalized catalog, start/resume episodes, switch devices, select audio/subtitles, and stream under account/device/concurrency rules. Studios deliver masters and timed metadata; operators schedule release and rights windows. Exclude ad auctions and recommendation-model internals.

Targets: playback authorization 99.99%, p95 start under two seconds, rebuffer under 1%, progress visible on another device in five seconds, and no new license outside verified entitlement, with existing playback bounded by the explicit license and revocation window. Immediate revocation of already issued offline licenses is not promised. Invariants: manifests reference complete renditions; rights/parental/concurrency checks precede license issuance; assets are immutable/versioned; ingest and progress updates are idempotent; CDN loss cannot broaden access.

docs.title: 3. Estimates
docs.text: Assume 250 million accounts, 100 million viewing hours/day, 3 Mbps mean delivered bitrate: about 135 PB/day egress. A 20,000-title catalog with episodes, 20 bitrate/device renditions, audio languages, subtitles, and regional replicas may consume tens of PB, modest beside egress. At 20 million concurrent streams and six-second segments, edges handle over 3 million segment requests/s. Browse traffic is cacheable; playback authorization and licenses scale with session starts, perhaps hundreds of thousands/s at premieres.

docs.title: 4. APIs and model
docs.text:
GET /v1/home?profileId=...&cursor=...
POST /v1/playback/sessions {profileId,titleId,deviceCapabilities}
  -> {sessionId,manifestUrl,drmChallenge,heartbeatInterval}
POST /v1/playback/{sessionId}/heartbeat {position,sequence,deviceTime}
POST /v1/playback/{sessionId}/license {challenge}

Title(title_id, type, metadata_version, maturity, availability_state)
Asset(asset_id, title_id, pipeline_version, codec, bitrate, language, object_prefix)
Rights(title_id, territory, starts_at, ends_at, plan, device_class, version)
PlaybackSession(session_id, account_id, profile_id, title_id, rights_version,
                device_id, started_at, lease_until, state)
Progress(profile_id, title_id, position, media_time, sequence, updated_at)
ManifestVersion(title_id, version, compatible_assets, checksums, state)

docs.title: 5. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  S[Studio delivery] --> I[Ingest workflow]
  I --> O[(Origin objects)]
  I --> C[(Catalog and rights)]
  U[TV or mobile] --> B[Browse API]
  U --> P[Playback control]
  P --> C
  P --> D[DRM license service]
  U --> E[Open Connect CDN]
  E --> Fetch[Origin fetch on cache miss]
  Fetch --> O
  U -. QoE/progress .-> Q[Event stream]
    subgraph ContentLane[Content preparation]
      S
      I
      O
      C
    end
    subgraph ControlLane[Playback authorization]
      P
      D
    end

Control plane owns catalog, rights, sessions, manifests, and CDN placement. Data plane serves encrypted segments from appliances near ISPs. They fail independently: existing bounded sessions can continue briefly during control-plane trouble without granting new rights.

docs.title: 6. Ingest, transcoding, and release
docs.text:
Studios upload encrypted masters through partner channels with checksums and delivery manifests. Ingest validates technical metadata, scans, performs quality control, and launches a DAG for per-shot/per-title encoding, HDR/SDR, codecs, audio normalization, subtitles, thumbnails, and device compatibility. Outputs use deterministic versioned keys. Human QC can gate premium releases.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant S as Studio
  participant I as Ingest
  participant O as Object store
  participant T as Transcoders
  participant C as Catalog
  S->>I: package manifest + checksums
  I->>O: verify durable master
  I->>T: versioned workflow
  T->>O: encrypted renditions
  T-->>I: checksums and QC
  I->>C: publish complete manifest + release state

Release is a metadata transition after assets, DRM keys, rights, localization, and CDN prepositioning pass readiness. A missing subtitle may block only affected locales; a missing baseline codec blocks compatible devices. Rollback selects the previous manifest without rewriting media.

docs.title: 7. Playback flow, ABR, and DRM
docs.text:
The client sends profile, title, network hints, and signed device capabilities. Playback control authenticates account, evaluates territorial/time/plan/device/parental rules, acquires a concurrency lease, and returns a short-lived signed manifest. The DRM service verifies session binding and device trust before wrapping the content key. Keys are separate from CDN objects.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant U as Player
  participant P as Playback control
  participant R as Rights and session store
  participant D as DRM
  participant E as Edge CDN
  U->>P: start(title, profile, capabilities)
  P->>R: authorize + conditional concurrency lease
  P-->>U: signed filtered manifest
  U->>D: license challenge + session
  D-->>U: bounded content license
  U->>E: encrypted segments
  U-->>P: sequenced heartbeat/progress

Manifests include only supported codec/HDR/audio/subtitle variants. ABR begins conservatively, uses throughput and buffer estimates, drops rapidly on congestion, and avoids oscillation. CDN serves immutable encrypted segments; regional shields and ISP appliances absorb premieres. Forecasts preposition likely title/language variants, while long-tail pulls through. Peer-to-peer delivery is rejected because privacy, ISP behavior, quality, and content-control costs outweigh origin savings.

docs.title: 8. Progress and concurrency deep dives
docs.text:
Heartbeats carry session identity, monotonic session sequence and media timestamp. Deduplicate within that session; never compare independent device sequence numbers. A versioned active-session ownership policy chooses which session updates (profile,title) resume state, allowing an intentional backward seek or rewatch. Greatest-ever media position is a completion/history signal, not always the desired resume position. Completion applies duration and credits policy, not simply the maximum timestamp.

Concurrency uses expiring leases per account. Start conditionally reserves a slot; heartbeat renews it; missed heartbeats expire. During partition, strict global limits harm availability while local limits can briefly oversubscribe. Choose bounded oversubscription with signed regional allocations for consumer plans, stricter consistency for high-value events. Do not terminate healthy playback solely because progress storage fails.

docs.title: 9. Rights, personalization, and CDN placement
docs.text:
Rights are interval records by territory, plan, and device. Evaluate authoritative current versions on session start and bind rights_version plus expiration into tokens/licenses. A policy revocation publishes deny epochs to playback and DRM; maximum token/license duration bounds propagation. Browse catalog is a projection filtered by region/profile, but playback always rechecks canonical rights.

Home rows are asynchronously materialized recommendation lists; cache keys include profile maturity and catalog epoch. Fallbacks are popular-in-region and continue-watching. Placement solves expected demand times origin cost under appliance capacity. Track hit rate by title/variant/ISP; avoid prepositioning every language or 4K asset.

docs.title: 10. Partitioning, consistency, failures, and regions
docs.text:
Partition catalog by title, sessions by account, progress by profile/title, and events by session. Hot premieres stress CDN and authorization caches, not one title row; signed versioned rights snapshots reduce reads. Salt QoE events. Reserve separate resources for browse and playback so recommendation overload cannot block starts.

Catalog and assets replicate globally; account home region owns subscription writes, while playback runs active-active using replicated entitlement snapshots and account lease coordination. Rights/manifests need strongly ordered versions; progress and recommendations are eventual. License issuance fails closed when rights are uncertain. Existing licenses remain valid only to their short bound.

DRM outage blocks new starts but not buffered media. CDN appliance failure reroutes within ISP then regional CDN with egress protection. Control-plane outage may renew existing session tokens only while the signed rights/revocation snapshot is fresh enough and within the original absolute rights deadline. Repeated local renewal cannot extend stale authorization indefinitely or create uncertain new entitlement. Queue failures delay future ingest only. Overload disables previews, reduces browse richness, and protects playback/license pools.

docs.title: 11. Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Encrypt media, separate keys, use hardware-backed DRM where available, rotate signing keys, watermark high-risk releases, attest devices, and detect credential sharing/account takeover without treating households as static IPs. Minimize viewing-history access, isolate child profiles, audit staff and studio operations, and honor regional privacy deletion. Rate-limit licenses and resist manifest/token replay by binding account, session, device, title, territory, and expiry.

Measure playback success/start time/rebuffer/fatal rate/bitrate by device-ISP-CDN, rights denials, license latency, session oversubscription, progress lag, CDN hit/origin egress, ingest stage age, QC failure, preposition accuracy, and cost per viewing hour. Player telemetry is the truth for QoE.

Test rights interval boundaries/time zones, device matrices, manifest completeness, heartbeat reorder/duplication, concurrency expiry, DRM binding, subtitle sync, and ABR with recorded network traces. Load premieres and household bursts. Chaos removes appliances, delays rights replicas, loses heartbeats, corrupts assets, and partitions account regions. Shadow new encoders and compare objective quality plus device playback before atomic manifest rollout.

docs.title: Release operations and capacity planning
docs.text:
A release readiness record joins facts without making one giant distributed transaction: approved asset manifest, territory rights, localization coverage, DRM keys, policy rating, and CDN placement each publish a versioned attestation. The release controller checks a compatible set and conditionally moves the title from scheduled to available. If an attestation is revoked, playback policy immediately blocks the affected territory/device while operators repair or roll back. Scheduled releases use server time and are tested around daylight-saving boundaries; clients never decide eligibility from their own clocks.

Capacity planning starts from expected concurrent streams by ISP and bitrate, not account totals. For a premiere, reserve origin shield and license-service headroom, prewarm only likely regional variants, and run a synthetic playback through each device/DRM combination. Admission control distinguishes a license retry from a new session so client storms do not multiply leases. Token-bucket limits are account-aware but avoid one shared global counter on every segment.

docs.title: L6 encoding optimization and playback controller
docs.text:
Per-title analysis first encodes representative complexity samples across resolution, codec, bitrate, and preset, computes VMAF plus encode cost, and removes Pareto-dominated candidates. Per-shot optimization then places scene boundaries on segment boundaries and assigns each shot a quality target or constrained bitrate. Calm dialogue can use fewer bits while grain, camera motion, and visual effects receive more; a constrained optimizer minimizes total bytes subject to a VMAF floor, peak bitrate, decoder level, segment-size variance, and encode budget. Shots are reassembled only when timestamp, GOP, audio, subtitle, and encryption boundaries remain aligned across every rung, allowing seamless ABR switches.

For example, fixed 1080p at 5.0 Mb/s uses about 4.5 GB for a two-hour film. Shot analysis may classify 70 quiet minutes at 2.2 Mb/s, 40 normal minutes at 3.5 Mb/s, and 10 action minutes at 7.0 Mb/s, averaging 3.03 Mb/s and about 2.73 GB, a 39% reduction. The optimizer rejects a cheaper plan if the fifth-percentile shot VMAF falls below 93 even when title-average VMAF passes. Encoder migrations shadow a reference corpus and a small title cohort; promotion requires byte saving, VMAF, decoder failures, startup, rebuffer, and manual golden-scene guardrails. Outputs carry source, optimizer, metric, encoder, and packaging versions for exact rollback.

flowchart TD
  M[Studio mezzanine] --> S[Shot boundary and complexity analysis]
  S --> C[Candidate encodes by shot]
  C --> P[Pareto and constrained optimizer]
  P --> E[Parallel shot encodes]
  E --> A[Aligned segment assembly]
  A --> Q{Objective and device QC pass?}
  Q -->|yes| R[Release attestation]
  Q -->|no| F[Fallback preset or human review]
  F --> E

The ABR controller combines conservative throughput and buffer occupancy rather than following throughput alone. It computes safe_bw = 0.85 * harmonic_mean(last 5 segment throughputs) and scores each candidate as quality - rebuffer_penalty - switch_penalty; any candidate whose predicted download time exceeds available buffer minus a two-second reserve is infeasible. Below 8 seconds the client steps down immediately, between 8 and 20 seconds it holds quality, and above 20 seconds it may step up one rung after two confirming downloads. Segment abandonment is allowed when the current segment would exhaust the buffer and a lower version can finish sooner. Device decode failures blacklist that codec for the session and retry the aligned baseline rung.

If recent segment rates are 8, 6, 5, 4, and 3 Mb/s, their harmonic mean is about 4.65 Mb/s and safe bandwidth is 3.95 Mb/s. Given rungs at 0.8, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, and 7.0 Mb/s, a client with 24 seconds buffered selects 3.0 Mb/s; it does not gamble on 4.5 Mb/s. For emergency low-buffer behavior, cap the rolling estimate by the latest measured segment throughput. If that measurement drops to 1.8 Mb/s with 7 seconds buffered, safe bandwidth is at most 1.53 Mb/s and the client immediately drops to 1.5 Mb/s. Rollout dashboards segment rebuffer, start time, average delivered VMAF, oscillations, abandonments, and decoder errors by device, ISP, CDN, and experiment cohort.

docs.title: DRM key lifecycle and outage containment
docs.text:
Use a key-encryption-key hierarchy: an offline/root HSM protects regional key-encryption keys, which wrap randomly generated per-title or per-epoch content encryption keys. Packaging obtains a short-lived grant, encrypts segments, stores only wrapped keys and key IDs in metadata, and never places plaintext keys beside media. License service instances unwrap inside HSM-backed boundaries after entitlement, device, concurrency, territory, policy epoch, and anti-replay checks. Licenses bind title, account/session, device security level, allowed tracks, offline flag, and absolute expiry.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant K as Key authority and HSM
  participant P as Packager
  participant C as Playback control
  participant L as License service
  participant D as Device DRM
  K->>P: content key grant and key ID
  P->>P: encrypt immutable segments
  P-->>K: destroy plaintext working key
  D->>C: start request and capabilities
  C->>C: rights and concurrency checks
  C-->>D: manifest and license challenge
  D->>L: attested challenge and session token
  L->>K: authorized unwrap request
  K-->>L: key in protected boundary
  L-->>D: device-wrapped bounded license

Keys transition through CREATED, PACKAGING, ACTIVE, RETIRED, REVOKED, and DESTROYED; transitions are audited and dual-controlled for premium releases. Rotation creates a new key epoch and manifest rather than mutating encrypted objects. Retirement stops new licenses but honors policy-approved existing offline licenses until their bound. Revocation increments a title/device/policy deny epoch distributed on a priority channel; license issuance fails closed on stale epoch, manifests stop refreshing, and device revocation lists address compromised DRM identities. Crypto-erasure happens only after contractual retention, rollback windows, and legal holds expire.

During a license-service outage, already buffered encrypted media and cached valid licenses continue until expiry, but new licenses fail closed. A multi-zone regional quorum, preloaded wrapped-key cache, and local signed rights snapshots remove database dependencies without bypassing authorization. Never extend a license merely because the service is unhealthy. Runbooks distinguish HSM saturation, unwrap failure, stale revocation feed, and entitlement dependency failure; shed previews and retries, reserve capacity for renewals near expiry, and deduplicate retries by challenge ID. For one million starts/minute with two license calls per start and 30% headroom, plan about 43,400 license operations/s; if an HSM partition sustains 5,000 unwraps/s, at least nine active partitions plus zonal failover reserve are required.

docs.title: Appliance placement, capacity, and regional lease reconciliation
docs.text:
For each ISP appliance, placement ranks an object bundle by forecast_requests * miss_cost - disk_bytes * storage_cost - fill_risk, subject to disk, NIC, codec/language demand, and minimum free-space constraints. Bundles include the popular audio/subtitle combinations but not every dub with every 4K codec. A two-hour title averaging 3 Mb/s is about 2.7 GB per video ladder path; ten video paths plus common audio/subtitles may consume 30 GB. A 100 TB usable appliance can hold roughly 3,300 such hot-title bundles before replication and reserve, so predicted title-ISP demand, not global popularity alone, drives placement.

NIC and fill bandwidth are separate constraints. Forty thousand concurrent streams at 4 Mb/s require 160 Gb/s; an appliance pair with 2x100 Gb/s links has only 100 Gb/s after either appliance fails. A strict one-appliance-loss target permits at most 50% aggregate steady utilization before further reserve, so 160 Gb/s requires more appliances or proven upstream overflow capacity. Placement simulates one-appliance loss and a cold premiere: peer appliances, regional CDN, and origin shield receive explicit overflow budgets. Operators track disk working-set hit ratio, per-port saturation, eviction churn, fill completion before release, peer-fill amplification, origin egress, thermal/power alarms, and forecast error. A failed box is drained from mapping, repaired, securely re-enrolled, and repopulated gradually to avoid a cache-fill storm.

Concurrency uses a home-account ledger plus signed regional lease budgets. The home region grants each playback region a short-lived allocation epoch and count; a region atomically spends a slot and creates (account_id, session_id, region, epoch, expiry). Heartbeats renew only the same session and never consume another slot. During partition, a region may spend only its remaining budget, bounding oversubscription; it cannot mint a new epoch. On recovery, regions submit active leases and spent counters, and the home ledger chooses the highest epoch, deduplicates session IDs, expires leases using server time, and issues corrected budgets only after prior regional grants can no longer authorize playback or their outstanding sessions have been counted against the new allowance. Selecting a higher epoch alone cannot revoke an isolated region's cached grant.

For a two-stream plan, the home region might allocate one slot to us-east and one to us-west. If both regions partition after starting one stream, neither can start a third; if policy allows one emergency slot per region, maximum oversubscription is explicitly bounded at two extra streams, not unbounded. Reconciliation does not abruptly kill all conflicts: rank sessions by valid epoch, start time, recent heartbeat, and device trust, stop renewing losers, and let their short lease expire. Alerts cover oversubscription age, budget divergence, stale epochs, heartbeat replay, reconciliation backlog, and forced-expiry rate; synthetic partition tests verify the promised bound.

docs.title: Catalog evolution and experimentation
docs.text:
Catalog metadata uses versioned schemas with tolerant readers. A new artwork or recommendation model is exposed through experiment assignment at profile level, but entitlement, maturity, and legal labels are never experimental. Assignment is sticky and logged with model/catalog versions so QoE and engagement results are reproducible. Guardrails include playback starts, rebuffering, title diversity, child safety, and cancellation, not only watch hours.

Device capability declarations are untrusted hints. The server intersects them with an observed compatibility registry, and clients can report decoder failure to retry a baseline manifest. Deprecating a codec requires usage measurement, a long device migration window, and retention of fallback assets until no supported client requests them.

docs.title: 12. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Long licenses improve outage tolerance but weaken revocation; bound by rights risk and allow shorter windows for live/premium content. Strict global concurrency prevents sharing but makes partitions user-visible; expiring bounded leases balance both. Prepositioning everything minimizes misses but wastes appliance disks; demand-aware placement wins.

Final design pre-ingests trusted masters into immutable, encrypted, versioned renditions; atomically releases complete manifests after rights/QC/CDN readiness; authorizes each playback against canonical policy; issues bound DRM licenses; and serves segments from ISP-adjacent CDN. Sequenced events update eventual progress and QoE. Control and media planes degrade independently.

docs.title: 13. Interview questions and levels
docs.text:
• How do rights revocations beat cached manifests?
  • What is the concurrency behavior during regional partition?
  • Which variants should be prepositioned before a premiere?
  • How can an encoder migration be rolled back safely?
  • Why is browse eligibility insufficient for playback authorization?

L5 should cover ingest/transcode, manifests, ABR/CDN, entitlement/DRM, progress, scaling, and failure. L6 should quantify egress economics, define rights/token bounds, regional concurrency semantics, release readiness, device/codec evolution, QoE experimentation, graceful control-plane isolation, and privacy/anti-sharing tradeoffs.

docs.title: 14. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Netflix is a rights-governed, preprocessed media system. Studio packages are checksum-verified, transformed by idempotent workflows into encrypted versioned ladders/audio/subtitles, quality-checked, prepositioned, then exposed by an atomic manifest release. Playback control rechecks account, profile, territory, plan, device, time window, and concurrency; DRM separately issues a short-lived session-bound content license. ISP-adjacent CDN appliances serve immutable segments, while ABR adapts to throughput and buffer.

Partition sessions by account and progress by profile/title; sequence heartbeats so duplicates and reordering are harmless. Strong versions govern rights/manifests; progress, browse lists, and QoE are eventual. Bound stale authorization through token/license duration and deny epochs. Protect playback resources before browse richness, and optimize from client QoE and egress cost. The key choices are revocation versus offline/outage tolerance, strict concurrency versus partition availability, and preposition hit rate versus disk cost.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will define paste lifecycle and privacy, size the object workload, separate metadata from immutable bodies, and trace create/read/delete flows. Deep dives cover content-addressed storage, expiration, syntax rendering, and abuse. Then we address partitioning, regional behavior, recovery, testing, and interview expectations.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
Users submit text and receive a compact URL. A paste may be public, unlisted, or private; may expire; and may optionally be protected by a password. Readers can request raw text or a safely rendered view with syntax highlighting. Authors can delete pastes. We exclude collaborative editing, comments, full-text public search, and arbitrary binary file hosting.

Paste bodies are substantially larger than URL-shortener values and are immutable after publication. The design therefore stores small canonical metadata in a transactional database and bodies in replicated object storage. Immutability enables caching, checksums, and simple repair.

docs.title: 3. Requirements and SLOs
docs.text:
• Create pastes up to 1 MB, with language hint, visibility, and expiration.
  • Read raw or rendered content; private reads require authorization.
  • Delete owned content and expire it automatically.
  • Return paginated owner history; collect delayed view counts.
  • Read availability 99.99%, create availability 99.9%, read p99 under 150 ms for cached bodies.
  • A successful create must never expose partial content. Private/password-protected content must pass authorization on every disclosure; public/unlisted takedown reaches all serving tiers within a declared 60-second maximum. Already downloaded copies cannot be recalled.

Public means discoverable only if a future listing product exists; unlisted means possession of a high-entropy ID grants access; private always requires identity. Password protection is not equivalent to private identity and must use a slow password hash.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. Published metadata references one complete body whose digest matches.
  2. A paste ID is never reassigned to different content.
  3. Authorization precedes body or rendered-cache disclosure.
  4. Expiration and deletion are monotonic terminal states unless an explicit restore window is designed.
  5. Retried creates with one idempotency key produce one paste.
  6. Rendering treats paste bytes as data, never executable markup.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 10 million creates/day and 500 million reads/day: 116 writes/s and 5,800 reads/s average, with 10x peaks. Average body size is 20 KB, p99 700 KB. New content is about 200 GB/day or 73 TB/year before replication; lifecycle expiration may halve retained bytes. Metadata at 500 bytes adds 1.8 TB/year.

Peak body egress at 58,000 reads/s times 20 KB is 1.16 GB/s. A CDN hit rate of 85% and regional object cache reduce origin traffic to 174 MB/s. IDs use 128 random bits encoded compactly, making guessing and collision negligible. View events around 100 bytes consume 50 GB/day before compression.

docs.title: 6. Core entities and data model
docs.text:
Paste(paste_id PK, owner_id?, body_key, sha256, byte_length, language,
      visibility, state, created_at, expires_at, password_hash?, version)
CreateRequest(principal_id, idempotency_key PK, request_hash, paste_id, outcome)
OwnerPaste(owner_id, created_at, paste_id)          // listing projection
ModerationDecision(paste_id, policy_version, action, reason, decided_at)
DailyView(paste_id, day, views, unique_estimate)

The metadata row is canonical for visibility and lifecycle. Object storage is canonical for body bytes only after metadata publishes it. CDN objects and highlighted HTML are projections. Keep the origin bucket private and authorize access through the read service or a bounded scoped capability. Non-guessable internal keys reduce discovery but are not access control: a leaked public storage URL would bypass application checks regardless of key entropy.

docs.title: 7. APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/pastes
Idempotency-Key: ...
Content-Type: application/json
{"content":"...","language":"go","visibility":"UNLISTED","expiresInSeconds":86400}

201 {"id":"p_7J...","url":"https://paste.example/p_7J...","sha256":"..."}
GET /v1/pastes/{id}                 # safe rendered representation
GET /v1/pastes/{id}/raw             # text/plain; nosniff
DELETE /v1/pastes/{id}
GET /v1/me/pastes?cursor=...&limit=50

For larger allowed bodies, issue a short-lived presigned staging upload and complete it with POST /v1/pastes/{id}:publish; the initial 1 MB product can proxy uploads to simplify clients. Return generic 404 for unauthorized private content to avoid existence leaks, and 410 for publicly known expired content if policy permits.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  U[User] --> E[Edge WAF and CDN]
  E --> P[Paste API]
  E --> V[Read service]
  P -->|write metadata and body| Data
  V -->|read metadata and body| Data
  V --> C[(Body and render cache)]
  P --> Q[Scan queue]
  Q --> X[Isolated scanners]
  V -. views .-> A[Analytics stream]
  subgraph Data[Separate durable stores]
    M[(Metadata DB)]
    O[(Object storage)]
  end
  subgraph Scan[Isolated content scanning]
    Q
    X
  end

The edge caches only unprotected content explicitly marked public/unlisted and uses surrogate keys for purge. Private and password-protected responses are Cache-Control: private, no-store; a public visibility flag must not bypass password verification. The API writes a staged object, then publishes metadata. Scanners consume staged or published content according to policy risk. Reads consult canonical metadata before fetching bytes.

docs.title: 9. Create and publish flow
docs.text:
The API authenticates optional identity, rate-limits, validates UTF-8 or explicitly records plain bytes, and computes a digest while streaming into a staging bucket. It never buffers 1 MB times thousands of concurrent requests in heap. If the final key differs, copy and verify the final immutable object before publishing metadata that references it. Alternatively retain the verified staging object's exact version as the final body and exempt it from abandoned-upload expiration. Only then transactionally insert metadata in ACTIVE or PENDING_SCAN state and the idempotency result. A failed metadata commit leaves an orphan, not a published pointer to a copy that may never complete.

To avoid metadata referencing a missing object, the strongest ordering is: upload immutable object, verify digest, commit metadata. Orphan objects are safe and garbage-collected by an inventory job. The inverse ordering can expose broken reads. If the metadata transaction fails, retry from the idempotency record or leave an unreferenced object.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant P as Paste API
  participant O as Object store
  participant D as Metadata DB
  C->>P: POST body + idempotency key
  P->>O: Stream staging object + checksum
  O-->>P: durable object version
  P->>D: Insert ACTIVE metadata + request result
  D-->>P: committed
  P-->>C: paste URL
  Note over P,O: Inventory later removes unreferenced objects

docs.title: 10. Read flow
docs.text:
The read service point-reads metadata or a short-lived metadata cache, checks state, expiry, visibility, identity, and password proof, then obtains the body by immutable object key. Raw responses force text/plain; charset=utf-8, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and content disposition policy. Rendered responses escape all text before adding syntax spans. A view event is emitted asynchronously.

Public cache keys include paste ID, metadata version, representation, and renderer version. Private content never enters shared caches. For deletion, update metadata first and purge CDN/cache by surrogate key. Because purge can fail, public cache TTL must fit the deletion SLO; highly sensitive takedowns use edge denylist checks independent of cached bodies.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: IDs, deduplication, and chunking
docs.text:
Generate 128-bit cryptographically random IDs. High entropy is part of unlisted-link confidentiality, unlike sequential IDs hidden by Base62. Conditional insertion handles the astronomically unlikely collision.

Content-addressing bodies by SHA-256 could deduplicate repeated text, but creates cross-tenant deletion and privacy problems: one physical object's reference count becomes canonical and digest equality leaks information. Prefer opaque object keys initially. At very large scale, deduplicate only public content through audited reference counting; private content remains tenant-isolated and encrypted with distinct keys.

One-megabyte bodies need no application multipart protocol; the API can stream a single bounded object upload. If the product grows to hundreds of MB, expose resumable parts with declared checksums and a manifest. Limits include total bytes, part count, upload lifetime, and concurrent parts to prevent resource exhaustion.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: expiration and garbage collection
docs.text:
Read-time expiry is authoritative. A time-wheel or database index on expiration emits deletion work, but a delayed worker only wastes storage; it cannot make expired content readable. Lifecycle proceeds ACTIVE -> EXPIRED/DELETED -> PURGED. Keep a minimal tombstone for replay safety and abuse evidence, then cryptographically erase body encryption keys when retention ends.

Object-store lifecycle rules are coarse and cannot alone honor metadata semantics. A reconciler compares metadata snapshots with object inventory and uses a durable staging lifecycle. Publication conditionally claims the exact staged object version before its deadline; GC atomically marks an unclaimed expired staging record deleting, which fences any late publisher, then removes the object. A grace period alone cannot stop a delayed commit from publishing a body just selected for deletion. It also detects referenced-but-missing bodies and restores from replicas or marks corruption rather than repeatedly returning 500.

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: safe highlighting
docs.text: Highlighting is CPU-heavy and parser inputs may be adversarial. Run versioned render workers in sandboxes with CPU, memory, recursion, and output-size limits. Escape first, tokenize second, and support a small language allowlist. Cache public rendered output by (body_digest, language, renderer_version); private render caches additionally isolate tenant/paste authorization scope and never bypass the read gate. A timeout falls back to escaped plain text, preserving availability. Never execute macros, fetch imports, or trust user language detection.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Hash-partition metadata by paste ID for even point access. Owner listings need a separate projection partitioned by owner; asynchronous creation of that projection is acceptable if list freshness is stated. Object stores partition internally, but random key prefixes avoid historical prefix hotspots. CDN shields absorb popular pastes; origin request coalescing prevents a cache miss stampede.

Viral content creates bandwidth rather than database pressure once metadata is cached. Enforce maximum egress per paste/tenant and degrade rendered views to raw text before rejecting reads. Creation overload receives 429 with retry hints, while read capacity is protected in separate pools. Scan queues use tenant-fair partitions; large spam campaigns cannot starve normal uploads.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Metadata state transitions and idempotency insertion need strong per-row consistency. Object storage must provide read-after-write for new immutable keys or publication waits until verification succeeds. The idempotency record stores request hash and outcome; same key plus different content is rejected. Delete retries compare versions and remain successful after terminal state.

View events are best effort before durable admission and may be redelivered afterward; their counts are non-critical. Aggregators deduplicate event IDs for a bounded window or document approximate totals. Listing projections, scan verdicts, and regional replicas are eventually consistent. Authorization and expiry cannot depend solely on those projections.

docs.title: 16. Reliability and multi-region behavior
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> STAGED: body durable
  STAGED --> PENDING_SCAN: metadata committed
  STAGED --> ACTIVE: low-risk publish
  PENDING_SCAN --> ACTIVE: allowed
  PENDING_SCAN --> BLOCKED: rejected
  ACTIVE --> EXPIRED: deadline
  ACTIVE --> DELETED: owner action
  ACTIVE --> BLOCKED: moderation
  EXPIRED --> PURGED
  DELETED --> PURGED
  BLOCKED --> PURGED

Use synchronous multi-zone metadata and object durability in each home region, then asynchronous cross-region replication. Reads route globally but check a replicated metadata record before using the nearest body replica. Immediately after create, route via a home-region hint until replication completes. If metadata is unavailable, private reads fail closed; public content may be served only with a still-valid signed authorization/status envelope bounded by the takedown SLO.

Object failure triggers replica fallback and checksum verification. Queue outage does not block low-risk creation unless moderation policy requires prepublication. Database outage permits cached public reads but rejects creates and uncertain authorization. Reconciliation repairs orphan/missing objects, stale projections, and incomplete multipart uploads.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text:
Enforce size limits before and during streams, quotas by account/IP/network, password attempt limits, and proof-of-work or challenges for anonymous bursts. Use Argon2id with per-paste salt for passwords; never place passwords in URLs. Malware, credential, secret, and CSAM classifiers run in isolated workers with controlled reviewer access and auditable takedowns. Reports and legal holds are separate from ordinary deletion.

Prevent XSS through escaping, strict CSP, no inline script, nosniff, and sandboxed previews. Use encryption at rest, TLS, scoped object credentials, key rotation, and redacted logs. Random IDs reduce enumeration but do not replace authorization. Avoid sending private paste contents to third-party detectors without explicit policy.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track create/read rates and latency by representation, bytes ingested/served, object and metadata errors, cache/CDN hit ratio, authorization denials, expiration lag, purge age, orphan bytes, checksum mismatch, renderer timeouts, scan backlog age, moderation false-positive samples, and per-tenant quota pressure. Trace a paste ID and object version without recording content.

Unit and property tests cover ID entropy, state transitions, checksums, request hashes, escaping, and expiration boundaries. Concurrency tests replay creates and deletes. Fuzz parsers and syntax highlighters. Load tests use heavy-tailed body sizes and Zipfian reads. Fault tests interrupt streams, lose commit responses, delay CDN purge, duplicate scan results, corrupt replicas, and verify no partial or unauthorized body is returned. Synthetic regional probes create, read, expire, and delete canary pastes.

docs.title: 19. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Storing bodies directly in a database simplifies atomicity but inflates replication, backup, and hot-row costs. Object storage plus metadata introduces reconciliation yet scales bytes and CDN delivery cleanly. Prepublication scanning minimizes exposure but increases create latency and scanner coupling; use it for anonymous/high-risk traffic and asynchronous revocation for trusted low-risk users.

The final design streams immutable bodies to object storage before atomically publishing canonical metadata and idempotency outcome. Reads authorize against metadata, then use body/render caches and CDN only under explicit visibility rules. Expiry is enforced inline; asynchronous workers scan, aggregate views, purge, and reconcile. Random IDs, sandboxed rendering, bounded caches, and policy denylisting protect confidentiality and takedown guarantees.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions and level expectations
docs.text:
• How would you add editable pastes while preserving immutable CDN caching?
  • When is serving cached public content during metadata failure acceptable?
  • How would you prove an object is safe to garbage-collect?
  • What changes for 5 GB binary uploads?
  • How do legal hold, privacy deletion, and abuse evidence interact?

An L5 candidate should separate metadata and blobs, define upload ordering, authorize before reads, handle expiry, caching, hot content, and idempotent retries. An L6 candidate should additionally reason about publication policy, cache revocation bounds, cryptographic deletion, regional fail-closed behavior, reconciler correctness, tenant fairness, cost per stored/served byte, and safe migrations of renderer or storage format.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Treat a paste as small canonical metadata plus one immutable object. With 10 million creates and 500 million reads daily, stream bodies into object storage, verify a checksum, then atomically publish metadata and an idempotency result. This ordering can leak harmless orphan objects but never publishes partial data; inventory reconciliation removes orphans later. Hash-shard metadata and put CDN plus regional caches before object storage.

Every read checks canonical state, expiry, visibility, and identity before selecting the object. Private content is never shared-cacheable. Raw output is text/plain; rendered output escapes input and uses bounded sandboxed highlighters. Deletion changes metadata before cache purge, and a fresh edge denylist meets urgent takedown bounds. Analytics and scanning use retryable asynchronous events, not the read critical path. Test skew, large bodies, interrupted upload, lost commit responses, stale purge, parser attacks, corruption, and regional lag. The central tradeoff is simple atomic database blobs versus scalable object storage plus explicit publication and reconciliation.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a service that watches products across merchants, records price history, and alerts users when conditions are met. Clarify acquisition methods, product matching, currency/tax semantics, freshness, alert guarantees, and merchant policy. Start with scheduled URL fetches and user alerts, then add adaptive crawling, canonical product identity, offer normalization, change detection, anti-abuse, regional compliance, and reconciliation.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Users submit supported product URLs, view normalized price history, and create threshold or percentage-drop alerts. Merchant integrations may be official APIs, feeds, or permitted web fetches. Prices include amount, currency, availability, seller, shipping, tax basis, membership requirement, and variant. We track facts and provenance; we do not purchase items or promise merchant accuracy.

Target p99 API reads below 200 ms, 99.9% watch creation, popular-offer freshness below five minutes, long-tail freshness below six hours, and 95% of eligible alerts emitted within two minutes of observing a qualifying price. Legal removals and merchant crawl rules override freshness. History can be eventual; an alert must be based on a durable observation.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• Every observation retains source, fetch time, parser version, currency, and price semantics.
  • Price comparisons occur only between compatible product variant and normalized total-price basis.
  • One observation causes at most one logical transition per alert version, despite redelivery.
  • Alert notification requires a committed qualifying observation and persisted trigger record.
  • A failed or suspicious parse never silently becomes a zero price.
  • Merchant robots, rate limits, authentication, and removal policy are enforced before fetch.
  • Canonical observations are immutable; corrections append superseding records.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 100 million users, 500 million active watches, 200 million distinct offers, and an average refresh every two hours: 200M * 12 / 86,400 = 27,778 fetches/s average, perhaps 100,000/s peak. Popular URLs are shared, so watches do not multiply fetches. This schedule produces 2.4 billion fetches/day. If every fetch yields one stored 2 KB observation, storage is 4.8 TB/day before compression; one billion stored observations/day and 2 TB/day instead require an explicit 41.7% retention/success fraction. At ten meaningful changes per thousand observations, the full-observation model produces 24 million changes/day, before alert fanout. Raw pages are retained briefly and sampled except for parser investigations. Alert fanout may spike around major sales, so queues need campaign-like smoothing.

docs.title: Data model and APIs
docs.text:
Product(product_id, brand, model, canonical_attributes, category)
Offer(offer_id, product_id, merchant_id, canonical_url, variant, seller, region)
Observation(observation_id, offer_id, fetched_at, amount_minor, currency,
            shipping_minor, tax_mode, availability, parser_version, confidence, raw_hash)
Watch(watch_id, user_id, offer_or_product_id, state, created_at)
Alert(alert_id, watch_id, version, rule, cooldown, state)
Trigger(trigger_id, alert_id, alert_version, observation_id, state)
FetchTask(merchant_id, url_hash, due_at, priority, lease_epoch)
EvidenceReport(report_id, offer_hint, source_cohort, observed_at, fields,
               evidence_hash, confidence, verification_state, expires_at)
VerificationCase(case_id, offer_hint, state, independent_cohorts, reason, version)

POST /v1/watches {"url":"...", "alert":{"total_below":{"USD":4999}}}
GET  /v1/products/{id}/offers
GET  /v1/offers/{id}/history?cursor=...
PATCH /v1/alerts/{id} If-Match: <version>
DELETE /v1/watches/{id}
POST /v1/merchants/{id}/feed-events

History pagination uses (fetched_at, observation_id) cursor. Creation returns PENDING_RESOLUTION if URL resolution or first fetch has not completed. Updating an alert increments its version, which fences triggers from the prior rule.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 U[Users] --> A[API]
 A --> D[(Watch and alert DB)]
 D --> O[URL resolver]
 O --> C[(Offer catalog)]
 S[Adaptive scheduler] --> Q[Merchant queues]
 Q --> F[API/feed/fetch workers]
 F --> P[Sandboxed parsers]
 P --> V[Normalizer and validator]
 V --> H[(Observation history)]
 V --> E[Change event log]
 E --> R[Alert evaluator]
 R --> N[Notification system]

docs.title: URL resolution and product matching
docs.text:
Normalize URLs using merchant-specific rules: allowlisted hosts, canonical parameters, redirect limits, and stable merchant product IDs. Never remove arbitrary query parameters globally because variant or seller identity may be encoded there. Resolve the offer, then match it to a product using GTIN/UPC where available; otherwise use normalized brand/model/attributes plus category-specific similarity. Auto-link only above a high threshold and keep match evidence/version. Ambiguous offers remain separate or enter review.

Product identity and offer identity are distinct. A laptop with different RAM is a different variant; several sellers can offer that variant. Product-level alerts define whether the cheapest eligible seller, shipping, condition, and membership prices count. This prevents a refurbished accessory from appearing as a dramatic price drop for a new device.

docs.title: Optional browser-extension acquisition plane
docs.text:
An opt-in extension can broaden discovery where contracts permit it, but its reports are untrusted evidence, never canonical observations. Local code extracts an allowlisted merchant product identifier, normalized variant, displayed amount/currency, availability, coarse event time, extension/parser version, and a hash of the evidence fields. It does not upload page bodies, browsing history, unrelated URLs, account identifiers, cookies, or merchant session tokens. A clear per-site permission, local preview, deletion control, short report retention, and regional privacy policy are product requirements. Private, logged-in, cart-only, negotiated, or membership prices are excluded unless the product explicitly models that audience and obtains consent.

The extension sends reports through a separately rate-limited collector. Rotating installation attestations and coarse source cohorts support abuse controls without becoming a durable cross-site identity. The collector strips network identifiers after short fraud retention, deduplicates (evidence_hash,time_bucket,source_cohort), and writes only the minimum evidence record. The normalizer cannot promote a report directly into Observation or trigger an alert.

flowchart LR
    X[Opt-in browser extension] --> C[Privacy and rate-limit collector]
    C --> E[(Untrusted evidence store)]
    E --> D[Discovery candidates]
    E --> K[Corroboration engine]
    D --> R[Canonical URL resolver]
    K --> V[Verification scheduler]
    F[Official feed or permitted fetch] --> V
    V --> Q{Evidence verified?}
    Q -->|Yes| O[(Canonical observation)]
    Q -->|No| Z[Reject or expire]
    O --> A[Alert evaluation]

Evidence follows an explicit state machine. REPORTED means syntactically valid but untrusted. CORROBORATING has matching reports from independent cohorts but still cannot alert. VERIFYING schedules an official API/feed lookup or permitted server fetch. Only that authoritative acquisition creates VERIFIED canonical observation provenance. Conflicts become REJECTED; unsupported or old evidence becomes EXPIRED. If server verification is impossible, corroborated reports may power a clearly labeled discovery hint, never price history, charts, or notifications.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> REPORTED
    REPORTED --> CORROBORATING: plausible evidence
    REPORTED --> REJECTED: invalid or abusive
    CORROBORATING --> VERIFYING: independent threshold met
    CORROBORATING --> EXPIRED: evidence window closes
    VERIFYING --> VERIFIED: official or server source agrees
    VERIFYING --> REJECTED: authoritative source conflicts
    VERIFYING --> EXPIRED: verification unavailable
    VERIFIED --> [*]
    REJECTED --> [*]
    EXPIRED --> [*]

Sybil resistance uses risk-weighted independence, not a raw report count. Reports sharing installation attestation, account, network prefix, device signals, identical timing, or evidence hash count as one cohort; per-installation, network, merchant, and offer quotas bound floods. New cohorts earn little weight, repeated agreement with later authoritative fetches increases bounded reputation, and no cohort can verify itself. Never expose exact reporter counts that make threshold gaming easy.

Extreme changes receive stricter treatment. A drop beyond both an absolute category bound and a relative threshold, such as 50 percent below the 30-day median, requires authoritative verification and a second fetch separated in time or an official feed. Cross-catalog simultaneous drops, parser-version changes, implausible decimal shifts, and prices below known shipping or tax floors quarantine the case. Reports can increase verification priority but cannot bypass these gates.

Discovery and monitoring are separate budgets and promises. Extension evidence may propose a new merchant URL or raise an unwatched offer's discovery score; discovery is sampled, aggressively expired, and paused first under load. Monitoring begins only after URL resolution, policy approval, product/variant matching, and one authoritative observation. Watched offers then use the normal adaptive scheduler and freshness SLO. Thus a report storm can create bounded verification work, not 500 million new scheduled watches or false alerts.

If 10 million installations send 20 sampled reports/day, the plane receives 200 million reports/day, about 2,300/s average and perhaps 12,000/s peak. At 500 bytes each that is 100 GB/day before replication. Deduplication, seven-day expiry for unverified evidence, and a per-merchant verification budget keep this optional signal materially smaller than canonical history. Sampling must happen on device or before durable write; collecting everything and deleting later is not equivalent privacy protection.

docs.title: Fetch scheduling and politeness
docs.text:
The scheduler maintains one next-due task per offer, not per watch. Priority approximates expected user value:

priority = watch_weight * change_probability * staleness_cost / expected_fetch_cost

Change probability derives from historical volatility, sale calendar, feed hints, and recent HTTP validators. Bound intervals by merchant policy. Apply hierarchical token buckets for merchant, host, credential, and IP, plus randomized timing. Conditional requests use ETag/Last-Modified. 429 and Retry-After multiplicatively reduce concurrency; repeated blocks open a circuit. Official feeds supersede crawling when their semantics and freshness are sufficient.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant S as Scheduler
 participant Q as Merchant queue
 participant F as Fetcher
 participant P as Parser
 participant H as History
 participant E as Evaluator
 S->>Q: due offer plus lease epoch
 Q->>F: token-granted fetch
 F->>P: response and metadata
 P->>P: extract typed candidates
 P->>H: validated immutable observation
 H-->>E: committed change event
 E->>E: evaluate current alert version
 E->>H: unique trigger(alert,version,observation)

docs.title: Parsing and validation
docs.text:
Prefer structured merchant APIs or JSON-LD, then merchant-specific selectors; generic extraction is fallback only. Parsers run in a networkless sandbox with CPU, memory, and output limits. They emit typed candidates and evidence, not database writes. The validator checks currency, realistic category bounds, decimal scale, availability, variant, shipping, tax mode, and discontinuity against recent history.

A huge price drop with parser-layout change, low confidence, or many simultaneous zero-like values enters quarantine. Compare a canary parser against production using stored permitted fixtures and a small live shadow sample. Parser versions deploy per merchant and roll back independently. Raw response hashes support deduplication; encrypted raw bodies have short retention and strict access.

docs.title: Change detection and alert evaluation
docs.text:
Normalize money in integer minor units. Preserve original currency and never compare using today's exchange rate to historical values without labeling the converted series. Define total as item plus known mandatory shipping and tax when available; unknown components make totals incomparable under strict rules.

Append every accepted observation, but emit a change only when normalized semantic fields differ or freshness requires it. Collapse repeated identical observations into run metadata for storage efficiency. Alert evaluator reads current alert version and applies threshold, percentage from a defined baseline, availability, seller, and cooldown. Percentage baseline may be previous stable price, rolling median, or user-created price; name it explicitly.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> ARMED
 ARMED --> QUALIFYING: rule true
 QUALIFYING --> TRIGGERED: trigger committed
 TRIGGERED --> COOLDOWN: notification enqueued
 COOLDOWN --> ARMED: price resets or cooldown expires
 ARMED --> PAUSED
 PAUSED --> ARMED
 ARMED --> DELETED
 COOLDOWN --> DELETED

Trigger insertion has unique (alert_id, alert_version, observation_id, transition_type). The transaction checks the current alert version, advances its armed/cooldown state with a conditional update, and writes trigger and outbox together. Serialize evaluation per alert and retain its last applied source position so delayed observations cannot roll the state backward. Per-observation uniqueness alone would still allow two different qualifying observations to race into the same cooldown window. Queue redelivery therefore cannot create another logical notification, though downstream providers may still duplicate. A hysteresis band prevents repeated alerts around the threshold. A user can choose one-shot or re-arm behavior.

docs.title: Popular offers and fetch deduplication
docs.text: Millions may watch one console. All watches reference one offer and observation stream. A coalescing cache allows one active fetch lease per URL hash; concurrent demand attaches waiters rather than causing a stampede. Sale events prewarm known popular offers but merchant quotas remain absolute. Freshness SLO is tiered by watch count and volatility so scarce requests maximize value fairly rather than favoring only the largest merchant.

docs.title: Price history compaction
docs.text:
Canonical immutable observations support audit, while a derived time-series projection stores change points and daily min/max/last. Recent detailed observations remain hot; older raw repeats compact into intervals. Queries merge tiers using stable cursors. Compaction records source ranges and checksum, and deletion occurs only after validation. Corrections append supersession links and rebuild projections instead of rewriting facts.

Chart serving chooses a resolution from requested range and pixel width rather than returning every observation. Keep raw change points for 48 hours, hourly open/high/low/close/availability buckets for 90 days, and daily buckets thereafter as an example policy. GET /history?from=&to=&resolution=auto&max_points=800 selects the finest tier producing at most 800 buckets; callers may request raw, 1h, or 1d within retention. A 365-day chart therefore returns at most 365 daily buckets instead of scanning millions of repeated fetches.

Buckets carry source count, first/last observation IDs, confidence floor, currency/tax basis, and completeness. The API never averages prices across variants, currencies, or incompatible total-price semantics. It returns min and max for the chart envelope and last for the line, labels gaps and stale intervals, and overlays superseding corrections by projection version. Cache keys include offer, range boundary, resolution, and projection version; stable cursors are needed for raw audit pages, while bounded chart windows return one immutable projection response.

docs.title: Feed and crawl reconciliation
docs.text: Feeds can be delayed, duplicated, or use different tax semantics. Assign source precedence per field and merchant contract; do not blindly let the newest timestamp win. Periodic sampled crawl compares feed values and raises drift alerts. Event IDs or content hashes deduplicate feed replay. Watermarks expose lag. If sources conflict beyond tolerance, lower confidence, pause alerts for the affected field, and retain both facts for operators.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and regions
docs.text:
Partition offers and latest observation by offer ID; partition append-only history by offer and month. Shard watches/alerts by user for management APIs, while an inverted index maps offer/product to alert partitions. Change events include offer ID and observation ID; evaluator fanout batches IDs and reads only potentially relevant rule buckets, such as currency plus threshold ranges, instead of all watches.

Merchant queues are isolated because one host's outage or legal pause must not consume global workers. Hot merchants receive dedicated partitions and credentials. Scheduler time wheels bucket due tasks, lease buckets with epochs, and checkpoint scans. Duplicate scheduling is safe; unique observation hashes and fetch leases reduce waste. Backpressure lengthens low-value intervals, pauses unwatched discovery, then delays low-priority alerts while preserving observation durability.

Fetches occur from permitted regions and IP ranges. User and alert data remain in a home region; public offer observations can replicate globally. Regional evaluators consume local copies and write triggers in the user's home region. The same observation may be evaluated in many regions, but alert-version uniqueness is authoritative. Merchant policy and parser configurations are signed control-plane artifacts with staged rollout.

docs.title: Consistency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Watches, alert versions, and triggers require transactional consistency. Catalog matching, history projections, exchange-rate views, and search are eventual. Observation commit plus event publication uses outbox. Fetching is at least once. Lease epochs fence slow schedulers. Notification effects are idempotent by trigger ID but not claimed exactly once.

Merchant outage serves stale data labeled with observation time and backs off. Scheduler loss rebuilds due tasks from canonical offers and checkpoints. Parser regression quarantines data and activates last good parser. History store failure buffers only bounded validated results in a durable log, then reduces fetch rate. Extension collector or corroboration failure drops or expires optional evidence and never blocks established monitoring; verification backlog is capped per merchant so it cannot starve watched-offer fetches. A chart projection failure falls back to a coarser verified tier or returns an explicit unavailable response rather than inventing buckets. Event lag delays alerts but cannot alert without committed observations. Notification outage retains trigger outbox. Region loss replays from replicated offsets; promote a writer only after fencing the old owner and recovering the acknowledged alert-state, trigger, and outbox prefix. Uniqueness collapses reevaluation only while that deduplication state survives. If recovery loses acknowledged triggers, pause effects and reconcile downstream trigger IDs before replay.

Reconciliation scans offers whose latest observation is older than policy, trigger rows lacking outbox delivery, alerts whose qualifying changes were skipped, feed sequence gaps, and evidence cases stuck in verification. Replay requires merchant/time/parser scope and dry-run counts. User deletion removes watches, alerts, notification addresses, extension installation state, and attributable evidence; public canonical observations remain because they were independently verified merchant facts, subject to source policy.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Fetch only allowlisted public merchant destinations to prevent SSRF; resolve DNS safely, block private ranges after redirects, restrict methods, and sandbox content. Encrypt user data, authenticate APIs, sign feed webhooks, isolate merchant credentials, and audit parser/config changes. Prevent watch spam, competitor scraping through the read API, alert bombing, affiliate manipulation, and malicious pages. Honor robots, contracts, deletion, copyright, and geographic restrictions.

Measure freshness by watch tier and merchant, fetch success/status/latency, quota utilization, queue age, conditional-hit rate, bytes, parser confidence and field missingness, quarantine rate, price discontinuities, observation-to-trigger latency, duplicate suppression, alert eligibility and delivery, feed watermark, catalog-match uncertainty, and cost per active watch. For extension evidence, measure consented active installations, reports accepted/dropped, cohort concentration, discovery yield, authoritative agreement, verification queue age/budget, extreme-change quarantine, deletion completion, and reports per verified offer without logging browsing detail. A sudden cross-catalog price collapse is a parser incident signal.

Property-test money comparison, threshold boundaries, hysteresis, alert-version fencing, URL normalization idempotence, and immutable observations. Golden merchant fixtures test parsers. Contract-test feeds. Fuzz HTML, redirects, compression bombs, and malformed currency. Forge many reports from one cohort, rotate apparent identities, coordinate extreme-price claims, replay evidence after expiry, and assert no unverified report reaches history or alerts. Privacy tests verify field allowlists, on-device sampling, consent revocation, and deletion. Compare raw, hourly, and daily chart buckets at tier boundaries and after corrections, including gaps and incompatible price semantics. Replay historical pages against parser releases. Load-test popular-product stampedes, evidence floods within verification budgets, and sale-wide alert fanout. Chaos-test queue duplication, scheduler clock skew, merchant throttling, history lag, and region failover. Synthetic known pages verify end to end.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Fetching per watch is simple but wasteful; shared offer observations win. Fixed refresh intervals are predictable but ignore volatility and value; adaptive scheduling improves freshness per dollar but needs fairness bounds. Generic parsers expand coverage but create false prices; merchant adapters and quarantine favor correctness. Extension reports expand discovery cheaply but add consent, privacy, and Sybil risk, so they remain expiring evidence and never alert without independent verification. Mutable latest-price rows are cheap but unauditable; immutable facts plus multi-resolution projections support alerts, efficient charts, and repair. Product-level matching improves comparison but false merges are dangerous, so uncertain identity remains separate.

flowchart TD
 W[User watch and versioned rule] --> C[Canonical offer or product]
 C --> S[Adaptive policy-aware scheduler]
 S --> M[Merchant-isolated acquisition]
 M --> P[Versioned sandbox parser]
 P --> V[Semantic validation and quarantine]
 V --> O[(Immutable observations)]
 O --> E[Idempotent change evaluation]
 E --> T[(Trigger and outbox)]
 T --> N[Notification delivery]
 O --> H[History projections]

The final design shares acquisition by canonical offer, enforces merchant limits before network work, validates typed parser output, and stores immutable provenance. A durable change stream evaluates versioned alerts into unique triggers. History, latest price, and catalog search remain rebuildable projections. Isolated merchant queues, adaptive schedules, quarantine, and reconciliation make the system operable.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. How do 10 million users watching one product affect fetch load?
  2. What exactly is a comparable price when shipping or tax is unknown?
  3. How do you prevent a parser bug from sending zero-price alerts?
  4. How are repeated threshold crossings deduplicated and re-armed?
  5. How does adaptive scheduling remain fair to long-tail products?
  6. How are feed and crawled observations reconciled?
  7. What does user deletion remove versus preserve?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should distinguish watch, offer, observation, and alert; estimate fetch/storage load; deduplicate popular URL work; explain scheduling, parsing, price comparison, trigger idempotency, partitioning, and main failures.

An L6 candidate should define price semantics and matching uncertainty, merchant governance, quarantine and parser rollout, adaptive cost/fairness policy, replay/reconciliation, regional data ownership, and overload stages. They should connect freshness tiers and raw-page retention to cost, contracts, privacy, and incident response.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Resolve each submitted URL into a canonical merchant offer and, only with strong evidence, a product variant. Many watches share one observation stream. An adaptive scheduler prioritizes watched, volatile offers but obeys hierarchical merchant quotas and backs off on throttling. Prefer feeds/APIs; sandbox versioned parsers for permitted pages and validate currency, variant, availability, shipping, tax, confidence, and discontinuities. Store immutable observations with provenance, then publish changes through an outbox. Evaluate current versioned alert rules into uniquely keyed triggers and notify idempotently, using cooldown and hysteresis. Partition offers/history by offer, alerts by user, and acquisition by merchant; isolate hot merchants and coalesce popular fetches. Quarantine suspicious parses, label stale data, reconcile feed/crawl drift and missing triggers, and measure freshness, quota, confidence, quarantine, trigger latency, and cost per watch.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will scope the product, establish redirect invariants, estimate traffic, define interfaces and storage, then design creation and redirect paths. Deep dives cover key generation, abuse-safe redirects, and expiration. We finish with scaling, failures, operations, and the L5/L6 bar.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
The service converts a long URL into a compact link such as https://sho.rt/aZ31Kq. Opening that link redirects a browser to the original URL. Users may request a custom alias and expiration; authenticated customers can inspect aggregate click statistics. We exclude page previews, ad interstitials, and a general analytics warehouse from the initial design.

The smallest correct system is a durable key-to-URL map plus an HTTP redirect service. Creation is modest write traffic, while redirects are latency-sensitive, cacheable reads. This asymmetry drives the architecture.

docs.title: 3. Requirements and SLOs
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Create random short links and optional custom aliases.
  • Redirect active links; return 404 for unknown and 410 for expired/deleted links.
  • Allow an owner to delete a link and read delayed aggregate statistics.
  • Prevent aliases that violate syntax, policy, or reserved-word rules.

Non-functional requirements:

  • Redirect availability: 99.99%; creation availability: 99.9%.
  • Redirect p99 below 80 ms from the nearest region, excluding client network time.
  • Acknowledged links survive a regional failure; deletion propagates globally within 60 seconds.
  • Analytics may lag by five minutes and must never delay redirects.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. An alias identifies at most one canonical destination over its lifetime. We do not immediately recycle deleted aliases.
  2. Successful creation returns only after the mapping is durably committed.
  3. Redirects never serve a known blocked or expired destination beyond the stated propagation window.
  4. Retried creates with the same owner and idempotency key return the same result.
  5. Click events are best-effort observations; they cannot alter redirect correctness.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 20 million new links per day and 2 billion redirects per day. That is about 230 creates/s and 23,000 redirects/s on average; design for 10x peaks: 2,500 writes/s and 250,000 reads/s. Five years yields 36.5 billion links. At roughly 500 bytes per mapping including indexes and replication, canonical storage is 18 TB before database overhead, perhaps 40 TB provisioned.

An eight-character Base62 namespace contains 62^8, about 218 trillion values, leaving ample occupancy headroom. Redirect responses average under 1 KB, so a 250,000/s peak is about 250 MB/s before TLS overhead. A 95% cache hit rate reduces database reads to 12,500/s. Two billion 150-byte click events produce 300 GB/day, retained cheaply in object storage after aggregation.

docs.title: 6. Core entities and data model
docs.text:
Link(alias PK, destination_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at,
     status, redirect_code, url_hash, version)
CreateRequest(owner_id, idempotency_key PK, request_hash, alias, result, expires_at)
AliasTombstone(alias PK, blocked_until, reason)
ClickEvent(event_id, alias, occurred_at, region, referrer_domain, device_class)
DailyStat(alias, day, clicks, unique_estimate, country_counts)

Link is canonical. Cache entries and DailyStat rows are derived. URLs are encrypted at rest but remain available to the redirect service. An owner-time secondary index supports listing with cursor pagination; it is not consulted on redirects.

docs.title: 7. API
docs.text:
POST /v1/links
Idempotency-Key: 8f...
{"url":"https://example.com/long","customAlias":"launch24","expiresAt":"2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"}

201 {"alias":"launch24","shortUrl":"https://sho.rt/launch24","expiresAt":"..."}
GET /{alias}                  -> 302 Location: https://example.com/long
DELETE /v1/links/{alias}      -> 204
GET /v1/links/{alias}/stats?from=...&to=... -> delayed aggregates

Use 302 with Cache-Control: no-store for browser-facing redirects so later requests return to the service for expiration and emergency-block checks. Status 302 alone does not prevent caching. This design keeps the destination immutable for an alias; changing it requires a new alias. Offer 301 only as a separate immutable-link product that explicitly cannot promise revocation of already cached browser redirects. Server-side mapping caches still use the bounded policy propagation window. Reject oversized URLs, unsupported schemes, credentials embedded in URLs, and invalid aliases. Listing APIs use opaque (created_at, alias) cursors rather than offsets.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> E[Edge and WAF]
  E --> R[Redirect service]
  E --> A[Link API]
  R --> K[(Distributed cache)]
  R --> D[(Sharded link store)]
  A --> I[ID allocator]
  A --> D
  R -. click .-> Q[Event stream]
  Q --> G[Aggregator]
  G --> S[(Analytics store)]

The edge rate-limits and routes redirects to a nearby stateless service. Link creation goes to the link's home region. The durable link store is partitioned by alias hash and replicated across zones. Cache-aside reads hold positive entries and short-lived negative entries. Analytics is intentionally downstream.

docs.title: 9. Creating links
docs.text:
For random links, the API validates and normalizes only what is safe: lowercase the scheme and host, but preserve path/query semantics. It checks the idempotency record, obtains an ID, bijectively encodes it in Base62, and transactionally inserts the mapping plus idempotency outcome. A conflict retries with another ID. The selected store must support the mapping-and-request transaction even when alias hash and owner/key route differently. Otherwise introduce a durable create-request owner that reserves one alias and reconciles its conditional insert; two independent writes are not an atomic idempotency implementation. Custom aliases use a conditional insert on the alias key; concurrent claimants produce one winner and 409 for others.

Do not deduplicate by destination by default: separate users need separate ownership, expiration, and analytics. A URL hash can support abuse investigation without changing identity.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant A as Link API
  participant I as ID allocator
  participant D as Link store
  C->>A: POST link + idempotency key
  A->>D: Read prior request
  alt first valid request
    A->>I: Lease ID range
    I-->>A: next ID
    A->>D: Conditional transaction: link + request
    D-->>A: committed
  else retry
    D-->>A: stored outcome
  end
  A-->>C: same short URL

docs.title: 10. Redirecting
docs.text:
The service validates alias length before any storage call. It checks an in-process blocklist and distributed cache. On a miss, it performs a bounded-deadline point read. Active rows produce a redirect; deleted, blocked, or expired rows produce 410; absence produces 404. The service emits a non-blocking click event with a random event ID. If the stream is unavailable, a bounded local buffer may drop events rather than exhaust memory or increase user latency.

Cache TTL is the minimum of five minutes and time to expiry. Deletion publishes invalidations and changes canonical status first. To meet the 60-second deletion as well as block contract, the separately refreshed denylist carries both owner deletions and security blocks. Its maximum accepted age fits inside that budget; a stale policy view fails closed for affected redirects. Five-minute mapping TTL alone would not meet the requirement.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: key generation
docs.text:
Random probing becomes inefficient and unpredictable as occupancy grows. A database sequence creates a central dependency and visibly adjacent links. Instead, regional allocators lease non-overlapping numeric ranges from a small strongly consistent control store. API nodes consume a range locally, apply a reversible keyed permutation to obscure sequence and region, then Base62-encode it. Losing a partially used range wastes IDs but cannot duplicate them.

This provides uniqueness without a write per ID. For exactly eight Base62 characters, allocate and permute within [0,62^8), not the full 64-bit range; an arbitrary 64-bit value can require eleven characters. Rotate permutation keys through disjoint versioned namespaces or rely on the canonical alias uniqueness check rather than assuming distinct keys produce disjoint outputs. The permutation obscures allocation, not a confidentiality guarantee. Random probing with conditional insertion is also acceptable at the stated low occupancy.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: expiry and deletion
docs.text: Absolute expiry is checked on every redirect, including cache hits and stale-serving paths, and also bounds cache TTL, so a delayed cleanup job cannot resurrect a link. A bucketed scanner deletes old rows later to reclaim space. Owner deletion is a state transition to DELETED, not immediate removal. Tombstones prevent accidental alias reuse and let replicas converge. Privacy deletion can cryptographically erase encrypted destination fields while retaining a minimal alias tombstone and audit facts.

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: malicious destinations
docs.text: Creation performs syntax checks, domain reputation lookup, and asynchronous malware scanning. Unknown URLs can be created in PENDING state for higher-risk tenants. Redirect-time policy must be locally available because calling an external scanner would violate latency and availability. Reports feed a moderation queue; emergency domain blocks are distributed as signed, versioned snapshots. Rate limits combine account, IP prefix, device, and destination domain to resist both mass creation and redirect amplification.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Partition canonical rows by a stable hash of alias. This evenly distributes popular namespaces, but one viral alias remains a hot cache key. Edge caching and request coalescing absorb it; replicas may serve immutable active mappings, while block status remains separately fresh. Consistent hashing allows gradual cache growth. Database shard maps are versioned; online migration dual-reads only during a bounded transition and verifies checksums before cutover.

Creation allocators partition by region. Analytics streams partition by alias for ordered per-link aggregation, but a celebrity alias can overload one partition. Salt event partitions by (alias, hash(event_id) mod N) and merge partial counters later. Apply per-tenant quotas and backpressure at ingress rather than allowing queues to grow without limit.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text: Alias claims, deletion state, and idempotency records require strongly consistent conditional writes. Redirects may read replicas and caches within an explicit staleness bound.
