An idempotency key stores a request hash: reuse with different parameters returns 422, preventing surprising outcomes. Events admitted to the durable stream may be delivered more than once, but events dropped before admission are lost. Aggregators deduplicate within a time window by event_id before counting; mergeable distinct-event sketches are an alternative when approximate unique event counts suffice, but ordinary mergeable counters do not deduplicate retries; analytics explicitly tolerates minor loss and duplication.

docs.title: 16. Reliability and multi-region behavior
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> ACTIVE: durable create
  ACTIVE --> EXPIRED: expires_at reached
  ACTIVE --> BLOCKED: policy action
  BLOCKED --> ACTIVE: reviewed and restored
  ACTIVE --> DELETED: owner delete
  EXPIRED --> TOMBSTONED: cleanup
  DELETED --> TOMBSTONED: retention elapsed

Run redirect capacity active-active across regions. To satisfy the requirement that acknowledged links survive regional loss, creation waits for durable mapping and idempotency state in a separate failure region as well as the home-region quorum; otherwise offer an explicitly weaker asynchronous-DR tier. This adds WAN latency to creation, not cache-hit redirects. Other read regions may still lag, so route immediate reads to an acknowledged replica. During failure serve cached active links only while policy freshness is acceptable; return 503 for uncertain misses rather than false 404s.

Allocator failure is survivable while leased ranges remain. Database overload triggers cache request coalescing, tighter admission control on creates, and stale-serving only for non-expired, non-blocked positive entries. Recovery drills include lost invalidations, replica lag, range loss, and stream backlog.

docs.title: 17. Security, privacy, and abuse
docs.text: Authenticate management APIs and enforce ownership server-side. Generated Base62 aliases are case-sensitive; lowercasing them would collapse distinct IDs and invalidate the namespace estimate. Custom aliases can have a separately defined normalization policy checked against the same canonical namespace. Reserve platform and trademark terms. Redirect workers never fetch destinations; scanners use isolated egress sandboxes. Strip sensitive query values from logs, encrypt destinations, and retain coarse analytics according to policy. Audit internal changes and require dual control for global blocks.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure redirect rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, status distribution, cache hit rate, database saturation, replica lag, stale age, invalidation delay, dropped click events, allocator range remaining, abuse decisions, and per-tenant cardinality. Trace cache misses and creation transactions, sampling successful viral redirects aggressively enough to diagnose hotspots without logging full URLs.

Tests include property tests for Base62/permutation round trips, concurrent alias claims, idempotency replay, boundary expiry, malicious parser inputs, and authorization. Load tests model Zipfian aliases rather than uniform traffic. Fault tests kill cache shards, delay replicas, duplicate events, exhaust allocator leases, and verify that store outages return 503, not false absence. Synthetic probes continuously create and resolve links in every region.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
A relational sharded store offers conditional transactions and operational familiarity; a managed key-value store offers simpler horizontal point access. Either works if alias uniqueness and lifecycle transitions are atomic. A global strongly consistent database simplifies read-after-create and deletion but costs latency and money on every write. Home-region writes plus bounded-stale reads match the workload.

The final design uses edge/WAF, active-active redirect services, cache-aside lookup, hash-sharded canonical mappings, leased-and-permuted IDs, transactional idempotency, tombstoned deletion, a fresh policy denylist, and a lossy-independent analytics stream. Complexity is attached to explicit requirements: global low latency, safe blocks, and high read skew.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions and level expectations
docs.text:
Questions to probe:

  • How would you support editable destinations without making cached 301 responses unsafe?
  • What happens during cache loss while the database is overloaded?
  • How do you prove aliases cannot collide after allocator failover?
  • How do GDPR deletion and permanent anti-reuse tombstones coexist?
  • When should analytics favor exact counts over sketches?

An L5 candidate should quantify read/write asymmetry, choose a key strategy, make alias claims atomic, design caching and expiration, and cover hot keys and failures. An L6 candidate should additionally define staleness contracts, policy distribution, regional ownership and migration, overload semantics, privacy deletion, cost controls, and operational evidence for safe evolution.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Build a durable alias-to-destination map optimized for point reads. At 2 billion redirects/day and 20 million creates/day, hash-shard canonical mappings and put edge plus distributed caches in front; expect high skew. Create links with conditional writes and durable idempotency, using locally leased, permuted IDs encoded in Base62. Redirect from cache or bounded database reads, checking status and expiry, and never block on analytics. Send clicks best effort to a durable stream, deduplicate its redelivery, and aggregate asynchronously with explicit loss metrics.

Aliases are never concurrently assigned and are not quickly recycled. Deletion writes canonical state before invalidating caches, while a fresh denylist gives emergency abuse blocks a tighter global bound. Active-active redirect regions use replicated data; dependency failure yields 503, not false 404. Test concurrency, expiry, skew, lag, event duplication, and cache loss. The decisive tradeoff is bounded staleness and low latency versus globally synchronous reads; reserve strong consistency for claims and lifecycle changes.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We design a crawler that continuously discovers and fetches public pages for a search index. After requirements, invariants, estimates, interfaces, and architecture, we deep-dive into URL canonicalization, politeness scheduling, duplicate detection, traps, and recrawling. We then cover partitioning, recovery, security, operations, and interview expectations.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
The crawler starts from seeds and discovered links, respects robots policy and host capacity, fetches HTTP content, stores immutable fetch artifacts, and emits parsed documents and new links. It is not the query engine or ranking system. Version one supports HTML, redirects, sitemaps, and selected text formats; browser rendering is a separate scarce tier.

The core tension is coverage versus responsible load. Raw throughput is not success if one domain is harmed, traps consume capacity, or stale pages crowd out useful recrawls.

docs.title: 3. Requirements and SLOs
docs.text:
• Accept seeds, discover links, fetch allowed pages, and refresh known pages.
  • Honor robots rules, crawl delay policy, redirects, noindex, and removals.
  • Prioritize valuable/fresh pages and expose per-URL fetch history.
  • At least 99.9% scheduler availability; never exceed configured per-origin concurrency/rate.
  • Newly submitted high-priority pages fetched within five minutes when allowed; broad corpus freshness is tiered.
  • Backpressure must bound queues and storage growth.

Out of scope: authenticated/private pages, bypassing paywalls, and executing arbitrary browser automation for every URL.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. A fetch lease is granted only after current robots policy permits it.
  2. Concurrent requests to an origin never exceed its effective policy.
  3. A URL has one canonical frontier identity; aliases may retain provenance.
  4. Fetch attempts are repeatable, but publishing a version is idempotent by fetch ID/content digest.
  5. Untrusted bytes never execute in the control plane.
  6. Queue priority cannot starve robots refresh, removal, or retry safety work.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Target 5 billion known canonical URLs and 500 million fetches/day: 5,800/s average, 25,000/s peak. At 150 KB average compressed response, ingress is 75 TB/day. Keeping compressed raw artifacts for 30 days costs 2.25 PB before replication; extracted text and metadata add roughly 20 TB/day. A 300-byte frontier record is 1.5 TB for five billion URLs.

With a 500 ms mean fetch, 25,000/s needs 12,500 concurrent sockets, but politeness rather than CPU dominates. DNS, TLS, and parser pools require separate budgets. Ten discovered links/page produce five billion candidate events/day, so early normalization and deduplication are mandatory.

docs.title: 6. Entities and interfaces
docs.text:
UrlRecord(url_id, canonical_url, origin_id, state, priority, next_fetch_at,
          last_status, content_digest, etag, last_modified, retry_count, version)
Origin(origin_id, scheme, host, port, robots_version, next_allowed_at,
       rate, concurrency, health_score)
FetchLease(fetch_id, url_id, origin_id, worker_id, leased_until, attempt)
FetchArtifact(fetch_id, url_id, fetched_at, status, headers, body_key, digest)
LinkEdge(source_url_id, target_url_id, discovered_at, attributes)

Internal interfaces include SubmitSeeds, LeaseReadyOrigins, LeaseUrl(origin), CommitFetch, and ReportRemoval. All accept idempotency identifiers. Cursor-based inspection APIs expose frontier state without scanning queues.

docs.title: 7. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  S[Seeds and sitemaps] --> N[Normalize and dedupe]
  N --> F[(URL frontier)]
  F --> H[Host politeness scheduler]
  H --> W[Fetcher workers]
  W --> I[Internet]
  W --> B[(Artifact object store)]
  W --> P[Sandbox parsers]
  P --> N
  P --> D[Document stream]
  R[Robots service] --> H
  W --> R

The frontier stores durable intent; the scheduler keeps only bounded ready windows in memory. Fetchers own network I/O, parsers own hostile content, and immutable artifacts support replay without refetching.

docs.title: 8. Discovery and canonicalization
docs.text:
Normalize scheme/host case, IDNs, default ports, dot segments, percent encoding, and fragments according to RFC semantics. Do not blindly sort query parameters or remove tracking-looking values: parameters can alter content. Maintain domain-specific rewrite rules only when evidence shows equivalence. Resolve relative links against the final response URL, cap links per document, and preserve source provenance.

Candidate URLs pass syntactic limits and a probabilistic seen filter, then an authoritative conditional insert. Bloom false positives would lose coverage if used alone; they may suppress only low-value rediscovery after durable history exists. The probabilistic data structures pattern shows how to size the filter from acceptable downstream lookup cost and preserve an authority-safe fallback.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant P as Parser
  participant N as Normalizer
  participant U as URL store
  participant F as Frontier
  P->>N: discovered URL + source
  N->>N: canonicalize and classify
  N->>U: conditional insert/read
  alt new or refresh-worthy
    U-->>N: canonical URL ID
    N->>F: schedule(url, priority, time)
  else duplicate
    U-->>N: existing state
  end

docs.title: 9. Politeness scheduling
docs.text:
Schedule by origin (scheme, host, effective port), not registrable domain: sibling hosts can have different robots policies. A registrable-domain or shared-infrastructure budget may additionally group origins without merging their policy identity. Each origin owns a FIFO/priority queue, token bucket, concurrency counter, and next_allowed_at. A global delay heap contains one entry per eligible origin, not every URL. The scheduler pops an origin, leases one URL, advances its deadline, and requeues it.

Robots rules are fetched with a crawler identity, cached by validators and bounded TTL, and evaluated using longest-match semantics. During unknown/expired policy, fail closed for new origins or use a conservative product-approved rule. 429 and Retry-After reduce origin rate; timeouts and 5xx apply jittered exponential backoff. Global demand never overrides per-origin limits.

RFC 9309 distinguishes unavailable robots (4xx, where crawling may be allowed) from unreachable robots (network/5xx, initially complete disallow), normally bounds cached policy to 24 hours, and requires at least a 500 KiB parsing limit. Crawl-delay is an extension, not an RFC-defined directive; noindex controls indexing separately. Our stricter throttling of 429 responses is deliberate operator policy (accessed 2026-09-08).

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> DISCOVERED
  DISCOVERED --> ROBOTS_WAIT
  ROBOTS_WAIT --> READY: allowed
  ROBOTS_WAIT --> DISALLOWED: denied
  READY --> LEASED
  LEASED --> FETCHED: committed
  LEASED --> READY: lease expired
  FETCHED --> READY: recrawl due
  FETCHED --> GONE: repeated terminal response

docs.title: 10. Fetch and parse flow
docs.text:
A worker resolves DNS through controlled resolvers, rejects private/link-local destinations, pins the validated address for the connection, and applies byte, redirect, decompression, and time limits. Conditional GET uses ETag/Last-Modified. It streams bytes to object storage while hashing, commits metadata, and acknowledges the lease. Parsers consume the artifact, detect type/charset, extract text, canonical hints, metadata, and links in a sandbox.

Redirects have a small hop limit and every target is revalidated against SSRF rules and robots. Disable automatic redirect following that bypasses scheduling: a different-origin target must acquire that origin's rate/concurrency permit at the egress gate before its HTTP request is sent. A 304 creates a lightweight observation referencing prior content. Failed parsing does not erase the valid fetch artifact.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: duplicates and traps
docs.text:
Exact duplicates share SHA-256 digests; near duplicates use SimHash/MinHash over normalized shingles. Keep one representative for indexing while preserving URL-specific metadata. Duplicate signals reduce recrawl and storage but must not collapse pages with distinct canonical/legal meaning.

Trap controls include maximum path depth/length, repeated path-token detection, query-key cardinality budgets, calendar-pattern detection, per-site URL quotas, low-novelty yield, and frontier growth ratios. Quarantine suspicious patterns rather than globally hard-coding them. A site-level circuit breaker stops discovery while allowing robots and manually submitted diagnostic fetches.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: recrawl priority
docs.text:
Estimate change probability from historical intervals, HTTP validators, sitemap dates, page importance, observed traffic, and publisher hints. Set next fetch so expected freshness value exceeds fetch cost. News pages may refresh in minutes; stable documentation in weeks. On 304, lengthen interval; meaningful changes shorten it. Reserve capacity classes for new discovery, refresh, removals, and retries so a discovery flood cannot age the corpus.

Use a capped priority score, not an unbounded global sort. Fair-share budgets by site and tenant prevent one giant domain from monopolizing workers. Recrawl models are advisory; hard minimum/maximum intervals protect sites and quality.

docs.title: 13. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Partition origin scheduler state by consistent hash of origin so one owner serializes token/concurrency decisions. Reassignment uses epoch-fenced leases: stale owners cannot grant valid work. Large origins remain intentionally bounded by politeness; shard only their URL queue behind one rate authority. Partition URL records by URL hash and artifacts by fetch ID.

Lease expiry does not stop a paused fetcher or an already sent HTTP request. Enforce send admission at a controlled egress gate that rejects old epochs and retains outstanding-request accounting across scheduler handoff; do not immediately recycle a timed-out worker's concurrency slot. Drain or expire its bounded network requests before replacement. This bounds our outbound in-flight work, not how long a remote server continues processing after a disconnect.

Document/link streams partition by URL ID. Hot output is controlled with bounded parser queues and admission backpressure to fetching. If storage approaches limits, stop low-priority discovery, retain metadata/checksums, and shorten raw retention before violating politeness or corrupting state.

docs.title: 14. Consistency, idempotency, and failures
docs.text:
Frontier transitions and leases require conditional version writes. Delivery is at least once: a lease timeout can duplicate a fetch, so CommitFetch(fetch_id) is idempotent and artifact keys are immutable. Robots versions accompany leases; the scheduler rejects stale policy epochs. Discovery duplicates are harmless conditional inserts. Persist scheduling intent (next_fetch_at and state) with the URL record and use an outbox or reconciliation to populate the frontier; a crash between insert and queue publication must not strand a newly discovered URL.

Scheduler loss reconstructs ready windows from durable next_fetch_at buckets. Worker loss expires leases. DNS or Internet failures back off per origin, not globally. Object-store failure pauses fetch issuance because publishing metadata without bytes violates the artifact invariant. Parser backlog backpressures new fetches. Never represent dependency failure as page deletion; only repeated policy-defined HTTP outcomes transition to gone.

Multi-region crawling assigns each origin a home region to prevent duplicate polite budgets. Standby regions acquire a fenced epoch after failure. Artifacts replicate asynchronously; frontier/control state uses cross-zone durability and periodic cross-region checkpoints.

docs.title: 15. Security and abuse
docs.text:
The crawler is an SSRF engine unless constrained. Block private, loopback, metadata, multicast, and newly rebound addresses at DNS and network layers; use egress proxies and destination ACLs. Sandboxed parsers have no network, credentials, or writable shared disk. Limit archive/decompression ratios, parser CPU, HTML nesting, and header sizes.

Authenticate seed submissions, rate-limit users and domains, reject crawl laundering, sign worker leases, and audit robots overrides. Honor removals, legal blocks, noindex, and retention policy. Publish crawler identity and operator contact; expose a site-owner verification and throttling channel.

docs.title: 16. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure fetches, useful bytes, statuses, latency, DNS/TLS errors, robots age/denials, per-origin concurrency violations (target zero), frontier age by class, lease expiry, change yield, duplicate ratio, trap quarantines, parser backlog, storage growth, and document publication lag. Cardinality-safe origin samples and trace IDs connect URL history without logging sensitive query values broadly.

Property-test canonicalization and robots matching against standards corpora. Model-test lease fencing and token buckets. Fuzz parsers, redirect chains, compressed bodies, and IDNs. Simulated origin servers assert request spacing, Retry-After, validators, and changing robots. Load tests use millions of tiny hosts plus a few huge hosts. Chaos tests kill scheduler owners, duplicate commits, delay storage, poison DNS, and verify bounded queues and zero politeness violations.

docs.title: 17. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
A single global URL priority queue is simple but cannot enforce per-origin scheduling efficiently. The two-level origin-plus-URL frontier makes politeness structural. Kafka alone is poor for delayed reprioritization and per-host leases; use a durable frontier database with bucketed time indexes, emitting bounded work streams.

The final system normalizes into a durable URL history, schedules through epoch-owned per-origin queues, validates robots and destinations, fetches into immutable artifacts, parses in sandboxes, and emits documents/links idempotently. Historical change drives recrawl; quotas, trap detection, and explicit overload classes bound cost.

docs.title: 18. Interview questions
docs.text:
• How is politeness preserved during scheduler failover?
  • When may a Bloom filter safely suppress work?
  • How do you detect infinite calendars without blocking legitimate archives?
  • What should happen when robots is temporarily unreachable?
  • How would JavaScript rendering fit without dominating cost?

docs.title: 19. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should separate frontier, scheduler, fetcher, parser, and storage; quantify bandwidth; enforce robots/per-host rates; deduplicate; retry safely; and discuss traps. An L6 answer should formalize lease fencing, policy epochs, capacity classes, recrawl economics, hostile-network containment, site-owner controls, regional ownership, corpus-quality metrics, and migrations without duplicate load.

docs.title: 20. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
At 500 million fetches/day, crawler design is governed by origins, not a flat URL queue. Normalize candidates, conditionally insert durable URL records, and place each in an origin queue. A delay heap selects eligible origins; token buckets, concurrency counters, robots versions, and epoch-fenced ownership make politeness invariant through retries and failover. Workers validate DNS against SSRF, stream bounded responses to immutable storage, then parsers sandbox hostile bytes and emit documents plus links.

Use content hashes and near-duplicate fingerprints, evidence-based trap quarantine, and historical change models for recrawl. At-least-once leases are safe because fetch commits are idempotent. Protect removal/robots work with reserved capacity, backpressure fetches behind parser/storage health, and never turn infrastructure errors into page deletion. Monitor request-spacing violations, frontier age, useful-change yield, trap growth, and publication lag. The key tradeoff is coverage and freshness versus responsible, bounded resource use.

docs.title: 21. Final checklist
docs.text: The design covers discovery, robots, fetch, parse, recrawl, immutable evidence, canonicalization, duplicate handling, traps, partition ownership, overload, security, and recovery. Its control plane decides what and when; its data plane performs bounded hostile I/O.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We scope text search over a crawled corpus, define relevance and freshness contracts, estimate query/index scale, and separate offline indexing from online serving. Deep dives cover inverted indexes, ranking, query execution, freshness, and deletion, followed by scaling, failures, abuse, testing, and level expectations.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
Given a textual query, return fast, relevant, diverse web results with title, URL, and snippet. The engine consumes fetched document versions from a crawler. It supports language detection, typo correction, filters, safe-search policy, and pagination. We exclude ads, personalized history, images/video, and a full browser-rendering crawler.

No single metric defines relevance. The design must preserve hard policy/removal rules while evolving retrieval and ranking independently.

docs.title: 3. Requirements and SLOs
docs.text:
• Index canonical documents and searchable fields; process updates and removals.
  • Return top results with snippets, spelling suggestions, and opaque continuation tokens.
  • Query availability 99.99%; p99 under 300 ms; policy removals globally effective within 15 minutes.
  • Important new pages searchable within five minutes; broad refresh within hours.
  • Results must not mix incompatible index generations, leak blocked documents, or depend on one ranking service.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. A document version is published only after all referenced index artifacts are durable.
  2. Query fanout uses one compatible index/schema generation.
  3. A current deny decision overrides cached retrieval and ranking.
  4. Retries of document updates are idempotent by (doc_id, source_version); older versions cannot overwrite newer ones.
  5. Pagination is stable against its index snapshot or explicitly best-effort, never offset-based across changing shards.
  6. Scores are comparable only under the same model/calibration version.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 5 billion indexed documents, 20 billion queries/day (231,000/s average, 1 million/s peak), and 500 million changed documents/day. Average extracted text is 30 KB, but a compressed inverted index may use 10-20% of source text: 150 TB of extracted text and roughly 15-30 TB of compressed postings at that assumed ratio. Positions, dictionary, stored fields, replicas, and headroom are additional measured components, potentially taking provisioned storage into hundreds of TB.

At three replicas and 1 million peak QPS, 90% query/result caching leaves 100,000 query executions/s. If each query fans to 200 shards, naive fanout is 20 million shard requests/s, motivating tiered retrieval, shard pruning, and replicas. A 200 ms budget might reserve 20 ms parsing, 100 ms retrieval, 50 ms reranking/snippets, and 30 ms network/edge margin.

docs.title: 6. Data model and interfaces
docs.text:
Document(doc_id, canonical_url, source_version, title, body, language,
         site_id, link_features, quality_features, policy_labels, fetched_at)
TermDictionary(term -> term_id, document_frequency)
Posting(term_id -> blocks[(doc_id_delta, term_frequency, positions, field_bits)])
StoredFields(doc_id -> url, title, compressed text offsets)
DocValues(doc_id -> rank features, timestamps, labels)
IndexManifest(generation, schema_version, model_compatibility, shard_files, checksums)

Indexer input is UpsertDocument(doc_id, source_version, artifact) or DeleteDocument. Query API:

GET /v1/search?q=distributed+systems&lang=en&safe=strict&pageToken=...
200 {"results":[{"url":"...","title":"...","snippet":"...","score":0.82}],
     "suggestion":null,"nextPageToken":"signed snapshot/shard cursors"}

docs.title: 7. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  C[Crawler document stream] --> N[Normalize and enrich]
  N --> I[Index builders]
  I --> O[(Immutable segment store)]
  I --> M[Index manifest controller]
  U[User] --> E[Edge and query cache]
  E --> Q[Query coordinator]
  Q --> R[Retrieval shard replicas]
  R --> O
  Q --> L[Reranker]
  Q --> S[Snippet service]
  P[Policy service] --> Q
  M --> R

Immutable segments and atomic manifests separate build from serve. The coordinator parses once, chooses shards/replicas, merges candidates, applies policy, reranks, and assembles snippets under deadlines.

docs.title: 8. Indexing pipeline
docs.text:
Normalization detects language, tokenizes with versioned analyzers, extracts fields, resolves canonical/duplicate groups, joins link and quality features, and emits a versioned document. Builders create immutable postings sorted by term then document, stored fields, doc values, and deletion bitmaps. Small near-real-time segments publish every few minutes; background compaction merges them into efficient larger segments.

A manifest references complete checksummed files. Replicas download, verify, warm, then atomically swap generations. Old files remain until no query snapshot references them. Duplicate update events compare source versions; late events are ignored.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Crawl pipeline
  participant B as Index builder
  participant O as Segment store
  participant M as Manifest controller
  participant R as Serving replica
  C->>B: doc_id + source_version
  B->>B: analyze and build segment
  B->>O: immutable files + checksums
  O-->>B: durable
  B->>M: publish manifest generation
  M-->>R: desired generation
  R->>O: fetch and verify
  R->>R: atomic generation swap

docs.title: 9. Query flow
docs.text:
The edge normalizes safe cache dimensions. The coordinator detects language, parses phrases/operators, expands synonyms or spelling candidates with limits, and retrieves lexical candidates. Each shard uses BM25-style scoring and returns top K with feature vectors. Shared corpus statistics or a defined shard calibration make these retrieval scores comparable; using the same formula with different local document frequencies alone does not. The coordinator merges top candidates, filters deny decisions, reranks perhaps 500 candidates with a learned model, enforces domain diversity, requests snippets, and returns before its deadline.

Every downstream call receives a shrinking deadline. Partial shard results are allowed above a coverage threshold and labeled in the API response as well as telemetry; policy service failure fails closed for risky classes using a locally replicated deny snapshot.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant U as User
  participant Q as Coordinator
  participant R as Retrieval shards
  participant L as Reranker
  participant P as Policy snapshot
  U->>Q: query and optional page token
  Q->>P: policy/model generation
  Q->>R: terms, filters, K, deadline
  R-->>Q: lexical candidates + features
  Q->>Q: merge and policy filter
  Q->>L: bounded candidate set
  L-->>Q: calibrated scores
  Q-->>U: diverse results + page token

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: inverted index execution
docs.text:
Postings are delta-encoded in compressed blocks with skip data and term upper bounds. Conjunctive queries intersect shortest lists first. Disjunctive queries use WAND/block-max WAND to skip blocks that cannot enter top K. Positions are loaded only for phrase/proximity verification. Doc values support fast filters without random document fetches.

Partition primarily by document ID: every query fans out, but indexing and document updates remain local and shard scores can be calibrated. Term partitioning reduces fanout for simple queries but hot terms and multi-term joins are difficult. Use document shards plus routing replicas and query caches. Very rare/vertical corpora can be pruned by language and market.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: ranking
docs.text:
Candidate generation prioritizes recall using lexical BM25 and optionally approximate-nearest-neighbor semantic retrieval. A lightweight first-stage score combines field matches, freshness, static page quality, and spam signals. A learned reranker consumes query-document interaction features only for bounded candidates. Final logic applies hard policy, near-duplicate collapse, host diversity, and freshness blending.

Offline NDCG/recall cannot guarantee user value. Online interleaving or guarded A/B tests track reformulation, long clicks, abandonment, latency, safety, and ecosystem concentration. Models and features are versioned; missing features have trained defaults. Never allow a model score to override legal removal.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: snippets, spelling, and pagination
docs.text:
Snippet service reads compressed stored fields and selects windows around matched terms, then escapes output. Precomputed passages reduce latency but increase index size. Highlighting uses token offsets from the same analyzer generation.

Spelling candidates come from a term lexicon and noisy-channel/popularity model; apply only when confidence is high and provide the original query path. Page tokens sign the query hash, index snapshot, model version, expiry, and per-shard search_after score/doc tie-breakers. For learned reranking and global diversity, lexical per-shard cursors alone do not preserve final order. Materialize a bounded ranked candidate session with a stable next-result offset, or specify and label best-effort pagination. Pin the candidate set and ranking inputs for the promised stable mode, while reapplying current removal policy on each page. Deep pagination is capped because candidate work and result quality degrade.

docs.title: 13. Freshness and deletion
docs.text:
Near-real-time mini-segments make important updates searchable quickly. A freshness overlay keyed by doc ID can hold urgent updates/deletes while full segment publication catches up. Compaction folds overlays into segments. Query replicas load signed deny/deletion snapshots frequently; cache keys include policy epoch, and emergency purges target document/query surrogate keys. Edge cache hits enforce the current minimum policy generation and freshness deadline too; the coordinator cannot filter a response that bypasses it.

State evolves from discovered to indexed to superseded or deleted. Tombstones carry source version so a delayed old upsert cannot resurrect a removed page. A privacy erase removes stored fields and source artifacts after retention while minimal non-content tombstones preserve ordering.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> RECEIVED
  RECEIVED --> INDEXED: segment published
  INDEXED --> SUPERSEDED: newer source version
  INDEXED --> DELETED: removal tombstone
  SUPERSEDED --> RECLAIMED: no snapshot references
  DELETED --> RECLAIMED: retention complete

docs.title: 14. Partitioning, scaling, and overload
docs.text:
Consistently hash doc IDs into logical shards; map logical shards to physical nodes so rebalancing moves bounded units. Replicate each shard across zones and select by queue depth, generation, and locality. Hedged requests fire only after a percentile threshold and within a global amplification budget. Hot queries are edge-cached; hot terms remain spread across document shards.

Under overload, stop semantic retrieval, reduce candidate K, skip expensive snippets, and return lexical results before rejecting queries. Admission control separates interactive, bot, and internal traffic. Indexing backpressure slows low-priority crawler consumption while preserving deletes and important fresh documents. Compaction has explicit I/O budgets so it cannot starve serving.

docs.title: 15. Consistency, reliability, and regions
docs.text:
Index input is at least once and idempotent by source version. Segment publication is atomic through manifests, not in-place file mutation. Queries pin a compatible generation; replicas that are behind are excluded. Counts and analytics may be eventual, but deletion overlays are strongly ordered per doc.

Serve queries active-active from regional index copies. Build globally or per corpus, replicate immutable segments, and switch manifests regionally after verification. If a shard fails, use another replica; if coverage stays below threshold, return a clear degraded response rather than fabricate completeness. Reranker failure falls back to lexical scores. Snippet failure returns title/URL. Control-plane outage leaves the last verified generation serving.

docs.title: 16. Security and abuse
docs.text:
Rate-limit automated queries, detect scraping, protect expensive operators, and cap token/Boolean expansion. Sanitize snippets and URLs to prevent XSS. Encrypt query logs, restrict access, minimize retention, and avoid joining identity unless personalization is explicitly scoped. Defend the corpus against keyword stuffing, link farms, cloaking, hacked pages, malicious structured data, and model-feature poisoning through multi-signal classifiers and human appeal workflows.

Signed manifests, checksums, least-privilege segment access, audited policy changes, and reproducible model lineage protect the supply chain. Safe-search and legal policy are versioned, explainable layers outside ranking.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track QPS, end-to-end and stage latency, timeout/partial rate, shard queue depth, cache hit rate, fanout, postings decoded, WAND skips, candidate count, generation skew, freshness lag, delete propagation, compaction debt, fallback rate, and cost/query. Quality dashboards cover NDCG, recall on judged sets, zero-result/reformulation rates, domain diversity, spam and safety escapes, with slices by language/device/market.

Test analyzers with golden multilingual corpora, posting codec round trips, deterministic scoring, late update/delete races, and signed tokens. Differential tests compare optimized retrieval to exhaustive scoring. Load tests use realistic head/tail queries. Chaos kills shards and model servers, corrupts segment downloads, delays manifests, and saturates compaction. Shadow traffic validates new generations and models before canary rollout.

docs.title: 18. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Database text indexes are excellent at modest corpus scale but lack cost-efficient immutable distribution and specialized ranking at billions of documents. In-place mutable indexes simplify freshness but complicate recovery and reproducibility. Immutable segments plus overlays create compaction work while making rollback and regional replication safe.

The final design consumes versioned crawler documents, builds immutable document-sharded inverted indexes, publishes atomic manifests, and serves through replicated retrieval shards. Coordinators execute bounded lexical recall, optional semantic recall, calibrated reranking, hard policy, diversity, and safe snippets. Mini-segments/overlays meet freshness and removal SLOs; graceful degradation protects latency.

docs.title: 19. Interview questions
docs.text:
• Why document-shard instead of term-shard the index?
  • How do WAND skips preserve exact top K?
  • How can deletion outrun normal index publication?
  • What is encoded in a stable pagination token?
  • How do you launch a ranker without trading safety or diversity for clicks?

docs.title: 20. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should explain inverted indexes, query fanout/merge, ranking stages, caching, replication, indexing updates, and latency degradation. An L6 candidate should define generation compatibility, model calibration, removal overlays, realistic quality experimentation, corpus abuse, compaction economics, regional rollout/rollback, tail amplification budgets, and organizational separation between relevance and policy.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
For five billion documents and million-QPS peaks, build immutable inverted-index segments from versioned crawler output and atomically publish checksummed manifests. Hash documents into logical shards, replicate across zones/regions, and pin each query to a compatible generation. Coordinators parse once, fan out with deadlines, merge BM25 candidates, apply current policy, rerank a bounded set, diversify, and generate escaped snippets. Block-max WAND, shard pruning, caches, and graceful feature shedding control fanout cost.

Mini-segments and doc-ID overlays provide five-minute freshness and faster deletes; tombstone versions prevent resurrection. At-least-once document updates are idempotent. Reranker or snippet failure degrades to lexical title/URL results, while policy failure fails closed. Measure both systems health and search quality, test optimized retrieval against exhaustive results, and shadow/canary every index or model generation. The central tradeoff is immutable, reproducible serving versus update immediacy; overlays bridge the two.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We design user video upload, processing, playback, discovery hooks, and moderation. We quantify bytes, define publication invariants, trace resumable upload and adaptive streaming, then examine transcoding, CDN delivery, counters, partitioning, failures, abuse, and L5/L6 expectations.

docs.title: 2. Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Creators upload videos, edit metadata, publish with public/unlisted/private visibility, watch on varied networks, and delete content. Viewers receive adaptive playback, captions, thumbnails, likes, and delayed view counts. Search/recommendation are downstream interfaces, not fully designed here; live streaming and ads are excluded.

SLOs: playback start p95 under 2 seconds on healthy broadband, rebuffer ratio under 1%, playback availability 99.99%, an illustrative annual retained-object durability objective of 99.999999999%, and p95 processing time under fifteen minutes after completion for ten-minute uploads. These are design targets, not verified YouTube service guarantees. Processing may be asynchronous, but no manifest may reference missing segments.

docs.title: 3. Invariants
docs.text:
1. A completed upload is checksum-verified and durable before acceptance.
  2. Publication exposes only an atomically selected, complete rendition manifest.
  3. Authorization is checked before private manifests or keys are issued.
  4. Source and renditions are immutable; edits create metadata/manifest versions.
  5. Upload completion, processing tasks, likes, and deletes are idempotent.
  6. View events never block playback and are not claimed exactly once.

docs.title: 4. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 5 million uploads/day averaging 300 MB: 1.5 PB/day ingress before replication. At 100 million hours watched/day and 3 Mbps average delivered bitrate, CDN egress is roughly 135 PB/day. Peak playback may reach 20 million concurrent sessions. Metadata for one billion videos at 3 KB is only 3 TB; media dominates cost. A ten-minute source may yield six bitrate/resolution ladders totaling about 2-3x source bytes. These numbers require direct object uploads, asynchronous compute, lifecycle tiers, and CDN offload above 95%.

docs.title: 5. APIs and data model
docs.text:
POST /v1/videos/uploads {size, contentType, partSize} -> {uploadId, signedPartUrls}
PUT signed-url (part bytes + checksum)
POST /v1/uploads/{id}:complete {parts, idempotencyKey} -> {videoId,state}
PATCH /v1/videos/{id} {title,visibility,expectedVersion}
GET /v1/videos/{id}/playback -> signed master manifest
DELETE /v1/videos/{id}

Video(video_id, owner_id, state, visibility, source_key, source_digest,
      active_manifest_version, metadata_version, policy_state, created_at)
Upload(upload_id, owner_id, expected_size, parts, expires_at, state)
Rendition(video_id, pipeline_version, codec, resolution, bitrate, segment_prefix, state)
Manifest(video_id, version, rendition_set, checksums, captions, state)
ProcessingTask(task_id, video_id, input_version, type, attempt, state)

Canonical metadata controls lifecycle; object storage contains immutable bytes; CDN and counters are projections.

docs.title: 6. High-level design
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  U[Uploader] --> A[Upload API]
  U --> O[(Object storage)]
  A --> M[(Metadata DB)]
  A --> Q[Workflow queue]
  Q --> T[Transcode workers]
  T --> O
  T --> M
  V[Viewer] --> P[Playback API]
  P --> M
  P --> V
  V --> CDN[CDN segment delivery]
  CDN --> O
  V -. events .-> E[Analytics stream]
    subgraph PrepareLane[Upload and processing]
      U
      A
      Q

    end
    subgraph PlaybackLane[Playback]
      V

docs.title: 7. Upload and processing flow
docs.text:
The API allocates an upload with byte/part quotas and short-lived scoped URLs. Clients upload parts in parallel, resume by listing acknowledged checksums, then complete with an ordered part manifest. Completion verifies size, per-part checksum, final digest, and ownership; a transaction creates the video plus workflow outbox. Replays return the same video. Abandoned multipart data expires automatically.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Creator
  participant A as Upload API
  participant O as Object store
  participant W as Workflow
  C->>A: create upload
  A-->>C: scoped part URLs
  C->>O: upload/resume checksummed parts
  C->>A: complete(parts, key)
  A->>O: verify composed source
  A->>A: commit video + outbox
  A-->>C: video ID, PROCESSING
  W->>O: transcode immutable source
  W->>A: atomically publish manifest

Probe extracts duration/codecs; malware and policy scans run before public availability. A workflow DAG creates mezzanine if needed, bitrate ladder, audio, thumbnails, captions, and manifests. Tasks use deterministic output keys (video,pipeline,task) and conditional completion, so retries duplicate computation but not state. Publication verifies every object/checksum then swaps active_manifest_version atomically. Failed optional captions do not block video; failed mandatory scan or base rendition does.

docs.title: 8. Playback and adaptive streaming
docs.text:
Playback authenticates visibility, region/age rights, and policy, then returns a short-lived signed HLS/DASH master manifest. The player chooses a conservative initial bitrate and estimates throughput from segment downloads, increasing slowly and decreasing quickly while considering buffer occupancy. Two-to-six-second segments balance switching agility against request overhead. Seek maps to segment boundaries; resume position is an asynchronous user projection.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant V as Player
  participant P as Playback API
  participant C as CDN
  participant O as Origin shield
  V->>P: playback request
  P-->>V: signed manifest + policy expiry
  V->>C: manifest and segment
  alt cache hit
    C-->>V: segment
  else miss
    C->>O: coalesced origin fetch
    O-->>C: immutable segment
    C-->>V: segment
  end

Segments are content-versioned and cache for months; manifests are shorter-lived. Multi-tier CDN with regional shields prevents origin stampedes. Signed cookies avoid one signature per segment. Popularity prediction prewarms launches; long-tail content stays pull-through. Origin failover uses replicated buckets and checksum validation.

docs.title: 9. Domain deep dives
docs.text:
Codec ladder: Build per-title ladders from complexity probes rather than fixed bitrates. Cap compute with presets; retain broadly supported H.264 while adding AV1 where expected egress savings exceed encode/storage/device costs. Never remove an old rendition until manifests no longer reference it.

Views and engagement: Emit session/start/heartbeat/complete events. A policy-defined watch threshold counts a view; deduplicate by event/session within a window and filter bots. Counters are delayed, mergeable projections. Likes use a unique (user,video) row plus transactional outbox; displayed totals may lag.

Deletion and reprocessing: Mark video unavailable first, revoke playback tokens within their bounded lifetime, purge manifests, then asynchronously erase renditions/source according to retention. Tombstone versions prevent late workflows from republishing. New codec pipelines build alongside old ones, shadow-check, atomically switch, and garbage-collect after token/cache expiry.

docs.title: 10. Partitioning, consistency, and regions
docs.text:
Hash metadata by video ID; index creator listings separately with cursors. A viral video is a CDN hot object, not a metadata-shard problem. Salt analytics partitions for viral IDs and merge partial aggregates. Queue partitions by video ID preserve workflow ordering, with priority/fairness so one creator cannot monopolize transcoders. Autoscale by queued media-minutes, codec, and GPU type, not task count.

Metadata writes use home-region single ownership and synchronous multi-zone durability; media replicates asynchronously before regional publication. Playback is active-active from replicated metadata/CDN. Strong consistency is required for lifecycle/version swaps and unique likes; feeds, views, processing progress, and search are eventual. Dependency uncertainty returns unavailable, never a false deletion or privacy grant.

docs.title: 11. Failure, security, and abuse
docs.text:
Lost completion responses replay safely. Worker death re-leases tasks; poison files enter quarantine after bounded attempts. Queue outage leaves videos processing but does not impair existing playback. CDN failure routes to another provider or shield with traffic budgets. Object corruption is detected by checksums and repaired from replicas. Overload sheds thumbnail variants and new low-priority encodes before playback.

Validate containers in sandboxes; cap duration, dimensions, decompression, and parser resources. Encrypt storage and transport, scope signed URLs by object/action/expiry, keep private media out of shared caches unless encrypted authorization is enforced, and audit staff access. Rate-limit uploads/comments/views; detect copyright matches, spam, synthetic views, harmful content, and coordinated reports. Appeals and legal holds are explicit states, not ad hoc database edits.

docs.title: 12. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure upload completion/checksum failures, processing latency by stage and media-minute, queue age, rendition success, publication lag, CDN hit/egress/origin load, playback start, fatal errors, bitrate, rebuffer ratio, policy denials, delete propagation, and cost per uploaded/watched minute. Correlate player QoE by ISP/device/codec without logging signed URLs.

Test multipart resume, completion races, workflow replay, manifest referential integrity, ABR under network traces, malformed media fuzzing, authorization, and tombstone races. Load with Zipfian popularity. Chaos kills encoders, delays replicas, loses queue acknowledgments, corrupts segments, and evacuates CDN regions. Canary every pipeline version on a codec corpus before gradual publication.

docs.title: Cost-aware capacity and overload
docs.text:
Transcoding is heterogeneous: a one-hour 4K AV1 job is not equivalent to a one-minute SD thumbnail task. Admission records normalized media-minutes and predicted CPU/GPU seconds. Separate queues by codec and hardware capability, reserve capacity for newly uploaded base renditions, and use weighted tenant fairness. During a celebrity upload burst, produce one widely compatible 360p/720p path first, publish only if product semantics allow partial ladders, then add premium renditions through new manifest versions. Backlog targets determine autoscaling, while maximum spot-instance share bounds interruption risk.

Storage policy distinguishes source, mezzanine, published rendition, abandoned upload, and superseded pipeline output. Sources may move to colder tiers after processing but must remain recoverable for future codecs. Renditions with negligible watch time can be generated on demand only when startup risk and compute economics justify it. Chargeback dashboards show bytes stored, encoded, and delivered by tenant and codec.

docs.title: L6 transcoding control plane and deterministic recovery
docs.text:
Represent each upload as a durable workflow execution keyed by (video_id, source_version, pipeline_version). Its DAG contains probe -> malware/policy scan -> complexity sample -> ladder plan -> parallel encode -> package -> verify -> publish; captions and thumbnails can branch after probe. A task record stores dependency versions, deterministic output key, attempt, lease owner/epoch, input checksum, encoder image digest, parameters, and terminal result checksum. A worker may commit only while holding the current lease epoch. Completion is a compare-and-set from RUNNING to SUCCEEDED, followed by an outbox event, so a lost acknowledgment causes a lookup rather than a second logical output.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> BLOCKED
  BLOCKED --> READY: dependencies satisfied
  READY --> LEASED: scheduler grants epoch
  LEASED --> RUNNING: worker starts
  RUNNING --> SUCCEEDED: checksum and QC pass
  RUNNING --> RETRY_WAIT: retryable failure
  RETRY_WAIT --> READY: deterministic backoff
  RUNNING --> QUARANTINED: poison input or attempt limit
  LEASED --> READY: lease expires
  RUNNING --> RETRY_WAIT: lease expires and stale completion fenced
  SUCCEEDED --> INVALIDATED: source or pipeline superseded
  INVALIDATED --> [*]
  QUARANTINED --> [*]

Retries are deterministic at the artifact boundary, not necessarily bit-identical inside every encoder. The logical artifact key is a hash of source checksum, rendition specification, encoder digest, and pipeline version; workers write to an attempt-scoped temporary key, verify duration, segment alignment, decodeability, and checksum, then conditionally install the canonical key. A speculative duplicate either observes the installed result or loses the conditional write. Retry only transient classes such as worker loss, rate limits, or storage timeout; malformed media and repeatable decoder crashes are quarantined. Backoff is derived from task ID plus attempt so replay does not synchronize a fleet-wide retry storm.

Partial ladders have an explicit publication policy. BASE_READY requires the baseline H.264 audio/video pair, aligned segments, thumbnails, policy approval, and rights state; only then may a manifest version expose 360p/720p. Optional 1080p, 4K, VP9, and AV1 tasks continue and produce a new immutable manifest version. A failed optional rung never leaves a dangling manifest reference. The controller stops retrying a rung when its predicted watch-value saving is below remaining encode cost, but failed mandatory outputs keep the video unpublished. Tombstone and source-version checks occur again at artifact commit and manifest swap, preventing a deleted or replaced upload from being resurrected.

flowchart TD
  S[Source checksum and probe] --> C[Complexity samples]
  C --> L[Per-title ladder planner]
  L --> B[Mandatory baseline tasks]
  L --> O[Optional premium tasks]
  B --> Q{Baseline QC complete?}
  Q -->|yes| M1[Publish manifest v1]
  Q -->|no| X[Hold or quarantine]
  O --> Q2{Optional QC and value pass?}
  Q2 -->|yes| M2[Publish manifest v2]
  Q2 -->|no| D[Drop rung or retry]
  M1 --> M2
  M1 --> P[Playback]
  M2 --> P
    subgraph BaseLane[Required baseline]
      B
      Q
      M1
      X
    end
    subgraph OptionalLane[Premium rungs]
      O
      Q2
      M2
      D
    end

docs.title: Per-title VMAF ladder and concrete ABR
docs.text:
The ladder planner samples scene boundaries plus difficult motion, texture, and dark regions, then encodes short clips across resolution/bitrate candidates. It computes VMAF and encode cost per candidate, removes dominated points, enforces device/codec floors, and chooses rungs whose quality gain exceeds a threshold such as 4 VMAF while bitrate grows by roughly 1.4x to 2x. Per-title constraints cap maximum source resolution, reject upscaling, preserve a low-bandwidth rung, and account for grain or animation where aggregate VMAF can mislead. Periodic subjective review calibrates VMAF thresholds, and planner/metric versions are recorded so a ladder can be reproduced.

For example, a 1080p animation probe might produce (360p, 0.35 Mb/s, VMAF 82), (480p, 0.60, 90), (720p, 1.10, 95), (1080p, 1.80, 97), and (1080p, 3.00, 98). The 3 Mb/s point costs 67% more for one VMAF point and is removed; a noisy sports title might retain 0.5, 1.2, 2.8, and 5.5 Mb/s instead. If one million viewing hours move from a fixed 3 Mb/s rendition to an equal-quality 1.8 Mb/s rendition, delivery falls by about 540 TB (1.2 Mb/s * 3,600 s * 1,000,000 / 8), easily justifying extra analysis encodes for a popular title.

At each segment boundary the client maintains harmonic-mean throughput over the last five successful downloads, applies a 15% safety margin for uncertainty, and combines it with buffer state. Let safe_bw = 0.85 * harmonic_mean; choose the highest rung below safe_bw, but use these guards: below 8 seconds of buffer, step down immediately; from 8 to 20 seconds, never step up; above 20 seconds, step up only one rung after two consecutive eligible segments; above 35 seconds, normal selection applies. Abandon an in-flight segment if its projected completion would drain the buffer and a lower rung can arrive sooner. Startup chooses a device/region prior capped at 720p and measures from the first media segment.

Numerically, samples of 6, 5, 4, 3, and 2 Mb/s have a harmonic mean near 3.45 Mb/s and safe_bw near 2.93 Mb/s. With 24 seconds buffered the player selects at most a 2.8 Mb/s rung and requires two confirmations before switching up; if the latest throughput drops to 1.4 Mb/s and buffer reaches 7 seconds, emergency selection caps the rolling estimate by that latest sample, so it immediately selects a rung below 1.19 Mb/s. Operations compare rebuffer ratio, start time, bitrate, switch frequency, and watch abandonment by player algorithm cohort; a QoE regression automatically halts rollout independently of server health.

docs.title: Rights lifecycle and media capacity
docs.text:
Rights are versioned intervals and predicates over owner, territory, age, product surface, monetization mode, device class, and allowed operations. The lifecycle is DRAFT -> SCHEDULED -> ACTIVE -> EXPIRED, with side transitions to BLOCKED, TAKEDOWN_PENDING, TAKEN_DOWN, APPEALED, and REINSTATED. Upload ownership does not imply universal playback rights. Playback binds the policy version and earliest rights expiry into a short-lived token; emergency takedown increments a deny epoch consumed by manifest authorization and token refresh. Every segment request, including a cache hit, must validate the scoped access token/cookie and its current policy or documented expiry bound; withholding the manifest alone does not protect a known segment URL. Encryption with controlled key delivery can provide an additional boundary. Previously downloaded or decrypted bytes cannot be recalled, and purge is defense in depth. Legal holds preserve evidence without making content playable, and every automated match, manual override, appeal, and territorial change is append-only audited.

Capacity uses media-seconds by codec/preset and delivered bitrate by geography. Suppose peak ingest is 500 hours/minute and the mix is 70% short H.264 at 6x real time, 20% HD VP9 at 1.5x, and 10% 4K AV1 at 0.25x. One minute of arrivals needs 350/6 + 100/1.5 + 50/0.25 = 325 encoder-hours, or 19,500 encoder-minutes. Sustaining arrivals therefore requires 19,500 continuously busy equivalent workers; at 65% target utilization and an additive 25% capacity margin, provision 19,500 / 0.65 * 1.25 = 37,500 worker equivalents. These rates cover one output path per input; producing multiple rungs adds their encode work. Scheduler reservations guarantee baseline H.264, while premium codecs consume elastic or spot capacity and are shed first.

CDN planning starts with peak traffic, cache hit, and shield amplification. Ten million concurrent viewers averaging 2.5 Mb/s require 25 Tb/s edge egress. At a 97% edge hit ratio, naive miss traffic is 750 Gb/s; regional shields with a 90% hit ratio reduce origin to about 75 Gb/s. Capacity must still reserve for correlated cold misses, so origin and inter-CDN failover are tested at a lower assumed edge hit such as 90%, not the steady-state average. Operators alarm on queued media-minutes by hardware class, deadline miss forecast, lease churn, QC failure fingerprint, partial-ladder age, edge/shield hit ratio, origin saturation, and rights-deny propagation. During shortage: protect playback, takedowns, and baseline encodes; pause backfills; then shed premium ladders and nonessential derivatives. A regional CDN evacuation uses weighted traffic ramps and origin budgets rather than instant global failover.

docs.title: Metadata and discovery integration
docs.text:
Search and recommendation consume a transactional outbox event containing video ID, metadata version, policy state, and active manifest version. They are projections and may lag; playback still checks canonical visibility. Title edits coalesce, while delete/block events use priority lanes. A subscriber stores the greatest version per video, making redelivery and reordering harmless. Thumbnail URLs include content versions so updates do not rely on global cache purge.

Comments and subscriptions would be separate bounded contexts: they can fail without affecting playback. This boundary prevents a broad social-product outage from consuming upload or playback pools and gives each feature an independent abuse model.

docs.title: 13. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Proxy uploads simplify clients but make API bandwidth the bottleneck; direct scoped multipart upload wins. Synchronous transcoding gives immediate answers but couples latency and expensive compute; durable workflows win. One universal ladder is operationally easy but wastes quality/bytes; per-title encoding is justified at watch scale.

Final design: direct verified upload to immutable object storage, transactional metadata/outbox, idempotent DAG transcoding, atomic complete-manifest publication, policy-gated signed playback, adaptive segmented delivery through multi-tier CDN, and asynchronous engagement. Immutable versions make retries, rollback, replication, and deletion races tractable.

docs.title: 14. Interview questions
docs.text:
• How does completion avoid publishing partial multipart data?
  • How would live streaming alter manifests and latency?
  • When is AV1 economically justified?
  • How does a delete beat stale workflow retries and CDN caches?
  • Which QoE signal matters more than server latency?

docs.title: 15. Level expectations
docs.text: L5 candidates should separate upload, processing, storage, metadata, CDN, and analytics; design resumability, ABR, retries, hot-video delivery, and privacy. L6 candidates should quantify media economics, model workflow state/fencing, define publication/deletion bounds, plan codec migrations, regional rights, overload priorities, moderation operations, and client-observed QoE.

docs.title: 16. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Media bytes dominate: direct checksummed multipart uploads into object storage and asynchronously transform immutable sources. Completion atomically creates canonical video state and an outbox; deterministic workflow tasks probe, scan, transcode a per-title bitrate ladder, create thumbnails/captions, verify artifacts, then swap a complete manifest version. Playback authorizes and returns short-lived HLS/DASH access; players adapt bitrate while CDN/shields serve immutable segments at above 95% hit rate.

Hash metadata by video, salt viral analytics, scale encoders by queued media-minutes, and preserve fair capacity. Lifecycle swaps are strongly consistent; views and progress are eventual/idempotent. Deletion marks unavailable first and tombstones the version before purge, defeating stale workers. Protect parsers, URLs, private cache behavior, moderation, and synthetic metrics. Operate from player QoE, publication lag, queue age, origin load, and cost per watched minute.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a platform that accepts ad impressions and clicks, produces advertiser reports within one minute, and later publishes billable totals. The key distinction is between a fast, revisable event-time view and a slower authoritative billing view. We will establish event identity and attribution rules first, estimate load, design ingestion and aggregation, then cover late data, hot campaigns, replay, fraud, and reconciliation.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
An ad exchange emits an impression when an ad is rendered and a click when a user interacts. Advertisers ask for counts, click-through rate (CTR), and spend grouped by campaign, creative, publisher, geography, and time bucket. The dashboard can tolerate recent corrections; invoices cannot silently change.

Assume this system starts after ad selection. Auction and creative serving are out of scope. We retain raw events for audit and reprocessing, provide near-real-time aggregates for 90 days, and finalize billing daily after a lateness window. Attribution is last eligible impression for the same ad opportunity or signed impression token, not arbitrary user-level multi-touch attribution.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Ingest impression, click, and optional conversion events.
  • Validate tenant, signature, schema, and event identity.
  • Attribute clicks to impressions and reject impossible or duplicate events.
  • Query counts, CTR, and estimated spend over dimensions and time ranges.
  • Produce daily finalized advertiser and publisher statements.
  • Replay raw data after bugs without double charging.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• Sustain 1 million events/second globally and 3x bursts.
  • Acknowledge valid ingestion in 100 ms p99; expose 99% of accepted events in 60 seconds.
  • Dashboard availability is 99.95%; acknowledged ingestion survives one zone failure under the configured quorum policy. Regional destruction has the separately stated replication RPO, not an undefined percentage durability promise.
  • Billing totals must be reproducible and traceable to accepted events.
  • Isolate advertisers and degrade queries before dropping accepted events.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. An event identity contributes at most once within the streaming deduplication horizon and at most once to finalized billing. Reports outside that horizon are provisional until canonical reconciliation.
  2. A billable click references one valid impression and satisfies the campaign's attribution and fraud policy version.
  3. Money uses integer micros and an explicit currency; currencies are never summed together.
  4. Finalized statements are immutable. Corrections create adjustment records linked to the prior statement.
  5. Every aggregate is derivable from immutable raw events plus versioned policy and reference data.
  6. Event time determines reporting buckets; processing time determines operational lag only.

These invariants do not require exactly-once transport. They require durable identities, deterministic computation, and idempotent sinks.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
At 1 million events/second and 350 bytes compressed per event, ingress is about 350 MB/s and 30 TB/day. Replicated raw storage at 3x is 90 TB/day, so lifecycle it: 30 days hot object storage and 13 months compressed archive. If impressions are 95%, clicks 4%, and conversions 1%, attribution state is driven mostly by impressions.

One-minute aggregates with 5 million distinct active combinations per hour produce between 5 million and 300 million occupied combination-minute rows per hour, depending on temporal occupancy, before rollups. Storing every possible dimension cube is explosive. We precompute common combinations and query uncommon combinations from a columnar analytics store. A 60-second visibility SLO implies stream capacity above peak, bounded state, and explicit late-event handling rather than hourly batch jobs.

docs.title: 6. Core entities and data model
docs.text:
AdEvent(event_id, type, event_time, received_time, advertiser_id,
        campaign_id, creative_id, publisher_id, impression_id,
        user_token, country, cost_micros, currency, schema_version,
        signature, source_region)
Aggregate(key_dimensions, window_start, window_size, impressions,
          clicks, conversions, spend_micros, revision, updated_at)
Attribution(impression_id, click_event_id, policy_version, decision, reason)
Statement(statement_id, account_id, date, currency, amount_micros,
          input_manifest_hash, policy_version, status)
Adjustment(adjustment_id, statement_id, amount_micros, reason, evidence_uri)

event_id is generated at the edge from source ID plus event type, or accepted from a trusted producer. A signed impression token carries immutable campaign, creative, publisher, price, expiry, and nonce. It prevents a compromised client from inventing a high-value click. Raw objects are partitioned by received date/hour/region, with event-time metadata in manifests so late partitions remain discoverable.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/events
Idempotency-Key: 01J...
{ "type":"CLICK", "eventId":"...", "eventTime":"...", "impressionToken":"..." }

GET /v1/reports?advertiserId=a1&from=...&to=...&groupBy=campaign,hour
GET /v1/statements/{statementId}
POST /internal/replays { "manifest":"s3://...", "codeVersion":"v42", "sink":"shadow" }

The event endpoint returns 202 Accepted after durable log replication, not after aggregation. Invalid signatures return 401; syntactic errors return 400; overload returns 429 before acceptance. Reports use opaque pagination tokens containing the query sort key and snapshot revision. Producers send batches with per-item outcomes to amortize network overhead.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  SDK[Ad SDK and servers] --> Edge[Regional collectors]
  Edge --> Log[(Partitioned event log)]
  Log --> Validate[Validation and dedupe]
  Validate --> Stream[Event-time aggregation]
  Validate --> Raw[(Immutable object store)]
  Stream --> RT[(Real-time OLAP)]
  Raw --> Batch[Daily canonical recompute]
  Batch --> Bills[(Statements and adjustments)]
  API[Reporting API] --> RT
  API --> Bills
    subgraph LiveLane[Live reporting]
      Stream
      RT
    end
    subgraph CanonicalLane[Canonical statements]
      Raw
      Batch
      Bills
    end

Collectors authenticate producers, apply admission control, add received_time, and append to a regional replicated log. Stream processors validate tokens, deduplicate, attribute, and update minute windows. Raw accepted and quarantined records land in object storage. A daily batch recomputes canonical totals independently; it never trusts a sum copied from the streaming projection.

docs.title: 9. Ingestion and attribution
docs.text:
Partition the log primarily by hash(advertiser_id, campaign_id) so campaign-relative order is usually preserved. A click can arrive before its impression due to separate client queues. The attribution operator keeps a bounded pending-click store and impression lookup keyed by impression_id. Signed token validation often permits attribution without waiting for the impression event, but the impression must eventually exist for billing.

The processor emits explicit decisions: ATTRIBUTED, PENDING, EXPIRED, DUPLICATE, or INVALID. Pending clicks expire after the allowed lateness plus attribution window. Reference data such as campaign status and price is consumed as a versioned changelog. Event-time evaluation uses the policy effective at the event, avoiding today's campaign configuration changing yesterday's bill.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Collector
  participant L as Event log
  participant P as Processor
  participant S as State store
  participant O as OLAP sink
  C->>L: append click(event_id, event_time)
  L-->>C: replicated offset
  L->>P: at-least-once delivery
  P->>S: begin atomic dedupe and effect transaction
  alt first observation
    P->>S: resolve impression and policy
    P->>S: commit seen ID, state and output intent together
    P->>O: relay idempotent aggregate effect
  else duplicate
    P->>S: resume any committed unpublished output
  end

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: event time and revisions
docs.text:
The dedupe marker, attribution/bucket changes, and durable output intent commit together. Marking an event seen before recording its output loses the effect if the processor crashes between the two. Revision sinks receive full replacement aggregates, or deltas with unique effect IDs; skipping older delta revisions is not equivalent to applying their contributions.

Mobile clients can be offline, clocks can be wrong, and inter-region links can lag. Each source partition advances a monotonic watermark from its observed progress and lateness policy, for example maximum valid observed event time minus an out-of-order allowance. A downstream operator generally takes the minimum watermark of active inputs. Idle-input exclusion must be explicit; a resumed source can then produce late events. A minute window emits when the watermark passes its end. Events up to 24 hours late revise the dashboard aggregate; later records go to a correction stream for batch handling.

Never drop merely because a producer timestamp is old. First validate it against token issuance and receipt bounds. A wildly future timestamp is quarantined. Each aggregate upsert carries (window_key, computation_version, revision); the sink applies only a newer revision. Consumers can show a provisional badge until the daily close.

Session windows are unnecessary: reporting uses fixed UTC minute/hour/day windows, while an advertiser's local day is a query or statement-calendar concern. Daylight-saving transitions therefore do not create ambiguous storage buckets.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: aggregation and hot keys
docs.text:
A celebrity campaign can dominate traffic. Directly partitioning only by campaign creates a hot task. Use two-stage aggregation: edge or first-stage processors aggregate by (campaign, minute, random_shard); a second stage merges shards. The random shard derives from event_id, making replay deterministic. Very low-volume dimensions bypass excessive sharding.

State stores retain dedupe IDs for at least maximum retry plus lateness. A compacted durable topic checkpoints aggregate updates; local RocksDB-like state is rebuildable. Backpressure propagates to collectors, which spool durably and shed untrusted debug events before paid traffic. Autoscaling reacts to input bytes, consumer lag, state write latency, and hot-partition skew, not CPU alone.

Common report keys are written to a distributed OLAP store sorted by tenant and time. High-cardinality fields such as raw user token are forbidden report dimensions. Approximate sketches can estimate unique reach, but billing counts remain exact after dedupe.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: canonical billing and reconciliation
docs.text:
After a 24-hour soft close, a batch job reads immutable manifests, deduplicates by event ID, joins versioned campaign data, runs the approved fraud model, and writes a candidate statement. It compares totals with streaming results by tenant, campaign, and hour. Differences over thresholds block finalization; differences under thresholds remain explained metrics, not silently ignored.

Maintain a durable billed-event identity registry across statement dates, not just a per-day dedupe set: a retry received tomorrow must not become tomorrow's new charge. The registry and finalization commit atomically or through a recoverable staged protocol with one authoritative owner. The statement stores input manifest hashes, code and policy versions, row counts, and amount. Finalization is a transactional state change from CANDIDATE to FINAL. Later valid events or fraud discoveries create debit or credit adjustments in the next cycle. Reprocessing first targets a shadow namespace; promotion swaps a version pointer rather than adding deltas into production and risking double count.

flowchart TD
  Raw[Immutable daily manifests] --> Recompute[Deterministic recompute]
  Recompute --> Candidate[Candidate totals]
  Live[Streaming totals] --> Compare{Within explained tolerance?}
  Candidate --> Compare
  Compare -->|yes| Final[Immutable statement]
  Compare -->|no| Hold[Hold and investigate]
  Late[Late or corrected evidence] --> Adj[Adjustment]
  Final --> Adj

docs.title: 13. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Log partitions are spread by campaign plus shard; raw data is time/region partitioned and compacted into healthy object sizes. OLAP data is tenant/time distributed, with campaign clustering for pruning. Tenant quotas stop one advertiser's broad query from exhausting the cluster. A query planner caps date range, dimensions, and estimated scanned bytes.

Regional collectors continue during WAN isolation. Their logs replicate asynchronously to a home analytics region. Globally duplicated events retain the same ID and collapse downstream. We avoid synchronous global writes on ingestion because availability and latency matter more than instant global dashboards. Statement finalization occurs in one elected control region with fenced leases.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text: The dashboard is eventually consistent and revision-aware. Statement metadata and finalization are strongly consistent. Dedupe is layered: collector batch IDs reduce retries, stream state removes event duplicates, and sink revision checks prevent duplicate effects. Retention expiry means extremely late duplicate events may reappear in streaming views, but canonical batch dedupe over the billing horizon corrects them before charging.

docs.title: 15. Reliability and failure modes
docs.text:
• Collector crash before acknowledgement causes producer retry; event ID dedupes it.
  • Processor crash restores checkpointed offsets and state, then re-emits revisions safely.
  • OLAP outage accumulates a durable output topic; freshness degrades while ingestion continues.
  • Poison records enter a bounded quarantine with reason and encrypted payload reference.
  • Reference-data lag pauses affected campaign partitions rather than evaluating with unknown policy.
  • Object-store manifest corruption blocks billing and is detected through checksums and independent counts.
  • Replay cannot write the live namespace until validation and an audited promotion.

Disaster recovery continuously copies raw objects and log segments cross-region. Recovery objectives are RPO under five minutes for dashboards, a separately measured cross-region accepted-event RPO of up to five minutes under normal replication lag, and RTO under one hour. A WAN outage can exceed that RPO; enforce an acknowledgement lag bound or explicitly widen the objective. Regional acknowledgement alone does not guarantee that every accepted event survives regional destruction. Restore drills prove checkpoints can rebuild, not merely that backups exist.

docs.title: 16. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text:
Use mTLS for server producers, rotating SDK credentials, signed short-lived impression tokens, tenant-scoped authorization, encryption in transit and at rest, and field-level protection for user tokens. Minimize user data: rotating pseudonymous identifiers are enough for fraud and reach. Retention and deletion operate on identity mapping where legally required; aggregate billing records remain under financial retention policy.

Rate limits combine producer, publisher, campaign, IP reputation, and device signals. Fraud detection flags click farms, impossible click latency, repeated nonces, and publisher spikes. Models produce versioned decisions with explainable reason codes. Administrative replay and statement actions require dual control and immutable audit logs.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure accepted, rejected, duplicated, quarantined, and attributed events; end-to-end event-time freshness; watermark delay; partition skew; state size; checkpoint duration; sink revision conflicts; and stream-versus-batch monetary variance. Trace a sampled event_id from collector offset through attribution to aggregate and statement evidence. Per-tenant dashboards avoid global averages hiding a large customer outage.

Tests include property tests for dedupe and window boundaries, deterministic replay golden sets, malformed-token fuzzing, skew and clock simulations, processor kill/restart tests, OLAP outage tests, and reconciliation fixtures with late and duplicated clicks. Canary code writes shadow aggregates and compares them before rollout. A production readiness test sustains 3x peak while one availability zone is unavailable.

docs.title: 18. Important tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Updating counters in a transactional database is simpler, but cannot absorb write volume, late revisions, or flexible dimensions.
  • Streaming-only billing is faster, but couples money to checkpoint and sink defects. Independent batch recomputation provides a correctness boundary.
