  • Global synchronous dedupe gives immediate convergence, but adds latency and an availability dependency. Stable IDs plus asynchronous regional processing are preferable.
  • Full cubes make reads cheap but create unbounded write amplification. Precompute popular dimensions and retain raw columnar facts.
  • A longer lateness window improves completeness but increases state and delays finality. Product-facing provisional data and explicit financial close separate these needs.

docs.title: 19. Final design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  subgraph Regions
    E1[Collector A] --> K1[(Regional log A)]
    E2[Collector B] --> K2[(Regional log B)]
  end
  K1 --> P[Validated event stream]
  K2 --> P
  P --> W[Watermarked sharded windows]
  W --> Q[(OLAP projections)]
  P --> R[(Raw immutable archive)]
  R --> C[Canonical billing job]
  C --> X{Reconciliation gate}
  X --> F[(Final statements)]
  X --> H[Investigation queue]
  Q --> A[Reporting API]
  F --> A

The selected design deliberately has two answer paths: low-latency, revisable projections for product use and deterministic, manifest-backed statements for money. Stable identities and idempotent effects make at-least-once infrastructure safe. Event-time watermarks, sharded aggregation, and regional buffering handle the actual distribution problems rather than assuming ordered traffic.

docs.title: 20. Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. How would you change attribution from signed impression ID to a 7-day user-level model?
  2. What happens when a campaign becomes a single hot key at 500,000 events/second?
  3. How do you prove a replay did not double charge an advertiser?
  4. Where is strong consistency necessary, and where is it harmful?
  5. How would privacy deletion interact with immutable billing evidence?
  6. How would you detect a stalled watermark caused by one idle partition?
  7. Which discrepancies should automatically block daily close?

docs.title: 21. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should clarify dashboard versus billing accuracy, estimate throughput and storage, choose a log and stream processor, explain dedupe, event-time windows, sharding, storage, and common failures. They should not claim that a broker magically provides end-to-end exactly once.

An L6 candidate should define policy versioning and financial finality, isolate tenants, reason about skew and backpressure, design independent reconciliation and safe replay, choose a multi-region ownership model, and connect SLOs to overload and recovery. They should identify organizational controls around fraud models and statement promotion, not only components.

docs.title: 22. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Accept signed impression and click events through regional collectors and acknowledge only after a replicated log append. Preserve immutable raw events. Process at least once, deduplicate by stable event ID, resolve clicks against versioned impression and campaign data, and aggregate by event-time windows. Watermarks close initial results; late events publish higher revisions. Two-stage deterministic sharding protects hot campaigns.

Serve recent reports from tenant/time-partitioned OLAP projections. Treat them as provisional. Each day, independently recompute billable totals from immutable manifests, compare them with streaming output, and finalize an immutable statement through a reconciliation gate. Corrections become adjustments, never statement mutation. Regional buffering favors available ingestion; one fenced control region owns close. Security centers on signed tokens, scoped access, privacy minimization, and audited administration. The essential idea is not exactly-once transport: it is reproducible inputs, versioned rules, idempotent effects, and explicit financial finality.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design the request-time platform that selects and serves an ad. We will define auction and pacing invariants, budget latency, separate control and data planes, and then explore targeting indexes, auctions, frequency caps, event-time feedback, partitioning, failures, privacy, and billing integration.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
When a page or app requests an ad, eligible campaigns compete. The winner must satisfy targeting, policy, budget, pacing, frequency, and creative constraints. The response includes a signed impression token used by measurement. Serving must remain fast when reporting is delayed, but it must not knowingly overspend or serve blocked creatives.

Scope includes campaign configuration, candidate retrieval, auction, pacing, creative selection, and impression/click emission. Creative media storage, advertiser billing aggregation, and sophisticated conversion attribution are external systems. We support CPM and CPC bids with a normalized expected-value auction.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
• Create/version campaigns, creatives, targeting, bids, schedules, and budgets.
  • Select an eligible ad for request context and return creative metadata.
  • Enforce campaign/account budgets, pacing, and frequency caps.
  • Emit signed impression and click evidence.
  • Apply policy blocks rapidly and provide explainable decisions.
  • Reconcile serving reservations with accepted impressions and billable events.

Peak is 5 million ad requests/second globally. Selection p99 is under 50 ms at 99.99% availability; control changes propagate in 60 seconds and emergency blocks in 10 seconds. Hard budget enforcement uses escrow with no overspend of the allocated limit. Separately specify the maximum stale spend after a budget reduction, bounded by outstanding grants, or explicitly choose a probabilistic budget with a quantified overspend target.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. A served creative is eligible under one immutable campaign/policy snapshot.
  2. Every response has a globally unique opportunity/impression token with authenticated campaign, price, creative, publisher, timestamp, and nonce.
  3. Budget consumption is idempotent by opportunity ID and bounded under regional concurrency.
  4. Frequency-cap decisions use documented staleness; duplicate impressions do not consume twice.
  5. Blocked campaigns/creatives disappear within the emergency SLO.
  6. Billable totals derive from accepted measurement events, while serving reservations are reconciled and released.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
At 5 million requests/second and 1 KB request/response, edge traffic is about 10 GB/s bidirectionally. Evaluating all one million active campaigns is impossible. If targeting retrieves 1,000 candidates and local filters reduce to 100 scored bids, fleets perform 500 million simple scoring operations/second.

Five million impressions/second at 300 compressed bytes produce 130 TB/day; measurement must batch and archive aggressively. A global per-impression budget write would require millions of coordinated writes/second, so budget authority allocates bounded regional/shard tokens. Frequency state for 500 million active users and hundreds of campaigns must be sparse and TTL-bound.

docs.title: 6. Data model
docs.text:
Campaign(campaign_id, advertiser_id, objective, bid_minor, currency,
         budget_minor, schedule, targeting_version, state, version)
Creative(creative_id, campaign_id, media_ref, policy_status, version)
ServingSnapshot(version, campaigns, targeting_index_ref, policy_hash, created_at)
BudgetGrant(grant_id, campaign_id, serving_cell, amount_minor, spent, expires_at)
AdOpportunity(opportunity_id, request_time, publisher, placement, context_hash)
Decision(opportunity_id, campaign_id, creative_id, score, clearing_price_minor,
         snapshot_version, grant_id, reason_codes)
Measurement(event_id, opportunity_id, type, event_time, received_time, signature)
FrequencyCounter(subject_token, campaign_id, bucket, count, revision)

Campaign configuration is versioned. Serving snapshots are immutable. Decisions and measurements are append-only. Reporting budget and frequency counters are projections with stable effect IDs; the grant ledger and active reservations are authoritative enforcement state.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/ad-requests
{ "opportunityId":"o1", "placement":"banner", "publisherId":"p1",
  "context":{"country":"IN","topics":["sports"]}, "consent":"..." }

200 { "creativeUrl":"...", "impressionToken":"signed...", "ttlMs":30000 }

PUT /v1/campaigns/{id} If-Match: "version-12"
POST /internal/policy/tombstones
POST /v1/measurement/events

Ad request retries with the same opportunity return the same cached decision when valid, avoiding double reservation. Configuration uses optimistic versions. Measurement acknowledges after durable log append and returns per-item validation status.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Adv[Advertiser UI] --> Control[Campaign control plane]
  Control --> Compile[Validate and compile snapshots]
  Compile --> Dist[Snapshot distribution]
  User[Publisher/app] --> Edge[Regional ad server]
  Dist --> Edge
  Edge --> Index[Local targeting index]
  Edge --> Pace[Local pacing/budget grants]
  Edge --> Auction[Auction + creative choice]
  Auction --> User
  Auction --> Log[(Decision/impression log)]
  Log --> Feedback[Event-time feedback]
  Feedback --> Control

The control plane validates campaigns, scans creatives, builds targeting indexes, allocates budget grants, and atomically distributes signed snapshots. The data plane is local and read-heavy; it performs no cross-region request-time calls.

docs.title: 9. Request-time selection
docs.text:
The edge validates publisher and consent, derives coarse context, and queries inverted indexes such as country, placement, device, topic, and schedule. Intersect the most selective posting lists, then filter campaign status, creative policy, grant availability, and frequency. A pre-ranker retains likely winners; the auction computes value and chooses a creative.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant P as Publisher
  participant S as Ad server
  participant I as Targeting index
  participant B as Budget/frequency state
  participant L as Event log
  P->>S: ad request(opportunity_id)
  S->>I: retrieve eligible candidates
  S->>S: auction selects tentative winner and price
  S->>B: reserve priced liability by opportunity ID
  B-->>S: reservation accepted or no budget
  alt reservation accepted
    S->>S: sign token
    S->>L: durable decision/impression intent
    S-->>P: creative + token
  else reservation rejected
    S-->>P: no-fill or bounded retry with another candidate
  end

The server enforces a 50 ms deadline: 5 ms edge/auth, 10 ms retrieval, 10 ms filters/features, 5 ms auction, 5 ms reservation/signing, and margin. If personalized state is late, serve contextual ads. If policy state is unknown, exclude affected candidates. If no safe candidate remains, return house ad or no-fill.

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: auction and pricing
docs.text:
Normalize bids to expected value per thousand impressions: CPM bid directly, CPC bid times predicted click probability times 1,000. Quality, policy, and user-experience terms can adjust ranking, but advertiser-visible charging rules must be stable and versioned. A generalized second-price-like auction charges the minimum value needed to beat the runner-up, bounded by bid and floor; first-price is operationally simpler and increasingly common.

Record candidates' coarse rejection reasons, winning score inputs, clearing price, model version, and snapshot. Do not log sensitive raw user features. Deterministic tie-breaking by hashed opportunity and campaign makes retries stable. Offline replay checks pricing arithmetic and counterfactual policy changes.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: budget and pacing
docs.text:
A globally linearizable campaign counter would add WAN latency and become a hot key. A budget authority debits a durable unallocated allowance when issuing monetary grants to regional cells. Maintain settled_spend + outstanding_granted_liability + unallocated <= campaign_budget. A cell atomically reserves a priced liability from its grant using opportunity ID. Grant expiry stops new reservations but does not erase impressions or clicks already authorized: reclaim only a verified unspent remainder after the cell is fenced and its accepted liabilities are reconciled. Unknown usage remains charged against the grant. Correct escrow prevents overspend of the allocated budget; outstanding grants instead bound stale spending after a budget reduction or emergency stop. Reissuing an entire expired grant without that proof can overspend repeatedly, not merely once by a fixed grant bound.

Pacing compares expected spend with a time-of-day curve. The server probabilistically admits a campaign using a deterministic hash of opportunity ID, avoiding synchronized bursts. Feedback updates observed spend, but grant reservation protects hard budget even when event aggregation lags. A hard CPC budget reserves the maximum charge still possible from the signed opportunity, not merely predicted click probability times price. Expected-value reservations improve utilization but provide only a probabilistic overspend target. Release liability only after its attribution/admissible-lateness window closes or authenticated evidence proves it cannot bill; late bills after close require an explicit adjustment policy.

flowchart TD
  Budget[Campaign daily budget] --> Auth[Budget authority]
  Auth --> G1[Cell A grant]
  Auth --> G2[Cell B grant]
  Auth --> G3[Cell C grant]
  G1 --> R1[Idempotent reservations]
  G2 --> R2[Idempotent reservations]
  G3 --> R3[Idempotent reservations]
  R1 --> Rec[Measurement reconciliation]
  R2 --> Rec
  R3 --> Rec
  Rec --> Auth

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: frequency and event time
docs.text:
Frequency caps may mean at most three impressions/user/campaign/day. A strict global counter is expensive and leaks availability across regions. Route a pseudonymous subject to a home cell where possible and atomically reserve cap capacity by opportunity ID before returning the ad, then settle or release it from measurement and expiry. Counting only delayed impressions permits an unbounded burst of decisions before feedback arrives. During roaming or partitions, allocate small cap grants by region or choose conservative exclusion. Document bounded overexposure.

Counters use fixed UTC event-time buckets with TTL. Signed tokens prevent invented timestamps. Duplicate measurement events dedupe by event ID/opportunity. Late impressions revise analytics but generally do not retract an already served ad; they affect future cap state if within the live window. Processing-time lag, watermark delay, and reservation age are separate metrics.

docs.title: 13. Control-plane publication
docs.text:
Campaign updates pass schema checks, budget authorization, targeting validation, creative malware/policy scans, and referential checks. A compiler produces a signed immutable snapshot and delta. Cells download, verify, build indexes off-path, then atomically switch pointers. They report version coverage. Emergency tombstones use a priority channel and are checked in a small local deny set before the main index and before returning a cached decision. A freshness lease shorter than the 10-second removal bound makes a disconnected cell stop affected paid serving; push alone cannot enforce the bound. Snapshot rollback preserves the newest tombstone generation.

Snapshots permit rollback and request-level version pinning. If a delta is missed, a cell fetches a complete snapshot. Unknown versions never partially merge. This separation keeps advertiser CRUD failures away from ad-request latency.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Traffic routes to nearby serving cells. Within a cell, requests distribute by opportunity hash; campaign grants shard large budgets among workers. Targeting indexes partition by market/placement and replicate for reads. Popular broad campaigns appear in many index partitions, so compilation compresses posting lists and caches common intersections.

Decision logs partition by opportunity ID; feedback aggregates by salted campaign ID to avoid hot campaigns. Control data partitions by advertiser but global account budgets use one authority. Backpressure drops optional debug traces first, returns no-fill before violating policy, and preserves accepted measurement in durable local spool.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Campaign editing and account budget allocation require strong control-plane consistency. Serving is snapshot-consistent per request, though cells may run adjacent versions within propagation SLO. Emergency policy blocks are stronger via push tombstones. Budget reservation is strongly consistent within its grant and globally bounded, not globally instant.

Opportunity ID deduplicates decision and reservation; event ID deduplicates measurement; aggregate sinks use revisions. At-least-once logs are expected. Billing consumes validated measurement and independently reconciles it with decisions and reservations rather than charging from mutable serving counters.

docs.title: 16. Reliability and multi-region strategy
docs.text:
• Index corruption fails checksum and leaves previous snapshot active.
  • Control-plane outage does not stop cells until snapshot/grants expire.
  • Budget authority outage spends only existing grants, then no-fills affected campaigns.
  • Measurement-log outage spools durably; if spool is full, stop paid serving rather than lose billable evidence.
  • Model timeout uses bid and contextual quality fallback.
  • Region loss fences new reservations and reconciles outstanding liabilities before reallocating a verified unspent remainder. Expiry alone does not prove money is unspent.

Campaign control has a single logical leader with replicated storage. Serving is active-active. Grant epochs fence stale cells; rapid disaster reallocation trades availability against overspend bound. Raw decision and measurement logs replicate for billing and audit.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse
docs.text:
Authenticate publishers and advertisers, authorize tenant-scoped changes, encrypt data, sign snapshots and impression tokens with rotated keys, and audit configuration and budget changes. Minimize identity through rotating pseudonymous tokens and consent-aware targeting. Never target forbidden sensitive categories.

Defend against click spam, impression laundering, domain spoofing, creative malware, budget-drain attacks, and scraper traffic. Use ads.txt-like publisher authorization, nonce replay detection, rate limits, supply-quality scoring, and separate fraud adjudication. Emergency policy controls require dual approval except pre-authorized kill switches.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure ad latency stages, fill rate, candidates before/after each filter, snapshot age/coverage, tombstone removal latency, grant remaining/expiry, pacing error, overspend bound, reservation-to-impression mismatch, frequency overage, model fallback, log spool depth, and event-time freshness. Slice by region, publisher, campaign tier, and snapshot.

Tests cover deterministic auctions and rounding, opportunity retry, concurrent grant exhaustion, snapshot atomicity, stale tombstones, late/duplicate impressions, hot campaigns, authority partition, full spools, and region fencing. Replay sampled auctions against recorded snapshots. Property tests prove spend never exceeds issued grants and one opportunity reserves once. Shadow snapshots compare eligibility and spend before rollout.

docs.title: 19. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Request-time global budget writes add coordination latency; durable escrow grants preserve the allocated budget while bounding stale spend after a reduction or stop. Explicit emergency allowances add separate slack.
  • Precomputed campaign matches are fast but explode across context combinations; inverted indexes plus local filtering are more flexible.
  • Strict global frequency caps reduce overexposure but require identity and coordination; home-cell state with bounded grants balances privacy and latency.
  • Serving from stale snapshots improves availability, but stale policy is unacceptable; separate ordinary expiry from priority tombstones.
  • Charging on reservation is simple but bills unrendered ads; charge validated measurement and reconcile reservations.

docs.title: 20. Final architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  CP[Versioned campaign control] --> SC[Snapshot compiler]
  SC --> Cells[Active-active serving cells]
  BA[Budget authority + grant epochs] --> Cells
  Kill[Priority policy tombstones] --> Cells
  Cells --> IDX[Local targeting and models]
  IDX --> OUT[Creative + signed token]
  Cells --> EV[(Decision/measurement logs)]
  EV --> AGG[Event-time reporting]
  EV --> REC[Reservation/billing reconciliation]
  REC --> BA

docs.title: 21. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. How is global overspend bounded without a global request-time counter?
  2. What is the behavior when measurement cannot be durably recorded?
  3. How do campaign blocks outrun normal snapshot publication?
  4. How are CPC and CPM bids compared?
  5. What event time governs frequency caps?
  6. How do retries avoid a second auction and reservation?
  7. How would stronger privacy constraints change targeting?

docs.title: 22. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should budget latency, retrieve candidates through indexes, filter and auction locally, define budget/frequency state, emit measurement, and discuss idempotency and failure. An L6 candidate should quantify grant overshoot, separate control/data planes and emergency policy, define snapshot rollout, event-time reconciliation, privacy boundaries, hot-campaign handling, and regional fencing.

docs.title: 23. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Compile validated campaign configuration into signed immutable snapshots and distribute them to active-active serving cells. For each request, use local inverted indexes to retrieve candidates, filter targeting, policy, budget, and frequency, pre-rank, run a versioned auction, reserve spend by opportunity ID, and return a creative with a signed impression token. No WAN dependency sits in the 50 ms path.

A budget authority durably debits escrow grants before issue; outstanding accepted liabilities remain allocated until reconciled, even after grant expiry. This preserves the allocated budget; outstanding grants bound stale spend after a budget reduction, not an excuse to reissue unknown usage. Event-time measurement deduplicates signed opportunities and reconciles valid impressions against reservations; billing uses those validated events, not serving counters. Frequency uses TTL buckets and documented regional staleness. Atomic snapshot swaps and a separate priority tombstone path balance availability with policy safety. During uncertainty the platform serves contextual or house ads, and stops paid serving before losing billable evidence.

docs.title: Design a Change Data Capture Platform
Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify source databases, log access, initial snapshots, ordering, schema evolution, delivery targets, and latency. State source-position and effect invariants before choosing a stream. Begin with one connector reading a durable database log into an immutable change stream. Then add snapshot handoff, transaction metadata, schema registry, partitioning, sink idempotency, backpressure, failover, and fleet operations.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Change data capture (CDC) converts committed source-database mutations into ordered events for search, caches, analytics, replication, and integration. It is not dual writing from applications: the database commit log is the authority. Consumers need row changes plus enough transaction, schema, and source-position context to replay and reconcile.

The platform supports relational write-ahead/binlogs first. Document stores can fit if they expose durable ordered change positions. It does not promise exactly-once network delivery or make arbitrary sinks transactional with a source database. It provides replayable events and protocols for idempotent business effects.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Register sources and selected tables with credentials, policy, and ownership.
  • Perform a consistent initial snapshot without gaps, allowing identifiable overlap duplicates at handoff.
  • Stream inserts, updates, deletes, transaction boundaries, and source positions.
  • Preserve required ordering and expose schema changes before dependent row events.
  • Deliver to durable topics and managed sinks with replay, backfill, pause, and reset.
  • Detect log loss, divergence, poison records, and silent data gaps.
  • Sustain millions of changes/s with low seconds-level end-to-end latency.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every emitted row event corresponds to a committed source mutation; rolled-back transactions are never published as committed changes.
  2. Within the declared ordering scope, source positions are monotonic and gaps are detected rather than silently skipped.
  3. Snapshot plus log replay covers the state at the snapshot boundary and every committed transition after that boundary, not historical transitions predating the snapshot; overlap duplicates are allowed and identified.
  4. A row event references a schema version sufficient to decode before/after data, and that schema is published first.
  5. Connector checkpoint never advances beyond durably published data.
  6. A stable event identity lets sinks apply one effective mutation despite retries and redelivery.
  7. Deletes remain representable through tombstones until every contracted consumer retention/replay window closes.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 10,000 source databases, one million tables, five million row changes/s peak, and 2 KB average event including before/after images: 10 GB/s ingress before replication. Seven days at that sustained rate is 6.048 PB logical, or 18.144 PB at three copies before compression; use average rate for retained bytes and peak for capture capacity. Compressed long retention moves to object storage. A single hot source can emit 500,000 changes/s, while thousands of idle connectors dominate connection and fleet overhead.

Latency budget might allocate 200 ms source-log availability, 300 ms read/decode, 500 ms durable publish, and one second sink application at p99. Large transactions violate per-event assumptions: a million-row transaction must stream bounded chunks while retaining transaction identity and atomic visibility policy. Snapshot throughput is separately capped so it does not overload production databases or starve live logs.

docs.title: Core Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Source(source_id, engine, endpoint_ref, log_identity, policy, owner_region)
CaptureAssignment(source_id, connector_id, epoch, lease_until)
SourcePosition(source_id, log_file_or_term, offset_or_lsn, transaction_id)
SchemaVersion(subject, version, fields, keys, compatibility, source_ddl_position)
ChangeEvent(event_id, source_id, table_id, primary_key, operation,
            before, after, schema_version, transaction, position, commit_time)
Checkpoint(source_id, assignment_epoch, durable_position, snapshot_state)
SnapshotRun(run_id, source_id, tables, low_watermark, high_watermark, state)
SinkCheckpoint(sink_id, input_partition, position, effect_token)
ReconciliationRun(source_id, scope, source_digest, target_digest, state)

Source logs and source database state are external canonical truth. The CDC platform's immutable raw event stream, schemas, and durable checkpoints are canonical evidence of capture. Search indexes, transformed topics, sink tables, lag views, and reconciliation summaries are projections.

docs.title: APIs and Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/sources                              {engine, credential_ref, tables, policy}
POST /v1/sources/{id}:snapshot                Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
POST /v1/sources/{id}:pause
POST /v1/sources/{id}:resume                  {expected_checkpoint}
POST /v1/sinks                                {input, connector_type, mapping, semantics}
POST /v1/replays                              {stream, start_position, end_position, target}
GET  /v1/sources/{id}/status
GET  /v1/events?source=...&table=...&after_position=...&limit=...

Administrative resets require expected current position, impact preview, authorization, and audit. Event envelopes are versioned and include source identity, stable table identity, schema reference, source position, transaction metadata, operation, before/after values subject to policy, and ingestion timestamps. Pagination uses source or stream cursors, never offset-based database queries.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DB[(Source database)] --> Log[WAL/binlog reader]
    DB --> Snap[Snapshot workers]
    Control[Connector control plane] --> Log
    Control --> Snap
    Log --> Decode[Transaction and schema decoder]
    Snap --> Decode
    Decode --> Raw[(Durable partitioned change log)]
    Decode --> Check[(Checkpoint store)]
    Raw --> Transform[Policy/format transforms]
    Transform --> Topics[(Consumer topics)]
    Topics --> Sinks[Idempotent sink workers]
    Raw --> Archive[Immutable replay archive]
    Reconcile[Reconciliation service] --> DB
    Reconcile --> Sinks

The data plane reads, decodes, and publishes. The control plane assigns connectors with fenced epochs, manages schemas and credentials, and orchestrates snapshots/replays. Raw capture is retained independently of sink transformations so consumers can recover from mapping bugs.

docs.title: Log Capture
docs.text: A connector authenticates using least-privilege replication credentials, verifies source log identity/timeline, and starts at its durable checkpoint. It groups records by transaction, discards rollback, publishes schema records before row records, then durably publishes row/transaction events. Only after broker acknowledgement does it advance checkpoint. On restart it rereads overlap; stable event IDs make this safe.

docs.title: Initial Snapshot
docs.text: For engines supporting MVCC, start a repeatable-read snapshot and record log low watermark L. Scan tables in primary-key ranges while concurrently retaining log changes after L. After snapshot chunks publish, emit a snapshot-complete barrier and replay buffered/log events in position order. Consumers deduplicate overlap and switch from snapshot image to live semantics at the barrier.

docs.title: Sink Application
docs.text: Sinks consume batches, decode pinned schema, and apply desired state. An upsert sink compares source position per key; older or duplicate events cannot overwrite newer state. A ledger-like sink inserts unique event IDs. After effects commit, it records input checkpoint transactionally where the sink supports it; otherwise deduplication must be atomic with the target effect, or the target must accept a stable idempotency key. A separate seen-ID table alone cannot bridge the crash between marking seen and applying a non-idempotent effect.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Snapshot-to-Log Handoff
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant D as Source DB
    participant S as Snapshot scanner
    participant L as Log reader
    participant B as Change stream
    O->>D: open consistent snapshot and obtain L
    O->>L: retain/read log after L
    O->>S: scan PK ranges at snapshot
    S->>B: snapshot rows(run, chunk, key)
    L->>L: retain live events(position > L), not yet visible
    S-->>O: all chunks checksummed
    O->>B: snapshot complete barrier
    L->>B: release ordered live stream

The exact database mechanism varies: exported snapshots, repeatable-read transactions, backup coordinates, or lock-assisted boundaries. The invariant is common: identify a log position consistent with the snapshot and retain logs until scanning catches up. A snapshot transaction cannot remain open for days without source impact; split into chunks only if the engine offers a consistent exported snapshot or use incremental snapshotting.

Incremental snapshotting injects low/high watermark markers into the log, scans a key range, buffers changes for that range, then reconciles snapshot rows with buffered events. Repeat for ranges. This limits source locks and restart cost but produces controlled overlap. Every chunk records key bounds, row count, checksum, schema version, and completion state. Retries rewrite the same snapshot identities.

Deletes during a snapshot are the classic gap: a row visible in snapshot may be deleted in the log. Applying snapshot first and ordered delete later converges. If a live update arrives before a delayed snapshot row at a sink, source-position comparison or phase barrier prevents the old image from winning.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Ordering and Transactions
docs.text:
Database logs usually provide total order per server/shard, not globally across a distributed database. Preserve and document that scope. A single log reader processes source positions monotonically; the output stream partitions by source shard to retain order. Repartitioning by table or primary key improves parallelism but loses cross-key transaction order unless an envelope and barrier protocol reconstruct it.

flowchart TD
    Log[Ordered source records] --> Buffer[Bounded transaction buffer]
    Buffer --> Size{Transaction bounded?}
    Size -->|yes| Tx[BEGIN, row events, COMMIT envelope]
    Size -->|no| Chunks[Spilled chunks with tx id and sequence]
    Tx --> Stream[Ordered source partition]
    Chunks --> Stream
    Stream --> Consumer{Needs atomic transaction visibility?}
    Consumer -->|yes| Stage[Stage until COMMIT then publish/apply]
    Consumer -->|no| Apply[Apply rows idempotently]

Large transactions spill encrypted chunks rather than exhaust connector memory. Consumers requiring atomic visibility stage chunks and expose only after commit. Other consumers may apply committed transaction rows progressively; speculative chunks read before source commit must remain invisible for every consumer and be discarded on rollback. Include a commit marker and complete chunk manifest so missing chunks cannot be mistaken for a completed transaction. Cross-source causal order does not exist unless applications provide correlation and a higher-level sequencer. Commit timestamp is not a unique cursor and clocks can skew.

Failover to a source replica must verify timeline/log identity and a common durable position. A promoted primary may use a new term. Position becomes (source_log_identity, term, offset), and divergence is quarantined for operator choice rather than merged by timestamp.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Schema Evolution and DDL
docs.text:
Where the engine exposes DDL, the decoder tracks it in source-log order and publishes a schema version before row events requiring it. This is not portable: PostgreSQL logical decoding does not emit a general DDL change stream, as the Debezium PostgreSQL connector documentation explains (accessed 2026-09-08). Its adapter must obtain decode metadata through supported relation/schema mechanisms and coordinate unsupported changes with migrations; it cannot promise a complete DDL audit from row events. Stable table and column identities are preferable to names; rename is not drop-plus-add when the source exposes identity. Events reference schema version and may include self-describing type metadata for long-term replay.

Compatibility policy differs by consumer. Adding nullable columns is commonly backward compatible; narrowing types, changing primary keys, or reinterpreting precision is not. Unsupported DDL pauses only the affected table/source partition, raises an actionable status, and retains logs. Skipping malformed DDL while decoding later rows risks silent corruption and is forbidden.

Online schema changes may create shadow tables, triggers, and swaps. Connector adapters recognize engine-specific patterns and map them to one logical table identity under explicit rules. During migration, dual schemas can coexist. Raw events preserve source representation; downstream normalization is versioned and replayable. Sensitive columns are filtered or tokenized before broad topics, but an encrypted restricted raw stream may remain for authorized recovery.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Exactly-Once Effects and Reconciliation
docs.text:
Exactly-once delivery across database log, broker, connector, network, and arbitrary sink is not credible. Define an event ID from immutable source identity, transaction/position, table, and row sequence. Brokers deliver at least once. A sink creates exactly-once effects through idempotent state transitions.

For a current-state table, store (primary_key, value, source_position) and conditionally upsert only newer positions; deletes write tombstones with positions. For append analytics, enforce unique event ID or merge periodic duplicates. For external APIs, persist an effect record and idempotency key before/reliably with invocation, then reconcile provider outcome. If the target cannot deduplicate, the contract is at-least-once side effects and must say so.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Sink consumer
    participant T as Target DB
    participant Q as Input topic
    Q->>C: batch with event IDs/positions
    C->>T: transaction conditional effects + input checkpoint
    alt commit succeeds, ack lost
        Q->>C: redelivered batch
        C->>T: duplicates/no older position changes
    else known transaction failure
        C->>T: rollback effects and checkpoint, retry same batch
        Note over C,Q: No acknowledgement on failure
    end
    opt target commit confirmed or safely resolved
        C-->>Q: acknowledge committed input prefix
    end

Reconciliation independently compares source and target by key-range counts and order-insensitive hashes at known watermarks. Mismatched ranges subdivide until row-level repair is practical. Deletes require tombstone awareness. Repair emits audited correction events or reruns a snapshot range; operators do not edit checkpoints blindly.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Assign one fenced active reader per source log partition. Shard connectors by source ID, while large sources receive dedicated workers. Raw topics partition by source shard to preserve order; downstream key-partitioned topics trade transaction order for parallel sink application. Include original position in every derived event. Schema topics are compacted and ordered relative to data through dependency barriers.

Hot sources use larger publish batches, compression, zero-copy buffers, and parallel decoding only where sequence can be reassembled. Slow sinks have independent consumer groups and cannot backpressure raw capture until broker/archive retention risk. Snapshot workers rate-limit source CPU, I/O, locks, and replication lag. Fair scheduling prevents a giant backfill from delaying small live sources.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Assignment epochs and checkpoint updates are strongly consistent per source. The connector lease is fenced: stale workers cannot publish into the active source epoch. Checkpoint update follows durable publication, deliberately allowing duplicates after crashes. Schema dependencies are durable before data references. Broker and sink delivery are at least once.

Event IDs survive replay into a new topic. Transform outputs include raw event ID and transform version. Sink checkpoints record both input position and effect semantics. Retention of dedup state must exceed maximum replay, outage, and tombstone windows; otherwise a replay uses a fresh target namespace or full rebuild protocol.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
Connector crash restarts from durable checkpoint and republishes overlap. Source outage freezes at last position. Broker outage stops checkpoint advancement and eventually pressures source-log retention; alerts estimate time-to-log-loss and pause snapshots first. If source logs are deleted before capture, mark a hard gap and require snapshot/reconciliation; never resume as if continuous.

Poison records quarantine with raw bytes, source position, schema, and error under restricted access. Policy decides whether the source partition pauses or emits an explicit gap marker; silent skip is disallowed. Sink outage grows consumer lag independently. Credential expiration, DDL incompatibility, disk spill exhaustion, large transactions, and replica promotion have dedicated states and runbooks.

Recovery restores schemas, raw log segments, connector checkpoints, and assignment epochs, then replays into empty test sinks and reconciles. Overload preserves log capture and raw durability first, then schema publication, live sinks, snapshots, backfills, and optional transforms in that order.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text:
Place capture near each source to avoid WAN latency and preserve residency. Replicate raw change streams and checkpoints to a recovery region according to RPO. Only one region owns a source epoch. Failover validates source connectivity, last durable raw position, replicated stream completeness, and fencing before resume.

Remote sinks consume replicated topics and tolerate bounded lag. For cross-region databases, capture each declared source shard and expose no fictional global order. Control-plane configuration and schemas replicate globally, while credentials remain region-scoped. A regional partition continues only if it can durably retain raw events and cannot conflict with another owner.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text:
Use least-privilege replication users, secret vault references, rotation, mTLS, workload identity, private networking, encryption, per-field policy, and immutable administrative audit. Raw before-images can expose deleted secrets and personal data; classify fields, minimize payloads, tokenize, restrict raw retention, and propagate erasure/retention tombstones under legal policy.

Validate table selection and sink destinations to prevent exfiltration. Sign connector artifacts and schema changes. Sandbox decoders and transforms; bound record, transaction, compression, and nesting sizes. Protect reset/replay APIs with dual approval, dry-run impact, quotas, and destination isolation because an accidental replay can duplicate financial or customer effects.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure source head minus read checkpoint, durable publish lag, end-to-end sink lag, transaction size/spill, duplicate rate, checkpoint age, broker retention margin, snapshot rows/bytes/range checksums, schema block time, tombstone age, sink conflicts, dead letters, reconciliation mismatch, and time-to-log-loss. Use source position and transaction IDs for tracing, not sensitive row values.

Test engine-specific logs with commits, rollback, savepoints, failover terms, DDL, large transactions, and log rotation. Property-test monotonic positions and idempotent sink application. Race snapshot scans with inserts, updates, deletes, and key changes. Inject lost acknowledgements, duplicate/reordered broker records, schema delay, source/broker outages, and stale connector epochs. Regularly reconcile seeded databases and prove deliberate corruption is found and repaired.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Publishing one transaction atomically simplifies consumers but large transactions create latency and memory risk; chunked envelopes preserve boundaries. Partitioning by source preserves transaction order but limits sink parallelism; derived key-partitioned topics make the trade explicit. Full before-images aid audit and transforms but increase privacy and bandwidth. Long raw retention improves recoverability but costs storage and expands data exposure. Trigger-based CDC is portable but burdens source transactions; native logs win where available. Advancing checkpoints after publish causes duplicates but prevents loss, the correct bias.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Sources[(Database logs and snapshots)] --> Readers[Fenced regional connector fleet]
    Control[Assignments, schemas, credentials, policy] --> Readers
    Readers --> Raw[(Immutable ordered raw change streams)]
    Readers --> CP[(Durable source checkpoints)]
    Raw --> Archive[Compressed replay archive]
    Raw --> Transform[Versioned policy transforms]
    Transform --> Derived[(Transaction or key partitioned topics)]
    Derived --> Sink[Idempotent sink adapters]
    Sink --> Targets[(Search, lakehouse, caches, replicas)]
    Recon[Watermarked reconciliation and repair] --> Sources
    Recon --> Targets
    Raw --> DR[Verified regional replica]

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. How do you prove there is no gap between snapshot and log capture?
  2. When may events be repartitioned by primary key?
  3. What happens when a million-row transaction exceeds memory?
  4. How does DDL become visible before dependent row events?
  5. Why does checkpoint-after-publish prefer duplicates over loss?
  6. How can a non-transactional external sink achieve idempotent effects?
  7. How do you detect and recover after source logs are truncated?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should use native logs, explain snapshot handoff, source positions, ordering, schema events, checkpoints, retries, and idempotent sinks. An L6 answer should formalize incremental snapshots, transaction chunking, failover timelines, schema identity, fenced connector epochs, hard-gap operations, watermarked reconciliation, privacy/retention, multi-region ownership, overload priorities, replay governance, and exactly-once effects without claiming exactly-once delivery.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Read committed mutations from the database's durable log, not application dual writes. A fenced connector decodes transaction and schema order, publishes immutable raw events, and advances its checkpoint only after durable acknowledgement; crashes therefore duplicate but do not lose. Initial load opens a consistent snapshot at log position L, scans bounded primary-key chunks while retaining later log records, emits a completion barrier, then releases ordered live changes. Every event carries stable source/log identity, transaction, row sequence, schema version, and before/after values under policy. Preserve source-shard order; repartition derived topics by key only when consumers accept loss of cross-key transaction order. Publish at least once and create exactly-once effects through event-ID uniqueness or source-position conditional upserts. Keep delete tombstones, detect hard gaps, pause on undecodable schema, reconcile source and target at known watermarks, and prioritize raw capture over snapshots and backfills during overload.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify batch versus streaming ingestion, analytical workloads, freshness, governance, and compatibility. State snapshot and schema invariants before naming formats or engines. Begin with immutable columnar files plus a transactional table log and catalog. Then evolve for concurrent writers, compaction, partition evolution, metadata scale, isolated compute, multi-region recovery, and safe migrations.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
A lakehouse provides warehouse-like tables and transactions over low-cost object storage while allowing multiple compute engines. Producers ingest files, database changes, and event streams. Analysts and applications run SQL against stable snapshots. Data owners publish schemas, quality expectations, retention, and access policy through a catalog.

The object store is not the table: a table is a versioned set of data and delete files described by metadata. The catalog resolves names, ownership, and current metadata pointers. Compute is replaceable. Dashboarding, model training algorithms, and source-database capture are adjacent but outside the core design.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Ingest batch files and streams with replay, quarantine, and lineage.
  • Create, append, update, merge, and delete table data atomically by snapshot.
  • Support snapshot-isolated reads, time travel, schema and partition evolution.
  • Serve interactive SQL, scheduled ETL, and large scans on independent compute pools.
  • Compact small files, expire snapshots, collect orphans, and control cost.
  • Enforce row, column, tenant, residency, retention, and audit policy.
  • Scale to exabytes, millions of tables, and thousands of concurrent commits.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. A published table snapshot references only immutable, checksummed files that are durably readable.
  2. A commit atomically changes one table from expected metadata version to one new version; conflicting writers retry or fail.
  3. Readers pin a snapshot for the query and never observe a partial file set.
  4. A source record identity has at most one effective table mutation under its ingestion contract, despite replay.
  5. Schema field identity is stable and independent of display name or ordinal; incompatible reuse is rejected.
  6. Snapshot expiration never deletes files reachable from a retained snapshot, branch, tag, or active query lease.
  7. Catalog authorization gates new plans and credentials; already issued object capabilities expire or are revoked at the data-serving boundary within a declared deadline.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 5 PB/day raw ingestion, 50 million new data files/day before compaction, 100,000 tables, 100,000 peak queries, and 10,000 table commits/s. At 1 GB target files, 5 PB/day is five million files even after healthy packing. Listing object-store prefixes cannot be a planning primitive; manifests and statistics must prune work.

A 10 PB fact table with 256 MB scan tasks has 40 million tasks if read completely, so query planning must prune partitions/files and aggregate manifests hierarchically. Metadata can dominate latency for small-file tables. Separate budgets for ingest bytes, commit rate, catalog QPS, planning CPU, object GETs, shuffle, and egress.

docs.title: Core Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Namespace(namespace_id, owner, properties, policy_version)
Table(table_id, name, format_version, current_metadata_ref, state)
Schema(schema_id, fields[(field_id,name,type,required)], compatibility)
PartitionSpec(spec_id, transforms[(field_id,transform)])
Snapshot(snapshot_id, parent_id, sequence, schema_id, spec_id,
         manifest_list_ref, summary, committed_at)
Manifest(manifest_id, entries[(file_ref,status,partition,stats,sequence)])
DataFile(file_id, uri, format, size, rows, bounds, checksum, encryption_key)
DeleteFile(file_id, type, target_scope, sequence, stats)
IngestionCommit(source_id, source_position_range, snapshot_id, request_hash)
QueryLease(query_id, snapshot_ids, expires_at)

Files and snapshot metadata are immutable. The catalog's current pointer and table lifecycle are canonical mutable state. Caches, materialized views, file indexes, query results, and usage statistics are projections.

docs.title: APIs and Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/tables                                  {namespace, schema, partition_spec}
GET  /v1/tables/{id}/metadata?snapshot=...
POST /v1/tables/{id}/commits                     Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
     {expected_metadata_version, new_files, delete_files, source_positions}
POST /v1/tables/{id}/snapshots/{id}:tag
POST /v1/tables/{id}:expire-snapshots
POST /v1/queries                                 {sql, catalog, warehouse, idempotency_key}
GET  /v1/queries/{id}/results?cursor=...

Engines usually use a table-format protocol rather than REST for every file. Commit requests include operation semantics, base snapshot, file checksums, and conflict scope. Result cursors bind query ID, result generation, and row offset; results expire explicitly. Object credentials are short-lived and restricted to files authorized by the planned snapshot.

Catalog revocation alone cannot revoke a bearer URL already issued by object storage. For an immediate-stop requirement, route reads through a policy-enforcing gateway or use a tested storage-policy/credential revocation path; otherwise the exposure bound includes credential lifetime and in-flight reads. Amazon S3 presigned URL documentation explicitly permits repeated use until expiry and downloads that continue past expiry if started earlier (accessed 2026-09-08). Snapshot isolation is a table-format mechanism, not an authorization revocation mechanism.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Sources[Files, streams, databases] --> Ingest[Ingestion plane]
    Ingest --> Stage[(Staging object storage)]
    Ingest --> Commit[Table commit service]
    Commit --> Catalog[(Catalog and metadata pointers)]
    Commit --> Lake[(Immutable data, delete, manifest files)]
    Users --> Gateway[SQL and API gateway]
    Gateway --> Planner[Query planner]
    Planner --> Catalog
    Planner --> Compute[Elastic compute pools]
    Compute --> Lake
    Catalog --> Maint[Compaction, expiry, quality]
    Maint --> Lake

The control plane owns names, metadata pointers, policy, and workload admission. Data planes ingest and compute against immutable artifacts. This separation lets engines fail or scale without changing table truth.

docs.title: Batch and Stream Ingestion
docs.text: Batch ingestion lands checksummed files in staging, validates schema and quality, writes target-sized columnar files, then commits them. Streaming workers checkpoint source positions only as part of or after successful table commit. A stable (source, partition, position range) deduplicates retries. Bad records enter a bounded quarantine with reason, schema version, and source identity; poison data does not block unrelated partitions.

docs.title: Query
docs.text: The planner resolves names and policy, pins table snapshots, reads manifest lists, prunes files using partition transforms and column bounds, and creates scan tasks. Workers read columnar ranges directly from object storage, push down predicates, shuffle only required columns, and write immutable result pages. A query lease protects its snapshots from expiration until completion or bounded timeout.

docs.title: Mutation
docs.text: Updates and deletes produce copy-on-write replacement files or merge-on-read delete files. The commit validates conflicts against snapshots after the writer's base. Equality deletes suit key-based changes; position deletes are precise but couple to file layout. Readers merge applicable deletes by sequence. Maintenance later rewrites clean files without changing logical rows.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Transactional Table Format
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Writer
    participant O as Object store
    participant C as Catalog/commit service
    W->>C: load table metadata version V
    W->>O: write immutable data and manifests
    W->>C: commit expected V, operation, new metadata
    C->>C: validate files, policy, conflicts
    C->>C: CAS current pointer V to V+1
    alt success
        C-->>W: snapshot S committed
    else concurrent conflict
        C-->>W: retry with latest metadata
    end

Publishing one metadata pointer is the linearization point. Files written before a failed CAS are invisible and later reclaimed. Append writers can often rebase if added files do not conflict. Overwrite, merge, and compaction inspect changed partitions/files or row-level conflict keys. Blind last-write-wins can lose rows and is rejected.

Iceberg's reliability documentation describes optimistic pointer replacement and revalidation of operation assumptions after a conflict; it does not make arbitrary rebasing safe (accessed 2026-09-08).

Snapshot metadata forms a parent chain with monotonically increasing sequence. Manifests summarize partitions and column bounds so planners avoid reading every file entry. Checkpoints or compact metadata files bound chain traversal. Branches support isolated maintenance or audit, while tags retain known snapshots.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Schema and Partition Evolution
docs.text:
Assign immutable field IDs. Renaming changes a label, not identity; dropping reserves the ID; adding a nullable field is generally compatible. Type widening follows an explicit matrix. Required-field additions need defaults/backfill or a new contract. Writers declare schema ID and map by field identity, preventing ordinal changes from silently swapping data.

Partitioning is metadata, not user-visible directory meaning. Transforms such as day(timestamp), bucket(tenant, 64), or truncate(country) receive spec IDs. New files may use a new partition spec while old files retain the old one; planners evaluate predicates across both. This hidden partitioning avoids rewriting an exabyte table merely to evolve layout.

Schema registry approval, producer compatibility checks, and table constraints are control-plane governance. Data quality rules run before publication for critical tables or asynchronously with a quarantine/quality state for lower tiers. A contract change canary writes to a branch and compares row counts, nulls, bounds, and representative queries.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Compaction, Deletes, and Garbage Collection
docs.text:
Small files inflate commits, planning, GET requests, and worker startup. Compaction selects a bounded partition/file group, reads at snapshot S, writes 256 MB-1 GB sorted files, and commits a rewrite only if inputs remain valid. It uses separate quotas so maintenance cannot starve ingestion. Sorting by common filters improves skipping but costs shuffle and can create skew.

Merge-on-read writes quickly but charges readers to apply delete files; copy-on-write makes writes expensive but reads simple. Use merge-on-read for high update rates, then compact based on delete ratio, file count, query heat, and cost. Position deletes must be rewritten when target files change.

flowchart TD
    Roots[Snapshots, tags, branches, query and writer pins] --> Mark[Traverse metadata and manifests]
    Mark --> Reachable[Reachable data/delete/metadata files]
    Inventory[Object inventory] --> Sweep{Older than grace and unreachable?}
    Reachable --> Sweep
    Sweep -->|no| Keep[Retain]
    Sweep -->|yes| Fence[Recheck pins and fence publication]
    Fence --> Delete[Delete with audit manifest]

Expiration first removes snapshot references under retention. GC uses object inventory plus mark-and-sweep, never a possibly stale refcount. Grace exceeds the declared bounded commit, retry, and inventory windows. Writers register durable staging pins before publication, including reused old files that a prior mark did not reach; commit and GC coordinate through a generation or conditional deletion protocol. Query lease acquisition/renewal is serialized with snapshot retirement: a query cannot acquire a new pin after its snapshot is retired, and a worker that loses its lease stops reading before the protected interval ends. Grace alone cannot protect an indefinitely paused writer or an old file newly referenced after the mark. Legal holds and tags are roots. Dry-run manifests, deletion rate limits, and sampled restore protect against catastrophic policy errors.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Catalog, Planning, and Compute Isolation
docs.text:
The catalog maps names to stable table IDs and metadata pointers, tracks ownership/policy, and emits change events. Cache immutable metadata aggressively, but validate the current pointer and authorization epoch. Namespace rename changes catalog mapping, not every file. Catalog unavailability can allow already-pinned read-only queries while rejecting commits and new authorization decisions.

Planner metadata work is bounded through manifest summaries, partition/file-stat pruning, cached snapshots, and planning timeouts. Cost/cardinality estimates are advisory, but min/max bounds used to skip files are correctness-critical: false bounds can omit matching rows. Validate their encoding and schema association; missing or untrusted pruning bounds must cause a scan, not exclusion. Query admission estimates scan bytes, CPU, memory, shuffle, and concurrency. Separate interactive, ETL, ingestion, and maintenance warehouses with tenant quotas.

Workers are disposable and read snapshots directly. Stage shuffles on encrypted local/remote storage and checkpoint long stages where useful. Straggler mitigation duplicates only deterministic tasks. Under overload, queue batch work, reject unbounded scans, spill within quota, and preserve catalog/commit capacity. Chargeback reports tie bytes and CPU to owner, query, and table.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Shard catalog and commit ownership by stable table ID; place extreme commit-rate tables on dedicated shards. Metadata files partition naturally by snapshot and manifest. Data files partition by table-defined transforms and target size, not object-store directory listing. Hash source partitions across ingestion workers while preserving position order per source partition.

Hot tables stress catalog, metadata planning, and object storage. Cache immutable manifests, fan out manifest evaluation, coalesce commits, and use hierarchical manifests. Coalescing adds latency and must preserve source-position identities. Skewed joins use heavy-key detection, salting, broadcast of genuinely small sides, and adaptive repartitioning. Fair admission prevents one tenant's Cartesian product from exhausting a warehouse.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Catalog pointer CAS and policy updates require strong consistency per table/namespace. Readers get snapshot isolation, not necessarily multi-table atomicity. A workflow needing a consistent set records explicit snapshot IDs or publishes a versioned dataset manifest after all table commits. Object-store reads must satisfy the durability/read-after-write assumptions required before publication.

Ingestion commits retain source ranges and request hashes. Stream delivery and catalog events are at least once; sinks compare versions. Exact range identity alone is insufficient if a restart changes batch boundaries: ranges [1,100] and [51,150] overlap without sharing an ID. Atomically advance a per-source-partition committed position with publication, reject gaps, and trim already committed prefixes, or deduplicate stable row-event IDs. Do not claim exactly-once transport. Materialized views record input snapshots and output snapshot for reproducibility.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
A worker crash before commit leaves reclaimable files; after commit it discovers the ingestion identity and advances its source checkpoint. Object-store slowdown triggers bounded retries, task backoff, and query cancellation rather than unbounded memory. Catalog failure freezes commits; pinned reads may continue. Metadata corruption first recovers an exact verified replica. Serving a parent snapshot is an explicit stale read; write promotion must recover the acknowledged commit prefix or reconcile lost commits and ingestion positions before accepting new mutations.

Compaction conflict discards output after grace. Lost catalog events are repaired by version scans. A bad schema rollout is stopped through compatibility checks and branch canary, then readers pin the prior snapshot while correction appends a new one. Restore verifies checksums, metadata reachability, row counts, and representative queries. Reconciliation finds source-position gaps, duplicate identities, orphan growth, manifest inconsistencies, and policy drift.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text:
Assign each table a metadata home region with synchronous zonal catalog replication. Replicate immutable objects according to residency and disaster tier. Remote engines read local replicas only when a snapshot replication manifest is complete; otherwise they route to home or fail explicitly. Cross-region egress is visible in planning cost.

Disaster failover promotes a fenced catalog epoch after object completeness is proven. Active-active independent table writes are possible with a consensus catalog but often add latency without product value. Dataset sharing publishes immutable snapshot references and policy rather than copying ad hoc directories. Migration copies objects, verifies manifests, catches up metadata versions, then atomically switches location descriptors.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text:
Use workload identity, short-lived object credentials, encryption with table/tenant keys, private networking, column masking, row filters, purpose-based roles, and immutable access/change audit. Policy is evaluated during planning and embedded in a signed plan; workers cannot request arbitrary paths. Recheck epochs for long queries where revocation requirements demand it.

Protect against malicious files, decompression bombs, parser exploits, SQL resource attacks, unauthorized exports, path injection, and poisoned statistics. Sandbox format readers and UDFs. Scan sensitive columns, tokenize where possible, enforce residency and retention, and make break-glass access time-bound and reviewed. Query results inherit source classification and expiration.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure ingest bytes/records, source lag, commit conflicts, commit and catalog latency, files per snapshot, file-size distribution, delete ratio, metadata planning time, prune ratio, scanned versus returned bytes, shuffle/spill, queue time, query failures, orphan age, snapshot retention, policy denials, and cost by owner. Track freshness as source position to published snapshot, not merely job success.

Property-test snapshot reachability, schema-ID mapping, partition transforms, conflict detection, and GC roots. Differential-test multiple engines against the same snapshots. Replay duplicate and reordered source batches. Chaos-test commit acknowledgements, object/catalog outages, worker loss, and region fencing. Scale-test million-file manifests, tiny files, skewed joins, and concurrent compaction. Regularly restore retained snapshots and execute golden queries.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Object storage lowers cost and decouples compute but makes metadata publication and small files critical. Copy-on-write favors reads; merge-on-read favors mutations. Strong multi-table transactions are convenient but impose coordination rarely justified for analytics; explicit dataset manifests are simpler. More statistics improve pruning but increase write and privacy cost. Global catalogs simplify names but can violate latency/residency goals; federated ownership with stable IDs adds discovery complexity. Open formats reduce lock-in but require rigorous compatibility testing.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Producers --> Ingestion[Batch and streaming ingestion cells]
    Ingestion --> Lake[(Immutable columnar data/delete/metadata)]
    Ingestion --> Commit[Per-table commit owners]
    Commit --> Catalog[(Catalog, pointer CAS, schema, policy)]
    Clients --> Gateway[Governed query gateway]
    Gateway --> Planner[Snapshot-pinning planner]
    Planner --> Catalog
    Planner --> Warehouses[Isolated elastic compute warehouses]
    Warehouses --> Lake
    Catalog --> Maintenance[Compaction, quality, expiry, GC]
    Maintenance --> Lake
    Lake --> Replica[Verified regional replicas/archive]

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. What is the linearization point of a table commit?
  2. How can two append writers commit without losing files?
  3. Why do field IDs matter during rename and reorder?
  4. How can partitioning evolve without rewriting old data?
  5. When should a table use merge-on-read versus copy-on-write?
  6. How do you prove a file is safe to garbage-collect?
  7. How do compute and control planes degrade independently?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should define immutable files, transactional snapshots, a catalog, schema evolution, ingestion checkpoints, query pruning, compaction, and retries. An L6 answer should formalize conflict scopes, field identity, partition evolution, query leases and GC proof, metadata scaling, workload isolation, source reconciliation, regional object completeness, migrations, governance, engine compatibility, and cost attribution.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: A lakehouse is a transactional metadata layer over immutable object-store files. Writers stage checksummed columnar data and manifests, then CAS one table metadata pointer from an expected version to a new snapshot. Readers pin that snapshot, prune hierarchical manifests with partition transforms and statistics, and run on isolated elastic compute. Record stable field IDs and versioned partition specs so schema and layout evolve without corrupting old files. Deduplicate ingestion by source-position range and commit checkpoints against published snapshots; delivery remains at least once. Use merge-on-read deletes for fast mutation or copy-on-write for fast reads, then compact under separate quotas. Expire snapshots before mark-and-sweep GC, preserving tags, branches, legal holds, and active query leases. Keep catalog/policy in a strongly consistent home region, verify immutable replica completeness before failover, and measure source-to-snapshot freshness, metadata scale, scan efficiency, and cost.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a stored-value wallet supporting top-up, peer transfer, merchant payment, refund, withdrawal, and transaction history. We will distinguish workflow state from immutable accounting, estimate scale, define APIs and ledger postings, then cover idempotency, external uncertainty, partitioning, limits, reconciliation, security, and recovery.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
A wallet holds a liability owed by the operator to a customer. Moving a number in a user row is not enough: customer liabilities, safeguarded bank cash, provider receivables, fees, and settlement must be balanced and reconciled. External rails can timeout after acting, so UNKNOWN is a valid workflow state.

Assume one country and currency initially, 100 million wallets, bank/card top-ups, internal transfers, and merchant settlement. Credit, foreign exchange, and offline payments are out of scope. KYC and AML services provide decisions but the wallet enforces their limits.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
• Create and verify wallets; freeze or close them.
  • Top up and withdraw through external providers.
  • Transfer internally and pay merchants.
  • Hold, capture, release, refund, and expose history.
  • Enforce balance, velocity, KYC, and risk limits.
  • Settle merchants and reconcile bank/provider statements.

Peak is 100,000 commands/second with p99 under 300 ms for internal transfers; external operations may remain pending. Reads are 99.99% available. No accepted value is created, destroyed, or posted twice. Financial history must be reproducible and externally reconcilable.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. Every value movement is an immutable, balanced ledger transaction in integer minor units.
  2. A command idempotency key and payload hash produce at most one semantic transfer.
  3. Available balance never falls below the configured floor.
  4. Workflow state never substitutes for ledger truth; each state names its accounting effect.
  5. Refunds and corrections append postings linked to originals; history is never edited.
  6. External success is booked only from authenticated evidence or confirmed status.
  7. Customer-liability control accounts reconcile to safeguarded bank cash plus documented in-flight items.

docs.title: 5. Estimates
docs.text:
One hundred million wallets at 2 KB account/profile state is 200 GB before replication. Ten transactions/user/month gives one billion workflows/month. With six postings average and 200 bytes/posting, journals add about 1.2 TB/month before indexes and replication. Bursts on salary days and merchant campaigns drive provisioning.

History reads use projections; spending checks use authoritative owner-shard balances. External callbacks and reconciliation files are retained independently. Partition capacity must account for celebrity and large-merchant hot wallets, not average users.

docs.title: 6. Data model
docs.text:
Wallet(wallet_id, customer_id, status, kyc_tier, home_shard, version)
Payment(payment_id, type, payer, payee, amount_minor, currency, state,
        idempotency_key, provider_ref, version, created_at)
JournalTxn(txn_id, business_ref, effective_at, reversal_of, sequence)
Posting(txn_id, ledger_account, asset, signed_amount, layer)
Hold(hold_id, wallet_id, amount_minor, state, expires_at, version)
ExternalAttempt(attempt_id, payment_id, provider, external_key, state, raw_ref)
SettlementBatch(batch_id, merchant_id, cutoff, amount_minor, bank_ref, state)
ReconBreak(source, external_ref, internal_ref, delta_minor, state, owner)

Wallet balance is a ledger-derived projection split into available, reserved, and pending. Payment is an orchestration state machine. Neither can mutate postings.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/transfers
Idempotency-Key: device-command-123
{ "from":"w1", "to":"w2", "amount":{"minor":5000,"currency":"INR"} }

POST /v1/topups
POST /v1/payments/{id}/refunds
GET /v1/payments/{id}
GET /v1/wallets/{id}/balance
GET /v1/wallets/{id}/transactions?cursor=...

The same key with a different canonical request hash returns conflict. Responses include workflow state, ledger transaction IDs, and asOfSequence. Cursors pin a history boundary. Callback endpoints authenticate provider signatures and deduplicate provider event IDs.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  App --> Gateway
  Gateway --> Pay[Payment orchestrator]
  Pay --> Risk[KYC/risk/limits]
  Pay --> Ledger[(Immutable ledger)]
  Pay --> Rails[Bank/card adapters]
  Ledger --> Views[(Balance/history views)]
  Rails --> Banks[External providers]
  Ledger --> Settle[Merchant settlement]
  Statements[Bank/provider statements] --> Recon[Reconciliation]
  Ledger --> Recon
  Pay --> Events[(Workflow outbox)]
    subgraph MoneyLane[Ledger and derived views]
      Ledger
      Views
      Settle
    end
    subgraph RailLane[External payment rails]
      Rails
      Banks
    end
    subgraph ReconLane[Reconciliation]
      Statements
      Recon
    end

docs.title: 9. Internal transfer
docs.text:
Route payer commands to its owner shard. In one serializable transaction, reserve idempotency, verify status and limits, lock account versions in deterministic order, validate available balance, append balanced postings from payer liability to payee liability, write workflow state, and append outbox. Acknowledgement follows commit.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant P as Payments
  participant L as Ledger shard
  participant N as Notifications
  C->>P: transfer(key, payer, payee, amount)
  P->>L: atomic post + idempotency
  L->>L: floor check, balanced append, and outbox
  L-->>P: committed sequence
  P-->>C: SUCCEEDED
  L->>N: at-least-once event
  N->>N: dedupe by payment ID

If wallets lie on different journal shards, use shard-local platform clearing accounts. Debit payer into outbound pending, credit payee from inbound pending, and advance a durable transfer workflow. Both shards remain balanced; the user sees PENDING until destination commit. A lost destination acknowledgement is UNKNOWN, not permission to refund the source: doing so after a successful destination credit would create spendable value twice despite each local journal balancing. Resolve the stable transfer ID at the destination and retry the same effect. Cancellation must durably fence future destination credit before releasing the source; after destination credit, use a new reverse-transfer workflow rather than a blind compensation. Clearing-account reconciliation finds stranded transfers. Prefer colocating common transfer populations before introducing this complexity.

docs.title: 10. External money movement
docs.text:
A top-up starts INITIATED, creates an external attempt with a stable provider key, and invokes the provider. A timeout becomes UNKNOWN, not failed. Poll provider status or await a signed callback. On confirmed success, post debit provider_receivable/cash_in_transit and credit customer_liability; on external settlement, move receivable to safeguarded-bank cash. A failed attempt has no customer-value posting, though fees may be separate.

A withdrawal first moves customer available liability to reserved. Confirmed provider success consumes the reserve and credits bank-cash/control; failure releases it. An unknown outcome keeps funds reserved. Retrying with a new external key can pay twice and is forbidden until status reconciliation.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> INITIATED
  INITIATED --> SUBMITTED
  SUBMITTED --> CONFIRMED
  SUBMITTED --> FAILED
  SUBMITTED --> UNKNOWN
  UNKNOWN --> CONFIRMED: provider evidence
  UNKNOWN --> FAILED: authoritative rejection
  CONFIRMED --> REVERSED: provider reversal

docs.title: 11. Ledger and refunds
docs.text:
Each transaction balances per currency. An internal INR 50 transfer debits payer customer-liability and credits payee customer-liability according to the chosen sign convention. Fees move customer liability to fee revenue. Holds transfer available to reserved layers. Product code uses approved posting templates rather than arbitrary accounts.

A refund is a new payment linked to the capture and bounded by captured amount minus completed refunds and outstanding refund reservations. Reserve refundable capacity atomically before any provider call; an unknown outcome keeps that capacity reserved. Concurrent refunds serialize through aggregate version or refundable-balance account. Provider reversals post explicit reversals; they do not change the original row. A card chargeback can arrive after credited funds were spent: record the resulting customer receivable or loss under an explicit posting policy, restrict further spending, and reconcile it rather than violating the available-balance floor or silently dropping the reversal. Authenticated top-up success is not a promise that a reversible rail is finally settled. Materialized balances update in the same local commit used for spending and asynchronously elsewhere.

docs.title: 12. Settlement and reconciliation
docs.text:
Merchant capture credits merchant payable. At cutoff, a batch freezes an immutable set of captures/refunds/fees and posts merchant payable to settlement payable. A stable bank transfer reference is created before submission. Confirmation posts settlement payable against safeguarded bank control.

Daily reconciliation independently compares: provider attempts to provider reports, bank-control postings to bank statements, merchant batches to bank transfers, customer-liability totals to wallet balance projections, and cross-shard clearing pairs. Match exact references first; constrained fuzzy matches require review. Breaks carry owner, age, amount, and evidence. No unexplained plug entry can make totals look correct.

flowchart TD
  PS[Provider statement] --> R[Reconciliation engine]
  BS[Bank statement] --> R
  L[Ledger control accounts] --> R
  SB[Settlement manifests] --> R
  R --> M[Matched evidence]
  R --> B[Break queue]
