  B --> I[Investigate]
  I --> A[Approved reversal/adjustment]
  A --> L
  M --> C[Daily control close]

docs.title: 13. Partitioning and consistency
docs.text:
Partition wallets by stable hash and give large merchants dedicated accounts/shards. Commands for one wallet route to one fenced owner. Ledger posting, balance floor, hold version, and idempotency are strongly consistent locally. Histories, notifications, analytics, and search are eventual and sequence-tagged.

Provider callbacks partition by payment ID. Settlement partitions by merchant and cutoff. At-least-once logs are safe because sinks deduplicate business IDs and compare sequence. Idempotency records live as long as financial records, not only in a cache.

Use one write region per regulated ledger/legal entity with synchronous replicas and fenced disaster standby. Stateless reads can run regionally. During isolation, avoid accepting spending against stale balances. External status and reconciliation restore workflows before clearing reservations.

docs.title: 14. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Unknown database commit resolves by idempotency lookup.
  • Duplicate callback finds provider event and payment IDs.
  • Provider timeout remains unknown and funds remain reserved.
  • Ledger outage stops value-changing commands but cached history remains readable.
  • Projection loss rebuilds from journal sequence.
  • Scheduler races capture using hold versions.
  • Settlement timeout queries bank reference before retry.
  • Cross-shard workflow resumes and clearing breaks alert.

Backpressure rejects before durable acceptance or queues after it; never return a generic timeout that invites a differently keyed retry. Disaster promotion also requires the acknowledged journal, holds, idempotency, and external-attempt prefix. Fencing alone cannot recover a lost debit or provider key; a standby with missing acknowledged state must pause spending and reconcile before reopening. Recovery drills prove journal restore, sequence fencing, and statement re-import.

docs.title: 15. Security and abuse
docs.text: Use strong authentication, device binding, step-up for new payees/withdrawals, encrypted/tokenized data, mTLS, HSM keys, rate and velocity limits, KYC tiers, AML monitoring, sanctions checks, and account freeze controls. Separate support, ledger, settlement, and reconciliation roles. Sensitive actions need dual approval and immutable audit. Signed deep links and payee confirmation reduce social engineering.

docs.title: 16. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure command latency, success/pending/unknown rates, idempotency conflicts, insufficient-fund rejects, ledger imbalance attempts, projection lag, holds and unknowns by age/value, external callback lag, settlement aging, clearing balances, reconciliation breaks, and customer-liability versus safeguarded-cash control totals.

Property tests prove conservation, retry stability, reversal, and concurrent refund bounds. State-machine tests cover callback/poll/timeout permutations. Test integer rounding, shard failover, hot merchants, provider duplication, corrupted files, and disaster restore. Recompute sampled balances from genesis and compare projections continuously.

docs.title: 17. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• One wallet row is simple but unauditable; immutable double entry plus projections is required for money.
  • Global synchronous balances simplify transfers but harm latency/availability; shard-local clearing exposes pending state safely.
  • Crediting top-up on client success improves UX but creates unfunded liabilities; wait for authenticated provider evidence.
  • Automatically retrying unknown withdrawals improves completion but risks duplicate payout; status resolution wins.
  • A long hold protects funds but frustrates users; age-based escalation and clear status are preferable to unsafe release.

docs.title: 18. Final architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  C[Authenticated command] --> O[Idempotent orchestrator]
  O --> K[KYC/risk/limits]
  O --> J[(Fenced balanced journal)]
  O --> A[Rail adapters with stable IDs]
  J --> P[Balances/history]
  A <--> X[Bank/card providers]
  J --> S[Merchant settlement]
  X --> R[Independent reconciliation]
  S --> R
  J --> R
  R --> Q[Owned break cases]

docs.title: 19. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. What balance is reserved during an unknown withdrawal?
  2. How does a cross-shard transfer conserve value?
  3. When may a top-up credit the customer?
  4. How do concurrent refunds remain bounded?
  5. Which external statements prove safeguarded funds?
  6. Why is workflow state not accounting truth?
  7. How do you fail over without double spending?

docs.title: 20. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should model idempotent workflows, integer amounts, balanced immutable postings, holds, provider unknowns, refunds, partitioning, and reconciliation. An L6 answer should define liability/control accounts, cross-shard clearing, safeguarded-fund proof, settlement manifests, legal-entity regional ownership, dual controls, and quantified unknown/break operations.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Treat wallet value as a customer liability in an immutable double-entry journal. Internal transfers atomically validate payer funds and append balanced postings; retries resolve through durable idempotency keys and payload hashes. Holds move value between available and reserved layers. Refunds and corrections append linked transactions rather than edit history. Sequence-tagged balances and histories are projections.

External calls use stable provider IDs. A timeout is UNKNOWN; withdrawals stay reserved until callback, status query, or reconciliation proves success or failure. Top-ups credit customers only from authenticated evidence. Merchant settlement freezes immutable manifests and records bank references before sending. Independently reconcile provider reports, bank statements, settlement batches, journal control accounts, and cross-shard clearing. Use one fenced write region per ledger and stop value-changing operations when authority is uncertain. Financial correctness comes from conservation, immutable evidence, idempotent workflows, and external proof.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a reusable multi-tenant ledger for wallets, payments, fees, and settlement. The interview should begin with accounting invariants, not database brands. We will define accounts and transactions, estimate load, design atomic posting and idempotency, then cover balances, holds, reversals, partitioning, close, external reconciliation, and audit controls.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
A ledger records economic facts. It does not call banks or decide payment workflow; upstream services move external money and ask the ledger to record known state. Every movement has equal and opposite postings. The ledger supplies authoritative balances as of a sequence and emits facts from which product views are built.

Support multiple legal entities, currencies, and balance layers such as available, pending, and reserved. Foreign exchange is represented as linked balanced transactions per asset with explicit rate and gain/loss accounts. We do not sum INR and USD into a fictional total.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Create chart-of-account definitions and ledger accounts.
  • Post balanced transactions idempotently.
  • Place, capture, release, and expire holds.
  • Reverse erroneous transactions without mutation.
  • Query current and historical balances and transaction history.
  • Close accounting periods and reconcile external accounts.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• 200,000 transactions/second, usually 2-8 postings each.
  • Post p99 under 50 ms within one region.
  • Zero acknowledged unbalanced or partially visible transactions.
  • Durable, tamper-evident history and reproducible balances.
  • 99.99% read availability; posting may fail closed if authority is uncertain.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. For each transaction and asset, signed posting amounts sum to zero.
  2. Journal transactions and postings are immutable; corrections append full reversals and replacements.
  3. A tenant-scoped idempotency key identifies one semantic request and payload hash.
  4. All postings in a transaction become visible atomically.
  5. An account's journal sequence is monotonic; balance at sequence N is deterministic.
  6. Available funds cannot go below the account's configured floor under serialized writes.
  7. Closed-period entries require a controlled adjustment in an open period.
  8. Internal control accounts reconcile to independent external statements; suspense is visible and owned.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
At 200,000 transactions/second and four postings average, the system writes 800,000 postings/second. At 180 bytes per posting, sustaining this rate produces 800,000 * 180 * 86,400 * 365 = 4.54 PB/year logical, or 13.62 PB/year at 3x replication before indexes and transaction metadata. If 200,000/s is only a peak, multiply retained bytes by the average-to-peak duty factor. Retain compact primary indexes, partition historical journals, and move immutable payload copies to archive without removing statutory records.

Balance reads may be ten times posting volume. Recomputing from genesis per request is impossible. Store materialized balances with the last applied journal sequence, periodically snapshot them, and retain the journal as authority. Ten thousand tenants and billions of accounts require tenant isolation and shard-aware account IDs.

docs.title: 6. Data model
docs.text:
LedgerAccount(account_id, tenant_id, legal_entity, asset, account_type,
              normal_side, status, shard_id, created_at)
JournalTransaction(txn_id, tenant_id, idempotency_key, request_hash, type,
                   effective_at, recorded_at, reversal_of, correlation_id)
Posting(posting_id, txn_id, account_id, asset, signed_amount, sequence, metadata)
Balance(account_id, settled, pending, reserved, journal_sequence, updated_at)
Hold(hold_id, account_id, asset, amount, state, expires_at, version)
Period(period_id, legal_entity, start_at, end_at, status, closed_at)
ReconciliationRun(run_id, external_account, statement_hash, status, cutoff)
ReconciliationBreak(break_id, run_id, internal_ref, external_ref, delta, state)

Amounts are signed integers in the asset's smallest unit. Asset precision is immutable once used. Metadata is schema-versioned and bounded; searchable business references receive explicit columns rather than arbitrary JSON indexes.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/transactions
Idempotency-Key: payment:p123:capture
{ "effectiveAt":"...", "postings":[
  {"accountId":"customer-available", "asset":"INR", "amount":-10000},
  {"accountId":"merchant-payable", "asset":"INR", "amount":10000}
] }

POST /v1/transactions/{id}/reverse
GET /v1/accounts/{id}/balance?asOfSequence=991
GET /v1/accounts/{id}/entries?cursor=...

The server verifies that an idempotency-key reuse has the same canonical payload hash; otherwise it returns conflict. Cursors encode account, sequence, direction, and snapshot boundary. Clients cannot directly post to protected equity or external-control accounts; posting templates authorize valid account combinations.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Clients --> API[Ledger API]
  API --> Validate[Schema, template, balance checks]
  Validate --> Shard[(Journal shard)]
  Shard --> Outbox[(Transactional outbox)]
  Outbox --> Proj[Balance and history projections]
  Proj --> Reads[Read API]
  Shard --> Archive[(Immutable archive)]
  Statements[Bank/provider statements] --> Recon[Reconciliation]
  Shard --> Recon
  Control[Period and account controls] --> Validate

docs.title: 9. Atomic posting path
docs.text:
Route by transaction shard. Inside one serializable database transaction: reserve idempotency key, lock or compare account versions in sorted order, verify account status/assets/templates, enforce balance floors, verify per-asset zero sums, allocate journal sequences, append transaction and postings, update materialized balances, and append an outbox record. Commit once, then acknowledge.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant L as Ledger API
  participant DB as Journal shard
  participant E as Event consumers
  C->>L: post(key, postings)
  L->>DB: begin + reserve key
  DB->>DB: validate assets, sum=0, floors
  DB->>DB: append journal/postings/balances/outbox
  DB-->>L: commit(sequence range)
  L-->>C: transaction + sequence
  DB->>E: relay outbox at least once
  E->>E: apply by transaction ID/sequence

If commit outcome is unknown, the client retries the same key; the ledger queries rather than repeats. Outbox publication can duplicate, so every consumer applies by transaction ID and sequence. The outbox never defines accounting truth; committed rows do.

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: holds and balance layers
docs.text:
A hold is not destruction of money. Placement transfers amount from available to reserved through balanced layer accounts and appends a hold state. Capture moves reserved funds toward the destination and releases excess. Release transfers reserved back to available. Expiry is a release with a scheduler-generated idempotency key. Capture and expiry race through expected hold version, with capture also requiring expires_at > authority_time and expiry requiring the opposite. A delayed scheduler cannot extend the spending authority of an expired hold.

Keep ledger balance and spendable policy separate. An overdraft account may have a negative floor; a prepaid wallet may not. Pending incoming funds can be visible but not spendable. Balance APIs return each layer, not one misleading number.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> ACTIVE: balanced reserve posting
  ACTIVE --> PARTIALLY_CAPTURED: capture part
  PARTIALLY_CAPTURED --> CAPTURED: capture remainder
  PARTIALLY_CAPTURED --> RELEASED: release remainder
  note right of PARTIALLY_CAPTURED
    Further partial captures keep this state
    until the remaining hold is exhausted.
  end note
  PARTIALLY_CAPTURED --> EXPIRED: scheduled release of remainder
  ACTIVE --> CAPTURED: full capture
  ACTIVE --> RELEASED: explicit release
  ACTIVE --> EXPIRED: scheduled release

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: reversals, time, and close
docs.text:
effective_at says when the economic event belongs; recorded_at and journal sequence say when the ledger learned it. Historical statements need both. Backdated entries are allowed only in open periods. Once closed, a discovered error creates a current-period adjustment referencing the original; the closed report remains reproducible.

A reversal duplicates all original postings with signs inverted and reversal_of. Enforce one full reversal per original transaction with an authoritative uniqueness constraint, regardless of caller idempotency key, and apply the normal floor/exception policy to the reversal. Partial refunds are new business transactions, not partial mutation. A mistaken reversal is itself reversed. This may appear verbose, but preserves an unbroken explanation of every balance.

Period close serializes the OPEN-to-CLOSING gate with posting validation, waits for already admitted workflows under a defined cutoff policy, freezes the cutoff sequence, recomputes control totals from postings, compares projections, completes external reconciliation, and publishes a signed close manifest. Reads "as of close" use that immutable cutoff.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: external reconciliation
docs.text:
For each bank or processor account, map internal control-account postings to independently downloaded statement lines. Match stable provider ID first, then constrained amount/date/reference rules. Compare opening balance, matched flows, unmatched flows, and closing balance. A difference enters suspense only through an explicit balanced transaction with evidence and owner; suspense aging is a high-severity metric.

flowchart TD
  S[Signed external statement] --> N[Normalize, hash, dedupe]
  J[Internal control postings] --> M[Exact then constrained matching]
  N --> M
  M --> OK[Matched evidence links]
  M --> BI[Internal-only break]
  M --> BE[External-only break]
  BI --> Case[Owned case + aging]
  BE --> Case
  OK --> Close[Control-account close]
  Case --> Adj[Approved reversal/adjustment]
  Adj --> J

Never reconcile only against a payment service derived from the same event stream; that is correlated evidence. Bank/provider statements must arrive through separately controlled channels and be hash-retained.

docs.title: 13. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
A transaction spanning accounts must fit one journal shard to remain atomic. Encode tenant/legal-entity shard affinity in account IDs and create local clearing accounts. High-volume tenants receive dedicated shards. Transfers across shards use a clearing workflow: source posts funds to outbound_pending, destination posts from inbound_pending, and a coordinator with stable transfer ID advances states. Each shard stays balanced even if the workflow pauses.

Cross-shard transfer is not atomically invisible; expose PENDING until both sides complete. Reconciliation of paired clearing accounts detects stranded transfers. An unknown destination outcome keeps source funds pending until the stable transfer ID is resolved; cancellation must fence any future destination credit before source release. Two-phase commit is an alternative when atomic cross-shard visibility is a real requirement, but it adds coordination, blocking and recovery cost; this product explicitly accepts pending transfers.

Read replicas serve immutable history; current balance reads requiring spend decisions go to the owner shard. Archival partitions and snapshots accelerate long histories without changing authority.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Posting, idempotency, floor checks, and sequence allocation are strongly consistent within a shard. Read projections are eventual and report asOfSequence. The API can request authoritative balance when making a spend decision. Consumers tolerate duplicate and out-of-order outbox messages using per-shard sequence gaps and replay.

Idempotency keys are retained for the financial record's life, not a 24-hour cache. The key namespace includes tenant and operation. Request hashes prevent accidental key reuse with a different amount.

docs.title: 15. Reliability and multi-region strategy
docs.text:
• Database timeout after commit resolves by idempotency lookup.
  • Projection loss rebuilds from snapshot plus journal.
  • Outbox relay retries; duplicate events have no duplicate effect.
  • Hold scheduler retries stable expiry keys and loses to concurrent capture safely.
  • Cross-shard coordinator resumes from durable state; clearing reconciliation finds omissions.
  • Corrupt external files fail checksum/schema checks and do not auto-adjust books.

Each legal entity has one fenced write region with synchronous in-region replicas and a tested standby. Uncoordinated global multi-writer accounting would permit conflicting floor checks; a globally serializable database can coordinate them, at the corresponding latency and availability cost. Disaster failover requires fencing old primaries and proving the journal sequence. In-region synchronous replication provides zero RPO for the covered zone failures, not destruction of the entire region. Zero RPO for regional loss additionally requires durable acknowledgement from a surviving region before acknowledging the posting, increasing latency by at least the inter-region round trip and blocking writes when that durability condition cannot be met. An asynchronous disaster standby instead has a nonzero, measured RPO; do not claim both local-only commit latency and unconditional regional zero RPO. See PostgreSQL 17 synchronous replication for the acknowledgement and latency boundary (accessed 2026-09-08). RTO is set by regulatory and business needs.

docs.title: 16. Security and governance
docs.text: Use workload identity, mTLS, encryption, HSM-managed keys, tenant isolation, posting-template authorization, and separation of duties. No general operator receives SQL mutation access. Privileged entries require dual approval and reason. Hash-chain journal batches and export signed manifests to write-once storage to expose tampering. Audit every read of sensitive account metadata.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track posting latency/rate, idempotency conflicts, balance-floor rejects, imbalance attempts, lock contention, shard skew, outbox and projection lag, sequence gaps, hold age, cross-shard pending age, suspense balances, reconciliation breaks, and close duration. Continuously compare sampled materialized balances with journal sums.

Property tests assert per-asset zero sum, reversal returns affected accounts to prior balances, retries are stable, and all capture/release/expiry interleavings conserve funds. Test integer boundaries, currency precision, shard failover, unknown commits, consumer replay, corrupted snapshots, and duplicate statement files. A formal state-machine test is valuable for holds and cross-shard transfers.

docs.title: 18. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Updating balances alone is fast but cannot prove history; journal plus transactional materialization gives both.
  • One database simplifies atomicity but limits scale; shard by legal ownership and model cross-shard transfers explicitly.
  • Two-phase commit hides pending transfers but adds blocking and uncertain recovery; balanced clearing workflows expose reality.
  • Event sourcing everything can overcomplicate account configuration; reserve immutability for financial facts and audited control changes.
  • Hash chains reveal tampering but do not prevent authorized fraud; access control, dual approval, and external reconciliation remain necessary.

docs.title: 19. Final design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  P[Posting templates] --> L[Ledger API]
  L --> J[(Fenced journal shards)]
  J --> B[(Transactional balances)]
  J --> O[Outbox]
  O --> H[History/search views]
  O --> W[Workflow consumers]
  J --> A[Signed archive]
  X[External statements] --> R[Independent reconciliation]
  J --> R
  R --> C[Break cases]
  C --> L

docs.title: 20. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. Why must postings balance per asset rather than overall?
  2. How does retry behave after an unknown commit?
  3. Can a current balance projection be authoritative?
  4. How do capture and expiry avoid releasing the same hold?
  5. How do cross-shard transfers remain balanced?
  6. What evidence makes reconciliation independent?
  7. How is a closed-period error corrected?

docs.title: 21. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should state balanced immutability, integer money, atomic posting, idempotency, balance projections, holds, reversals, and reconciliation. An L6 candidate should solve shard-local atomicity, clearing workflows, bitemporal close, unknown outcomes, tamper evidence, external control accounts, RPO/fencing, and operational segregation.

docs.title: 22. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
The authoritative object is an immutable journal transaction containing postings that sum to zero for every asset. Route its accounts to one fenced shard; in one serializable commit reserve the durable idempotency key, validate templates and floors, append transaction and postings, update balances, and write an outbox. Unknown commit outcomes resolve by key lookup. Projections expose fast sequence-tagged reads and can always rebuild.

Holds are balanced transfers among available and reserved layers; capture, release, and expiry race through versions. Corrections are linked reversals and replacements. Cross-shard money uses independently balanced pending clearing accounts and explicit workflow states, not an unbounded distributed transaction. Period close pins a sequence and external reconciliation compares internal control accounts to independently sourced bank/provider statements. Append-only data alone is insufficient: correctness also needs authorization, fencing, dual control, reconciliation, and tested recovery.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a payment risk platform that returns ALLOW, CHALLENGE, or BLOCK before authorization, then detects slower fraud patterns and feeds confirmed outcomes back into models. We will define decision accountability, estimate load and latency, design online features and rules/models, then cover event time, case management, replay, consistency, degradation, and privacy.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
Fraud detection minimizes expected loss while controlling false declines and customer friction. It does not move money; the payment orchestrator owns authorization. The platform supplies a versioned decision and evidence. Some facts, such as chargebacks, arrive weeks later, so low-latency decisions and retrospective learning have different clocks.

Assume card and wallet payments across regions. Regulatory screening is adjacent but separate. Manual investigators review selected cases. A block policy must be explainable and reversible; a model score alone is not the audit record.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Score payment attempts using transaction, account, device, merchant, and graph signals.
  • Execute deterministic rules and versioned models.
  • Return reason codes and required challenge.
  • Update velocity features within seconds.
  • Ingest chargebacks, authentication outcomes, and investigator labels.
  • Create cases, replay decisions, and support shadow policies.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• 100,000 decisions/second peak; p99 under 80 ms with 99.99% availability.
  • No duplicate attempt may inflate velocity counters.
  • High-risk emergency rules propagate globally in under 30 seconds.
  • Decisions and evidence remain auditable for the required retention period.
  • Graceful degradation must be explicit by product and risk tier.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. A caller-scoped payment_attempt_id pins one policy version and one effective decision; retries cannot select a newer policy.
  2. Feature values used, rule/model versions, threshold, decision, and reasons are durably recorded.
  3. Duplicate or reordered events do not double-increment velocity features.
  4. Features respect event time and never use information learned after the decision in replay evaluation.
  5. A request never mixes policy artifacts: it pins one immutable bundle even while a fleet canary runs multiple versions.
  6. Fail-open or fail-closed behavior is configured and audited per instrument, amount, and regulation.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
At 100,000 peak decisions/second and 4 KB request plus evidence, ingress is 400 MB/s. Sustaining that peak for 30 days produces 1.037 PB before compression, replication, and indexing; actual retention uses measured average rate, not peak. Keep a narrow query index and archive full evidence in object storage. Ten velocity reads per request require one million reads/s; three writes add 300,000 writes/s, before retries and stream maintenance.

With an 80 ms p99, reserve about 10 ms gateway, 25 ms parallel feature fetch, 10 ms rules, 15 ms model, 10 ms persistence/network, and 10 ms margin. Cross-region calls do not fit. Models and hot features must be local. Expensive graph computation is precomputed; the request path fetches compact signals.

These are stage deadline allocations, not additive p99 measurements: component p99s do not generally sum to end-to-end p99. Measure correlated feature stalls, audit latency, and queued requests together under the full workload. A feature group's deadline includes pool wait and retries, not just service execution.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
RiskRequest(attempt_id, account_id, merchant_id, device_id, amount_minor,
            currency, event_time, channel, context)
DecisionAttempt(caller_id, attempt_id, request_hash, policy_version, state, version)
Decision(attempt_id, policy_version, outcome, score, reasons,
         feature_snapshot_ref, decided_at, degraded_flags)
FeatureValue(entity_key, feature_name, window, value, event_time, revision)
RiskEvent(event_id, type, entity_keys, event_time, payload, source)
PolicyBundle(version, rules_hash, model_version, schema_hash, effective_at, status)
Case(case_id, subject_keys, evidence_refs, state, assignee, disposition)
Label(attempt_id, type, observed_at, effective_event_time, source, confidence)

Amounts use integer minor units with currency. Raw risk events and decisions are immutable. Feature stores, graph indexes, and case search are projections. Investigators append state transitions and notes rather than rewriting prior evidence.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/risk/decisions
Idempotency-Key: payment-attempt-123
{ "attemptId":"...", "amount":{"minor":250000,"currency":"INR"}, ... }

200 { "outcome":"CHALLENGE", "decisionId":"...", "policyVersion":81,
      "reasons":["DEVICE_NEW","VELOCITY_HIGH"] }

POST /v1/risk/events
POST /v1/cases/{id}/transitions

The decision API is synchronous. First conditionally create a caller-scoped attempt record containing the canonical request hash, pinned policy version, and PENDING state. A retry reads this record before looking up the currently active policy; changed payloads conflict. Workers compute under the stored version and conditionally finalize one decision. A losing worker returns the committed winner, not its own computation; an unfinished attempt returns an explicit retryable pending outcome. Event APIs are durable asynchronous ingestion with stable IDs. Case transitions require expected version to prevent investigators overwriting concurrent work.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  Pay[Payment service] --> API[Risk API]
  API --> Features[(Online feature store)]
  API --> Rules[Rule engine]
  API --> Model[Local model server]
  Rules --> Decide[Decision combiner]
  Model --> Decide
  Decide --> Audit[(Decision audit log)]
  Sources[Payments, login, chargebacks] --> Log[(Risk event log)]
  Log --> Stream[Event-time feature jobs]
  Stream --> Features
  Log --> Lake[(Evidence lake)]
  Lake --> Train[Training and graph jobs]
  Audit --> Cases[Case platform]
    subgraph ServeLane[Online decision]
      Pay
      API
      Rules
      Model
      Decide
      Audit
      Cases
    end
    subgraph FeatureLane[Feature pipeline]
      Sources
      Log
      Stream
      Features
    end
    subgraph EvidenceLane[Offline evidence]
      Lake
      Train
    end

The API fetches independent feature groups in parallel, evaluates one pinned policy bundle, persists the decision, and returns. Streaming updates near-real-time velocities. Batch jobs create graph and long-horizon features, training sets, and reconciliation reports.

docs.title: 9. Decision execution
docs.text:
Authenticate the caller, validate amount and event time, and first check the idempotency store. For a new attempt, pin the active policy bundle in its durable claim; for a retry, load the bundle already stored in that claim. Fetch account, device, merchant, and network features with deadlines. Rules can immediately block impossible states or require strong authentication; the model estimates risk for remaining traffic. A deterministic combiner maps evidence to outcome.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant P as Payment service
  participant R as Risk API
  participant F as Feature store
  participant E as Rules/model
  participant D as Decision store
  P->>R: score(attempt_id)
  R->>D: lookup or claim scoped attempt, hash, pinned policy
  alt terminal decision exists
    D-->>R: prior decision
  else new claim or resumable PENDING attempt
    R->>F: parallel feature batch
    F-->>R: values + ages
    R->>E: pinned bundle + features
    E-->>R: outcome + reasons
    R->>D: conditional finalize under attempt version
    D-->>R: committed winner or pending outcome
  end
  R-->>P: decision

Persist evidence before returning a decision, as required by invariant 2. A replicated append log can replace the decision store only if attempt claims and finalization are serialized by one fenced partition owner with replayable deduplication; an offset plus a read-through cache alone cannot prevent concurrent conflicting decisions. Never recompute a retry under a newer policy without an explicit new attempt. On recovery, retain the pinned bundle or escalate the pending attempt rather than silently switching versions.

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: velocity features and event time
docs.text:
Examples include payments per card in 10 minutes, distinct accounts per device in 24 hours, and failed authentication amount per merchant in one hour. Stream processors deduplicate event IDs and update fixed event-time buckets. Querying a window sums current buckets. Expiration subtracts old buckets; exact distinct values use bounded sets for small windows and sketches when approximation is acceptable.

A payment may be scored before its accepted event updates the stream. To avoid a burst slipping through, the decision path performs an atomic reservation/increment for critical short-window counters keyed by attempt ID. The stream later observes the reservation and does not increment twice. Less critical features tolerate seconds of lag.

Late events revise historical features for training and investigation, but do not time-travel a completed decision. Replay asks what was known at decision time, using bitemporal records: event time and knowledge/receipt time. Watermarks close operational windows while retaining revisions for a configured horizon.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: rules, models, and policy rollout
docs.text:
A policy bundle contains rule bytecode, model artifact, feature schema/defaults, thresholds, and degradation matrix. It is signed, immutable, validated offline, loaded into memory, and atomically activated. Rules return named evidence, not just booleans. Model explanations can provide bounded feature contributions but must not expose exploitable detail to customers.

New bundles run on shadow traffic. Compare block/challenge rates, latency, missing features, decision flips, and later fraud labels. Canary by stable account hash, then expand. An emergency deny rule uses the same signed publication path with expedited approval and expiry; ad hoc database flags are too difficult to audit. Its independently monotonic emergency generation also gates new payment authorization, including reuse of an older ALLOW decision. Preserve the historical decision unchanged and record any current emergency veto separately. A freshness lease within the 30-second propagation bound makes disconnected authorities stop affected authorization; rollback of an ordinary bundle cannot roll back emergency blocks.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: delayed labels and reconciliation
docs.text:
Authorization success is not a fraud label. Chargebacks arrive days later and may be disputed. Labels store source, observation time, event-effective time, and confidence. Training applies a maturity window and handles censored transactions. Investigator decisions supplement but do not overwrite network outcomes.

Daily reconciliation joins payment attempts, risk decisions, actual authorization actions, challenges, and outcomes. It detects payments with no risk decision, callers that ignored BLOCK, duplicate decisions, missing audit payloads, and policy mismatches. Exceptions create cases. This reconciliation validates integration correctness independently of model quality.

flowchart TD
  P[Payment attempt manifest] --> J[Daily reconciliation]
  D[Immutable decisions] --> J
  A[Authorization/challenge outcomes] --> J
  J --> M{Matched semantics?}
  M -->|yes| Metrics[Loss and friction metrics]
  M -->|no| Case[Operational case]
  C[Chargebacks and reviews] --> Labels[Versioned labels]
  Labels --> Metrics
  Labels --> Train[Point-in-time training]
    subgraph MatchLane[Decision reconciliation]
      P
      D
      A
      J
      M
      Case
    end
    subgraph LabelLane[Delayed labels]
      C
      Labels
      Train
    end

docs.title: 13. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Decision workers are stateless and scale by request rate. Feature keys partition by a hashed entity prefix. Hot merchants or devices use salted write buckets and read fan-in, but critical atomic account counters remain unsalted with strict rate controls. Co-locate regional replicas with scoring fleets.

Event logs partition by primary entity while carrying all related keys; separate jobs update card, device, account, and merchant projections. This duplicates stream work but avoids one impossible ordering key. Graph features compute from immutable edges in batch and publish versioned snapshots.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Decision identity and policy activation need strong consistency. Most features are eventually consistent with recorded age. Critical reservations use linearizable conditional writes. Events are delivered at least once; ID retention exceeds retry and chargeback ingestion windows. Sink writes compare revisions. No claim of end-to-end exactly once is needed.

Multi-region decision commands route a caller-scoped attempt to one fenced authority, normally the account's home region. Local replicas serve global merchant and device signals with bounded lag. During partition, a non-owner cannot durably finalize a competing decision; return an explicit unavailable/pending outcome or execute a separately identified, audited caller fallback. Quarantining conflicting decisions after both were returned would not preserve the one-decision invariant. Ownership transfer requires fencing and recovery of committed attempt claims before new decisions; local scoring latency therefore depends on keeping the caller near its authority.

docs.title: 15. Reliability and overload
docs.text:
• Feature group timeout applies its declared default and records degraded flags.
  • Model server failure falls back to deterministic rules, usually increasing challenges.
  • Policy load failure retains the last verified bundle.
  • Event lag freezes stale-sensitive features or tightens thresholds.
  • Audit append failure returns unavailable/pending rather than an unaudited finalized decision. High-value callers stop authorization; any lower-tier challenge fallback must be separately identified and durably audited by its owning caller.
  • A hot-key attack is rate-limited before it exhausts the feature store.

Bulkheads separate merchants and feature groups. Requests have one bounded retry only when no decision is known. Load shedding prioritizes payment decisions over case search and shadow evaluation. Region evacuation uses tested policy and feature snapshots; recovery reconciles all attempts accepted during isolation.

docs.title: 16. Security and privacy
docs.text:
Use mTLS workload identity, tenant authorization, encryption, key rotation, field tokenization, and strict investigator roles. Separate decision evidence from raw personal data with reference-based access. Display access is audited. Retention differs for financial evidence and behavioral features. Subject deletion removes eligible behavioral data while legally retained decision records remain restricted.

Protect model and rule endpoints from extraction; rate-limit scoring and reveal customer-safe reason families only. Policy publication requires code review, signed artifacts, dual approval for broad blocks, and a tamper-evident audit log.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure end-to-end and per-stage latency, decision mix, score distribution, feature age/null/default rates, reservation conflicts, event and watermark lag, policy version coverage, caller compliance, fraud loss, false-positive proxies, challenge completion, and reconciliation exceptions. Slice by region, merchant, instrument, and policy while enforcing privacy thresholds.

Tests include idempotent retry races, rule determinism, feature event-time boundaries, point-in-time leakage, malformed payload fuzzing, stale feature chaos, model timeouts, policy rollback, hot keys, and regional partitions. Replay historical manifests against old and candidate bundles. Red-team both adversarial input manipulation and investigator access.

docs.title: 18. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Synchronous fresh counters improve burst detection but add a latency and availability dependency; reserve only critical velocities and stream the rest.
  • Fail-open protects conversion but increases loss; fail-closed protects money but harms users. A risk-tier degradation matrix is better than one global answer.
  • A single opaque model is flexible but hard to audit; deterministic rules plus a model and reasoned combiner provide control.
  • Global strong feature consistency is too slow; local scoring with explicit staleness and reconciliation fits the latency budget.
  • Exact unique counts are costly; sketches are valid for model features, not deterministic regulatory thresholds unless error is accounted for.

docs.title: 19. Final design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  GW[Regional risk gateway] --> ID[(Idempotency/decision store)]
  GW --> FF[Parallel feature fetch]
  FF --> PB[Signed policy bundle]
  PB --> OUT[Allow/challenge/block]
  OUT --> ID
  ID --> AUD[(Immutable audit stream)]
  EVT[(Risk events)] --> V[Event-time velocities]
  V --> FS[(Regional feature store)]
  FS --> FF
  EVT --> RAW[(Evidence archive)]
  RAW --> BT[Graph, training, reconciliation]
  AUD --> BT
  BT --> REG[Model/policy registry]
  REG --> PB

docs.title: 20. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. Which features must be synchronously updated?
  2. How do you score when the feature store is unavailable?
  3. How do event time and knowledge time differ in model replay?
  4. How do you prove a caller enforced a block?
  5. How do you deploy an emergency rule safely?
  6. What partition key handles a device shared by many accounts?
  7. How do delayed chargebacks affect evaluation?

docs.title: 21. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should produce a latency-budgeted online path, feature store, rules/model split, idempotent decisions, streaming velocities, failure fallback, and audit storage. An L6 candidate should define bitemporal replay, policy atomicity, critical reservations, caller reconciliation, label maturity, multi-region degradation, and governance around blocking decisions.

docs.title: 22. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Place stateless regional risk workers in the payment path. A durable caller-scoped attempt claim pins a signed policy bundle, then workers fetch local features in parallel, evaluate explainable rules and a versioned model, combine them into allow/challenge/block, and durably finalize one winner with evidence. Retries resolve the attempt before consulting active policy. Critical burst counters reserve synchronously; other velocity and graph features update from an immutable event log with event-time buckets and idempotent revisions.

Policies deploy through shadow, canary, atomic activation, and rollback. Missing dependencies follow an explicit risk-tier degradation matrix. Chargebacks and reviews are delayed, versioned labels, not immediate truth. Daily reconciliation verifies every payment had one decision and that the caller enforced it. Partition features by entity, salt hot aggregate keys, and keep scoring local rather than paying global coordination latency. The design's core is accountable decisions under uncertainty, not merely a high-AUC model.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a home-feed recommender for 100 million daily users. We will clarify objectives and safety constraints, estimate online and training load, separate candidate generation from ranking, then examine feature freshness, event-time training, experimentation, failures, privacy, and multi-region serving.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
For a user and context, return 50 eligible items likely to create long-term value. The system combines follows, collaborative similarity, content understanding, and popularity. It is not a single machine-learning model: it is a data and serving system whose output must remain useful when models or features fail.

Out of scope are item creation, media delivery, and moderation internals. Moderation and inventory systems supply eligibility. The objective balances meaningful engagement, retention, creator diversity, and negative feedback rather than optimizing clicks alone.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Record impressions, clicks, dwell, likes, follows, hides, and reports.
  • Generate candidates from several independent sources.
  • Rank, filter, diversify, and paginate recommendations.
  • Incorporate fresh activity within minutes and train models daily or hourly.
  • Support experiments, explanations, deletion, and model rollback.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• 1 million recommendation requests/second at peak, p99 under 200 ms.
  • 5 million engagement events/second, at-least-once delivery.
  • 99.99% availability; safe fallback if dependencies fail.
  • No blocked item served after a 10-second propagation SLO.
  • Reproducible training sets without future-data leakage.

docs.title: 4. Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every response contains only items eligible for that user, region, age policy, and request time.
  2. Pagination does not repeat an item within a feed session.
  3. Training features use information available at the example's event time, never future state.
  4. Model, feature schema, candidate-source, and policy versions are recorded for each impression.
  5. At-least-once events produce idempotent feature effects.
  6. User deletion removes personal online state and future training eligibility within policy deadlines.

Recommendations are projections, not canonical state. Availability may use stale features, but safety cannot.

docs.title: 5. Estimates
docs.text:
At one million requests/second and 50 results, ranking 50 million final items/second is plausible; scoring the entire catalog is not. If each of five candidate sources returns 500 IDs, the ranker evaluates up to 2,500 candidates/request, or 2.5 billion scores/second, requiring lightweight models, batching, and regional fleets. A 5 KB response produces 5 GB/s before compression.

Five million 200-byte events/second are 86.4 TB/day raw if sustained. Retain compressed immutable events in object storage and compact online features. For 500 million users with 10 KB online state, feature storage is 5 TB logical, or 15 TB at three replicas before overhead. Embeddings at 256 float16 dimensions consume 512 bytes each: one billion items require roughly 512 GB plus ANN indexes.

docs.title: 6. Data model
docs.text:
Interaction(event_id, user_id, item_id, type, event_time, received_time,
            request_id, position, model_version, consent_scope)
UserFeature(user_id, feature_name, value, event_time, revision, ttl)
ItemFeature(item_id, embedding, quality, locale, updated_at, schema_version)
Eligibility(item_id, policy_tags, status, version, effective_at)
FeedSession(session_id, user_id, experiment, served_item_ids, cursor, expires_at)
ModelArtifact(version, schema_hash, training_manifest, metrics, status)

Immutable interactions are canonical evidence. Online features, vector indexes, and session state are rebuildable projections. Offline tables use event-date partitions plus point-in-time snapshots. Personally identifying attributes are excluded or tokenized.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/recommendations
{ "userId":"u1", "surface":"home", "sessionId":"s1", "cursor":"...", "limit":50 }

POST /v1/interactions
Idempotency-Key: e1
{ "requestId":"r1", "itemId":"i9", "type":"CLICK", "eventTime":"..." }

The response includes requestId, opaque cursor, model version, and items with coarse explanation codes. Cursor state references a feed session and signed generation; clients cannot alter offsets. Interaction ingestion acknowledges after durable append. Batch APIs return per-record errors.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Client --> Gateway
  Gateway --> Orchestrator
  Orchestrator --> Follow[Follow candidates]
  Orchestrator --> ANN[Embedding ANN]
  Orchestrator --> Trend[Trending candidates]
  Orchestrator --> Ranker
  Features[(Online features)] --> Ranker
  Safety[(Eligibility)] --> Ranker
  Ranker --> Session[(Feed sessions)]
  Client --> Events[(Event log)]
  Events --> Stream[Feature updates]
  Stream --> Features
  Events --> Lake[(Offline lake)]
  Lake --> Train[Training pipeline]
  Train --> Registry[Model registry]
  Registry --> Ranker

The online path fans out candidate requests under strict deadlines, deduplicates IDs, fetches batched features, scores, applies policy and diversity, and stores session results. The offline path builds point-in-time datasets, trains and evaluates artifacts, then deploys through a registry.

docs.title: 9. Candidate generation
docs.text:
Independent sources improve coverage: recent items from followed creators, item-to-item ANN neighbors, user-embedding ANN retrieval, regional trends, editorial inventory, and exploration. Each receives a quota and 20-40 ms deadline. Partial results are acceptable. Candidate records include source and retrieval score for ranking features and diagnostics.

ANN indexes are partitioned by language or broad market, replicated, and refreshed incrementally. New items enter a fresh-item index immediately and the main index after compaction. Cold users receive contextual popularity plus declared interests; cold items use content embeddings and exploration budget.

docs.title: Choosing and operating HNSW versus IVF/PQ
docs.text:
HNSW keeps a navigable multi-layer proximity graph. It is a strong default for tens of millions of vectors per shard when high recall, low single-query latency, incremental insertion, and sufficient RAM matter. Build-time controls M set graph degree and memory, efConstruction trades build CPU for graph quality, and query efSearch trades latency for recall. Inserts are online, but deletes become tombstones and repeated embedding updates create graph churn, so replicas periodically rebuild from a pinned snapshot and swap generations.

IVF partitions vectors into trained coarse centroids; a query probes nprobe nearby lists. Product quantization stores compact residual codes and computes approximate distances, often reducing vector memory by an order of magnitude. IVF/PQ fits hundreds of millions or billions of mostly stable vectors where memory cost and scan throughput dominate, but centroid/codebook training, batch-oriented rebuilds, and weaker fresh-item behavior add complexity. A small exact or HNSW delta index absorbs new and updated items; queries merge its results with the immutable IVF/PQ base, and compaction folds the delta into the next generation.

Choose from measurements on production-shaped vectors, filters, and hardware, not catalog size alone. Establish exact top-K neighbors for a stratified query sample, then sweep HNSW efSearch or IVF nprobe and PQ code size. Record recall@K, p50/p99 latency, queries/core, resident bytes/vector, build time, update visibility, filtered-query recall, and merge overhead. Recommendation evaluation then checks whether retrieval loss changes downstream outcomes; ANN recall is diagnostic, not the product objective.

Situation Preferred starting point Main operational cost 20M vectors/shard, frequent inserts, high recall HNSW RAM and rebuilds after deletes/updates 1B stable vectors, tight memory budget IVF/PQ Training, quantization loss, batch compaction Large base plus minute-fresh inventory IVF/PQ base + HNSW delta Dual-query merge and generation control 
flowchart TD
  S[Embedding snapshot] --> T[Train centroids and PQ codebooks]
  T --> B[Build immutable IVF/PQ generation N]
  U[Fresh and updated items] --> D[Mutable HNSW delta]
  Q[User query vector] --> P[Probe IVF lists]
  Q --> D
  B --> P
  P --> M[Merge exact IDs and approximate scores]
  D --> M
  M --> E[Eligibility and pre-ranker]
  D --> C[Compaction]
  B --> C
  C --> N[Generation N plus 1]
    subgraph BaseLane[Immutable generation]
      S
      T
      B
      P
    end
    subgraph DeltaLane[Recent items]
      U

Worked ANN benchmark. For 100 million 256-dimensional vectors, raw float16 embeddings alone use 51.2 GB. Assume a hypothetical HNSW profile using 78 GB with recall@100 0.96 and p99 18 ms. A hypothetical 32-byte IVF/PQ profile uses 3.2 GB plus 0.8 GB of lists/centroids, with recall 0.90 and p99 11 ms at nprobe=16, or recall 0.95 and p99 31 ms at nprobe=64. These are invented planning inputs, not results of a cited benchmark or a measurement performed for this book. Under a 25 ms deadline they illustrate choosing the higher-memory profile; actual selection requires a reproducible corpus, implementation, hardware and filter workload.

docs.title: 10. Ranking and serving
docs.text:
A cheap pre-ranker reduces 2,500 candidates to 300; a richer ranker scores those; a deterministic post-ranker enforces safety, author caps, diversity, freshness, and already-seen suppression. A feed session stores a bounded ordered oversupply, perhaps 200 IDs, allowing cheap pagination and stable experiments. When exhausted, the next cursor generates more while carrying an exact bounded seen set. Atomically advance session generation, its seen set, and page publication so concurrent cursors cannot publish overlapping pages. Return the winning stored page on a retry. Set an explicit session length/expiry bound; a Bloom filter may suppress unseen items and an evicting set permits old repeats, so neither supports an unlimited exact no-repeat promise.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant G as Candidate sources
  participant F as Feature store
  participant R as Ranker
  participant S as Session store
  C->>O: recommendations(session, cursor)
  par bounded fanout
    O->>G: retrieve candidates
    O->>F: batch user/context features
  end
  O->>R: candidates + features + versions
  R->>R: score, safety, diversify
  R->>S: atomic page and seen-set generation update
  S-->>R: committed winner page or conflict
  R-->>O: committed page
  O-->>C: items + signed cursor

Deadline budgets prevent retry storms. If ANN times out, use follows and trends. If online features fail, use cached user state and item priors. Every page, cached cohort and retry rechecks current eligibility, with backfill advancing past scanned positions. Enforce a policy-freshness lease within the 10-second removal bound and fail closed when it expires; push invalidation alone cannot guarantee that deadline. This gate also applies to non-sensitive blocked inventory and survives model rollback. Cache anonymous cohort lists, but personalized lists have short TTLs and must respect deletion.

docs.title: Feature and inference batching capacity
docs.text:
The orchestrator deduplicates item IDs before feature access and sends one multi-get per storage shard, not one RPC per candidate. If 2,500 retrieved candidates collapse to 1,800 unique items spread over 16 shards, the request issues at most 16 parallel shard RPCs. At 1 million requests/s this logical workload is 1.8 billion item lookups/s, but microbatching 32 requests for up to 2 ms lets a feature worker deduplicate shared hot items across roughly 57,600 keys and amortize transport. Batch size is capped by bytes and deadline; batchers flush immediately for near-expiry requests.

Inference follows the ranking cascade. Suppose pre-ranking 2,500 candidates costs 4 microseconds/candidate on one CPU core: that is 10 ms CPU/request or 10,000 CPU-seconds/s at 1 million requests/s. At 65% utilization, it needs about 15,385 cores before redundancy. The full ranker scores 300 candidates/request in batches of 64 requests, or 19,200 rows/batch. If an accelerator sustains 1.2 million rows/s at that shape, demand is 300 million rows/s, requiring 250 accelerators; 30% failure/rollout headroom raises this to 325. Measure queueing and padding because theoretical FLOPS do not establish serving capacity.

Worked deadline budget. From a 200 ms deadline, reserve 20 ms for edge/network, 10 ms for serialization, and 20 ms fallback margin. Candidate fanout receives 40 ms, feature multi-get 35 ms, pre-rank 20 ms, full inference 45 ms, and policy/session work 10 ms. Fanout closes when its 40 ms stage allowance ends, not at a conflicting 35 ms cutoff; late sources are omitted without retry. These allocations sum to 200 ms but require end-to-end measurement to establish p99. Dynamic batchers use absolute request deadlines.

docs.title: Deterministic diversification
docs.text:
Diversification is a constrained re-ranking stage after safety filtering. First enforce hard constraints such as eligibility, block lists, and maximum one item from a sensitive category. Then greedily select the item maximizing lambda * relevance - (1-lambda) * max_similarity_to_selected - author_penalty - exposure_penalty, subject to per-author, topic, format, and freshness quotas. Maximum marginal relevance is explainable and bounded for hundreds of candidates; a learned slate model can improve interactions but is harder to debug and must still pass the hard constraint layer.

With pinned candidates, features, exposure state and policy, stable score quantization and item-ID tie-breaks make the algorithm deterministic. The committed session page supplies retry identity when those inputs change. Relaxation is explicit: if fewer than 50 items remain, relax soft topic targets, then format targets, but never safety or block constraints. Track unique authors/topics, concentration indexes, pairwise embedding similarity, freshness, relevance loss against the un-diversified list, and guardrail outcomes by cohort.

Worked diversification example. The top five scores are three near-identical posts from author A at 0.94, 0.93, and 0.92, a different-topic post from B at 0.89, and a fresh post from C at 0.84. With an author cap of two and similarity penalty 0.20, an illustrative slate is A1, B1, C1, A2 if the actual pairwise similarities and remaining penalties make that greedy order win; scores and one penalty constant alone do not determine the order. In that slate, A3 is rejected by the cap. The slate gives up 0.03-0.08 pointwise score for broader coverage, and the impression records both raw rank and final selection reason.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: streaming and event-time features
docs.text:
Stream processors deduplicate event_id and maintain features such as 10-minute topic clicks, 7-day creator affinity, and recent seen items. Fixed event-time buckets allow expiration by subtracting old buckets. Watermarks handle delayed clients; revisions carry (user, feature, event_time, revision) so stale writes cannot overwrite newer state.

Late data may update durable offline features but should not unexpectedly reorder an active session. New requests use the latest valid feature snapshot; an existing page remains immutable. High-volume celebrity-item counters use salted partial aggregation. User keys distribute naturally but bot users receive quotas to protect state.

The online and offline feature definitions share declarative transformations. Materialization differs, semantics do not. Monitoring compares sampled online values with point-in-time offline recomputation to detect training-serving skew.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: leakage-free training
docs.text:
Training examples join an impression with outcomes in a defined label window. Each feature is looked up "as of" impression time. A daily snapshot joined by current value is wrong because it leaks later popularity or user behavior. Immutable manifests pin input partitions, feature definitions, label horizon, consent state, and code.

Constrain knowledge time as well as event time: a correction backdated to yesterday but first available tomorrow was not available to yesterday's ranker. Feast's point-in-time join documentation distinguishes these conditions and documents created-timestamp filtering where supported. Retain an availability timestamp reflecting the online path and validate the chosen offline store's behavior, rather than assuming an event-time join prevents all leakage (accessed 2026-09-08).

Negative examples come from impressed-but-not-engaged items, not arbitrary catalog items. Position and prior model influence are logged to reduce selection bias. Exploration traffic supplies less biased evidence. Delayed outcomes require waiting for label maturity or marking censored examples.

flowchart TD
  I[Immutable impressions] --> Join[Point-in-time join]
  E[Outcome events] --> Label[Label-window builder]
  Label --> Join
  Hist[Versioned feature history] --> Join
  Join --> Data[Training manifest]
  Data --> Train[Train]
  Train --> Eval[Offline + safety evaluation]
  Eval --> Shadow[Shadow/canary]
  Shadow --> AB[A/B experiment]
  AB --> Promote[Registry promotion]

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: experimentation and feedback loops
docs.text:
Assignment is deterministic by user and experiment salt, with mutually exclusive layers for conflicting tests. Log assignment even when serving falls back. Guardrails include hides, reports, latency, creator concentration, and retention, not only CTR. Promotion requires statistical and operational review.

Recommendations influence future data. Over-exploitation narrows inventory and starves challengers. Reserve controlled exploration slots, cap repeated exposure, and monitor exposure distribution. Models are rolled out shadow, then 1%, 10%, and broader. The registry can atomically return a surface to the last known-good artifact.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning and consistency
docs.text:
User features and sessions partition by user ID; item features and embeddings by item ID; ANN indexes by market and vector centroid. Replicate read-heavy item state. Cache feature batches close to rankers. Heavy users are bounded by feature TTL and event-rate quotas.

Interactions and feature projections are eventually consistent. Session page creation uses conditional write so request retries return the same generation. Eligibility uses a strongly controlled source and push invalidation. Model registry promotion is strongly consistent; workers pin an artifact per request, preventing mixed-model scoring.

docs.title: 15. Failures and multi-region strategy
docs.text:
• Candidate timeout yields partial ranking with source quotas redistributed.
  • Feature-store outage uses bounded stale cache and baseline ranker.
  • Model load failure leaves the previous artifact active.
  • Event lag harms freshness but not request availability; surface lag explicitly.
  • Session-store outage can return a non-personalized cached feed with a new degraded session.
  • Bad features trigger circuit breakers based on null and distribution drift.

Users have a home region for mutable features; events accepted elsewhere replicate there asynchronously. Regional serving uses local replicas and tolerates bounded staleness. Eligibility tombstones and model rollback distribute globally on priority channels. Raw logs replicate to the training region; a region failure does not retrain from partial data.

docs.title: Dual-index and model migration
docs.text:
An embedding-model change alters the vector space, so new query vectors cannot safely search an old item index. Build index B from a complete item snapshot using model B, then continuously apply ordered embedding changes after the snapshot watermark. Keep model/index bundles explicit: (query_model_A, item_index_A) and (query_model_B, item_index_B). Workers never mix those halves. Readiness requires checksum and cardinality reconciliation, update lag within SLO, benchmark gates, and successful load on every serving shard.

Shadow a sampled set of live queries against bundle B, logging latency, recall against an exact sample, candidate overlap, source yield, downstream score distributions, eligibility loss, and business guardrails. Canary traffic pins the whole request to one bundle and feed sessions retain that assignment. Ramp 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%; retain A until active sessions expire and rollback time passes. Rollback atomically changes the registry pointer, while dual-write continues long enough to avoid rebuilding under incident pressure.

flowchart TD
  E[Canonical item changes] --> IA[Index A updater]
  E --> IB[Index B updater]
  MA[Query model A] --> BA[Bundle A]
  IA --> BA
  MB[Query model B] --> BB[Bundle B]
  IB --> BB
  R[Version registry] --> X[Request router]
  X -->|control and existing sessions| BA
  X -->|shadow then canary| BB
  BA --> O[Comparable logs and guardrails]
  BB --> O
  O --> R

Worked migration. Index B is built from snapshot offset 900 and catches up through offset 1,240 while live is at 1,250, so its lag is 10 events. Reconciliation finds 99,998,700 of 100,000,000 eligible items; the missing 1,300 exceed the 100-item gate, so shadowing may continue but canary serving cannot start. After repair reaches the gate, 1% canary traffic uses model and index B together. A latency regression rolls the bundle pointer back to A; no request sends model-B vectors to index A.

docs.title: Runaway-source overload containment
docs.text:
A candidate source can become runaway by returning too many IDs, expanding fanout recursively, retrying, or consuming shared feature/inference capacity after its usefulness falls. Enforce source-specific concurrency, QPS, response-byte, candidate-count, and CPU budgets at both caller and callee. The orchestrator accepts only the first bounded, schema-valid response before the source deadline, truncates excess deterministically, and never retries within the same recommendation request. Bulkheads give core follows/trends and active ranking separate queues from experimental sources.

Admission uses per-source token buckets plus a global cost budget measured in candidates entering each downstream stage. Circuit breakers trip on timeout, malformed-size, marginal-yield, and resource-saturation signals. Under pressure, shed shadow traffic, exploration sources, expensive ANN probes, and extra candidates in that order; preserve eligibility and the safe fallback. Autoscaling may follow sustained demand but is not the first response to positive feedback, because scaling every downstream service amplifies cost and recovery time.

Use the Applied AI Systems track to extend this design into model pipelines, serving, vector retrieval, evaluation, adaptation, reliability, and governed data flywheels.

Worked overload example. An experimental graph source normally returns 300 candidates for 10% of requests, or 30 million candidates/s. A bug returns 30,000 and retries twice, attempting 9 billion candidates/s. A 500-ID response cap, 50,000-request/s source token bucket, and no-retry rule limit admission to 25 million candidates/s; its isolated queue fills and the breaker opens. Other sources retain their reserved inference lanes, and affected requests redistribute quota to trends rather than exhausting the shared feature store.

docs.title: 16. Security, privacy, and abuse
docs.text:
Authenticate event producers, authorize internal feature access by purpose, encrypt stores, and audit model/data access. Consent is evaluated both at collection and dataset construction. Deletion writes a tombstone to online stores, embedding indexes, caches, and future training filters; immutable audit data is access-restricted and aged out according to policy.

Adversaries may poison interactions or scrape recommendations. Apply device/account rate limits, trust-weight events, detect coordinated behavior, sign cursors, and avoid exposing raw scores. Safety policy cannot be overridden by model output.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track request latency by stage, candidate count/source/timeout, feature age and null rate, model score drift, eligibility-filter count, diversity, cache hit rate, session duplicates, event-time lag, online-offline feature parity, and business guardrails. Join sampled impressions to eventual outcomes by request_id.

Tests include feature transformation parity, point-in-time leakage checks, deterministic session pagination, model contract tests, ANN recall benchmarks, chaos timeouts, stale eligibility tests, skewed event loads, and deletion end-to-end audits. Replay a fixed event manifest and assert feature hashes. Load-test fallback paths, since they receive the most traffic during incidents.

docs.title: 18. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Precomputing full feeds makes reads cheap but becomes stale and expensive for inactive users; online composition balances freshness and cost.
  • One large ranker may improve relevance but threatens latency; cascaded ranking spends computation selectively.
  • Fresh mutable features improve response but amplify instability; immutable sessions provide user-visible continuity.
  • Central global features simplify semantics but add WAN latency; home-region writes with local replicas fit bounded staleness.
  • Rich personal history can improve accuracy but increases privacy and deletion cost; use minimum necessary, TTL-bound features.

docs.title: 19. Final architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB

    FR --> PF[Policy + diversity]

docs.title: 20. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. How do you prevent point-in-time leakage?
  2. What is the latency budget for candidate fanout and ranking?
  3. How do cold users and cold items enter the system?
  4. What happens when the feature store is stale for an hour?
  5. How do you evaluate ANN recall versus recommendation quality?
  6. How does deletion propagate into trained models?
  7. How do you limit feedback loops and creator concentration?

docs.title: 21. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should separate retrieval, ranking, post-filtering, event collection, training, and online features; estimate fanout; explain caching, fallback, partitioning, and model rollout. An L6 candidate should reason about leakage, feedback loops, experimentation validity, feature parity, safety priority, privacy lifecycle, multi-region ownership, and degradation budgets.

docs.title: 22. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Use several bounded candidate sources so no model must search the full catalog. Merge and deduplicate candidates, pre-rank cheaply, score a smaller set with versioned online features, then apply non-negotiable eligibility and deterministic diversity. Store immutable session pages for stable, duplicate-free pagination. Under dependency failure, return safe trends or cached cohorts rather than fail the request.

Interactions enter an immutable log. Idempotent event-time processors update TTL-bound online features; the same definitions produce point-in-time offline histories. Training manifests pin data, labels, consent, schema, and code, preventing future leakage and enabling replay. Model artifacts move through offline checks, shadowing, canaries, and experiments with guardrails. Partition mutable state by user, item state by item, and ANN by market/centroid. The L6 insight is that recommendation quality depends as much on data semantics, safety, experimentation, and failure behavior as on model choice.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a retail brokerage for cash equities: fund an account, view quotes, place/cancel orders, receive executions, maintain positions and cash, and reconcile with exchange, clearing broker, bank, and depository. We will separate order truth, execution truth, and accounting truth, then cover risk, event ordering, market-data fanout, settlement, failures, and regulation.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
The brokerage is an agent between customers and venues. An accepted order is not a trade; a venue execution creates an obligation; settlement later exchanges securities and cash. Quotes may be stale without changing ownership. Orders can partially fill, and cancel acknowledgement can race a fill.

Scope includes limit/market orders and T+1 settlement in one market. Options, margin lending, matching-engine design, and tax-lot optimization are extensions. A broker may route through an exchange gateway and clear through an external clearing member.

The venue boundary is a protocol contract, not a reliable RPC. Assume each trading session has one fenced sender, durable outbound sequence numbers, replay or gap-fill support, stable client order IDs, venue-assigned order IDs, execution IDs unique within a venue, and a status or drop-copy channel independent of the order-entry session. An acknowledgement confirms venue acceptance, not execution. A timeout is an unknown outcome unless the venue explicitly guarantees that an unacknowledged request was not processed. If a real venue lacks any of these capabilities, the adapter must document the weaker guarantee and compensate with tighter reconciliation or manual review.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Open funded brokerage accounts and expose buying power.
  • Stream quotes and account updates.
  • Place, cancel, and query orders with partial fills.
  • Apply pre-trade limits and reserve cash or quantity.
  • Book executions into immutable cash and security ledgers.
  • Settle and reconcile against venue, clearer, bank, and depository files.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• 100,000 order requests/second at market open; p99 broker acceptance under 100 ms excluding venue.
  • No accepted execution lost or booked twice.
  • Account views available at 99.99%; trading can fail safe under uncertainty.
  • Full auditability with synchronized clocks and retained raw external messages.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. Client order ID is unique per account; retry returns the existing order.
  2. Order filled quantity equals the sum of unique venue executions and never exceeds order quantity.
  3. Cancellation never erases a fill received before or after cancel acknowledgement.
  4. Every accounting transaction balances debits and credits per currency or security unit.
  5. Ledger entries are immutable; correction is a linked reversal and replacement.
  6. Available cash equals settled cash plus approved credit minus holds and obligations, according to policy.
  7. Internal books reconcile to independently obtained venue, clearing, bank, and depository records.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Ten million active accounts placing ten orders/day gives 100 million orders/day, but open and news bursts dominate. At 100,000 requests/second and 1 KB audit payloads, the order ingress is 100 MB/s. Executions may exceed orders due to partial fills.

For market data, one million active symbols at 10 normalized updates/second produce 10 million updates/second internally. Suppose two million concurrent clients each watch 20 symbols: that is 40 million active subscriptions. Delivering every source update at the same 10 Hz would require 400 million client messages/second. At 200 bytes/message before TLS and WebSocket overhead, payload egress alone is 80 GB/s. Conflating each symbol to at most one update every 250 ms caps a continuously changing subscription at 4 messages/second, or 160 million messages/second and 32 GB/s in the worst case. Actual load is lower because many symbols update less often, but gateways must be sized from the measured subscription-weighted update rate, not symbol count. At a measured safe limit of 40,000 outbound messages/second per gateway, the 160 million messages/second bound requires 160,000,000 / 40,000 = 4,000 gateways before failover and burst headroom. At the worst-case 4 Hz this output limit admits only 10,000 continuously changing subscriptions per gateway; a larger subscription count is safe only when measurement proves a lower subscription-weighted update rate.

Ledger volume includes holds, releases, trades, fees, settlement, deposits, and withdrawals. At 20 postings/order lifecycle and 200 bytes/posting, 100 million orders imply 400 GB/day before replication and indexes. Keep primary account indexes narrow and archive journal payloads.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
Order(order_id, account_id, client_order_id, symbol, side, type, quantity,
      limit_price_minor, status, current_attempt_id, filled_qty, version, created_at)
VenueOrderAttempt(attempt_id, order_id, attempt_no, venue, session_id,
                  broker_client_order_id, outbound_sequence, state,
                  venue_order_id, last_evidence_at, version)
VenueOrderMap(venue, session_id, venue_order_id, broker_order_id, attempt_id)
Execution(venue, execution_id, order_id, quantity, price_minor, trade_time,
          received_time, settlement_date, raw_message_hash)
JournalTxn(txn_id, business_ref, type, effective_at, recorded_at, status)
Posting(posting_id, txn_id, ledger_account, asset, amount_signed, layer)
Hold(hold_id, order_id, account_id, asset, amount, state, version)
Position(account_id, symbol, settled_qty, unsettled_buy, unsettled_sell, revision)

VenueOrderAttempt owns routing and transport state: QUEUED, SENT, UNKNOWN, ACKNOWLEDGED, or REJECTED. Order.status is the customer-visible lifecycle derived from attempt evidence and executions; it does not overwrite the attempt history. Posting uses integer minor currency units or integer security units; never floating point. A journal transaction must sum to zero independently for each asset. Orders, attempts, and projections are mutable state machines, while executions, journal transactions, and postings are append-only.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/accounts/{account}/orders
Idempotency-Key: client-order-77
{ "symbol":"ACME", "side":"BUY", "type":"LIMIT", "quantity":10,
  "limitPrice":{"minor":12550,"currency":"INR"} }

POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel
If-Match: "order-version-4"
GET /v1/orders/{id}
GET /v1/accounts/{id}/positions?asOf=...

GET /v1/quotes/{symbol}
200 { "symbol":"ACME", "bidMinor":12545, "askMinor":12550,
      "stream":"venue-a:eq", "sequence":91822, "asOf":"...", "stale":false }

WS /v1/quotes/stream
SUBSCRIBE { "symbols":["ACME","WIDGET"], "requestId":"sub-9" }
SNAPSHOT { "subscriptionId":"s-41", "stream":"retail-eq-12",
           "sequence":4401, "quotes":[...] }
UPDATE { "subscriptionId":"s-41", "sequence":4402, "changes":[...] }

Acceptance means the broker durably recorded and queued the order, not that the venue accepted it. Responses distinguish BROKER_ACCEPTED, ROUTE_UNKNOWN, VENUE_ACCEPTED, PARTIALLY_FILLED, FILLED, CANCEL_PENDING, CANCELLED, and REJECTED. ROUTE_UNKNOWN means the current VenueOrderAttempt is UNKNOWN: the venue may have accepted the order, the hold remains, and the order is neither rejected nor safe to route under a new economic identity. WebSocket account events carry sequence numbers; clients detect gaps and resnapshot.

A quote GET returns a point-in-time value with source stream, sequence, exchange time, receive time, and staleness. A subscription begins with a snapshot and then deltas whose sequence is scoped to the returned retail stream, not necessarily the raw venue feed. The gateway buffers deltas while taking the snapshot, sends the snapshot at sequence S, then releases only deltas greater than S. A client seeing a gap or reconnecting without a retained resume window requests a new snapshot; replaying arbitrary old deltas onto a fresh snapshot is invalid. Duplicate sequences are ignored.
