This contract preserves convergence without pretending that quotes are transactionally current.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  App --> API[Trading API]
  API --> Risk[Pre-trade risk]
  Risk --> OMS[(Order state + outbox)]
  OMS --> Router[Venue router]
  Router <--> Venue[Exchange]
  Venue --> Exec[Execution ingest]
  Exec --> OMS
  Exec --> Ledger[Immutable ledger]
  Ledger --> Views[(Cash/position projections)]
  Market[Market-data feeds] --> MD[Normalizer + conflation]
  MD --> Bus[Partitioned quote streams]
  Bus --> SG[Subscription gateways]
  SG --> App
  External[Clearer/bank/depository] --> Recon[Reconciliation]
  Ledger --> Recon

docs.title: 9. Order lifecycle and pre-trade risk
docs.text:
The API authenticates the account, validates market rules, and executes account-level risk serially or with fenced optimistic versions. A buy places a cash hold for bounded principal, fees, and slippage; a market order needs an enforceable price collar, protected-limit conversion, or explicitly authorized credit because its execution price otherwise has no finite worst case. A sell reserves available quantity. The transaction inserts the order, hold, first VenueOrderAttempt, and an outbox route command atomically. The router is the sole writer of attempt transport state and sends its stable broker_client_order_id according to venue protocol. On acknowledgement it atomically binds the attempt and reverse mapping from (venue, session, venue_order_id) to broker_order_id. Execution and cancel reports often carry only venue identifiers, so adapters resolve this map before touching order state. Reports that precede the acknowledgement remain durably parked by venue key and are replayed after mapping appears; they are never discarded as unknown orders.

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  [*] --> BROKER_ACCEPTED
  BROKER_ACCEPTED --> VENUE_ACCEPTED
  BROKER_ACCEPTED --> ROUTE_UNKNOWN: attempt outcome ambiguous
  ROUTE_UNKNOWN --> VENUE_ACCEPTED: acknowledgement or execution
  ROUTE_UNKNOWN --> BROKER_ACCEPTED: absence proven and retry safe
  BROKER_ACCEPTED --> REJECTED
  ROUTE_UNKNOWN --> REJECTED: authoritative venue rejection
  VENUE_ACCEPTED --> PARTIALLY_FILLED
  VENUE_ACCEPTED --> FILLED: full execution
  ROUTE_UNKNOWN --> FILLED: full execution before acknowledgement
  ROUTE_UNKNOWN --> PARTIALLY_FILLED: execution precedes acknowledgement
  PARTIALLY_FILLED --> PARTIALLY_FILLED
  PARTIALLY_FILLED --> FILLED
  VENUE_ACCEPTED --> CANCEL_PENDING
  PARTIALLY_FILLED --> CANCEL_PENDING
  CANCEL_PENDING --> CANCELLED
  CANCEL_PENDING --> FILLED
  CANCEL_PENDING --> CANCEL_PENDING: partial fill while cancel unresolved
  CANCEL_PENDING --> VENUE_ACCEPTED: cancel rejected, no fills
  CANCEL_PENDING --> PARTIALLY_FILLED: cancel rejected, some fills

States do not assume message order. UNKNOWN belongs to the attempt; ROUTE_UNKNOWN is the corresponding derived order status exposed while recovery is in progress. An execution is accepted by unique (venue,execution_id) even if the venue acknowledgement is delayed. A cancel means "cancel remaining quantity" and can race fills. The derived order status follows filled quantity and venue facts, not arrival order. A cancel acknowledgement releases only the confirmed unfilled remainder using venue cumulative quantity and a reconciled execution prefix; reserve any known-but-not-yet-booked fills until their executions arrive. A late report of an already executed fill must not spend cash that cancellation incorrectly released.

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: immutable brokerage ledger
docs.text:
Use a double-entry, multi-asset journal. When reserving INR 1,260.00, debit customer:available:INR and credit customer:held:INR as balance-layer transfers. On a fill, release the proportional hold, recognize unsettled cash payable, security receivable, broker fee revenue, and taxes through balanced transactions. At settlement, move unsettled to settled accounts. Security postings balance units just as cash postings balance currency.

The ledger accepts a business idempotency key such as execution:venue:123. It validates all accounts and balanced sums, appends transaction and postings in one database transaction, then emits via transactional outbox. No update or delete exists. A correction posts a reversal referencing the original and a corrected transaction. Materialized balances are caches; authoritative balance is the sum of postings through a journal sequence.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant V as Venue
  participant E as Execution service
  participant L as Ledger
  participant P as Projections
  V->>E: execution X, partial fill
  E->>E: transaction: execution identity and PENDING_BOOKING intent
  E->>L: book(execution:X)
  L->>L: validate balanced postings
  L->>L: append journal + outbox atomically
  L-->>E: committed sequence 991
  E->>E: mark booking complete and retry pending intents after crash
  L->>P: posting event 991
  P->>P: apply if sequence is next

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: settlement and external reconciliation
docs.text:
At trade date, the clearing broker confirms obligations. At T+1, cash moves through a bank and securities through a depository. Internal settlement batches reference immutable execution sets. External transfer IDs are recorded before submission; retries query status before resending. Unknown outcomes freeze affected withdrawals or quantity rather than guessing.

Reconciliation has independent inputs: venue drop copy versus OMS executions, clearer contract notes versus trade ledger, bank statement versus cash settlement accounts, and depository position file versus security ledger. Match by external ID, date, asset, amount, and account mapping. Breaks become owned cases with aging and severity. A balancing "reconciliation adjustment" without evidence is prohibited.

flowchart TD
  OMS[OMS executions] --> V{Venue drop-copy match}
  VD[Venue records] --> V
  V --> C{Clearing obligation match}
  CF[Clearer file] --> C
  C --> B{Bank cash match}
  BS[Bank statement] --> B
  C --> D{Depository units match}
  DP[Depository file] --> D
  B --> Close[Settlement close]
  D --> Close
  V -->|break| Case[Reconciliation case]
  C -->|break| Case
  B -->|break| Case
  D -->|break| Case

docs.title: 12. Market data and event time
docs.text:
Adapters normalize redundant feeds and retain source sequence numbers, exchange event time, receive time, and quality. A per-symbol order book requires sequence continuity; gaps trigger snapshot recovery. The broker publishes conflated latest quotes to retail clients rather than every tick. Trading risk uses a feed-age threshold and can reject market orders when prices are stale.

The normalizer partitions by symbol and emits compact latest-value records. A subscription gateway authenticates the account, enforces symbol and connection quotas, groups requested symbols by stream partition, and maintains one shared upstream subscription per partition rather than one per client. It builds each connection's snapshot from a sequence-consistent latest-value store, then fans out changed symbols. Conflation happens before per-client serialization so a burst replaces an unsent quote for the same symbol instead of growing a queue.

Each connection has byte and message limits plus a write deadline. A slow consumer first receives more aggressive conflation, then a RESYNC_REQUIRED control message; if it still cannot drain, the gateway closes it with the last delivered sequence. It never drops an arbitrary delta while claiming sequence continuity. Resume tokens are short-lived and bind account, subscription set, stream generation, and last sequence. Gateways shed unauthenticated connections and oversized subscriptions before healthy streams, while a separate non-conflated product uses dedicated capacity and a different contract.

Trade and execution accounting uses venue trade time plus recorded receipt time. Reporting can order by event time; recovery and audit use receipt sequence. Late corrections never overwrite executions: bust and correct messages create reversal/replacement journal activity.

docs.title: 13. Partitioning, consistency, and scaling
docs.text:
OMS ownership partitions by account so holds and buying power serialize locally. Venue sessions partition by protocol session and preserve outbound sequence. Ledger partitions may use account affinity, but each balanced transaction must remain within one shard; use broker clearing accounts per shard and periodic balanced consolidation. Cross-shard transfers use paired pending transactions and a coordinator, not unbalanced writes.

Orders and ledger commits require strong consistency in their ownership shard. Quotes and account projections are eventually consistent and sequence-tagged. Execution ingestion, ledger booking, and outboxes are idempotent. Avoid distributed transactions with venues: durable intent, stable external IDs, status queries, and reconciliation handle the boundary.

docs.title: 14. Reliability and multi-region operation
docs.text:
• API retry finds the order by client key.
  • Router crash recovers unsent outbox rows and venue sequence.
  • Unknown venue send status queries/drop-copy reconciles before resend.
  • Duplicate execution is ignored by venue execution ID only after its durable booking workflow is complete; otherwise resume that workflow.
  • Projection lag shows asOfSequence; trading risk reads authoritative holds.
  • Market-data gaps mark quotes stale and trigger feed failover.
  • Ledger failure stops new risk reservations; it never accepts unbookable trades deliberately.

An unknown venue outcome follows a stateful recovery protocol:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant R as Venue router
  participant O as OMS
  participant V as Venue order session
  participant D as Status or drop copy
  R->>O: mark attempt SENT with stable client ID and sequence
  R->>V: submit order
  Note over R,V: connection fails before acknowledgement
  R->>O: mark attempt UNKNOWN and expose ROUTE_UNKNOWN
  Note over R,O: hold remains reserved
  R->>D: query stable client order ID
  alt venue proves accepted
    D-->>R: venue order ID and current state
    R->>O: bind reverse map and apply venue facts
  else venue proves absent
    D-->>R: NOT_FOUND at reconciled session watermark
    R->>V: resend same stable identity if contract permits
  else still ambiguous
    D-->>R: unavailable or incomplete
    R->>O: retain attempt UNKNOWN and escalate by age
  end

NOT_FOUND is sufficient only after the venue has reconciled through the original outbound sequence; an immediate lookup miss can race ingestion. While ambiguous, the attempt remains UNKNOWN, the order reports ROUTE_UNKNOWN, and the router must not release the hold, send a new client order ID, or report rejection. Only authoritative absence can return the order to BROKER_ACCEPTED for a protocol-safe resend of the same identity; a different venue or identity requires a new attempt only after non-acceptance is proved. Executions from drop copy resolve acceptance even if the order-session acknowledgement never arrives. Recovery workers repeatedly compare outbound sequence, reverse mappings, open-order snapshots, and executions, with bounded retries and an operator queue for aged unknowns.

Each regulated market has an active trading region near its venue and a hot standby with fenced session ownership. Stateless reads can be active-active. Synchronous ledger replication covers only the failure domains that acknowledge the commit. A regional standby with asynchronous copies can lose acknowledged orders, holds, venue keys and postings; recover that complete prefix from surviving logs and external evidence before resuming trading, or require synchronous cross-region durability for a regional zero-RPO contract. Failover requires venue session recovery and sequence reconciliation before order flow resumes.

docs.title: 15. Security and controls
docs.text: Use strong customer authentication, device binding, withdrawal step-up, mTLS to venues, encryption, HSM-backed keys, least privilege, and immutable operator audits. Separate trading, ledger administration, and reconciliation duties. Apply account takeover, wash-trading, market-abuse, and sanctions controls. Mask personal data from engineering logs. Time sources are monitored and signed external messages retained.

docs.title: 16. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track order acceptance and venue latency, state-transition anomalies, duplicate executions, outstanding holds, ledger imbalance attempts, projection lag, market-data gaps/age, unsettled obligations, reconciliation breaks and age, and bank/depository transfer unknowns. Trace by client order, broker order, venue order, execution, journal transaction, and settlement batch IDs.

Tests model every order/cancel/fill interleaving, duplicate and reordered venue messages, balanced-posting properties, integer rounding, partial-fill hold release, bust/correct, venue disconnect, database failover, and settlement-file corruption. Contract tests run each venue adapter against acknowledgements delayed past executions, duplicate IDs, sequence gaps, session reset, status-query races, and an order accepted immediately before disconnect. Property tests assert that an unknown attempt never causes a second economic order and that every execution eventually resolves through the reverse map or an owned exception.

Quote tests join snapshot and live updates while injecting a delta at the handoff boundary, duplicates, gaps, feed failover, gateway restart, and expired resume tokens. Load tests use measured symbol popularity and burst rates, then throttle clients to prove bounded gateway memory, deterministic resync, and isolation of healthy consumers. Daily proof sums all posting assets to zero and compares projection balances to journal recomputation. Disaster drills recover venue sequences and open orders.

docs.title: 17. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Account partitioning simplifies buying power but can hotspot institutional accounts; isolate them or serialize through dedicated owners.
  • Immediate cross-region active-active order writes improve availability but risk duplicate venue actions; one fenced market owner is safer.
  • Mutable balances are fast but unauditable alone; immutable journal plus projections provides speed and proof.
  • Reserving worst-case cash reduces overspend but lowers buying power; product policy may permit controlled credit, explicitly ledgered.
  • Conflated quotes scale retail fanout but are unsuitable for professional tick consumers, which need a separate tier.
  • A long quote replay window improves reconnect success but consumes gateway or stream storage; a short window plus snapshot is simpler for retail clients.
  • Retaining holds during unknown venue outcomes reduces buying power, but releasing them can fund a duplicate order; resolution safety wins over temporary availability.

docs.title: 18. Final design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  T[Trading API] --> AR[Account risk + holds]
  AR --> O[(OMS + outbox)]
  O --> VR[Fenced venue router]
  VR <--> EX[Exchange]
  EX --> EI[Idempotent executions]
  EI --> JL[(Balanced immutable journal)]
  JL --> CP[Cash and position views]
  EI --> ST[Settlement obligations]
  ST --> EXT[Bank/clearer/depository]
  EXT --> RC[Independent reconciliation]
  JL --> RC
  O --> RC

docs.title: 19. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. What does cancel success mean when a fill races it?
  2. How is buying power computed for partial fills?
  3. How do cash and security postings balance?
  4. What happens after a venue send times out?
  5. Which external sources reconcile each lifecycle stage?
  6. How do you recover a FIX-like session after failover?
  7. Why are positions projections rather than truth?

docs.title: 20. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should distinguish orders, fills, and settlement; model partial fills and cancellation races; reserve funds; book immutable balanced entries; and handle venue idempotency and reconciliation. An L6 answer should define shard accounting, external unknown outcomes, drop-copy controls, market-data quality, regulated failover, settlement close, and segregation of duties.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Serialize order risk by account, atomically record an order, hold, and route outbox, then send a stable broker ID through a fenced venue session. Treat venue executions as immutable facts keyed by venue execution ID; accept them despite reordered acknowledgements. Partial fills consume proportional holds, and cancellation affects only remaining quantity.

Book every execution, fee, hold, release, and settlement in a balanced append-only multi-asset journal using integer units. Cash and position screens are sequence-tagged projections, never authority. T+1 settlement moves explicit unsettled obligations through bank and depository. Independently reconcile OMS to venue drop copy, ledger to clearer, cash to bank, and units to depository; breaks create cases, not invented adjustments. Keep market trading single-owner with a fenced standby, and prefer safe rejection when authoritative risk or market-data quality is unknown.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will rank the most rapidly trending topics, videos, or products for a region and category over 5-minute, 1-hour, and 24-hour windows. We first define "trending," then separate exact event accounting from approximate candidate discovery. We will cover event-time windows, hot keys, ranking, serving, replay, abuse, and multi-region operation.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
Trending is not simply the largest lifetime count; that would permanently favor old popular items. It measures recent momentum, optionally normalized against an item's baseline and diversity rules. The product accepts engagement events and serves a fresh ordered list by scope. It need not expose a perfectly exact global order, but it must be stable enough not to flicker and resistant to manipulation.

Out of scope are personalized ranking and content search. Assume eligibility, safety status, category, and creator metadata come from upstream systems. Deletes and safety blocks must remove an item quickly even if historical events remain.

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• Consume views, clicks, likes, shares, purchases, and negative feedback.
  • Compute top 100 by country, category, and configured window.
  • Return ranked items with score explanation and update time.
  • Apply eligibility, moderation, diversity, and minimum-volume policies.
  • Support deterministic replay and offline quality evaluation.

docs.title: Non-functional
docs.text:
• 2 million events/second average, 5x bursts.
  • New legitimate trends visible within 30 seconds; read p99 below 100 ms.
  • 99.99% serving availability and no loss of accepted source events.
  • Bounded cost as items and dimensions grow; one viral item cannot stall a partition.
  • Event-time semantics for delayed mobile events.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants and SLOs
docs.text:
1. An engagement ID contributes at most once per scoring version.
  2. A score uses the policy and metadata effective for the intended computation version.
  3. Blocked or ineligible content is absent within 10 seconds, independent of ranking freshness.
  4. Every served list identifies its scope, window end, score version, and generation.
  5. Approximation may miss an item only within a documented error budget; final candidate scores are computed exactly from retained window buckets.

The freshness SLO is measured from event time for on-time events and from receipt for late events. "Top K" is therefore a versioned projection, not canonical business state.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
At 2 million events/second and 150 compressed bytes, the log receives 300 MB/s or 26 TB/day. Ninety percent are views. Ten million items may be active daily, but only a small fraction can enter any top-100 list. With 200 countries, 100 categories, three windows, and 100 results, published lists are only six million entries; intermediate cardinality is the challenge.

One-second raw counters for every item and dimension would create excessive state. Use 10-second buckets for the 5-minute window and one-minute buckets for longer windows. Retaining 24 hours of compact counters for ten million active scope-item pairs can still require hundreds of GB, distributed across workers. Candidate sketches sharply reduce global shuffle.

docs.title: 6. Entities and model
docs.text:
Engagement(event_id, item_id, actor_hash, event_type, event_time,
           received_time, country, source, metadata_version)
ScorePolicy(version, event_weights, decay, baseline_formula,
            eligibility_rules, diversity_rules, effective_at)
Bucket(scope, item_id, bucket_start, weighted_count, unique_sketch,
       negative_count, revision)
TrendList(scope, window, generation, window_end, policy_version,
          items[{item_id, score, rank, reason}], expires_at)
Eligibility(item_id, allowed_scopes, status, version, effective_at)

Scopes are bounded product configurations such as country=IN,category=sports, not user-defined arbitrary dimensions. Raw events are immutable. Buckets and lists are replaceable projections. Actor hashes have short retention and are used for abuse controls and approximate uniques, not displayed.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
GET /v1/trending?country=IN&category=sports&window=1h&limit=50
If-None-Match: "generation-8492"

200 { "asOf":"...", "policyVersion":17, "items":[...] }

POST /internal/eligibility-events
POST /internal/recompute { "from":"...", "to":"...", "policyVersion":18 }

Engagement arrives through a durable event bus rather than a public synchronous API. Reads use a bounded limit, return an ETag, and fall back from category-country to country only when the product explicitly allows it. Opaque generation IDs prevent clients mixing pages from different lists; normally top 100 needs no pagination.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Apps[Product services] --> Log[(Engagement log)]
  Log --> Clean[Validate and dedupe]
  Clean --> Local[Local bucket counters]
  Local --> Cand[Candidate merge]
  Cand --> Rank[Exact scoring and policy]
  Meta[Eligibility changelog] --> Rank
  Rank --> Lists[(Versioned trend lists)]
  Lists --> Cache[Regional cache]
  Cache --> API[Trending API]
  Clean --> Raw[(Raw archive)]

The data plane is append, local aggregation, candidate generation, exact scoring, and atomic list publication. The serving plane reads immutable list generations from regional caches. A separate control plane owns policy versions, scope definitions, moderation, and rollout.

docs.title: 9. Core requirement: counting recent engagement
docs.text:
Partition input by a salted item key. First-stage tasks deduplicate IDs and update fixed event-time buckets. A deterministic salt from actor or event ID spreads a viral item. At bucket close, each task sends compact partials rather than individual events. Second-stage workers merge salts by (scope,item,bucket).

Weights should not invite opaque arithmetic in an interview. A sample score is:

raw = max(0, 1*views + 3*likes + 6*shares + 10*purchases - 4*negative)
momentum = raw_recent / max(expected_baseline(item, scope), floor)
score = log1p(raw_recent) * momentum^0.3 * freshness_decay

The baseline prevents a huge established item from always winning, while the volume term prevents one event on a tiny baseline from dominating. Policy versions capture coefficients and thresholds.

docs.title: 10. Deep dive: approximate candidates, exact final ranking
docs.text:
Sending every active item to one global sorter is untenable. Each partition maintains a heavy-hitter structure, such as Space-Saving, for each active scope/window and emits top M, where M might be 500 for final K=100. The merger unions local candidates, retrieves their exact bucket totals, computes scores, filters eligibility, and sorts.

This is approximate only at candidate discovery. Set M using replay experiments so recall@100 exceeds 99.9%. Count-Min Sketch alone is unsuitable for final ranking because collisions overestimate counts. For small scopes, exact heaps are simpler. The system records candidate cutoff and error bounds, allowing operators to detect when skew invalidates assumptions. See Probabilistic Data Structures for the CMS/Space-Saving selection boundary, merge constraints, and validation gates.

Count-heavy-hitter guarantees do not automatically apply to the final baseline-normalized, decayed score. An item with fewer views but a much lower expected baseline can win this score while missing every count-based candidate list; exact rescoring cannot recover an absent candidate. Maintain separate positive-engagement candidates, momentum/baseline-stratified candidates, and recent entrants, then measure recall against an exhaustive final-score oracle on bounded scopes. Ordinary insertion-only sketches cannot ingest negative feedback as arbitrary decrements with unchanged guarantees: keep negative counts separately and apply them during exact scoring. The clamp above also keeps log1p(raw_recent) and fractional powers defined when negative feedback dominates.

flowchart TD
  P1[Partition top M] --> U[Union candidates]
  P2[Partition top M] --> U
  P3[Partition top M] --> U
  U --> E[Fetch exact window buckets]
  E --> S[Score and filter]
  S --> D[Diversity rerank]
  D --> Pub[Atomic generation publish]

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: event time, windows, and stability
docs.text:
Workers advance watermarks from source partitions. An event updates the bucket containing its event time. Publish provisional rolling lists at most every 10 seconds using open-bucket contributions; waiting for a full one-minute bucket and then another 20 seconds would violate the 30-second freshness target. A 20-second watermark delay controls initial bucket closure, not whether open-window trends can be shown; events arriving up to six hours late revise affected buckets and may produce a new list generation. Older events remain in raw storage for offline training but do not rewrite the live trend.

Sliding windows are implemented as sums of fixed buckets, subtracting the bucket leaving the window. This bounds state and avoids scanning raw events. Bucket IDs are UTC instants, avoiding daylight-saving ambiguity. When a source partition is idle, explicit idle markers keep its watermark from freezing all output.

Pure ranks flicker around equal scores. Add hysteresis: an entrant must exceed the current item by a small margin, and retain a previous item for a minimum dwell unless blocked. This stability rule is part of policy and measured against freshness; it must never override urgent moderation.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant E as Event log
  participant W as Window worker
  participant R as Ranker
  participant S as List store
  E->>W: event at t, delivered at t+12s
  W->>W: dedupe and update bucket(t)
  W->>R: revised candidate partial
  R->>R: exact score + eligibility + hysteresis
  R->>S: compare-and-set generation N+1
  S-->>R: published

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: eligibility, diversity, and abuse
docs.text:
Ranking and eligibility are separate. A moderation tombstone is pushed to regional serving caches and checked on every read, including cached generation and conditional-GET responses, so removal does not wait for recomputation. A policy freshness lease bounded by the 10-second removal SLO makes isolated replicas fail closed; rollback and stale-list fallback retain the latest safety generation. Rankers also consume the ordered eligibility changelog for complete future generations.

After scoring, a deterministic reranker enforces limits such as at most two items per creator and minimum category diversity. It records whether an item was omitted by score, eligibility, or diversity. This provides explainability and prevents debugging a policy outcome as a data outage.

Bot defense uses trusted-source weights, rate limits, account age, repeated-device patterns, and unique-actor sketches. Suspicious activity enters a separate feature stream and can contribute zero or reduced weight. Never delete raw evidence. A policy update triggers shadow ranking and comparison before promotion.

docs.title: 13. Partitioning, skew, and scaling
docs.text:
Input is salted by item; aggregation state is partitioned by hash of (scope,item). Scope fanout is bounded: enrich an event only into a small configured hierarchy. A global event may update global, country, and one category-country scope, not every possible combination.

Rankers own groups of scopes. Very large global scopes receive dedicated workers; tiny categories share workers. Consistent hashing reduces movement during scaling. Backpressure first delays ranking generations while durable counting continues. If state stores approach limits, spill closed buckets and reduce optional scope frequency rather than discard accepted events.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Event transport is at least once. A state-store put-if-absent(event_id) with retention beyond maximum live lateness removes duplicates; bucket updates and consumed offsets checkpoint atomically within the processor. Downstream partials carry (computation_epoch, partition, scope, item, bucket, revision) and a complete replacement value; mergers retain only the highest revision for that identity and adjust totals by the replacement difference. A newer delta cannot simply replace an older delta. List publication writes a complete immutable generation then atomically updates a scope pointer, so readers never see half a list.

Serving is eventually consistent across regions. Strong global ordering is unnecessary; clients receive asOf and generation. Eligibility blocks are stronger and distributed on a priority path.

docs.title: 15. Reliability and multi-region operation
docs.text:
• Processor failure restores state and offsets, replaying idempotently.
  • Cache failure falls back to the regional list store or the last unexpired generation.
  • Ranker overload slows publication but does not lose buckets.
  • Metadata lag freezes promotion for affected scopes; unknown safety state fails closed.
  • A bad score policy rolls back by repointing to the prior version.
  • Region loss serves a nearby region's slightly older lists while logs replicate and recover.

Each region computes local scopes. A designated region merges global candidates asynchronously, avoiding cross-region coordination per event. Raw archives and policy histories replicate. Recovery drills rebuild a chosen hour using pinned input watermarks, clock values, metadata/policy versions and prior hysteresis state, then compare generation hashes. Raw events and policy alone do not determine a list whose dwell rules depend on its previous generation.

docs.title: 16. Security and privacy
docs.text: Authenticate event producers with workload identity and authorize list management separately. Encrypt data and logs, rotate keys, validate schemas, and reject dimensions that could leak sensitive attributes. Actor hashes are rotating, purpose-limited, and access-controlled. Public APIs enforce quotas and only expose approved metadata. Policy changes, moderation overrides, and replays require audit trails and least-privilege roles.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track source-to-list event-time freshness, watermark lag, duplicate rate, bucket revision count, candidate recall on sampled exact computations, score distributions, rank churn, eligibility-removal latency, cache age, hot-key skew, and per-scope generation failures. Alerts should distinguish empty because no events, all content filtered, and pipeline failure.

Property tests cover bucket add/subtract, dedupe, deterministic reranking, and monotonic revisions. Replay tests compare known event sets and policy versions. Load tests inject a single viral item, 5x bursts, late events, and region isolation. Abuse tests generate coordinated actors. Shadow policies measure overlap@K, rank correlation, freshness, diversity, and safety violations before rollout.

docs.title: 18. Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Exact distributed sorting maximizes precision but wastes shuffle on millions of losers; approximate candidates plus exact rescoring meets a measurable recall target.
  • Processing-time windows are simple but punish delayed mobile traffic; event time gives meaningful trends at the cost of revisions.
  • Updating a mutable sorted set per event offers low latency but creates hot keys and poor replay semantics; bucketed stream state is safer.
  • Active-active global ranking is fresher locally but can diverge; regional counting with one asynchronous global merge is operationally clearer.
  • More hysteresis reduces flicker but hides fast changes. Treat it as a policy with an SLO, not an implementation accident.

docs.title: 19. Final architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  L[(Regional logs)] --> D[Dedupe + enrich]
  D --> B[Salted event-time buckets]
  B --> H[Per-partition heavy hitters]
  H --> M[Scope candidate union]
  B --> X[Exact candidate counts]
  M --> X
  X --> P[Policy, safety, diversity]
  P --> G[(Immutable generations)]
  G --> C[Regional caches]
  C --> API[Read API]
  T[Priority tombstones] --> C
  D --> A[(Raw archive)]

This design spends precision where users see it: candidate discovery is bounded and approximate, final scores are exact over retained buckets, and list publication is atomic. Immutable inputs and versioned policy make rankings reproducible; a separate priority safety path prevents freshness mechanics from delaying removal.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. How do you choose candidate count M and prove recall?
  2. What happens when one item receives half of all traffic?
  3. How would you add personalized trends without leaking user data?
  4. Can a late event remove an item from a previously served list?
  5. How do you distinguish organic virality from coordinated abuse?
  6. Which components require strong consistency?
  7. How would you handle a worldwide event during a regional partition?

docs.title: 21. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 answer should define a score, estimate event volume, use logs and windows, handle dedupe and hot items, publish cached lists, and discuss late data and failure recovery. It should separate ingestion from serving.

An L6 answer should quantify approximation quality, bound scope fanout, define watermark and policy-version behavior, separate moderation from rank freshness, reason about overload and multi-region ownership, and propose replay-based quality gates. It connects ranking correctness to product metrics and abuse controls.

docs.title: 22. Five-minute summary
docs.text:
Consume immutable engagement events into regional logs. Deduplicate and aggregate them in fixed event-time buckets, salted so viral items cannot hot-spot one worker. Each partition emits a bounded heavy-hitter candidate set. Union those candidates, retrieve exact bucket totals, apply a versioned momentum score, safety and diversity rules, then atomically publish an immutable top-K generation. Regional caches make reads fast; priority tombstones remove unsafe content independently.

Watermarks provide timely initial output and bounded revisions for late events. Revision IDs make retries and replay idempotent. Small scopes can rank exactly; large scopes use approximate discovery with measured recall. During overload, preserve counting and delay optional list generations. Regional scopes compute locally, while one region asynchronously merges global candidates. The central tradeoff is controlled approximation for scale without making correctness unmeasurable.

docs.title: Yelp: Local Business Search and Reviews
docs.text:
This chapter develops an end-to-end design for a Yelp-like service. It is intended both as a study guide and as a structure for a 45-60 minute system design interview.

The core challenge is not storing business pages or reviews. It is serving relevant, geographically constrained search results with low latency while reviews, ratings, and business data continue to change.

docs.title: 1. Interview Roadmap
docs.text:
A strong interview discussion can use this order:

Phase Time Goal Requirements 5 minutes Establish the product boundary and scale Entities and APIs 5 minutes Define the contract and data ownership High-level design 15 minutes Satisfy each functional requirement Deep dives 15-20 minutes Search, geo-indexing, ratings, consistency, and scale Wrap-up 5 minutes Failures, tradeoffs, and final architecture

docs.title: 2. Understanding the Problem
docs.text:
Yelp lets users discover nearby businesses, inspect business details and reviews, and contribute reviews. Search may combine:

  • Free text: good ramen, Blue Bottle, or dentist.
  • A category: restaurants, plumbers, hotels, or salons.
  • A location: latitude/longitude, city, neighborhood, or map area.
  • Filters: rating, price, open now, distance, or attributes.
  • Ranking signals: textual relevance, distance, quality, popularity, and personalization.

We will design the core public product, not the business-owner administration platform.

docs.title: Core requirements
docs.text:
1. Users can search for businesses by name, free text, category, and location.
  2. Users can view a business and its paginated reviews.
  3. Authenticated users can create or update a review with a mandatory 1-5 rating and optional text.

docs.title: Clarifications
docs.text:
• A user may have at most one review per business.
  • Search results show a business summary: name, category, location, rating, review count, and optionally a representative image.
  • Search uses the user's coordinates or a resolved named location.
  • Newly created reviews should appear on the business page immediately or within seconds.
  • Aggregate ratings and search results may lag briefly.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Business onboarding and owner verification.
  • Ads and sponsored ranking.
  • Social feeds, follows, reactions, and review comments.
  • Reservations, food ordering, and payments.
  • Personalized recommendations.
  • Full moderation and fraud-detection design.
  • Turn-by-turn maps and routing.

docs.title: 3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Target Reasoning Search latency p95 under 500 ms Search is the primary interactive path Business-page latency p95 under 300 ms Business reads are frequent and cacheable Availability 99.99% for reads Users should still browse during partial failures Review durability No acknowledged review loss Reviews are user-authored source data Consistency Strong for review ownership; eventual for search and aggregates Prevent duplicate reviews without coupling all reads Scale 100M daily active users, 10M businesses Establishes read-heavy internet scale Geographic support Global, location-aware Nearby results require spatial indexing

docs.title: 3.3 Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
• An acknowledged review is durably stored and is never lost because a cache, stream, aggregate, or search index fails.
  • A user has at most one current review per business; retries with the same idempotency key return the original mutation result.
  • Only eligible review states contribute to rating_sum, review_count, and average_rating, and each review version affects those aggregates at most once.
  • Review updates, deletions, and moderation changes preserve a versioned audit history and cannot be overwritten by delayed older events.
  • Canonical business and review databases are authoritative; ratings, caches, and search documents are rebuildable projections.
  • Search pagination remains bound to a stable sort tuple or point-in-time view so page traversal does not repeat or omit results solely due to concurrent index updates.
  • Authorization is checked against canonical ownership for every review mutation; possession of an ID or stale cache entry grants no write access.

docs.title: 3.4 Back-of-the-Envelope Estimates
docs.text:
These estimates establish orders of magnitude rather than exact capacity plans.

Assume:

  • 100M daily active users.
  • 10 searches per active user per day.
  • 5 business-page views per user per day.
  • 1M review writes per day.
  • 10M businesses.
  • 1B total reviews.
  • 2 KB average review record including metadata, excluding secondary indexes and replicas.
  • 5 KB average business search document, excluding images.

Traffic:

Searches/day          = 100M * 10 = 1B
Average search QPS    = 1B / 86,400 ~= 11,600
Peak search QPS       = 5 * average ~= 58,000

Business views/day    = 100M * 5 = 500M
Average view QPS      ~= 5,800
Peak view QPS         ~= 29,000

Review writes/day     = 1M
Average review QPS    ~= 12
Peak review QPS       ~= 100-200

Storage:

Reviews               = 1B * 2 KB ~= 2 TB raw
With indexes/replicas  ~= 6-10 TB
Search documents      = 10M * 5 KB ~= 50 GB raw
With shards/replicas   ~= 150-300 GB

The ratio confirms a read-heavy design. Search throughput and hot-business traffic matter more than average review-write throughput.

docs.title: 3.5 Sensitivity and headroom
docs.text:
Capacity should be expressed as a formula so a changed interview assumption does not invalidate the design:

peak_search_qps = DAU * searches_per_user_per_day * peak_factor / 86,400

At 100M DAU, 10 searches/day, and 5x peak:       57,900 QPS
If searches rise to 20/day:                     115,700 QPS
If peak factor also rises from 5x to 8x:        185,200 QPS

Suppose one OpenSearch data node sustains 800 representative queries/s at the target p95 with 30% safety headroom already included. The initial 58K peak needs roughly 58,000 / 800 ~= 73 query-serving node equivalents before replica topology, zone-failure reserve, and indexing capacity. If 800 were instead a saturation benchmark, the denominator would be 800 * 0.70; use one convention, not both. This is a planning input, not a universal node benchmark; replay production query mixes to measure the real denominator.

Review projections also amplify writes. At 200 peak review mutations/s, an aggregate update, search-document update, cache invalidation, moderation task, and audit event produce about 200 * 5 = 1,000 downstream operations/s. A ten-minute consumer outage creates roughly 200 * 600 = 120,000 review events to drain. If consumers can safely process 2,000/s while 200/s continue arriving, recovery takes about 120,000 / (2,000 - 200) ~= 67 seconds.

docs.title: 4. Core Entities
docs.text:
erDiagram
    USER ||--o{ REVIEW : writes
    BUSINESS ||--o{ REVIEW : receives
    CATEGORY ||--o{ BUSINESS_CATEGORY : classifies
    BUSINESS ||--o{ BUSINESS_CATEGORY : belongs_to
    BUSINESS ||--|| RATING_AGGREGATE : has

    USER {
        uuid user_id PK
        string display_name
        string status
        timestamp created_at
    }

    BUSINESS {
        uuid business_id PK
        string name
        string description
        decimal latitude
        decimal longitude
        string address
        string city
        string timezone
        string status
        timestamp updated_at
    }

    REVIEW {
        uuid review_id PK
        uuid user_id FK
        uuid business_id FK
        int rating
        string text
        string status
        timestamp created_at
        timestamp updated_at
    }

    RATING_AGGREGATE {
        uuid business_id PK
        bigint rating_sum
        bigint review_count
        decimal average_rating
        bigint version
    }

    CATEGORY {
        int category_id PK
        string name
        int parent_category_id
    }

docs.title: Why keep the aggregate?
docs.text: Computing AVG(rating) across thousands or millions of reviews on every business read or search is too expensive. RATING_AGGREGATE provides an incrementally maintained value that can be copied into the cache and search index.

docs.title: 5.1 Search businesses
docs.text:
GET /v1/businesses/search?q=ramen&lat=37.7749&lon=-122.4194&radius_m=5000&category=restaurant&min_rating=4&cursor=...

Response:

{
  "businesses": [
    {
      "businessId": "b_123",
      "name": "Marufuku Ramen",
      "categories": ["Ramen", "Japanese"],
      "location": { "lat": 37.785, "lon": -122.432 },
      "distanceMeters": 1520,
      "averageRating": 4.5,
      "reviewCount": 2841,
      "thumbnailUrl": "https://cdn.example.com/business/b_123/cover.jpg"
    }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "opaque-token"
}

Notes:

  • Use an opaque cursor instead of an offset for stable pagination at scale.
  • Cap radius_m, page size, and query complexity.
  • Coordinates may be replaced by a location_id produced by geocoding.

docs.title: 5.2 Get business details
docs.text:
GET /v1/businesses/{business_id}

The response contains the business profile, categories, opening hours, attributes, aggregate rating, and media references. Images themselves are served by a CDN.

docs.title: 5.3 Get reviews
docs.text:
GET /v1/businesses/{business_id}/reviews?sort=recent&limit=20&cursor=...

Possible sort modes include recent, highest, lowest, and useful. Each sort mode needs a corresponding index or a precomputed ranking strategy.

docs.title: 5.4 Create a review
docs.text:
POST /v1/businesses/{business_id}/reviews
Idempotency-Key: 765899d0-...
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "rating": 5,
  "text": "Excellent noodles and fast service."
}

Return 201 Created after the durable database commit. The response should include the canonical review and current processing state.

docs.title: 5.5 Update a review
docs.text:
PUT /v1/businesses/{business_id}/reviews/me
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "rating": 4,
  "text": "Updated after a second visit."
}

PUT is naturally idempotent. Optimistic concurrency can use an If-Match header or a review version.

docs.title: 6.1 Start with one synchronous PostgreSQL/PostGIS system
docs.text:
For a new product, OpenSearch and Kafka are not prerequisites. One multi-AZ PostgreSQL cluster with PostGIS can own businesses, categories, reviews, rating aggregates, and an outbox table. A synchronous review transaction inserts or updates the review, adjusts rating_sum and review_count, and inserts a versioned cache-refresh event in the outbox. After commit, the outbox relay invalidates or refreshes the cache; no network cache call runs inside the SQL transaction. Search uses a GiST location index plus PostgreSQL full-text or trigram indexes:

SELECT business_id, name, average_rating,
       ST_Distance(location, :point) AS distance_m
FROM businesses
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND ST_DWithin(location, :point, :radius_m)
  AND search_text @@ websearch_to_tsquery('simple', :query)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_text, websearch_to_tsquery('simple', :query)) DESC,
         distance_m ASC, business_id ASC
LIMIT :limit;

Use a generated tsvector, a GIN text index, a GiST geography index, and the pinned keyset pagination described below. This baseline gives immediate ratings, simple transactions, and one repair surface. It is appropriate while representative load tests remain below roughly 2,000 peak searches/s, p95 stays below 300 ms, database CPU stays below 60% at peak, replica lag stays below one second, and review writes do not create visible lock waits. These are measured trigger examples, not laws; hardware and query shape determine the actual limits.

Do not migrate merely because the business count crosses a round number. Migrate when at least one sustained signal appears despite query/index tuning: search p95 exceeds 500 ms, search consumes over 50% of primary capacity, text/geo relevance requires typo tolerance or facets PostgreSQL cannot economically provide, synchronous rating lock p99 exceeds 100 ms, or projection work threatens the review-write SLO.

docs.title: 6.2 Evolve projections without changing the source of truth
docs.text:
First introduce a transactional outbox while still applying the rating synchronously. Next relay outbox events to Kafka and build OpenSearch in shadow mode. Compare result quality, counts, and latency, then switch search reads with an alias or feature flag. Finally move rating and cache projections asynchronous only after consumers are idempotent and reconciliation exists. The review row remains authoritative throughout.

flowchart LR
    A[Stage 1: PostgreSQL and PostGIS] -->|Search pressure measured| B[Stage 2: Outbox and Kafka]
    B -->|Shadow index validated| C[Stage 3: OpenSearch reads]
    C -->|Write contention measured| D[Stage 4: Async aggregates and caches]
    A --- A1[Synchronous review and rating transaction]
    B --- B1[Durable change stream]
    C --- C1[SQL remains canonical]
    D --- D1[Rebuildable projections with lag SLOs]

During migration, dual-read comparisons are safe; application dual writes are not. Populate OpenSearch from a database snapshot at watermark W, replay outbox events after W, verify sampled documents and deletions, then cut over. If OpenSearch regresses, route reads back to bounded PostGIS queries while the data volume still permits it.

docs.title: 6.3 Scaled architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[Web and Mobile Clients] --> CDN[CDN and Edge]
    CDN --> GW[API Gateway]
    GW --> AUTH[Authentication Service]
    GW --> SS[Search Service]
    GW --> BS[Business Service]
    GW --> RS[Review Service]

    SS --> RC[(Search Result Cache)]
    SS --> SEARCH[(OpenSearch Cluster)]
    SS --> GEO[Geocoding Service]

    BS --> BC[(Business Cache)]
    BS --> BDB[(Business Database)]

    RS --> RDB[(Review Database)]
    RS --> OUTBOX[(Transactional Outbox)]

    OUTBOX --> RELAY[Outbox Relay]
    RELAY --> KAFKA[Kafka]
    KAFKA --> AGG[Rating Aggregator]
    KAFKA --> INDEXER[Search Indexer]
    KAFKA --> MOD[Moderation Pipeline]

    AGG --> BDB
    AGG --> BC
    INDEXER --> SEARCH

    MEDIA[Object Storage] --> CDN

docs.title: Service responsibilities
docs.text: Component Responsibility API Gateway Authentication enforcement, routing, rate limits, request IDs Search Service Query parsing, geo filtering, ranking, pagination Business Service Canonical business metadata and detail reads Review Service Review validation, ownership, durable writes, review reads Search index Denormalized read model optimized for text and geo queries Kafka Decouples durable writes from derived updates Rating Aggregator Maintains rating sum, count, and average Search Indexer Projects business and rating changes into search documents Redis Absorbs hot reads and short-lived repeated searches Object storage/CDN Stores and serves images independently of application servers

docs.title: 7.1 Search read path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant S as Search Service
    participant Geo as Geocoder
    participant Cache as Search Cache
    participant OS as OpenSearch

    C->>G: Search query and location
    G->>S: Validated request
    opt Named location supplied
        S->>Geo: Resolve city/neighborhood
        Geo-->>S: Point, bounding box, or polygon
    end
    S->>Cache: Lookup normalized query key
    alt Cache hit
        Cache-->>S: Result page
    else Cache miss
        S->>OS: Text + filters + geo query
        OS-->>S: Ranked business documents
        S->>Cache: Cache briefly
    end
    S-->>C: Business summaries and cursor

docs.title: 7.2 Why not query the primary database?
docs.text:
A relational database can filter a small dataset using a spatial extension such as PostGIS, but the complete query combines:

  • Fuzzy and prefix text matching.
  • Category and attribute filters.
  • Distance calculations.
  • Relevance and popularity scoring.
  • Faceting and aggregations.

A search engine is designed for this combination. It stores denormalized business documents and provides inverted and spatial indexes. The primary database remains the authoritative source.

docs.title: 7.3 Search document
docs.text:
{
  "business_id": "b_123",
  "name": "Marufuku Ramen",
  "description": "Japanese ramen restaurant",
  "categories": ["restaurant", "japanese", "ramen"],
  "location": { "lat": 37.785, "lon": -122.432 },
  "city_id": "sf",
  "neighborhood_ids": ["lower-pacific-heights"],
  "average_rating": 4.5,
  "review_count": 2841,
  "price_tier": 2,
  "is_open": true,
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "popularity_score": 0.82,
  "updated_at": "2026-09-05T12:00:00Z"
}

Copying display fields into this document avoids making one database request per search result. is_open is only a dated projection: an open-now filter needs business-local schedules, holiday exceptions, timezone data and an explicit query-time instant. Recheck freshness or calculate from the schedule at serving time; a boolean indexed hours ago cannot mean open now.

docs.title: 7.4 Geo-indexing
docs.text:
Common options:

Technique Strength Limitation Geohash Easy bucketing and prefix-based locality Cell boundaries require neighbor lookup Quadtree Adaptive hierarchical partitioning More index-management complexity R-tree Efficient geometric range queries Commonly provided by spatial databases Search-engine geo point Built-in distance and polygon queries Couples query behavior to search engine

For this design, use the search engine's geo_point index. Internally it divides the world into cells and examines only cells intersecting the requested region.

Exact distance can use the Haversine formula after coarse cell filtering:

a = sin^2(delta_lat / 2)
  + cos(lat1) * cos(lat2) * sin^2(delta_lon / 2)

a = clamp(a, 0, 1)  # floating-point roundoff guard
distance = 2R * atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1-a))

The important idea is to avoid calculating distance against all 10M businesses.

docs.title: 7.5 Ranking
docs.text:
A simplified ranking function is:

final_score =
    w1 * text_relevance
  + w2 * distance_decay
  + w3 * bayesian_rating
  + w4 * log(1 + review_count)
  + w5 * popularity
  + w6 * business_quality

Raw average rating should not dominate ranking. A business with one five-star review should not necessarily outrank one with 2,000 reviews averaging 4.7.

A Bayesian-adjusted rating helps:

weighted_rating = (v / (v + m)) * R + (m / (v + m)) * C

R = business average rating
v = business review count
C = global or category average
m = confidence threshold

In a real system, ranking evolves into a learned model, but explaining the initial deterministic signals is sufficient for the core design.

docs.title: 7.6 Search pagination
docs.text:
Offset pagination (page=500) forces the search engine to collect and discard many preceding results. Stable keyset pagination needs both an immutable read snapshot and the last item's sort tuple; a tuple plus a vague "query version" is insufficient while documents change. In OpenSearch, page one opens a point-in-time snapshot and the signed cursor contains {pit_id, query_hash, expires_at, last_score, last_distance, last_business_id}. Every continuation uses the same PIT and search_after tuple:

(score, distance, business_id)

For the equivalent ordering score DESC, distance ASC, business_id ASC, the relational keyset predicate is:

WHERE score < :last_score
   OR (score = :last_score AND distance > :last_distance)
   OR (score = :last_score AND distance = :last_distance
       AND business_id > :last_business_id)
ORDER BY score DESC, distance ASC, business_id ASC
LIMIT :limit;

The predicate is evaluated only inside the pinned PIT or an equivalent immutable result generation. PostgreSQL cannot safely carry an ordinary MVCC snapshot through stateless pooled requests. For the baseline implementation, page one therefore materializes a bounded, expiring SearchSnapshot(snapshot_id, query_hash, ordinal, business_id, score, distance) result set; later pages use WHERE snapshot_id = :snapshot_id AND ordinal > :last_ordinal ORDER BY ordinal LIMIT :limit. The cursor is opaque, signed, query-bound, and expiring. If its PIT or materialized snapshot expires, return an explicit restart response instead of silently querying current data. business_id is the deterministic tie-breaker.

docs.title: 7.7 Cache strategy
docs.text:
Search queries have a large key space because coordinates differ. Improve hit rate by normalizing:

  • Lowercase and canonicalize query text.
  • Sort filter parameters.
  • Cache coarse candidate sets by geocell, not final distances or exact-radius results shared across different coordinates. Expand the candidate radius by the maximum cell displacement, then recompute distance and enforce the caller's original radius before final ranking.
  • Cache only the first result page for 15-60 seconds.
  • Include search-index version or schema version in the key.

Do not depend on caching for correctness. Cached/PIT candidates still pass a current business-removal and review-visibility gate within a declared freshness bound; if that policy cannot be established, omit affected content. Keep next cursors after the last scanned candidate so all-filtered pages advance. Caching is an optimization for hot locations and queries.

docs.title: 8.1 Business detail path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant B as Business Service
    participant Cache as Redis
    participant DB as Business DB
    participant CDN as CDN

    C->>B: GET /businesses/b_123
    B->>Cache: GET business:b_123
    alt Cache hit
        Cache-->>B: Business projection
    else Cache miss
        B->>DB: Read business and aggregate
        DB-->>B: Business record
        B->>Cache: SET with TTL
    end
    B-->>C: Details and media URLs
    C->>CDN: Fetch images
    CDN-->>C: Cached media

Use cache-aside because the database remains authoritative and business details are naturally keyed by ID. Popular businesses can become hot keys; Redis clustering, local in-process caching, and request coalescing can spread the load.

docs.title: 8.2 Review storage and access pattern
docs.text:
The dominant query is:

SELECT ...
FROM reviews
WHERE business_id = ? AND status = 'VISIBLE'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, review_id DESC
LIMIT 20;

Create an index equivalent to:

CREATE INDEX reviews_by_business_recent
ON reviews (business_id, status, created_at DESC, review_id DESC);

At moderate scale, sharded relational storage is attractive because it provides transactions and uniqueness constraints. At very large scale, a wide-column store can efficiently keep reviews clustered by business, but enforcing one review per user and supporting updates becomes more complicated.

docs.title: 8.3 Sharding reviews
docs.text:
Shard by a stable hash of business_id:

shard = hash(business_id) mod number_of_logical_shards

Benefits:

  • A business's review pages require one shard.
  • Rating-rebuild jobs can scan one business locally.
  • The access pattern aligns with the partition key.

Risk:

  • A globally famous business can create a hot partition.

Mitigations:

  • Cache its first review pages.
  • Add read replicas.
  • Store old review pages in object storage or a secondary read model.
  • If necessary, split an extreme business by (business_id, bucket) and fan out reads. Do this only for exceptional hot keys because it complicates ordering.

docs.title: 8.4 Consistent review pagination
docs.text:
Use a cursor containing (created_at, review_id). A query for the next page becomes:

WHERE business_id = :business_id
  AND status = 'VISIBLE'
  AND (created_at, review_id) < (:last_created_at, :last_review_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, review_id DESC
LIMIT :limit;

Concurrent new reviews appear before the cursor and do not shift already visited pages.

docs.title: 9.1 Write path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant R as Review Service
    participant DB as Review DB
    participant O as Outbox
    participant K as Kafka
    participant A as Rating Aggregator
    participant I as Search Indexer
    participant Cache as Cache projector

    C->>G: POST review + idempotency key
    G->>R: Authenticated user request
    R->>R: Validate rating and content
    R->>DB: Begin transaction
    R->>DB: Insert review
    R->>O: Insert ReviewCreated event
    R->>DB: Commit transaction
    R-->>C: 201 Created
    O-->>K: Relay committed event
    K-->>A: ReviewCreated
    A->>DB: Atomically update aggregate
    K-->>I: RatingUpdated / ReviewCreated
    I->>I: Update search document
    K-->>Cache: Review and aggregate version
    Cache->>Cache: Invalidate or replace if newer

The review, synchronous aggregate change when enabled, and versioned outbox event are committed in the same local database transaction. This avoids the dual-write failure in which the review commits but event publication fails. Cache invalidation or replacement occurs only after commit and applies max(current_version, event_version), so a delayed event cannot overwrite a newer cached object. Preserve a version high-watermark or conditional fill token even while the value is absent; otherwise an old in-flight load can refill the cache after deletion. Unconditional eviction itself is harmless to correctness but cannot establish version fencing.

docs.title: 9.2 One review per user per business
docs.text:
Enforce the invariant in storage:

ALTER TABLE reviews
ADD CONSTRAINT one_review_per_user_business
UNIQUE (user_id, business_id);

An application-side SELECT followed by INSERT is insufficient because two concurrent requests may both observe no review and then insert.

If resubmission means update, perform an upsert or expose a separate update API. Preserve review history in an audit table or immutable change log if moderation requires it.

docs.title: 9.3 Idempotency
docs.text:
Mobile clients retry after timeouts. The service should store the (user_id, idempotency_key) and response for a bounded period. Repeating the same key returns the original result rather than performing another mutation.

The uniqueness constraint protects the domain invariant; the idempotency key gives retries predictable API semantics.

The review, request hash, and stored idempotency outcome commit together. For sharded reviews, route (business_id,user_id) to a stable bucket so two requests for one pair cannot reach independent uniqueness constraints. PostgreSQL unique and exclusion constraints apply inside their database boundary, not across unrelated shards (accessed 2026-09-08). The baseline spatial columns and query point use geography when radius is in meters, as specified by ST_DWithin; latitude/longitude geometry would otherwise use angular units.

docs.title: 10.1 Incremental calculation
docs.text:
Store:

rating_sum
review_count
average_rating = rating_sum / review_count if review_count > 0 else null

For a new visible review with rating r:

rating_sum   = rating_sum + r
review_count = review_count + 1

For an update from old_rating to new_rating:

rating_sum = rating_sum - old_rating + new_rating

For deletion or moderation removal:

rating_sum   = rating_sum - old_rating
review_count = review_count - 1

docs.title: 10.2 Avoiding lost updates
docs.text:
Two consumers can update the same aggregate concurrently. Options include:

  1. Atomic SQL increments.
  2. Optimistic concurrency using a version field and retry.
  3. Kafka partitioning by business_id, giving ordered processing for each business.

Use Kafka ordering plus atomic updates. Partition ordering reduces races, while atomic storage operations protect against deployment mistakes or multiple consumers.

docs.title: 10.3 Exactly-once effect
docs.text:
Kafka commonly provides at-least-once delivery. Consumers must tolerate duplicate events.

Maintain processed event IDs for a complete, ordered delta stream. If events can be reordered or versions skipped, store the last applied (review_id, version, visible_rating_or_null) contribution, not just the version. For each newer full-state event, subtract the stored contribution if visible, add the new contribution if visible, and update contribution/version in the same transaction as the aggregate. An older event does nothing. For example, if visible rating 2 at v1 jumps directly to rating 5 at v3, add 3 relative to stored v1; applying v3's producer delta of only +1 from unseen v2=4 would undercount. Visibility transitions update both sum and count, and removing the last visible review yields null, not division by zero.

BEGIN
  INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES (?)
  -- If duplicate key, stop.
  UPDATE rating_aggregate ...
COMMIT

This produces an exactly-once effect even when delivery is repeated.

docs.title: 10.4 Reconciliation
docs.text:
Incremental aggregates can drift due to bugs or historical data corrections. Run periodic reconciliation:

  1. Recompute sums and counts from authoritative visible reviews.
  2. Compare them with stored aggregates.
  3. Correct mismatches.
  4. Emit an event to refresh caches and search documents.

docs.title: 11. Deep Dive: Named Locations
docs.text:
A user may search for pizza in Brooklyn rather than provide coordinates.

flowchart LR
    Q[Query: pizza in Brooklyn] --> P[Query Parser]
    P --> G[Geocoding and Place Service]
    G --> L[(Location Index)]
    G --> Shape[Brooklyn Polygon or Bounding Box]
    P --> Text[Text: pizza]
    Shape --> Search[Search Engine]
    Text --> Search
    Search --> Results[Ranked Businesses]

The location service stores canonical places, aliases, hierarchy, centroids, bounding boxes, and polygons:

United States > New York > New York City > Brooklyn > Williamsburg

Use polygon filtering when boundaries matter. Use a center point plus radius for simpler product behavior. Cache place resolution heavily because names and boundaries change infrequently.

Ambiguous names such as Springfield require country, region, user location, and popularity as disambiguation signals.

docs.title: 12. Deep Dive: Hot Businesses and Skew
docs.text: A celebrity venue, viral review, or city-wide event can concentrate reads and review activity on one business_id, defeating capacity plans based only on average traffic.

docs.title: 12.1 Read-path isolation
docs.text:
• Cache the business summary and first review pages as versioned objects, with request coalescing and TTL jitter to prevent stampedes.
  • Serve images through the CDN and bound review-page size so a hot page does not create per-review hydration fan-out.
  • Use read replicas for colder pages, but cap concurrency and serve a stale safe page rather than allowing one business to exhaust database connections.
  • Detect hot keys from per-business QPS and latency instead of permanently adding a special storage path for every business.

docs.title: 12.2 Write and aggregate hot keys
docs.text:
Review writes remain authoritative SQL transactions, partitioned by business_id. Partitioning Kafka by the same key preserves per-business event order but makes a viral business one hot consumer partition. The aggregator should use atomic deltas, micro-batch consecutive changes for that business, and scale unrelated partitions independently; it must not shard one aggregate blindly because updates and moderation reversals still need one auditable result.

If one business exceeds a single aggregate writer, maintain bucketed partial sums keyed by (business_id, bucket_id) and derive the displayed total from versioned partials. Reconciliation still recomputes the canonical aggregate from eligible reviews, so bucket movement or duplicate delivery cannot silently corrupt the rating.

docs.title: 12.3 Overload behavior
docs.text: Prioritize durable review commits and ownership checks over immediate aggregate, search, and cache refresh. Bound queues, expose source-to-projection lag, and degrade to a slightly stale rating or cached first page. Never bypass uniqueness, acknowledge an uncommitted review, or run an unbounded primary-database query because the search or cache tier is overloaded.

docs.title: 13. Data Consistency Model
docs.text:
Data Consistency Explanation Review creation Strong Never acknowledge before durable commit One-review invariant Strong Enforced by a unique constraint Review read-after-write Prefer strong/session consistent User should see their own submission Average rating Eventual, normally seconds Derived asynchronously Search document Eventual, normally seconds Search is a projection Search cache Eventual with short TTL Slightly stale results are acceptable Business administration changes Eventual in search; strong in source DB Removed businesses need priority invalidation

For read-your-write behavior, the review creation response includes the review, and the client can optimistically insert it into the review list. Alternatively, route the user's immediate read to the primary or a causally caught-up replica.

docs.title: 14. Search Index Synchronization
docs.text:
Business metadata and aggregate rating arrive as events. The indexer creates one denormalized document per business.

flowchart TD
    BDB[(Business DB)] --> BO[Business Outbox]
    RDB[(Review DB)] --> RO[Review Outbox]
    BO --> K[Kafka]
    RO --> K
    K --> A[Rating Aggregator]
    A --> K
    K --> I[Idempotent Indexer]
    I --> OS[(OpenSearch)]
    BDB --> Backfill[Snapshot and Backfill Job]
    Backfill --> OS
    subgraph BusinessLane[Business changes]
      BDB
      BO
      Backfill
    end
    subgraph ReviewLane[Review changes]
      RDB
      RO
    end

Business metadata and rating aggregates have independent version spaces. Apply partial fields under their own source versions, or have one materializer join them into a new unified document generation. Comparing an aggregate version directly with a business revision can discard valid updates or regress unrelated fields. Aggregate publication itself uses a transactional outbox.

Operational requirements:

  • Include entity version and event ID in every event.
  • Ignore stale events that arrive after newer versions.
  • Send repeatedly failing records to a dead-letter queue with alarms.
  • Track source-to-index lag.
  • Support complete index rebuilds without downtime.

docs.title: Zero-downtime reindexing
docs.text:
1. Create businesses_v2 with the new mapping.
  2. Backfill documents from a database snapshot.
  3. Replay events generated after the snapshot watermark.
  4. Verify counts and sampled records.
  5. Atomically move the businesses_read alias from v1 to v2.
  6. Retain v1 briefly for rollback.

docs.title: 15.1 Search cluster unavailable
docs.text:
• Serve recently cached first-page results when available.
  • Optionally degrade to category-based popular businesses by region.
  • Do not fall back to an unbounded relational text query.
  • Apply circuit breakers so failures do not exhaust service threads.

docs.title: 15.2 Redis unavailable
docs.text:
• Treat Redis as optional and read from the source database/search cluster.
  • Rate-limit and shed nonessential traffic to protect databases.
  • Use bounded local caches for the hottest immutable projections.

docs.title: 15.3 Kafka delayed or unavailable
docs.text:
• Review writes continue because events remain safely in the outbox.
  • Ratings and search documents become stale.
  • Alert on outbox age and consumer lag.
  • Relay events after Kafka recovers.

docs.title: 15.4 Database primary unavailable
docs.text:
• Business reads can continue from cache and replicas.
  • Review writes pause or fail over to a synchronous replica.
  • Prefer rejecting writes over acknowledging data that may be lost.

docs.title: 15.5 Poison events
docs.text:
• Retry with exponential backoff.
  • After a threshold, move the event to a dead-letter queue.
  • Keep processing unrelated partitions where possible.
  • Provide replay tooling after correcting the bad data or consumer bug.

docs.title: 16. Multi-Region Design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    DNS[Geo DNS / Anycast] --> US[US Region]
    DNS --> EU[EU Region]
    DNS --> AP[APAC Region]

    US --> USC[(Regional Cache)]
    EU --> EUC[(Regional Cache)]
    AP --> APC[(Regional Cache)]

    US --> USS[(Regional Search Replica)]
    EU --> EUS[(Regional Search Replica)]
    AP --> APS[(Regional Search Replica)]

    US --> Home[Home-Region Write Routing]
    EU --> Home
    AP --> Home
    Home --> DB[(Authoritative Databases)]
    DB --> Stream[Global Change Stream]
    Stream --> USS
    Stream --> EUS
    Stream --> APS
    subgraph USLane[US region]
      US
      USC
      USS
    end
    subgraph EULane[EU region]
      EU
      EUC
      EUS
    end
    subgraph APLane[APAC region]
      AP
      APC
      APS
    end

Search and business reads should be served regionally. Review writes can route to a user's or business's home region to avoid multi-primary conflicts. Events replicate derived data globally.

Tradeoff:

  • A single write region simplifies correctness but increases distant write latency.
  • Multi-primary writes improve latency but complicate uniqueness, ordering, and conflict resolution.

Since review writes are infrequent compared with reads, favor simpler home-region ownership and globally replicated reads.

docs.title: 17. Abuse, Privacy, and Security
docs.text:
Although full moderation is outside the core design, mention the boundaries:

  • Authenticate review mutations and authorize updates by ownership.
  • Rate-limit by user, device, IP, and business.
  • Scan text and media asynchronously for policy violations.
  • Track review status: PENDING, VISIBLE, REMOVED, or QUARANTINED.
  • Encrypt traffic and sensitive data; avoid storing unnecessary location history.
  • Keep audit records for moderation actions.
  • Support privacy deletion while retaining legally required anonymous accounting data.
  • Detect coordinated spam using account age, velocity, device signals, similarity, and graph features.

Reviews awaiting moderation may be visible only to the author. Rating aggregation must include only eligible review statuses.

docs.title: 18. Observability
docs.text: Track service-level indicators rather than only machine health.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
• QPS and p50/p95/p99 latency.
  • Zero-result and error rates.
  • Cache hit rate.
  • Search cluster CPU, heap, rejected queries, and shard skew.
  • Geocoder latency and ambiguity rate.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Write success and conflict rates.
  • Database commit latency.
  • Idempotency replays.
  • Outbox age and relay failures.
  • Kafka lag by consumer and partition.

docs.title: Correctness
docs.text:
• Aggregate reconciliation mismatch rate.
  • Search-index freshness and source/index version gaps.
  • Missing or duplicate document counts.
  • Read-after-write visibility delay.

Use end-to-end request IDs and propagate trace context through Kafka event headers.

docs.title: Correctness and contract tests
docs.text:
• Race concurrent creates and updates for the same (user_id, business_id) and assert one current review with deterministic idempotent responses.
  • Duplicate, delay, and reorder review events; each eligible review version must affect the aggregate and search document at most once.
  • Exercise moderation, deletion, and update transitions and compare incremental ratings with a full authoritative recomputation.
  • Page through reviews and search while concurrent writes occur, asserting cursor stability, tie-break ordering, and documented read-your-write behavior.
  • Test authorization, named-location ambiguity, Unicode normalization, geo-boundary cases, and API/schema compatibility.

docs.title: Search quality and migration tests
docs.text:
• Maintain labeled query sets for text relevance, category, typo tolerance, distance, named places, boundaries, and Bayesian ranking.
  • Shadow new mappings and ranking versions, then compare zero-result rate, relevance judgments, latency, and source/index version gaps before alias cutover.
  • Rebuild an index from a snapshot plus event watermark and verify counts, sampled records, deletions, and rollback to the old alias.

docs.title: Load and failure tests
docs.text:
• Load-test peak geo searches, one hot business, first-page cache stampedes, skewed Kafka partitions, and synchronized client retries.
  • Inject Redis, search, Kafka, geocoder, and database failures and verify bounded fallback behavior rather than unbounded primary-store queries.
  • Pause consumers and outbox relays, then verify lag alarms, replay, reconciliation, and recovery without acknowledged review loss.

docs.title: Search cluster
docs.text:
• Partition primarily for capacity, then use replicas for read throughput and availability.
  • Avoid too many tiny shards; shard count should reflect data size and node count.
  • Route queries to regional replicas.
  • Separate heavy indexing from user query capacity where needed.

docs.title: Review database
docs.text:
• Start with logical shards substantially exceeding physical hosts, such as 1,024 logical buckets.
  • Map buckets to physical database clusters through a routing layer.
  • Move buckets during rebalancing without changing external IDs.
  • Replicate each shard across availability zones.

docs.title: Business IDs and review IDs
docs.text: Use UUIDv7, ULID, or a Snowflake-style identifier to generate unique IDs without a central database round trip. Avoid exposing shard topology directly in IDs unless operational simplicity justifies it.

docs.title: SQL versus NoSQL for reviews
docs.text:
Choose sharded SQL initially because:

  • Review writes need uniqueness and transactions.
  • Writes are far lower than reads.
  • The main access pattern has a clear composite index.

Choose a wide-column store when review volume or availability requirements exceed the relational setup and the team accepts application-managed uniqueness and secondary read models.

docs.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous rating updates
docs.text: Synchronous updates provide immediate aggregate consistency but increase write latency and contention. Asynchronous updates keep review writes isolated and resilient. Yelp-like search can tolerate a few seconds of rating staleness, so asynchronous processing is the better default.

docs.title: Cache invalidation versus TTL
docs.text: Business status changes, especially closure or policy removal, should trigger active invalidation. Ordinary rating updates can rely on event-driven refresh plus a TTL safety net.

docs.title: Database geo queries versus search engine
docs.text: PostGIS is sufficient for smaller products or simple distance queries. A dedicated search engine is justified when text relevance, typo tolerance, facets, filters, and geo-ranking are all required at high throughput.

docs.title: 22. Final Design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Client[Clients] --> Edge[CDN / WAF / Load Balancer]
    Edge --> Gateway[API Gateway]

    Gateway --> SearchSvc[Search Service]
    Gateway --> BusinessSvc[Business Service]
    Gateway --> ReviewSvc[Review Service]

    SearchSvc --> QueryCache[(Redis Search Cache)]
    SearchSvc --> Geocoder[Place and Geocoding Service]
    SearchSvc --> Search[(OpenSearch)]

    BusinessSvc --> ObjectCache[(Redis Business Cache)]
    BusinessSvc --> BusinessDB[(Sharded Business SQL)]

    ReviewSvc --> ReviewDB[(Sharded Review SQL)]
    ReviewSvc --> Outbox[(Outbox Table)]

    Outbox --> Relay[Event Relay]
    Relay --> Bus[Kafka]

    Bus --> AggregateWorker[Rating Aggregator]
    Bus --> IndexWorker[Search Indexer]
    Bus --> ModerationWorker[Moderation]

    AggregateWorker --> BusinessDB
    AggregateWorker --> Bus
    AggregateWorker --> ObjectCache
    IndexWorker --> Search

    BusinessMedia[(Object Storage)] --> Edge
