    Reconciler[Reconciliation Jobs] --> ReviewDB
    Reconciler --> BusinessDB
    BusinessDB -->|snapshot for rebuild| Reindexer[Backfill / Reindex Jobs]
    Reindexer --> Search
    subgraph SearchLane[Search reads and indexing]
      SearchSvc
      QueryCache
      Geocoder
      Search
      Reindexer
    end
    subgraph BusinessLane[Business reads and ratings]
      BusinessSvc
      ObjectCache
      BusinessDB
    end
    subgraph ReviewLane[Review authority and events]
      ReviewSvc
      ReviewDB
      Outbox
    end
    subgraph EventLane[Event processing]
      Relay
      Bus
      IndexWorker
      AggregateWorker
      ModerationWorker
    end

docs.title: End-to-end behavior
docs.text:
1. Search requests go to a geo-aware, denormalized OpenSearch index.
  2. Business details come from Redis or the authoritative business database.
  3. Reviews are read from a database partitioned by business and paginated by cursor.
  4. Review writes commit with an outbox event in one transaction.
  5. Kafka consumers update rating aggregates, invalidate caches, moderate content, and refresh search documents.
  6. Reconciliation and reindex jobs repair drift and support schema evolution.
  7. Regional caches and search replicas keep the dominant read paths fast and available.

docs.title: How do you prevent a business with one five-star review from ranking first?
docs.text: Use Bayesian rating, a minimum-review confidence threshold, and separate textual relevance from quality signals.

docs.title: What happens immediately after a user submits a review?
docs.text: The authoritative review is visible through the review service, while aggregate ratings and search may remain stale for several seconds. The response or client-side optimistic update provides read-your-write behavior.

docs.title: How do you guarantee only one review per user and business?
docs.text: Use a database unique constraint on (user_id, business_id). API idempotency alone is not enough.

docs.title: How do you avoid losing the rating update event?
docs.text: Write the review and outbox event in the same database transaction, then relay the outbox asynchronously.

docs.title: How do you handle a celebrity business receiving huge traffic?
docs.text: Cache its details and first review pages, use read replicas, coalesce concurrent cache misses, and isolate pathological hot partitions only when observed.

docs.title: How do you rebuild the search index?
docs.text: Backfill a versioned index from a source snapshot, replay events after the snapshot watermark, validate it, and atomically switch an alias.

docs.title: Why is eventual consistency acceptable?
docs.text: Search rank and average rating can be slightly stale without violating a financial or ownership invariant. Durable review storage and uniqueness remain strongly consistent.

docs.title: L5 Expectations: Core
docs.text:
• Clarifies the three core requirements.
  • Defines reasonable APIs and entities.
  • Separates search from the transactional database.
  • Uses caching and cursor pagination.
  • Explains the basic review-write and rating-update flow.

docs.title: L5 Expectations: Strong Signals
docs.text:
• Quantifies traffic and storage.
  • Explains geo indexing, denormalized search documents, and ranking.
  • Handles concurrency for one-review uniqueness and aggregate updates.
  • Uses an outbox, idempotent consumers, sharding, and failure degradation.
  • Discusses consistency explicitly.

docs.title: L6 Expectations
docs.text:
• Drives requirement and product tradeoffs rather than listing technology.
  • Designs operational paths: index rebuilds, reconciliation, regional ownership, and hot-key handling.
  • Connects architecture to SLOs, capacity, cost, and failure isolation.
  • Identifies evolution paths instead of prematurely adding maximum complexity.

docs.title: 25. Five-Minute Interview Summary
docs.text:
Yelp is a read-heavy system whose hardest path is low-latency text and geographic search. I would store canonical businesses and reviews in transactional databases, partition reviews by business, and enforce one review per user and business with a unique constraint. A denormalized OpenSearch document supports text, filters, geo-distance, and ranking without joining the primary database for every result.

Business details and popular review pages are cached in Redis, while images are served from object storage through a CDN. Review creation commits the review and a transactional outbox event together. Kafka consumers then update the rating aggregate, moderation state, cache, and search index asynchronously. This gives durable and strongly consistent review ownership while accepting short-lived eventual consistency for ratings and search.

The design scales reads through regional search replicas, caches, and database replicas. It handles retries with API idempotency and idempotent consumers, protects against dual-write loss with the outbox pattern, and repairs derived-state drift through reconciliation and zero-downtime search reindexing.

docs.title: 26. Final Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Use the database for durable truth and invariants.
  2. Use a search engine for combined text, filter, ranking, and geo workloads.
  3. Denormalize the search read model to avoid per-result database calls.
  4. Partition review data according to its dominant access pattern: business_id.
  5. Enforce one review per user and business at the database layer.
  6. Update ratings incrementally, process events idempotently, and reconcile periodically.
  7. Use a transactional outbox instead of unsafe database-plus-Kafka dual writes.
  8. Accept eventual consistency only for derived data, not acknowledged user content or ownership rules.
  9. Design explicit degraded behavior for cache, search, Kafka, and database failures.
  10. Explain tradeoffs and evolution paths rather than naming technologies without justification.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design real-time online chess with matchmaking, authoritative clocks, legal moves, reconnection, ratings, spectators, tournaments, and anti-cheat. Clarify time controls, scale, fairness, and correspondence play. Start with one authoritative game server and durable move log, then add regional routing, queues, hot-event fanout, clock compensation, rating pipelines, and trust systems.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Players seek rated or casual games, accept matches, make legal moves, resign, offer draws, and reconnect. Spectators watch with optional anti-cheat delay. The platform stores game history and updates ratings. Tournaments and computer analysis are secondary consumers. We support standard chess first; variants require versioned rules engines.

Move acknowledgement should be below 150 ms p99 in-region, matchmaking below 10 seconds for common pools, clock disagreement below 100 ms under normal networks, and 99.99% active-game availability. A game must have one authoritative move order and result. Clients render optimistically but never decide legality, clock, or rating.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• One game generation has one fenced authority and a totally ordered sequence of legal moves.
  • Move n+1 applies only to the exact position hash after move n and the side to move.
  • Clock time never increases except an increment/delay credit defined by the pinned time control or an explicit versioned adjustment; elapsed time is charged exactly once per accepted turn.
  • A terminal result is immutable unless an auditable adjudication creates a superseding administrative record.
  • Rated game pairing rules and rating algorithm version are fixed when the game starts.
  • Duplicate client commands produce one logical move or result.
  • Spectators and opponents never receive private anti-cheat evidence or hidden pairing attributes.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 50 million daily players, 5 million concurrent connections, 500,000 active games, and 200,000 move commands/s at peak. A game averages 80 plies. At 300 bytes/event, 10 million games/day produce 240 GB/day of canonical moves before replication, while WebSocket fanout dominates bandwidth. A championship with five million spectators and a 1 KB update creates 5 GB of edge egress per move, or 40 Gbit/s at one move/second before protocol overhead. Keep one canonical move and replicate through regional/gateway fanout; one game ID is both a sequencing hot key and a potentially large egress burst. Presence heartbeats at one/minute produce 83,000/s; avoid second-level durable writes.

Pool fragmentation must be measured before adding dimensions. If 120,000 players seek games concurrently, splitting into 4 regions, 6 time controls, 2 rated modes, and 5 broad rating bands leaves an average 120,000 / 240 = 500 tickets/cell, but demand is skewed. If the quietest region has 5% of traffic and a niche time control has 2%, that combination sees only 120,000 * 0.05 * 0.02 / (2 * 5) = 12 tickets per rated/rating cell before variant, trust, or latency constraints. At one arrival every 2 seconds and only 20% mutually compatible opponents, expected compatible arrival is roughly one per 10 seconds. Dashboards therefore track live cardinality and arrival rate per effective pool, and the product merges or widens sparse pools rather than assuming global averages.

docs.title: Data model and interfaces
docs.text:
Game(game_id, generation, white_id, black_id, rules_version, time_control,
     rated, rating_version, state, result, authority_epoch, event_seq)
GameEvent(game_id, seq, command_id, type, move_uci, position_hash,
          white_ms, black_ms, server_time, actor_id)
Snapshot(game_id, seq, fen, clocks, checksum)
QueueEntry(player_id, pool, rating_band, region, constraints, lease_until)
RatingChange(game_id, player_id, old_rating, new_rating, algorithm_version)
FairPlayCase(case_id, game_id, signals_version, state, decision)

POST /v1/matchmaking/tickets
DELETE /v1/matchmaking/tickets/{id}
GET /v1/games/{id}
GET /v1/games/{id}/events?after=42
WSS /v1/games/{id}/play
POST /v1/games/{id}/moves {command_id, expected_seq, move, client_sent_at}

WebSocket messages carry game generation, authority epoch, expected sequence, command ID, and connection epoch. HTTP move submission is a recovery path. History pagination uses sequence cursors. The client clock is display guidance only.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Players] --> E[Edge WebSocket gateways]
 E --> G[Authoritative game servers]
 G --> D[(Game event store)]
 M[Matchmaker] --> G
 C --> M
 D --> B[Fanout bus]
 B --> E
 B --> S[Spectator/CDN gateway]
 D --> R[Rating service]
 D --> F[Fair-play pipeline]
 D --> A[Analysis and archive]

docs.title: Matchmaking
docs.text:
Queue entries are grouped by variant, rated flag, time control, region, and rough skill band. A matcher scans oldest entries and computes eligible opponents. The acceptable rating distance expands with wait time, for example band = min(max_band, base + growth * wait_seconds). Cost combines rating difference, estimated RTT, color balance, repeated-opponent penalty, and wait fairness. Choose mutual minimum cost within hard constraints.

Tickets use leases and compare-and-set state from WAITING to MATCHED; a unique player-active-game constraint prevents double pairing. Match creation transactionally fixes rules, time control, ratings, region, and game generation, then emits an outbox event. Bots and suspected collusion cohorts may enter separate pools, but opaque trust policy must not leak through API responses.

The primary queue index is ordered by (pool_id, rating_bucket, enqueue_time, ticket_id). A secondary (pool_id, region, enqueue_time) index supports latency-first scans, and (player_id, state) enforces one live ticket. A matcher claims the oldest unleased anchor, computes its widening window, scans adjacent rating buckets up to a fixed candidate cap, and batch-fetches RTT, color history, block lists, and recent opponents. Hard filters run first. Eligible candidates sort deterministically by total cost, then oldest enqueue_time, smaller rating difference, lower predicted maximum RTT, and lexical ticket_id; this tie-break order makes replay and incident diagnosis possible.

Widening is piecewise and policy-versioned. One common pool might allow +/-50 rating for 0-5 seconds, add 25 points every 5 seconds to +/-200, then permit adjacent regions below a 120 ms RTT ceiling after 20 seconds. Both players' windows and region consent must accept the pair. The scan budget remains bounded, for example four buckets and 128 candidates per attempt, so an old impossible ticket cannot monopolize a shard. Rejected anchors back off briefly while new candidates arrive.

Worked matchmaking example. Ticket A, rating 1510, has waited 17 seconds, so its window is +/-125. Candidates B at 1580 and C at 1490 both accept A. Their costs after normalization are 23 and 23. B enqueued at 10:00:03 and C at 10:00:01, so C wins the oldest-ticket tie-break. If C does not mutually allow the predicted 95 ms region, B wins without changing the ordering formula.

docs.title: Atomic pair reservation across partitions
docs.text:
Queue indexes may be partitioned by pool and rating bucket, so the two tickets need not share a transactional shard. Do not lock two shards synchronously in arbitrary order. A reservation coordinator creates a durable PairIntent(pair_id, ticket_a, ticket_b, policy_version, expires_at, state) on a consensus-backed match ledger, then conditionally changes each ticket from WAITING to RESERVED(pair_id) using its ticket version. Claims execute in canonical ticket-ID order. If either compare-and-set fails, the coordinator releases any successful claim with matching pair_id; expiry sweepers do the same after a bounded lease.

After both claims are visible, one idempotent ledger transaction creates game_id, fixes game policy, changes the intent to COMMITTED, and writes an outbox record. Ticket shards consume that record and mark their rows MATCHED. A player-active-game uniqueness record keyed by player ID is also claimed before commit. Recovery treats the match ledger as authority: a committed intent is completed, never compensated into two fresh tickets; an uncommitted expired intent is released. This is a small saga with a linearizable decision record, not a claim of distributed exactly-once execution.

Cleanup first wins a conditional PREPARING -> ABORTED decision in the match ledger, competing with PREPARING -> COMMITTED; only then may it release matching ticket claims. Ticket shards must not independently recycle a claim merely because its wall-clock lease elapsed while the coordinator could still commit. Active-player keys remain protected by the same terminal decision. The later client-to-matchmaker sequence assumes both tickets and active-player keys are colocated; it is not a cross-shard SQL transaction.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Pair coordinator
  participant L as Match ledger
  participant A as Ticket shard A
  participant B as Ticket shard B
  participant O as Outbox
  C->>L: create PREPARING pair intent
  C->>A: CAS WAITING to RESERVED pair
  A-->>C: reserved with version
  C->>B: CAS WAITING to RESERVED pair
  B-->>C: reserved with version
  C->>L: commit game and active-player keys
  L->>O: GAME_CREATED
  O-->>A: mark MATCHED
  O-->>B: mark MATCHED

Worked reservation failure. A is reserved, but B was matched by another coordinator one millisecond earlier. The CAS on B fails. The intent remains uncommitted, and release on A succeeds only if its state still names this pair_id; a stale cleanup cannot release a later reservation. If the coordinator crashes after ledger commit but before notifications, replaying the outbox completes both ticket projections with the same game_id.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant P as Player clients
 participant M as Matchmaker
 participant D as Match DB
 participant G as Game authority
 participant E as Event store
 P->>M: queue tickets
 M->>D: CAS both tickets and create game
 D-->>P: game ID and region
 P->>G: connect scoped game tokens
 G->>E: append GAME_STARTED seq 0
 P->>G: move(command, expected seq, epoch)
 G->>G: validate turn, clock, legality
 G->>E: conditional append next sequence
 E-->>P: authoritative move and clocks

docs.title: Legal moves and event sourcing
docs.text:
The authority reconstructs position from a recent checksummed snapshot plus subsequent events. A pure, versioned rules engine validates side to move, piece movement, check, castling rights, en passant, promotion, repetition, fifty-move rule, and insufficient material. It returns new position hash and terminal status. Persist the event with expected prior sequence and authority epoch before acknowledging.

Pin the exact draw policy. FIDE Laws effective 2023, articles 5, 6.9 and 9, distinguish claimable threefold/50-move draws from automatic fivefold/75-move draws and make a timeout a draw if the opponent cannot possibly mate by any legal sequence. Dead position is broader than a simple piece-count test. These are over-the-board laws; online auto-claim, lag compensation and disconnect policies are explicitly versioned product adaptations, not claims of FIDE online certification (accessed 2026-09-08).

Position hashing uses Zobrist keys as a lookup accelerator, but a candidate repetition match compares the exact rule-relevant position identity, including side to move, castling and applicable en-passant rights. A hash collision must not decide a draw. Snapshots retain repetition history/counts and the halfmove counter as well as FEN; a position FEN alone does not encode how often it has occurred. Generate legal moves by applying pseudo-legal candidates and rejecting positions leaving the king in check. Rules engine determinism is tested exhaustively with perft positions. Upgrades do not alter running or historical games; each game pins rules_version.

docs.title: Authoritative clocks
docs.text:
At turn start store each remaining duration and a monotonic server timestamp. On a move, compute elapsed = now_monotonic - turn_started, optionally subtract bounded server-observed network compensation under a published policy, then apply increment/delay and persist resulting clocks with the move. Client timestamps cannot be trusted. The move and charged time commit atomically, so retries do not charge twice.

Monotonic timestamps from different hosts or boots are not comparable. Recovery records a clock/authority epoch and reconstructs remaining duration from the last committed clocks plus an explicitly bounded outage-time policy. If elapsed-time mapping cannot be trusted, pause/adjudicate under that policy rather than subtracting a new host's monotonic clock from the old host's value. Normal move increments are allowed increases under the pinned time-control version.

For a timeout, schedule an in-memory timer but verify against authoritative state when it fires. A delayed timer cannot flag a player who already moved. If move and timeout arrive concurrently, the authority serializes them; policy defines whether arrival before authoritative deadline wins. Gateways continuously estimate RTT and show a smooth local countdown, corrected by server events.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> CREATED
 CREATED --> ACTIVE
 ACTIVE --> ACTIVE: legal move plus clock charge
 ACTIVE --> DRAWN: agreement or rule
 ACTIVE --> WHITE_WON: mate, resign, timeout
 ACTIVE --> BLACK_WON: mate, resign, timeout
 ACTIVE --> ABORTED: policy before rated threshold
 DRAWN --> [*]
 WHITE_WON --> [*]
 BLACK_WON --> [*]
 ABORTED --> [*]

docs.title: Reconnection and command idempotency
docs.text: Each device connection has an epoch. A reconnect fetches snapshot and events after the client's last sequence, then atomically supersedes its older socket. Commands deduplicate by (game_id, actor_id, command_id) and require expected event sequence. A stale command receives current state, not blind retry. If acknowledgement is lost, retry returns the prior move result. Disconnection does not pause rated clocks unless the predefined format says so.

docs.title: Spectators and tournaments
docs.text:
Canonical events enter a fanout bus. Ordinary games use gateway subscriptions; hot games write compact event objects to an origin cache and CDN/WebSocket tree. A configurable delay queue withholds events for anti-cheat. Reconnect uses sequence from durable history. Spectator chat has separate moderation, partitions, and overload policy; it cannot affect the game authority.

Tournament control assigns rounds, tie-break policy, pairings, and start deadlines. It references games rather than embedding play state. Swiss pairing is a constrained optimization using score groups, color balance, previous opponents, byes, team/country constraints, and deterministic tie-breaks. Pairing inputs and algorithm version are immutable and auditable. If computation fails, operators can publish a signed replacement pairing generation.

docs.title: Full Swiss pairing and tournament recovery
docs.text:
At the round deadline, freeze an input generation containing eligible players, scores, opponent history, color history, withdrawals, prior byes, ranking seed, and pairing-policy version. Sort by score, then configured tournament tie-breaks and stable player ID. Assign an odd player a bye by scanning from the lowest score for the lowest-ranked eligible player who has not received one; the bye and its points are explicit pairing records.

Process score groups high to low. Float the lowest-ranked compatible player from an odd group into the next group according to the policy's float history. Split an even group into upper and lower halves, then search pairings between halves. A legal edge forbids previous opponents and violates no absolute color, team, federation, club, or availability constraint. Edge cost penalizes score difference, repeated float direction, color imbalance, same-affiliation pairings when soft, and deviation from seed order. Solve minimum-cost perfect matching; for typical groups, branch-and-bound with most-constrained-player-first and deterministic candidate order is practical. If no perfect matching exists, backtrack floats and exchanges across adjacent groups. Relax only constraints listed as soft, in a fixed order, and record each relaxation. Color assignment then minimizes alternation and imbalance, with deterministic lot/seed tie-breaks.

flowchart TD
  F[Freeze round input generation] --> B{Odd field}
  B -->|yes| Y[Assign eligible deterministic bye]
  B -->|no| G[Build score groups]
  Y --> G
  G --> O[Float odd groups by policy]
  O --> H[Split upper and lower halves]
  H --> M[Minimum-cost legal matching]
  M --> P{Perfect matching found}
  P -->|no| X[Backtrack floats and ordered soft constraints]
  X --> M
  P -->|yes| C[Assign colors]
  C --> V[Validate every player exactly once]
  V --> R[Publish signed pairing generation]

Worked Swiss round. A four-player score group contains seeds A,B,C,D; A-C and B-D are rematches. The initial upper/lower pairing is rejected. The alternative A-D,B-C avoids rematches; if both opponents' color histories allow assigning A Black, it also avoids a third White for A, so no color relaxation is needed. If neither color assignment meets the hard rules, backtrack rather than declaring the pair legal. This is an illustrative configurable pairing heuristic, not a complete implementation of a named FIDE Swiss system.

Tournament recovery operates at round scope, not game scope alone. The controller is stateless over a consensus-backed tournament log and acquires a fenced (tournament_id, round, controller_epoch) lease. Pairing publication is compare-and-set from DRAFT to one immutable PUBLISHED generation; game creation is idempotent by (tournament_id, round, board). A replacement controller reconciles every board into not-created, created-not-started, active, or terminal, replays missing outbox messages, and starts only games referencing the published generation. It never recomputes pairings merely because some game creation calls timed out.

If published pairings are provably corrupt before play begins, an authorized operation cancels all not-started board allocations and publishes a superseding signed generation linked to the original. Once any game starts, repair policy preserves completed/active games and creates explicit administrative results or a tournament-wide pause; silently changing opponents would corrupt standings. Round advancement requires all boards terminal or adjudicated, a standings checksum, and one committed next-round input snapshot.

Worked tournament-wide recovery. The controller crashes while creating 5,000 round-three games. The ledger shows one published pairing generation, 4,930 GAME_CREATED outbox records, 40 games committed without delivered notifications, and 30 boards absent. The new epoch replays the 40 notifications and idempotently creates only the 30 absent boards. It does not rerun Swiss pairing, so no player can receive a different opponent after partial publication.

docs.title: Rating updates
docs.text: Game completion writes a unique rating-work item. A per-player ordered processor applies Glicko-2 or Elo with pinned algorithm version. Two simultaneous games must not overwrite each other; lock/order by player or transactionally compare rating version. Multi-player transaction across both players can use a database transaction when colocated; otherwise write an immutable rating ledger and materialize balances in deterministic event order. A correction never edits historical entries. Elo/Glicko updates are path-dependent: reversing one old delta does not reproduce the ratings that later games would have produced. Either apply an explicitly defined current-rating adjustment policy or replay the affected deterministic rating history into a new generation and append the resulting adjustments with provenance.

docs.title: Fair play
docs.text: Signals include move agreement with engines at multiple depths, think-time correlation, accuracy conditional on position difficulty, tab/device behavior where lawful, account graph, rating trajectory, and collusion patterns. No single signal proves cheating. Online rules may delay suspicious tournament broadcasts or rate-limit accounts; punitive decisions use versioned models, calibrated thresholds, human review, and appeals. Keep raw sensitive telemetry access restricted and retention bounded. Never run invasive analysis in the move critical path.

docs.title: Authority placement and migration
docs.text: Consistent hashing places games by ID on regional authority shards, but an allocator accounts for player RTT and shard load. A shard holds leases from a quorum store with epoch. To drain, stop accepting new games, snapshot active games, stop and fence old writes, transfer the final acknowledged tail and clock handoff state, increment epoch, and have clients reconnect. The old process cannot append after losing its epoch. Live migration may cost a short pause; silently running two authorities is worse.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and regions
docs.text:
Partition canonical events by game ID, preserving order. Snapshot every 10-20 plies to bound recovery. Archive completed games to object storage while retaining query indexes. WebSocket gateways shard by connection and subscribe through regional buses. Rating processing partitions by player ID; tournament standings by tournament ID. Presence uses expiring leases and approximate counts.

Home a game in the region minimizing the maximum player RTT subject to residency and capacity. Both players connect through nearby edges to that region. Cross-region synchronous move replication would add latency; instead commit to zonal quorum in the home region and asynchronously replicate events to a paired region. On regional loss, increment authority epoch in surviving quorum, recover from replicated log, and expose possible RPO according to mode. High-stakes tournaments can pay for synchronous dual-region commits or a dedicated venue region.

Hot spectator fanout never changes game partition load. Cache snapshots and events by sequence, use hierarchical pub-sub, and degrade chat, analysis overlays, then spectator freshness before player moves. Matchmaking can widen region/rating bands only with explicit user policy. Admission stops new games before active-game headroom is consumed.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and failures
docs.text:
Move order, clock, result, and game authority require linearizable behavior per game. Lobby presence, spectator count, search, analysis, and fair-play features are eventual. Match and move creation use transactional outboxes. Queue redelivery is absorbed by command/game IDs. Rating effects are idempotent by game and player. We do not claim exactly-once WebSocket delivery; sequence-based catch-up is the contract.

Gateway loss reconnects without stopping clocks. Game-process loss reconstructs from snapshot/log under a higher lease epoch. Event-store unavailability stops move acknowledgement rather than accepting uncommitted play. Fanout failure does not block canonical appends; players poll/catch up. Matchmaker partition may create no new matches, never duplicate active games. Rules-engine crash quarantines a game for recovery. Clock source uses monotonic time; wall-clock changes affect display/audit timestamps, not elapsed duration.

Reconciliation finds active games without leases, expired clocks lacking terminal events, terminal games missing rating work, rating work with mismatched versions, and gaps between event store and archive. Manual adjudication is signed, reasoned, and emits superseding events. Replay cannot alter ratings twice.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Use short-lived game-scoped tokens, TLS, command authorization, invite entropy, DDoS protection, and account/device risk controls. Validate all moves server-side. Defend against engine assistance, sandbagging, boosting, collusion, multi-accounting, disconnect abuse, chat harassment, spectator scraping, and tournament disruption. Protect minors and minimize behavioral telemetry. Moderation and adjudication are auditable with separation of duties.

Measure matchmaking wait/quality, abandoned tickets, move round-trip, validation time, stale/duplicate commands, clock compensation and disputes, reconnect recovery, authority lease health, event append latency, active-game headroom, spectator lag/fanout, rating backlog, rules-version errors, and fair-play model drift/appeals. Synthetic bots play legal scripted games continuously across regions.

Property-test legal move generation, repetition, terminal states, clock monotonicity, command idempotency, and epoch fencing. Perft suites verify rules. Model-check move-versus-timeout races. Replay historical games across storage and rating versions. Load-test synchronized tournament starts and championship spectators. Chaos-test process death between append/ack, gateway loss, bus lag, region partition, delayed timers, and duplicate rating events. Canary rules changes only on new unrated games.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Peer-to-peer play is cheap but cannot provide trusted clocks or legality; server authority wins. A relational row per game is simple but loses an auditable move history; append-only events plus snapshots provide both. Global strong replication improves RPO but hurts blitz latency; zonal commits with tier-specific regional durability are practical. A single matchmaking queue maximizes choice but ignores RTT and variants; segmented pools with widening balance quality and wait.

flowchart TD
 Q[Leased matchmaking ticket] --> M[Atomic pair and fixed game policy]
 M --> A[Fenced regional game authority]
 A --> V[Versioned legal-move and clock engine]
 V --> E[(Append-only game events)]
 E --> P[Player sequence catch-up]
 E --> S[Delayed hierarchical spectator fanout]
 E --> R[Ordered rating ledger]
 E --> F[Offline fair-play analysis]

The final architecture gives each game one fenced regional authority that validates commands, computes clocks, and conditionally appends ordered events before acknowledgment. Snapshots accelerate recovery. Gateways provide reconnect and sequence catch-up. Matchmaking and tournaments create immutable policy generations. Rating, fair play, archive, and spectator fanout consume events independently, keeping the move path small.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. Who wins a race between a move and the server timeout timer?
  2. How does reconnect avoid duplicate moves and double clock charge?
  3. How do five million spectators avoid creating a hot game-server key?
  4. How is a live game migrated without split-brain authority?
  5. How do simultaneous completed games update one player's rating?
  6. Which anti-cheat signals are safe for automatic action?
  7. What durability would you buy for a world championship versus casual blitz?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should establish server authority, model ordered moves and clocks, choose event log plus snapshots, explain matchmaking, reconnect, command idempotency, partitioning, spectator fanout, rating, and process failure.

An L6 candidate should define move/timeout semantics, epoch fencing and migration, regional durability tiers, tournament auditability, rating ordering, anti-cheat governance, overload priorities, and privacy. They should quantify latency/headroom tradeoffs and connect high-stakes modes to additional cost and operational controls.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Atomically match leased tickets and pin rules, rating, time control, and region. Route each game to one fenced authority. For every command, verify identity, connection/authority epoch, expected sequence, side to move, legality, and authoritative monotonic clock; append the move and resulting clocks before acknowledging. Deduplicate command IDs and let reconnect fetch a snapshot plus events after sequence N. Timers recheck canonical state, so stale timeout callbacks cannot end a moved game. Partition events by game and snapshot periodically. Keep spectator fanout, analysis, ratings, chat, and anti-cheat off the move path; use delayed hierarchical fanout for hot matches and ordered idempotent rating work. Commit zonally for normal latency, replicate for recovery, and buy stronger durability for high-stakes events. Degrade spectators before active play and measure move latency, clock disputes, stale commands, lease health, recovery, rating lag, and fanout delay.

docs.title: API Gateway
docs.text: This case study owns the gateway design. Use Proxies and Load Balancing and Deadlines, Retries, and Pools for data-path and overload mechanics.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design an edge gateway that terminates client connections, authenticates requests, routes to services, and enforces cross-cutting policy. We clarify which features belong on the synchronous path, estimate connections and bandwidth, define route and policy models, and separate configuration management from stateless regional proxies. Deep dives cover routing, retries, overload, streaming, policy rollout, and regional failover.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: The gateway is the public front door for HTTP, gRPC, and WebSocket APIs. It centralizes TLS, identity verification, routing, quotas, request limits, and telemetry. It should not contain business workflows or become the canonical source of user authorization; services still enforce resource-level authorization. Because every request passes through it, simplicity, bounded work, and safe degradation matter more than feature count.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Terminate TLS and support HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, and selected WebSocket routes.
  • Match host, method, path, headers, and API version to weighted upstream clusters.
  • Authenticate tokens/API keys, enforce coarse authorization, quotas, CORS, and size limits.
  • Apply deadlines, circuit breakers, safe retries, transformations, and canary traffic splits.
  • Publish access logs, metrics, traces, and per-request diagnostic IDs.
  • Manage certificates, routes, policies, and staged rollouts.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 5 million requests/s globally, 2 Tb/s peak, and 10 million concurrent connections.
  • Added p99 latency below 5 ms excluding TLS handshake and upstream time.
  • 99.999% availability for healthy routes; no control-plane dependency on requests.
  • Configuration propagation below 30 seconds, emergency revocation below 5 seconds.

Business composition, payload persistence, and fine-grained resource authorization are out of scope.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. A request is evaluated against one immutable configuration snapshot.
  2. A route can forward only to endpoints authorized for its tenant, protocol, and trust zone.
  3. Authentication failure never degrades to anonymous access unless the route explicitly permits anonymous clients.
  4. The gateway retries only operations declared replay-safe and only within one end-to-end deadline and retry budget.
  5. Request and response bodies never exceed configured limits, including after decompression.
  6. Configuration activation and certificate changes are auditable and rollbackable.

The gateway guarantees at-most-one downstream attempt only when retries are disabled. With retries, downstream effects require idempotency.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Five million requests/s at 50 KB average response is 250 GB/s, or 2 Tb/s, making bandwidth the primary fleet dimension. At 20 Gbit/s safe egress per proxy, at least 100 proxies are needed before regional distribution, maintenance, and headroom. If average request duration is two seconds, Little's Law gives ten million in-flight requests, not ten million transport connections: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex streams while idle keep-alive sockets carry none. Independently assuming ten million open connections and a tested 50,000-connection limit per proxy gives a 200-proxy connection floor. Also qualify concurrent-stream limits, per-stream buffers and TLS/packet CPU before selecting the larger fleet requirement. Access logs at 300 bytes/request produce 1.5 GB/s, so logs must be asynchronous and sampled for successful high-volume routes while retaining errors according to policy. A 100 MB global configuration distributed to 500 proxies is 50 GB per full rollout; deltas and regional relays reduce fan-out.

docs.title: 6. Entities and configuration model
docs.text:
Listener(listener_id, address, port, protocols, certificate_refs)
Route(route_id, tenant_id, match, priority, cluster_id, policies[], version)
Cluster(cluster_id, protocol, discovery_ref, locality_policy,
        health_policy, circuit_breaker)
Endpoint(endpoint_id, cluster_id, address, zone, weight, health, epoch)
Policy(policy_id, type, parameters, failure_mode, version)
Snapshot(snapshot_version, listeners[], routes[], clusters[], policies[], checksum)

Canonical configuration lives in a transactional control database. The compiler emits validated, signed, immutable regional snapshots. Endpoint health and load are rapidly changing data-plane state delivered separately from slower route configuration.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
Management:

PUT  /v1/routes/{id}                 If-Match: version
POST /v1/configs/{id}:validate
POST /v1/configs/{id}:stage
POST /v1/configs/{id}:activate
POST /v1/configs/{id}:rollback
GET  /v1/proxies/{id}/status

Discovery and proxy streams carry version, nonce, resource type, delta, and checksum; proxies ACK or NACK with error details. Client-facing interfaces preserve protocol semantics. Gateway-generated errors use a stable envelope containing status, code, request ID, and retryability without leaking internal addresses.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Client --> DNS[Anycast/DNS and DDoS edge]
  DNS --> Proxy[Regional gateway proxies]
  Proxy --> Service[Upstream services]
  Discovery[Endpoint discovery] --> Proxy
  Admin --> API[Gateway control API]
  API --> DB[(Config DB)]
  DB --> Compiler[Snapshot compiler]
  Compiler --> Relay[Regional config relays]
  Relay --> Proxy
  Proxy --> Telemetry[Async telemetry pipeline]

The control plane authorizes edits, validates references, compiles snapshots, and monitors rollout. The data plane consists of edge protection, proxies, endpoint discovery, and local policy engines. Proxies keep last-known-good snapshots and endpoint caches. A control outage prevents new configuration but must not interrupt established traffic.

docs.title: 9. Request hot path
docs.text:
On accept, the proxy negotiates TLS using an in-memory certificate map, parses with strict bounds, captures one snapshot pointer, and assigns a request ID. It normalizes host/path safely, matches a precompiled route trie, authenticates, checks policy, chooses a healthy endpoint, and forwards with propagated deadline and trace context. Response streaming uses bounded buffers and backpressure rather than reading complete bodies.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant G as Gateway
  participant I as Identity cache/provider
  participant U as Upstream
  C->>G: request + credentials
  G->>G: parse, normalize, capture snapshot
  G->>I: verify key/JWKS cache on miss
  I-->>G: verified claims
  G->>G: authorize route, quota, choose endpoint
  G->>U: request + deadline + identity context
  U-->>G: streaming response
  G-->>C: response
  G-->>G: enqueue telemetry without blocking

Avoid remote calls where possible: JWT verification uses cached signed keys; API key lookups use bounded caches with revocation feeds; rate limiting uses local/distributed leases. Introspection-only tokens have an explicit fail policy.

docs.title: 10. Routing and service discovery
docs.text:
Compile exact hosts, wildcard hosts, path prefixes, methods, and headers into deterministic precedence; ambiguous routes are rejected before publication. Weighted routing hashes a stable key for sticky canaries when supplied, otherwise uses random weighted choice. Endpoint selection first chooses locality and priority, then power-of-two choices weighted by observed load. Passive health combines connection failures and latency; active probes verify idle endpoints.

Discovery updates have epochs and endpoint TTLs. A disappearing endpoint drains existing streams for a bounded period but receives no new requests. Outlier ejection has maximum-ejection limits so correlated upstream failure does not remove every endpoint. Panic mode may broaden locality or fail fast according to route policy.

docs.title: 11. Authentication and policy chain
docs.text:
Policy order is explicit: connection and request bounds, authentication, coarse authorization, rate limit, transformations, routing, retry, and response filters. Authentication establishes a typed principal. The gateway signs or mTLS-protects forwarded identity headers and strips client-supplied copies. Services validate gateway identity and still authorize the object being accessed.

JWT verification refreshes cached keys according to bounded freshness rules and validates issuer, audience, allowed algorithm, and token time claims. Planned key rotation may retain old keys through token lifetime; compromised or explicitly revoked keys must be rejected sooner through the revocation policy. Revocation-sensitive routes use short tokens or introspection. CORS is browser policy, not authentication. Transformations are declarative and bounded; arbitrary user code is not run on gateway workers.

docs.title: 12. Deadlines, retries, and circuit breaking
docs.text:
The client deadline is capped by route maximum. Each attempt gets only remaining time. Retry only connect failures, resets before response headers, and selected statuses for idempotent methods or requests carrying a downstream-supported idempotency key. Use exponential jitter and a global retry budget, for example retries below 10% of successful traffic. Hedging is reserved for idempotent latency-sensitive reads and consumes the same budget.

Circuit breakers bound concurrent requests and pending connection queues per endpoint/cluster. When full, fail fast with retry guidance. Adaptive concurrency uses latency gradients but retains hard safety caps. Retries must not jump across data-residency boundaries.

flowchart TD
  Req[Matched request] --> Deadline{Deadline remains?}
  Deadline -->|no| Fail[Fail timeout]
  Deadline -->|yes| Endpoint[Choose healthy endpoint]
  Endpoint --> Attempt[Send one attempt]
  Attempt --> Result{Success or potentially retryable outcome?}
  Result -->|success| Return[Stream response]
  Result -->|nonretryable| Error[Return original error]
  Result -->|retryable| Budget{Replay safe and budget available?}
  Budget -->|yes| Deadline
  Budget -->|no| Error

docs.title: 13. Partitioning, overload, and hot routes
docs.text:
Traffic partitions geographically through anycast or latency DNS, then by connection across proxies. Proxies are stateless except caches, so scale horizontally. Long-lived connections skew load; load balancers consider active connections and bytes, not only request count. A hot route or tenant gets explicit concurrency, QPS, and bandwidth limits plus dedicated pools when isolation matters.

Overload defense is layered: DDoS filtering, connection caps, header/body limits, per-client quotas, route admission, bounded upstream queues, and load shedding. Preserve health, control, and critical APIs before bulk endpoints. Reject early before authentication work where safe. Backpressure streamed responses and cap slow-client connection time.

docs.title: 14. Configuration consistency and rollout
docs.text:
The compiler validates references, route ambiguity, trust-zone constraints, policy types, secret availability, and resource limits. Regional relays distribute snapshots. Proxies build indexes off-thread, validate checksum/signature, then atomically swap pointers. Requests in flight finish on their captured version. A delta names its base; mismatch triggers full snapshot repair.

Rollout proceeds through test, one proxy, one zone, then percentages, with automated rollback on NACK, 5xx, latency, or authentication anomalies. Emergency deny/certificate revocation uses a small reserved channel. Rollback republishes known-good content under a new monotonic version while preserving current mandatory deny rules and revoked credentials. Revocation freshness has its own enforcement gate so an in-flight old route snapshot cannot bypass it. Endpoint discovery changes independently and faster than route snapshots.

docs.title: 15. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Proxy crash: connection-level load balancer removes it; clients retry according to protocol.
  • Control plane unavailable: existing snapshots and certificates continue; edits stop.
  • Bad config: preflight, NACK, canary, and automatic rollback contain it.
  • Identity provider unavailable: cached verification continues; routes requiring live introspection fail closed when identity cannot be established. A route may explicitly allow anonymous access, but provider failure does not turn an unverified token into an authenticated principal.
  • Discovery stale: endpoint TTL expires; fail fast rather than route indefinitely to removed hosts.
  • Upstream overload: breakers, queues, retry budgets, and local shedding prevent amplification.
  • Telemetry outage: bounded buffers sample/drop normal logs; security audit policy may reject sensitive operations.
  • Zone loss: locality routing shifts gradually within regional capacity and global traffic manager drains the region if needed.

docs.title: 16. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Every region has independent proxies, relays, discovery, identity caches, and rate-limit budgets. Anycast/DNS steers clients; health considers synthetic end-to-end requests, not process liveness. Stateless requests can fail over automatically. WebSockets and streams reconnect and resume at application level. Global rate limits use escrowed regional budgets rather than WAN checks.

Configuration bundles replicate globally from a home writer. Promotion requires a higher publisher epoch. Certificates and trust bundles are prepositioned. Residency policy is compiled into allowed region-to-cluster edges, so failover cannot accidentally export data. Capacity reserves determine whether a full-region evacuation is credible.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use hardware-backed private keys where justified, automated certificate rotation, modern TLS, mTLS upstream, least-privilege workload identity, and signed configuration. Normalize paths once to defeat traversal and route-confusion attacks. Defend against request smuggling by consistent parser rules and never forwarding ambiguous framing. Cap decompression, regex, headers, streams, and connection duration. Strip hop-by-hop and identity headers. Audit configuration and privileged diagnostics; redact credentials from logs and traces.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure request/connection/byte rates, handshake failures, route match failures, auth reasons, limiter decisions, upstream latency, retries, ejections, queue time, resets, snapshot age/version distribution, NACKs, and telemetry drops. Bound metric cardinality through route IDs rather than paths. Distributed traces distinguish gateway queue, connect, TLS, and upstream phases. Synthetic probes traverse public DNS and real identity.

Golden tests verify route matching and normalization. Differential tests compare compiler and proxy policy behavior. Fuzz parsers for smuggling and malformed protocols. Load tests include slow clients, large streams, WebSockets, hot tenants, and retry storms. Fault tests expire discovery, rotate certificates, partition control plane, and remove zones. Canary replay compares new snapshots against sampled sanitized requests.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: Central gateways simplify policy but enlarge blast radius and add latency. Sidecars reduce central network concentration but multiply operations. Local JWT verification is available but revocation is delayed. More retries hide transient faults but amplify overload. Rich transformations speed teams initially but turn infrastructure into business code. Atomic snapshots consume memory during rollout but avoid mixed configuration. Anycast fails over quickly but may move connections unexpectedly; DNS is slower but controllable.

docs.title: 20. Final design, questions, and expectations
docs.text:
Use stateless regional proxies behind DDoS protection and locality-aware balancing. Proxies evaluate one signed immutable snapshot, verify identity locally, enforce bounded policy, and route to discovered endpoints with deadlines, retry budgets, and breakers. A transactional control plane compiles and canaries snapshots; endpoint discovery remains a separate fast stream. Last-known-good operation, regional independence, and layered shedding protect availability.

Questions: When is retry safe? How does config rollback affect in-flight requests? How are long-lived connections balanced? What happens when JWKS refresh fails? How do you prevent request smuggling? How does region failover preserve residency?

An L5 candidate should design routing, authentication, rate limiting, discovery, retries, and scaling. An L6 candidate should bound amplification, separate planes and update cadences, stage policy/certificate changes, reason about protocols, overload priority, trust boundaries, regional capacity, and organizational ownership.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: The gateway is a minimal synchronous policy and routing layer, not a business workflow engine. Regional stateless proxies terminate TLS, strictly parse and normalize requests, capture one immutable signed configuration snapshot, verify identity from local key caches, enforce quotas and bounds, and select healthy locality-aware endpoints. Deadlines and retry budgets prevent amplification; only replay-safe operations retry. Breakers and bounded queues fail fast under upstream overload. A transactional control plane validates and canaries route snapshots, while endpoint discovery updates independently. Proxies survive control outages on last-known-good state. Regions have independent capacity and escrow quotas; failover obeys compiled residency constraints. Protocol fuzzing, request replay, synthetic probes, staged rollouts, and version-distribution metrics control the gateway's unusually large blast radius.

docs.title: Primary source boundary
docs.text: JWT Best Current Practices, RFC 8725 sections 3.1 and 3.8-3.10 supports explicit algorithm, issuer/key, audience, and untrusted-claim validation (accessed 2026-09-19). Cache freshness, revocation propagation, and rollback gates here are proposed deployment contracts, not guarantees supplied by a JWT signature.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a service that runs untrusted user code for online judges, notebooks, and automation. We begin with the threat model and execution semantics, estimate concurrent CPU/memory demand, define submissions and sandbox leases, and separate image/policy management from scheduling and runtime isolation. Deep dives cover sandboxing, artifact preparation, fairness, output streaming, retries, and regional containment.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Clients submit source or an approved artifact, language/runtime, resources, inputs, and timeout. The platform compiles if needed, runs in an isolated sandbox, captures bounded output, and reports status. Untrusted code may be malicious: it can fork, exhaust memory, exploit kernels, probe networks, or leak neighboring data. Security is a primary correctness property. The platform offers at-least-once scheduling but one logical result; it does not promise arbitrary side effects because outbound network is denied by default.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Submit, cancel, inspect, and rerun code in approved language/runtime versions.
  • Compile source, run test cases or commands, stream bounded logs, and persist results/artifacts.
  • Set CPU, memory, wall-time, process, filesystem, network, and output limits.
  • Support interactive sessions as a separate pool with idle timeout.
  • Manage runtime images, policy versions, secrets, and tenant quotas.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 20,000 submissions/s peak, 200,000 concurrent sandboxes, and burst queueing.
  • Queue delay p95 below 2 seconds for standard jobs when capacity exists.
  • Strong tenant isolation; compromise of one sandbox must not expose host or peer data.
  • 99.95% platform availability, with deterministic result classification.

Building arbitrary internet-derived dependencies and unrestricted outbound access are out of scope.

docs.title: 4. Correctness and security invariants
docs.text:
1. A sandbox sees only its immutable inputs, scoped secrets, scratch space, and explicitly allowed network destinations.
  2. CPU, memory, process, disk, output, and wall-clock budgets are enforced outside guest control.
  3. A stale or duplicate worker lease cannot publish over a terminal result.
  4. Runtime image digest and policy version are fixed for an attempt and recorded with its result.
  5. Tenant data is erased or cryptographically discarded before capacity is reused.
  6. Result state is monotonic; retries create attempts and one fenced winner.
  7. Control services never parse or execute untrusted code with their own privileges.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: At 20,000 submissions/s and an average 10-second runtime, Little's Law gives 200,000 concurrent sandboxes. At 0.25 effective CPU and 256 MB average memory each, demand is 50,000 cores and 51.2 TB RAM before headroom, using decimal units consistently. At 64 usable cores and 256 GB per worker, CPU needs 782 hosts and memory 200; roughly 1,200 hosts across three balanced zones leave 800 after one zone fails, only a small margin over that CPU floor. Memory admission must reserve enforceable per-job limits and host overhead rather than assuming every adversarial job stays at average usage. Source plus input averages 50 KB, or 1 GB/s ingress. Output capped at 1 MB could reach 20 GB/s worst case, so stream backpressure and truncation are essential. Runtime images at 1 GB cannot be pulled per job; workers need prewarmed content-addressed layers.

docs.title: 6. Entities and state model
docs.text:
Submission(submission_id, tenant_id, source_ref, runtime_digest,
           command, resource_profile, policy_version, idempotency_key, state)
Attempt(attempt_id, submission_id, number, worker_id, lease_epoch,
        lease_expires_at, started_at, finished_at, outcome, usage, result_ref)
Runtime(runtime_id, version, image_digest, compiler, status, sbom, signature)
ExecutionPolicy(policy_version, syscalls, network_rules, mounts,
                max_resources, isolation_class)
Worker(worker_id, pool, zone, capabilities, image_cache, health, epoch)

Submission states are QUEUED -> ASSIGNED -> PREPARING -> RUNNING -> SUCCEEDED|FAILED|TIMED_OUT|CANCELLED|INFRA_ERROR. Infrastructure failures before execution may create a fresh attempt within a bounded budget; failures during execution retry only under the side-effect policy below. INFRA_ERROR is terminal when no safe retry remains. Infrastructure retries are not unbounded or necessarily free of resource charges.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> QUEUED
  QUEUED --> ASSIGNED: fenced lease
  ASSIGNED --> PREPARING
  PREPARING --> RUNNING
  RUNNING --> SUCCEEDED
  RUNNING --> FAILED
  RUNNING --> TIMED_OUT
  ASSIGNED --> CANCELLED
  PREPARING --> CANCELLED: supervisor confirms stop
  ASSIGNED --> INFRA_ERROR: retry budget exhausted
  RUNNING --> QUEUED: infrastructure retry explicitly safe
  QUEUED --> CANCELLED
  RUNNING --> CANCELLED: supervisor kill
  ASSIGNED --> QUEUED: lease lost / infra retry
  PREPARING --> QUEUED: pre-execution infrastructure retry allowed
  RUNNING --> INFRA_ERROR: no safe retry remains
  PREPARING --> INFRA_ERROR: retry budget exhausted

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/submissions                 Idempotency-Key: ...
GET  /v1/submissions/{id}
POST /v1/submissions/{id}:cancel
GET  /v1/submissions/{id}/events     Last-Event-ID: ...
GET  /v1/submissions?state=&cursor=
POST /v1/runtimes/{id}:stage
POST /v1/runtimes/{id}:activate

The create request references uploaded immutable source/input objects, runtime digest, resource profile, and optional allowed capability profile. It never accepts host paths or raw privileged container options. Worker APIs claim leases, report phase/progress, upload bounded result manifests, and complete with epoch. Cursor pagination uses creation time and submission ID.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Client --> API[Submission API]
  API --> DB[(Submission DB)]
  API --> Obj[(Encrypted object storage)]
  DB --> Queue[Fair scheduling queues]
  Scheduler --> Queue
  Scheduler --> Worker[Sandbox worker pools]
  Worker --> Runtime[MicroVM/container sandbox]
  Runtime --> Logs[Bounded output stream]
  Worker --> Obj
  Worker --> Results[Result coordinator]
  Results --> DB
  Control[Runtime and policy control plane] --> Scheduler
  Control --> Worker

The control plane builds and signs runtimes, defines policies, registers pools, and rolls versions. The data plane accepts immutable inputs, fairly schedules, executes, streams output, and commits results. Untrusted bytes remain in object storage and sandbox processes; schedulers manipulate references and metadata only.

docs.title: 9. Submission and scheduling path
docs.text:
The API authenticates tenant, validates runtime and resource profile, checks quota, stores object references, and commits QUEUED plus an outbox row before acknowledging. Queue messages are hints; sweepers repair missing notifications. The scheduler chooses isolation pool, tenant, priority, and a worker that has resources and preferably cached image layers. It conditionally assigns an epoch-bound lease in the database.

Use hierarchical weighted deficit round robin so large tenants cannot starve small ones. Token buckets bound starts, semaphores bound concurrency, and CPU-second budgets control sustained cost. Interactive sessions and batch judges use distinct pools because latency, duration, and abuse patterns differ. Reservations leave capacity for security-critical and internal health work.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant A as API
  participant S as Scheduler
  participant W as Worker supervisor
  participant V as Sandbox
  participant R as Result coordinator
  C->>A: submit(refs,runtime,limits)
  A-->>C: durable submission ID
  S->>W: attempt lease + signed manifest
  W->>W: verify digest/policy, prepare isolation
  W->>V: boot and execute
  V-->>W: bounded stdout/stderr + exit
  W->>R: result manifest + lease epoch
  R->>R: conditional terminal commit
  R-->>C: observable terminal event

docs.title: 10. Sandbox isolation
docs.text:
Isolation has layers. Dedicated worker operating systems expose no control-plane credentials. A hardware-virtualized microVM gives each sandbox a kernel and is preferred for hostile multi-tenant workloads; a hardened container pool may serve trusted or low-risk code at lower startup cost. Never rely on language sandboxing alone. The supervisor runs outside the guest, configures cgroups/VM limits, read-only root images, ephemeral encrypted scratch, minimal devices, seccomp, capabilities, user namespaces, and mandatory access control.

Default network is none. Allowed egress traverses an identity-aware proxy with DNS pinning, destination allowlists, byte limits, and request logs; metadata and private control ranges are always blocked. Inputs mount read-only. Secrets are short-lived, job-scoped, delivered after boot through a memory channel, never baked into images or command arguments. Hosts are frequently patched and rotated.

docs.title: 11. Runtime supply chain and compilation
docs.text:
Runtime images are reproducibly built in an isolated pipeline, scanned, signed, assigned an SBOM, and referenced only by digest. Staging runs conformance, escape, resource-limit, and performance tests. Activation changes the default for new submissions; each accepted submission pins a digest, so rollout cannot mutate queued work. Emergency revocation prevents new starts and may terminate running attempts when severity warrants.

Compilation happens in the same or a stricter sandbox. Cache compiled artifacts by hash of source, compiler digest, flags, architecture, and dependency lockfile, scoped to tenant unless artifacts are provably public. Cache entries are untrusted outputs and are verified before execution. Dependency packages come from an internal curated mirror with hashes; arbitrary install scripts and internet access are denied.

docs.title: 12. Resource enforcement and output
docs.text:
CPU quotas and usage accounting come from hypervisor/cgroup counters; guest clocks are not trusted. Wall timeout is a supervisor monotonic timer. Memory has a hard limit and no host-wide overcommit beyond safe policy. PID limits stop fork bombs; filesystem quotas stop sparse or inode attacks. On violation, the supervisor first marks cause, then kills the VM/process tree, waits a bounded grace, and destroys it.

Stdout and stderr flow through byte-counting pipes into bounded chunks. Slow clients do not backpressure the guest indefinitely: after the output cap, retain a truncation marker and drain/discard or terminate according to policy. Structured result manifests include exit code, signal, timeout phase, peak resources, truncation, runtime digest, and policy version. Large artifacts require declared output paths and size checks.

flowchart TD
  Manifest[Signed attempt manifest] --> Verify[Worker verifies epoch, image, policy]
  Verify --> Boot[Boot isolated sandbox]
  Boot --> Mount[Read-only inputs + ephemeral scratch]
  Mount --> Run[Run under external limits]
  Run --> Monitor{Exit or limit?}
  Monitor -->|normal| Collect[Collect bounded result]
  Monitor -->|CPU/memory/time/output| Kill[Supervisor terminates tree]
  Kill --> Collect
  Collect --> Wipe[Destroy VM and discard scratch key]
  Wipe --> Publish[Publish fenced result]

docs.title: 13. Leases, retries, and result consistency
docs.text:
Workers heartbeat attempt leases. Lease expiry allows an infrastructure retry, but a paused old worker might resume. Each assignment increments epoch; result coordinator accepts a terminal result only for the current epoch and atomically transitions submission state. The stale sandbox is killed when it reconnects. Outputs upload under attempt-specific immutable paths, so duplicates cannot overwrite.

Infrastructure failures proven to precede all untrusted execution may retry within the bounded platform budget. Compilation can itself execute plugins or build logic, so PREPARING is not automatically effect-free. Failure during execution is ambiguous and retries only if product semantics allow it. Since outbound effects are normally denied, duplicate execution is contained. For approved egress jobs, callers supply idempotency keys and targets must support them. Cancel commits desired state, signals the worker, and fencing prevents later success publication; it cannot undo an already completed external action.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning, pools, and overload
docs.text:
Partition submissions by tenant plus ID and scheduling queues by isolation class, runtime architecture, region, and priority. Too many narrow queues fragment capacity, so capabilities are indexed and matched rather than creating every combination. Workers advertise allocatable CPU, memory, VM slots, image cache, and health. Bin-packing memory too tightly increases correlated OOM risk; maintain reserve.

During overload, admission rejects low-priority jobs with retry-after before upload, queue age caps expire stale work, tenant concurrency prevents capture, and autoscaling uses queued resource-seconds rather than item count. Prewarm common runtime digests based on forecast. Rare images pay cold-start latency without evicting the entire hot cache. Scheduler and result traffic have reserved capacity independent of user output.

docs.title: 15. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• API crash after commit: transactional outbox and sweeper enqueue the durable row.
  • Scheduler crash: assignment leases and conditional state survive; another scheduler resumes.
  • Worker loss: lease expires, attempt becomes infrastructure failure, and capacity is quarantined until host health is known.
  • Sandbox escape signal: isolate host at network layer, stop scheduling, preserve forensic evidence, rotate any exposed credentials, and rebuild from trusted image.
  • Object storage unavailable: stop new large submissions; bounded workers finish metadata locally only within disk limits.
  • Result coordinator unavailable: workers retain signed manifests in bounded spool; leases extend only while canonical ownership is valid.
  • Runtime vulnerability: revoke digest, drain/terminate affected attempts, and rebuild patched images.

Host cleanup is not trusted as the sole boundary. MicroVM destruction plus encrypted scratch with per-job keys makes data remanence less dependent on perfect deletion.

docs.title: 16. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Route submissions to a home region based on latency, capacity, and residency. Inputs and results stay regional unless policy permits replication. Scheduling and workers are region-local so WAN failure cannot strand leases. Submission metadata replicates to a standby, but failover obtains a higher regional epoch before retrying queued work. Running jobs are treated as ambiguous; a grace period alone does not prove they stopped. Retry only after the applicable side-effect policy is satisfied, preserve effect keys, and enforce the regional fence at result and dispatch authorities. Missing acknowledged metadata under asynchronous replication must be recovered or declared as an RPO loss before recreating intent.

Global admission allocates tenant quota budgets to regions and rebalances periodically. Runtime images and policy bundles replicate by signed digest. Disaster recovery capacity must include image cache warm-up and object replication, not only database promotion. Interactive sessions generally reconnect and restart; transparent VM migration adds risk and is not required.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text:
Assume every submission is hostile. Separate public ingress, control services, builders, workers, artifact stores, and egress proxies into trust zones with least-privilege identities. No worker has database admin or image-signing credentials. Signed attempt manifests prevent workers accepting forged policy. Rate-limit submissions and output; inspect archive depth, compression ratio, filenames, and declared dependencies. Protect against side channels with dedicated pools for high-assurance tenants, CPU scheduling controls, and no cross-tenant cache where required.

Audit source access, secret grants, runtime/policy changes, egress, cancellation, and operator debugging. Do not place source, inputs, secrets, or raw output in ordinary control-plane logs. Security response includes host quarantine, fleet revocation, key rotation, and evidence retention.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track admission rejects, queue delay by pool/tenant class, queued CPU-seconds, sandbox startup, image pulls, runtime, result classes, limit violations, lease expiry, stale completion, host pressure, output truncation, egress denies, cleanup latency, and per-runtime failure shifts. Trace control phases using IDs, not source. Independent probes submit known programs that test CPU, memory, filesystem, network denial, output, and result retrieval.

Conformance tests run every runtime against golden compile/execute outputs. Adversarial tests include fork bombs, memory bombs, decompression bombs, filesystem exhaustion, syscall fuzzing, malformed binaries, and network escape attempts. Red teams target VM and management boundaries. Fault tests kill workers at every phase, delay object storage, duplicate messages, and fail regions. Soak tests detect leakage and host degradation across repeated reuse. Restore drills validate signed runtime and policy provenance.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: MicroVMs improve kernel isolation but cost startup time and memory; containers improve density but share a kernel. Pooling warm microVM shells lowers latency but complicates guaranteed cleanup. Internet access improves usability but dramatically expands abuse and exfiltration risk, so curated mirrors win by default. Aggressive bin packing lowers cost but worsens noisy neighbors. Retrying ambiguous attempts improves availability but can duplicate approved egress effects. Dedicated pools improve assurance at lower utilization.

docs.title: 20. Final design, questions, and expectations
docs.text:
The final platform durably accepts immutable submission references, schedules them through tenant-fair resource queues, and leases each attempt to hardened workers. Signed runtime and policy digests boot inside microVM sandboxes with external resource enforcement, no network by default, read-only input, encrypted scratch, and bounded output. Fenced result commits, outbox repair, host quarantine, and home-region epochs handle failures.

Questions: Why is a container alone insufficient? What happens when a lease expires during execution? How are wall and CPU limits different? How do you safely cache compilation? How is output flooding contained? What is the response to a suspected escape? How does region failover treat running jobs?

An L5 candidate should cover queues, workers, limits, isolation, state transitions, retries, artifacts, and scaling. An L6 candidate should articulate the threat model, trust zones, supply-chain controls, fencing, ambiguous execution, fairness by resources, forensic recovery, regional residency, and cost/security segmentation.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: The platform treats code as hostile data until it enters a short-lived sandbox. The API durably records immutable source/input references and pinned runtime/policy digests. A hierarchical fair scheduler allocates CPU, memory, and concurrency, then grants a fenced attempt lease to a worker. The worker verifies a signed manifest and runs code in a microVM with a separate kernel, read-only inputs, encrypted ephemeral scratch, external CPU/memory/PID/time limits, and no network by default. Output is byte-bounded and never blocks control traffic. Result commits require the current lease epoch; duplicate or stale attempts cannot overwrite terminal state. Runtime images have reproducible builds, signatures, SBOMs, staged tests, and emergency revocation. Regional execution preserves residency and uses higher epochs for failover. Escape drills, adversarial programs, host quarantine, and independent probes validate security as an operational property, not merely a sandbox setting.

docs.title: Design a Content Delivery Network
docs.text: This case study owns the CDN design. Use HTTP Semantics and Caching and BGP, Anycast, and Global Routing for cache protocol and edge-routing mechanics.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a CDN for static files, video segments, and cacheable API responses. Clarify object size, freshness, purge guarantees, origins, geography, TLS, and dynamic acceleration. Begin with regional edge caches pulling from origin, then add anycast/request mapping, hierarchical caching, signed delivery, shield selection, revalidation, purge generations, overload controls, and multi-provider recovery. Separate customer configuration from the request path.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Customers map hostnames to origins and define cache, routing, TLS, and security policy. Viewers fetch objects from nearby points of presence (PoPs). The CDN reduces origin load and latency; the origin remains canonical. Cached bytes and logs are projections. We target 99.99% delivery availability, under 50 ms p99 edge overhead on hits, over 95% byte hit ratio for cacheable media, and ordinary global purge within 30 seconds. Private content must never cross authorization or tenant boundaries.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text: Support GET/HEAD, byte ranges, conditional requests, compression, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, origin failover, custom domains/certificates, cache rules, signed URLs/cookies, purge by URL/tag/version, WAF and rate limits, logs, and usage reports. Support 100-byte API objects through multi-GB media, but not arbitrary origin writes. Configuration must roll out safely; edge delivery must survive control-plane failure.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A cache key includes every request attribute allowed to change the representation.
  • A private response is served only after current authorization policy succeeds and is never stored in a public partition.
  • A verified object is atomically visible; partial or checksum-invalid bytes are never hits.
  • Freshness follows explicit policy and bounded clock assumptions; stale serving is labeled and limited.
  • A purge generation prevents an older fill from resurrecting invalidated content.
  • Tenant TLS identity and configuration are isolated by hostname and version.
  • Billing and logs may be delayed, but delivery is never blocked on them.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 20 million requests/s, 200 Tb/s peak egress, 100 PB global cache, one million customer hostnames, and 100,000 configuration changes/s during bulk automation. A 95% byte hit ratio still sends 10 Tb/s to upper tiers/origins. Request hit ratio can be lower because tiny dynamic objects dominate count. Cache capacity is not evenly useful: a viral 5 GB release can create synchronized misses worldwide, while a long tail should not displace repeatedly accessed regional content.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
Distribution(id, tenant, hostnames, origins[], policy_version, state)
CachePolicy(key_fields, ttl_rules, stale_rules, vary_allowlist, negative_ttl)
RoutePolicy(origin_groups, shields, geo_rules, failover)
Certificate(hostname, key_ref, state, activate_at, expires_at)
CacheEntry(key_hash, object_hash, metadata, expires_at, purge_generation)
Purge(id, scope, generation, submitted_at, status)

Configuration is canonical and versioned. Edge bundles are immutable compiled projections. Object bodies are content-addressed locally; metadata owns freshness and tenant namespace. Query APIs paginate with opaque version-bound cursors.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
PUT  /v1/distributions/{id}       If-Match: config-version
POST /v1/distributions/{id}/purges  {urls|tags|all}, Idempotency-Key
GET  /v1/purges/{id}
GET  https://customer.example/path  Range, If-None-Match

The edge normalizes scheme, authority, path, query, selected headers, encoding, and method into the configured cache key. It rejects ambiguous host/path encodings before routing. Purge returns an ID and coverage, not a false claim that every intermediary browser cache has forgotten the object.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 U[Users] --> M[Anycast/DNS mapping]
 M --> E[Edge PoP]
 E --> R[Regional cache]
 R --> S[Origin shield]
 S --> O[Customer origin]
 C[Config API] --> D[(Versioned config store)]
 D --> B[Bundle compiler/distributor]
 B --> E
 P[Purge service] --> E
 E --> L[Async logs and metrics]

Control-plane services manage hostname ownership, certificates, policy, purge, and placement. The data plane terminates connections, enforces policy, caches, and proxies using local bundles. Regional and shield tiers collapse misses before origin.

docs.title: 9. Request and cache flow
docs.text:
The edge selects configuration by SNI and Host, authenticates private requests, applies WAF/rate policy, computes the cache key, and checks metadata. A fresh hit streams local bytes. A stale entry may be revalidated with ETag/Last-Modified. A miss acquires a short singleflight lease; one request fetches while peers wait, receive stale content, or are rejected according to policy.

The fetch goes through the chosen regional cache and shield. Response policy decides cacheability, TTL, allowed Vary, negative caching, and size. Bytes stream to the viewer while writing a temporary file and checksum. Only a successful complete response atomically installs metadata. Client disconnect need not cancel a useful fill, but fill budgets prevent attackers from forcing unlimited downloads.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant U as Viewer
 participant E as Edge
 participant R as Regional cache
 participant S as Shield
 participant O as Origin
 U->>E: GET cache key K
 E->>E: miss, acquire fill lease
 E->>R: fetch K with generation
 R->>S: collapsed miss
 S->>O: conditional GET
 O-->>S: bytes and validators
 S-->>R: response stream and validators
 R-->>E: response stream and validators
 E->>E: atomic install if generation current
 E-->>U: response

docs.title: 10. Freshness, revalidation, and ranges
docs.text:
TTL derives from customer policy and safe origin headers.
