Under RFC 9111 sections 3 and 5.2.2.7, unqualified private forbids storage by a shared HTTP cache; a tenant partition in a CDN is not automatically a single-user private cache. no-store forbids storage. Any separately contracted application-level personalized cache needs explicit authorization and isolation, not reinterpretation of this header. Stale extensions obey their age bounds and cannot bypass mandatory revalidation. Age includes inherited upstream age plus local residence time (accessed 2026-09-08).

Range requests can use a complete object or independently verified chunks. Caching arbitrary overlapping ranges causes fragmentation, so normalize media into fixed-size segments or fill the complete object below a size limit. Revalidation returning 304 refreshes metadata without moving bytes. Negative caching of 404/5xx is short and explicit; caching errors too long turns a brief origin incident into an outage.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: cache keys and poisoning
docs.text:
Under-keying leaks or serves wrong variants; over-keying destroys hit ratio. Start with host, normalized path/query, method, negotiated encoding, and an allowlist of Vary headers. Never allow unconstrained Vary, forwarded host, or attacker-selected headers into origin routing. Normalize percent encoding and reject duplicate/conflicting headers consistently at every tier to prevent request smuggling and cache deception.

If an origin varies on an unsupported header, bypass shared caching rather than silently ignoring that dimension. Vary: * cannot match a later request. Combine stored byte ranges only when they share a strong validator; equal URLs and lengths do not prove the same representation.

Authenticated responses are uncacheable by default. Private caching keys on a stable authorization partition, not raw credentials, and has tighter eviction. Origin response headers cannot override platform safety policy. A customer preview tool shows the computed key and cache decision.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: eviction and admission
docs.text:
LRU alone admits one-hit scans and evicts valuable objects. Use TinyLFU-style frequency admission plus segmented LRU: a small probation segment receives new entries, frequently reused entries enter protected storage, and large objects pay size-aware cost. Memory stores metadata and tiny hot bodies; SSD stores larger objects. Content-addressed bodies can be shared only where policy permits, while metadata remains tenant-separated.

Eviction is local and needs no global coordination. Popularity differs by geography, so central placement loses. Predictive prefetch is reserved for known release manifests; arbitrary prefetch wastes bandwidth. Cache warming is rate-limited against both shield and disk.

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: purge without resurrection
docs.text:
URL purges are exact keys; tag purges consult a bounded tag index; purge-all increments a distribution epoch. The purge service durably assigns a monotonically increasing generation and fans it out. Edges record generation tombstones before deleting metadata. A fill captures the generation at start and may install only if unchanged, preventing a slow pre-purge origin response from reappearing.

Apply the fence at regional caches and shields too. A post-purge edge miss must not label an old upper-tier hit with the new generation: require an upper-tier purge acknowledgement or bypass/revalidate that tier before installing the response. Report purge coverage for every serving tier, not only edge nodes.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> MISS
 MISS --> FILLING: acquire lease at G
 FILLING --> FRESH: complete and current generation
 FILLING --> MISS: purge generation greater than G
 FRESH --> STALE: TTL expires
 STALE --> FRESH: 304 and generation still current
 STALE --> MISS: purge tombstone
 STALE --> FILLING: replacement
 FRESH --> MISS: purge tombstone

Purge delivery is at least once and idempotent by (distribution,generation). Offline PoPs compare high-water marks before serving after restart. Versioned URLs remain the strongest content release mechanism because they avoid races with external caches.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning, scaling, and overload
docs.text:
Map users by anycast or DNS latency policy, then keep each PoP autonomous. Within a PoP, rendezvous hashing maps keys to cache nodes with bounded-load alternatives. Replicate only very hot objects; ordinary misses can refill. Regional cache and shield keys use the same normalization contract.

Overload order matters. Limit connections, header bytes, request rate, fill concurrency, origin bandwidth, and per-tenant disk. Serve cheap fresh hits first, stale eligible hits next, then controlled misses; reject speculative prefetch and expensive transforms. Queueing is bounded by request deadline. Origin protection uses singleflight, token buckets, circuit breakers, retry budgets, and Retry-After. Retries never amplify an already overloaded origin.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text: Configuration writes are linearizable per distribution; edge rollout is eventual and version-observed. Cache content is intentionally eventual under TTL. Purge offers bounded global propagation inside our network, not immediate client-cache invalidation. Config and purge APIs use idempotency keys and conditional versions. Fetch retries are safe for GET/HEAD; ordinary asynchronous logs may be lost or duplicated. Billing uses a separately specified durable metering path with request/event deduplication and loss reconciliation; the existence of an access log is not that guarantee.

docs.title: 16. Reliability, failover, and multi-region
docs.text:
PoP loss shifts traffic through anycast withdrawal or DNS remapping. A partially unhealthy PoP drains new connections but allows existing streams to finish. If a cache disk fails, keys remap and refill under strict origin budgets. Regional-cache failure bypasses to another region or shield. Origin failover requires explicit eligibility, health hysteresis, and content compatibility; blindly retrying a second mutable origin can return a different object.

Control outage freezes last-known-good bundles and certificates. Bundles have compatibility and stale deadlines; safety-critical revocation uses a separately replicated emergency channel. Multi-region control ownership is per distribution with fenced transfer. Customers can configure a second CDN, but DNS failover and TLS/config parity are tested continuously.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use mTLS internally, HSM-backed certificate keys, automated renewal, hostname proof, scoped APIs, encrypted disks, log redaction, and signed bundles. Signed URLs bind path, expiry, audience, and optional IP with clock-skew allowance; planned key rotation overlaps verification keys, while compromise revocation removes trust according to its separate propagation deadline. Defend against DDoS, hotlinking, cache poisoning, request smuggling, origin discovery, SSRF in origin configuration, decompression bombs, oversized ranges, and purge abuse. Egress ACLs permit only validated origins.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure request/byte hit ratio separately, edge latency, time to first byte, cache age, stale serves, fill coalescing, eviction/admission, disk errors, shield/origin QPS, retry amplification, purge/config coverage, TLS expiry, WAF decisions, PoP catchment, and per-tenant cost. Propagate request, config version, cache key hash, purge generation, and origin attempt IDs.

Property-test key normalization and generation races. Fuzz HTTP parsers and compare tiers. Load-test viral cold objects, many tiny keys, ranges, slow clients, disk saturation, and origin collapse. Chaos-test PoP/region loss, corrupt cache bytes, delayed purge, certificate distributor outage, and partial origin failure. Synthetic probes validate public/private variants and fresh/stale/purged behavior from many networks.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: Push distribution is ideal for planned releases but cannot cover the long tail; pull with optional manifests wins. Longer TTL raises hit ratio but increases staleness. Anycast reacts quickly yet makes catchments opaque; DNS mapping is controllable but cached. One global cache is operationally impossible; autonomous tiers contain failure. Serving stale improves availability but may violate correctness for personalized or revoked content, so policy must classify objects.

docs.title: 20. Final architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
 V[Versioned config and TLS] --> B[Signed edge bundles]
 B --> P[Autonomous edge PoPs]
 U[Viewer mapping] --> P
 P --> RC[Regional caches]
 RC --> SH[Per-origin shields]
 SH --> O[Canonical origins]
 G[Generation-fenced purge] --> P
 G --> RC
 G --> SH
 P --> T[Async telemetry and billing]

The final design uses locally enforced immutable policy, tiered pull caches, deterministic keys, atomic verified fills, generation-fenced purge, and origin-aware overload controls.

docs.title: 21. Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text: How is a cache key proven safe? Can purge race a fill? How do range requests cache? What happens when a viral object is cold? When is stale serving forbidden? How does origin failover preserve content semantics? How are private objects isolated? Why measure byte and request hit ratio separately?

docs.title: 22. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate explains routing, cache keys, TTL/revalidation, eviction, shields, purge, overload, and failure. An L6 candidate defines freshness and privacy invariants, separates planes, prevents resurrection and retry amplification, plans certificate/provider migration, and reasons about cost and regional policy.

docs.title: 23. Five-minute summary
docs.text: Five-minute summary: compile customer policy into signed local bundles; map viewers to autonomous PoPs; serve verified fresh bytes locally; collapse misses through regional caches and one origin shield. Use explicit stale policy, size-aware admission, deterministic cache keys, and generation tombstones for purge. Keep logs and control services off the hot path, bound every queue and retry, protect origins during cold bursts, and test externally across networks and failure domains.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a multi-tenant distributed key-value cache used by services to reduce database latency and load. We first define cache semantics because a cache is not canonical storage, estimate memory and network needs, expose get/set/delete and bulk APIs, and build a partitioned in-memory data plane. Deep dives cover placement, eviction, stampede prevention, invalidation, and failure recovery before adding optional cross-region warming.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: The platform stores derived or reproducible values with TTLs. Callers choose cache-aside, read-through, or write-through integration, but the default is cache-aside: miss, read the source of truth, then populate. The service optimizes availability and latency; it does not promise durable retention. A missing key may mean absent, expired, evicted, or temporarily unavailable, so business correctness must remain in the backing system.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Get, multi-get, set with TTL, add-if-absent, compare-and-set, increment, and delete.
  • Namespaces with quotas, maximum object size, eviction policy, and authorization.
  • Optional negative caching and request coalescing.
  • Online node addition/removal with bounded disruption.
  • Usage, hot-key, and hit-rate diagnostics.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 10 million reads/s and 2 million writes/s globally; 95% expected hit ratio.
  • p99 under 2 ms in-zone and 99.99% service availability.
  • Objects up to 1 MB, median 1 KB; TTL from one second to seven days.
  • No noisy tenant may exhaust shared memory or network.

Durable databases, arbitrary queries, and cross-key transactions are out of scope.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. The cache never fabricates a value: returned bytes correspond to a mutation applied by the authoritative owner for that key and namespace; the writer may have lost its response.
  2. Ordinary reads do not serve an entry after logical expiration, allowing the documented bounded clock error. Explicit stale-if-error reads use a separate maximum stale deadline and return a stale marker.
  3. Compare-and-set succeeds only against the observed version on the authoritative shard.
  4. Namespace isolation applies to storage, bandwidth, and authorization.
  5. Rebalancing never creates two accepted writers for one shard epoch.
  6. Add-if-absent has one linearization point on the primary: among concurrent callers, at most one creates the live key.
  7. Increment atomically applies to the current integer value on one key and returns the resulting value; it never silently converts arbitrary bytes.

Read-after-write and delete visibility are configurable. The default is eventual across replicas, while primary reads provide session-level freshness. Cache loss must not violate application correctness.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: At 10 million reads/s with 1 KB values on hits and 95% hit ratio, payload egress is 9.5 GB/s before protocol overhead; 10 GB/s is a conservative all-hit bound. Two million client writes/s plus one replica write per mutation bring aggregate node work to 14 million operations/s, requiring at least 140 node equivalents at a measured 100,000 operations/s each, before failure and skew reserve. At 8 Gbit/s usable egress per node, client-read bytes alone require ten nodes; include replication traffic separately. Suppose 2 billion entries average 1 KB value plus 150 bytes metadata: 2.3 TB logical. Replication factor two with 30% of RAM kept free requires 2.3 * 2 / 0.70 = 6.57 TB, or 103 nodes with 64 GB allocatable RAM each. A 95% hit rate still sends 500,000 reads/s to backing stores. For three balanced zones, preserving the 140-node work floor after one zone fails requires at least 210 nodes, before hot-shard and maintenance reserve; validate the operation mix rather than treating a reads-only benchmark as universal.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
Namespace(namespace_id, owner, memory_quota, qps_quota,
          max_value_bytes, default_ttl, eviction_policy, version)
Entry(namespace_id, key_bytes, value_bytes, value_version,
      created_at, expires_at, flags, size_bytes)
ShardMap(map_version, shard_id, primary, replicas[], epoch, state)

Namespace configuration is canonical in a transactional metadata store. Entry state resides only in RAM, optionally with a local append log to speed restart but not to claim durability. Shard maps are versioned control-plane projections distributed to clients and proxies.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
GET /v1/namespaces/{ns}/keys/{base64Key}
PUT /v1/namespaces/{ns}/keys/{base64Key}?ttl=300
DELETE /v1/namespaces/{ns}/keys/{base64Key}
POST /v1/namespaces/{ns}:multiGet
POST /v1/namespaces/{ns}/keys/{key}:add?ttl=300
POST /v1/namespaces/{ns}/keys/{key}:increment
POST /v1/namespaces/{ns}/keys/{key}:compareAndSet

Responses include value_version, remaining TTL, shard-map version, and hit/miss. Binary clients use multiplexed RPC, deadlines, and bounded batches. Writes accept an idempotency token for safe retries. A lease-based getOrLoad(key, loader_id) interface returns either a value or temporary fill ownership; arbitrary loader code never executes inside cache nodes.

add treats an expired entry as absent after expiration is checked under the same key lock or owner-thread turn as insertion. It returns STORED or EXISTS plus the observed version. increment(delta, initial, ttl) accepts signed 64-bit integer values only, checks overflow, creates initial when absent if requested, and preserves the existing TTL unless the create path supplies one. Both operations are linearizable on the current primary. Their result may still be lost after a primary-only acknowledgement and failover, so they are coordination conveniences for disposable state, not durable uniqueness or billing counters. An idempotency token is required to retry increment after an unknown response; otherwise a retry can apply the delta twice.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  App --> Client[Smart client]
  Client --> P[Primary shard]
  Client --> R[Replica shard]
  P --> R
  Admin --> Control[Cache control plane]
  Control --> Meta[(Metadata DB)]
  Control --> Maps[Signed shard maps]
  Maps --> Client
  P --> Metrics[Metrics and access samples]

The control plane owns namespaces, placement, node health, and migrations. The data plane consists of smart clients and cache nodes. Smart clients avoid proxy hops; a thin proxy option supports untrusted or simple clients. Each client keeps a persistent, multiplexed connection pool per selected node, with bounded pending requests, idle and maximum connection ages, health probes, TLS session reuse, and a global connection budget. Map changes drain obsolete pools rather than reconnecting every request; retries choose only the owner for the required epoch and consume a retry budget. Nodes keep serving under the last shard map during a metadata outage. Start with primary-plus-replica partitions; add persistence or regional replication only for measured warm-up pain.

docs.title: 9. Read and write paths
docs.text:
A client hashes namespace and key to a virtual shard, checks its local map, and sends a deadline-bound request. Default reads go to the primary for predictable freshness; relaxed reads may choose a healthy replica. On a miss, the application loads canonical storage and sets a TTL with jitter. Writes mutate the primary, receive a monotonically increasing per-entry version, and replicate asynchronously. A stricter namespace can require one replica acknowledgment.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant A as Application
  participant C as Cache client
  participant P as Primary
  participant D as Database
  A->>C: get(key)
  C->>P: GET key, mapVersion
  P-->>C: MISS + fill token
  C-->>A: miss + fill ownership
  A->>D: read canonical row
  D-->>A: value, sourceVersion
  A->>C: set(key,value,ttl,fillToken)
  C->>P: conditional SET
  P-->>C: stored version

Writes from cache-aside applications should usually update the database first and then delete the cache. Updating cache before database commit can expose uncommitted values. Delete-after-write narrows stale time, and CDC invalidation provides a second defense.

docs.title: From one node to a distributed cache
docs.text:
First make one node correct. Hash (namespace, key) to a bucket array whose entries reference immutable key bytes and value metadata. Resolve collisions with open addressing or bucket chains; resizing is incremental so one request does not pause the process. Values come from slab or size-class allocators, while entry headers track version, expiry, size, and recency pointers. This avoids per-object allocator overhead and makes fragmentation measurable, but wastes space when values sit just above a class boundary.

Requests run on sharded owner loops or fine-grained bucket locks. Under that serialization point, set, add, increment, CAS, and delete update the hash index, byte accounting, expiration structure, and recency/admission metadata as one mutation. Reads check expiration before returning bytes. Expired entries are unlinked lazily on access and proactively through timing-wheel buckets; delayed cleanup may consume memory but must never make expired data visible. Exact LRU rewrites shared recency state on every hit, so production nodes sample accesses into per-thread buffers and periodically update segmented recency lists. TinyLFU-style frequency sketches decide admission; recency structures choose a victim.

Distribution adds placement above this node-local engine rather than changing key semantics. A virtual shard owns an independent hash-table slice, memory budget, expiration wheel, replication stream, and epoch. This gives migration and failover a bounded unit while the node-level allocator still shares physical pages under namespace quotas.

docs.title: 10. Placement and rebalancing
docs.text:
Use thousands of virtual shards, far more than nodes. Rendezvous hashing maps each shard to failure-domain-aware nodes and moves only affected shards when membership changes. The control plane publishes map epoch E+1 with a migrating state. The old primary snapshots entries to the new node while forwarding recent mutations; after catch-up, the controller grants a higher fencing epoch and switches clients. Old nodes redirect requests carrying new map versions and reject writes after fencing.

Placement choices differ operationally:

Method Lookup Membership change Operational fit hash(key) mod N O(1) Most keys move when N changes Fixed, uniform fleets or a teaching baseline Consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes O(log V) Roughly the added or removed capacity moves Familiar, but token balancing and failure-domain replicas need care Rendezvous hashing over candidate nodes O(N), or less with hierarchy Only keys preferring changed nodes move Simple deterministic ranking, weighting, and replica selection

Direct modulo hashing is unacceptable for an elastic fleet because changing N remaps nearly every key. Rings and rendezvous both limit movement. This design hashes keys to a fixed virtual-shard ID first, then uses rendezvous hashing for shard-to-node assignment. Clients perform constant-time key-to-shard lookup and consume a precomputed map, so they do not score every node on every request.

Cold movement is often preferable because entries are disposable: assign the new owner and accept misses. Warm copy is justified for expensive backing stores or very large working sets. Rate-limit migration so it does not consume latency headroom.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Old[Old owner memory]
    OH[Shard hash index]
    OS[Size-class slabs]
    OT[Expiry wheel]
    OR[Recency and frequency]
    OH --> OS
    OH --> OT
    OH --> OR
  end
  subgraph New[New owner memory]
    NH[Rebuilt hash index]
    NS[Allocated slabs]
    NT[Rebuilt expiry wheel]
    NR[Cold recency metadata]
    NH --> NS
    NH --> NT
    NH --> NR
  end
  OH -->|snapshot live entries at epoch E| NH
  OS -->|copy key, value, version, expiry| NS
  Mutations[Buffered mutations after snapshot] -->|ordered catch-up| NH
  Fence[Control plane grants epoch E+1] --> New
  Fence -->|reject later writes| Old

The copy excludes already expired entries and transfers absolute expiry, not a fresh TTL. It preserves value and source versions but need not preserve exact recency: the destination can start copied entries in a probation segment to avoid declaring the entire moved set hot. Migration reserves destination memory before copying, accounts copy buffers outside tenant capacity, validates key counts and byte checksums, then closes old-owner writes, captures their final watermark, and switches only after the target has applied that complete prefix. A small nonzero lag is a preparation gate, not proof of safe writer transfer. Cold movement can discard values but must still fence the former owner. If headroom is insufficient, choose cold movement instead of risking fleet-wide eviction.

docs.title: 11. Eviction and memory management
docs.text:
TTL expiration uses a coarse timing wheel plus lazy checks on access; scanning all keys is too expensive. When memory crosses a watermark, evict within each namespace quota. Exact global LRU requires lock-heavy updates. Sampled LRU or segmented LRU approximates recency cheaply; TinyLFU admission plus a small recency window protects frequent values from one-hit scans. Objects larger than the namespace threshold are rejected because a few large entries can create allocator fragmentation and bandwidth spikes.

Reserve memory for metadata and replication buffers. Slab or size-class allocation reduces fragmentation. Eviction is observable by cause: TTL, quota, pressure, manual delete, or rebalance.

docs.title: 12. Stampedes, hot keys, and invalidation
docs.text:
For a cold popular key, millions of misses can overload the database. A short fill lease allows one caller to load while others wait briefly, receive stale-if-allowed data, or fail fast. Lease holders publish only if their token and source version remain current. TTL jitter avoids synchronized expiry. Probabilistic early refresh lets a caller refresh before expiry with probability increasing as expiration approaches.

A single hot key can saturate one shard. Replicate detected immutable hot values to read replicas or host-local near caches, with short TTL and versioned invalidations. This is safe only when bounded staleness is acceptable, values carry versions, invalidation loss expires naturally, and authorization is identical at every copy. Never near-cache secrets with immediate revocation requirements, one-time tokens, lock ownership, or values whose stale reuse can spend money. A mutable hot key remains single-owner for CAS, add, and increment; replicas can serve only explicitly stale reads. Split counters into independently owned stripes only when the caller accepts an approximate aggregate, never to preserve a linearizable counter contract. Negative results use short TTLs and distinguish not found from backend failure.

flowchart TD
  Miss[Cache miss] --> Lease{Fill lease acquired?}
  Lease -->|yes| Load[Load source of truth]
  Load --> Publish[Conditional publish]
  Lease -->|no| Stale{Stale allowed?}
  Stale -->|yes| Return[Return stale + refresh pending]
  Stale -->|no| Wait[Bounded wait with jitter]
  Wait --> Retry[Retry cache once]

CDC invalidations carry namespace, key, and source version. Nodes ignore older invalidations and keep bounded version high-watermarks or invalidate outstanding fill tokens even when the value is absent. Otherwise delete followed by a slow old loader can resurrect stale data. Define the retention window against maximum loader and CDC delay; beyond it revalidate with the source. Whole-namespace purges are asynchronous jobs with progress, not an unbounded request.

docs.title: 13. Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Partition by hash of (namespace_id, key) for even spread. Large tenants have namespace quotas but share shards until isolation is needed. Dedicated pools support regulated or extremely hot tenants. Multi-get groups keys by shard and executes in parallel with a concurrency bound; output preserves input order and marks per-key errors. Admission control limits operations, bytes, and CPU because QPS alone misses large-value abuse.

Autoscaling watches sustained CPU, network, allocator pressure, and eviction rate. Adding empty RAM does not instantly improve hit rate; warm-up and movement are explicit rollout states.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Primary operations are ordered per key. Asynchronous replicas may lag, so relaxed reads can return older values. Quorum replication improves failover freshness but raises write latency; it still does not make the cache a database. CAS compares opaque versions containing the shard epoch and an entry generation that is not reused after eviction or delete/recreate; resetting a per-entry counter would allow an ABA match. Add-if-absent and increment share the same primary serialization point as CAS. Failover can lose any operation acknowledged before replication, and a client with an unknown increment response must retry with the same idempotency token or read and reconcile at the application layer.

Set retries with the same idempotency token return the original result for a bounded window. Delete retries carry the original mutation token or expected generation: an unconditional delayed retry could otherwise erase a newly populated entry. Fill tokens prevent a slow loader from overwriting a newer fill. Source versions, when supplied, reject regression from delayed CDC or loaders.

docs.title: 15. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Node crash: clients refresh maps and retry once on the promoted replica; misses refill naturally.
  • Network partition: only the fenced primary epoch accepts writes. Isolated replicas may serve explicitly stale reads.
  • Control-plane outage: existing maps continue; topology changes pause.
  • Memory pressure: enforce tenant quotas, reject writes before reads, and evict by policy.
  • Backend slowdown: coalescing, stale-if-error, circuit breakers, and miss-rate admission protect it.
  • Bad client retry storm: deadlines, exponential jitter, retry budgets, and server load shedding.
  • Corrupt local snapshot: discard it and start cold; canonical data is elsewhere.

Recovery promotes the most up-to-date replica when practical, increments epoch, and rebuilds redundancy in the background. Never block fleet recovery on restoring every disposable entry.

Failure alerts should expose customer and dependency impact, not just dead nodes. Track unavailable and stale-read rates by namespace class, failover duration, promoted-replica lag in operations and bytes, estimated acknowledged writes lost, epoch mismatch rejects, redirect loops, retry amplification, connection-pool saturation, migration copy/catch-up lag, memory reservation failures, refill QPS, and backend error/latency after misses. Page when error budget burns or backing-store protection approaches its limit; ticket isolated replica rebuild lag before it removes failover margin.

docs.title: 16. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Deploy independent regional caches close to applications. Canonical database replication determines application freshness; cache invalidations follow CDC into each region. Cross-region synchronous cache writes add latency without creating durable correctness. For disaster recovery, the destination starts cold, optionally prewarmed from access-frequency sketches or a safe snapshot. Limit prewarming so it does not overload databases or links.

If clients move between regions, they may observe older cached data. Applications requiring monotonic reads include a minimum source version; the cache returns miss when its value is older. Namespace metadata replicates globally, while one home control plane coordinates writes and promotes through a new epoch.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use mTLS workload identity, namespace ACLs, encryption in transit, and optional value encryption for sensitive tenants. Cache keys and sampled values must not leak into ordinary logs. Operators get metadata-only diagnostics unless break-glass access is audited. Quotas cover memory, requests, ingress, egress, key length, and object size. Validate compression ratios to prevent decompression bombs and isolate parsers from the data process.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure hit ratio by namespace and status, but pair it with saved backend work; a high hit ratio on cheap keys may be useless. Track p50/p99 latency, evictions and rejected admissions by cause, expirations pending cleanup, fill waits, replication lag, hot-key share, memory fragmentation by size class, slab utilization, timing-wheel backlog, recency-buffer drops, bytes, redirects, pool queue time, and backend load after misses. Trace sampled cache-aside flows without value contents.

Unit tests cover TTL boundaries, add races, increment overflow and retry deduplication, CAS, allocator class boundaries, and eviction accounting. Property tests model map epochs and ensure fenced writers cannot commit. Deterministic node tests race access with expiry cleanup and assert that hash, slab, timing-wheel, quota, and recency accounting converge. Load tests use Zipfian popularity, varied sizes, synchronized expiries, slow client pools, and node churn. Fault tests kill primaries during replication, interrupt warm migration at every phase, and disconnect control plane. Replay tests compare eviction policies on production access samples. Capacity drills rehearse a full regional cold start without collapsing databases.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: Smart clients remove a hop but require library rollout; proxies centralize behavior but add cost and a bottleneck. Replication improves availability and read scale but consumes RAM. Primary reads give freshness; replica reads lower latency. Exact LRU costs more than its benefit at scale, so approximate admission wins. Warm rebalancing preserves hit rate but consumes network; cold movement is simpler. Persistence accelerates restart but risks callers treating cache as durable.

docs.title: 20. Final design, questions, and expectations
docs.text:
The final design uses versioned virtual shards, zone-aware primary and replicas, smart clients, in-memory entries, timing-wheel expiration, TinyLFU-style admission, per-namespace quotas, fill leases, and CDC invalidation. The transactional control plane publishes fenced shard maps; data nodes survive its outage. Regions remain independent and recover by refill.

Interview questions: How do you stop a stampede? What happens to acknowledged writes on primary failure? How is a hot key detected and mitigated? Why does adding nodes cause misses? How do delete and database commit order interact? How would minimum-version reads work?

An L5 answer should estimate RAM/QPS, define cache-aside paths, hash partitions, choose eviction, and handle node loss and hot keys. An L6 answer should distinguish saved work from hit ratio, fence rebalancing, isolate tenants by bytes, protect backing stores during cold start, define freshness contracts, and justify operational complexity with measured requirements.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: This is a disposable, multi-tenant in-memory cache, not a database. Canonical namespace metadata lives in a control plane that publishes versioned, fenced shard maps. Smart clients hash namespace and key to zone-replicated primaries; optional replica reads trade freshness for latency. Entries expire through lazy checks and timing wheels, while sampled admission and eviction avoid exact-LRU overhead. Fill leases, TTL jitter, early refresh, and stale-if-error protect databases from stampedes. Virtual shards and rendezvous placement limit movement; hot keys gain read replicas or near-cache copies. Per-tenant memory, byte, and QPS quotas prevent noisy neighbors. Regional caches operate independently and consume versioned CDC invalidations. Failures produce misses or explicitly stale reads, never invented durability. The design is validated with skewed traffic, churn, synchronized expiry, and cold-region recovery tests.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a multi-tenant store for Get, Put, conditional update, delete, and range scan. Clarify value size, consistency, latency, transactions, durability, and regions. Start with range-sharded replicated state machines using a write-ahead log and LSM storage. Then add MVCC, snapshots, rebalancing, split/merge, overload control, repair, and explicit geo modes. The challenge is maintaining observable semantics through leader, disk, and network failure.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Applications store opaque values under ordered keys. The store is canonical, unlike a cache. We support linearizable single-key operations and snapshot-consistent scans in-region; optional transactions span a bounded number of ranges. Cross-region replicas are asynchronous by default. Targets: 99.99% writes, 99.999% reads where stale reads are allowed, 10 ms p99 small operations in-region, and no acknowledged-write loss under the configured failure model.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text: Support get/put/delete, compare-and-swap, batch, scans with continuation, TTL, watches, backups, quotas, encryption, and idempotent mutations. Values are at most 1 MB, typical 1 KB. Preserve ordered scans. Avoid claiming unlimited transactions, exactly-once delivery, or availability during loss of quorum.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• Each range has one current epoch and one quorum-approved leader/lease holder.
  • An acknowledged write is committed to a quorum and survives any allowed minority failure.
  • Reads at timestamp T return the newest committed version at or before T.
  • Split/merge and replica movement never create two writable owners for one key/epoch.
  • CAS evaluates and writes atomically at one serialization point.
  • Version and tombstone reclamation preserves every supported replica, live snapshot, transaction, incremental backup chain, and restore policy.
  • Retry deduplication never maps one token to two effects.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 10 PB logical retained data, 10 billion keys, 5 million reads/s, 1 million writes/s, and 3x replication. Those storage and key counts imply 1 MB retained per key, not 1 KB. Separately assume incoming values average 1 KB plus 100 bytes metadata: logical ingest is 1.1 GB/s before replication and compaction. Reconcile this difference through a measured size distribution, retained MVCC versions, and retention period; if instead each key has only one 1.1 KB version, the logical dataset is 11 TB. Three durable copies require 3.3 GB/s aggregate replica writes; leader-to-follower replication alone is about 2.2 GB/s, excluding ingress. Hot keys invalidate uniform assumptions. At 10 PB, 10-50 GB ranges yield 200,000-1,000,000 ranges; target 50% disk and 60% CPU utilization to preserve repair and failover headroom.

docs.title: 6. Core entities and data model
docs.text:
Range(start_key, end_key, range_id, epoch, replicas[], leader, state)
Version(key, commit_ts, value_or_tombstone, expiry, checksum)
LogEntry(index, term, command, client_id, sequence)
Transaction(txn_id, read_ts, priority, writes, status)
Snapshot(range_id, index, files[], checksum)

The metadata directory maps ordered key spans to range descriptors. Data uses an LSM: mutable memtable, immutable memtables, sorted-string tables, Bloom filters, sparse indexes, and a WAL. MVCC keys encode (user_key, descending_timestamp).

This LSM is not a relational heap plus B+ tree: it trades background compaction and read amplification for buffered sequential writes. Database Indexing explains B+ tree and heap access paths, while Relational Databases explains PostgreSQL-style WAL, checkpoints, transactions, and replicas.

docs.title: 7. Interface
docs.text:
Get(key, consistency, read_timestamp?) -> value, version
Put(key, value, idempotency_token, precondition?) -> version
Delete(key, token, precondition?) -> version
Scan(start, end, limit, cursor, read_timestamp?) -> rows, cursor
Txn(reads, conditions, writes, token) -> committed|aborted
Watch(prefix, after_revision) -> changes|compacted

Opaque scan cursors bind range end, last key, read timestamp, directory epoch, and expiry. Clients retry NOT_LEADER and stale-epoch responses after refreshing descriptors, under one deadline.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Clients] --> G[Smart client/gateway]
 G --> M[Metadata directory]
 G --> R[Range leaders]
 R --> F[Range followers]
 R --> W[WAL and LSM]
 M --> P[Placement control plane]
 P --> R
 R --> B[Backup/change stream]
 X[Compaction and repair] --> W

The control plane places ranges and coordinates epochs. The data plane replicates each range through consensus and serves reads/writes. Placement outages stop movement but not operations on healthy ranges.

docs.title: 9. Write and read paths
docs.text:
A gateway locates the range and sends a mutation to its leader with client sequence. The leader validates epoch/precondition, appends to its WAL, replicates the log, waits for majority durable acknowledgement, applies in order to memtable/MVCC, and responds. Followers reject stale leader terms. Group commit batches fsync without weakening quorum durability.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant L as Range leader
 participant F1 as Follower 1
 participant F2 as Follower 2
 C->>L: Put key, token, precondition
 L->>L: append and durably flush local WAL
 par replicate
  L->>F1: log entry
  L->>F2: log entry
 end
 F1-->>L: durable ack
 L->>L: quorum commit and apply
 L-->>C: committed version

Linearizable reads go through the leader after confirming its lease/quorum or a read-index round. Snapshot reads at a sufficiently old closed timestamp can use followers. Bloom filters skip SSTables for absent point keys; reads merge memtable and SSTable versions. Read repair is not a substitute for consensus.

docs.title: 10. LSM storage and compaction
docs.text:
WAL provides recovery; memtables batch random writes into sorted sequential SSTables. Leveled compaction bounds read amplification, while size-tiered compaction favors write throughput but uses more space. Per-level checksums detect corruption. Block cache and Bloom filters accelerate reads, but canonical bytes remain WAL/SSTables.

Compaction is correctness-sensitive: it can drop an overwritten version only below the global safe timestamp, and a tombstone only when no older value can reappear from covered storage levels or supported replica recovery. A self-contained old backup does not pin live tombstones forever: backup retention and restore-time deletion replay enforce its separate lifecycle. Incremental backup chains must retain their required bases and changes. Scheduler budgets disk and CPU so foreground latency wins. Emergency disk fullness rejects writes before WAL safety is endangered and prioritizes flush/space reclamation.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: consensus, leases, and clocks
docs.text:
Raft-like consensus orders writes per range. Election terms fence old leaders. A lease avoids quorum reads only when clock uncertainty and maximum pause are bounded; otherwise use read index. Lease expiration is conservative under clock jumps. Committed log entries survive leader change, while uncommitted suffixes may be truncated and must never have been acknowledged.

Thousands of ranges share processes, so elections use jitter and capped concurrency. A node outage must not trigger every range election simultaneously. Leaders are spread by load/failure domain, not simply count.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: range split, merge, and movement
docs.text:
When size/QPS crosses thresholds, choose a sampled key boundary. The parent commits a SPLITTING record at index, creates child descriptors with higher epochs, snapshots shared files, then atomically updates directory ownership. Requests with old epochs receive both child hints. Shared immutable SSTables avoid immediate copying.

Replica movement first adds a learner, streams a snapshot plus log tail, catches up, promotes it through consensus, then removes the old replica. Never reduce quorum during transfer. Merge requires adjacent ranges, compatible replicas, low load, and one committed transition. Reconciliation repairs stuck transitions.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> ACTIVE
 ACTIVE --> SPLITTING: size or QPS
 SPLITTING --> ACTIVE: abort safely
 SPLITTING --> RETIRED: children installed
 ACTIVE --> MOVING: add learner
 MOVING --> ACTIVE: promote then remove
 ACTIVE --> MERGING: adjacent cold range
 MERGING --> RETIRED: merged range installed

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: transactions
docs.text:
Single-range transactions execute in one replicated command. For cross-range transactions, MVCC plus two-phase commit writes intents at participants and a transaction record at a coordinator range. Reads encountering intents resolve committed/aborted status. Wound-wait priorities or wait queues handle conflicts; deadlock is bounded by transaction deadlines.

The coordinator's commit decision is durable before participants finalize, so a crash leaves resolvable intents. Background recovery aborts expired pending transactions only after proving no commit. Transactions have limits on keys, bytes, ranges, and duration because old read timestamps block garbage collection.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning, hot keys, and overload
docs.text:
Ordered range partitioning enables scans but a sequential key pattern hotspots the final range. Encourage hash prefixes for non-scan workloads, pre-split known tenants, and split by QPS as well as bytes. One key cannot be split while retaining linearizability; mitigate with application sharding, commutative counters, batching, caching reads, or a dedicated range.

Admission controls exist per node, tenant, and range. Separate read/write/maintenance queues; bound them by deadline and weighted fairness. Backpressure starts before memtable/WAL/disk saturation. Reject optional stale reads last if cheap, preserve replication and heartbeats, and stop accepting writes when quorum durability or disk reserve is threatened.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Linearizable operations serialize through the range leader. Snapshot isolation prevents inconsistent scans but permits write skew unless serializable conflict checks are enabled. Cross-range serializability uses timestamp ordering and read/write conflict tracking at added latency. Watches are at least once; resume from revision or receive compaction reset.

Dedup records (client_id,sequence)->result replicate with the write and expire after a documented retry window. After expiry, clients need application idempotency. TTL is a logical tombstone based on server/HLC time; physical deletion is asynchronous.

docs.title: 16. Reliability and recovery
docs.text:
Leader loss elects a follower; minority partitions stop writes, avoiding split brain. Corrupt blocks retry another replica, quarantine the file, and repair from checksummed snapshots. Anti-entropy compares range/index and file hashes, but consensus determines authoritative history. Node replacement uses throttled learners. Backups combine periodic snapshots with ordered logs and are restored into an isolated cluster before promotion.

The control plane continuously reconciles descriptor ownership, replica count/diversity, learner age, disk skew, and unavailable ranges. Disaster drills prove restore point and restore time rather than merely checking backup job success.

docs.title: 17. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
For strong global data, place quorum replicas across regions, accepting WAN write latency and correlated network partitions. More commonly, each keyspace has a home region with synchronous multi-zone replicas and asynchronous remote logs. Promotion requires an explicit fenced epoch and known recovery point; acknowledged writes not replicated remotely may be lost under region destruction according to stated RPO.

Active-active is offered only with constrained semantics such as LWW, CRDT counters/sets, or application conflict resolution. Calling conflicting opaque values "eventually consistent" does not solve them. Tenant policy selects latency, RPO, and conflict model.

docs.title: 18. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use mTLS workload identity, tenant/key-prefix ACLs, envelope encryption, HSM-backed keys, audit logs, signed backups, network isolation, and redacted diagnostics. Defend against oversized values, scan amplification, hot-key denial, transaction/intents exhaustion, watch fanout, and noisy neighbors with quotas. Key rotation rewrites wrapped data keys without blocking reads; deletion uses tombstones, retention, compaction, and backup lifecycle.

docs.title: 19. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure latency by operation/consistency, QPS/bytes, proposal-to-commit time, leader changes, quorum health, WAL fsync, compaction debt, read/write/space amplification, cache/Bloom efficacy, range skew, hot keys, split/move duration, transaction conflicts/intents, safe timestamp, replication lag, disk errors, and rejected work.

Model-check election, reconfiguration, split, and transaction races. Property-test MVCC visibility, CAS, cursors, dedup, and tombstone GC. Fuzz WAL/SSTable corruption. Load-test sequential keys, one hot key, scans during compaction, node replacement, and retry storms. Chaos-test partitions, pauses, clock changes, disk-full, torn writes, and restore.

docs.title: 20. Important tradeoffs
docs.text:
Hash shards balance writes but lose range scans; ordered ranges win the required interface. Replication is simpler than erasure coding for small mutable values. Leaderless quorum can improve availability but conflict/read-repair semantics complicate conditional writes; consensus ranges win. Transactions add coordination and GC pressure, so bound them. Follower reads lower latency but expose staleness.

flowchart TD
 D[Range directory with epochs] --> C[Smart routing]
 C --> L[Consensus range leader]
 L --> Q[Zonal quorum]
 Q --> S[WAL plus MVCC LSM]
 P[Placement and split controller] --> L
 S --> A[Snapshots, logs, repair]
 A --> R[Async disaster-recovery region]

docs.title: 21. Final architecture
docs.text: The final design uses epoch-fenced ordered ranges, per-range consensus, quorum-durable WAL commits, MVCC LSM storage, controlled split/move workflows, and asynchronous disaster-recovery replication.

docs.title: 22. Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text: When is a write acknowledged? Can a follower serve linearizable reads? How does a split avoid dual ownership? When may tombstones disappear? What happens to 2PC after coordinator failure? How is one hot key handled? What RPO follows asynchronous geo replication?

docs.title: 23. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate covers sharding, consensus, LSM, read/write paths, hot keys, recovery, and consistency. An L6 candidate states durability proofs, handles reconfiguration and GC invariants, quantifies overload/repair headroom, separates placement from serving, and offers explicit geo products rather than one vague consistency mode.

docs.title: 24. Five-minute summary
docs.text: Five-minute summary: partition ordered keys into epoch-fenced ranges; replicate each through consensus; acknowledge after quorum-durable WAL commit; store MVCC versions in an LSM; route linearizable reads through a valid leader and safe snapshot reads to followers. Split and move through logged transitions, retain tombstones until safe, bound transactions and queues, reserve repair capacity, and expose region failure as a deliberate latency/RPO choice.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a service that coordinates mutually exclusive work across unreliable clients. Clarify whether callers protect an external resource, lease duration, fairness, reentrancy, throughput, and failure semantics. Start with a consensus-replicated lock record and expiring lease, then add fencing tokens, watches, queues, sessions, multi-region boundaries, deadlock guidance, and operational repair. The key insight is that a lease alone cannot stop a paused former owner from writing to another system.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Clients create a session, acquire a named lock with TTL and wait deadline, renew, release, and observe ownership. The service supports exclusive locks first; shared/read locks, semaphores, and multi-lock transactions are separate products. Locks coordinate jobs and leadership, not every database row. Protected resources must validate fencing tokens when stale-owner safety matters.

This design specializes the distributed coordination pattern: sessions provide ephemeral ownership, CAS serializes transfer, revisions order waiters, and watches only prompt authoritative rechecks. The lock service adds fairness, reentrancy policy, contention handling, and a fencing-token contract with each protected resource.

Target acquire/renew p99 below 20 ms in-region, 99.99% availability, millions of held locks, and hundreds of thousands of operations/s. The service provides linearizable lock state within a region. During loss of quorum it refuses ownership changes. Availability never justifies two valid owners. Fairness is bounded FIFO where configured, not strict real-time fairness across cancelled/networked clients.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• At most one unexpired committed exclusive lease exists for a lock generation.
  • Every successful ownership change returns a monotonically increasing fencing token that is never reused.
  • Only matching session, lease ID, and lock generation can renew or release.
  • Expiry and acquire are committed by the consensus authority, not inferred from a client clock.
  • A stale leader or delayed client cannot grant/renew after its consensus term or session generation is fenced.
  • An acquire retry with the same request ID returns the same outcome while retained.
  • Queue cancellation or timeout cannot later acquire invisibly; request generation determines validity.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 10 million clients, 20 million held locks, 500,000 acquire/release operations/s, and TTL 30 seconds. Renewing each lock only once per TTL would already require about 670,000 renewals/s and leave no safety margin. A chosen 10-second renewal interval requires 20 million / 10 = 2 million renewals/s before retries. Session leases covering many locks or batched renewals reduce this traffic, though they enlarge correlated expiry; name the renewal interval separately from TTL. At 500 bytes canonical state per held lock, live data is 10 GB before replication; wait queues and changelogs may dominate. Hot global locks serialize by definition and cannot scale through sharding. Namespace admission and contention limits prevent one key from exhausting a consensus group.

docs.title: Data model and interfaces
docs.text:
Session(session_id, client_generation, lease_expiry, state, last_request_seq)
Lock(name_hash, name, owner_session, lease_id, lock_generation,
     fencing_token, expires_at, reentrancy_count, revision)
Waiter(lock_name, request_id, session_id, mode, enqueue_revision,
       deadline, state, waiter_generation)
Event(revision, lock_name, type, owner_session, fencing_token)

POST /v1/sessions {ttl_ms}
POST /v1/locks/{name}:acquire {session_id, request_id, ttl_ms, wait_ms}
POST /v1/locks/{name}:renew {session_id, lease_id, generation}
POST /v1/locks/{name}:release {session_id, lease_id, generation}
GET  /v1/locks/{name}
GET  /v1/locks/{name}/watch?after_revision=...

Acquire returns lease_id, lock generation, fencing token, authoritative expiry, and revision. Names are normalized, length-bounded, namespace-scoped, and opaque; hierarchical path semantics are not implied. The API distinguishes NOT_OWNER, EXPIRED, CANCELLED, and DEADLINE_EXCEEDED.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Clients] --> G[Authenticated gateways]
 G --> R[Lock shard leaders]
 R --> F[Consensus followers]
 R --> T[Server-time expiry wheel]
 R --> W[Wait/watch fanout]
 W --> C
 R --> A[(Audit snapshots and log)]
 P[Namespace/policy control plane] --> G
 C --> X[Protected resources]
 R -. fencing token .-> X

docs.title: Acquire and fencing
docs.text:
Gateway routes the normalized lock name to one consensus shard. The leader checks session, namespace policy, deadline, and current record. If free or authoritatively expired, it appends a transaction assigning a new random lease ID, incremented lock generation and fencing token, owner session, and expiry based on leader time. It responds only after quorum commit.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant L as Lock leader
 participant Q as Quorum followers
 participant X as Protected database
 C->>L: acquire(name, request_id, session)
 L->>Q: append owner, expiry, token 734
 Q-->>L: quorum durable
 L-->>C: lease and fencing token 734
 C->>X: conditional write with token 734
 X->>X: atomically check token, mutate, store max 734
 Note over C,X: token 733 rejected after X observes 734

The protected resource atomically checks the token, applies the mutation, and persists the highest token per protected object. If A has 733 and pauses, B acquiring 734 alone does not make the resource reject A: the resource must first observe 734. For a handoff that revokes A before B begins work, install 734 at the resource and acknowledge that installation before declaring transfer complete. Retry installation idempotently after a lost reply; do not report a completed handoff from the lock-service commit alone. See the stronger handoff trace and fixture. The lock service cannot retract A's process or packets. If the resource cannot validate tokens or another equivalent authority condition, accept only best-effort stale-owner safety.

Fencing token must be monotonic for the lock/protected scope and durably preserved across restore. A random lease ID authenticates a particular ownership but is not an ordering token. Consensus term alone may reset/misorder across shard migrations; store a persistent generation/token allocation scheme.

docs.title: Renewal, release, and expiry
docs.text:
Renew checks exact session generation, lease ID, lock generation, unexpired state, and policy, then commits a later expiry. A renew received after authoritative expiry fails even if no successor exists; the client must reacquire and obtain a higher fence. Release uses the same compare-and-set and is idempotent. It advances generation or records release so delayed renewals cannot revive ownership.

Expiry timers are hints. The leader places deadlines in a hierarchical timing wheel. When a timer fires it reads current state and appends an expiry only if generation and deadline still match. A leader change rebuilds near-term timers by scanning indexed expiry buckets. Time derives from a monotonic component anchored to bounded wall time; leadership is not granted when clock uncertainty exceeds safety margin. Conservative uncertainty may delay availability, never overlap leases.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> FREE
 FREE --> HELD: committed acquire
 HELD --> HELD: valid renew
 HELD --> FREE: valid release
 HELD --> EXPIRED: committed expiry
 EXPIRED --> HELD: next token acquire
 HELD --> ORPHANED: session revoked
 ORPHANED --> EXPIRED: cleanup commit

Clients renew well before expiry with jitter and stop protected work immediately after renewal uncertainty. They do not assume temporary connectivity means ownership. A safe client library exposes a cancellation context when lease confidence is lost and passes the fencing token to every protected operation.

docs.title: Wait queues and fairness
docs.text:
If a held lock permits waiting, append a waiter with request ID, session, enqueue revision, and deadline. On release/expiry, select the oldest eligible waiter, skip cancelled/expired sessions, and atomically transfer ownership with the next fence. Long polling or watch informs the winner; the committed state, not notification delivery, grants ownership.

Cancellation is a versioned state transition. If cancellation races transfer, exactly one committed order wins and the response tells the client whether it acquired then must release, or cancellation prevailed. Disconnected winners receive a short acquisition-confirmation window or rely on session liveness, preventing a long unused lease at queue head. Strict FIFO can let slow/dead waiters reduce throughput; bounded FIFO may skip ineligible heads while recording reason.

Watch streams carry revisions and are advisory. Slow watchers receive reset/snapshot instructions. A client seeing a free notification still performs acquire; it never treats observation as ownership. This prevents a thundering herd from all acting after release, though they may all contend. Queue mode or randomized retry reduces that load.

docs.title: Sessions and reentrancy
docs.text:
A session amortizes liveness across locks and is bound to client generation. Session expiry marks all owned locks eligible for committed cleanup. Batch heartbeats reduce writes, but a network issue now loses many locks simultaneously; cap locks/session and spread renew timing. Explicit per-lock leases are safer for long critical sections.

Reentrancy is allowed only for the same session and explicit reentrant API, incrementing a count under one generation/token. Release decrements until zero. Process/thread identity is not inferred across distributed clients. Prefer non-reentrant locks because hidden nested ownership causes leaks. Session handoff is forbidden; use release/reacquire with a new fence.

docs.title: Multi-lock operations and deadlock
docs.text:
Atomic acquisition of arbitrary lock sets turns shards into a distributed transaction manager and invites deadlock. The baseline API requires clients to sort normalized lock names globally and acquire in order with one overall deadline; failure releases acquired locks. For a small same-shard set, one consensus transaction can grant all and allocate a transaction fence. Cross-shard atomic locks require two-phase commit, durable coordinator recovery, and wound-wait/timeout policy; offer only with a demonstrated requirement.

Detect prolonged wait-for cycles from queue telemetry for diagnostics, but prevention through ordering is simpler. Never automatically revoke a live lock merely to break a deadlock unless protected operations are designed for fencing and abort.

docs.title: Hot locks and herd control
docs.text: A single lock cannot process critical sections in parallel. Report contention, queue length, hold time, and owner. Encourage partitioning the protected resource, optimistic concurrency, work queues, semaphores, or leader election with local batching. Gateways coalesce status reads; wait queues notify one next owner rather than broadcasting. Per-lock waiter caps and acquisition rates reject pathological contention before exhausting shard memory.

docs.title: Shard movement and token continuity
docs.text: Lock names hash to consensus groups. Copy records, maximum fencing tokens, session state, receipts, and waiters while the source remains authoritative. At cutover, fence every source mutation for the range, including renewals, releases, expiry, session cleanup, and queue transfer, not only new acquires. Resolve in-flight transactions, capture the final committed watermark F, then apply and verify its complete prefix at the target before enabling the new authority. A control-plane routing update alone cannot make an isolated old store reject writes. Token ranges can include a migration epoch in high bits plus per-lock counter, ensuring all new tokens compare above old tokens. Protected external sinks need their own fence installation for immediate revocation; moving lock records does not install that fence. Clients refresh routing on epoch errors. Reverse transfer must drain and fence the current writer and preserve its final prefix under a fresh epoch, as in the canonical migration protocol.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and multi-region
docs.text:
Hash locks across many consensus groups; keep lock, waiters, idempotency records, and revision together. Replicate each group across zones. Gateways cache routing but not ownership decisions. Separate CPU pools for acquire/renew/release, watches, and audit. Reserve capacity for renew and release so an acquire flood cannot make healthy owners lose leases. Cells isolate namespaces and cap blast radius.

The default is region-scoped locks because cross-ocean consensus latency harms every acquire/renew and network partitions reduce availability. Globally protected resources either use a home region lock service and accept latency, or a multi-region consensus group with explicit quorum placement. Independent regional locks with asynchronous replication are not a global lock. Disaster failover must preserve consensus log and maximum fencing token; if safety cannot be proven, block acquisition until operator recovery rather than reset tokens.

Backpressure rejects non-waiting acquire attempts first, caps waiters, coalesces watches, and protects established renewals and cleanup. Overloaded clients receive retry-after with jitter. A hot lock is isolated but remains serialized. Audit export and metrics may lag; canonical lease operations may not.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Acquire, renew, release, queue transfer, expiry, and fencing token are linearizable per lock. Metrics, watches, and cross-region audit are eventual. Request IDs plus session sequence make retries idempotent. A lost acquire response is resolved by querying/retrying the same request; never issue a new request ID blindly, because the first may own the lock.

Leader loss elects a quorum member and fences the old term. Minority partitions cannot grant or renew. Client pause is handled by expiry plus protected-resource fencing. Gateway loss is harmless. Timer loss is rebuilt. Session service outage pauses new/renew operations if liveness cannot be established. Disk corruption triggers replica replacement and log checksum verification. Clock uncertainty extends no ownership; it delays expiry/acquire conservatively.

Reconciliation scans expired records not cleaned, owners with expired sessions, waiters past deadline, idempotency outcomes missing final replies, fencing monotonicity, and routing/shard epoch mismatch. Snapshot restore validates maximum token high-watermarks against an external durable backup/control record. Manual force-release increments generation/token and is audited; it does not make the old process stop, so fencing remains mandatory.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Authenticate workloads with mutual TLS, authorize namespace/name prefixes, encrypt state, sign routing metadata, audit ownership and force operations, and avoid sensitive data in lock names. Prevent namespace enumeration, lock squatting, massive TTLs, waiter floods, renew abuse, watch amplification, and compromised clients releasing others' leases. Bound TTL, name length, locks/session, waiters/lock, and operations/tenant.

Measure acquire/renew/release latency, success/failure reason, contention, queue wait, hold duration, lease remaining at renew, expiration and late-renew rates, stale-owner rejection at integrated resources, fencing-token gaps/regressions, session fanout, timer lag, watch resets, leader elections, quorum availability, shard/hot-key skew, force releases, and client-library versions. Alert before renew p99 approaches the safety margin.

Property-test exclusivity, monotonic fencing, request idempotency, generation checks, expiry/renew races, cancellation/transfer ordering, and reentrancy counts. Model-check consensus-level lock transitions and multi-lock ordering. Use fake monotonic clocks for boundaries. Load-test one hot lock, millions of cold locks, renewal storms, and waiter disconnects. Chaos-test client pauses, packet delay, leader partition, clock uncertainty, timer loss, shard migration, and restore. Integration tests prove protected databases reject stale tokens.

docs.title: Important tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Database conditional rows may be sufficient at modest scale and inherit database operations; a dedicated service is justified by many languages, leases, watches, and isolation. Lease-only designs improve liveness but do not stop paused owners; fencing is non-negotiable for destructive work. Short TTL detects failure quickly but increases renew load and false expiry. FIFO is fair but can reduce throughput. Multi-region locks increase latency and partition unavailability; scope coordination regionally whenever possible.

flowchart TD
 C[Authenticated idempotent acquire] --> R[Name-sharded consensus leader]
 R --> L[Generation-bound expiring lease]
 L --> F[Monotonic fencing token]
 F --> X[Protected resource token check]
 R --> Q[Bounded revision-ordered wait queue]
 T[Server-time verified expiry] --> R
 S[Session generation and renewal reserve] --> R
 R --> W[Advisory watch and audit]

The final architecture hashes names to zonal consensus groups. Leaders commit generation-bound leases and durable monotonic fencing tokens, verify renew/release exactly, and transfer bounded queues in revision order. Server-timed expiry is revalidated before commit. Safe client libraries cancel work on uncertainty and pass tokens to protected resources. Sessions, watches, control routing, and audit support the core without weakening it.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. Why is an expiring lease insufficient after a client process pauses?
  2. What should a client do after losing an acquire response?
  3. How do renew and expiry races resolve safely?
  4. Can independent regional lock clusters implement one global lock?
  5. How are fencing tokens preserved during shard migration or restore?
  6. What should happen when a FIFO waiter disconnects as ownership transfers?
  7. When is a work queue or optimistic transaction better than a lock?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should choose consensus per shard, model leases/generations, explain idempotent acquire/renew/release, server-time expiry, fencing tokens, client pause, wait queues, partitioning, and leader failure. They must not equate a lease with control of an external resource.

An L6 candidate should define clock and quorum assumptions, resource integration, migration/token continuity, restore proof, overload reserves, fairness semantics, session correlated risk, multi-lock boundaries, and regional scope. They should challenge whether locking is the right primitive and connect TTL/fairness choices to throughput and operational safety.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Hash each normalized lock name to a zonally replicated consensus group. A leader grants only through a quorum commit, binding owner session, random lease ID, lock generation, authoritative expiry, and a never-reused monotonically increasing fencing token. Protected systems atomically check tokens with mutations; an old token is rejected after the sink observes a newer token, not simply when a lease expires. Strong handoff installs the new token before reporting transfer complete. Renew and release compare exact session/lease/generation; timer callbacks re-read state before committing expiry. Idempotency request IDs resolve lost responses. Bounded revision-ordered wait queues transfer ownership atomically and watches are advisory only. Reserve capacity for renew/release, cap hot-lock queues, jitter client renewal, and prefer resource partitioning over contending on one key. Keep locks regional unless global consensus latency is justified. Observe renew margin, expiry races, stale-token rejection, contention, timer lag, quorum, and token monotonicity; test client pauses, migration, and restore explicitly.

docs.title: Primary source boundary
docs.text: Vendor (etcd 3.6, accessed 2026-09-08): API guarantees specifies KV atomicity, revision ordering, lease APIs, and the weaker watch contract. These are coordination-service guarantees, not a claim that etcd atomically commits a mutation in an external database. The sink integration and sizing numbers above are requirements of this proposed design, not published etcd benchmarks.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a shared rate-limiting platform for APIs running across many hosts and regions. Start with policy semantics and the safety invariant, estimate the request and key cardinality, define the check interface, and then separate policy management from enforcement. We will evolve a single Redis counter into local admission plus distributed quota accounting, examine hot keys and failure policy, and close with regional operation and rollout.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: A rate limiter protects dependencies, enforces customer plans, and allocates scarce capacity fairly. It answers whether an operation may proceed, usually in less than a millisecond inside a gateway or service. Limits may apply by tenant, user, API, IP, or combinations, with burst and sustained rates. Billing-grade metering is separate: this system makes fast admission decisions and emits auditable usage, but should not become a synchronous billing ledger.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Create, version, stage, and disable policies such as 100 requests/second with burst 200.
  • Evaluate hierarchical limits: global, tenant, route, and user. Denial by any applicable policy denies the request.
  • Return allow/deny, retry delay, remaining approximation, and policy version.
  • Support shadow evaluation and emergency overrides.
  • Produce usage and decision events for debugging and capacity planning.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 5 million checks/second globally, p99 enforcement overhead below 2 ms.
  • 99.99% limiter availability; bounded over-admission during failures.
  • Policy changes visible within 10 seconds, emergency revocation within 2 seconds.
  • Fair behavior under skew and explicit fail-open or fail-closed per route.

Out of scope are bot detection, authentication, and exact monthly invoicing.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. A decision evaluates one complete policy version, never a mixture of fields from two versions.
  2. Within the declared error budget, accepted cost for a quota does not exceed limit + burst + distributed_slack per window.
  3. Retries of a lease reservation with the same reservation token do not allocate twice within its retention horizon. Local checks are charged per invocation unless the SDK explicitly retains a bounded decision-token result.
  4. A policy scoped to tenant A cannot affect tenant B.
  5. Denial is conservative when any fail-closed dependency is unavailable; fail-open behavior is explicit policy, not an accidental timeout.

Rate limits are not naturally exactly consistent at global scale. Exact global admission is possible through a shared serialization authority, at the cost of coordination latency and unavailability when that authority cannot be reached. This local fast-path design instead exposes bounded slack.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 5 million checks/s peak, 25 million active keys in a minute, average key plus state 120 bytes, and three replicas. Active state is roughly 9 GB, including the three replicas once; allocator overhead, expiry indexes, and headroom motivate an illustrative 40 GB fleet for that key population. State explicitly whether each region holds the full population or a partition before multiplying this budget. At 250-byte decision events and 10% sampling, telemetry is 125 MB/s; all denials and policy changes are retained. A gateway making an 800 microsecond network call would consume 4,000 concurrent requests at peak, motivating in-process checks. Ten regions receiving cached policy snapshots need little control-plane bandwidth: 100,000 policies at 1 KB is 100 MB per full snapshot, while normal deltas are small.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
Policy(policy_id, scope_pattern, algorithm, rate, period_ms, burst,
       failure_mode, priority, version, status, effective_at)
PolicyBundle(bundle_version, checksum, generated_at, policies[])
Lease(lease_id, policy_id, bucket_id, owner, tokens, consumed,
      expires_at, fencing_token)
DecisionEvent(request_id, policy_id, version, key_hash, cost,
              outcome, reason, region, timestamp)

Policy definitions are canonical in a transactional database. Signed bundles in object storage and local agent memory are projections. Issued-grant identities, amounts, and expiry are durable until no grant can be spent; losing this accounting cannot justify recreating a full bucket. Local consumption can be volatile only if restart discards the old grant without recrediting it. Events are append-only. Sensitive raw identities are converted to keyed hashes before telemetry.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
Management API:

PUT /v1/policies/{id}  If-Match: 41
POST /v1/policies/{id}:stage
POST /v1/policies/{id}:activate
GET /v1/bundles/latest?region=eu-west

Hot-path library interface:

check(DecisionRequest {
  request_id, subject_attributes, route, cost, deadline
}) -> Decision { allowed, retry_after_ms, reason, policy_version }

The request ID is stable across safe retries. Batch checks are allowed only when all items share a deadline; partial outcomes are explicit.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Admin --> API[Policy API]
  API --> DB[(Policy DB)]
  DB --> Compiler[Bundle compiler]
  Compiler --> Blob[(Signed bundles)]
  Blob --> Agent[Host agent]
  Agent --> SDK[In-process limiter]
  Client --> Gateway
  Gateway --> SDK
  SDK --> LeaseSvc[Regional lease service]
  LeaseSvc --> Store[(Sharded token store)]
  SDK --> Events[Decision event stream]

The control plane validates and distributes immutable policy bundles. The data plane is the SDK, host agent, and regional lease service. A control-plane outage does not stop checks because agents retain the last valid bundle. The simplest deployment starts with direct atomic counters in a regional store; leases are introduced only when call volume or latency requires them.

docs.title: 9. Policy lifecycle
docs.text:
The API checks scope syntax, conflicting priorities, positive rates, and maximum burst. A compiler resolves inheritance into a deterministic ordered decision graph, signs it, and publishes a monotonically versioned bundle. Agents poll and subscribe to invalidations, verify signature and checksum, then atomically swap an immutable in-memory pointer. Activation records desired and observed rollout percentages. Canary hosts shadow the new bundle before enforcement; rollback means republishing the prior known-good content under a new monotonic version.

Emergency deny rules use a small high-priority channel with short TTL and stronger propagation SLO. Temporary traffic overrides may expire back to the normal bundle. Security revocations have a separate durable generation and freshness rule: a stale agent fails closed for affected operations, and neither rollback nor TTL expiry silently restores revoked access.

docs.title: 10. Admission algorithms
docs.text:
A token bucket models sustained rate plus burst. For elapsed time dt, refill min(capacity, tokens + rate * dt) and allow cost c only when at least c tokens remain. A single owner updates timestamp and balance atomically. A sliding-window log is exact but stores every request; a fixed window is cheap but allows twice the nominal rate at boundaries. A sliding-window counter interpolates adjacent windows and is useful where approximate smoothing suffices.

Use token buckets for traffic shaping, concurrency semaphores for simultaneous expensive work, and daily counters for coarse plan quotas. Policies name their semantics so operators do not mistake one for another. For hierarchical checks, this baseline may conservatively charge an earlier bucket when a later bucket denies; document that loss of utilization. Exact all-or-nothing charging needs co-located atomic reservation or a durable multi-bucket protocol, not an unsafe ad hoc refund.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant G as Gateway SDK
  participant A as Host agent
  participant L as Lease service
  participant S as Token shard
  G->>A: resolve policy bundle
  A-->>G: immutable policy graph
  G->>G: consume local lease token
  alt lease below threshold
    G->>L: replenish(policy,key,request_id)
    L->>S: atomic reserve N tokens
    S-->>L: reservation + fencing token
    L-->>G: token lease
  end
  G-->>G: allow or deny

docs.title: 11. Distributed leases and bounded overshoot
docs.text:
Every host asking a central store per request creates latency and hot-key pressure. Instead, the regional owner reserves chunks from a canonical bucket and leases them to hosts.
