For a fixed-window escrow quota, grants debit the authoritative allowance before issue and cannot create overspend merely because a host crashes; a crash strands capacity. For a continuously refilled bucket of capacity B and rate r, delayed consumption of previously issued grants can shift up to H * L admissions into an interval of duration dt, giving accepted_cost <= r * dt + B + H * L, assuming at most H holders each have at most L total outstanding tokens, grants cannot be duplicated, and clients enforce expiry. Add emergency budgets separately. Repeated unbounded fail-open replenishment or lost grant accounting invalidates this bound. Choose small grants near exhaustion; short expiry bounds stale consumption, but a new allocator epoch alone cannot revoke tokens already held by an isolated SDK.

RFC 2697 section 3 specifies token refill and consumption for a single-rate traffic marker (accessed 2026-09-08). It supports the local token model, not this proposed distributed lease bound; the latter follows from the explicitly bounded outstanding grants.

The SDK replenishes asynchronously below a threshold without exceeding its total outstanding-token cap. If its lease empties, it may synchronously request a small lease until the deadline. Strict policies deny on timeout; availability-oriented policies use a bounded, nonrenewable emergency budget and mark the event degraded. Unreported tokens are treated as consumed, not returned on expiry. Only verified unspent capacity may be reclaimed after the old holder is fenced from consumption; otherwise normal rate refill or the next quota window restores capacity.

docs.title: 12. Hot keys, partitioning, and scaling
docs.text:
Hash (policy_id, normalized_subject) to virtual shards. Replicate each shard across zones, with one writer at a time. Ordinary tenants distribute naturally; a global policy is a hot key. Split global capacity into per-shard or per-region sub-budgets and periodically rebalance based on demand. Heavy tenants receive dedicated shards, and admission queues cap work before the storage fleet.

Consistent hashing minimizes movement, but rebalancing uses epochs: the old owner stops granting leases, the coordinator advances a fencing token, and the new owner starts from durable bucket state. Do not let both allocators mint grants from the same restored balance. Existing bounded grants may remain spendable within declared slack, but new grant ownership transfers only after fencing the old allocator and carrying its final bucket and issued-grant prefix.

docs.title: 13. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Policy state is strongly consistent at publication and eventually propagated. A request uses the bundle version captured at check start. Regional token mutation is linearizable per bucket through a leader or atomic script. Cross-region totals are intentionally escrowed: each region owns a budget and cannot spend another region's allocation without transfer.

Lease reservation deduplicates request_id for a short horizon. Keeping every request ID is too expensive, so direct per-request deduplication is limited to synchronous reservations; local lease consumption relies on the caller invoking check once. Downstream services must still be idempotent because an allow decision does not guarantee one execution.

docs.title: 14. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Policy database unavailable: reads and checks continue from bundles; writes stop.
  • Corrupt bundle: signature/checksum validation rejects it and retains last-known-good.
  • Agent unavailable: SDK uses its embedded bundle until max staleness, then follows route failure mode.
  • Token shard leader loss: quorum elects a leader; no grants occur without fencing.
  • Lease service overload: shed shadow checks first, shrink expensive cardinality, and deny or consume emergency budget.
  • Clock skew: token timestamps come from shard owners; monotonic process clocks measure local lease expiry.
  • Event pipeline outage: decisions continue through a bounded buffer; audit-required policies can switch to fail-closed.

Recovery reconciles granted lease records and advances shard epochs. Operators can freeze policy rollout, drain a bad shard, or lower local lease sizes to tighten overshoot.

docs.title: 15. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Serve checks locally. For a global quota Q, an allocator escrows regional budgets summing to at most Q; regions spend independently. Every few seconds they report utilization, and the allocator moves unspent future capacity. A partition preserves safety but may reduce utilization. If product preference is availability, permit a documented regional emergency allowance and include it in global slack.

Policies replicate globally through signed bundles. The home region accepts writes; failover requires a database promotion and a new publisher epoch. Active-active policy editing is unnecessary complexity unless administrators require it.

flowchart TB
  Allocator[Global budget allocator]
  Allocator -->|escrow 45%| R1[Region A token shards]
  Allocator -->|escrow 45%| R2[Region B token shards]
  Allocator -->|reserve 10%| R3[Failover reserve]
  R1 --> G1[Gateways A]
  R2 --> G2[Gateways B]
  R1 -. utilization .-> Allocator
  R2 -. utilization .-> Allocator

docs.title: 16. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Management APIs require SSO, RBAC, tenant-scoped authorization, approval for global policies, and immutable audit records. Bundles are signed and agents use mTLS. Keys are normalized with explicit schema to prevent attackers bypassing limits through Unicode, path variants, or header casing. Hash secrets rotate with overlap. Cardinality guards reject unbounded user-controlled dimensions, while separate IP and credential limits resist distributed and account-based abuse.

docs.title: 17. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure decision latency, allow/deny counts, degraded decisions, bundle age, lease utilization, overshoot estimate, hot shards, and replenishment errors. Avoid high-cardinality raw keys; provide sampled hashed exemplars and a privileged explain endpoint. Alert on policy propagation lag and unexpected denial-rate changes, not merely CPU.

Unit tests cover boundary refill and precedence. Property tests assert tokens never become negative and accepted cost stays within modeled slack. Deterministic simulations vary clocks, retries, host crashes, and shard reassignment. Load tests use Zipfian subjects, not uniform keys. Canary and shadow comparisons quantify changed decisions before activation. Regional game days isolate the allocator and kill shard leaders.

docs.title: 18. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: Direct central checks maximize per-key precision but add latency and create hot keys. Local-only buckets maximize availability but cannot enforce shared quotas. Leases trade bounded over-admission for low latency and scale. Fixed windows are operationally simple but have boundary bursts; token buckets express burst explicitly. Global synchronous consensus gives tighter quotas but makes every request depend on inter-region latency. Escrowed regional budgets preserve safety and locality at the cost of temporary unused capacity.

docs.title: 19. Final design
docs.text: Use a transactional policy control plane that compiles signed immutable bundles. Agents distribute bundles to in-process SDKs. SDKs evaluate hierarchy locally and consume adaptive token leases reserved atomically from zone-replicated regional shards. Hash normal keys, isolate heavy tenants, and split global hot limits into escrow budgets. Events flow asynchronously to audit and analytics. Policy-specific failure modes, fencing, last-known-good bundles, bounded queues, and emergency budgets make degradation intentional.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions and L5/L6 expectations
docs.text:
Questions: How is maximum overshoot calculated? What happens when 1,000 hosts hit one tenant? How do policy rollback and stale agents interact? Why not use a sliding log? How would you support request cost greater than one? Can a global quota remain available through a partition without exceeding its bound?

An L5 candidate should clarify algorithms, estimate QPS and state, define atomic updates, shard keys, handle retries and store failure, and discuss hot tenants. An L6 candidate should make slack a product contract, separate planes, derive lease sizing, design escrow and fencing, stage policy migrations, set overload priorities, and connect precision choices to dependency capacity and revenue risk.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: The limiter performs millions of checks on the local request path. Canonical policies live in a strongly consistent database and compile into signed versioned bundles, so a control-plane failure does not stop enforcement. Gateways evaluate applicable policies in process. For shared quotas, they consume short adaptive leases atomically reserved from sharded regional token buckets. Lease size controls the explicit overshoot bound. Hot global limits are split into regional escrow budgets rather than requiring cross-region consensus. Immutable bundle swaps prevent mixed versions; request IDs deduplicate reservations; fencing protects shard movement. Failure behavior is per policy, with strict routes denying and availability-oriented routes using bounded emergency capacity. Telemetry, shadow rollout, Zipfian load tests, and game days verify decisions and propagation. The key tradeoff is precision versus latency and availability, stated quantitatively rather than hidden.

docs.title: Design a Global DNS Service
docs.text: This case study owns the service design. Use DNS and Service Discovery and BGP, Anycast, and Global Routing for protocol mechanics and path evidence.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design authoritative DNS hosting, not the public recursive resolver ecosystem. Clarify record types, update frequency, DNSSEC, routing policy, propagation, and availability. Start with a strongly consistent source of truth that compiles zones into immutable snapshots served by anycast nameservers. Then add delegation, negative answers, health-based routing, DNSSEC signing, overload controls, regional isolation, and safe rollouts. The hard problem is preserving protocol-correct answers globally while the control plane or network is impaired.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
Tenants create zones and records and delegate their domains to our nameservers. Resolvers issue UDP or TCP queries; authoritative servers answer from local memory without contacting the control plane. Operators support weighted, latency, geolocation, and failover policies. DNS maps names to records; it is not a strongly consistent service registry. Recursive caches, TTL floors, and client pinning mean an accepted update cannot instantly redirect every user.

Targets are 99.999% data-plane availability, 20 ms p99 server processing, ordinary change publication within 30 seconds, and DNSSEC-valid authoritative answers and denial proofs for signed zones. Referral and glue handling follows the protocol; not every record in a response is signed. Control-plane availability may be 99.99% because existing zones remain servable during its outage.

docs.title: 3. Functional and non-functional requirements
docs.text:
Functional: create/delete zones; CRUD A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, CAA, SRV, and alias records; import/export; routing policies; health checks; DNSSEC; audit history; idempotent changes; paginated listing.

Non-functional: globally low latency; tolerate region loss and DDoS; protocol correctness over UDP/TCP; bounded propagation; durable zone history; tenant isolation; safe key rotation; predictable cost. Zone transfer and query logging may be optional. We do not build recursive resolution or domain registration.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A published zone snapshot is internally complete and advances its 32-bit SOA serial under DNS serial-number arithmetic, including wraparound.
  • One RRset exists per (zone, owner, type); a CNAME owner cannot also hold ordinary data RRsets, with DNSSEC metadata exceptions handled by the protocol validator.
  • Delegation, apex SOA/NS, wildcard, and negative responses obey DNS semantics.
  • An edge serves one validated snapshot, never a mixture of generations.
  • DNSSEC signatures and denial-of-existence proofs correspond to the served generation and remain valid beyond propagation margin.
  • A tenant can mutate only zones it owns; every accepted mutation is durably audited.
  • Health automation changes only synthesized policy output, never silently destroys canonical records.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 20 million zones, 2 billion record sets, 10 million steady queries/s and 100 million/s under attack. At 300 bytes per normalized record, canonical data is about 600 GB before indexes and versions; replicated in-memory serving snapshots are larger. Writes average only thousands/s, but a major customer can update a million records at once. A 1,200-byte average response at 10 million QPS is 96 Gbit/s before attack traffic. Popularity is extremely skewed, so CPU, packet rate, and network capacity rather than storage dominate.

docs.title: 6. Core entities and data model
docs.text:
Zone(zone_id, tenant_id, name, state, serial, dnssec_policy, version)
RecordSet(zone_id, owner, type, ttl, values[], routing_policy, version)
ChangeSet(change_id, zone_id, base_version, operations[], state, idempotency_key)
Snapshot(zone_id, serial, object_uri, checksum, compiled_at)
HealthCheck(check_id, target, regions, thresholds, status, generation)
SigningKey(zone_id, key_id, role, state, activate_at, retire_at)

Canonical rows retain names in normalized lowercase wire form while preserving presentation separately. Large lists use opaque cursors binding tenant, filter, last key, and snapshot version. Deletion writes a tombstone and retains history for recovery and audit.

docs.title: 7. API and DNS interface
docs.text:
POST /v1/zones
POST /v1/zones/{zone}/changes  Idempotency-Key: ...
GET  /v1/zones/{zone}/records?name=&type=&cursor=
GET  /v1/changes/{change}
POST /v1/zones/{zone}/rollback
DNS  QNAME/QTYPE over UDP, TCP, and optionally DoT

A change is conditionally applied against base_version, returns PENDING, and later becomes PUBLISHED with serial and propagation evidence. Retrying the key returns the same outcome. The DNS response includes AA, RCODE, answer/authority/additional sections, EDNS size handling, and truncation for TCP retry.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Customers] --> API[Control API]
 API --> Z[(Consensus zone store)]
 Z --> V[Validator and compiler]
 V --> S[(Immutable snapshot store)]
 S --> F[Global distribution]
 F --> E[Anycast edge cells]
 R[Recursive resolvers] --> E
 H[Health probes] --> P[Policy evaluator]
 P --> V
 K[Offline/HSM signer] --> V

The control plane authenticates, validates, versions, compiles, and distributes. The data plane is a fleet of independent anycast cells serving local immutable snapshots. Query processing has no synchronous dependency on the database, health system, or signer.

docs.title: 9. Zone publication
docs.text:
The API validates syntax, quotas, CNAME exclusivity, delegation, and optimistic version. One transaction appends the change and advances canonical version. A compiler reads that version, constructs a radix-tree snapshot, synthesizes policy records, validates the entire zone, signs it if needed, and stores content-addressed bytes.

Distribution announces a manifest (zone, serial, hash, minimum-reader-version). Each edge downloads, verifies, memory-maps, and atomically swaps its pointer. It acknowledges the serial; publication status aggregates acknowledgements by geography. Deltas reduce bandwidth, but periodic complete snapshots and hashes repair missed events. An incompatible binary rejects the manifest and continues serving the previous valid generation.

Keep an internal monotonic publication generation separate from the wire SOA serial. Under RFC 1982 sections 3 and 7, 0 follows 4294967295, and a distance of exactly 2^31 has undefined ordering (accessed 2026-09-08). Compare by the RFC rule, not unsigned >; reject ambiguous jumps and resynchronize stale secondaries explicitly. Rollback republishes old record content with a new generation and advancing serial, not the old serial. Test wraparound, half-range ambiguity, and a secondary offline across multiple updates.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant U as Tenant
 participant A as API
 participant D as Zone store
 participant C as Compiler/signer
 participant E as Edge cell
 U->>A: change set, base version, key
 A->>D: conditional commit
 D-->>A: version
 D->>C: ordered change
 C->>C: validate, compile, sign
 C->>E: manifest and snapshot
 E->>E: verify then atomic swap
 E-->>C: serial acknowledged
 A-->>U: published coverage

docs.title: 10. Authoritative query algorithm
docs.text:
An edge parses with allocation and label limits, finds the longest matching hosted zone, then performs exact lookup. If absent, it checks empty non-terminals and closest-encloser wildcard rules. It follows in-zone aliases only where explicitly supported; a CNAME normally returns the target name for recursion elsewhere. Delegation returns referral NS plus in-bailiwick glue. Nonexistent names produce NXDOMAIN; existing names lacking the type produce NODATA. Both include SOA for negative caching.

UDP responses honor advertised EDNS size and amplification limits. Oversized responses set TC, causing TCP retry. Rate limiting occurs before expensive DNSSEC work. Responses are cached inside a cell by (snapshot hash, qname, qtype, EDNS/DNSSEC attributes), so publication naturally invalidates them.

docs.title: 11. Routing and health policies
docs.text:
Weighted routing uses deterministic hashing of resolver/client subnet and policy generation, avoiding random answer churn while approximating weights. Latency routing selects among measured regional buckets, and geolocation uses a versioned IP map. EDNS Client Subnet improves locality but leaks location and fragments caches; support it only with truncated prefixes and tenant opt-in.

Health probes run from several failure domains. A target changes state only after quorum-like thresholds and hysteresis. Policy evaluation emits a new synthesized snapshot. During probe-system failure, freeze the last state rather than declare everything unhealthy. A failover answer has a TTL compatible with recovery goals, but resolvers may retain old answers, so applications still need retries and multi-address responses.

For DNSSEC zones, per-query weighted/geographic answers must select from complete pre-signed RRset variants, or use an explicitly secured online signer. Arbitrarily deleting addresses from a signed RRset invalidates its signature. Include routing bucket and applicable client-subnet scope in the response-cache key so geographic policy cannot leak a cached variant to another routing context.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: DNSSEC lifecycle
docs.text:
Use a key-signing key protected by an HSM and shorter-lived zone-signing keys. Sign offline from serving. Pre-publish a new public key, wait at least cache/delegation safety windows, activate it, overlap signatures, then retire the old key. DS changes at the parent require a tracked external workflow. NSEC3 can reduce easy zone walking but costs CPU and still permits dictionary attacks; narrow proofs or NSEC may be operationally simpler.

Signatures are generated with inception skew allowance and enough expiry margin to survive signer outages. Edges alert on minimum remaining validity and reject expired snapshots. Emergency behavior is to serve the last valid signed generation. If none remains valid, return an explicit failure such as SERVFAIL for affected answers; an expired signature cannot become safe by calling its snapshot last-known-good. Never silently downgrade to unsigned.

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: delegation and negative caching
docs.text: Authority changes cross organizational boundaries. Creating a hosted zone does not make it reachable until the registrar publishes parent NS and, where needed, glue and DS. The product exposes checks for lame delegation and DNSSEC chain mismatch. Removing a name may remain negatively or positively cached according to the prior TTL. Safe migration lowers TTL before changing authority, waits the old TTL, dual-serves identical data, changes delegation, then retains old service through the parent TTL.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning, hot zones, and overload
docs.text:
Shard canonical state by zone ID; one zone change is serialized, while bulk import compiles outside the transaction and conditionally installs one version. Distribution partitions by snapshot hash and uses hierarchical relays. Edge storage partitions zones across worker processes, but every site can answer every zone.

Anycast spreads normal traffic but route changes can move floods abruptly. Cells use packet-level filters, source and response-rate limiting, cookies where supported, minimal-any responses, per-zone budgets, and upstream scrubbing. Reserve capacity for TCP and legitimate cache misses. Under CPU pressure, drop malformed and abusive classes first, shed expensive ANY/DNSSEC responses next, and preserve ordinary A/AAAA. Never query the control plane on a miss.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text: Canonical zone writes are linearizable per zone. Edge views are eventually consistent with measured serial lag. Atomic snapshot swap guarantees local consistency. Idempotency keys and base versions make retries safe; events are at least once, and compiler/distributor deduplicate by (zone, version, hash). DNS itself provides no read-your-writes guarantee through recursive caches. The API reports control publication, not universal cache expiry.

docs.title: 16. Reliability, recovery, and multi-region
docs.text:
Control shards replicate across zones and store snapshots in multi-region object storage. A region losing quorum rejects mutation; other regions remain writable only for zones they authoritatively own. Ownership transfer uses a fenced epoch. Edges continue serving their last valid snapshot during control outages.

Bad publication is contained by canary cells, automated protocol validation, and serial rollback to a newly compiled higher serial. Edge crash restarts from local durable snapshot; distributor loss triggers manifest reconciliation. Region or provider loss is handled by anycast withdrawal after both internal and external probes. Because BGP convergence is imperfect, sites fail independently rather than depending on a global primary.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use strong tenant identity, scoped roles, MFA for destructive/DNSSEC actions, mTLS internally, HSM-backed keys, encrypted snapshots, immutable audits, approval policy for critical zones, and domain-ownership proof. Defend against zone takeover, dangling delegation, unauthorized transfer, cache-amplification abuse, parser exploits, oversized TXT data, cross-tenant leakage, and compromised distribution nodes. Signed manifests and least-privilege edge credentials prevent an edge from authoring data.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure QPS/RCODE/type, processing and network latency, UDP truncation/TCP fallback, packet drops, amplification ratio, anycast catchment, per-zone skew, snapshot age, serial lag, rejected manifests, DNSSEC expiry, probe disagreement, policy flaps, and delegation health. Trace a change ID through canonical version, compiled hash, and edge acknowledgements without logging sensitive query names by default.

Use golden protocol vectors, fuzz parsers and compression pointers, property-test wildcard/delegation logic, and differential-test against mature servers. Load-test packet rate, hot names, TCP floods, and mass publication. Chaos-test signer outage, expired key, bad snapshot, lost region, BGP withdrawal, clock skew, and distributor partition. Synthetic probes resolve signed, wildcard, delegated, failover, NXDOMAIN, and TCP cases from external networks.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: Mutable edge records publish faster but risk partial generations; immutable snapshots win correctness. Very low TTL improves failover only while increasing query cost and cannot defeat resolver floors. Anycast lowers latency and supports failover but complicates debugging and traffic engineering. Dynamic request-time policy is current but adds dependencies; precompiled policy wins predictable serving. Multi-primary global zone writes appear available but conflict ordering is difficult; per-zone authority with explicit transfer is clearer.

docs.title: 20. Final architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
 W[Versioned zone writes] --> C[Whole-zone compiler]
 H[HSM DNSSEC signing] --> C
 P[Hysteretic health policy] --> C
 C --> O[Content-addressed snapshots]
 O --> D[Regional relays]
 D --> A[Anycast isolated cells]
 A --> Q[UDP/TCP authoritative answers]
 M[Serial and validity reconciliation] --> A

The final design uses linearizable per-zone authoring, full-zone validation, immutable signed generations, asynchronous measured distribution, and self-contained anycast cells. It sacrifices instant global visibility to ensure every answer is generated from one valid generation.

docs.title: 21. Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text: How do wildcard and delegation lookup interact? What does successful publication promise? How do you rotate DNSSEC keys through a parent? How do you prevent health-check flapping? What happens when one zone is 40% of QPS? How do you migrate providers without an outage? Why can a 5-second TTL still fail over slowly?

docs.title: 22. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate scopes authoritative DNS, estimates packet load, explains snapshots, TTLs, DNS semantics, DNSSEC, anycast, overload, and edge staleness. An L6 candidate separates control/data failure budgets, identifies delegation and signature-expiry invariants, quantifies publication and attack behavior, designs key/provider migration, and connects privacy, cost, and operations to policy.

docs.title: 23. Five-minute summary
docs.text: Five-minute summary: store canonical zones in per-zone ordered state; validate and compile complete immutable snapshots; sign away from the query path; distribute and atomically swap them into independent anycast cells. Answer protocol-correctly from memory over UDP/TCP. Treat health routing as versioned synthesis, caches as unavoidable, and propagation as measurable rather than instantaneous. Protect packet capacity under attack, serve last-known-good during control failure, and continuously reconcile serials, signatures, delegation, and external reachability.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a feature-management service that lets teams change behavior without redeploying code. We begin with evaluation semantics and blast-radius invariants, estimate policy distribution and evaluation volume, define flag models and APIs, then separate a strongly governed control plane from an in-process data plane. Deep dives cover deterministic targeting, snapshots and streaming, dependencies, stale state, experimentation, and multi-region recovery.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: A flag maps an evaluation context to a typed variation. Teams use flags for release ramps, kill switches, entitlements, configuration, and experiments. Most evaluations must happen in-process to avoid adding a remote dependency to every request. The platform distributes signed, versioned configuration to SDKs and records exposure events asynchronously. It is not an authorization system: security decisions require a dedicated policy engine and server-side trusted attributes.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Create boolean, string, number, and JSON flags with environments and owners.
  • Target by attributes, segments, prerequisites, percentage rollout, and schedules.
  • Stage, approve, activate, rollback, archive, and audit changes.
  • Evaluate through server/client SDKs and a remote API for thin clients.
  • Emit exposure events and support experiment assignment without metric analysis itself.

Non-functional requirements:

  • One million flags across tenants, 20 million evaluations/s, and 10 million connected SDK instances.
  • In-process p99 below 100 microseconds; remote p99 below 20 ms.
  • Normal changes propagate in 10 seconds; kill switches in 2 seconds.
  • Evaluations continue during control-plane and network outages.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. One evaluation uses one immutable environment snapshot and returns a variation valid for that snapshot.
  2. Percentage assignment is deterministic for the same flag salt, subject key, and rollout definition.
  3. Tenant and environment boundaries are enforced before configuration reaches an SDK.
  4. A stale SDK follows the declared fallback policy; staleness never silently becomes authorization.
  5. Audit history is append-only and links every activation to actor, prior version, and review state.
  6. Exposure events do not alter evaluation and are deduplicable; analytics loss cannot block requests.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Twenty million evaluations/s cannot afford network calls, confirming local SDK evaluation. Suppose one million flag definitions average 2 KB: 2 GB total, but each environment subscribes only to relevant projects, perhaps 5 MB per server snapshot. Ten million clients receiving 5 MB full snapshots would imply 50 TB per fleet refresh, not 50 PB; repeated refreshes and reconnect storms still justify deltas and CDN distribution. Mobile/web clients receive only public, client-enabled flags; server agents use deltas. If 1% of evaluations emit 300-byte sampled exposures, telemetry is 60 MB/s. A kill-switch update to one million subscribed instances in two seconds needs hierarchical fan-out rather than one control server holding every connection.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
Flag(flag_id, project_id, key, type, owner, purpose, archived)
FlagVersion(flag_id, version, variations[], rules[], prerequisites[],
            fallthrough, off_variation, salt, created_by, checksum)
Environment(env_id, tenant_id, name, active_bundle_version, policy)
Segment(segment_id, version, included_keys, excluded_keys, rules[])
Bundle(bundle_version, env_id, flags[], segments[], checksum, signature)
Change(change_id, env_id, base_version, patch, state, approvals[], audit)
Exposure(event_id, flag_id, flag_version, subject_hash, variation, reason)

The transactional control database is canonical. Immutable bundles in object storage/CDN and SDK memory are projections. Audit events are durable and separate from best-effort exposure telemetry.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/projects/{p}/flags
PUT  /v1/flags/{key}/versions/{v}       If-Match: etag
POST /v1/changes/{id}:approve
POST /v1/changes/{id}:activate
POST /v1/environments/{id}:rollback
GET  /v1/sdk/bundles/latest             If-None-Match: checksum
GET  /v1/sdk/stream                     Last-Event-ID: bundle-version
POST /v1/evaluate

SDK call:

evaluate(flagKey, expectedType, subjectContext, callerDefault)
  -> Detail{value, variationId, reason, flagVersion, bundleVersion, stale}

Unknown flags, type mismatches, missing attributes, cycles, and stale snapshots return typed reasons plus the caller-supplied default.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Admin --> API[Flag management API]
  API --> DB[(Control DB)]
  DB --> Compiler[Validator/compiler]
  Compiler --> Blob[(Signed bundles)]
  Compiler --> Fanout[Regional stream fan-out]
  Blob --> CDN
  Fanout --> Relay[Host relay/agent]
  Relay --> SDK[In-process SDK]
  CDN --> ClientSDK[Client SDK]
  App --> SDK
  SDK --> Events[Exposure pipeline]

The control plane owns authoring, review, compilation, and publication. The data plane is bundle distribution and deterministic SDK evaluation. Host relays multiplex connections for server processes. SDKs retain a validated last-known-good bundle, so control-plane unavailability does not enter application hot paths.

docs.title: 9. Authoring and publication
docs.text:
An edit creates a change against a base environment version. Validation checks types, missing variations, segment references, prerequisite cycles, unreachable rules, client-visible sensitive attributes, and maximum evaluation complexity. A simulator runs saved contexts and reports changed decisions. High-risk environments require a second approver and scheduled activation window.

The compiler resolves references, produces deterministic ordering, signs a complete immutable bundle, stores it, then atomically advances the environment's active pointer. Distribution begins only after durable publication. Rollback activates a prior bundle's content as a new monotonic version, preserving audit chronology. Flag changes and code deploys should not be coupled transactionally; teams use defaults and staged rollout.

docs.title: 10. Deterministic evaluation algorithm
docs.text:
Given a captured snapshot: locate flag; verify type and on/off status; recursively evaluate prerequisites with a depth and visited-set bound; evaluate rules in order; then use fallthrough. A rule checks clauses against trusted context and segment membership. First matching rule wins. A percentage rollout hashes a canonical, length-prefixed encoding of (flag_salt, stable_subject_key, optional_group_key) into a fixed bucket, then selects the cumulative weight range. Specify UTF-8 normalization and field presence so concatenation cannot confuse distinct tuples.

Never use language-native hash functions because versions may differ. Specify an algorithm such as SHA-256 first 64 bits modulo 100,000 and publish cross-language golden vectors. Changing variation weights preserves assignments in unchanged bucket ranges; changing salt intentionally reshuffles. Mutually exclusive experiments first hash into a shared allocation group with disjoint enrollment ranges, then select a variation inside the assigned experiment. Sharing a salt alone does not prevent two experiments from enrolling the same subject.

flowchart TD
  Start[Capture bundle pointer] --> Exists{Flag exists and type matches?}
  Exists -->|no| Default[Caller default + reason]
  Exists -->|yes| Enabled{Flag enabled?}
  Enabled -->|no| Off[Off/fallback variation]
  Enabled -->|yes| Pre[Evaluate prerequisites]
  Pre -->|failed| Off[Off/fallback variation]
  Pre -->|passed| Rules[Rules in order]
  Rules --> Match{Rule matched?}
  Match -->|yes| Split[Variation or deterministic bucket]
  Match -->|no| Fall[Fallthrough]
  Split --> Detail[Value + version + reason]
  Fall --> Detail
  Off --> Detail
  Default --> Detail

docs.title: 11. Distribution and propagation
docs.text:
Regional fan-out nodes consume active-pointer events and notify relays through long-lived streams. Notifications can carry compact deltas, but each delta names base and target checksum. If a relay missed a version or checksum fails, it downloads the full signed bundle from object storage/CDN. SDKs parse and validate off-thread, then atomically swap one immutable pointer. Existing evaluations finish against the old snapshot.

Connections use jittered reconnect and exponential backoff. Hierarchical relays reduce connection count and absorb bursts. Polling remains a repair path even when streaming works. The service measures publication-to-observation latency using relay acknowledgments and SDK heartbeat samples, not merely server publish time.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant U as Operator
  participant C as Compiler
  participant O as Bundle store
  participant R as Regional relay
  participant S as SDK
  U->>C: activate approved change
  C->>O: store signed bundle V42
  C->>C: CAS active pointer to V42
  C-->>R: version notification
  R-->>S: delta V41 to V42
  S->>S: verify, compile, atomic swap
  S-->>R: observed V42

docs.title: 12. Segments, prerequisites, and complexity
docs.text:
Small static segments can compile into sorted hashed-key sets or Bloom filter plus exact set. Very large dynamic segments may be delivered as versioned snapshots to server SDKs; remote lookup on every evaluation violates availability and latency. If freshness demands remote membership, expose that weaker mode explicitly and cache with fail behavior. Sensitive segment membership never ships to untrusted browser SDKs.

Prerequisites form a directed acyclic graph checked at publish time. Evaluation memoizes flag results within one call and caps depth, clauses, regex complexity, and segment size. Cyclic or excessive bundles are rejected, not handled recursively in production.

docs.title: 13. Partitioning, scaling, and hot paths
docs.text:
Control data partitions by tenant/project; bundle compilation queues isolate tenants. The distribution plane partitions subscriptions by environment and relay. A global kill switch is a fan-out hot key, addressed by CDN caching, relay trees, and reserved emergency bandwidth. Client SDK snapshots use cache-control plus versioned URLs; never personalize a CDN bundle with server-only rules.

Evaluation allocates no objects on the common path where practical. Precompile clause accessors and regexes, canonicalize rules, and keep snapshots immutable. Exposure emission uses a bounded nonblocking buffer. If full, sample or drop according to purpose and increment a local loss metric; evaluation never waits.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Management writes are strongly consistent and use optimistic concurrency. Activation is linearizable at the environment pointer, while SDK visibility is eventual. Every evaluation reports its bundle and flag versions, making mixed fleet state diagnosable. There is no global instant at which all processes switch.

Activation requests carry idempotency keys. Bundle content is content-addressed, so repeat compilation is harmless. Stream events are at least once and SDK application is monotonic within a publisher epoch; resync validates the current authorized epoch/version and cannot silently accept a stale signed bundle as current. Exposure IDs derive from request/decision identity where available; analytics deduplicates but tolerates loss. Experiment assignment is deterministic rather than stored per request.

docs.title: 15. Failure modes and recovery
docs.text:
• Control database outage: evaluation and distribution of existing bundles continue; edits pause.
  • Compiler bug or corrupt bundle: signature/schema checks retain last-known-good; canary relays block broad rollout.
  • Stream outage: SDKs poll CDN with jitter and continue stale.
  • CDN outage: relays serve cached bundles; new instances use packaged bootstrap defaults if no cache exists.
  • SDK memory pressure: reject oversized bundle before swap and report health.
  • Exposure pipeline outage: bounded buffers drop analytics, never application traffic.
  • Operator misconfiguration: approvals, simulations, percentage ramps, automated guardrails, and one-click rollback limit blast radius.

Kill switches need a safe compiled default and regular drills. A stale-age policy may force a safety-critical flag to its off variation after a deadline, while ordinary release flags stay last-known-good.

docs.title: 16. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Run active regional distribution and remote evaluation, backed by globally replicated immutable bundles. Keep one home writer for each environment to avoid conflicting activation order; failover acquires a higher publisher epoch before accepting writes. Regions can distribute cached bundles throughout a control outage. CDN snapshots cover mobile clients globally.

Data residency applies to contexts and exposure events. Local SDK evaluation keeps attributes in-process. Exposure events hash stable keys with tenant-specific salts and remain regional unless approved. A region disconnected during activation keeps its prior bundle and reports stale; it does not synthesize a version.

flowchart TB
  Writer[Home control writer, epoch 8] --> Global[(Replicated bundle store)]
  Global --> RA[Region A relays]
  Global --> RB[Region B relays]
  RA --> SA[SDK fleet A]
  RB --> SB[SDK fleet B]
  Witness[Failover coordinator] -->|grant epoch 9| Standby[Standby writer]
  Standby --> Global

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Management uses SSO, RBAC, environment-scoped roles, mandatory approval for production, and immutable audits. SDK credentials are project/environment scoped and rotated. Server secrets and rules never enter client-visible bundles. Bundle signatures prevent tampering; TLS protects transport. Context values are minimized and redacted from diagnostics. Attribute names are schema-governed to prevent teams targeting protected characteristics without review. Rate limits and bundle-size limits stop accidental fan-out abuse.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track evaluation count and reason, default/error rate, SDK latency, snapshot age, version distribution, propagation percentiles, stream reconnects, full-resync rate, bundle size, compiler failures, exposure loss, and per-flag variation ratios. Avoid raw subject labels. An explain tool evaluates a supplied context against a specified historical bundle and returns clause decisions without changing state.

Golden vectors run in every SDK language for hashing, type coercion, semver, dates, and regex behavior. Property tests guarantee bucket stability and total variation weights. Differential tests compare SDKs against a reference interpreter. Publication tests crash between object upload and pointer activation. Scale tests fan out emergency changes and reconnect all clients with jitter. Game days block control plane and CDN, rotate signing keys, and rehearse kill switches.

docs.title: 19. Important tradeoffs
docs.text: Remote evaluation centralizes logic and fresh data but adds latency and a hard dependency. Local evaluation wins for availability but accepts propagation delay and SDK complexity. Deltas save bandwidth but need full-snapshot repair. Ordered first-match rules are understandable but make reordering behavioral. Large static segments consume memory; remote segments weaken availability. Last-known-good favors continuity, while stale-to-off favors safety; choose per flag purpose.

docs.title: 20. Final design, questions, and expectations
docs.text:
The final design stores governed, versioned flags in a transactional control plane, compiles signed immutable environment bundles, distributes them through regional relay trees and CDN, and evaluates against atomic in-memory snapshots. Deterministic hashing provides stable rollout. Polling repairs streams, defaults handle bootstrap, and exposure telemetry remains asynchronous.

Interview questions: How do ten million SDKs receive a kill switch? How is percentage stability tested across languages? What happens if a prerequisite changes mid-evaluation? Why are flags not authorization? How does rollback interact with monotonic versions? How do large segments work?

An L5 candidate should define rules, local evaluation, versioned distribution, deterministic rollout, fallbacks, and auditing. An L6 candidate should separate planes, quantify propagation, design governance and blast-radius controls, specify stale semantics by purpose, handle cross-language compatibility, residency, migrations, and fleet-wide emergency operations.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: The system keeps feature evaluation off the network hot path. A strongly consistent control plane validates changes, checks dependency cycles and complexity, requires approvals, compiles signed immutable bundles, and atomically advances an environment pointer. Regional relay trees stream checksum-based deltas; polling and CDN full snapshots repair gaps. SDKs validate off-thread and atomically swap one bundle pointer, so an evaluation never mixes versions. Ordered rules and a specified hash produce deterministic targeting and percentage rollout across languages. Last-known-good bundles preserve availability, while safety flags may expire to off. Exposure telemetry uses bounded asynchronous buffers and cannot block requests. Home-region publication establishes total order; regional distribution continues from cached bundles. Golden vectors, simulations, canaries, propagation metrics, and kill-switch drills control the operational risk.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a scheduler for one-time, recurring, and dependency-driven background jobs. We clarify whether the promise is durable intent or exactly-once effects, quantify jobs and executions, define state machines and leases, and separate scheduling control from worker execution. Deep dives cover time indexing, claiming, retries, DAGs, fairness, and regional failover.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Clients submit work to run now or later. The scheduler durably records intent, determines when an execution becomes eligible, assigns it to a compatible worker, and tracks completion. Worker code may run for milliseconds or hours. For eligible, uncancelled work within its retry/deadline policy and stated availability assumptions, the platform guarantees at-least-once attempt delivery after acceptance; applications use idempotency or transactional effect patterns. It does not claim exactly-once side effects across arbitrary external systems.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Create, update, pause, resume, cancel, and inspect one-time or cron schedules.
  • Execute jobs with priorities, deadlines, resource requirements, retries, and timeouts.
  • Support DAG dependencies and tenant concurrency/rate quotas.
  • Expose execution history, logs references, manual retry, and dead-letter handling.
  • Allow graceful worker draining and version-targeted jobs.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 100 million schedules, 50,000 starts/s peak, and one million concurrent executions.
  • Eligible jobs start within 5 seconds at p99 when capacity exists.
  • Accepted jobs survive process, zone, and storage-node failures.
  • Fairness prevents one tenant from monopolizing workers.

Interactive workflows, arbitrary container building, and log storage are separate systems.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. Every accepted execution intent is durable before success is returned.
  2. One execution attempt has at most one valid lease owner at an epoch, although a timed-out attempt may overlap its retry.
  3. A terminal execution never returns to runnable without an explicit new execution ID.
  4. A DAG node becomes eligible only after its declared dependency predicate is durably satisfied.
  5. Cancellation prevents future assignment after its commit; an already running external effect may require cooperative cancellation.
  6. Retry count, backoff, and deadline are evaluated from canonical state.

At-least-once delivery is explicit. Exactly-once business effects require an idempotency key or a database transaction owned by the application.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: At 50,000 starts/s with three scheduler writes per start, storage sees 150,000 writes/s before completion, retry, and heartbeat work. One million concurrent executions heartbeating every 15 seconds add 67,000 updates/s if each renews independently. Batch or session-scope renewals; a volatile heartbeat cache may assist liveness, but accepted lease epochs and terminal-state checks require durable authority. If 20 million executions/day retain 2 KB metadata for 30 days, history is 1.2 TB before indexes and replication. Dividing a five-second dispatch horizon into ten 500 ms buckets puts 25,000 due jobs in each bucket globally at peak, or about 25,000 / shard_count per balanced shard before skew. Payloads averaging 10 KB add 200 GB/day; store large payloads in object storage and keep references in rows.

docs.title: 6. Entities and state model
docs.text:
Schedule(schedule_id, tenant_id, type, expression, timezone,
         next_fire_at, definition_version, status)
Execution(execution_id, schedule_id, scheduled_for, state, priority,
          queue, attempt, max_attempts, deadline, idempotency_key, version)
Attempt(attempt_id, execution_id, lease_owner, lease_epoch,
        lease_expires_at, started_at, finished_at, outcome)
Dependency(parent_execution_id, child_execution_id, predicate)
Worker(worker_id, pool, capabilities, region, state, last_seen)

States are PENDING -> READY -> LEASED -> RUNNING -> SUCCEEDED|FAILED|CANCELLED|DEAD. Lease expiry transitions a nonterminal execution back to READY if policy permits. State changes append events and update a current-state row transactionally.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> PENDING
  PENDING --> READY: due and dependencies met
  READY --> LEASED: fenced claim
  LEASED --> READY: offer lease expired
  LEASED --> RUNNING: worker accepted
  RUNNING --> SUCCEEDED
  RUNNING --> READY: lease expired / retry
  RUNNING --> FAILED: non-retryable
  RUNNING --> DEAD: retryable failure, attempts exhausted
  PENDING --> CANCELLED
  READY --> CANCELLED
  LEASED --> CANCELLED: cancel before worker start
  RUNNING --> CANCELLED: cooperative stop

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/schedules                 Idempotency-Key: ...
PATCH /v1/schedules/{id}           If-Match: version
POST /v1/schedules/{id}:pause
POST /v1/jobs:run
POST /v1/executions/{id}:cancel
GET  /v1/executions?tenant=&cursor=&state=

Workers use long polling or a bidirectional stream:

poll(pool, capabilities, max_jobs, available_resources)
ackStart(attempt_id, lease_epoch)
heartbeat(attempt_id, lease_epoch, progress)
complete(attempt_id, lease_epoch, outcome, result_ref)

Pagination cursors contain stable sort keys, not offsets. Create idempotency keys map retries to the original schedule or execution.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Client --> API[Scheduler API]
  API --> DB[(Schedule and execution DB)]
  DB --> Timer[Time-index scanners]
  Timer -->|materialize and append outbox| DB
  DB --> Relay[Outbox relay]
  Relay --> Ready[Partitioned ready queues]
  Worker --> Dispatch[Dispatch service]
  Dispatch --> Ready
  Dispatch -->|conditional claim and lease epoch| DB
  Dispatch --> Lease[(Derived lease cache)]
  Worker --> Results[Result service]
  Results --> DB
  DB --> Events[Execution event stream]
  Admin --> Control[Pool and policy control plane]

The control plane owns definitions, quotas, pools, and worker versions. The data plane materializes due work, queues it, leases it, and records outcomes. The database is canonical; a queue message is a wake-up hint and may be duplicated or lost because reconciliation repairs it.

docs.title: 9. Creating schedules and materializing runs
docs.text:
Creation validates cron syntax, timezone, deadline, retry policy, payload limits, and tenant authorization in one transaction. A one-time job creates its execution immediately. A recurring schedule stores next_fire_at. Time-index scanners claim ranges by shard and generate an execution keyed by (schedule_id, scheduled_for, definition_version), whose unique constraint makes retries harmless. They advance next_fire_at and append the ready outbox record in that same transaction. The transaction also validates the scanner epoch and current definition ownership. Across an edit, define an effective-time boundary so old and new versions cannot both materialize the same logical occurrence; uniqueness including version alone does not prevent that.

Missed-run policy is explicit: skip, run latest once, or catch up up to a bound. Daylight-saving behavior is also explicit: cron can mean wall-clock timezone or fixed interval. Updating a definition affects future occurrences only; existing executions retain their immutable definition version.

docs.title: 10. Time indexing and dispatch hot path
docs.text:
Indexing all schedules by next_fire_at allows range scans but creates a concentrated write edge. Partition by a hash of schedule ID and time bucket. Each scanner owns fenced shard leases, reads the next bucket, and writes ready executions. A hierarchical timing wheel is useful for volatile timers, but durable database rows remain authoritative.

Ready queues partition by pool and priority. Dispatchers long-poll queues, check tenant tokens and concurrency, then atomically create a lease using execution version. A worker must acknowledge quickly; otherwise the short offer lease expires. Running jobs renew longer leases with jitter.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant T as Timer scanner
  participant D as Execution DB
  participant R as Outbox relay
  participant Q as Ready queue
  participant S as Dispatcher
  participant W as Worker
  T->>D: validate owner, insert execution, advance schedule, append outbox
  D-->>T: READY execution
  R->>D: read committed outbox
  R->>Q: enqueue execution ID
  Q-->>S: ready hint
  W->>S: poll(capacity, capabilities)
  S->>D: conditional claim + lease epoch
  D-->>S: attempt
  S-->>W: job + lease
  W->>S: complete(epoch, result)
  S->>D: terminal transition if epoch valid

docs.title: 11. Retries, leases, and idempotent effects
docs.text:
A lease is ownership, not proof that a process stopped after expiry. A paused worker can resume while a retry runs. Fencing epochs ensure stale completions cannot overwrite current scheduler state, but they cannot retract an email or charge. Every execution carries a stable business idempotency key. Well-designed handlers insert that key with the effect in one local transaction, or use an outbox to call external systems that support idempotency.

Retryable failures use exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum deadline. Infrastructure loss does not necessarily consume an application attempt. Poison jobs enter a dead-letter state after bounded retries. Operators can replay into a new execution ID while preserving the business key and audit link.

docs.title: 12. DAG execution
docs.text:
For a DAG, store immutable edges and a remaining-dependency counter per child. A parent's terminal execution transition emits an event; failed intermediate attempts do not satisfy execution dependencies. A dependency processor conditionally changes the edge (parent_execution_id, child_execution_id) from unsatisfied to satisfied and decrements the counter in the same transaction. Deduplicating only by parent attempt is insufficient because two attempts could decrement the same edge twice. When the predicate is met and the counter reaches zero, move the child to READY. Periodic reconciliation compares edge state with execution state to repair missed events.

Large fan-out is paged into batches to avoid one transaction touching millions of children. Failure policy can fail-fast descendants, continue with partial inputs, or run compensation nodes. Cycle detection occurs at definition time; dynamic DAG expansion has strict node and depth limits.

docs.title: 13. Fairness, backpressure, and partitioning
docs.text:
Hash schedules and executions by tenant plus ID, while ready queues partition by worker pool. Pure global priority starves small tenants. Dispatch uses hierarchical weighted deficit round robin: select a pool, then a tenant with positive quota, then highest-priority eligible work. Tenant token buckets bound starts and semaphores bound concurrency. Reserved capacity supports critical workloads; unused reserve may be borrowed with preemption rules.

Backpressure starts at admission. When ready age or worker saturation exceeds thresholds, reject optional immediate jobs, delay catch-up runs, and cap DAG fan-out. Queue depth alone is misleading; oldest eligible age and capacity deficit drive scaling.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Execution state requires linearizable conditional transitions per row. Schedule listing and history may use eventually consistent indexes. Queue delivery is at least once; duplicate entries lose the conditional claim. API retries deduplicate by tenant and idempotency key. Completion retries return the stored terminal result if attempt and epoch match.

Database and queue cannot share a transaction cheaply. Use a transactional outbox: state transition and outbox row commit together; relays publish repeatedly; consumers deduplicate. A sweeper finds READY rows lacking recent enqueue evidence, ensuring lost wake-ups do not strand work.

docs.title: 15. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Scanner crash: its fenced range lease expires; another scanner rematerializes idempotently.
  • Queue outage: canonical ready rows accumulate; outbox and sweeper refill after recovery.
  • Dispatcher crash after claim: offer lease expires and job returns to ready.
  • Worker partition: lease eventually expires; duplicate effects are contained by handler idempotency.
  • Database failover: dispatch pauses rather than lease from stale replicas.
  • Retry storm: jitter, tenant budgets, dead-letter thresholds, and admission shedding protect the platform.
  • Bad schedule creates huge catch-up: per-schedule generation caps quarantine it.

Reconciliation scans bounded state partitions for expired leases, impossible counters, stale pending jobs, and missing queue notifications. All repair actions are monotonic and audited.

docs.title: 16. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Give each schedule a home region and route writes there. Its executions run locally unless a pool is explicitly global. Metadata replicates to a standby region. During failover, a coordinator obtains a higher regional epoch before scanners and dispatchers start; the claim and completion authorities reject old-region epochs even while that region remains isolated. The standby first proves it has the required committed intent and effect-key prefix; an asynchronous replica with missing acknowledged records cannot silently promise zero loss or safely recreate ambiguous effects. In-flight external effects may overlap, so idempotency remains required.

Active-active is feasible by assigning disjoint tenant homes, not by concurrently scheduling the same job in two regions. Global workers pull from regional queues through local dispatchers. Data residency constrains payload placement; object references use region-specific replicas.

flowchart TB
  Global[Home-region directory]
  Global --> A[Region A scheduler epoch 12]
  Global --> B[Region B standby]
  A --> ADB[(A execution DB)]
  A --> AW[Workers A]
  ADB -. replicated metadata .-> BDB[(B standby DB)]
  Global -->|promote epoch 13| B
  B --> BW[Workers B]

docs.title: 17. Security and isolation
docs.text: Authenticate workloads with mTLS and authorize tenant-scoped actions. Encrypt payload references and secrets; workers receive short-lived scoped credentials at assignment, never long-lived credentials embedded in jobs. Separate untrusted execution pools with sandboxing and network policy. Validate resource requests, payload size, cron frequency, and DAG fan-out. Cancellation, replay, definition changes, and secret access produce immutable audit events.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track eligible-to-start delay (started_at - eligible_at) for the stated SLO and scheduled-time lateness (started_at - scheduled_for) separately; dependency or quota waits can make these differ. Also track, ready age, runtime, success by failure class, retries, lease expirations, duplicate claims, worker saturation, quota denials, reconciliation repairs, and outbox lag. Correlate schedule, execution, attempt, and trace IDs. Avoid tenant IDs as unconstrained metric labels.

Model-based tests generate state transitions and assert terminal monotonicity and fencing. Fake-clock tests cover cron, leap days, DST, deadlines, and backoff. Integration tests crash components between database and queue operations. Load tests include synchronized midnight schedules, giant fan-outs, long jobs, and skewed tenants. Game days isolate a region and rehearse promotion. Handler certification tests verify idempotency for critical business jobs.

docs.title: 19. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Database polling is simple and durable but can overload indexes; queues dispatch efficiently but are not canonical. Combining canonical rows, outbox hints, and reconciliation gives repairability. Push dispatch uses workers efficiently; pull/long-poll naturally reports capacity. Leases give availability but permit overlapping attempts. Home-region ownership is simpler than global consensus. DAG counters are fast but need event deduplication and repair.

The final design stores versioned schedules and execution state in a partitioned transactional database, materializes due occurrences through fenced scanners, publishes ready hints through an outbox, and dispatches with tenant-fair queues. Conditional leases and epochs protect scheduler state. Workers use stable idempotency keys for effects. Reconciliation, dead letters, quotas, and home-region failover complete the operational design.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions and expectations
docs.text:
Questions: Why can leases not guarantee exactly once? How do you avoid duplicate cron runs? What happens after queue loss? How do you fairly schedule one huge tenant? How are DST and missed runs defined? How do million-node DAG fan-outs behave? What is the regional failover fence?

An L5 candidate should define state transitions, durable acceptance, polling or queues, leases, retry backoff, worker heartbeats, and partitioning. An L6 candidate should expose effect semantics, separate canonical state from notifications, design fencing and reconciliation, quantify fairness and overload, address schedule version migration, and connect regional ownership to recovery objectives.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: The scheduler durably records execution intent and promises at-least-once attempts, not exactly-once external effects. Versioned schedules generate uniquely keyed executions through fenced time scanners. Execution rows are canonical; outbox-backed ready queues are replaceable wake-up hints. Dispatchers use hierarchical tenant fairness, quotas, and worker-advertised capacity, then claim jobs with conditional leases and fencing epochs. Expired leases may overlap retries, so handlers use stable business idempotency keys or transactional outboxes. DAG counters are updated by deduplicated terminal events and repaired by reconciliation. Home-region ownership keeps routine execution local; failover still requires a shared, enforced regional authority and a higher epoch. Metrics center on schedule delay and oldest ready age. Fault, fake-clock, skew, and failover tests verify the hidden boundaries.

docs.title: Design a Global Load Balancer
docs.text: This case study owns the product and control-plane design. Use Proxies and Load Balancing for connection handling, backend selection, health, and draining mechanics.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design L4/L7 load balancing for internet and internal services. Clarify protocols, health, affinity, locality, TLS, configuration rate, and failure policy. Start with stateless regional proxies and a strongly versioned control plane, then add global traffic steering, connection-aware algorithms, passive health, overload protection, draining, and safe rollout. The core tension is keeping the data plane fast and autonomous while routing state changes safely.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Owners define virtual services, listeners, backend pools, health checks, routing, and security policy. Clients connect to a stable VIP/hostname and are sent to healthy capacity. The balancer proxies or forwards traffic; service discovery supplies candidates, and application state remains canonical elsewhere. Targets: 99.999% regional forwarding availability, under 2 ms p99 L4 and 10 ms L7 overhead, health removal within 10 seconds, and configuration rollout within 30 seconds.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text: Support TCP/UDP, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, optional QUIC, TLS termination/passthrough, host/path/header routes, weights, affinity, retries, timeouts, canaries, health checks, connection draining, WAF/rate hooks, access logs, and global/regional failover. Preserve client identity where required. Configuration must be auditable and rollbackable. We exclude service implementation and authoritative discovery.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A request is evaluated against one complete configuration generation.
  • Only eligible endpoints for the selected route, subset, and security policy receive new traffic.
  • Draining stops new assignment before terminating existing work.
  • Retry attempts share one deadline and bounded budget; non-idempotent requests are not retried without an idempotency contract.
  • Affinity is bounded and cannot override health or authorization.
  • A listener never presents another tenant's certificate or route.
  • Control-plane unavailability does not interrupt established forwarding.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 50 million requests/s, 10 million concurrent connections, a 5 Tb/s provisioned egress budget, one million virtual services, and 20 million endpoints. At 10 KB average response, payload demand is 50M * 10 KB * 8 = 4 Tb/s; 5 Tb/s adds 25% for protocol overhead and reserve rather than following directly from the payload calculation. At small RPC sizes packet and TLS CPU may dominate instead. A proxy with 100,000 concurrent connections needs roughly gigabytes for socket state. Provision cells at no more than 50-60% steady CPU so a zone can fail without queue collapse in a three-zone balanced topology. A global backend fleet restart can generate millions of health and discovery changes.

docs.title: 6. Entities and configuration model
docs.text:
VirtualService(id, tenant, listeners[], routes[], generation)
Route(match, priority, backend_pool, retry, timeout, affinity)
BackendPool(id, discovery_ref, algorithm, locality, outlier_policy)
Endpoint(id, address, zone, weight, health_generation, drain_state)
Certificate(hostnames, key_ref, activation, expiry)
Bundle(cell, generation, checksum, minimum_binary_version)

Canonical configuration is versioned; compiled bundles are read-only projections. Endpoint health and load are ephemeral, versioned observations, not customer configuration. APIs use conditional versions, idempotency keys, and opaque pagination cursors.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
PUT  /v1/virtual-services/{id} If-Match: generation
POST /v1/backend-pools/{id}:drain {endpoint, deadline}
GET  /v1/rollouts/{generation}
Data plane: TCP/UDP listeners and HTTP/gRPC proxy

Responses expose accepted, validated, canary, and globally deployed states. Backend requests carry trace/request IDs, forwarded identity under a trusted contract, and remaining deadline. Configuration validation catches overlapping routes, missing pools, redirect loops, and invalid certificates.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Clients] --> G[DNS/anycast global steering]
 G --> E[Regional LB cells]
 E --> B[Service backends]
 A[Config API] --> S[(Versioned store)]
 S --> K[Compiler and rollout]
 K --> E
 D[Service discovery] --> E
 H[Health system] --> E
 E --> T[Async telemetry]

The control plane compiles routes, certificates, and policy. Each data-plane cell has multiple zones and local endpoint/config snapshots. No request waits for discovery, rollout, logs, or global health.

docs.title: 9. Connection and request flow
docs.text:
At L4, a frontend hashes the connection tuple plus service into a forwarding table entry and sends packets to a proxy/backend using direct server return or full NAT. At L7, the proxy accepts TLS, validates SNI/Host, parses bounded headers, selects the highest-priority route, authenticates, chooses a pool and endpoint, enforces deadline, and streams with backpressure.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant L as Load balancer
 participant H as Local health/load
 participant B as Backend
 C->>L: request or connection
 L->>L: pin config generation, route
 L->>H: choose eligible endpoint
 L->>B: attempt 1 with deadline
 alt safe retryable failure and budget
  L->>B: attempt 2 elsewhere
 end
 B-->>L: response stream
 L-->>C: response with backpressure

docs.title: 10. Endpoint selection algorithms
docs.text:
Round robin is simple but ignores unequal work. Weighted round robin handles declared capacity, not live queueing. Least-connections works for long connections but a connection may carry many multiplexed streams. Weighted least-request uses (active_requests+1)/weight; power-of-two choices approximates it with less shared contention. EWMA latency captures performance but can punish endpoints receiving harder requests.

Use power-of-two weighted least-request within the preferred healthy locality, with EWMA as an outlier signal. Consistent hashing is opt-in for caches or affinity; bounded-load rendezvous hashing spills from overloaded owners. Algorithms operate on locally observed state to avoid a centralized scheduler bottleneck.

docs.title: 11. Health, ejection, and recovery
docs.text:
Active probes establish readiness from multiple balancers. Passive observations detect failures visible to real traffic. One client's network problem must not globally eject a backend, so local outlier detection uses minimum volume, consecutive failure/rate thresholds, exponential ejection duration, and a cap on ejected capacity. Control health aggregates only corroborated evidence.

Endpoint states are WARMING, HEALTHY, DRAINING, EJECTED, and REMOVED. Recovery ramps weight gradually to avoid sending a cold instance full load. Panic mode is explicit: if healthy capacity falls below a threshold, either use degraded endpoints or fail closed depending on service class.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> WARMING
 WARMING --> HEALTHY: readiness and ramp
 HEALTHY --> EJECTED: outlier threshold
 EJECTED --> WARMING: probation succeeds
 HEALTHY --> DRAINING: owner request
 DRAINING --> REMOVED: grace expires
 REMOVED --> [*]

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: retries, hedging, and deadlines
docs.text:
Retries improve transient failures but multiply load. The proxy derives each attempt timeout from the client's remaining deadline, retries only safe methods/statuses, excludes the failed endpoint, and consumes a retry token replenished by successful originals. A 10% retry budget bounds amplification. POST requires a declared idempotency key understood by the backend; transport failure after bytes were sent is ambiguous.

Hedging sends a second attempt only after a percentile delay and only for cheap idempotent requests. Cancel losers, but assume cancellation may not prevent effects. Circuit breakers cap endpoint/pool concurrent requests and pending queues. Immediate bounded rejection is safer than waiting beyond useful deadlines.

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: affinity and consistent hashing
docs.text: Cookie affinity is easy but signs pool and expiry to prevent tampering. Source-IP affinity performs poorly behind NAT and mobile networks. Consistent hashing minimizes movement on membership change but can overload the new owner and makes zone failover disrupt many sessions. Use virtual nodes or rendezvous hashing with bounded load and short-lived cookies. Affinity never selects unhealthy/draining nodes. Stateful applications still need shared state or resumable sessions.

docs.title: 14. Deep dive: configuration rollout
docs.text: The compiler resolves references and emits an immutable bundle. Validators check semantics and resource limits. Roll out to test cells, then one canary per region, compare errors/latency/no-route metrics, and expand. Each worker verifies signature/hash and atomically swaps; existing connections may remain pinned while new requests use the new generation. Rollback publishes a higher generation based on old content, avoiding clocks and generation reversal, while retaining current certificate revocations and mandatory deny rules. Dangerous changes support approvals and dry-run traffic simulation.

docs.title: 15. Partitioning, scaling, and overload
docs.text:
Partition global traffic into regional cells via DNS or anycast. Inside a cell, flow hashing spreads connections across workers; consistent hashing minimizes disruption. Endpoint snapshots partition by service, while hot services receive dedicated workers/cells. Connection tables replicate only where failover requirements justify their cost; usually connection loss is retried by clients.

Overload controls are hierarchical: listener connection limits, tenant token buckets, header/body caps, route concurrency, bounded pending queues, backend circuit breakers, and egress bandwidth. Preserve health/config traffic and established streams; reject new low-priority requests first. Load shedding returns protocol-specific overload signals and Retry-After. Autoscaling is slower than queue growth, so admission control is mandatory.

docs.title: 16. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text: Configuration writes are linearizable per virtual service; edge rollout and discovery are bounded eventual. Atomic generation swap prevents mixed routing state. Health is intentionally local and eventual. API retries deduplicate by operation ID. Request retry does not imply exactly-once effects; application idempotency does. Access logs are best effort unless a durable acknowledgement path is explicitly designed. A durable exporter may redeliver, so downstream consumers deduplicate stable event IDs; billing cannot infer complete usage from a lossy asynchronous log.

docs.title: 17. Reliability, failover, and multi-region
docs.text:
A worker crash loses its connections unless flow state is replicated; frontends remap new flows. Zone loss is absorbed by spare capacity in surviving zones. Region loss shifts traffic only after destination capacity checks; otherwise global failover converts one outage into two. DNS has cache delay, while anycast can reroute abruptly and requires route dampening.

Control loss freezes last-known-good bundles. Discovery loss retains endpoints to a stale deadline and combines passive health. Bad rollout auto-halts/rolls back. TLS keys remain locally available with expiry alarms. Regional control ownership uses fenced epochs; data cells remain autonomous.

docs.title: 18. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use mTLS to backends, HSM-backed TLS keys, hostname ownership, scoped APIs, signed bundles, secret-free logs, network segmentation, and trusted identity-header stripping/reinjection. Defend against DDoS, Slowloris, malformed HTTP, request smuggling, TLS exhaustion, route injection, SSRF routes, header spoofing, cross-tenant certificates, and health endpoint abuse. Limit parsing and decompression before allocation.

docs.title: 19. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure accepted/rejected connections, requests, bytes, handshake and proxy latency, route/pool/status, active/pending load, retries/hedges, deadline exhaustion, ejections, panic mode, endpoint skew, config/endpoint age, rollout coverage, TLS expiry, and regional capacity. High-cardinality IDs are sampled, not metric labels.

Property-test route precedence and hashing movement. Fuzz protocol parsers. Replay shadow traffic against bundles. Load-test long connections, HTTP/2 multiplexing, hot routes, retry storms, slow clients, and zone evacuation. Chaos-test stale discovery, half-open backends, config corruption, certificate distributor loss, and regional capacity shortage. Synthetic probes traverse every listener and failover path.

docs.title: 20. Important tradeoffs
docs.text:
Proxying enables rich policy but costs CPU and adds a hop; direct return wins high-throughput L4. Central load knowledge is current but unscalable; local choices win. Aggressive ejection reacts quickly but can amplify correlated failure. Stateful failover preserves connections at major complexity; most services accept reconnect. Anycast is fast but less controllable than DNS.

flowchart TD
 P[Versioned policy] --> C[Validated signed bundle]
 C --> R[Autonomous regional cells]
 D[Local discovery snapshots] --> R
 H[Active plus passive health] --> R
 R --> A[Bounded-load endpoint choice]
 A --> B[Deadline and retry budget]
 B --> S[Service backends]

docs.title: 21. Final architecture
docs.text: Global steering selects a capacitated region; autonomous cells atomically consume bundles and endpoint snapshots; workers use local bounded-load selection, layered admission, and conservative retries.

docs.title: 22. Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text: Why power-of-two? How does draining race discovery? When is panic mode safe? Can a POST retry? How does HTTP/2 alter least-connections? How do you evacuate a region without overload?

docs.title: 23. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate covers routing, algorithms, health, TLS, retries, draining, scaling, and failure. An L6 candidate separates planes, quantifies spare capacity and amplification, defines safety modes, handles migrations and bad rollout, and ties isolation to cost and organization.

docs.title: 24. Five-minute summary
docs.text: Five-minute summary: version and compile policy away from traffic; route clients to a healthy region; atomically load local config and endpoint snapshots; select endpoints with weighted power-of-two choices; combine hysteretic active health with local outlier detection. Bound connections, queues, retries, and affinity. Drain before removal, ramp recovery, preserve last-known-good state through control outages, and fail over only into proven spare capacity.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a multi-tenant platform that collects application and infrastructure logs, supports near-real-time search and tailing, and retains data economically. We establish loss and ordering contracts, size ingestion and storage, separate schema/retention control from collection, and follow a record through agents, durable buffering, indexing, object storage, and query. Deep dives cover overload, indexing, late data, deletion, and regional isolation.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Logs are timestamped events with text and optional structured fields. Engineers use them for incident response, debugging, audit, and analytics. The platform must accept bursts without blocking applications, make dropped data visible, and offer recent search quickly. It is not a transactional database, metrics engine, or permanent compliance archive by default. Audit streams can purchase stricter durability and immutable retention.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Collect files, stdout, syslog, and structured events through host agents and direct APIs.
  • Search by time, service, severity, indexed fields, and full text; aggregate and paginate results.
  • Live-tail selected streams with bounded lag.
  • Manage schemas, parsing rules, redaction, retention, saved queries, and access controls.
  • Export, legal-hold, and delete tenant data with progress.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 15 TB/hour peak raw ingress, 500 billion events/day at 500 bytes/event, and bursts of 3x peak for ten minutes.
  • Searchable recent logs within 30 seconds; p95 common query under 5 seconds.
  • 30 days searchable and one year archive for selected streams.
