  • Collection must not exhaust host disk or CPU; acknowledged durability is tier-specific.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. Every record is assigned to exactly one tenant before storage and query authorization.
  2. An acknowledged durable-tier batch survives a single-zone failure; best-effort tiers disclose weaker guarantees.
  3. Retries may duplicate transport, but stable event IDs deduplicate query results within the documented horizon.
  4. Search results never silently cross tenant or field-level authorization boundaries.
  5. Partial, truncated, sampled, or delayed query results are labeled.
  6. Retention deletion removes both data and indexes by policy deadline; legal hold overrides automated deletion with audit.

Global event ordering is not required here; imposing one would require a shared ordering authority and still would not reveal the exact physical occurrence order across independent clocks. Ordering is best effort per source sequence.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text:
At 500 billion 500-byte events/day, raw volume is 250 TB/day, averaging 10.42 TB/hour or 2.89 GB/s. A 5 TB/hour peak would be impossible for that daily volume. Choose a 15 TB/hour peak: 4.17 GB/s and 8.33 million events/s. Three-way replicated hot buffers then need 12.5 GB/s aggregate writes. At an illustrative 5:1 compression ratio, retained bodies add 50 TB/day, or 1.5 PB over 30 days; a 30% index adds 450 TB before replicas. Archiving every stream for a year would add 18.25 PB compressed, reduced by the selected-stream fraction.

At 100 MB/s safe aggregate replica writes per broker, the peak floor is 125 broker equivalents before failure reserve. A ten-minute 3x peak with drain capacity fixed at ordinary peak accumulates (45 - 15) TB/hour * (10/60) hour = 5 TB logical backlog, or 15 TB replicated; double-sized compute alone does not absorb a sustained 3x burst without queues. Bound backlog by reserved storage and drain it using capacity above live arrivals. Host agents need a strict disk cap, perhaps 5 GB, because fleet-wide unlimited buffering transfers an outage into disk exhaustion.

docs.title: 6. Entities and data model
docs.text:
LogEvent(tenant_id, event_id, event_time, ingest_time, source_id,
         source_sequence, stream_id, severity, body, attributes)
Stream(stream_id, tenant_id, schema_version, retention_class,
       durability_tier, index_policy, redaction_policy)
Segment(segment_id, tenant_id, partition, min_time, max_time,
        object_uri, checksum, schema_versions, index_uri)
DeletionJob(job_id, selector, requested_by, state, watermark, audit_ref)

Immutable segments in object storage are canonical retained data. Recent broker and index-node copies are transient. A metadata catalog maps time, tenant, stream, and partition to segments. Schemas and policies live in a transactional control database and compile into signed agent/gateway configurations.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/logs:ingest                 Idempotency-Key: batch-id
POST /v1/search {query,start,end,limit,cursor,partialPolicy}
GET  /v1/tail?selector=...
PUT  /v1/streams/{id}                If-Match: version
POST /v1/deletions
GET  /v1/deletions/{id}

Agents use compressed batches carrying source sequence ranges and checksums. Ingest responses return accepted, rejected, sampled, and last-durable sequence. Search cursors encode the exact merge key (event_time, ingest_time, event_id) plus query identity and catalog snapshot generation and expire; offsets would become inconsistent and expensive. Large exports are asynchronous jobs writing encrypted objects.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Apps --> Agent[Node log agent]
  Agent --> Gateway[Regional ingest gateway]
  Gateway --> Bus[(Durable partition log)]
  Bus --> Parser[Parse/redact pipeline]
  Parser --> Hot[Hot index shards]
  Parser --> Writer[Segment writer]
  Writer --> Obj[(Object storage)]
  Writer --> Catalog[(Segment catalog)]
  Query[Query frontend] --> Hot
  Query --> Obj
  Query --> Catalog
  Control[Policy control plane] --> Agent
  Control --> Parser

The control plane owns streams, quotas, parser/redaction versions, retention, and index policies. The data plane collects, buffers, transforms, stores, and queries. Agents retain last-known-good policy, so a control outage does not block collection. Durable-tier acceptance occurs after replicated broker append; an economical tier may acknowledge gateway memory or local agent disk with a clear contract.

docs.title: 9. Collection and ingestion hot path
docs.text:
Agents tail files using inode and offset, capture container metadata, add source sequence and event ID, batch, compress, and checkpoint only after acknowledgment. They never block application writes. Their bounded spool evicts according to stream priority and records exact dropped byte/event estimates. Backoff includes jitter and a global retry budget.

Gateways authenticate workload and tenant, enforce bytes/events/new-field quotas, validate timestamps and compressed size, then partition by (tenant, stream, hash(source_id)). Partitioning preserves source order while spreading streams. Brokers replicate across zones. Producers retry batches; consumers deduplicate event IDs during segment creation and queries.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant A as Agent
  participant G as Gateway
  participant B as Broker quorum
  participant P as Parser
  participant O as Object storage
  participant M as Segment catalog
  A->>G: batch(sequence range, checksum)
  G->>G: auth, quota, timestamp checks
  G->>B: append by stream/source
  B-->>G: quorum durable offset
  G-->>A: durable sequence
  B->>P: consume at least once
  P->>O: immutable segment + index
  P->>M: atomically publish verified segment manifest
  M-->>P: committed catalog generation
  P->>B: checkpoint after catalog publish

docs.title: 10. Parsing, redaction, and schema evolution
docs.text:
Raw bytes first pass mandatory redaction at the agent when secrets are recognizable, then again at the trusted parser. Policy versions are attached to records. JSON, regex, and grok parsers have CPU and depth limits; malformed logs retain parse status and a safely redacted body. If mandatory redaction cannot complete, quarantine the record behind restricted access instead of exposing the original body through search. A parser rollout runs in shadow against sampled traffic and compares extracted fields.

Dynamic fields can explode mappings. Each stream has typed approved fields, a cap on new fields, and a fallback attributes blob. Schema changes create new segment metadata versions; queries coerce compatible types or require explicit casts. Redaction cannot be undone, so suspicious rule changes require staged approval.

docs.title: 11. Storage and indexing
docs.text:
Consumers sort bounded batches by event time, encode columns, compress repeated fields, build indexes, upload data and index objects, then atomically publish a segment manifest. Object creation without catalog publication is garbage collected; catalog publication only references checksum-verified objects. Late events create patch segments and query merge handles overlap.

Index every event's tenant, time, stream, and service. Use inverted indexes for selected low/medium-cardinality fields and token indexes for body text. Bloom filters cheaply skip segments for rare terms. Indexing arbitrary fields is expensive, so stream owners choose fields and see estimated cost. Recent hot indexes live on SSD for fast incidents; older queries scan object segments with predicate pushdown.

docs.title: 12. Query and live-tail paths
docs.text:
The frontend authenticates, expands authorized streams, parses the expression, estimates bytes/segments, selects hot and object tiers, and fans out by time partition. Workers prune through catalog statistics and indexes, scan matches, and merge by (event_time, ingest_time, event_id). Result limits, scanned-byte budgets, deadlines, and per-tenant concurrency prevent query-of-death. Partial shard failures return warnings and continuation state if policy allows.

Live tail subscribes to a post-redaction stream after tenant/field authorization and applies bounded filters. Subscribing directly to pre-parser broker payloads would bypass mandatory server-side redaction. It is best effort, rate-limited, and disconnects slow consumers rather than retaining unbounded buffers. It does not replace durable search.

flowchart TD
  Q[Authorized query] --> Cost[Cost and policy check]
  Cost --> Plan[Time/partition plan]
  Plan --> H[Recent SSD indexes]
  Plan --> C[Catalog pruning]
  C --> O[Object segment scans]
  H --> Merge[K-way ordered merge]
  O --> Merge
  Merge --> Page[Page + cursor + completeness]

docs.title: 13. Partitioning, skew, and backpressure
docs.text:
Broker partitions combine tenant and stream with source hashing. A single chatty source remains a hot partition, so agents can split only when per-source order is not required. Heavy tenants get dedicated partitions and query pools. Storage segments partition by tenant, time bucket, and hash bucket, balancing query fan-out against segment count. Tiny segments create catalog pressure; compact them in the background.

Overload policy is tiered: reject malformed data, throttle new cardinality, sample debug logs, then shed low-priority streams while preserving security/audit streams. Sampling is deterministic by event ID so retries agree. Every loss path emits counters through an independent channel. Query admission isolates incident users from bulk exports.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Ingestion is at least once. Batch IDs and source sequences prevent repeated broker append within a retention window; event IDs collapse downstream duplicates. Stable IDs are generated from source identity, boot ID, and sequence, not event content, because identical legitimate lines can repeat. Search freshness is eventually consistent as broker data reaches hot indexes. Read-your-own-log can poll a returned durable offset watermark.

Catalog manifests use compare-and-swap generation. Compaction writes new immutable segments, publishes a replacement set atomically, then deletes old objects after readers' cursor generations expire. Saved-query and policy updates use optimistic concurrency.

docs.title: 15. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Agent restart: resume from persisted inode/offset and acknowledged source sequence.
  • Host disk full: honor spool cap, shed by priority, and alert outside local logs.
  • Gateway or broker loss: clients reroute; quorum acknowledgment protects durable tier.
  • Parser poison record: quarantine one event, not the partition; retain raw reference.
  • Index lag: search reports freshness watermark; durable segments continue building.
  • Object-store outage: brokers and local segment buffers absorb a bounded window, then admission sheds lower tiers.
  • Catalog corruption: restore the committed catalog/checkpoint and replay its ordered manifest log, including replacements and deletions. Enumerated signed objects are candidates for reconciliation, not proof of committed membership; blindly importing them can resurrect orphans or deleted records.
  • Query worker loss: retry a shard once within deadline or return explicit partial results.

Recovery prioritizes ingestion, then security streams, recent indexing, and finally historical compaction. Replays are idempotent by event and segment IDs.

docs.title: 16. Retention, deletion, and multi-region
docs.text:
Lifecycle workers mark expired segments in catalog, wait for reader grace, then delete data and indexes. Selective deletion writes tombstones consulted by all queries and rewrites affected segments asynchronously. Legal hold moves references to immutable retention policy; release is audited. Deletion jobs expose scanned and remaining ranges.

Each region ingests and queries locally to avoid WAN dependency and satisfy residency. Selected streams replicate compressed immutable segments to a disaster-recovery region. Global search fans out to authorized regional frontends and merges pages; it reports unreachable regions. Control metadata has a home writer and global read replicas. During regional failure, agents may route only streams whose residency and durability policy allows it; source sequences continue to deduplicate.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use mTLS workload identity, tenant-scoped tokens, field-level authorization, encryption, and separate keys for regulated streams. Redact credentials before broad storage and block common secret patterns, while acknowledging redaction is defense in depth. Search and export are audited; sensitive queries can require reason codes. Defend parsers from regex denial of service, decompression bombs, oversized fields, and forged timestamps. Quotas cover bytes, events, fields, indexes, scans, exports, and live tails.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track source-to-search lag, accepted and dropped bytes by reason, spool utilization, broker under-replication, consumer lag, parser failures, redaction matches, segment size, catalog lag, index selectivity, query bytes and partials, tail disconnects, and deletion SLO. Synthetic records with canary IDs traverse collection, search, retention, and alerting through an independent monitor.

Golden tests verify parsers and redaction. Property tests exercise event identity, cursor ordering, and compaction equivalence. Load tests include bursty multiline logs, one hot source, field explosions, expensive wildcard searches, and late timestamps. Fault tests fill agent disks, lose brokers after acknowledgment, stall object storage, and replay consumers. Security tests seed known secrets and verify absence from raw, index, export, and diagnostics.

docs.title: 19. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Indexing everything speeds discovery but multiplies cost and cardinality risk; selective indexing plus object scans is sustainable. A broker absorbs bursts and enables replay but adds latency and expense. Local agent acknowledgment minimizes loss on network failure but cannot survive host loss. Sorting by event time improves search but requires bounded lateness. Regional independence improves availability and residency but complicates global search.

The final design uses bounded agents, authenticated regional gateways, a replicated partition log, versioned parse/redaction workers, hot SSD indexes, immutable columnar object segments, and a catalog-driven query engine. Policies and schemas are control-plane artifacts. Priority shedding, explicit completeness, idempotent replay, and manifest-based recovery handle overload and failure.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions and expectations
docs.text:
Questions: What does ingest acknowledgment guarantee? How do duplicates arise? Why are event and ingest time both needed? How do you stop mapping explosion? How does selective deletion work inside immutable segments? What happens when object storage is unavailable? How does a global query paginate?

An L5 candidate should size throughput/storage, batch and partition ingestion, define indexes and retention, and handle agent/broker failure. An L6 candidate should tier durability, quantify burst buffers, design schema and redaction rollout, expose loss and partial results, isolate incident queries, support deletion/legal hold, and reason about residency and cost.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: Agents collect without blocking applications, assign stable source sequences, compress batches, and use bounded priority spools. Regional gateways authenticate, quota, and append durable-tier logs to a zone-replicated broker. Versioned consumers parse and redact, build recent SSD indexes, and publish immutable compressed object segments through atomic catalog manifests. Queries estimate cost, prune segments, fan out across hot and archive tiers, merge stable pages, and label partial or stale results. Selective indexes control cost and schema explosion. Event IDs make replay harmless; source ordering is local, not global. Regions ingest independently, with policy-approved segment replication and explicit partial global search. Tiered shedding preserves audit logs and reports every loss path. Retention, tombstone deletion, secret tests, and disaster drills make the platform operable.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: We will design a platform that ingests numeric time series, supports dashboards and ad hoc queries, and evaluates alerts. We define cardinality and alert correctness first, estimate points and storage, separate metadata/control functions from ingestion/query data planes, then explore write routing, compression, downsampling, query fan-out, alert evaluation, and multi-region operation.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text: Services emit counters, gauges, histograms, and summaries tagged with dimensions such as region and status. Engineers query recent high-resolution data, retain coarse history, build dashboards, and receive alerts. Metrics favor aggregate numerical analysis over exact event retrieval. Logs and traces are linked but stored elsewhere. The platform may drop low-priority telemetry under extreme overload; it must make loss visible and protect critical alerts.

docs.title: 3. Requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements:

  • Ingest tagged samples through push and scraping gateways.
  • Query selectors, ranges, aggregations, rates, percentiles, and groupings.
  • Define recording rules, dashboards, and alert rules with routing and silences.
  • Discover metric names and labels with tenant isolation.
  • Apply retention, downsampling, quotas, and deletion policies.

Non-functional requirements:

  • 20 million samples/s peak, 100 million active series, 30-day raw and 13-month downsampled retention.
  • Ingest acknowledgment p99 under 500 ms; dashboard query p99 under 3 seconds.
  • Alerts evaluated every 30 seconds with under 60-second notification delay.
  • 99.99% ingest availability and explicit completeness indicators.

Arbitrary log search and exact billing are out of scope.

docs.title: 4. Correctness invariants
docs.text:
1. Tenant A cannot write, discover, query, or alert on tenant B's series.
  2. A series identity is metric name plus a canonical sorted label set.
  3. Duplicate samples with the same series and timestamp resolve deterministically; retries do not multiply counters.
  4. Query results identify partial data rather than silently presenting it as complete.
  5. Alert state transitions use a stable rule version and suppress duplicate notifications within the configured policy.
  6. Retention and deletion eventually remove all indexed and object data within a stated compliance SLO.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: At 20 million samples/s and an effective 2 bytes/sample after delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR values, and block compression, samples require 3.5 TB/day. Indexes, labels, replicas, and object overhead can triple that to roughly 10 TB/day raw. Thirty days is 300 TB. Ingest batches of 1,000 samples reduce request rate to 20,000/s. One hundred million active series at 200 bytes of head metadata require 20 GB logical, distributed and replicated. A dashboard with 20 panels, each scanning 10,000 series over 1,000 points, could process 200 million points; query budgets and recording rules are mandatory.

docs.title: 6. Data model
docs.text:
Series(tenant_id, fingerprint, metric_name, labels, created_at)
Sample(series_id, timestamp_ms, value)
Block(tenant_id, shard, min_time, max_time, object_uri, checksum,
      resolution, compaction_level)
RuleGroup(group_id, tenant_id, interval, version, rules[], owner)
AlertInstance(rule_id, label_fingerprint, state, active_since,
              last_evaluated, last_notified, value)

Recent mutable samples live in write-ahead logs and in-memory head blocks. Immutable compressed blocks in object storage are canonical for retained history. A metadata index maps label matchers and time ranges to series and blocks. Rule definitions are canonical in a transactional control database.

docs.title: 7. Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/metrics:write              Content-Encoding: snappy
GET  /v1/query?expr=&time=
GET  /v1/query_range?expr=&start=&end=&step=
GET  /v1/labels/{name}/values?match=&cursor=
PUT  /v1/rule-groups/{id}           If-Match: version
POST /v1/silences

Write batches include tenant identity, source ID, sequence, and samples. Responses report accepted, rejected, and throttled counts. Queries carry deadlines, maximum resolution, and partial-response policy. Pagination uses label/value cursors. Remote-read and remote-write protocols support agents, but server-side limits override client hints.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  Agents --> Gateway[Regional ingest gateways]
  Gateway --> Distributor
  Distributor --> Ing1[Ingester shards]
  Distributor --> Ing2[Ingester replicas]
  Ing1 --> Obj[(Object storage blocks)]
  Ing2 --> Obj
  Query[Query frontend] --> Qry[Query workers]
  Qry --> Ing1
  Qry --> Obj
  Qry --> Index[(Series/block index)]
  Rules[Rule evaluators] --> Query
  Rules --> Notify[Notification router]
  Control[Control plane] --> Gateway
  Control --> Rules

The control plane manages tenants, quotas, schemas, rule versions, and placement. The write data plane validates and shards samples. The query data plane plans and merges reads. Immutable object blocks decouple compute from storage, while recent heads supply low latency.

docs.title: 9. Ingestion hot path
docs.text:
Gateways authenticate, decompress with ratio limits, normalize labels, reject timestamps beyond allowed skew, and enforce samples, bytes, and active-series quotas. A fingerprint hashes the canonical label set for routing/indexing, but full tenant, metric name, and labels are retained and compared so a hash collision cannot merge distinct series. Distributors use consistent hashing to send each series to a replication set. An acknowledgment requires a configurable quorum of ingesters to append to local WAL; asynchronous object upload is not on the hot path.

Ingester heads append ordered chunks. Slightly out-of-order samples fit a bounded reorder window; older samples enter a separate patch block or are rejected. Duplicate timestamp policy is deterministic, such as the maximum (source_generation, source_sequence, source_id) under a specified total ordering for that series, with ties requiring identical bytes. Local arrival order at independent replicas is not deterministic; alternatively reject conflicting writers under a fenced single-source contract. WAL segments replicate across zones and replay after restart. Once a time window closes, ingesters encode immutable blocks, upload them, and publish metadata.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant A as Agent
  participant G as Gateway
  participant D as Distributor
  participant I1 as Ingester A
  participant I2 as Ingester B
  A->>G: compressed batch + sequence
  G->>G: auth, canonicalize, quota
  G->>D: accepted samples
  par replicated append
    D->>I1: append by series
    D->>I2: append by series
  end
  I1-->>D: WAL durable
  I2-->>D: WAL durable
  D-->>A: accepted/rejected counts

docs.title: 10. Compression, compaction, and retention
docs.text:
Within a series chunk, delta-of-delta compresses regular timestamps and XOR encoding compresses slowly changing floating values. Blocks contain postings indexes for label pairs, chunk metadata, bloom filters where useful, and checksums. Background compactors merge small overlapping blocks, deduplicate samples, and produce larger non-overlapping blocks per shard and time range. Compaction uses leases and output manifests so duplicate workers are harmless.

Downsampling generates 1-minute and 1-hour aggregates including count, sum, min, max, and mergeable histogram buckets. Averages alone lose weighting; percentiles cannot be averaged. Lifecycle rules delete raw blocks after 30 days and retain aggregates. Tombstones hide deleted series immediately from queries; compaction physically removes bytes later.

Downsampling is type-specific. A counter needs reset-aware increases and boundary samples; the arithmetic mean or sum of cumulative counter readings cannot reconstruct its rate. Histogram buckets must use compatible boundaries or an explicit common coarsening before merging, and a summary's precomputed quantiles are not aggregatable. These boundaries follow Prometheus histogram/summary guidance (accessed 2026-09-08). If a retained tier lacks the required information, reject or label an approximate query rather than claim raw-resolution equivalence.

docs.title: 11. Query planning and execution
docs.text:
The frontend parses and bounds the expression, chooses raw or downsampled resolution based on requested step, and splits long ranges by time and series shard. Workers fetch postings, prune blocks, scan chunks, execute vector operations, and stream partial aggregates to a reducer. Associative functions such as sum push down well; non-associative operations retain sufficient intermediate state.

Cache immutable block indexes, query plans, and final results keyed by tenant, expression, range, step, and block generation. Recent ranges are not cached long. Deduplicate concurrent identical dashboard queries. Enforce scanned-series, samples, wall-time, and concurrency budgets; return a typed limit error rather than exhaust the cluster.

flowchart TD
  Expr[Range expression] --> Parse[Parse and cost estimate]
  Parse --> Plan[Choose resolution and split]
  Plan --> S1[Recent head query]
  Plan --> S2[Object block shard 1]
  Plan --> S3[Object block shard N]
  S1 --> Merge[Merge and deduplicate]
  S2 --> Merge
  S3 --> Merge
  Merge --> Result[Result + completeness metadata]

docs.title: 12. Alerting and recording rules
docs.text:
Rule groups are assigned by consistent hash to evaluators with fenced leases. One evaluator executes a group sequentially at each interval against a fixed rule version and evaluation timestamp. Recording rules write derived series back with source and timestamp deduplication. Alert conditions progress inactive -> pending -> firing; for: 5m requires continuous true evaluations, with an explicit tolerance for missing evaluations. Missing or partial data is an explicit unknown state, not an implicit healthy result; each rule defines whether to hold state, reset its pending timer, or emit a separate telemetry-loss alert.

Notification routers group by labels, inhibit child symptoms, apply silences, and deduplicate using (alert fingerprint, state, route, repeat interval). They persist a pending delivery intent before sending, then record confirmed or unknown outcome. Marking an intent delivered before the network call can lose the alert on crash; an unknown response may duplicate unless the receiver honors the same idempotency key. HA evaluator replicas may both send during partitions; router deduplication bounds duplicates.

docs.title: 13. Cardinality, partitioning, and overload
docs.text:
Partition writes by tenant and series fingerprint, with many virtual tokens and zone-aware replicas. Object blocks also include time windows so queries parallelize. One high-volume series cannot split naturally; enforce per-series sample rates or shard instrumentation counters with an explicit aggregation label. Cardinality explosions usually come from labels such as request ID. Gateways maintain sketches and per-label budgets, reject new series before existing ones, and show top contributors.

Under overload, preserve critical tenants and rule queries, then interactive dashboards, then bulk queries. Drop or sample explicitly designated low-priority metrics at gateways and increment durable loss counters outside the affected path. Backpressure agents through retry-after and bounded local buffers; never permit unbounded queues.

docs.title: 14. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text:
Writes are quorum durable in recent replicas, then eventually visible in object blocks. Queries merge heads and blocks by series/timestamp and deduplicate overlap during compaction. A write retry with the same source sequence is ignored; without a sequence, identical timestamp/value duplicates collapse but conflicting values follow documented policy. Metadata discovery may lag samples.

Rule updates use optimistic concurrency and take effect atomically per group. An evaluation captures rule version and data cutoff. Alert notifications are at least once with deduplication, not exactly once. Query responses include watermark and missing-shard warnings.

docs.title: 15. Failures and recovery
docs.text:
• Agent disconnect: bounded disk buffer and age-based shedding; expose dropped samples.
  • Ingester crash: quorum replicas serve; WAL replay restores head; ring tokens remain fenced.
  • Object store slowdown: retain closed blocks locally within a limit and throttle low-priority ingestion before disk fills.
  • Index corruption: rebuild from immutable block manifests.
  • Compactor duplication: deterministic output ranges and manifest compare-and-swap select one result.
  • Query worker loss: retry only failed shards within deadline and mark partial when allowed.
  • Rule evaluator loss: lease reassignment may repeat an evaluation; stable timestamps deduplicate outputs.
  • Notification provider outage: bounded durable retry queues and escalation-channel isolation.

docs.title: 16. Multi-region strategy
docs.text:
Agents write to the nearest region and optionally duplicate critical series to a second region. Independent regional ingestion avoids WAN dependence. Global object storage replication provides disaster recovery, but block catalogs include region and generation to avoid double counting. Global queries fan out only when requested and merge by replica labels or deduplication metadata.

Alert rules normally evaluate in one home region against local data. A standby evaluates in shadow and takes over after a fenced epoch. For region-loss alerts, an external witness monitors both regions. Control metadata replicates, while tenant residency policies constrain metric movement.

docs.title: 17. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text: Use workload identity and tenant claims at every hop, encryption in transit and at rest, and scoped object-store credentials. Label and expression parsers have depth, regex, and expansion limits. Prevent query-of-death patterns before execution through cost estimation. Audit rule, silence, dashboard permission, and retention changes. Metrics often leak customer IDs in labels, so provide linting, hashing guidance, deletion, and restricted metadata discovery.

docs.title: 18. Observability and testing
docs.text:
The monitoring system must monitor itself through an independent minimal path. Track accepted/dropped samples, active-series churn, WAL fsync latency, replication shortfall, block upload and compaction lag, query scanned samples, cache efficacy, partial responses, rule lateness, alert delivery, and tenant quota rejection. Synthetic canary series traverse write, query, rule, and notification paths.

Property tests cover label canonicalization and block merge deduplication. Golden tests validate query semantics and downsample equivalence. Load tests model churn and adversarial regex, not only steady counters. Fault tests kill ingesters after acknowledgment, corrupt blocks, delay object storage, and partition evaluators. Shadow rule evaluation compares versions before rollout. Restore drills rebuild indexes solely from object manifests.

docs.title: 19. Tradeoffs and final design
docs.text:
Quorum WAL acknowledgment balances durability and latency; object-store acknowledgment would be slower. Local storage databases simplify reads but couple retention to compute. Immutable blocks reduce cost and enable independent query scaling. Precomputed recording rules spend write/storage to reduce repeated query cost. High availability alert replicas increase duplicate risk. Downsampling saves cost but cannot reconstruct raw quantiles.

The final design uses regional gateways, a consistent-hash replicated ingester ring with WAL-backed heads, immutable object blocks, separate metadata indexes, horizontally scaled query workers, and fenced rule evaluators. Control-plane quotas and versions are off the sample hot path. Completeness metadata, tiered overload, and independent synthetic monitoring make degradation visible.

docs.title: 20. Interview questions and expectations
docs.text:
Questions: Why is cardinality more dangerous than sample rate? How do heads and compacted blocks avoid duplicates? How do you compute percentiles after downsampling? What protects alerts when query traffic spikes? How is partial data represented? What changes for out-of-order samples?

An L5 candidate should estimate samples and storage, shard series, batch writes, compress data, build range queries, and explain alerts. An L6 candidate should budget cardinality, separate planes and workloads, design completeness semantics, compaction fencing, regional alert ownership, cost controls, deletion, and self-monitoring independence.

docs.title: 21. Five-minute summary
docs.text: The platform ingests 20 million tagged samples per second into regional gateways that authenticate, canonicalize labels, enforce cardinality quotas, and route each series to zone-replicated ingesters. Quorum WAL append acknowledges writes; recent head chunks later become compressed immutable object blocks. Compactors deduplicate, merge, downsample with mergeable statistics, and enforce retention. Query frontends estimate cost, choose resolution, split by time and series shard, merge heads with blocks, and report partial results explicitly. Fenced evaluators run versioned rule groups; notification routers group and deduplicate alerts. Independent regions avoid WAN coupling, with home-region alert ownership and replicated blocks for recovery. Priority isolation protects alerts from expensive dashboards. Synthetic end-to-end series, adversarial-cardinality tests, and restore drills verify the design.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design an S3-like service for durable blobs addressed by bucket and key. Clarify object size, consistency, versioning, multipart upload, durability, regions, and cost tiers. Start with metadata plus replicated immutable chunks, then add erasure coding, checksums, background repair, lifecycle, multi-region replication, hot-key scaling, and a separate control plane. The main challenge is proving durable, atomic object semantics over fallible disks and networks.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Clients create buckets, put/get/head/delete objects, list by prefix, perform multipart uploads, use conditional requests, and configure versioning, retention, lifecycle, and replication. Objects range from bytes to 5 TB. We support strong read-after-write and list consistency within a region. Cross-region replication is asynchronous unless a premium synchronous class is selected.

Target 99.99% request availability, first-byte latency below 100 ms p99 for small hot objects, and eleven-nines annual durability for standard storage. Durability is a statistical objective, not a guarantee that malformed client data is correct. Successful PUT means metadata and required failure-domain fragments are durable. CDN, inventory, and analytics are projections.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A committed object version maps to one immutable manifest and content checksum.
  • Namespace updates for one (bucket,key) are linearizable in-region and ordered by generation.
  • A reader sees either the previous complete version or the new complete version, never a partial upload.
  • Fragment placement satisfies the storage class's zone/rack/device diversity policy.
  • Deletes create versioned tombstones; retention/legal hold can forbid physical deletion.
  • Multipart completion includes each declared part exactly once in declared order.
  • Repair never promotes unverified bytes and never reduces the number of independent durable fragments below policy intentionally.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 10 exabytes stored, 10 trillion objects, 100 million writes/s at extreme global scale, and a 10:1 read/write byte ratio. The retained average is 10 EB / 10 trillion = 1 MB/object. If new writes also averaged 1 MB and the extreme peak were sustained, ingestion would be 100 TB/s or 8.64 EB/day before coding; a 10:1 read/write byte ratio would imply 1 PB/s reads. Treat that as a peak envelope and specify its duration, incoming size distribution, overwrite rate, and retention rather than silently assuming steady state. Tiny objects stress metadata while huge videos stress bandwidth. At 4 KB metadata/object, canonical metadata alone is 40 PB before indexes and replication. A 10+4 erasure code has 1.4x raw overhead versus 3x replication, but small-object packing and repair reads matter. Design cells of perhaps 50-100 PB so failures, scans, and blast radius remain bounded.

docs.title: Data model and interfaces
docs.text:
Bucket(bucket_id, account_id, name, region, policy_version, versioning, state)
ObjectVersion(bucket_id, key_hash, key, generation, version_id, state,
              manifest_id, etag, size, storage_class, created_at)
Manifest(manifest_id, chunks[(chunk_id, offset, length, checksum, coding_scheme)])
Fragment(chunk_id, fragment_index, node_id, device_id, checksum, placement_epoch)
Multipart(upload_id, bucket_id, key, state, parts, expiry, initiator)
ReplicationTask(version_id, destination, state, source_generation)

PUT    /{bucket}/{key}              If-Match / If-None-Match
GET    /{bucket}/{key}              Range: bytes=...
HEAD   /{bucket}/{key}
DELETE /{bucket}/{key}?versionId=...
GET    /{bucket}?prefix=&cursor=
POST   /{bucket}/{key}?uploads
PUT    /{bucket}/{key}?partNumber=1&uploadId=...
POST   /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId=...  complete ordered parts

Opaque list cursors bind bucket, prefix, last key, namespace snapshot/generation, and expiry. ETag semantics are documented: it may be a content checksum for simple uploads but is not universally MD5, especially for multipart or encrypted objects.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Clients] --> E[Edge auth and routing]
 E --> M[Metadata cell]
 E --> I[Upload/download coordinators]
 I --> N[Storage nodes]
 M --> D[(Replicated metadata log)]
 M --> P[Placement service]
 P --> N
 N --> R[Repair and scrub pipeline]
 D --> L[Lifecycle and replication]
 N --> K[Key management]
 G[Global control plane] --> M

docs.title: Put and atomic commit
docs.text:
The edge authenticates and authorizes bucket/key action, validates quota and retention headers, and assigns request/version IDs. A coordinator streams bytes, computes end-to-end checksums, chunks large objects, and sends fragments to nodes selected by a placement plan. Nodes fsync fragment plus checksum and return durable receipts. Only after enough policy-compliant receipts exist does metadata atomically recheck the current precondition and commit the immutable manifest and namespace generation. Receipts bind the upload, immutable fragment identity, checksum, placement generation, and durability class; validation at initiation alone cannot serialize two concurrent conditional uploads.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant M as Metadata leader
 participant P as Placement
 participant W as Write coordinator
 participant N as Storage nodes
 C->>M: initiate PUT and precondition
 M->>P: reserve placement
 M-->>C: upload token and coordinator
 C->>W: stream bytes
 W->>N: encoded fragments plus checksums
 N-->>W: durable receipts
 W->>M: commit manifest and receipts
 M->>M: quorum append namespace version
 M-->>C: version ID and ETag

If data upload succeeds but metadata commit fails, fragments are orphans collected after a grace period. If the response is lost after commit, retry with idempotency token returns the version. A coordinator cannot invent placement receipts; nodes sign them. Small objects may be packed into immutable extents to avoid filesystem and coding overhead, while the manifest points to byte ranges. Extent compaction is copy-on-write.

docs.title: Get, ranges, and integrity
docs.text:
Metadata resolves the requested/latest visible version and returns a signed manifest. The read coordinator chooses nearby healthy fragments, issues hedged reads only after delay, reconstructs if necessary, verifies each returned chunk or authenticated stripe before releasing its bytes, decrypts, and streams ranges. A whole-object checksum is verified when a full object is read; it cannot alone validate an arbitrary partial range before streaming. For erasure code k+m, any k fragments reconstruct data. Range reads map to chunk stripes and avoid reading the whole object.

A checksum mismatch marks the replica suspect, retries another fragment, emits a high-priority repair signal, and never returns corrupt bytes. Client-provided checksums validate transit and accidental wrong content. Encryption is envelope-based: per-object data keys are wrapped by tenant/region master keys; cryptographic erasure can complement physical deletion but does not override retention policy.

docs.title: Multipart uploads
docs.text:
Parts are immutable objects scoped to upload ID. A retry with the same operation token and checksum returns the existing part generation. Deliberately replacing a part number uses a new operation token and a conditional higher generation; reuse of a token with different content is rejected. Completion transactionally verifies ownership, expiry, ordered part list, checksums, total size, and preconditions, then creates one object manifest referencing part chunks. Concurrent complete/abort is serialized by multipart state. Uncompleted parts are invisible and lifecycle-collected after expiry.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> INITIATED
 INITIATED --> UPLOADING
 note right of UPLOADING
   Put or replace parts while uploading.
 end note
 UPLOADING --> COMPLETING
 COMPLETING --> COMMITTED
 COMPLETING --> UPLOADING: validation failure
 INITIATED --> ABORTED
 UPLOADING --> ABORTED
 COMMITTED --> [*]
 ABORTED --> [*]

docs.title: Placement, coding, and repair
docs.text:
Placement uses weighted rendezvous hashing over eligible devices, constrained by region, zone, rack, power domain, media class, free-space watermark, and correlated-failure labels. Deterministic candidates aid retry, while a placement epoch and load correction prevent full disks. Never place two required fragments in one prohibited failure domain.

For k+m coding, acknowledging any k fragments is reconstructible now but does not necessarily survive the promised next failure. Require the acknowledged fragment set to retain at least k after every covered failure domain is removed. For 10+4, fourteen fragments spread across four zones as 4/4/3/3 survive one zone; 5/5/4 across three zones does not. Placement, acknowledgement threshold and repair reserve jointly define the durability contract, not the coding ratio alone.

New/hot objects can use three replicas for fast writes and reads, then transition to erasure coding after an age threshold. Encoding reads verified replicas, writes a complete coded set, commits a new manifest atomically, then retires old replicas. Repair priority approximates probability of loss times value: fragments below safety threshold first, then correlated-risk devices, then routine rebalance. Rate limits protect foreground I/O and avoid a failed rack causing a repair storm that overloads remaining racks.

Scrubbers continuously read and checksum statistically selected fragments; device telemetry predicts failures but checksum remains authority. A lost fragment is rebuilt from independent sources into a new placement, verified, then metadata changes. Repair work is idempotent by (chunk, target coding epoch) and uses leases.

docs.title: Namespace, list, and deletion
docs.text:
Partition metadata by bucket and key range/hash. Point lookup benefits from hash; ordered prefix listing needs lexicographic ranges, so use range partitioning with automatic split and hot-key caching. A bucket directory maps ranges to metadata groups. Each group is consensus replicated. Huge single buckets split into many ranges while preserving ordered merge for list.

Delete without version ID writes a delete marker when versioning is enabled; deleting a version writes a tombstone subject to retention. Listing reads a consistent namespace snapshot or generation watermark and returns a cursor; concurrent writes after that point need not appear until a new listing. Garbage collection waits for tombstone durability, replication policy, active read leases, multipart references, and retention. Mark/sweep derives reachability from canonical manifests, with quarantine before physical deletion.

docs.title: Partitioning, cells, and multi-region
docs.text:
Cells contain metadata groups, coordinators, storage pools, repair capacity, and independent failure budgets. Buckets are assigned to a home cell; very large buckets span range groups within a cell or explicitly migrate. Cell routing metadata is globally replicated but tiny. A cell cannot consume another cell's repair budget. Add capacity by adding nodes and gradually adjusting placement weights; background movement is capped.

Asynchronous cross-region replication consumes committed version events, copies verified chunks, then commits destination metadata with source version/generation. Replication preserves ordering per key and deduplicates version ID. A destination read may lag; expose replication status. Active-active writes need conflict semantics: either choose a home region per bucket, or retain concurrent versions and deterministic last-writer metadata without pretending wall clocks are causal. Synchronous classes wait for durable receipts in multiple regions and cost more latency.

Hot keys are handled by edge/CDN caching, read replicas, and coordinators using signed manifests; metadata leader load remains bounded. Write-hot single keys are inherently serialized by generation and should receive 409/429 rather than unsafe concurrency. Backpressure rejects new low-priority bulk writes, slows lifecycle transitions, and reserves I/O for reads, metadata, and safety-critical repair.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and failure recovery
docs.text:
Metadata consensus gives linearizable namespace operations within a region. Data fragments are immutable and become visible only through committed manifests. Idempotency tokens bind account, bucket, key, operation, and body/checksum intent. Conditional headers compare version/ETag atomically. Inventory and replication are eventual.

Node loss triggers alternate reads and repair. Metadata leader loss elects a new leader; stale leaders are term-fenced. Coordinator loss leaves resumable multipart parts or orphan fragments. Network partition favors the metadata quorum and prevents minority commits. Full device moves to read-only and placement excludes it. Key-service outage may permit bounded reads using cached unwrapped keys in secure memory but blocks writes/rotations according to policy. Region loss follows bucket replication/RPO class.

Reconciliation scans committed manifests for insufficient/incorrect placement, fragments absent from manifests, replication gaps, expired multiparts, lifecycle tasks, stuck deletes, and billing byte counts. It repairs through normal versioned workflows. Disaster tests restore metadata logs, placement maps, key references, and sampled objects, then validate checksums. Durability modeling tracks annualized fragment loss, repair time, and correlated domains, not just replica count.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Use scoped signed requests, bucket policies, object ACLs only if necessary, private-by-default settings, TLS, envelope encryption, KMS audit, retention locks, access logs, and short-lived presigned URLs. Prevent path canonicalization bugs, confused deputy access, credential stuffing, public-bucket leaks, zip bombs, storage exhaustion, egress abuse, and enumeration. Rate-limit by account and bucket, validate content length, and make policy evaluation fail closed.

Measure request latency/availability by operation and cell, first byte, throughput, metadata quorum health, fragment write success, checksum mismatch, degraded reads, coding overhead, repair backlog/time-to-safety, device error trends, capacity watermarks, replication lag, orphan bytes, multipart age, GC backlog, hot ranges, KMS errors, and durability risk. Billing meters logical, physical, request, and egress bytes with reconciliation.

Property-test namespace/version/tombstone state, conditional writes, multipart races, and placement diversity. Fault-inject torn writes and checksum corruption. Model erasure-code tolerance. Load-test tiny objects, giant ranges, hot keys, and prefix listing during splits. Chaos-test disk/rack/zone loss, leader changes, coordinator death after receipts, KMS outage, and repair storms. Restore drills validate real objects, not merely metadata. Canary firmware and coding migrations by cell.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Three replicas simplify reads/repair but cost 3x; erasure coding lowers cost with reconstruction and repair amplification. Hash metadata spreads writes but hurts list; lexicographic range shards support prefix APIs and require hot-range splitting. Direct-to-node uploads reduce proxy bandwidth but need signed placement tokens and commit receipts. Global active-active namespace sounds available but creates conflict and latency; home-region buckets plus explicit replication classes are understandable.

flowchart TD
 A[Authorized conditional request] --> M[Consensus metadata range]
 M --> P[Failure-domain-aware placement]
 P --> W[Streaming checksum and encoding]
 W --> N[Immutable fragments and receipts]
 N --> C[Atomic manifest commit]
 C --> R[Verified reads and range reconstruction]
 C --> L[Replication, lifecycle, inventory]
 N --> S[Scrub and priority repair]
 S --> N

The final design uses cell-local consensus for bucket namespace and immutable manifests, while coordinators stream checksummed replicated or coded fragments to diverse storage nodes. Visibility changes only through atomic metadata commit. Reads verify and reconstruct. Versioned deletion, lifecycle, cross-region replication, scrub, and repair operate asynchronously under strict safety and foreground budgets. The global control plane routes cells and signs policy but is not on bulk data paths.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. What exactly must be durable before PUT returns success?
  2. How are orphan fragments distinguished from live data safely?
  3. Why does erasure coding make repair more complex than replication?
  4. How can LIST be strongly consistent while ranges split?
  5. What happens when multipart completion races abort?
  6. How does a region failover avoid conflicting latest versions?
  7. Which metrics actually support an eleven-nines durability claim?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should separate metadata/data, model immutable chunks/manifests, estimate metadata and bytes, explain multipart, checksums, replication/coding, partitioning, conditional writes, deletion, and disk/node failures.

An L6 candidate should define the durability proof, correlated placement, repair economics and overload, namespace migration, cell blast radius, region conflict policy, lifecycle/retention safety, KMS behavior, and staged coding changes. They should connect storage classes to latency, durability, and cost.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Authenticate and check preconditions in a consensus-backed metadata range, then stream bytes through a coordinator that checksums, chunks, and writes replicated or erasure-coded immutable fragments across required failure domains. Commit the manifest and new key generation only after enough signed durable receipts; readers therefore see the old or complete new version. Reads choose healthy fragments, hedge selectively, verify end-to-end checksums, and reconstruct ranges. Multipart parts stay invisible until atomic completion. Versioned tombstones plus retention-aware mark/sweep make deletion safe. Partition metadata lexicographically for listing, split hot ranges, organize infrastructure into bounded cells, cache hot reads, and serialize write-hot keys. Scrub continuously and prioritize repair by loss risk without starving foreground traffic. Replicate committed versions across regions with explicit lag or synchronous cost. Observe degraded reads, checksum errors, placement diversity, repair time-to-safety, replication lag, orphans, capacity, and restore correctness.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a durable multi-tenant pub-sub platform where producers publish to topics and subscriptions deliver messages to consumers. Clarify ordering, retention, replay, pull versus push, filtering, throughput, and delivery semantics. Begin with partitioned append-only logs, then add replicated brokers, consumer leases, acknowledgements, retry/dead-letter policy, quotas, schema governance, transactions where justified, and geo-replication.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Producers create topics and publish keyed messages. Consumers create independent subscriptions, pull batches or receive pushes, acknowledge, extend leases, seek to time/offset, and configure retention, filters, retry, and dead letters. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition or explicit ordering key. Delivery is at least once by default. Exactly-once effects require cooperation with a transactional sink and are not a universal network guarantee.

Target publish durability acknowledgement below 20 ms p99 in-region, 99.99% availability, millions of topics, tens of millions of partitions, and aggregate terabytes/s. Retain messages from hours to months. Control-plane changes may take seconds; an acknowledged publish and subscription cursor are canonical data-plane state.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• Within one partition, committed records have immutable monotonically increasing offsets.
  • An acknowledged publish exists on the configured quorum and survives allowed failures.
  • A subscription never advances its committed cursor past an unacknowledged gap unless policy explicitly skips/dead-letters it.
  • Producer retries with the same producer epoch and sequence do not create a second logical record.
  • One active consumer lease generation owns a partition at a time; stale owners cannot commit acknowledgements.
  • Retention never removes data still protected by stronger configured replay/subscription policy.
  • Filters and schemas are versioned; replay uses recorded payload and documented current/original policy.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 100 million messages/s globally, 1 KB average, or 100 GB/s ingress and perhaps 500 GB/s egress at fanout five. With replication factor three, brokers sustain 300 GB/s sequential writes. Seven-day retention is 60 PB logical. One million active subscriptions over one million topic partitions can create billions of cursor relationships if modeled naively, so store sparse partition assignments/cursors and isolate high fanout topics. A 10 MB/s partition cap implies 10,000 busy partitions for 100 GB/s, plus headroom for skew and failures.

docs.title: Entities and interfaces
docs.text:
Topic(topic_id, tenant_id, partition_count, retention, schema_policy, state)
Partition(topic_id, partition_id, leader_epoch, replicas, start_offset, high_watermark)
Record(offset, timestamp, key, headers, payload, producer_id, producer_epoch, sequence)
Subscription(subscription_id, topic_id, mode, filter_version, retry_policy, state)
Cursor(subscription_id, partition_id, committed_offset, lease_generation)
Delivery(subscription_id, partition_id, offset, attempt, lease_deadline)

POST /v1/topics/{topic}:publish
POST /v1/topics/{topic}:publishBatch
POST /v1/subscriptions/{sub}:pull {max_messages, max_bytes, wait_ms}
POST /v1/subscriptions/{sub}:ack {delivery_tokens}
POST /v1/subscriptions/{sub}:modifyAckDeadline
POST /v1/subscriptions/{sub}:seek {timestamp|offset|snapshot}

Publish responses include partition, offset, and leader epoch. Delivery tokens bind subscription, partition, offset, attempt, lease generation, and expiry, preventing acknowledgements for another assignment.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 P[Producers] --> G[Protocol gateways]
 G --> B[Partition leaders]
 B --> R[Partition followers]
 B --> L[(Segment storage)]
 B --> D[Dispatchers]
 D --> C[Pull/push consumers]
 D --> X[(Cursor and lease store)]
 M[Metadata quorum] --> G
 M --> B
 O[Object archive] --> D
 B --> O

docs.title: Publish, partitioning, and replication
docs.text:
Gateway authorizes topic, enforces message/schema/tenant limits, then chooses partition. A key hashes consistently to a partition for order; unkeyed traffic uses sticky batches to avoid tiny requests while balancing load. The leader appends a batch to the current segment, replicates to followers, and advances high watermark after quorum durability. Only committed offsets are readable.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant P as Producer
 participant G as Gateway
 participant L as Partition leader
 participant F as Followers
 participant D as Dispatcher
 participant C as Consumer
 P->>G: batch, producer epoch, sequences
 G->>L: routed batch
 L->>F: append at offsets
 F-->>L: durable acknowledgements
 L-->>P: committed offsets
 L->>D: high watermark advanced
 D->>C: records plus delivery tokens
 C->>D: acknowledge tokens
 D->>D: commit cursor under lease generation

Producer idempotency stores the latest sequence and recent mapping per producer/partition. A duplicate sequence returns its old offset; a gap is rejected or requires producer recovery. Producer epoch fences a restarted or duplicated producer. This prevents duplicates caused by publish retries within retention of sequence state, but cannot deduplicate semantically identical events with new IDs.

Segments are append-only, indexed sparsely by offset/time, checksummed, and rolled by size/time. Hot data lives on broker disks; old sealed segments upload to object storage with manifests and local cache. Retention deletes only whole eligible segments after topic policy, subscription protection where offered, archive verification, and legal hold.

docs.title: Consumer assignment and delivery
docs.text:
For shared subscriptions, a coordinator assigns partitions to consumers using sticky balancing to minimize movement while respecting capacity. Each assignment has a lease generation. Cooperative rebalance asks consumers to revoke incrementally rather than stopping all partitions. Consumers fetch bounded bytes, process, then acknowledge. Cursor updates coalesce contiguous acknowledgements; an interval/bitmap tracks temporary gaps.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> AVAILABLE
 AVAILABLE --> LEASED: deliver
 LEASED --> ACKED: valid ack
 LEASED --> AVAILABLE: deadline expires
 LEASED --> RETRY_DELAY: retry policy
 RETRY_DELAY --> AVAILABLE
 LEASED --> DEAD_LETTERED: attempts exhausted
 ACKED --> [*]
 DEAD_LETTERED --> [*]

An ack deadline balances duplicate probability and recovery speed. Consumers can extend it within a cap; repeated extension is observable. When a lease expires, redelivery increments attempt. Ordering subscriptions cannot deliver later records past a failed ordered key without violating order; they block, skip by explicit policy, or move the poison record to a dead-letter topic and record the gap. Unordered subscriptions can continue around sparse failures.

Dead-letter handoff must durably publish the original record and its identity before the source cursor skips it, or commit both through the broker's transaction protocol. A crash after DLQ publication may repeat the DLQ record, deduplicated by source identity; a DLQ outage must not advance the source cursor and lose the only copy.

Push delivery uses the same lease model. The dispatcher signs requests, limits per-endpoint concurrency, interprets only configured success codes as acknowledgement, and applies circuit breakers. A slow endpoint has isolated backlog and cannot consume dispatcher threads globally.

docs.title: Backpressure and fairness
docs.text:
Hierarchical token buckets enforce tenant, topic, producer, subscription, and egress quotas in bytes and messages. Weighted fair queues prevent a high-volume subscription from starving others. Dispatch respects consumer-advertised credits. When consumers lag, data remains in the log rather than broker memory. When disk approaches watermark, throttle producers whose retention/backlog drives usage, reject low-priority publishing, and preserve replication traffic. Never accept writes that cannot meet durability policy.

Hot partition mitigation begins with good keys and producer aggregation. A single ordering key is inherently serial. Offer virtual key sharding only if the application can merge order, or a dedicated high-capacity partition. Increasing partition count changes key mapping; preserve existing key-to-partition mapping through a partition-map version or accept that only post-change order is local to the new partition. State this migration contract.

docs.title: Filtering, schemas, and transactions
docs.text:
Broker-side filters evaluate bounded header/attribute predicates, not arbitrary code. Compile and version filters, charge CPU to the subscription, and send malformed evaluations to metrics rather than dropping silently. Payload schemas live in a registry with compatibility policy at publish. Store schema ID on each record. Validation outage may fail closed for strict topics or accept into quarantine for explicitly permissive topics.

Transactions across several partitions add a coordinator, transaction IDs, prepare markers, and read-committed visibility. They increase latency and recovery complexity; use them only for workloads needing atomic publication. A common consume-transform-produce flow can atomically commit output records and source offsets if all use the platform transaction protocol. External database effects still require an inbox/outbox or sink connector with idempotent keys.

docs.title: Leader election and truncation
docs.text: Partition metadata stores replicas, leader, and epoch in a quorum control plane. A new leader must contain all committed offsets. It fences old leaders and truncates uncommitted tails to the chosen log. Followers fetch sequentially and report durable offset. Allowing an out-of-sync replica to lead improves availability but can lose acknowledged records, violating the invariant; only an explicit lower-durability topic class may choose that tradeoff.

docs.title: Replay and seek
docs.text: Seeking pauses assignments, increments subscription generation, resolves timestamp to offsets using segment indexes, writes a complete immutable cursor manifest for the new generation, atomically switches the subscription pointer to that manifest, then resumes. A million partition cursors need not fit in one database transaction; incomplete manifests stay invisible and are retried or garbage-collected. In-flight acknowledgements from the old generation fail. Replay can create duplicate downstream effects, so tooling requires scope, dry-run estimated bytes/messages, rate cap, and confirmation. A forked subscription is safer when production processing must continue.

docs.title: Geo-replication
docs.text: A replicator consumes committed source offsets and publishes destination records with source topic/partition/offset identity. Destination deduplicates that identity and checkpoints only after commit. Preserve per-source-partition order, but merging two active regions has no universal total order. Global topics either assign each key a home region, expose region-partitioned order, or use expensive consensus. Loop-prevention metadata stops circular replication.

docs.title: Partitioning and scaling
docs.text:
Partitions are the unit of ordering, replication, throughput, placement, and consumer parallelism. Place replicas across racks/zones with disk and network awareness. Metadata scales through hierarchical namespaces and sharded watch streams; clients cache routing and refresh on epoch errors. Brokers isolate page cache, network, replication, and dispatch pools. Large tenants receive dedicated quotas or cells.

Split control and data planes: metadata quorum manages topics, ACLs, assignments, schemas, and placement, while brokers continue existing traffic during short control outages. Cells contain brokers and coordinators with bounded blast radius. Cross-cell topics use explicit replication. Autoscaling cannot instantly move terabytes, so maintain disk/network headroom and add brokers ahead of forecast demand.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Record order and high watermark are strongly consistent per partition. Topic lists, consumer lag dashboards, and geo-replicated views are eventual. Publish retries use producer sequence. Delivery and broker processing remain at least once. Ack commit uses lease generation. Transactional read-process-write offers stronger platform-local semantics, not magical external exactly once.

Leader loss elects an in-sync follower. Broker disk loss triggers replica rebuild with throttled copying. Coordinator loss reconstructs assignments/cursors and increments generations. Cursor-store outage pauses new ack commits and delivery rather than losing position. Object archive outage retains local segments until capacity policy forces producer throttling. Poison records follow explicit retry/dead-letter policy. Region loss uses replicated topics and documented RPO; subscriptions resume from replicated checkpoints and may redeliver.

Reconciliation compares segment manifests, replica high watermarks, checksums, archive copies, producer sequence state, cursor bounds, dead-letter linkage, and billing. Scrubbers verify sealed segments. Repair is rate-limited and prioritized below quorum restoration but above rebalance. Operators can inspect and replay a partition without mutating canonical records.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Authenticate workloads with short-lived identities, authorize topic/subscription actions, encrypt transport and disks, isolate tenant keys when required, sign push deliveries, audit seeks and policy changes, and redact payloads. Defend against oversized messages, decompression bombs, topic explosion, partition abuse, schema attacks, replay storms, slow consumers, and egress theft. Enforce quotas before allocation and cap headers/filter complexity.

Measure publish latency/error by acknowledgement class, batch size, bytes, leader changes, replication lag, under-replicated partitions, disk/network saturation, segment flush, consumer lag in offsets/time/bytes, redelivery and ack-expiry rate, stuck ordered keys, rebalance duration, push health, dead-letter volume, archive lag, quota rejection, fairness, and cost. Trace metadata and IDs, not arbitrary payloads.

Property-test offsets, producer sequencing, ack-gap compression, lease fencing, retention safety, and seek generations. Model-check election/truncation. Fuzz protocols, schemas, and filters. Load-test tiny and maximum messages, skewed keys, high fanout, slow consumers, and rebalance storms. Chaos-test leader death after quorum append, disk corruption, metadata partition, cursor outage, archive lag, and regional failover. Restore archived segments and replay checksums regularly.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Per-message queues simplify ack state but duplicate storage for fanout; a shared log plus independent cursors is efficient. More partitions increase parallelism but raise metadata, open-file, and rebalance cost. Synchronous replication protects acknowledged data but adds latency. Long retention on brokers is fast but expensive; tiered immutable segments reduce cost with replay latency. Server filtering saves egress but spends shared CPU and complicates policy.

flowchart TD
 P[Authorized idempotent producer] --> L[Partition leader and sequence check]
 L --> Q[Quorum replicated append]
 Q --> H[Committed high watermark]
 H --> D[Credit-aware fair dispatcher]
 D --> C[Generation-fenced subscription cursor]
 H --> A[Tiered immutable archive]
 H --> G[Ordered geo-replicator]
 M[Metadata and schema control plane] --> L
 M --> D

The final architecture uses partitioned replicated logs as canonical records, a quorum control plane for epochs and policy, and independent generation-fenced subscription cursors. Producers batch and sequence retries; consumers receive credit-bounded leases and acknowledge contiguous progress. Tiered segments support retention/replay, while geo-replication preserves source-partition identity. Quotas and cells bound overload and tenant blast radius.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. When can a producer retry without creating a duplicate record?
  2. How do sparse acknowledgements interact with ordered delivery?
  3. Can partition count increase without breaking key order?
  4. Which replica may become leader after a partition?
  5. What does exactly-once mean for an external database sink?
  6. How is a production subscription replayed safely?
  7. How does tiered storage affect retention and recovery?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should choose partitioned logs, estimate bytes, explain leader/follower replication, ordering scope, producer idempotency, consumer leases/acks, retries, partitioning, retention, and broker failures without claiming universal exactly once.

An L6 candidate should define data-loss policy in election, partition migration, fairness and disk overload, control/data-plane and cell boundaries, geo-order semantics, transaction scope, replay governance, tiered repair, and schema evolution. They should quantify operational and cost consequences.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Hash keyed records to a partition and append producer-batched, sequenced records at its fenced leader. Acknowledge only after quorum durability and expose only offsets through the committed high watermark. Store immutable checksummed segments, tiering sealed data to object storage. Shared subscriptions assign partitions with generation leases; dispatch respects credits, acknowledgements advance contiguous cursors, and deadline expiry causes at-least-once redelivery. Poison records use bounded retry and explicit dead letters. Hierarchical byte/message quotas, fair queues, disk watermarks, and isolated cells protect replication and active consumers. Metadata quorum controls epochs, schemas, ACLs, and placement but stays off payload paths. Replicate regions using source partition/offset identity and admit that active-region merges lack total order. Observe replication, disk, consumer lag, redelivery, rebalances, archive, hot keys, and fairness; model-check leader truncation and restore/replay regularly.

docs.title: 1. Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a service that stores, issues, rotates, and revokes credentials for workloads and humans. Clarify secret types, identity authority, read availability, revocation speed, audit, and disaster recovery. Start with encrypted versioned secrets behind authenticated APIs, then add workload identity, envelope encryption, dynamic credentials, leases, rotation workflows, edge agents, policy compilation, and break-glass recovery. Security invariants dominate convenience: a highly available service that discloses the wrong secret has failed.

docs.title: 2. Product framing
docs.text:
Tenants store API keys, certificates, database passwords, and encryption material, or request short-lived credentials generated for downstream systems. Workloads retrieve by logical path and version; operators define policy and rotation. The service is not a general configuration store, KMS replacement, or place to put large blobs. KMS protects root keys; secrets management applies identity, policy, lifecycle, and delivery.

Targets: 99.99% control writes, 99.999% cached workload reads for eligible secrets, under 50 ms p99 regional retrieval, routine revocation propagation within 60 seconds, complete durable audit, and zero plaintext in logs/backups. Availability modes differ: payment signing keys may fail closed, while a replicated read-only database password may use bounded stale cache.

docs.title: 3. Functional and non-functional requirements
docs.text: Support create/read/version/delete, CAS, metadata listing, access policy, workload and human login, dynamic database/cloud credentials, leases, renew/revoke, rotation, certificate issuance, audit, notifications, import/export, and recovery. Non-functional requirements include least privilege, tenant isolation, key separation, tamper evidence, bounded blast radius, secure deletion, and operability during identity/KMS/downstream outages. We exclude arbitrary secret sharing links and direct storage of root HSM keys.

docs.title: 4. Correctness and security invariants
docs.text:
• Every disclosure is authorized against authenticated identity, resource, action, context, and a known policy generation.
  • Plaintext exists only in bounded trusted memory and is never persisted outside encrypted envelopes.
  • A secret version is immutable; rotation creates a new version and explicit activation state.
  • Lease/revocation generation fences stale renewals and issuers.
  • Dynamic credential issuance has one durable request identity and a reconciled downstream effect.
  • Audit records are append-only, ordered per tenant, and independently tamper-evident.
  • Deletion respects retention/legal hold and eventually removes all ciphertext/data-key references and backups per policy.
  • No control-plane outage silently broadens access.

docs.title: 5. Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 100 million secret objects, 20 versions average, 5 million workload reads/s at fleet start, 20,000 writes/s, and 100,000 dynamic leases/s. At 2 KB ciphertext plus metadata per version, stored data is about 4 TB before replication and audit. Reads are bursty: deployment or node restart can multiply normal QPS by 100. KMS cannot unwrap per request at this rate; regional key caches, agents, and envelope encryption are required. Audit volume may exceed secret storage and must have independent capacity.

docs.title: 6. Core entities and data model
docs.text:
Secret(path, tenant, type, metadata, current_version, policy_ref, state)
SecretVersion(secret_id, version, ciphertext, wrapped_DEK, checksum, state, created_at)
Policy(policy_id, statements[], generation, compiled_hash)
Identity(subject, issuer, claims, session_generation)
Lease(lease_id, secret/version, subject, expiry, renewable, generation, state)
Rotation(job_id, secret, old_version, new_version, phase, deadline)
AuditEvent(event_id, tenant_sequence, actor, action, resource_hash, decision, chain_hash)

Canonical metadata is separate from encrypted payloads. Paths are normalized and bounded. Listing returns metadata only through opaque, policy-bound cursors; it never decrypts values. Deletion writes a tombstone and queues cryptographic and physical erasure.

docs.title: 7. API and delivery interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/secrets/{path}/versions  Idempotency-Key, If-Match
GET  /v1/secrets/{path}?version=
DELETE /v1/secrets/{path}/versions/{v}
POST /v1/engines/{name}/credentials {role, ttl, request_id}
POST /v1/leases/{id}:renew
POST /v1/leases/{id}:revoke
POST /v1/secrets/{path}:rotate

Responses include version, lease ID, expiry, renewable flag, policy generation, and a non-secret request ID. Workloads preferably use a node-local agent over a protected Unix socket. The agent authenticates workload identity and either serves an in-memory API or atomically replaces a tightly permissioned file on a memory-backed mount with swap and core dumps disabled. Do not write plaintext to an ordinary persistent volume, include that mount in backups, or assume atomic rename supplies confidentiality. Consumers must reopen the file on rotation; already copied plaintext cannot be recalled by changing the mount.

docs.title: 8. High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 W[Workloads and operators] --> I[Identity gateway]
 I --> A[Regional secret API]
 A --> P[Policy decision]
 A --> M[(Consensus metadata)]
 A --> O[(Encrypted object store)]
 A --> K[KMS/HSM]
 A --> E[Dynamic secret engines]
 E --> D[Databases/cloud/PKI]
 A --> U[Node-local agents]
 A --> L[Immutable audit pipeline]
 C[Global control plane] --> P

The control plane manages tenants, policies, engines, key hierarchy, and replication. The data plane authenticates, authorizes, decrypts/leases, and delivers from regional cells. Agents may cache specifically permitted values, but policy and ciphertext remain canonical centrally.

docs.title: 9. Static secret write and read paths
docs.text:
On write, the API authenticates the caller, evaluates write policy, validates CAS/version limits, generates a random data-encryption key (DEK), encrypts plaintext with AEAD using tenant/path/version as associated data, wraps the DEK under a tenant-region key in KMS, and zeroizes plaintext buffers. One metadata transaction commits immutable ciphertext reference, checksum, current version, and operation ID. A lost response can be retried safely.

On read, authenticate fresh workload credentials, evaluate compiled policy, fetch ciphertext, unwrap or retrieve a short-lived cached DEK, verify associated data/tag, emit audit, and return over mTLS. To meet the stated complete-audit target, durably append the disclosure decision before releasing plaintext and fail closed if the tamper-evident spool cannot accept it. A best-effort audit tier is a separately named weaker contract. The event proves authorized release was attempted, not that the client received the bytes.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant W as Workload
 participant A as Secret API
 participant P as Policy engine
 participant M as Metadata/ciphertext
 participant K as KMS
 participant L as Audit spool
 W->>A: read path with workload token
 A->>P: subject, action, path, context
 P-->>A: allow at generation G
 A->>M: fetch immutable version
 A->>K: unwrap DEK if not cached
 A->>L: append disclosure decision
 A-->>W: plaintext, version, lease/expiry

docs.title: 10. Identity and authorization
docs.text:
Bootstrap is the hardest dependency. Workload identity should derive from an attested orchestrator identity, hardware identity, or short-lived signed service account token, not a baked-in shared secret. The gateway validates issuer, audience, nonce, expiry, workload generation, and channel binding. Human access uses SSO, MFA, reason/ticket, and stronger approval for production or break-glass operations.

Policies are deny-by-default statements over tenant, path, action, identity attributes, environment, and optional network/device context. Compile and distribute signed policy bundles. A data cell may continue using a bounded-age bundle; emergency deny/revocation uses a high-priority channel. Avoid fetching group membership synchronously on each read.

docs.title: 11. Deep dive: envelope encryption and key hierarchy
docs.text:
