An HSM-backed root protects regional/tenant key-encryption keys (KEKs); KEKs wrap per-version DEKs; DEKs encrypt data. This limits HSM throughput and blast radius. Associated data prevents moving ciphertext between tenants or paths. Cache unwrapped KEKs/DEKs only in locked memory for short periods, with process isolation and explicit zeroization; cache misses are rate-limited so a KMS outage does not become a storm.

KEK rotation rewraps DEKs without exposing or rewriting plaintext. Root rotation rewraps KEKs under dual control. Compromise response identifies all descendants, disables issuance, rotates affected material, and preserves forensic audit. Cryptographic deletion destroys wrapping keys only when no unrelated secret shares them; otherwise delete the per-version wrapped DEK and ciphertext through retention workflows.

docs.title: 12. Deep dive: dynamic credentials and leases
docs.text:
For a database role, the engine reserves a durable issuance record keyed by request ID, creates a unique username/password with constrained grants and expiry, records downstream identity, then marks the lease active. A timeout after database creation is ambiguous; reconciliation queries by deterministic username/request tag rather than creating duplicates. If creation cannot be proven, reconcile or revoke candidates under the same issuance identity. Do not issue a fresh identity until a late old create cannot leave an active orphan; require downstream request fencing, an authoritative terminal result, or continued quarantine with native expiry.

Renewal verifies subject, lease generation, maximum lifetime, and downstream state. Serialize renewal and revocation in the canonical lease workflow and ensure downstream ordering or reconciliation prevents a delayed renew from restoring revoked access. Revocation is idempotent and retries until the downstream confirms removal. Expiry uses a timing wheel to schedule work, but a durable lease state drives correctness. Downstream outage means leases may outlive control metadata; short native database TTLs and reconciler scans limit exposure.

Native expiry often blocks only new authentication, not sessions already established with the credential. Verify each backend's session semantics; strict revocation may require terminating sessions or an authorization proxy checking a current lease. Do not certify a sixty-second access-revocation bound solely from a password expiry or a queued revoke job.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> REQUESTED
 REQUESTED --> CREATING: durable reservation
 CREATING --> ACTIVE: downstream confirmed
 CREATING --> RECONCILING: timeout/unknown
 ACTIVE --> RENEWING: valid request
 RENEWING --> ACTIVE: renewed under current generation
 RENEWING --> RECONCILING: unknown outcome
 RENEWING --> REVOKING: revoke wins
 ACTIVE --> REVOKING: expiry or revoke
 RECONCILING --> ACTIVE: credential found
 RECONCILING --> REVOKING: abort
 REVOKING --> REVOKED: downstream confirmed
 REVOKED --> [*]

docs.title: 13. Deep dive: rotation without downtime
docs.text:
Rotation is a state machine, not UPDATE password. Generate a candidate, install it downstream, verify it independently, publish version N+1, wait for consumers to acknowledge/reload, then revoke N after a bounded overlap. For systems supporting two active credentials this is safe. For single-password accounts, create a replacement principal or coordinate a maintenance window.

Agents write secret.tmp, fsync, rename atomically, and signal/reload the process. Consumers report version, but absence of acknowledgement is not proof of absence. Rollback before old revocation restores routing to N; after revocation it requires generating another credential. Rotation jobs are resumable and each phase is idempotent.

docs.title: 14. Partitioning, scaling, and overload
docs.text:
Partition metadata by tenant/path hash while colocating one secret's versions and leases where practical. Large tenants receive dedicated cells. Reads scale through stateless APIs, encrypted object storage, policy caches, DEK caches, and node agents. Dynamic engines shard by backend/role to enforce downstream quotas. Audit partitions by tenant sequence and fans out asynchronously.

Overload priority is revoke/emergency deny, established lease renewal, ordinary reads, writes, then bulk list/rotation. Bound authentication, KMS unwrap, engine creation, and audit queues separately. Use singleflight for identical cache misses, jitter agent renewal, issue server retry windows, and apply per-tenant fairness. Never fail open authorization because policy/KMS is slow. Eligible agents may serve a bounded cached secret, clearly exposing version/age.

docs.title: 15. Consistency and idempotency
docs.text: Secret metadata/version activation and lease generations are linearizable per secret/lease. Policy and agent caches are bounded eventual; revocation SLO includes their maximum age. Read-after-write through the API can pin minimum version, while an agent may lag. Mutation tokens map retries to one version/job. Dynamic issuance uses durable request records and reconciliation, not exactly-once claims. Audit transport is at least once with stable event IDs and sequence-gap detection.

docs.title: 16. Reliability, failure modes, and recovery
docs.text:
Metadata consensus spans zones; loss of quorum stops writes and sensitive uncached reads. Encrypted object replicas are checksummed. KMS outage allows only explicitly cached decryptions until key-cache expiry. Identity outage permits existing short-lived sessions only within policy. Engine outage blocks issuance but not static reads; revocation queues persist and alert.

Backups contain ciphertext, metadata, policy, and audit checkpoints, encrypted under separate recovery keys held with dual control. Restore into an isolated cell, validate audit/key references, reconcile dynamic credentials, and rotate high-risk secrets before serving. A compromised region is fenced by control epoch and identities, not merely removed from DNS.

docs.title: 17. Multi-region strategy
docs.text: Each secret has a home region for writes and asynchronous encrypted replicas elsewhere. Reads may occur in approved regions only, respecting residency policy. Promotion uses a fenced ownership epoch and documented RPO; concurrent active writers are avoided. Globally needed secrets can use synchronous metadata across regions at WAN latency, but plaintext never replicates, only envelopes. Regional KEKs isolate wrapping authority, but a region authorized to decrypt a replicated secret can disclose that same plaintext. Key separation alone does not isolate the secret value shared across regions.

docs.title: 18. Security and abuse prevention
docs.text:
Apply least privilege, separation of duties, two-person recovery/root operations, mTLS, HSM keys, memory hardening, no swap/core dumps, restricted debug endpoints, signed binaries/bundles, dependency provenance, and immutable external audit copies. Defend against confused deputy paths, token replay, SSRF through engines, policy wildcard mistakes, secret enumeration, response caching, log leakage, clipboard/UI exposure, malicious plugins, and administrator misuse. Honey secrets can detect unexpected access but never replace controls.

Deletion first denies reads, tombstones versions, revokes dynamic effects, removes agent caches, then expires ciphertext and backups. Legal hold prevents physical erasure and is itself audited. Rate and anomaly controls can require step-up approval, but automated workload retrieval must not depend on brittle behavior models.

docs.title: 19. Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure auth/policy decisions, read/write/issue/revoke latency, denial reasons, secret/policy version age, cache/stale use, KMS calls/errors, audit spool lag/gaps, lease expiry/revocation lag, rotation phase/age, engine reconciliation, plaintext response bytes by class, and unusual subject/path access. Never put secret paths, values, tokens, or decrypted data in broad metric labels/traces; use keyed hashes and restricted correlation maps.

Property-test policy precedence, lease fencing, CAS, rotation transitions, and deletion retention. Fuzz parsers and engine responses. Use known-answer crypto and ciphertext-swapping tests. Load-test fleet bootstrap, KMS cold cache, mass rotation, and audit backpressure. Chaos-test identity/KMS/database outage, clock skew, lost responses, stuck revocation, region compromise, corrupt backup, and agent restart. Red teams test exfiltration, privilege escalation, and operator pathways.

docs.title: 20. Important tradeoffs
docs.text:
Central fetch gives fresher revocation but makes every startup dependent on the service; bounded agents improve availability with exposure windows. Static credentials are operationally simple but long-lived; dynamic credentials reduce blast radius while adding downstream reconciliation. Global active-active writes improve convenience but complicate ownership and revocation; home-region authority wins. Durable audit-before-read improves assurance but can reduce availability, so expose it as a tenant policy.

flowchart TD
 ID[Attested short-lived identity] --> PD[Local policy decision]
 CP[Versioned policy control plane] --> PD
 PD --> SC[Regional secret cell]
 SC --> EM[Envelope decrypt via KMS/HSM]
 SC --> DE[Reconciled dynamic engines]
 SC --> AG[Bounded node-agent delivery]
 SC --> AU[Tamper-evident audit]
 RV[Emergency revoke channel] --> PD

docs.title: 21. Final architecture
docs.text: The final design combines attested identity, immutable secret versions, envelope encryption, linearizable activation/leases, compiled deny-by-default policy, reconciled dynamic engines, resumable rotation, bounded agents, and independent audit.

docs.title: 22. Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text: How does a workload obtain its first credential? What if DB creation succeeds but the response is lost? When may an agent serve stale? How do you rotate a one-password system? What does KMS outage do? How are revocations prioritized? How is a restored region prevented from issuing old leases?

docs.title: 23. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate covers identity, policy, envelope encryption, versions, leases, rotation, availability, audit, and threat modeling. An L6 candidate finds bootstrap and revocation invariants, separates planes and failure modes, designs downstream reconciliation and disaster fencing, quantifies stale exposure, and addresses governance, migration, residency, and human operations.

docs.title: 24. Five-minute summary
docs.text: Five-minute summary: authenticate with attested short-lived identity; authorize locally against signed versioned policy; store only immutable AEAD ciphertext with per-version DEKs wrapped by HSM-backed keys; make activation and leases linearizable. Generate dynamic credentials through durable request records and reconciliation, rotate through overlap and acknowledgement, prioritize revoke under overload, and permit only explicitly bounded agent caching. Keep audit tamper-evident, test recovery and compromise, and fail closed whenever uncertainty could disclose to the wrong principal.

docs.title: Design a Service Discovery System
docs.text: This case study owns the registry and control-plane design. Use DNS and Service Discovery for resolver caches, endpoint selection, stale state, and wire-level discovery behavior.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a platform that lets service clients find healthy instances by logical name. Clarify registration authority, health semantics, consistency, DNS versus API discovery, zones, metadata, and control-plane outages. Start with a strongly consistent registry and client polling, then add leases, watches, DNS compatibility, locality-aware resolution, caching, overload protection, federated regions, and safe rollout.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Workloads register instances or are registered by an orchestrator, renew leases, deregister, and resolve service names into endpoints plus metadata. Clients can watch changes. Operators define namespaces, access policy, health gates, traffic weights, subsets, and maintenance drains. Discovery supplies candidates; load balancing chooses among them. It is not a general configuration database or service mesh data path.

This design specializes the distributed coordination pattern: instance registrations are generation-bound ephemeral ownership, registry versions are ordered revisions, and endpoint watches are advisory. Discovery additionally owns health precedence, stale endpoint policy, DNS projection, locality, and load-balancing metadata; those concerns do not belong in the generic coordination layer.

Target registry write availability of 99.99%, regional lookup availability of 99.999%, cached lookup below 5 ms p99, new healthy endpoint visibility within 10 seconds, and failed endpoint removal within 15 seconds under normal conditions. During partition, serving a recently verified set is usually safer than returning empty. Staleness bounds and behavior are explicit by service criticality.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• An instance identity is unique within namespace/service and tied to one owner generation.
  • Only the current lease generation may renew or deregister an instance.
  • Registry revisions are monotonically ordered within a regional namespace shard.
  • A watch resumes after a revision or receives an explicit compaction/reset response; it never silently skips changes.
  • Authorization and namespace boundaries apply before endpoint disclosure.
  • Health state has provenance and version; stale agents cannot overwrite newer orchestrator decisions.
  • Traffic weight zero/drain excludes new selections before endpoint removal, according to bounded propagation SLO.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 10 million service instances, 1 million logical services, five million clients, and 30-second lease renewals: 330,000 renewals/s if every instance writes independently. Batch agent renewals and orchestrator integration can reduce consensus writes by orders of magnitude. At 1 KB/instance, current registry data is 10 GB raw, but watches and QPS dominate. If each client resolves 100 services every minute, origin would receive 8 million lookups/s; local caches and push watches must absorb most. A fleet restart can create millions of simultaneous registrations and watches.

docs.title: Entities and interfaces
docs.text:
Service(namespace, service_name, policy_version, owner, home_region)
Instance(instance_id, service, address, port, zone, protocol, subset,
         owner_generation, lease_id, health, weight, metadata, revision)
Lease(lease_id, owner_generation, ttl, expires_at, last_batch_revision)
HealthReport(instance_id, source, source_generation, status, observed_at)
Change(revision, service, instance_id, operation, value_hash)

PUT    /v1/namespaces/{ns}/services/{svc}/instances/{id}
POST   /v1/leases/{lease}:renew
DELETE /v1/.../instances/{id}       If-Owner-Generation: ...
GET    /v1/.../services/{svc}/endpoints?zone=...
GET    /v1/.../services/{svc}/watch?after_revision=...
DNS    _grpc._tcp.service.namespace.discovery

Registration returns lease generation and registry revision. Endpoint responses include revision, TTL, expiry/stale deadline, locality, protocol, weight, and health provenance. Metadata size and indexed fields are bounded.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 O[Orchestrator/agents] --> G[Regional registry gateways]
 G --> R[(Consensus registry shards)]
 R --> W[Watch fanout]
 W --> C[Node-local/client caches]
 C --> A[Applications and load balancers]
 R --> D[DNS adapters]
 H[Health evaluators] --> R
 P[Policy control plane] --> G
 F[Cross-region federation] <--> R

docs.title: Registration and lease lifecycle
docs.text:
Prefer orchestrator-driven registration because the scheduler already knows desired identity, placement, and process generation. For external workloads, an authenticated agent registers after proving ownership. The registry conditionally creates (service,instance) under owner generation and attaches it to a lease. Batched heartbeats renew many instances with one write and response bitmap.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant A as Node agent
 participant G as Registry gateway
 participant R as Registry leader
 participant W as Watch fanout
 participant C as Client cache
 A->>G: register instances, owner generation
 G->>R: conditional transaction
 R->>R: quorum commit revision
 R-->>A: lease and revision
 R->>W: ordered changes
 W->>C: delta revision
 A->>G: batched lease renewal
 G->>R: renew if generation current

Lease expiry uses server time and a timing wheel for candidates, but expiration is committed through consensus before publishing removal. A delayed timer rechecks lease generation and deadline. After process restart, a higher owner generation fences old heartbeats. Explicit drain first sets weight to zero, waits propagation plus in-flight grace, then deregisters. Immediate deletion is reserved for known-bad endpoints.

TTL selection trades detection speed against renewal/control load. Add random jitter to renewal at roughly one-third TTL and maintain multiple missed-renewal tolerance. A registry outage should not cause all healthy leases to expire at once: any authoritative lease-grace extension must be predeclared and quorum committed while writes remain possible. Without quorum, no leader invents a renewal; clients may independently retain last-known-good endpoints to a declared stale deadline. The policy is visible because excessive staleness can route to dead instances.

docs.title: Health aggregation
docs.text:
Health is not one Boolean. Sources include process readiness, orchestrator state, active probes, passive request failures, and operator drain. Apply precedence: administrative deny and terminated owner dominate; readiness gates new traffic; passive health affects local ejection rather than globally removing an endpoint based on one client's network. Each report includes source generation and timestamp.

A regional evaluator uses hysteresis, requiring several failures to mark unhealthy and several successes to restore, avoiding flaps. Global registry changes should represent broadly verified health. Client load balancers perform fast outlier ejection with bounded duration and share aggregated hints only through an authenticated pipeline resistant to a faulty client. Distinguish STARTING, HEALTHY, DRAINING, UNHEALTHY, and EXPIRED.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> STARTING
 STARTING --> HEALTHY: readiness threshold
 STARTING --> UNHEALTHY: startup deadline
 HEALTHY --> EXPIRED: lease expires
 STARTING --> EXPIRED: lease expires
 HEALTHY --> DRAINING: owner/operator
 HEALTHY --> UNHEALTHY: verified failures
 UNHEALTHY --> HEALTHY: recovery threshold
 DRAINING --> EXPIRED: grace/deregister
 UNHEALTHY --> EXPIRED: lease expires
 EXPIRED --> [*]

docs.title: Resolution, caching, and load balancing
docs.text:
Clients read through a node-local agent or library cache. Cache entries include revision, TTL, stale deadline, and negative-cache status. Singleflight coalesces simultaneous misses. Watches update popular entries; infrequent services poll with conditional revision. On watch disconnect, resume from last applied revision. If history was compacted, fetch a full snapshot and atomically replace the set.

The snapshot must carry revision S; subscribe or resume after S while retaining/buffering that suffix. A plain list followed by a watch of only future events can lose an endpoint update in between. etcd 3.6 API guarantees make watches revision-ordered and resumable within retained history, but not linearizable or bounded-delay. The ten-second propagation target is an operational SLO, not a watch API guarantee (accessed 2026-09-08).

Resolver first filters authorization, protocol, healthy/draining state, compatible subset, and required metadata. Then it prefers same zone, region, and healthy failure domains. Endpoint selection belongs to the load balancer: weighted least-request, power-of-two choices, or consistent hashing for affinity. Discovery weights are coarse rollout intent, not live per-request load. Clients cap connection attempts and use circuit breakers so a stale set does not trigger storms.

DNS provides broad compatibility through A/AAAA/SRV records with TTL. It cannot express rich health generations, authorization per workload, or immediate watches reliably, and recursive resolvers may ignore low TTLs. Use DNS for simple clients; use the native xDS/API path for advanced metadata and fast propagation. Negative DNS caching is bounded because a temporary empty service can otherwise remain invisible.

docs.title: Watch fanout
docs.text: Registry commits append compact change events by revision. Fanout nodes subscribe once per shard and multiplex to clients by service. Clients advertise watched service sets and flow-control credits. Slow watchers receive coalesced latest snapshots or a reset marker instead of retaining unbounded deltas. Periodic full hashes detect drift. Watch events are hints to fetch canonical state when correctness requires; caches atomically apply complete service endpoint generations.

docs.title: Thundering herds
docs.text: A regional restart can align registration, renewal, DNS expiry, and watch reconnect. Use jittered leases/TTLs, exponential reconnect with full jitter, server-issued retry windows, admission queues, batched agent operations, and stale-while-revalidate. Gateways reserve capacity for deregistration/health and established lease renewal before new watches. Clients never tight-loop on an empty answer. Load tests include cold fleet bootstrap, not merely steady state.

docs.title: Sharding and hot services
docs.text: Partition registry by hash of namespace/service so all endpoints and revisions for one service share a shard. A service with hundreds of thousands of endpoints becomes hot; split endpoint storage into buckets under one service generation, then publish a manifest so clients swap a complete set. Watch fanout, not consensus reads, serves millions of consumers. Large platform services receive dedicated fanout trees and node-local snapshots.

docs.title: Safe metadata and protocol evolution
docs.text: Unbounded labels turn discovery into a database and expose secrets. Define typed, size-limited fields and an allowlist of routable metadata. Schema versions support old/new clients. To migrate endpoint identity or shard mapping, dual-publish views from one canonical record, compare them, move consumers, then retire the old projection. Never let two writable registries independently own the same instance generation.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and multi-region
docs.text:
Consensus shards replicate across zones. Gateways route by service hash and cache shard maps. Read/watch fanout scales independently from writes. A tiny control plane manages namespaces, ACLs, shard placement, and federation; regional data planes continue cached resolution during control interruption. Cells cap service count, watch connections, and failure blast radius.

Most services are region-local. Cross-region discovery exports only explicitly global services through federation. Each region remains authority for its instances and publishes namespaced endpoint records with origin region/revision. Consumers merge sets according to routing policy; no last-write conflict exists because ownership is disjoint. A globally named service can prefer local endpoints and fail over to remote after health and capacity checks.

If a regional registry loses quorum, it stops authoritative writes but clients serve last-known-good within stale bounds. Another region does not take over local instance ownership unless the orchestrator also moves workloads and issues a higher federation epoch. This avoids advertising endpoints whose liveness cannot be established.

Backpressure drops verbose metadata and coalesces watch updates before rejecting reads. New registrations may be rate-limited during floods, but established renewals and explicit unhealthy/drain events reserve capacity. Node-local clients use endpoint-set age and error rate to decide whether to fail open to stale endpoints or fail closed for sensitive services.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Registration, lease generation, health precedence, and revision are linearizable per service shard. Caches, DNS, federation, passive health, and endpoint metrics are eventual within bounds. Requests carry operation IDs; owner generation makes registration/renewal idempotent and fences stale agents. Watch delivery is at least once; clients ignore revisions already applied.

Leader loss pauses writes while a quorum elects, but cached reads continue. Agent/network loss eventually expires leases after grace. Fanout loss reconnects/resumes or snapshots. DNS adapter failure affects compatibility clients only. Bad health probes use hysteresis and source isolation. A metadata shard overload isolates affected services; routing maps direct others normally. Clock skew uses leader/server expiry time, not agent clocks.

Reconciliation compares orchestrator desired/running instances with registry ownership, leases without instances, instances without valid owners, fanout snapshot hashes, DNS views, and federation lag. Operators can force drain or revoke an owner generation. Snapshots and consensus logs are backed up and restored into an isolated cell; clients must not trust a restored registry until orchestrator reconciliation and a new cell epoch complete.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Use workload identity and mutual TLS, namespace ACLs, signed agent credentials, encrypted metadata, audit for policy/drain changes, and network controls preventing external access. Do not store secrets in labels. Defend against fake registration, endpoint poisoning, lease theft, namespace enumeration, watch amplification, metadata bombs, and compromised health reporters. Quotas bound services, instances, labels, watches, and renewal rates.

Measure registration/renewal latency, lease expiry reason, endpoint propagation delay, registry revision and apply lag, stale-cache age, empty responses, watch connections/resets/backlog, DNS TTL behavior, health flaps, fanout amplification, shard skew, quorum state, orchestrator drift, federation lag, load-balancer no-endpoint errors, and traffic to draining/dead endpoints. Trace revisions and identities, not sensitive metadata.

Property-test owner/lease fencing, expiry races, revision application, snapshot replacement, health precedence, and drain ordering. Model-check leader and timer races. Fuzz metadata and DNS names. Load-test fleet restart, one hot service, millions of watches, and synchronized TTL expiration. Chaos-test quorum loss, fanout partition, stale agents, clock changes, bad probes, DNS cache behavior, and regional isolation. Synthetic services continuously register, resolve, connect, drain, and verify propagation SLOs.

docs.title: Important tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Self-registration is simple but can leave stale identity; orchestrator authority is stronger where available. Aggressive TTL removes failures quickly but increases writes and mass-expiry risk. Strong reads on every request are current but make discovery a latency dependency; watched local caches win. DNS is universal but semantically weak. Globally writable registry promises convenience but risks split ownership; region-owned endpoints with federation are clearer.

flowchart TD
 O[Orchestrator or authenticated agent] --> L[Generation-fenced lease]
 L --> R[Zonal consensus registry shard]
 H[Versioned health sources] --> R
 R --> W[Credit-aware watch fanout]
 W --> C[Atomic node-local endpoint cache]
 C --> B[Locality-aware client load balancer]
 R --> D[DNS compatibility projection]
 R --> F[Region-owned federation]

The final architecture stores instance ownership, lease, health, and service revision in zonally replicated shards. Orchestrators or agents batch generation-fenced updates. Fanout nodes transform ordered changes into bounded watches; node-local caches provide stale-aware, low-latency resolution. Native clients perform locality-aware load balancing, while DNS is a constrained projection. Federation merges region-owned records without shared writes.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. Should clients return no endpoints or stale endpoints during registry failure?
  2. How does lease expiry avoid a stale timer deleting a new process?
  3. Why should one client's passive failures not globally remove an endpoint?
  4. How do millions of clients watch one platform service?
  5. What breaks when DNS TTL is treated as a strict freshness guarantee?
  6. How is a service drained without dropping in-flight requests?
  7. How does cross-region federation prevent split ownership?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should define registration, leases, health, resolution, watches, caches, TTL, sharding, DNS tradeoffs, and main failures. They should separate discovery from load balancing and explain stale behavior.

An L6 candidate should define ownership/health precedence, propagation and stale budgets, herd control, hot-service fanout, control/data-plane and cell isolation, region federation, migration, and restore reconciliation. They should connect TTL, availability, operational load, security, and service criticality.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Register endpoints through an orchestrator or authenticated agent into a zonal consensus shard. Tie each instance to an owner generation and server-timed lease so stale processes and expiry callbacks cannot overwrite replacements. Aggregate versioned health sources with precedence and hysteresis; drain by publishing zero weight, waiting propagation, then deregistering. Publish ordered revisions through credit-aware multiplexed watches into atomic node-local caches. Clients filter compatible healthy endpoints and perform locality-aware balancing; they can serve last-known-good endpoints to a policy-specific stale deadline during control outages. Use DNS only as a limited projection. Hash services across shards, dedicate fanout for hot services, batch renewals, and jitter lease/watch recovery to prevent herds. Regions own their endpoints and federate explicit global services. Observe propagation, cache age, renewals, watch resets, health flaps, shard skew, and orchestrator drift; reserve overload capacity for renewals and removals.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Scope rich-text or plain-text documents, concurrent editing, presence, comments, offline work, history, and sharing. First define convergence and authorization, then compare operational transformation (OT) with conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs). This design chooses server-ordered OT for bounded online documents, while showing when a CRDT is better.

docs.title: Requirements, invariants, and estimates
docs.text:
Multiple users edit a document and see remote changes within 200 ms normally. Clients reconnect and catch up without losing acknowledged edits. Owners share/revoke access, history supports recovery, and periodic snapshots bound replay. Presence and cursors are ephemeral. Assume 10 million daily editors, one million concurrent connections, 20 operations per concurrently connected editor per minute, or roughly 330,000 ops/s while that one-million-editor concurrency holds. At 200 bytes/op, ingress is 66 MB/s; retained operation logs and snapshots reach petabytes over years. One viral document creates a hot key independent of global averages.

  • Every acknowledged operation is durable and belongs to one document revision.
  • Authorized replicas converge to identical content after receiving the same accepted operations.
  • Revision numbers increase monotonically per document; gaps may occur after failover.
  • Operation IDs make retries idempotent.
  • Revocation blocks future operations and sync; it cannot erase content already downloaded.
  • Snapshots correspond to a known log revision and are checksum-verifiable.
  • Presence loss never affects document correctness.

docs.title: Data model and APIs
docs.text:
Document(doc_id, owner_id, title, head_revision, snapshot_revision, state, acl_version)
Acl(doc_id, principal_id, role, version)
Operation(doc_id, revision, op_id, actor_id, session_id, connection_epoch,
          base_revision, payload, created_at)
Snapshot(doc_id, revision, object_key, checksum, format_version)
Comment(comment_id, doc_id, anchor, body, state, version)
ClientSession(session_id, doc_id, actor_id, last_ack_revision, lease_expiry)
GatewayLease(gateway_id, region, state, capacity, lease_expiry)
SessionRoute(session_id, gateway_id, doc_id, connection_epoch, lease_expiry)
SessionFence(doc_id, session_id, current_connection_epoch)

POST /v1/documents
GET  /v1/documents/{id}?revision=...
POST /v1/documents/{id}/operations   Idempotency-Key: <op_id>
GET  /v1/documents/{id}/operations?after_revision=...
PUT  /v1/documents/{id}/acl/{principal}
POST /v1/documents/{id}/comments
GET  /v1/collaboration?doc_id=...     WebSocket

Operations express retain/insert/delete for text or typed tree edits for rich text. A schema version makes migrations explicit.

docs.title: Architecture and flows
docs.text:
flowchart TD
 C[Editor clients] --> G[Collaboration gateways]
 G --> S[Document session service]
 S --> A[ACL service]
 S --> L[Document leader]
 L --> D[(Operation log + outbox)]
 D --> B[Regional event bus]
 B --> G
 D --> P[Snapshot workers]
 P --> O[(Object storage)]
 C --> H[History API]
 H --> D
 H --> O
    subgraph LiveLane[Live collaboration]
      G
      S
      A
      L
      D
      B
    end
    subgraph HistoryLane[Snapshots and history]
      P
      O
      H
    end

The WebSocket connection plane is independent of document ordering. Global edge routing chooses a healthy regional gateway, which authenticates the handshake, owns socket backpressure and heartbeats, and forwards edit frames to the document plane. Gateways never become revision authority. A session registry stores a short lease from session_id to gateway_id, document, user, and monotonically increasing connection epoch. A gateway registry advertises READY, DRAINING, or UNHEALTHY, current sockets, and capacity. A compact fanout directory maps doc_id to the set of gateways with local subscribers, so each committed operation crosses the bus once per interested gateway rather than once per socket.

flowchart LR
    C[Clients] --> E[Global edge]
    E --> W[WebSocket gateway pool]
    W --> SR[(Session and gateway registry)]
    W --> R[Document router]
    R --> L[Fenced document leaders]
    L --> D[(Revision log and outbox)]
    D --> B[Regional broadcast bus]
    B --> FD[Document fanout directory]
    FD --> W
    W --> C
    P[Presence service] <--> W

With one million concurrent sockets and a tested limit of 10,000 sockets per gateway, the floor is 100 gateways. Provisioning 40 percent failover and drain headroom gives 140. At roughly 32 KB of socket buffers and protocol state, the fleet holds about 32 GB before process overhead. A 200-byte leased route per connection is about 200 MB raw and can be regionally sharded; it is reconstructible from gateway heartbeats, so it is not part of document durability.

On planned drain, the gateway changes its registry state before rejecting new sockets, sends clients a RECONNECT(target_region,resume_token,last_ack_revision,connection_epoch) control frame, and keeps existing connections for a bounded grace period. The edge excludes draining gateways. The reconnect presents the signed resume token; the registry compare-and-swaps to a higher connection epoch, making late frames from the old socket stale. Every edit carries both session_id and that connection_epoch. The receiving gateway checks that it owns the current route, and the document leader checks the current session epoch again immediately before append; therefore a frame already forwarded by the old socket cannot commit after the document authority has durably advanced its session fence. The registry CAS alone is not that linearization point. The new gateway subscribes, requests replay after last_ack_revision, then enables sends. On an abrupt gateway loss there is no redirect frame: lease expiry and missed heartbeats remove it, clients reconnect with jitter, resend unacknowledged operation IDs under the new epoch, and rebuild lossy presence.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Old gateway
    participant R as Route registry
    participant C as Client
    participant N as New gateway
    participant L as Document leader
    O->>R: Mark DRAINING
    O-->>C: RECONNECT with signed resume token
    C->>N: Open socket with token and last revision
    N->>R: CAS to next connection epoch
    R-->>N: session ID and new connection epoch
    N->>L: Advance durable session fence to new epoch
    N->>L: Replay after last acknowledged revision
    L-->>N: Missing operations and current head
    N-->>C: RESUMED at current head
    C->>N: Resend IDs with session ID and new epoch
    N->>L: Forward edit with session ID and new epoch
    L->>L: Conditional append against durable session fence
    O->>O: Close after grace period
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant A as Client A
 participant L as Document leader
 participant D as Operation log
 participant B as Client B
 A->>L: op X with session ID and connection epoch, based on r10
 L->>L: transform X through revisions 11..12
 L->>D: append r13 only if durable session fence matches
 D-->>A: ack op X, revision 13
 L-->>B: operation revision 13
 B->>B: transform against unacknowledged local ops

The leader serializes accepted operations, validates the current (session_id, connection_epoch) fence, ACL, document-leader epoch, version, and schema, transforms stale-base operations, and commits before broadcast. SessionFence is colocated with the operation authority: reconnect advances it before the new socket may send, and every append conditionally requires the supplied epoch to equal current_connection_epoch. Thus a takeover that wins first makes an old frame's append fail; a cache-only gateway or non-atomic registry lookup is insufficient. Clients retain unacknowledged local operations and rebase incoming operations through them.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Offline client
 participant S as Sync service
 participant O as Snapshot store
 participant L as Operation log
 C->>S: reconnect(last revision, pending ops)
 alt history retained
   S->>L: operations after revision
   S-->>C: catch-up operations
 else history compacted
   S->>O: latest snapshot
   S-->>C: snapshot + subsequent operations
 end
 C->>S: pending ops with original IDs/bases

docs.title: OT versus CRDT
docs.text:
OT transforms concurrent operations relative to a server-defined order. For text, insert and delete pairs need complete, tested transform functions satisfying convergence properties. It uses compact positions and gives the server a natural revision, ACL, undo, and audit boundary. Its weaknesses are central sequencing, difficult transform correctness, and complicated offline branches when base history is compacted.

A sequence CRDT gives each element a stable identifier and defines commutative merge rules. Replicas can edit offline and exchange operations without one total-order leader; duplicates are harmless when operation IDs are unique. Costs include identifier/tombstone metadata, garbage collection requiring causal knowledge, less intuitive undo, schema evolution, and potentially unbounded document overhead. Rich-text tree CRDT semantics remain product-specific rather than automatic.

Concern OT CRDT Online client/server editing Natural fit Good fit Long offline, peer-to-peer Complex rebasing Strong fit Metadata size Usually compact Larger IDs/tombstones Central authority/audit Natural Must be layered on Algorithm risk Transform matrix Merge/GC/schema rules Undo Server revision based Intent-preserving undo is harder

Choose OT here because sessions are server-mediated, ACL changes require authority, documents have bounded size, and low metadata overhead matters. Choose a CRDT if local-first multi-day offline editing or peer-to-peer operation is a primary requirement. Do not combine both without a precise semantic boundary.

flowchart TD
 A{Primary requirement?} -->|Server-mediated, low latency| B[Server-ordered OT]
 A -->|Offline-first or peer-to-peer| C[CRDT]
 B --> D[Transform against accepted revisions]
 C --> E[Merge stable element IDs]
 D --> F[Periodic snapshot and compact log]
 E --> G[Causal GC and metadata control]

docs.title: Transform correctness and rich text
docs.text: Text OT defines deterministic tie-breaking for insert/insert at one position, overlap rules for delete/delete, and position shifts for insert/delete. Property tests check convergence for every operation pair and permutations of concurrent edits. Rich text should use typed tree operations such as insert node, delete range, and set mark; manipulating serialized HTML creates invalid structures. Unsupported schema versions are rejected or translated at a version gateway.

docs.title: Offline sync and compaction
docs.text: Clients persist a base revision, local operation IDs, and pending operations. If the base remains in the log, the server transforms them through intervening history. If compacted, the client loads a snapshot and may reapply intent; for complex stale edits, present an explicit conflict copy instead of silently dropping content. Snapshot creation reads through revision R, writes checksum and format, then conditionally publishes the pointer. Logs before the oldest supported client/session revision can be archived.

docs.title: Hot documents and backpressure
docs.text: One leader establishes order, so a viral document has a finite write ceiling. Batch keystrokes over 20-50 ms, coalesce presence, and cap collaborators/edit rate. Separate read-only viewers into broadcast relays. If overloaded, drop cursor updates first, reduce rendering frequency, then switch excess users to read-only rather than accepting edits that cannot meet durability. Splitting one document by sections works only if cross-section operations and global undo semantics are constrained.

docs.title: Active-document memory residency
docs.text:
A document leader is a durable ordering role; its materialized document is a bounded cache. On the first editor, the owner acquires or confirms its epoch, enters LOADING, reads the latest checksum-valid snapshot, and replays the tail to the current head before admitting edits. ACTIVE state is pinned while sockets, pending commands, snapshot work, or replay consumers reference it. After the final session leaves, an idle timer allows quick reconnects. Eviction first stops admission for that local instance, flushes committed outbox progress and optional snapshot work, records the head revision, and only then releases memory; durability never depends on the heap image.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ABSENT
    ABSENT --> LOADING: first session or command
    LOADING --> ACTIVE: snapshot and tail verified
    LOADING --> FAILED: corrupt state or lost epoch
    ACTIVE --> IDLE: no sessions or pending work
    IDLE --> ACTIVE: reconnect before timeout
    IDLE --> EVICTING: idle timeout or memory pressure
    EVICTING --> ABSENT: pins zero and checkpoint recorded
    EVICTING --> ACTIVE: new session cancels eviction
    ACTIVE --> DRAINING: leader move or shutdown
    DRAINING --> ABSENT: successor ready and old epoch fenced
    FAILED --> ABSENT: release ownership

Use a weighted LRU within a hard per-cell memory budget, charging tree bytes, transform tail, undo metadata, and subscriber indexes to the document and tenant. If an average resident document consumes 120 KB, 10,000 active documents require about 1.2 GB; reserve additional headroom for a few large documents and reject or relocate before the process swaps. Oversized documents can retain only a bounded transform window in memory and page cold tree sections if product operations permit it. Memory pressure evicts idle documents first, then rejects new opens; it does not discard acknowledged operations or silently move active leaders.

docs.title: Comments, anchors, and undo
docs.text: Anchors are logical ranges transformed alongside text operations; deleted ranges collapse according to product rules. Comments have canonical lifecycle records and versioned anchors. Undo should invert the user's intent relative to subsequent operations, not simply restore an old snapshot. The server retains enough authored-operation metadata to transform inverse operations.

docs.title: Partitioning, regions, consistency, and failure
docs.text:
Partition documents by ID into cells; operation storage further ranges by revision. Huge tenants can receive dedicated cells. Snapshots use immutable object keys. Assign each open document a leased leader in its home region. Gateways are global but forward edits to that leader. Synchronous zonal replication precedes acknowledgement; async disaster-recovery replication follows. Thus acknowledged-edit durability covers the synchronous failure domains only; a regional-loss no-loss promise requires surviving synchronous acknowledgement or recovery of the complete acknowledged prefix before promotion. Failover uses epochs so the old leader cannot append. Clients resend unacknowledged operation IDs after reconnect.

Document operations are strongly ordered per document. Presence, search, notifications, comments counters, and cross-region replicas are eventual. ACL updates are strongly checked before every accepted operation; gateways receive invalidations but socket membership is not authority. Operation uniqueness prevents duplicate append. An outbox guarantees committed broadcasts can replay.

Leader loss causes reconnect, fencing, and resend. Gateway loss loses only presence and unacknowledged transport. Registry loss prevents optimized routing but gateways can retain existing sockets and the edge can use health-based placement; leases rebuild from heartbeats. Bus loss delays broadcasts; clients catch up from the log. Snapshot corruption falls back to the prior checksum-verified snapshot and replay. A poison operation is rejected before append. Cell overload has per-document and tenant admission limits. Backups plus immutable logs enable point-in-time recovery and audit.

docs.title: Security, privacy, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Authenticate sessions and authorize open, edit, comment, share, export, and history independently. Encrypt transport/storage, isolate tenant keys where required, audit shares and administrative access, sanitize pasted rich content, scan attachments, and rate-limit share spam. Revocation terminates sessions promptly. Data deletion includes snapshots, operation logs, search, comments, exports, and backups under published retention. Client-side E2EE would prevent server transforms/search and requires a different trust architecture.

Measure operation acceptance and broadcast latency, transform depth, pending-client queue, duplicate retries, leader moves, hot-document rates, snapshot duration/failure, replay length, reconnects, ACL-denied operations, presence drops, and convergence mismatches from sampled client hashes. Trace by doc/op IDs without content.

Test OT algebra with property-based concurrent operation permutations, fuzz rich-text trees, replay duplicates/reorder, race ACL revocation with edits, crash leaders after commit before ack, corrupt snapshots, and reconnect from every compaction boundary. Drain gateways while edits are in flight, kill them without notice, expire registry leases, duplicate resume tokens, and assert that connection epochs plus operation IDs prevent split sessions and duplicate commits. Repeatedly hydrate and evict documents at snapshot boundaries, inject memory pressure and lost leader epochs, and verify that no leader admits edits before replay reaches the recorded head. Load-test one viral document, one million mostly idle sockets, reconnect storms with jitter, and many normal documents. Run cross-version client compatibility, schema migration, chaos, and restore drills. CRDT implementations additionally test arbitrary merge order, causal GC, and tombstone resurrection.

Document-format migration uses an explicit reader/writer compatibility window. New servers first read both formats, snapshot workers produce shadow snapshots, and validators render both to normalized trees for comparison. Only then do leaders emit new operations. Old clients receive a capability error or a translated safe subset rather than corrupting unknown node types. Rollback remains possible until the old log and snapshots pass the retention boundary.

Sampled replica hashes provide an additional convergence alarm, but mismatches trigger evidence capture and repair from canonical revisions rather than automatic client overwrite.

docs.title: L6 mechanisms: transforms, protocol, and compaction
A worked OT transform matrix
docs.text:
Use half-open text positions over Unicode code points in one normalized text leaf. Let I(p,s,id) insert string s before position p, and D(p,n) delete [p,p+n). T(a,b) rewrites operation a so it preserves its intent after concurrent operation b. Inserts at the same position are ordered by (actor_id,op_id); the lower key appears first. Deletes never delete concurrently inserted text, and overlapping deletes remove each original character once.

a transformed against b I(q,t) D(q,m) I(p,s) Shift to p+len(t) when q<p, or when q=p and b wins the tie; otherwise keep p Keep p when p<=q; shift to p-m when p>=q+m; clamp to q when insertion falls inside the deleted range D(p,n) Keep when q>=p+n; shift start by len(t) when q<=p; when p<q<p+n, split into D(p,q-p) and D(q+len(t),p+n-q) so inserted text survives Map both endpoints through x -> x for x<=q, q for q<x<q+m, and x-m for x>=q+m; the new delete is the mapped half-open interval and may become a no-op

Worked insert/insert: replicas start with cat. A sends I(1,"X",A7) and B sends I(1,"Y",B2). If A7 < B2, the server accepts A as revision 11 (cXat), transforms B to I(2,"Y",B2), and reaches cXYat. A first processes its ordered acknowledgement of A at r11, then applies canonical B at r12 without shifting B through A again. B first processes canonical A at r11 and rebases its pending B, then retires B on its r12 acknowledgement. Both render cXYat.

Worked delete/insert: start with abcdef; A sends D(1,4) to remove bcde, while B sends I(3,"X",B9) after c. If A is first, B's position is clamped to 1 and the result is aXf. If B is first, A becomes a compound deletion of transformed intervals [1,3) and [4,6), applied right-to-left: it removes bc and de, but not concurrent X, again producing aXf. A production implementation represents a compound result as one retain/delete component list and normalizes adjacent components before append.

The matrix is necessary but not sufficient. Tests enumerate every pair around boundaries 0, document length, equal positions, full overlap, containment, and empty output. Property tests assert apply(apply(S,a),T(b,a)) == apply(apply(S,b),T(a,b)); three-way tests assert transformation-path independence for all permutations. All implementations explicitly convert positions to the same Unicode code-point coordinate system; normalization alone does not reconcile UTF-16 code units with code points. Normalize inserted strings by the agreed rule before assigning positions, and do not renormalize an entire document after every operation without an explicit position-remapping operation.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant A as Client A
 participant L as Fenced leader
 participant B as Client B
 A->>L: I(1,X,A7), base 10
 B->>L: I(1,Y,B2), base 10
 L->>L: append A at r11
 L->>L: transform B through r11 to I(2,Y)
 L-->>A: ACK A r11 and OP B r12
 L-->>B: OP A r11 and ACK B r12
 A->>A: retire A7, then apply canonical B at r12
 B->>B: retire B2 and render through r12
 Note over A,B: Both render cXYat

docs.title: Wire payload, acknowledgement, and resync
docs.text:
An edit frame is {doc_id, session_id, connection_epoch, leader_epoch, op_id, actor_id, base_revision, client_seq, schema_version, components, base_hash}. connection_epoch fences an older socket for the same session; leader_epoch fences an old document owner. Both must match current authority before append. client_seq detects a missing local send but does not determine document order. The acknowledgement is {op_id, accepted_revision, transformed_components, head_revision, session_id, connection_epoch, leader_epoch, result_hash}. Returning canonical transformed components lets the sender replace its optimistic form rather than infer what the server committed. An OP broadcast carries revision, original ID, canonical components, author, and resulting hash. NACK is typed: ACL_STALE, SCHEMA_UNSUPPORTED, BASE_COMPACTED, CONNECTION_EPOCH_STALE, LEADER_EPOCH_STALE, or INVALID_OPERATION; clients must not retry all failures blindly.

The client keeps shadow at last_ack_revision, one in-flight batch, and a buffered local batch. A remote operation applies to shadow, then transforms through in-flight and buffered operations before applying to the visible document. ACK retires exactly the matching IDs and advances the shadow using the server's canonical operation. A revision gap, connection- or leader-epoch change, or hash mismatch pauses edits and sends RESYNC(session_id,connection_epoch,last_ack_revision,last_hash,pending_ids).

flowchart TD
 A[Receive ACK or remote OP] --> B{Expected session, epochs, and next revision?}
 B -->|Yes| C[Apply to shadow]
 C --> D[Transform through in-flight and buffer]
 D --> E[Update visible tree and hash]
 B -->|No| F[Freeze outbound edit frames]
 E --> G{Hash agrees?}
 G -->|Yes| H[Continue]
 G -->|No| F
 F --> I{Base retained?}
 I -->|Yes| J[Replay missing canonical ops]
 I -->|No| K[Load checksum snapshot plus tail]
 J --> L[Rebase pending IDs]
 K --> L
 L --> M{Intent validates?}
 M -->|Yes| H
 M -->|No| N[Open conflict copy for user recovery]

Resync returns either {snapshot_revision:null, operations, head_hash} or {snapshot_url, snapshot_revision, snapshot_checksum, operations_after_snapshot, head_hash}. The server deduplicates pending IDs already committed and transforms only the remainder. The client verifies the server hash against canonical shadow, then atomically replaces it, reapplies valid pending intent, and only then unfreezes transmission. The visible tree with unacknowledged local edits is not expected to equal the server hash.

docs.title: Throughput, snapshots, undo, and offline bounds
docs.text:
At the stated 330,000 ops/s, 200-byte logical operations become about 66 MB/s raw and roughly 5.7 TB/day. With three synchronous copies plus index/outbox overhead of 2x, provision roughly 66 MB/s * 3 * 2 = 396 MB/s sustained writes and about 34 TB/day before compression and expiry. Across one million active documents this is easy to shard; a single document remains serialized. Batching 20 keystrokes/s from 1,000 editors into 50 ms frames yields at most 20,000 primitive edits/s but about 20 leader batches/s per editor, so transform CPU is controlled by limiting both accepted batches/s and maximum components/batch. A 10,000-component pending window triggers read-only overload before quadratic transform work grows without bound.

Snapshot on whichever comes first: 10,000 accepted components, 5 MB of log tail, or five minutes for active documents. A worker reads immutable revision R, materializes the typed tree, writes {format_version,R,root_hash} to object storage, then compare-and-swaps the document pointer only if it advances the prior snapshot. Keep a 24-hour hot tail and 30-day compressed archive as an example product policy. Compaction watermark is min(oldest supported session base, undo horizon, migration hold, replication checkpoint), not simply the latest snapshot.

Undo records an intent group {actor_id, authored_op_ids, before_context, after_context}. To undo, fetch each canonical authored operation, invert it in reverse order, and transform the inverse through every later operation. Deleted content needed by the inverse lives in encrypted undo metadata until the undo horizon. Undo never rewinds another user's changes: undoing A's insertion deletes the surviving descendants of A's inserted span, while concurrently inserted B text remains. If later structure makes the inverse invalid, disable that undo entry instead of restoring a historical snapshot.

Offline clients compact adjacent local inserts/deletes only while preserving stable operation IDs through a supersedes list. Fold only operations known never to have been submitted; resolve possibly committed IDs first, since partially accepting a composite would duplicate or erase intent. For example, typing hello, deleting lo, and adding p in one untouched leaf can upload I(p,"help") with the original IDs; crossing a remote anchor, comment boundary, or tree node forbids that fold. Once the server's history no longer covers the base, plain positional operations cannot be safely rebased from the snapshot alone. The client performs a three-way intent merge using its saved base, current snapshot, and local result, or creates a conflict document. This is the explicit offline bound that avoids pretending OT is a CRDT.

docs.title: Rich-text tree operations
docs.text:
The canonical document is a schema-versioned tree with stable node IDs: block nodes contain inline leaves, and marks are normalized attributes rather than overlapping HTML tags. Operations include insert_node(parent_id,index,node), delete_node(node_id), move_node(node_id,new_parent,index), splice_text(leaf_id,pos,delete_count,text), and set_mark(leaf_id,start,end,key,value). The leader rejects cycles, unknown parents, invalid child types, and edits against deleted node IDs.

Transforms use identity before position. Concurrent text splices in one leaf use the text matrix. Sibling inserts shift indexes with the same deterministic tie-break. A node edit against deletion becomes a no-op with an audit reason; concurrent moves of one node use last ordered move while preserving a single parent. Marks are interval operations transformed with text, split around deletions, and coalesced when adjacent values match. Structural normalization, such as merging adjacent equivalent text leaves, runs deterministically after each canonical operation and emits an ID-remap table in the ACK so cursors, comments, and pending edits retain anchors.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Server OT provides compact operations, authoritative revisions, and straightforward enterprise policy, but limits one document's write throughput and offline independence. CRDTs improve decentralized convergence but spend metadata and add causal cleanup complexity. Snapshotting bounds startup but creates compaction compatibility obligations. A separate connection plane allows independent socket scaling and graceful gateway drains, at the cost of leased registries, reconnect protocol, and one more routing hop. Bounded document residency protects cells from memory exhaustion but makes hydration latency and eviction correctness explicit. Section sharding scales only when the product accepts weaker cross-section semantics. Durable operations must never share a fate with lossy presence.

flowchart TD
 A[Global authenticated gateway] --> B[Fenced home-region document leader]
 B --> C[OT transform and schema validation]
 C --> D[(Replicated revision log + outbox)]
 D --> E[Regional broadcast relays]
 D --> F[Checksum snapshots and archive]
 G[Strong ACL versions] --> B
 H[Reconnect/offline rebase] --> B
 I[Ephemeral presence] --> E

docs.title: Questions, levels, and five-minute summary
docs.text:
1. Which transform properties guarantee convergence?
  2. When does a CRDT beat OT for this product?
  3. How can logs be compacted while offline clients exist?
  4. What happens after commit but before sender acknowledgement?
  5. Can a viral document be partitioned without changing semantics?
  6. How does revocation interact with already downloaded content?

L5 candidates should define operations, per-document ordering, retry IDs, snapshots, realtime reconnect, ACL checks, and OT/CRDT tradeoffs. L6 candidates should make convergence testable, negotiate offline and undo semantics, design fencing/compaction/migrations, quantify hot-document ceilings, isolate presence, and connect residency, audit, and deletion to product guarantees.

In five minutes: route each document to a fenced home-region leader. Clients send idempotent operations based on a revision; the leader checks current ACL and schema, transforms through intervening OT operations, durably appends the next revision and outbox, then broadcasts. Clients transform incoming operations against pending local edits and reconnect by cursor; snapshots plus subsequent logs bound recovery. Keep presence lossy and separate. OT fits server-mediated, compact, auditable editing; choose a CRDT when long offline or peer-to-peer editing justifies stable element IDs, tombstones, and causal GC. Partition by document, protect viral documents with batching/read-only relays, and continuously property-test convergence, failover, compaction, and revocation races.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a multi-tenant service that accepts transactional and bulk email, renders templates, enforces consent, sends through public mail infrastructure, and tracks delivery. Start with durable acceptance and one outbound provider, then add scheduling, reputation isolation, retries, inbound feedback, and regional operation. The hard part is not SMTP; it is preserving intent while handling ambiguous delivery, hostile input, changing policy, and mailbox-provider throttling.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Clients submit single messages or campaigns, select an immutable template, schedule delivery, cancel unsent work, and query status. Recipients can unsubscribe by category. Operators manage domains, DKIM keys, IP pools, provider routes, quotas, and suppression lists. We support attachments by reference, webhooks, bounces, complaints, and opens only where privacy policy permits.

Transactional mail should be accepted in 200 ms p99 and normally handed to a remote server within 10 seconds. Campaigns may complete over hours. Availability is 99.99% for acceptance and 99.9% for status. A successful API response means durable acceptance, never inbox placement. Search, analytics, and open tracking are projections and may lag.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• (tenant_id, idempotency_key) identifies one immutable logical message and request hash.
  • A message references one immutable template version and one normalized recipient set.
  • Current suppression and legal policy win over queued promotional work.
  • Each SMTP/provider submission has a stable attempt ID; retries create auditable attempts.
  • Status is monotonic within a defined lattice; late bounces may refine DELIVERED to BOUNCED but cannot resurrect cancelled work.
  • Transactional capacity is reserved and cannot be consumed by campaigns.
  • A sending domain uses only authorized identities and current signing keys.
  • We promise at-least-once processing, not exactly-once arrival.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 5 billion single-recipient messages/day, 58,000/s average, 500,000/s peak, with 2 KB metadata and 12 KB rendered body on average. Metadata is 10 TB/day; bodies add 60 TB/day before compression and replication. Attachments live in object storage and are referenced, avoiding queue inflation. Reusing each SMTP connection for 20 sequential deliveries reduces connection establishments to about 25,000/s, not recipient deliveries: 500,000 recipient outcomes/s still require tracking. Concurrent sockets equal delivery rate times mean transaction duration for non-pipelined workers; connection reuse alone does not divide that concurrency by 20. Multi-recipient SMTP transactions are a separate optimization limited to compatible bodies and destination routing. Domain-specific throttles, not global bandwidth, set effective capacity. Retain detailed attempts for 30 days, aggregate metrics for 13 months, and suppression hashes until policy allows deletion.

docs.title: Data model and interfaces
docs.text:
Message(message_id, tenant_id, idempotency_key, template_version, category,
        sender_identity, scheduled_at, state, policy_version, created_at)
Recipient(message_id, recipient_id, address_ciphertext, address_hash, state)
Attempt(attempt_id, recipient_id, route, remote_domain, try_no, state, response, next_at)
Template(template_id, version, subject, body_uri, variables_schema, checksum)
Suppression(address_hash, tenant_scope, category, reason, version, expires_at)
Domain(domain_id, tenant_id, dkim_key_ref, dns_state, reputation_pool)
Feedback(event_id, attempt_id, type, occurred_at, raw_uri)

POST   /v1/messages                 Idempotency-Key: 7f...
POST   /v1/campaigns
GET    /v1/messages/{message_id}
DELETE /v1/messages/{message_id}
PUT    /v1/suppressions/{address_hash}
POST   /v1/feedback/{provider}

Creation transactionally writes the message, recipients, and outbox record. Pagination uses opaque (created_at,message_id) cursors, not offsets. Cancellation is conditional on state/version and cannot recall bytes already accepted by a remote mail server.
