docs.title: Acceptance, rendering, and delivery
docs.text:
Validate sender ownership, template variables, size, recipient limits, and tenant budget before acceptance. Store encrypted addresses and a keyed hash for suppression lookup. Rendering consumes the immutable template and bounded variables, writes the body to object storage, and emits a recipient task. Workers fetch bodies just in time, preventing large payloads in the broker.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant A as API
 participant D as Database
 participant O as Orchestrator
 participant W as Sender
 participant X as Remote MX
 C->>A: message plus idempotency key
 A->>D: commit message and outbox
 D-->>C: accepted(message_id)
 D->>O: committed intent
 O->>O: consent, render, route
 O->>W: recipient task and deadline
 W->>X: SMTP transaction with attempt ID
 X-->>W: 2xx, 4xx, 5xx, or timeout
 W->>D: conditional attempt transition

The scheduling algorithm uses weighted deficit round robin across tenants inside separate transactional and bulk lanes. Each remote domain has an adaptive token bucket. Success slowly increases concurrency; 421/450 responses decrease it multiplicatively and add jitter. A tenant cannot borrow reserved transactional capacity. Expired password-reset mail is discarded rather than delivered late.

docs.title: Suppression and consent
docs.text: At send time, join category policy, tenant opt-out, global hard-bounce/complaint suppression, and jurisdiction. Promotional messages fail closed when the policy store is unavailable. Transactional mail may proceed from a recent signed policy snapshot only for explicitly approved categories. One-click unsubscribe tokens bind recipient hash, tenant, category, and expiry. Changes emit versioned events. The authoritative send claim atomically checks current policy/cancellation generation and changes QUEUED to SUBMITTING; stale cache comparison alone is insufficient. Define cancellation as preventing claims ordered after its commit. An already claimed or in-flight SMTP transaction may still complete and must be reported as too late or uncertain, since a database check cannot atomically revoke bytes at an external MX.

docs.title: Attempt state machine and retry
docs.text:
The diagram shows the logical recipient lifecycle; each network submission also retains a separate immutable attempt identity and outcome history.

stateDiagram-v2
 direction LR
 state Cancellable {
   ACCEPTED --> RENDERED
   RENDERED --> QUEUED
   DEFERRED --> QUEUED
 }
 Cancellable --> CANCELLED: cancellation wins before submission
 [*] --> ACCEPTED
 ACCEPTED --> SUPPRESSED
 QUEUED --> SUPPRESSED
 DEFERRED --> SUPPRESSED
 QUEUED --> SUBMITTING
 SUBMITTING --> ACCEPTED_REMOTE
 SUBMITTING --> UNKNOWN: final acknowledgement lost
 UNKNOWN --> ACCEPTED_REMOTE: provider evidence
 UNKNOWN --> DEFERRED: explicit duplicate-tolerant retry policy
 SUBMITTING --> DEFERRED
 SUBMITTING --> FAILED
 ACCEPTED_REMOTE --> BOUNCED
 ACCEPTED_REMOTE --> DELIVERED
 DELIVERED --> BOUNCED: later authoritative failure evidence

Cancellable groups the four pre-submission states. It is a visual grouping, not an additional persisted status. Cancellation must win the dispatch ownership check before a worker submits to the provider.

SMTP 4xx is transient and 5xx is normally permanent; provider-specific classifiers are versioned. Backoff is exponential with full jitter and bounded by message expiry. A timeout after DATA is ambiguous: the remote server may have accepted the message. Reusing a message identifier helps deduplication but does not guarantee it. Query provider status when possible; otherwise retry according to product duplicate tolerance and record UNKNOWN evidence. Never retry malformed addresses or policy rejection.

RFC 5321, sections 2.1 and 4.5.3.2.6, defines responsibility transfer at the final successful DATA reply and warns that losing that reply can cause duplicates. An internal attempt ID is not a standard SMTP deduplication facility. Distinguish remote acceptance from evidence of final delivery (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Reputation and routing
docs.text: Reputation is partitioned by customer class, sender domain, IP pool, destination domain, and traffic type. New identities warm gradually. Routing scores eligible pools by health, reputation, cost, residency, and quota, while hard policy filters precede scoring. Complaints immediately reduce or pause promotional traffic for that identity. Dedicated pools isolate large trusted tenants; shared pools are cheaper but impose admission controls so one abuser cannot poison everyone.

docs.title: Campaign expansion
docs.text: A campaign stores an immutable audience snapshot URI, template version, cancellation generation, and budget. Expanders lease deterministic audience ranges and derive recipient IDs from (campaign_id, audience_row_id). Duplicate leases collapse at a uniqueness constraint. Checkpoints permit restart without rescanning. Cancellation increments a generation checked by expanders, scheduler, and sender; already accepted remote messages remain irreversible.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and regions
docs.text:
Shard message metadata by tenant and time, placing very large tenants on dedicated shards. Partition send queues by priority and destination-domain hash so one worker owns local domain concurrency, then split hot domains into virtual shards coordinated by a shared quota lease. Suppression is hash-partitioned and heavily cached with versioned invalidation. Object storage serves bodies through short-lived credentials.

Each tenant has a home region for residency. Acceptance uses zonal quorum and asynchronously copies encrypted canonical records to a paired region. Outbox offsets and campaign checkpoints replicate. A recovering region must restore the acknowledged message, idempotency, suppression and attempt prefix or expose the measured data-loss window and hold uncertain work for reconciliation. An asynchronous copy alone cannot guarantee all acknowledged mail survives regional destruction. Failover increments a region epoch; workers reject leases from older epochs. Duplicate enqueues are expected and absorbed by recipient/attempt uniqueness, but a failover during SMTP remains ambiguous. DNS, DKIM key metadata, and policy form a strongly governed control plane; message delivery is the elastic data plane.

Backpressure propagates from mailbox domains to domain queues, campaign expansion, and API tenant budgets. Shed analytics first, pause low-reputation campaigns next, and reject new bulk work with 429 and retry guidance before affecting transactional acceptance. Queue byte limits prevent attachment references or poison tasks from exhausting brokers.

docs.title: Reliability and failure modes
docs.text:
Database/broker dual writes use an outbox. Queue redelivery is ordinary. If rendering fails deterministically, quarantine the message; if object storage fails, retry without advancing attempt count. Provider or MX outage opens a per-route circuit, not a global breaker. Lost feedback is recovered by provider reconciliation and age scans. A suppression outage pauses marketing. Clock skew is handled with database time and tolerant lease expiry. Corrupt templates are checksum rejected.

Dead letters retain reason, classifier version, and replay eligibility. Replay requires tenant, time, category, and maximum-count scope plus dry-run approval. A reconciliation job compares accepted recipients, terminal outcomes, outbox publication, provider billing, and old ambiguous attempts. It writes normal events so webhooks and projections converge. Disaster exercises restore DB, keys, bodies, and offsets into an isolated environment before traffic switching.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Authenticate tenants, authorize sender identities, verify DNS ownership, rotate DKIM keys, encrypt addresses and bodies, isolate credentials, malware-scan attachments, verify feedback signatures, and redact logs. Defend against phishing, list bombing, spoofing, header injection, tracking abuse, and enumeration with reputation onboarding, per-recipient frequency caps, complaint thresholds, CAPTCHA on public forms, and emergency kill switches. Retention and deletion workflows cover queues, object versions, analytics, and backups.

Measure API durability latency, outbox lag, render failures, queue age by lane/domain, SMTP response classes, connection reuse, adaptive limits, retry amplification, unknown outcomes, bounce/complaint rate, suppression freshness, campaign completion, inbox proxy signals, cost, and tenant fairness. Trace IDs connect intent to attempts without exposing addresses.

Property-test state transitions, idempotency, generation cancellation, and suppression precedence. Contract-test SMTP/provider adapters and webhook signatures. Fuzz MIME and headers. Load-test campaign cliffs plus password-reset bursts and hot-domain throttling. Chaos-test DB leader loss, broker duplication, stale policy caches, object-store latency, credential rotation, and regional fencing. Canary new classifiers and routes against controlled mailboxes before gradual tenant rollout.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Direct SMTP provides control and lower marginal cost but demands reputation operations; external providers accelerate launch but add cost and opaque throttling. Rendering at request time gives immediate validation but increases latency and stores PII longer; asynchronous rendering keeps acceptance fast. Per-domain queues improve throttling but risk hot partitions; virtual shards plus a domain quota coordinator preserve control. Strong global suppression reads are safer but slower; versioned regional replicas with fail-closed promotional behavior are practical.

flowchart TD
 I[Idempotent durable intent] --> T[Immutable template rendering]
 T --> P[Current consent and policy]
 P --> F[Fair priority scheduler]
 F --> Q[Destination-domain quota]
 Q --> R[Reputation-aware route]
 R --> X[SMTP or provider attempt]
 X --> N[(Canonical attempt state)]
 Y[Signed feedback and reconciliation] --> N
 Z[Metrics, replay, audit] --> N

The final design keeps canonical intent and attempts in a transactional store, bodies in object storage, and analytics in replaceable projections. An outbox feeds policy/rendering and fair scheduling. Domain-partitioned workers enforce adaptive quotas and reputation-aware routes. Signed feedback and reconciliation close asynchronous gaps. The control plane governs identity, policy, keys, and routing; the data plane can scale and fail independently.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. What does a timeout after SMTP DATA mean, and when should we retry?
  2. How does a billion-recipient campaign avoid delaying password resets?
  3. How are opt-outs enforced for already queued work?
  4. How would destination-domain throttling survive repartitioning?
  5. Which state is canonical when callbacks and synchronous responses disagree?
  6. How do you warm a new IP pool without damaging shared reputation?
  7. What is restored and fenced during regional failover?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should clarify transactional versus bulk semantics, estimate storage and peak send rate, model message/recipient/attempt state, use outbox and idempotency, explain suppression, domain throttles, retries, queues, and major outages. They should not claim inbox delivery or exactly once.

An L6 candidate should define the ambiguity policy, legal and reputation invariants, adaptive overload behavior, tenant isolation, control/data-plane separation, regional epochs, replay safety, cost routing, classifier migration, and abuse governance. They should connect dedicated pools and retention choices to economics and policy, and propose measurable rollout and reconciliation plans.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Durably accept an idempotent message and outbox record, referencing an immutable template and object-stored body. Before sending, enforce current suppression and category policy. Expand campaigns deterministically, reserve transactional capacity, schedule tenants fairly, and throttle adaptively per destination domain. Record explicit attempts and classify SMTP outcomes; treat post-submission timeout as ambiguous rather than promising exactly once. Route by eligibility, reputation, health, residency, and cost. Normalize signed bounces and complaints into monotonic canonical state and reconcile missing feedback. Partition by tenant/time and destination domain, split hot domains with coordinated quotas, and fence regional failover using epochs. Operate queue age, retry amplification, unknown outcomes, complaint rate, suppression freshness, fairness, and cost. Pause campaigns before degrading critical mail.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Scope the feed rather than all of Facebook. Clarify sources, ranking, privacy, freshness, and interaction writes. Build a candidate-generation pipeline over posts and social edges, then add hybrid fanout, ranking, and policy filtering. The central distinction from a chronological timeline is that ranking combines many source types while privacy can change after materialization.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Users publish posts, create friendship or follow edges, join groups, and consume a personalized feed containing eligible posts from friends, followed pages, and groups. They react, comment, hide, or report. This chapter owns post metadata, candidate generation, ranking, pagination, and visibility enforcement; media processing, recommendations beyond connected sources, ads, and comment internals are excluded.

Feed reads should complete under 400 ms p99, post creation under 300 ms p99, and ordinary posts should become candidates within ten seconds. Availability favors reads, but never at the expense of showing content the viewer cannot currently access. Ranking may be eventually consistent. Deletes, blocks, group removal, and audience changes must take effect within a bounded policy SLO.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A post has one canonical audience policy and lifecycle state.
  • Candidate presence never implies authorization; reads re-evaluate policy.
  • An idempotency key identifies one mutation and request body.
  • A reaction from one user has one current state per post.
  • Deleted content cannot be resurrected by delayed events or stale caches.
  • Feed cursors use stable boundaries, not offsets.
  • Model failure has a deterministic eligible chronological fallback.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 1 billion daily users, 300 million posts/day, 20 feed sessions/user/day, and 20 items/page. That is 20 billion feed requests/day, around 230,000/s average and 1.5 million/s peak. At 2 KB metadata per post, new canonical metadata is 600 GB/day before replication. If each post were pushed to 500 recipients, 150 billion candidate entries/day would result. A 24-byte candidate reference is 3.6 TB/day. Groups and pages create extreme skew, so fanout must be selective. Media dominates bytes and uses object storage and CDN.

The read path should fetch perhaps 500 candidates to return 20 after filtering and ranking. At peak this is too expensive without precomputed candidate inboxes, caches, and bounded retrieval.

docs.title: Entities and data model
docs.text:
Post(post_id, author_id, body_ref, audience_id, created_at, state, version)
Audience(audience_id, type, owner_id, rule, version)
Edge(src_id, dst_id, edge_type, state, affinity, updated_at)
Candidate(owner_id, bucket, post_id, source_id, reason, created_at)
Interaction(post_id, user_id, type, state, updated_at)
FeedSession(session_id, user_id, model_version, boundary, expires_at)

Posts partition by ID, with author-time indexes. Edges maintain viewer-to-sources and source-to-viewers projections. Candidate stores partition by viewer and time bucket. Interaction keys make updates naturally idempotent. Audience rules are versioned because retroactive access decisions need an auditable input.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/posts                       Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
PATCH /v1/posts/{id}/audience
DELETE /v1/posts/{id}
GET /v1/feed?cursor=<opaque>&limit=20
PUT /v1/posts/{id}/reactions/me      {"type":"LIKE"}
DELETE /v1/posts/{id}/reactions/me
POST /v1/feed/{post_id}/feedback     {"action":"HIDE"}

The feed response explains source reason at a product-safe level and returns a signed cursor containing session, rank boundary, and expiry. Mutation retries with the same key and different payload receive 409.

docs.title: Publishing and candidate generation
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant P as Post service
    participant D as Post DB
    participant K as Event log
    participant G as Candidate generator
    participant C as Candidate store
    U->>P: Create post + audience
    P->>D: Commit post, key, outbox
    P-->>U: Post ID
    D->>K: Relay committed event
    K->>G: PostCreated
    G->>G: Resolve eligible source shards
    G->>C: Idempotent candidate inserts

Small friend audiences are pushed. Large pages and groups publish into source-specific recent-post indexes and are pulled during reads. Medium sources may push only to recently active, high-affinity followers. Candidate generation stores reason and source, not a copied post or permanent authorization decision.

docs.title: Feed read and ranking
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant F as Feed service
    participant C as Candidate sources
    participant V as Visibility
    participant R as Ranker
    participant D as Post DB/cache
    U->>F: Get feed(cursor)
    F->>C: Fetch pushed + pull candidates
    F->>V: Batch eligibility check
    V-->>F: Allowed IDs and policy versions
    F->>R: Features for bounded candidates
    R-->>F: Scores
    F->>D: Batch hydrate selected posts
    F-->>U: Items + cursor

Candidate generation optimizes recall; ranking optimizes ordering. Retrieval imposes quotas per source class so one active group cannot monopolize the page. The ranker consumes precomputed features with point-in-time definitions; request-time features have strict latency budgets. Filtering occurs before and after ranking to handle races.

docs.title: Candidate generation and diversity
docs.text: Sources include friend posts, pages, and groups. Each generator emits a common envelope with post ID, reason, event time, and source score. A mixer applies per-source caps, author deduplication, and freshness windows. This prevents a prolific source from occupying all retrieval slots before the expensive ranker. Missing one generator yields a partial but valid feed; the service records which source classes contributed.

docs.title: Ranking lifecycle
docs.text: Offline pipelines train models from impression and interaction logs while guarding against leakage and feedback loops. A feature registry defines ownership, freshness, defaults, and privacy classification. Online inference is versioned and shadowed before serving. If feature fetches or inference exceed budget, use cached features or a lightweight model, then chronology. Feed sessions pin a model version briefly, but do not promise immutable pages because new blocks and deletes override rank stability.

docs.title: Privacy-aware materialization
docs.text: Audience choices include public, friends, custom lists, and group membership. Expanding every custom audience into candidates is optional optimization, never the source of truth. Visibility evaluates current edge state, audience version, blocks in both directions, geographic policy, age restrictions, and moderation state. A deny cache receives priority invalidations. Positive authorization caches are short-lived and keyed by all relevant versions. Their freshness lease and the final response gate must fit the declared removal bound; knowing a cached version number alone does not prove it is current. Public content still requires fresh deletion, block and moderation state.

docs.title: Interactions and feedback
docs.text: Reaction updates are upserts on (post_id,user_id) and emit change events. Counters are eventually consistent sharded aggregates, so the displayed count can lag while the user's own reaction reads from canonical interaction state. Hide/report feedback immediately affects that viewer's feed through a viewer suppression store; asynchronous safety systems investigate broader action.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and regions
docs.text:
Hash posts by ID and retain author indexes separately. Partition candidate inboxes by viewer plus time bucket; split unusually active viewers into sub-buckets merged at read. Partition social reverse edges by source and range so large pages enumerate in parallel. Cache post bodies by immutable version, but never cache a cross-user assembled feed without viewer and policy identity.

Use a user's home region for interaction and post writes, with regional ID allocation. Replicate canonical state and events. Build candidate inboxes locally because they are disposable. Membership and block changes travel on a priority stream; if their freshness cannot be proven, fail closed for restricted content. Region evacuation restores reads from replicated posts and rebuilds recent candidates, accepting lower personalization before full recovery.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and failure recovery
docs.text:
Post and audience updates are linearizable per post shard. Feed candidates, counters, and features are eventual. Outbox publication closes the database/broker dual-write gap. Consumers use event IDs and unique candidate keys. Event versions reject stale updates; tombstones dominate creates with lower versions.

Broker lag delays freshness but not posting. Candidate-store loss triggers bounded pull from connected sources and asynchronous rebuild. Ranker failure falls back. Visibility failure fails closed for nonpublic content and can serve only already-proven public posts. Feature-store overload sheds expensive feature families. Circuit breakers and per-stage deadlines prevent retries from multiplying load. Recovery tools can replay by source, viewer shard, event range, and model version.

docs.title: Security, abuse, and privacy
docs.text: Authenticate sessions, authorize post mutations, encrypt data, and audit policy or employee access. Rate-limit publishing, interactions, group invitations, and scraping using account and device reputation. Safety classifiers can quarantine distribution while preserving canonical evidence. Explanations must not reveal private edge information. Data export and deletion traverse posts, interactions, indexes, training datasets, and caches with lineage-based completion records. Logs avoid post bodies and protected audience membership.

docs.title: Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure feed latency by stage, candidate count and age by source, eligibility rejection, model and feature fallback, diversity, empty-page rate, duplicate impressions, post-to-feed delay, deletion/block propagation, fanout cost, queue age, shard skew, and CDN egress. Business metrics need guardrails for reports, hides, and demographic quality, not only engagement.

Contract-test each candidate generator. Property-test audience matrices and cursor boundaries. Replay duplicated, delayed, and reordered events. Load-test graph and page-size distributions rather than uniform traffic. Chaos-test loss of ranker, visibility cache, broker, and a region. Use offline evaluation, shadow traffic, canaries, and holdbacks for ranking changes. Synthetic private groups continuously verify no unauthorized exposure.

docs.title: L6 mechanisms: bounded retrieval, ranking, and stable delivery
Candidate quotas and quantitative fanout choice
docs.text:
For a request that needs 20 results, retrieve at most 600 candidates: 240 friend posts, 120 groups, 80 followed pages, 60 connected-source recency, and 100 reserve slots redistributed to generators that meet deadlines. Within a class, cap one author at 20 retrieval candidates and one group at 30. Deduplicate by post ID before visibility checks. Quotas are configuration by cohort and are logged with the request; they constrain infrastructure and concentration, not final page counts. An underfilled class lends unused quota rather than forcing low-quality items.

Choose push versus pull from measured cost, not a label such as celebrity. For source s, let F_s be eligible followers, a_s the fraction active during the candidate TTL, P_s posts/day, e=24 bytes per inbox reference, and r_s expected reads/day. Push storage bytes are P_s * F_s * a_s * e. Compare monetary or normalized resource cost by applying write/storage prices, then compare with bounded source-index reads and ranking cost under expected read rate r_s; raw bytes cannot be compared directly with a per-lookup cost. A pull reads only the bounded recent candidate slice, not necessarily every daily post. With a 24-hour inbox, a_s=0.2, and a per-post fanout budget of 10 MB, push only while F_s * 0.2 * 24 <= 10 MB, or about 2.08 million followers. Operationally use a lower 1 million threshold to reserve retry/index headroom. Also switch to pull whenever predicted fanout completion exceeds the ten-second freshness SLO. Recompute the class from trailing seven-day active-follower and post-rate estimates; use hysteresis, for example enter pull above 1 million and return to push below 700,000, to prevent flapping.

flowchart LR
 A[Friend quota 240] --> M[Deduplicate and quota mixer]
 B[Group quota 120] --> M
 C[Page quota 80] --> M
 D[Connected recency quota 60] --> M
 E[Reserve quota 100] --> M
 M --> V[Batch current visibility]
 V --> P[Lightweight pre-rank top 200]
 P --> H[Heavy rank top 80]
 H --> X[Diversity constrained selection of 20]
 X --> F{Enough eligible items?}
 F -->|Yes| R[Return page]
 F -->|No| Y[Borrow reserve then chronological fallback]
 Y --> R

docs.title: Ranking, diversity, and fallback ladder
docs.text:
Stage one uses cheap freshness, affinity, source quality, and negative-feedback features to reduce 600 eligible candidates to 200. Stage two scores at most 80 with the full model. Selection then greedily maximizes model_score - lambda_author * author_count - lambda_source * source_count - lambda_topic * recent_topic_count, subject to an author cap of at most two items per page, a soft target of at most five from one source class, relaxed when fewer than four eligible classes exist, no exact duplicate media, and at least two source classes when inventory permits. Fairness and integrity constraints are evaluated as launch guardrails by geography and cohort; they are not inferred from engagement score.

Fallback is deterministic and preserves eligibility: full model with fresh features, full model with registered defaults, lightweight model, then reverse chronological order over the already authorized mixed set. A timeout never bypasses visibility or block checks. If fewer than 20 safe candidates survive, return fewer than 20. The response records the fallback level so experiments do not treat degraded traffic as normal model output.

docs.title: Latency and feature budgets
docs.text:
The 400 ms endpoint deadline allocates 25 ms for edge/auth, 70 ms for parallel candidate reads, 55 ms for visibility, 45 ms for lightweight feature fetch and pre-rank, 65 ms for heavy features plus inference, 45 ms for diversity selection and hydration, 25 ms for serialization/network, and 70 ms contingency. These sum to 400 ms; they are deadline allocations, not a proof obtained by summing measured component p99s. Deadlines are absolute from request start, so a late stage cannot consume another stage's reserve. Candidate generators have a 60 ms soft deadline and 70 ms hard deadline; late classes are omitted and recorded.

Feature payload is capped at 80 candidates times 128 dense values, about 40 KB using 32-bit values before protocol overhead. At most 16 request-time features may perform remote reads, all through two batch calls with a combined 30 ms deadline. The rest come from a point-in-time online vector keyed by (viewer_id,post_id,feature_version) or viewer/source vectors. Missing-feature bitsets accompany defaults so the model can distinguish zero from unavailable. Shed semantic embeddings first, then cross features, while retaining block, audience, moderation, and age controls outside the feature system.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant F as Feed service
 participant C as Candidate stores
 participant V as Visibility
 participant X as Feature store
 participant R as Ranker
 participant H as Hydrator
 F->>C: Parallel quotas, deadline 70 ms
 C-->>F: Up to 600 envelopes
 F->>V: Batch authorize, deadline 55 ms
 V-->>F: Eligible IDs and policy versions
 F->>X: Top 200 cheap vectors, deadline 20 ms
 X-->>F: Values plus missing bitsets
 F->>R: Pre-rank then top-80 heavy rank, 65 ms
 R-->>F: Scores and model version
 F->>H: Diversity-selected top 20, 45 ms
 H-->>F: Immutable post versions
 Note over F,H: Absolute endpoint deadline 400 ms p99

docs.title: Impression provenance and mutation-safe pagination
docs.text:
Persist one deduplicated record per rendered card, not merely per response:

Impression(impression_id, request_id, feed_session_id, viewer_id,
           post_id, post_version, author_id, source_type, source_id,
           candidate_reason, candidate_event_time, generator_version,
           retrieval_quota, pre_rank_score, final_score, rank_position,
           model_version, feature_snapshot_id, policy_version,
           mixer_version, fallback_level, experiment_ids, rendered_at)

The client emits VISIBLE(impression_id) after a defined viewport/time threshold; server-return and client-visible events remain separate. Interaction training joins through impression_id, preserving which generator, policy, features, and model caused exposure. Logs are access-controlled and retention-limited because source and experiment provenance can reveal graph information.

The signed cursor contains {session_id, viewer_id, issued_at, expires_at, model_version, mixer_version, as_of_time, last_score_bucket, last_event_time, last_post_id, seen_digest}. First-page as_of_time freezes the upper creation-time boundary: newer posts appear only after refresh, preventing inserts from shifting later pages. Seek with the total key (score_bucket DESC,event_time DESC,post_id DESC), never offset. Scores are quantized and the model/mixer version is pinned for the short session. Deletes and lost authorization are filtered immediately, so pages may shrink; the service over-fetches but never backfills with an item above the cursor boundary. Server page publication atomically advances the session generation and exact seen set; concurrent requests return the winning stored page or retry from the current cursor. Client and server retain exact seen IDs for the short session; the digest detects cursor tampering or state loss.

If mutable features reorder an unseen post below the boundary, it may appear later; if they move it above, it waits for refresh. This yields no unauthorized or duplicate item within retained session state, but not a globally immutable ranking. Expired sessions start a new snapshot. A deterministic retry key (session_id,page_boundary) returns the same impression IDs where cached, preventing retries from double-counting exposure.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Push-only candidate generation minimizes read work but amplifies writes and bakes in stale eligibility. Pull-only keeps graph changes simple but cannot meet feed latency for users with thousands of sources. Hybrid materialization plus read-time policy checks separates performance from correctness. A single end-to-end model is potentially optimal but hard to debug and expensive; retrieval, mixing, and ranking stages provide budgets and graceful degradation. Session snapshots improve pagination but consume state; short-lived signed cursors and client deduplication are usually enough.

flowchart TD
    E[Canonical posts, edges, interactions] --> L[Versioned event log]
    L --> P[Push candidates for bounded audiences]
    L --> S[Recent-source indexes for large audiences]
    P --> M[Candidate mixer]
    S --> M
    M --> V[Current visibility gate]
    V --> R[Ranker with fallback ladder]
    R --> H[Hydrate immutable post versions]
    H --> Gate[Final current policy gate]
    Gate --> U[Viewer feed]
    L --> O[Features, counters, moderation]

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. Which eligibility checks happen at fanout and which must happen at read?
  2. How do you stop a large group from dominating candidate retrieval?
  3. What cursor semantics are offered when model scores change?
  4. How do you roll back a model without invalidating every session?
  5. What is served when visibility or feature systems are unavailable?
  6. How do deletion guarantees extend into training data?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: L5 candidates should separate posts from candidates, estimate fanout, design hybrid push/pull, explain ranking fallback, and cover retries and privacy filtering. L6 candidates should define stage budgets and overload policy, version authorization inputs, handle regional evacuation, reason about model governance and feedback loops, build replay/migration paths, and balance relevance against safety, fairness, latency, and infrastructure cost.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Keep posts, relationships, and interactions canonical; treat feed candidates, counters, and features as rebuildable projections. Commit posts with an outbox, push candidates for bounded audiences, pull from recent indexes for large pages and groups, and mix source classes under explicit quotas. On every read, batch-check current visibility, rank a bounded eligible set, hydrate immutable post versions, and issue a signed boundary cursor. Partition inboxes by viewer and time and reverse edges by source ranges. Make every consumer idempotent and every lifecycle update versioned. Prioritize block and deletion propagation, degrade inference to simpler models and chronology, and fail closed when restricted-content authorization is uncertain. Operate stage latency, fanout skew, candidate quality, policy propagation, and recovery independently.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text:
Clarify which activities and devices are supported, whether recording must work without a network, how accurate distance must be, who can see routes, and whether live location is in scope. State the local-durability and activity-lifecycle invariants before choosing databases. Start with one phone recording an activity into a durable local journal and synchronizing it to a canonical backend. Then add GPS quality processing, resumable uploads, wearable handoff, social feeds, live sharing, regional scale, privacy controls, and operational recovery.

A useful 45-minute interview allocation is five minutes for scope and invariants, five for estimates and APIs, ten for the device and upload protocol, ten for backend ingestion and GPS processing, five for feeds and live sharing, and ten for partitioning, reliability, privacy, and tradeoffs. The most important distinction is that recording and uploading are separate: losing connectivity must not lose the workout.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
The product records runs, rides, walks, hikes, and indoor workouts from phones or wearables. It computes elapsed and moving time, distance, pace, elevation, heart-rate summaries, route maps, and personal records. A user may keep an activity private, share it with followers or friends, or publish it. Friends can view a feed and react. Optionally, a user can share a short-lived live location with explicitly selected viewers.

The source evidence is the ordered sensor record captured on the device. The backend owns the canonical synchronized activity and immutable raw sample objects; summaries, route polylines, achievements, search indexes, and feeds are rebuildable projections. The system does not provide medical diagnosis, emergency dispatch, turn-by-turn navigation, or competition-grade timing. Payment, ad ranking, and detailed recommendation design are out of scope.

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text:
• Start, pause, resume, finish, discard, and recover an activity on a phone or wearable.
  • Continue recording for hours while offline or while the app is backgrounded.
  • Capture ordered GPS, altitude, heart rate, cadence, power, and device events when available.
  • Synchronize large activities with resumable, duplicate-safe uploads.
  • Compute distance, pace, moving time, splits, elevation, route, and quality indicators.
  • List a user's history and show a self feed with read-your-writes behavior.
  • Show authorized friend activities and support idempotent reactions and comments.
  • Apply activity visibility, blocks, route redaction, deletion, export, and retention policy.
  • Optionally share low-latency live progress with a small authorized audience.

docs.title: Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text:
• A locally acknowledged sample survives process death and ordinary device restart.
  • Activity recording works without network access for at least 24 hours.
  • Backend activity reads target 99.99% availability and p99 under 300 ms.
  • Activity completion becomes visible to the owner within two seconds after finalization; friend-feed propagation targets under 30 seconds at p99.
  • Upload can resume after arbitrary interruption without resending the entire activity.
  • Battery, storage, and mobile data use are bounded and visible to the user.
  • Location data is encrypted, access-controlled, auditable, and minimized.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. Each activity has one stable client-generated activity_id; retries and device restarts never create another logical activity.
  2. Within a recording source, journal sequence numbers are unique and strictly increasing. An acknowledged journal record is never silently omitted from recovery.
  3. Local recording state follows legal transitions. FINISHED and DISCARDED are terminal for recording; no new sensor sample may be created after FINISHED, although bytes durably recorded by another source before finish may arrive later. Server lifecycle is separate, and DELETED is terminal there.
  4. A chunk identity binds activity, source, sequence range, encoding version, byte length, and checksum. The same identity cannot later represent different bytes.
  5. Finalization succeeds only against a complete upload manifest, or explicitly records known gaps. Summary generation references the exact manifest revision it consumed.
  6. Retries may redeliver commands and chunks, but stable keys create one canonical effect.
  7. Raw sensor evidence is immutable after acceptance. Corrections produce a new processing version, not an in-place rewrite of evidence.
  8. Visibility reduction, blocking, and deletion dominate stale feed, cache, notification, and live-session state.
  9. Derived distance never claims greater precision than input quality supports; rejected points remain explainable through quality metadata.
  10. Live sharing expires without a heartbeat and never broadens the audience beyond the current activity policy and explicit share grant.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100 million registered users and 20 million daily active users. If 10% record one activity per day, the system receives 2 million activities/day, about 23 finalizations/s average and perhaps 20x peak, or 460/s. Activity metadata writes are not the dominant load; sensor bytes and social reads are.

For a 60-minute outdoor workout sampled every second, there are 3,600 GPS samples. At 40 bytes/sample after delta encoding and compression, GPS consumes about 144 KB. Heart rate and motion metadata can add 100 KB, while indexes, manifests, and summaries add roughly 20 KB. Budget 300 KB/activity average:

2,000,000 activities/day * 300 KB = 600 GB/day raw and derived ingress
600 GB/day * 365 days = 219 TB/year before replication
3 copies of this raw-and-derived budget = 657 TB/year
Additional indexes, versions and reserve may bring provisioned storage near 1 PB/year

Sampling every five seconds lowers bytes but can destroy corner and interval fidelity. Instead, use adaptive sampling and compact delta encoding. A heavy five-hour ride at one-second sampling may be several MB, so protocols must not assume one request per activity.

Assume each daily active user opens the feed eight times and reads two pages. That is 320 million page reads/day, about 3,700/s average and 40,000/s peak. Two million activities/day averaging 60 minutes imply 2,000,000 * 60 / 1,440 ~= 83,000 concurrent recordings on an average day. Applying a 3x time-of-day peak gives about 250,000 concurrent recordings. If 1% enable live sharing, 2,500 sessions at one update every five seconds produce 500 updates/s; ten viewers per session creates 5,000 deliveries/s. Regional pub/sub can handle that baseline, but celebrity fanout must still be capped because live sharing is designed for trusted small groups.

At 256 KB chunks, a normal activity is roughly one or two chunks depending on sensor payload and sealing policy; the 300 KB estimate includes derived data that is not necessarily uploaded. A long activity may require tens of chunks. Upload bandwidth at a 20x activity peak is modest on average, but reconnect after a widespread mobile outage can release hours of backlog. Capacity planning therefore includes queued bytes and concurrent resumptions, not only normal QPS.
