RouteSegment(activity_id, processing_version, segment_no, encoded_polyline,
             bounds, redaction_class)
FeedItem(viewer_bucket, rank_key, activity_id, activity_version, author_id)
Reaction(activity_id, user_id, type, state, version)
LiveGrant(grant_id, activity_id, owner_id, audience, expires_at, revoked_at)
AuditEvent(actor_id, action, resource_id, policy_version, occurred_at)

Activity, accepted chunk metadata, immutable raw chunk objects, manifests, visibility, and relationship state are canonical. ActivitySummary, route segments, leaderboards, achievements, notification records, and feed items are projections. Raw samples need not be expanded into one database row each; compressed immutable chunk objects are cheaper, while sparse metadata and time-range indexes support processing and diagnosis.

Partition keys and uniqueness constraints should be visible in the schema:

CREATE TABLE activity_chunk (
  activity_id UUID NOT NULL,
  source_id UUID NOT NULL,
  first_seq BIGINT NOT NULL,
  last_seq BIGINT NOT NULL,
  object_key TEXT NOT NULL,
  byte_length INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sha256 CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  encoding VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
  sample_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (activity_id, source_id, first_seq),
  UNIQUE (activity_id, source_id, last_seq, sha256),
  CHECK (first_seq <= last_seq)
);

The database transaction records object metadata only after object storage confirms durable bytes. Alternatively, upload to a temporary object key, verify it, transactionally install the chunk row, then promote or retain the content-addressed object. Orphan temporary objects are removed after their durable staging lease expires and a conditional deletion state fences descriptor publication. Age alone is insufficient if a delayed completion can still install the object.

docs.title: APIs and Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/activities
Idempotency-Key: 1dbb...
{ "activity_id": "client-uuid", "sport": "RUN", "started_at": "...",
  "visibility": "FRIENDS", "sources": [{"source_id": "phone-uuid"}] }

POST /v1/activities/{id}/upload-sessions
Idempotency-Key: 655e...
{ "manifest_revision": 3, "encoding": "fit-delta-v2" }

PUT /v1/upload-sessions/{session}/chunks/{source}/{first_seq}
Content-Length: 238112
Digest: sha-256=<base64>
If-None-Match: *
<binary chunk bytes>

GET /v1/upload-sessions/{session}
-> { "accepted": [{"source_id": "...", "first_seq": 1, "last_seq": 4096,
                    "sha256": "..."}], "missing": [[4097, 8192]] }

POST /v1/activities/{id}/finalize
Idempotency-Key: 9e5a...
{ "manifest_revision": 3, "root_checksum": "...", "ended_at": "...",
  "sources": [{"source_id": "...", "last_seq": 7210}], "declared_gaps": [] }

GET /v1/activities/{id}
GET /v1/users/me/activities?before=<opaque_cursor>&limit=20
GET /v1/feed?before=<opaque_cursor>&limit=20
PATCH /v1/activities/{id}  If-Match: <activity_version>
{ "visibility": "PRIVATE", "title": "Morning run" }
DELETE /v1/activities/{id} Idempotency-Key: ...
PUT /v1/activities/{id}/reactions/me
POST /v1/activities/{id}/live-grants
GET /v1/live/{grant_token}  Upgrade: websocket

The chunk response distinguishes 201 Created, 204 Already Present, and 409 Checksum Conflict. A repeated idempotency key with a different request hash is rejected. List cursors encode a stable sort key such as (completed_at, activity_id) and query watermark; offset pagination would duplicate or skip activities as new ones arrive. Every read authorizes against current owner, relationship, block, and activity policy rather than trusting feed membership.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Sensors[Phone and wearable sensors] --> Recorder[Offline recorder]
    Recorder --> Journal[(Encrypted local journal)]
    Journal --> Sync[Resumable sync engine]
    Sync --> Edge[Regional API edge]
    Edge --> Meta[Activity metadata service]
    Edge --> Upload[Upload coordinator]
    Upload --> Objects[(Immutable object storage)]
    Meta --> Canon[(Canonical activity DB and outbox)]
    Upload --> Canon
    Canon --> Bus[(Durable event stream)]
    Bus --> Process[GPS and summary pipeline]
    Process --> Views[(Summary and route stores)]
    Bus --> Feed[Feed materializer]
    Feed --> FeedStore[(Feed projections)]
    Edge --> Query[Authorized query service]
    Canon -->|canonical read result| Query
    Views -->|summary read result| Query
    FeedStore -->|feed read result| Query
    subgraph DeviceLane[Offline recording]
      Sensors
      Recorder
      Journal
      Sync
    end
    subgraph UploadLane[Object upload]
      Upload
      Objects
    end
    subgraph CanonLane[Canonical activity]
      Meta
      Canon
    end
    subgraph ProcessLane[Derived views]
      Bus
      Process
      Views
      Feed
      FeedStore
    end

The mobile data plane records locally without waiting for the backend. The backend control path creates activities and upload sessions, while bulk chunk bytes go directly or through an upload edge to object storage. A canonical transaction finalizes the manifest, moves activity state, and writes an outbox event. At-least-once consumers derive summaries and social projections by activity and processing version.

Requirement Authoritative flow Durable boundary Result Offline recording sensors -> local writer -> encrypted journal forced journal frame recoverable local activity Resumable upload sealed chunks -> coordinator -> object store and chunk metadata checksum-bound object plus canonical descriptor missing ranges can be queried and retried Finish and summarize /finalize -> manifest validation -> canonical DB/outbox -> processor manifest, server state, and outbox transaction versioned summary and route Feed visibility finalized event -> hybrid fanout -> authorization-first hydration canonical activity and current policy stale projections cannot grant access Live sharing coarse device updates -> authorized regional relay expiring grant, not each delivery bounded ephemeral location stream

docs.title: Offline-First Device Architecture
docs.text:
The recorder owns the activity state machine and one append-only journal per active activity. Sensor adapters normalize platform callbacks but do not decide durability. A single writer assigns sequence numbers, validates the current state, frames records with length and CRC, encrypts them, appends them, and periodically forces data to stable storage. UI counters are projections from acknowledged records and may be recomputed.

flowchart TD
    GPS[GPS adapter] --> Queue[Bounded sensor queue]
    HR[Heart-rate adapter] --> Queue
    Motion[Motion adapter] --> Queue
    Controls[Pause and finish commands] --> Writer[Single journal writer]
    Queue --> Writer
    Writer --> WAL[(Encrypted append journal)]
    WAL --> Index[(Local activity index)]
    WAL --> View[Live metrics projector]
    WAL --> Chunker[Immutable chunk builder]
    Chunker --> Outbox[(Local upload outbox)]
    Outbox --> Sync[Background sync worker]
    Sync --> Cloud[Backend upload API]

The queue is bounded. Under overload, control events and coarse GPS fixes are retained before redundant high-frequency motion samples. The recorder emits an explicit SAMPLE_GAP record with sensor and interval rather than hiding loss. Platform background execution limits require foreground-service or workout-session APIs where available, wake locks used sparingly, and a user-visible warning when the operating system revokes recording capability.

Phones and wearables can both record. Give each source its own sequence space and clock model; do not interleave samples by arrival time. On merge, estimate monotonic-time offset using synchronization exchanges and wall-clock anchors, then choose source precedence per sensor. If a watch transfers data after the phone is FINISHED, accept only samples the watch durably recorded before the finish cutoff, append a new server manifest revision, and reprocess rather than mutating accepted chunks. This extends synchronized evidence; it does not reopen local recording.

docs.title: Durable Local Journal and Crash Recovery
docs.text:
Each journal frame contains (format_version, activity_id, source_id, seq, event_type, monotonic_time, wall_time, payload_length, payload, crc). Files use an authenticated encryption key held by the device keystore. A segment header records nonce material and previous-segment hash. Segment rotation bounds recovery scanning and lets completed prefixes become immutable upload chunks.

Acknowledgement semantics must be honest. For a user command such as pause or finish, return success only after the record and required metadata are committed to SQLite WAL or forced to the journal file. Sensor callbacks may be batched for battery efficiency; document that the last small batch, for example up to five seconds, can be lost on sudden power failure. Process death after an OS callback but before local acknowledgement is not preventable.

SQLite WAL alone is not a power-loss durability setting: SQLite's synchronous pragma states that WAL with NORMAL can lose a committed transaction after power/system failure, while FULL synchronizes after each commit. Use WAL plus synchronous=FULL and verified storage behavior for acknowledged control records; apply the documented lossy batch policy only to unacknowledged samples (accessed 2026-09-08).

On startup, recovery performs these steps:

  1. Read the local activity index and locate every activity not terminally discarded or fully synchronized.
  2. Scan from the last verified segment boundary, checking frame length, sequence, authentication tag, and CRC.
  3. Truncate only an incomplete or corrupt trailing frame. Quarantine mid-file corruption and preserve later bytes for support tooling.
  4. Replay state transitions and metrics from the journal; never trust an independently updated UI-state row over the log.
  5. Resume an activity only if the platform still has sensor ownership and product policy allows it; otherwise mark INTERRUPTED and ask the user to finish or continue.
  6. Rebuild the local upload outbox from sealed segments and query server upload status before sending.

Compaction is copy-on-write. After server finalization and a verified retention delay, create a compact summary record, atomically swap the local index to it, then delete old segments. A crash before the swap leaves old data authoritative; a crash after the swap leaves orphan files that a sweeper can safely remove. Disk pressure first drops regenerable map tiles and feed caches, then pauses new recordings with a clear error; it never silently deletes an active journal.

docs.title: Activity Lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Local_recording
        DRAFT -->|durable START| RECORDING
        RECORDING -->|durable PAUSE| PAUSED
        PAUSED -->|durable RESUME| RECORDING
        RECORDING -->|sensor loss| INTERRUPTED
        PAUSED -->|process loss| INTERRUPTED
        INTERRUPTED -->|explicit recovery| RECORDING
        INTERRUPTED -->|durable FINISH and seal| FINISHED
        INTERRUPTED -->|confirmed discard| DISCARDED
        RECORDING -->|durable FINISH and seal| FINISHED
        PAUSED -->|durable FINISH and seal| FINISHED
        DRAFT -->|discard| DISCARDED
        RECORDING -->|confirmed discard| DISCARDED
        PAUSED -->|confirmed discard| DISCARDED
    end
    subgraph Server_lifecycle
        CREATED -->|first chunk| UPLOADING
        UPLOADING -->|validated finalize| PROCESSING
        PROCESSING -->|summary published| READY
        PROCESSING -->|declared gap or quality failure| PARTIAL
        CREATED -->|delete| DELETED
        UPLOADING -->|delete| DELETED
        PROCESSING -->|delete fences publication| DELETED
        READY -->|delete| DELETED
        PARTIAL -->|delete| DELETED
    end
    FINISHED -. sync sealed manifest .-> UPLOADING

Local recording, local sync progress, and server lifecycle are related but not identical. FINISHED is terminal for local sample creation; a separate sync status can remain PENDING, UPLOADING, or SYNCED. The server can be UPLOADING or PROCESSING while the device is locally FINISHED, and the API returns canonical server state plus upload completeness. Durable finish seals the ending timestamp and source high-watermarks. Evidence recorded by another source before that cutoff but transferred later requires a new manifest revision; post-cutoff samples are rejected.

Pause is a durable control event, not absence of samples. Elapsed time spans start to finish minus policy-defined exclusions; moving time derives from quality-filtered motion and can differ from user pauses. Auto-pause creates separate inferred events so a later algorithm version can recompute moving time without rewriting user commands.

Discard writes a local tombstone before deleting bytes and, if any server object exists, synchronizes a deletion command. Delete after publication immediately hides the activity in canonical policy, writes a tombstone to the outbox, evicts feeds and caches asynchronously, revokes live grants, and schedules physical erasure according to backup and legal-retention policy.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: GPS Distance and Route Quality
docs.text:
For consecutive valid points (lat1, lon1) and (lat2, lon2) in radians, a Haversine baseline estimates great-circle distance:

dlat = lat2 - lat1
dlon = lon2 - lon1
a = sin(dlat/2)^2 + cos(lat1) * cos(lat2) * sin(dlon/2)^2
a = clamp(a, 0, 1)  # protect floating-point roundoff
c = 2 * atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1-a))
distance = R * c, where R ~= 6,371,000 meters

Summing every raw pair overcounts distance when a stationary GPS fix jitters. The processor first validates time order and coordinate bounds, then associates each fix with horizontal accuracy, provider, speed, altitude quality, and motion evidence. It applies a quality pipeline rather than one magic smoothing constant.

flowchart LR
    Raw[Immutable fixes] --> Validate[Bounds and time validation]
    Validate --> Accuracy[Accuracy and stale-fix gate]
    Accuracy --> Speed[Acceleration and impossible-speed gate]
    Speed --> Drift[Stationary drift and outlier filter]
    Drift --> Match{Map match useful?}
    Match -->|yes| Roads[Candidate roads and path scoring]
    Match -->|no| Free[Free-form route]
    Roads --> Distance[Distance and moving-time model]
    Free --> Distance
    Distance --> Simplify[Multi-resolution simplification]
    Simplify --> Publish[Versioned summary and route]

docs.title: Accuracy and Drift
docs.text:
A reported 50-meter-accuracy point should not move a runner 35 meters merely because it arrived next. Reject fixes outside configured accuracy bounds or down-weight them in a Kalman-like state estimator. During likely stationary periods, require displacement to exceed a noise envelope derived from both fixes before adding distance. Keep raw points and rejection reasons so processing can be audited and improved.

Tunnels, urban canyons, tree cover, and battery-saving modes create long gaps or biased fixes. Do not draw a confident straight line across every gap. Mark uncertain segments, cap interpolation by duration and plausible route, and expose a quality score. Barometric altitude, when calibrated, is usually better for elevation change than noisy GPS altitude. Elevation gain needs smoothing and minimum ascent thresholds; it is not the sum of every positive centimeter.

docs.title: Impossible Speed and Clock Errors
docs.text: Compute implied speed from distance divided by monotonic-time delta. Reject zero or negative deltas and quarantine clock jumps. Thresholds vary by sport: a 20 m/s point may be impossible for a run but ordinary for cycling downhill. Acceleration, neighboring points, motion sensors, and road constraints distinguish a single teleport from a real fast segment. Never use client wall time alone because users, networks, and daylight-saving changes can move it.

docs.title: Map Matching
docs.text: Map matching is optional and versioned. A hidden Markov model can score road or trail candidates by perpendicular distance, heading, road class, and path plausibility between fixes. It improves sparse road cycling tracks but can damage trail runs, open-water activities, or newly built roads. Apply it only when sport, map coverage, and confidence justify it. Retain both measured and matched geometry and show users when a route was corrected.

docs.title: Route Simplification
docs.text:
Serving thousands of raw points to every feed card wastes bandwidth and leaks precision. Douglas-Peucker or a streaming equivalent creates multiple route levels with explicit error tolerances, for example 5 meters for activity detail and 50 meters for feed thumbnails. Preserve segment boundaries, redaction boundaries, pauses, and critical turns. Simplification runs after privacy clipping so it cannot recreate a removed endpoint by connecting across it.

Distance algorithm upgrades write processing_version=N+1, compare old and new results in shadow, and atomically publish a complete new summary and route generation. Personal records and achievements reference the version used and are reconciled if a material correction changes eligibility.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Idempotent Resumable Upload
docs.text:
The client seals journal segments into deterministic chunks. A chunk should contain one source and contiguous sequence range, use a pinned encoding version, and have a SHA-256 checksum over exact transmitted bytes. The client persists the chunk descriptor and checksum before enqueueing upload. It never regenerates different bytes under the same descriptor.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Device sync engine
    participant U as Upload coordinator
    participant O as Object storage
    participant C as Canonical DB
    participant P as Processing pipeline
    D->>U: create session(activity, manifest revision, key)
    U->>C: upsert session and return accepted ranges
    C-->>D: session, accepted chunks, expiry
    loop only missing chunks
        D->>U: PUT chunk(range, length, checksum)
        U->>O: write temporary or content-addressed object
        O-->>U: durable object checksum
        U->>C: install descriptor if absent
        U-->>D: created or already present
    end
    D->>U: finalize(manifest, root checksum, high-watermarks)
    U->>C: verify coverage and atomically finalize plus outbox
    C-->>D: canonical activity revision
    C->>P: at-least-once ActivityFinalized

The manifest lists all sources, each expected sequence high-watermark, ordered chunk descriptors, declared gaps, and a root checksum over canonical descriptor serialization. Finalization validates that accepted chunks exactly cover each required range without overlap, that checksums match, and that no unexpected source appears. Missing ranges return a machine-readable response; they do not produce a silently shorter workout.

The sample SQL constraints alone do not reject overlapping ranges such as [1,100] and [50,150]. Serialize descriptor insertion and finalization under an activity/source lock, reject overlap with installed descriptors, and freeze the manifest revision while checking coverage and publishing it. Chunk uploads cannot race a completed coverage check to mutate the manifest being finalized.

Session expiry does not delete installed content-addressed chunks immediately. A new session for the same activity and manifest revision discovers them through canonical chunk metadata. Concurrent retries race on the primary key; the winner installs the checksum, and identical losers receive Already Present. Different bytes for the same range produce a hard conflict requiring a new manifest revision or client repair.

The critical crash windows are explicit:

  • Object write succeeds but metadata insert fails: the object is an orphan and later retried or swept.
  • Metadata commits but acknowledgement is lost: the retry finds the same checksum and succeeds without another effect.
  • Finalization commits but response is lost: the idempotency key returns the prior activity revision.
  • Processing publishes twice: projection keys include (activity_id, processing_version) and publication uses compare-and-set.
  • The device deletes local bytes too early: forbidden until it observes finalized manifest revision and persists that acknowledgement locally.

Direct-to-object-storage presigned URLs reduce API bandwidth but complicate checksum enforcement and completion authorization. The coordinator can issue a URL bound to object key, maximum length, content hash, activity, and short expiry; the client must call complete, and the server independently verifies object metadata before installing the descriptor. For small normal activities, proxy upload may be simpler and safer.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Backend Storage and Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
The metadata service performs strongly consistent per-activity transitions. Chunk bytes live in object storage, not a relational database. A transactional outbox emits ActivityFinalized, ActivityVisibilityChanged, and ActivityDeleted. Stream consumers are at least once and use source version checks.

Processing stages decode and validate chunks, normalize source clocks, select sensor sources, run GPS quality logic, calculate summaries and splits, generate route resolutions, evaluate achievements, and publish a generation. Expensive map matching uses a separate bounded pool so its backlog cannot delay basic summaries. An activity can become READY with baseline geometry and receive an enhanced route later if the product allows; the API labels versions so readers never combine incompatible pieces.

Pipeline records include input manifest revision, algorithm version, map-data version, stage status, output checksums, and error category. Deterministic stages can replay from raw chunks. Poisoned or unsupported chunks quarantine the activity as PARTIAL without blocking a stream partition. Operator repair selects a new processing version; it never edits output rows blindly.

Use lifecycle-aware storage tiers. Recent metadata and summaries remain in a low-latency database. Raw chunks begin in standard object storage, transition to colder classes after the reprocessing window, and are physically deleted according to policy. Route thumbnails may be CDN-cached only under a signed authorization decision and short TTL; public activities are not assumed permanently public.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Self Feed and Friend Feed
docs.text:
The self feed is an owner-indexed activity query ordered by (completed_at, activity_id). It reads canonical metadata or an owner projection with a fallback, so a newly finalized activity is visible immediately. This is cheaper and more correct than routing the owner's own activity through social fanout.

For friends, use a hybrid feed:

  • Ordinary accounts fan out activity IDs on write into follower inboxes.
  • High-fanout accounts remain in an author outbox and are merged on read.
  • The feed row stores only a reference, author, rank key, and source version, not an authorization grant.
  • Hydration fetches current activity summary and rechecks visibility, friendship/follow state, blocks, and deletion.
  • Ranking may mix recency and affinity, but the cursor pins a query generation or stable rank boundary.
flowchart TD
    Final[Activity finalized] --> Classify{Author fanout class}
    Classify -->|ordinary| Fanout[Bounded fanout workers]
    Fanout --> Inboxes[(Viewer inbox shards)]
    Classify -->|high fanout| Author[(Author activity outbox)]
    Viewer[Viewer feed request] --> Merge[Candidate merge and rank]
    Inboxes --> Merge
    Author --> Merge
    Merge --> Auth[Current policy hydration]
    Graph[(Follow, friend, block graph)] --> Auth
    Activities[(Canonical visibility and tombstones)] --> Auth
    Auth --> Page[Authorized cursor page]
    subgraph CandidateLane[Candidate preparation]
      Final
      Classify
      Fanout
      Inboxes
      Author
      Viewer
      Merge
    end
    subgraph PolicyLane[Current authorization]
      Graph
      Activities
      Auth
      Page
    end

Fanout events are duplicate-safe by (viewer_id, activity_id, activity_version). Visibility reduction emits high-priority invalidation, but correctness does not depend on deletion reaching every inbox before a read. Hydration filters stale rows. To avoid empty pages after filtering, fetch bounded extra candidates and continue until the page fills or scan budget is exhausted.

Reactions are canonical idempotent upserts keyed by (activity_id, user_id). Aggregate counts are eventual and can be sharded for hot activities. A user sees their own reaction from canonical state. Notifications are retryable delivery based on durable reaction events; delayed notifications recheck that the activity remains visible and the reaction still exists.

docs.title: Optional Live Sharing
docs.text:
Live sharing is a separate ephemeral path, not a reason to weaken durable recording. The owner creates a short-lived grant for named users, a trusted group, or an unguessable link according to product policy. The device sends coarser updates, for example every five seconds, containing activity ID, monotonic sequence, location, elapsed time, and optional heart rate. Every update is also recorded locally if it belongs in the final activity.

Regional gateways authorize the grant at connection time and subscribe to an activity channel. They keep only the latest update plus a bounded replay window. Viewers tolerate gaps and discard lower sequences. No database write is required for every viewer delivery. The durable final route still arrives through normal upload and may differ after quality processing.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Owner device
    participant G as Live ingest gateway
    participant A as Authorization service
    participant R as Regional relay
    participant V as Authorized viewer
    O->>G: update(activity, grant, seq, location)
    G->>A: validate owner, grant, expiry, policy version
    A-->>G: allow with redaction policy
    G->>R: publish latest redacted update
    V->>A: exchange share token for short session
    A-->>V: scoped subscription token
    V->>R: subscribe(activity, token, last seq)
    R-->>V: latest then monotonic updates
    Note over G,R: missing heartbeat closes session

Live route redaction can delay location by a configurable interval and withhold points inside privacy zones. Revocation increments a grant epoch distributed on a priority channel; gateways reject older tokens and close sockets. Every grant has a hard expiry, viewer cap, rate cap, and owner-visible audience. Under overload, reduce update frequency and history first; never bypass authorization or affect the durable recorder.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition canonical activity metadata by owner_id so user history, privacy defaults, and ordinary writes are colocated; retain a globally unique activity ID lookup or encode shard routing in the ID. Chunk metadata can partition by activity_id, while object keys distribute by a hash prefix to avoid storage-listing hotspots. Processing streams partition by activity ID so one activity's manifest and policy events remain ordered.

Owner partitioning creates skew for prolific or imported accounts but normal activities are small metadata records. Very large imports and bulk reprocessing use separate quotas and worker pools. Feed inboxes partition by viewer ID, author outboxes by author ID, and reactions by activity with hash-suffixed counter shards. Live relays partition by (region, activity_id) and enforce audience caps.

Hot keys arise from celebrity posts, challenge leaderboards, and mass reconnect. Celebrity activities use read caches for public summaries, pull-on-read feed candidates, sharded reaction aggregation, and notification budgets. Leaderboards consume versioned summaries into a separate ranking system and are not transactionally updated with activity completion.

Reshard canonical owners with an ownership epoch: snapshot owner data at sequence S, copy it, replay later changes, fence the old shard, and switch routing. Upload sessions include the current home shard but can be redirected without changing object identity. Processing and feed events carry ownership and source versions so stale workers cannot publish over newer state.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Activity lifecycle, manifest installation/finalization, visibility, deletion, idempotency records, and live-grant state require strong consistency per activity or owner. Raw objects are immutable. Summaries, achievements, feed membership, reaction counts, search, and notifications are eventual projections. The owner gets read-your-writes through canonical metadata and a direct self-feed path.

Use optimistic revisions for user edits. PATCH visibility with If-Match either installs the next version and outbox event or returns current state. A deletion tombstone has a version and retention greater than cache, event replay, backup-restore, and feed rebuild windows. Consumers apply only events newer than their stored source version; deletion and block policy still receive explicit precedence.

Network delivery is at least once; the system does not claim exactly-once execution or delivery. Duplicate-safe business effects come from activity IDs, request idempotency keys with body hashes, chunk range and checksum uniqueness, conditional processing-version publication, feed-row uniqueness, and reaction upserts. Deduplication state must live at least as long as clients can retry or old events can replay.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
Device failure is the first reliability domain. Process death recovers from the local journal. Battery death can lose only the documented unforced tail. Sensor permission revocation appends an interruption when possible and warns the user. Low disk blocks recording before corruption. Keystore loss makes encrypted data unrecoverable by design; the UI should distinguish it from an empty activity.

Backend failures degrade independently. Metadata outage leaves devices recording and retrying with jitter. Object-store outage pauses chunk completion without losing journals. Stream outage delays processing and feeds but not finalization if the outbox remains durable. Processor failure replays immutable inputs. Feed-store loss rebuilds from canonical activities and graph snapshots. Authorization-store uncertainty fails closed for private or friends-only data.

docs.title: Reconnect Storms
docs.text:
After a carrier outage or backend recovery, millions of devices may retry together. Clients use exponential backoff with full jitter, persist next-attempt time, honor Retry-After, and query upload status before retransmitting. The edge issues per-user upload concurrency limits and admission tokens. Separate metadata control requests from bulk-byte capacity so clients can learn what is missing even when data upload is throttled.

The server publishes load tiers. At moderate pressure, it reduces presigned URL issuance and lowers per-device parallelism. Next it delays map matching, achievements, feed fanout, and notifications while preserving chunk acceptance and manifest finalization. At severe pressure, it prioritizes expiring active journals and final chunks over historical imports. Recovery ramps token issuance gradually to avoid a second wave.

docs.title: Corruption and Reconciliation
docs.text: End-to-end checksums detect in-transit and at-rest corruption. Periodic jobs compare manifest descriptors with object existence, length, and checksums; missing objects move activities to repair state and request retained device data where possible. Projection reconciliation compares the canonical finalized manifest and processing version with summary, route, feed, and achievement generations. Backups restore tombstones and privacy versions before serving reconstructed projections.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text:
Assign each user a home region with synchronous multi-zone canonical writes. Record and upload traffic routes home, while object storage replicates according to durability and residency policy. Authorized summaries and feed projections replicate near readers. Cross-region follows are asynchronous workflows; feed freshness can lag without changing visibility correctness.

On regional loss, promote a replica under a higher ownership epoch. If replication has nonzero RPO, only devices that still retain journals can repair missing uploads; a client that already deleted finalized bytes cannot be assumed to do so. Bind permission to discard local bytes to the promised backend durability tier, and recover the acknowledged metadata/object prefix before claiming no activity loss. Object inventory may help recover candidate chunks but cannot by itself establish which manifest or privacy state was committed. Do not allow simultaneous activity owners in two regions. Privacy tombstones, blocks, and live-grant revocations use a priority replicated deny channel; when current deny state cannot be established, non-public reads fail closed.

docs.title: Privacy, Authorization, and Abuse Prevention
docs.text: Location is sensitive even when an activity is public. Visibility values such as PRIVATE, FOLLOWERS, FRIENDS, and PUBLIC are insufficient alone; evaluate owner blocks, viewer blocks, age and regional policy, club membership, live grant, and field-level sharing. Feed rows are hints, not authority. A signed CDN URL is a bearer capability until expiry unless every edge hit also checks a current authorization epoch. For immediate revocation of future reads, use a policy-enforcing gateway with authoritative checks and defined handling of in-flight responses; otherwise declare a bound covering token/cache lifetime and deny-state freshness. Already downloaded routes cannot be recalled. Service-to-service access uses workload identity, least privilege, encryption, audited break-glass, and purpose-limited raw-location roles.

docs.title: Route Redaction
docs.text:
Users can define privacy zones around home, work, schools, or arbitrary places. Store zones encrypted and restrict which services can access centers. At publication time, clip raw or processed route points inside zones and optionally trim a configurable distance from start and end. Add randomized boundary treatment carefully: deterministic per activity avoids a mosaic of repeated outputs revealing the exact center, while excessive noise makes routes misleading.

Redaction creates a new derived route with a policy version. Summary distance can still use the full private route, but public maps and segment achievements use policy-defined geometry. Simplify only after clipping and split the polyline at removed intervals; otherwise a straight connector can reveal the hidden path. Bounding boxes, thumbnails, start labels, timestamps, photos, and live updates must use the same or stricter redaction. Cache keys include activity and privacy version.

Visibility reduction first updates canonical authorization and a deny epoch, then invalidates routes, CDN objects, feeds, search, notifications, and live grants. Stale projections may exist physically but must not be readable. Data export includes raw evidence and processing versions for the owner. Deletion has an immediate logical phase and an asynchronous physical phase across objects, replicas, caches, derived data, and backups with auditable completion.

Abuse controls cover fake GPS, leaderboard manipulation, scraping, stalking, reaction spam, malicious compressed chunks, and denial-of-wallet uploads. Bound chunk sizes, decompression ratio, sample counts, coordinate rates, activity duration, and manifest revisions. Validate parsers in isolated workers. Fraud signals can label or exclude achievements, but should not delete personal workout history without policy and appeal.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure device journal append latency, force frequency, queue drops, recovered tails, active-journal age, local disk pressure, upload bytes pending, session retries, checksum conflicts, missing ranges, finalization latency, object orphans, and reconnect admission. Backend service-level indicators include activity-read latency and availability, processing lag by stage, PARTIAL rate, feed fanout/hydration latency, authorization denials, stale-policy cache blocks, live update age, socket count, and revocation propagation.

GPS quality metrics include points by accuracy bucket, rejected-point reasons, implied-speed outliers, stationary drift, raw versus processed distance delta, map-match confidence, route simplification error, and processing-version change distribution. Avoid logging coordinates, zone centers, health values, or share tokens. Trace with salted activity identifiers and manifest/processing versions under controlled retention.

Test the device state machine with deterministic simulated sensor and storage failures. Property-test sequence monotonicity, legal lifecycle transitions, journal prefix recovery, CRC truncation, idempotent replay, manifest range coverage, and root-checksum stability. Kill the process before and after append, force, segment seal, upload, finalization, and local deletion. Test full disk, permission loss, clock jumps, reboot, old app versions, watch handoff, and corrupt encrypted frames.

Build GPS corpora for stationary jitter, straight runs, switchbacks, tunnels, urban canyons, out-and-back routes, dateline crossing, poles, bad accuracy, impossible teleports, and sparse samples. Compare Haversine and processing outputs against surveyed or simulator ground truth with sport-specific tolerances. Shadow algorithm and map-data upgrades before publishing.

Integration tests inject duplicate, reordered, missing, conflicting, and partially uploaded chunks. Chaos tests cover object storage, metadata database, stream, processing stage, feed store, graph service, authorization service, and regional failure. Load tests include one celebrity, many long activities, a 24-hour outage followed by reconnect, and slow live viewers. Privacy tests verify the declared revocation bound for stale feed, direct URL, CDN, export, and live access, including policy-channel isolation and already-issued capabilities.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text:
Recording directly to network simplifies the client but loses workouts offline; a durable local journal wins despite recovery complexity. One mutable activity blob is easy to upload but makes interruption expensive and conflict-prone; immutable checksummed chunks plus a manifest make retries bounded. One-second GPS captures shape but costs battery and amplifies jitter; adaptive sensing preserves important movement while reducing idle samples.

Summing Haversine distances is transparent but noisy. Filtering improves quality but introduces algorithm-dependent results; retain raw evidence and version outputs. Map matching can repair road tracks but invents paths in weak map coverage, so it must be confidence-gated and optional. Fanout-on-write gives fast friend feeds but creates celebrity amplification; hybrid push/pull isolates skew. Live sharing adds safety and social value but materially expands privacy and operational risk, so keep it optional, short-lived, audience-capped, and separate from durable recording.

Strong global consistency would make mobile and cross-region operation brittle. Strong per-activity state plus immutable bytes and eventual projections matches the actual invariants. Keeping raw location forever maximizes future reprocessing but increases cost and privacy exposure; tiered, policy-bound retention with explicit quality-version limits is preferable.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Device[Offline-first device]
        Sensors[Sensor adapters] --> Writer[Single state and journal writer]
        Writer --> Local[(Encrypted journal and local outbox)]
        Local --> Sync[Checksummed chunk sync]
    end
    Sync --> Edge[Regional authenticated edge]
    Edge --> Coordinator[Upload coordinator]
    Edge --> Activity[Activity and privacy service]
    Coordinator --> Blob[(Immutable replicated object store)]
    Coordinator --> Canon[(Owner-sharded metadata, manifest, outbox)]
    Activity --> Canon
    Canon --> Stream[(At-least-once versioned stream)]
    Stream --> Geo[GPS quality and map pipeline]
    Stream --> Social[Hybrid feed and notification pipeline]
    Geo --> Derived[(Versioned summaries and redacted routes)]
    Social --> Feed[(Viewer inboxes and author outboxes)]
    Edge --> Read[Authorization-first query service]
    Read --> Canon
    Read --> Derived
    Read --> Feed
    Policy[Privacy, graph, blocks, deny epochs] --> Read
    Policy --> Live[Ephemeral live gateways and relays]
    Local -. optional coarse updates .-> Live
    Control[Algorithms, map versions, quotas, ownership epochs] --> Geo
    Control --> Coordinator
    subgraph AuthorityLane[Upload and canonical state]
      Coordinator
      Activity
      Blob
      Canon
    end
    subgraph DerivedLane[Versioned projections]
      Stream
      Geo
      Social
      Derived
      Feed
    end
    subgraph ReadLane[Current authorization]
      Read
      Policy
    end

The smallest correct design is a device journal, resumable chunk uploader, owner-sharded activity metadata store, immutable object storage, and one deterministic summary worker. Add the stream, social projections, map matching, multi-region replicas, and live relays only when scale and product requirements justify them. Across every layer, canonical activity and policy versions override convenient caches.

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. What exactly is durable when the app says a sample, pause, or finish was recorded?
  2. How does recovery distinguish a torn trailing write from corruption in the middle of a journal?
  3. Why are device sequence and monotonic time safer than arrival time and wall time?
  4. How can a phone and watch contribute samples without inventing a global device clock?
  5. Why does summing every Haversine segment overcount a stationary workout?
  6. When should map matching be disabled even if road data is available?
  7. What prevents the same chunk upload from creating duplicate bytes or conflicting content?
  8. How does finalization prove that every expected sequence is present?
  9. What happens if finalization commits but the device never receives the response?
  10. How does the owner see a completed activity before friend-feed fanout finishes?
  11. How is a private activity protected if a stale feed row or CDN object remains?
  12. What is shed first during a reconnect storm, and what must remain available?
  13. How do route simplification and privacy-zone clipping interact?
  14. Which state must be strongly consistent, and which projections can be rebuilt?
  15. How would a GPS algorithm migration avoid silently changing historical records?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text:
An L5 answer should separate recording from upload, define a durable local journal and legal lifecycle, estimate sensor storage, use stable activity IDs and chunk checksums, explain resumable finalization, give a defensible GPS filtering pipeline, partition by owner/activity, make feeds eventual but authorization current, and cover retries, deletion, observability, and major failures.

An L6 answer should negotiate device acknowledgement and battery-loss semantics, formalize multi-source clocks and manifest coverage, identify every crash window, design reconnect admission and overload priorities, version GPS and map outputs, quantify feed and live-sharing amplification, separate control and data planes, define regional ownership and fencing, make privacy denial dominate stale distribution, plan algorithm and schema migrations, and connect raw-location retention to cost, regulation, abuse, and organizational access boundaries.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text:
A fitness tracker must preserve the workout before it can synchronize it. A single device writer appends sequenced control and sensor records to an encrypted durable journal; crash recovery validates the journal prefix, reconstructs lifecycle state, and resumes a local outbox. Sealed source-specific ranges become immutable checksummed chunks. The backend accepts retries idempotently, reports missing ranges, and finalizes only a complete versioned manifest, then emits an outbox event. Raw chunks remain immutable while versioned workers validate clocks and accuracy, reject drift and impossible speed, calculate a Haversine baseline, optionally map-match confident routes, simplify geometry, and atomically publish summaries.

Store canonical activity, manifest, visibility, and deletion state strongly consistently per owner/activity. Keep raw bytes in object storage and rebuild summaries, achievements, routes, feeds, and notifications from versioned events. Give owners a direct history path and friends a hybrid push/pull feed whose hydration always reauthorizes. Optional live sharing uses expiring grants, coarse updates, bounded regional relays, and fast revocation without entering the durable recording path. Partition metadata by owner, processing by activity, and feeds by viewer; isolate celebrity and import skew. During outages, devices continue journaling. During reconnect storms, admit uploads with jitter and tokens while delaying map matching and social work. Clip privacy zones before simplifying routes, version every redaction, fail closed on uncertain authorization, and make deletion and blocks dominate every cache and projection.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Clarify whether the focus is photo/video publishing, profiles, following, home feed, likes, and comments. This design covers those surfaces and the media pipeline; Stories, Reels recommendation, ads, and direct messages are excluded. Begin with durable media ingest and canonical post metadata, then design hybrid feed fanout and globally efficient delivery.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
A user uploads media, creates a captioned post, follows accounts, browses profiles and a personalized home feed, and likes or comments. Uploads must survive client retries and weak networks. A post becomes visible only after required media variants are ready and policy checks pass. Feed reads target 300 ms p99 excluding media transfer; images and video start quickly through a CDN. Private-account and block rules are mandatory. Deletes should stop new delivery within minutes and purge retained copies according to policy.

The minimum viable home feed is reverse chronological over posts from accepted follow relationships, ordered by (created_at, post_id). Ranking is an optional product layer, not a correctness dependency. If the ranker is disabled, overloaded, or being evaluated, chronology remains a complete and explainable fallback.

The design supports 500 million daily users, creator skew, viral media, and phones that retry after ambiguous responses. It prioritizes availability for public reads while failing closed for uncertain private access.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• An upload session owns immutable source bytes identified by checksum.
  • A published post references only media assets in a publishable state.
  • Post metadata is canonical; feeds contain references, not copies.
  • Current privacy, block, moderation, and deletion state overrides cached feed entries.
  • One idempotency key and payload produce one post.
  • Likes have one state per (user, post); displayed counts may lag.
  • Delayed processing cannot republish a deleted or rejected asset.
  • At most one active follow edge exists per (follower, followee), and self-follow is rejected.
  • A private account contributes posts only after an accepted request; unfollow, block, or revocation wins over stale fanout entries at read time.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 100 million new posts/day with two media objects on average. At 4 MB uploaded per post, ingress is 400 TB/day, roughly 4.6 GB/s average and perhaps 40 GB/s peak. Several responsive image sizes and video renditions can double or triple stored bytes, yielding hundreds of petabytes over years before lifecycle tiering. Twenty feed opens per daily user and two pages/open produce 20 billion page requests/day. Metadata writes average 1,200/s but media and engagement peaks are much larger. A viral 5 MB asset viewed 100 million times represents 500 TB of egress; CDN hit rate is a first-order cost and reliability concern.

Fanout sizing makes the hybrid threshold concrete. If a creator publishes p posts/day to F followers and each inbox reference averages 40 logical bytes before replication and indexes, push cost is p * F logical writes/day and 40 * p * F logical bytes/day. A creator with 5M followers and two posts/day causes 10M writes and about 400 MB of logical writes per day for one author. Three copies require at least 1.2 GB/day before indexes and compaction. More importantly, completing within a 60-second freshness SLO requires about 83K logical writes/s for that post.

Set the push cutoff from measured worker capacity rather than status. With 20K safe writes/s allocated to one fanout job and a 60-second target, the hard bound is 20,000 * 60 = 1.2M active recipients. Applying 50% headroom gives a starting cutoff near 600K active followers. Recompute it from active-follower ratio, publish rate, queue lag, and read amplification; a dormant 2M-follower account may be cheaper than a highly active 400K-follower account.

docs.title: Entities and data model
docs.text:
User(user_id, handle, account_state, privacy, profile_version, created_at)
UploadSession(upload_id, owner_id, object_key, checksum, state, expires_at)
MediaAsset(media_id, owner_id, source_key, variants[], state, moderation_version)
Post(post_id, author_id, caption, media_ids[], visibility, created_at,
     publication_seq, state, version)
Follow(follower_id, followee_id, state, relationship_version, updated_at)
FeedEntry(owner_id, bucket, post_id, author_id, created_at)
FeedCandidateSnapshot(snapshot_id, owner_id, post_watermark, graph_watermark,
                      ordered_post_ids[], expires_at)
Like(post_id, user_id, state, updated_at)
Comment(comment_id, post_id, author_id, body, state, created_at)

Metadata databases partition posts and assets by ID, with author-time indexes. Object keys are opaque and never confer authorization. Feed entries partition by viewer and time bucket. Comments partition by post and bucket; pathological viral posts need subpartitions. Counters are sharded projections.

Follow.state is PENDING, ACCEPTED, REJECTED, or REVOKED. Following a public account conditionally creates ACCEPTED; following a private account creates PENDING and notifies the followee. Only the followee can accept or reject. Unfollow changes an accepted or pending edge to REVOKED; it does not delete audit history. A block atomically records an authoritative pair-level deny policy. Both directional relationship projections are then revoked idempotently; if they live on different shards, read and accept paths consult the deny authority until those projections catch up. Each mutation increments relationship_version, allowing delayed accept and fanout work to detect that it lost a race.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/uploads                    {"content_type":"image/jpeg","size":...}
POST /v1/uploads/{id}/complete      {"checksum":"..."}
POST /v1/posts                      Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
GET  /v1/feed?cursor=<opaque>&limit=20
GET  /v1/users/{id}/posts?cursor=...
PUT  /v1/users/{id}/follow          Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
DELETE /v1/users/{id}/follow
GET  /v1/follow-requests?cursor=...
POST /v1/follow-requests/{id}/accept If-Match: <relationship-version>
POST /v1/follow-requests/{id}/reject If-Match: <relationship-version>
PUT  /v1/posts/{id}/likes/me
DELETE /v1/posts/{id}/likes/me
POST /v1/posts/{id}/comments
DELETE /v1/posts/{id}

The upload API returns short-lived multipart signed URLs restricted to key, size, and content type. Completion verifies object metadata server-side. Post creation returns 202 Processing or 201 Published depending on product semantics; status polling and push events expose progress.

Follow endpoints return the canonical relationship state. Repeating an idempotency key with the same body returns the prior result; reusing it for a different target is rejected. Accepting an already revoked or superseded request returns 409 Conflict, while repeated unfollow succeeds without recreating the edge. Profile and follower-list APIs apply block and privacy policy before returning data.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Mobile clients] --> A[API gateway]
    C --> O[(Object storage upload)]
    A --> U[Upload service]
    A --> P[Post service]
    A --> F[Feed service]
    U --> O
    U --> K[Media job log]
    K --> X[Transcode and resize workers]
    X --> O
    X --> M[Safety scan]
    P --> D[(Metadata DB + outbox)]
    D --> E[Domain event log]
    E --> W[Feed fanout]
    W --> I[(Feed inboxes)]
    F --> I
    F --> D
    O --> CDN[Media CDN]

docs.title: Upload and publish
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant U as Upload service
    participant O as Object storage
    participant X as Media pipeline
    participant P as Post service
    C->>U: Create upload session
    U-->>C: Signed multipart URLs
    C->>O: Upload parts and complete
    C->>U: Complete(checksum)
    U->>O: Verify object metadata
    U->>X: Enqueue immutable media ID
    X->>O: Write variants
    X->>U: Asset READY or REJECTED
    C->>P: Create post(media IDs, key)
    P->>P: Validate ownership and READY state
    P-->>C: Published post ID

The media pipeline is a state machine: CREATED -> UPLOADED -> SCANNING -> PROCESSING -> READY, with FAILED, REJECTED, and DELETED terminal controls. Workers conditionally advance versions, so duplicated or reordered jobs cannot regress state. Source objects remain private; only approved variants enter CDN-backed namespaces.

docs.title: Feed read
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant F as Feed service
    participant I as Inbox
    participant H as High-fanout source index
    participant P as Policy and post store
    participant R as Optional ranker
    C->>F: GET feed(cursor)
    F->>P: Pin graph and publication watermarks
    F->>I: Fetch pushed IDs through watermark
    F->>H: Fetch large-creator IDs through watermark
    F->>F: Seal deduplicated candidate snapshot
    F->>P: Batch hydrate and authorize
    opt Ranking enabled and healthy
        F->>R: Rank eligible candidates
        R-->>F: Scored candidates
    end
    F->>F: Stable chronological fallback or ranked order
    F-->>C: Metadata, CDN URLs, cursor

CDN URLs may be public for public approved media or signed and short-lived for private media. The origin authorization layer never relies solely on an old signature after a privacy change; revocation must deny old URLs at an authenticated edge on cache hits as well as misses, or wait for their explicitly bounded capability lifetime. Rotating a path only changes new references and does not revoke a known old cached URL. Public-to-private changes use the same gate; already downloaded bytes cannot be recalled.

docs.title: Follow, unfollow, and private approval
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Follower
    participant G as Graph service
    participant D as Relationship DB and outbox
    participant B as Private followee
    participant F as Feed service
    A->>G: PUT follow(id, key)
    G->>D: Conditional create PENDING
    D-->>B: Follow-request notification
    B->>G: Accept(request, expected version)
    G->>D: PENDING to ACCEPTED and emit event
    D-->>F: RelationshipAccepted(version)
    F->>F: Optionally backfill recent post IDs
    A->>G: DELETE follow
    G->>D: ACCEPTED to REVOKED, increment version
    D-->>F: RelationshipRevoked(version)
    F->>F: Tombstone or lazily filter stale entries

Acceptance and unfollow are conditional updates. If they race, exactly one expected-version transition wins; a delayed acceptance cannot resurrect the edge. Product policy must state whether acceptance backfills recent posts. A bounded window such as the latest 100 posts or 30 days avoids unbounded fanout, and read-time authorization still controls visibility.

docs.title: Publish and fanout
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant P as Post service
    participant D as Post DB and outbox
    participant Q as Fanout queue
    participant G as Graph store
    participant I as Feed inboxes
    P->>D: Commit published post and event
    D-->>Q: PostPublished(post version)
    Q->>G: Page accepted active followers
    loop Follower pages
        Q->>I: Put if absent(owner, post)
        Q->>Q: Persist page checkpoint
    end
    Note over Q,I: High-fanout authors stay in pull index

Fanout is at least once, so (owner_id, post_id) is unique. Workers checkpoint the last follower-page token only after inbox writes complete. On crash they replay a page safely. A relationship version captured during enumeration is advisory, not authorization: feed hydration checks current privacy, block, follow, post, moderation, and deletion state before returning content.

docs.title: Resumable media ingest
docs.text: Clients upload directly to object storage to keep API fleets out of the byte path. Multipart sessions resume individual parts and expire abandoned uploads. Completion compares declared size, checksum, owner, and object generation. Content-addressable deduplication can save storage, but cross-user dedup must not leak whether another user uploaded identical content. Garbage collectors remove expired staging objects only after checking session state and generation.

docs.title: Media processing and delivery
docs.text: Workers produce format, resolution, crop, thumbnail, and video rendition manifests. Jobs are idempotent by (media_id, pipeline_version, variant). New codecs run alongside old variants, and manifests switch only after validation. CDN keys include immutable content or variant versions, allowing year-long caching. Origin shielding prevents a viral miss from stampeding object storage. Negative caching is short because a variant may still be processing.

docs.title: Feed fanout and creator skew
docs.text: Push post IDs for ordinary private and public accounts into active followers' inboxes. Pull posts from high-fanout creators at read time. Private creators may favor push for efficiency but still require read authorization. Fanout tasks enumerate follower shards through fair queues, with dynamic thresholds based on follower count, activity, and write cost. Ranking overfetches before filtering and applies creator diversity.

docs.title: Stable chronological merge and recovery
docs.text:
Page one must establish a bounded candidate snapshot before returning any item. With independently sharded graph and post authorities, G and W are consistent retained version vectors or a materialization barrier over the relevant shards, not unexplained scalar global sequences. Define a finite history horizon and maximum session depth; if the completeness scan exceeds its budget, return an explicit partial/retry response rather than promise a complete chronology. The feed service obtains a graph watermark G and publication watermark W, freezes the accepted author set at G, and admits only posts with publication_seq <= W. It reads pushed inbox entries, high-fanout timelines, and canonical timelines for any author whose fanout checkpoint is below W; therefore an entry delayed in the push queue cannot appear behind the reader later or be skipped forever. The service k-way merges these sources by (created_at DESC, post_id DESC), deduplicates by post_id, and seals the ordered IDs as a short-lived FeedCandidateSnapshot.

Every page, including chronological fallback, must reference that snapshot. The signed cursor contains {snapshot_id, feed_mode, next_ordinal, query_hash, expires_at}; the next page reads ordinal >= next_ordinal, never recomputes a union from current push and pull stores. Current authorization, block, moderation, and deletion policy still runs during hydration, so policy removals can intentionally shorten a page, but source lag cannot create chronology gaps. Snapshot expiry produces an explicit restart response. Implementations may store the bounded ordered IDs or an equivalent immutable per-source boundary manifest, but an optional watermark alone is not sufficient.

Ranking, when enabled, seals a stored ordered ID list using pinned features and scores at session creation and uses (score DESC, created_at DESC, post_id DESC) over the same mandatory candidate snapshot. The cursor identifies the snapshot and model version. If the snapshot expires, return an explicit restart cursor rather than mixing incompatible pages. If the ranker fails before page one, order the sealed candidates chronologically; if it fails mid-session, continue the stored ranked order or ask the client to restart, never change ordering semantics invisibly.

Missing fanout is recoverable because feeds store references and author timelines remain canonical. When queue lag breaches the freshness SLO, read-time pull includes authors whose fanout watermark trails their latest post. A sweeper compares outbox publication, fanout checkpoints, and inbox samples, then replays idempotently. Rebuilding an inbox scans accepted follows and bounded author timelines at a relationship watermark; hydration removes any edge revoked during the rebuild.

docs.title: Viral comments and counts
docs.text: Likes use canonical per-user rows and asynchronous sharded counters. Comments on ordinary posts can partition by post; viral posts add a hash suffix and merge by (created_at, comment_id). Moderation tombstones comments rather than rewriting pages. Counter accuracy is bounded, and user-specific state is fetched separately so a stale count never changes whether the button appears selected.

docs.title: Partitioning and multi-region
docs.text:
Hash metadata by IDs and maintain author indexes. Feed inboxes use viewer plus monthly or sequence buckets. Follower reverse indexes use source plus ranges. Object storage partitions through high-entropy prefixes, while CDN cache keys use immutable versions. Dedicated shards can isolate celebrity comment and engagement traffic.

Upload to the nearest region, then replicate source media according to residency rules before publication in additional geographies. Assign user metadata a home region and replicate events globally. Regional feed projections are rebuildable. Public media can be globally cached; private media honors residency and access controls. During home-region failure, reads use replicas and uploads may enter a region-owned pending state; avoid conflicting post updates by fencing the old owner before failover.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and failures
docs.text:
Post publication and idempotency mapping are strongly consistent on one shard. Media processing, fanout, moderation, counters, and replication are eventual state machines. The post service transactionally stores an outbox event. Consumers use event IDs or unique target keys; version checks make delete win over delayed ready/publish events.

Object-store completion without API acknowledgement is recovered by retrying completion. A failed processor retries with bounded attempts and quarantine; original bytes remain for replay. If fanout lags, profile reads remain correct and feed reads pull recent posts. If ranking fails, use chronology. If CDN origin is overloaded, stale public variants may be served, but private authorization cannot be bypassed. Storage corruption is detected by checksums and repaired from replicas. Queue backpressure rejects or delays noncritical transformations before source uploads.

docs.title: Security, abuse, and privacy
docs.text: Signed upload URLs restrict object key, byte range, type, and expiry. Scan malware and malformed codecs in sandboxed workers. Rate-limit follows, comments, likes, and uploads by account, device, IP, and reputation. Detect credential stuffing, scraping, spam, and coordinated engagement. Strip sensitive image metadata such as GPS unless explicitly retained. Private media never uses guessable URLs as security. Blocks and account privacy changes invalidate access promptly. Deletion workflows cover originals, variants, CDN caches, backups by retention policy, search indexes, and ML datasets with auditable lineage.

docs.title: Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure upload completion and abandonment, checksum failure, processing duration by variant, moderation lag, publish success, post-to-feed age, fanout amplification, inbox and creator skew, feed stage p99, CDN hit ratio, origin egress, time-to-first-byte, unauthorized-deny rate, comment hot partitions, and delete completion. Correlate an upload ID through object generation, jobs, media ID, and post.

Test multipart resume and ambiguous completion, duplicate/reordered jobs, decompression bombs and corrupt media, variant golden outputs, privacy relationship matrices, cursor stability, and deletion races. Race private accept against unfollow, block against fanout, privacy-publication changes against feed hydration, duplicate follow requests, post deletion against inbox insertion, and a fanout checkpoint crash after writes but before acknowledgement. Assert that revoked edges never revive, inbox keys remain unique, pages have no duplicates or gaps within their declared snapshot, and ranker failure follows the documented restart or chronology behavior. Load tests use realistic media sizes and Zipfian creators around the hybrid cutoff. Chaos experiments remove a processor pool, broker partition, CDN shield, metadata shard, fanout worker, ranker, or region. Synthetic private accounts continuously assert that unauthorized principals cannot fetch metadata or bytes.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Proxying uploads simplifies clients but makes application servers costly and failure-prone; direct signed upload wins with more state-machine complexity. Mutable CDN URLs simplify references but make cache invalidation unsafe; immutable variant URLs plus manifests win. Push-only feed fanout fails on celebrities, while pull-only raises every read's graph cost; hybrid wins. Serving private objects through globally shared public caches is cheap but unsafe; authenticated edge delivery costs more and satisfies the invariant.

flowchart TD
    A[Resumable direct upload] --> B[(Private immutable source)]
    B --> C[Versioned media pipeline]
    C --> D[(Approved immutable variants)]
    D --> E[CDN and authorized edge]
    F[Canonical post + outbox] --> G[Durable event log]
    G --> H[Hybrid feed projections]
    H --> I[Merge, policy filter, rank]
    F --> I
    I --> J[Metadata plus safe media URLs]

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. How does upload completion recover when the client times out?
  2. How can a private-media URL be revoked after it reaches a device?
  3. What prevents delayed processing from reviving deleted media?
  4. How do comment partitions preserve stable pagination on viral posts?
  5. How do you roll out a new image or video codec?
  6. Where does media residency constrain replication and CDN use?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should separate byte and metadata paths, define resumable upload, model media states, design hybrid feed fanout, and cover CDN, retries, and privacy. An L6 candidate should quantify egress and skew, version pipelines and policy, design fencing and regional residency, explain revocation limits, isolate overload domains, provide migration and replay plans, and connect safety, deletion, quality, and cost to operations.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Upload immutable source bytes directly to object storage through constrained multipart URLs. Verify checksum and ownership, then run idempotent, versioned processing and safety jobs before allowing a post to reference READY assets. Store post metadata canonically with an outbox. Push post IDs for normal creators and pull recent IDs for high-fanout creators; merge, authorize against current relationship and moderation state, rank, and paginate by stable boundaries. Deliver approved immutable variants through CDN, with authenticated edge controls for private media. Partition metadata by ID, inboxes by viewer and time, follower lists by source ranges, and viral comments by post plus suffix. Let derived counters and feeds lag, but make publication, user engagement state, deletion precedence, and access decisions explicit. Operate upload integrity, processing lag, fanout skew, feed latency, CDN behavior, and deletion end to end.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design comments attached to a live stream, sports event, or launch. Clarify ordering, audience size, moderation, replay, and whether every viewer must see every message. The key is separating durable comment acceptance from best-effort realtime distribution. At million-viewer scale, sampling and ranking are product requirements, not merely optimizations.

docs.title: Requirements, invariants, and estimates
docs.text:
Users post comments, receive a continuously updating stream, react, report, and replay recent history. Moderators remove comments and mute users. Post acknowledgement targets 200 ms p99. For eligible comments selected into a viewer's subscribed distribution tier, delivery normally targets one second from selection; measure acceptance-to-eligibility delay separately. Acceptance does not promise broadcast to every viewer, and held comments have a separate moderation latency objective. The service remains available under celebrity-event bursts and protects the player from comment-system failures.

  • Accepted comments are durable before acknowledgement and have an event-local sequence.
  • A request key creates at most one canonical comment.
  • Authorization and moderation state override caches and delayed delivery.
  • Durable distribution consumers process at least once, but live socket delivery is best effort with bounded replay; clients deduplicate by comment ID.
  • A removal version dominates delayed create/index events.
  • Per-viewer ordering is monotonic by server sequence, with documented gaps.
  • Viewer backpressure never blocks canonical ingestion.

Assume 10 million concurrent viewers for a top event, 2% commenting once/minute: 3,300 writes/s, with 20x bursts. Sending every comment to every viewer is billions of deliveries/s. Therefore channels produce one durable stream but viewer tiers receive ranked, sampled, localized subsets. At 500 bytes/comment, canonical storage is small compared with realtime egress and connections.
