docs.title: Massive fanout and selection
docs.text: The durable event stream is consumed once into regional relays. Gateways subscribe to topic variants such as moderator-approved highlights, locale, friends, or sampled general chat. A mixer enforces author diversity, rate caps, freshness, quality, and deterministic sampling so reconnects are less jarring. Hosts and moderators may receive an unsampled stream. Hierarchical relay prevents cross-region multiplication and sends one frame per gateway, which then multiplexes local sockets.

docs.title: Ordering, pagination, and replay
docs.text: An event shard assigns increasing sequences. Sampling creates intentional gaps, so clients order received items and use a server watermark rather than assume contiguity. History uses (event_id, seq) cursor pagination. During reconnect, gateways replay a bounded regional buffer; older gaps use durable history. Edits and removals are separate versioned control events at the same comment identity, not newly ordered comments, and must apply even when their original comment sequence is below the display watermark. A held comment released after the topic has advanced beyond its original sequence appears in authorized history but is not injected backward into the live ordered tier; alternatively the product must define a separate eligibility/delivery sequence.

docs.title: Moderation and viral abuse
docs.text: Admission applies authentication, per-account/device/IP token buckets, duplicate-text detection, URL policy, and lightweight classifiers. Async systems aggregate reports, reputation, and coordinated behavior. Moderation commands use a priority topic distributed to every gateway; gateways keep a compact tombstone cache and remove already-rendered items. Human tooling records actor, policy version, evidence, and appeal outcome. Slow moderation reduces distribution volume rather than allowing unchecked backlog.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text: Each socket has a bounded queue. Slow consumers lose typing/reaction updates first, then receive coarser comment samples, and finally a resync marker. Gateways never push back into canonical logs. Event-level admission budgets isolate hot events, while fair queues preserve small streams. If egress capacity falls, the mixer lowers sample rates transparently.

docs.title: Partitioning, regions, consistency, reliability, and recovery
docs.text:
Partition canonical comments by event and time bucket. A hot event uses one logical sequencer with partitioned storage writers; any leased sequence ranges need a committed-prefix frontier and explicit sealed gaps before publication, since allocating disjoint ranges does not establish commit order. if strict total order is unnecessary, shard by lane and expose (lane,sequence) partial order. Reactions partition by comment plus hash suffix. Gateways and relays partition by event and geography.

Write an event in its home region with synchronous zonal replicas. Replicate logs and moderation commands to viewing regions. Fenced failover prevents two sequencers; gaps are acceptable after lease loss. Distribution is regional and disposable. Comment append is strongly consistent per event; moderation, reactions, ranking, and delivery are eventual. Idempotency mappings and outbox commits close retry and dual-write gaps.

Reliability objectives follow the product hierarchy: preserve video playback first, accepted-comment durability and moderation commands second, and complete realtime distribution last. Canonical comments use an RPO of zero within the home region because acknowledgement follows a synchronous zonal commit; regional disaster recovery targets an RPO under one minute from the replicated log and a 15-minute RTO for posting. Realtime relays are disposable and target a two-minute RTO by reconnecting viewers to healthy capacity with a lower initial sample rate.

Bus failure delays realtime but history remains correct. Operators detect it from event-age and outbox-age SLO burn, pause nonessential reaction consumers, restore or reroute partitions, and replay from committed outbox offsets; idempotent comment IDs and tombstone versions make replay safe. Gateway loss reconnects clients with cursors, while admission jitter and replay budgets prevent a recovery storm. Regional relay loss shifts subscriptions to another relay at a lower sample rate. Sequencer loss acquires a higher fenced epoch before appends resume; ambiguous requests retry with their original idempotency keys. Cache loss invokes stricter load shedding. Poison messages are quarantined without blocking the partition. After regional recovery, reconciliation compares canonical sequence ranges, moderation-version watermarks, and sampled gateway delivery receipts before quality tiers are raised. Replays always honor current tombstones.

docs.title: Security, privacy, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Do not expose viewer lists or raw IPs. Apply age/region policy, blocks, mutes, and streamer controls. Escape rendered text, scan links, restrict moderator APIs, encrypt and audit evidence, and define retention for chat replay. Protect against bot floods, Unicode impersonation, brigading, and report abuse.

Measure accept and end-to-end latency, outbox age, moderation decision/removal propagation, accepted/held/rejected rates, comments per event, fanout amplification, relay/gateway saturation, socket drops, sample ratio, replay rate, duplicates, ordering regressions, and report outcomes. Correlate by comment ID and policy version.

Property-test tombstone precedence and cursor ordering. Replay duplicates and version reorder. Load-test flash crowds, one hot event, many small events, slow sockets, and spam bursts. Chaos-test sequencer, relay, bus, and region loss. Safety changes run shadow evaluation and canaries; synthetic comments verify removals reach every regional gateway.

docs.title: Event lifecycle, replay, and capacity control
docs.text:
An event moves through SCHEDULED, WARMING, LIVE, ENDED, and ARCHIVED. Warming preallocates sequencer capacity, regional topics, moderation staff/tools, and CDN-independent gateway pools based on expected audience. Live transition is idempotent. Ending rejects new ordinary comments, drains accepted work, records the final watermark, and converts hot storage into a replay index. Archival applies retention and legal policies to bodies, author mappings, reports, and moderation evidence separately.

Replay is not simply the live stream saved forever. It may return a stable chronological subset, highlighted comments, and tombstones at the viewer's playback timestamp. Each record carries media time as well as ingestion sequence. Late moderation updates the replay projection and remains effective even though the original live packet was delivered. Rebuilders scan canonical comments plus versioned moderation actions up to a checkpoint, then atomically switch an index generation.

Capacity planning uses connections, frames, and bytes rather than comment writes alone. If ten million viewers receive two 400-byte frames per second, edge egress is roughly 8 GB/s before protocol overhead. Batching several comments per frame cuts headers and CPU. Compression helps text but can increase latency and security risk if contexts mix principals; gateway policies choose bounded independent frames. Regional relays expose subscription counts so placement can add gateways before queues fill.

A flash-crowd runbook establishes explicit thresholds. At moderate pressure, coalesce reactions and presence. Next, lower general-chat sample rates and reserve full feeds for moderators. Then disable expensive personalization, cap history replay, and reject comments from low-reputation unauthenticated sessions. At severe pressure, preserve the video product, canonical moderation commands, and accepted-comment durability while returning a clear degraded indicator. Recovery raises quality gradually to avoid a reconnect and replay storm.

Privacy controls include per-viewer blocks and muted terms. Applying them at every regional relay would explode state, so gateways maintain compact viewer policy or clients apply convenience mutes; safety-critical blocks are checked during history hydration and distribution-token construction. The design must distinguish privacy authorization, which cannot be delegated to a client, from display preferences, which can.

Reactions use a separate lossy aggregation path. A user reaction is an idempotent canonical upsert, but the animated count shown during the event is a windowed approximation produced from regional deltas. Periodic durable reconciliation corrects drift. This avoids turning a popular comment into a single counter hot key and prevents reaction storms from competing with moderation traffic. Clients render an approximate marker and fetch the user's own reaction state separately.

Deployments drain gateways instead of dropping all sockets simultaneously. New connections move to the new version while old gateways stop accepting subscriptions and retain existing ones for a deadline. Protocol envelopes advertise supported versions, and unknown optional fields are ignored. Changes to ordering, cursor, or tombstone semantics require a negotiated protocol version and mixed-client tests. This operational detail prevents an otherwise harmless rollout from becoming the largest reconnect storm of the day.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Broadcasting everything preserves chat completeness but collapses at large audiences and harms usability. Ranked deterministic sampling is scalable but creates different viewer experiences. Pre-moderation is safer but adds latency; risk-tiered synchronous gates plus fast async removal balance both. Strict total order simplifies replay but creates a sequencer bottleneck; retain it while rate is feasible, then explicitly move to lane ordering rather than pretending global order.

flowchart TD
 A[Rate and safety gated ingest] --> B[Fenced event sequencer]
 B --> C[(Canonical log + outbox)]
 C --> D[Async moderation and tombstones]
 D -->|eligible only| E[Regional hierarchical relays]
 D -->|priority removals| E
 E --> F[Ranked/sampled topic variants]
 F --> G[Bounded gateway queues]
 H[Durable history] --> I[Cursor replay]

docs.title: Questions, levels, and five-minute summary
docs.text:
1. Can every viewer see every comment at ten million concurrency?
  2. How do removals reach clients that already rendered content?
  3. What ordering contract survives sampling and failover?
  4. Which load is shed first during a flash crowd?
  5. How do moderator and ordinary streams differ?

L5 candidates should separate ingest from fanout, quantify amplification, design bounded sockets, idempotency, cursor replay, and moderation. L6 candidates should negotiate completeness versus relevance, define overload tiers, sequence/failover semantics, regional relay topology, policy auditability, and a migration to partial ordering.

In five minutes: durably append rate- and safety-gated comments to an event-local ordered log with an outbox. Consume that log into moderation and hierarchical regional distribution. Do not broadcast every item at huge scale; create policy-controlled, ranked, localized, or deterministically sampled topic variants and multiplex each once per gateway. Bound socket queues and degrade ephemeral reactions, sample density, then require resync without affecting ingestion. Use versioned tombstones that override stale events, opaque sequence cursors for history, fenced regional failover, and explicit gaps under sampling. Operate event skew, moderation latency, fanout amplification, queue drops, and replay correctness.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design a multi-tenant platform that accepts notification intents and delivers push, email, SMS, and in-app messages. Clarify transactional versus promotional traffic, user preferences, scheduling, templates, provider callbacks, and delivery semantics. The core is controlled at-least-once workflow with idempotent effects, suppression, and channel-specific overload policy.

docs.title: Requirements, invariants, and estimates
docs.text:
Producers submit immediate or scheduled intents. The platform resolves recipients, consent, template, locale, channel policy, and provider; sends; consumes callbacks; and exposes status. Transactional traffic targets seconds, while campaigns may take hours. No claim of exactly-once delivery is possible because external providers and devices can duplicate.

  • One tenant idempotency key creates one logical notification intent.
  • Current legal suppression and user opt-out override queued promotional work.
  • Every attempt is auditable with redacted payload and provider response.
  • Transactional traffic cannot be starved by campaigns.
  • State transitions are monotonic and versioned; callbacks cannot regress terminal state.
  • Retry uses the same logical identity but a distinct attempt ID.
  • Templates are immutable once referenced by a send.

Assume 10 billion logical notifications/day, 115,000/s average and 1 million/s peak. With 1.5 channels selected on average, there are 15 billion initial channel sends/day before suppression. Total provider attempts additionally multiply by the eligible fraction and mean attempts per eligible send; at 100% eligibility and 1.1 attempts/send, this is 16.5 billion attempts/day. A 1 KB intent is 10 TB/day before replication. Campaigns can enqueue hundreds of millions at once, and provider quotas differ by country, sender, and channel, so smoothing and partition fairness matter more than average throughput.

docs.title: Preference and policy resolution
docs.text: At execution time, resolve category, tenant policy, user preference, quiet hours, frequency caps, destination validity, legal suppression, and regional rules. Promotional consent is fail-closed. Atomically serialize the send claim with current suppression and cancellation generation before provider submission. A later opt-out prevents later claims but cannot recall an already claimed or in-flight external request; expose this boundary explicitly. A cached policy generation alone is not proof of current consent. Transactional categories may bypass marketing preference only if explicitly classified and audited. Snapshot the policy versions used on the attempt.

docs.title: Scheduling, priority, and backpressure
docs.text: Near-term schedules live in partitioned delay queues or time buckets; long-term schedules remain in the database and are promoted into queues by scanners with leases. Separate priority lanes reserve capacity for OTP/security, transactional, and bulk work. Weighted fair queuing across tenants prevents one campaign from monopolizing workers. Provider token buckets account for sender, region, and destination constraints. When overloaded, expire stale OTPs, pause campaigns, and reject new bulk batches before delaying critical alerts.

docs.title: Idempotency and retries
docs.text: Ingress stores (tenant,key,request_hash) uniquely. Create one logical delivery operation per intent/channel under a pinned routing generation, then create numbered transport attempts for that operation. A policy update must not accidentally create a second send for an already submitted intent. A timeout after provider submission is ambiguous: retrying may duplicate delivery. Retries use distinct diagnostic attempt IDs but retain the logical provider idempotency key within its documented retention window. Otherwise query status, delay retry, and explicitly accept at-least-once delivery semantics where unavoidable. Exponential backoff with jitter applies only to classified transient errors. Permanent invalid destinations update suppression lists. Dead letters include replay tooling and reason ownership.

docs.title: Templates and personalization
docs.text: Templates are versioned, reviewed, immutable artifacts with typed variables and locale fallback. Rendering happens before channel queues so malformed variables fail consistently, but secrets are not persisted in rendered logs. Large campaigns can pre-render common fragments while per-user values remain bounded. Links use tenant-controlled domains and signed, privacy-aware tracking policy.

docs.title: Provider routing and callbacks
docs.text: Routing considers health, cost, destination, regulatory sender, quota, and capabilities. Circuit breakers operate per route, not globally. Callback ingress verifies signatures, deduplicates provider event IDs, maps provider statuses into a monotonic internal lattice, and tolerates callback-before-response races. DELIVERED means the provider/device reported delivery, not that a human read it.

docs.title: Partitioning, regions, and failures
docs.text:
Partition intents by tenant plus ID/time; attempts by intent or destination hash depending on query needs; scheduled buckets by due time and shard. Keep high-volume tenants in dedicated partitions. Channel queues partition by provider route and priority, with enough partitions to scale without losing destination-level rate control.

Accept in a tenant's region for residency. Critical regional services use zonal quorum. Replicate intent/outbox state to a paired region. Schedulers use leases and epochs; failover can enqueue duplicates, which attempt uniqueness absorbs. Providers are region-specific and credentials never cross unauthorized boundaries.

Database/broker dual writes are solved by outbox. Queue redelivery is normal. Provider outage opens route circuit breakers and reroutes only when sender identity and semantics match and the original submission is proven absent or a documented duplicate-tolerant policy allows it. Provider A's idempotency key does not deduplicate a submission to provider B; otherwise retain UNKNOWN and delay. Preference outage suppresses promotional work. Template outage can use immutable cached versions. Callback loss is reconciled through provider status APIs where available. Every queue has age and byte limits; replay is scoped by tenant, channel, and time.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Authenticate producers with tenant-scoped credentials, authorize template/category use, encrypt destinations, tokenize PII, separate credential vaults, verify callbacks, audit exports, and redact bodies. Defend against spam tenants, SMS pumping, OTP bombing, phishing templates, destination enumeration, and unsubscribe tampering. Apply tenant budgets, reputation, approval workflows, and global emergency suppression.

Measure acceptance and end-to-end latency by priority/channel, queue age, scheduled lateness, suppression reasons, preference lookup health, render errors, provider acceptance/delivery, callback lag, retry amplification, ambiguous outcomes, cost per delivered message, tenant fairness, and OTP expiry-before-send. Trace intent to attempts without logging sensitive payloads.

Test state-machine properties, idempotent batches, callback reorder/duplication, cancellation races, quiet-hour boundaries and time zones, provider timeout ambiguity, quota exhaustion, and suppression propagation. Load-test campaign cliffs plus OTP bursts. Chaos-test provider, queue, DB, and region loss. Provider adapters use contract sandboxes and canaries; templates use schema and snapshot rendering tests.

docs.title: Campaign expansion, migrations, and reconciliation
docs.text:
Campaigns are control-plane objects, not billions of synchronous API requests. A campaign stores an immutable audience snapshot reference, template version, policy category, budget, schedule, and cancellation generation. Expansion workers claim audience partitions, emit deterministic recipient intent IDs, and checkpoint progress. Duplicate claims collapse at the intent uniqueness constraint. Cancellation increments a generation checked during expansion and immediately before provider send; already submitted provider requests cannot always be recalled, which the API states clearly.

Audience membership and consent are separate. The snapshot answers whom the campaign selected, while execution-time policy answers whom it may contact now. This permits reproducibility without violating a later opt-out. Frequency counters use reservation tokens: the orchestrator atomically reserves a slot with expiry, attempts delivery, then commits or releases according to policy. Do not release an expired reservation while its external outcome is unknown if that would permit violating a hard frequency cap. Approximate counters are acceptable for soft product caps, but statutory limits require a stronger destination-scoped store.

Adding a provider begins with a dark adapter that validates mapping and records hypothetical routes. Then canary traffic uses destinations controlled by the operator, followed by a low percentage of one eligible route. Compare acceptance, callback completeness, latency, cost, and complaint rates. Routing configuration is versioned and instantly reversible. Migrating queue partitions uses dual-read or stop-copy-resume with unique attempt IDs; never dual-submit merely to compare providers.

Reconciliation closes gaps that callbacks cannot. Periodic jobs scan old SENT_TO_PROVIDER attempts, query provider status where supported, and classify irreducibly unknown outcomes. They also compare campaign expanded counts, scheduled bucket checkpoints, suppression versions, and billing records. Reconciliation writes normal versioned events so downstream status views and customer webhooks recover consistently. Manual replay requires tenant/channel/time scope, dry-run counts, approval, and a diagnostic replay generation while retaining original logical delivery/provider keys. A new generation must not by itself authorize resending completed notifications; an intentional resend is a separate explicit operation.

Data retention separates intent metadata, rendered payload, provider identifiers, delivery analytics, and legal suppression hashes. Suppression may need to outlive ordinary customer data to prove that an address must not be contacted, but it should be minimized and one-way keyed. Tenant deletion workflows revoke credentials, stop schedules, tombstone payloads, and track completion across queues, provider exports, analytics, and backups.

Customer webhooks form another delivery channel with the same semantics. Sign each event, include a stable event ID and monotonic notification version, retry with bounded backoff, and provide a pull API for recovery. A slow customer endpoint receives an isolated queue and cannot delay provider callbacks or other tenants. Webhook status describes platform state transitions; it does not redefine provider truth.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
One global queue is simple but destroys priority and tenant isolation. Route-specific priority queues plus a control-plane orchestrator are operable. Checking preference only at enqueue is fast but unsafe for scheduled sends; execution-time checks win. Aggressive retry improves nominal delivery but creates duplicates and cost; classify outcomes and expose uncertainty. Building every provider feature into the core couples releases; stable adapters isolate channel semantics.

 A[Durable idempotent intent] --> B[Policy and immutable template resolution]
 B --> C[Priority/fair scheduling]

 D --> E[Provider adapters]

 F --> G[(Monotonic attempt state)]

docs.title: Questions, levels, and five-minute summary
docs.text:
1. What does success mean when a provider times out?
  2. How do OTPs remain fast during a billion-message campaign?
  3. When are preferences checked for scheduled notifications?
  4. How are out-of-order callbacks normalized?
  5. How does regional failover avoid duplicate schedules?

L5 candidates should model intents/attempts, queues, preferences, templates, provider adapters, retries, and priority isolation. L6 candidates should define legal suppression semantics, uncertainty and cost policy, fair scheduling, regional residency/fencing, provider migrations, global abuse controls, and operational replay boundaries.

In five minutes: durably accept an idempotent intent and outbox event, then resolve current consent, suppression, immutable template, locale, channel, and deadline. Schedule through separately reserved priority lanes with tenant fairness and route-specific provider quotas. Create explicit attempts, use provider idempotency where possible, and otherwise admit at-least-once delivery under ambiguous timeouts. Normalize signed, deduplicated callbacks into monotonic states. Partition by tenant/time and route/priority, lease scheduled buckets, and let duplicate failover work collapse through unique attempt keys. Shed campaigns before transactional and OTP traffic, fail promotional consent closed, and operate queue age, retry amplification, provider health, delivery cost, and suppression propagation.

docs.title: Interview Roadmap
docs.text: Clarify communities, posts, comments, votes, ranking, moderation, and anonymous reading. State visibility and vote invariants before discussing feeds. Start with transactional community content and an asynchronous ranking projection, then evolve for celebrity threads, vote manipulation, moderator workflows, deletion, and regional reads. The difficult boundary is between canonical user actions and policy-dependent views.

docs.title: Product Framing
docs.text:
Reddit is a collection of independently governed communities. A user submits a link or text post, comments in a tree, votes, subscribes, reports abuse, and reads ranked listings such as hot, new, top, and personalized home. Moderators define community rules and remove content; platform administrators enforce global safety and legal policy.

The system does not promise that ranking is stable or globally identical. It must promise that authorized content, one user's effective vote, and moderation precedence are correct. Search, recommendation, karma, and displayed scores are projections. Chat, advertising, and media transcoding are out of scope.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Create communities, memberships, posts, nested comments, votes, saves, and reports.
  • List community and home feeds by new, top, and hot with opaque cursor pagination.
  • Apply moderator and platform actions, locks, bans, quarantines, and appeals.
  • Show edits and deletion semantics without resurrecting removed content.
  • Support 99.99% read availability, 99.9% writes, and feed p99 below 300 ms.
  • Absorb breaking-news bursts and coordinated abuse without losing canonical actions.

docs.title: Correctness Invariants
docs.text:
1. A (principal_id, target_id) has one effective vote; changing direction replaces rather than adds another vote.
  2. A post or comment belongs to exactly one community and has an immutable author and creation identity.
  3. Visibility requires every applicable policy layer to allow access. Moderator approval cannot override platform removal or restore author-deleted/private content; within each layer, delayed lower versions cannot undo newer decisions.
  4. A comment's parent is in the same post, and its materialized path is acyclic.
  5. A mutation idempotency key and request hash produce one canonical effect.
  6. Feed position is not canonical state; it may change as votes, age, and policy change.
  7. Deleted user data follows retention policy, while necessary moderation evidence remains access-restricted and auditable.

docs.title: Capacity Estimates
docs.text:
Assume 500 million monthly readers, 80 million daily active users, 20 billion feed item impressions/day, 30 million posts/comments/day, and 2 billion vote mutations/day. At 20 displayed items/page, impressions correspond to one billion page reads/day, about 11,574/s average and 116,000/s at 10x peak. Vote writes average about 23,000/s independently. Prefetches and short/filtered pages change the item-to-request ratio and must be measured. A major live thread can receive 50,000 actions/s and millions of readers, so global averages hide the principal scaling risk.

At 1 KB average metadata/body after compression, new canonical text is tens of GB/day; votes add roughly 100 GB/day before replicas and indexes. Feed egress and caches dominate storage. Keep recent vote state and aggregates hot, archive mutation history by retention, and budget ranking computation by candidate count rather than total corpus size.

docs.title: Core Entities and Data Model
docs.text:
Community(community_id, name, policy_version, visibility, owner_region)
Membership(community_id, user_id, role, state, version)
Post(post_id, community_id, author_id, type, body_ref, state, version, created_at)
Comment(comment_id, post_id, parent_id, author_id, depth, path_key, body, state, version)
Vote(target_id, voter_id, direction, weight_class, version, updated_at)
Score(target_id, up_weight, down_weight, confidence, computed_at, generation)
ModerationAction(action_id, target_id, scope, action, precedence, version, actor, reason)
Report(report_id, target_id, reporter_id, category, state)
Outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, type, version, payload)

Posts, comments, effective votes, and moderation actions are canonical. Score, karma, search, recommendation candidates, and listings are rebuildable projections. Public score may be fuzzed for anti-abuse, but authorization and internal aggregates are not derived from the fuzzed value.

docs.title: APIs and Interfaces
docs.text:
POST /v1/communities/{id}/posts                 Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
POST /v1/posts/{id}/comments                    {parent_id, body}
PUT  /v1/targets/{id}/vote                      {direction: UP|DOWN|NONE, expected_version}
GET  /v1/communities/{id}/feed?sort=hot&cursor=...&limit=50
GET  /v1/posts/{id}/comments?sort=best&cursor=...&depth=3
POST /v1/targets/{id}/reports
POST /v1/moderation/actions                      {target_id, action, reason, expected_version}

Mutation responses include canonical ID, version, and visibility. Feed cursors encode sort mode, ranking generation, last score tuple, and tie-breaking ID; clients must not construct them. Ranking pages may omit or repeat items across long sessions, while new pagination provides stable creation-order semantics within retention.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Client --> Edge[Edge auth and abuse gate]
    Edge --> Content[Content service]
    Edge --> Vote[Vote service]
    Content --> DB[(Canonical content shards)]
    Vote --> VDB[(Effective vote shards)]
    DB --> Outbox[(Outbox and event log)]
    VDB --> Outbox
    Outbox --> Rank[Ranking processors]
    Outbox --> Mod[Moderation pipeline]
    Rank --> Lists[(Feed and comment projections)]
    Mod --> Policy[(Visibility projection)]
    Edge --> Feed[Feed service]
    Lists -->|ranked candidates| Feed
    Policy -->|current visibility| Feed
    subgraph ContentLane[Authoritative writes]
      Content
      Vote
      DB
      VDB
      Outbox
    end
    subgraph RankLane[Ranking projections]
      Rank
      Lists
    end
    subgraph ModLane[Visibility]
      Mod
      Policy
    end

The smallest correct system uses relational transactions for content and effective votes, an outbox for asynchronous work, and cached sorted listings. Feed reads hydrate candidate IDs through current visibility policy so stale ranking never bypasses removal.

docs.title: Submit and Read
docs.text: Submission checks membership, community policy, rate limits, duplicate fingerprints, and synchronous high-confidence safety rules. One transaction inserts content and outbox. The response can be VISIBLE, HELD, or REJECTED; uncertain content is not broadly distributed until asynchronous checks finish. Feed services fetch a bounded candidate window, filter current authorization and blocks, hydrate objects, and return an opaque cursor.

docs.title: Vote
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant V as Vote service
    participant D as Vote shard
    participant R as Rank stream
    U->>V: PUT direction, key
    V->>D: conditional upsert effective vote
    D->>D: append old-to-new delta and outbox
    D-->>U: vote version
    D->>R: at-least-once delta
    R->>R: dedupe event and update aggregate
    R-->>U: eventual displayed score/rank

A transition from up to down emits up -1, down +1, not a second vote. The transactional vote row is authoritative. Stream aggregates deduplicate event IDs and periodically reconcile against vote snapshots.

docs.title: Comment Tree
docs.text: Comments retain parent identity and a bounded depth. Reads fetch top-level ranked comments, then bounded child pages; they never load a million-node tree at once. A stable path_key supports chronological traversal, while separate per-parent ranking indexes support best-first expansion. Deleted comments may leave a structural placeholder when visible descendants exist.

docs.title: Deep Dive 1: Ranking Algorithms
docs.text:
new orders by (created_at, id). top can rank by Wilson lower bound rather than raw up-minus-down, preventing a two-vote item from appearing equally trustworthy as a thousand-vote item. For positive fraction p, observations n, and confidence constant z, Wilson's lower bound discounts small samples. Comments use this confidence score plus policy features and deterministic tie breaks. The usual binomial confidence interpretation assumes independent unweighted observations; applying it to correlated or fractional risk-weighted votes is a ranking heuristic unless an appropriate effective-sample-size model is justified.

hot balances quality and age. One proposed score, not a claim about Reddit's deployed algorithm, is sign(net_votes) * log10(max(abs(net_votes),1)) - age_seconds / decay_constant, where age is nonnegative elapsed time since creation and the decay constant is positive. The former placement of the sign on the age term would reward older positively voted posts and larger negative vote magnitudes. Test that aging any fixed-vote item never increases its score and that adding downvotes cannot improve a negative item's score. Compute from trustworthy weighted counts, not displayed fuzzed counts. Ranking generations pin formula and feature versions. Incremental processors update affected items, while periodic full recomputation catches drift.

Home feed generation is hybrid. Precompute recent candidates from subscribed communities into community lists; at request time merge a bounded number using a heap, then apply freshness, language, seen-item suppression, safety, and community diversity. Fanout-on-write to every subscriber loses for huge communities and inactive users. Candidate fan-in costs more per active reader but bounds write amplification; cache the merged first page by coarse subscription cohort where privacy permits.

docs.title: Deep Dive 2: Vote Integrity and Manipulation
docs.text:
Raw vote count is not rank weight. A risk pipeline evaluates account age, verified status, device clusters, timing, reciprocal rings, shared networks, and community raids. Suspicious votes remain canonical user actions but may receive zero or reduced ranking weight pending review. This distinction preserves auditability and allows model reversal without rewriting user history.

Per-account, device, IP prefix, target, and community token buckets stop floods. Detection uses graph and time-window features, with delayed labels from moderator outcomes. Do not reveal exact suppression logic. Score fuzzing reduces reverse engineering but must be explicitly a presentation defense, never a consistency mechanism. Reconciliation compares effective votes, weighted aggregates, and ranking inputs by sampled target.

docs.title: Deep Dive 3: Moderation and Visibility
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HELD
    HELD --> VISIBLE: checks pass
    HELD --> REMOVED: rule or review
    VISIBLE --> LOCKED: moderator lock
    LOCKED --> VISIBLE: unlock
    LOCKED --> REMOVED: scoped removal
    VISIBLE --> REMOVED: scoped action
    REMOVED --> VISIBLE: valid appeal at higher version
    REMOVED --> LEGAL_HOLD: evidence retention

The diagram is a simplified visibility workflow. Lock state and legal-hold retention are separate fields in implementation: a removed item can remain locked, and releasing a legal hold does not republish it. Visibility is evaluated as layered policy: platform/legal, community, author state, viewer age/region, viewer blocks, and content state. Each action is append-only with precedence and version. A platform ban cannot be undone by a community moderator. Removal events travel on a priority stream and purge feed/search/cache entries, but every read still checks a compact current visibility record because purge is not instantaneous.

Moderator queues prioritize reports by severity, confidence, virality, and age while preserving fair capacity for small communities. Actions require scoped roles, reasons, audit records, and optional dual control for mass operations. Appeals append decisions. Moderator bots receive capability-scoped APIs, quotas, signed webhooks, and a sandboxed rule environment.

docs.title: Deep Dive 4: Hot Posts and Comment Ranking
docs.text:
A hot post concentrates votes, comment writes, and reads on one ID. Content is immutable by version and edge-cacheable. Vote rows partition by voter hash within target buckets; aggregate processors combine bucket deltas. Comment writes partition by post plus lane, because strict total order across comments is unnecessary; IDs and creation time provide deterministic merge order. Per-parent child indexes avoid one giant list.

Cache a versioned thread skeleton and hydrate mutable score/visibility separately. Readers get a ranking generation and continuation cursor. Under overload, reduce deep-child hydration, disable expensive personalization, serve a slightly older ranked snapshot, then require login for writes. Moderation removals and locks retain reserved capacity and bypass ordinary ranking queues.

docs.title: Partitioning and Scaling
docs.text:
Partition posts and comments by community or post hash, with very large communities assigned dedicated shards and split posts by stable lanes. Effective votes partition by (target_id, hash(voter_id)); aggregates use hierarchical combining to avoid one counter key. Community listings partition by community and time bucket. Home requests merge only active subscriptions and cap candidate work.

Detect skew through per-key QPS, queue age, and fanout. Reshard using routing epochs: dual-read during copy, one fenced write owner, verify counts and versions, then switch. Separate read, write, moderation, and backfill pools. Backpressure slows ranking freshness before canonical acceptance; if outbox retention approaches its limit, reject low-trust writes rather than acknowledge unrecoverable events.

docs.title: Consistency and Idempotency
docs.text:
Content state, effective votes, locks, and role transitions need strong consistency per aggregate. Scores, karma, search, feeds, report priority, and recommendations are eventual and expose freshness. Outbox publication and consumers are at least once. Consumers atomically deduplicate vote deltas with their aggregate effects; they buffer version gaps or reconcile full replacements, because discarding an older unseen delta loses its contribution. Full-state consumers compare aggregate version; a tombstone or higher policy version dominates stale creation.

Retries use idempotency key plus request hash. A reused key with different content is rejected. Vote APIs naturally upsert desired state, making retries safe. Cache invalidation is advisory: reads validate visibility versions. Ranking cursor generations expire; clients restart rather than mixing incompatible score formulas.

docs.title: Reliability and Failure Modes
docs.text:
Database failure rejects writes but cached public reads continue with a degraded banner and current compact deny list. Ranking outage freezes lists; new can read canonical indexes. Event-stream failure grows outbox lag and disables nonessential recommendation updates. Cache loss uses request coalescing and conservative limits to prevent database collapse. A poison event is quarantined while its partition advances, with a repair record preserving order semantics.

A lost write response is resolved by idempotency lookup. Duplicate vote deltas are ignored. Missing ranking events are found through version gaps and snapshot reconciliation. Moderator-stream lag pages immediately and can force direct deny-list polling. Disaster restore replays canonical snapshots plus logs and validates content counts, effective vote totals, and maximum moderation version before publication.

docs.title: Multi-Region Strategy
docs.text:
Assign each community a home region for writes, synchronously replicated across zones. Global edges serve cached public content and route mutations home. Vote acceptance may occur in regional cells if each voter-target identity has one deterministic owner; otherwise route it home to avoid conflicting effective votes. Ranking and feed projections replicate asynchronously.

During home-region failure, promote a fenced replica at a known epoch. If fencing is uncertain, keep reads and temporarily reject community mutations rather than create two moderator histories. Legal removals propagate globally on a separate high-priority control plane. Region evacuation is tested with ranking lag and cold-cache budgets, not only database recovery time.

docs.title: Security and Abuse Prevention
docs.text:
Use TLS, workload identity, hardened sessions, MFA for moderators, scoped RBAC, encrypted data, key rotation, and immutable action audit. Escape Markdown/HTML, proxy and scan links, sandbox media metadata, block SSRF, and rate-limit expensive tree expansion. Protect private and quarantined communities through authorization at origin and signed, short-lived media URLs.

Address spam, bots, brigading, vote rings, ban evasion, moderator-account takeover, report abuse, doxxing, scraping, and enumeration. Store network identifiers under short retention and restricted access. Separate public deletion, privacy erasure, legal hold, and safety evidence so one broad delete job neither leaks nor destroys mandatory records.

docs.title: Observability and Testing
docs.text:
Measure submit/vote/feed latency, ranking and outbox lag, candidate count, cache hit rate, hot-key load, score reconciliation error, duplicate events, removal propagation, report age, moderator queue SLA, false-positive appeals, and degraded responses. Slice by community size, region, client, policy/ranking generation, and trust tier while applying privacy thresholds.

Property-test one-effective-vote transitions, moderation precedence, cursor ordering, comment acyclicity, and tombstone dominance. Model-test randomized create/edit/delete/vote/retry sequences. Replay duplicates and reorder versions. Load-test a front-page post, raid, cache flush, and slow consumers. Chaos-test owner failover and stream outage. Shadow ranking changes and inspect quality, abuse, latency, and community-size fairness before canary rollout.

docs.title: Important Tradeoffs
docs.text: Raw score is transparent but easy to game; weighted internal score plus limited display fuzzing improves resistance at trust cost. Fanout-on-read controls amplification but increases read work; bounded precomputed community lists make it practical. Strict global comment order simplifies pagination but creates a hot sequencer with little product value. Pre-moderation is safest but suppresses conversation; risk-tiered holding plus priority removal balances latency and harm. Home-region writes trade mutation latency for understandable moderation history and recovery.

docs.title: Final Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Users --> Cells[Regional edge and feed cells]
    Cells --> Owners[Community/post write owners]
    Owners --> Canon[(Canonical content, votes, actions, outbox)]
    Canon --> Events[(Partitioned event log)]
    Events --> Integrity[Vote integrity and aggregates]
    Events --> Moderation[Layered moderation]
    Events --> Ranking[Versioned ranking]
    Integrity --> Proj[(Scores and candidate lists)]
    Ranking --> Proj
    Moderation --> Vis[(Current visibility)]
    Cells --> Proj
    Cells --> Vis
    Canon --> Archive[Snapshots, audit, reconciliation]
    subgraph AuthorityLane[Canonical state and recovery]
      Owners
      Canon
      Archive
    end
    subgraph RankLane[Ranking and integrity]
      Integrity
      Ranking
      Proj
    end
    subgraph ModLane[Moderation]
      Moderation
      Vis
    end

docs.title: Interview Deep-Dive Questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a user's effective vote different from a score delta?
  2. How would Wilson ranking change early comment ordering?
  3. How do removals override stale feed and cache entries?
  4. What breaks if every home feed is fanout-on-write?
  5. How do you partition a post receiving 50,000 actions/s?
  6. Which behavior degrades first when ranking falls behind?
  7. How do platform and community moderation precedence interact?

docs.title: L5 and L6 Expectations
docs.text: An L5 answer should separate canonical content from feeds, define idempotent vote transitions, explain hot/top ranking, paginate comment trees, handle hot posts, moderation, caching, and retries. An L6 answer should additionally formalize policy precedence, weighted-vote reversibility, ranking generations, skew migration, overload tiers, regional fencing, reconciliation, moderator governance, and the trust/cost implications of anti-abuse choices.

docs.title: Five-Minute Summary
docs.text: Reddit is canonical community content and effective user actions feeding policy-dependent projections. Store posts, comments, one effective vote per voter-target, moderation actions, and outbox records transactionally. Rank new by stable time, top with confidence such as Wilson lower bound, and hot with a versioned vote-and-age formula. Build home feeds by merging bounded community candidate lists rather than pushing every post to every subscriber. Keep ranking eventual, but check current layered visibility on every hydration so stale caches cannot resurrect removals. Split hot vote targets into voter buckets and combine deltas idempotently; split comment writes into lanes and paginate the tree. Preserve suspicious votes while changing their rank weight so decisions are reversible. Reserve capacity for locks and removals, degrade personalization and depth before canonical writes, own community mutations in one fenced region, and continuously reconcile votes, scores, and policy versions.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Cover organizations, channels, threaded messages, real-time delivery, history, search indexing, and multi-device unread state. Exclude calls and app marketplace internals. Unlike consumer chat, workspace tenancy, retention, legal holds, enterprise authorization, and searchable history are central.

docs.title: Requirements, invariants, and capacity estimates
docs.text:
Members send/edit/delete messages in public or private channels and DMs, receive real-time updates, page history, search permitted content, and track reads. Target 200 ms p99 sends, subsecond online delivery, and 99.99% history reads. Search may lag seconds. Tenant policy controls retention and exports.

  • A committed message has one channel-local sequence and stable ID.
  • Current membership and policy gate every history/search result.
  • Message versions are auditable according to tenant policy.
  • Event delivery is at least once; clients deduplicate by event ID.
  • Read cursors advance monotonically; unread counts are projections.
  • Tenant data, keys, quotas, and indexes remain isolated.
  • Delete/retention tombstones dominate stale index events.

Assume 50 million daily users, 100 messages/user/day, or 5 billion messages/day: 5B / 86,400 = 58,000 writes/s average and roughly 290,000 writes/s at 5x peak. At 2 KB/message, canonical message metadata grows by 10 TB/day, or 3.65 PB/year before replication, revisions, attachments, and index expansion. With three zonal copies and a search projection budgeted at 1.5x canonical bytes, messages alone require about 16.4 PB/year; retention tiers and per-workspace deletion are therefore storage architecture requirements.

Five million concurrent sockets dominate realtime capacity. If one gateway safely holds 40,000 connected devices, steady state needs 125 gateways; provisioning 40% reconnect and failure headroom raises the regional fleet target to about 175 gateway equivalents. At an illustrative average of two 700-byte delivered events/s per connected device, edge egress is 7 GB/s before TLS and WebSocket overhead. These estimates justify gateway-level multiplexing, bounded per-device queues, hierarchical topics for large channels, and cell-level capacity admission rather than per-user broker fanout. A 10x burst concentrated in one enterprise channel does not imply 10x canonical writes, but it can saturate fanout and must trigger channel-specific sampling of ephemeral events and resync behavior.

docs.title: Data model and interfaces
docs.text:
Workspace(workspace_id, plan, region, policy_version)
Channel(channel_id, workspace_id, type, home_shard, membership_version)
Membership(channel_id, user_id, role, joined_seq, left_seq)
Message(channel_id, seq, message_id, author_id, body_ciphertext, version, state)
MessageRevision(message_id, version, body, actor, created_at)
ReadCursor(user_id, channel_id, last_read_seq)
Event(event_id, workspace_id, channel_id, seq, type, payload_ref)

POST /v1/channels/{id}/messages       Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
PATCH /v1/messages/{id}
DELETE /v1/messages/{id}
GET /v1/channels/{id}/messages?before_seq=...&limit=50
PUT /v1/channels/{id}/read-cursor     {"through_seq":123}
GET /v1/search?q=...&cursor=...
GET /v1/events?cursor=...             WebSocket transport

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Clients] --> E[Edge/API]
 E --> M[Message service]
 E --> H[History service]
 E --> G[Realtime gateways]
 M --> D[(Partitioned message DB + outbox)]
 D --> K[Event log]
 K --> F[Realtime fanout]
 F --> G
 K --> I[Search indexer]
 I --> S[(Tenant-aware search)]
 K --> U[Unread projector]
 U --> R[(Read/unread store)]
 H --> D
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant M as Message service
 participant D as Channel shard
 participant K as Event log
 participant G as Gateway
 C->>M: send(key, body)
 M->>D: authorize and append seq + outbox
 D-->>C: committed message
 D->>K: relay event
 K->>G: at-least-once channel event
 G-->>C: event to subscribed devices
 C->>G: cumulative event ack

Gateways hold subscriptions, not history truth. On reconnect, a device supplies its workspace event cursor, represented by an opaque per-partition offset vector or a separately ordered delivery stream rather than a fictional workspace-wide message sequence; gaps are filled from a durable regional event buffer, then channel history if the buffer expired.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant Q as Search service
 participant S as Search index
 participant A as Authorization
 participant D as Message store
 C->>Q: query + cursor
 Q->>S: retrieve over tenant partition
 Q->>A: batch authorize channels and versions
 Q->>D: hydrate current message revisions
 Q-->>C: filtered results + cursor

docs.title: Channel ordering and threads
docs.text: Each channel has one logical append leader assigning sequences. Database ranges or log partitions preserve order. Threads store parent_message_id but remain sequenced in the channel, enabling one event stream and consistent retention. Hot all-company channels can shard reactions and read traffic, but writes requiring strict channel order remain bounded by one sequencer; product limits or a relaxed broadcast mode handle the extreme.

docs.title: Real-time fanout
docs.text: The fanout service maps channels to gateway subscription shards. It sends one event per gateway, not per user, and the gateway multiplexes local sockets. Large channels use hierarchical topics. Slow devices have bounded buffers and receive a resync_required marker instead of consuming server memory indefinitely. Presence and typing are lossy ephemeral events with TTL and aggressive rate limits; messages are durable.

docs.title: Search and authorization
docs.text: Indexers consume versioned message events. Documents carry workspace, channel, message version, and tombstone state. Search first restricts tenant and candidate channels, then reauthorizes and hydrates current versions, because index membership can lag. Private-channel names must not leak through facets or timing. Tombstones use a priority lane, and periodic reconciliation compares index versions with canonical state.

docs.title: Unreads, edits, and retention
docs.text: Canonical read cursor is max(last_read_seq, incoming) after validating the caller, channel, current membership and that the requested sequence does not exceed the known channel head. Otherwise a forged future cursor could mark future messages read indefinitely. Unread count is estimated from sequence/counter projections and excludes inaccessible or deleted messages, so it can briefly disagree. Edits append revisions; tenant settings choose visible edit history. Retention jobs write tombstones before physical deletion, preserving legal-hold copies in a separately authorized vault. Delayed create/index events cannot outrank a higher deletion version.

docs.title: Partitioning and multi-region
docs.text:
Place a workspace in a policy-selected home region. Partition message tables by workspace then channel hash and time range; this improves isolation and deletion. Very large tenants receive dedicated cells. Search indexes are tenant-routed, with large tenants isolated. Event gateway pools partition subscriptions by workspace/channel hash.

Synchronously replicate channel writes across zones. Replicate encrypted logs to a disaster-recovery region subject to residency. Failover fences channel leaders by epoch. Global users connect to nearby gateways, which forward writes to the home region and consume replicated delivery streams. Read replicas may serve history only when authorization and retention versions are fresh enough.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and failures
docs.text:
Messages and membership changes are strongly ordered per channel shard; search, unreads, notifications, and realtime delivery are eventual. The send key maps to a request hash and committed ID. Outbox events and consumer uniqueness prevent dual-write loss and duplicate effects.

Gateway failure reconnects clients and replays. Search outage does not affect messaging. Broker lag preserves history but delays live delivery and projections. A channel leader failure retries after epoch fencing. If authorization is unavailable, private reads fail closed; already open clients do not gain continued access merely because a socket subscription exists. Cell overload applies tenant quotas, sheds typing/presence/search first, and maintains message writes and history. Backups and logs support point-in-time restore; event replay rebuilds projections.

docs.title: Security, abuse, and privacy
docs.text: Enforce workspace SSO, MFA, SCIM deprovisioning, channel roles, app scopes, and policy versions centrally. Encrypt per tenant or cell, protect exports and legal holds with separate approvals, audit administrative reads, and redact message bodies from logs. Rate-limit spam, mentions, file uploads, search scraping, and bot tokens. Malware-scan files and rotate download URLs. Enterprise retention and deletion promises must explicitly describe backups, exports, and connected applications.

docs.title: Control plane, migrations, and enterprise recovery
docs.text:
Separate the control plane that places workspaces, configures residency, rotates keys, and changes quotas from the data plane that sends and reads messages. A control-plane outage should freeze placement changes but leave existing cell routing functional through signed, cached maps. Routing records carry generations; gateways reject stale moves rather than write to both cells. Cell health, capacity, tenant size, and compliance constraints inform placement.

Moving a workspace begins with a consistent source checkpoint. Copy immutable message ranges and snapshots, stream the outbox tail, build search in a shadow index, and validate message/revision counts plus ACL samples. Briefly fence source writes, apply the final tail, increment the routing generation, and retain the source read-only for rollback. Once the destination accepts writes, rollback must copy its acknowledged tail back, fence the destination and promote a complete source prefix; changing routing back to the old copy alone loses messages. External apps and exports use stable workspace IDs, so physical movement remains invisible. Large migrations are rate-limited to preserve customer traffic and have explicit abort criteria.

A SCIM deprovision race illustrates authorization precedence. Once identity state marks a member disabled, new API calls and socket subscriptions fail regardless of stale channel membership. Gateways receive a high-priority session-revocation event and close existing sockets. Gate every new delivery under a current identity/policy epoch or a bounded freshness lease; a disconnected gateway stops delivery when that lease expires. Push alone does not prove a revocation deadline. Search and history still perform current authorization, so delayed gateway invalidation cannot leak new content. Legal-hold readers use a separate role and audited endpoint rather than weakening normal membership checks.

Disaster recovery must be exercised at workspace granularity as well as cell granularity. Restoring a cell from backup establishes a log checkpoint, replays canonical mutations, rebuilds unreads and search, then compares sampled document hashes and membership versions before serving. Recovery objectives differ: message history and ACLs have strict durability, while presence, typing, cached unreads, and search ranking can be discarded or rebuilt. This classification controls replication cost and prevents teams from treating every projection as equally critical.

Apps and bots introduce a second noisy-neighbor dimension. Events destined for integrations enter tenant-scoped queues after the message commit, and app acknowledgements never gate user-visible sends. Each installation has scopes, rate limits, retry budgets, and a revocation version. Duplicate webhook events carry stable IDs. If an app is slow, its queue is compacted or dead-lettered according to subscription semantics rather than retaining an unbounded copy of workspace history. Bot-authored mutations pass through the same channel sequencer and audit trail as human mutations.

Operators expose per-installation lag and replay controls so workspace administrators can diagnose integrations without receiving access to another tenant's metadata.

docs.title: Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure send/commit latency, channel sequence gaps, outbox age, realtime event age, connected sockets, resync frequency, slow-consumer drops, history p99, search indexing/deletion lag, unauthorized candidate filtering, unread drift, tenant throttling, and hot channels. Attribute cost and SLOs by cell and tenant without exposing content.

Test idempotent send/edit/delete races, membership boundary sequences, monotonic reads, index reorder, retention versus legal hold, gateway reconnect storms, and large-channel skew. Chaos-test cell dependencies and region failover. Authorization uses generated tenant/channel matrices and continuous synthetic former-member checks. Search upgrades use dual indexes, shadow queries, relevance comparison, and reversible alias switches.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Per-workspace databases maximize isolation but waste resources for small tenants; multi-tenant cells with dedicated escape hatches balance cost. Direct per-user realtime fanout explodes work; gateway-level topic fanout exploits multiplexing. Serving search results directly from the index is fast but unsafe; reauthorization and canonical hydration cost latency but preserve policy. Channel-local ordering is useful, while workspace-global order is needless.

flowchart TD
 A[Tenant-routed edge] --> B[Home-region channel leader]
 B --> C[(Canonical messages, revisions, outbox)]
 C --> D[Durable workspace event log]
 D --> E[Hierarchical realtime fanout]
 D --> F[Versioned search projection]
 D --> G[Unread/notification projections]
 H[History/search reads] --> I[Current authorization gate]
 I --> C
 I --> F

docs.title: Questions, levels, and five-minute summary
docs.text:
1. How do large channels avoid per-user realtime fanout?
  2. How does search avoid leaking former private-channel membership?
  3. What happens to edit history under retention and legal hold?
  4. How are a noisy tenant and a hot channel isolated?
  5. How does regional failover fence old channel leaders?

L5 candidates should define ordered channel storage, realtime reconnect, search projection, idempotency, tenant-aware partitioning, and failure fallbacks. L6 candidates should drive residency and legal-hold semantics, cell isolation, overload tiers, leader fencing, search migrations, authorization-version propagation, and enterprise operability.

In five minutes: route each workspace to a regional cell and each channel to an ordered append shard. Commit message, idempotency key, and outbox together. Fan committed events hierarchically to subscribed gateways; reconnecting clients replay from cursors. Store history canonically, index versioned projections asynchronously, and reauthorize every history/search result against current membership. Track read cursors canonically while treating unread counts as projections. Shard by tenant, channel, and time; isolate huge tenants and degrade presence, typing, search, and notifications before messaging. Use tombstone versions for deletion and retention, fenced leaders for failover, and explicit enterprise controls for residency, audit, and legal hold.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Scope profile creation, preference/discovery, swipe decisions, reciprocal matches, and post-match messaging handoff. Exclude media transformation details, subscription billing, and chat internals. The core challenge is producing safe, fresh candidates under geography and preference constraints while creating exactly one match from concurrent reciprocal likes.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Users maintain profiles and discovery preferences, receive ranked candidate cards, swipe left/right, and match when likes are mutual. Discovery targets 300 ms p99 and must not repeatedly show decided profiles unless product policy resets them. Location is approximate and highly sensitive. Blocks, bans, age gates, and visibility controls must apply promptly.

  • A swipe ID has one durable outcome under retry.
  • At most one active match exists for an unordered user pair.
  • A user never receives themselves, blocked users, ineligible ages, or current prior decisions.
  • Match creation is atomic with reciprocal-like verification.
  • Candidate pools and rank scores are projections, not eligibility truth.
  • Precise location is never returned to another user.
  • Delete/ban state dominates delayed pool and notification events.

Assume 50 million daily users, 100 swipes/day: 5 billion/day, 58,000/s average and 300,000/s peak. Ten discovery pages/day produce 500 million ranking requests/day. Profiles average 10 KB metadata plus media references; media uses object storage/CDN. Swipe history grows by terabytes/day and needs lifecycle tiers. Dense cities and popular profiles create hot geographic cells and impression skew.

docs.text:

POST /v1/swipes                 Idempotency-Key: <swipe_id>
GET  /v1/matches?cursor=...
DELETE /v1/matches/{id}
