PATCH /v1/profile
PUT  /v1/location               {latitude, longitude, observed_at}

docs.title: Architecture and flows
docs.text:
flowchart LR
 C[Client] --> E[API edge]
 E --> D[Discovery service]
 E --> S[Swipe service]
 D --> P[(Candidate pool)]
 D --> R[Ranker]
 D --> A[Eligibility/policy]
 A --> G[(Profile, preference, geo indexes)]
 S --> W[(Decision/like store)]
 S --> M[(Pair-keyed match store)]
 S --> O[(Outbox)]
 O --> N[Notification/chat bootstrap]
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant U as User A
 participant S as Swipe service
 participant D as Decision store
 participant M as Match store
 participant O as Outbox
 U->>S: RIGHT on B, swipe_id
  Note over D,O: Logical tables in one pair-owned transaction
  S->>D: begin, lock pair, write idempotent A decision
  S->>D: check active B->A like under same lock
 alt reciprocal like exists
   S->>M: conditional create unordered pair
    S->>O: append MatchCreated
    S->>D: commit decision, match, outbox and response
   S-->>U: matched(match_id)
  else no reciprocal like
    S->>D: commit decision and accepted response
   S-->>U: accepted
 end

Serialize operations by canonical pair_key = hash(min(A,B),max(A,B)), or use a unique constraint and transaction spanning pair-scoped likes/match. Concurrent likes serialize; only one match is created. Each swipe retry returns its originally stored result, while the current matches endpoint exposes the subsequently created match to both users.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant U as User
 participant D as Discovery
 participant P as Pool generator
 participant E as Eligibility
 participant R as Ranker
 U->>D: discovery(cursor)
 D->>P: candidates from geo cells/interests
 D->>E: batch current checks
 E-->>D: eligible candidates
 D->>R: score with bounded features
 R-->>D: ranked cards
 D-->>U: coarse distance + cursor

docs.title: Candidate retrieval and geography
docs.text: Map recent locations to hierarchical cells such as S2/geohash. Query the user's cell and expanding neighbors until enough candidates exist, then calculate exact distance server-side. Sparse areas expand radius gradually; dense cells sample and diversify rather than scanning all profiles. Index only discoverable, moderated profiles with coarse attributes. Before response, canonical policy checks age, preferences in both directions where required, blocks, prior decisions, visibility, freshness, and rate limits.

docs.title: Ranking, fairness, and pool exhaustion
docs.text: Rankers combine preference fit, activity, distance bands, quality, and exploration. Apply exposure caps so popular profiles and dense neighborhoods do not absorb all impressions. Candidate pools cache IDs briefly but not authorization. A cursor includes pool generation and boundary; clients deduplicate across regenerated pools. When exhausted, the product may widen constraints with consent, wait for new users, or clearly return no candidates, never silently violate hard filters.

docs.title: Reciprocal match transaction
docs.text: Decision writes use (actor,target) plus swipe idempotency. A right swipe creates an active like; left may suppress future discovery. Match creation is unique by unordered pair. Unmatch transitions the match state and revokes chat access; whether future rematching is allowed is explicit policy. Notifications consume outbox events idempotently and recheck active match so delayed pushes do not announce an already-unmatched pair.

docs.title: Privacy and safety
docs.text: Store exact coordinates encrypted with tightly scoped access; retain only as long as needed. Return distance bands and add jitter where appropriate. Do not expose candidate-list membership, read-like status, or precise activity. Blocks are directional records but eligibility checks both directions. Safety systems detect spam swiping, automated scraping, underage accounts, impersonation, harassment, and coordinated abuse. Reports preserve evidence under restricted access.

docs.title: Partitioning, consistency, and regions
docs.text:
Partition profiles and actor-history projections by actor, candidate indexes by region/cell and attribute buckets, and canonical directed decisions plus matches by unordered pair key. Both reciprocal decisions must share the match transaction described below; independently actor-sharded authoritative likes would reintroduce the cross-shard race. Popular profile versions are read-cacheable and impressions use sharded counters. Split hot cells, merge cold cells, and bound candidate generation and online filtering.

Profiles have a home region; location updates go to the nearest compliant region and update geo projections asynchronously. Pair operations route deterministically to one owning region, avoiding active-active match races. During owner-region failure, queue swipes or fail over only after fencing. Discovery can serve stale pools but must recheck current blocks/bans; if that check is unavailable, fail closed.

Swipe and match transaction state is strongly consistent per pair/decision keys. Geo indexes, candidate pools, rank features, impressions, and notifications are eventual. Outbox records make match notifications recoverable. Versioned events and tombstones prevent deleted profiles from re-entering pools.

Failures include stale location, ranker outage, pool generation lag, and notification duplication. Use location TTL, chronological/simple-score fallback, on-demand bounded retrieval, and idempotent notification keys. Queue age and per-cell work budgets drive admission control. Rebuild projections from profiles, preferences, decisions, and blocks without modifying canonical matches.

docs.title: Observability and testing
docs.text:
Measure discovery stage p99, eligible yield, empty pools, cache generation age, geo-cell skew, repeat-card rate, swipe and match transaction latency, duplicate match attempts, notification delay, block/ban propagation, profile exposure distribution, report rate, and precise-location access audits. Monitor quality by geography and cohort without optimizing only matches.

Property-test pair uniqueness and symmetric eligibility. Race reciprocal likes, right/unmatch, block/match, and deletion/pool events. Replay duplicate/reordered events. Load-test dense and sparse geographies, popular profiles, and bots. Chaos-test pair-owner failover and policy dependency loss. Red-team enumeration, distance triangulation, screenshots/API scraping, and age-filter bypass.

docs.title: Product evolution, moderation, and recovery
docs.text:
Discovery changes require more than an offline ranking score. New models first replay historical point-in-time features, then run in shadow without changing cards. A small canary receives the model under exposure, safety, latency, and geography guardrails. Holdbacks measure long-term match quality and reports, while dashboards detect whether a cohort or sparse region loses supply. Rollback switches a versioned routing rule; short-lived pools naturally expire instead of requiring a global cache purge.

Profile review is a versioned workflow: draft, automated checks, visible, limited, suspended, and deleted. Every candidate carries the profile version used during generation. Online eligibility compares it with canonical state, preventing a pool entry from bypassing a later suspension. Media hashes and moderation decisions may be retained under restricted policy to stop repeat abuse, but deletion and appeal rules must distinguish safety evidence from ordinary profile data. Human actions include reason, evidence, policy version, and dual control for sensitive access.

Account deletion writes a priority deny record, closes discovery eligibility, revokes active sessions, and emits work for geo indexes, pools, matches, notifications, media, analytics, and backups. Match/chat policy determines what counterparties retain. Completion is tracked as a saga with per-system checkpoints; retries are idempotent, and missed consumers are found by reconciliation. This is stronger than assuming one broadcast instantly erases every copy.

Suppose a pair-owner shard fails after persisting a match but before responding. Both clients may retry their swipes. Unique swipe and pair keys return the existing outcome after the new leader is fenced in. The outbox eventually creates chat access and notifications once. If notification arrives after an immediate unmatch, its consumer checks match version and suppresses it. These races are useful interview probes because they connect database uniqueness, lifecycle versions, asynchronous effects, and user safety.

Cost controls include bounded candidates per rank call, cache reuse of immutable profile versions, tiered swipe-history retention, and separate impression aggregation. They must not weaken block checks or secretly change hard preferences. Under overload, reduce expensive ranking features and pool refresh frequency, then return fewer cards; never widen age or safety constraints to improve availability.

Pagination must also reserve impressions carefully. Returning a card records a deterministic impression token tied to user, candidate, pool generation, and expiry. A retry returns the same page when practical and does not repeatedly charge exposure caps. The swipe API accepts only a valid recent token, reducing arbitrary target enumeration without making the token an authorization grant. Expired tokens can still produce a safe rejection or a fresh eligibility check. Analytics deduplicates impressions by token, while ranking experiments retain the model and policy versions that selected each card.

docs.title: L6 mechanisms: geo retrieval, constrained exposure, and pair atomicity
Concrete geo candidate algorithm
docs.text:
Store discoverable users in S2 cells at level 14, roughly neighborhood-sized, with postings segmented by coarse age band, discovery mode, and activity bucket. Keep the encrypted exact point in a separate location service. For viewer u, compute the covering cells for concentric rings [0,5], (5,15], (15,30], and (30,R] km, intersecting the configured maximum radius. Query ring cells in deterministic pseudo-random order seeded by (u,pool_generation) so repeated generation is stable but cells do not receive positional bias.

For each ring, request at most ceil(target_remaining / estimated_yield) postings, capped at 2,000 scanned IDs and 200 IDs per cell. Cell metadata maintains count and trailing eligible-yield estimates by coarse filter. Oversized cells subdivide to level 16; sparse adjacent cells are fetched in one batch. Merge postings, remove self and decisions with a Bloom filter followed by canonical lookup, batch-fetch profiles, then evaluate exact Haversine distance and mutual hard preferences server-side. Stop once 400 eligible IDs are found or the scan reaches 10,000 IDs/80 ms. Never infer supply by exposing cell IDs or exact distance to clients.

flowchart TD
 A[Viewer point and hard radius] --> B[Build ordered S2 ring covering]
 B --> C[Estimate postings from cell metadata]
 C --> D[Scan capped cell postings]
 D --> E[Bloom prefilter self and prior decisions]
 E --> F[Canonical block ban age visibility checks]
 F --> G[Exact server-side distance and mutual preferences]
 G --> H{400 eligible or budget spent?}
 H -->|No| I[Expand to next ring]
 I --> C
 H -->|Yes| J[Constrained rank and pool write]
 J --> K[Return only distance band]

docs.title: Estimate-driven pools and fair exposure
docs.text:
To return 20 cards with expected online eligibility yield y, rank acceptance a, and a 25% reserve, request N = min(400,ceil(20 * 1.25 / (y*a))). If canonical filtering historically yields y=0.55 and rank policy accepts a=0.8, request 57 candidates. Persist estimates as exponentially weighted rates by cell/ring/filter bucket, with a conservative floor of 0.1 for new buckets. Pool generation stops at 400 eligible IDs, 10,000 scanned postings, 80 ms geo work, or 2 MB intermediate data. Sparse markets may produce fewer cards; hard age, block, ban, visibility, and distance settings never relax automatically.

Ranking first predicts compatibility/quality, then applies constrained selection. Give each candidate an exposure debt d = target_impressions(cohort,window) - actual_impressions, clipped to prevent low-quality promotion, and rank by base_score + alpha*d + exploration_bonus. Hard controls cap impressions per candidate per city/time window and at two cards from the same fine cell in any ten-card span. Reserve, for example, 10% of eligible slots for calibrated exploration among candidates above a safety and quality floor. For hard caps, reserve exposure capacity atomically before issuing a card token, settle it once on the deduplicated visible impression, and release only when the token can no longer become valid exposure under the defined window. Counting delayed impressions alone can overshoot a hard cap; approximate local counters provide only a declared soft cap. Audit exposure distributions by gender, age band, geography, account age, and subscription tier while withholding tiny cohorts; product fairness policy defines targets rather than the model inventing them.

If the ranker fails, use a versioned deterministic score over activity band, distance band, profile completeness, and exposure debt. If the exposure authority is unavailable, spend only previously escrowed cap grants or return fewer cards; an arbitrary local cap is not a proof of a global bound. If canonical eligibility is unavailable, return no cards. Pool exhaustion returns exhausted_reason such as HARD_FILTERS, RECENT_DECISIONS, or SUPPLY_DELAY; widening requires an explicit user action.

docs.title: Pair-owned atomic match boundary
docs.text:
Route canonical pair_key = H(min(A,B),max(A,B)) to one transactional shard and store both directed decisions plus the match row in that pair partition. The transaction for swipe (A,B,swipe_id) performs: insert idempotency result if absent; lock/read pair state; upsert A's decision; if it is RIGHT and B has an active RIGHT, insert the unique match; append MatchCreated to the same shard's outbox; commit the swipe result. The idempotency row stores the final response, including existing match_id, so timeout retries cannot return a contradictory outcome.

Actor-keyed swipe history remains a projection fed from the pair transaction; it is not used to decide reciprocity. This avoids an impossible atomic write between independently actor-sharded likes and a pair-sharded match. Per-actor rate limiting can precede routing, but the pair owner is the correctness boundary. A monotonically increasing pair version orders right swipe, unmatch, block, and rematch transitions. Chat creation consumes (pair_key,match_version) and checks that exact active version. Chat access also checks current pair/block authority on every new operation or under a declared bounded freshness lease: a pre-creation check alone races unmatch after the check and before the grant is installed.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant A as User A
 participant P as Pair owner shard
 participant T as Pair transaction
 participant O as Outbox
 participant C as Chat and notification
 A->>P: RIGHT B, swipe_id S9, impression I7
 P->>T: Verify token and begin pair_key(A,B)
 T->>T: Insert S9 result slot and upsert A to B
 T->>T: Read active B to A under same lock
 alt Reciprocal right exists
  T->>T: Insert unique match and increment pair version
  T->>O: Append MatchCreated in transaction
  T-->>P: Commit matched M42
 else No reciprocal right
  T-->>P: Commit accepted
 end
 P-->>A: Stored idempotent outcome
 O->>C: M42 and pair version
 C->>P: Recheck exact active version

Pair-owner failover requires a new routing epoch and quorum fencing before writes resume. Requests sent to an old epoch receive a redirect and do not queue locally. If commit succeeds but response fails, the new owner reads the persisted swipe_id. Concurrent reciprocal swipes serialize; the first commits a like and its accepted response, and the second creates the match. Retrying the first swipe returns that original response; the caller discovers the later match through event delivery or GET /v1/matches, not by changing a stored idempotency outcome.

docs.title: Cursor and impression-token contract
docs.text:
The discovery cursor is signed and encrypted because even pool membership is sensitive: {viewer_id,pool_generation,offset,last_rank_key,policy_version,model_version,issued_at,expires_at,nonce}. It references a short-lived immutable ordered pool. Regeneration creates a new generation and subtracts durable decisions plus recent impression IDs; it never accepts an offset from another generation. The service caches (generation,offset,page_size) -> card IDs and tokens through the retry window so retries retain the same page identity and tokens, while current eligibility and prior decisions can remove cards. Cached payloads never bypass a new block or swipe.

Each card carries a single-use-looking but idempotent signed token {token_id,viewer_id,candidate_id,pool_generation,rank_position,profile_version,policy_version,model_version,issued_at,expires_at}. Rendering records token_id with a unique constraint and charges exposure once. Swipe verifies signature, viewer, target, expiry, and profile version, then repeats current block/ban/age/visibility checks; the token proves the card was issued, not that it remains eligible. Reusing the same token with the same swipe_id returns the prior outcome; a different target or payload is rejected. Tokens reduce arbitrary-ID swipes and tie training data to selection provenance without becoming authorization capabilities.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Precomputed pools reduce latency but stale quickly; short pools plus canonical read-time eligibility balance speed and safety. Exact distance improves ranking but leaks location; bands preserve utility. Global active-active pair writes maximize availability but complicate uniqueness; deterministic ownership with fenced failover preserves the core invariant. Pure engagement ranking causes concentration and unsafe incentives; constrained ranking makes policy and exposure first-class.

flowchart TD
 A[Versioned profiles/preferences/location] --> B[Regional candidate indexes]
 B --> C[Short-lived candidate pools]
 C --> D[Canonical eligibility and abuse gate]
 D --> E[Constrained ranker with fallback]
 F[Idempotent swipe] --> G[Pair-owned atomic match state]
 G --> H[Outbox notifications/chat grants]
 G --> D
 I[Blocks/bans/deletes] --> D
 I --> B

docs.title: Questions, levels, and five-minute summary
docs.text:
1. How do simultaneous reciprocal likes create one match?
  2. How do you prevent distance triangulation?
  3. What happens when candidate pools are exhausted?
  4. How are popular profiles and dense cells kept from becoming hot keys?
  5. Can discovery continue if block state is unavailable?

L5 candidates should model discovery, geo indexing, read-time filters, idempotent swipes, unique matches, partitioning, and abuse. L6 candidates should define pair ownership and fencing, rank constraints and exposure policy, privacy threat models, regional residency, overload behavior, projection rebuilds, and safe product behavior under uncertainty.

In five minutes: generate short-lived pools from coarse geo and preference indexes, then recheck canonical mutual eligibility, decisions, blocks, bans, and profile versions before constrained ranking. Never return exact location. Persist swipes idempotently and route an unordered pair to one transactional owner that conditionally creates a unique match when reciprocal likes exist. Publish match events through an outbox and recheck active state before notifications or chat grants. Partition actor history, pair matches, and geographic cells separately; split dense cells and cap popular-profile exposure. Treat pools, rank scores, counters, and notifications as projections, while profile policy, decisions, blocks, and match state remain canonical.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Clarify whether the interview covers posting, following, home timelines, search, trends, and direct messages. This design serves tweets and home timelines; search, ads, and DMs are extensions. Start with chronological feeds, then add ranking. The decisive issue is asymmetric fanout: most authors are small, while a celebrity can have hundreds of millions of followers.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Users create, delete, and read tweets; follow or unfollow accounts; and page through a home timeline. Tweets may contain text and references to uploaded media. Replies, reposts, and likes are modeled as typed edges or tweets, but notification delivery is outside the critical posting path.

The system should sustain bursty global traffic, return a first timeline page in under 300 ms at p99, make ordinary tweets visible to most online followers within five seconds, and remain readable during partial failures. Deleted or access-revoked content must disappear quickly. A user must never receive a protected tweet without authorization. Ordering may be approximate across authors, but each tweet has a stable identity and an author's own sequence cannot reverse.

Out of scope are full-text search, ad auctions, trend computation, and media transcoding internals.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A successful create maps an idempotency key to exactly one tweet ID.
  • Canonical tweet state lives in the tweet store; timeline entries are disposable projections.
  • Authorization is checked at read time even when fanout happened earlier.
  • A delete tombstone dominates delayed fanout and cache entries.
  • Pagination never depends on mutable page numbers; cursors describe a stable boundary.
  • Follow state changes affect future eligibility, while policy defines whether historical tweets appear.
  • Queue delivery is at least once; consumers make effects idempotent.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text:
Assume 500 million daily users, 200 million tweets/day, and 50 billion timeline item reads/day. At 50 delivered items/page, this is one billion page requests/day, about 11,574/s average and 116,000/s at 10x peak; the page-read/tweet-write API ratio is 5:1. A 20:1 ratio would instead require four billion pages/day averaging 12.5 delivered items/page. Do not equate item reads with page requests. Average tweet metadata is 1 KB, or about 200 GB/day before replication and indexes. At three replicas and one year online, tweet metadata approaches 220 TB. If an average author has 300 followers, naive fanout creates 60 billion entries/day; at 32 bytes each that is 1.9 TB/day before replication. Tweet-write peak at 10x average is about 23,150/s. Media bytes dominate storage and egress, so clients upload directly to object storage through signed URLs and consume via a CDN.

These estimates justify separate canonical and derived stores, asynchronous fanout, and special treatment for high-fanout authors.

docs.title: Entities and data model
docs.text:
User(user_id, handle, visibility, status, profile_version)
Tweet(tweet_id, author_id, author_seq, body, media_ids[], created_at, state)
Follow(follower_id, followee_id, state, updated_at)
TimelineEntry(owner_id, rank_time, tweet_id, author_id, source)
Idempotency(principal_id, key, request_hash, tweet_id, expires_at)
Tombstone(tweet_id, deleted_at, reason, policy_version)

Tweet IDs can be time-sortable 128-bit IDs allocated regionally. Tweet partitions by tweet_id; an author-time index supports profiles. Follow edges need both directions: followees by follower for reads and followers by followee for fanout. Timeline entries partition by owner and bucket by month or sequence range to avoid unbounded partitions.

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/tweets                 Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
GET  /v1/tweets/{tweet_id}
DELETE /v1/tweets/{tweet_id}
PUT  /v1/users/{id}/following/{followee_id}
DELETE /v1/users/{id}/following/{followee_id}
GET  /v1/users/{id}/timeline?cursor=<opaque>&limit=50
POST /v1/media/uploads

Creation returns 201 with the stable ID, or the original response on retry. A timeline cursor contains the last rank key, snapshot/ranking version, and a signed expiry; it is not a raw offset. Responses include content and policy versions so caches cannot resurrect older visibility.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    C[Clients] --> E[Edge and API gateway]
    E --> W[Tweet service]
    E --> T[Timeline service]
    E --> G[Social graph service]
    W --> TS[(Tweet store)]
    W --> O[(Transactional outbox)]
    O --> K[Event log]
    K --> F[Fanout workers]
    G --> GS[(Graph store)]
    F --> TI[(Timeline store)]
    T --> TI
    T --> TS
    T --> P[Policy service]
    T --> R[Ranker]
    T --> RC[(Timeline cache)]
    C --> CDN[Media CDN]
    subgraph ClientLane[Client and static media]
      C
      CDN
    end
    subgraph WriteLane[Tweets and fanout]
      W
      TS
      O
      K
      F
      TI
    end
    subgraph GraphLane[Social graph]
      G
      GS
    end
    subgraph ReadLane[Timeline reads]
      T
      P
      R
      RC
    end

The write service commits tweet and outbox record atomically. Event-log consumers update profile indexes, notifications, counters, and timeline projections independently. Reads fetch candidate IDs, remove tombstones and unauthorized items, hydrate canonical tweets in batches, rank, and cache only short-lived pages.

docs.title: Create and fan out
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant W as Tweet service
    participant D as Tweet DB
    participant K as Event log
    participant F as Fanout workers
    participant T as Timeline store
    C->>W: POST tweet + idempotency key
    W->>D: transaction: key, tweet, outbox
    D-->>W: committed tweet ID
    W-->>C: 201 Created
    W->>K: relay outbox event
    K->>F: tweet-created (at least once)
    F->>T: conditional insert(owner, tweet)

For ordinary authors, workers enumerate follower shards and push an entry to each home timeline. Fanout is parallel but bounded; lag is measured by event age. For celebrities, the event records a pull candidate instead of writing millions of entries. The home read merges precomputed inbox entries with recent tweets from followed celebrity accounts, then ranks the combined set. Thresholds should use measured fanout cost and posting rate, not a permanent celebrity flag.

docs.title: Read a timeline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant T as Timeline service
    participant I as Timeline index
    participant H as Hot-author index
    participant S as Tweet store
    participant P as Policy
    C->>T: GET timeline(cursor)
    T->>I: scan pushed candidates
    T->>H: fetch pull candidates before boundary
    T->>S: batch hydrate IDs
    T->>P: batch authorize(viewer, authors, tweets)
    P-->>T: allowed set
    T-->>C: ranked page + next cursor

The service overfetches because deletion, blocking, and moderation remove candidates. It applies a strict work budget; if filtering empties a page, it may return fewer items rather than scan without bound. Ranking can start with reverse chronology, then incorporate relationship affinity and quality. The cursor freezes the ranking model version for a short session to reduce duplicates and jumps.

docs.title: Fanout, hot keys, and backpressure
docs.text: Follower lists are range-sharded, and each fanout task addresses one shard. A scheduler uses weighted queues so a viral account cannot starve ordinary authors. When lag exceeds the SLO, it degrades large accounts from push to pull, coalesces fanout tasks by author while retaining every distinct tweet reference, and postpones noncritical counters. Per-user timeline writes can also be hot when a user follows many prolific accounts; append buckets and write combining spread load.

docs.title: Deletes, edits, and privacy
docs.text: Deletion first marks canonical state and commits a tombstone event. Reads always honor canonical state or a compact tombstone cache, so physical removal from every timeline can lag. Sweepers remove projections and CDN objects. Protected-account changes and blocks increment policy versions; timeline cache keys include viewer and policy version. Cache hits still validate current policy freshness and deny state; a stored version number or delayed invalidation cannot alone prove the removal bound. If edits are allowed, immutable revisions preserve moderation evidence while only the latest authorized revision is served.

docs.title: Pagination and ranking stability
docs.text: Offset pagination fails under concurrent insertion. The cursor records (score, created_at, tweet_id) and the oldest candidate window already considered. Ranked scores change, so sessions either freeze candidates and the computed ordered scores briefly or accept clearly documented at-least-once appearance. Clients deduplicate by tweet ID. Refill logic limits scans and exposes an is_partial signal during dependency degradation.

docs.title: Partitioning and multi-region
docs.text:
Tweets partition by hash of tweet ID with an author index; graphs partition by followee for fanout and maintain an asynchronously built reverse view. Timeline partitions use owner ID plus time bucket. Virtual shards permit rebalancing, and heavy owners can receive dedicated shards.

Route writes to a user's fenced home authority to preserve author sequence. Replicate tweets, author-sequence high-watermarks, idempotency and graph changes; timeline projections are rebuildable. Failover fences the old writer and restores that authority before accepting new posts. A new random/time-sortable ID range alone cannot restore acknowledged author order or lost idempotency state; asynchronous disaster recovery must expose its RPO and cannot silently reorder prior acknowledgements by ID. Privacy and delete events use a priority lane and read-time deny lists.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and failures
docs.text:
Tweet creation is strongly consistent within its shard. Timelines, counts, and notifications are eventually consistent. Follow creation uses a compare-and-set state machine so retries cannot duplicate edges. Consumers store event IDs or use naturally unique keys such as (owner_id, tweet_id). Outbox relay retries forever; poison events enter quarantine with alarms and replay tooling.

If the graph store is unavailable, posting still succeeds and fanout waits. If the timeline store fails, reads can fall back to pull from a bounded set of followees, returning a partial marker. If ranking fails, reverse chronology is valid. Cache failures cause load shedding, not unbounded database traffic. Every queue has retention sized for recovery, age-based alerts, and admission control. Rebuilding a timeline scans recent posts from current followees, while canonical tweets remain untouched.

docs.title: Abuse, security, and privacy
docs.text: Authenticate at the edge; authorize every mutation against the principal. Rate-limit by account, device, IP reputation, and action. Separate spam scoring from durable acceptance so false positives can be appealed, but block known malicious media before distribution. Encrypt transport and storage, isolate media upload credentials, audit employee access, and minimize viewer-specific cache sharing. Blocking, muted words, legal holds, geographic restrictions, and account deletion are policy inputs, not client filters.

docs.title: Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track API p50/p99, create success, event age, fanout amplification, per-shard saturation, timeline empty/partial rate, hydration misses, policy-deny rate, cache hit rate, and delete propagation latency. Trace from tweet ID through outbox and fanout tasks. Synthetic accounts continuously post, follow, block, delete, and verify visibility across regions.

Test model invariants with property tests; retry every mutation under injected timeouts; replay duplicate and reordered events; load-test Zipfian follower distributions; chaos-test broker, cache, and region loss; and verify authorization with a generated relationship matrix. Shadow ranking models and compare candidate loss before rollout.

docs.title: Important tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Pure push gives cheap reads but catastrophic celebrity writes and stale privacy projections. Pure pull avoids amplification but makes every read proportional to followee count. Hybrid fanout bounds both. Storing full tweets in timelines improves locality but multiplies edits and deletions; storing IDs preserves one canonical copy at the cost of hydration. Global synchronous writes simplify semantics but damage availability and latency; home-region writes plus explicit eventual projections fit the product.

flowchart TD
    A[Regional edge] --> B[Home-region write path]
    B --> C[(Canonical tweets + outbox)]
    C --> D[Global durable event log]
    D --> E[Priority policy/delete consumers]
    D --> F[Adaptive fanout scheduler]
    F --> G[(Regional pushed timelines)]
    D --> H[(Hot-author recent-post index)]
    I[Timeline read] --> G
    I --> H
    I --> J[Hydration + authorization]
    J --> K[Ranker or chronological fallback]

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. How do you choose and dynamically change the push/pull threshold?
  2. What happens when a user blocks an author while fanout is delayed?
  3. How does cursor pagination behave when ranking scores change?
  4. How would you rebuild one corrupted timeline without replaying all history?
  5. Which workloads create hot partitions despite hashing?
  6. How do you prove deletion propagation meets policy?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate should estimate amplification, separate canonical tweets from timelines, propose hybrid fanout, define cursor pagination, and explain retries, deletion, and cache fallback. An L6 candidate should make policy propagation an invariant, design adaptive overload behavior, articulate regional write ownership and recovery, quantify skew, provide migration and replay mechanisms, and connect ranking, moderation, privacy, and cost to operational ownership.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Store tweets once as canonical records and publish committed outbox events. Push ordinary authors' tweet IDs into follower timelines, but pull recent posts for accounts whose fanout cost is excessive. Timeline reads merge both candidate sources, batch-hydrate canonical tweets, enforce current policy, rank, and paginate with an opaque boundary cursor. Hash and bucket timeline data, shard follower enumeration, isolate viral fanout with fair queues, and degrade ranking to chronology. Use idempotency keys for writes and unique projection keys for at-least-once consumers. Treat deletes and access revocations as priority tombstones checked at read time. Keep each region's projections rebuildable from canonical state and the event log, and operate the design through lag, skew, partial-result, privacy, and recovery metrics.

docs.title: Design a Video Conferencing System
docs.text: This case study owns the meeting product and architecture. Use Realtime and Media for RTP/WebRTC transport, congestion, NAT traversal, and packet-level failure behavior.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Design interactive meetings with audio, video, screen sharing, chat, recording, and joining by link. Clarify participant limits, latency, quality, privacy, and whether webinars are included. Begin with WebRTC clients and regional selective forwarding units (SFUs), then add signaling, congestion control, cascaded regions, recording, moderation, and failure recovery. Media quality under changing networks is the central problem; metadata storage is secondary.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text: Users create and join meetings, publish tracks, subscribe to selected tracks, mute, share a screen, chat, and optionally record. Hosts admit or remove participants and lock meetings. Assume interactive meetings up to 1,000 participants, with a 25-person gallery; webinars with 100,000 viewers use a separate broadcast path. Target under 150 ms one-way media latency in-region, under 300 ms cross-region, join p99 below 3 seconds, and 99.99% signaling availability. Graceful quality reduction is preferable to synchronized failure.

docs.title: Correctness invariants
docs.text:
• A meeting ID maps to one active meeting generation; stale signaling cannot mutate a newer generation.
  • A participant session has one authenticated identity and monotonically increasing connection epoch.
  • Only authorized publishers can create tracks; subscription never grants publication.
  • Host/moderation commands are ordered by meeting control revision and are auditable.
  • Media encryption keys are scoped by meeting and epoch and revoked membership cannot obtain future keys.
  • Recording consent and indicator state precede captured media according to policy.
  • Signaling retries are idempotent; media packets are intentionally lossy and never retried after their playout deadline.

docs.title: Capacity estimates
docs.text: Assume 50 million daily participants, 2 million concurrent, and 100,000 meetings. A publisher sends scalable video layers totaling about 2.5 Mbps plus 50 Kbps audio. An SFU does not transcode ordinary calls but may egress 25 selected streams per receiver; bandwidth dominates CPU. Two million users averaging 3 Mbps down consume 6 Tbps. Signaling at ten events/user/minute averages 330,000 events/s. Store roughly 20 KB meeting metadata and chat per participant, but recording at 1 GB/hour makes object storage and lifecycle policy decisive. Capacity is reserved by region and failure headroom, not global averages.

docs.title: Entities and interfaces
docs.text:
Meeting(meeting_id, generation, host_id, policy, home_region, state, revision)
Participant(session_id, meeting_id, user_id, role, connection_epoch, state)
Track(track_id, session_id, kind, codec, simulcast_layers, state)
Subscription(session_id, track_id, preferred_layer, effective_layer)
ControlEvent(meeting_id, revision, actor, command, result, timestamp)
Recording(recording_id, meeting_id, consent_revision, state, manifest_uri)

POST /v1/meetings
POST /v1/meetings/{id}:join        -> signed session token, ICE servers
POST /v1/meetings/{id}:admit
POST /v1/meetings/{id}:record
GET  /v1/meetings/{id}/events?after=<revision>
WSS  /v1/sessions/{session_id}/signal

Signaling messages include session_id, connection epoch, client sequence, command ID, and meeting revision. SDP and ICE negotiation are carried over the socket. Media uses SRTP over UDP where possible and TURN/TLS as fallback.

docs.title: Join and negotiation
docs.text:
The edge authenticates the invite and user, applies waiting-room policy, and asks the allocator for an SFU with regional proximity, available egress, codec support, and failure-domain diversity. The join response contains a short-lived, meeting-scoped token. Clients exchange SDP offers and ICE candidates through signaling, attempting direct UDP to the SFU, then TURN/UDP, then TURN/TLS. Reconnection increments the connection epoch so delayed commands from the old socket are ignored.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant G as Edge
 participant S as Signaling
 participant A as Allocator
 participant F as SFU
 C->>G: join invite and capabilities
 G->>S: authenticated join
 S->>A: allocate(region, codecs, load)
 A-->>S: SFU and reservation
 S-->>C: session token and ICE config
 C->>F: ICE, DTLS, SRTP
 F-->>C: subscribed media layers
 C->>S: joined(command_id, epoch)
 S->>S: publish ordered meeting event

docs.title: Media forwarding and congestion control
docs.text:
Publishers encode simulcast layers, for example 180p/300 Kbps, 360p/700 Kbps, and 720p/1.8 Mbps. For each receiver, the SFU estimates available bitrate from transport feedback, reserves audio and screen share, then selects video layers using a bounded utility function. Active speaker, pinned tiles, and viewport visibility assign utility. Additive increase and loss/delay-triggered multiplicative decrease prevent persistent queues. Layer changes use hysteresis to avoid oscillation. If overloaded, reduce resolution, then frame rate, then pause off-screen video; never sacrifice audio first.

Packet retransmission is useful only within the jitter-buffer deadline. NACK requests recent packets from a small SFU cache; forward error correction helps burst loss at bandwidth cost. Keyframe requests are coalesced so a new subscriber wave does not trigger every publisher simultaneously. Lip sync uses RTP timestamps and sender reports. With ordinary hop encryption, the SFU terminates each DTLS-SRTP association, accesses RTP payloads and re-encrypts for the receiver, but avoids codec decoding. With additional frame E2EE it forwards opaque encrypted frames. It should avoid decoding except where server-side recording or moderation explicitly requires it.

docs.title: Meeting control and moderation
docs.text:
Control commands use optimistic concurrency against meeting revision. The authoritative leader for a meeting orders admit, remove, lock, mute-request, role change, and recording events. Muting another user disables server forwarding and sends a signed command; clients cannot be trusted to stop capture. A removed session token is revoked and its track routes are deleted. SFUs enforce current control epochs or bounded authorization leases and stop affected forwarding when freshness expires. Push-only revocation cannot meet a deadline across a partition. Chat is a durable ordered stream per meeting; media is not coupled to chat persistence.

stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> CREATED
 CREATED --> WAITING
 WAITING --> JOINING: admitted
 JOINING --> CONNECTED: media established
 CONNECTED --> RECONNECTING: path failure
 RECONNECTING --> CONNECTED: higher epoch
 RECONNECTING --> LEFT: grace expired
 CONNECTED --> REMOVED: host action
 WAITING --> REMOVED: denied or removed
 JOINING --> REMOVED: revoked during negotiation
 RECONNECTING --> REMOVED: host action
 CONNECTED --> LEFT: leave
 REMOVED --> [*]
 LEFT --> [*]

docs.title: Recording and webinars
docs.text:
Recording is a separate subscriber. It receives tracks, records individually for later composition or composites a layout live, writes short immutable segments, and checkpoints a manifest. Individual tracks preserve editing flexibility but cost more storage; composition is cheaper to play. Consent revision and visible/audible indicators must be committed before subscription starts. Crashes resume at a new segment; manifests tolerate gaps and never rewrite completed segments.

For very large webinars, forwarding one interactive stream per viewer is uneconomic. Presenters stay on SFUs; a transcoder creates an adaptive bitrate ladder distributed through a CDN using low-latency HLS/DASH. Viewers trade several seconds of latency for scale. A smaller interactive cohort can remain on WebRTC. This explicit product boundary avoids forcing incompatible latency and fanout requirements into one path.

docs.title: SFU placement and cascading
docs.text: The allocator scores (network RTT, available egress, CPU, participant affinity, zone risk), rejecting candidates below headroom. Small meetings use one SFU. Large meetings shard participants across SFUs; publishers send to a local SFU and selected layers traverse an SFU mesh. Cross-region meetings use regional SFUs with one copy of each needed layer over inter-region links, not one stream per remote receiver. A topology controller caps mesh degree and elects relay paths. Extra hops add latency but sharply reduce publisher uplink and backbone duplication.

docs.title: Encryption choices
docs.text: Transport encryption protects each client-SFU hop and allows routing by RTP metadata. True end-to-end encryption encrypts encoded frames with meeting epoch keys while leaving minimal routing headers visible. A membership service distributes keys to authenticated devices and rotates on joins/removals according to policy. E2EE conflicts with server recording, transcription, some moderation, and PSTN interop; offer explicit modes rather than claiming all simultaneously. Removal rotates to fresh key material distributed only to remaining authenticated members, using a protocol with post-removal secrecy. Merely hashing a shared old key into the next key lets a removed member compute it too.

docs.title: Reconnection and SFU failure
docs.text: Clients maintain last meeting revision and track identities. On socket failure they reconnect with a higher epoch and request events after that revision. If only signaling fails, media continues. If an SFU fails, the allocator chooses a replacement; publishers renegotiate and subscribers preserve stable logical track IDs. A shadow SFU for every meeting doubles cost, so reserve hot standby only for high-value meetings and optimize ordinary recovery to seconds. Brief media loss is accepted; control events remain durable.

docs.title: Partitioning, scaling, and multi-region
docs.text:
Partition signaling and metadata by meeting ID so one logical leader orders control. Presence is ephemeral and rebuilt from session leases. Very large meetings use child media partitions while retaining one control revision stream. SFUs are stateless beyond short-lived routes, packet caches, and measurements; drain them before deploy. Autoscaling watches reserved egress, packet rate, and join rate, not CPU alone. Admission control keeps 30-40% regional network headroom for machine or zone failure.

Route users to nearby media regions while meeting metadata has a home region. A globally replicated directory maps meeting generation to home and media topology. Control writes go to the home leader; cross-region participants accept extra control latency while media remains local. If the home region fails, a quorum-backed failover increments generation and fences old leaders. Existing media can continue temporarily, but new moderation waits for authoritative control rather than creating split-brain hosts.

Hot meetings are isolated through dedicated signaling partitions, SFUs, and TURN quotas. Backpressure rejects new video publications before joins, defaults newcomers to audio, and moves passive users to webinar delivery. Clients receive explicit quality constraints rather than inferring failure.

docs.title: Consistency, idempotency, and reliability
docs.text:
Meeting policy and ordered control are strongly consistent per meeting; participant presence, quality statistics, active speaker, and analytics are eventual. Commands deduplicate by (meeting_id, session_id, command_id) and compare connection epoch. Event consumers checkpoint revision. Media packet sequence numbers handle reorder; duplicate packets are discarded. There is no reason to put media in a durable queue.

Failures include NAT traversal failure, signaling disconnect, SFU overload, packet loss, TURN exhaustion, regional backbone impairment, recorder lag, and key-service outage. TURN capacity is pre-provisioned and regionally isolated. Circuit breakers stop allocating unhealthy SFUs. If key distribution fails, E2EE joins fail closed while existing epochs continue for a bounded window. If recording storage slows, buffer only bounded segments, surface degraded recording, and protect the live call. Malformed optional analytics can be quarantined, but an undecodable authoritative control revision blocks dependent control application until repaired or replaced by a verified snapshot. Skipping an unknown removal or recording-consent event would violate policy.

docs.title: Security, abuse, observability, and testing
docs.text:
Use short-lived scoped join tokens, invite entropy, waiting rooms, role authorization, meeting locks, rate limits, signed clients where appropriate, and encrypted transport. Protect against meeting bombing, credential sharing, chat spam, malicious SDP, oversized packets, TURN bandwidth theft, and denial through repeated joins. Minimize media retention, make recording obvious, audit moderation, honor deletion across manifests and replicas, and treat biometric/transcription features as separate consented products.

Observe join success by ICE path, time to first audio/video, RTT, jitter, loss, bitrate, freeze ratio, audio concealment, quality limitation reason, SFU egress saturation, TURN allocation, keyframe storms, reconnection success, control lag, recording gaps, and regional capacity. Use privacy-preserving session correlation rather than media payload logging.

Test control-state properties and epoch fencing, adapter compatibility across browser/device matrices, malformed SDP/RTP fuzzing, network simulation for loss/reorder/bandwidth changes, and long-call memory stability. Load-test synchronized joins and gallery changes. Chaos-test SFU death, signaling leader loss, TURN exhaustion, region isolation, clock skew, and object-store throttling. Synthetic robots continuously join, publish known audio/video, and score received quality.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Mesh calls avoid servers but publisher bandwidth grows with participants; SFUs win beyond tiny calls. MCUs simplify clients and bandwidth but transcode expensively and fix layout; use them for composition, not ordinary forwarding. One global SFU minimizes topology logic but increases latency and blast radius; regional SFUs with controlled cascading win. Strong presence is costly and unnecessary, while strong moderation ordering is essential. E2EE improves confidentiality but intentionally removes server features.

flowchart TD
 U[Authenticated join] --> C[Meeting control leader]
 C --> A[Capacity-aware regional allocator]
 A --> L[Local SFU and TURN]
 L --> B[Bandwidth estimator]
 B --> S[Per-receiver layer selection]
 L --> X[Regional SFU cascade]
 L --> R[Consent-gated recorder]
 C --> E[(Ordered control events)]
 E --> O[Audit, chat, projections]

The final system separates durable meeting control from ephemeral media forwarding. A home-region leader orders policy and moderation; regional allocators place participants on capacity-reserved SFUs. Clients publish simulcast, SFUs choose layers per receiver, TURN handles restrictive networks, and regional cascades limit backbone fanout. Recording is an explicit subscriber, and webinar scale exits through a transcoder and CDN.

docs.title: Interview deep-dive questions
docs.text:
1. Why choose an SFU over mesh or MCU, and when does that change?
  2. How does the system preserve audio during an egress overload?
  3. What happens when signaling fails but media still flows?
  4. How are host commands fenced during regional failover?
  5. How do 100,000 viewers change the architecture?
  6. Which features conflict with end-to-end encryption?
  7. How would you diagnose freezes seen only on one ISP?

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 candidate should separate signaling from media, estimate bandwidth, choose SFU and TURN, explain join negotiation, simulcast, congestion handling, meeting partitioning, retries, and common failures. They should preserve audio under overload and distinguish durable control from lossy packets.

An L6 candidate should quantify regional headroom, design cascaded topology and hot-meeting isolation, define control generations and key epochs, negotiate E2EE product limits, handle migrations and draining, and tie quality, privacy, recording cost, and webinar boundaries to business policy. They should propose rollout metrics and failure exercises rather than only components.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Use an authenticated signaling plane to allocate nearby SFUs and exchange WebRTC negotiation; send encrypted media directly to SFUs, with TURN fallback. Keep one ordered, durable control stream per meeting, fencing reconnects and failover by epochs, while treating presence and quality as ephemeral. Publishers send simulcast layers. Each SFU reserves audio and screen share, estimates receiver bandwidth, and chooses visible video layers with hysteresis. Shard media for large meetings and cascade only required layers between regions. Record through a consent-gated subscriber writing immutable segments. Move massive passive audiences to transcoding and CDN delivery. Scale on egress and packet rate, reserve failure headroom, isolate hot meetings, and degrade video before audio. Measure join success, first media, loss, freezes, TURN use, saturation, control lag, and recording gaps; test real network impairment and zonal failure.

docs.title: Interview roadmap
docs.text: Scope one-to-one and group text/media messaging, delivery receipts, offline sync, and multiple devices. Exclude calls, payments, public channels, and cryptographic protocol internals, but preserve end-to-end encryption (E2EE) constraints. Start with durable store-and-forward delivery, then add groups, device fanout, ordering, and regional failover.

docs.title: Product framing and requirements
docs.text:
Users send messages to contacts and groups, receive them online or after reconnecting, and observe sent, delivered, and read states. Each registered device receives encrypted payloads. The service should accept messages under 200 ms p99 within a region, deliver to connected recipients within one second normally, retain offline messages for a defined period, and support billions of users. Availability is high, but authentication, membership, and cryptographic device identity cannot be bypassed.

E2EE means servers route ciphertext and limited metadata; they cannot search or moderate plaintext. Abuse controls rely on rate, graph, reports, and privacy-preserving signals.

Source boundary: Meta's 2021 multi-device explanation documents per-device identity keys, client-side pairwise encryption/fanout, Sender Keys for groups and encrypted history transfer. It says delivered messages are not retained on the server. This chapter's server-side conversation sequencer and optional 30-day canonical archive are proposed product choices, not verified WhatsApp architecture or retention policy (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Invariants and estimates
docs.text:
• A client-generated message ID is unique within a sender identity and conversation.
  • Accepted ciphertext is durably stored before acknowledgement.
  • Each conversation has a server-assigned monotonic sequence, though clients may display provisional sends.
  • Delivery is at least once; device clients deduplicate.
  • Only devices eligible at send time receive group sender-key material under the protocol policy.
  • A receipt advances monotonically per device/conversation.
  • Membership removal prevents future messages but cannot retract decrypted history.

Assume 2 billion daily users, 100 messages/user/day: 200 billion/day, 2.3 million/s average and 10 million/s peak. At 1 KB envelope average, ingress is 200 TB/day before replicas. Connections may exceed one billion concurrently. Media bypasses messaging servers via encrypted object storage. Metadata retention and offline TTL dominate durable queue size.

Conversation(conversation_id, type, home_shard, membership_version)

GET  /v1/sync?cursor=<device_cursor>&limit=...
POST /v1/receipts                      {conversation_id, delivered_through, read_through}

WebSocket or QUIC carries the same typed envelopes as the HTTP fallback. Cursors are opaque per-device log positions.

docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

The sender retries ambiguous requests; (conversation,sender_device,client_msg_id) returns the original sequence. Fanout inserts unique (device,conversation,seq) rows. Gateways lease batches, send, and retain entries until cumulative delivery acknowledgement or expiry.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber

 participant G as Gateway
 participant I as Device inbox
 participant M as Message log
 C->>G: sync(cursor)
 G->>I: scan after cursor

docs.title: Ordering and duplicates
docs.text: A conversation home shard serializes appends and assigns sequence numbers. This gives deterministic group order without global ordering. Failover fences the previous leader with epochs; a sequence may have gaps, never reuse. Clients merge provisional local sends with acknowledged sequences and deduplicate by client ID. Cross-conversation ordering is intentionally undefined.

docs.title: Groups and device fanout
docs.text: Small groups expand synchronously into device inbox tasks after commit. Large groups shard membership snapshots and fan out asynchronously with fair scheduling. The message records membership version; workers evaluate joined_seq/left_seq against the message's accepted membership epoch. A removed user never receives messages accepted after removal; delivery of older already-authorized ciphertext follows the explicit history/revocation policy. Adding a companion device requires key transfer/verification and a bounded history policy, not silent server plaintext recovery.

docs.title: Presence, connections, and push
docs.text: Gateways keep soft presence in an expiring distributed map. Presence is advisory and aggressively privacy-limited. Consistent hashing routes a device to a gateway region; reconnect resumes by durable cursor, so losing gateway memory is harmless. Mobile push contains only a wake-up token, not plaintext. Backpressure slows sync batches, coalesces wakes, and rejects abusive senders before durable queues exhaust.

docs.title: Encrypted media
docs.text: The client encrypts media with a random key, uploads ciphertext using a constrained signed URL, and sends the encrypted key and content hash in the message envelope. CDN/object storage sees opaque bytes. Expired unreferenced uploads are collected. Integrity checks detect corruption without revealing plaintext.

docs.title: Partitioning and regions
docs.text:
Partition conversations by ID and map each to a home region/shard; split exceptionally large broadcast-like groups or move them to a channel product with weaker semantics. Device inboxes partition by device and time bucket. Membership partitions by conversation. Gateways partition live connections by device hash.

Keep synchronous replicas across failure zones within the home region and async replicas to a paired region. Failover requires quorum/lease fencing to avoid two sequencers. During isolation, non-home regions can retain encrypted client retries locally but should not assign conflicting order. Device inboxes are regional projections rebuilt from the message log.

docs.title: Consistency, failures, and recovery
docs.text:
Message append and idempotency mapping are strongly consistent per conversation. Delivery, receipts, presence, and push are eventual. Receipts use max(current,incoming) after verifying device ownership, eligible delivered ranges and a known delivery frontier. Cumulative receipt N covers eligible messages through N, with server-certified sequence gaps; it cannot acknowledge an unseen future sequence or skip an unresolved eligible envelope. A transactionally written outbox prevents accepted messages from disappearing before fanout.

Gateway loss causes reconnect and replay. Bus outage increases event age while accepted messages remain safe. Inbox loss triggers replay from conversation events for affected devices. Slow or offline devices have quotas and TTLs; policy decides archive retrieval after queue expiry. Poison envelopes are quarantined without blocking a partition. Overloaded groups receive per-conversation token buckets so one chat cannot starve the fleet.

docs.title: Security, abuse, privacy
docs.text: Bind sessions to registered device keys, rate-limit registration and sends, detect enumeration, and protect key-directory updates with transparency/audit mechanisms. Minimize and expire IP, social graph, and delivery metadata. Group invite controls, blocking, unknown-sender requests, report flows, and forwarding limits mitigate spam. Reports may include user-selected decrypted messages; this must be explicit. Encrypt storage and logs, isolate keys, and never log ciphertext payloads unnecessarily.

docs.title: Lifecycle, migrations, and overload drills
docs.text:
Account and device lifecycle deserves its own state machine. Registering a device proves control of the account and establishes a new identity key; removing it revokes future envelopes and key updates. A phone-number reassignment must not expose the former owner's graph or queued messages. The identity service therefore separates stable account identity from reusable address, waits through a quarantine period where policy permits, and requires contacts to observe a safety-number change. Backup restoration is a client-side encrypted import, not a server shortcut around E2EE.

Schema changes use envelope versions understood by both old and new clients. Writers initially emit the old representation while readers accept both, then capability telemetry permits dual-write or new emission. A conversation-log repartition is performed by fencing writes briefly at a revision, copying immutable history, tailing changes, validating counts/checksums, and switching the routing epoch. Inbox projections can simply be rebuilt after the cutover. Key protocol changes require a longer compatibility window and explicit downgrade prevention.

Consider a regional broker outage during a major holiday. Send acceptance continues while the replicated message log and outbox have capacity. Delivery lag alarms trigger push coalescing, disable presence and read-receipt chatter, reserve workers for one-to-one and small groups, and slow large-group fanout. If retained outbox bytes approach the safety limit, admission control first rejects abusive and broadcast-like traffic; it does not acknowledge work that cannot be retained. Recovery drains with fair per-conversation scheduling so recent interactive chats are not trapped behind one old group backlog.

Retention is also semantic. Expiring a device inbox does not necessarily delete canonical encrypted history; the product must define whether history is server-retained, client-backup-only, or available for a bounded window. Message deletion can distribute a tombstone, but a recipient may already have decrypted or copied content. UI wording and compliance guarantees must reflect that physical limit rather than imply remote erasure.

Large attachment download is independently resumable. A recipient validates ciphertext chunks and the authenticated content hash before exposing plaintext. Signed object URLs are short-lived and can be refreshed only by a currently eligible device, but revocation cannot claw back bytes already downloaded. CDN cache keys identify encrypted immutable objects, so tenants never share plaintext and origin retries cannot alter message meaning. Media reference counts are projections; garbage collection requires both retention expiry and a safety delay to survive delayed message fanout.

docs.title: L6 mechanisms: key lifecycle, device semantics, and failover
Identity keys, signed prekeys, and one-time prekeys
docs.text:
Each device generates its long-lived identity signing/DH key material locally and registers a public bundle containing {account_id,device_id,identity_public_key,signed_prekey_public,signature,prekey_id,one_time_prekeys[],key_version}. The server verifies proof of account/device registration and the signed-prekey signature but never receives private keys. Signed prekeys rotate on a schedule and overlap long enough for delayed initiations. One-time prekeys are atomically claimed at most once; low-watermark telemetry asks the device to replenish them. If none remain, initiation may use the signed prekey with reduced initial forward secrecy, and the client surfaces/records that protocol state rather than silently fabricating a one-time key.

An initiating device fetches the recipient device list plus one bundle per device, verifies signatures and transparency proofs, and performs the protocol's authenticated asynchronous key agreement. The initial ciphertext includes the public material and prekey IDs needed by each recipient. The directory returns monotonic device-list and key versions; rollback, unknown-device addition, identity-key replacement, or reused one-time-prekey IDs trigger safety-number change handling and security telemetry. The server can rate-limit claims but cannot choose alternate keys without detection by signed identities and key transparency.

That detection requires an authenticated identity anchor and independently checked log consistency, such as previously verified device keys, security-code comparison, or trusted-device approval. A signature under a newly substituted identity and an inclusion proof from a server-controlled log do not alone defeat a malicious server. Protocol libraries and test vectors, not this architectural sketch, must define the ratchet cryptography.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant A as Initiating device
 participant K as Key directory
 participant T as Transparency log
 participant B as Recipient device
 B->>K: Identity key, signed prekey, one-time prekeys
 K->>T: Commit device-list and key version
 A->>K: Fetch B device bundle
 K-->>A: Signed prekey plus atomically claimed OPK
 A->>T: Verify inclusion and latest consistency
 A->>A: Authenticated prekey agreement
 A->>B: Initial encrypted envelope with prekey IDs
 B->>B: Consume OPK and derive session
 B-->>K: Replenish below low watermark

docs.title: Double Ratchet and group sender keys
docs.text:
After initial agreement, each device pair runs a Double Ratchet session. A DH ratchet advances the root key when the peer's ratchet public key changes; sending and receiving chain KDFs derive a unique message key per message and erase prior chain keys. Headers carry ratchet public key, previous-chain length, and message number. A bounded skipped-key cache permits out-of-order delivery; exceeding the bound requires session repair rather than retaining unlimited keys. Retransmission resends the same ciphertext envelope and message key result for the same client message ID; it never encrypts a different plaintext under a reused key/nonce.

Pairwise encryption of every group message is O(m*d) ciphertexts. Instead, each sending device creates a group sender-key state containing a signing public key and symmetric chain seed, distributes it over existing pairwise encrypted sessions to every currently eligible member device, and then sends one group ciphertext. Every message advances the sender chain and is signed by that sending device. Sender keys are scoped to (group_id,membership_epoch,sender_device_id).

flowchart TD
 A[Membership or device-list change] --> B[Commit new membership epoch]
 B --> C[Invalidate affected sender-key distributions]
 C --> D[Each active sender device creates or rotates sender key]
 D --> E[Pairwise encrypt distribution to eligible devices]
 E --> F[Recipient records group epoch and sender device]
 F --> G[One ciphertext per group message]
 G --> H{Epoch and sender chain valid?}
 H -->|Yes| I[Verify signature, derive key, erase old key]
 H -->|No| J[Request bounded key redistribution or sync]

Removing a member increments the membership epoch before later sends are accepted. Active senders rotate and distribute new sender keys excluding removed devices; adding a member also starts a new epoch so it does not gain old sender chains. Messages accepted under epoch E use the membership snapshot for E; delayed fanout cannot substitute current membership. A server cannot force already offline senders to rotate, so it rejects their stale-epoch sends and clients refresh membership/key distribution first.

docs.title: Multi-device membership and key rotation
docs.text:
Account membership is a signed device-list state, separate from group membership. Linking device D2 requires an existing trusted device or explicit account recovery to authorize D2's identity key. Contacts fetch a versioned list and establish independent pairwise sessions to D2; servers fan out future one-to-one messages to each eligible recipient device and the sender's companion devices. History transfer is an E2EE device-to-device or encrypted-backup operation with a visible time boundary.

Adding or removing a device increments device_list_version. Removal immediately stops server envelope fanout, revokes its unclaimed prekeys, rotates account-scoped distribution state, and causes group sender-key redistribution according to policy. A group records both membership_epoch and recipient device-list versions used for a send. Rapid device churn is batched only within a short explicit window; security-critical removal is never delayed for batching. Clients retain old chain keys only for the bounded out-of-order window and erase them after advancement, so rotation protects future messages but cannot retract keys already delivered.

docs.title: Storage sizing and receipt semantics
docs.text:
At 200 billion messages/day and a 1 KB canonical encrypted envelope, raw ingress is 200 TB/day. Three in-region copies plus one asynchronous DR copy consume about 800 TB/day before compression and metadata. A 30-day canonical retention example is 24 PB; adding 25% indexes/outbox overhead reaches roughly 30 PB. Device inboxes store references, not ciphertext: with an average 2.5 recipient devices and a 32-byte reference, they add 200B * 2.5 * 32, or 16 TB/day raw. For pairwise multi-device encryption, the canonical record contains distinct recipient ciphertexts or references to them; the 1 KB average must include that multiplicity or be multiplied by its measured envelope expansion. Group fanout can dominate that estimate, so apply per-device offline TTLs, time-bucket compaction, and a separate bounded-history product policy. At 10 million peak messages/s, provision at least 10 GB/s raw append bandwidth, about 30 GB/s across three synchronous copies, before headroom.

accepted(seq) means the home quorum durably stored ciphertext and outbox, not that any recipient received it. A device-level delivered receipt means that named recipient device authenticated, durably stored, and acknowledged all messages through sequence N; read means its UI crossed the product-defined read boundary through N. Store monotonic (delivered_through,read_through) per recipient device and conversation. User-level “delivered” can mean any device or all active devices, but the API/UI must choose and name one; a practical policy shows delivered after any current device and exposes no device detail to senders. Group receipts are sparse per (message,user) near the recent read window and aggregate to counts for large groups rather than creating an unbounded sender-visible matrix. Removed devices stop affecting “all active devices” after the removal version, and delayed lower receipts never regress state.

docs.title: Regional failover boundary
docs.text:
Each conversation has {home_region,shard,epoch} in a quorum-backed directory. The home leader accepts and sequences writes only with a current lease; synchronous zonal replicas acknowledge locally and a paired region tails ciphertext, idempotency rows, membership epochs, and outbox. On regional failure, the control plane proves the old lease expired or obtains quorum fencing, promotes the paired replica, increments epoch, and publishes routing. The new leader may leave sequence gaps but never reuses a sequence. Clients resend ambiguous (sender_device,client_msg_id) requests and receive the committed result if replication included it.

Prevent reuse of sequence numbers from a lost asynchronous tail by reserving sequence ranges durably in the surviving quorum before allocation, or by defining sequence identity as (authority_epoch, local_sequence) throughout messages, receipts and cursors. Merely incrementing an ownership epoch without changing or protecting the sequence space is insufficient. Missing idempotency records after nonzero-RPO recovery also require explicit uncertain-history reconciliation rather than an unconditional once-only claim.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
 participant C as Client
 participant O as Old home epoch 17
 participant D as Quorum directory
 participant N as Paired region
 C->>O: Send M9
 O->>N: Async replicate log and idempotency
 Note over O: Region becomes unreachable
 N->>D: Request promotion
 D->>D: Prove lease expiry, fence epoch 17
 D-->>N: Grant epoch 18
 C->>N: Retry M9 with same client ID
 N->>N: Resolve M9 against recovered acknowledged prefix
 alt complete prefix proves result or absence
   N->>N: Return stored result or append once
 else missing asynchronous tail
   N-->>C: Uncertain history, pause and reconcile
 end
 opt accepted result established
   N-->>C: accepted sequence under epoch 18
 end
 O-->>D: Stale leader returns
 D-->>O: Writes rejected for stale epoch

If replica lag exceeds the declared recovery point, failover pauses acceptance or returns retryable uncertainty rather than risk two outcomes for one client ID. Non-home regions may spool client ciphertext in an unsequenced encrypted ingress queue, but only the fenced owner converts it into accepted messages. After promotion, rebuild device inbox projections from the canonical log/outbox, prioritize interactive conversations, and bound reconnect waves with jitter and per-device leases. Failback is another fenced migration, never an automatic reversal.

docs.title: Observability and testing
docs.text:
Track accept latency, durable-append errors, delivery latency percentiles, undelivered age, duplicate suppression, receipt lag, connections/gateway, reconnect storms, membership fanout cost, hot conversations, push effectiveness, queue bytes, and regional replication lag. Use opaque IDs in traces.

Property-test membership interval eligibility and monotonic receipts. Inject duplicate/reordered bus events, timeout every acknowledgement boundary, kill gateways during sync, partition sequencer replicas, rotate devices, and load-test Zipfian groups plus reconnect storms. Cryptographic implementations need protocol vectors, independent review, and downgrade tests.

docs.title: Tradeoffs and final architecture
docs.text:
Per-recipient copies simplify sync but amplify group storage; references in device inboxes keep ciphertext canonical. Global sequencing is unnecessary and would add coordination cost; conversation-local sequencing matches user expectations. Active-active conversation writes invite split-brain order, so home-region ownership plus fenced failover wins. E2EE reduces server features and moderation visibility but is a product privacy requirement.

flowchart TD
 A[Authenticated encrypted send] --> B[Home conversation leader]
 B --> C[(Replicated ordered message log + outbox)]
 C --> D[Version-aware device fanout]
 D --> E[(Durable regional device inbox)]
 E --> F[Connection gateway or push wake]
 F --> G[Client dedupe and decrypt]
 G --> H[Monotonic cumulative receipts]

docs.title: Questions and level expectations
docs.text:
1. How does leader failover avoid duplicate sequences?
  2. Which membership snapshot controls a delayed group fanout?
  3. What happens when one device remains offline for months?
  4. How does adding a device affect historical keys?
  5. How is a reconnect storm contained?

L5 candidates should define store-and-forward, local ordering, device inboxes, idempotent retry, offline sync, and group skew. L6 candidates should design fencing, membership-version semantics, reconnect overload policy, metadata privacy, key lifecycle boundaries, replay operations, and regional disaster recovery while explaining product compromises imposed by E2EE.

docs.title: Five-minute summary
docs.text: Assign each conversation to a fenced home shard that durably appends encrypted envelopes and an outbox before acknowledging. Use client message IDs for idempotency and conversation-local sequences for order. At-least-once consumers expand committed messages into per-device inbox references using membership versions; gateways stream them to connected devices or issue content-free push wakes. Reconnecting devices resume from durable cursors and acknowledge cumulative monotonic receipts. Store encrypted media directly in object storage. Partition logs by conversation, inboxes by device and time, and protect large groups with shardable fair fanout. Keep E2EE keys on devices, minimize metadata, and degrade presence or push without losing accepted messages.

docs.title: Engineering Foundations and Practice
docs.text:
This track explains what must be true underneath a convincing architecture diagram. It complements, rather than replaces, the canonical foundations. Its scope is selected mechanisms and engineering practice, not a complete operating-systems, database, security, or distributed-computing course.

Work through the calculations, reproduce the experiments, and explain each failure before checking the answer. The capstone is an evolving design exercise, not a claimed production deployment. All workload numbers are illustrative assumptions unless explicitly attributed.

docs.title: Three waves
docs.text:
Wave Read in order Produce before advancing 1: Mechanisms Machine and runtime, distributed theory, performance science, storage internals Resource budget, event history, workload experiment, crash-boundary table 2: Contracts and operations Temporal data, API lifecycle, authorization and privacy, service operations As-of query, compatibility matrix, revocation contract, incident runbook 3: Evolution and evidence Architecture decisions, brownfield migration, correctness methods Decision record, cutover proof obligations, counterexample and regression 
flowchart LR
    M[Machine budgets] --> P[Performance experiments]
    D[Failure model] --> S[Storage and authority]
    S --> C[Data and API contracts]
    C --> O[Operations]
    P --> O
    O --> E[Migration and retirement]
    E --> T[Executable evidence]
    T --> M

docs.title: Practice, not just reading
docs.text:
Use the eight executable labs to predict a broken result, inspect an independent oracle, apply the guarded path, and rerun regressions. Python 3.9+ and the standard library are sufficient; no service, container, account, or network is needed. Each fixture can be selected independently. The durable-counter fixture uses a real local SQLite file and subprocess termination; the other fixtures are deterministic state-machine simulations.

The Atlas capstone carries one product from a single process through scaling, an incident, a storage migration, and decommission. Keep earlier decisions visible: changing an assumption must cause a specific contract or design change. Do not replace every stage with a fresh unrelated diagram.

The assessment contains prompts, answer checks, and L5/L6 evidence gates. The coverage guide explains the machine-readable registry, explicit gaps, and why an entry is not a claim of mastery. Use the study routes for pacing.

For broader organizational scope, continue to Staff Architecture; for deeper testing strategy, pair correctness methods with distributed systems testing. This track supplies concrete mechanism evidence without replacing those curricula.

docs.title: Entry diagnostic
docs.text:
Without looking ahead, answer these in ten minutes:

  1. A process reports an increment then exits. What evidence distinguishes an acknowledged durable increment from a buffered write?
  2. An old worker resumes after its lease expires. Which component must reject its write?
  3. At 90% utilization, why might a 10% traffic increase be much worse than 10% more latency?
