  4. A correction arrives today but applies to last month. Which two times must a query specify?
  5. Can a binary rollback reverse a storage-authority change after the new store accepts writes?

If the answers are only technology names, start at Wave 1. If the contracts are clear but tests are missing, start at correctness methods. For interview-level application, return to the practice system after each wave.

docs.title: API Contract Lifecycle
docs.text: An API has consumers that evolve at different times. Compatibility includes meaning, ordering, retry behavior, authorization, and failure semantics, not only JSON parsing. Prerequisites: API and data modeling and HTTP semantics.

docs.title: Write the operation contract
docs.text:
For Atlas, POST /v1/jobs accepts a job, not proof that the job ran. Authentication establishes a principal; authorization binds it to a tenant and operation; validation bounds the request before expensive allocation. Define an operation resource for later resolution.

POST /v1/jobs
Idempotency-Key: tenant7-import42
Content-Type: application/json

{"dataset_id":"d9","kind":"EXPORT","schema_version":1}

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Location: /v1/operations/op42
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"op42","state":"ACCEPTED","version":1}

Principle: RFC 9110 (June 2022), section 15.3.3 defines 202 as accepted for processing, not completed processing. The specific operation resource, idempotency-key scope, and expiry below are our application contract, not requirements imposed by that RFC.

Store (principal, tenant, operation_kind, key, normalized_request_hash, result) atomically with acceptance and an outbox event. Enforce the scoped key with a unique constraint. Concurrent first submissions race inside the acceptance transaction; the loser rolls back its attempted job and resolves the winning receipt. Same key and same intent returns the original operation. Same key with different intent is a conflict. If the key expires before the permitted retry horizon, the same retry can create another operation; retention is a semantic choice.

Assumption (2026-09): Clients may retry for 24 hours. Keep receipts at least that long, plus clock/processing margin, or expose a stronger permanent operation identity. At 100 accepted jobs/s and 300 bytes/receipt, one day is 100 * 86400 * 300 = 2.592 GB before indexes and replication. This makes retention a capacity input, not a reason to quietly shorten the guarantee.

docs.title: Compatibility is directional
docs.text:
Change Old client to new server New client to old server Required gate Optional response field often safe, strict decoder may fail field absent test shipped decoders New request field old client omits it old server may reject it deploy reader support first New enum member exhaustive switches may fail old server may reject command unknown-value policy and consumer inventory Milliseconds changed to seconds parses but meaning breaks parses but meaning breaks new field/version, never silent reinterpretation Required authorization scope callers can be denied may have inconsistent enforcement policy rollout coordinated with clients New pagination ordering duplicates/skips across pages mixed-server cursor failure versioned cursor semantics

"Tolerant reader" is not permission to ignore unknown security commands or malformed data. Distinguish ignored optional response fields from strict command validation. Also distinguish absent, explicit null, and default values; a patch omitting a field need not clear it.

docs.title: Preconditions and replay
docs.text:
Use a resource version for concurrent edits, not the client's clock. A strong ETag with If-Match supports conditional updates under RFC 9110, section 13.1.1. The server still must bind the comparison and mutation atomically. Rechecking in application code before a separate write is insufficient.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API
    participant D as Canonical transaction
    participant P as Projection
    C->>A: Submit command with key K
    A->>D: Accept plus receipt plus outbox
    D-->>A: Operation O committed
    A--xC: Response lost
    C->>A: Retry K with same intent
    A->>D: Resolve stored receipt
    D-->>A: Original O
    D->>P: Event may be delivered repeatedly
    A-->>C: O, still not a completion promise

The outbox/inbox lab teaches receipt/effect atomicity under crash and duplicate delivery. It does not make a non-idempotent external email or payment effect atomic with your database. External systems require their own idempotency or reconciliation protocol.

docs.title: Lifecycle runbook
docs.text:
1. Inventory consumers by authenticated client identity and version, including batch jobs and disaster-recovery tooling. Zero recent traffic is not proof a quarterly client is gone.
  2. Add new readers/fields while preserving old meanings. Record default and null behavior in executable contract tests.
  3. Shadow normalized semantic outcomes, not byte-for-byte payloads containing timestamps. Sample safely and redact secrets.
  4. Enable new writers for a small cohort; compare error and outcome ratios by client version. Stop on a correctness mismatch, even when aggregate availability is healthy.
  5. Publish deprecation dates and owners. Measure unsupported usage, offer migration diagnostics, and retain an exception path with an expiry.
  6. Remove old behavior only after agreed observation and retry horizons. Retire keys, routes, documentation, and compatibility tests deliberately.
Failure Detection Response Regression Unknown enum crashes old SDK client-version error rate stop new enum emission oldest supported decoder Mixed deployment rejects new cursor cursor-version rejection route/pin version or rollback emission paginate across old/new nodes Receipt expires during outage duplicate operation audit reconcile and extend supported horizon retry at exact retention boundary Response leaks a hidden field schema/privacy review remove exposure and assess impact least-privileged contract snapshot

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Specify idempotency, preconditions, partial failure, pagination, and the four old/new client/server combinations. L6: Own consumer discovery, migration budget, exception expiry, and decommission evidence across teams.

Exercise: can GET /operations/op42 after a timeout safely return 404 from a lagging replica? Only if the contract distinguishes not-yet-visible from definitively absent. Otherwise route resolution to canonical state or require a visibility watermark. A client must not interpret projection lag as permission to create a second job.

For the data-authority transition behind this lifecycle, continue to brownfield migrations. Return to engineering foundations for the full route.

docs.title: Architecture Decisions Under Uncertainty
docs.text: Prerequisites: delivery framework, cost engineering, and service operations. Architecture work reduces consequential uncertainty. A decision document should explain what evidence would change the decision, not make the original choice look inevitable.

docs.title: Separate constraints from preferences
docs.text:
For Atlas, "no unauthorized export may be published" is a correctness constraint. "Small exports complete in 60 seconds" is a proposed product objective. "Use the team's familiar database" is a preference with real training and operational costs. "We need microservices" is a proposed solution. Put them in different columns before evaluating options.

Input Evidence needed What changes if false One tenant owns each job domain and authorization review cross-tenant transaction boundaries 100 submissions/s expected forecast plus measured pilot capacity and receipt storage Recovery within 30 minutes restore drill backup/standby design Team can operate one DB well on-call experience and staffing managed service or narrower scope

Use quality-attribute scenarios: source of stimulus, environment, stimulus, affected artifact, response, and measurable response criterion. "Scalable" becomes "during a twofold tenant burst, admit no more than its budget, preserve another tenant's dispatch bound, and report rejections explicitly." This can be tested.

docs.title: Worked decision record
docs.text:
ADR-003: Keep job acceptance and receipt in one relational transaction
Status: accepted for stage 1; review after measured contention threshold
Context: tenant-scoped jobs, ambiguous client retries, small operations team
Invariant: one command ID creates at most one accepted job and one outbox event
Options: relational transaction; independent DB and broker writes; new event store
Decision: transaction with unique command key and outbox row
Why: local atomicity fits the invariant and existing operational capability
Costs: relay and inbox code; receipt retention; DB write capacity; replay tooling
Rejected: independent writes leave a crash gap; event store adds unneeded ownership
Revisit: sustained measured contention exceeds headroom after index/batch tuning
Owner: job platform lead; security and data owners review authority/retention
Evidence: outbox/inbox counterexample, restore drill, workload experiment
Exit: preserve IDs, event semantics, deletion ledger, and consumer compatibility

The record does not claim outbox delivery is exactly once. It moves the atomicity boundary to a place where a local transaction can enforce it, leaving duplicates and external effects explicit. See messaging and the lab.

docs.title: Quantify the tradeoff without false precision
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): Option A costs 2 engineer-weeks plus 2 hours/month of recurring operation. Option B costs 6 engineer-weeks plus 0.5 hour/month. At 40 hours/week, B adds 160 initial hours and saves 1.5 hours/month: labor-only break-even is about 107 months. This excludes reliability impact, growth, licensing, and strategic value, so it does not prove A is better. It exposes which missing benefits would have to justify B.

A weighted score is useful for recording preferences but can hide a veto. A security-incompatible option cannot compensate with a high performance score. Apply hard constraints first, then compare viable alternatives by sensitivity. If a small change to arbitrary weights reverses the decision, collect evidence instead of presenting the ranking as objective fact.

flowchart TD
    Q[Decision question] --> I[Invariants and constraints]
    I --> V[Viable alternatives]
    V --> U[Most consequential uncertainty]
    U --> E[Small discriminating experiment]
    E --> D[Decision with owner and expiry trigger]
    D --> R[Review measured outcomes]
    R --> Q

docs.title: Reversibility is a property of state
docs.text:
Changing a stateless timeout may be quickly reversible, though it can still trigger a retry storm. Changing a persisted field's meaning, exposing an API, or accepting writes in a new store creates obligations that a binary rollback cannot erase. A decision is reversible only if the old system can interpret the new state and the reverse path preserves accepted effects.

Use a small experiment to resolve the largest uncertainty: a query plan on representative skew, a process-restart drill, or a consumer compatibility test. A large prototype that implements the preferred solution without testing an alternative often measures enthusiasm rather than reducing uncertainty.

docs.title: Adversarial design review
docs.text:
Challenge Weak answer Required evidence Why not one process? scale measured bottleneck and simpler alternatives What if traffic is 10x smaller? same architecture cost/ownership sensitivity What survives rollback? old image persisted schema, receipts, accepted effects Who owns the new dependency? platform team explicit agreement, SLO, escalation What retires after launch? later consumer horizon and removal checklist

Record uncertainty as a risk with a trigger and owner. "Might be slow" is not actionable; "if p99 pool wait exceeds 50 ms under the agreed burst, stop expansion and inspect saturation" is. Keep proposed thresholds labeled as assumptions until measurements justify them.

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Defend a choice with constraints, alternatives, and failure behavior. L6: Lead conflicting stakeholder priorities, quantify uncertainty and operating cost, and make change/retirement ownership explicit.

Exercise: a vendor promises 10x throughput but the current service is dominated by a serial policy check. Use Amdahl's bound to challenge the benefit, then design an experiment that includes the policy path. Write the evidence that would justify adopting the vendor and the condition that would stop adoption.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (2011): original lightweight decision-record proposal; our acceptance and retirement gates extend that format for this course.
  • SEI, Quality Attribute Workshops, Third Edition (2003): structured quality-attribute elicitation, not a guarantee that a weighted matrix chooses the correct architecture.

Continue with brownfield migrations and record evolving decisions in the capstone.

docs.title: Engineering Evidence Assessment
docs.text: Use these prompts blind, then compare with the answer checks. They assess selected concepts in engineering foundations, not the entire course. Run the labs and keep a decision journal through the capstone. Do not assign a correctness-critical pass because an aggregate score is high.

docs.title: A1: Machine and runtime
docs.text:
Prompt (10 minutes): A 2 GiB instance has 700 MiB baseline, 300 MiB reserve, 1.25 MiB retained/request, and 40 DB permits. Traffic doubles; CPU is low but queue age rises. Diagnose and propose admission and cancellation behavior.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: 838 is a memory-derived ceiling, not the execution target; DB wait can dominate with low CPU; bound retained work, inspect pool wait and oldest request, and release permits once on every exit. Distinguish heap from RSS and user buffers from persistent storage. L5 provides the resource model; L6 adds tenant isolation, recovery reserve, and an experiment to validate runtime assumptions.

docs.title: A2: Distributed theory
docs.text:
Prompt (15 minutes): An old worker resumes after a lease expires. The new owner has not yet written. A five-node group is also changing membership. Explain which operations can remain safe and which assumptions permit progress.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: install new authority at the protected sink before completing transfer for the stated strict handoff; atomic token/effect comparison; reject invented authority; explain three-of-five overlap and why disjoint configurations invalidate that argument. Lamport timestamp order is not proof of causality, and FLP limits guaranteed termination under its specific asynchronous crash model. L6 identifies read authority, durable voting state, and safe reconfiguration as separate obligations.

docs.title: A3: Performance science
docs.text:
Prompt (15 minutes): At 90 arrivals/s and 10 ms mean service time, predict M/M/1 mean response time. Then assess a claimed p99 improvement from a closed-loop, success-only benchmark during overload.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: 100 ms under the stated M/M/1 assumptions; not a p99 result. Record offered/admitted/completed/rejected rates, generator scheduling lag, all-outcome latency and end-of-run backlog. Little's law uses matching averages and boundaries. Amdahl's law requires a fixed-workload serial fraction. L6 challenges workload skew, uncertainty, correlated tails, and failure-evacuation capacity.

docs.title: A4: Storage and queries
docs.text:
Prompt (15 minutes): An increment commits, its response is lost, and a query slows after one tenant becomes 1,000 times larger than estimated. Give separate correctness and performance diagnoses.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: replay the original receipt, do not increment twice, and retain the original response even after later commands. Inspect the earliest estimated/actual cardinality divergence, index probe amplification, spills, and waits. A checkpoint is not an independent backup. L6 budgets restore plus replay, corruption escalation, maintenance load, and hardware assumptions beyond process-kill evidence.

docs.title: A5: Temporal data
docs.text:
Prompt (10 minutes): Price 100 applies on [1,31). A correction recorded on day 20 makes it 80 on [10,15). Answer for valid day 12 known on day 15, valid day 12 known on day 25, and valid day 15 known on day 25.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: 100, 80, 100. Preserve valid and recorded axes, half-open boundaries, stable identity and units. Corrections replace or compensate contributions instead of double-counting. L6 covers concurrent corrections, reproducible published reports, recomputation capacity, and privacy constraints on history.

docs.title: A6: API lifecycle
docs.text:
Prompt (15 minutes): Add a new job state, cursor format, and optional request field while old mobile clients and old servers remain. A retry receipt expires after one hour but clients retry for a day.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: test all client/server directions; optional syntax does not guarantee semantic compatibility; preserve enum and cursor meanings; deploy readers before writers; receipt retention contradicts the stated retry horizon. 202 is acceptance, not completion. L6 inventories infrequent consumers, manages exceptions and deprecation, and defines a reversible write window.

docs.title: A7: Authorization and privacy
docs.text:
Prompt (15 minutes): A queued export was authorized, then membership is revoked. The policy service is partitioned. A backup predates a deletion request. Define publication, download, and restore behavior.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: stale authorization cannot commit a protected post-revocation effect under the strict contract; fail closed or pause that path; already delivered bytes cannot be recalled. Scope decisions by tenant/resource/action and bind checks to effects. Restore into quarantine and reapply deletion obligations before exposure. L6 negotiates precise revocation semantics and accountable retention exceptions rather than promising universal immediate deletion.

docs.title: A8: Operations
docs.text:
Prompt (15 minutes): Admission 900/s, completion 600/s for five minutes, then completion recovers to 1,000/s. An index rebuild caused the incident. State impact, containment, drain estimate, and recovery gates.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: 90,000 extra jobs, then 900 s drain at a net 100/s. Stop the rebuild, bound new admission and retries, preserve accepted work, audit old jobs and policy-sensitive effects, and expire emergency configuration. Count overload rejection as a user outcome under the declared SLI. L6 assigns incident authority, customer priorities, operating-debt investments, and post-incident ownership.

docs.title: A9: Decisions and migration
docs.text:
Prompt (20 minutes): A 2 TiB migration copies at 100 MiB/s while 8 MiB/s of changes accumulate; catchup applies 20 MiB/s. A new schema can express a state the old binary cannot. Plan cutover and rollback.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: about 5.83 hours copy and 3.88 hours subsequent catchup under the sequential illustrative model. Reserve retention and foreground headroom. Verify a contiguous applied watermark, versions, tombstones, receipts, and policy state; fence the old writer before activation. After new writes, rollback requires reverse data and semantic compatibility. L6 states when forward repair is the only valid option and names consumer/retirement gates and owners.

docs.title: A10: Correctness evidence
docs.text:
Prompt (20 minutes): A seed sweep passes, but the oracle reads expected values from the same function that updated state. Fix the test strategy and explain what the shipped eight fixtures do not prove.

Answer checks: open after your attempt

Answer checks: independent input-derived or hand-specified oracle; known-broken mutation must fail; positive useful work must pass; deterministic fault cuts and minimized traces precede more seeds. The counter exercises actual SQLite process restart, while seven labs simulate state transitions. No general linearizability checker, real CDC, distributed policy service, power-loss test, or production scheduler benchmark is supplied. L6 proposes approved integration evidence for the highest-risk unmodeled assumptions.

docs.title: Scoring and progression
docs.text:
Score each attempted prompt from 0 to 3: 0 is absent or unsafe; 1 names the concept without a concrete contract; 2 gives a correct worked mechanism and failure test; 3 adds quantified limits, alternatives, operational ownership, and evidence limitations. This is a local evidence rubric, not a hiring standard or a validated psychometric scale.

For L5 progression, require at least 2 on the selected route's prompts, no unresolved invariant violation, and one independently explained lab regression. For L6 progression, additionally require level-3 evidence on decisions, operations, and migration, plus a capstone defense that preserves earlier accepted effects. Reattempt weak areas after a spaced interval with changed numbers or fault order.

docs.title: Adversarial final defense
docs.text:
Have a reviewer choose three pivots without warning: the policy authority is down; a delayed snapshot arrives after deletion; the old client returns after a month; a receipt is missing; the load generator is saturated; the new store accepts an old-unrepresentable state. The learner must identify the invariant, unavailable path, independent evidence, and responsible owner. A longer diagram is not evidence of a better answer.

Record outcomes in the existing learner scorecard, with these prompt IDs and fixture seeds as supporting notes. The registry maps concepts to these assessments but does not record or infer a learner's competence.

docs.title: Authorization, Revocation, and Privacy
docs.text: Prerequisite: security architecture. Authentication answers who presented a credential. Authorization answers whether that principal may perform this action on this resource under the relevant policy and context. Encryption protects a channel or stored bytes; it does not answer the authorization question.

docs.title: Model the decision boundary
docs.text:
Define a decision tuple:

(principal, tenant, resource, action, policy_version, resource_version, context)

RBAC assigns permissions through roles. ABAC evaluates attributes such as resource classification and device posture. Relationship-based models express links such as document membership and group nesting. Each still needs a trusted source of facts, cycle/size bounds for graph expansion, and a revocation policy. Do not accept a tenant identifier from a request as proof of membership.

Boundary Invariant Counterexample Object lookup tenant and object identity are checked together valid token accesses another tenant's guessed ID Cache decision scoped by principal/resource/action/policy shared result reused for a less privileged user Worker dispatch service identity does not replace user authority export worker acts as a confused deputy Effect commit policy still permits protected effect permission revoked after a preflight check Audit minimal evidence without secrets tokens and document contents copied into logs

docs.title: State the revocation promise
docs.text:
"Revocation is immediate" is ambiguous. One implementable strict contract is: once the revocation transaction completes, no protected effect that serializes after it may commit using the old policy. An effect serialized before revocation might still be delivered later. Already downloaded bytes cannot be recalled.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant W as Export worker
    participant P as Policy authority
    participant S as Protected effect store
    W->>P: Authorize under policy 4
    P->>S: Revoke and install policy 5
    W->>S: Commit export with expected policy 4
    S-->>W: Reject stale policy
    W->>P: Reauthorize or cancel

The policy-version check and protected effect must share a serializable boundary, or another protocol must establish equivalent ordering. A check over RPC followed by an unguarded write has a time-of-check/time-of-use race. A sink that only remembers the maximum version it has seen has a propagation window before it learns version 5. The permission-revocation fixture models an already-installed authoritative policy and atomic effect-time checking, not a globally distributed implementation.

For low-risk reads, a bounded-staleness policy may be acceptable. Assumption (2026-09): Decision cache TTL is 60 seconds. A revocation just after refresh permits nearly 60 seconds of stale decisions, plus any separately allowed in-flight effects. That bound assumes every refresh reads an up-to-date authority. Refreshing from a lagging replica or using stale-while-revalidate can extend stale permission beyond 60 seconds. Bind entries to a policy revision, require the authority freshness promised by the contract, and do not renew an old decision indefinitely. This is not "immediate" and must be disclosed in the product contract. Shorter TTL increases authority load: 100,000 independently active keys refreshed every 60 s imply roughly 1,667 checks/s under a uniform steady workload, before churn and misses.

docs.title: Failure policy and least privilege
docs.text:
If the policy authority is unavailable, privileged exports fail closed or pause under a documented policy. Serving a public landing page may continue. Do not globally fail open to preserve an availability graph. Partition behavior is operation-specific, just as in distributed consistency.

Use short-lived, scoped worker capabilities where appropriate: tenant, action, resource, expiry, and intended sink. Signatures prevent tampering but do not solve revocation or validate a stale policy snapshot. Separate the ability to request an export, read source data, write an artifact, and issue a download URL. A compromised scheduler should not automatically gain every tenant's storage rights.

docs.title: Privacy is a data lifecycle
docs.text:
Inventory collection purpose, fields, access, replicas, projections, exports, logs, backups, retention, and deletion ownership. Pseudonymous identifiers can remain linkable personal data; hashing is not automatically anonymization. Data minimization often reduces both blast radius and storage cost.

collect -> canonical row -> event -> cache/index -> export -> backup
                     deletion request -> obligations at every retained copy

An operational deletion ledger can record a minimal subject token, scope, request time, and completion checkpoints without retaining the deleted payload. Restore procedures must apply outstanding deletions before exposing restored data. Legal holds and statutory retention are jurisdiction- and context-specific; involve the responsible privacy/legal owner rather than inventing a universal deletion deadline.

Failure Detection Recovery Test Stale permission cache deny/allow divergence sampling invalidate and enforce sink policy revoke between check and effect Nested group explosion evaluation budget exceeded bounded deny or explicit error cyclic and high-fanout groups Deleted data restored deletion-ledger reconciliation quarantine and re-delete before serve restore pre-deletion snapshot Signed URL outlives membership expiry/invalidation audit short lifetime or gateway enforcement revoke after URL issuance Audit contains secrets secret scanning and field allowlist restrict and rotate exposed credentials synthetic token never logged

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Prevent cross-tenant access, explain stale decisions and effect-time checks, and trace deletion through projections. L6: Negotiate revocation semantics, define fail-closed exceptions, connect privacy obligations to restore and decommission, and assign accountable owners.

Exercise: a user starts an export while authorized, loses membership, then requests the completed artifact. Specify separately whether computation may finish, whether the artifact may persist, and whether download is allowed. A defensible contract can allow internal cleanup/computation but deny publication and download under the current policy.

docs.title: Sources and claim boundaries
docs.text:
• Saltzer and Schroeder (1975), The Protection of Information in Computer Systems: complete mediation, least privilege, and fail-safe defaults; our operational policies are applications of these principles.
  • Pang et al. (2019), Zanzibar: a primary system paper on relationship-based authorization and consistency. Its production properties do not transfer automatically to a homemade permission cache.
  • NIST Privacy Framework 1.0 (2020): privacy risk-management framework, not a legal-compliance certification or universal retention schedule.

Apply these boundaries in service operations and the capstone.

docs.title: Brownfield Migrations and Decommission
docs.text: Prerequisites: partitioning and sharding, API lifecycle, and architecture decisions. A migration preserves promises while implementations coexist. The most dangerous question is not "did the copy finish?" but "which system may acknowledge the next write?"

docs.title: Inventory the existing contract
docs.text:
List writers, readers, scheduled jobs, exports, admin scripts, change streams, backups, retention, and direct database consumers. Include undocumented behavior that real clients depend on. Decide explicitly which behavior remains supported and which gets a managed breaking change. A strangler facade can route operations incrementally, but routing alone does not reconcile shared state.

The canonical source is not whichever database has the most rows. It is the store authorized to accept writes for a particular key range and epoch. Keep routing metadata and storage-side authority checks connected. A stale client must not be able to write the old store after cutover.

docs.title: Expand, copy, catch up, transfer, contract
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Expand
    Expand --> Snapshot: compatible readers and versioned records
    Snapshot --> Catchup: captured source watermark
    Catchup --> Verify: contiguous changes applied
    Verify --> Fence: semantic reconciliation passes
    Fence --> FinalCatchup: old writes drained, final watermark captured
    FinalCatchup --> NewOwner: final prefix applied and verified
    NewOwner --> Retire: rollback horizon and consumer gates pass
    Catchup --> Aborted: source stays authoritative
    Verify --> Aborted: mismatch
    NewOwner --> ReverseCatchup: need to return authority
    ReverseCatchup --> Fence: reverse data verified

At snapshot start, capture a consistent relationship between snapshot contents and the change-log position. A timestamp guessed by a client is not necessarily that relationship. Apply changes after the snapshot watermark without gaps, preserving deletions and transaction ordering where needed. Copying may race with change application, so compare authoritative row revisions at the destination.

Preflight catchup is not sufficient for transfer while the source still writes. After freezing admission and resolving in-flight transactions, record the final committed source watermark F. Apply and verify the complete prefix through F, including tombstones and receipts, while old writes remain fenced; only then activate the target. If final catchup fails, retain the fenced state until an explicit recovery restores exactly one authority. Reverse transfer needs the same final-prefix step.

Counterexample: snapshot reads version 4, source commits version 5, change capture applies version 5 to target, then delayed backfill overwrites it with version 4. "Backfill succeeded" now means the target is wrong. A conditional install that refuses older versions fixes this race. Deletions need versioned tombstones so old snapshots cannot resurrect missing rows. The shard-movement fixture reproduces both.

docs.title: Cutover proof obligations
docs.text:
Gate Evidence If it fails Snapshot/log relationship exact captured watermark and retained log restart copy from valid boundary Catchup complete contiguous applied watermark, not max observed offset repair gaps before transfer Semantic equivalence per-key versions, tombstones, totals, sampled invariants quarantine divergent ranges Old owner fenced storage rejects old epoch and in-flight writes drained/resolved do not activate new owner New owner ready capacity, authorization, receipts, deletion ledger before fencing, keep source active; after fencing, pause until an explicit recovery establishes one authority Reverse path ready post-cutover writes reproducible in old-compatible form declare rollback unavailable; use forward repair

Checksums can identify differences efficiently but are not alone a semantic proof. Normalize intentional schema differences and compare domain invariants. Matching row counts can hide one missing row and one extra row. Sampling reduces cost but can miss rare corruption; disclose sample selection and residual risk.

docs.title: Capacity and convergence
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): Copy 2 TiB at 100 MiB/s: 2 * 1024 * 1024 / 100 = 20,971.52 s, about 5.83 hours. Source changes accrue at 8 MiB/s, producing about 163.84 GiB during copy. If catchup can apply 20 MiB/s while new changes remain 8 MiB/s, net drain is 12 MiB/s and catchup takes about 3.88 hours. Reserve log retention beyond copy, catchup, retries, and investigation, not merely six hours.

If apply capacity drops to 6 MiB/s, lag grows indefinitely under that arrival rate. Options include throttling writes, increasing isolated catchup capacity, changing the copy method, or choosing a controlled pause. Increasing foreground retries worsens the convergence problem. Run performance calculations before setting the migration window.

docs.title: Rollback is another migration
docs.text:
Before new-owner writes begin, abort can discard the target and leave the source authoritative. After they begin, routing back to an old snapshot loses accepted data. Reverse replication, an append-only command ledger, or an explicit reconciliation process must carry new writes and deletions back. Install a fresh authority epoch for the reverse transfer; do not resurrect an old epoch.

Some new schema states have no old representation. An export status added in v2 may be unknown to v1. Either keep writes old-compatible during the rollback window, define a tested down-conversion, or state that rollback is unavailable once those writes occur. "Roll back the image" is not an answer to irreversible state.

docs.title: Retirement runbook
docs.text:
1. Confirm no active or scheduled consumers depend on the old path across the agreed business cycle. Observe retry, replay, offline-client, and disaster-recovery horizons.
  2. Make the old path read-only or deny writes, then observe attempted use with caller identity and clear diagnostics. Do not silently forward mutations forever.
  3. Validate restored backups can run without the old dependency, or record a time-bounded restore adapter and owner.
  4. Reconcile retention and deletion obligations, revoke credentials, remove network access, and dispose of data through the approved policy.
  5. Remove flags, routes, alerts, dashboards, queues, scheduled jobs, runbooks, and billing resources. Close the decision record with evidence, not only a launch date.

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Explain snapshot/change races, guarded backfill, and write fencing. L6: Own consumer inventory, capacity, authority transfer, rollback irreversibility, retention, and removal across teams.

Exercise: a target reports offset 100 but has not applied offset 97. Is it caught up to 100? No: a maximum observed offset is not a contiguous applied watermark. Explain how a per-partition gap tracker or ordered transactional application establishes the needed prefix, and what cross-partition invariants remain outside that proof.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Sadalage and Fowler, Evolutionary Database Design (2003; maintained essay): incremental schema change and database evolution; our fencing protocol is a separate requirement.
  • Fowler, Strangler Fig Application (2004): incremental replacement pattern, not a data-consistency protocol.
  • Raft extended paper (2014), section 6: safe replicated membership transition; do not equate application shard routing with implementing Raft reconfiguration.

Use the migration practice and capstone stages 5-6 for end-to-end application.

docs.title: Atlas: One System Through Its Lifetime
docs.text:
Atlas is a fictional multi-tenant dataset export service. Teams register datasets, request bounded exports, inspect status, download authorized artifacts, correct metadata, and eventually close their workspace. This is a longitudinal advanced exercise with reference design checkpoints, not a production system or a claim that the fixtures implement the whole service.

Start each stage from the preceding design. Preserve a decision journal, schema versions, command IDs, capacity sheets, failure traces, and operational obligations. When a new requirement changes a decision, record why the previous decision was reasonable under its earlier assumptions. Use architecture decisions and the assessment rubric.

docs.title: Product framing and invariants
docs.text:
In scope: tenant-scoped job acceptance, idempotent retries, asynchronous local effects, export publication, status projection, corrections, revocation, and migration. Out of scope: actual data transformation engines, billing settlement, general workflow programming, and a multi-region write protocol.

tenant(id, policy_version, state)
dataset(tenant_id, id, schema_version, revision, classification)
job(tenant_id, id, command_id, request_hash, state, version, source_revision)
receipt(tenant_id, principal_id, command_id, request_hash, operation_id, result)
outbox(event_id, tenant_id, aggregate_id, aggregate_version, payload_version)
inbox(consumer_id, event_id)
artifact(tenant_id, job_id, object_key, source_revision, policy_version, state)
metadata_assertion(entity_id, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, revision, value)

This is a conceptual schema, not executable DDL. Worker ownership also needs an authoritative epoch record and an atomic publication check against it; the ordinary job version cannot substitute for an ownership protocol.

Unique receipt scope prevents one caller's key from colliding with another caller's unrelated request. Every tenant-scoped foreign reference must remain within the tenant. Large payloads live outside acceptance rows, but publication of their references is guarded.

ID Invariant or objective Evidence owner I1 One accepted job per scoped command ID and normalized intent API owner I2 Every accepted job has a recoverable outbox event storage owner I3 Stale worker or policy epoch cannot publish a protected artifact worker and security owners I4 Projection revisions do not regress or resurrect deleted state data owner I5 At most one store may acknowledge writes for a shard; older ownership epochs are rejected after transfer migration owner I6 Required deletions remain enforced after restore privacy and recovery owners O1 Submission and completion SLOs are separately measured service owner 
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Accepted
    Accepted --> Running: current worker epoch
    Accepted --> Cancelled: cancellation wins
    Running --> Ready: artifact prepared
    Running --> Failed: terminal failure
    Running --> Cancelled: cancellation wins before publication
    Ready --> Published: current policy authorizes effect
    Ready --> Cancelled: revoked or cancelled before publication
    Published --> Retired: retention or deletion workflow

Define cancellation as a serialized state transition, not a promise to recall already downloaded bytes. A worker may finish computation after cancellation, but its publication CAS must fail and its temporary object must be cleaned up.

docs.title: Stage 1: One process and one database
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): 10 submissions/s, one operator, 99.5% submission target, and a 30-minute restore objective. Begin with one process, one relational store, and one local worker loop. Do not add a broker or shard map before an actual need.

flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> P[One process: API and worker]
    P --> D[(Transactions, receipts, jobs, outbox)]
    P --> B[(Artifact bytes)]
    D --> R[Backup and restore drill]

Acceptance transaction: validate tenant and command, reserve its ID, create job and outbox row, commit, then respond 202 with an operation resource. Worker publication compares job version and policy version at the protected metadata boundary. Temporary object upload can occur earlier; an uploaded but unpublished object is not a downloadable artifact.

Submission interface: use the API contract. Status reads may be canonical initially. Include stable errors for conflicting intent, forbidden access, invalid size, and temporary admission rejection. A timeout remains unknown; retry the same key or query the operation.

Deliverables: ADR choosing the local transaction, four crash boundaries, a resource budget, and durable-counter evidence. Add a second command to catch a deduplicator that rejects everything. Exit gate: describe what the fixture proves about process termination and what a 30-minute restore claim still needs.

docs.title: Stage 2: Separate workers and repeated delivery
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): Exports become slow and bursty; 100 submissions/s, average 2 CPU-seconds/job. CPU demand is 200 CPU-seconds/s. If the initial instance has eight usable cores, its CPU-only ceiling is four jobs/s at 100% utilization, before overhead. At least 25 such instances would be needed just to match demand; keeping 30% of CPU capacity unused raises that lower bound to ceil(200 / (8 * 0.70)) = 36. One process on a sufficiently large host could use many cores if its work is parallelizable; the constraint is usable CPU and execution structure, not process count itself.

Separate worker execution from acceptance. The outbox relay may publish repeatedly; consumers deduplicate local effects with inbox receipts. Partition job dispatch by a stable key only if ordering is needed; do not imply ordering across all tenants. For long jobs, use resumable checkpoints and a retry budget rather than replaying unlimited computation.

flowchart LR
    A[API] --> D[(Canonical acceptance and outbox)]
    D --> R[Relay]
    R --> Q[Duplicate-prone delivery]
    Q --> W[Bounded workers]
    W --> P[Policy and worker epoch check]
    P --> M[(Published artifact metadata)]
    W --> O[(Temporary object bytes)]

Deliverables: outbox/inbox and fenced-worker traces; a command/event/version envelope; producer and consumer retention horizons; an external-object cleanup runbook. Exit gate: show how an old worker is rejected even if it resumes before the new worker's first effect.

Reference tradeoff: a broker improves decoupling and buffering but adds retention, replay, access control, and ownership. It does not remove the transactional outbox gap or make object-store publication atomic with a local DB.

docs.title: Stage 3: Scale reads and model corrections
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): Status reads reach 20,000/s. Most can tolerate two seconds of projection lag, but operation resolution after an ambiguous submission must remain authoritative. Add a status projection and versioned cache only to the tolerant path.

For a 1 KiB status response, response payload traffic is 20.48 MB/s (about 19.53 MiB/s) at 20,000/s, before protocol overhead. At a 95% hit ratio, canonical/projection misses remain 1,000/s; a full cache loss exposes the whole 20,000/s. Reserve miss capacity or shed tolerant reads rather than letting cache failure collapse acceptance.

Metadata corrections now require valid-time and knowledge-time queries. A completed export retains the source revision used when it ran. A corrected dataset description does not silently change the contents or provenance of an already published artifact.

Deliverables: versioned-cache and temporal-corrections results, a query compatibility table, a cache-loss load experiment specification, and the exact behavior when a projection cannot meet a requested watermark. Exit gate: demonstrate that a delayed fill cannot resurrect a deleted status after cache eviction.

docs.title: Stage 4: Incident and recovery
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): An index rebuild reduces completion from 1,000/s to 600/s while admission remains 900/s. The incident lasts five minutes before containment. Queue growth is 90,000 jobs. A large tenant monopolizes waiting memory, and one queued export's permission is revoked.

Use the operations runbook. Stop the rebuild, preserve evidence, bound admission, isolate tenant queues, and keep policy checks available. At restored 1,000/s completion and 900/s admission, backlog drain takes 15 minutes. If admission can be reduced to 700/s, the arithmetic lower bound is five minutes; negotiate who is rejected and how clients retry.

Deliverables: bounded-scheduling and permission-revocation traces; incident timeline; bad-event accounting; temporary configuration owner and expiry; customer communications; recovery assertions for accepted jobs and unpublished objects.

Exit gate: no revoked export becomes published merely because it was authorized when queued. Distinguish computation, publication, and download. Reject a proposed mitigation that disables authorization to improve completion rate. Do not declare recovery from a green CPU graph while old accepted jobs remain unresolved.

docs.title: Stage 5: Migrate a live shard
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): One large tenant needs storage isolation and a new schema representation. Move that tenant's shard while other tenants continue. Do not introduce a universal sharding scheme merely to move one hot tenant.

Follow brownfield migration: consumer inventory, compatible expansion, consistent snapshot/log boundary, guarded backfill, contiguous catchup, semantic verification, old-owner fencing, new authority activation, and monitored expansion. Copy receipts, policy state, tombstones, and outbox/inbox obligations as well as business rows.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Source owner
    participant M as Migration controller
    participant T as Target owner
    M->>S: Capture snapshot and log boundary
    S->>T: Copy and versioned changes
    M->>T: Preflight contiguous catchup and semantic checks
    M->>S: Freeze and resolve writes, revoke old epoch
    S-->>M: Old writes fenced, final committed watermark F
    M->>T: Apply through F including deletions and receipts
    T-->>M: Contiguous F and final reconciliation verified
    M->>T: Install fresh authority epoch
    T-->>M: Ready for authoritative writes

Deliverables: shard-movement evidence; per-range reconciliation; copy/catchup capacity sheet; a cutover checklist; a post-cutover write followed by reverse-catchup exercise. Exit gate: identify the moment a routing-only rollback stops being safe, and explain whether all new schema states remain representable in the old system.

The target's preflight watermark is not the final transfer boundary: the source may commit more work before the freeze. Do not activate the target until it has applied the final committed prefix recorded after source writes and in-flight transactions are resolved. The fixture's complete input set does not test this live log-capture obligation.

Reference alternative: a controlled write pause may be safer and cheaper than dual-write complexity when the tenant accepts the downtime. Quantify the pause, retry horizon, and owner sign-off rather than treating zero downtime as an unstated requirement.

docs.title: Stage 6: Decommission a workspace and old platform
docs.text:
Close one tenant workspace, revoke future export authority, deny new commands, drain or cancel accepted jobs according to contract, retire artifacts, and record deletion checkpoints. Retain only justified minimal audit facts under the applicable policy. Restored data must remain quarantined until deletion obligations are reapplied.

Then retire the old storage platform after the migration rollback and consumer horizons expire. Remove credentials, queues, dashboards, routes, flags, scheduled jobs, and bills. A read-only old database with permanent production credentials is not decommissioned.

Deliverables: consumer census including infrequent jobs, deletion/restore test plan, retirement checklist, final ADR outcome, and a ledger of remaining exceptions with owners and expiry. Exit gate: demonstrate a restore procedure that does not revive the deleted tenant or depend unexpectedly on the retired system.

docs.title: Final review and five-minute summary
docs.text:
Pivot L5 evidence L6 evidence One process to workers local atomicity, retries, bounded execution operating cost and new failure-domain ownership Read scaling projection contract, version guard cache-loss admission and capacity policy Incident measured queue recovery and invariant checks customer priorities, incident authority, corrective investments Migration guarded copy, catchup, fencing reverse compatibility, cross-team consumer gates Retirement cleanup and restore obligations retention exceptions, costs, and ownership closure

In five minutes, tell the causal story: local transactions were enough at first; CPU demand justified worker separation; read load justified projections; overload required explicit admission and fairness; authorization remained a commit-time constraint; migration transferred authority as well as data; retirement closed the lifecycle. Cite one failed fixture and one real-world evidence gap at every major transition.

The primary sources for these mechanisms are scoped in the linked chapters and the concept registry. Atlas numbers and decisions are original teaching assumptions, not attributed production reports.

docs.title: Executable Correctness and Fault Methods
docs.text: Prerequisites: distributed theory and storage recovery. Testing is a search for counterexamples under a model. A passing suite is evidence about those tested histories, not proof that every real deployment preserves the invariant.

docs.title: Start with a specification independent of implementation
docs.text:
A counter specification is "one effect for each unique accepted command ID, with stable replay results." It is not "the counter equals the sum of rows returned by the same buggy update code." An independent oracle can be simpler, slower, hand-enumerated, or based on separately recorded commands.

For concurrent APIs, record invocation time, completion time, arguments, identity, and outcome. A linearizability checker searches for a legal sequential history respecting nonoverlapping real-time precedence. Pending operations require care: a timeout may have committed. A checker that assumes every timed-out call aborted can report false failures or hide duplication through the wrong specification.

Principle: Herlihy and Wing (1990) define linearizability using concurrent histories and a real-time-constrained sequential explanation. Our fixtures do not implement a general linearizability checker; they test narrower state-transition invariants.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
Method What it can establish What it does not establish Hand-worked history one counterexample or legal trace all interleavings Deterministic simulation behavior for explicit modeled transitions kernel, disk, network, or runtime semantics Bounded exhaustive search all states within the encoded finite bound unbounded proof or model fidelity Seeded randomized test reproducible exploration of generated schedules uniform coverage of all failures Subprocess termination process-level restart behavior on this stack power-loss durability Real fault/load experiment measured behavior under actual injected conditions untested environments or future versions Formal proof theorem under explicit model assumptions truth of every physical assumption 
flowchart LR
    I[Invariant] --> O[Independent oracle]
    O --> B[Known broken implementation]
    B --> C[Minimal counterexample]
    C --> F[Guarded implementation]
    F --> R[Regression and boundary cases]
    R --> L[Document unmodeled limits]
    L --> I

docs.title: Faults at transitions, not arbitrary sleeps
docs.text:
Place deterministic cuts before/after a mutation, persistence, acknowledgment, authority transfer, and projection update. For a transaction with four relevant boundaries, inspect all four before increasing the random seed count. A thousand runs that never pause between effect and receipt cannot discover that crash gap.

Use event schedules and seeded randomness rather than wall-clock sleeps to reproduce a known race. Preserve the seed and the smallest failing input. Shrink a failure by removing events while retaining the violation. Do not remove the independent oracle or alter the contract until the implementation passes; that changes the question rather than fixing the bug.

docs.title: Mutation checks prevent vacuous success
docs.text:
The fixture runner expects each deliberately broken variant to violate the same oracle used for its fixed variant. If a broken implementation passes, --mode verify fails. Unexpected SQL errors, subprocess failures, and programming exceptions are not counted as successful detection of the intended bug.

Also test positive behavior. An implementation that rejects every write trivially avoids duplicates but violates useful progress. The counter applies distinct commands; the fence accepts current authority; permission checks accept authorized effects before revocation and after fresh regrant; the cache permits newer recreation; the scheduler drains admitted work.

Counterexample to a weak cache oracle: "returned versions never decrease" passes if the cache always returns nothing. Add a known newest-value query and a recreation assertion. Conversely, insisting every cache lookup returns a value after eviction would reject a safe cache miss. The oracle must reflect the stated contract, not maximum availability.

docs.title: Safety and liveness need different tests
docs.text:
An invariant can be checked at every transition. Liveness usually needs a progress assumption and bound for the finite experiment. For the scheduler, finite admitted work and a functioning dispatcher imply eventual drain in the model. That does not prove fairness with continuous arrival, variable execution time, priority inversion, or stuck tasks.

Assumption (2026-09): An integration drill permits at most 10 seconds for a child process to finish; the runner fails if it exceeds that bound. This is a test timeout to prevent a hung suite, not a service SLO or proof that storage always responds in ten seconds.

docs.title: Review matrix
docs.text: Attack the test Required correction Oracle calls the implementation's update helper derive expected state from inputs or hand outcomes Broken mode exits zero despite intended violation use nonzero standalone broken mode; verify mode explicitly catches only oracle failure Seed changes nothing enumerate schedules or vary payload/burst; disclose what varies Tests run only under assert use explicit checks that survive python -O Crash is an exception that triggers cleanup terminate child without normal transaction cleanup Every replay result is read from final state check stable original receipt as well as final total Cache watermark unbounded in production state its retention/memory limit and rebuild protocol

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Write an invariant, reproduce a counterexample, and demonstrate a fixed regression without sleeps. L6: Review oracle independence, model fidelity, test coverage gaps, and production evidence needed before accepting the guarantee.

Exercise: the counter passes after os._exit. What next supports a machine-failure durability claim? Document database mode/version, filesystem and device persistence semantics; use an approved power-loss or storage-fault environment with acknowledged-command evidence outside the failing machine; verify recovery and corruption behavior across repeated cuts. Even then, report tested conditions rather than universal proof.

Additional primary reading: Lamport, Specifying Systems (2002) for state machines, invariants, and temporal reasoning. Continue to labs, then defend the capstone using the assessment.

docs.title: Concept Coverage and Evidence Registry
docs.text: The downloadable concepts.json maps selected concepts to a canonical explanation, prerequisites, worked example, optional executable lab, assessment, authoring depth, and primary source records. Paths are relative to docs/. It is an initial scoped registry for this expansion, not a complete inventory of every concept in the masterclass.

docs.title: What an entry means
docs.text:
Field Meaning What it does not claim id stable concept identifier universal taxonomy canonical preferred explanation for this route other existing chapters are obsolete prerequisites IDs to understand first every prerequisite in computer science is included example worked artifact or trace production evidence lab runner selector, or null an executable exists when null assessment prompt with answer checks the learner has passed it depth core or advanced authoring tier certified competence or flagship completeness sources scoped primary references source endorses every local design decision limitations known evidence boundary all possible gaps have been discovered

Some concepts retain an existing foundation as canonical, notably caching and distributed transactions. The new chapters supply mechanism-level explanation, experiments, or evolution practice without reducing the depth of that material. The registry's source records state what the reference supports; many exact algorithms and all Atlas numbers are local teaching choices.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python3 scripts/validate-engineering.py
python3 docs/engineering/fixtures.py --seed 1 --seeds 20
npm run validate
mkdocs build --strict

The registry validator checks schema fields, unique IDs, local documents and anchors, prerequisite existence and acyclicity, source references, lab selectors, ASCII, and assessment/example targets. It includes negative self-tests that deliberately break those properties. It does not judge prose quality, prove correctness, or check external URL availability. The repository content and Mermaid validators cover the authored site surface.

docs.title: Deliberate gaps
docs.text:
The expansion contains eleven cohesive chapters, eight executable fixture selectors, a six-stage capstone, and evidence assessments. It does not supply a full OS, consensus implementation, query engine, real service benchmark, general linearizability checker, real CDC transport, or production authorization system. The counter uses actual SQLite process restart; the other seven fixtures simulate their stated transitions. No power-loss proof is claimed.

Specific gaps remain explicit in registry entries: no runtime memory-model stress fixture; no clock synchronization service; no multi-version SDK harness; no calendar/time-zone fixture; no executable privacy erasure proof; no production continuous-arrival scheduler fairness test. Existing Java concurrency, networks, and canonical foundations remain relevant deeper routes.

docs.title: Maintaining coverage honestly
docs.text:
Add a concept only with a real explanation, example, and assessment target. Use null for a missing lab rather than linking an unrelated passing command. Record partial coverage in limitations. When splitting a concept, keep IDs stable or explicitly migrate registry consumers. When changing a fixture's semantics, update the chapter, lab guide, oracle, and assessment together.

Use engineering foundations for the reading route, assessment for learner evidence, and the capstone for integration. A green registry check means the map is internally connected, not that the territory is complete.

docs.title: Distributed Theory, Clocks, and Authority
docs.text: Prerequisite: consistency, consensus, and CAP. That chapter defines application promises; this one derives the assumptions needed to implement them. A proof without a fault model is not yet an engineering argument.

docs.title: Name the model
docs.text:
Model dimension Possibilities Design consequence Process failure crash-stop, crash-recovery, Byzantine recovery needs durable protocol state; arbitrary faults need a different protocol Network delay, loss, duplication, reordering, partition timeout cannot establish that a peer is dead Timing synchronous, asynchronous, partially synchronous liveness depends on which timing assumptions eventually hold Storage durable atomic records, torn writes, corruption voting/log state may need validation and recovery Membership fixed or changing intersecting quorums must remain meaningful across configurations

Safety says something bad never happens: two different values are not committed at one log position. Liveness says something good eventually happens: a valid command eventually completes under stated conditions. Fair scheduling and eventual message delivery are assumptions, not consequences of repeated retries.

Principle: Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson (1985) show impossibility of guaranteed termination for deterministic consensus in a fully asynchronous model permitting even one crash failure. This does not say consensus is unusable or that every run fails. Real systems preserve safety while using additional assumptions for progress.

docs.title: Three kinds of time
docs.text:
Wall time answers calendar questions and can be corrected. Monotonic elapsed time is appropriate for a local duration, but is not a globally comparable timestamp and should not be persisted as a portable absolute deadline across reboot. Logical time describes ordering rather than seconds.

Lamport clocks increment on local events; receiving timestamp t sets the local clock above both the previous clock and t. If a causally precedes b, then L(a) < L(b). The converse is false. Independent events can have ordered numbers without a causal relationship. Adding a node ID creates a deterministic total order, not knowledge that one event caused another. See Lamport (1978), Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events.

Worked history:

A: local write x (clock 1); send notification (clock 2)
B: independent edit y (clock 1); receive notification (clock 3)
C: independent edit z (clock 9)

A.send -> B.receive is causal. B.receive < C.edit numerically does not establish causality. Vector clocks can distinguish concurrent histories when all relevant updates carry the required components, at metadata cost related to tracked participants. They still do not pick the domain-correct merge for concurrent reservations.

Assumption (2026-09): Each wall clock is within 20 ms of reference time. Two timestamps differing by 25 ms do not prove real order: their uncertainty intervals overlap. A difference greater than 40 ms permits an order conclusion under that bound. If the bound is unavailable, the conclusion is unavailable too. Clock monitoring is part of the protocol premise.

docs.title: Leases need fencing
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Worker A
    participant C as Authority
    participant B as Worker B
    participant S as Protected storage
    A->>C: Acquire epoch 7
    Note over A: Paused beyond lease duration
    B->>C: Acquire epoch 8
    C->>S: Install current epoch 8
    B->>S: Write with epoch 8
    A->>S: Late write with epoch 7
    S-->>A: Reject stale authority

A lock service cannot stop a paused process from resuming. The protected sink must compare authority at the mutation boundary. A monotonic maximum-seen token rejects old workers after a newer token reaches the sink; it does not necessarily reject an expired worker before that happens. For immediate transfer semantics, install the new epoch at the sink before declaring transfer complete. The fenced-worker lab models this stronger handoff.

The epoch check and effect must be atomic. Checking an epoch, pausing, and then writing recreates the race. Fencing is also not authorization: a malicious caller must not be able to invent a larger epoch. Epoch allocation and propagation require authenticated authority.

docs.title: Derive a consensus commitment
docs.text:
In a fixed five-member crash-fault group, majority size is three. Any two such majorities overlap in at least one member. That intersection helps only if the member preserves the protocol's durable vote/log rules. Acknowledging persistence before it exists defeats the argument after restart.

Raft, extended paper (2014), sections 5-6 specifies election restrictions, log matching, commitment, and joint configuration changes. In Raft, a leader does not infer commitment of an old-term entry merely from its replica count; committing an entry from its current term can commit the preceding prefix. This is a protocol-specific rule, not a generic property of all majority replication.

term 4: A appends X at index 10, not yet committed
term 5: another leader may have a competing suffix
unsafe shortcut: count three copies of X later and declare it committed
required reasoning: apply election and current-term commitment rules together

Reads need authority too. A disconnected old leader can serve stale state even without accepting writes. A linearizable read requires a protocol that establishes current authority and that the state machine has applied the relevant committed prefix; merely reading local memory is insufficient.

For a configuration change from {A,B,C} to {D,E,F}, independent majorities can be disjoint. Do not atomically replace a client routing file and call it safe consensus reconfiguration. Joint consensus is one solution; other algorithms have their own proof obligations. Loss of quorum means stop authority-sensitive progress, not force-promote an arbitrary replica.

docs.title: Failure and verification
docs.text:
Counterexample Safety guard Measurement Liveness boundary Paused old worker resumes sink-side epoch stale-token rejection count authority reachable for transfer Voter forgets its vote durable protocol metadata restart/replay audit functioning storage quorum Old leader reads stale state read authority protocol read index and applied index gap quorum reachable Membership replacement loses overlap protocol reconfiguration configuration epoch on requests required old/new quorums

Exercise: enumerate all three-member subsets of five nodes and show overlap. Then repeat with three old and three new nodes. This establishes a set property, not the full consensus proof. For model-checking scope and history oracles, use correctness methods.

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Distinguish ordering, elapsed time, and calendar time; explain stale-worker rejection and majority intersection. L6: State precise progress assumptions, identify read and membership protocols, and plan recovery when the timing or storage premise is violated.

Assessment: a system advertises a 30-second lease and a 10-second GC target. Is double execution impossible? No: the GC target is not a hard pause bound, network messages can be late, and execution is not the same as a protected effect. Demonstrate the old token failing at the sink, then identify any external sink that cannot enforce the token. Return to canonical coordination to apply this boundary.

docs.title: Eight Executable Fault Labs
docs.text:
These are offline-first teaching fixtures, not production libraries. Download fixtures.py, or run the repository copy from its root. Python 3.9+ and its standard library are the only requirements. SQLite support must be present in the Python installation. Temporary databases are isolated and automatically removed; no existing service or user database is modified.

python3 docs/engineering/fixtures.py
python3 docs/engineering/fixtures.py --lab durable-counter --seed 17 --seeds 1
python3 docs/engineering/fixtures.py --lab versioned-cache --seed 1 --seeds 20
python3 docs/engineering/fixtures.py --lab fenced-worker --mode broken --seeds 1
python3 docs/engineering/fixtures.py --lab fenced-worker --mode fixed --seeds 1

The standalone broken command intentionally exits 1. verify is the default: it requires an oracle failure from the broken variant for every seed, then requires the fixed variant to pass. It emits one JSON result per lab and exits zero only when all selected checks pass. Unexpected implementation errors are not accepted as proof that the intended mutation was caught. Fixed paths use explicit comparisons, not Python assertions that vanish under optimization.

docs.title: Evidence protocol
docs.text:
For every lab, first write the invariant and predict the shortest failure trace without reading the implementation. Run broken mode and capture the reported seed and counterexample. Inspect the oracle separately from the update path. Explain the guard, run fixed mode, then run verify across multiple seeds. Add a new regression and write one limitation that would matter in deployment.

Each lab is independently selectable. Randomness varies payloads, epochs, arrival counts, or delivery order; it is not a claim of exhaustive exploration. The cache fixture explicitly enumerates all six orders of three updates. The outbox fixture crosses two producer and two consumer crash boundaries. The counter tests four process termination boundaries.

docs.title: Durable counter
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: storage recovery. Fixture: durable-counter. Model: actual file-backed SQLite, independent child processes, abrupt os._exit, explicit journal_mode=DELETE, and synchronous=FULL in the worker. The runtime's actual SQLite version and filesystem still matter.

Invariant: acknowledged effects survive process restart; unique command IDs apply once; repeated IDs return the original result; conflicting reuse is rejected. The parent oracle chooses the delta and expected state by crash boundary, records the child response, then reopens the DB. It does not derive the expected total from the tested receipts.

Seed 17 selects an illustrative increment. The broken child mutates within a transaction, prints success, and exits before commit. The parent observes a success response but a recovered zero. Fix: commit the mutation and receipt before acknowledgment. A lost response after commit remains ambiguous to the caller but is resolved by retrying the same ID.

Regressions include termination before work, after update, after commit, and after acknowledgment; two retries; different intent under one ID; a second independent ID; and replay of the first ID after the second increments the counter. The second ID returns the new total while replay of the first must keep its old response.

Limitations: This is not power-loss testing, disk-corruption injection, concurrent-writer stress, or a new WAL implementation. SQLite's transaction protocol supplies the durability mechanism. The kernel and device remain alive during a process exit. A successful fixture is not actual machine-failure durability proof.

docs.title: Fenced worker
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: leases need fencing. Fixture: fenced-worker. Model: serialized authority installation and atomic sink mutations.

Invariant: only the currently installed epoch may mutate protected state. The independent expected acceptance list contains the initial owner and the new owner, not stale or invented future epochs. Broken mode trusts the worker's earlier authorization; a paused worker overwrites newer work.

Fix: compare the presented epoch with installed authority atomically with the effect. Regressions issue stale writes both before and after the new worker's first write and reject an arbitrary larger token. Current-epoch writes must still succeed.

Limitations: No real lease clock, consensus allocator, network authentication, or multi-sink atomicity. Exact installed-epoch equality is stronger than a maximum-seen-token design; do not confuse the two. An external sink without fencing remains an unresolved side-effect boundary.

docs.title: Outbox and inbox
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: API replay and distributed transactions. Fixture: outbox-inbox. Model: explicit atomic transaction versus split-write transitions; simulated persistent dictionaries survive logical process crashes.

Invariant: every accepted source command has an event, and each event causes one local effect with one receipt. The oracle is the original command list and its multiset, independent of outbox and inbox contents. Broken producer commits business state before creating an event; retry sees the business row and never emits it. Broken consumer commits an effect before its receipt; redelivery repeats it.

Fix both boundaries: business plus outbox in one transaction, inbox receipt plus local effect in another. Delivery remains duplicate-prone. Regressions cross producer and consumer cut points, shuffle triple deliveries, verify all source IDs, and require exactly one effect per ID rather than only the correct aggregate sum. Broken-mode checks require both the producer-only gap and the consumer-only gap to be detected, so the first cannot mask the second.

Limitations: Atomic commit is assumed in this model; only the counter exercises a real database transaction. This does not prove broker retention, relay liveness, consumer concurrency, or external exactly-once effects. A full broker outage needs explicit retry, retention, and reconciliation tests.

docs.title: Versioned cache
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: caching and migration version guards. Fixture: versioned-cache. Model: per-key authoritative revisions, retained version knowledge, and cache eviction.

Invariant: late fills cannot replace newer state or resurrect a deletion. The independent oracle requires revision 3 after all three authoritative updates, absence after deletion/eviction, and the new payload after revision 4 recreates the object. Broken mode uses arrival order.

Fix: install only a newer revision and retain the deletion/version watermark when evicting cached payloads. Regressions enumerate all six delivery permutations, evict the payload, deliver an old fill, recreate with a newer revision, and replay the same version without mutating its payload.

Limitations: Revision allocation is assumed authoritative, and conflicting payloads with the same revision are ignored rather than diagnosed. Retained watermarks consume memory; deleting them needs a safe replay/expiry boundary or a canonical revalidation path. No TTL timing or cache stampede is simulated.

docs.title: Shard movement
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: brownfield migration. Fixture: shard-movement. Model: snapshot, shuffled change records, versioned tombstones, epoch transfer, and reverse catchup.

Invariant: the target at cutover equals the source command ledger, and the old route cannot acknowledge writes after transfer. The oracle is a hand-derived key/value map, not a count or checksum of copied rows. Broken backfill overwrites a newer change or resurrects a deleted row.

Fix: compare revisions when merging snapshot and change records; preserve tombstones; fence old-owner writes. Regressions include reordered changes, a duplicate record, stale routing, a post-cutover write, and reverse copying that preserves the new write and deletion.

Limitations: There is no real CDC connector, distributed routing propagation, or contiguous-watermark tracker. The input change set is complete by construction. Learners must separately test missing offsets and snapshot/log consistency before claiming a safe migration implementation.

docs.title: Temporal corrections
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: temporal data. Fixture: temporal-corrections. Model: immutable valid-time assertions with knowledge cutoffs and explicit precedence.

Invariant: answering a past-valid-time query respects both validity and what was known then. The oracle is a hand-written set of point answers. Broken mode chooses the latest known assertion even when it does not apply to the requested valid time.

Fix: filter by half-open valid interval and knowledge cutoff before selecting precedence. Regressions cover before/inside/after the correction, exact boundaries, a query before any knowledge, shuffled insertion order, and duplicate assertions.

Limitations: One entity, integer-day timestamps, no calendar/time-zone conversion, no competing-authority corrections, and no real incremental aggregate. A versioned correction policy is still needed for concurrent domain updates.

docs.title: Permission revocation
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: revocation contract. Fixture: permission-revocation. Model: policy installed at the effect sink and atomic effect-time comparison.

Invariant: an old decision cannot authorize an effect after revocation or across tenant boundaries. The independent acceptance list includes only the pre-revocation effect and a fresh capability after regrant. Broken mode trusts a cached allow decision.

Fix: scope policy by tenant/principal and compare current version and permission at the effect boundary. Regressions include unknown principal, cross-tenant replay, revoke then regrant, rejection of an old capability after regrant, and successful current authorization.

Limitations: No cryptographic credentials, distributed policy propagation, object/action hierarchy, or data already downloaded by a user. The simulation checks only its scoped effect contract; it cannot prove globally instantaneous revocation.

docs.title: Bounded scheduling
docs.text:
Canonical explanation: runtime ownership and operations. Fixture: bounded-scheduling. Model: finite tenant burst, bounded waiting queues, cancellation, round-robin dispatch, and drain.

Invariant: global queued work is at most four, each tenant queues at most two, every admitted ID completes or cancels once, and rejected work never executes. The oracle checks bounds and conservation from the original arrivals, not the scheduler's own success counter. Broken mode admits the full burst without bounds.

Fix: reject before enqueue when either budget is exhausted; dispatch across tenant queues. Regressions vary burst size, ensure the small tenant runs within two dispatches, cancel queued work twice, reuse the released slot, verify ID conservation, and drain all remaining work.

Limitations: Queue bounds exclude active workers because dispatch completes immediately in this model. There are no variable job durations, deadlines, byte budgets, continuous arrivals, or preemption. Finite round-robin dispatch evidence is not a proof of production fairness. Extend to explicit active permits and deadline/cancellation races before adapting the idea to a real executor.

docs.title: Assessment handoff
docs.text: For L5, submit the failing trace, guard, independent oracle, and one added boundary regression. For L6, additionally identify an unmodeled physical or organizational assumption and design a safe integration drill to test it. Use the assessment gates and capstone; passing the default command alone is not completion of the learning exercise.
