docs.title: Machine and Runtime Foundations
docs.text: An RPC handler is also a program sharing processors, memory, file descriptors, and storage queues. Adding replicas cannot repair an unbounded per-request allocation or a broken publication protocol. Prerequisites: estimation and the network request journey.

docs.title: Resource ownership before capacity
docs.text:
A process has an address space; its threads share that space but each has execution state and a stack. Virtual memory separates addresses from physical placement. Allocating an address range does not imply all pages are resident. A page fault can mean allocating a zero page, mapping an existing page, or waiting for storage; treating all faults as disk I/O is incorrect.

CPU caches reduce access cost through locality, but coherence is not an application synchronization protocol. Two threads can both read counter 7 and both write 8 even if every load sees a coherent value. Atomic read-modify-write or exclusive ownership is required. A language memory model also constrains which writes become visible after synchronization; hardware intuition cannot replace it.

Principle: Identify the owner and lifetime of every scarce resource. A task is not finished for capacity accounting until its buffers, permits, sockets, and cancellation callbacks are released.

Resource Owner Release condition Failure symptom Request buffer admitted request body consumed or rejected retained heap grows with queued work DB permit executing transaction commit/rollback and connection return low CPU but high pool wait File descriptor open handle all references closed unrelated opens fail CPU budget tenant scheduler work yields or terminates one tenant delays all others Native memory runtime/library explicit close or allocator reclamation RSS rises with stable heap 
flowchart LR
    A[Arrival] --> Q{Admission budget}
    Q -->|accept| B[Bounded buffer]
    Q -->|reject| R[Retryable rejection]
    B --> C[CPU and allocation]
    C --> I[I/O wait]
    I --> F[Finish or cancel]
    F --> P[Release permits and references]

docs.title: Worked resource budget
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): One instance has a 2 GiB resident-memory budget, a 700 MiB baseline, and needs 300 MiB reserve for bursts and native allocations. Each admitted request retains 256 KiB plus a 1 MiB decoded object graph. The request-memory ceiling is:

available = 2048 - 700 - 300 = 1048 MiB
per request = 0.25 + 1 = 1.25 MiB
memory ceiling = floor(1048 / 1.25) = 838 requests

This is a ceiling, not the chosen concurrency. If every admitted request immediately needs the DB and the pool permits only 40 simultaneous transactions, admitting 838 requests mostly creates waiting and stale deadlines. When requests spend substantial time in other phases, choose separate bounded request and DB limits from phase residence times; the pool size is not automatically the correct whole-request concurrency. If decoded size doubles, the ceiling falls to floor(1048 / 2.25) = 465. Bound compressed input, decoded input, fanout, and queue occupancy separately; compressed size alone does not bound memory.

Assumption (2026-09): CPU demand is 2 ms/request at 2,000 requests/s. Demand is 4 CPU-seconds/second. Eight usable cores imply 50% average utilization only if scheduling, serialization, and memory stalls do not reduce usable capacity. Container CPU quota, competing workloads, and a one-thread hot path can invalidate that estimate.

docs.title: Scheduling is not parallelism
docs.text:
An event loop multiplexes waits but one blocking callback can stall unrelated work. A thread pool contains blocking but can deadlock when every worker waits for child work queued into the same pool. Lightweight tasks reduce task-management cost; they do not manufacture database connections or make a sequential critical section parallel.

Counterexample: eight workers each submit a child task to an eight-worker pool and wait. All eight children are queued; no parent releases a worker. Queue growth is not necessary for deadlock. Fix ownership by executing the child inline when appropriate, composing asynchronous completion, or using a separately bounded execution boundary. A larger pool merely shifts the failure threshold if nesting remains unbounded.

Allocation rate and live-set size are different. A high allocation rate can cause frequent collection even with a small retained set. A large live set can make reclamation expensive even at modest allocation rates. GC pauses can expire leases and deadlines, so connect runtime behavior to fencing, not just latency graphs.

docs.title: Visibility is not persistence
docs.text:
application object -> library buffer -> kernel page cache -> device -> recovery-visible state

Each arrow has different completion semantics. A process exit leaves the kernel running; a machine failure does not. Flushing a language buffer is not necessarily an OS persistence request. An atomic rename may protect readers from a partial replacement but is not, by itself, proof that the directory entry survives power loss.

Vendor (accessed 2026-09-07): SQLite's atomic commit documentation, sections 2 and 3 explicitly describes buffering, reordering, flushing assumptions, and rollback-journal commit. It does not describe its WAL-mode commit algorithm. Use the storage chapter and durable-counter lab to distinguish these layers.

docs.title: Measurement and failure exercise
docs.text:
Collect offered/admitted/completed rate, queue wait, execution time, CPU time, resident memory, allocation rate, major faults where available, and pool wait on the same interval. CPU utilization alone cannot distinguish useful work from spinning. RSS alone cannot distinguish a leak from a cache that deliberately retains reusable pages.

Inject Predict Observe Recovery check Tenfold body expansion allocation rejection decoded-size failures, stable RSS bound next small request succeeds Worker pauses after DB acquisition pool starvation active permits and wait age cancellation releases permit once CPU quota halved queue age rises CPU throttling and completion rate shedding stops backlog growth Close callback runs twice double release risk permit count exceeds configured maximum idempotent cleanup

Reproduce the admission invariant with bounded scheduling. Then sketch a real load experiment with one-variable changes. Do not infer runtime overhead or GC behavior from the simulation.

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Explain why a 40-connection pool should constrain admitted work, trace cancellation ownership, and distinguish heap, RSS, and buffered I/O. L6: Set per-tenant budgets, reserve capacity for recovery, and decide which measurements justify changing the execution model rather than scaling replicas.

Exercise: reserve 200 MiB more for an index build and double decoded object size. Recalculate the memory ceiling and identify whether memory or DB concurrency is binding. Answer: floor(848 / 2.25) = 376; DB concurrency still limits executing transactions to 40. The remaining space is not permission to queue 336 expired requests.

docs.title: Sources and next steps
docs.text:
• Java Language Specification 21, chapter 17: language-specific synchronization and happens-before; not a universal CPU memory model.
  • Linux kernel cgroup v2 documentation: reference for resource-controller measurements; verify host/kernel support before using counters.
  • Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: authors' chapters on address spaces, scheduling, concurrency, and persistence; deeper reading, not a latency benchmark.

Continue to performance science, or return to engineering foundations.

docs.title: Performance Science and Queueing
docs.text: Prerequisites: estimation and machine budgets. A capacity estimate predicts a constraint. An experiment tries to falsify the prediction. A plausible number without workload and measurement boundaries is neither a benchmark nor a capacity guarantee.

docs.title: Define the measured system
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    O[Offered arrivals] --> A[Admission]
    A --> Q[Queue]
    A --> R[Rejections]
    Q --> S[Service]
    S --> C[Completions]
    S --> T[Timeouts and failures]

Count offered, admitted, started, completed, rejected, and timed-out requests separately. Include queue wait in user latency. A service that returns only its fastest 10% of requests can report an excellent success-only p99 while being nearly useless. Report latency distributions alongside outcome ratios and in-flight work at the end of the run.

docs.title: Little's law is a boundary equation
docs.text:
For a stable system with compatible long-run averages, L = lambda * W: average work in the boundary equals arrival/completion rate through that boundary times mean residence time. It is not a percentile formula and does not require exponential service times. Use admitted rate if the boundary starts after rejection.

Assumption (2026-09): 800 admitted requests/s and 50 ms mean residence time imply L = 800 * 0.050 = 40 average in-flight requests. This does not imply a safe maximum concurrency of 40. Burstiness, tail service times, and admission policy determine the upper distribution. If in-flight requests rise indefinitely, a steady-state application of the law is inappropriate.

docs.title: Why utilization bends latency
docs.text:
For an ideal M/M/1 queue with Poisson arrivals, independent exponential service times, one server, and lambda < mu:

rho = lambda / mu
mean response time W = 1 / (mu - lambda)
mean queue wait Wq = rho / (mu - lambda)

Assumption (2026-09): Mean service time is 10 ms, so mu = 100/s. At lambda = 50/s, W = 20 ms; at 90/s, W = 100 ms; at 99/s, W = 1 s. At or above 100/s, this infinite-buffer model has no finite steady-state mean. Finite queues instead reject work.

For a GI/G/1 queue, Kingman's heavy-traffic approximation highlights variability:

Wq approximately ((Ca^2 + Cs^2) / 2) * (rho / (1 - rho)) * E[S]

Ca and Cs are coefficients of variation of inter-arrival and service time. This is an approximation under queueing assumptions, not a p99 predictor. At rho = 0.8, E[S] = 10 ms, and Ca = Cs = 1, estimated queue wait is 40 ms. If Cs = 3, it becomes 200 ms. Same mean service demand, much worse waiting. Sources: Little (1961) and Kingman (1961); formulas here are illustrative applications, not measured service results.

docs.title: Parallelism has a serial floor
docs.text:
Amdahl's fixed-workload model gives speedup(N) = 1 / (s + (1-s)/N). With 20% serial work and eight workers, speedup is 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/8) = 3.33, not eight. The infinite-worker ceiling is five. This omits extra coordination and contention, which can make scaling worse. If only the parallel 80% becomes ten times faster, total speedup is 1/(0.2+0.8/10) = 3.57, even without overhead. Use the fraction of elapsed work affected by a proposed optimization, not the vendor's component speedup as the whole-service gain. Amdahl (1967) motivates reasoning about the nonparallel portion; it is not a universal cloud sizing formula.

Fanout also amplifies tails. If 20 independent branches each meet a latency threshold with probability 0.99, all meet it with probability 0.99^20 = 0.818. Independence is an assumption; shared pauses create correlation. Do not add or average branch p99s to obtain the end-to-end p99.

docs.title: A benchmark contract
docs.text:
Before measuring, fill this artifact:

Field Example experimental choice Question Does bounded admission preserve small-tenant latency during a large-tenant burst? Workload Open-loop arrivals, explicit skew, payload-size distribution, 10% writes State Dataset size, hot/cold cache condition, initial backlog Environment CPU quota, RAM, runtime/database version, storage type Interventions Change only admission bound; keep dataset and offered trace fixed Outcomes Goodput, rejection fraction, all-outcome latency, queue age, CPU, memory Repetition Multiple runs and seeds, warmup disclosed, uncertainty and raw counts retained Stop condition Memory ceiling, queue age beyond deadline, or generator overload

An open-loop generator schedules arrivals independently of completions; it must record scheduling lag if it cannot maintain offered load. A closed-loop client waits for responses, so stalls lower its offered rate. Closed-loop tests are useful for a fixed-user population but can hide overload through coordinated omission when interpreted as a fixed-arrival experiment. The wrk2 author's explanation describes this measurement problem and its rate-controlled approach; adopting a tool does not validate its setup.

Do not average p99 values across hosts. Merge compatible histograms or raw samples with request weights, then compute the percentile. Record histogram resolution. For very high percentiles, report the sample count and observation period: ten thousand requests provide only about ten observations beyond p99.9, and autocorrelation makes naive independent-sample confidence claims suspect.

docs.title: Reproducible experiment and failures
docs.text:
Run the bounded-scheduling fixture. Predict the exact queue-capacity violation before inspecting output. Its dispatch steps are not milliseconds and its counts are not a benchmark. Use its invariants as load-test assertions for a real scheduler.

Failure in experiment Misleading result Correction Generator CPU saturates target appears to plateau safely record scheduled versus sent arrivals Timeouts omitted latency improves during outage include outcome counts and censoring Warm cache compared to cold false optimization gain control and disclose cache state Autoscaling changes mid-run incomparable resource budgets freeze or explicitly study the controller Retry traffic uncounted goodput confused with attempt rate label original commands and attempts

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Calculate mean concurrency and saturation sensitivity, define a reproducible benchmark, and separate throughput from goodput. L6: Challenge workload representativeness, include tenant fairness and failure evacuation, and gate rollout on user outcomes rather than a microbenchmark win.

Exercise: a backlog of 36,000 jobs sees 900 new jobs/s and 1,000 completions/s. Drain time is 36,000 / (1,000-900) = 360 s, not 36 s. If completions fall to 850/s, it never drains under sustained arrivals. Propose an admission or capacity policy and account for retries. Continue with service operations.

docs.title: Service Operations as a Design Discipline
docs.text: Prerequisites: reliability engineering and performance science. A service is operable when an on-call engineer can detect user harm, contain it, recover trustworthy state, and return authority to normal operation without guessing.

docs.title: A service ownership contract
docs.text:
Record a primary and backup owner for code, data, capacity, policy, dependencies, and retirement. Include escalation contacts and access paths that work during the primary identity or network outage. A runbook requiring the failed service to authenticate its own operator is circular.

Separate the data plane, which serves established operations, from the control plane, which changes routing, policy, membership, and limits. A control-plane outage need not stop all data-plane work if cached configuration remains valid. But expiry or a security-sensitive policy may require stopping selected operations. Define validity, not just last-known-good behavior.

docs.title: User outcomes and budgets
docs.text:
Principle: The Google SRE Workbook, Implementing SLOs (2018) recommends specifying good events over total events and establishing an agreed error-budget policy. The targets below are teaching assumptions, not Google's targets or measured Atlas performance.

Assumption (2026-09): Atlas targets 99.9% successful valid submissions over 28 days and 99% of accepted small exports completed within 60 s. Rejections caused by our overload count as bad submissions; invalid or unauthorized commands are tracked separately. Accepted jobs that disappear are not excluded because there is no completion event.

SLI Numerator / denominator Window Owner action Submission success successful valid submissions / valid attempts 28 days; short windows for alerts on-call gates rollout and sheds optional work Completion timeliness accepted small jobs completed by 60 s / accepted small jobs old enough to judge 28 days worker owner inspects queue age and capacity Projection freshness eligible reads with lag within contract / eligible reads 1 hour data owner pauses stale-sensitive features Revocation safety protected effects violating policy / checked protected effects continuous audit security incident, stop affected effects

At 10 million valid submissions, a 99.9% objective allows 10,000 bad events. A 1% error ratio burns budget at 0.01/0.001 = 10 times the sustainable rate. If traffic were uniform, sustaining that ratio consumes a 28-day budget in 2.8 days. Traffic is not generally uniform; event counts remain the authoritative accounting.

A zero-tolerance correctness invariant is not traded against an availability budget. One unauthorized artifact is a security issue even if the availability SLO is green. Monitor both outcome budgets and invariant sentinels.

docs.title: Change and configuration safety
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Prepared
    Prepared --> Canary: compatibility and recovery checks
    Canary --> Expanded: cohort evidence passes
    Canary --> Halted: invariant or SLO regression
    Expanded --> Stable: full observation window
    Expanded --> Halted: regression
    Halted --> Prepared: corrected artifact and reviewed recovery
    Stable --> [*]

A canary must receive representative traffic and have comparable control data. A quiet tenant does not validate a hot-tenant code path. Keep code, schema, feature flags, and policy versions in incident evidence. Configuration can be as dangerous as code: validate ranges and relationships, version changes, bound rollout, and preserve emergency overrides with owners and expiry.

Readiness means the instance can safely accept its advertised work. Liveness means it should be restarted if unhealthy under a specific policy. Making liveness depend on a failing shared database can restart the whole fleet and amplify the incident. During drain, stop admission, deregister, allow bounded completion, then cancel or persist resumable work before termination.

docs.title: Incident runbook with gates
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): A new index rebuild causes I/O contention. Offered jobs remain 900/s, completion falls from 1,000/s to 600/s, and the queue grows by 300/s. After five minutes, 90,000 jobs have accumulated, excluding the original queue.

  1. Declare impact using accepted-job age and failed-submission counts. Assign incident lead, technical operator, and communications owner; record timestamps and configuration versions.
  2. Stop the rebuild and freeze unrelated rollout. Preserve logs/metrics needed for diagnosis without dumping personal payloads.
  3. Enforce admission and tenant fairness. Do not increase retries while the bottleneck is saturated. Retain accepted work durably or report explicit failure under its contract.
  4. Measure restored completion and admitted rates. At 1,000/s completion and 900/s arrival, 90,000 backlog takes 900 s to drain. Reserve resources for reconciliation and policy checks.
  5. Verify receipts, projection offsets, and protected effects against independent samples before declaring recovery. Healthy CPU alone is not recovery.
  6. Remove temporary limits gradually, observe queue-age decay, and expire emergency settings. Publish customer-impact accounting and owner-assigned corrective actions.
Failure Detection Containment Exit criterion Queue overload oldest eligible job age, admission ratio shed new optional work backlog drains with margin Policy outage authorization error and deny-path probes pause privileged effects authoritative checks healthy Bad routing config version/cohort mismatch stop config rollout single valid authority per shard Restore needed missing/corrupt canonical records isolate affected partition validated snapshot plus logs plus deletion ledger Dependency brownout pool wait and timeout ratio bounded attempts, circuit policy successful probes and sustainable goodput

docs.title: Drills and operational debt
docs.text:
Run bounded scheduling and permission revocation together as separate drills. Then challenge the assumption that shedding a tenant is acceptable while a legal export deadline is pending. Scheduling policy needs business priorities as well as fairness.

Track toil as recurring manual work with frequency, duration, and risk. Assumption (2026-09): A 20-minute manual repair occurring 15 times/month costs five engineer-hours/month, before interruptions and error risk. Automation is valuable only if its invariant checks, audit trail, and rollback are safer than the manual path. Remove obsolete alerts and runbooks when their system is retired.

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Define measurable SLIs, trace overload recovery, and write a safe drain/rollback sequence. L6: Set incident authority, negotiate budget policy, identify correlated failure domains, and budget operational work and retirement ownership across teams.

Exercise: a deployment reduces mean latency but doubles policy-check failures for one small tenant. Should it expand? No: inspect cohort outcomes and correctness boundaries rather than letting aggregate traffic hide the regression. Record the decision in architecture decisions, then test the capstone incident.

docs.title: Storage Recovery and Query Execution
docs.text: Prerequisites: relational databases, indexing, and machine persistence layers. An index is an access path; a recovery protocol explains which state that path is allowed to expose after failure.

docs.title: Commit is a recoverability claim
docs.text:
For a redo-log design, data-page writes must not reach durable storage ahead of the log needed to recover them. A transaction's acknowledgment policy determines which durable boundary is promised. Buffering log bytes and returning success early silently changes that promise.

Vendor (PostgreSQL 17, accessed 2026-09-08): Write-ahead logging, section 28.3 specifies log-before-data persistence and explains group commit: one log synchronization may make several concurrent transactions durable. This amortizes sync cost; it does not permit acknowledging a durable commit before its required log records are persisted.

flowchart LR
    T[Transaction changes] --> L[Append log records]
    L --> F[Required log persistence]
    F --> A[Acknowledge commit]
    F --> P[Flush data pages later]
    P --> C[Checkpoint progress]

This is a conceptual redo path, not SQLite's rollback-journal algorithm. Undo/redo systems may persist uncommitted page changes and need undo information. Recovery must distinguish committed transactions from incomplete ones and tolerate recovery being interrupted again. ARIES uses analysis, redo that repeats history, and undo with compensation log records; see Mohan et al. (1992). Not every database implements ARIES.

Vendor (accessed 2026-09-07): SQLite atomic commit, sections 3-4, explains saving original pages in a rollback journal and recovering a hot journal. Its hardware and filesystem assumptions are explicit. The counter fixture uses a SQLite transaction rather than inventing a production WAL.

docs.title: A crash-boundary table
docs.text:
Invariant: every acknowledged increment survives a process restart, and retrying a command ID never increments twice. A commit with a lost response may survive too; unacknowledged does not mean aborted.

Termination point Permitted recovery Retry behavior Before transaction starts no effect apply command After update, before commit no effect for this transaction apply command After commit, before response effect may already exist return stored result After response acknowledged effect exists return same result

For the before-commit row, termination is known to occur before the commit call begins. Termination during the commit call has an unknown outcome until recovery resolves the receipt.

The command receipt and counter mutation must share one transaction. Storing the receipt first can lose an effect; storing it later can duplicate one. An independent oracle records intended unique command IDs and accepted responses outside the tested database. Reading the database twice is not an independent correctness check.

docs.title: Checkpoints are not backups
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09): Recovery starts from a 200 GiB snapshot and has 30 GiB of required log. At an effective snapshot restore rate of 400 MiB/s, copying takes 200 * 1024 / 400 = 512 s. Replay at 50 MiB/s takes another 30 * 1024 / 50 = 614.4 s. Sequential lower-bound recovery is 1,126.4 s, about 18.8 minutes, before provisioning, validation, and routing.

Parallel work may reduce elapsed time; storage contention may increase it. A checkpoint limits some recovery work but does not necessarily create an independent failure-domain copy. Replicating an accidental delete rapidly is not protection from that delete. Restore drills must verify data versions, application invariants, permissions, and deletion obligations before serving traffic.

Torn writes need detection or reconstruction. A checksum detects some corruption; it does not recover missing bytes or prove that a logically valid record belongs at this position. Include length, sequence, identity, and checksum where a log format requires them. Distinguish a truncated uncommitted tail from corruption in a previously acknowledged prefix; silently skipping both can lose data.

docs.title: From SQL to physical work
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    SQL[Query and parameters] --> L[Logical operators]
    L --> O[Estimate cardinality and choose plan]
    O --> S[Scan or index access]
    S --> J[Join and filter]
    J --> G[Sort or aggregate]
    G --> R[Rows returned]

Consider orders JOIN customers filtered by tenant and recent time. A nested-loop join is attractive if the outer side is small and the inner side has an index. A hash join pays to build a hash table, then probes it; insufficient memory may spill partitions. A merge join can exploit ordering but may require expensive sorts. The best choice depends on cardinality and distribution, not a universal ranking.

Assumption (2026-09): The optimizer predicts 100 outer rows but a hot tenant produces 100,000. With one inner probe per row, work becomes 1,000 times the estimate before cache effects. If a probe costs an illustrative 0.2 ms and runs sequentially, probe time is 20 s rather than 20 ms. Real probes may overlap; measure rather than adopting this as a benchmark.

Statistics can miss correlation: country and currency are not independent, nor are tenant and event type. Parameter distributions can differ enough that one cached plan is unsuitable for both small and large tenants. Inspect estimated versus actual rows at the earliest divergent operator, buffer activity, spill bytes, and lock wait. Total query time alone does not locate the error.

Vendor (PostgreSQL 17 documentation, accessed 2026-09-07): Using EXPLAIN distinguishes estimates from actual execution statistics. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement; do not use it casually on production writes. Product-specific plan costs are not milliseconds.

docs.title: Storage structures under maintenance load
docs.text:
B-trees pay page-update and split costs; log-structured merge designs trade sequential ingestion for compaction and read amplification. Neither eliminates maintenance. Tombstones cannot be dropped safely while an older replica or snapshot can reintroduce the deleted value. Long-lived snapshots can retain versions and increase storage pressure. A read-heavy benchmark with no compaction or vacuum debt is incomplete for a write-heavy deployment.

Trigger Signal Safe response Recovery assertion Log disk fills free bytes and append failures reject before acknowledging previous receipts still resolve Replay hits corrupt prefix validation error at known sequence stop and restore/repair from trusted copy no silent skipped commit Hash join spills temporary bytes and latency reduce batch or correct plan same result multiset Snapshot pins old versions oldest snapshot age, retained bytes expire controlled readers retention bounds restored

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Name the durable boundary, explain ambiguous commit outcomes, and diagnose a cardinality error. L6: Budget restoration and maintenance alongside foreground traffic, define corruption escalation, and refuse a durability claim based only on process-kill tests.

Exercise: construct a fixture where a transaction commits but its response disappears. The correct counter is one after two submissions of the same command, and both successful responses identify the same original result. Then test two different IDs and require two effects: a deduplicator that suppresses everything is not correct. Continue to correctness methods and non-relational storage.

docs.title: Temporal and General Data Modeling
docs.text: Prerequisite: API and data modeling. The central question is not just "what is the value?" It is "for which identity, in which unit, valid when, and according to knowledge available when?" These distinctions matter in entitlements, addresses, pricing, organizational structure, and scientific observations, not only finance.

docs.title: Identity, value, and evidence
docs.text:
Use stable internal identity for an entity whose name can change. A person's email address is an attribute and access channel, not necessarily permanent identity. Scope natural keys: (tenant_id, external_id) may be unique while external_id alone is not. Preserve provenance for imported facts so a correction can identify the assertion it supersedes.

Modeling choice Invariant Counterexample Quantity plus unit comparisons use compatible dimensions 10 kilograms treated as 10 pounds Integer minor units plus currency amounts retain interpretation every currency assumed to have two decimals Explicit unknown value unknown differs from zero and absent missing measurement counted as zero Stable ID plus aliases rename does not create a new entity email change breaks history joins State machine plus version only legal transitions commit cancelled task becomes running on replay

Choose exact decimal or scaled integer representation when exact decimal arithmetic is required; binary floating point is useful for approximate numerical work but should not silently become a billing policy. Specify rounding mode and when rounding occurs. round(a)+round(b) can differ from round(a+b).

docs.title: Two time axes
docs.text:
Valid time says when a fact applies in the modeled world. Recorded time says when the system learned it. Event time, ingestion time, and processing time may add distinct pipeline concerns, but are not interchangeable with those two axes.

Assumption (2026-09): Atlas records a plan price of 100 credits valid on days [1,31), known from day 1. On day 20, an authorized correction says the price was actually 80 credits on [10,15).

price_assertion(id, tenant, valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at, revision, amount)
A: [1,31), recorded=1, revision=1, amount=100
B: [10,15), recorded=20, revision=2, amount=80

The fixture uses immutable assertions and a deterministic latest-recorded/revision precedence rule among matching assertions. This is a deliberately small policy, not a general database temporal standard. Production systems must also define conflicting corrections, authority, withdrawal, and open-ended intervals.

Query Expected amount Why Valid day 12, known day 15 100 correction was not known yet Valid day 12, known day 25 80 correction now applies Valid day 9, known day 25 100 outside correction interval Valid day 15, known day 25 100 half-open end excludes day 15 
flowchart LR
    A[Original assertion] --> H[Immutable history]
    C[Authorized correction] --> H
    H --> Q{Valid time and knowledge cutoff}
    Q --> P[Historical answer]
    H --> R[Recompute affected projection]
    R --> D[Versioned downstream delta]

Half-open intervals [start,end) make adjacent intervals unambiguous: exactly one includes a shared boundary. They do not prevent overlaps; enforce nonoverlap where the domain requires one active assertion, or specify precedence where corrections deliberately overlap. Avoid pretending that a wall-clock timestamp alone resolves simultaneous conflicting edits.

docs.title: Correction is not replay blindness
docs.text:
A daily aggregate cannot just add the new 80-credit assertion to a previous 100-credit result. It must replace the affected contribution or apply an explicit -100,+80 correction with idempotent identity. If readers must never observe a half-applied correction, commit both delta legs together with their receipt, or atomically upsert the complete revised contribution. Preserve the original report if the question is "what did we publish then?" Recompute if the question is "what do we now believe applied then?" Both can be valid products.

Assumption (2026-09): A correction affects five daily partitions with 2 million rows each. At 50,000 rows/s, a full 10-million-row replay needs at least 200 s of processing, excluding I/O and joins. An index on entity and validity can reduce the affected set. Do not recompute all tenants when lineage can identify one tenant's range.

Deletion complicates immutable history. "Append-only" is an application update policy, not permission to retain personal data indefinitely. Separate minimal audit facts from sensitive payloads, define retention and legal holds, and ensure restored backups reapply required tombstones. See authorization and privacy.

docs.title: Migration and validation
docs.text:
Failure Detection Recovery Test Arrival order used as effective order historical answer changes incorrectly rebuild from valid-time assertions late correction outside queried interval Endpoints both inclusive two prices at boundary normalize interval convention exact start/end and adjacent ranges Duplicate correction repeated delta deduplicate by correction ID same correction twice Backfill overwrites newer edit revision falls guarded update or replay concurrent edit during scan Unit changes in place impossible aggregate preserve unit/version and convert explicitly mixed-unit rejection

Run temporal corrections. Its oracle uses hand-specified point answers, not the same filtering expression as the implementation. Add a correction at an interval boundary and a query before any recorded knowledge. A missing value must remain None, not become zero.

docs.title: L5/L6 and assessment
docs.text:
L5: Model identity, units, valid/recorded time, and boundary behavior; trace a late correction into a projection. L6: Decide which historical questions the business must reproduce, bound recomputation cost, and reconcile auditability with deletion and organizational ownership.

Exercise: an address is corrected on day 20 to apply from day 10. Which address should an already dispatched package retain? Preserve the dispatch snapshot as evidence of the action, even if the current effective address changes. Correcting master data should not rewrite physical history.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Snodgrass, Developing Time-Oriented Database Applications in SQL (1999): author's treatment of valid and transaction time, intervals, and temporal queries. Our assertion precedence is a local teaching contract, not a claim that SQL engines implement it automatically.
  • IEEE 754-2019: floating-point arithmetic standard; the decision to use decimal or minor units is domain judgment, not a prohibition on floating-point systems.

Connect this model to API lifecycle and the capstone.

docs.title: API and Data Modeling
docs.text:
Engineering extensions: Temporal and general data modeling develops identity, units, valid/recorded time, and late corrections. API contract lifecycle develops compatibility, retry horizons, rollout, and retirement with assessment and executable evidence.

An API is a concurrency and failure contract. A data model is an encoded set of invariants and access paths. Design them together from user operations, not independently from entity nouns.

docs.title: Example: reservation service
docs.text:
Requirements: create a five-minute hold, confirm it after payment, cancel it, and list a user's reservations. No seat may have two active owners.

POST /v1/holds
Idempotency-Key: 8f2...
{"show_id":"s1","seat_ids":["A10","A11"]}

201 Created
{"hold_id":"h7","status":"HELD","expires_at":"2026-09-05T12:05:00Z"}

The following is a schema sketch, not executable DDL; a concrete database migration must declare types, foreign keys, and its partial-index syntax.

reservation(id, user_id, show_id, status, expires_at, version, created_at, confirmed_at)
reserved_seat(show_id, seat_id, reservation_id, state)
idempotency(principal_id, key, request_hash, response, expires_at)

UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id) WHERE state IN ('HELD', 'CONFIRMED')
INDEX reservation_by_user (user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)

The database constraint is the final guard; a read-then-write availability check is not atomic. Expiry should transition ownership through a transaction or conditional write, not rely solely on a delayed timer.

docs.title: Interface decisions
docs.text:
Concern Recommended contract Why retries idempotency key scoped to caller and operation resolves lost responses safely concurrency version or ETag on updates detects lost updates pagination opaque cursor over stable sort (time,id) avoids offset drift and deep scans async work 202 plus operation resource separates acceptance from completion errors stable machine code plus retryability clients should not parse prose bulk calls per-item outcomes and bounded batch size partial failure is inevitable

Reject reuse of an idempotency key with a different request hash. Store the final status and response atomically with the business write where possible.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API
    participant DB as Database
    C->>A: POST hold + key K
    A->>DB: transaction: claim seats + save K
    alt seats free
        DB-->>A: hold H
        A-->>C: 201 H
    else conflict
        DB-->>A: constraint violation
        A-->>C: 409 SEAT_UNAVAILABLE
    end

docs.title: Canonical state and projections
docs.text:
Canonical state answers correctness-sensitive questions. Projections optimize specific reads and may lag. For example, reservation rows are canonical; "available seats by section" in Redis and a search index are projections. Label this boundary explicitly.

flowchart LR
    API --> DB[(Canonical rows)]
    DB --> O[Transactional outbox]
    O --> S[Event stream]
    S --> P1[(Availability projection)]
    S --> P2[(User history projection)]

Choose normalization for invariants and updates; denormalize for proven read paths. Every duplicate needs an owner, freshness expectation, and rebuild path.

docs.title: Evolution rules
docs.text:
• Add fields as optional before making them required.
  • Use tolerant readers, but validate commands strictly.
  • Deploy dual-read or shadow verification before changing canonical storage.
  • Backfill with checkpoints, throttling, and per-row version guards.
  • Never reuse enum values or change field meaning in place.
  • Treat deletion as a workflow across canonical rows, caches, indexes, backups, and audit policy.

docs.title: Failure semantics
docs.text:
Event Client-visible result Recovery validation fails 400, no state change correct request business conflict 409, no state change refresh or choose another seat timeout before commit unknown retry same idempotency key commit succeeds, response lost retry returns original response idempotency record projection update fails write remains committed replay outbox; expose lag partial bulk failure item-level success/error retry only failed items

Model states and legal transitions, not free-form status strings. Authorization belongs at both API and data access boundaries: a valid reservation ID must not permit cross-tenant reads.

docs.title: Derive the contract from commands and queries
docs.text:
Start with user intent, not CRUD. POST /reservations says less than POST /holds: a hold has a duration, ownership rule, conflict outcome, and legal next actions. Separate commands that change canonical state from queries that may use projections.

For each operation, write six facts before choosing HTTP, gRPC, or messaging:

Fact Hold example principal and authorization authenticated buyer may hold at most eight seats precondition all requested seats are unowned at commit time invariant a seat has at most one active owner successful effect one HELD reservation with five-minute expiry retry identity (principal_id, idempotency_key) observable failure validation, conflict, throttling, unknown outcome

This framing prevents an attractive API from requiring an impossible storage operation. For example, atomically holding arbitrary seats across independently owned partitions requires distributed coordination. The product can instead limit a hold to one show partition, allocate seat pools to owners, or pay for a cross-partition transaction. The API boundary and partition boundary should agree.

flowchart TD
    UI[User intent] --> CMD[Commands]
    UI --> QRY[Queries]
    CMD --> INV[Preconditions and invariants]
    QRY --> AP[Sort, filter, and freshness]
    INV --> TX[Transaction and partition boundary]
    AP --> IDX[Indexes and projections]
    TX --> CONTRACT[API contract]
    IDX --> CONTRACT

docs.title: Model the state machine explicitly
docs.text:
A reservation is not a row whose status can take any string. It is a state machine. Assume the legal transitions are HELD -> CONFIRMED, HELD -> EXPIRED, and HELD -> CANCELLED; a confirmed reservation may later become REFUNDED, but never EXPIRED. Enforce transitions with conditional updates such as:

UPDATE reservation
SET status = 'CONFIRMED', version = version + 1, confirmed_at = :now
WHERE id = :id
  AND user_id = :principal
  AND status = 'HELD'
  AND expires_at > :now
  AND version = :expected_version;

Zero updated rows can mean not found, unauthorized, expired, wrong state, or stale version. Do not leak resource existence across tenants. The service can first query through an authorization-scoped access path or return one stable conflict code where disclosure is unsafe.

The :now above is an authority-sampled decision time, not a caller-supplied timestamp or an application time captured before waiting for a lock. Define expiry as evaluated when the storage authority grants the transition. If a transaction can wait, lock the ownership row and sample a fresh trusted time before evaluating the predicate. Transaction-start timestamps alone can admit a hold that expired during the wait. This contract does not promise that the response reaches the buyer before expiry.

Expiry races illustrate why the transition belongs in storage. At 12:05:00, a confirmation worker and expiry worker may run together. If both read HELD then update unconditionally, the last writer wins and can produce an illegal state. Conditional transitions ensure only one changes the row. The loser rereads and maps the current state to a deterministic response.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HELD: seats claimed
    HELD --> CONFIRMED: payment accepted before expiry
    HELD --> CANCELLED: buyer cancels
    HELD --> EXPIRED: conditional expiry
    CONFIRMED --> REFUNDED: refund workflow completes
    CANCELLED --> [*]
    EXPIRED --> [*]
    REFUNDED --> [*]

The seat ownership row should become CONFIRMED in the same transaction that confirms the reservation, and be released in the same transaction that transitions a hold to EXPIRED or CANCELLED. A timer merely proposes the transition. Correctness comes from the predicate and transaction, so duplicate and late timer delivery is harmless.

docs.title: Idempotency is stored protocol state
docs.text:
An idempotency key is not just a header forwarded to the database. Define scope, payload equality, lifetime, and concurrent behavior. A robust algorithm is:

  1. Canonicalize the command and compute request_hash.
  2. Attempt to insert (principal, operation, key, hash, IN_PROGRESS) under a uniqueness constraint.
  3. If the row exists with another hash, return 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED.
  4. If it exists with a final response, return that response exactly.
  5. If it is IN_PROGRESS, wait briefly, poll an operation resource, or return a retryable conflict; do not execute concurrently.
  6. In one transaction, perform the business change and store the final response or stable result reference.

When the idempotency table and business data cannot share a transaction, use a domain-unique command ID in the canonical record and reconcile incomplete protocol rows. Do not promise atomicity from two ordinary writes to separate systems.

For a local transaction, include the initial key claim in that same transaction; otherwise a crash between steps 2 and 6 strands IN_PROGRESS. An intentionally separately committed claim needs a lease, takeover fencing, and canonical-outcome lookup. Expiry alone must not permit repeating an unknown effect. PostgreSQL 17 isolation also means a duplicate insert can wait on an uncommitted contender; bound that wait and retry the entire aborted transaction, not only its final statement (accessed 2026-09-08).

Retention must exceed the maximum credible retry period. If mobile clients retry for 24 hours, expiring keys after ten minutes reopens duplicate creation. Storing full responses for 24 hours has a cost: at 20,000 commands/s and 600 bytes/record, one day is roughly 20,000 * 86,400 * 600 = 1.04 TB before indexes and replicas. Store compact result references where possible, partition expiry data, and document what happens after expiration.

docs.title: Pagination under concurrent writes
docs.text:
Offset pagination is simple but unstable. If a client requests rows 1-20 ordered newest-first and a new row arrives, OFFSET 20 may repeat the old row 20. Deletions can cause omissions, and deep offsets scan discarded rows.

Use keyset pagination over a unique stable order:

SELECT id, show_id, status, created_at
FROM reservation
WHERE user_id = :user
  AND (created_at, id) < (:cursor_time, :cursor_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT :page_size_plus_one;

The opaque cursor should encode the last (created_at,id), query filters, sort version, and optionally an expiry, then be integrity-protected. Fetch one extra row to determine has_more. Keyset pagination gives traversal stability relative to the cursor, not a full snapshot: later status changes can still appear. If export requires snapshot semantics, issue a snapshot watermark and retain the necessary versions, or create an asynchronous export job.

docs.title: Indexes are executable access paths
docs.text:
For every query, show the leading index fields and expected cardinality. reservation_by_user(user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) supports one user's history. It does not efficiently answer "all expiring holds" because user_id is absent. Add an expiry work index such as (status, expires_at, id), or publish delayed work, but account for write amplification and cleanup.

Use Database Indexing to validate left-prefix, equality-before-range, covering, selectivity, and planner behavior. Use Relational Databases when the access path also depends on MVCC visibility, constraints, WAL, replicas, or schema evolution.

Suppose 15,000 holds/s update the reservation table, seat table, three secondary indexes, and one outbox row. The logical write amplification is at least six records per request, or 90,000 record mutations/s before replication. This may change the partition and storage decision even though API QPS looks modest. Remove speculative indexes; projections can serve access paths that do not require transactional freshness.

Hot partitions also follow the API. Partitioning reservations by user_id spreads history reads, but seat claims for one popular show must coordinate by (show_id,seat_id). One table need not satisfy both. Keep canonical ownership partitioned for its invariant and build user history as an asynchronously rebuildable projection.

docs.title: Asynchronous APIs need observable operations
docs.text:
For work exceeding a request deadline, return acceptance only after durable intent:

POST /v1/exports
Idempotency-Key: exp-91

202 Accepted
Location: /v1/operations/op-44
Retry-After: 5
{"operation_id":"op-44","status":"PENDING"}

202 does not mean completion. The operation resource needs terminal states, progress if meaningful, error codes, creation and expiry timestamps, and authorization. Cancellation is another command with race semantics: it may return that cancellation was requested while the worker concurrently completes. Define whether completed output remains downloadable.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API
    participant DB as Canonical DB and outbox
    participant W as Worker
    C->>A: POST export, key K
    A->>DB: commit operation PENDING + job event
    DB-->>A: operation op-44
    A-->>C: 202, Location op-44
    DB-->>W: job event (at least once)
    W->>DB: claim op-44 if PENDING
    W->>DB: mark SUCCEEDED, output reference
    C->>A: GET op-44
    A-->>C: SUCCEEDED, signed download URL

Workers claim with a lease or conditional state change and make output publication idempotent. A lease expiry can cause two workers; it is not proof the first stopped. Fence writes with an attempt number so an old worker cannot overwrite the newer result.

docs.title: Schema and API evolution without a flag day
docs.text:
Use expand-migrate-contract. To replace full_name with given_name and family_name:

This is a representation example, not a rule that names always have two parts. Do not split legacy names on the first space: preserve the original display name and ask for structured fields only where the product genuinely needs them. Mark uncertain backfills instead of inventing identity data.

  1. Add nullable new columns and deploy readers that understand both forms.
  2. Write the new representation while preserving the old compatibility path through one owner, not unrelated dual writes.
  3. Backfill in small primary-key ranges with checkpoints and a predicate that avoids overwriting newer rows.
  4. Compare old and new reads in shadow traffic; measure mismatch by reason.
  5. Switch reads progressively behind a reversible flag.
  6. Stop old writes only after every deployed client is compatible.
  7. Enforce new constraints, then remove old data in a later release.

Event schemas require the same order. Add optional fields, preserve old meanings, and version genuinely incompatible semantics. A database rollback does not undo events already consumed, so rollout plans must include consumer compatibility and replay.

For a storage migration, make one store canonical. Change capture is safer than application dual writes because it gives an ordered repair source. Backfill to a watermark, tail live changes, shadow-read, shift a small cohort, and retain reverse routing until confidence is high. Define rollback before cutover, including whether writes made on the new store can be replayed back.

docs.title: Failure and abuse scenarios
docs.text:
• A client times out after commit and retries: return the prior result through the idempotency record.
  • Two users claim the same seat: one conditional claim commits; the other receives 409, regardless of stale availability views.
  • The outbox consumer is down for six hours: canonical writes continue if outbox storage and recovery SLO permit; queue age alerts before retention is exhausted.
  • A backfill overwrites a recent edit: prevent it with source version predicates and record mismatches for repair.
  • A tenant enumerates IDs: authorization-scoped queries and non-disclosing errors prevent cross-tenant reads; random IDs alone are not authorization.
  • A caller submits a 100,000-item bulk request: enforce byte and item limits, bound parallelism, and return per-item results or an asynchronous operation.

Rate limits should reflect scarce resources. A flat requests-per-second limit does not protect a bulk endpoint or expensive search. Charge weighted units by items, bytes, or estimated work, isolate tenants, and include a machine-readable Retry-After response.

docs.title: Interview traps and L5/L6 reasoning
docs.text:
• CRUD-only modeling: entity endpoints omit transitions, preconditions, and conflict meaning.
  • Read then write: application checks do not enforce uniqueness under concurrency; use constraints or conditional writes.
  • Exactly-once claims: retries and consumers duplicate; design idempotent commands and effects.
  • Offset by default: concurrent inserts and deep pages produce drift and cost.
  • Dual writing casually: partial success creates two truths without an authoritative repair log.
  • Cache as canonical: derived availability must not decide the final seat claim.
  • Status as free text: illegal transitions and ambiguous terminal states become production bugs.

An L5 answer links each command to an invariant, transaction, index, failure code, and retry behavior. It distinguishes canonical rows from projections and traces a timeout after commit. An L6 answer finds the product constraint hidden in the partition key, estimates index and protocol-state cost, defines tenant isolation and abuse controls, and presents a reversible migration with compatibility windows, shadow verification, and rollback. L6 reasoning also assigns ownership: the API team owns compatibility, the domain team owns state transitions, and projection consumers own freshness SLOs and rebuild procedures.

docs.title: Caching Without Losing Correctness
docs.text:
Executable extension: The versioned-cache lab enumerates reordered updates, deletion, eviction, and late-fill resurrection. Its retained-watermark assumption and production limits are explicit; apply it in Atlas read scaling.

A cache trades freshness and operational complexity for latency, cost, or dependency protection. It is derived state unless the design explicitly makes it durable and authoritative.

docs.title: Start with the objective
docs.text:
For a product service at 30,000 reads/s, 2 KB responses, 80% repeated keys, and a database safe limit of 8,000 reads/s, a 75% hit rate reduces database load to 7,500 reads/s. The cache is justified by dependency capacity, not fashion.

Pattern Use when Main risk cache-aside general read caching stale data and miss races read-through centralized loading policy library/platform coupling write-through immediate cache visibility needed dual-system write latency write-behind write coalescing is acceptable data loss and ordering refresh-ahead predictable hot keys wasted refresh and stale refresh races request memoization duplicate work within one request limited reuse

docs.title: Cache-aside flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Service
    participant K as Cache
    participant D as Database
    C->>S: GET product/42
    S->>K: get(42)
    alt hit
        K-->>S: value, version
    else miss
        S->>D: read product 42
        D-->>S: value, version 9
        S->>K: set if newer(version 9, TTL)
    end
    S-->>C: product

Use versioned values so a slow miss cannot overwrite a newer invalidation or refresh. TTL limits how long an entry can remain resident after its fill. It does not by itself bound age relative to the latest canonical write: a lagging replica or delayed fill can supply an already-old value. Correctness-sensitive reads need a stronger contract.

docs.title: Invalidation choices
docs.text:
Requirement Approach seconds of staleness acceptable TTL plus jitter read-your-writes update/invalidate after commit plus session bypass many derived keys version namespace or event-driven invalidation correctness-critical decision read canonical store or validate version negative lookup protection short negative cache, never indefinite

For a price shown in search, stale cache may be acceptable; checkout must re-read canonical price and inventory. Separate display correctness from transaction correctness.

docs.title: Stampedes, hot keys, and overload
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    M[Concurrent misses] --> C[Per-key request coalescing]
    C --> R[One origin read]
    R --> J[TTL with jitter]
    R --> S[Serve stale on bounded error]
  • Coalesce concurrent misses per key, but bound waiters and loader time.
  • Randomize TTLs to avoid synchronized expiry.
  • Replicate or locally cache hot keys; adding shards does not split one key.
  • Apply admission policies so one-hit objects do not evict frequently reused data.
  • Reserve origin capacity and shed optional traffic when cache hit rate collapses.

docs.title: Failure semantics
docs.text:
Failure Safe behavior cache unavailable bypass under a strict origin budget; otherwise fail fast invalidation lost expire the resident entry, reload from a sufficiently fresh source, and replay the change stream origin unavailable serve stale only for explicitly stale-safe reads cache returns corrupt data schema/version validation, evict, fetch canonical regional cold start warm top keys gradually; rate-limit origin access

Measure hit rate by endpoint and key popularity, origin requests saved, p99 latency, eviction rate, value age, loader concurrency, and stale-served count. A high global hit rate can hide a zero-hit expensive endpoint.

docs.title: Quantify the cache contract
docs.text:
Define what the cache protects and what freshness the caller can observe. "Cache product data for five minutes" is incomplete. A useful contract says: product description reads may be five minutes stale; price display may be 30 seconds stale; checkout must validate price and stock against canonical state; cache loss may increase browse latency but must not corrupt orders.

Work the load before selecting a pattern. At 30,000 reads/s and a 75% hit ratio, origin load is 7,500 reads/s. If one expensive endpoint contributes 6,000 of those reads at 4 ms database CPU each and all other misses cost 0.5 ms, the expensive endpoint uses 24 CPU-seconds/s by itself. Weighted hit ratio is therefore more useful:

origin work saved = sum(request_rate * hit_rate * origin_cost)
origin work remaining = sum(request_rate * (1 - hit_rate) * origin_cost)

Memory also includes keys, metadata, allocator fragmentation, replication, and headroom. Ten million 2 KB values with 300 bytes overhead, two total copies, and 25% free headroom need about 10M * 2,300 B * 2 / 0.75 = 61.3 GB, not the 20 GB of single-copy payload. If only 5% of keys receive 90% of reads, admission and eviction can provide most benefit without caching the full corpus.

flowchart TD
    R[Read requirements] --> F[Freshness by field or operation]
    R --> C[Origin cost and safe capacity]
    R --> W[Working-set distribution]
    F --> P[Cache pattern]
    C --> P
    W --> P
    P --> O[Overload and invalidation contract]
    O --> M[Metrics and rollout gates]

docs.title: Cache-aside race: the stale fill
docs.text:
Versioning in the baseline flow prevents a common race:

  1. Reader A misses cache key product:42 and reads database version 9.
  2. Writer B commits version 10 and invalidates the key.
  3. Reader A, delayed in the network, stores version 9 after the invalidation.
  4. Every later reader sees stale version 9 until TTL expiry.

Deleting after the database write is not enough because the delayed fill occurs after the delete. set-if-newer(version=9) works if the cache retains a version-10 tombstone or value. Alternatives include short TTLs, invalidation sequence watermarks, or double deletion after a delay, but delayed deletion only narrows the race and must be treated as probabilistic.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Reader A
    participant K as Cache
    participant D as Database
    participant B as Writer B
    A->>K: get product 42
    K-->>A: miss
    A->>D: read
    D-->>A: value v9
    B->>D: commit value v10
    B->>K: invalidate / tombstone v10
    A->>K: set-if-newer value v9
    K-->>A: rejected because 9 < 10

A database version, log sequence number, or monotonic entity revision is safer than a wall-clock timestamp. Two hosts' clocks can disagree, and last-write-wins timestamps may let an older value dominate. If versions are only ordered within a shard, include shard identity and epoch.

Eviction must not erase the only rejection watermark while an older loader remains in flight. Retain the watermark beyond the maximum loader/replay lifetime, or use a cache-generation change that invalidates old fills after cache loss. The comparison and fill must be atomic. For invalidation from PostgreSQL CDC, logical decoding can resend recent changes after a crash; never advance the durable consumer cursor ahead of applied invalidations (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Write-path choices and their failure windows
docs.text:
Cache-aside writes usually commit canonical state and then invalidate. If invalidation fails, stale data remains until TTL or replay. Use a transactional outbox or database change stream to make invalidation recoverable, accepting propagation lag. Invalidation events should carry the entity version, and consumers must be idempotent.

Write-through puts a caching layer on the synchronous path. It can make subsequent reads immediately visible, but a cache acknowledgment must not precede the required durable database commit. If database succeeds and cache update fails, invalidate and recover rather than roll back an already visible business transaction through an unrelated write.

Write-behind makes the cache temporarily authoritative. This is suitable only when lost/coalesced updates match the product contract, such as approximate telemetry. Acknowledging a bank transfer from a non-durable cache is not safe. If write-behind is justified, persist a log, define ordering per key, fence stale workers, expose drain lag, and reconcile the destination.

Sequence Failure window Consequence Mitigation DB commit, then cache delete process dies before delete stale cache change stream/outbox plus TTL cache update, then DB commit DB commit fails cache shows nonexistent state avoid for canonical writes DB commit, then cache update slow old update races new update version regression set-if-newer durable log, cache apply, async DB worker outage or reorder lag or lost ordering per-key sequence, replay, fencing

docs.title: TTL is a probability and load decision
docs.text:
TTL controls an upper bound only when entries expire correctly and readers do not refresh from lagging sources. It also determines miss load. If one million keys are populated uniformly with a 300-second TTL, steady expiration causes roughly 3,333 reloads/s. If all keys were warmed at deployment and receive the same TTL, they can expire together and overwhelm origin.

Apply jitter, for example a uniformly random TTL from 240 to 360 seconds. This spreads expiration but does not solve a single hot key. For a key receiving 50,000 reads/s, use request coalescing so one loader refreshes while others wait or receive bounded stale data. Bound the waiter count and loader deadline; otherwise one failed loader consumes memory and request threads.

Probabilistic early refresh avoids a sharp edge. As an item nears expiry, a small increasing fraction of callers attempts refresh under a per-key lock. Refresh-ahead should use popularity: refreshing every cold key wastes origin work and cache capacity.

Negative caching protects origin from repeated misses for nonexistent IDs. Keep negative TTL short because object creation must become visible. Never turn an authorization failure into a shared negative cache entry; cache keys must include every dimension that changes the result.

docs.title: Key design and invalidation graphs
docs.text:
A safe key includes namespace, tenant, logical identity, representation version, and material variants such as language or authorization class. Omitting tenant_id can leak data. Omitting schema version can make old serialized values crash new code. Do not place secrets or raw personal data in keys because keys appear in logs and metrics.

Derived pages create invalidation fan-out. Updating one product might affect product:42, category pages, search results, recommendations, and promotion summaries. Tracking and deleting every derived key becomes fragile. Prefer one of these:

  • Cache smaller canonical fragments and assemble the page.
  • Put a version in a namespace, such as category:7:v83:page:2, and advance the namespace pointer.
  • Consume canonical change events into rebuildable projections.
  • Accept bounded staleness for discovery while validating on the transaction path.

Version namespaces make old entries unreachable immediately but do not free memory immediately. TTL and eviction reclaim them, so budget temporary duplication during high update rates.

flowchart LR
    DB[(Canonical DB)] --> O[Outbox or change stream]
    O --> I[Invalidation consumer]
    I --> E[Entity keys]
    I --> V[Version namespace pointer]
    I --> T[Version tombstones]
    O --> R[Replay checkpoint]
    R --> I

docs.title: Eviction, admission, and hot keys
docs.text:
LRU assumes recent access predicts reuse and can be polluted by scans. A one-time analytics scan can evict the product working set. Admission policies such as TinyLFU estimate frequency and reject low-value newcomers; segmented policies protect frequently reused entries from transient bursts. Match policy to traces, not intuition.

Sharding distributes many keys but not one key. A celebrity profile at 100,000 reads/s still lands on one cache shard. Replicate hot values into process-local caches, read from replica keys, or have the cache platform replicate based on measured heat. Local caches reduce network latency but make invalidation slower and memory usage multiplicative. Include process restarts and fleet-wide cold starts in the origin budget.

Large values can create network and eviction problems. A 5 MB object requested 2,000/s is 10 GB/s of cache egress. Compression trades CPU for bandwidth; chunking complicates atomic versioning. Often a CDN or object store is the right cache tier while Redis-like storage keeps metadata.

docs.title: Failure scenarios and controlled degradation
docs.text:
Cache outage. Blind bypass converts 30,000 reads/s into origin traffic against an 8,000/s safe limit. Reserve perhaps 5,000/s for cache misses, admit only that budget during outage, serve bounded stale local values where allowed, and reject optional browse traffic early. Protect checkout's canonical capacity in a separate pool.

Regional cold start. Warming every object competes with user traffic and caches cold data. Prewarm a measured top-key set, ramp instances gradually, coalesce misses, and cap warmup to origin headroom. Persisting snapshots can help, but validate age and schema before loading.

Invalidation stream lag. Continue serving only if each endpoint's staleness budget exceeds observed lag. Expose value version/age internally, alarm on the oldest unprocessed event, and bypass cache for correctness-sensitive reads. Catch-up should be rate-limited so replay does not evict hot values or overload origin.

Poisoned or corrupt value. Validate schema and checksums, evict the specific key, and fetch canonical state. Add a circuit breaker if a bad writer repeatedly repopulates it. Never deserialize untrusted cached objects with unsafe polymorphic types.

Hot-key expiry. One absent key creates thousands of waiters. Elect one bounded loader, serve stale within a declared grace window, and fail quickly after the grace period. "Serve stale" must not apply to permissions, revocations, inventory decisions, or legal deletion.

docs.title: Migration and rollout
docs.text:
Introduce caching as a reversible optimization:

  1. Measure origin request shape, safe capacity, key popularity, and acceptable age.
  2. Deploy cache writes or fills while reads still use origin; validate serialization and memory estimates.
  3. Shadow cache reads and compare value version and semantics without serving them.
  4. Enable a stale-safe endpoint for 1% of traffic, then ramp while watching origin work saved, p99, value age, and errors.
  5. Inject cache failure and invalidation lag before full rollout; confirm admission control protects origin.
  6. Keep a kill switch that stops cache reads without causing unrestricted bypass.
  7. Change key schemas with a new namespace. Read old then new only for a bounded migration, and avoid permanent compatibility branches.

For cache-cluster resharding, consistent hashing reduces movement but does not remove miss bursts. Add nodes gradually, limit migration bandwidth, and account for temporary replication. If clients have an outdated ring, they can produce split caches; version topology and observe misses by client version.

docs.title: Interview traps and L5/L6 reasoning
docs.text:
• "Add Redis" without an objective: quantify latency, origin protection, or cost and the required hit ratio.
  • TTL as correctness: expiration reduces stale duration but cannot enforce an inventory or authorization invariant.
  • Global hit ratio: segment by endpoint, tenant, key heat, bytes, and origin work.
  • Unlimited bypass: cache failure becomes an origin outage.
  • Deleting after write solves races: a delayed fill can reinsert old data; use versions or ordered invalidation.
  • Ignoring cache-key authorization dimensions: shared values can leak tenant or permission-specific responses.
  • Caching large objects in a general KV: bandwidth and memory fragmentation may dominate; choose the right tier.

An L5 candidate identifies canonical state, chooses a fitting pattern, explains stale-fill and stampede defenses, calculates origin load, and gives safe outage behavior. An L6 candidate defines freshness per operation, models weighted cost and hot-key skew, chooses admission and eviction from workload evidence, designs versioned invalidation and replay, and stages a reversible rollout with failure injection. L6 reasoning explicitly reserves capacity for critical paths and challenges whether a cache should exist at all when a projection, index, CDN, or query redesign better addresses the bottleneck.

docs.title: Consistency, Consensus, and CAP
docs.text:
Engineering extension: Distributed theory, clocks, and authority adds explicit fault models, FLP scope, logical-clock counterexamples, durable consensus assumptions, and a fenced-worker fixture.

Consistency is an operation-specific promise. Ask "consistent for which read after which write, under what failure?" before selecting a mechanism.

docs.title: Useful guarantees
docs.text:
Guarantee Example Typical mechanism read-your-writes profile edit is immediately visible to editor sticky leader read or version token monotonic reads order status never moves backward session watermark causal ordering reply does not precede parent causal metadata or partition ordering linearizability one username has one owner leader/consensus conditional write serializability inventory and reservation obey transaction rules serializable transaction eventual convergence like count becomes accurate idempotent events plus reconciliation

Linearizability concerns one operation appearing atomic in real time. Serializability concerns transaction equivalence to a serial order; without strict serializability it need not honor wall-clock order.

docs.title: CAP without slogans
docs.text:
CAP's consistency property is linearizability, not every useful consistency guarantee. Its availability property requires every request received by a non-failing node to complete, not merely a high uptime percentage. During a partition, a replicated read/write object cannot guarantee both properties. Rejecting a request or waiting indefinitely sacrifices this availability. "CA" is not a meaningful partition-time choice for such an object.

The diagram below is an application-invariant decision aid, not a proof that every invariant requires coordination. Mergeable operations and preallocated escrow rights can preserve some invariants without global linearizability. See Gilbert and Lynch (2002), formal model and impossibility result.

flowchart TD
    P[Network partition] --> Q{Operation requires coordination?}
    Q -->|yes, preserve invariant| CP[Reject or wait]
    Q -->|accept availability| AP[Record concurrent state]
    AP --> M[Detect and merge conflict]
    Q -->|no| L[Serve partition-local operation]

A checkout inventory decrement against a single global stock owner usually rejects on the minority side to preserve its linearizable conditional-update contract. A cart add may remain available if concurrent additions can merge. A single product can therefore use different guarantees per operation; stock sold from preallocated regional rights is a different contract, discussed below.

docs.title: Quorums are conditional
docs.text:
With replication factor N, writes to W, and reads from R, W + R > N creates overlap only under assumptions about replica membership, clocks/versioning, sloppy quorums, and repair. It does not automatically provide linearizability.

Design Benefit Cost/risk leader writes simple total order leader latency and failover pause quorum reads/writes tunable availability conflict resolution and tail latency consensus group durable ordered decisions cross-node coordination CRDT deterministic merge only fits mergeable semantics escrow/leases local operations within allocated rights rebalancing and expiry complexity

docs.title: Concrete example: unique usernames
docs.text:
Invariant: at most one account owns a normalized username. Route a username to one consensus-backed partition and perform put-if-absent. During loss of quorum, reject claims rather than create two owners. Profile reads can still come from stale replicas if the UI tolerates it.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Region A
    participant L as Username leader
    participant B as Region B
    A->>L: claim("sam", account1)
    L-->>A: committed at version 42
    B-xL: partitioned
    B->>B: reject claim because uniqueness cannot be proven

docs.title: Failure semantics and repair
docs.text:
• A timeout is an unknown outcome, not proof of failure; retry with the same command ID.
  • Leader failover can expose stale followers unless promotion checks committed logs.
  • Asynchronous replication has a measurable recovery point objective: acknowledged writes may be lost after region loss.
  • Last-write-wins can discard valid concurrent updates and depends on clocks; use only when that policy matches the domain.
  • Anti-entropy repairs replicas but does not repair external side effects. Reconcile payments, emails, and indexes separately.

Choose the weakest guarantee that preserves each invariant, then offer session-level guarantees where users notice anomalies. State the unavailable path explicitly instead of hiding it behind "eventual consistency."

docs.title: Define the history you need
docs.text:
Consistency models constrain observable histories. Begin with an operation and an invariant, not a database label. For a username claim, clients need a single real-time order for conditional writes. For a user's profile, read-your-writes may be enough. For a collaborative counter, convergence may be enough if increments commute.

These guarantees are related but not interchangeable:

  • Linearizability: each operation appears to occur atomically between invocation and response, respecting real-time precedence. It composes across individual objects.
  • Sequential consistency: operations fit one total order that preserves each client's program order, but the order need not respect wall-clock precedence between clients.
  • Serializability: committed transactions are equivalent to some serial execution. Plain serializability may reorder transactions in a way that violates real-time expectations.
  • Strict serializability: combines serializability with real-time order and is the strongest common transaction contract.
  • Snapshot isolation: transactions read a stable snapshot and conflicting writes are detected, but write skew can violate multi-row invariants.

Availability is also scoped. A system that serves stale reads during a partition but rejects writes is available for one operation and unavailable for another. State the behavior per API and failure domain.

flowchart TD
    OP[Operation] --> INV{Cross-request invariant?}
    INV -->|No, mergeable| EV[Eventual or causal merge]
    INV -->|Yes| OBJ{Single object conditional?}
    OBJ -->|Yes| LIN[Linearizable conditional operation]
    OBJ -->|No| TX[Serializable transaction or redesigned boundary]
    EV --> UX[Add session guarantees where visible]
    LIN --> FAIL[Reject when quorum cannot prove safety]
    TX --> FAIL

This second decision tree is also a conservative coordination aid, not a necessity theorem: cross-request numeric invariants may admit escrow, and some causal dependencies span partitions. A serializable transaction does not inherently require a distributed quorum if all data is local. Check the actual engine and fault model rather than treating every edge as a universal implication.

docs.title: Quorum overlap does not eliminate stale reads
docs.text:
Take N=3, W=2, R=2, with replicas A, B, and C. A write of value v2 reaches A and B, so it is acknowledged. A later read from B and C sees v2 and old v1; with a correct comparable version, the coordinator returns v2. The inequality W + R > N ensures at least one overlap between successful sets.

Now inspect the assumptions. If acknowledgments occur before durable persistence, A and B can both restart and lose v2. If versions use unsynchronized wall clocks, v1 may carry a later timestamp. If the read coordinator returns the first response rather than reconciling all R, overlap is irrelevant. If membership changed between operations without joint coordination, the sets may not belong to the same replica universe. Quorums improve overlap; they do not by themselves establish one-copy linearizable semantics.

Even a normal quorum can return stale data with concurrent writes. Client X writes v2 to A and B while client Y's read contacts B and C before B receives v2; it returns v1. This is allowed because the write had not completed before the read began. If the write completed first, a properly implemented strict quorum read should encounter v2, but sloppy membership or failed durability can break that assumption.

A sharper counterexample is a partial write present only on A. Read 1 from A+B returns v2, then Read 2 from B+C returns v1 after Read 1 completed. Both use R=2, but the completed reads regress. A linearizable register protocol must prevent that new-old inversion, for example with protocol-defined read write-back; asynchronous repair alone is insufficient. This does not contradict etcd's strict-serializable KV contract, which is stronger than bare quorum counting (accessed 2026-09-08).

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant X as Writer
    participant A as Replica A
    participant B as Replica B
    participant C as Replica C
    participant Y as Reader
    X->>A: put v2, version 8
    X->>B: put v2, version 8
    A-->>X: durable ack
    B-->>X: durable ack (W=2)
    Y->>B: get
    Y->>C: get
    B-->>Y: v2, version 8
