    C-->>Y: v1, version 7
    Y-->>Y: reconcile and return v2
    Y->>C: async repair to v2

docs.title: Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff
docs.text:
During a partition, suppose A and B are the natural replicas for key K but unavailable from the coordinator. A sloppy quorum may store v2 on fallback nodes D and E and acknowledge W=2. A read routed through another coordinator may query natural replicas A, B, and C after A recovers but before hinted handoff. It can collect R=2 old responses and return v1, even though W + R > N. The write and read quorums overlapped numerically but not in node membership.

Sloppy quorum improves write availability and is reasonable where temporary stale reads and conflict reconciliation are accepted. It is not appropriate evidence for strict uniqueness. Hints need durable storage, expiry policy, backpressure, and observability. If D is down when A returns, handoff can be delayed further. If concurrent writes occur on both sides, version vectors or another causal version can preserve siblings for domain resolution; last-write-wins silently discards one.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C1 as Coordinator 1
    participant A as Natural A
    participant B as Natural B
    participant D as Fallback D
    participant E as Fallback E
    participant C2 as Coordinator 2
    Note over C1,B: A and B unreachable
    C1->>D: store v2 as hint for A
    C1->>E: store v2 as hint for B
    D-->>C1: ack
    E-->>C1: ack, write accepted
    Note over A,B: natural replicas later reachable
    C2->>A: read before hinted handoff
    C2->>B: read before hinted handoff
    A-->>C2: v1
    B-->>C2: v1
    Note over C2: stale despite nominal W=2, R=2

docs.title: Read repair and anti-entropy
docs.text:
When a quorum read sees versions 8, 8, and 7, it can return version 8 and asynchronously write it to the stale replica. Blocking repair waits for repair before responding; asynchronous repair improves latency but leaves a wider stale window. Read repair only touches keys that are read. Cold keys need background anti-entropy, often Merkle-tree comparison by key range followed by transfer of differing records.

Repair must not overwrite concurrent siblings when the domain requires preserving them. A scalar total order, even one constructed from logical timestamps and writer IDs, does not distinguish concurrency from causality. In multi-writer systems that must retain concurrent updates, use causal metadata and a merge policy. Tombstones must remain until every relevant replica has observed deletion; removing a tombstone too early can resurrect an old value during repair. Set tombstone grace from maximum outage and repair time, then alert when a replica exceeds it.

docs.title: Leader election and committed logs
docs.text:
Consensus protocols such as Raft establish one ordered log per group while a quorum is connected. Terms or ballots distinguish leadership epochs. A simplified election proceeds:

  1. A follower misses heartbeats, increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes.
  2. A voter grants at most one vote per term and rejects a candidate whose log is less up to date.
  3. A majority elects the candidate. Two leaders cannot each hold a majority in the same term because majorities overlap.
  4. The leader appends a command and sends it to followers.
  5. Once the entry is stored on a majority under the protocol's commit rules, it becomes committed and is applied in order.

In Raft, the leader advances commitment by counting replicas for an entry from its current term. That commitment also commits preceding log entries; it must not declare an old-term entry committed solely because that old entry now appears on a majority. The distinction prevents unsafe failover histories. See the Raft paper, section 5.4.2.

An acknowledgment should mean the entry is committed, not merely present on the leader. Suppose leader A appends entry 12 locally and responds before replication. A fails; B, without entry 12, wins an election and commits a different entry at that index. The client observed a write that vanished. Majority commit and election log checks prevent this history.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant L as Leader term 7
    participant F1 as Follower 1
    participant F2 as Follower 2
    C->>L: conditional claim command K
    L->>L: durably append index 42, term 7
    L->>F1: AppendEntries(42, term 7)
    L->>F2: AppendEntries(42, term 7)
    F1-->>L: durable ack
    Note over L,F1: majority has entry 42
    L->>L: advance commit index and apply
    L-->>C: committed result
    L-->>F1: commit index 42
    L-->>F2: retry replication

Leader leases can make reads cheaper, but consensus safety and read freshness are separate. A follower read may lag. A leader read needs proof it still leads, commonly a quorum round or a valid bounded lease. On failover, an old leader may continue accepting requests while partitioned; followers reject its stale term, and it must not acknowledge without quorum. Clients retry commands with IDs because failover timeouts leave outcomes unknown.

Committed log entries survive minority failure, not every disaster. If a three-node group places all nodes in one region, region loss defeats the durability claim. Placement determines the failure model. Cross-region quorums improve disaster tolerance but add wide-area latency to every coordinated write.

docs.title: Transaction isolation anomalies
docs.text:
Single-key linearizability does not automatically preserve a multi-key invariant. Consider two doctors, Alice and Bob, each on call. The rule is that at least one remains on call.

Under snapshot isolation:

  1. Transaction T1 reads Alice=on and Bob=on.
  2. Transaction T2 reads the same snapshot.
  3. T1 sets Alice=off; T2 sets Bob=off.
  4. They write different rows, so no write-write conflict occurs.
  5. Both commit, leaving nobody on call.

This is write skew. Serializable isolation, explicit locking of a shared invariant row, or encoding the rule into one conditional object prevents it when every writer follows that protocol. With explicit locking, acquire the lock before the decision reads and use a snapshot that includes the preceding holder's committed changes; a pre-lock snapshot can remain stale. PostgreSQL 17, transaction isolation, sections 13.2.2-13.2.3 documents snapshot isolation and whole-transaction retries (accessed 2026-09-08).

Other anomalies matter:

Isolation weakness Trace Risk dirty read T2 reads T1's uncommitted value; T1 aborts action based on state that never existed non-repeatable read T1 reads row twice; T2 changes it between reads inconsistent decision inside transaction phantom T1 repeats a predicate query and sees new matching rows broken range/count invariant lost update T1 and T2 read 10, both write 11 one increment disappears write skew transactions update different rows from same snapshot cross-row invariant fails 
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant T1 as Txn 1
    participant DB as Snapshot-isolated DB
    participant T2 as Txn 2
    T1->>DB: read Alice=on, Bob=on
    T2->>DB: read Alice=on, Bob=on
    T1->>DB: write Alice=off
    T2->>DB: write Bob=off
    T1->>DB: commit (no row conflict)
    T2->>DB: commit (no row conflict)
    Note over DB: invariant violated: nobody on call

Do not answer "the database is ACID" without naming isolation, retry behavior, and invariant encoding. Serializable databases may abort transactions to prevent anomalies; applications must retry the entire transaction with a stable command ID and avoid repeating non-transactional side effects.

docs.title: Session tokens make weak replication usable
docs.text:
Users notice when their own update disappears or an order status moves backward. Session guarantees can hide those anomalies without making every read globally linearizable.

After a write, return a token containing the shard, committed version or log position, topology epoch, and integrity protection. On a later read, the router chooses a replica whose applied position is at least the token. If none has caught up before the deadline, it can wait, route to the leader, or return a retryable response. It must not silently return an older version when read-your-writes is promised.

For monotonic reads, the client carries the greatest observed watermark and never accepts a lower one. For causal consistency across shards, a single scalar may be insufficient; dependency vectors or a causal service track that a reply depends on a parent write. Keep tokens opaque and signed so callers cannot demand impossible positions or cross tenant boundaries.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant W as Write leader
    participant R as Read router
    participant F as Follower
    C->>W: update profile
    W-->>C: success + token(shard 3, pos 918, epoch 12)
    C->>R: get profile + token
    R->>F: applied position?
    F-->>R: 912
    R->>R: wait, choose leader, or retry
    F-->>R: advances to 918
    R->>F: read with minimum position 918
    F-->>R: value from snapshot at or beyond 918
    R-->>C: value at position >= 918

Tokens need lifecycle rules. A resharding epoch maps old positions to the new ownership or forces a leader read. A token from deleted history cannot be honored forever; document expiration. Browser multi-tab and multi-device sessions may not share tokens, so decide whether the guarantee is per request chain, account, device, or global user experience.

docs.title: Leases, fencing, and clock hazards
docs.text:
A lease grants temporary authority, but expiry does not stop the old holder. Consider worker A holding a 30-second lease. A pauses for 40 seconds during garbage collection. The lease service expires A and grants worker B a new lease. A resumes and writes to storage. Without fencing, both act as owner.

Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token with every lease: A has token 41 and B has 42. The protected storage atomically checks and records the highest token with each mutation. It rejects A after observing 42, but may still accept 41 before 42 reaches it. If transfer must immediately revoke A, install 42 at the sink before reporting transfer complete; see the authority handoff protocol. A lease library alone cannot fence an external system.

Wall clocks create additional hazards. Clock steps from NTP correction, VM suspension, leap handling, or drift can make a client believe a lease remains valid after the authority expired it. Use the lease service's ordered epochs and monotonic elapsed time for local deadlines, allow drift margins, and keep lease duration much larger than expected timing uncertainty. Do not use client timestamps to order money movement or resolve concurrent writes unless clock assumptions and error bounds are part of the protocol.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Worker A token 41
    participant LS as Lease service
    participant B as Worker B token 42
    participant S as Protected store
    A->>LS: acquire lease
    LS-->>A: token 41
    Note over A: long pause beyond expiry
    B->>LS: acquire expired lease
    LS-->>B: token 42
    B->>S: write with token 42
    S-->>B: accepted, highest=42
    A->>S: late write with token 41
    S-->>A: rejected as fenced

docs.title: Failure choices by operation
docs.text:
For a network partition, explicitly walk both sides:

  • Username claim: only the side with consensus quorum may accept. The minority returns unavailable because two accepted owners cannot be merged.
  • Shopping-cart add: both sides may accept an operation ID and merge a grow-only set or observed-remove structure, subject to product deletion semantics.
  • Inventory decrement: coordinate against one owner or preallocate escrow rights. If region A has 60 rights and region B has 40, each may sell locally within allocation; transferring rights requires coordination.
  • Profile read: a stale replica may respond, but a session token can require read-your-writes for the editor.
  • Payment notification: record idempotent intent locally, but reconcile the external provider because replica repair cannot undo or rediscover every side effect safely.

Last-write-wins is a business policy, not a neutral repair algorithm. Two users concurrently changing a delivery address can lose valid work, and a fast clock can dominate. Use LWW only where replacing one register is acceptable; preserve siblings, field-level merges, or user conflict resolution otherwise.

docs.title: Migrate from eventual state to consensus safely
docs.text:
Suppose an eventually consistent username store has accumulated duplicates and must move to consensus-backed ownership. A flag-day switch can strand writes or canonize conflicts arbitrarily. Use a staged migration:

  1. Define normalization precisely, including case folding and Unicode policy, and create a stable owner identifier.
  2. Inventory all existing values and detect conflicts. Resolve them with an explicit product policy before enforcement; do not let migration timing choose winners.
  3. Create consensus partitions keyed by normalized username and import resolved ownership with source versions.
  4. Start shadow claims: the old path remains authoritative while the new service evaluates each request and records disagreement without responding.
  5. Introduce one durable command log or outbox from the authoritative path. Avoid independent dual writes whose partial failures cannot be ordered.
  6. Catch up to a recorded watermark, verify counts and sampled ownership, then make the consensus service authoritative for a small tenant or hash cohort.
  7. During cutover, route both claim and release for a username to the same authority. Reads can fall back only if fallback cannot violate the new guarantee.
  8. Expand cohorts while monitoring rejection differences, quorum latency, unavailable rate, and reconciliation backlog.
  9. Roll back routing through the command log. Do not accept new claims in both stores during rollback.
  10. After the compatibility window, stop old writes and retain an audited mapping for support and recovery.
flowchart LR
    OLD[(Eventual store)] --> SCAN[Conflict inventory]
    SCAN --> POLICY[Product resolution]
    POLICY --> NEW[(Consensus ownership)]
    OLD --> LOG[Ordered change log]
    LOG --> NEW
    NEW --> SHADOW[Shadow comparison]
    SHADOW --> COHORT[Authority by cohort]
    COHORT --> FULL[Consensus authoritative]
    COHORT -->|rollback| LOG

The same pattern applies to counters or configuration: resolve historical ambiguity, establish one ordered source, backfill to a watermark, shadow, cut over by disjoint ownership, and retain a rollback path. Consensus does not repair past external effects; duplicates already used in emails, URLs, or ACLs need domain reconciliation.

docs.title: Interview traps and concrete level signals
docs.text:
• "Choose CP": CAP is not a whole-system database personality. Name the operation, partition behavior, and invariant.
  • R + W > N means strong consistency: overlap depends on stable membership, durable acknowledgments, version comparison, and non-sloppy placement; linearizability needs a protocol.
  • Follower promotion by health check: a reachable follower may lack committed entries. Election terms, log checks, and quorum define safe leadership.
  • Snapshot isolation means serializable: write skew can violate cross-row rules.
  • Lease expiry means old owner stopped: pauses and partitions require fencing at the protected resource.
  • Timestamps solve conflicts: clock skew and concurrent valid writes make LWW lossy.
  • Eventual means random: convergence requires deterministic merge, idempotency, repair, tombstone policy, and bounded operational lag.
  • Consensus means no duplicates: client retries still repeat commands; the state machine needs command deduplication.

An L5 candidate maps each operation to a guarantee, explains quorum overlap and leader failover, handles timeout as unknown, and distinguishes canonical correctness from stale reads. They can trace one transaction anomaly and select a mechanism that preserves the stated invariant.

An L6 candidate tests protocol assumptions: durable acknowledgments, membership epochs, clock bounds, placement failure domains, repair of cold keys, tombstone retention, and side effects outside the replicated log. They offer session guarantees where global coordination is unnecessary, quantify the availability cost of quorum, and design an eventual-to-consensus migration with explicit conflict policy, single authority per key, rollout cohorts, and rollback. The L6 answer connects the mechanism to product policy: who wins an existing username conflict is not a Raft decision.

docs.title: Cost Engineering for System Design
docs.text: Cost is a resource constraint and a design signal. A system that meets latency and availability goals but cannot sustain its unit economics is not production-ready. Cost engineering connects workload, architecture, reliability, and ownership in one model.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • build a unit-cost model from requests, bytes, compute time, and retention;
  • calculate storage, replication, egress, standby, observability, and compute cost drivers;
  • separate fixed, variable, step, and risk costs;
  • run sensitivity and break-even analyses rather than quote one forecast;
  • define cost-aware SLOs and overload/degradation policy; and
  • show L5 service optimization and L6 portfolio and commitment judgment.

docs.title: First principles: price the workload path
docs.text:
Cloud bills are outputs. Begin with resource consumption per business unit:

cost per successful operation = allocated monthly cost / successful operations
contribution per operation = revenue per operation - variable cost per operation

Choose a unit tied to product value: successful checkout, active tenant, streamed hour, indexed GB, or completed job. Requests alone can hide fan-out and failures. Keep unsuccessful and retried work visible.

Contribution is not accounting gross margin, and a nonmonetary value proxy cannot be subtracted from dollars. FinOps Unit Economics distinguishes resource-efficiency metrics from business-unit metrics. Record the allocation boundary and time window; a zero-success interval has undefined cost per success, not zero cost (accessed 2026-09-08).

flowchart LR
    D[Business demand] --> W[Requests and bytes]
    W --> C[Compute and memory]
    W --> S[Storage and I/O]
    W --> N[Network and egress]
    W --> O[Logs metrics and traces]
    C --> T[Total cost]
    S --> T
    N --> T
    O --> T
    R[Reliability topology] --> T
    T --> U[Cost per successful unit]

Classify cost behavior:

  • Fixed: control plane, minimum database cluster, baseline on-call tooling.
  • Variable: request CPU, bytes stored, egress, per-operation fees.
  • Step: another shard, NAT gateway, license tier, or reserved capacity block.
  • Risk: unplanned failover, incident egress, emergency scaling, penalties.
  • Opportunity: engineering complexity and delivery delay.

Allocation is not optimization. Tags and account boundaries can assign spend, but only workload drivers explain how to change it.

docs.title: Build a transparent monthly model
docs.text:
Use one worksheet with units and assumptions:

requests_month = requests_per_second * seconds_month
compute_hours  = instance_count * hours_month
stored_GB      = ingest_GB_day * retained_days * replication / compression
transfer_GB    = sum(bytes in mutually exclusive billable route classes)
monthly_cost   = compute + storage + IOPS + egress + managed_fees
               + observability + support + allocated_shared_cost

Use disjoint transfer rows, such as internet delivery, cross-zone replication, cross-region replication, and backup export. A replicated byte crossing a region must not be counted once as replication and again as an additional cross-region byte. Separate charges can still apply to that same byte, such as network transfer and gateway processing; model those as separate price components.

Use 2,592,000 seconds for a 30-day month and 720 hours. Keep decimal GB versus binary GiB consistent with the price sheet. Taxes, support, committed-use discounts, free tiers, and negotiated rates belong in separate explicit rows.

Do not hard-code public list prices into architecture claims. Prices vary by provider, region, tier, date, contract, and traffic direction. Store each input with source URL, region, retrieval date, and owner; rerun the model during reviews.

docs.title: Steady footprint versus GB-months
docs.text: Storage capacity and storage billing are different quantities. With no expiry, replication, or compression, a new system ingesting 4 TB/day reaches 120 TB after 30 days. Under continuous uniform ingestion, its average footprint over that month is 60 TB, so the month consumes about 60 TB-months, not 120 TB-months. The next month starts with the retained first-month data. Integrate the occupied or provisioned capacity over time and apply the provider's actual metering rules. A retention-sized steady-state estimate is appropriate only after the window fills.

docs.title: Compute and memory
docs.text:
Compute demand follows useful work, headroom, and topology:

cores_needed = peak_requests_per_second * CPU_seconds_per_request
provisioned_cores = cores_needed / target_peak_utilization

At 40,000 requests/s and 2.5 ms CPU/request, demand is 100 CPU-seconds/s, or 100 fully utilized cores. At a 60% target peak utilization, the starting provision is 100 / 0.60 = 167 cores. Then add N-1 zone or host failure policy, deployment surge, skew, and background work.

Memory can be the actual constraint. Include heap or process working set, caches, connection buffers, queues, page cache, sidecars, and fragmentation. Right-sizing CPU while paging or triggering long GC cycles increases both cost and user harm.

Autoscaling reduces variable idle capacity only when startup and signal delay fit the workload. A ten-minute boot cannot absorb a one-minute flash crowd. Keep warm headroom, scheduled scaling, admission control, or queueing for work whose deadlines allow it. Scale on demand signals such as concurrency or queue age, not CPU alone.

Spot or interruptible capacity suits checkpointable, retryable work. It is not automatically cheap if interruption causes large replay, egress, missed deadlines, or simultaneous fallback to expensive capacity. Commitments lower unit price but convert variable cost into a forecast obligation. Cover stable baseline first and preserve flexibility for uncertain growth.

docs.title: Storage: retained bytes are only the start
docs.text:
Monthly storage cost includes logical data, replicas, indexes, versions, metadata, WAL/logs, snapshots, temporary compaction space, and API/I/O charges.

Suppose ingest is 4 TB/day, retention 90 days, compression is 2.5:1, replication factor 3, indexes add 25% of compressed primary bytes, and operational free-space reserve is 30%:

compressed primary = 4 TB/day * 90 / 2.5 = 144 TB
replicated data    = 144 TB * 3 = 432 TB
with indexes       = 432 TB * 1.25 = 540 TB
provisioned at 70% = 540 TB / 0.70 = 771.4 TB

This is a steady-state physical-capacity estimate after the 90-day retention window fills. It excludes backups and write amplification. Provider-billed storage can differ: some managed prices already include durability copies, and usage-priced object storage does not bill an empty 30% disk reserve like provisioned block capacity. Do not multiply a provider's per-GB price by internal replica count unless that is its billing contract. Object-storage lifecycle tiers can reduce old-data price, but retrieval fees, minimum storage duration, restore latency, and request charges may dominate during reprocessing. Tie storage class to access distribution and RTO, not age alone.

Retention is a product, legal, reliability, and cost decision. Cutting raw retention from 90 to 30 days may save storage but make a 45-day fraud investigation impossible. A tiered design can retain aggregates online, raw data in colder storage, and deletion evidence separately.

docs.title: Network and egress
docs.text:
Use the Network Calculations Workbook to make bandwidth, serialization, connection, retry, and failover assumptions explicit before pricing the topology.

Network cost depends on direction and topology: internet egress, cross-zone, cross-region, CDN origin traffic, NAT processing, load-balancer bytes, private links, and provider-to-provider transfer can have different rates.

At 20,000 responses/s averaging 120 KB:

payload rate = 20,000 * 120 KB = 2.4 GB/s
per day      = 2.4 * 86,400 = 207,360 GB/day
per month    = 6,220,800 GB/month

Protocol overhead, retries, cache misses, and TLS do not make this smaller. If an edge cache raises byte hit ratio from 70% to 90%, origin payload falls from 30% to 10%, a 66.7% reduction in origin bytes. Request hit ratio and byte hit ratio differ; large-object misses can dominate egress.

Compression trades CPU and latency for bytes. Measure by content type and device. Moving compute near data can reduce transfer, but duplicating datasets across regions may cost more storage and replication. Include traffic during resharding, repair, restore, replay, and region evacuation.

docs.title: Replication, standby, and reliability cost
docs.text:
Replication pays for durability and availability, but replicas also incur compute, storage, log transfer, backups, and operations. A read replica is not free merely because it serves queries.

Compare three patterns:

Topology Normal cost Failure behavior Hidden cost single region, multi-zone lower survives zone faults no regional continuity warm regional standby medium scale and promote within RTO data lag, untested capacity, failover egress active-active regions high lower routing failover time conflict, duplicated baseline, coordination and testing

A standby sized at 20% is cheap only if it can reach required capacity before the RTO. If failover requires 15 minutes to provision but the RTO is 5 minutes, the cost model is buying an invalid design. Conversely, a fully active duplicate may be unjustified for a journey with a four-hour RTO.

N-1 capacity is a billable requirement. Three equal zones at 50% normal utilization rise to 75% after one zone fails. At 65%, survivors rise to 97.5% before skew. Model the failure workload and degradation policy, not only normal average.

docs.title: Observability cost and signal value
docs.text:
Observability cost comes from collection CPU, agents, network, ingestion, indexing, cardinality, retention, queries, archives, and human attention. More telemetry is not automatically more observable.

For 100,000 requests/s with one 4 KB log per request:

log ingest = 100,000 * 4 KB = 400 MB/s
per day    = 34.56 TB/day

At 30-day hot retention, that is over 1 PB before replication and indexes. Prefer structured low-volume outcome logs, metrics for aggregate health, sampled traces, and temporary targeted debug telemetry. Never sample away rare correctness or audit evidence by accident.

Metrics cardinality approximates the product of label dimensions that coexist. IDs, URLs with identifiers, and unbounded error text can bankrupt a time-series backend. Set per-team budgets for active series, log GB/day, trace spans, and retention. Provide dashboards that connect telemetry cost to owning service and signal use.

docs.title: Managed service versus self-managed
docs.text:
Compare total cost of ownership, not hourly node price:

TCO = infrastructure + licenses + support + engineering labor
    + incident loss + migration cost + compliance work + opportunity cost

A managed database may cost more per unit but reduce patching, backups, failover, and specialized staffing. It may also add egress, feature, quota, or lock-in constraints. Self-management can be rational at scale when workload-specific efficiency and internal expertise exceed the operating burden. Include 24x7 ownership and upgrade/recovery testing in both cases.

docs.title: Sensitivity and break-even analysis
docs.text:
A forecast without sensitivity is a disguised guess. Identify variables with uncertainty and cost leverage:

Variable Base Low High Cost effect peak requests/s 40k 25k 80k compute and quotas response size 120 KB 70 KB 200 KB CDN and egress cache byte hit ratio 85% 70% 93% origin compute and network retention 90 d 30 d 365 d storage and compliance compression 2.5x 1.5x 4x storage versus CPU

Use tornado analysis: vary one input while holding others fixed, rank the monthly deltas, then test correlated scenarios. Traffic and telemetry often rise together; treating them as independent understates the high case.

For build-versus-buy, let managed fixed cost be $30,000/month plus $0.10 per million operations, and self-managed cost be $80,000/month plus $0.02 per million. Ignoring omitted risks, break-even volume V in millions is:

30,000 + 0.10V = 80,000 + 0.02V
0.08V = 50,000
V = 625,000 million operations/month

The illustrative break-even is 625 billion operations/month, about 241,000 operations/s averaged over 30 days. These are invented prices for the algebra, not provider quotes.

The result is only as useful as included labor, commitments, support, migration, and reliability assumptions. Use it to locate questions, not manufacture certainty.

docs.title: Cost-aware SLOs
docs.text:
An SLO defines user value; cost constrains how it is delivered. Do not weaken correctness silently to save money. Segment journeys: checkout may need 99.99% while historical export can be queued with a 24-hour completion SLO.

Calculate the marginal cost of a reliability target. Moving from 99.9% to 99.99% may require multi-region capacity, stronger replication, lower-risk deployment, and more on-call investment. Compare that increment with expected user, contractual, and business harm. The cheapest valid design meets the required SLO with recovery evidence; it does not maximize availability everywhere.

Create degradation ladders tied to cost and overload:

  1. Disable expensive optional enrichment.
  2. Reduce result depth or freshness within the product contract.
  3. Queue deferrable work.
  4. Preserve paid or critical tenant fairness without starving control traffic.
  5. Reject quickly above the safe envelope.

Track cost per good request alongside availability and latency. A retry storm can increase spend while successful throughput falls. A useful operational guardrail is:

cost efficiency = good operations / consumed resource unit

Alert on abrupt efficiency drops, not on spending alone.

docs.title: Decision framework
docs.text:
1. Define business unit, demand distribution, SLO, RTO/RPO, and data lifecycle.
  2. Draw the request and data path, including retries, replication, telemetry, and recovery.
  3. Convert each path into CPU-seconds, GB-months, operations, and transferred bytes.
  4. Add failure headroom, standby, commitments, shared services, support, and labor.
  5. Calculate unit cost at low, base, high, and failure scenarios.
  6. Rank sensitivities and optimize the largest controllable driver.
  7. Validate changes against latency, correctness, availability, privacy, and operability.
  8. Assign budget ownership and calibrate forecast against actual usage monthly.

docs.title: Failure cases and tradeoffs
docs.text: Cost action Possible regression Guardrail raise utilization p99 and failover saturation load test and N-1 ceiling reduce replicas lower availability or durability explicit SLO, RPO, and restore evidence shorten retention lost investigation or replay legal/product review and tiered archive sample telemetry missed rare failures preserve audit and error exemplars reserve capacity stranded commitment cover stable baseline; scenario analysis use spot capacity interruption and replay checkpointing and fallback budget centralize tenants larger blast radius cells, quotas, isolation, restore units compress aggressively CPU and latency increase end-to-end benchmark by payload

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate quantifies service unit cost, sizes capacity from measurements, identifies dominant drivers, and preserves SLOs while optimizing. An L6 candidate also models portfolio commitments, shared-cost allocation, tenancy tiers, regional topology, migration economics, marginal reliability cost, budget policy, and how architecture standards prevent spend from becoming unowned externality.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Quoting a monthly cloud bill without a per-unit model.
  • Using average traffic and forgetting peak, skew, and failure headroom.
  • Counting logical storage but not replicas, indexes, WAL, backups, and free space.
  • Ignoring cross-zone, cross-region, NAT, and observability charges.
  • Declaring serverless or managed services cheaper at every scale.
  • Cutting telemetry without protecting audit and rare-error evidence.
  • Buying commitments before separating stable baseline from uncertain growth.
  • Optimizing cost by violating an unstated SLO.

docs.title: 1. Compute sizing
docs.text:
A handler needs 4 ms of CPU per request at 25,000 peak requests/s. Target peak CPU is 50%, and one zone out of three must be survivable without shedding. Estimate total provisioned cores before skew and deployment surge.

Answer: Peak demand is 25,000 * 0.004 = 100 cores. At 50% target utilization, 200 active cores are required under normal policy. To lose one of three equal zones while retaining 200 cores, each zone needs 100 cores, for 300 total. Add skew, background work, sidecars, and deployment surge after measurement.

docs.title: 2. Retention sensitivity
docs.text:
A stream ingests 2 TB/day, compresses 4:1, uses replication factor 3, and has 20% index overhead. Compare 30-day and 180-day stored footprints before free-space reserve.

Answer: At 30 days: 2 * 30 / 4 * 3 * 1.2 = 54 TB. At 180 days: 324 TB. The extra 150 days costs 270 TB of replicated indexed footprint, before backups and compaction. Evaluate colder tiers and retrieval/RTO rather than assuming all 180 days must remain hot.

docs.title: 3. Cache economics
docs.text:
Origin traffic is 1 PB/month at a 60% byte hit ratio. A cache change reaches 85% without changing demand. What happens to origin bytes?

Answer: Total demand is 1 PB / (1 - 0.60) = 2.5 PB/month. At 85% hit ratio, origin is 2.5 * 0.15 = 0.375 PB/month, a 62.5% reduction from 1 PB. Subtract added cache storage, invalidation, request, and compute cost, and verify freshness and tail latency.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Express spend per successful business unit and preserve units in every equation.
  • Model compute, memory, storage, I/O, egress, reliability, and telemetry together.
  • Include failure capacity and recovery traffic, not only normal averages.
  • Use sensitivity and break-even analysis to expose uncertain assumptions.
  • Optimize the largest controllable driver without violating correctness or SLOs.
  • Assign architecture and budget ownership, then calibrate forecasts with actuals.

docs.title: Authoritative sources
docs.text:
• FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework
  • FinOps Foundation, FOCUS Specification
  • Google, Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives
  • Google Cloud Architecture Center, Cost Optimization Framework
  • AWS, Well-Architected Cost Optimization Pillar
  • Microsoft Azure, Well-Architected Cost Optimization
  • CNCF, OpenCost Specification

docs.title: Database Indexing
docs.text:
Engineering extension: From SQL to physical work traces cardinality estimation, joins, spills, and maintenance load; performance science explains how to measure the resulting bottleneck without misleading percentile claims.

An index is a second physical representation of selected table values. It trades storage and write work for a cheaper way to locate rows. Good indexing starts with a concrete query shape, expected cardinality, and measured plan; it does not start with indexing every filterable column.

This chapter uses PostgreSQL 17-style examples, but the page, fanout, selectivity, and write-amplification reasoning applies broadly. For transaction, WAL, replica, and schema context, see Relational Databases. Search-engine inverted indexes are a different projection described in Search and Indexing.

docs.title: Heap storage versus clustered storage
docs.text:
In a heap-organized table, rows live in data pages without being physically ordered by a secondary index. A B+ tree leaf entry normally contains the indexed key plus a row locator. Finding one row is therefore two access paths: traverse the index, then fetch the heap page. PostgreSQL tables are heap-organized; an index scan can touch heap pages in scattered order.

A clustered table stores rows in primary-key order, or stores full rows in the primary B+ tree leaves. Range scans gain locality, but every secondary index must identify the primary key and primary-key changes become expensive. Some engines cluster by primary key continuously. PostgreSQL's CLUSTER rewrites a heap once in index order; later writes do not preserve that order automatically.

Layout Leaf points to Strength Cost heap plus secondary index physical or logical row locator stable row placement; multiple peers extra heap lookup; random I/O clustered primary index full row or clustered key primary-key ranges are local secondary leaves are wider; page splits move layout index-only access projected values in leaf avoids many heap reads wider index; visibility checks and writes remain

PostgreSQL's MVCC can leave multiple tuple versions in a heap page. An index entry may lead to a dead or invisible tuple until vacuum reclaims it. An index-only scan can avoid heap access only when all required columns are in the index and the visibility map proves the heap page is visible to all relevant snapshots. Heap Fetches: 0 in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) is evidence; the words Index Only Scan alone are not.

flowchart LR
    Q[Predicate] --> R[Root page]
    R --> I[Internal page]
    I --> L[Leaf page with key and row locator]
    L --> H[Heap page]
    H --> T[Visible tuple version]

docs.title: B+ tree pages, fanout, and height
docs.text:
A B+ tree stores separator keys and child pointers in root and internal pages; leaves store sorted keys and row locators and are linked for ordered traversal. All leaves are at the same depth. A lookup does one binary search per visited page, while the page cache and storage device determine whether that visit is memory-speed or an I/O.

Suppose an 8 KiB internal page has 256 bytes of headers and safety space. If an average separator plus child pointer consumes 24 bytes, the rough fanout is:

fanout = floor((8192 - 256) / 24) = 330

Real pages reserve free space, keys vary, and prefix compression differs by engine, so use a conservative fanout of 250. Here, a page level includes the root and leaf, while a branch step is one parent-to-child edge. A three-page-level tree (root, one internal level, leaves) has two branch steps and addresses about 250^2 = 62,500 leaf pages. If each leaf averages 200 entries, that is about 62,500 * 200 = 12.5 million rows. A four-page-level tree (root, two internal levels, leaves) has three branch steps and covers about 250^3 * 200 = 3.125 billion rows. Point lookup visits three or four index pages respectively, plus a heap page when the index does not cover the query. This is why B+ tree lookup height grows slowly. The bigger operational cost is often random heap access, cache misses, or returning many rows, not a handful of page-local comparisons.

Wide keys reduce fanout and cache density. Replacing a 48-byte text key with a compact surrogate may remove a level at large scale, but a surrogate is not automatically useful: the query may still need a separate wide-key index and a heap lookup. Calculate complete access paths rather than optimizing one tree in isolation.

docs.title: Equality and range mechanics
docs.text:
For customer_id = 42, the tree descends to the first matching leaf entry and reads adjacent entries until the value changes. For created_at >= T1 AND created_at < T2, it descends once to T1, then follows leaf pages sequentially until T2. Sorting is free only when the required order matches the index ordering, including direction and tie-breakers.

CREATE INDEX order_customer_history
ON customer_order (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

SELECT id, total_cents, created_at
FROM customer_order
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND (created_at, id) < (TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-01 10:00:00+00', 9000)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;

The equality on customer_id selects one contiguous section. The tuple range starts at the cursor, and the ordering matches the index. This supports bounded keyset pagination. An index on (created_at, customer_id) would mix every customer in the time range and filter afterward.

docs.title: Composite indexes and the left prefix
docs.text:
For a B+ tree on (a, b, c), rows are ordered by a, then by b within equal a, then by c. Efficient navigation generally uses a contiguous left prefix:

Predicate Useful navigation on (tenant_id, status, created_at) tenant_id = ? yes, first key tenant_id = ? AND status = ? yes, first two keys tenant_id = ? AND status = ? AND created_at >= ? yes, equality prefix then range tenant_id = ? AND created_at >= ? only tenant_id bounds navigation; status is a gap status = ? usually cannot seek by the leading key

Place equality columns before the first range or ordering column when that matches the workload. After a range begins, later columns usually cannot narrow the contiguous leaf interval, although they may be checked in the index and avoid heap work. "Most selective first" is not a universal composite-index rule. Leading equality, required ordering, reusable query prefixes, and range position matter together.

Two superficially similar queries can need different indexes:

-- Operations queue: equality, equality, then oldest first.
CREATE INDEX job_claim_path
ON job (region, state, available_at, id)
WHERE state IN ('READY', 'RETRY');

-- Tenant audit history: equality, then newest range.
CREATE INDEX audit_tenant_time
ON audit_event (tenant_id, occurred_at DESC, event_id DESC);

The queue example assumes one fixed region and one fixed state in each scan. If the query instead asks for state IN ('READY', 'RETRY') ORDER BY available_at, the index contains separate state-ordered runs, not one global time order. The planner may need a sort or merged scans. A partial index on (region, available_at, id) with the same active-state predicate is an alternative when both states share one queue and the query predicate permits that index.

Do not append every output column to the key portion. Key columns determine ordering and can enlarge internal separators as well as leaves; PostgreSQL may truncate unnecessary trailing key columns from upper levels. Payload columns that only support index-only reads belong in an INCLUDE clause where supported.

docs.title: Selectivity, cardinality, and correlation
docs.text:
Selectivity is the fraction of rows expected to pass a predicate. If a table has 100 million rows and state = 'READY' selects 18 million, an index may cause millions of row locators and scattered heap reads; a sequential scan can be cheaper. If tenant_id = 71 AND state = 'READY' selects 900 rows, a composite index is likely valuable.

The break-even point is not a fixed percentage. It depends on row width, cached pages, physical correlation, storage latency, parallelism, and whether the index covers the query. A rough cold-I/O comparison illustrates the decision:

table: 80 GiB / 8 KiB = 10,485,760 heap pages
sequential scan at 1.5 GiB/s: about 53 seconds before CPU
index result: 120,000 rows on about 95,000 scattered heap pages
random reads at effective 25,000 IOPS: about 3.8 seconds

At 5 million matching rows scattered over 3.8 million pages, the same estimate is 152 seconds, so the table scan wins. If matching rows are physically correlated and occupy 70,000 adjacent pages, the index range can win again. Estimates must model pages, not just row percentages.

Planners estimate cardinality from sampled statistics: distinct counts, null fraction, common values, histograms, and sometimes cross-column dependency or correlation statistics. Independent-column assumptions fail for facts such as country = 'IN' and currency = 'INR'. Create extended statistics where supported, increase statistics targets for skewed columns, and refresh statistics after material distribution changes. An index cannot repair a cardinality estimate the planner does not understand.

docs.title: Covering indexes
docs.text:
A covering index contains every column needed by a query. In PostgreSQL, INCLUDE carries non-key values without making them part of ordering:

CREATE INDEX invoice_account_due
ON invoice (account_id, due_at, id)
INCLUDE (amount_cents, currency, status);

Coverage can remove heap reads for stable pages, but it widens leaves, lowers fanout, consumes cache, and amplifies updates. Included columns still have maintenance cost. Cover a frequent, latency-sensitive query after measuring heap fetches; do not cover SELECT *.

docs.title: Partial indexes
docs.text:
A partial index stores only rows satisfying a predicate:

CREATE INDEX payment_unsettled_retry
ON payment_attempt (next_retry_at, id)
WHERE settled_at IS NULL AND terminal = false;

It is smaller and avoids indexing rows outside the active set. Moving a row out of that set still creates cleanup work for its old index entry. The planner must be able to prove that the query predicate implies the index predicate. Parameterized or logically equivalent but opaque expressions can prevent use. Partial unique indexes can enforce scoped invariants, such as one active lease per resource.

docs.title: Hash indexes
docs.text: Hash indexes map equality keys to buckets and do not support ordering, prefix, or range scans. They can suit equality-only access, but a B+ tree also handles equality and is usually more versatile. Choose hash only from measured engine-specific behavior, collision handling, durability, and operational support, not from an assumed O(1) slogan.

docs.title: Bitmap access
docs.text:
A bitmap represents candidate row locations compactly and combines predicates with bitwise AND or OR. PostgreSQL commonly builds transient bitmaps from ordinary indexes, then visits heap pages in physical order:

Bitmap Index Scan on color_idx ----+
                                    +--> BitmapAnd --> Bitmap Heap Scan
Bitmap Index Scan on region_idx ---+

This can beat independent random row fetches for medium-selectivity predicates. Some analytical systems maintain persistent bitmap indexes, which compress low-cardinality values well but can be costly under high-concurrency updates. Distinguish a bitmap execution plan from a persisted bitmap index.

docs.title: GIN and GiST
docs.text:
GIN is an inverted mapping from contained keys to rows. It fits arrays, document keys, and full-text terms where one row emits many index entries. Reads can be excellent; writes and pending-list cleanup can be expensive.

GiST is a framework for hierarchical, possibly overlapping predicates. Operator classes define concepts such as bounding boxes and distance. It supports spatial, range-overlap, and nearest-neighbor access where ordinary total ordering is insufficient. Because internal bounds may be lossy, the engine can return candidates and recheck the original predicate.

The operator and operator class must match. "Create a GIN/GiST index" is incomplete without naming the query operators, data distribution, recheck behavior, and update rate.

docs.title: Write amplification and page splits
docs.text:
Every secondary index turns one logical row change into more physical work: WAL records, dirty index pages, cache pressure, replica bytes, backup growth, and vacuum or cleanup. If 12,000 updates/s touch a table and four indexes, a lower-bound logical count is 12,000 * (1 table + 4 indexes) = 60,000 structure mutations/s before WAL, full-page images, replication, and page rewrites.

An insert into a full leaf page splits it, allocates a sibling, moves entries, and inserts a separator into the parent. A parent can split recursively. Random keys spread insert pressure but fragment many pages; monotonically increasing keys concentrate writes at the right edge but preserve locality. Fill factor reserves space to reduce splits for update-heavy or randomly inserted indexes at the cost of a larger tree.

In PostgreSQL, an update that changes no indexed column may use a heap-only tuple update when the page has room, avoiding new entries in every index. Adding a frequently changing column to an index disables that advantage for those updates. Dead entries persist until vacuum can remove them; long transactions delay cleanup and can turn a logically small table into a large physical one.

docs.title: Read plans as evidence
docs.text:
Use a controlled loop rather than intuition:

  1. Capture the exact SQL, bind-value distribution, result count, frequency, and latency objective.
  2. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL, SETTINGS, FORMAT TEXT) in a safe environment with representative data and parameters.
  3. Read from the leaves upward: actual rows, loops, time, buffer hits/reads, sorts, heap fetches, and rows removed by filters.
  4. Compare estimated rows with actual rows per execution. Multiply actual rows and node time by loops only to estimate cumulative work; multiplying only the actual side falsely reports a cardinality error. A large per-execution error points to stale statistics, correlation, or parameter sensitivity before a missing index.
  5. Create the smallest candidate index in a test environment, refresh statistics, rerun warm and cold-enough trials, and compare total write/storage cost.
  6. Test worst credible tenants, common values, empty results, large ranges, and prepared-statement behavior. One fast literal is not a workload.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL, SETTINGS)
SELECT id, amount_cents, created_at
FROM payment_attempt
WHERE merchant_id = 771
  AND state = 'FAILED'
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-09-01 00:00:00+00'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 100;

Key evidence:

Signal Interpretation sequential scan with many rows removed candidate access-path problem, unless predicate is broad index scan returning far more rows than output weak bounds or filtering after the scan estimate 50, actual 500,000 statistics/distribution problem that can distort joins and memory large shared reads, few hits working set is not resident; test realistic cache state sort spills to temporary blocks ordering/index or memory decision, not just scan time index-only scan with many heap fetches visibility churn limits actual coverage benefit fast node repeated many loops cumulative nested-loop cost may dominate

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Use an isolated writable test database for mutations; a read-only replica is suitable only for supported reads. A rollback does not undo sequence increments or external trigger effects. Never run an unbounded expensive plan on production merely to inspect it; plain EXPLAIN does not execute. PostgreSQL 17, Using EXPLAIN documents per-loop averages and execution side effects (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Online index lifecycle
docs.text:
An index is an operated object, not a one-time DDL statement.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Proposed
    Proposed --> Building: workload evidence
    Building --> Validating: online build complete
    Validating --> Serving: plan and latency gates pass
    Validating --> Dropped: regression or invalid build
    Serving --> Rebuilding: bloat or definition change
    Rebuilding --> Serving: replacement validated
    Serving --> Dropped: observation window proves unused

A PostgreSQL-style rollout is:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY payment_merchant_failed_v2
ON payment_attempt (merchant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)
INCLUDE (amount_cents)
WHERE state = 'FAILED';

ANALYZE payment_attempt;

SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid, indisready
FROM pg_index
WHERE indexrelid = 'payment_merchant_failed_v2'::regclass;

Concurrent creation avoids a long write-blocking table lock, but it takes longer, performs extra scans, consumes I/O, waits on old transactions, and can leave an invalid index after failure. Verify validity, build progress, replica lag, disk reserve, WAL rate, and query plans. Throttle or cancel when foreground SLOs or recovery headroom are threatened.

Before removal, identify overlapping definitions and observe query plans over a full business cycle. Usage counters reset and prepared plans can hide dependencies, so zero scans is evidence, not proof. Remove with the engine's online form where available:

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY payment_merchant_failed_v1;

Changing a definition is normally create-new, validate, shift, then drop-old. Preserve enough disk for both indexes and build workspace. Rehearse cancellation and cleanup; schema migration tools need non-transactional handling for concurrent index commands.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Name the query, predicates, order, limit, selected columns, and expected rows.
  • Draw the complete index-to-heap path and estimate pages, not only Big-O.
  • Use equality prefixes before the first range when the access pattern supports it.
  • Check selectivity, skew, correlation, and estimate error with representative binds.
  • Treat coverage and partial predicates as write/storage tradeoffs.
  • Match specialized structures to operators, not data type names alone.
  • Quantify table, WAL, replica, vacuum, and page-split amplification.
  • Validate with actual rows, loops, buffers, heap fetches, spills, and latency.
  • Build, verify, observe, replace, and drop through an online lifecycle.

docs.title: Check the plan you expect
docs.text:
A tenant history index is (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC). Your query fixes tenant_id, filters no status, and requests the newest 50 rows across every status. Does this index inherently provide the requested order?

Trace the sorted runs

No. Within that tenant, rows are grouped by status before time. The first 50 entries can belong to one status rather than the newest 50 across all statuses. A (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) index fits this query and supplies a deterministic tie-breaker. The original index may still help other queries, but retaining both has a write and storage cost. Verify the actual plan and representative tenants before adding it.

Vendor scope (PostgreSQL 17, accessed 2026-09-19): The left-prefix discussion follows multicolumn indexes. Coverage still requires the visibility-map condition, and online DDL follows the restrictions in CREATE INDEX. Optimizer features differ across versions; this is not a promise that every later planner uses the same access path.

docs.title: A Delivery Framework for System Design
docs.text:
Engineering extension: Architecture decisions under uncertainty supplies a worked ADR, sensitivity analysis, reversibility tests, and an adversarial review. Carry those decisions through the Atlas capstone, rather than restarting from a new diagram at each scale.

System design interviews test decision quality, not diagram density. A strong answer turns ambiguity into requirements, invariants, numbers, and an architecture whose failure behavior is explicit.

Read the diagram guide to distinguish architecture, message order, and durable acceptance before using the diagrams as a design contract.

docs.title: The 45-minute loop
docs.text: Time Deliverable Failure to avoid 0-5 min users, use cases, exclusions, SLOs solving an unstated problem 5-10 min invariants and estimates choosing storage by fashion 10-20 min API, data model, baseline design drawing boxes without flows 20-35 min bottlenecks and requirement-led scaling premature global complexity 35-42 min failures, recovery, operations treating retries as recovery 42-45 min tradeoffs and summary ending without a recommendation

docs.title: Start with a design contract
docs.text:
Ask who performs each action, what must be synchronous, expected geography, retention, and what may be stale. Convert answers into testable statements:

  • Functional: a buyer can place an order and retrieve its status.
  • Invariant: one accepted checkout creates at most one chargeable order.
  • SLO: 99.9% of checkout responses complete within 800 ms monthly.
  • Scale: 5,000 average and 25,000 peak checkouts/s.
  • Exclusion: catalog authoring and payment-rail internals.

Do not call availability or consistency "high." Give a target and scope. A 99.99% read SLO does not imply writes, every region, or every dependency share that target.

docs.title: Work from requirements to components
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    R["1. Frame the problem<br/>Requirements, invariants, SLOs"] --> D["2. Build a baseline<br/>Data, APIs, one end-to-end flow"]
    D --> X["3. Stress the design<br/>Estimate the limiting resource"]
    X --> E["4. Evolve with evidence<br/>Address the measured bottleneck"]
    E --> F["5. Test the promise<br/>Failure, recovery, tradeoffs"]
    F -.->|revise the assumption| X

For every box, state its contract: input, output, durable state, timeout, retry owner, and overload response. Then trace one success and one failure end to end.

docs.title: A concrete walkthrough
docs.text:
For ticket reservation, assume 1 million seats, 20,000 peak attempts/s, and ten celebrity events receiving 80% of traffic. The key invariant is confirmed + held <= capacity; overselling is unacceptable, while search results may be 30 seconds stale.

Baseline: one relational database transaction conditionally decrements availability and inserts a five-minute hold. Scale reads using a cache and search projection. Scale hot writes only after measuring lock waits: serialize commands per event or partition seats into independently owned pools. This reasoning is stronger than starting with Kafka because each mechanism answers a stated constraint.

docs.title: Decision record
docs.text: Question Default Escalate when synchronous or async? sync for user-visible acceptance work exceeds latency budget or can be deferred SQL or distributed KV? SQL for constraints and transactions partition-local access dominates and scale exceeds one cluster cache? no cache initially repeated reads or computation justify invalidation cost queue? direct call buffering, fan-out, or temporal decoupling is required multi-region writes? one write region measured RTO, regulation, or latency requires more

docs.title: Failure semantics
docs.text:
Define outcomes, not merely faults:

  • Before durable acceptance: return failure; the client may retry with an idempotency key.
  • After acceptance but before response: return unknown; retry returns the stored result.
  • Async handler failure: retry with bounded backoff, then quarantine; never silently discard.
  • Projection lag: canonical reads remain correct; expose lag and degrade nonessential views.
  • Overload: shed optional work and reject early rather than consume all threads and time out.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API
    participant D as Canonical DB
    C->>A: command(key)
    A->>D: transaction(command, key)
    D-->>A: committed
    A--xC: response lost
    C->>A: retry(key)
    A->>D: read prior result
    A-->>C: same result

docs.title: L5 versus L6
docs.text: An L5 answer is coherent, quantified, and covers primary bottlenecks and recovery. An L6 answer also surfaces hidden policy, hot-key skew, migration steps, ownership boundaries, cost, and which complexity can be postponed. End with the recommendation, its limiting assumption, and the first metric that would force redesign.

docs.title: Turn ambiguity into a scored contract
docs.text:
Interview prompts are intentionally underspecified. Do not spend five minutes collecting every conceivable requirement. Ask questions that can reverse an architectural choice. For a ticketing system, these are high-value questions: Is a seat selected or automatically assigned? Is overselling forbidden or merely undesirable? Does payment happen before or after the hold? How concentrated is demand per event? Can users buy across regions? A question about profile avatars is low value because its answer is unlikely to change the core design.

Write a compact contract with four columns:

Statement Scope Measurement Design consequence no confirmed seat has two owners confirmation command invariant violations = 0 serialize or conditionally claim each seat hold response is fast successful hold API p99 under 500 ms keep payment and email off the synchronous path availability may lag browse API age under 10 s for 99.9% permit a cache or projection recover after zone loss regional service RTO 2 min, RPO 0 for confirmations synchronously replicate canonical writes across zones

The distinction between an invariant and an SLO matters. An invariant has no percentile: allowing 0.1% double booking is not a latency tradeoff. An SLO has a window and an error budget. At 10 million monthly hold requests, 99.9% availability permits 10,000 failed requests. The design must say whether overload rejections and dependency failures consume that budget.

flowchart TD
    P[Ambiguous prompt] --> Q[Questions that change choices]
    Q --> FR[Functional requirements]
    Q --> INV[Correctness invariants]
    Q --> SLO[Latency and availability SLOs]
    Q --> EX[Explicit exclusions]
    INV --> M[Required coordination]
    SLO --> B[Capacity and failure budget]
    FR --> AP[API and access paths]
    M --> BASE[Smallest correct baseline]
    B --> BASE
    AP --> BASE

docs.title: Build and stress the smallest correct system
docs.text:
Start with one deployable service and one transactional database when that can meet the stated scale. This is not naivety; it exposes the actual consistency boundary. Split components only when a measured property requires independent scaling, isolation, ownership, or release cadence.

For the ticket example, suppose peak demand is 20,000 attempts/s, but 80% targets ten events. An average partition calculation is misleading. Each hot event receives about 20,000 * 0.8 / 10 = 1,600 attempts/s. If one database transaction for an event takes 4 ms while holding a shared event-level lock, that lock permits at most 250 serial operations/s. More database replicas do not remove this write bottleneck. Seat-level conditional writes, partitioned inventory pools, or an event command sequencer address it; a read cache does not.

Use this stress loop for every major component:

  1. Name the resource: CPU, bandwidth, IOPS, connections, lock time, queue age, or storage.
  2. Calculate demand under normal peak and one credible failure.
  3. Identify the saturation signal and safe operating limit.
  4. Choose an overload action before saturation.
  5. State the next design and the threshold that activates it.

If three zones each provide 10,000 requests/s and peak load is 20,000 requests/s, normal utilization is 67%. Losing one zone leaves exactly 20,000 requests/s, or 100% theoretical capacity. That is unsafe because retries, maintenance, and imbalance need headroom. Either provision each zone above 12,500 requests/s, reduce admitted work, or accept that the target RTO is impossible.

docs.title: Trace protocols, not arrows
docs.text:
An architecture diagram becomes useful when every arrow has semantics. For a create operation, state request identity, deadline propagation, authentication context, retry policy, and whether acknowledgment means buffered, replicated, or committed. For an event, state partition key, ordering scope, delivery semantics, retention, poison-message handling, and consumer idempotency.

Consider hold creation:

  1. The client sends command ID K, seat list, and a 700 ms deadline.
  2. The API authenticates the principal, validates the request, and hashes its canonical form.
  3. One transaction claims K under a uniqueness constraint, conditionally claims the seats, inserts the hold and outbox row, and records the response for K.
  4. The transaction commits after synchronous replicas acknowledge.
  5. An outbox publisher later emits HoldCreated; notification and search consumers deduplicate by event ID.
  6. If the response is lost after step 4, a retry with K reads the recorded result. Reuse of K with a different hash returns a client error.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Hold API
    participant DB as Canonical DB
    participant O as Outbox relay
    participant N as Notification
    C->>A: create seats, command K, deadline
    A->>DB: claim seats + result K + outbox E atomically
    DB-->>A: committed hold H
    A-->>C: 201 H
    DB-->>O: committed outbox row
    O->>N: HoldCreated(event E)
    N->>N: dedupe E and send
    N-->>O: acknowledged

Do not claim that the queue makes the workflow exactly once. The transaction makes canonical acceptance atomic, while command IDs and event IDs make repeated effects harmless. External effects such as sending email may still need provider idempotency keys and reconciliation.

State the provider horizon when defending that last claim. Stripe's primary contract retains executed responses, including 500, but may prune keys after at least 24 hours. A retry with the same key after pruning can be a new effect; an unknown outcome then needs reconciliation rather than an unbounded retry promise (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Failure table before exotic scaling
docs.text:
Walk through failures at boundaries, including ambiguous outcomes:

Failure point What the caller knows Safe response Recovery evidence API dies before transaction no acceptance retry K no idempotency row database commits, API dies outcome unknown retry K stored response and commit record outbox relay stops hold exists, event delayed restart from checkpoint outbox age and unpublished rows consumer poison event one projection stalls or skips only by policy bounded retry then quarantine dead-letter alert plus replay tool cache fleet fails canonical state intact budgeted bypass or reject browse traffic origin saturation and cache health entire region fails depends on replication promise fail over after fencing old writer replication position and epoch

Retries consume capacity precisely when dependencies are unhealthy. Give each call one deadline smaller than its caller's remaining deadline, exponential backoff with jitter, and a retry budget. If a dependency normally sees 10,000 calls/s and clients retry 20% of timeouts twice, it can receive 14,000 calls/s while already degraded. Admission control, bounded queues, and circuit breaking prevent this positive feedback loop.

docs.title: Evolve with reversible rollout steps
docs.text:
A mature answer includes how the baseline becomes the scaled design without a flag day. To replace direct availability reads with a projection:

  1. Define the projection schema and include canonical version or event position.
  2. Publish changes through a transactional outbox while existing reads stay unchanged.
  3. Backfill historical state with checkpoints; consumers must tolerate backfill and live events arriving out of order.
  4. Shadow-read both stores and compare results by age and semantic equivalence.
  5. Enable projection reads for employees, then 1%, 10%, and 50% of traffic while watching mismatch, lag, and origin load.
  6. Keep checkout on canonical validation regardless of browse rollout.
  7. Roll back by routing reads to the database; continue publishing so the projection does not fall further behind.
  8. Remove the old read path only after a defined observation window.

Schema and partition migrations need the same discipline: dual-compatible software first, bounded backfill second, cutover third, cleanup last. Dual writes from application code are dangerous because one side can succeed alone. Prefer one canonical write plus change capture, or record repairable intent atomically.

docs.title: Interview traps and course corrections
docs.text:
• Naming technology before invariants: saying "use Cassandra for scale" does not establish whether uniqueness, range scans, or transactions are needed. Recover by listing access paths and invariants first.
  • Scaling averages: a uniform 20,000 QPS says nothing about a celebrity event. Add a hottest-key estimate and show where serialization occurs.
  • Treating a queue as durability: define acknowledgment, replication, retention, replay, and what happens after poison messages.
  • Confusing high availability with no errors: specify failure scope, SLO window, RTO, RPO, and degraded behavior.
  • Putting all work on the request path: separate acceptance from deferrable effects, but retain an observable operation status.
  • Adding multi-region active-active by reflex: if one write region meets latency and recovery goals, active-active adds conflict policy without product value.
  • Ignoring deletion: deleting canonical rows while retaining caches, search documents, outbox payloads, and backups violates the user-visible contract.

docs.title: Concrete L5 and L6 reasoning
docs.text:
At L5, the candidate should drive a coherent vertical slice: clarify two or three decisive requirements, quantify peak and storage, define APIs and schema, trace success and ambiguous timeout, identify a bottleneck, and choose a justified scaling mechanism. "I use a conditional seat claim because overselling is forbidden; browse is a stale projection because it is advisory" is concrete L5 reasoning.

At L6, the candidate changes the shape of the problem. They ask whether fairness, bot resistance, regional regulation, or event-operator isolation is part of correctness. They distinguish the inventory data plane from the event-admission control plane, calculate failure capacity, and explain migration and rollback. They might recommend a waiting room that issues signed admission grants for exceptional events rather than permanently overbuilding the reservation database. They also identify ownership: commerce owns canonical inventory, the platform team owns the event stream, and an explicit schema contract prevents either team from silently breaking replay.

Finish in five sentences: the product contract, the canonical write path, the derived read path, the principal failure behavior, and the threshold for the next evolution. This ending demonstrates prioritization instead of merely reciting components.

docs.title: Distributed Transactions and Workflows
docs.text:
Executable extension: Run the outbox/inbox fixture, then review correctness methods to separate simulated atomicity, actual process-restart evidence, and unsupported external-effect guarantees.

A distributed transaction coordinates one business outcome across state owned by different failure and concurrency domains. The central problem is not making every step atomic. It is preserving explicit invariants when messages, responses, processes, and coordinators fail at inconvenient times.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • define local ACID boundaries and avoid distributing an invariant unnecessarily;
  • explain two-phase commit, blocking, recovery, and heuristic danger;
  • implement transactional outbox and idempotent inbox protocols;
  • choose sagas, TCC, escrow, or reconciliation from business semantics;
  • handle unknown outcomes and retries without duplicate effects; and
  • demonstrate L5 protocol depth and L6 cross-domain operating policy.

docs.title: First principles: invariants and knowledge
docs.text:
Start with a business invariant, not a workflow diagram:

I1: available inventory never becomes negative
I2: one checkout request creates at most one charge
I3: every accepted order eventually becomes fulfilled, cancelled, or escalated

I1 and I2 are safety properties: a forbidden outcome must never occur. I3 is a liveness property: accepted work must eventually make progress. A system can preserve safety by refusing all work and still fail liveness. State the recovery assumptions and escalation deadline that make I3 achievable.

Classify each business requirement:

  • Immediate: must hold before success is acknowledged.
  • Convergent: may be temporarily false but must repair within a bound.
  • Compensatable: a later semantic action can offset an earlier action.
  • Reconciled: independent evidence can detect and repair divergence.

Atomicity does not eliminate uncertainty for a remote caller. If a server commits and its response is lost, the caller cannot distinguish commit from failure. Stable command identity and outcome lookup are therefore part of the protocol.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Received
    Received --> Committed: local transaction commits
    Received --> Rejected: validation or conflict
    Committed --> Returned: response delivered
    Committed --> UnknownToCaller: response lost
    UnknownToCaller --> Returned: retry with same key reads outcome

docs.title: Local ACID before distributed coordination
docs.text:
Put data that participates in one tight invariant in one transactional boundary when scale and ownership allow it. A local transaction can atomically write canonical state, command outcome, and an outbox record:

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO command_result(command_key, request_hash, state)
VALUES (:key, :hash, 'IN_PROGRESS');

UPDATE inventory
SET available = available - :quantity
WHERE sku = :sku AND available >= :quantity;
-- Require exactly one affected row.

INSERT INTO reservation(reservation_id, sku, quantity, state)
VALUES (:reservation_id, :sku, :quantity, 'HELD');

INSERT INTO outbox(event_id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload)
VALUES (:event_id, :reservation_id, 'InventoryHeld', :payload);

UPDATE command_result SET state = 'SUCCEEDED', result_id = :reservation_id
WHERE command_key = :key;

COMMIT;

The unique command key prevents duplicate execution. Scope it to the authenticated tenant and operation, validate a strictly positive quantity before mutation, and enforce nonnegative inventory and positive reservation quantities with database constraints. Store a request hash so reuse of the same key with different input is rejected. The affected-row check must abort the transaction on zero rows; a SQL comment does not implement that branch. On a duplicate key, roll back this attempt and read the committed outcome rather than continuing with the stock update. No broker transaction is needed for the invariant.

docs.title: Two-phase commit
docs.text:
Two-phase commit, or 2PC, coordinates participants that can prepare and later commit or abort.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Coordinator
    participant A as Participant A
    participant B as Participant B
    C->>A: PREPARE transaction X
    C->>B: PREPARE transaction X
    A-->>C: YES, durable prepared state
    B-->>C: YES, durable prepared state
    C->>C: Durably record COMMIT X
    C->>A: COMMIT X
    C->>B: COMMIT X
    A-->>C: ACK
    B-->>C: ACK

In phase one, each participant validates and durably records enough state to commit later while retaining required locks or reservations. If all vote yes, the coordinator durably chooses commit; otherwise it chooses abort. Phase two communicates the decision. Participants recover prepared transactions from durable logs and query the coordinator or recovery peers for the outcome.

2PC provides atomic commitment under its model; it does not provide arbitrary distributed serializability unless concurrency control across participants does so. It can block a prepared participant while the decision is unavailable. Long-lived locks amplify tail latency and deadlocks. Operationally dangerous manual outcomes can create heuristic mixed states.

Use 2PC when participants expose compatible prepare/commit semantics, the transaction is short, availability loss during coordinator uncertainty is acceptable, and atomicity is more valuable than loose coupling. Avoid holding a prepared database transaction while waiting for a human, shipping provider, or unbounded remote API.

docs.title: Transactional outbox and idempotent inbox
docs.text:
The dual-write problem appears when a service writes its database and broker separately. Either order has a crash window. An outbox writes the business state and event in one local transaction. A relay publishes unprocessed rows and records progress. Publication is at least once, so consumers deduplicate.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant API
    participant DB as Orders and outbox DB
    participant R as Relay
    participant B as Broker
    participant C as Consumer
    API->>DB: Commit order plus event E
    R->>DB: Read unsent E
    R->>B: Publish E
    B--xR: acknowledgment lost
    B->>C: deliver E
    C->>C: commit effect and inbox E atomically
    R->>B: publish E again
    B->>C: deliver duplicate E
    C->>C: inbox E exists, skip repeated effect

An inbox is a unique (consumer, event_id) record written in the same transaction as the consumer's database effect. Acknowledgment follows commit. Retain dedup evidence for the maximum redelivery and replay horizon, or use permanent business identity/version semantics.

Outbox details matter:

  • preserve aggregate ID, aggregate version, event ID, schema version, and occurred time;
  • partition relay work without publishing two versions of one aggregate out of order;
  • monitor oldest unpublished age, attempts, poison rows, and table growth;
  • delete or archive only after publication evidence and replay requirements permit;
  • rebuild downstream projections from canonical state or retained events.

docs.title: Sagas
docs.text:
A saga is a sequence of local transactions connected by messages, with compensating actions for completed steps. Compensation is business logic, not database rollback. A refund does not erase that a charge occurred; a cancellation may incur a fee; an email cannot be unsent.

flowchart TD
    O[Create order] --> I[Reserve inventory]
    I --> P[Authorize payment]
    P --> F[Confirm fulfillment]
    I -->|fails| C1[Cancel order]
    P -->|fails| C2[Release inventory]
    F -->|fails| C3[Void or refund payment]
    C3 --> C2
    C2 --> C1

Orchestration centralizes state transitions, deadlines, and visibility. Choreography lets services react to events but can hide the global state machine and create cycles. Prefer an explicit durable workflow for long or high-value processes. Store current state, step attempts, next wake time, external references, and compensation state.

Every forward and compensating command needs stable identity. Model terminal states including SUCCEEDED, COMPENSATED, FAILED_MANUAL, and EXPIRED. Do not retry permanent business rejection. Bound retries and escalate when automation cannot restore the invariant.

docs.title: Try-confirm-cancel
docs.text:
Try-confirm-cancel, or TCC, asks each participant to reserve a resource, then confirm or cancel it.

TRY:     create hold H with quantity, owner, and expires_at
CONFIRM: consume H exactly once and create final allocation
CANCEL:  release H exactly once

TCC exposes reservation semantics and avoids holding database locks across services. It needs capacity reserved during the decision window, idempotent operations, authorization of the holder, expiry, and a sweeper. Expiry races with confirm: use an atomic state transition such as HELD -> CONFIRMED only if current time and policy permit, and make the caller observe the definitive result.
