Compression and TTL reduce retained bytes but do not erase ingest I/O. A 7-day raw retention is 272.16 TB logical before replication and overhead. Validate per-node network, WAL, flush, compaction, repair, and disk-free-space limits.

Define the measured amplification numerator before multiplying: the 12.96 GB/s example assumes the 8x engine factor excludes the separately budgeted overhead. If a metric already includes WAL or replicas, do not add them again. PostgreSQL's WAL description illustrates why sequential log bytes and eventual data-page writes are distinct resource streams even outside an LSM engine (accessed 2026-09-08).

For a bucketed wide-column table receiving 2,000 events/s from one hot device at 500 bytes/event, one day produces 172.8 million rows and 86.4 GB before overhead. Daily bucketing is still too large; hash or hour sub-buckets may be needed, at the cost of read fan-out.

docs.title: Failure cases and operations
docs.text: Failure Consequence Design response hot partition one shard saturates while fleet is idle better key, sub-buckets, admission and migration compaction debt p99 and disk usage climb reserve I/O, throttle writes, prioritize compaction, add headroom tombstone storm reads scan deleted versions bucket TTL data, repair, compact, cap pathological queries stale replica rejoins deleted value can return enforce repair horizon; rebuild unsupported stale nodes Bloom filter mis-sizing avoidable disk reads or excess memory size from key count and target false-positive rate secondary projection lag stale query results expose lag, session fallback, rebuild and reconcile small-file explosion metadata and scan overhead compaction, writer coordination, file-size targets backup without restore test false durability confidence restore by partition and verify checksums/invariants

docs.title: Decision framework
docs.text:
1. Write invariants and exact read/write operations.
  2. Choose ownership and atomicity keys.
  3. Estimate item, partition, series, index, and retained sizes.
  4. Select an engine family from access paths, not schema aesthetics.
  5. Trace WAL, replication, acknowledgment, read, delete, repair, and restore.
  6. Budget amplification, compaction, rebalancing, and N-1 capacity.
  7. Define canonical state and projection freshness/rebuild.
  8. Load-test skew, TTL cliffs, node outage, stale rejoin, and disk pressure.

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 candidate provides concrete keys and records, calculates partition size and amplification, chooses consistency per operation, and handles compaction, repair, and hot keys. An L6 candidate also defines fleet tiers, multi-tenant fairness, schema and topology migrations, restore units, deletion across projections, cost ceilings, organizational ownership, and when to standardize or reject another datastore.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Choosing a document store because the API uses JSON.
  • Saying NoSQL scales horizontally without a partition key or rebalance plan.
  • Treating eventual consistency as one fixed delay.
  • Claiming R + W > N proves linearizability.
  • Ignoring tombstone retention and stale replicas.
  • Estimating retained bytes but not compaction and repair I/O.
  • Creating an index for every query without write and storage cost.
  • Calling every copy canonical and leaving reconciliation undefined.

docs.title: 1. Model device history
docs.text:
Design storage for 50 billion immutable device events retained for 30 days. Events average 500 bytes before storage overhead. The dominant query reads one device's last 24 hours. Some devices produce 5,000 events/s.

Worked answer

Fleet average ingest is 50 billion / (30 * 86,400) = 19,290 events/s, or about 9.65 MB/s of logical payload, but placement must handle the much larger per-device skew. At 500 bytes/event, a 5,000/s device produces 216 GB/day before overhead. Use a wide-column or time-series layout keyed by tenant, device, and bounded time bucket, ordered by event time plus unique event ID; use hour buckets and, if one hour remains too hot for a node, deterministic hash sub-buckets. An arbitrary half-open rolling 24-hour range can intersect 25 hourly buckets, so budget up to 25 * sub-bucket count reads, not only 24. Apply TTL, time-window compaction, per-device admission, and an analytical projection for fleet-wide scans.

docs.title: 2. Compaction bandwidth
docs.text:
A cluster ingests 80 MB/s logical, replication factor 3. Measured SSTable-write amplification is 10, excluding WAL and repair. What write bandwidth must the storage fleet absorb before other overhead?

Worked answer

80 MB/s * 3 * 10 = 2.4 GB/s. Add WAL, metadata, repair, snapshots, burst headroom, and failure capacity. If disks provide only the average requirement, compaction debt will grow during peaks or node loss.

docs.title: 3. Delete safety
docs.text:
A replica was offline for 10 days, but tombstones are removed after 7 days. May it rejoin directly?

Worked answer

Not safely without engine-specific proof. It can contain pre-delete values after tombstones have disappeared elsewhere, allowing resurrection during repair. Rebuild it from a current trusted replica or snapshot, or use a supported repair procedure that prevents stale data from winning. Align maximum outage, repair cadence, and tombstone retention.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Select storage from invariants, access paths, lifecycle, and operations.
  • LSM trees trade sequential writes for compaction and read/space amplification.
  • Tombstones are correctness state, not disposable garbage.
  • Bound partition size, time-series cardinality, and analytical file count.
  • Make one source canonical and every secondary representation rebuildable.
  • Quantify replication, amplification, repair, failure headroom, and restore.

docs.title: Authoritative sources
docs.text:
• O'Neil et al., The Log-Structured Merge-Tree
  • Google, Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
  • Amazon, Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
  • Apache Cassandra, Storage Engine
  • RocksDB, Compaction
  • InfluxData, Time Series Database Storage Engine
  • Apache Parquet, File Format
  • Abadi, Boncz, and Harizopoulos, Column-Oriented Database Systems

docs.title: Partitioning and Sharding
docs.text:
Engineering extension: Brownfield migrations and the shard-movement fixture connect guarded backfill, tombstones, catchup, authority transfer, reverse migration, and decommission.

Partitioning divides data or work into independently manageable units. It improves parallelism and fault isolation only when the partition key matches access patterns and distributes load.

This chapter uses partition for a logical ownership unit that may move between nodes. Table partitioning inside one relational database is different from sharding across independent database authorities; Relational Databases compares those boundaries.

docs.title: Choose from operations
docs.text:
Suppose a messaging service stores 10B messages, accepts 100K writes/s, reads conversations in time order, and has rare conversations at 20K messages/s. Candidate keys:

Key Strength Weakness message_id hash even writes conversation reads scatter conversation_id hash ordered local reads celebrity conversation hot key (conversation_id, time_bucket) bounds partitions cross-bucket pagination and late writes user ID inbox locality duplicates group messages and complicates membership

A practical key is (hash(conversation_id), monthly_bucket) with logical ordering by (sent_at, message_id). Smaller buckets bound storage and retention work, but all current writes can still hit one bucket. Split an exceptionally hot conversation across lane suffixes when parallel write capacity is required, with a directory describing the active lanes.

flowchart LR
    R[Request] --> K[Partition function]
    K --> P1[(Partition 1)]
    K --> P2[(Partition 2)]
    K --> P3[(Partition 3)]
    M[Partition map] --> K

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Best for Cost hash point access and uniformity range scans scatter range ordered scans and locality moving hotspots directory custom placement and tenants map availability and lookup consistent hash changing node count uneven virtual-node load compound/time bucket high-volume entity histories query fan-out and lifecycle metadata

Separate logical partitions from physical nodes. Many logical partitions permit movement, balancing, and isolation without changing application keys.

docs.title: Rebalancing safely
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Coordinator
    participant O as Old owner
    participant N as New owner
    C->>O: snapshot partition at offset 80
    O->>N: copy snapshot
    O->>N: stream changes after 80
    N-->>C: caught up at 126
    C->>O: gate writes and drain in-flight mutations
    O-->>C: final committed offset 130, old authority fenced
    O->>N: replay through 130
    N-->>C: durable through 130, new epoch installed
    C->>C: atomically switch routing epoch
    C->>N: enable writes under new epoch

Routing carries an epoch; stale routers are redirected rather than allowed to write both owners. Copy, catch up, cut over, verify, then delete. Throttle movement so repair does not consume foreground I/O.

docs.title: Cross-partition operations
docs.text:
Avoid distributed transactions by changing boundaries: colocate data that changes together, reserve rights per shard, or use a saga with compensations. When an invariant genuinely spans partitions, consensus or a transaction coordinator may be justified; state its latency and availability cost.

Secondary indexes introduce a choice: colocated local indexes make writes cheap and global queries fan out; global indexes make reads cheap but add distributed writes and asynchronous lag.

Within each shard, index ordering, selectivity, covering, and page maintenance still apply. See Database Indexing; sharding does not make a poor local access path efficient.

docs.title: Failure semantics
docs.text:
• One shard down should fail only its keys; cap retries to prevent fleet-wide amplification.
  • Split brain can violate uniqueness; fenced epochs or consensus must reject stale owners.
  • A poisoned hot key can saturate one shard despite low fleet utilization; isolate or split it.
  • Partial fan-out reads need an explicit contract: fail whole query, return partial results with a token, or retry missing shards.
  • Rebuild from canonical data or a durable log; do not assume replicas are independent backups.

Measure per-partition QPS, bytes, p99, queue depth, largest-to-median load, fan-out width, move duration, and routing errors. Repartition before a hard storage limit, because migration itself needs spare capacity.

docs.title: Start with invariants and access paths
docs.text:
Partitioning is not primarily a node-placement decision. It is a statement about which operations can remain local. Write the required operations before choosing a function:

  • Fetch one message by ID within 50 ms.
  • Append a message while preserving order within a conversation.
  • Page a conversation forward and backward without duplicates.
  • Delete all data for a tenant within a bounded compliance window.
  • Survive one node loss without acknowledging data that cannot be recovered.

These requirements conflict. Hashing message_id distributes point reads but scatters every conversation page. Hashing only conversation_id colocates pages but allows one celebrity conversation to dominate a partition. A time bucket bounds storage and deletion work, but a page crossing midnight or month-end must read two buckets. The design should name which cost is paid rather than claiming one key is universally balanced.

Keep three identities separate. The logical key belongs to the product, such as conversation_id. The logical partition is a movable unit, such as one of 4,096 partition IDs. The replica set is the current physical placement. Applications should not embed host names in durable records. A routing service maps logical partitions to replica sets under a monotonically increasing epoch.

flowchart TD
    O[Required operations] --> L[Choose locality boundary]
    L --> H{Hot-key risk acceptable?}
    H -->|Yes| P[Hash logical key]
    H -->|No| B[Add bucket or lane]
    P --> V[Map to many logical partitions]
    B --> V
    V --> R[Place replicas across failure domains]
    R --> M[Measure skew and fan-out]

docs.title: Worked hash-partition example
docs.text:
Assume 64 logical partitions and use an unsigned stable 64-bit hash:

partition_id = hash64(conversation_id) mod 64

If hash64("conversation-817") = 14,981, the partition is 14,981 mod 64 = 5. Every router must use the same hash algorithm and byte encoding; language-default hash functions are unsafe because they can change between processes or releases. Store the hash-function version in routing metadata when a future replacement is plausible.

Uniform hashing balances many similarly sized keys probabilistically, not deterministically. Suppose ordinary conversations produce 10 writes/s, while one live event produces 20,000 writes/s. Moving that partition merely moves the hotspot. Split only the exceptional logical key into, for example, eight lanes:

lane = hash64(message_id) mod 8
physical_key = (conversation_id, hour_bucket, lane)

The write rate falls toward 2,500 writes/s per lane, but a time-ordered read now merges eight sorted iterators. A deterministic display order can use (sent_at, message_id), but client timestamps do not establish acceptance order or causality. If the product promises one append order, allocate a conversation sequence through its authority and budget that serialization point. A directory records that this conversation has eight lanes for the affected hours. Do not impose lanes on every conversation: they increase metadata, fan-out, and p99 latency for no benefit to normal keys.

docs.title: Worked rendezvous-hashing example
docs.text:
Rendezvous, or highest-random-weight, hashing scores every candidate node for a key and selects the highest score. For partition p17, suppose the stable scores are:

Candidate Score for p17 Initial rank node A 0.42 3 node B 0.91 1 node C 0.63 2

The owner is B; with replication factor two, B and C hold replicas. Add node D and calculate only its score, 0.95. D now ranks first and B second, so the desired replica set becomes D and B, matching the diagram. Keep C until D is caught up and the membership transition commits. If D scores 0.30 for another partition, that partition does not move. This limited movement is the main advantage over hash(key) mod node_count, where changing the divisor remaps most keys.

Weighted rendezvous adjusts scores according to capacity so a node with twice the safe disk and I/O receives roughly twice the partitions. Weight is not a substitute for load feedback: equal byte counts can hide expensive tenants, large values, or read-heavy partitions. Use rendezvous hashing to produce a desired placement, then let the control plane enforce anti-affinity, drain states, and movement limits.

flowchart LR
    K[Logical partition p17] --> A[Score A: 0.42]
    K --> B[Score B: 0.91]
    K --> C[Score C: 0.63]
    K --> D[Score D: 0.95]
    D --> P[Primary: D]
    B --> S[Secondary: B]

With three replicas across three zones, do not simply choose the top three hosts if two share a rack or zone. Rank candidates, then select the highest candidate satisfying placement constraints. The placement algorithm must be deterministic for a routing epoch, but only the coordinator should publish assignments; otherwise independent routers can disagree during membership churn.

docs.title: Range partitions and split policy
docs.text:
Range partitioning is appropriate when scans dominate: events by time, users by normalized name, or orders by tenant and creation time. Boundaries such as [A, F), [F, M), and [M, Z] preserve locality but rarely preserve load. Sequential timestamps direct all new writes to the final range. Prefix the timestamp with a stable entity hash when entity-local range scans matter, or pre-split future time ranges and distribute them.

A split should use observed bytes and service demand. If a 200 GB range sustains 7,000 QPS against a safe 8,000 QPS limit, waiting for 8,000 leaves no headroom for copying. Split near a sampled median key, copy children in the background, and retain the parent mapping until all routers understand the children. Merge tiny adjacent ranges only when doing so will not recreate a hotspot.

docs.title: Worked online migration
docs.text:
Consider moving logical partition 23 from replica set {A, B, C} to {D, E, F} while writes continue. Assume a 600 GB snapshot, a 12 MB/s change stream, and 30 MB/s of effective migration capacity. In a simple copy-then-replay plan, the snapshot takes 600,000 / 30 = 20,000 seconds, about 5.56 hours. It accumulates 20,000 * 12 = 240,000 MB of changes. Catch-up has 30 - 12 = 18 MB/s net drain and takes another 240,000 / 18 = 13,333 seconds, about 3.70 hours. Total time is roughly 9.26 hours before validation and cutover. This assumes retained changes, steady rates, and that 30 MB/s already accounts for target replication and application costs. Concurrent copy and replay need a separate shared-bandwidth budget; they cannot each consume the full 30 MB/s.

  1. Publish epoch 41 with A as owner and D as a non-serving learner. Keep writes single-owned.
  2. Record snapshot offset 8,400, copy immutable files, and checksum every range.
  3. Stream changes after offset 8,400 to D. Apply idempotently by log position or record version.
  4. When D remains within the cutover threshold, gate new writes for partition 23, drain in-flight mutations, fence A's authority, and record final committed position F. Verify the target replica set is durably caught up through F before promotion. Routing through A alone does not establish a final boundary while A still commits writes.
  5. Publish epoch 42 with D as owner. Requests carrying epoch 41 receive a redirect containing epoch 42; A must not independently accept them.
  6. Observe read checksums, error rate, lag, and p99. Keep old replicas readable but fenced for a rollback window.
  7. After the rollback window and backup verification, remove old copies gradually.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Planned
    Planned --> Copying: add learner
    Copying --> CatchingUp: snapshot verified
    CatchingUp --> CutoverReady: lag below threshold
    CutoverReady --> ServingNew: fence old, replay final F, publish epoch
    ServingNew --> Verified: checksums and SLO healthy
    ServingNew --> RolledBack: cutover guard fails
    Verified --> RetiredOld: rollback window ends

Dual writing from clients is a weaker migration strategy because partial failures create two truths. If unavoidable, establish one canonical side, attach a monotonic version, repair discrepancies from a durable log, and specify which side wins. Never compare only row counts; compare key ranges, versions, and sampled or full checksums.

After target writes begin, rollback also gates and fences the target, reverse-replays its accepted tail, verifies the old set through that final position, and grants a fresh epoch. PostgreSQL logical decoding supplies a concrete snapshot-to-stream boundary and explicitly warns that crash recovery can repeat changes. It does not supply this application authority-transfer protocol automatically (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Secondary indexes and scatter-gather tails
docs.text:
A local secondary index is partitioned with canonical rows. It preserves atomic updates, but a query without the partition key contacts every shard. If each of 50 shards independently meets p99 at 40 ms, the chance that all 50 finish below their individual p99 is 0.99^50, about 60.5%. The aggregate query therefore encounters a shard-level one-percent tail roughly 39.5% of the time. Parallelism reduces mean latency, not tail probability.

Bound scatter width through a directory, time predicate, tenant key, or dedicated global projection. Give fan-out requests one deadline and cancellation signal; do not allow each shard its own full timeout and retries. A global index can route directly, but its asynchronous lag means the result may omit a just-written record. For correctness-sensitive lookup, validate candidates against canonical storage or use a synchronously maintained uniqueness index.

docs.title: Capacity, skew, and operational limits
docs.text:
Average capacity is insufficient. For 100,000 writes/s over 100 partitions, the mean is 1,000 writes/s. If the measured median is also near 1,000/s and the largest-to-median ratio is 6, the hottest partition receives about 6,000 writes/s while fleet utilization looks low. A mean alone does not establish the median. Provision and alert against per-partition disk, CPU, queue age, and I/O. Track the top tenants contributing to each hot partition so operators can distinguish random imbalance from a single hot key.

Set explicit limits for partition size, movement concurrency per node and zone, learner lag, routing-map staleness, and repair bandwidth. Movement should pause automatically when foreground p99, disk queue depth, or replication lag crosses a guardrail. A node loss during rebalance must not trigger unbounded concurrent repair.

docs.title: Design review checklist
docs.text:
• Name the locality and ordering scope before selecting the key.
  • Quantify expected key cardinality, skew, largest key, and growth horizon.
  • Separate logical partitions from nodes and version the routing map.
  • Explain hot-key splitting and the resulting read merge.
  • Define stale-router behavior and fence old owners.
  • Budget temporary storage, bandwidth, and foreground headroom for migration.
  • State partial-result semantics for cross-partition reads.
  • Rehearse split, move, rollback, rebuild, and node-loss procedures.
  • Treat replicas as availability copies; maintain separately tested backups.

docs.title: Relational Databases
docs.text:
Engineering extension: Storage recovery and query execution connects commit boundaries, interrupted recovery, checkpoint/restore budgets, and physical query work to a file-backed durable-counter fixture.

A relational database is a concurrency-control and durability system with a declarative query engine. Its central advantage is not merely tables: it can enforce invariants across related data while exposing transactions, constraints, indexes, recovery logs, and an optimizer through one coherent boundary.

This chapter uses PostgreSQL 17-style terminology to make internals concrete. Exact lock, replication, and DDL behavior varies by engine. See Database Indexing for access-path mechanics and Partitioning and Sharding for distributed placement.

docs.title: When relational wins
docs.text:
Prefer a relational system when several of these are true:

  • Correctness depends on uniqueness, references, checks, or atomic changes across rows.
  • Commands update a bounded set of related records and must expose a clear commit point.
  • Access paths will evolve and a query optimizer is more valuable than one fixed key API.
  • Operators need ad hoc reconciliation, audits, joins, and repair queries.
  • Data size and write rate fit one primary or a deliberately partitioned/sharded topology.
  • The team benefits from mature backup, point-in-time recovery, migration, and observability tools.

A key-value store can be better for a narrow key API, independently partitionable records, extreme horizontal write scale, or predictable tail latency without joins. A search engine is better for text relevance and broad candidate retrieval. An analytical column store is better for scans and aggregations over large immutable histories. These systems are often projections around relational canonical state, not replacements for every responsibility.

Start with invariants and failure semantics. "No two active bookings own the same seat" is a reason for a unique constraint and transaction. "Fetch a document by ID" alone is not a reason to require a relational database.

docs.title: Logical model and enforced invariants
docs.text:
Normalization gives each fact one authoritative owner. Foreign keys prevent dangling relationships; unique and exclusion constraints serialize conflicting claims; checks constrain row-local facts. Denormalize only for a measured read path and define freshness and repair.

CREATE TABLE account (
    account_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id bigint NOT NULL,
    external_ref text NOT NULL,
    balance_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (balance_cents >= 0),
    version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_ref),
    UNIQUE (account_id, tenant_id)
);

CREATE TABLE transfer (
    transfer_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id bigint NOT NULL,
    request_key text NOT NULL,
    debit_account_id bigint NOT NULL,
    credit_account_id bigint NOT NULL,
    amount_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
    state text NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('POSTED', 'REVERSED')),
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, request_key),
    CHECK (debit_account_id <> credit_account_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (debit_account_id, tenant_id)
        REFERENCES account(account_id, tenant_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (credit_account_id, tenant_id)
        REFERENCES account(account_id, tenant_id)
);

The composite foreign keys make a cross-tenant transfer unrepresentable even when account IDs are globally unique. The database must still be given the right invariant. A nonnegative balance check on each account cannot prove conservation across two accounts. Put both balance updates and the immutable transfer record in one transaction; verify that the lock query found exactly two accounts and that each balance update affected exactly one row. For ledgers, balanced postings and append-only correction entries provide stronger evidence than mutable balances alone.

This teaching schema assumes one fixed currency/asset. For multiple assets, carry an immutable asset code on accounts and postings, reject cross-asset transfers on this path, and balance each asset independently. Equal integer amounts in two currencies do not prove conservation; foreign exchange needs its own quoted-rate and posting contract.

Constraints are executable concurrency controls, not documentation. Application-side SELECT followed by INSERT races under concurrency. Let a unique constraint arbitrate, then map its specific violation to a stable domain conflict. Use NOT NULL, foreign keys, and checks after validation/backfill rather than relying indefinitely on optional application checks.

docs.title: PostgreSQL-style physical path
docs.text:
PostgreSQL stores table tuples in fixed-size heap pages. A tuple carries transaction visibility metadata; an update commonly writes a new tuple version and leaves the old version for existing snapshots. Index leaves point to heap tuple locations. Vacuum later marks dead space reusable after no active snapshot can observe those versions.

flowchart LR
    C[Client transaction] --> B[Shared buffers]
    B --> H[Dirty heap and index pages]
    B --> W[WAL records]
    W --> F[WAL flush]
    F --> A[Commit acknowledged]
    H --> K[Checkpoint writes pages]
    F --> R[Streaming replica]
    K --> D[(Data files)]

The write-ahead rule requires relevant WAL to reach durable storage before dirty data pages may be considered safely persisted. Commit ordinarily waits for the commit WAL record according to configured durability. The heap page itself may be written later. Recovery replays WAL from a checkpoint to reproduce committed changes and discard incomplete transactions logically.

docs.title: WAL, checkpoints, and group commit
docs.text:
WAL turns scattered page mutations into an ordered append path and supports crash recovery, physical replication, and point-in-time recovery. It does not remove storage cost: indexes, full-page images after checkpoints, large transactions, and replication slots can produce substantial WAL volume.

A checkpoint establishes a recovery starting point and schedules dirty-page writes. Frequent checkpoints shorten recovery but increase write pressure and full-page-image frequency. Infrequent checkpoints need more WAL and longer replay. Spread checkpoint I/O to avoid a burst that competes with foreground reads and fsync.

Group commit lets transactions arriving close together share a durable flush. If an fsync takes 2 ms, serially flushing every commit caps one path near 500 commits/s. Batching 40 ready commits behind one flush can theoretically expose about 40 / 0.002 = 20,000 commits/s on that path, although lock, WAL insertion, CPU, and storage bandwidth impose lower real limits. Group commit amortizes flush latency; it does not acknowledge before the required flush.

Durability settings define product semantics. Asynchronous commit can lose recently acknowledged transactions on process or machine failure. It can be valid for disposable telemetry, not for a payment merely because latency improved.

docs.title: MVCC and transaction boundaries
docs.text:
MVCC gives each statement or transaction a visibility snapshot while writers create new row versions. Readers often avoid blocking writers, but concurrency anomalies still depend on isolation level and write predicates. Keep transactions short: an idle transaction retains snapshots, delays vacuum, holds locks, and may prevent WAL or schema cleanup.

Use one transaction for one invariant boundary:

BEGIN;

-- Lock both tenant-owned accounts in one deterministic order. Require exactly
-- two rows; otherwise abort before either balance changes.
SELECT account_id
FROM account
WHERE tenant_id = 8
  AND account_id IN (101, 202)
ORDER BY account_id
FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE account
SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 2500,
    version = version + 1
WHERE account_id = 101
  AND tenant_id = 8
  AND balance_cents >= 2500;

-- Require exactly one affected row; zero means missing account or insufficient funds.
UPDATE account
SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 2500,
    version = version + 1
WHERE account_id = 202
  AND tenant_id = 8;

-- Require exactly one affected row; otherwise roll back the whole transaction.

INSERT INTO transfer
    (tenant_id, request_key, debit_account_id, credit_account_id, amount_cents, state)
VALUES
    (8, 'req-774', 101, 202, 2500, 'POSTED');

COMMIT;

The transaction runner checks all three cardinalities before commit: two locked rows, one debited row, and one credited row. Any mismatch causes ROLLBACK, so an absent credit account cannot leave a lone debit. Acquire multiple explicit row locks in a stable key order to reduce deadlocks. Deadlocks remain normal recoverable outcomes: the database aborts one participant, and the application retries the entire idempotent transaction with bounded backoff.

The unique transfer key rolls back a duplicate attempt, but returning the prior result also requires comparing its debit account, credit account, amount, tenant, and currency policy with the new request. A key reused for different input is not a successful duplicate. Store that request fingerprint and result durably. Use checked integer arithmetic for the credit as well as the debit. PostgreSQL 17 transaction isolation documents whole-transaction retries; WAL documents the flush-before-data rule, not external-provider atomicity (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Anomaly and remedy matrix
docs.text:
Anomaly Example Common exposure Remedy dirty read observe a balance another transaction later aborts read-uncommitted semantics read committed or stronger; PostgreSQL maps read uncommitted to read committed non-repeatable read rereading one row returns a newer committed value statement snapshots under read committed repeatable read snapshot or lock/validate version phantom rerunning a predicate finds newly matching rows read committed predicate reads repeatable read for stable snapshot; serializable for predicate-dependent writes lost update two clients derive a value and last writer overwrites first read-modify-write without guard atomic update, FOR UPDATE, or optimistic version predicate write skew two doctors each go off call after seeing the other on call snapshot isolation across different rows serializable isolation, explicit lock on shared guard row, or remodel constraint serialization failure engine rejects a dangerous dependency cycle serializable execution retry the complete transaction with same command identity deadlock transfers lock accounts in opposite order any lock-based level stable lock order plus full-transaction retry

Isolation names alone are insufficient across products. State the anomaly to prevent and test the chosen engine behavior. PostgreSQL's serializable isolation uses dependency tracking and can abort transactions that would form a nonserializable history. Applications must treat serialization failures as expected retryable outcomes; swallowing them or retrying only the last statement breaks the abstraction.

Optimistic concurrency is useful when conflicts are rare:

UPDATE document
SET body = :body, version = version + 1
WHERE document_id = :id AND version = :expected_version;

Zero affected rows means conflict or absence. Pessimistic row locking fits short high-contention decisions, but queues waiters and can amplify latency. Neither strategy fixes a predicate-wide invariant unless the locked or validated data represents that predicate.

docs.title: Indexes and query planning
docs.text:
The planner chooses scans, joins, ordering, and parallelism from estimated row counts and cost parameters. An index is useful only if its ordering and columns reduce the work of a real query enough to repay maintenance. Composite left prefixes, equality-before-range, covering, partial, and specialized indexes are developed in Database Indexing.

Use EXPLAIN for estimates and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for measured execution in a safe environment. Compare estimated and actual cardinality at every node. A join problem that looks like insufficient memory can begin with a 10,000x estimate error; a slow index scan can actually be millions of random heap fetches.

docs.title: Connections, sessions, and pooling
docs.text:
A database connection consumes backend memory, process/thread scheduling, session state, and lock-table participation even while idle. Setting the maximum to thousands does not create database throughput. Once CPU, cache, WAL, or storage saturates, more active queries increase queueing and p99.

Use a bounded pool per service and a fleet-wide connection budget. A rough initial concurrency bound follows Little's Law. If one database can safely complete 6,000 simple operations/s and average database service time is 8 ms:

useful in-flight work = throughput * service time
                      = 6,000/s * 0.008 s
                      = 48 operations

This is not a prescription for exactly 48 connections: transactions make several calls, workload classes differ, and headroom matters. It shows why 2,000 simultaneously active connections are likely a queue, not capacity. Load-test pool size, use short acquisition deadlines, reject or shed before requests pile up, and reserve connections for migrations, operators, and correctness-critical work.

Transaction-level proxies improve multiplexing but can break assumptions about session variables, temporary tables, prepared statements, advisory locks, and LISTEN/NOTIFY. Know whether affinity is session, transaction, or statement scoped before introducing a proxy.

docs.title: Replicas, positions, and read-your-writes
docs.text:
Physical streaming replicas replay WAL from a primary. They provide read scale and availability copies, but asynchronous replicas can be stale and are not backups. A long replica query can conflict with replay cleanup; delaying replay preserves the query while increasing staleness.

Track freshness by WAL/log position, not wall-clock guesswork. A write response can carry an integrity-protected session token containing topology epoch and commit position P. A later read follows this policy:

flowchart TD
    Q[Read with required position P] --> C{Replica replay position at least P?}
    C -->|Yes| R[Read through a fresh replica snapshot]
    C -->|No| D{Deadline permits waiting?}
    D -->|Yes| W[Wait for replay up to budget]
    D -->|No| H{Current primary contains required history?}
    H -->|Yes| P[Read fresh snapshot on primary]
    H -->|No| E[Return unavailable or explicit lost-write outcome]
    W --> C

This provides read-your-writes only if the chosen snapshot includes the required position on a compatible timeline. Check replay before acquiring a fresh read snapshot; a repeatable-read transaction opened earlier can remain stale even after the replica catches up. Following asynchronous failover, the new primary may lack the acknowledged write, so primary fallback must not silently return old data as if the token had been honored. Sticky routing by itself fails after topology changes, and "replica lag below one second" does not prove one particular commit is visible.

Synchronous replication can require one or more standbys to durably receive WAL before commit returns. It reduces acknowledged-loss risk but couples write availability and latency to those standbys. Define whether acknowledgement means remote memory, remote durable flush, or replay/application.

docs.title: Failover without two primaries
docs.text:
Failover is a fencing problem, not only promotion:

  1. Determine that the old primary cannot continue accepting writes through a lease, quorum, or external fence.
  2. Choose an eligible replica from durable replay/receive positions and timeline history.
  3. Promote it under a new topology epoch and redirect writers.
  4. Rewind or rebuild the old primary before allowing it to rejoin; never attach two divergent timelines casually.
  5. Reconcile connection pools, replication slots, backup lineage, and read-your-writes tokens.

With asynchronous replication, data acknowledged by the old primary but absent from the promoted replica can be lost. State that RPO explicitly. Automatic failover cannot manufacture missing WAL.

docs.title: Partitioning versus sharding
docs.text:
These terms describe different boundaries:

Technique Location Transaction/query implication Primary purpose table partitioning child tables inside one database system planner can prune; one transaction manager remains lifecycle, pruning, maintenance sharding rows split across independent database authorities cross-shard joins and transactions coordinate or move to application capacity, write scale, fault isolation replication copies of the same logical data writes coordinate; reads choose freshness availability and read scale

Partitioning a 2 TB event table monthly does not add write capacity if every partition uses the same WAL, CPU, and storage bottleneck. It can make retention a metadata operation, bound vacuum/index work, and prune time queries. Too many partitions increase planning, metadata, and connection overhead; predicates must include partition bounds for pruning.

Sharding introduces routing, resharding, cross-shard constraints, backups at a common point, and failover per shard. Choose a shard key from transaction locality and access paths. Global uniqueness may need key construction, a synchronously owned registry, or acceptance of scoped uniqueness. See Partitioning and Sharding for placement and migration mechanics.

docs.title: Extensions and projections
docs.text:
Relational systems can stretch through extensions: spatial operator classes, full-text search, time-series helpers, vector types, foreign data access, and logical decoding. An extension runs inside or beside a critical state system, so evaluate upgrade compatibility, WAL/replica behavior, backup/restore, crash safety, resource isolation, and operational ownership. Syntax convenience is not an architecture proof.

Keep canonical tables narrow and correctness-focused. Build read models through materialized views, summary tables, caches, warehouses, or search indexes when a workload needs another layout. A projection needs:

  • A source position or entity version that rejects stale replay.
  • A freshness SLO and observable lag.
  • Delete/tombstone handling.
  • A complete rebuild path from canonical data and ordered changes.
  • Validation at the canonical source for correctness-sensitive decisions.

Triggers can maintain local invariants atomically but add hidden work and deployment coupling. Transactional outboxes make external projection intent durable in the same commit and let asynchronous consumers retry. Do not dual-write the database and an external index and call both authoritative.

docs.title: Schema evolution and constraint rollout
docs.text:
Use expand, migrate, validate, contract. Adding a nullable metadata-only column may be fast; adding a volatile default, rewriting a type, validating a large constraint, or building an index can scan/rewrite data and generate WAL. Test with production-like size and locks.

Example: require every transfer to have a purpose without a flag day:

ALTER TABLE transfer ADD COLUMN purpose text;

-- Deploy writers that populate purpose and readers that tolerate NULL.
-- Backfill bounded primary-key ranges with commits and throttling.

ALTER TABLE transfer
ADD CONSTRAINT transfer_purpose_present
CHECK (purpose IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;

ALTER TABLE transfer
VALIDATE CONSTRAINT transfer_purpose_present;

ALTER TABLE transfer
ALTER COLUMN purpose SET NOT NULL;

NOT VALID is PostgreSQL-specific: new writes are checked while historical rows can be validated separately. Lock behavior still matters, and converting to NOT NULL should be rehearsed for the exact server version. For foreign keys, indexes on referencing columns often prevent expensive parent deletes/updates; they are not automatically created by the foreign key declaration.

Backfills should be idempotent, checkpointed, and guarded against overwriting newer writes:

UPDATE transfer
SET purpose = 'legacy-import'
WHERE transfer_id > :low
  AND transfer_id <= :high
  AND purpose IS NULL;

Use short batches, pause on replica lag/WAL/disk/latency guardrails, and record progress outside an unbounded transaction. Deploy tolerant readers first, dual-read or shadow-compare when semantics change, and remove old columns only after rollback and old-binary windows end.

docs.title: Capacity calculations
docs.text:
Estimate the physical system rather than table payload alone. Suppose 18,000 transactions/s each produce:

heap tuple and metadata             700 bytes
three index entries                 3 * 80 = 240 bytes
logical change before WAL           940 bytes
WAL bytes / logical-change bytes    2.4x (illustrative assumption)
primary WAL stream                18,000 * 940 * 2.4 = 40.6 MB/s
two physical replicas               about 81.2 MB/s additional network receive

This models WAL volume only. Dirty heap/index writes, vacuum, checkpoints, and storage replication add physical work and need their own budget. The 2.4x factor is an assumption to replace with observed WAL bytes per transaction.

At 40.6 MB/s, the primary generates about 40.6 * 86,400 = 3.51 TB/day of WAL before compression and workload variation. A replication slot stalled for 18 hours could pin roughly 40.6 * 64,800 = 2.63 TB. Disk alerts must include retained WAL and time-to-full, not only table growth.

For recovery, if the latest base backup leaves 900 GB of WAL to replay and sustained recovery throughput is 250 MB/s, replay alone is about 900,000 / 250 = 3,600 seconds, or one hour, before restore download, verification, and service warmup. Recovery objectives must be proved by restore drills.

docs.title: Operations and failure semantics
docs.text:
Monitor transaction rate and latency by workload; active/waiting/idle-in-transaction sessions; lock waits and deadlocks; buffer hit/read/write rates; checkpoint duration; WAL generation, flush latency, and retained bytes; replica receive/replay positions; vacuum age and dead tuples; table/index growth; estimate errors and plan changes; pool acquisition time; backup age; and tested restore time.

Failure Required behavior client timeout after commit retry through idempotency key; do not infer rollback primary process crash recover from checkpoint plus WAL; reconnect with bounded jitter replica lag enforce position token or route to primary for freshness-sensitive read disk nearly full preserve WAL/recovery reserve; stop optional writes and maintenance safely long transaction blocks vacuum identify owner, cancel by policy, repair bloat after snapshots release online DDL waits on lock use lock timeout, inspect blocker, retry later rather than queue the fleet asynchronous failover loses tail expose stated RPO and reconcile external effects backup job says success restore and validate constraints/checksums in isolation

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• State why relational constraints and transactions fit the invariants.
  • Put one command's invariant inside one bounded transaction where feasible.
  • Name the required isolation behavior and retryable aborts.
  • Trace heap, index, WAL flush, checkpoint, vacuum, and recovery paths.
  • Bound application and fleet connections from measured database capacity.
  • Define replica positions, freshness tokens, synchronous acknowledgement, and failover RPO.
  • Distinguish table partitioning, sharding, and replication.
  • Treat extensions and external stores as operated projections with rebuild paths.
  • Roll out constraints and schema changes through expand, backfill, validate, and contract.
  • Calculate WAL, replica traffic, retained-log risk, restore time, and maintenance headroom.

docs.title: Reliability Engineering for Designs
docs.text:
Engineering extension: Service operations turns reliability into SLI definitions, incident authority, configuration and drain gates, and a quantified recovery runbook. Practice the bounded scheduler and Atlas incident.

Reliability is the probability that a defined operation succeeds within its contract. Build it from user journeys, failure domains, and recovery paths rather than a collection of retries.

docs.title: Turn goals into budgets
docs.text:
A 99.9% time-based SLO permits 43.2 bad minutes in a 30-day month. A request-based SLO instead permits 0.1% of eligible requests to be bad; converting that to outage minutes assumes uniform traffic. Define the SLI precisely: eligible checkout attempts receiving a terminal accepted or business-rejected response within 800 ms. Exclude invalid requests, not dependency failures.

Goal Mechanism Hidden cost higher availability redundancy across failure domains correlated software/config failures remain lower RTO automated failover false failover and split brain lower RPO synchronous replication write latency and partition unavailability graceful overload admission control and prioritization rejected optional work safe retries idempotency and budgets state and dedup retention

docs.title: Failure-oriented architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> A[Admission control]
    A --> S[Stateless service]
    S --> D[(Replicated DB)]
    S --> Q[(Durable queue)]
    Q --> W[Workers]
    S -. timeout/breaker .-> X[Dependency]

Use deadlines propagated from the caller. A service with 200 ms remaining must not start a dependency call with a 500 ms timeout. Retries need exponential backoff, jitter, a cap, and a shared attempt budget. Retry only transient and idempotent operations.

docs.title: Overload is a correctness problem
docs.text:
When arrival rate exceeds service rate, queues increase latency until all requests time out while still consuming work. Reject before expensive work, bound every queue, reserve capacity for health/control traffic, and prioritize core operations.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Healthy
    Healthy --> Degraded: saturation threshold
    Degraded --> ShedOptional: queue age grows
    ShedOptional --> Healthy: sustained recovery
    Degraded --> FailClosed: invariant dependency unavailable

docs.title: Failure semantics table
docs.text: Failure point Semantics Recovery server proves rejection before durable commit not accepted safe retry with same command identity response lost after commit unknown to caller same idempotency key returns result cache lost performance degradation bounded bypass and gradual warmup async consumer down accepted but delayed durable backlog and replay database replica lost continue within quorum replace and verify replication entire region lost RTO/RPO-specific failover fence old writer before promotion bad deployment correlated errors canary, automatic halt, rollback/roll-forward

docs.title: Recovery is a product feature
docs.text:
Backups are useful only after restore tests. Specify snapshot interval, log retention, encryption keys, restore duration, and consistency checks. Reconciliation compares independent evidence: orders versus payments, object metadata versus blobs, source tables versus projections.

Game days should test dependency latency, partial packet loss, expired credentials, full disks, queue poison, zone loss, and operator mistakes. Fault injection without assertions merely creates outages.

docs.title: Observability and ownership
docs.text:
Track user-success rate and latency first, then saturation, dependency outcomes, queue age, replication lag, and invariant violations. Logs need correlation IDs but must not leak secrets. Alerts should be actionable and budget-based; page on user harm or imminent exhaustion, ticket on trends.

An L6 design names degradation policy and authority: who declares failover, what operations become unavailable, how tenant isolation works, and how a migration is aborted. Reliability includes runbooks, capacity ownership, and a path to return from degraded state.

docs.title: Define reliability per user journey
docs.text:
A service is not simply "up." Browse, checkout, cancellation, and administration can have different contracts. Define an SLI as a ratio over eligible events:

availability = good eligible requests / total eligible requests

For checkout, a good request may be one that receives an accepted or valid business rejection within 800 ms. A card decline is a successful system outcome; a timeout caused by the payment dependency is not. Excluding all 4xx responses without classifying them can hide authentication or validation regressions. Measure at the boundary closest to the user, then retain internal SLIs to localize failures.

Time-window aggregation matters. Request-based availability weights busy minutes more heavily. Time-slice availability might mark each minute good only if at least 99.9% of eligible requests succeed. The latter prevents a quiet, completely broken hour from disappearing beneath peak volume. State which method the SLO uses.

docs.title: Worked availability and error budgets
docs.text:
A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. The approximate unavailable time permitted by common availability goals is:

SLO Error fraction Monthly budget Average daily budget 99.0% 1% 432 min 14.4 min 99.9% 0.1% 43.2 min 86.4 sec 99.95% 0.05% 21.6 min 43.2 sec 99.99% 0.01% 4.32 min 8.64 sec

For a request-based 99.9% SLO over 200 million eligible requests, the budget is 200,000 bad requests. If 80,000 have failed ten days into the window, 40% of the budget is consumed while 33% of time has elapsed. At uniform traffic, this pace would exhaust the budget before the window ends. For seasonal traffic, compare failures with the eligible-request forecast rather than elapsed time alone.

Burn rate compares observed error rate with the allowed error rate. For a 99.9% SLO, the allowed rate is 0.1%. An observed 1.4% error rate is a 14x burn. At constant traffic, a 30-day budget disappears in about 30 / 14 = 2.14 days. Google's multiwindow, multi-burn-rate example pages on (burn_1h > 14.4 AND burn_5m > 14.4) OR (burn_6h > 6 AND burn_30m > 6). The short window confirms the error is still occurring; the two pairs catch different burn speeds. These are starting thresholds, not universal defaults (accessed 2026-09-08).

flowchart LR
    R[Eligible requests] --> G[Good within contract]
    R --> B[Bad or too slow]
    G --> S[SLI ratio]
    B --> S
    S --> E[Error budget remaining]
    E -->|Healthy| C[Normal change velocity]
    E -->|Fast burn| F[Freeze risky rollout]
    E -->|Exhausted| P[Reliability work and exception process]

Budgets guide decisions; they are not permission to schedule outages until every minute is consumed. Keep planned maintenance in the same user-impact accounting unless the product contract explicitly excludes it.

docs.title: Compose dependency availability carefully
docs.text:
For independent serial dependencies required on every request, availability multiplies. If the API, database, and payment adapter are each 99.9%, the path is 0.999^3 = 99.7003%, before network and client failures. The product is valid only for independent success events under a common observation boundary. Shared outages can overlap rather than add: perfect correlation here yields 99.9%, while disjoint outages yield about 99.7%. Model the joint failure behavior; independence is not a guaranteed upper or lower bound for a required serial path.

Parallel redundancy helps only when failures are sufficiently independent and failover works. Two independent 99% replicas with successful failover yield 1 - (0.01 * 0.01) = 99.99%. Shared power, a bad schema migration, or a malformed request can defeat both. Redundancy addresses component failure; canaries, compatibility, and blast-radius controls address correlated failure.

Optional dependencies should not sit in the critical path. If recommendations fail, return checkout without recommendations. For correctness dependencies, failing open can violate an invariant; fraud authorization or entitlement checks may need to fail closed. Record this as a product decision.

docs.title: Deadlines, retries, and amplification
docs.text:
For the transport, connection-pool, and retry-budget mechanics behind this reliability policy, use Deadlines, Retries, and Pools.

Propagate one end-to-end time budget through the call graph. Use local monotonic clocks and transmit remaining duration rather than comparing unsynchronized absolute clocks; gRPC deadline propagation subtracts elapsed time. Suppose the client budget is 800 ms. The edge consumes 40 ms and the service has spent 110 ms, leaving 650 ms. Reserve 100 ms to form and transmit the response, so downstream work has at most 550 ms. Starting three sequential calls with 500 ms timeouts ignores the contract.

Retries consume both time and capacity. If a frontend makes one call to service A, which retries service B up to three total attempts, and B retries database operations up to three attempts, one user request can create 3 * 3 = 9 database attempts. At 10,000 requests/s, a total dependency failure can drive 90,000 attempts/s before client retries. This retry amplification can prevent recovery.

flowchart TD
    U[10k user requests/s] --> A[Service A: up to 3 attempts]
    A --> B[Service B: up to 30k calls/s]
    B --> D[Database: up to 90k attempts/s]
    D --> X[Saturation extends failure]
    X -->|timeouts trigger more retries| A

Prefer retries at one layer, usually the layer with end-to-end context. Use an attempt budget carried with the request, exponential backoff with full jitter, and a retry cap. Retry only when the remaining deadline permits useful work and the operation is idempotent. Hedged reads send a second attempt after a latency percentile, not immediately; cap them globally because they deliberately add load.

A circuit breaker prevents repeated work against a known failing dependency, but it does not create capacity. Its open state should fail quickly or use an explicitly safe fallback. Probe recovery with limited half-open traffic. A fleet of synchronized probes can itself overload a recovering dependency, so jitter and centrally bound them.

docs.title: Capacity, queues, and graceful degradation
docs.text:
Little's Law states L = lambda * W: average work in the system equals arrival rate multiplied by time in system. At 5,000 requests/s and 200 ms average latency, about 1,000 requests are in flight. If latency rises to two seconds at unchanged arrival rate, 10,000 are in flight, consuming connections and memory. Unbounded queues turn a capacity shortage into latency, timeout, and retry failures.

Admission should happen before expensive parsing, allocation, and downstream calls. Bound queues by time as well as count. Reserve capacity for health checks, lease renewal, operator access, and high-value operations. Degrade deliberately: omit recommendations, lower result depth, serve bounded stale data, or delay analytics. Never degrade an invariant silently.

Load shedding should return a clear retryable status quickly. Fairness controls prevent one tenant from occupying all workers. Adaptive concurrency can lower in-flight limits as latency rises, but retain static safety ceilings and test oscillation behavior.

docs.title: Failure domains and zonal evacuation
docs.text:
Deploying three replicas across three zones does not guarantee survival of one zone if each zone normally runs at 70% utilization. With 100 capacity units per zone, total demand is 210 units and surviving capacity is 200, producing 105% utilization. To survive one of three equal zones without shedding, normal fleet utilization must stay at or below roughly 66.7%, and lower in practice for skew and repair.

A zonal evacuation is controlled load transfer, not just instance replacement:

  1. Detect zone-specific symptoms using independent signals: request errors, network reachability, and infrastructure health.
  2. Stop placing new work and new leaders in the suspect zone.
  3. Verify healthy zones have headroom; shed optional traffic before shifting if needed.
  4. Drain traffic gradually while watching p99, queue age, connection pools, and dependency quotas per destination zone.
  5. Fence stateful leaders and restore replication factor without violating anti-affinity.
  6. Hold the zone out until a defined stable period passes. Reintroduce a small canary, then ramp.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Balanced
    Balanced --> Suspect: zone signals disagree
    Suspect --> Evacuating: incident authority confirms
    Evacuating --> Evacuated: traffic and leaders drained
    Evacuating --> Balanced: false alarm and healthy
    Evacuated --> CanaryReturn: repair verified
    CanaryReturn --> Balanced: ramp guardrails pass
    CanaryReturn --> Evacuated: regression

Avoid automatic evacuation on one noisy metric. A traffic shift can overload healthy zones and convert a partial incident into a regional outage. Define who can override automation and how routing converges.

docs.title: Data durability, RPO, and recovery
docs.text:
Availability and durability differ. A replicated database can serve requests while an operator mistake deletes data from every replica. Backups need separate credentials and failure domains, immutable retention where appropriate, and tested restore procedures.

Quantify recovery. Hourly snapshots plus continuous logs can offer an RPO near zero only if logs are durable, complete, and replayable. If restoring a 20 TB snapshot at an effective 500 MB/s, transfer alone takes about 11.1 hours, before validation and log replay. An RTO of two hours is incompatible with that method; use incremental snapshots, parallel restore, a warm standby, or a smaller recovery unit.

A restore test must verify more than process startup. Compare record counts by partition, checksums, referential integrity, business totals, encryption key availability, and application read/write behavior. Preserve evidence about uncertain requests around the failure boundary and reconcile with external systems.

docs.title: Safe change and blast radius
docs.text:
Changes can cause correlated incidents that hardware redundancy does not contain. Progressive delivery sends a small representative slice to the new version, compares success and latency, and halts automatically on guardrail breaches. Include schema, configuration, credentials, feature flags, and traffic policy in change control; rolling back application code may not reverse an incompatible data migration.

Use expand-contract database migrations. Add a field or table first, deploy code that handles both forms, backfill under throttles, switch reads, and remove the old form only after rollback and old-version windows end. Assign idempotent checkpoints to backfills and pause them when foreground SLOs burn.

Limit blast radius by cell, tenant, zone, or shard. A global control plane can publish configuration, but data planes should continue with the last valid version during a control-plane outage. Validate configuration before publication and support rapid rejection of a bad epoch.

docs.title: Observability and game-day assertions
docs.text:
Dashboards should connect user harm to causes: SLI and latency, admitted and shed rates, saturation, dependency outcomes, queue age, replica lag, and remaining error budget. High-cardinality dimensions such as tenant or shard need controlled aggregation but are essential for blast-radius analysis.

Every game day needs expected assertions. During a zone-loss exercise, verify that error rate remains within the test budget, no stale leader accepts writes, healthy-zone utilization stays below its evacuation ceiling, replication factor recovers, and traffic can return safely. Stop conditions protect production if assumptions are wrong.

docs.title: Design review checklist
docs.text:
• Define good, bad, eligible, and too-slow events per journey.
  • Calculate monthly budget, current burn rate, and alert windows.
  • Quantify serial dependency composition and correlated risks.
  • Show deadline allocation and worst-case retry multiplication.
  • Bound queues, concurrency, fallback freshness, and shedding priority.
  • Demonstrate N-1 zone capacity with skew and repair headroom.
  • State RTO and RPO alongside measured restore and replay time.
  • Fence old writers before promotion or evacuation.
  • Make rollout, rollback, reconciliation, and return-to-normal executable.

docs.title: Security Architecture
docs.text:
Engineering extension: Authorization, revocation, and privacy develops effect-time policy checks, stale decisions, tenant isolation, deletion/restore obligations, and an independently checked permission-revocation fixture.

Security architecture controls who can cause which state transition, on whose data, under what evidence and limits. Encryption and login are mechanisms inside that system. Begin with assets, adversaries, trust boundaries, and abuse cases.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • produce a threat model tied to concrete controls and residual risk;
  • separate authentication, authorization, session, and tenant-isolation decisions;
  • trace OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect without confusing tokens or actors;
  • design workload identity, mTLS, key rotation, privacy, deletion, and audit paths;
  • reason about abuse and software-supply-chain failures; and
  • distinguish L5 implementation depth from L6 program and blast-radius ownership.

docs.title: First principles: assets, actions, and boundaries
docs.text:
Security preserves confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and accountability for defined assets. It is risk management, not a claim that compromise is impossible.

risk = likelihood * impact
residual risk = inherent risk reduced by effective controls

Use a data-flow diagram before selecting controls:

flowchart LR
    U[User agent] -->|public network| E[Edge]
    E -->|authenticated request| A[Application]
    A -->|workload identity| D[(Tenant data)]
    A --> K[Key service]
    A --> Q[(Audit log)]
    O[Operator] -->|privileged path| P[Admin plane]
    P --> A

Mark where data changes owner, privilege, protocol, persistence, or administration domain. For each flow, ask STRIDE-style questions: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege. Add product abuse that STRIDE may not reveal, such as account farming, scraping, credential stuffing, or refund fraud.

Threat Prevent Detect Recover stolen user credential phishing-resistant MFA, rate limits impossible-travel and device signals revoke sessions; recover account cross-tenant access tenant-bound authorization and storage keys denied-access and invariant metrics contain tenant scope; investigate reads service impersonation workload identity and mTLS identity and policy audit revoke identity; rotate trust material malicious release reviewed provenance and admission policy deployment and runtime evidence halt rollout; restore known-good artifact destructive operator action least privilege and dual control immutable admin audit revoke access; restore and reconcile

docs.title: Authentication, sessions, and authorization
docs.text:
Authentication establishes an identity with a confidence level. Authorization decides whether that principal may perform one action on one resource in one context. Do not encode authorization only in UI visibility or trust caller-supplied roles.

Centralize policy semantics while enforcing close to the resource. A useful decision tuple is:

allow(principal, action, resource, tenant, context, policy_version)

RBAC assigns permissions to roles and is operationally simple. ABAC evaluates attributes such as tenant, ownership, device posture, region, and time. ReBAC derives access from relationships such as document member or team parent. Most systems combine them. Default deny, make precedence explicit, and version policy so an audit can reconstruct a decision.

Session cookies should be Secure, HttpOnly, and use an appropriate SameSite policy. Rotate session identifiers after privilege changes. Protect state-changing browser requests against CSRF. Short token lifetime limits exposure but increases dependency on refresh and identity availability; revocation needs session state, a deny list, or short expiry plus risk-based controls.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
docs.text:
OAuth delegates authorization. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer. The actors are resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server. An ID token tells the client about authentication. An access token is presented to the resource server. They are not interchangeable.

For browser and mobile clients, use Authorization Code with PKCE (S256). This OIDC example additionally requests the openid scope; an OAuth-only response need not contain an ID token. Bind the redirect URI and transaction state to the initiating client session:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User agent
    participant C as Client
    participant AS as Authorization server
    participant API as Resource server
    C->>U: Redirect with state, nonce, code challenge
    U->>AS: Authenticate and consent
    AS-->>U: Authorization code
    U->>C: Code and state
    C->>AS: Code plus PKCE verifier
    AS-->>C: ID token and access token
    C->>API: Access token
    API-->>C: Authorized resource

For JWT tokens, validate issuer, audience, signature algorithm, signature, expiry, and required claims. Opaque access tokens instead require the authorization server's supported validation or introspection contract. The client also validates state and OIDC nonce. Pin accepted algorithms; never accept a token merely because it decodes. Resource servers should receive audience-restricted, scope-minimized tokens. Sender-constrained tokens reduce bearer-token replay when the ecosystem supports them.

Do not put secrets or excessive personal data in JWT claims: signed does not mean encrypted, and issued tokens persist until expiry. Opaque tokens permit central introspection and rapid revocation at the cost of a runtime dependency and cache-consistency choices.

docs.title: Workload identity and mTLS
docs.text:
For handshake evidence, trust distribution, and mesh data/control-plane failure, use TLS and PKI and Service Mesh and Zero Trust.

Static service credentials spread, age, and survive ownership changes. Prefer short-lived workload identities issued from attested runtime facts: workload, namespace, service account, environment, and deployment identity. Authorize the workload, not only its network address.

mTLS authenticates both transport peers and encrypts the hop. It does not decide whether service A may read tenant B's invoices; an authorization policy must bind identity, method, resource, and tenant. If a sidecar terminates mTLS, define how the application trusts identity metadata and prevent direct bypass to its plaintext port.

A rotation plan overlaps trust safely:

  1. Publish a new trust root or issuer while retaining the old one.
  2. Verify every verifier has accepted the new trust bundle.
  3. Issue leaf credentials from the new authority.
  4. Observe old-credential use until bounded lifetime drains it.
  5. Remove the old root and retain audit evidence.

Emergency revocation needs shorter leaf lifetimes, policy denial, or both. Certificate revocation mechanisms alone may not meet the response time of an internal fleet.

docs.title: Key and secret lifecycle
docs.text:
Keys pass through generation, distribution, activation, use, rotation, revocation, archival, and destruction. Generate strong keys in an approved cryptographic module or managed KMS. Separate key-encryption keys from data-encryption keys and use envelope encryption:

ciphertext = Encrypt(DEK, plaintext, authenticated_context)
wrapped_DEK = Encrypt(KEK, DEK)

Authenticated context should bind stable metadata such as tenant ID, object ID, schema version, and purpose. A ciphertext copied to another tenant or field then fails authentication. Store key IDs and algorithm versions with ciphertext, but not plaintext keys.

That claim assumes an authenticated-encryption construction and that the decryptor derives expected context from trusted identity and metadata. If the attacker can copy both ciphertext and a caller-controlled tenant context, context binding does not authorize access. Check authorization before key use, and ensure every nonce satisfies the chosen algorithm's uniqueness requirements. As with the OWASP authorization guidance, encryption is not a substitute for restricting the application's authority (accessed 2026-09-08).

Rotation does not always require rewriting all data. New writes use the current key; old data can be rewrapped or lazily re-encrypted under a measured migration. Deletion by destroying a dedicated key works only when the key's scope matches the deletion subject and no plaintext copies, caches, logs, backups, or derived datasets remain.

Secrets must not appear in source, images, logs, metrics labels, crash dumps, or broad environment inspection. Deliver them at runtime, scope them narrowly, rotate automatically, and alert on anomalous access.

docs.title: Tenant isolation
docs.text:
Tenant isolation is defense in depth across identity, policy, queries, storage, encryption, quotas, and operations.

Layer Control Failure it contains API derive tenant from authenticated context caller changes tenant_id parameter authorization action and resource check authenticated user crosses role boundary data access tenant predicate or row policy missing application filter schema/database composite tenant keys or dedicated database cross-tenant reference and blast radius cryptography tenant-scoped key where justified storage snapshot or key-scope compromise capacity per-tenant quotas and fair queues noisy-neighbor denial of service operations tenant-scoped support tools and audit broad operator access

Shared tables maximize efficiency but demand excellent policy and testing. Separate schemas, databases, accounts, or cells increase isolation and restore flexibility at operational cost. Choose tiers from impact and regulatory needs, not customer size alone. Test guessed IDs, stale memberships, confused-deputy calls, cache-key omissions, exports, and support tooling.

docs.title: Privacy, retention, and deletion
docs.text:
Create a data inventory with category, purpose, legal basis, owner, location, residency, retention, recipients, and deletion method. Minimize collection and purpose. Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a scoped surrogate; pseudonymized data can still be personal data if re-identification remains possible.

Deletion is a workflow across canonical records, indexes, caches, search, streams, analytical copies, vendor systems, and backups:

flowchart TD
    R[Verified deletion request] --> I[Inventory affected objects]
    I --> C[Atomically tombstone canonical state and record deletion intent]
    C --> P[Outbox relay retries deletion intent]
    P --> D[Derived stores and vendors]
    D --> V[Verify completion]
    V --> A[Record minimal audit evidence]
    C --> B[Backup expiry policy]

Commit the canonical denial/tombstone and durable deletion intent together where possible. If those stores cannot transact together, persist a recoverable workflow before acknowledging the request. Otherwise a crash after canonical deletion but before publication can strand a still-visible search copy. Record a separate receipt for each sink and retry idempotently.

State whether backups are selectively edited, cryptographically erased, or allowed to expire under a documented isolation and restoration policy. A restore must not resurrect deleted records; replay deletion evidence before reopening service.

docs.title: Audit and repudiation resistance
docs.text:
An audit event records actor, effective identity, action, target, tenant, decision, policy version, request ID, time source, outcome, and privileged justification. Avoid secrets and unnecessary payloads. Protect append paths with restricted writers, immutable retention, hashes or signatures where required, independent export, and monitored gaps.

Application logs are not automatically audit logs. Debug logs may be sampled, mutable, and short-lived. Audit availability also matters: decide whether a sensitive action fails closed when durable audit recording is unavailable, or writes through a local durable buffer with a strict recovery objective.

docs.title: Abuse resistance and availability
docs.text:
Rate limiting must bind the scarce resource and likely attacker dimension: account, credential, device, IP prefix, tenant, endpoint, or expensive backend key. IP-only limits punish shared networks and are easy to distribute around. Layer coarse edge limits, authenticated quotas, per-tenant fairness, concurrency limits, and business invariants.

Prevent enumeration with uniform external errors while retaining internal reason codes. Bound decompression ratios, parser depth, regex work, upload size, fan-out, pagination, and query complexity. Challenge or delay suspicious traffic before expensive dependencies. Abuse controls need appeal, false-positive, and emergency-disable paths.

docs.title: Software supply chain
docs.text:
Treat source, build service, dependencies, artifact registry, deployment controller, and runtime as one trust chain. Pin dependencies and verify integrity; generate an SBOM; isolate builds; minimize build credentials; sign provenance and artifacts; enforce admission policy; scan, patch, and monitor runtime drift.

Signing an artifact proves association with a key, not that code is safe. Protect signing identity, make builds reproducible or attestable, require reviewed source provenance, and support rapid revocation. Avoid unreviewed install scripts and mutable tags in production manifests.

docs.title: Quantitative security decisions
docs.text:
Suppose 10 million active sessions have 24-hour access tokens. Reducing lifetime to 15 minutes lowers the maximum lifetime of a stolen access token by 96x, assuming the attacker cannot refresh it. With all sessions continuously active and evenly distributed, the steady-state average is 10,000,000 / 900 = 11,111 refreshes/s; synchronized expiry can create a much larger peak. Add jitter, scalable refresh infrastructure, device-bound sessions where appropriate, and emergency revocation.

For online guessing, an account with 20 allowed attempts/hour and a uniformly random six-digit code faces an upper-bound success probability near 20 / 1,000,000 = 0.002% per hour before expiration and telemetry effects. Distributed attacks require account-based limits, not only IP limits. Use standards-approved authenticators rather than inventing code schemes.

docs.title: Decision framework
docs.text:
1. List assets, sensitive actions, adversaries, regulations, and impact tiers.
  2. Draw data and admin flows with trust boundaries.
  3. Enumerate misuse and failure cases; rank inherent risk.
  4. Bind identities to least-privilege authorization at each resource.
  5. Minimize data and choose encryption, retention, deletion, and audit semantics.
  6. Add abuse, tenant, operator, and supply-chain controls.
  7. Define prevention, detection, containment, recovery, owner, and residual risk.
  8. Validate with design review, tests, staged attack exercises, and incident drills.

docs.title: Failure cases and tradeoffs
docs.text: Failure Why it happens Response signing key exposed broad CI or operator access revoke, rotate, invalidate sessions/artifacts, investigate provenance authorization cache stale policy changed before cache expiry version decisions; short TTL; push invalidation for high-risk changes mTLS sidecar bypass application port reachable directly network policy, loopback binding, application verification deletion misses search index incomplete data inventory durable workflow, per-sink receipt, periodic reconciliation audit pipeline down synchronous sink unavailable fail closed for critical actions or durable local buffer by policy one tenant exhausts workers shared queue without fairness tenant quotas, weighted scheduling, admission control security control causes outage global policy or certificate rollout canary, overlap trust, break-glass with expiry and audit

docs.title: L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: An L5 design gives a concrete threat model, protocol-correct identity flow, resource-level authorization, tenant-safe data access, key rotation, abuse limits, and recovery for likely compromise. An L6 design also defines control ownership across teams, impact tiers, policy distribution and rollback, cell boundaries, organization-wide identity migration, audit evidence, regulatory lifecycle, supply-chain trust, and accepted residual risk.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Saying "JWT is secure" without validation, audience, storage, expiry, and revocation.
  • Using an ID token to call an API.
  • Treating mTLS as authorization.
  • Accepting tenant IDs from request bodies without binding them to identity.
  • Claiming encryption at rest solves application or operator misuse.
  • Describing deletion only in the primary database.
  • Logging full tokens or personal payloads for audit.
  • Adding rate limits without naming the scarce resource or attacker key.
  • Trusting signed artifacts without protecting the signer and source-to-build path.

docs.title: 1. Cross-tenant document API
docs.text:
An API receives /tenants/{tenant}/documents/{id} and checks only that the caller is logged in. Repair the design.
