Answer: Derive allowed tenant memberships from authenticated identity; authorize read on the document; query by both tenant_id and document_id; bind cache keys and encryption context to tenant; prevent cross-tenant references with schema constraints where possible; audit denied and privileged access; and test guessed IDs, stale roles, support impersonation, exports, and caches. The path tenant is a requested scope, not authority.

docs.title: 2. OAuth token choice
docs.text:
A single-page application sends its OIDC ID token to three internal APIs because it contains the user's email.

Answer: The ID token is intended for the client and may have the wrong audience and permissions. Obtain access tokens audience-restricted to the resource APIs, validate issuer/audience/signature/expiry at each trust boundary, minimize scopes and claims, and keep user profile data separate from authorization. Use Authorization Code with PKCE and protect browser session/token storage.

docs.title: 3. Key rotation
docs.text:
A database holds one billion envelope-encrypted objects. The key-encryption key must rotate within seven days.

Answer: Introduce the new KEK, make new writes use it, and rewrap DEKs without decrypting every plaintext where the KMS and format permit. Process in resumable partitions with rate limits, record key version per object, verify counts and failed objects, retain the old key for rollback until coverage is proven, then disable and finally destroy it according to policy. Emergency compromise may require a faster path and wider containment. Rewrapping does not undo exposure if an attacker already obtained the old KEK and wrapped DEKs or plaintext. In that case, assess which data keys and ciphertext copies are compromised; recovery may require new DEKs and data re-encryption as well as access revocation.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Start with assets, actions, adversaries, and trust boundaries.
  • Authentication names a principal; authorization governs a resource action.
  • Scope short-lived user and workload credentials and plan rotation before issuance.
  • Enforce tenant identity in policy, query, key, quota, and operator paths.
  • Treat privacy deletion and audit as distributed workflows with verification.
  • Protect the source-to-runtime supply chain and design compromise recovery.

docs.title: System Design Readiness
docs.text:
For deeper mechanism and lifecycle practice, follow Engineering Foundations and Practice. Its three waves connect runtime budgets, distributed theory, performance, storage recovery, contracts, operations, and safe evolution to eight executable fault fixtures and an evolving capstone. This is an extension to the canonical route below, not a replacement.

System design interviews test structured engineering judgment under incomplete information. Readiness means you can derive architecture from requirements, quantify limits, trace protocols, preserve invariants through failures, and communicate tradeoffs at the expected scope. Memorized diagrams are not enough.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • diagnose prerequisite gaps before practicing more case studies;
  • connect requirements, estimates, data, protocols, reliability, security, and cost;
  • answer component and end-to-end questions at L5 depth;
  • add organizational scope, migrations, and policy at L6 depth;
  • use a repeatable practice and review loop; and
  • score diagnostic answers against an explicit key.

docs.text:
Follow dependencies rather than reading every topic in arbitrary order:

flowchart TD
    E[Estimation] --> D[Delivery framework]
    N[Networking] --> D
    A[API and data modeling] --> R[Relational databases]
    A --> NR[Non-relational storage]
    R --> P[Partitioning and sharding]
    NR --> P
    C[Consistency and CAP] --> P
    P --> MR[Multi-region]
    M[Messaging and streams] --> T[Distributed transactions]
    R --> T
    C --> T
    D --> X[Case studies]
    P --> X
    MR --> X
    T --> X
    S[Security architecture] --> X
    REL[Reliability] --> X

Recommended sequence:

  1. Delivery Framework and Estimation
  2. Networking, API and Data Modeling, and Database Indexing
  3. Relational Databases, Non-Relational Storage, and Caching
  4. Consistency and CAP, Partitioning and Sharding, and Messaging and Streams
  5. Distributed Transactions, Reliability, and Multi-Region
  6. Security Architecture and Cost Engineering
  7. Pattern drills and complete case studies under time constraints

Do not wait for perfect mastery before integrating topics. Learn enough to apply one concept, then revisit it when a case study exposes a gap.

docs.title: The first-principles design model
docs.text:
A defensible design connects five artifacts:

requirements -> invariants -> operations -> resource model -> failure policy
  1. Requirements: user journeys, scale, latency, availability, geography, privacy, and exclusions.
  2. Invariants: safety facts that must never become false. State eventual-progress and bounded-freshness requirements separately.
  3. Operations: commands, queries, events, identities, and consistency needs.
  4. Resource model: QPS, bytes, CPU, memory, connections, partitions, and cost.
  5. Failure policy: deadlines, idempotency, retries, degradation, recovery, and ownership.

An architecture box is justified only when it implements one of these. "Kafka for scale" is weak. "A partitioned log decouples ingestion from three replayable projections; order ID scopes ordering; seven-day retention exceeds the four-hour outage plus six-hour rebuild objective" is design reasoning.

docs.title: Readiness dimensions
docs.text: Dimension Ready behavior Warning sign requirements prioritizes journeys and SLOs asks only DAU and QPS estimation keeps units and models peaks/skew guesses machine counts data states invariants, keys, indexes, retention lists databases by brand protocols traces commit, ack, retry, and timeout order draws arrows without semantics distribution names partition key, consistency, failover says "eventual" without operation scope reliability quantifies budgets, queues, RTO/RPO adds retries and replicas generically security binds identity, tenant, resource, and action says "encrypt everything" cost calculates dominant unit drivers treats price as post-design concern communication records decisions and revises visibly silently changes assumptions

docs.title: Calculation baseline
docs.text:
You should derive these without prompts:

requests/day          = requests/s * 86,400
ingest/day            = writes/s * bytes/write * 86,400
retained storage      = ingest/day * retention * replicas / compression
concurrency           = throughput * time in system
backlog growth        = arrival rate - service rate
drain time            = backlog / (service rate - new arrival rate)
availability in series = product of required independent component availability
error budget          = eligible events * (1 - SLO)

Always add peak-to-average ratio, replication, indexes, protocol overhead, write amplification, failure headroom, and uncertainty where relevant. A correct formula with unsupported inputs is not evidence; state how benchmarks and production measurements will calibrate it.

docs.title: Protocol-tracing baseline
docs.text:
For every state-changing request, answer:

  1. What identity authorizes it?
  2. What stable command or idempotency key names it?
  3. Where is the invariant checked under concurrency?
  4. What exact durable write defines acceptance?
  5. What is published, and before or after which commit?
  6. What happens if the response or acknowledgment is lost?
  7. Which layer retries, with what deadline and budget?
  8. How are duplicates, stale events, and gaps handled?
  9. How does an operator reconcile and repair it?
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API
    participant D as Canonical DB
    participant B as Broker
    participant P as Projection
    C->>A: Command plus idempotency key
    A->>D: Transaction: invariant, result, outbox
    D-->>A: Commit position
    A-->>C: Accepted result
    D->>B: Relay event at least once
    B->>P: Event plus aggregate version
    P->>P: Deduplicate and apply

If you cannot explain the crash before and after each arrow, the design is not finished.

docs.title: Decision framework: the 45-minute execution loop
docs.text:
Time Output 0-5 min top journeys, constraints, assumptions, and explicit non-goals 5-10 min scale worksheet and SLO/RTO/RPO targets 10-18 min API, data model, invariants, and primary access paths 18-28 min smallest end-to-end architecture and one protocol trace 28-36 min bottleneck evolution, partitioning, caching, async work, multi-region 36-42 min failure table, security, observability, cost, and operations 42-45 min tradeoff summary, migration path, and unanswered risks

This is a control loop, not a script. Spend more time where the interviewer probes. Keep a visible decision log:

Decision Why Rejected alternative Revisit trigger partition by account ID account-local ordering and writes region key creates hot partitions cross-account workload dominates async analytics outside checkout latency contract synchronous write couples failure legal rule requires immediate evidence

docs.title: L5 expectations
docs.text:
An L5 answer owns a service or bounded system deeply:

  • converts product requirements into measurable APIs and SLOs;
  • estimates scale with distributions and identifies the first bottleneck;
  • gives concrete schemas, keys, indexes, partitioning, and retention;
  • traces one write and one read through all dependencies;
  • explains concurrency control, idempotency, deadlines, and backpressure;
  • handles instance, zone, dependency, and data-recovery failures;
  • includes tenant-safe authorization, abuse limits, and observability;
  • compares at least one credible alternative and states migration triggers.

L5 depth is not the number of technologies. It is the precision of one coherent system.

docs.title: L6 expectations
docs.text:
An L6 answer adds scope and durable organizational judgment:

  • separates control and data planes and defines degraded operation;
  • establishes cells, regions, tenants, and administrative blast radii;
  • chooses standards for identity, APIs, events, SLOs, and migrations across teams;
  • models correlated failures and N-1 or regional evacuation capacity;
  • provides versioned rollout, rollback, reconciliation, and decommission paths;
  • explains cost allocation, capacity commitments, and platform leverage;
  • names owners, decision authority, audit evidence, and incident recovery;
  • recognizes where consistency or availability is a product decision.

L6 breadth without protocol depth is hand-waving. Show one path at L5 precision, then expand its fleet and organizational implications.

docs.title: Exercises with worked answers: diagnostic questions
docs.text: Answer these in 45 to 90 seconds each before reading the key. Show calculations where requested.

docs.title: Requirements and estimation
docs.text:
1. A service averages 20,000 requests/s, peaks at 5x, and returns 8 KB. Estimate peak response bandwidth.
  2. Why is daily active users insufficient for capacity planning?
  3. At 6,000 jobs/s arriving and 5,000 jobs/s processing, how large is the backlog after 20 minutes?
  4. A handler sustains 2,000 requests/s per instance at the target p99. How many instances serve a 30,000 requests/s peak while keeping 40% of provisioned capacity spare, before zone-loss and deployment reserve?

docs.title: Data and consistency
docs.text:
1. Design a key for fetching a user's newest 100 notifications without one unbounded partition.
  2. When is a relational database a better canonical store than a document store?
  3. What does a tombstone do in an LSM store, and why can early removal resurrect data?
  4. Does R + W > N prove linearizability? Explain.
  5. A user writes then immediately reads from a replica. Give two ways to provide read-your-writes.
  6. Why can a secondary index turn a one-shard query into scatter-gather?

docs.title: Protocols and transactions
docs.text:
1. The database commits but the client times out. What should retry do?
  2. Explain the outbox pattern and its delivery semantics.
  3. When is 2PC a defensible choice over a saga?
  4. Distinguish saga compensation from rollback.
  5. Design expiry for a seat hold without racing confirmation.
  6. Why does broker-level exactly-once not guarantee exactly one payment charge?

docs.title: Networking and reliability
docs.text:
1. Why does lowering a DNS TTL immediately before migration not guarantee fast convergence?
  2. At 10,000 requests/s and 40 ms mean service time, estimate useful mean concurrency.
  3. A client, gateway, and service each make three attempts. What is the worst-case dependency amplification?
  4. Why can one HTTP/2 connection be a bottleneck or failure domain despite multiplexing?
  5. Three equal zones run at 70% utilization. Can the service survive one zone loss without shedding?
  6. A 99.9% SLO sees 1.5% errors. What is the burn rate?

docs.title: Security and cost
docs.text:
1. Distinguish an OIDC ID token from an OAuth access token.
  2. Why is mTLS insufficient for tenant authorization?
  3. List four places a deletion workflow must consider beyond the primary row.
  4. What must an audit record contain to reconstruct an authorization decision?
  5. A service logs 5 KB/request at 50,000 requests/s. Estimate daily raw log volume.
  6. Why can raising utilization reduce cost but violate an availability design?
  7. What is the difference between request hit ratio and byte hit ratio?
  8. Name the minimum inputs for cost per successful operation.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text: Reveal the diagnostic answer key after your first attempt

docs.title: Requirements and estimation
docs.text:
1. Peak is 20,000 * 5 = 100,000 requests/s. Payload bandwidth is 100,000 * 8 KB = 800 MB/s, or about 6.4 Gbit/s before protocol overhead and retries.
  2. DAU hides requests per user, object size, peak-to-average ratio, geography, skew, session concurrency, background work, and growth. Convert journeys into per-second and byte distributions.
  3. Growth is 1,000 jobs/s. In 1,200 seconds the backlog reaches 1.2 million jobs, assuming rates remain constant.
  4. Keeping 40% of provisioned capacity spare means a 60% target utilization. Required capacity is 30,000 / 0.60 = 50,000 requests/s, so the service needs 50,000 / 2,000 = 25 instances. Zone-loss and deployment surge are separate reserves. If a problem instead defines "40% extra over demand," the result would be 21; always state which convention is used.

docs.title: Data and consistency
docs.text:
1. Use a partition key such as (tenant_id, user_id, time_bucket) and a descending sort key (created_at, notification_id). Query current then prior buckets until 100 results are collected. Choose bucket size from hot-user rate and retention.
  2. Choose relational when correctness needs cross-row uniqueness/references/transactions, access paths evolve, joins and reconciliation matter, and the workload fits its scaling plan. Document shape alone is not a reason to abandon constraints.
  3. A tombstone is a newer delete marker that masks older immutable values. If removed before old replicas/files are repaired or compacted, an older value can reappear and win during merge or repair.
  4. No. Overlap is insufficient without assumptions about membership, version selection, concurrent operations, sloppy quorums, and topology change. Cite the engine's operation-level guarantee.
  5. Route to the current authority that contains the acknowledged write, or carry a commit position/session token and wait or route to a replica that has replayed at least that position. Acquire a fresh snapshot after this check. An asynchronous failover may lose the required history; report that explicitly instead of silently returning stale data. Sticky routing alone is not a proof across topology changes.
  6. If the index is not colocated or partitioned by the query predicate, every shard may need to search its local index and return candidates, increasing latency and work with shard count.

docs.title: Protocols and transactions
docs.text:
1. Retry with the same idempotency key and request hash. The server returns the stored committed outcome or continues the in-progress command; it must not create a second command because timeout is an unknown outcome.
  2. Commit canonical state and an outbox row in one local transaction. A relay publishes later and may publish duplicates. Consumers apply with inbox deduplication or versioned idempotency. The end-to-end default is at least once plus idempotent effects.
  3. Use 2PC when all short-lived participants support prepare/commit, atomic commitment is required, blocking during uncertainty is acceptable, and one coordinator/recovery domain is operationally manageable. Atomic cross-participant visibility additionally requires suitable reader isolation; 2PC alone does not provide it. Use a saga for long, autonomous, compensatable steps.
  4. Rollback removes uncommitted database effects. Saga compensation is a new committed business action, such as refunding a charge, and may be incomplete or irreversible.
  5. Inventory owns an atomic transition from HELD to CONFIRMED only if the hold is eligible under its authoritative time/policy. Expiry transitions HELD to EXPIRED. Exactly one wins; retries read the terminal state.
  6. The broker transaction does not include the external payment provider and local database crash window. Use a stable provider idempotency key, durable local state, outcome lookup, and reconciliation.

docs.title: Networking and reliability
docs.text:
1. Resolvers can retain the previous long TTL, impose cache floors, and clients can reuse old connections. Lower TTL before migration, wait out the prior TTL, overlap endpoints, and drain connections.
  2. Little's Law gives 10,000 * 0.040 = 400 active requests on average. Tail, bursts, and headroom require testing around a bounded limit.
  3. 3 * 3 * 3 = 27 attempts. Choose one retry owner and propagate deadline and attempt budget.
  4. All streams share one TCP congestion and loss domain; connection flow control, server stream limits, CPU, or one reset can affect many requests. A few bounded connections may improve isolation.
  5. No. Losing one-third of capacity raises survivor utilization to 70% / (2/3) = 105% before skew. Keep lower normal utilization or define shedding.
  6. Allowed error is 0.1%. Burn rate is 1.5 / 0.1 = 15x; a 30-day budget would exhaust in about two days if sustained at uniform eligible traffic.

docs.title: Security and cost
docs.text:
1. An ID token tells the client about the user's authentication and is audience-bound to that client. An access token conveys delegated authorization to a resource server. An API should not accept an ID token as a substitute.
  2. mTLS authenticates the peer workload and encrypts the hop. Authorization must still decide whether that workload and effective user may perform one action on one tenant resource.
  3. Any four of caches, search indexes, streams, analytical stores, object blobs, vendor systems, logs, materialized views, and backups/restores, subject to legal retention policy.
  4. Actor and effective identity, action, resource, tenant, context, decision, policy version, outcome, request/correlation ID, trustworthy timestamp, and privileged justification where applicable, without secrets.
  5. 50,000 * 5 KB = 250 MB/s; multiplied by 86,400 gives 21.6 TB/day raw, before replication and index overhead.
  6. Higher normal utilization leaves less capacity for peaks, retries, deployments, and zone loss. Queueing sharply increases p99 near saturation. Validate target utilization against the failure SLO.
  7. Request hit ratio counts requests, including repeated requests for one object; byte hit ratio weights by bytes. Many tiny cache hits can coexist with expensive large misses, so egress and origin load follow byte hit ratio more closely.
  8. Allocated monthly fixed and variable costs, count of eligible operations, successful-operation count, and a consistent definition of success. Useful decomposition also needs resource use, shared-cost policy, and failure/retry waste.

docs.title: Scoring and remediation
docs.text:
These bands are course self-assessment heuristics, not validated predictors of hiring outcomes. Record the actual reasoning and failed checks alongside the number.

Score each answer:

  • 0: absent, materially incorrect, or only a product name.
  • 1: correct concept but no mechanism, scope, or failure reasoning.
  • 2: correct, concrete, scoped, and includes the key tradeoff or calculation.
Score Interpretation Next action 52-60 strong integrated readiness run timed mocks and tighten communication 42-51 interview-capable with visible gaps drill every zero and weak protocol trace 30-41 foundations not yet integrated follow prerequisite map and repeat diagnostics below 30 foundational gaps dominate study core chapters before case-study memorization

Any zero on questions 8, 11, 12, 19, 21, 23, or 24 is a correctness risk even if the total is high. Revisit the linked foundation and explain one real workflow aloud from request to recovery.

Keep the first attempt and elapsed time before opening the key. Re-answer missed questions on a new scenario rather than editing the recorded attempt. In particular, compare question 13 against the PostgreSQL isolation contract: commit decisions and the snapshot a reader observes are separate promises (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Practice loop
docs.text:
1. Pick one case and write a five-line design contract.
  2. Estimate load, storage, concurrency, and failure headroom.
  3. Model one command, one query, and their data structures.
  4. Trace commit, publish, retry, and unknown outcomes.
  5. Inject dependency latency, zone loss, bad rollout, and tenant abuse.
  6. Calculate one cost sensitivity and one migration trigger.
  7. Score using Interview Scorecard.
  8. Record the weakest reasoning step and drill that foundation next.

Use retrieval practice. Redraw from a blank page, explain aloud, and compare against invariants. Reading a polished solution feels fluent but does not prove you can produce one.

docs.title: Common interview traps
docs.text:
• Beginning with architecture before defining the design contract.
  • Optimizing for global scale when one primary and a migration path suffice.
  • Listing caches, queues, and databases without data ownership.
  • Using average estimates and ignoring skew, tails, and failure capacity.
  • Claiming exactly once, strong consistency, or zero downtime without scope.
  • Adding retries without idempotency, deadline, and amplification math.
  • Discussing happy-path scale while omitting recovery and deletion.
  • Treating security and cost as closing remarks rather than constraints.
  • Giving an L6 platform answer without one precise end-to-end protocol.

docs.title: Failure cases and course corrections
docs.text: Failure mode Evidence during the interview Course correction scope explosion every feature becomes mandatory restate top journeys and move the rest to non-goals architecture by habit components appear before operations return to invariants, access paths, and measured constraints arithmetic drift units disappear or totals contradict write units, recompute one baseline, and state uncertainty protocol ambiguity commit, publish, and acknowledgment order is unclear trace one command and inject a crash after each step premature distribution multi-region machinery hides the core design establish the smallest correct single-region path first hidden overload queues and retries are unbounded calculate concurrency and amplification; add admission control correctness hand-wave "eventual consistency" replaces an invariant state what may be stale, for whom, and for how long shallow L6 breadth policy language lacks a working protocol zoom into one path at L5 depth, then expand ownership and migration

docs.title: Final readiness checklist
docs.text:
• I can turn an ambiguous prompt into prioritized journeys and non-goals.
  • I can calculate traffic, bytes, concurrency, backlog, and N-1 capacity.
  • I can state invariants and show where concurrency enforces them.
  • I can provide concrete API, schema, partition, index, and event examples.
  • I can trace DNS, connection, deadline, commit, publish, and retry behavior.
  • I can classify timeout outcomes and design idempotent recovery.
  • I can explain consistency per operation and multi-region authority.
  • I can define SLI/SLO, degradation, RTO/RPO, restore, and reconciliation.
  • I can bind identity, authorization, tenant, privacy, audit, and abuse controls.
  • I can calculate cost per unit and test its most sensitive assumption.
  • I can compare alternatives and name a reversible migration trigger.
  • I can finish with risks, owners, and evidence required before launch.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Readiness is integrated reasoning, not architecture recall.
  • Requirements, invariants, operations, resources, and failures must connect.
  • L5 demonstrates precise ownership of one system; L6 extends it across domains and time.
  • Calculations expose bottlenecks and invalid promises early.
  • Protocol traces and crash points reveal correctness gaps hidden by diagrams.
  • Practice from a blank page, score evidence, and remediate the weakest prerequisite.

docs.title: Java Concurrency for LLD Interviews
docs.text:
Java concurrency questions are small system-design interviews. The objects may fit on a whiteboard, but the design still needs explicit state, invariants, ownership, failure behavior, and tests. This track develops those skills from thread mechanics through the Java Memory Model, synchronization, executors, asynchronous composition, and production diagnostics.

The code targets Java 21. Unless a chapter explicitly discusses virtual threads, examples use platform threads so scheduling and shared-memory hazards remain visible.

Core examples target Java 21; several test fixtures intentionally use virtual threads for independently blocked actors. Complete class blocks, method sketches requiring surrounding types/imports, and intentionally broken examples are different artifacts. The targeted review runner extracts an explicit allowlist, adds imports and explicitly declared fake dependency methods for lifecycle sketches, compiles with --release 21, and runs bounded child JVMs. Run it with JAVA_HOME set to JDK 21 or newer. JDK 24 execution does not validate Java 21 monitor pinning or Java 21 preview APIs; JDK 17 cannot compile the full baseline. JUnit and JCStress snippets require their own harness/dependencies and are not all exercised by this runner.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
By the end of the track, you should be able to:

  • turn an underspecified concurrency prompt into state, invariants, and a synchronization policy;
  • distinguish atomicity, visibility, ordering, progress, and cancellation requirements;
  • explain correctness with explicit interleavings and happens-before edges;
  • select locks, concurrent collections, atomics, executors, or immutability for stated reasons;
  • identify a design's linearization points and liveness risks;
  • write deterministic tests for safety properties and useful stress tests for races;
  • discuss Java 21 platform threads and virtual threads without mixing their cost models.

docs.title: Prerequisite map
docs.text:
You should be comfortable with Java syntax, classes, interfaces, exceptions, generics, and collections. The track introduces concurrency concepts from first principles, but it assumes you can read ordinary Java 21 code.

flowchart LR
    J[Core Java] --> M[Interview method]
    J --> T[Threads and tasks]
    M --> MM[Thread safety and JMM]
    T --> MM
    MM --> L[Locks and conditions]
    L --> E[Executors and queues]
    E --> A[Atomics and concurrent collections]
    E --> V[Virtual threads and structured tasks]
    A --> P[Patterns and diagnostics]
    V --> P

Before Chapter 3, make sure these terms are precise:

Term Working definition State Data whose value can affect later behavior or results. Shared Reachable by more than one thread during overlapping lifetimes. Mutable Able to change after construction. Invariant A predicate that must hold at every externally observable boundary. Synchronization policy The rule that says which mechanism protects each piece of state and when callers must use it. Linearization point The conceptual instant at which a concurrent operation takes effect. Safety Nothing bad happens, such as a duplicate allocation or corrupted value. Liveness Something good eventually happens, such as a blocked caller making progress.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Chapter Core question Interview deliverable 1. The 45-minute method How do I structure the discussion? Contract, state model, invariants, policy, linearization points, liveness, tests 2. Threads, tasks, and lifecycle What actually executes, blocks, and stops? Correct lifecycle and cancellation reasoning 3. Thread safety and the Java Memory Model When may another thread observe a write? Data-race analysis and happens-before proof 4. Synchronization, locks, and conditions How should compound state transitions be protected? Locking protocol and wait-condition design 5. Coordination primitives How do threads rendezvous, hand off permits, and advance phases? Primitive selection, interruption policy, and group-completion proof 6. Atomics and concurrent collections When is one atomic transition or concurrent collection enough? CAS loop, per-operation atomicity boundary, and collection tradeoff 7. Executors, capacity, and backpressure How is work admitted, bounded, rejected, and stopped? Executor ownership, capacity calculation, overload policy, and shutdown protocol 8. Async composition, parallelism, and virtual threads Which execution model fits waiting, CPU work, and fan-out? Completion/failure graph, end-to-end deadline, and resource-bound design 9. Liveness, debugging, and concurrency testing How do I prove progress and investigate failures? Deadlock analysis, diagnostic workflow, and deterministic race tests 10. Concurrency patterns Which reusable ownership and coordination shape fits the state? Pattern choice with invariants, failure modes, and lifecycle semantics 11. Classic problems: solved workbook Can I apply the method to canonical synchronization exercises? Complete solution, correctness argument, and adversarial test plan 12. Concurrent LLD problems: solved workbook Can I combine concurrency semantics with component design? Interview-ready API, implementation, operational limits, and evaluation rubric

Later chapters should build on the same proof discipline rather than replacing it with API memorization.

docs.title: How to study each chapter
docs.text:
1. Predict every broken example before running it.
  2. Write one failing interleaving as numbered thread steps.
  3. State the invariant independently of the implementation.
  4. Mark the synchronization action or API contract that establishes ordering.
  5. Identify the operation's linearization point.
  6. Name at least one safety test and one liveness test.
  7. Re-deliver the design aloud under a five-minute limit.

One successful run proves almost nothing

A race may need a rare schedule, a different processor, or a different JIT decision. Tests can reveal concurrency defects, but a correctness argument must cover all permitted executions.

docs.title: A running example: bounded seat allocation
docs.text:
Suppose multiple threads call reserve() on a pool with one remaining seat.

final class BrokenSeatPool {
    private int remaining = 1;

    boolean reserve() {
        if (remaining > 0) {
            remaining--;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

The desired invariant is:

0 <= remaining <= initialCapacity
successfulReservations + remaining == initialCapacity

An invalid execution is:

Step Thread A Thread B remaining 1 reads remaining == 1 1 2 reads remaining == 1 1 3 writes 0; returns true 0 4 writes 0; returns true 0

Both callers report success for one seat. The final field value looks plausible, so an assertion on remaining alone misses the violation. A corrected design must make the check and decrement one atomic state transition:

final class SeatPool {
    private int remaining = 1;

    synchronized boolean reserve() {
        if (remaining == 0) {
            return false;
        }
        remaining--;
        return true;
    }

    synchronized int remaining() {
        return remaining;
    }
}

The monitor protects every access to remaining. The successful call linearizes at remaining--; an unsuccessful call linearizes at its observation of zero while holding the same monitor. Monitor release happens-before a later acquisition of that monitor, so callers using these methods receive both atomicity and visibility.

docs.title: Tool-selection preview
docs.text: Need Likely starting point Main cost or trap Publish fixed configuration Immutable object plus safe publication A final reference does not freeze mutable children. Protect a small compound invariant synchronized Blocking and accidental lock scope. Timed or interruptible lock acquisition ReentrantLock Unlock must be in finally; fairness reduces throughput. One independent numeric update AtomicLong Multiple atomics do not create one multi-field transaction. High-contention statistics LongAdder sum() is not an atomic snapshot for control decisions. Per-key atomic map operation ConcurrentHashMap.compute Mapping functions must remain short and non-recursive. Bound asynchronous work ThreadPoolExecutor plus bounded queue Rejection and shutdown are part of the design. Many blocking I/O tasks Virtual threads in Java 21 They do not make CPU work faster or remove shared-state races.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Saying "thread-safe" without naming the protected state and invariant.
  • Treating volatile as a general replacement for locking.
  • Assuming thread-safe methods compose into a thread-safe workflow.
  • Using sleep as coordination or as proof that another thread finished.
  • Catching InterruptedException and continuing without a cancellation policy.
  • Optimizing contention before establishing correctness.
  • Claiming an API is lock-free, fair, or linearizable without knowing its contract.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Why can remaining == 0 coexist with two successful reservations?
  2. What is the difference between a safety property and a liveness property?
  3. Why must a synchronization policy cover readers as well as writers?
  4. What does a linearization point let an interviewer reason about?
  5. Why are virtual threads not a fix for data races?

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Write a two-minute opening for this prompt: "Design an in-memory component that allocates at most ten permits to concurrent callers and allows permits to be returned." Include state, two invariants, one policy decision, and one question for the interviewer.

Solution

I will model ten interchangeable permits. The canonical mutable state is either an available count or a set of checked-out permit IDs; I would choose IDs only if ownership or duplicate returns must be diagnosed. The safety invariants are 0 <= available <= 10 and one permit cannot be checked out to two callers. A return must not increase capacity after a duplicate or foreign release. I will put every allocation and return transition under one private lock first, then consider a semaphore or a more scalable representation only if requirements justify it. Do callers wait, time out, or fail immediately when exhausted, and must cancellation remove waiting callers promptly?

This opening exposes the ambiguity around waiting and return identity. If duplicate returns are impossible by contract, a count may suffice. If the component must detect them, track lease IDs or owner tokens.

docs.title: Sources and originality
docs.text:
The curriculum is independently authored. Its interview-oriented organization was informed by the broad educational goals of AlgoMaster System Design and the repository curation style of awesome-low-level-design. No prose or examples are copied from either source.

Normative Java semantics should be checked against Java Language Specification, Chapter 17: Threads and Locks and the Java SE 21 java.util.concurrent package documentation.

Next: The 45-minute concurrency interview method

docs.title: The 45-Minute Concurrency Interview Method
docs.text: A concurrency design answer needs a proof, not merely a class diagram. Start with observable behavior and state. Derive invariants. Assign every shared mutable field to a synchronization policy. Only then choose APIs and optimize contention.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • structure a 45-minute concurrency LLD interview;
  • separate required behavior from implementation choices;
  • inventory state, ownership, invariants, and wait conditions;
  • define synchronization and cancellation policies;
  • identify linearization points for successful and failed operations;
  • evaluate safety, liveness, fairness, and performance separately;
  • propose deterministic unit tests and bounded stress tests.

docs.title: 1. Use the interview clock deliberately
docs.text:
Time Deliverable Questions to answer 0-5 min Contract What operations exist? May they block? What are capacity and failure semantics? 5-10 min State and invariants What changes? What must never be observed? Who owns each value? 10-18 min Baseline API and model What are the public methods, results, and lifecycle states? 18-28 min Synchronization proof What protects each field? Where does each operation linearize? 28-34 min Liveness and cancellation Can threads deadlock, starve, wait forever, or ignore shutdown? 34-40 min Tests Which schedules prove boundaries, and how will tests terminate? 40-45 min Tradeoffs and summary Why this primitive? What changes under different load or semantics?

Do not force every interview into exact minute boundaries. The purpose of the clock is to prevent ten minutes of class modeling followed by an unexamined synchronized keyword.

docs.title: 2. Establish a concurrency contract
docs.text:
Consider this prompt:

Design an in-memory key pool. A caller acquires an unused key, uses it, and releases it. At most capacity keys may be checked out. Callers may wait up to a timeout.

Ask questions whose answers change correctness or the API:

  • Are keys interchangeable, or does the caller receive a stable identity?
  • Is a duplicate release an error, a no-op, or undefined behavior?
  • Must acquisition be first-in-first-out?
  • Does timeout include time spent contending for internal locks?
  • How does shutdown affect current holders and waiters?
  • Must waiting acquisition react to thread interruption?
  • Can capacity change after construction?

Turn answers into explicit operations and outcomes:

interface KeyPool extends AutoCloseable {
    KeyLease acquire(Duration timeout)
            throws InterruptedException, TimeoutException;

    @Override
    void close();
}

A lease can make ownership and one-time return explicit:

interface KeyLease extends AutoCloseable {
    String key();

    @Override
    void close();
}

The signature already encodes three decisions: acquisition can block, interruption remains visible, and release is attached to a lease that supports try-with-resources.

docs.title: 3. Inventory state before choosing a primitive
docs.text:
Write a state table on the whiteboard:

State Mutable? Shared? Owner or guard Relevant invariant availableKeys yes yes pool lock no key appears twice checkedOut yes yes pool lock disjoint from available closed yes yes pool lock no acquire succeeds after close lease released yes potentially lease monitor complete return takes effect once configured capacity no yes final field, safely published positive and fixed

Thread confinement means state is reachable by only one thread during the period it is mutable. Guarded state is shared mutable state accessed only while holding a designated lock. Ownership transfer moves exclusive responsibility from one thread or component to another using a publication mechanism.

Do not say "the class is synchronized." Say, for example:

The private lock guards availableKeys, checkedOut, and closed. Every read and write of those fields occurs while holding that lock. The lease monitor guards its release flag and the entire return, because clients may close the same lease concurrently.

That statement is a synchronization policy. It is reviewable and testable.

docs.title: 4. Write invariants as predicates
docs.text:
For a fixed key universe allKeys:

availableKeys intersection checkedOut == empty
availableKeys union checkedOut == allKeys
availableKeys.size + checkedOut.size == capacity
each lease returns at most one key
closed implies no future acquire succeeds

Distinguish three types of condition:

Type Meaning Example Representation invariant Internal state is valid whenever no operation is mid-transition. Available and checked-out sets are disjoint. Safety property An externally bad result never occurs. Two live leases never expose the same key. Liveness property Progress eventually occurs under stated assumptions. A waiter completes after a key is released, unless interrupted, timed out, or closed.

Liveness needs assumptions. "Every waiter eventually succeeds" is false if leases are never returned or an unfair scheduler never runs a thread.

docs.title: 5. Show the broken design and an interleaving
docs.text:
final class BrokenCounterPool {
    private final int capacity;
    private int inUse;

    BrokenCounterPool(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    boolean tryAcquire() {
        if (inUse == capacity) {
            return false;
        }
        inUse++;
        return true;
    }

    void release() {
        inUse--;
    }
}

With capacity == 1, the check-then-act sequence is not atomic:

Step Thread A Thread B inUse 1 reads inUse == 0 0 2 reads inUse == 0 0 3 computes and writes 1 1 4 computes and writes 1 1 5 returns true returns true 1

The field does not exceed capacity, yet two permits were issued. Internal state alone cannot reconstruct the externally visible violation. Also, an unmatched release() can make inUse negative.

docs.title: 6. Build the smallest correct baseline
docs.text:
The following sketch uses a fair ReentrantLock because the contract includes blocking acquisition and a timeout. Fairness is a policy choice, not a universal improvement.

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

final class LockedKeyPool implements KeyPool {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(true);
    private final Condition keyReturnedOrClosed = lock.newCondition();
    private final ArrayDeque<String> available;
    private final Set<String> checkedOut = new HashSet<>();
    private boolean closed;

    LockedKeyPool(Set<String> keys) {
        if (keys.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("keys must not be empty");
        }
        available = new ArrayDeque<>(Set.copyOf(keys));
    }

    @Override
    public KeyLease acquire(Duration timeout)
            throws InterruptedException, TimeoutException {
        if (timeout.isNegative()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("timeout must not be negative");
        }

        long budgetNanos = saturatedNanos(timeout);
        long startedNanos = System.nanoTime();
        if (!lock.tryLock(budgetNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            throw new TimeoutException("timed out acquiring pool lock");
        }
        try {
            while (available.isEmpty() && !closed) {
                long remaining = remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos);
                if (remaining == 0L) {
                    throw new TimeoutException("no key became available");
                }
                keyReturnedOrClosed.awaitNanos(remaining);
            }
            if (closed) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("pool is closed");
            }

            String key = available.removeFirst();
            boolean added = checkedOut.add(key);
            if (!added) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("pool invariant violated");
            }
            return new Lease(this, key);
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    private void release(String key) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            if (!checkedOut.remove(key)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("key is not checked out");
            }
            available.addLast(key);
            keyReturnedOrClosed.signal();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            closed = true;
            keyReturnedOrClosed.signalAll();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    private static long saturatedNanos(Duration timeout) {
        try {
            return timeout.toNanos();
        } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            return Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
    }

    private static long remainingNanos(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
        long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
        return elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
                : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
    }

    private static final class Lease implements KeyLease {
        private final LockedKeyPool pool;
        private final String key;
        private boolean released;

        private Lease(LockedKeyPool pool, String key) {
            this.pool = pool;
            this.key = key;
        }

        @Override
        public String key() {
            return key;
        }

        @Override
        public synchronized void close() {
            if (!released) {
                pool.release(key);
                released = true;
            }
        }
    }
}

For interview code, call out the deliberate simplifications:

  • Extreme positive durations are clamped to Long.MAX_VALUE nanoseconds. The elapsed-time calculation avoids overflow from adding a budget to System.nanoTime().
  • Closing prevents new acquisition and wakes waiters, but existing leases remain valid and return normally.
  • Fair locking gives waiting threads a stronger admission preference under contention, but costs throughput and still does not promise perfect end-to-end FIFO completion.
  • Lock acquisition and every condition wait consume one end-to-end timeout. The condition wait uses a while loop because wakeups can be spurious and another thread can consume the key first.

docs.title: 7. Mark linearization points
docs.text:
An operation is linearizable when each completed call can be viewed as taking effect once, between invocation and response, while respecting real-time order.

Operation outcome Linearization point Successful acquire Removal from available while holding lock Timed-out acquire Failed timed lock acquisition, or protected empty observation after the wait budget expires Acquire rejected by close Protected observation of closed == true First lease close Removal from checkedOut while holding lock Duplicate lease close Observation of released under the lease monitor, after the first return completed Pool close Protected write closed = true

The lease monitor serializes complete returns, not merely election of a returning caller. An atomic flag set before pool.release would allow a second close to return while the key was still unavailable, violating a completed-close return contract. Lock order is lease monitor then pool lock; no pool path acquires a lease monitor. The lease's key() must not be used after close: returning a key cannot revoke a string already held by the caller.

docs.title: 8. Explain memory ordering, not just mutual exclusion
docs.text:
Unlocking a ReentrantLock happens-before a later successful lock of that same lock. Therefore, writes to available, checkedOut, and closed made before unlock become visible to the next holder.

The lease monitor publishes released; the pool lock publishes pool state. Timeout bounds waiting, not a hard real-time response: after a wake the implementation may take an available key even if scheduling delayed reacquisition beyond the budget. A strict deadline-wins contract would check remaining time again before removal, while retaining a separate zero-budget immediate-attempt policy.

An interviewer may ask whether signal() publishes the returned key. The complete answer is:

  1. The releaser changes the predicate while holding lock.
  2. It signals a waiter before unlocking.
  3. The waiter cannot return from awaitNanos and inspect the predicate until it reacquires the lock.
  4. The releaser's unlock happens-before that successful reacquisition.

The signal is notification; the lock edge provides memory visibility.

docs.title: 9. Analyze liveness and cancellation
docs.text:
Ask these questions explicitly:

  • Deadlock: Does any path acquire multiple locks in inconsistent order?
  • Starvation: Can a runnable waiter be bypassed indefinitely?
  • Livelock: Can threads keep changing state without completing useful work?
  • Bounded waiting: Is there a timeout, cancellation path, or shutdown policy?
  • Notification: Does every transition that can make a wait predicate true signal appropriate waiters?
  • Interruption: Is interruption propagated, translated, restored, or intentionally consumed?

The corrected pool uses timed interruptible tryLock and interruptible condition waits. If interrupted during either wait, acquire throws InterruptedException and issues no lease. Interruption after acquisition can race with success. close() uses signalAll() because every waiter must wake to observe terminal state. release() can use signal() because one returned key enables at most one acquisition.

docs.title: 10. Test the contract
docs.text:
Prefer orchestration primitives over sleeps. A safety test can align contenders at a start gate and record leases. The gates control when work is admitted and released; scheduling among contenders remains nondeterministic:

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class LockedKeyPoolTest {
    @Test
    void neverIssuesMoreThanCapacity() throws Exception {
        var pool = new LockedKeyPool(Set.of("k1", "k2"));
        var start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        var release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        var holdersReady = new CountDownLatch(2);
        var active = new AtomicInteger();
        var maximum = new AtomicInteger();
        var keys = ConcurrentHashMap.<String>newKeySet();

        var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(12);
        var futures = new java.util.ArrayList<java.util.concurrent.Future<Void>>();
        try {
            for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
                futures.add(executor.submit(() -> {
                    start.await();
                    try (var lease = pool.acquire(Duration.ofSeconds(2))) {
                        int now = active.incrementAndGet();
                        maximum.accumulateAndGet(now, Math::max);
                        if (!keys.add(lease.key())) {
                            throw new AssertionError("duplicate live key");
                        }
                        holdersReady.countDown();
                        release.await();
                        keys.remove(lease.key());
                        active.decrementAndGet();
                    }
                    return null;
                }));
            }
            start.countDown();
            assertTrue(holdersReady.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            release.countDown();
            for (var future : futures) future.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        } finally {
            start.countDown();
            release.countDown();
            for (var future : futures) future.cancel(true);
            executor.shutdownNow();
            pool.close();
            assertTrue(executor.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
        }

        assertEquals(2, maximum.get());
    }
}

The holders latch replaces an unbounded spin, every future is observed, and cleanup releases gates before cancelling workers. Timed waits bound the cooperative paths. Still use a child-JVM timeout for deliberately mutated non-interruptible deadlocks: an in-process test cannot forcibly terminate arbitrary Java code.

Build a test matrix:

Property Controlled setup Assertion Capacity safety Hold all keys, start one more acquire No additional lease before release Uniqueness Run many holders and track live keys No duplicate live key Timeout Exhaust pool, use a short budget TimeoutException, no state change Interruption Block a known waiter, interrupt it Prompt InterruptedException, no lease Shutdown Block several waiters, call close All terminate with closed outcome Idempotent lease close Concurrently close one lease One return only; capacity unchanged Reuse Release then reacquire Returned key becomes available

Stress tests increase schedule coverage by repeating operations with randomized yields or durations. They do not replace the invariant and happens-before proof. Tools such as jcstress are useful when testing Java Memory Model outcomes; ordinary unit tests are poor at proving an outcome impossible.

docs.title: 11. Compare design options
docs.text:
Design Strength Cost Choose when One intrinsic lock Small proof surface No timed lock acquisition or multiple conditions State and waiting rules are simple ReentrantLock plus Condition Interruptible/timed lock, explicit conditions More code; unlock discipline required Wait predicates or lock features matter Semaphore plus key queue Capacity primitive is explicit Must keep permit count and queue consistent Permits are independent or composition is carefully designed BlockingQueue<String> take, timed poll, and return map naturally Shutdown and duplicate returns need extra policy Keys themselves are the bounded resources Lock-free structure Potential progress under narrow contention Hard proof, retries, allocation, ABA concerns Measurement shows blocking is the bottleneck and algorithm is well understood

For this prompt, a bounded BlockingQueue may be the simplest production answer if duplicate return and shutdown semantics are wrapped correctly. In an interview, presenting the lock-based baseline first makes invariants and linearization visible; then comparing the queue demonstrates API knowledge without outsourcing the proof.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Drawing classes before deciding whether operations block or fail.
  • Naming a lock without listing every field it guards.
  • Protecting writes but exposing unsynchronized getters or iterators.
  • Defining a linearization point only for successful operations.
  • Equating fairness with guaranteed FIFO completion.
  • Calling signal outside the lock or waiting with if rather than while.
  • Ignoring timeout accounting across lock acquisition and condition waiting.
  • Testing with Thread.sleep and assuming the desired state has been reached.
  • Forgetting that task exceptions submitted to an executor are often captured in Future.
  • Discussing throughput while cancellation and shutdown remain undefined.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. What belongs in a synchronization policy?
  2. Why is available.size() <= capacity insufficient as the only invariant?
  3. Where does a timed-out operation linearize?
  4. Why does a condition wait always recheck its predicate?
  5. Which edge publishes a released key to an awakened waiter?
  6. When is signal() preferable to signalAll(), and what must be true?
  7. How can a test fail inside a worker without failing the test method?
  8. Why might a fair lock reduce throughput?

docs.title: Exercise 1: Repair the synchronization policy
docs.text: A cache protects entries with synchronized put, but get and size are unsynchronized. State the defect and propose a complete policy.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Find the linearization points
docs.text: For a bounded queue, identify plausible linearization points for successful offer, failed offer, successful poll, and timed-out poll.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Design a cancellation test
docs.text:
Describe a deterministic test proving that a blocked acquisition reacts to interruption without consuming a key.

Solutions

Previous: Java Concurrency track | Next: Threads, tasks, and lifecycle

docs.title: Solution 1
docs.text: The lock does not protect a field; a protocol does. Unsynchronized reads can race with writes, observe stale state, and interact unsafely with a non-concurrent collection. Guard every access to entries, including compound iteration and size reads, with the same private lock. Alternatively, replace the representation with a suitable concurrent map, then separately prove any multi-call invariant because thread-safe map methods do not automatically compose.

docs.title: Solution 2
docs.text:
• Successful offer: insertion into the queue's protected representation.
  • Failed immediate offer: protected observation that capacity is exhausted.
  • Successful poll: removal from the protected representation.
  • Timed-out poll: final protected observation that the queue is empty after the remaining wait budget reaches zero.

Exact points depend on the implementation contract, but each must occur between invocation and response and produce an order consistent with real time.

docs.title: Solution 3
docs.text:
1. Create a capacity-one pool and acquire its only key.
  2. Start a waiter and use a latch immediately before it calls blocking acquire.
  3. Establish that the task has started; where possible, add an injectable test hook or inspect a documented waiting state rather than sleeping.
  4. Interrupt the waiter thread.
  5. Require the future to complete within a short outer deadline with InterruptedException as its cause.
  6. Release the original lease and acquire once successfully.
  7. Assert no second key or duplicate lease exists.

The outer deadline protects the suite from a broken implementation. Cleanup closes the first lease and pool in finally.

docs.title: Threads, Tasks, and Lifecycle
docs.text: A thread is an execution path scheduled by the runtime and operating system. A task is a unit of work. Keeping those concepts separate lets a design change execution policy without rewriting business logic.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish processes, threads, concurrency, and parallelism;
  • explain Java thread states without treating them as an application state machine;
  • use start, join, sleep, interruption, and daemon status correctly;
  • separate task definitions with Runnable or Callable from thread creation;
  • choose execution strategies for CPU-bound and I/O-bound work;
  • define lifecycle, failure, cancellation, and shutdown behavior;
  • explain Java 21 virtual-thread caveats at interview depth.

docs.title: 1. Process, thread, and task
docs.text:
A process is an operating-system isolation boundary with its own virtual address space and resources. Processes communicate through mechanisms such as sockets, pipes, files, or shared memory. A crash or memory corruption is usually contained more strongly across processes than across threads.

Threads inside one Java process share the heap and process resources. Each thread has its own call stack, program counter, and execution state. Sharing makes communication cheap, but an unsafely shared object can be corrupted by any participating thread.

Concept Owns Shares Typical design concern Process Address space, OS identity, resource limits Explicit IPC endpoints Isolation, deployment, crash boundary Thread Stack, instruction position, scheduling state Heap and process resources Races, blocking, scheduling, lifecycle Task Inputs, logic, result or failure Depends on captured references Cancellation, idempotency, execution policy

In Java, creating new Thread(task) binds one task to one thread directly. Submitting a task to an ExecutorService separates what should run from where and when it runs.

docs.title: 2. Concurrency is not parallelism
docs.text:
Concurrency means multiple tasks can make progress over overlapping time. Parallelism means multiple computations execute at the same physical instant, usually on different cores.

One core can run concurrent tasks by time-slicing. Many cores can run parallel tasks. A concurrent program is not necessarily faster: coordination, cache misses, allocation, and context switching can dominate.

Concurrent on one core:  A A | B B | A | B B | A
Parallel on two cores:   A A A A A
                         B B B B B

Interview answers should connect the goal to the workload:

  • Use concurrency to keep serving other work while one task waits.
  • Use parallelism to reduce elapsed time for divisible CPU computation.
  • Use isolation even when throughput is unchanged, for example a dedicated thread for a single-writer state machine.

docs.title: 3. Java thread states
docs.text:
Thread.State reports six JVM-level states:

State Meaning Common cause NEW Constructed but not started new Thread(...) RUNNABLE Eligible to run or running in the JVM Computation, native execution, or scheduler-ready BLOCKED Waiting to enter a synchronized monitor Another thread owns that monitor WAITING Waiting indefinitely for a defined action Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park() TIMED_WAITING Waiting up to a deadline sleep, timed join, timed wait, timed park TERMINATED run completed normally or abruptly Return or uncaught exception 
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NEW
    NEW --> RUNNABLE: start
    RUNNABLE --> BLOCKED: monitor unavailable
    BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE: monitor acquired
    RUNNABLE --> WAITING: indefinite wait or join
    WAITING --> RUNNABLE: notification, completion, interrupt
    WAITING --> BLOCKED: Object.wait must reacquire monitor
    RUNNABLE --> TIMED_WAITING: sleep or timed wait
    TIMED_WAITING --> RUNNABLE: timeout, notification, interrupt
    TIMED_WAITING --> BLOCKED: timed Object.wait must reacquire monitor
    RUNNABLE --> TERMINATED: run returns or throws
    TERMINATED --> [*]

This is an observation model, not a protocol for coordinating application logic. A sampled state may change immediately. RUNNABLE does not prove that a thread is on a CPU, and an I/O implementation may report states differently. Never spin until another thread's state equals WAITING as the production coordination mechanism.

docs.title: 4. start() is not run()
docs.text:
Broken code:

Thread worker = new Thread(() -> importFile(), "import-worker");
worker.run();
System.out.println("caller continues");

Calling run() is an ordinary method call. importFile executes on the current thread and completes before the print. Calling start() requests a new execution thread, which later invokes run():

Thread worker = new Thread(() -> importFile(), "import-worker");
worker.start();
System.out.println("caller may continue before import finishes");

A Thread can be started at most once. Calling start() again throws IllegalThreadStateException; terminated threads are not restartable. Reuse tasks or create new threads through an execution service.

docs.title: Happens-before reasoning
docs.text:
The Java Memory Model gives start() a crucial guarantee: actions in the calling thread before worker.start() happen-before actions in the started thread. Therefore, initialization before start is visible to the worker.

final class StartVisibility {
    private int value;

    void runExample() throws InterruptedException {
        value = 42;
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            if (value != 42) {
                throw new AssertionError();
            }
        });
        worker.start();
        worker.join();
    }
}

Do not reverse the edge. Writes performed after start() are not automatically ordered before worker reads.

docs.title: 5. join() waits and publishes completion
docs.text:
Broken code assumes scheduling order:

int[] result = {0};
new Thread(() -> result[0] = 42).start();
System.out.println(result[0]);

The caller can print 0; it neither waits for completion nor establishes the required visibility edge.

Corrected code:

int[] result = {0};
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> result[0] = 42);
worker.start();
worker.join();
System.out.println(result[0]);

All actions in a terminated thread happen-before another thread returns from join after observing that termination. Joining a thread that has not started does not establish completion of future work. join supplies both completion coordination and visibility.

join does not propagate the worker's exception. An uncaught exception terminates the worker; the joining thread returns normally. If a result or failure must cross the task boundary, use Future, CompletableFuture, or another explicit result channel.

Timed join can return while the worker remains alive. Check the postcondition:

worker.join(500);
if (worker.isAlive()) {
    worker.interrupt();
    throw new IllegalStateException("worker exceeded deadline");
}

The timeout does not stop the worker. Interruption is only a request, and the caller still needs a policy for final cleanup or bounded escalation.

docs.title: 6. sleep() pauses; it does not coordinate
docs.text:
Thread.sleep makes the current thread temporarily not runnable. It does not release monitors the thread owns. Its timing depends on system timers and scheduling, and interruption can end it early; it is not an exact wake-time guarantee.

Broken coordination:

worker.start();
Thread.sleep(100);
assert cache.isReady();

This test can fail on a slow machine and waste 100 ms on a fast one. Use a completion mechanism:

var ready = new java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch(1);
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
    initializeCache();
    ready.countDown();
});
worker.start();

if (!ready.await(2, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("cache initialization timed out");
}

The CountDownLatch contract also supplies memory consistency: actions before countDown() happen-before actions after a corresponding successful await() return.

Never sleep while holding a lock to "give another thread time." The other thread may need that same lock and be unable to make progress.

docs.title: 7. Interruption is cooperative cancellation
docs.text:
Calling interrupt() does not forcibly kill a Java thread. It sets the target's interrupt status, unless the thread is blocked in certain interruptible methods. Methods such as sleep, join, and BlockingQueue.take respond by clearing the status and throwing InterruptedException.

Broken code loses the cancellation request:

try {
    queue.take();
} catch (InterruptedException ignored) {
    // Continue as if nothing happened.
}

If the method cannot propagate InterruptedException, restore the status and terminate or return:

void consumeUntilStopped() {
    try {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            Message message = queue.take();
            process(message);
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

If the method can propagate it, prefer that:

Message nextMessage() throws InterruptedException {
    return queue.take();
}

docs.title: Interrupt-status API distinctions
docs.text:
API Which thread? Clears status? thread.interrupt() Target thread Not by itself thread.isInterrupted() Target thread no Thread.interrupted() Current thread yes

The static Thread.interrupted() is often used when code intentionally acknowledges and consumes an interrupt. Accidental calls can erase cancellation evidence.

docs.title: Interleaving: interrupt before blocking
docs.text:
Interruption is not merely a wakeup delivered only after blocking:

Step Controller Worker 1 calls worker.interrupt() running computation 2 later calls queue.take() 3 interruptible call detects status and throws

A sound cancellation design handles requests that arrive before, during, or after a blocking boundary. Also, CPU loops must poll status at useful intervals:

for (int i = 0; i < records.size(); i++) {
    if ((i & 1023) == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
        throw new java.util.concurrent.CancellationException();
    }
    transform(records.get(i));
}

The polling interval trades cancellation latency against checking overhead.

docs.title: 8. Daemon threads are not a shutdown strategy
docs.text:
The JVM begins shutdown when no started non-daemon thread remains, or when shutdown is otherwise initiated. Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive. They can stop without completing finally blocks when the process exits.

Thread metrics = new Thread(this::publishLoop, "metrics-publisher");
metrics.setDaemon(true);
metrics.start();

setDaemon must occur before start. Use daemon threads only for work that may be abandoned at process termination. Never rely on a daemon thread to flush critical records, commit data, or release an external lease. Prefer explicit close, interruption, executor shutdown, bounded wait, and a documented final policy.

Work Daemon appropriate? Reason Best-effort local diagnostics sampler possibly Losing the final sample is acceptable Payment settlement writer no Abandonment violates durability Lock-renewal loop no as sole policy Requires explicit release/fencing and shutdown Test-only leak detector possibly Must not keep a failed suite alive

docs.title: 9. Runnable and Callable
docs.text:
Runnable.run() returns no value and declares no checked exception. Callable<V>.call() returns V and may throw Exception.

Runnable refresh = () -> cache.refresh();

java.util.concurrent.Callable<Report> buildReport =
        () -> reportService.build(reportId);

These interfaces describe task shape, not scheduling. Avoid embedding thread creation in domain methods:

// Broken ownership: every call creates an unmanaged thread.
void sendReceipt(Order order) {
    new Thread(() -> mailer.send(order)).start();
}

Inject an execution policy or return a task:

final class ReceiptService {
    private final java.util.concurrent.Executor executor;

    ReceiptService(java.util.concurrent.Executor executor) {
        this.executor = executor;
    }

    void sendReceipt(Order order) {
        executor.execute(() -> mailer.send(order));
    }
}

The corrected design still needs answers for overload, rejection, retries, exception reporting, shutdown, and whether asynchronous acceptance is valid. Dependency injection makes those policies selectable; it does not define them.

docs.title: 10. CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work
docs.text:
A CPU-bound task spends most time computing. An I/O-bound task spends substantial time waiting for storage, network, or another blocking resource.

Workload Starting execution policy Constraint to measure CPU-bound independent calculations Pool near available processor count Core utilization, task size, memory bandwidth Blocking I/O with scarce downstream connections Concurrency bounded by downstream capacity Connection count, latency, queue age, timeout rate Mixed CPU and blocking I/O Separate pools or isolate stages Head-of-line blocking and saturation Many simple blocking I/O tasks on Java 21 Virtual thread per task Downstream limits, pinning, memory, task admission

For CPU work, adding threads beyond cores usually increases context switching rather than throughput. For blocking work, more concurrent tasks can hide wait time, but only until another resource saturates.

A rough sizing intuition for platform threads is:

threads ~= cores * targetUtilization * (1 + waitTime / computeTime)

This is a measurement hypothesis, not a configuration theorem. Request bursts, service-time variance, memory, connection pools, and downstream quotas still matter.

docs.title: Java 21 virtual threads
docs.text:
Virtual threads are final in Java 21. They make thread-per-task style practical for large numbers of mostly blocking tasks. They do not:

  • provide extra CPU cores;
  • make unsafe shared mutation safe;
  • remove the need for timeouts, cancellation, or admission control;
  • increase database connection limits;
  • justify creating unbounded work.

Long blocking operations while inside synchronized or native/foreign calls can pin a virtual thread to its carrier in Java 21. Later JDKs may improve implementation details, so state the version when discussing pinning. Prefer APIs whose semantics fit the design, measure with Java 21 tooling, and avoid rewriting correct locking solely from folklore.

docs.title: 11. Lifecycle is part of the API
docs.text:
A component that starts threads owns these decisions:

  1. When are threads created?
  2. Who requests shutdown?
  3. Are new tasks rejected after shutdown?
  4. Are queued tasks drained, cancelled, or returned?
  5. How are running tasks asked to stop?
  6. How long does the owner wait?
  7. Where do uncaught failures go?

A raw-thread component can expose explicit lifecycle:

final class Poller implements AutoCloseable {
    private enum State { NEW, RUNNING, STOPPING, TERMINATED }

    private final Object lifecycle = new Object();
    private final Thread worker;
    private State state = State.NEW;

    Poller() {
        worker = new Thread(this::runLoop, "event-poller");
    }

    void start() {
        synchronized (lifecycle) {
            if (state != State.NEW) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("poller cannot start from " + state);
            }
            state = State.RUNNING; // Linearizes start before the thread is launched.
            worker.start();
        }
    }

    private void runLoop() {
        try {
            while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
                Event event = source.next();
                handle(event);
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        } catch (RuntimeException failure) {
            reportFailure(failure);
            throw failure;
        } finally {
            synchronized (lifecycle) {
                state = State.TERMINATED;
            }
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        synchronized (lifecycle) {
            if (state == State.NEW) {
                state = State.TERMINATED;
                return;
            }
            if (state == State.RUNNING) {
                state = State.STOPPING; // Linearizes shutdown against start.
            }
        }
        worker.interrupt();
        try {
            worker.join(5_000);
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            return;
        }
        if (worker.isAlive()) {
            reportFailure(new IllegalStateException("poller did not stop"));
        }
    }
}

This is illustrative, not universal. source.next() and handle must honor the chosen cancellation policy. Starting in the constructor would publish this before construction completes, a defect covered in Chapter 3. The lifecycle monitor prevents double start and makes concurrent start/close deterministic: whichever guarded transition wins decides whether the worker is launched, and close before start permanently terminates the component.

docs.title: Lifecycle invariants and linearization points
docs.text:
For a component with states NEW, RUNNING, STOPPING, and TERMINATED, state the legal transitions before writing synchronization code:

NEW -> RUNNING -> STOPPING -> TERMINATED
NEW -> TERMINATED
RUNNING -> TERMINATED (unexpected worker exit)

Useful invariants are:

  • at most one worker thread is started;
  • no task is accepted after the component commits to stopping;
  • TERMINATED implies the worker can perform no more component work;
  • every accepted task either completes or receives the documented cancellation outcome;
  • resource closure happens at most once, after no code can begin using that resource.

Guard the lifecycle state and task-admission decision with one policy. If close() writes STOPPING under a lock but submit() checks state without that lock, a task can slip in after shutdown appears to succeed.

Plausible linearization points are the guarded NEW -> RUNNING transition for start, the guarded RUNNING -> STOPPING transition for close, and the guarded insertion into an accepted-work queue for submission. A failed submission linearizes at its protected observation that state is no longer RUNNING.

The liveness contract also needs bounds. For example: after close, an interruptible idle worker reaches TERMINATED within five seconds unless a named external call violates its cancellation contract. This is more useful than promising that shutdown is "graceful" without defining completion, abandonment, or a deadline.

docs.title: 12. Tests for lifecycle and cancellation
docs.text:
Use controlled dependencies. A fake source can announce entry into next() and block interruptibly on a latch. Then a test can:

  1. start the poller;
  2. wait until the fake confirms it is blocked;
  3. call close;
  4. assert that close returns within a deadline;
  5. assert that no event runs after closure;
  6. assert that failure reporting receives unexpected runtime failures.

Every concurrency test needs an outer timeout and cleanup. Capture task failures through Future.get, an uncaught-exception handler, or a test-owned error queue. Do not let worker failures disappear on background threads.

docs.title: Tradeoffs
docs.text: Choice Benefit Cost or caveat Raw Thread Explicit mechanics and naming Manual lifecycle; one thread per task Fixed platform-thread pool Bounded execution concurrency Queueing and thread starvation under blocking Cached/unbounded pool Absorbs short bursts Can create excessive threads and overload dependencies Virtual thread per task Simple blocking code at high task counts Requires explicit resource bounds; Java 21 pinning caveats Interrupt cancellation Standard cooperative signal Code and dependencies must respond correctly Custom cancellation token Domain-specific reasons/deadlines Must integrate with interruptible Java APIs Daemon thread Does not delay JVM exit Work may be abandoned

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Calling run() and claiming a new thread was started.
  • Assuming start() means the worker has already executed.
  • Assuming join() forwards the worker's exception.
  • Using sleep for readiness or mutual exclusion.
  • Swallowing InterruptedException.
  • Calling Thread.interrupted() without realizing it clears status.
  • Treating daemon threads as graceful cleanup.
