  • Choosing thread count from request rate while ignoring task service time and downstream capacity.
  • Saying virtual threads make blocking free or CPU work parallel without bound.
  • Starting a worker in a constructor and leaking a partially constructed object.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Can concurrent work happen on one CPU core? Can parallel work happen without concurrency?
  2. What is the difference between BLOCKED and WAITING in Thread.State?
  3. Which happens-before edges do start and successful join provide?
  4. Why does timed join require an isAlive check?
  5. Does sleep release an intrinsic lock?
  6. What should code do when it catches InterruptedException but cannot throw it?
  7. Why can a virtual-thread design still overload a database?
  8. Why should a task not decide unilaterally to create a new thread?

docs.title: Exercise 1: Diagnose a visibility and lifecycle bug
docs.text:
final class BrokenService {
    private boolean stop;
    private final Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
        while (!stop) {
            doOneUnit();
        }
    });

    void start() {
        worker.start();
    }

    void stop() throws InterruptedException {
        stop = true;
        worker.join(1_000);
    }
}

List at least four problems and produce a corrected version.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Choose an execution policy
docs.text: An API performs 2 ms of CPU validation, waits about 80 ms for a database, and the database permits 100 concurrent requests. Should Java 21 use a 100-thread platform pool, virtual threads, or a CPU-sized pool?

docs.title: Exercise 3: Preserve interruption
docs.text:
Write a helper that waits for a worker to finish and returns false after a timeout. If the caller is interrupted, it must not erase the request.

Solutions

Previous: The interview method | Next: Thread safety and the Java Memory Model

docs.title: Solution 1
docs.text:
Problems include a data race on stop, unbounded shutdown if doOneUnit blocks despite the timed join returning, failure to check isAlive, no response to interruption in blocking operations, no double-start policy, and no reporting for worker failure.

final class Service implements AutoCloseable {
    private final Thread worker;
    private boolean started;
    private boolean closed;

    Service() {
        worker = new Thread(this::runLoop, "service-worker");
        worker.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, failure) ->
                reportFailure(thread.getName(), failure));
    }

    synchronized void start() {
        if (started || closed) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("already started or closed");
        }
        started = true;
        worker.start();
    }

    private void runLoop() {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            doOneInterruptibleUnit();
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        synchronized (this) {
            closed = true;
            if (!started) {
                return;
            }
        }
        worker.interrupt();
        try {
            worker.join(1_000);
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            return;
        }
        if (worker.isAlive()) {
            reportFailure("service-worker",
                    new IllegalStateException("shutdown timed out"));
        }
    }
}

This assumes doOneInterruptibleUnit either uses interruptible operations or checks status. The shared monitor serializes start with closing admission, including close-before-start. Call close from the external lifecycle owner, not the worker itself, which cannot join its own termination. The earlier enum lifecycle makes intermediate stopping and terminated states explicit.

docs.title: Solution 2
docs.text: The database's limit is the binding resource. Either a platform pool of at most 100 database-active tasks or virtual threads gated by a 100-permit semaphore can work. Virtual threads simplify blocking composition and may support many waiting requests, but they must not bypass the 100-call limit or admission control. A CPU-sized pool would underuse the database because each task spends most time waiting. Also bound queued/admitted requests and apply deadlines; do not allow unlimited virtual threads to accumulate.

docs.title: Solution 3
docs.text:
static boolean joinWithin(Thread worker, Duration timeout) {
    if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
    try {
        return worker.join(timeout);
    } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        return false;
    }
}

This Java 21 helper requires an already-started worker and intentionally translates interruption to false while restoring status. join(Duration.ZERO) only checks termination; converting a sub-millisecond duration to join(0) would instead wait forever. A successful termination observation publishes worker writes; a timeout does not. See the Thread.join(Duration) contract.

docs.title: Thread Safety and the Java Memory Model
docs.text:
Thread safety is not "the program usually prints the right value." A class is thread-safe when it preserves its contract under every permitted interleaving of its public operations, without requiring callers to add undocumented coordination.

The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines which writes a read may observe and which reorderings are legal. It is a language-level contract across compilers, the JIT, processors, and caches. Hardware intuition alone is not a correctness proof.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish atomicity, visibility, and ordering;
  • identify conflicting accesses and data races;
  • construct a happens-before proof using Java's rules;
  • explain safe uses and limits of final and volatile;
  • design immutable objects and safe publication paths;
  • diagnose lost updates, check-then-act races, and unsafe compound actions;
  • prevent this escape during construction;
  • implement and justify double-checked locking correctly in Java 21.

docs.title: Atomicity
docs.text:
An operation is atomic relative to other operations when no thread can observe it partially completed. Reading or writing an individual int is atomic, but count++ is a read-modify-write sequence:

read count
compute count + 1
write result

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: A write is visible to another thread when the JMM requires the later read to observe that write or a still later write. Elapsed wall-clock time does not create visibility.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
The compiler, JIT, and processor may reorder actions as long as single-thread behavior remains legal and the JMM's inter-thread constraints are preserved. A happens-before relationship constrains which effects must be visible and ordered across threads.

Requirement Broken assumption Mechanism examples Atomicity "The statement is one line." Lock, atomic read-modify-write, thread confinement Visibility "The other core will refresh eventually." Volatile edge, monitor/lock edge, start/join, concurrent API contract Ordering "Source order is global order." Happens-before relationships

A mechanism may solve one requirement but not another. A volatile counter write is visible, but counter++ on a volatile field is still not an atomic increment.

docs.title: 2. Conflicting accesses and data races
docs.text:
Two accesses conflict when they access the same variable, at least one is a write, and they occur in different threads. A program has a data race when conflicting accesses are not ordered by happens-before.

Data-race freedom is a powerful design target. Correctly synchronized programs appear sequentially consistent: their actions can be understood as an interleaving that preserves each thread's program order and synchronization rules.

Do not confuse a data race with a higher-level race condition:

  • A data race is defined by unsafely ordered conflicting memory accesses.
  • A race condition is a broader outcome that depends on timing or ordering.
  • A program can have no data race and still violate a compound business invariant because individually synchronized methods are composed incorrectly.

docs.title: 3. Lost updates
docs.text:
Broken counter:

final class BrokenCounter {
    private int value;

    void increment() {
        value++;
    }

    int get() {
        return value;
    }
}

A possible interleaving from zero:

Step Thread A Thread B value 1 reads 0 0 2 reads 0 0 3 computes 1 0 4 computes 1 0 5 writes 1 1 6 writes 1 1

Two increments produce one. Marking value volatile fixes neither the read-modify-write atomicity nor the lost update.

If the state is one independent counter:

final class Counter {
    private final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong value =
            new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong();

    long increment() {
        return value.incrementAndGet();
    }

    long get() {
        return value.get();
    }
}

incrementAndGet is one atomic read-modify-write and is the operation's linearization point. If the invariant spans the counter and another field, one AtomicLong is not enough; put the compound state under one lock or encode it in one immutable value updated atomically.

docs.title: 4. Check-then-act and method composition
docs.text:
Even thread-safe method calls can form an unsafe compound action:

var users = java.util.Collections.synchronizedMap(
        new java.util.HashMap<String, User>());

if (!users.containsKey(id)) {
    users.put(id, loadUser(id));
}

Interleaving:

Step Thread A Thread B 1 containsKey(id) returns false 2 containsKey(id) returns false 3 computes user A computes user B 4 put(id, userA) 5 put(id, userB) overwrites A

Each method is synchronized, but the invariant "initialize once" spans two calls. Use a compound API whose contract provides per-key atomicity:

private final java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, User> users =
        new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();

User user(String id) {
    return users.computeIfAbsent(id, this::loadUser);
}

Tradeoffs matter. The mapping function should be short, must not recursively update the same mapping, and may be invoked again if an invocation fails or does not establish a mapping. Do not perform irreversible external effects and assume exactly-once execution. If loading is slow, consider caching a future, explicit single-flight state, timeout, and failure eviction policy.

docs.title: 5. Happens-before: the proof vocabulary
docs.text:
If action A happens-before action B, A's effects are visible to B and A is ordered before B for JMM reasoning. The relation is transitive.

Core rules used in interviews:

Rule Edge Program order Earlier action in one thread -> later action in that thread Monitor Unlock of monitor M -> every later lock of M Explicit lock Unlock of lock L -> later successful lock of L Volatile Write to volatile V -> every subsequent read of V that observes that order Thread start Actions before t.start() -> actions in thread t Thread termination Actions in t -> successful return from t.join() Transitivity A -> B and B -> C implies A -> C Concurrent utilities Library-specific edges for submission, Future.get, latch, queue handoff, and others

The JLS defines additional details, including synchronization order and default initialization. In an interview, use the smallest chain that proves the relevant read.

docs.title: Example proof
docs.text:
final class ResultBox {
    private int result;

    int calculate() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> result = 42);
        worker.start();
        worker.join();
        return result;
    }
}

Proof:

  1. The worker's write result = 42 precedes its termination by program order.
  2. All actions in the worker happen-before the successful return from join.
  3. The return reads result after join by caller program order.
  4. By transitivity, the write happens-before the read, which must see 42 absent another write.

docs.title: 6. Visibility failure in a stop flag
docs.text:
final class BrokenRunner {
    private boolean stop;

    void run() {
        while (!stop) {
            doWork();
        }
    }

    void stop() {
        stop = true;
    }
}

The read and write conflict and have no happens-before edge. The worker may observe a stale value. The JIT is also allowed to optimize under the JMM's data-racy semantics in ways that invalidate the intuition "it rereads on every loop."

For a single independent flag:

final class Runner {
    private volatile boolean stop;

    void run() {
        while (!stop) {
            doWork();
        }
    }

    void stop() {
        stop = true;
    }
}

A write to stop happens-before a subsequent read that observes it. This design assumes doWork returns often enough to check the flag. If it blocks in interruptible APIs, interruption may be the appropriate cancellation mechanism. A volatile flag does not wake a blocked socket read, condition wait, or queue operation by itself.

docs.title: 7. Volatile: publication and state flags
docs.text:
A volatile field provides:

  • atomic reads and writes for that field;
  • visibility and ordering through the volatile happens-before rule;
  • no mutual exclusion;
  • no automatic atomicity for compound expressions or invariants across fields.

docs.title: Publishing related data with a volatile flag
docs.text:
final class SnapshotPublisher {
    private int[] snapshot;
    private volatile boolean ready;

    void publish(int[] source) {
        snapshot = source.clone();
        ready = true;
    }

    int[] current() {
        if (!ready) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("not ready");
        }
        return snapshot.clone();
    }
}

The write to snapshot precedes the volatile write to ready by program order. A reader's subsequent volatile read of ready == true creates an edge from the volatile write. By transitivity, the initialized array reference and contents are visible. Cloning on both boundaries prevents callers from mutating the published representation.

This one-time publication design would be wrong if a publisher later wrote ready = false, replaced snapshot, and allowed readers to infer versions from one Boolean. Prefer a single volatile immutable snapshot reference:

record Snapshot(long version, java.util.List<String> values) {
    Snapshot {
        values = java.util.List.copyOf(values);
    }
}

final class Snapshots {
    private volatile Snapshot current = new Snapshot(0, java.util.List.of());

    Snapshot current() {
        return current;
    }

    void publish(Snapshot next) {
        current = next;
    }
}

Each read obtains one coherent immutable version. Writers still need coordination if version monotonicity or compare-and-set semantics matter.

docs.title: 8. Final fields and immutability
docs.text:
final prevents reassignment after construction. The JMM also gives final fields special initialization safety: when an object is properly constructed and its reference does not escape during construction, another thread that obtains the reference is guaranteed to see the initialized final fields, including the reachable state covered by the final-field rule.

Final does not recursively make an object immutable:

final class BrokenConfig {
    private final java.util.List<String> hosts;

    BrokenConfig(java.util.List<String> hosts) {
        this.hosts = hosts;
    }

    java.util.List<String> hosts() {
        return hosts;
    }
}

The caller can mutate the original list or the returned list. Correct it with defensive copies:

final class Config {
    private final java.util.List<String> hosts;

    Config(java.util.List<String> hosts) {
        this.hosts = java.util.List.copyOf(hosts);
    }

    java.util.List<String> hosts() {
        return hosts;
    }
}

List.copyOf rejects null elements and produces an unmodifiable list, which is suitable only if element objects are themselves immutable or safely shared. Deep immutability is a property of the entire reachable object graph.

docs.title: Immutable-object checklist
docs.text:
• Make state private and final.
  • Validate constructor arguments.
  • Copy mutable inputs before storing them.
  • Do not expose mutable internals.
  • Ensure referenced elements are immutable or copied.
  • Do not let this escape during construction.
  • Place mutable caches outside the value or synchronize them separately.

docs.title: 9. Safe publication
docs.text:
Publication makes an object reference reachable by another thread. Safe publication uses a JMM mechanism that guarantees the receiving thread sees a valid initialized state.

Common safe publication mechanisms include:

  • storing the reference into a properly used volatile field;
  • storing it under a lock and reading it under the same lock;
  • completing construction before placing it in a thread-safe collection;
  • static initialization;
  • passing state to a thread before calling start();
  • using concurrent utility methods with documented memory-consistency effects.

Broken publication:

final class Registry {
    private Config config;

    void initialize() {
        config = new Config(java.util.List.of("a", "b"));
    }

    Config config() {
        return config;
    }
}

If different threads call these methods without ordering, there is a data race on config. Make the reference volatile for independently replaceable immutable snapshots:

final class Registry {
    private volatile Config config;

    void initialize() {
        config = new Config(java.util.List.of("a", "b"));
    }

    Config config() {
        Config value = config;
        if (value == null) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("not initialized");
        }
        return value;
    }
}

The volatile write publishes the constructed immutable object to a subsequent volatile read. If initialization must happen exactly once, add a lock, static holder, or atomic transition; volatile alone permits multiple writers. In the broken version, the reference race can keep a reader seeing null; it does not negate Config's properly constructed final-field guarantees when a non-null reference is observed. Do not generalize this final-field exception to mutable or non-final state. The earlier SnapshotPublisher is strictly one-shot; even a second publish without resetting ready would race on the ordinary array reference.

docs.title: 10. this escape
docs.text:
An object escapes when another thread can reach it before construction and initialization are complete.

Broken registration from a constructor:

final class BrokenListener {
    private final String topic;

    BrokenListener(EventBus bus, String topic) {
        bus.register(this);
        this.topic = topic;
    }

    void onEvent(Event event) {
        System.out.println(topic.length());
    }
}

The bus may invoke onEvent before topic is assigned. Final-field guarantees require proper construction; publishing this during construction defeats that premise.

Use a factory that publishes only after construction:

final class Listener {
    private final String topic;

    private Listener(String topic) {
        this.topic = java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(topic);
    }

    static Listener createAndRegister(EventBus bus, String topic) {
        Listener listener = new Listener(topic);
        bus.register(listener);
        return listener;
    }

    void onEvent(Event event) {
        System.out.println(topic.length());
    }
}

The bus itself must safely publish registrations to dispatch threads. Moving code out of the constructor fixes premature escape but does not excuse the bus from its own synchronization policy.

Other escape routes include:

  • starting a thread with this::run in a constructor;
  • submitting a lambda that captures this;
  • assigning this to a static or externally reachable field;
  • invoking an overridable method from a constructor when a subclass can expose state.

docs.title: 11. Double-checked locking
docs.text:
The historical broken form lacks volatile:

final class BrokenLazyService {
    private Service instance;

    Service get() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (this) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new Service();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

The unsynchronized outer read races with the write. Without the required ordering, a reader is not guaranteed to observe a properly initialized Service.

Correct Java 21 form:

final class LazyService {
    private volatile Service instance;

    Service get() {
        Service value = instance;
        if (value == null) {
            synchronized (this) {
                value = instance;
                if (value == null) {
                    value = new Service();
                    instance = value;
                }
            }
        }
        return value;
    }
}

Reasoning:

  1. Construction completes before instance = value by program order.
  2. The assignment is a volatile write.
  3. A fast-path volatile read that sees the non-null reference occurs after that write in synchronization order.
  4. The volatile write happens-before that read, publishing construction effects.
  5. The inner check under the monitor ensures only one value is installed.
  6. The local variable avoids repeated volatile reads on the fast path.

This idiom relies on the memory model in Java 5 and later; for pre-Java-5 code, its semantics were not sufficient. In Java 21, prefer simpler initialization when possible:

final class Services {
    private Services() {}

    static Service instance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;
    }

    private static final class Holder {
        private static final Service INSTANCE = new Service();
    }
}

Class initialization is synchronized by the JVM and safely publishes static fields. Use an enum singleton or eager static final field when laziness is unnecessary. Complexity is not free merely because the idiom is valid.

docs.title: 12. Multi-field invariants and volatile snapshots
docs.text:
Broken attempt:

final class BrokenRange {
    private volatile int lower;
    private volatile int upper;

    void set(int lower, int upper) {
        if (lower > upper) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        }
        this.lower = lower;
        this.upper = upper;
    }
}

Each field is visible, but a reader can combine values from different updates. For transitions (0, 10) -> (20, 30), a reader might observe (20, 10), violating lower <= upper.

Publish one immutable value:

record Range(int lower, int upper) {
    Range {
        if (lower > upper) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("lower exceeds upper");
        }
    }
}

final class Ranges {
    private volatile Range current = new Range(0, 10);

    Range get() {
        return current;
    }

    void set(int lower, int upper) {
        current = new Range(lower, upper);
    }
}

The reference update is atomic and volatile-published. If writers must reject stale versions or derive updates from the current value, use an AtomicReference compare-and-set loop or a lock.

docs.title: 13. API memory-consistency reasoning
docs.text:
High-level concurrency APIs document ordering guarantees. Use them instead of reverse-engineering implementations.

Examples from Java 21 contracts include:

  • Actions before submitting a task to an Executor happen-before its execution begins.
  • Actions in an asynchronous computation happen-before actions following a successful Future.get() in another thread.
  • Actions before CountDownLatch.countDown() happen-before actions after a corresponding successful await().
  • Actions before placing an element into a concurrent collection happen-before another thread's access or removal of that element where the API specifies it.

Example handoff:

Message message = new Message(payload);
queue.put(message);

// In another thread:
Message received = queue.take();
received.process();

The BlockingQueue memory-consistency contract safely hands off actions before insertion to actions after removal. If Message remains mutable and both threads continue changing it after handoff, those later accesses need another policy.

docs.title: 14. Testing memory-model claims
docs.text:
This test is suggestive but not a proof:

for (int round = 0; round < 100_000; round++) {
    // Start racing operations and assert observed outcomes.
}

Passing means only that sampled executions did not reveal a defect. Failing once is useful evidence. For low-level JMM questions, jcstress provides a harness designed to classify outcomes across generated schedules and runtime optimizations.

At the class-design level:

  1. Prove every conflicting access is ordered or intentionally atomic.
  2. Write deterministic tests for public invariants using barriers and latches.
  3. Add stress tests for schedule diversity.
  4. Bound every wait so broken code fails rather than hanging the suite.
  5. Capture worker exceptions.
  6. Run on more than one core and, when practical, more than one supported JDK and architecture.

docs.title: Tradeoffs
docs.text:
Technique Best fit Strength Limitation Immutability Read-mostly values and snapshots Minimal synchronization after publication Copying and update allocation Volatile field Independent flag or snapshot reference Cheap visibility and ordering No compound mutual exclusion Intrinsic/explicit lock Multi-field invariant Simple atomic transition proof Blocking and contention Atomic variable One value with CAS-friendly updates Non-blocking atomic RMW Retry cost; awkward compound state Concurrent collection Shared collection operations Scalable documented compound APIs Cross-operation invariants still need design Thread confinement Per-request or single-owner state Removes sharing and races Handoff and ownership limits

Choose the mechanism from the invariant. Do not choose atomics because they appear more advanced, or locks because they feel safer without defining scope.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Saying an int counter is safe because reads and writes are atomic.
  • Adding volatile to count++ and claiming lost updates are fixed.
  • Using thread-safe collection methods in a non-atomic check-then-act sequence.
  • Treating happens-before as elapsed-time order.
  • Assuming final makes referenced collections immutable.
  • Publishing a fully constructed object through an ordinary raced field.
  • Starting a thread or registering a callback inside a constructor.
  • Writing double-checked locking without volatile.
  • Using two volatile fields for one cross-field invariant.
  • Quoting hardware cache behavior instead of a JMM or API guarantee.
  • Assuming a stress test proves race freedom.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. How do atomicity, visibility, and ordering differ?
  2. What two conditions make memory accesses conflicting?
  3. Why can a program without data races still have a race condition?
  4. Why does volatile not make counter++ atomic?
  5. Build the happens-before chain from task submission to Future.get.
  6. What must be true for final-field initialization safety to apply?
  7. Why is a final List reference not enough for immutability?
  8. What exactly does the volatile field do in double-checked locking?
  9. How does an immutable volatile snapshot preserve a multi-field invariant?
  10. Why is one million successful stress iterations not proof of correctness?

docs.title: Exercise 1: Fix a check-then-act race
docs.text:
final class CouponBook {
    private final java.util.Set<String> used =
            java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

    boolean redeem(String code) {
        if (used.contains(code)) {
            return false;
        }
        used.add(code);
        chargeDiscount(code);
        return true;
    }
}

Make one in-process redemption win, and discuss whether the external discount effect is exactly once.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Prove publication
docs.text: A builder thread creates an immutable Rules object, submits a task that reads it, and the caller later obtains the task's result with Future.get. Write the happens-before chain.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Repair a torn logical snapshot
docs.text: A metrics object has volatile fields requests and failures. Readers require a pair from one update generation. Produce a correct design and state its tradeoff.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Find this escape
docs.text:
class BaseProcessor {
    BaseProcessor(Registry registry) {
        registry.register(this::process);
    }

    void process(Item item) {}
}

final class Processor extends BaseProcessor {
    private final Validator validator;

    Processor(Registry registry, Validator validator) {
        super(registry);
        this.validator = validator;
    }

    @Override
    void process(Item item) {
        validator.validate(item);
    }
}

Explain the failure and redesign construction.

Solutions

docs.title: Solution 1
docs.text:
Use the return value of the atomic set operation:

boolean redeem(String code) {
    if (!used.add(code)) {
        return false;
    }
    chargeDiscount(code);
    return true;
}

The successful add is the in-memory linearization point. Exactly one thread in this process reaches chargeDiscount for a code. This is not end-to-end exactly once: the process can crash after recording the code but before charging, or charging can succeed before an ambiguous exception. Durable redemption requires a transactional record, idempotency key accepted by the discount system, and reconciliation or an outbox-style workflow. If charging fails permanently, define whether the code remains consumed or whether a guarded rollback permits retry.

docs.title: Solution 2
docs.text:
1. Builder actions initialize the immutable Rules before submission by program order.
  2. Actions before task submission happen-before task execution under the executor contract.
  3. Task reads and result production occur before task completion by program order.
  4. Task actions happen-before actions after successful Future.get under the Future contract.
  5. By transitivity, construction is visible both inside the task and to caller actions after get that consume the result.

Immutability prevents later mutation from introducing a new race.

docs.title: Solution 3
docs.text:
record Metrics(long requests, long failures) {
    Metrics {
        if (requests < 0 || failures < 0 || failures > requests) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid metrics");
        }
    }
}

final class MetricsView {
    private volatile Metrics current = new Metrics(0, 0);

    Metrics current() {
        return current;
    }

    void publish(long requests, long failures) {
        current = new Metrics(requests, failures);
    }
}

One volatile reference yields a coherent pair. The tradeoff is allocation per publication. Multiple writers need a lock or AtomicReference update protocol if updates derive from current state; blind publication can otherwise lose a newer generation.

docs.title: Solution 4
docs.text:
The base constructor registers a method reference that captures the not-yet-completed subclass object. A dispatch can invoke overridden process before Processor.validator is assigned, causing a null dereference and violating proper-construction assumptions.

Construct first, then register through a factory:

final class Processor {
    private final Validator validator;

    private Processor(Validator validator) {
        this.validator = java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(validator);
    }

    static Processor create(Registry registry, Validator validator) {
        Processor processor = new Processor(validator);
        registry.register(processor::process);
        return processor;
    }

    void process(Item item) {
        validator.validate(item);
    }
}

The registry must safely publish the callback and define deregistration/lifecycle. Avoid calling overridable methods from constructors; composition makes the initialization boundary clearer.

docs.title: Chapter summary
docs.text:
1. Start from shared mutable state and invariants.
  2. Treat atomicity, visibility, and ordering as distinct requirements.
  3. Order every conflicting access with a happens-before edge or an atomic API contract.
  4. Prefer immutable snapshots and safe publication for read-heavy state.
  5. Use volatile for independent state or immutable references, not arbitrary compound transactions.
  6. Prevent construction-time escape.
  7. Use double-checked locking only with volatile and only when simpler initialization is unsuitable.

Previous: Threads, tasks, and lifecycle | Next: Synchronization, locks, and conditions

docs.title: 04. Synchronization, Locks, and Conditions
docs.text: Mutual exclusion is not the goal by itself. The goal is to preserve an invariant while making state changes visible as one atomic operation. This chapter develops that reasoning from intrinsic monitors to explicit locks, conditions, read-write locks, and optimistic reads.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • identify the shared state and invariant before choosing a lock;
  • explain monitor ownership, reentrancy, visibility, and linearization points;
  • use wait, notify, and notifyAll with guarded loops;
  • implement bounded queues with both a monitor and Condition objects;
  • select lock, lockInterruptibly, tryLock, and fairness deliberately;
  • compare ReadWriteLock with StampedLock;
  • prevent deadlock through ordering, granularity, and encapsulation; and
  • write deterministic concurrency tests without relying on sleep.

docs.title: Conceptual model: protect transitions, not fields
docs.text:
A lock protects a protocol over shared state. State may span several fields, and an invariant usually relates them.

For a bounded queue:

  • Shared state: the element array, read index, write index, and count.
  • Invariant: 0 <= count <= capacity; exactly count logical slots contain queued elements; indices remain in range.
  • Linearization point for put: while holding the lock, the element is stored and count is incremented.
  • Linearization point for take: while holding the lock, the element is removed and count is decremented.

The linearization point is the instant at which a concurrent operation appears to take effect. Naming it makes an LLD answer testable. If the fields are guarded by different locks, or callers can mutate the backing array, no single atomic transition exists.

Happens-before

An unlock of a monitor or Lock happens-before a later successful lock of the same object. This gives both mutual exclusion and visibility. A lock on one object does not publish state to code locking another object.

docs.title: Intrinsic monitors and synchronized
docs.text: Every Java object can act as an intrinsic monitor. A thread entering a synchronized method locks this; a static synchronized method locks the Class object; a synchronized block locks its explicit monitor.

docs.title: Broken: check and act under different locks
docs.text:
final class BrokenInventory {
    private int remaining = 1;

    synchronized boolean inStock() {
        return remaining > 0;
    }

    void reserve() {
        if (inStock()) {
            remaining--; // Outside the monitor.
        }
    }
}

Two threads can both observe stock and decrement. Synchronizing an accessor does not make a multi-call workflow atomic.

docs.title: Corrected: one transition under one monitor
docs.text:
final class Inventory {
    private int remaining;

    Inventory(int initialStock) {
        if (initialStock < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative stock");
        }
        remaining = initialStock;
    }

    synchronized boolean tryReserve(int quantity) {
        if (quantity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        }
        if (remaining < quantity) {
            return false;
        }
        remaining -= quantity; // Linearization point.
        return true;
    }

    synchronized int remaining() {
        return remaining;
    }
}
  • Shared state: remaining.
  • Invariant: remaining >= 0.
  • Linearization point: remaining -= quantity.

Keep the monitor private in effect: do not call unknown code while holding it, and do not expose mutable protected state.

docs.title: Reentrancy
docs.text:
Java monitors and ReentrantLock are reentrant. A thread that already owns a lock may acquire it again. The lock tracks a hold count and becomes available only after matching releases.

final class Account {
    private long cents;

    synchronized void credit(long amount) {
        requirePositive(amount); // Reentrant call on the same receiver.
        cents = Math.addExact(cents, amount);
    }

    private synchronized void requirePositive(long amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
    }
}

Reentrancy prevents self-deadlock during nested synchronized calls. It does not make a compound operation across two objects atomic, and it can hide callbacks that execute while an outer lock remains held.

docs.title: Guarded suspension with wait and notification
docs.text:
wait, notify, and notifyAll operate on an object's wait set. The caller must own that object's monitor.

wait atomically releases the monitor and suspends the thread. Before returning, it reacquires the monitor. It releases only this monitor, not any other locks held by the caller. Entering a synchronized block is not interruptible, so the monitor-based queue cannot promise prompt cancellation while blocked on monitor entry. notify moves one arbitrary waiter toward lock reacquisition; notifyAll does so for all waiters. Neither transfers ownership immediately.

docs.title: Broken: testing once and waiting on if
docs.text:
synchronized E take() throws InterruptedException {
    if (count == 0) {
        wait();
    }
    return remove();
}

This fails because:

  • a thread may wake spuriously;
  • another consumer may remove the item before this thread reacquires the monitor;
  • a notification means "state may have changed," not "your predicate is true."

The rule is always:

synchronized (monitor) {
    while (!predicate()) {
        monitor.wait();
    }
    changeState();
}

docs.title: Monitor-based bounded queue
docs.text:
import java.util.Objects;

public final class MonitorBoundedQueue<E> {
    private final Object[] elements;
    private int head;
    private int tail;
    private int size;

    public MonitorBoundedQueue(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        }
        elements = new Object[capacity];
    }

    public synchronized void put(E element) throws InterruptedException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(element, "element");
        while (size == elements.length) {
            wait();
        }
        elements[tail] = element;
        tail = (tail + 1) % elements.length;
        size++; // Linearization point.
        notifyAll();
    }

    public synchronized E take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (size == 0) {
            wait();
        }
        @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
        E element = (E) elements[head];
        elements[head] = null;
        head = (head + 1) % elements.length;
        size--; // Linearization point.
        notifyAll();
        return element;
    }

    public synchronized int size() {
        return size;
    }
}

Both producers and consumers share one wait set. notifyAll avoids waking only producers when the queue is full or only consumers when it is empty. Awakened threads recheck their predicates in while loops. The cost is unnecessary wakeups.

Interruption is part of the contract

wait throws InterruptedException after the thread reacquires the monitor. Do not swallow it. A low-level blocking method should usually propagate it. Code that cannot propagate should restore status with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and terminate or return a documented cancellation result.

docs.title: ReentrantLock and Condition
docs.text: ReentrantLock separates locking from lexical scope and adds interruptible acquisition, timed acquisition, optional fairness, and multiple condition queues. That flexibility creates a new obligation: every successful acquisition must have a finally-guarded unlock.

docs.title: Broken: leaked lock on failure
docs.text:
lock.lock();
update();
lock.unlock();

If update throws, all future callers may block forever.

docs.title: Correct lock shape
docs.text:
lock.lock();
try {
    update();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Do not place lock.lock() inside the try: if an interruptible or custom acquisition fails before ownership, finally must not unlock a lock the thread does not own.

docs.title: Condition-based bounded queue
docs.text:
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public final class ConditionBoundedQueue<E> {
    private final Object[] elements;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();
    private int head;
    private int tail;
    private int size;

    public ConditionBoundedQueue(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        }
        elements = new Object[capacity];
    }

    public void put(E element) throws InterruptedException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(element, "element");
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (size == elements.length) {
                notFull.await();
            }
            elements[tail] = element;
            tail = (tail + 1) % elements.length;
            size++; // Linearization point.
            notEmpty.signal();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public E take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (size == 0) {
                notEmpty.await();
            }
            @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
            E element = (E) elements[head];
            elements[head] = null;
            head = (head + 1) % elements.length;
            size--; // Linearization point.
            notFull.signal();
            return element;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            return size;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

The invariants and linearization points match the monitor implementation. Two condition queues make signaling selective. Conditions still permit spurious wakeups, so await belongs in a guarded while loop.

docs.title: Interruptible locking
docs.text:
Use lockInterruptibly() when waiting for a lock is cancellable. A request with an expired deadline should not remain stuck behind an owner.

lock.lockInterruptibly();
try {
    performShortTransition();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Plain lock() does not abort acquisition on interruption. The thread's interrupt status is restored after it eventually acquires the lock.

docs.title: Timed tryLock
docs.text:
Timed acquisition bounds waiting and can help avoid deadlock when several locks cannot share a global order.

if (!lock.tryLock(50, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    return false;
}
try {
    return performShortTransition();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Untimed tryLock() is immediate. A failed acquisition changes no protected state and is not a linearization point for the requested mutation; it linearizes as a failed attempt at the read of lock availability.

docs.title: Fairness
docs.text: new ReentrantLock(true) prefers the longest-waiting contender under contention. It reduces starvation risk but often lowers throughput by reducing barging and increasing context switches. Fairness does not imply scheduler-level strict FIFO, and untimed tryLock() may barge even on a fair lock. Start non-fair unless the requirement is bounded overtaking or starvation resistance.

docs.title: ReadWriteLock
docs.text:
ReentrantReadWriteLock allows concurrent readers and one exclusive writer. It helps only when reads are frequent and long enough to offset bookkeeping. Tiny getters often perform better with a plain lock or immutable snapshot.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

final class PriceBook {
    private final Map<String, Long> cents = new HashMap<>();
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

    long priceOf(String sku) {
        rw.readLock().lock();
        try {
            Long value = cents.get(sku);
            if (value == null) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown sku");
            }
            return value;
        } finally {
            rw.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    void setPrice(String sku, long value) {
        if (value < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price");
        }
        rw.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            cents.put(sku, value); // Linearization point.
        } finally {
            rw.writeLock().unlock();
        }
    }
}
  • Shared state: the mutable map.
  • Invariant: every stored price is non-negative.
  • Linearization point: put for writes; successful map read while the read lock is held for reads.

Lock upgrading from read to write is unsafe with ReentrantReadWriteLock: two readers can both wait forever for a write lock while retaining read locks. Release the read lock, acquire the write lock, and recheck the predicate. Downgrading is possible by acquiring the read lock before releasing the write lock.

docs.title: StampedLock optimistic reads
docs.text:
StampedLock is not reentrant. Its optimistic read does not lock; it copies state and then validates that no writer acquired the lock during the copy.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock;

final class Point {
    private final StampedLock lock = new StampedLock();
    private double x;
    private double y;

    void move(double dx, double dy) {
        long stamp = lock.writeLock();
        try {
            x += dx;
            y += dy; // The pair becomes visible as one write transition.
        } finally {
            lock.unlockWrite(stamp);
        }
    }

    double distanceFromOrigin() {
        long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead();
        double currentX = x;
        double currentY = y;
        if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {
            stamp = lock.readLock();
            try {
                currentX = x;
                currentY = y;
            } finally {
                lock.unlockRead(stamp);
            }
        }
        return Math.hypot(currentX, currentY);
    }
}

Validation must occur after all fields are copied. A failed validation discards the snapshot and retries under a read lock. Do not perform irreversible actions, dereference temporarily inconsistent object graphs, or call unknown code before validation. StampedLock has no ownership concept, so the correct stamp and unlock mode are essential.

docs.title: Granularity, ordering, and encapsulation
Deterministic tests
docs.text:
Concurrency tests should establish ordering with latches, barriers, futures, or observable states. Thread.sleep is neither an assertion nor a reliable scheduler.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertFalse;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class MonitorBoundedQueueTest {
    @Test
    void producerBlocksUntilConsumerCreatesCapacity() throws Exception {
        var queue = new MonitorBoundedQueue<Integer>(1);
        queue.put(10);
        var entered = new CountDownLatch(1);

        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var blockedPut = executor.submit(() -> {
                entered.countDown();
                queue.put(20);
                return null;
            });

            entered.await();
            assertFalse(blockedPut.isDone());
            assertEquals(10, queue.take());
            blockedPut.get();
            assertEquals(20, queue.take());
        }
    }

    @Test
    void waitingConsumerRespondsToInterruption() throws Exception {
        var queue = new ConditionBoundedQueue<Integer>(1);
        var started = new CountDownLatch(1);

        Thread consumer = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            started.countDown();
            try {
                queue.take();
                throw new AssertionError("take should not complete");
            } catch (InterruptedException expected) {
                // Expected termination path.
            }
        });

        started.await();
        consumer.interrupt();
        consumer.join(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        assertFalse(consumer.isAlive());
    }
}

isDone() immediately after a latch is useful here because the queue is already full and no consumer exists; completion would violate the queue contract. A timeout belongs at the test boundary to fail a hang, not to manufacture ordering.

The examples are test sketches, not hang-safe harnesses: bound entered.await and Future.get, capture raw-thread failures through a future or error queue, and release/cancel tasks before closing an executor. Executor close() may otherwise wait forever after a timed assertion fails. Use child-JVM isolation when deliberately testing non-interruptible monitor deadlock.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating a thread-safe field or getter as proof that a compound action is safe.
  • Using if around wait or await instead of a guarded while loop.
  • Calling wait or signal without owning the corresponding monitor or lock.
  • Assuming notify selects the waiter whose predicate became true.
  • Forgetting finally around explicit lock release.
  • Swallowing interruption and continuing an operation with a cancelled caller.
  • Holding locks across I/O, callbacks, or another subsystem's lock.
  • Upgrading a read lock directly to a write lock.
  • Using an optimistic snapshot before validating its stamp.
  • Splitting one invariant across independently acquired locks.

docs.title: Exercise 1: add timed offer
docs.text:
Add boolean offer(E element, Duration timeout) to ConditionBoundedQueue. It must tolerate spurious wakeups and preserve the remaining timeout.

Complete solution 
public boolean offer(E element, java.time.Duration timeout)
        throws InterruptedException {
    Objects.requireNonNull(element, "element");
    if (timeout.isNegative()) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
    }
    long budgetNanos = saturatedNanos(timeout);
    long startedNanos = System.nanoTime();

    if (!lock.tryLock(budgetNanos, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
        return false;
    }
    try {
        while (size == elements.length) {
            long remaining = remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos);
            if (remaining == 0L) {
                return false;
            }
            notFull.awaitNanos(remaining);
        }
        elements[tail] = element;
        tail = (tail + 1) % elements.length;
        size++;
        notEmpty.signal();
        return true;
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

private static long saturatedNanos(java.time.Duration timeout) {
    try {
        return timeout.toNanos();
    } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
        return Long.MAX_VALUE;
    }
}

private static long remainingNanos(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
    long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
    return elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
            : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
}

Lock acquisition and condition waiting consume the same timeout. Recomputing from monotonic elapsed time prevents spurious wakeups from restarting the budget, and avoids overflow from constructing an absolute nanosecond deadline. The insertion and size++ form the successful operation's linearization point. Timeout failure changes no queue state. As with the key pool, this bounds waiting rather than enforcing a deadline-wins result: if space is available after delayed reacquisition, this implementation may still insert.

docs.title: Exercise 2: repair a two-lock transfer
docs.text:
Two threads transfer in opposite directions and sometimes deadlock. Define a locking protocol and state its invariant.

Complete solution 
static boolean transfer(AccountLocking from, AccountLocking to, long amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("positive amount required");
    if (from == to) {
        return true;
    }
    AccountLocking first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
    AccountLocking second = from.id() < to.id() ? to : from;

    first.lock();
    second.lock();
    try {
        if (from.balanceUnderLock() < amount) {
            return false;
        }
        Math.addExact(to.balanceUnderLock(), amount);
        from.debitUnderLock(amount);
        to.creditUnderLock(amount);
        return true;
    } finally {
        second.unlock();
        first.unlock();
    }
}

All callers acquire by immutable ID, eliminating a circular wait. Shared state is both balances. The invariants are non-negative balances and conservation of their sum for successful transfers. The successful linearization point is completion of the paired mutations while both locks remain held. A failed transfer linearizes at the insufficient-funds check.

docs.title: Exercise 3: explain optimistic-read safety
docs.text:
Why is computing Math.hypot after validation preferable to doing arbitrary work before validation?

Complete solution

Before validation, copied fields may represent different write epochs. Pure local computation is harmless but may be wasted. Arbitrary work can publish, persist, or act on an invalid snapshot and cannot be undone by falling back to a read lock. Copy the minimum primitive or safely dereferenceable state, validate, retry under a read lock if needed, and only then perform side effects.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
1. What does synchronized provide beyond mutual exclusion?
  2. Why must wait and Condition.await use a while loop?
  3. When is notifyAll safer than notify, and what does it cost?
  4. How does reentrancy work, and which deadlocks does it not prevent?
  5. Why is unlock placed in finally?
  6. When would you choose lockInterruptibly or timed tryLock?
  7. What practical guarantee does a fair ReentrantLock provide?
  8. Why can read-to-write lock upgrading deadlock?
  9. What may be read before StampedLock.validate, and what should wait until after it?
  10. State the shared state, invariant, and linearization points of a bounded queue.
  11. How would you test that a producer blocks without using sleep?
  12. What API design keeps a lock protocol encapsulated?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A lock protects an invariant and its state transition, not an isolated variable.
  • Intrinsic monitors are reentrant and provide visibility through monitor release and acquisition.
  • wait and await release the lock, may wake spuriously, and require guarded loops.
  • Conditions separate wait sets; monitor code often needs notifyAll when predicates differ.
  • Explicit locks add cancellation, timeout, fairness, and condition choices at the cost of manual release.
  • Read-write and stamped locks help only when workload shape justifies their complexity.
  • Stable lock ordering, small critical sections, and private ownership prevent many deadlocks.
  • Deterministic tests control phases with synchronization primitives and reserve timeouts for hang detection.

Previous: Thread Safety and the Java Memory Model | Next: Coordination Primitives

docs.title: 05. Coordination Primitives
docs.text: Locks protect state. Coordination primitives control when work may proceed. An interview-quality design distinguishes resource capacity from phase completion, reusable rendezvous, and pairwise handoff instead of using one primitive for every problem.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish permits from lock ownership;
  • choose among Semaphore, CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Phaser, and Exchanger;
  • model one-shot and reusable coordination explicitly;
  • implement alternating output, zero-even-odd, and H2O grouping;
  • define shared state, invariants, and linearization points for each design;
  • handle interruption without leaking permits or stranding peers;
  • explain broken barriers and recovery policy; and
  • test coordination deterministically without timing guesses.

docs.title: Conceptual model
docs.text:
Coordination answers one of four questions:

Question Primitive May another operation enter a capacity-limited region? Semaphore Have a fixed number of one-time events completed? CountDownLatch Have all fixed participants reached this reusable phase? CyclicBarrier Which dynamic participants have reached this phase? Phaser Can two peers swap values at a rendezvous? Exchanger

Every design should identify:

  • Participants: which threads or tasks coordinate.
  • Shared state: counters, queues, phase numbers, or output.
  • Invariant: what must remain true across interleavings.
  • Linearization point: when admission, arrival, or handoff logically occurs.
  • Failure policy: what interruption, timeout, or participant failure means to peers.

docs.title: Semaphore: permits are not ownership
docs.text: A semaphore maintains a permit count. acquire decrements it when positive or waits; release increments it. Unlike a lock, the releasing thread need not be the acquiring thread. That makes a semaphore suitable for capacity and signaling, but dangerous if code assumes ownership.

docs.title: Broken: unconditional release
docs.text:
void callRemote() throws InterruptedException {
    try {
        permits.acquire();
        client.call();
    } finally {
        permits.release();
    }
}

If interruption occurs before acquisition succeeds, finally creates a permit. Capacity silently grows.

docs.title: Corrected: release only after successful acquisition
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

final class Bulkhead {
    private final Semaphore permits;

    Bulkhead(int maximumConcurrentCalls) {
        if (maximumConcurrentCalls <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        }
        permits = new Semaphore(maximumConcurrentCalls);
    }

    <T> T execute(java.util.concurrent.Callable<T> task) throws Exception {
        boolean acquired = false;
        try {
            permits.acquire();
            acquired = true; // Record that successful acquisition already admitted us.
            return task.call();
        } finally {
            if (acquired) {
                permits.release();
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Shared state: semaphore permit count and in-flight calls.
  • Invariant: availablePermits + inFlight = capacity when each operation holds one permit.
  • Linearization point: successful permit acquisition for admission; release for departure.

A fair semaphore reduces barging for blocking acquisition but costs throughput. Multi-permit acquisition can create head-of-line blocking. availablePermits() is an observation, not a reservation; never check it and then assume a later acquisition will succeed.

Semaphores do not protect arbitrary invariants

A binary semaphore can limit entry to one participant, but it has no thread ownership and is not reentrant. Prefer a lock for ownership-based mutual exclusion.

docs.title: CountDownLatch: one-shot completion
docs.text:
A latch starts with a non-negative count. await blocks until countDown has reduced the count to zero. It cannot reset.

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

final class ServiceGate {
    private final CountDownLatch ready;

    ServiceGate(int dependencies) {
        ready = new CountDownLatch(dependencies);
    }

    void dependencyReady() {
        ready.countDown(); // Linearizes one completion if count was positive.
    }

    void awaitReady() throws InterruptedException {
        ready.await();
    }
}
  • Shared state: latch count.
  • Invariant: count never increases and never becomes negative.
  • Linearization point: a successful decrement; for await, observation of zero.

Actions before countDown happen-before actions after another thread successfully returns from await. Additional countDown calls at zero do nothing, which can hide duplicate completion signals. If identity matters, track completed dependency IDs separately.

docs.title: Start gate and finish gate
docs.text:
Tests often use one latch to release workers together and another to observe completion:

var start = new CountDownLatch(1);
var done = new CountDownLatch(workerCount);

for (int i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
    executor.submit(() -> {
        try {
            start.await();
            runCase();
        } finally {
            done.countDown();
        }
        return null;
    });
}
start.countDown();
done.await();

The finally prevents one failed worker from stranding the observer. It does not report the failure; retain futures or collect exceptions separately.

docs.title: CyclicBarrier: fixed reusable rendezvous
docs.text:
A cyclic barrier releases a fixed number of parties when all have called await. It then advances to the next generation and can be reused.

import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier;

var barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> publishCompletedBatch());

void processPartition() throws Exception {
    loadPartition();
    barrier.await();
    consumePublishedBatch();
}

The barrier action runs once per generation in the last arriving thread before other participants are released.

  • Shared state: arrival count, generation, and any phase data.
  • Invariant: no participant starts the next phase before all parties complete the current phase.
  • Linearization point: the last arrival trips the barrier and advances its generation.

docs.title: Broken barriers
docs.text:
If a waiting participant is interrupted or times out, that generation becomes broken. Other waiters receive BrokenBarrierException; later await calls also fail until reset begins a new generation.

try {
    barrier.await();
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    cancelWholeRound();
} catch (java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException e) {
    cancelWholeRound();
}

Do not blindly retry await: the failed participant may never arrive. Decide whether to cancel the round, reconstruct the workers and barrier, or reset only after all old-generation tasks are contained. A reset while old tasks continue can mix logical rounds.

docs.title: Phaser: dynamic, multi-phase coordination
docs.text:
A phaser combines a phase number with dynamic registration. Participants register, arrive, and optionally deregister. Unlike CyclicBarrier, its party count can change.

import java.util.concurrent.Phaser;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;

final class TwoStagePipeline {
    private final Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1); // Coordinator.

    void submit(Runnable stageOne, Runnable stageTwo,
                java.util.concurrent.Executor executor) {
        phaser.register();
        try {
            executor.execute(() -> {
                try {
                    stageOne.run();
                    phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
                    stageTwo.run();
                } finally {
                    phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
                }
            });
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException rejected) {
            phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
            throw rejected;
        }
    }

    void runPhases() {
        phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
        phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
        phaser.arriveAndDeregister();
    }
}

This sample assumes submission completes before the coordinator advances. If registration races with phase advance, a task may join a later phase. Close registration through an external lifecycle protocol when phase membership matters. Registration occurs before submission, so rejection must deregister synchronously; otherwise the coordinator waits forever for a task that cannot run.

The executor must run every admitted party concurrently; a small fixed pool can deadlock with running tasks awaiting queued parties. A stage-one exception currently deregisters that task and allows surviving tasks into stage two: this is a drop-failed-party policy, not an all-inputs-succeeded guarantee. If stage two requires every stage-one output, record shared failure, terminate the phaser, and check termination before consuming results. Never run this pipeline on a direct executor.

  • Shared state: registered, unarrived, and phase counts.
  • Invariant: a phase advances only when every registered party for that phase arrives or deregisters.
  • Linearization point: arrival that reduces unarrived parties to zero and advances phase.

arriveAndAwaitAdvance is not interruptible. Use awaitAdvanceInterruptibly(phase) when cancellation is required:

int phase = phaser.arrive();
try {
    phaser.awaitAdvanceInterruptibly(phase);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    phaser.forceTermination(); // Policy: cancel this whole pipeline.
    throw e;
}

Be careful: after arrive, the party has already fulfilled its obligation for that phase. Failure handling must not arrive twice. This example terminates the whole protocol. A design that cancels only one party needs an external lifecycle that deregisters it in a phase where it has not already arrived.

docs.title: Exchanger: pairwise handoff
docs.text:
Exchanger<V> pairs two threads. Each supplies a value and receives the other's value. It is useful for double buffering, where a producer hands off a full buffer and receives an empty one.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Exchanger;

final class BufferHandoff {
    private final Exchanger<List<String>> exchanger = new Exchanger<>();

    List<String> exchange(List<String> mine) throws InterruptedException {
        return exchanger.exchange(mine); // Pairwise handoff linearization point.
    }

    static List<String> emptyBuffer() {
        return new ArrayList<>();
    }
}

The invariant is exclusive logical ownership after each successful exchange: each buffer belongs to one side. Timeout or interruption means no successful exchange for that caller. It is a poor fit for more than two participants, unbalanced arrival rates, or cases where a queue should absorb bursts.

docs.title: Pattern: alternating printer
docs.text:
Two semaphores encode whose turn it is. One initial permit lets the first printer run; the other starts at zero.

import java.util.function.IntConsumer;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

final class AlternatingPrinter {
    private final Semaphore oddTurn = new Semaphore(1);
    private final Semaphore evenTurn = new Semaphore(0);
    private final int maximum;

    AlternatingPrinter(int maximum) {
        if (maximum < 0 || maximum > Integer.MAX_VALUE - 2)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("maximum out of range");
        this.maximum = maximum;
    }

    void printOdd(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int value = 1; value <= maximum; value += 2) {
            oddTurn.acquire();
            try {
                output.accept(value); // Output linearization point.
            } finally {
                evenTurn.release();
            }
        }
    }

    void printEven(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int value = 2; value <= maximum; value += 2) {
            evenTurn.acquire();
            try {
                output.accept(value); // Output linearization point.
            } finally {
                oddTurn.release();
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Shared state: turn permits and the output sink.
  • Invariant: before each output, exactly the required side can proceed; values appear in ascending order.
  • Linearization point: each call to output.accept.

The finally permits one more peer turn after callback failure; it does not prevent that peer from becoming stranded on its following turn. Both callbacks must return normally for this compact protocol. A coordinator must observe any failure and cancel both tasks. Interruption before handoff can also strand the peer. Limit maximum to 0..Integer.MAX_VALUE-2 here so the int step cannot wrap; the same bound applies to n below.

docs.title: Pattern: zero-even-odd
docs.text:
One thread prints zero before every integer. Separate semaphores make the legal transitions explicit.

import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

final class ZeroEvenOdd {
    private final int n;
    private final Semaphore zero = new Semaphore(1);
    private final Semaphore odd = new Semaphore(0);
    private final Semaphore even = new Semaphore(0);

    ZeroEvenOdd(int n) {
        if (n < 0 || n > Integer.MAX_VALUE - 2)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("n out of range");
        this.n = n;
    }

    void zero(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int value = 1; value <= n; value++) {
            zero.acquire();
            output.accept(0);
            (value % 2 == 0 ? even : odd).release();
        }
    }

    void odd(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int value = 1; value <= n; value += 2) {
            odd.acquire();
            output.accept(value);
            zero.release();
        }
    }

    void even(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int value = 2; value <= n; value += 2) {
            even.acquire();
            output.accept(value);
            zero.release();
        }
    }
}
  • Shared state: the three permit counts and output.
  • Invariant: legal states cycle from zero-enabled to exactly one parity-enabled and back.
  • Linearization point: each output callback.

In an interview, mention failure semantics. The compact solution assumes callbacks do not fail and all three tasks remain alive. Production code should coordinate cancellation because permit protocols do not automatically propagate failure.

docs.title: Pattern: H2O grouping
docs.text:
The requirement is not merely "at most two hydrogen threads and one oxygen thread run." Output must be partitionable into complete groups containing exactly two H and one O. A barrier closes each molecule before permits for the next one are released.

import java.util.concurrent.Phaser;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.Objects;

final class H2O {
    private final Semaphore hydrogenSlots = new Semaphore(2, true);
    private final Semaphore oxygenSlots = new Semaphore(1, true);
    private final Phaser molecule = new Phaser(3);

    void hydrogen(Runnable releaseHydrogen) throws InterruptedException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(releaseHydrogen, "releaseHydrogen");
        hydrogenSlots.acquire();
        releaseHydrogen.run();
        molecule.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
    }

    void oxygen(Runnable releaseOxygen) throws InterruptedException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(releaseOxygen, "releaseOxygen");
        oxygenSlots.acquire();
        releaseOxygen.run();
        molecule.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
        hydrogenSlots.release(2);
        oxygenSlots.release();
    }
}

This compact interview solution has an explicit precondition: each callback is a short, non-blocking output action that does not throw. Interruption can abort semaphore acquisition before a slot is owned. After admission there is no interruptible wait: Phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance completes the participant's generation even when its interrupt flag is set, so interruption cannot leak a slot or strand peers. If callbacks can fail or block, this is not a sufficient service design; use a generation object that buffers output and atomically commits or aborts all three participants instead of pretending a partial molecule can be repaired.

  • Shared state: two slot semaphores, one phaser generation, and output.
  • Invariant: only two hydrogen and one oxygen participant enter a generation; the next generation receives no slots until all three current callbacks finish and arrive.
  • Linearization point: the third barrier arrival commits the molecule group. Individual character output occurs earlier and should remain buffered if externally visible atomic grouping is required.

Group completion versus output order

The barrier guarantees groups of two hydrogen participants and one oxygen participant. It does not require HHO order within a group. If exact order is required, model another turn protocol or buffer the three symbols and publish the completed group in the barrier action.

docs.title: One-shot versus reusable coordination
docs.text:
Primitive Parties Reusable Ownership Typical failure effect Semaphore dynamic yes no caller must avoid permit leak CountDownLatch fixed count no no missing countdown waits forever CyclicBarrier fixed parties yes no generation becomes broken Phaser dynamic parties yes no application decides termination Exchanger pairs yes no unmatched peer waits or times out

Choose from lifecycle semantics, not surface syntax. A latch cannot represent repeated rounds. A barrier should not model a capacity pool. A semaphore does not tell you that a whole cohort has completed.

docs.title: Interruption and cancellation rules
docs.text:
1. Decide whether interruption cancels one participant or the whole protocol.
  2. Release only resources that were definitely acquired.
  3. Do not count down a success latch for work that did not satisfy its contract; use a separate completion latch if failures also unblock an observer.
  4. Treat a broken barrier as a failed generation, not a transient wakeup.
  5. Deregister abandoned phaser parties so surviving participants can advance.
  6. Bound waits at system boundaries and surface timeout as a domain outcome.
  7. Retain futures so coordinator code can observe worker failures.

docs.title: Deterministic tests
docs.text:
The output sequence itself is the assertion for turn-taking algorithms. Launch tasks together and place one timeout around completion.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class CoordinationTest {
    @Test
    void alternatesOddAndEven() throws Exception {
        var printer = new AlternatingPrinter(6);
        List<Integer> output = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        var start = new CountDownLatch(1);

        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var odd = executor.submit(() -> {
                start.await();
                printer.printOdd(output::add);
                return null;
            });
            var even = executor.submit(() -> {
                start.await();
                printer.printEven(output::add);
                return null;
            });
            start.countDown();
            odd.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            even.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        }

        assertEquals(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), output);
    }

    @Test
    void formsCompleteMolecules() throws Exception {
        var h2o = new H2O();
        List<Character> output = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        List<Character> input = List.of('O', 'H', 'H', 'H', 'O', 'H');

        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var futures = input.stream().map(atom -> executor.submit(() -> {
                if (atom == 'H') {
                    h2o.hydrogen(() -> output.add('H'));
                } else {
                    h2o.oxygen(() -> output.add('O'));
                }
                return null;
            })).toList();
            for (var future : futures) {
                future.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            }
        }

        for (int start = 0; start < output.size(); start += 3) {
            List<Character> group = new ArrayList<>(output.subList(start, start + 3));
            Collections.sort(group);
            assertEquals(List.of('H', 'H', 'O'), group);
        }
    }
}

The H2O test validates each contiguous group, not only global totals. Global totals would miss an illegal output such as HHHHOO. Oxygen alone releases the next group's slots after phase advance; onAdvance is too early because the new phase has not yet been installed. Interrupting an atom before admission can still leave an insufficient mix; the caller must supply replacement participants or terminate the whole exercise. See the Phaser lifecycle contract.

These test sketches need process-level isolation for a broken non-interruptible barrier: a timed Future.get does not bound try-with-resources executor closure. Cancel cooperative tasks in finally, release test gates, and use a child-JVM timeout for deliberately broken monitor/barrier code.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Releasing a semaphore permit after failed or interrupted acquisition.
  • Treating availablePermits() as an atomic admission check.
  • Using a semaphore as a reentrant ownership lock.
  • Forgetting that CountDownLatch is one-shot.
  • Hiding worker failure by counting down only a completion signal.
  • Retrying a broken barrier without rebuilding the logical round.
  • Registering with a phaser after the intended phase has already advanced.
  • Arriving twice during phaser interruption cleanup.
  • Using an exchanger when producers and consumers need buffering.
  • Validating only aggregate H2O counts instead of group boundaries.
  • Ignoring the fact that one failed turn-taking participant can strand peers.

docs.title: Exercise 1: bounded, timed bulkhead
docs.text:
Implement a bulkhead that rejects an operation if no permit is available within a duration. Ensure interruption does not change capacity.

Complete solution 
final class TimedBulkhead {
    private final java.util.concurrent.Semaphore permits;

    TimedBulkhead(int capacity) {
        permits = new java.util.concurrent.Semaphore(capacity);
    }

    <T> java.util.Optional<T> execute(
            java.time.Duration timeout,
            java.util.concurrent.Callable<T> task) throws Exception {
        boolean acquired = permits.tryAcquire(
                timeout.toNanos(), java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        if (!acquired) {
            return java.util.Optional.empty();
        }
        try {
            return java.util.Optional.ofNullable(task.call());
        } finally {
            permits.release();
        }
    }
}

The permit is released only on the path where tryAcquire returned true. Admission linearizes at successful acquisition. Rejection linearizes when timed acquisition reports failure.
