Optional cannot distinguish a successful null result from rejection, so a production API should prohibit null or return a dedicated result type.

docs.title: Exercise 2: reusable three-stage workers
docs.text:
Three fixed workers must all finish stage A before any starts stage B, and all finish B before any starts C. Choose and use a primitive.

Complete solution 
final class ThreeStageWorker implements java.util.concurrent.Callable<Void> {
    private final java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier barrier;
    private final Runnable stageA;
    private final Runnable stageB;
    private final Runnable stageC;

    ThreeStageWorker(java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier barrier,
                     Runnable stageA, Runnable stageB, Runnable stageC) {
        this.barrier = barrier;
        this.stageA = stageA;
        this.stageB = stageB;
        this.stageC = stageC;
    }

    @Override
    public Void call() throws Exception {
        stageA.run();
        barrier.await();
        stageB.run();
        barrier.await();
        stageC.run();
        return null;
    }
}

The barrier is reusable and party count is fixed. Each last arrival advances a generation and is the phase transition's linearization point. If any worker fails before arrival, cancel all peers; otherwise they wait forever. Futures and a coordinator should implement that cancellation policy.

docs.title: Exercise 3: repair a flaky latch test
docs.text:
A test starts workers, sleeps for 100 ms, and checks a counter. Replace timing with explicit coordination.

Complete solution 
var start = new java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch(1);
var done = new java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch(workerCount);
var counter = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger();

try (var executor = java.util.concurrent.Executors
        .newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            try {
                start.await();
                counter.incrementAndGet();
            } finally {
                done.countDown();
            }
            return null;
        });
    }
    start.countDown();
    if (!done.await(1, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
        throw new AssertionError("workers did not finish");
    }
}
org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals(workerCount, counter.get());

The start latch creates a defined release point. The done latch proves every worker reached completion. The timeout detects a defect rather than attempting to schedule the workers.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a semaphore permit different from lock ownership?
  2. How can interruption accidentally increase semaphore capacity?
  3. When is a latch preferable to joining futures?
  4. Why can a CountDownLatch not model repeated rounds?
  5. What breaks a CyclicBarrier, and what happens to its peers?
  6. When would you choose a Phaser over a barrier?
  7. What registration race exists with dynamic phaser participants?
  8. Where is an exchanger useful, and when is a queue better?
  9. State the state machine behind zero-even-odd.
  10. Why do H2O semaphores alone not prove molecule grouping?
  11. How should failure propagate in an alternating protocol?
  12. How do you test a barrier or turn-taking algorithm deterministically?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Semaphores represent permits, not thread ownership.
  • Latches represent one-shot completion; barriers and phasers represent phases.
  • A broken barrier is a failed generation that needs an explicit recovery policy.
  • Phasers support dynamic registration but require careful lifecycle control.
  • Exchangers provide pairwise handoff, not buffering.
  • Turn-taking algorithms are small state machines whose permits encode legal transitions.
  • H2O grouping needs a generation boundary, not only aggregate capacity limits.
  • Interruption handling must preserve permit counts, party counts, and peer liveness.
  • Deterministic tests use explicit start and completion gates plus bounded hang detection.

docs.title: 06. Atomics and Concurrent Collections
docs.text: Lock-free APIs do not remove synchronization; they move it into atomic instructions and library protocols. Correct use still starts with shared state, an invariant, and a precise linearization point. This chapter covers Java 21 atomics and collections as building blocks for interview-grade low-level designs.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • explain compare-and-set and retry loops;
  • select AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference, or LongAdder;
  • keep atomic update functions pure because they may run repeatedly;
  • identify and prevent ABA with AtomicStampedReference;
  • use ConcurrentHashMap atomic compound methods correctly;
  • explain computeIfAbsent recursion and blocking hazards;
  • choose copy-on-write, concurrent, or blocking collections by workload;
  • reason about weakly consistent iteration;
  • identify linearization points in counters, state machines, reservations, and registries; and
  • test concurrent behavior deterministically.

docs.title: Conceptual model: one atomic transition
docs.text:
An atomic variable provides indivisible operations on one logical location. A concurrent collection provides atomicity for documented operations, usually one key or one queue action at a time. Neither automatically preserves an invariant spanning several independent locations.

For every operation, state:

  1. Shared state: the atomic reference, counter, map entry, or queue.
  2. Invariant: the legal values or relationships.
  3. Transition: old state to new state.
  4. Linearization point: the successful CAS or documented atomic collection operation.
  5. Contention policy: retry, block, reject, stripe, or serialize.

Atomic does not mean transaction

Two atomic increments are two atomic operations, not one transaction. If available + reserved must remain constant, represent them in one immutable state behind one AtomicReference, or use a lock.

docs.title: Compare-and-set
docs.text:
Compare-and-set (CAS) means: if the current value equals the expected value, replace it with the update atomically; otherwise report failure. A CAS loop reads, derives a candidate, and retries after interference.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

final class CappedCounter {
    private final int maximum;
    private final AtomicInteger value = new AtomicInteger();

    CappedCounter(int maximum) {
        if (maximum < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative maximum");
        }
        this.maximum = maximum;
    }

    boolean tryIncrement() {
        while (true) {
            int current = value.get();
            if (current == maximum) {
                return false;
            }
            if (value.compareAndSet(current, current + 1)) {
                return true; // Successful CAS is the linearization point.
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Shared state: value.
  • Invariant: 0 <= value <= maximum.
  • Linearization point: successful compareAndSet; a failure due to the cap linearizes at the read that observes maximum.

Assuming the underlying CAS has non-blocking progress, a failed strong CAS here means another increment won. Generic CAS retry loops are normally lock-free rather than wait-free: an individual caller may repeatedly lose. This particular capped, increment-only example has a stronger bound because only finitely many increments can succeed before every caller observes the cap. Do not transfer that bound to a counter that can decrease or reset. Expensive candidate computation and hot single locations can still create retry storms.

docs.title: Atomic number and reference types
docs.text: AtomicInteger and AtomicLong support increments, additions, swaps, CAS, and functional updates. AtomicReference<T> atomically replaces object references and can hold an immutable aggregate state.

docs.title: Broken: check then increment
docs.text:
if (reserved.get() < capacity) {
    reserved.incrementAndGet();
}

The read and increment are separate. Several threads can pass the check and exceed capacity.

docs.title: Corrected stock reservation
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

final class Stock {
    private final AtomicInteger remaining;

    Stock(int quantity) {
        if (quantity < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative quantity");
        }
        remaining = new AtomicInteger(quantity);
    }

    boolean tryReserve(int quantity) {
        if (quantity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        }
        while (true) {
            int current = remaining.get();
            if (current < quantity) {
                return false;
            }
            if (remaining.compareAndSet(current, current - quantity)) {
                return true; // Reservation linearization point.
            }
        }
    }

    int remaining() {
        return remaining.get();
    }
}
  • Shared state: remaining stock.
  • Invariant: remaining stock never becomes negative.
  • Linearization point: successful CAS; rejected reservation linearizes at an observed insufficient value.

This only reserves in memory inside one process. Durable inventory requires an authoritative database transition, idempotency, and failure recovery.

docs.title: Functional updates must tolerate retries
docs.text: updateAndGet, getAndUpdate, and accumulateAndGet may reapply their functions after CAS contention. Keep these functions deterministic from their arguments and free of externally visible side effects. Map contracts differ: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent invokes the mapping function at most once per call, while other concurrent-map implementations may retry a computation. Even with ConcurrentHashMap, a later call may load again after removal, failure, or a null result; no map callback supplies durable exactly-once effects.

docs.title: Broken: side effect inside retryable update
docs.text:
balance.updateAndGet(current -> {
    auditLog.append("charged");
    return current - charge;
});

If CAS loses, the function may append again. The final atomic value can be correct while the audit log contains duplicates.

docs.title: Corrected: CAS first, side effect after success
docs.text:
boolean charge(AtomicInteger balance, int amount, java.util.function.IntConsumer audit) {
    if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("positive amount required");
    while (true) {
        int current = balance.get();
        if (current < amount) {
            return false;
        }
        int updated = current - amount;
        if (balance.compareAndSet(current, updated)) {
            audit.accept(amount);
            return true;
        }
    }
}

This prevents duplicate audit calls due to CAS retry, but a crash between CAS and audit still loses the audit. If both effects must be atomic, an in-memory atomic cannot provide that guarantee; use a transactional store or durable outbox.

docs.title: Immutable state machine with AtomicReference
docs.text:
One reference can atomically replace a state containing several related values.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

final class Job {
    enum Status { CREATED, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED }

    record Snapshot(Status status, int attempts, String result) {
        Snapshot {
            if (attempts < 0) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative attempts");
            }
            if (status == Status.SUCCEEDED && result == null) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("success requires result");
            }
            if (status != Status.SUCCEEDED && result != null) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("result only on success");
            }
        }
    }

    private final AtomicReference<Snapshot> state =
            new AtomicReference<>(new Snapshot(Status.CREATED, 0, null));

    boolean start() {
        while (true) {
            Snapshot current = state.get();
            if (current.status() != Status.CREATED
                    && current.status() != Status.FAILED) {
                return false;
            }
            Snapshot next = new Snapshot(
                    Status.RUNNING, current.attempts() + 1, null);
            if (state.compareAndSet(current, next)) {
                return true;
            }
        }
    }

    boolean succeed(String result) {
        java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(result, "result");
        while (true) {
            Snapshot current = state.get();
            if (current.status() != Status.RUNNING) {
                return false;
            }
            Snapshot next = new Snapshot(
                    Status.SUCCEEDED, current.attempts(), result);
            if (state.compareAndSet(current, next)) {
                return true;
            }
        }
    }

    Snapshot snapshot() {
        return state.get();
    }
}
  • Shared state: one reference to an immutable snapshot.
  • Invariant: attempts are non-negative; only success carries a result; transitions follow the allowed graph.
  • Linearization point: successful CAS for each transition.

Immutability prevents a caller from changing fields behind the atomic reference. Validate transitions against the current snapshot on every retry.

docs.title: LongAdder versus AtomicLong
docs.text:
AtomicLong maintains one linearizable value. Under heavy write contention, all writers compete on that location. LongAdder spreads updates across cells and sums them when read.

Requirement Prefer sequence number or unique ID AtomicLong compare-and-set transition AtomicLong exact value used for admission AtomicLong or lock high-rate metrics increment LongAdder approximate live telemetry LongAdder

LongAdder.sum() is not an atomic snapshot with concurrent updates. It may miss or include updates racing with the sum. sumThenReset() is also not atomic with concurrent increments and is unsuitable when losing counts is forbidden.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

final class RequestMetrics {
    private final LongAdder completed = new LongAdder();

    void recordCompletion() {
        completed.increment();
    }

    long approximateCompleted() {
        return completed.sum();
    }
}

The increment is thread-safe, but do not claim one global linearization point for a concurrent sum. This makes LongAdder a poor stock counter.

docs.title: ABA and stamped references
docs.text:
CAS compares the observed value with the current value. If state changes from A to B and back to A, value-only CAS cannot detect the intermediate change. That is the ABA problem.

Consider a reusable slot represented by node reference A:

  1. Thread T1 reads A.
  2. T2 replaces A with B, retires A, then reuses A as the head.
  3. T1 sees A again and its CAS succeeds, although assumptions about A's history may be invalid.

Garbage collection prevents raw memory reuse errors common in unmanaged languages, but ABA still matters when identity can leave and re-enter a logical state.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference;

final class VersionedValue<T> {
    private final AtomicStampedReference<T> value;

    VersionedValue(T initial) {
        value = new AtomicStampedReference<>(initial, 0);
    }

    record View<T>(T value, int stamp) {}

    View<T> view() {
        int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
        T current = value.get(stampHolder);
        return new View<>(current, stampHolder[0]);
    }

    boolean replace(View<T> expected, T update) {
        return value.compareAndSet(expected.value(), update,
                expected.stamp(), expected.stamp() + 1);
    }
}
  • Shared state: reference and stamp as one atomic pair.
  • Invariant: each successful replacement advances the stamp.
  • Linearization point: successful stamped CAS.

An int stamp can wrap. Decide whether wrap is plausible within the lifetime of a stale operation. Another approach is an immutable wrapper containing a wider logical version and value.

The caller must retain the stamp from the original observation. Reading a fresh stamp inside replace(expectedValue, update) only detects interference during that call, not an A-B-A cycle since the caller read A.

docs.title: ConcurrentHashMap: atomicity is per operation
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap supports concurrent retrievals and updates without one global map lock. Its compound methods provide atomic behavior for a key.

docs.title: Broken frequency counter
docs.text:
counts.put(word, counts.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1);

Two threads can read the same count and overwrite one increment.

docs.title: Frequency counter with LongAdder
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

final class FrequencyCounter {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counts =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    void record(String key) {
        counts.computeIfAbsent(key, ignored -> new LongAdder()).increment();
    }

    long count(String key) {
        LongAdder adder = counts.get(key);
        return adder == null ? 0 : adder.sum();
    }
}
  • Shared state: key-to-adder registry and each adder's cells.
  • Invariant: each key maps to at most one installed adder at a time.
  • Linearization point: map installation for a new key; increments are thread-safe, while concurrent sums are not exact snapshots.

If exact linearizable counts per key are required, use AtomicLong values. If exact consistency across keys is required, this map is insufficient by itself.

docs.title: Useful atomic map methods
docs.text: Method Use putIfAbsent publish one value if no mapping exists computeIfAbsent derive and install a missing value computeIfPresent update or remove an existing mapping compute derive mapping from present or absent state merge combine an existing and supplied value replace(key, old, next) conditional per-key transition remove(key, value) conditional removal

docs.title: Cache registry
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

final class CacheRegistry<K, V> {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, V> values = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    V getOrLoad(K key, Function<? super K, ? extends V> loader) {
        return values.computeIfAbsent(key, loader);
    }

    boolean invalidate(K key, V expectedValue) {
        return values.remove(key, expectedValue);
    }
}
  • Shared state: map entries.
  • Invariant: each key has at most one current non-null mapping.
  • Linearization point: successful installation/removal performed by the map operation.

ConcurrentHashMap forbids null keys and values. A mapping function that returns null installs nothing.

Keep remapping functions short and non-recursive

computeIfAbsent may block other updates to the same internal region while computing. Do not perform slow I/O when latency isolation matters. Do not recursively update the same map from the mapping function; detectable recursive computation can throw IllegalStateException, and cross-key recursion can create cycles or deadlock-like stalls. For expensive asynchronous loads, store futures and define failure eviction explicitly.

docs.title: Asynchronous single-flight registry
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

final class AsyncRegistry<K, V> {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> loads =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    CompletableFuture<V> getOrLoad(
            K key, Supplier<CompletableFuture<V>> loader) {
        CompletableFuture<V> future = loads.computeIfAbsent(key, ignored -> {
            try {
                return java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(loader.get(), "loader future");
            } catch (Throwable failure) {
                return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(failure);
            }
        });
        future.whenComplete((value, failure) -> {
            if (failure != null) {
                loads.remove(key, future);
            }
        });
        return future.copy();
    }
}

This shares one installed future per key and conditionally evicts only that failed future. A loader that itself calls getOrLoad for the same key can still recurse. Also, loader.get() runs during map computation; a stronger design inserts an incomplete future quickly, starts I/O outside map computation, and completes the future afterward.

Return a dependent copy so one caller cannot cancel or complete the shared root for everyone. The loader still owns the root; document its lifecycle and bound registry cardinality. The Job snapshot above is a one-run example with no fail method: adding retries requires passing the claimed attempt/version to completion, or a late old worker could succeed a newer RUNNING attempt. An atomic snapshot alone does not fence stale actors.

docs.title: Copy-on-write collections
docs.text:
CopyOnWriteArrayList creates a fresh backing array for each mutation. Reads require no lock and iterators observe an immutable snapshot taken when the iterator was created.

import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;

final class ListenerRegistry<E> {
    private final CopyOnWriteArrayList<java.util.function.Consumer<E>> listeners =
            new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    void add(java.util.function.Consumer<E> listener) {
        listeners.addIfAbsent(listener);
    }

    void publish(E event) {
        for (var listener : listeners) {
            listener.accept(event);
        }
    }
}
  • Shared state: current immutable backing-array snapshot.
  • Invariant: with addIfAbsent, a listener appears at most once by equality.
  • Linearization point: publication of the replacement array for mutation; iterator creation fixes its snapshot.

Use copy-on-write when reads and traversals vastly outnumber writes and the collection is modest. Avoid it for frequent writes, large lists, or memory-sensitive bursts. Iterator remove is unsupported, and an existing iterator does not see later changes.

docs.title: Concurrent and blocking queues
docs.text:
Queue choice encodes backpressure and ordering semantics.

Type Capacity Waiting behavior Typical use ConcurrentLinkedQueue unbounded non-blocking offer/poll lightweight shared work list ArrayBlockingQueue bounded blocking and timed methods fixed-memory producer-consumer LinkedBlockingQueue optional bound blocking and timed methods buffered pipeline PriorityBlockingQueue unbounded blocking take, priority order priority scheduling without backpressure SynchronousQueue zero producer meets consumer direct handoff DelayQueue unbounded take waits for delay expiry and delayed tasks

For BlockingQueue:

  • add throws if capacity is unavailable;
  • offer returns false immediately;
  • timed offer waits up to a bound;
  • put waits until capacity exists;
  • remove throws if empty;
  • poll returns null immediately;
  • timed poll waits up to a bound;
  • take waits for an element.
boolean submit(java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue<Job> queue, Job job)
        throws InterruptedException {
    return queue.offer(job, 100, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

The successful offer that links or stores the element is the enqueue linearization point. A successful poll or take removal is the dequeue linearization point. Queue internal state is shared; its invariant is that each enqueue occurrence is removed at most once and capacity is not exceeded for bounded queues.

An unbounded queue does not provide overload control. It converts overload into growing memory and latency. Prefer a bounded queue plus explicit reject, caller-runs, drop, or shed policy when producers can outrun consumers.

docs.title: Weakly consistent iteration
docs.text:
Iterators from ConcurrentHashMap and many concurrent queues are weakly consistent. They do not throw ConcurrentModificationException; they may reflect some updates that happen after iterator creation and may omit others. They do not provide one atomic snapshot.

Use weak iteration for diagnostics, best-effort maintenance, or approximate metrics. Do not use it to enforce invariants such as "sum all balances, then authorize a withdrawal" or to perform exactly-once processing. For a stable snapshot, coordinate writers, copy under the relevant protocol, use immutable snapshots, or query a transactional source.

Bulk map operations such as forEach, reduce, and search also observe concurrent state. Their functions should not depend on encounter order and should avoid side effects that require exactly-once execution.

docs.title: Choosing locks, atomics, and concurrent collections
docs.text:
Situation First choice Reason one numeric independent transition atomic number direct linearizable operation several related fields lock or immutable atomic snapshot preserve cross-field invariant per-key independent updates ConcurrentHashMap compound method atomic key-scoped operation hot metrics counter LongAdder spreads write contention bounded producer-consumer bounded BlockingQueue storage plus backpressure rare listener changes CopyOnWriteArrayList cheap stable traversal complex blocking protocol lock and conditions explicit predicates and waits

Lock-free is not automatically faster. Measure contention, allocation, retry rate, and tail latency. Prefer the simplest mechanism that expresses the invariant.

docs.title: Stock cannot oversell
docs.text:
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class AtomicExamplesTest {
    @Test
    void stockNeverOversells() throws Exception {
        int initial = 100;
        var stock = new Stock(initial);
        var successes = new AtomicInteger();
        var start = new CountDownLatch(1);

        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var futures = java.util.stream.IntStream.range(0, 500)
                    .mapToObj(ignored -> executor.submit(() -> {
                        start.await();
                        if (stock.tryReserve(1)) {
                            successes.incrementAndGet();
                        }
                        return null;
                    })).toList();
            start.countDown();
            for (var future : futures) {
                future.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            }
        }

        assertEquals(initial, successes.get());
        assertEquals(0, stock.remaining());
    }

    @Test
    void oneCacheValueIsPublishedPerKey() throws Exception {
        var registry = new CacheRegistry<String, Object>();
        var loadCalls = new AtomicInteger();
        var start = new CountDownLatch(1);

        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            var futures = java.util.stream.IntStream.range(0, 100)
                    .mapToObj(ignored -> executor.submit(() -> {
                        start.await();
                        return registry.getOrLoad("key", key -> {
                            loadCalls.incrementAndGet();
                            return new Object();
                        });
                    })).toList();
            start.countDown();
            Object expected = futures.getFirst().get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            for (var future : futures) {
                org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertSame(
                        expected, future.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            }
        }

        assertEquals(1, loadCalls.get());
    }
}

The start latch increases overlap without claiming a specific scheduler order. Future timeouts detect hangs. Final invariants, not observed thread interleavings, determine correctness.

docs.title: Deterministically force one CAS failure
docs.text: Production classes can accept a package-private test hook immediately before CAS. A test uses barriers to let both threads read the same old value, allows one CAS, then verifies the other retries. Do not retain such hooks in public APIs; alternatively test a small CAS-loop helper whose candidate function counts invocations and whose atomic is changed at a controlled barrier.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Splitting check-and-act across separate atomic operations.
  • Assuming multiple atomic fields form an atomic snapshot.
  • Putting I/O, logging, metrics, random generation, or mutation in retryable update functions.
  • Using LongAdder.sum() for admission or exact sequencing.
  • Ignoring ABA when a value can leave and return to the same representation.
  • Treating ConcurrentHashMap.get followed by put as a compound atomic action.
  • Recursively mutating a map from computeIfAbsent.
  • Running slow loaders inside map computation without considering contention.
  • Assuming a weakly consistent iterator is a snapshot.
  • Using copy-on-write for a write-heavy or large collection.
  • Selecting an unbounded queue without an overload policy.
  • Assuming thread-safe callbacks make a compound workflow safe.

docs.title: Exercise 1: reserve and release with one invariant
docs.text:
Extend stock so reservations can be released without exceeding the initial capacity. Keep the transition in one atomic value.

Complete solution 
final class ReleasableStock {
    private final int capacity;
    private final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger remaining;

    ReleasableStock(int capacity) {
        if (capacity < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative capacity");
        }
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.remaining = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger(capacity);
    }

    boolean tryReserve(int quantity) {
        if (quantity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        }
        while (true) {
            int current = remaining.get();
            if (current < quantity) {
                return false;
            }
            if (remaining.compareAndSet(current, current - quantity)) {
                return true;
            }
        }
    }

    void release(int quantity) {
        if (quantity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        }
        while (true) {
            int current = remaining.get();
            if (quantity > capacity - current) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("release exceeds reservations");
            }
            if (remaining.compareAndSet(current, current + quantity)) {
                return;
            }
        }
    }
}

Shared state is remaining capacity. The invariant is 0 <= remaining <= capacity. Each successful CAS is a linearization point. This API trusts callers to release each reservation once. A robust domain model would return a reservation token with idempotent lifecycle state rather than expose an uncorrelated quantity release.

docs.title: Exercise 2: exact per-key frequency
docs.text:
Implement exact linearizable counts per key and explain what remains non-atomic.

Complete solution 
final class ExactFrequencyCounter {
    private final java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<
            String, java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong> counts =
            new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    long record(String key) {
        return counts.computeIfAbsent(
                key, ignored -> new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong())
                .incrementAndGet();
    }

    long count(String key) {
        var counter = counts.get(key);
        return counter == null ? 0 : counter.get();
    }
}

Installation is atomic per key, and each increment is linearizable on that key's AtomicLong. Reading several keys is not one atomic snapshot. Removal concurrent with increment would require an additional lifecycle protocol because a thread could increment an atomic no longer installed in the map.

docs.title: Exercise 3: safe state transition with a version
docs.text:
Model a document that transitions from DRAFT to PUBLISHED. It may return to DRAFT after retraction, but an editor must detect that a publish-retract cycle occurred.

Complete solution 
final class VersionedDocument {
    enum Status { DRAFT, PUBLISHED }

    private final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference<Status> state =
            new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference<>(Status.DRAFT, 0);

    record View(Status status, int version) {}

    View view() {
        int[] stamp = new int[1];
        Status status = state.get(stamp);
        return new View(status, stamp[0]);
    }

    boolean publish(View expected) {
        if (expected.status() != Status.DRAFT) {
            return false;
        }
        return state.compareAndSet(
                Status.DRAFT, Status.PUBLISHED,
                expected.version(), expected.version() + 1);
    }

    boolean retract(View expected) {
        if (expected.status() != Status.PUBLISHED) {
            return false;
        }
        return state.compareAndSet(
                Status.PUBLISHED, Status.DRAFT,
                expected.version(), expected.version() + 1);
    }
}

The state and version form one atomic pair. Every successful transition increments the stamp. An editor holding the original DRAFT view cannot publish after another publish-retract cycle because the status matches but the stamp does not. Successful stamped CAS is the linearization point.

docs.title: Exercise 4: choose a queue
docs.text:
A service accepts image jobs, has 16 consumers, must cap memory at 1,000 queued jobs, and should reject after waiting 50 ms. Choose an API and state the overload behavior.

Complete solution

Use an ArrayBlockingQueue<Job> with capacity 1,000 and timed offer:

final class ImageJobBuffer {
    private final java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<Job> queue =
            new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000);

    boolean submit(Job job) throws InterruptedException {
        return queue.offer(job, 50, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }

    Job take() throws InterruptedException {
        return queue.take();
    }
}

A successful offer linearizes at insertion. A false result is explicit overload and must become a stable caller response such as rejection or retry-after; it must not be silently dropped. take blocks consumers without polling. The queue bounds queued jobs, not executing jobs, so total in-flight capacity is up to 1,016 plus producer-local references.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
1. Explain CAS and why a CAS loop can invoke its update logic repeatedly.
  2. What progress guarantee does a simple CAS loop provide?
  3. Why is check-then-increment unsafe even with an atomic counter?
  4. When should related fields be placed in one immutable atomic snapshot?
  5. Why must atomic functional updates avoid side effects?
  6. When is LongAdder better than AtomicLong, and when is it incorrect?
  7. What is ABA, and how does a stamp help?
  8. Which ConcurrentHashMap operations make per-key compound actions atomic?
  9. What can go wrong inside computeIfAbsent?
  10. When is CopyOnWriteArrayList a strong choice?
  11. What does weakly consistent iteration guarantee and not guarantee?
  12. How does bounded queue selection express backpressure?
  13. State the invariant and linearization points of stock reservation.
  14. How would you test a cache registry without sleep?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• CAS atomically commits a transition only when the observed state is still current.
  • A failed CAS requires recomputation; retryable functions must not perform side effects.
  • Atomic variables preserve one-location invariants, while immutable snapshots can combine related fields.
  • LongAdder improves hot metric writes but does not provide an exact concurrent snapshot.
  • Stamps or versions detect value histories hidden by ABA.
  • ConcurrentHashMap compound methods are atomic per key, not across the map.
  • Copy-on-write favors frequent traversal and rare mutation.
  • Blocking queues combine transfer semantics with explicit capacity and waiting policy.
  • Weakly consistent iteration is useful for observation, not transactional decisions.
  • The simplest mechanism that directly expresses the invariant is usually the strongest interview answer.

Previous: Coordination Primitives | Next: Executors and Backpressure

docs.title: 07. Executors, Capacity, and Backpressure
docs.text: Executors separate task submission from task execution. That separation is useful only when the queue, rejection behavior, and shutdown protocol are part of the design. An executor with an accidental unbounded queue is not a capacity plan.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • choose between Executor, ExecutorService, Callable, and Future;
  • predict how every ThreadPoolExecutor parameter affects admission;
  • derive a starting pool size from measured workload data;
  • design bounded overload behavior instead of hiding overload in a queue;
  • explain scheduled task semantics and failure behavior;
  • implement graceful and forced shutdown correctly;
  • prevent ThreadLocal state from leaking between pooled tasks; and
  • build and test a bounded worker service.

docs.title: 1. The execution model
docs.text:
Executor has one operation:

void execute(Runnable command);

The interface does not specify which thread runs the command or when it starts. ExecutorService adds lifecycle control and result-bearing submission. A Callable<V> may return a value or throw a checked exception. Future<V> represents the eventual completion of one submitted task.

submit -> admission -> queued/running -> completed
                 |                       |-- value
                 |                       |-- failure
                 |                       `-- cancellation
                 `-- rejected

docs.title: Completion semantics
docs.text: For a successful Future.get(), actions in the task happen-before actions after get() returns. get() wraps task failure in ExecutionException. Interrupting the waiting caller does not cancel the task. cancel(true) requests interruption if the task has started; it does not forcibly stop Java code.

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
A useful conceptual state machine is:

NEW -> QUEUED -> RUNNING -> SUCCESS
  |       |         |------> FAILED
  |       |         `------> CANCELLED (cooperative)
  |       `----------------> CANCELLED
  `------------------------> REJECTED (no Future-owned execution)

The exact internal FutureTask states are implementation details. The interview invariant is simpler:

A one-shot task submitted once to a standard ExecutorService is invoked at most once for that submission. Its future reaches a terminal outcome only if it completes or is explicitly cancelled; accepted work can otherwise remain pending forever.

Do not confuse that with exactly-once business processing. A process crash can occur after an external side effect but before durable acknowledgement.

CANCELLED is a future outcome, not proof that the task body stopped. A running body can ignore interruption and continue after get() reports cancellation. Executor.execute also permits caller-thread execution; the interface alone promises no queue or thread creation.

docs.title: Broken: fire-and-forget with no lifecycle
docs.text:
public final class BrokenIndexer {
    private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);

    public void index(Document document) {
        pool.submit(() -> repository.save(document));
    }
}

Problems:

  • newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue;
  • failures disappear inside ignored Future objects;
  • callers cannot observe completion or rejection;
  • the service has no shutdown contract; and
  • accepted work can be lost when the process exits.

docs.title: Corrected: explicit result and lifecycle
docs.text:
public final class Indexer implements AutoCloseable {
    private final ExecutorService pool;

    public Indexer(int workers, int capacity) {
        this.pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                workers,
                workers,
                0L,
                TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity),
                Thread.ofPlatform().name("indexer-", 0).factory(),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
    }

    public Future<IndexResult> index(Document document) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(document);
        return pool.submit(() -> repository.save(document));
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        ExecutorShutdown.graceful(pool, Duration.ofSeconds(20));
    }
}

This is better because queue capacity and rejection are visible design choices. Production code should also expose active threads, queue depth, completed tasks, rejected tasks, and task latency.

docs.title: 3. ThreadPoolExecutor admission algorithm
docs.text:
Given corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, keepAliveTime, and a work queue, execute broadly follows this order:

  1. If fewer than corePoolSize workers exist, start a worker for the task.
  2. Otherwise, try to enqueue the task.
  3. If the queue is full and fewer than maximumPoolSize workers exist, start another worker.
  4. Otherwise, invoke the rejection handler.

This ordering causes a common interview trap: maximumPoolSize has no practical effect with an unbounded queue because step 2 almost always succeeds.

docs.title: Parameter interactions
docs.text:
Choice Admission effect Operational consequence Small core, bounded queue, larger max Queues before growing past core Can add queue delay before using spare threads Core equals max, bounded queue Fixed concurrency and bounded backlog Predictable capacity and simpler tuning SynchronousQueue No storage; direct handoff only Grows toward max quickly, rejects when all workers are busy Unbounded queue Almost every task queues Max is ineffective; latency and memory can grow without bound allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) Even core workers may retire Saves idle resources but adds cold-start cost

Non-core workers retire after keepAliveTime while idle. Core workers do so only when core timeout is enabled. Prestarting core threads trades startup cost for idle resource use.

docs.title: Bounded versus unbounded queues
docs.text:
A bounded queue turns capacity into a finite quantity:

in-flight capacity = active workers + queue slots

It does not solve overload by itself. It creates the point at which the system must shed, block, redirect, or degrade work. An unbounded queue delays that decision until latency or memory fails elsewhere.

Queue choice also changes scheduling:

  • ArrayBlockingQueue is bounded and allocation-stable. Optional fairness reduces barging but usually costs throughput.
  • LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) is bounded when a capacity is supplied, but allocates linked nodes.
  • PriorityBlockingQueue is unbounded and does not preserve FIFO among equal priorities unless tasks include a sequence tie-breaker.
  • SynchronousQueue has zero capacity and pairs producers with workers.

docs.title: 4. Rejection and backpressure
docs.text:
The built-in policies express different contracts:

Policy Behavior Appropriate when AbortPolicy Throws RejectedExecutionException Caller can fail fast, retry elsewhere, or return overload CallerRunsPolicy Submitter runs the task Slowing that submitter safely propagates pressure DiscardPolicy Silently drops the task Rarely; only explicitly disposable, measured work DiscardOldestPolicy Drops queue head and retries Rarely; semantics tolerate loss and ordering changes

CallerRunsPolicy is not universally safe. It may execute blocking work on an event-loop thread, hold a lock while running user code, or make request latency unbounded. Also, after shutdown it silently discards under the JDK implementation. Prefer an explicit rejection contract.

docs.title: Broken: retry storm
docs.text:
while (true) {
    try {
        executor.execute(task);
        break;
    } catch (RejectedExecutionException overloaded) {
        // Immediate retry adds more load and burns CPU.
    }
}

docs.title: Corrected: bounded admission wait
docs.text:
public final class BoundedExecutor {
    private final ThreadPoolExecutor executor;
    private final Semaphore inFlight;

    public BoundedExecutor(int workers, int queueCapacity) {
        if (workers <= 0 || queueCapacity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        }
        int capacity = Math.addExact(workers, queueCapacity);
        inFlight = new Semaphore(capacity, true);
        executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                workers, workers, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(queueCapacity),
                new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
    }

    public boolean execute(Runnable task, Duration budget)
            throws InterruptedException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(task, "task");
        Objects.requireNonNull(budget, "budget");
        if (budget.isNegative()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative budget");
        }
        long nanos;
        try {
            nanos = budget.toNanos();
        } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            nanos = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
        if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(nanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            return false;
        }
        try {
            executor.execute(() -> {
                try {
                    task.run();
                } finally {
                    inFlight.release();
                }
            });
            return true;
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException rejected) {
            inFlight.release();
            return false;
        }
    }

    public void shutdown() {
        executor.shutdown();
    }
}

The semaphore bounds running plus queued work and makes producers wait only for their admission budget. After a permit is obtained, execute remains the sole executor-admission operation. Therefore a shutdown race is resolved by ThreadPoolExecutor: either submission commits before shutdown, or rejection releases the permit and returns false. A permit does not guarantee a queue slot at that instant: a finishing worker may release its permit before taking the next queued task, so a permitted submission can still be rejected. Never repair rejection with executor.getQueue().offer(...); a direct enqueue can race with shutdown and leave work in a queue that has no worker allowed to start it.

docs.title: Backpressure options
docs.text:
1. Reject quickly and return a retryable overload result.
  2. Wait for a bounded admission budget.
  3. Make the producer perform safe work.
  4. Drop explicitly classified low-value work and count every drop.
  5. Reduce work quality, batch, or route to durable storage.

The invariant is:

Running work plus queued work never exceeds the declared in-process bound, and every non-accepted request receives an explicit outcome.

docs.title: 5. Pool sizing with Little's Law
docs.text:
Little's Law states L = lambda * W for a stable system:

  • L: average number of requests in the system;
  • lambda: average arrival or completion rate; and
  • W: average time in the system.

If a dependency sustains 800 operations/second and each operation occupies a worker for 25 ms, expected concurrency is:

L = 800/s * 0.025s = 20 concurrent operations

Twenty is a measured starting point, not a promise. Account for tail latency, burst tolerance, dependency quotas, CPU, connection-pool capacity, and memory per task. A downstream connection pool of 12 makes a 100-thread pool mostly a waiting room.

For CPU-bound work, begin near the number of available processors and benchmark. For mixed blocking work, a traditional approximation is:

threads = processors * target_utilization * (1 + wait_time / compute_time)

The formula assumes measured, reasonably stable times. Validate it with load tests. Virtual threads change the cost of waiting threads, not downstream capacity or Little's Law.

Queue capacity should follow an explicit latency budget. If the pool completes 500 tasks/second and at most 100 ms of queueing is acceptable, a rough average queue bound is 50 tasks. Bursts and service-time variance require measurement, not arbitrary multiplication.

docs.title: 6. Scheduled executors
docs.text:
ScheduledExecutorService supports delayed and periodic work.

  • schedule runs once after at least the delay.
  • scheduleAtFixedRate targets a cadence measured from planned start times. It does not overlap executions of the same periodic task. A slow run can cause subsequent runs to start late.
  • scheduleWithFixedDelay waits the delay after one run completes before scheduling the next.

If a periodic task throws, later executions are suppressed. Catch and report expected failures at the task boundary.

ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("lease-renewer").factory());

ScheduledFuture<?> handle = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> {
    try {
        renewLeases();
    } catch (Exception failure) {
        failureReporter.accept(failure);
    }
}, 0, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Scheduled delays use relative timing. Wall-clock jumps can still affect application logic that reads calendar time. Keep scheduled tasks short or hand off bounded work to a separate executor. Otherwise one slow maintenance action delays unrelated schedules.

Cancellation of a scheduled task should usually remove it from the delay queue:

ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor scheduler = new ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(2);
scheduler.setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true);
scheduler.setExecuteExistingDelayedTasksAfterShutdownPolicy(false);
scheduler.setContinueExistingPeriodicTasksAfterShutdownPolicy(false);

docs.title: 7. Shutdown is a protocol
docs.text:
shutdown() rejects new tasks but lets accepted tasks finish. shutdownNow() attempts to interrupt running tasks and returns tasks that never started. Neither method waits.

public final class ExecutorShutdown {
    private ExecutorShutdown() {}

    public static void graceful(ExecutorService executor, Duration timeout) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(executor);
        Objects.requireNonNull(timeout);
        if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        long nanos;
        try { nanos = timeout.toNanos(); }
        catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) { nanos = Long.MAX_VALUE; }
        executor.shutdown();
        boolean interrupted = false;
        try {
            if (!executor.awaitTermination(nanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
                cancelQueued(executor.shutdownNow());
                if (!executor.awaitTermination(nanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
                    System.err.println("Executor did not terminate");
                }
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException interruptedException) {
            interrupted = true;
            cancelQueued(executor.shutdownNow());
        } finally {
            if (interrupted) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }
    }

    static void cancelQueued(java.util.List<Runnable> queued) {
        for (Runnable task : queued) {
            if (task instanceof Future<?> future) future.cancel(false);
        }
    }
}

The service-level order usually is:

  1. stop external admission;
  2. mark the component as draining;
  3. stop producers and periodic submissions;
  4. call shutdown on workers;
  5. await a bounded grace period;
  6. call shutdownNow and cancel outstanding work;
  7. close dependencies after tasks stop; and
  8. report work that did not complete.

Tasks must cooperate with interruption. Restore interrupt status when a layer cannot complete the cancellation policy itself.

The helper grants two separate waits of timeout, so total grace plus forced wait may approach twice that duration, excluding scheduling delays. It handles queued standard FutureTask wrappers; custom wrappers need their own completion hook. shutdownNow alone does not cancel returned futures. A running task may outlive both waits, so the diagnostic is not permission to close dependencies still in use.

docs.title: Broken interruption handling
docs.text:
try {
    queue.put(item);
} catch (InterruptedException ignored) {
    // Cancellation was consumed, so shutdown may hang.
}

docs.title: Corrected interruption handling
docs.text:
try {
    queue.put(item);
} catch (InterruptedException cancelled) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    throw new CancellationException("worker interrupted");
}

docs.title: 8. ThreadLocal hygiene
docs.text:
Pool threads outlive tasks. A value left in a ThreadLocal can be observed by an unrelated request and can retain a large object graph.

private static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>();

public static Runnable withRequestId(String requestId, Runnable task) {
    return () -> {
        String previous = REQUEST_ID.get();
        try {
            REQUEST_ID.set(requestId);
            task.run();
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) {
                REQUEST_ID.remove();
            } else {
                REQUEST_ID.set(previous);
            }
        }
    };
}

Restoring the previous value makes nesting safe. Clearing in afterExecute can add defense in depth, but it must know every context holder and does not replace lexical cleanup. Prefer explicit parameters where practical.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
The service processes jobs with these semantics:

  • at most workers + queueCapacity jobs are admitted;
  • submission never waits indefinitely;
  • every accepted submission returns a Future;
  • rejected submissions fail immediately;
  • task failure completes only that task exceptionally;
  • close stops admission, drains, then interrupts; and
  • business actions must be idempotent because process failure can cause external retries.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

public final class BoundedWorkerService implements AutoCloseable {
    public record Stats(long accepted, long completed, long failed, long rejected,
                        int active, int queued) {}

    private final ThreadPoolExecutor executor;
    private final Duration shutdownTimeout;
    private final LongAdder accepted = new LongAdder();
    private final LongAdder completed = new LongAdder();
    private final LongAdder failed = new LongAdder();
    private final LongAdder rejected = new LongAdder();

    public BoundedWorkerService(int workers, int queueCapacity,
                                Duration shutdownTimeout) {
        if (workers <= 0 || queueCapacity <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be positive");
        }
        this.shutdownTimeout = Objects.requireNonNull(shutdownTimeout);
        if (shutdownTimeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        this.executor = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                workers,
                workers,
                0L,
                TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
                new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(queueCapacity),
                Thread.ofPlatform().name("bounded-worker-", 0).factory(),
                (task, ignored) -> {
                    rejected.increment();
                    throw new RejectedExecutionException("worker service overloaded");
                });
    }

    public <T> Future<T> submit(Callable<T> job) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(job);
        Future<T> future = executor.submit(() -> {
            try {
                T value = job.call();
                completed.increment();
                return value;
            } catch (Exception | Error failure) {
                failed.increment();
                throw failure;
            }
        });
        accepted.increment();
        return future;
    }

    public Stats stats() {
        return new Stats(accepted.sum(), completed.sum(), failed.sum(),
                rejected.sum(), executor.getActiveCount(), executor.getQueue().size());
    }

    public List<Runnable> forceShutdown() {
        List<Runnable> queued = executor.shutdownNow();
        ExecutorShutdown.cancelQueued(queued);
        return queued;
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        ExecutorShutdown.graceful(executor, shutdownTimeout);
    }
}

docs.title: Linearization and accounting
docs.text:
For an accepted task, submission linearizes when ThreadPoolExecutor.execute commits it to a worker or queue. Rejection linearizes when the rejection handler runs. accepted increments after submit returns, so snapshots are intentionally approximate: a task can complete before its accepted counter increments. This is valid for telemetry, not billing.

The exact capacity invariant applies at executor admission. Metrics observed concurrently need not satisfy accepted = completed + failed + queued + active because counters and executor gauges are not one atomic snapshot, cancellation is omitted, and a running task can finish between reads.

docs.title: Failure and cancellation
docs.text:
• A thrown exception is stored in the Future; it does not kill the worker.
  • Future.cancel(false) prevents a queued task from running when cancellation wins.
  • Future.cancel(true) also interrupts a running worker, but the callable must cooperate.
  • shutdownNow returns queued FutureTask instances. The service must define whether callers, a durable queue, or a recovery process owns them.
  • A JVM crash bypasses close; durable jobs require durable intake and idempotent effects.

docs.title: 10. Tests without timing guesses
docs.text:
The following JUnit 5 tests use latches as deterministic gates. Timeouts bound a broken test; they are not assertions about scheduler speed.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

final class BoundedWorkerServiceTest {
    @Test
    void rejectsBeyondWorkersAndQueue() throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch started = new CountDownLatch(1);
        CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);

        try (var service = new BoundedWorkerService(1, 1, Duration.ofSeconds(1))) {
            Future<Integer> running = service.submit(() -> {
                started.countDown();
                release.await();
                return 1;
            });
            assertTrue(started.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            Future<Integer> queued = service.submit(() -> 2);

            assertThrows(RejectedExecutionException.class,
                    () -> service.submit(() -> 3));

            release.countDown();
            assertEquals(1, running.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            assertEquals(2, queued.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            assertEquals(1, service.stats().rejected());
        } finally {
            release.countDown();
        }
    }

    @Test
    void cancellationInterruptsCooperativeTask() throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch started = new CountDownLatch(1);
        CountDownLatch interrupted = new CountDownLatch(1);

        try (var service = new BoundedWorkerService(1, 1, Duration.ofSeconds(1))) {
            Future<Void> future = service.submit(() -> {
                started.countDown();
                try {
                    new CountDownLatch(1).await();
                    return null;
                } catch (InterruptedException expected) {
                    interrupted.countDown();
                    throw expected;
                }
            });
            assertTrue(started.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            assertTrue(future.cancel(true));
            assertTrue(interrupted.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            assertThrows(CancellationException.class, future::get);
        }
    }
}

Also test: task exceptions, rejection after close, restoration of interrupt status, queued-task cancellation, metric monotonicity, and absence of worker threads after shutdown.

docs.title: 11. Tradeoffs
docs.text: Decision Benefit Cost or risk Fixed bounded pool Predictable concurrency and memory Rejects bursts; may underuse variable capacity Elastic pool with handoff Handles short bursts without queue delay Thread growth and downstream overload Caller-runs Natural producer throttling Unsafe on event loops or while holding locks Fail-fast rejection Preserves latency and resources Callers need retry, fallback, or error handling Large queue Absorbs brief bursts Stale work, high tail latency, retained memory Small queue Fast overload signal More rejection during harmless microbursts Platform pool Mature controls for CPU and bounded concurrency Blocking consumes expensive OS threads

docs.title: Exercise 1: explain an idle maximum
docs.text:
A pool has core 8, max 64, and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Under load it has 8 active workers and 50,000 queued tasks. Why did it not grow to 64, and what is the smallest defensible correction?

Solution

ThreadPoolExecutor queues after all core workers are busy. Because the queue accepts every task, the executor never reaches the branch that creates workers above core. If the required concurrency is fixed, set core and max to the measured worker count and use a bounded queue plus explicit rejection. If elasticity is required, use a bounded queue or SynchronousQueue, set a justified max, and cap the downstream dependency separately. Reducing the queue without defining rejection behavior is incomplete.

docs.title: Exercise 2: write a safe context wrapper
docs.text:
Wrap a Callable<T> so it installs a request ID and always restores the previous ThreadLocal value.

Solution 
static <T> Callable<T> withRequestId(String id, Callable<T> task) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(task);
    return () -> {
        String previous = REQUEST_ID.get();
        try {
            REQUEST_ID.set(id);
            return task.call();
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) {
                REQUEST_ID.remove();
            } else {
                REQUEST_ID.set(previous);
            }
        }
    };
}

The finally block handles success, exception, and interruption. Restoration, rather than unconditional removal, preserves nested scope.

docs.title: Exercise 3: choose a schedule
docs.text:
A cache refresh takes 2 to 20 seconds. The requirement is to wait 30 seconds after each refresh ends before starting another. Choose the API and show failure containment.

Solution 
ScheduledFuture<?> refresh = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> {
    try {
        cache.refresh();
    } catch (Exception failure) {
        metrics.refreshFailure();
        logger.log(System.Logger.Level.ERROR, "refresh failed", failure);
    }
}, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Fixed delay matches completion-to-next-start semantics. Catching expected operational failures prevents one failure from suppressing all future executions. Cancellation and scheduler shutdown still stop it.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Saying max threads limits an executor that has an unbounded queue.
  • Treating queue capacity as backpressure without defining rejection behavior.
  • Assuming Future.cancel(true) kills arbitrary code.
  • Calling shutdownNow and assuming running tasks have stopped.
  • Swallowing InterruptedException.
  • Ignoring periodic-task suppression after an exception.
  • Using CallerRunsPolicy from an event loop or lock-protected path.
  • Treating executor telemetry as an atomic accounting ledger.
  • Forgetting that pooled ThreadLocal values outlive requests.

docs.title: Questions to practice
docs.text:
1. Walk through admission for core 4, max 16, queue 100 at the 1st, 5th, 105th, and 117th simultaneous submissions.
  2. How would you expose overload to an HTTP caller and prevent retry amplification?
  3. Which capacity should dominate: worker threads, queue slots, database connections, or dependency quota?
  4. What is the linearization point for accepted submission and for rejection?
  5. How do graceful shutdown and process-crash recovery differ?
  6. When is a SynchronousQueue better than a bounded buffer?
  7. Why can a long queue reduce throughput even before memory exhaustion?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Executors are admission and lifecycle components, not just thread factories.
  • Queue type determines whether and when a pool can grow beyond its core size.
  • Bound both concurrency and backlog, then make overload explicit.
  • Use Little's Law and dependency limits to establish a measured starting size.
  • Cancellation is cooperative, and shutdown must be a bounded service protocol.
  • Scheduled tasks need explicit cadence, failure, cancellation, and shutdown semantics.
  • Clean ThreadLocal state in lexical finally blocks.
  • Test concurrency with deterministic gates and bounded test timeouts, not sleeps.

Previous: Atomics and Concurrent Collections | Next: Async, Parallelism, and Virtual Threads

docs.title: 08. Async Composition, Parallelism, and Virtual Threads
docs.text: Asynchrony is about waiting without tying up the caller. Parallelism is about executing work at the same time. Virtual threads make blocking code cheaper to scale, but they do not increase CPU, connection limits, or dependency quotas. Strong interview answers separate these concerns before choosing an API.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • compose and combine CompletableFuture stages without accidental serialization;
  • control execution placement and exception semantics;
  • implement end-to-end deadlines and explain cancellation limits;
  • reason about work stealing, blocking, and nested fork/join work;
  • use parallel streams only where their ownership and cost are acceptable;
  • design Java 21 thread-per-task services with virtual threads;
  • bound scarce dependencies with semaphores rather than pooling virtual threads;
  • discuss pinning and version-specific preview APIs accurately;
  • build a fan-out aggregator and parallel merge sort; and
  • test completion, failure, timeout, cancellation, and shutdown behavior.

docs.title: 1. Choose the model from the work
docs.text:
Work Primary need Typical Java 21 tool One blocking request per task Scalable waiting Virtual thread per task Several independent remote calls Composition and deadlines CompletableFuture with explicit executor Recursive CPU computation Parallel divide and conquer ForkJoinPool / RecursiveTask Pure bulk collection transform Data parallelism Carefully evaluated parallel stream Limit calls to scarce dependency Admission control Fair or non-fair Semaphore

Do not select an asynchronous API merely to avoid blocking syntax. A synchronous call on a virtual thread is often simpler than a graph of callbacks. Conversely, virtual threads do not provide result composition, deadlines, or sibling cancellation by themselves.

docs.title: 2. CompletableFuture completion model
docs.text:
A stage reaches one terminal outcome:

INCOMPLETE -> NORMAL(value)
           -> EXCEPTIONAL(cause)
           `-> CANCELLED(CancellationException)

Ordinary completion is single-winner. Attempts to complete or completeExceptionally an already completed future return false and do not replace its outcome. The exceptional recovery methods obtrudeValue and obtrudeException can override later observations and must not be part of this normal protocol. Actions before completion happen-before dependent actions triggered by that completion.

docs.title: Transformation, composition, and combination
docs.text:
• thenApply: transform T into U; analogous to map.
  • thenCompose: use T to start a future CompletionStage<U> and flatten it; analogous to flatMap.
  • thenCombine: wait for two independent stages and combine both values.
  • allOf: wait for all stages, but does not collect typed results.
  • anyOf: complete from one stage, returning Object.

docs.title: Broken: nested future and accidental serialization
docs.text:
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> nested =
        loadCustomer(id).thenApply(customer -> loadLatestOrder(customer.id()));

Customer customer = loadCustomer(id).join();
Order order = loadLatestOrder(customer.id()).join();

The first form leaves a nested future. The second blocks before launching the second operation. If the operations are dependent, use composition; if independent, start both before combining.

docs.title: Corrected composition
docs.text:
CompletableFuture<Order> order = loadCustomer(id)
        .thenCompose(customer -> loadLatestOrder(customer.id()));

docs.title: Corrected combination
docs.text:
CompletableFuture<CustomerView> view(String id) {
    CompletableFuture<Customer> customer = loadCustomer(id);
    CompletableFuture<List<Order>> orders = loadOrders(id);
    return customer.thenCombine(orders, CustomerView::new);
}

The combination completes normally only after both inputs complete normally. If either fails, the combined stage completes exceptionally. Do not rely on which failure wins when both fail concurrently.

docs.title: 3. Execution placement must be explicit
docs.text:
Non-Async continuations may run on the thread that completes the previous stage, or immediately on the caller if the stage is already complete. Async variants without an executor normally use ForkJoinPool.commonPool().

ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32);
ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(
        Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());

CompletableFuture<Report> report = CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> repository.load(id), io)
        .thenApplyAsync(this::calculateReport, cpu);

Execution placement is part of correctness when a stage blocks, consumes substantial CPU, requires thread context, or shares a bounded resource. Passing an executor only to the first stage does not make every later Async stage use it.

docs.title: Broken: blocking the common pool
docs.text:
return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.blockingGet(uri));

This sends blocking I/O to the common fork/join pool, which is shared by unrelated code and parallel streams.

docs.title: Corrected: owned executor
docs.text:
return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.blockingGet(uri), ioExecutor);

For Java 21 blocking I/O, an owned virtual-thread-per-task executor is another clear option:

try (ExecutorService tasks = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<Response> response = tasks.submit(() -> httpClient.blockingGet(uri));
    return response.get();
}

docs.title: 4. Exception semantics
docs.text:
join() throws unchecked CompletionException; get() throws checked ExecutionException and is interruptible. Both preserve the underlying cause.

Method Runs on success Runs on failure Can recover thenApply Yes No No exceptionally No Yes Yes, with fallback value handle Yes Yes Yes, transforms either outcome whenComplete Yes Yes No intended transformation

docs.title: Broken: converting every bug to an empty result
docs.text:
return fetchAccount(id).exceptionally(failure -> Account.empty());

This hides programming errors, cancellation, authentication failures, and overload behind the same fallback.

docs.title: Corrected: classify causes
docs.text:
return fetchAccount(id).exceptionally(failure -> {
    Throwable cause = unwrap(failure);
    if (cause instanceof AccountNotFoundException) {
        return Account.empty();
    }
    if (cause instanceof CancellationException cancellation) {
        throw cancellation;
    }
    throw new CompletionException(cause);
});

static Throwable unwrap(Throwable failure) {
    Throwable current = failure;
    while ((current instanceof CompletionException
            || current instanceof ExecutionException)
            && current.getCause() != null) {
        current = current.getCause();
    }
    return current;
}

whenComplete is useful for telemetry, but if its callback throws while the input succeeded, the returned stage fails. Keep observability hooks defensive.

docs.title: 5. Deadlines, timeouts, and cancellation
docs.text:
A timeout is local to one wait or stage. A deadline is an absolute end-to-end budget. Recomputing a fresh timeout at every layer can exceed the caller's total budget.

public record Deadline(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
    public Deadline {
        if (budgetNanos < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative budget");
    }

    public static Deadline after(Duration budget) {
        if (budget.isNegative()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative budget");
        }
        long nanos;
        try {
            nanos = budget.toNanos();
        } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            nanos = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
        return new Deadline(System.nanoTime(), nanos);
    }

    public Duration remaining() {
        long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
        long remaining = elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
                : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
        return Duration.ofNanos(remaining);
    }
}

Use monotonic System.nanoTime() for elapsed budgets. Storing start plus budget instead of adding them avoids absolute-deadline overflow; extreme positive durations saturate at Long.MAX_VALUE nanoseconds. Pass the remaining budget to dependency clients that can enforce their own connect, request, and read timeout.

orTimeout completes the same CompletableFuture exceptionally with TimeoutException. completeOnTimeout completes it normally with a fallback. Neither guarantees interruption or termination of the underlying supplier.

CompletableFuture<Quote> bounded = quoteFuture
        .orTimeout(deadline.remaining().toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);

docs.title: Cancellation limitations
docs.text:
CompletableFuture.cancel(true) completes the future with cancellation, but its mayInterruptIfRunning argument has no interrupting effect on tasks created through ordinary CompletableFuture async methods. The supplier may continue consuming resources. Incomplete dependent stages complete exceptionally as specified by their combinators; this is downstream outcome propagation, not interruption of their running work. Cancellation does not automatically cancel upstream or sibling work. See the Java 21 CompletableFuture cancellation contract.

For interruptible blocking work, retain the Future returned by an ExecutorService, cancel it, and make the task interruption-aware. Prefer clients with native deadline/cancellation support. Design side effects as idempotent because timeout at the caller does not prove non-execution remotely.

docs.title: Contract and invariants
docs.text:
The aggregator requests inventory, price, and recommendations in parallel.

  • inventory and price are required;
  • expected recommendation I/O failures and timeouts degrade to an empty list; unexpected bugs remain failures;
  • all calls receive one shared deadline;
  • remaining time is checked before task submission and again before dependency invocation; scheduling can still cross the deadline after a check;
  • executor ownership belongs to the aggregator;
  • close rejects new work and interrupts outstanding tasks after a grace period.

Completion semantics:

  • success linearizes when the final combined future is completed with all required values;
  • required-call failure completes the aggregate exceptionally;
  • expected optional-call failure is recorded and converted to its documented fallback;
  • caller cancellation of the returned CompletableFuture does not reliably stop suppliers.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

public final class ProductAggregator implements AutoCloseable {
    public record Inventory(boolean inStock) {}
    public record Price(long minorUnits, String currency) {}
    public record Recommendation(String sku) {}

    public interface CatalogClient {
        Inventory inventory(String sku, Duration timeout) throws Exception;
        Price price(String sku, Duration timeout) throws Exception;
        List<Recommendation> recommendations(String sku, Duration timeout)
                throws Exception;
    }

    public record ProductView(Inventory inventory, Price price,
                              List<Recommendation> recommendations) {}

    private final CatalogClient client;
    private final ExecutorService executor;

    public ProductAggregator(CatalogClient client) {
        this.client = Objects.requireNonNull(client);
        this.executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    }

    public CompletableFuture<ProductView> aggregate(String sku, Duration budget) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(sku);
        Deadline deadline = Deadline.after(budget);

        CompletableFuture<Inventory> inventory = call(deadline,
                () -> client.inventory(sku, requireTime(deadline)));
        CompletableFuture<Price> price = call(deadline,
                () -> client.price(sku, requireTime(deadline)));
        CompletableFuture<List<Recommendation>> recommendations =
                this.<List<Recommendation>>call(deadline,
                        () -> client.recommendations(sku, requireTime(deadline)))
                        .exceptionally(failure -> {
                            Throwable cause = failure;
                            while (cause instanceof CompletionException
                                    && cause.getCause() != null) {
                                cause = cause.getCause();
                            }
                            if (cause instanceof IOException
                                    || cause instanceof TimeoutException) {
                                System.err.println("Recommendations unavailable: "
                                        + cause.getClass().getSimpleName());
                                return List.of();
                            }
                            throw new CompletionException(cause);
                        });

        CompletableFuture<ProductView> result = inventory
                .thenCombine(price, Required::new)
                .thenCombine(recommendations,
                        (required, optional) -> new ProductView(
                                required.inventory(), required.price(), optional));

        long remaining = deadline.remaining().toNanos();
        return result.orTimeout(remaining, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
    }

    private <T> CompletableFuture<T> call(Deadline deadline, CheckedSupplier<T> supplier) {
        try {
            requireTime(deadline);
            return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
                try {
                    return supplier.get();
                } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    throw new CompletionException(interrupted);
                } catch (Exception failure) {
                    throw new CompletionException(failure);
                }
            }, executor);
        } catch (TimeoutException | RejectedExecutionException failure) {
