            return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(failure);
        }
    }

    private static Duration requireTime(Deadline deadline) throws TimeoutException {
        Duration remaining = deadline.remaining();
        if (remaining.isZero()) {
            throw new TimeoutException("aggregate deadline expired");
        }
        return remaining;
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        executor.shutdown();
        boolean restoreInterrupt = false;
        try {
            if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                executor.shutdownNow();
                if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
                    System.err.println("Aggregator tasks did not terminate");
                }
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            restoreInterrupt = true;
            executor.shutdownNow();
        } finally {
            if (restoreInterrupt) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }
    }

    private record Required(Inventory inventory, Price price) {}

    @FunctionalInterface
    private interface CheckedSupplier<T> {
        T get() throws Exception;
    }
}

Replace the example's bounded failure-class diagnostic with production metrics and use clients whose timeout aborts network work. thenCombine is not a fail-fast sibling-cancellation mechanism: a failed required call can still wait for other inputs, bounded here by the aggregate timeout. Submission rejection is represented by a failed future; already submitted work is not rolled back. The virtual-thread executor removes the need to size threads around blocking duration, but dependency concurrency remains unbounded unless separately limited.

docs.title: 7. Fork/join and work stealing
docs.text:
A ForkJoinPool gives each worker a deque. A worker usually processes its own tasks in stack-like order and steals older tasks from other workers when idle. This reduces contention and suits recursively generated CPU work.

The usual pattern is:

  1. stop splitting below a measured threshold;
  2. fork one subproblem;
  3. compute the other directly;
  4. join the forked result; and
  5. combine.

Forking both halves can create unnecessary queueing. Tiny thresholds create overhead; huge thresholds lose parallelism.

docs.title: Managed blocking concern
docs.text:
Fork/join parallelism assumes workers mostly compute. Blocking a worker can reduce available parallelism. ForkJoinPool.managedBlock lets the pool compensate for recognized blocking, but adapters are difficult to make correct and do not raise downstream capacity. Prefer moving blocking work to a suitable executor or using virtual threads for blocking workflows.

Nested parallel operations on the common pool can interfere with unrelated components. Although fork/join joins are cooperative, external locks, I/O, and cyclic waits can still starve progress. Own a pool when isolation is a requirement.

docs.title: State, invariant, and completion
docs.text:
Each task owns the half-open range [low, high) of one array. Child ranges do not overlap, so they may sort concurrently. After both children complete, merge writes one sorted permutation into the parent range.

Invariants:

  • elements outside [low, high) are untouched by that task;
  • after task completion, its range is sorted;
  • the completed range contains exactly the input multiset from that range; and
  • no merge begins until both child ranges complete.

The task's completion point is return from compute after the merge. join establishes visibility of child writes.

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveAction;

public final class ParallelMergeSort {
    private ParallelMergeSort() {}

    public static void sort(int[] values, int threshold, ForkJoinPool pool) {
        if (threshold < 2) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("threshold must be at least 2");
        }
        int[] scratch = new int[values.length];
        pool.invoke(new SortTask(values, scratch, 0, values.length, threshold));
    }

    private static final class SortTask extends RecursiveAction {
        private final int[] values;
        private final int[] scratch;
        private final int low;
        private final int high;
        private final int threshold;

        private SortTask(int[] values, int[] scratch, int low, int high,
                         int threshold) {
            this.values = values;
            this.scratch = scratch;
            this.low = low;
            this.high = high;
            this.threshold = threshold;
        }

        @Override
        protected void compute() {
            int size = high - low;
            if (size <= threshold) {
                Arrays.sort(values, low, high);
                return;
            }

            int middle = low + size / 2;
            SortTask left = new SortTask(values, scratch, low, middle, threshold);
            SortTask right = new SortTask(values, scratch, middle, high, threshold);
            left.fork();
            right.compute();
            left.join();
            merge(values, scratch, low, middle, high);
        }
    }

    private static void merge(int[] values, int[] scratch,
                              int low, int middle, int high) {
        System.arraycopy(values, low, scratch, low, high - low);
        int left = low;
        int right = middle;
        int target = low;
        while (left < middle && right < high) {
            values[target++] = scratch[left] <= scratch[right]
                    ? scratch[left++] : scratch[right++];
        }
        while (left < middle) {
            values[target++] = scratch[left++];
        }
        while (right < high) {
            values[target++] = scratch[right++];
        }
    }
}

This implementation has one shared scratch array, but sibling tasks write disjoint ranges. Benchmark the threshold for representative arrays. Sorting mutates the input; callers must not read or write it concurrently.

docs.title: 9. Parallel streams
docs.text:
Parallel streams use the common fork/join pool in ordinary usage. They are concise for large, in-memory, CPU-heavy, stateless transformations with associative reductions.

Avoid them when:

  • operations block on I/O or locks;
  • encounter order matters and ordered operations dominate;
  • input is small or splitting is poor;
  • lambdas mutate shared state;
  • request isolation or executor ownership matters;
  • the code already runs inside constrained parallel work; or
  • latency predictability matters more than aggregate throughput.

docs.title: Broken shared mutation
docs.text:
List<Result> output = new ArrayList<>();
inputs.parallelStream().map(this::compute).forEach(output::add);

ArrayList mutation races, and encounter order is not guaranteed by forEach.

docs.title: Corrected reduction
docs.text:
List<Result> output = inputs.parallelStream()
        .map(this::compute)
        .toList();

Correct does not imply faster. Measure against a sequential stream with production-like data and co-tenant load.

docs.title: 10. Virtual threads in Java 21
docs.text:
Virtual threads are final in Java 21. The JVM schedules many virtual threads onto a smaller set of carrier platform threads. Blocking in supported JDK operations usually parks the virtual thread and releases its carrier.

try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<Response>> futures = requests.stream()
            .map(request -> executor.submit(() -> client.call(request)))
            .toList();
    for (Future<Response> future : futures) {
        consume(future.get());
    }
}

Virtual threads improve thread scalability for blocking workloads. They do not make CPU work faster and do not make unsafe shared state safe.

docs.title: Why not pool virtual threads
docs.text:
Pooling is primarily a way to reuse expensive platform threads and limit concurrency. Virtual threads are cheap and intended to be created per task. Pooling them adds queueing and obscures task identity without solving scarce-resource admission.

Use a semaphore, rate limiter, connection pool, or dependency-native limit around the scarce operation:

public final class LimitedClient {
    private final Semaphore permits;
    private final RemoteClient client;

    public LimitedClient(int maxConcurrent, RemoteClient client) {
        this.permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent);
        this.client = client;
    }

    public Response call(Request request) throws InterruptedException {
        permits.acquire();
        try {
            return client.call(request);
        } finally {
            permits.release();
        }
    }
}

Permit ownership invariant: every successful acquire has exactly one release in finally; a failed or interrupted acquire has no release. The linearization point for admission is successful permit acquisition. Fair semaphores reduce barging but can lower throughput.

For bounded waiting, use tryAcquire(timeout, unit) and return an explicit overload or deadline result. Do not hold a permit across unrelated computation.

docs.title: Pinning and version caveats
docs.text:
In Java 21, a virtual thread can be pinned to its carrier while blocking inside a synchronized method or block, and in some native or foreign-function calls. Long, frequent pinned blocking can reduce scalability. Short uncontended synchronized sections remain reasonable; do not replace every monitor blindly. Java Flight Recorder and Java 21's jdk.tracePinnedThreads property help locate some problematic pinning cases.

Version boundary (accessed 2026-09-08): JEP 491, delivered in JDK 24, removes monitor-related pinning and removes the effect of jdk.tracePinnedThreads. Remaining native/callback and class-initialization cases still need version-appropriate diagnostics, including JFR. Keep the Java 21 baseline distinct from JDK 24 behavior; an old pinning workaround is not automatically required on a newer runtime.

ThreadLocal works with virtual threads, but millions of per-thread values can consume substantial memory. Prefer explicit context and avoid expensive thread-local caches.

Preview and version-specific APIs

In Java 21, ScopedValue and Structured Concurrency are preview APIs. They require --enable-preview at compile and run time, their package/API shapes may change, and production use requires an explicit upgrade policy. They are not used by the Java 21 baseline examples in this chapter. Structured concurrency aims to make child-task lifetime, failure propagation, and cancellation follow a lexical parent scope; it is not safe to present a later JDK API signature as Java 21 code.

docs.title: Aggregator completion tests
docs.text:
Use controllable fakes rather than sleeping network stubs.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

final class ProductAggregatorTest {
    @Test
    void launchesRequiredCallsBeforeEitherCompletes() throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch entered = new CountDownLatch(2);
        CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ProductAggregator.CatalogClient fake = new StubClient(
                timeout -> { entered.countDown(); release.await(); return inStock(); },
                timeout -> { entered.countDown(); release.await(); return tenDollars(); },
                timeout -> List.of());

        try (var aggregator = new ProductAggregator(fake)) {
            CompletableFuture<ProductAggregator.ProductView> result =
                    aggregator.aggregate("sku-1", Duration.ofSeconds(2));
            assertTrue(entered.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
            assertFalse(result.isDone());
            release.countDown();
            assertEquals(tenDollars(), result.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).price());
        } finally {
            release.countDown();
        }
    }

    @Test
    void requiredFailurePropagates() {
        ProductAggregator.CatalogClient fake = new StubClient(
                timeout -> inStock(),
                timeout -> { throw new IllegalStateException("pricing unavailable"); },
                timeout -> { throw new IOException("recommendations unavailable"); });

        try (var aggregator = new ProductAggregator(fake)) {
            CompletionException failure = assertThrows(CompletionException.class,
                    () -> aggregator.aggregate("sku-1", Duration.ofSeconds(1)).join());
            assertEquals("pricing unavailable", rootCause(failure).getMessage());
        }
    }

    @Test
    void optionalFailureDegradesToEmptyRecommendations() {
        ProductAggregator.CatalogClient fake = new StubClient(
                timeout -> inStock(),
                timeout -> tenDollars(),
                timeout -> { throw new IOException("recommendations unavailable"); });

        try (var aggregator = new ProductAggregator(fake)) {
            ProductAggregator.ProductView view = aggregator
                    .aggregate("sku-1", Duration.ofSeconds(1)).join();
            assertEquals(tenDollars(), view.price());
            assertEquals(List.of(), view.recommendations());
        }
    }

    private static ProductAggregator.Inventory inStock() {
        return new ProductAggregator.Inventory(true);
    }

    private static ProductAggregator.Price tenDollars() {
        return new ProductAggregator.Price(1_000, "USD");
    }

    private static Throwable rootCause(Throwable failure) {
        Throwable current = failure;
        while (current.getCause() != null) {
            current = current.getCause();
        }
        return current;
    }

    @FunctionalInterface
    private interface TimedCall<T> {
        T call(Duration timeout) throws Exception;
    }

    private record StubClient(
            TimedCall<ProductAggregator.Inventory> inventory,
            TimedCall<ProductAggregator.Price> price,
            TimedCall<List<ProductAggregator.Recommendation>> recommendations)
            implements ProductAggregator.CatalogClient {
        @Override
        public ProductAggregator.Inventory inventory(String sku, Duration timeout)
                throws Exception {
            return inventory.call(timeout);
        }

        @Override
        public ProductAggregator.Price price(String sku, Duration timeout)
                throws Exception {
            return price.call(timeout);
        }

        @Override
        public List<ProductAggregator.Recommendation> recommendations(
                String sku, Duration timeout) throws Exception {
            return recommendations.call(timeout);
        }
    }
}

The fixture makes every dependency independently controllable. Tests should additionally verify timeout classification, fallback metrics, rejection after close, interrupt-aware client cancellation, and absence of virtual threads owned by the component after close.

docs.title: Merge sort property test
docs.text:
@Test
void parallelSortMatchesJdkSort() {
    SplittableRandom random = new SplittableRandom(42);
    ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(4);
    try {
        for (int size = 0; size < 2_000; size += 37) {
            int[] actual = random.ints(size, -100, 101).toArray();
            int[] expected = actual.clone();
            Arrays.sort(expected);
            ParallelMergeSort.sort(actual, 64, pool);
            assertArrayEquals(expected, actual);
        }
    } finally {
        pool.shutdownNow();
    }
}

This checks sorted order and multiset preservation against a trusted oracle across duplicates, negatives, empty input, and uneven partitions.

docs.title: 12. Tradeoffs
docs.text: Choice Strength Cost or limitation CompletableFuture graph Rich non-blocking composition Complex cancellation and execution placement Virtual thread per task Direct blocking style and cheap waiting Dependency limits still required; pinning can matter Fork/join Efficient recursive CPU parallelism Poor fit for unmanaged blocking and isolation Parallel stream Compact bulk parallelism Common-pool coupling and weak operational control Explicit platform pool Strong concurrency and resource bounds Expensive blocked threads and tuning burden Semaphore around dependency Limits the actual scarce resource Adds waiting/rejection policy and fairness choice

docs.title: Exercise 1: compose a dependent call
docs.text:
authenticate(token) returns CompletableFuture<User>. loadCart(userId) returns CompletableFuture<Cart>. Return one future without blocking or nesting.

Solution 
CompletableFuture<Cart> cart(String token) {
    return authenticate(token)
            .thenCompose(user -> loadCart(user.id()));
}

thenCompose preserves the dependency and flattens CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Cart>> into one completion stage. Failure or cancellation of authentication prevents the cart function from running.

docs.title: Exercise 2: bound virtual-thread calls
docs.text:
Allow at most 20 concurrent calls and wait no more than the caller's remaining deadline for a permit.

Solution 
Response call(Request request, Deadline deadline) throws Exception {
    long nanos = deadline.remaining().toNanos();
    if (nanos == 0 || !permits.tryAcquire(nanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
        throw new TimeoutException("dependency admission deadline expired");
    }
    try {
        Duration remaining = deadline.remaining();
        if (remaining.isZero()) {
            throw new TimeoutException("deadline expired after admission");
        }
        return client.call(request, remaining);
    } finally {
        permits.release();
    }
}

The permit bounds dependency concurrency, not virtual-thread creation. The second remaining-time calculation prevents permit waiting from resetting the downstream timeout.

docs.title: Exercise 3: repair exceptional recovery
docs.text:
The code future.exceptionally(error -> null).thenApply(Item::id) fails later with an unhelpful null dereference. Preserve absence explicitly.

Solution 
CompletableFuture<Optional<String>> id = future
        .thenApply(item -> Optional.of(item.id()))
        .exceptionally(error -> {
            Throwable cause = unwrap(error);
            if (cause instanceof ItemNotFoundException) {
                return Optional.empty();
            }
            throw new CompletionException(cause);
        });

The type now represents documented absence. Unexpected failure still remains exceptional.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Calling thenApply when the function already returns a future.
  • Assuming every continuation runs on the supplied first-stage executor.
  • Blocking the common fork/join pool with remote I/O.
  • Treating orTimeout as cancellation of the remote operation.
  • Pooling virtual threads to protect a database instead of limiting database calls.
  • Claiming virtual threads improve CPU-bound throughput.
  • Mutating shared state from a parallel stream.
  • Forking recursively below useful granularity.
  • Presenting preview structured-concurrency APIs as stable Java 21 APIs.
  • Ignoring that optional fallback can hide an outage without metrics.

docs.title: Questions to practice
docs.text:
1. When do thenCompose and thenCombine express different dependency graphs?
  2. Which thread can execute a non-async continuation?
  3. How would you propagate one request deadline through three dependencies?
  4. Why can a timed-out CompletableFuture still consume a connection?
  5. When is a virtual thread preferable to a future chain?
  6. How do you cap a virtual-thread service against a 50-connection database pool?
  7. State the invariants that make shared-scratch parallel merge sort safe.
  8. How would you detect and investigate virtual-thread pinning on your deployed JDK?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Composition models dependency; combination models independent results.
  • Explicitly own executors for blocking, CPU-heavy, or isolated work.
  • Preserve typed failure and define optional fallback narrowly.
  • A deadline is end-to-end; stage timeouts do not guarantee work cancellation.
  • Fork/join fits recursive CPU work when task granularity is measured.
  • Parallel streams trade control for concision and share global resources.
  • Create a virtual thread per task; limit scarce dependencies directly.
  • Treat pinning diagnostics and preview APIs as JDK-version-specific.
  • Test completion graphs with controllable gates and observable terminal outcomes.

Previous: Executors, Capacity, and Backpressure | Next: Liveness, Debugging, and Testing

docs.title: 09. Liveness, Debugging, and Concurrency Testing
docs.text: Safety asks whether something bad happens. Liveness asks whether something good eventually happens. A design can preserve every data invariant and still fail because no thread can make progress. Production diagnosis and deterministic tests are therefore part of low-level design, not afterthoughts.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish deadlock, livelock, starvation, and priority inversion;
  • repair multi-lock code with global ordering or timed rollback;
  • identify lock cycles and blocked owners from thread dumps;
  • use jcmd and Java Flight Recorder for live investigation;
  • reproduce races with deterministic gates rather than sleeps;
  • design stress, invariant, history, shutdown, and leak tests;
  • explain what JCStress proves and does not prove; and
  • state linearization points and completion semantics in an interview.

docs.title: 1. Progress properties
docs.text:
Failure What happens Typical signal Deadlock Participants wait in a cycle; none can proceed Stable blocked threads and a wait-for cycle Livelock Participants keep changing state but make no useful progress CPU/activity without completed operations Starvation One participant is repeatedly denied service Overall throughput exists, one request waits excessively Priority inversion High-priority work waits for lower-priority work holding a resource Priority and latency do not align

Java thread priorities are scheduler hints and are platform-dependent. Do not build correctness around them. Priority inversion also occurs at the application level: a latency-critical task can wait behind bulk work in one FIFO executor even without OS thread priorities.

docs.title: Safety, liveness, and bounded liveness
docs.text:
• Safety: an account balance never reflects a half-transfer.
  • Liveness: an admitted transfer eventually reaches a terminal result.
  • Bounded liveness: it reaches a terminal result before its deadline.

Interviews should make the bound explicit. "Eventually" is not useful to a caller with a 200 ms budget.

docs.title: 2. Deadlock as a wait-for cycle
docs.text:
Four conditions commonly characterize lock deadlock:

  1. mutual exclusion;
  2. hold and wait;
  3. no forced lock preemption; and
  4. circular wait.

Breaking any one prevents that deadlock class. Global lock ordering breaks circular wait. tryLock with complete rollback breaks indefinite hold-and-wait. Removing nested acquisition can eliminate the structure entirely.

docs.title: Broken transfer
docs.text:
public static void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) {
    synchronized (from) {
        synchronized (to) {
            from.debit(cents);
            to.credit(cents);
        }
    }
}

Two threads executing transfer(a, b, 10) and transfer(b, a, 20) can each hold one monitor and wait forever for the other.

docs.title: State and invariants
docs.text:
For an in-memory transfer:

  • account IDs are immutable and unique;
  • balances do not become negative;
  • the sum of the two balances is unchanged by a successful transfer;
  • either both balance changes become visible as one operation or neither does; and
  • every acquired lock is released on every exit path.

The linearization point is the mutation performed while both account locks are held. If readers acquire the same locks, no reader can observe the intermediate debit-only state.

docs.title: Corrected: global lock order
docs.text:
public final class Transfers {
    private Transfers() {}

    public static void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(from);
        Objects.requireNonNull(to);
        if (cents <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("cents must be positive");
        }
        if (from == to) {
            return;
        }

        Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
        Account second = first == from ? to : from;
        synchronized (first) {
            synchronized (second) {
                if (from.balance() < cents) {
                    throw new InsufficientFundsException(from.id());
                }
                long credited = Math.addExact(to.balance(), cents);
                from.setBalance(from.balance() - cents);
                to.setBalance(credited);
            }
        }
    }
}

Identity hash codes can collide and mutable business attributes cannot define order. Prefer a unique immutable key. If keys can be equal for distinct objects, add a tie lock or a unique sequence.

docs.title: Corrected alternative: tryLock with rollback
docs.text:
public static boolean transferBefore(
        LockingAccount from,
        LockingAccount to,
        long cents,
        Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException {
    if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("positive cents required");
    if (timeout.isNegative()) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
    }
    long budgetNanos = saturatedNanos(timeout);
    long startedNanos = System.nanoTime();
    boolean fromLocked = false;
    boolean toLocked = false;
    try {
        fromLocked = from.lock().tryLock(
                remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos),
                TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        if (!fromLocked) {
            return false;
        }

        long remaining = remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos);
        toLocked = to.lock().tryLock(remaining, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        if (!toLocked) {
            return false;
        }

        if (from.balance() < cents) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException(from.id());
        }
        if (from == to) return true;
        long credited = Math.addExact(to.balance(), cents);
        from.setBalance(from.balance() - cents);
        to.setBalance(credited);
        return true;
    } finally {
        if (toLocked) {
            to.lock().unlock();
        }
        if (fromLocked) {
            from.lock().unlock();
        }
    }
}

private static long saturatedNanos(Duration timeout) {
    try {
        return timeout.toNanos();
    } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
        return Long.MAX_VALUE;
    }
}

private static long remainingNanos(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
    long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
    return elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
            : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
}

Both acquisitions use one elapsed-time budget, not a fresh timeout per lock. This avoids overflow from constructing an absolute nanosecond deadline. Reverse-order release is conventional and important when lock relationships evolve. Returning false means no transfer occurred.

If callers immediately retry in lockstep, deadlock can become livelock. Add bounded randomized backoff outside all locks, impose a retry limit, or prefer global ordering.

docs.title: 3. Starvation and priority inversion
docs.text:
Starvation can result from:

  • an unfair lock under sustained contention;
  • a hot producer filling a shared queue;
  • readers continuously delaying a writer;
  • tasks blocking all workers while waiting for tasks queued behind them; or
  • one tenant monopolizing a shared pool.

Fair ReentrantLock and Semaphore variants reduce barging but generally reduce throughput. Fairness is not a real-time guarantee. Better designs often isolate workloads, use per-tenant admission limits, avoid nested executor waits, and monitor queue age by class.

docs.title: Broken: thread-pool starvation deadlock
docs.text:
ExecutorService one = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
Future<String> outer = one.submit(() -> one.submit(this::load).get());

The only worker waits for an inner task that only that worker can run.

docs.title: Corrected: compose or execute directly
docs.text:
Future<String> result = one.submit(this::load);

For asynchronous APIs, return and compose the inner stage rather than blocking a worker on work submitted to the same constrained executor.

Priority inversion should be handled structurally: keep critical sections short, avoid performing I/O under locks, separate latency classes, and apply admission control. Raising Java thread priority is not a portable repair.

docs.title: 4. Failure, cancellation, and lock hygiene
docs.text:
Locks do not release automatically when a method throws unless the language construct guarantees it. Monitors exit automatically; explicit locks require finally.

lock.lockInterruptibly();
try {
    updateState();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Prefer lockInterruptibly when cancellation while waiting is meaningful. A thread blocked on monitor entry cannot be interrupted out of that acquisition. Never call unknown code, remote I/O, listener callbacks, or blocking queue operations while holding a lock unless the contract and bound are explicit.

Shutdown can expose liveness defects. A task that ignores interruption, waits for a callback that shutdown has disabled, or holds a lock needed by the shutdown thread can prevent termination. Design cancellation paths alongside normal paths.

docs.title: Step 1: preserve evidence
docs.text: Before restarting, capture at least two or three thread dumps several seconds apart. A single dump shows state; repeated dumps show whether stacks and lock ownership are stable. Also preserve process metrics, request latency, queue depth, CPU, GC, and deployment events.

docs.title: Step 2: capture thread information with jcmd
docs.text:
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > thread-dump-1.txt
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info

Run another Thread.print -l after a short diagnostic interval. -l includes ownable synchronizer information. jcmd <pid> help shows commands supported by that exact JDK.

Look for:

  • BLOCKED threads waiting to enter monitors;
  • WAITING or TIMED_WAITING threads parked on locks, futures, queues, or conditions;
  • locked objects and waiting to lock object IDs;
  • the thread that owns each required lock;
  • repeated stacks across dumps;
  • executor workers waiting on child futures; and
  • a deadlock report emitted by the JVM at the end of a thread dump.

Thread state alone is not guilt. Healthy idle workers are often WAITING. Build the ownership chain.

docs.title: Step 3: draw the wait-for graph
docs.text:
thread transfer-a -> waits for Account B -> held by transfer-b
thread transfer-b -> waits for Account A -> held by transfer-a

A cycle is evidence of deadlock. A long chain without a cycle may be contention, slow I/O under a lock, or starvation.

docs.title: Step 4: record JFR
docs.text:
Use settings, duration, and filenames approved for the environment:

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=liveness settings=profile duration=120s \
  filename=/safe/path/liveness.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.check

Inspect Java monitor blocked events, thread park events, socket/file I/O, CPU samples, allocation pressure, and virtual-thread events available in the deployed JDK. JFR event names and virtual-thread diagnostics vary by JDK release. Verify with the exact runtime and Mission Control version.

Continuous JFR with conservative settings often provides better pre-incident context than starting a recording after saturation. Protect recordings because they may contain class, thread, path, or application data.

docs.title: Step 5: repair the design
docs.text: Do not stop at changing a timeout. Determine whether the root cause is lock order, I/O under lock, nested executor dependence, missing admission control, an unbounded retry loop, or cancellation that cannot reach the blocked operation. Add a regression test for the progress property.

docs.title: 6. Making races reproducible
docs.text: Thread.sleep does not establish a happens-before relationship and does not prove another thread reached a line. It creates slow, flaky tests.

docs.title: Broken race test
docs.text:
executor.submit(counter::increment);
Thread.sleep(50);
assertEquals(1, counter.get());

docs.title: Corrected completion test
docs.text:
Future<?> completion = executor.submit(counter::increment);
completion.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
assertEquals(1, counter.get());

To expose a particular interleaving, add gates to a test seam.

public final class TransferProbe {
    private final CountDownLatch firstLockHeld = new CountDownLatch(2);
    private final CountDownLatch continueToSecond = new CountDownLatch(1);

    public void afterFirstLock() throws InterruptedException {
        firstLockHeld.countDown();
        continueToSecond.await();
    }

    public boolean bothAtBoundary(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException {
        return firstLockHeld.await(timeout.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
    }

    public void release() {
        continueToSecond.countDown();
    }
}

The gate belongs in injected test instrumentation, not in production synchronization. A test timeout is still needed so a defect fails the suite instead of hanging it.

docs.title: Useful deterministic primitives
docs.text:
• CountDownLatch: one-shot event or start gate;
  • CyclicBarrier: repeated rendezvous among a fixed party count;
  • Phaser: phased coordination with dynamic parties;
  • Semaphore: control when an operation may enter;
  • Future.get(timeout): observe completion with a test bound; and
  • controllable fakes: hold dependency completion until the test releases it.

docs.title: 7. A deterministic deadlock-repair test
docs.text:
The corrected transfer should complete opposite-direction operations and preserve total value.

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

final class TransfersTest {
    @Test
    void oppositeTransfersCompleteAndPreserveMoney() throws Exception {
        Account left = new Account(1, 1_000);
        Account right = new Account(2, 1_000);
        CyclicBarrier start = new CyclicBarrier(3);

        try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
            Future<?> one = executor.submit(() -> {
                await(start);
                Transfers.transfer(left, right, 100);
            });
            Future<?> two = executor.submit(() -> {
                await(start);
                Transfers.transfer(right, left, 200);
            });

            start.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            assertTimeoutPreemptively(Duration.ofSeconds(1), () -> {
                one.get(900, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
                two.get(900, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            });
        }

        assertEquals(2_000, left.balance() + right.balance());
        assertEquals(1_100, left.balance());
        assertEquals(900, right.balance());
    }

    private static void await(CyclicBarrier barrier) {
        try {
            barrier.await();
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            throw new CancellationException("test worker interrupted");
        } catch (BrokenBarrierException broken) {
            throw new AssertionError(broken);
        }
    }
}

assertTimeoutPreemptively runs its body on a different thread and interrupts it on timeout. Avoid it around code that depends on test-thread ThreadLocal state or performs non-rollbackable external effects. Plain timed Future.get is often enough.

This test demonstrates completion for one controlled start, not mathematical deadlock freedom. The argument for freedom comes from the global order; repeated and stress tests defend the implementation.

If the transfer regresses to monitor deadlock, executor close() can hang after the timed assertion. Interruption cannot break monitor acquisition. Run deliberately deadlocking variants in a child JVM with an external timeout; neither Future.get(timeout) nor JUnit preemptive interruption can forcibly stop those workers. Account setters in these sketches must be non-throwing after validation, and pair snapshots must hold both account locks.

docs.title: 8. Stress testing
docs.text:
A stress test repeats many operations across many threads and checks invariants after coordinated completion. It increases the probability of harmful interleavings but cannot prove their absence.

@Test
void concurrentTransfersPreserveTotalAndNonNegativeBalances() throws Exception {
    int accountCount = 16;
    Account[] accounts = IntStream.range(0, accountCount)
            .mapToObj(id -> new Account(id, 10_000))
            .toArray(Account[]::new);
    long expectedTotal = 160_000;
    int workers = 8;
    int operationsPerWorker = 20_000;
    CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);

    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers)) {
        List<? extends Future<?>> futures = IntStream.range(0, workers)
                .mapToObj(worker -> executor.submit(() -> {
                    SplittableRandom random = new SplittableRandom(worker);
                    start.await();
                    for (int i = 0; i < operationsPerWorker; i++) {
                        Account from = accounts[random.nextInt(accountCount)];
                        Account to = accounts[random.nextInt(accountCount)];
                        if (from != to) {
                            try {
                                Transfers.transfer(from, to, 1);
                            } catch (InsufficientFundsException allowed) {
                                // Rejection preserves state.
                            }
                        }
                    }
                    return null;
                }))
                .toList();
        start.countDown();
        for (Future<?> future : futures) {
            future.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        }
    }

    assertEquals(expectedTotal,
            Arrays.stream(accounts).mapToLong(Account::balance).sum());
    assertTrue(Arrays.stream(accounts).allMatch(account -> account.balance() >= 0));
}

Use several deterministic seeds in normal CI and broader randomized seeds in a dedicated stress job. Record the seed on failure. Avoid adding logging in hot race windows because it changes scheduling.

docs.title: 9. JCStress overview
docs.text:
JCStress is the OpenJDK concurrency stress harness for testing outcomes under the Java Memory Model. It repeatedly runs small actor methods under varied generated conditions and classifies observed outcomes.

A conceptual lost-update test is:

@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "2", expect = Expect.ACCEPTABLE, desc = "Both increments visible")
@Outcome(id = "1", expect = Expect.FORBIDDEN, desc = "Lost update")
@State
public class AtomicIncrementStress {
    private final AtomicInteger value = new AtomicInteger();

    @Actor
    public void actor1() {
        value.incrementAndGet();
    }

    @Actor
    public void actor2() {
        value.incrementAndGet();
    }

    @Arbiter
    public void observe(I_Result result) {
        result.r1 = value.get();
    }
}

Use the JCStress Maven archetype/plugin and version compatible with the target JDK; annotations and result-holder imports come from the harness. Do not run a JCStress test as an ordinary JUnit test.

JCStress is strong for small memory-model litmus tests: publication, reordering, atomicity, and allowed outcomes. It does not prove a large service linearizable, validate remote side effects, or replace lifecycle and load tests.

docs.title: 10. Linearizability and invariant testing
docs.text:
An invariant constrains valid states. Linearizability additionally requires each concurrent operation to appear atomic at one point between invocation and response, while respecting real-time order.

For a bounded counter:

  • invariant: 0 <= value <= limit;
  • successful increment linearizes at the winning compare-and-set;
  • rejected increment linearizes at the read/CAS attempt that establishes the limit;
  • history records invocation, response, arguments, result, and operation ID.

docs.title: History record
docs.text:
record Event(long operationId, String phase, String operation,
             int argument, Object result, long sequence) {}

Use an AtomicLong sequence only to capture recorder order; do not mistake it for the data structure's linearization order. A checker searches for a legal sequential history that respects observed results and the real-time precedence of non-overlapping calls.

For small histories, exhaustive backtracking is practical:

  1. collect invocation and response events; for this simple checker, require all invocations to have completed;
  2. derive happens-before constraints from response-before-invocation;
  3. choose an operation whose predecessors are already chosen;
  4. apply it to a simple reference model;
  5. reject branches whose model result differs; and
  6. succeed if one complete legal order exists.

If a captured history has pending operations, do not simply discard them: a pending write may explain a completed read. A full checker considers legal completions of some pending calls and removal of the others under the linearizability definition. Keep histories small because the search can grow factorially. Use model-based random command generation and shrink failing histories. Invariant checks are cheaper and scale farther, but may miss a non-linearizable history whose final state is valid.

docs.title: 11. Shutdown and thread-leak tests
docs.text:
Lifecycle tests need positive evidence that admission stops, queued work is handled by policy, running work sees cancellation, and owned threads terminate.

@Test
void closeInterruptsBlockedWorkerAndLeavesNoOwnedThread() throws Exception {
    String prefix = "shipment-worker-test-";
    CountDownLatch started = new CountDownLatch(1);
    CountDownLatch interrupted = new CountDownLatch(1);
    ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(
            Thread.ofPlatform().name(prefix, 0).factory());

    executor.submit(() -> {
        started.countDown();
        try {
            new CountDownLatch(1).await();
        } catch (InterruptedException expected) {
            interrupted.countDown();
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    });

    assertTrue(started.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
    executor.shutdown();
    if (!executor.awaitTermination(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        executor.shutdownNow();
    }
    assertTrue(interrupted.await(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
    assertTrue(executor.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
    assertTrue(Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream()
            .noneMatch(thread -> thread.isAlive() && thread.getName().startsWith(prefix)));
}

The 50 ms grace period is policy input, not a claim that work should finish in 50 ms. The assertions depend on latches and termination. Use unique prefixes to avoid confusing unrelated threads. For virtual threads, thread enumeration APIs and observability differ; assert executor termination and component-owned task completion rather than relying only on global enumeration.

Also test:

  • rejection after shutdown begins;
  • repeated close if idempotence is promised;
  • shutdown while the queue is full;
  • task that restores interrupt status;
  • task that ignores interruption, to verify bounded close behavior;
  • scheduled-task cancellation; and
  • resource closure only after workers stop using the resource.

docs.title: 12. A reusable race harness
docs.text:
This harness starts actors together, stores actor failures in futures, and applies a completion bound. It propagates the first failure encountered while joining; it does not aggregate every concurrent failure.

public final class ConcurrentHarness {
    private ConcurrentHarness() {}

    public static void run(List<? extends Runnable> actors, Duration timeout)
            throws Exception {
        if (timeout.isNegative()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        }
        if (actors.isEmpty()) return;
        long budgetNanos = saturatedNanos(timeout);
        long startedNanos = System.nanoTime();
        CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(actors.size());
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(actors.size(),
                Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("race-actor-", 0).factory());
        try {
            List<? extends Future<?>> futures = actors.stream()
                    .map(actor -> executor.submit(() -> {
                        ready.countDown();
                        start.await();
                        actor.run();
                        return null;
                    }))
                    .toList();

            if (!ready.await(remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos),
                    TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
                throw new TimeoutException("actors did not become ready");
            }
            start.countDown();
            for (Future<?> future : futures) {
                long remaining = remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos);
                future.get(remaining, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
            }
        } finally {
            start.countDown();
            executor.shutdownNow();
            if (!executor.awaitTermination(
                    budgetNanos,
                    TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
                throw new AssertionError("test actors leaked");
            }
        }
    }

    private static long saturatedNanos(Duration timeout) {
        try {
            return timeout.toNanos();
        } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            return Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
    }

    private static long remainingNanos(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
        long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
        return elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
                : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
    }
}

One overflow-safe elapsed-time budget bounds readiness and every get rather than granting each phase a fresh timeout. Cleanup gets a separate bounded termination allowance so an operation timeout does not skip leak detection. Future.get surfaces actor exceptions. This harness coordinates starts; it does not force an exact operation-level interleaving. Use injected gates for that.

Daemon actors prevent a leaked test worker from keeping a child JVM alive; they do not make continuing in the same JVM safe after a leak. Run hostile actors in an isolated process and terminate it on timeout. Cleanup failure may mask the original actor exception in this compact harness; retain both as suppressed causes in a diagnostic runner.

docs.title: 13. Tradeoffs
docs.text: Technique Strength Limitation Global lock order Simple proof against order-cycle deadlock Every code path must follow the same stable order Timed tryLock Bounded waiting and cancellation opportunity Rollback and retry can cause livelock Fair lock Reduces barging Lower throughput; no strict timing guarantee Thread dump Low-cost lock and stack snapshot Transient races may disappear between samples JFR Time-correlated production evidence Requires event knowledge, storage, and privacy controls Deterministic gate Reproduces a chosen boundary Instrumentation can perturb behavior Stress test Explores many schedules Passing does not prove correctness JCStress Tests JMM outcomes rigorously Best for small state machines, not whole services Linearizability checker Validates observable histories Search cost and modeling complexity

docs.title: Exercise 1: repair two-lock update
docs.text:
Two objects have unique immutable string IDs. Write a helper that acquires their ReentrantLock values in one global order and runs an update. It must handle the same object.

Solution 
static void withBoth(Node left, Node right, Runnable update) {
    Objects.requireNonNull(left);
    Objects.requireNonNull(right);
    Objects.requireNonNull(update);
    if (left == right) {
        left.lock().lock();
        try {
            update.run();
        } finally {
            left.lock().unlock();
        }
        return;
    }

    Node first = left.id().compareTo(right.id()) < 0 ? left : right;
    Node second = first == left ? right : left;
    first.lock().lock();
    try {
        second.lock().lock();
        try {
            update.run();
        } finally {
            second.lock().unlock();
        }
    } finally {
        first.lock().unlock();
    }
}

Unique IDs make the order total. If IDs were not unique, equal IDs for distinct nodes would need a tie-break mechanism.

docs.title: Exercise 2: test a lost update without sleep
docs.text:
Create two actors that start together, each increments a thread-safe counter 10,000 times, and assert completion and final value.

Solution 
@Test
void atomicCounterDoesNotLoseUpdates() throws Exception {
    AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
    int increments = 10_000;
    Runnable actor = () -> {
        for (int i = 0; i < increments; i++) {
            counter.incrementAndGet();
        }
    };

    ConcurrentHarness.run(List.of(actor, actor), Duration.ofSeconds(2));
    assertEquals(2 * increments, counter.get());
}

The harness supplies simultaneous release, exception propagation, and bounded completion. Repeating this against a plain int may reveal a race but cannot prove it on every run.

docs.title: Exercise 3: diagnose a dump
docs.text:
Thread A owns lock X and waits for Y. Thread B owns Y and waits for X. Thread C is parked on an empty executor queue. Which thread is part of the deadlock, and what evidence should be captured before restart?

Solution

A and B form the lock-ownership cycle and are deadlocked. C is likely an idle worker and is not implicated merely because it is WAITING. Capture multiple jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l dumps, relevant metrics and queue depths, runtime flags and command line, and a bounded JFR recording if operationally safe. Preserve object IDs, owner names, and full stack frames that establish both edges of the cycle.

docs.title: Exercise 4: state a completion contract
docs.text:
Define terminal outcomes for a cancellable queued command.

Solution

An admitted command reaches exactly one caller-visible terminal outcome: success, application failure, or cancellation. Cancellation before execution prevents its body from starting when cancellation wins. Cancellation after start requests cooperative termination and may race with normal completion. A timeout while waiting is not itself proof of cancellation. Rejection occurs before admission and is not a command completion. External side effects require idempotency because local cancellation cannot roll them back automatically.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Calling every long wait a deadlock without finding a cycle.
  • Treating WAITING as inherently unhealthy.
  • Repairing deadlock with retries that create livelock.
  • Ordering locks by a mutable field or a non-unique hash.
  • Using a fresh timeout for every acquisition or future wait.
  • Writing sleep-based assertions.
  • Checking only final state when operation histories may be non-linearizable.
  • Assuming one successful stress run proves thread safety.
  • Ignoring exceptions thrown inside worker futures.
  • Testing shutdown without asserting owned threads or tasks terminate.
  • Relying on thread priorities for correctness.

docs.title: Questions to practice
docs.text:
1. Draw the wait-for graph for a three-lock cycle and break it by design.
  2. When is tryLock preferable to global ordering, and how do you avoid livelock?
  3. How do starvation and priority inversion differ from deadlock?
  4. What would you inspect in three consecutive thread dumps?
  5. Which JFR events would help distinguish CPU spin, monitor contention, and blocked I/O?
  6. How do deterministic gates change the probability of reproducing a race?
  7. State a linearization point for a CAS counter, a lock-based transfer, and a rejected queue offer.
  8. What can JCStress establish that a JUnit loop usually cannot?
  9. How do you prove shutdown is bounded when a task ignores interruption?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Liveness failures differ: find cycles, activity, service denial, or priority dependencies.
  • Global lock ordering provides a clean deadlock-freedom argument when the order is total and universal.
  • Timed acquisition needs one deadline, complete rollback, and bounded retry.
  • Diagnose from repeated thread dumps, ownership chains, metrics, and JFR evidence.
  • Coordinate tests with latches, barriers, futures, and controllable fakes, not sleeps.
  • Stress and invariant tests find bugs but do not prove linearizability.
  • JCStress targets small Java Memory Model outcomes; history checking targets observable atomic behavior.
  • Shutdown tests must verify rejection, cancellation policy, termination, and resource order.

Previous: Async, Parallelism, and Virtual Threads | Next: Concurrency Patterns

docs.title: 10. Concurrency Patterns
docs.text: Concurrency patterns are reusable answers to recurring ownership, coordination, and shutdown problems. The interview skill is not naming a pattern. It is choosing the smallest library-backed mechanism whose correctness argument fits the requirements.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • map a requirement to an ownership and synchronization strategy;
  • state shared state, invariants, and linearization points before writing code;
  • compare blocking, lock-free reads, partitioned locking, and message passing;
  • reason about contention, starvation, interruption, cancellation, and shutdown;
  • test protocols with barriers and controlled dependencies rather than sleeps; and
  • recognize when a custom concurrency primitive is an unnecessary risk.

docs.title: The interview framework
docs.text:
Use SCALE for every concurrent component:

  1. S - State: Which fields are shared? Who may mutate them?
  2. C - Contract: What must always be true? What may block or fail?
  3. A - Atomic event: At which instruction does each operation logically occur?
  4. L - Liveness: Can callers deadlock, starve, or wait forever? How does cancellation propagate?
  5. E - Evidence: Which deterministic test forces each important interleaving?
Requirement Prefer Avoid by default Bounded handoff with backpressure BlockingQueue hand-written wait/notify queue Many reads, occasional whole-state update immutable snapshot + atomic publication locking every getter One owner per mutable object actor-style mailbox or confinement sharing internals across workers Independent keys with hot-key risk striping or ConcurrentHashMap one global lock Duplicate expensive requests memoization/single-flight check-then-act around a plain map Cooperative service shutdown two-phase termination Thread.stop, swallowed interrupts Irregular CPU work ForkJoinPool blocking I/O inside common pool tasks

docs.title: 1. Producer-consumer
docs.text:
A producer-consumer pipeline separates submission rate from processing rate. A bounded queue is usually part of the correctness contract: it limits retained work and turns overload into backpressure.

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;
import java.util.function.Consumer;
import java.util.Objects;

public final class BoundedWorker<T> implements AutoCloseable {
    private final BlockingQueue<T> queue;
    private final Consumer<T> handler;
    private final Consumer<? super Throwable> failureReporter;
    private final AtomicBoolean accepting = new AtomicBoolean(true);
    private final List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>();
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock lifecycle = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

    public BoundedWorker(int capacity, int workerCount, Consumer<T> handler,
                         Consumer<? super Throwable> failureReporter) {
        if (capacity <= 0 || workerCount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        this.queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(capacity);
        this.handler = Objects.requireNonNull(handler, "handler");
        this.failureReporter = Objects.requireNonNull(failureReporter, "failureReporter");
        for (int i = 0; i < workerCount; i++) {
            Thread worker = Thread.ofPlatform().name("bounded-worker-" + i).start(this::run);
            workers.add(worker);
        }
    }

    public boolean submit(T item, Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException {
        Objects.requireNonNull(item, "item");
        Objects.requireNonNull(timeout, "timeout");
        if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        long budgetNanos = saturatedNanos(timeout);
        long startedNanos = System.nanoTime();
        if (!lifecycle.readLock().tryLock(
                budgetNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return false;
        try {
            if (!accepting.get()) return false;
            return queue.offer(item,
                    remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos),
                    TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        } finally {
            lifecycle.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    private void run() {
        try {
            while (accepting.get() || !queue.isEmpty()) {
                T item = queue.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
                if (item != null) {
                    try {
                        handler.accept(item);
                    } catch (Throwable failure) {
                        reportFailure(failure);
                    }
                }
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    private void reportFailure(Throwable failure) {
        try {
            failureReporter.accept(failure);
        } catch (Throwable reportingFailure) {
            if (reportingFailure != failure) {
                failure.addSuppressed(reportingFailure);
            }
            failure.printStackTrace();
        }
    }

    private static long saturatedNanos(Duration timeout) {
        try {
            return timeout.toNanos();
        } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            return Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
    }

    private static long remainingNanos(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
        long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
        return elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
                : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
    }

    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        lifecycle.writeLock().lockInterruptibly();
        try { accepting.set(false); }
        finally { lifecycle.writeLock().unlock(); }
        for (Thread worker : workers) worker.join();
    }
}
  • Shared state: queue contents and accepting.
  • Invariant: queue size is in [0, capacity]; accepted items are either queued or handed to one consumer. This implementation is at-most-once after process failure, not durable delivery.
  • Linearization: successful offer; queue removal inside poll; shutdown begins at accepting.set(false) under the lifecycle write lock.
  • Cost/contention: O(1) queue operations; producers and consumers contend on queue coordination. A small capacity rejects bursts; a large one increases memory and stale work.
  • Liveness: one timeout covers lifecycle-lock acquisition and queue admission. The lifecycle lock makes admission atomic with respect to closing; close then drains accepted work. A blocked handler can still delay shutdown, so a production API should offer a bounded close and forced-stop policy.
  • Failure policy: a handler failure is reported and contained at the item boundary, so one bad item cannot silently kill a worker and strand accepted queue entries. Even a broken reporter is contained with a last-resort uncaught-style print; production code should route this fallback to service health telemetry.
  • Deterministic test: block the handler on a latch, fill the queue, assert a timed third submission fails, release the latch, close, and assert all accepted items ran exactly once. Also submit a throwing handler item and assert its failure is reported while a later item still runs.

docs.title: 2. Guarded suspension
docs.text:
An operation waits until a predicate over shared state becomes true. Always test the predicate in a loop: signals are hints, and another thread may consume the condition first.

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public final class OneShotGate<T> {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition completed = lock.newCondition();
    private boolean done;
    private T value;

    public void complete(T result) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            if (done) throw new IllegalStateException("already completed");
            value = result;
            done = true;
            completed.signalAll();
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    public T await(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException {
        if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        long budgetNanos = saturatedNanos(timeout);
        long startedNanos = System.nanoTime();
        if (!lock.tryLock(budgetNanos, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("timed out");
        }
        try {
            while (!done) {
                long remaining = remainingNanos(startedNanos, budgetNanos);
                if (remaining == 0L) throw new IllegalStateException("timed out");
                completed.awaitNanos(remaining);
            }
            return value;
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    private static long saturatedNanos(Duration timeout) {
        try {
            return timeout.toNanos();
        } catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            return Long.MAX_VALUE;
        }
    }

    private static long remainingNanos(long startedNanos, long budgetNanos) {
        long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - startedNanos;
        return elapsed <= 0L ? budgetNanos
                : elapsed >= budgetNanos ? 0L : budgetNanos - elapsed;
    }
}
  • Invariant: done == false implies no observable result; done == true never becomes false.
  • Linearization: completion occurs when done becomes true while holding the lock; a completed read occurs while observing that state under the same lock.
  • Liveness: one overflow-safe elapsed-time budget bounds interruptible lock acquisition and condition waiting. signalAll is correct when several waiters need the one-shot result.
  • Tradeoff: CompletableFuture<T> already implements this one-shot protocol and should normally replace this educational class.

docs.title: 3. Reader-writer locking
docs.text:
Use a reader-writer lock only when reads are frequent, read-side work is long enough to amortize lock overhead, and concurrent reads materially improve throughput.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;

public final class ReadMostlyCatalog {
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true);
    private final Map<String, String> values = new HashMap<>();

    public String get(String key) {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try { return values.get(key); }
        finally { lock.readLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public void put(String key, String value) {
        java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(key);
        java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(value);
        lock.writeLock().lock();
        try { values.put(key, value); }
        finally { lock.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }

    public Map<String, String> snapshot() {
        lock.readLock().lock();
        try { return Map.copyOf(values); }
        finally { lock.readLock().unlock(); }
    }
}
  • Invariant: every map mutation holds the write lock; returned snapshots cannot mutate the catalog.
  • Linearization: Map.get under the read lock and Map.put under the write lock.
  • Contention: get and put are O(1) average; copying a snapshot is O(n) and keeps the read lock for that copy. A writer excludes all readers. Fair mode reduces starvation risk and usually reduces throughput.
  • Trap: Java's ReentrantReadWriteLock does not support safe read-to-write upgrade. Release the read lock and revalidate under the write lock.

docs.title: 4. Immutable snapshot
docs.text:
If readers need a coherent whole-state view, publish a new immutable value atomically. Readers perform no locking and never observe a partially updated configuration.

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;
import java.util.function.UnaryOperator;

public final class RoutingTable {
    public record Snapshot(long version, Map<String, String> routes) {
        public Snapshot { routes = Map.copyOf(routes); }
    }

    private final AtomicReference<Snapshot> current =
            new AtomicReference<>(new Snapshot(0, Map.of()));

    public Snapshot current() { return current.get(); }

    public Snapshot update(UnaryOperator<Map<String, String>> change) {
        while (true) {
            Snapshot before = current.get();
            Snapshot after = new Snapshot(Math.incrementExact(before.version()), change.apply(before.routes()));
            if (current.compareAndSet(before, after)) return after;
        }
    }
}
  • Invariant: a snapshot's map never changes; versions increase by one per successful publication.
  • Linearization: successful compareAndSet.
  • Cost/contention: reads are O(1); writes copy affected state and may retry. The updater must be side-effect-free because CAS retries can invoke it repeatedly.
  • Use when: state is modest, reads dominate, and cross-field consistency matters. Avoid for huge, frequently rewritten maps.

docs.title: 5. Thread confinement and actor-style ownership
docs.text:
One thread owns mutable state. Other threads submit messages and receive futures. This replaces data races with queue ordering, but does not make multi-actor workflows atomic.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;

public final class AccountActor implements AutoCloseable {
    private final ExecutorService mailbox = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
    private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>();

    public CompletableFuture<Long> add(String account, long delta) {
        CompletableFuture<Long> reply = new CompletableFuture<>();
        mailbox.execute(() -> {
            try {
                long next = Math.addExact(balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L), delta);
                if (next < 0) throw new IllegalStateException("negative balance");
                balances.put(account, next);
                reply.complete(next);
            } catch (Throwable failure) {
                reply.completeExceptionally(failure);
            }
        });
        return reply;
    }

    @Override public void close() { mailbox.close(); }
}
  • Invariant: only the mailbox thread touches balances; balances are non-negative.
  • Linearization: mutation in the mailbox task, not task submission or future completion.
  • Cost/contention: O(1) average operations; no lock contention inside the actor, but one mailbox is a serial bottleneck. Partition actors by stable key to scale.
  • Shutdown: ExecutorService.close() waits for orderly termination in Java 21. Define admission behavior during closure and bound waits at the application boundary.

Cancelling or completing the returned CompletableFuture does not retract the mailbox mutation. Submission after close throws synchronously. A callback attached to reply may execute inline on the mailbox worker, so it must not call blocking close() on that same mailbox. The unbounded mailbox and account map make this an ownership example, not a production capacity policy.

docs.title: 6. Striped locking
docs.text:
Striping maps many keys onto a fixed number of locks. It bounds lock memory while allowing unrelated stripes to proceed concurrently.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public final class StripedCounter<K> {
    private final ReentrantLock[] locks;
    private final Map<K, Long>[] maps;

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public StripedCounter(int stripes) {
        if (stripes <= 0 || Integer.bitCount(stripes) != 1)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("positive power of two");
        locks = new ReentrantLock[stripes];
        maps = (Map<K, Long>[]) new Map<?, ?>[stripes];
        for (int i = 0; i < stripes; i++) {
            locks[i] = new ReentrantLock();
            maps[i] = new HashMap<>();
        }
    }

    public long add(K key, long delta) {
        int stripe = spread(key.hashCode()) & (locks.length - 1);
        locks[stripe].lock();
        try {
            long next = Math.addExact(maps[stripe].getOrDefault(key, 0L), delta);
            maps[stripe].put(key, next);
            return next;
        } finally { locks[stripe].unlock(); }
    }

    private static int spread(int hash) { return hash ^ (hash >>> 16); }
}
  • Invariant: keys retain stable equality and hash codes, so a key always maps to one stripe; that stripe's map is accessed only under its lock.
  • Linearization: map update while holding the stripe lock.
  • Complexity: O(1) average and O(stripes + keys) memory. Colliding hot keys serialize. Resizing the stripe array would change ownership and requires global coordination.
  • Multi-key operations: acquire distinct stripe locks in ascending index order, deduplicate equal stripes, and release in reverse order to avoid deadlock.

docs.title: 7. Memoization and single-flight
docs.text:
Memoization reuses completed results. Single-flight additionally ensures concurrent requests for one key share one in-flight computation.

import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.function.Function;

public final class SingleFlight<K, V> {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> flights = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public CompletableFuture<V> execute(K key, Function<K, V> loader) {
        CompletableFuture<V> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
        CompletableFuture<V> existing = flights.putIfAbsent(key, mine);
        if (existing != null) return existing.copy();

        try {
            Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
                try { mine.complete(loader.apply(key)); }
                catch (Throwable failure) { mine.completeExceptionally(failure); }
                finally { flights.remove(key, mine); }
            });
        } catch (RuntimeException | Error failure) {
            mine.completeExceptionally(failure);
            flights.remove(key, mine);
            throw failure;
        }
        return mine.copy();
    }
}
  • Invariant: at most one mapped future exists per key; only its elected owner invokes the loader.
  • Linearization: putIfAbsent elects the owner. Removal uses (key, value) so an old completion cannot remove a newer flight.
  • Semantics: this deduplicates only overlapping calls; it is not a cache. Dependent copies isolate caller cancellation/completion from the root. Loader lifetime, distinct-key admission, and shutdown remain unbounded; a stronger service owns an executor and retains cancellation handles. Completion callbacks can run inline before root removal, so recursive same-key loads must not block awaiting themselves.
  • Test: hold the loader on a latch, issue 100 same-key calls, assert one invocation, release, and compare every result.

docs.title: 8. Balking
docs.text:
Balking rejects an operation when the object is not in a state where the operation makes sense. It does not wait for the state to change.

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

public final class StartOnceService {
    enum State { NEW, RUNNING, STOPPED }
    private final AtomicReference<State> state = new AtomicReference<>(State.NEW);

    public boolean start() {
        if (!state.compareAndSet(State.NEW, State.RUNNING)) return false;
        // Publish or launch resources only for the elected starter.
        return true;
    }

    public boolean stop() {
        return state.compareAndSet(State.RUNNING, State.STOPPED);
    }

    public State state() { return state.get(); }
}
  • Invariant: legal transitions are NEW -> RUNNING -> STOPPED; no restart.
  • Linearization: successful CAS.
  • Tradeoff: a boolean result is suitable for an expected duplicate command. Throw when the state indicates caller misuse. If startup can fail after the CAS, add a STARTING state and explicit rollback/failure semantics.

docs.title: 9. Two-phase termination
docs.text:
First request stop; then let the worker observe that request, clean up, and terminate. Interruption is a wake-up/cancellation signal, not a substitute for state.

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;

public final class PollingService implements AutoCloseable {
    private final AtomicBoolean stopping = new AtomicBoolean();
    private final CountDownLatch terminated = new CountDownLatch(1);
    private final Thread worker;

    public PollingService(Runnable pollOnce) {
        worker = Thread.ofPlatform().name("polling-service").start(() -> {
            try {
                while (!stopping.get()) pollOnce.run();
            } finally {
                terminated.countDown();
            }
        });
    }

    public boolean stop(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException {
        if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        long nanos;
        try { nanos = timeout.toNanos(); }
        catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) { nanos = Long.MAX_VALUE; }
        stopping.set(true);
        worker.interrupt();
        return terminated.await(nanos, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
    }

    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        if (!stop(Duration.ofSeconds(10))) throw new IllegalStateException("shutdown timed out");
    }
}
  • Invariant: the latch announces that the poll loop has exited and reached its final cleanup, not that the Java thread has terminated. An uncaught-exception handler may still run afterward.
  • Linearization: stop is requested when stopping becomes true; successful latch waiting publishes actions before countDown. Use join as well if the contract requires actual thread termination.
  • Caveat: pollOnce must cooperate with interruption or return regularly. Preserve interrupt status when catching InterruptedException at a layer that cannot complete cancellation.

docs.title: 10. Work stealing
docs.text:
Work stealing gives each worker a deque. Idle workers steal tasks from others, which balances irregular recursive work with less contention than one central queue. Java's ForkJoinPool implements this strategy.

import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask;

public final class ParallelSum extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    private final long[] values;
    private final int from;
    private final int to;

    public ParallelSum(long[] values, int from, int to) {
        this.values = values;
        this.from = from;
        this.to = to;
    }

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += values[i];
            return sum;
        }
        int middle = (from + to) >>> 1;
        ParallelSum left = new ParallelSum(values, from, middle);
        left.fork();
        long right = new ParallelSum(values, middle, to).compute();
        return right + left.join();
    }

    public static long sum(long[] values, int parallelism) {
        try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(parallelism)) {
            return pool.invoke(new ParallelSum(values, 0, values.length));
        }
    }
}
  • Invariant: leaf ranges are disjoint and cover [0, values.length) exactly once.
  • Linearization: a pure aggregate has no shared-state update; invoke completion publishes the result.
  • Complexity: O(n) work, O(log n) span for balanced splits, plus task overhead. Tune the threshold from measurements.
  • Liveness: do not perform unmanaged blocking I/O in fork/join tasks. Use virtual threads for blocking request-style work or managedBlock for exceptional cases.
