docs.title: When not to create a custom concurrency primitive
docs.text:
Do not build a lock, semaphore, future, queue, executor, scheduler, or barrier in an interview solution unless implementing that primitive is the problem.

Prefer a JDK primitive when it already provides:

  • a documented Java Memory Model happens-before relationship;
  • interruption and timeout behavior;
  • protection against spurious wakeups and lost notifications;
  • years of race, overflow, and cancellation fixes; and
  • operationally familiar behavior.

A custom abstraction can be justified when the policy is domain-specific, such as per-tenant admission or dependency scheduling. Build that policy on java.util.concurrent; do not recreate its mechanism. If requirements include fairness, reentrancy, condition queues, lock-free progress, or recovery after owner death, explicitly narrow scope rather than casually promising them.

docs.title: Deterministic testing checklist
docs.text:
• Inject executors, clocks, loaders, and blocking dependencies.
  • Use CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, or Phaser to establish a known interleaving.
  • Assert externally visible state and invariants, not thread names or incidental timing.
  • Give every blocking assertion a deadline so a failure terminates.
  • Repeat stress tests as additional evidence, not as the only proof.
  • Test interruption before waiting, during waiting, and during shutdown.
  • Test admission racing with shutdown.
  • Test exceptions at the point where ownership has changed.
  • Run static analyzers and race-oriented tools where available, but retain a written correctness argument.

docs.title: Interview follow-ups
docs.text:
1. How would queue capacity follow from service time, memory budget, and latency SLO?
  2. When does StampedLock optimistic reading help, and what validation is mandatory?
  3. How would you prevent one hot actor or stripe from monopolizing capacity?
  4. Should single-flight cache failures? How do retry storms change the answer?
  5. What happens when an updater passed to a CAS loop has a side effect?
  6. How would you make two-phase termination drain accepted work without accepting new work?
  7. Why can a fair lock reduce throughput?
  8. How do virtual threads change thread-per-task economics without removing data races?
  9. Which operations in your design are linearizable, and which offer only eventual observation?
  10. What evidence would convince you that a custom primitive is necessary?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Start with ownership and invariants, then select synchronization.
  • Bounded queues encode backpressure; unbounded queues hide overload.
  • Immutable publication and confinement often remove more races than intricate locking.
  • Striping improves independent-key concurrency but needs lock ordering for multi-key work.
  • Single-flight coordinates in-flight work; it is not automatically a cache.
  • Liveness, cancellation, and shutdown are API semantics, not cleanup details.
  • Prefer JDK concurrency primitives and keep custom code at the policy layer.

docs.title: 11. Classic Concurrency Problems: Solved Workbook
docs.text: These exercises are protocol-design drills. For each one, say what may happen next, encode that rule with a standard primitive, and identify the state transition that makes an operation take effect.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• translate output-order and resource constraints into explicit invariants;
  • produce complete Java 21 solutions with interruption and termination behavior;
  • compare semaphores, conditions, barriers, and fork/join decomposition;
  • identify linearization points and contention costs; and
  • design deterministic tests that do not rely on arbitrary sleeps.

docs.title: Workbook framework
docs.text: For each prompt use SCALE: shared State, correctness Contract, Atomic event, Liveness, and test Evidence. Unless stated otherwise, callbacks must return normally, remain short, and not re-enter the coordinator. A propagated failure stops only that caller, not its peers: the owner must observe failures promptly, cancel all peer tasks, and bound cleanup. These compact protocols are not reusable after partial failure unless explicitly stated.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Two threads share one object. One calls printLeft and the other calls printRight. Invoke the supplied callbacks in the sequence L R L R ... exactly rounds times. Do not busy-spin.

docs.title: Constraints and reasoning
docs.text:
• rounds >= 0; exactly one caller invokes each method.
  • A binary semaphore is a turn token. Initially the left side owns it.
  • Acquiring the next token before printing prevents duplicate turns; releasing transfers ownership.
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public final class Alternator {
    private final int rounds;
    private final Semaphore left = new Semaphore(1);
    private final Semaphore right = new Semaphore(0);

    public Alternator(int rounds) {
        if (rounds < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative rounds");
        this.rounds = rounds;
    }

    public void printLeft(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 0; i < rounds; i++) {
            left.acquire();
            output.run();
            right.release();
        }
    }

    public void printRight(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 0; i < rounds; i++) {
            right.acquire();
            output.run();
            left.release();
        }
    }
}
  • State/invariant: permit ownership alternates; total permits are one between callbacks. The output prefix is always a prefix of (LR)^rounds.
  • Linearization: successful acquisition claims a turn; callback completion followed by release hands it over.
  • Complexity/contention: O(rounds) work, O(1) state, one handoff per symbol.
  • Liveness/cancellation: interruption cancels a waiter, but can strand its peer. A reusable library component would share a failure flag and release both waiters.
  • Deterministic test: append callbacks to a synchronized buffer, launch right before left through an executor, join with a deadline, and assert the exact string.

Alternative: one ReentrantLock, one Condition per side, and a leftTurn boolean make lifecycle failure handling easier. Use while (!leftTurn) condition.await() and signal the opposite condition after toggling.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For positive n, three threads call zero, even, and odd. Produce 0 1 0 2 ... 0 n, using the supplied integer consumer.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

public final class ZeroEvenOdd {
    private final int n;
    private final Semaphore zeroTurn = new Semaphore(1);
    private final Semaphore oddTurn = new Semaphore(0);
    private final Semaphore evenTurn = new Semaphore(0);

    public ZeroEvenOdd(int n) {
        if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative n");
        this.n = n;
    }

    public void zero(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (long value = 1; value <= n; value++) {
            zeroTurn.acquire();
            output.accept(0);
            (value % 2 == 0 ? evenTurn : oddTurn).release();
        }
    }

    public void odd(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (long value = 1; value <= n; value += 2) {
            oddTurn.acquire();
            output.accept((int) value);
            zeroTurn.release();
        }
    }

    public void even(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        for (long value = 2; value <= n; value += 2) {
            evenTurn.acquire();
            output.accept((int) value);
            zeroTurn.release();
        }
    }
}
  • Invariant: after every nonzero value, zero owns the next permit; after zero, exactly the required parity owns one permit.
  • Linearization: each permit acquisition fixes the next output position.
  • Cost: O(n) output and handoffs, O(1) state. The protocol intentionally serializes output.
  • Shutdown: interrupt all three tasks if any callback fails. Do not swallow InterruptedException.
  • Test: submit the methods in every launch order for n values 0, 1, 2, and 101; collect under a lock and compare with a sequential oracle.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Four worker methods print numbers, fizz, buzz, or fizzbuzz for the range 1..n. Every value must produce exactly one output in numeric order.

docs.title: Reasoning and solution
docs.text:
The shared counter determines both eligibility and completion. One shared condition wakes waiters to recheck their individual predicates. Every waiter loops because a signal does not reserve the condition.

import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
import java.util.function.IntConsumer;

public final class ConcurrentFizzBuzz {
    private final int n;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition changed = lock.newCondition();
    private long current = 1;

    public ConcurrentFizzBuzz(int n) {
        if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative n");
        this.n = n;
    }

    public void fizz(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        runWhen(v -> v % 3 == 0 && v % 5 != 0, ignored -> output.run());
    }

    public void buzz(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        runWhen(v -> v % 5 == 0 && v % 3 != 0, ignored -> output.run());
    }

    public void fizzBuzz(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        runWhen(v -> v % 15 == 0, ignored -> output.run());
    }

    public void number(IntConsumer output) throws InterruptedException {
        runWhen(v -> v % 3 != 0 && v % 5 != 0, output);
    }

    private void runWhen(java.util.function.IntPredicate eligible, IntConsumer output)
            throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            lock.lockInterruptibly();
            try {
                while (current <= n && !eligible.test((int) current)) changed.await();
                if (current > n) {
                    changed.signalAll();
                    return;
                }
                output.accept((int) current);
                current++;
                changed.signalAll();
            } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        }
    }
}
  • Invariant: current is the smallest unprinted value; exactly one predicate matches each value.
  • Linearization: incrementing current after the callback.
  • Contention: O(n) work and broadcasts. Four dedicated conditions reduce wakeups but increase protocol code.
  • Race to discuss: callbacks run under the lock to preserve output order. Slow callbacks block all workers. A sequenced output sink or prepared result can move safe work outside the lock.
  • Test: use callbacks that append tokens; start all workers behind a barrier; compare with a sequential FizzBuzz list and enforce a deadline.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Hydrogen and oxygen threads arrive independently. Release callbacks in groups containing exactly two H callbacks and one O callback. Groups must not overlap. Order inside a group does not matter.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import java.util.concurrent.Phaser;

public final class H2O {
    private final Semaphore hydrogens = new Semaphore(2, true);
    private final Semaphore oxygens = new Semaphore(1, true);
    private final Object terminationLock = new Object();
    private volatile Throwable failure;
    private final Phaser molecule = new Phaser(3);

    public void hydrogen(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        participate(hydrogens, output);
    }

    public void oxygen(Runnable output) throws InterruptedException {
        participate(oxygens, output);
    }

    private void participate(Semaphore slots, Runnable output)
            throws InterruptedException {
        try {
            slots.acquire();
            throwIfTerminated();
            output.run();
            int phase = molecule.arrive();
            int next = molecule.awaitAdvanceInterruptibly(phase);
            if (next < 0) throwIfTerminated();
            if (slots == oxygens) {
                synchronized (terminationLock) {
                    throwIfTerminated();
                    hydrogens.release(2);
                    oxygens.release();
                }
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            terminate(interrupted);
            throw interrupted;
        } catch (RuntimeException | Error failed) {
            terminate(failed);
            throw failed;
        }
    }

    private void throwIfTerminated() {
        Throwable cause = failure;
        if (cause != null) throw new IllegalStateException("H2O coordinator terminated", cause);
    }

    private void terminate(Throwable cause) {
        synchronized (terminationLock) {
            if (failure != null) return;
            failure = cause;
            molecule.forceTermination();
            // Wake current and future semaphore callers so they observe termination.
            hydrogens.release(Integer.MAX_VALUE - hydrogens.availablePermits());
            oxygens.release(Integer.MAX_VALUE - oxygens.availablePermits());
        }
    }
}
  • Invariant: at most two H and one O pass permits in a phase; the next phase receives permits only after all three arrive.
  • Linearization: semaphore acquisition assigns a thread to a molecule; phase advance completes that molecule.
  • Complexity/contention: O(1) per atom and a three-party barrier per molecule. Fair semaphores reduce overtaking at a throughput cost.
  • Liveness/failure: insufficient atoms wait forever while the coordinator is healthy. Interruption or callback failure is fail-stop: one synchronized termination transition records the cause, terminates the phaser, and wakes semaphore waiters. Peers fail rather than forming later molecules from an uncertain phase. awaitAdvanceInterruptibly makes barrier waiting cancellable; the interrupted caller separately rethrows InterruptedException.
  • Test: submit shuffled atoms, block callbacks at a test barrier, and verify each consecutive completed phase contains exactly two H and one O.

Only the oxygen participant replenishes the next group's slots, and only after observing phase advance. Releasing slots inside onAdvance is unsafe: that hook runs before the next phase is installed, so a newly admitted atom could arrive in the exhausted old phase. Cancellation can leave partial output and a callback already past its failure check may finish; termination is not rollback of output.

flowchart LR
    S[Acquire two H slots and one O slot] --> C[Three callbacks finish]
    C --> A[Three arrivals advance phase]
    A --> O[O observes advance and releases next slots]
    O --> S
    S -. interrupt or callback failure .-> F[Fail stop and wake peers]
    C -. failure .-> F

The arrows describe normal phase order, not atomic visibility of three characters. Chapter 5 develops a smaller non-cancellable-after-admission variant with the same Phaser; see Pattern: H2O grouping.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Five philosophers repeatedly need their left and right forks before eating. Prevent deadlock. The API should not hold one fork while waiting without a global ordering rule.

docs.title: Solution: resource ordering
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public final class DiningTable {
    private final ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[5];

    public DiningTable() {
        for (int i = 0; i < forks.length; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock(true);
    }

    public void dine(int philosopher, Runnable pickLeft, Runnable pickRight,
                     Runnable eat, Runnable putLeft, Runnable putRight)
            throws InterruptedException {
        if (philosopher < 0 || philosopher >= 5) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        int left = philosopher;
        int right = (philosopher + 1) % 5;
        int first = Math.min(left, right);
        int second = Math.max(left, right);

        forks[first].lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            forks[second].lockInterruptibly();
            try {
                if (first == left) { pickLeft.run(); pickRight.run(); }
                else { pickRight.run(); pickLeft.run(); }
                eat.run();
                putLeft.run();
                putRight.run();
            } finally { forks[second].unlock(); }
        } finally { forks[first].unlock(); }
    }
}
  • Invariant: a fork is held by at most one philosopher; all threads acquire lower-numbered fork before higher-numbered fork.
  • Deadlock proof: a wait-for cycle would require strictly increasing fork numbers around a cycle, which is impossible.
  • Linearization: there is no single atomic dine; ownership of both forks becomes established at the second lock acquisition.
  • Liveness: fair locks reduce starvation risk but do not promise bounded completion under arbitrary scheduling. Interruptible acquisition supports cancellation.
  • Cost: O(1) work; neighbors contend while non-neighbors can eat concurrently.
  • Alternative: a four-permit waiter semaphore prevents all five philosophers from holding one fork. It is simpler but centralizes contention and still needs careful release on interruption.
  • Test: start five workers on a barrier, execute thousands of meals, track fork ownership atomically, fail on duplicate ownership, and require every worker to finish by a deadline.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a fixed-capacity FIFO queue with interruptible put and take. Do not use BlockingQueue for this exercise. Handle spurious wakeups.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public final class BoundedQueue<E> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Deque<E> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();

    public BoundedQueue(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("non-positive capacity");
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    public void put(E item) throws InterruptedException {
        if (item == null) throw new NullPointerException("item");
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await();
            items.addLast(item);
            notEmpty.signal();
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public E take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await();
            E item = items.removeFirst();
            notFull.signal();
            return item;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public int size() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return items.size(); }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}
  • Invariant: 0 <= size <= capacity; removals preserve insertion order; all deque access holds the lock.
  • Linearization: addLast for put, removeFirst for take.
  • Complexity/contention: O(1) per operation, O(capacity) memory, one lock for both ends. Separate locks can improve throughput but complicate empty/full transitions.
  • Cancellation/shutdown: interrupted waiters make no state change. A closable queue needs a closed flag under the same lock, signalAll, rejection of future puts, and a documented drain policy.
  • Test: force full and empty states with latches; interrupt blocked producers/consumers; run multiple producers with unique sequence ranges and verify no loss, duplication, or per-producer reordering.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build a small integer register that allows concurrent reads and exclusive writes. Prevent a continuous stream of new readers from indefinitely bypassing a waiting writer.

docs.title: Solution: writer-aware monitor
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
import java.util.function.IntSupplier;

public final class WriterAwareRegister {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(true);
    private final Condition mayRead = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition mayWrite = lock.newCondition();
    private int readers;
    private int waitingWriters;
    private boolean writing;
    private int value;

    public int read() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (writing || waitingWriters > 0) mayRead.await();
            readers++;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        try { return value; }
        finally {
            lock.lock();
            try {
                readers--;
                if (readers == 0) mayWrite.signal();
            } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        }
    }

    public int write(IntSupplier update) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            waitingWriters++;
            try {
                while (writing || readers > 0) mayWrite.await();
            } finally {
                waitingWriters--;
                if (!writing && waitingWriters == 0) mayRead.signalAll();
                else if (!writing && readers == 0) mayWrite.signal();
            }
            writing = true;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }

        try { return value = update.getAsInt(); }
        finally {
            lock.lock();
            try {
                writing = false;
                if (waitingWriters > 0) mayWrite.signal();
                else mayRead.signalAll();
            } finally { lock.unlock(); }
        }
    }
}
  • State/invariant: writing excludes readers and another writer; readers >= 0; new readers wait behind queued writers.
  • Visibility: lock release/acquisition publishes value, although reading outside the bookkeeping lock makes the proof subtle. The active-reader protocol ensures no writer overlaps that read.
  • Linearization: read samples value; write assigns value while holding logical write ownership.
  • Liveness: writer preference bounds reader bypass but can starve readers under a continuous writer stream. Fair ReentrantReadWriteLock is the normal library choice.
  • Cancellation: removing the last waiting writer can make the reader predicate true without a write completing. Signal readers on that transition, including interruption; otherwise readers can remain asleep forever. The update callback must not re-enter read or write, which would wait on its own logical ownership.
  • Test: inject update callbacks blocked on latches, assert no reader enters during a write, assert two readers can overlap using a test hook in an extended API, and place a writer between reader waves.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Sort an int[] using divide-and-conquer parallelism. Bound task creation and avoid allocating a new array at every merge.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool;
import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveAction;

public final class ParallelMergeSort {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 8_192;

    public static void sort(int[] values, int parallelism) {
        if (parallelism <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("parallelism");
        int[] scratch = new int[values.length];
        try (ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(parallelism)) {
            pool.invoke(new SortTask(values, scratch, 0, values.length));
        }
    }

    private static final class SortTask extends RecursiveAction {
        private final int[] a;
        private final int[] scratch;
        private final int lo;
        private final int hi;

        SortTask(int[] a, int[] scratch, int lo, int hi) {
            this.a = a; this.scratch = scratch; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi;
        }

        @Override protected void compute() {
            if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
                java.util.Arrays.sort(a, lo, hi);
                return;
            }
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            invokeAll(new SortTask(a, scratch, lo, mid),
                      new SortTask(a, scratch, mid, hi));
            merge(a, scratch, lo, mid, hi);
        }
    }

    private static void merge(int[] a, int[] scratch, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
        int i = lo, j = mid, k = lo;
        while (i < mid && j < hi) scratch[k++] = a[i] <= a[j] ? a[i++] : a[j++];
        while (i < mid) scratch[k++] = a[i++];
        while (j < hi) scratch[k++] = a[j++];
        System.arraycopy(scratch, lo, a, lo, hi - lo);
    }
}
  • Invariant: sibling tasks own disjoint array and scratch ranges; both halves are sorted before their parent merges.
  • Linearization: sorting is a batch mutation rather than a concurrent object operation; successful invoke completion publishes the sorted array to the caller.
  • Complexity: O(n log n) work and O(n) scratch. With sequential merges, span satisfies S(n) = S(n/2) + O(n), hence O(n), not O(log n). Parallel speedup is limited by the serial root merge and memory bandwidth.
  • Cancellation/shutdown: pool closure follows completion. ForkJoinTask.cancel(true) does not interrupt its worker. Responsive cancellation needs an explicit shared token checked in splitting and merge loops, plus joining all children before returning the mutable array to the caller.
  • Test: compare random, sorted, reverse, duplicate-heavy, empty, and singleton arrays against Arrays.sort. Fix the random seed. Verify the input multiset as well as ordering.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Model turns, eligibility predicates, resource ownership, and phase membership explicitly.
  • Wait in predicate loops and make interruption part of the contract.
  • Identify whether the linearization point is token acquisition, state mutation, or phase advance.
  • Deadlock freedom does not imply starvation freedom.
  • Deterministic barriers and injected callbacks expose interleavings more reliably than sleeps.
  • Outside a primitive-building exercise, prefer BlockingQueue, executor, future, and lock implementations from the JDK.

docs.title: 12. Concurrent LLD Problems: Solved Workbook
docs.text: This workbook combines concurrency reasoning with low-level design. Each solution is intentionally scoped for an interview: it is complete core Java 21 code for the stated contract, not a claim of production readiness. Real systems also need metrics, configuration, abuse controls, persistence, and integration-specific failure policy.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• clarify concurrent APIs before choosing classes;
  • isolate mutable state and write explicit invariants;
  • locate races and linearization points;
  • design cancellation, backpressure, and shutdown as first-class behavior;
  • construct deterministic tests with injected time and dependencies; and
  • evaluate solutions with a repeatable interview rubric.

docs.title: LLD answer framework
docs.text:
1. Scope: callers, workload, ordering, durability, and failure semantics.
  2. Contract: method results, blocking, timeout, and cancellation behavior.
  3. State: ownership, invariants, and legal transitions.
  4. Coordination: library primitive and lock granularity.
  5. Proof: linearization point, happens-before edge, and deadlock argument.
  6. Operations: bounded resources, overload, observability, and shutdown.
  7. Tests: force races with controlled clocks, barriers, and fakes.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: Design an in-process limiter that admits an operation only when one token is available. Tokens refill continuously at a configured rate up to a fixed capacity. Multiple threads may call it concurrently. Support a non-blocking attempt and a timed blocking attempt.

docs.title: Clarified API and scope
docs.text:
• One limiter represents one bucket. Per-user limiting composes buckets in a registry.
  • tryAcquire() does not wait for refill, but may briefly block acquiring the bookkeeping lock. It is not a lock-free or strict immediate-return API.
  • acquire(timeout) waits until one token is available, the deadline expires, or the caller is interrupted.
  • Time is monotonic. The implementation is local to one process and provides no distributed quota.
  • Fractional refill is retained as nanosecond-scaled credit.

docs.title: Invariants and class design
docs.text:
• 0 <= storedNanos <= capacityNanos.
  • lastRefillNanos stores the latest monotonic clock tick; elapsed time uses wrap-safe subtraction.
  • State refill and token consumption happen under one lock.
  • Waiting does not reserve a future token; contenders recheck the predicate.
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

public final class TokenBucket {
    private static final long TOKEN = 1_000_000_000L;
    private final long capacityNanos;
    private final long refillPerSecond;
    private final LongSupplier nanoTime;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(true);
    private final Condition changed = lock.newCondition();
    private long storedNanos;
    private long lastRefillNanos;

    public TokenBucket(long capacity, long refillPerSecond, LongSupplier nanoTime) {
        if (capacity <= 0 || refillPerSecond <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        this.capacityNanos = Math.multiplyExact(capacity, TOKEN);
        this.refillPerSecond = refillPerSecond;
        this.nanoTime = nanoTime;
        this.storedNanos = capacityNanos;
        this.lastRefillNanos = nanoTime.getAsLong();
    }

    public boolean tryAcquire() {
        lock.lock();
        try { return consumeIfAvailable(); }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    public boolean acquire(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException {
        if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative timeout");
        long timeoutNanos;
        try { timeoutNanos = timeout.toNanos(); }
        catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) { timeoutNanos = Long.MAX_VALUE; }
        long deadline = nanoTime.getAsLong() + timeoutNanos;
        boolean acquired = lock.tryLock(timeoutNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        if (!acquired) return false;
        try {
            if (timeoutNanos == 0) return consumeIfAvailable();
            while (true) {
                long remaining = deadline - nanoTime.getAsLong();
                if (remaining <= 0) return false;
                if (consumeIfAvailable()) return true;
                long untilToken = nanosUntilToken();
                changed.awaitNanos(Math.min(remaining, untilToken));
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    private boolean consumeIfAvailable() {
        refill();
        if (storedNanos < TOKEN) return false;
        storedNanos -= TOKEN;
        return true;
    }

    private void refill() {
        long now = nanoTime.getAsLong();
        long elapsed = Math.max(0, now - lastRefillNanos);
        if (elapsed == 0) return;
        long credit;
        try { credit = Math.multiplyExact(elapsed, refillPerSecond); }
        catch (ArithmeticException overflow) { credit = capacityNanos; }
        storedNanos = Math.min(capacityNanos, saturatedAdd(storedNanos, credit));
        lastRefillNanos = now;
    }

    private long nanosUntilToken() {
        long missing = TOKEN - storedNanos;
        long whole = missing / refillPerSecond;
        return Math.max(1, whole + (missing % refillPerSecond == 0 ? 0 : 1));
    }

    private static long saturatedAdd(long a, long b) {
        return Long.MAX_VALUE - a < b ? Long.MAX_VALUE : a + b;
    }
}

docs.title: Races, linearization, and cost
docs.text: The check and decrement must not be split; otherwise two callers can spend one token. A successful call linearizes at storedNanos -= TOKEN; a failed immediate call linearizes at the underflow check after refill. Operations are O(1). One lock makes the bucket a contention point, which is inherent for one strict quota. Sharding changes semantics by allowing bounded oversubscription.

docs.title: Liveness, cancellation, and shutdown
docs.text: acquire computes one overflow-safe absolute deadline before attempting the lock. Wrap-safe subtraction from the monotonic clock charges lock contention and every spurious or refill wake to the same budget. The zero-timeout path uses timed tryLock(0, NANOSECONDS) so pre-existing interruption and the fair-lock policy are respected even for an immediate attempt. It wakes on its computed refill time; no background thread is required. The condition also permits an extension where administrative refill or close calls signalAll. A closable version would guard a closed flag under the lock, signal all waiters, and reject future acquisition.

docs.title: Deterministic tests
docs.text: Use a fake LongSupplier backed by an AtomicLong. Drain the initial capacity, advance exactly one token interval, and assert one success. Start 100 callers behind a barrier against a one-token bucket and assert exactly one success. For timed waiting, coordinate clock advancement with a test-only wake method or a controllable condition abstraction; never wait on wall-clock seconds.

docs.title: Extensions and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Add tryAcquire(long permits) with overflow-safe arithmetic.
  • Store per-key buckets in a bounded, expiring registry; define eviction races.
  • Return retry-after duration for caller backoff.
  • For distributed enforcement, use server-side atomic state and accept latency/availability tradeoffs.
  • Fixed-point arithmetic is deterministic; a double implementation is shorter but accumulates rounding error.

docs.title: Evaluation rubric (10 points)
docs.text:
• 2: clear burst and refill semantics;
  • 2: atomic refill plus consumption and bounded credit;
  • 2: monotonic injectable time and overflow awareness;
  • 2: interruption/deadline behavior and contention analysis;
  • 2: race-focused deterministic tests and distributed-scope caveat.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: Design a concurrent in-memory cache with per-entry TTL. Reads must never return an expired entry. A background sweeper may remove expired entries, but an old expiry record must never delete a newer value for the same key.

docs.title: Clarified API and invariants
docs.text:
• put(key, value, ttl) replaces the key with a distinct immutable entry.
  • get(key) returns empty after expiration and may lazily remove the entry.
  • remove(key) conditionally removes the entry it observed.
  • TTL zero is rejected; expiry uses monotonic time.
  • The map contains at most one current entry per key. An expiry task can delete only the exact entry instance it was created for.
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.DelayQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Delayed;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock;
import java.util.function.LongSupplier;

public final class TtlCache<K, V> implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final long MAX_TTL_NANOS = Long.MAX_VALUE / 2;

    private static final class Entry<V> {
        private final V value;
        private final long expiresAt;
        Entry(V value, long expiresAt) {
            this.value = value;
            this.expiresAt = expiresAt;
        }
        V value() { return value; }
        long expiresAt() { return expiresAt; }
    }

    private static final class Expiry<K, V> implements Delayed {
        final K key;
        final Entry<V> expected;
        final LongSupplier nanoTime;
        Expiry(K key, Entry<V> expected, LongSupplier nanoTime) {
            this.key = key;
            this.expected = expected;
            this.nanoTime = nanoTime;
        }
        @Override public long getDelay(TimeUnit unit) {
            return unit.convert(expected.expiresAt() - nanoTime.getAsLong(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
        }
        @Override public int compareTo(Delayed other) {
            Expiry<?, ?> that = (Expiry<?, ?>) other;
            long difference = expected.expiresAt() - that.expected.expiresAt();
            return Long.compare(difference, 0);
        }
    }

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, Entry<V>> entries = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final DelayQueue<Expiry<K, V>> expiries = new DelayQueue<>();
    private final ReentrantReadWriteLock lifecycle = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
    private final LongSupplier nanoTime;
    private final Thread sweeper;
    private volatile boolean running = true;
    private boolean closed;

    public TtlCache(LongSupplier nanoTime) {
        this.nanoTime = nanoTime;
        this.sweeper = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ttl-cache-sweeper").start(this::sweep);
    }

    public void put(K key, V value, Duration ttl) {
        if (key == null || value == null) throw new NullPointerException();
        long ttlNanos;
        try { ttlNanos = ttl.toNanos(); }
        catch (ArithmeticException tooLarge) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("TTL is too large", tooLarge);
        }
        if (ttlNanos <= 0 || ttlNanos > MAX_TTL_NANOS)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("TTL must be in (0, 2^62) nanoseconds");
        lifecycle.readLock().lock();
        try {
            ensureOpen();
            long expiresAt = nanoTime.getAsLong() + ttlNanos;
            Entry<V> entry = new Entry<>(value, expiresAt);
            entries.put(key, entry);
            expiries.offer(new Expiry<>(key, entry, nanoTime));
        } finally {
            lifecycle.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    public Optional<V> get(K key) {
        lifecycle.readLock().lock();
        try {
            ensureOpen();
            while (true) {
                Entry<V> entry = entries.get(key);
                if (entry == null) return Optional.empty();
                if (nanoTime.getAsLong() - entry.expiresAt() < 0)
                    return Optional.of(entry.value());
                if (entries.remove(key, entry)) return Optional.empty();
            }
        } finally {
            lifecycle.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    public boolean remove(K key) {
        lifecycle.readLock().lock();
        try {
            ensureOpen();
            Entry<V> entry = entries.get(key);
            return entry != null && entries.remove(key, entry);
        } finally {
            lifecycle.readLock().unlock();
        }
    }

    private void ensureOpen() {
        if (closed) throw new IllegalStateException("cache is closed");
    }

    private void sweep() {
        try {
            while (running) {
                Expiry<K, V> expiry = expiries.take();
                entries.remove(expiry.key, expiry.expected);
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        lifecycle.writeLock().lock();
        try {
            if (!closed) {
                closed = true;
                running = false;
                sweeper.interrupt();
            }
        } finally {
            lifecycle.writeLock().unlock();
        }
        try {
            sweeper.join();
        } finally {
            expiries.clear();
            entries.clear();
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Races, linearization, and cost
docs.text:
The critical race is put(k, old), put(k, new), then old expiry. remove(k, expected) uses entry identity to protect the replacement. An expired get retries if removal loses to replacement: returning empty then could invent a cache miss even though an unexpired mapping existed throughout the call. Successful get linearizes at its map read (the later clock check proves it was unexpired then); a miss linearizes at a null read or successful expired-entry removal. put linearizes at map replacement. Map work is average O(1), but put also inserts an O(log n) expiry record; get can retry under replacement contention. Old expiry records remain until due, so frequent replacement can grow the delay queue.

Signed deadline subtraction assumes elapsed intervals remain below 2^63 ns and compared deadlines are less than that far apart. Bounded TTL alone is insufficient if expired records survive a centuries-long pause. Values and keys must be immutable or separately synchronized; immutable entry wrappers do not freeze user objects. Close interrupted during join rejects future operations and clears data but does not prove sweeper termination; retry close to join it.

docs.title: Cancellation, shutdown, and deterministic tests
docs.text: The lifecycle read/write lock makes admission and close atomic: once close obtains the write lock, no operation can be admitted, and all post-close put, get, and remove calls fail. Close stops the sole sweeper and clears process-local data. A fake clock alone does not wake DelayQueue.take, so unit-test stale protection by exposing package-private expiry logic or by factoring scheduling behind an interface. Test replacement, exact-boundary, wraparound, close-versus-put, and post-close rejection races.

docs.title: Extensions and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Bound memory with weight-based admission/eviction; TTL alone is not a capacity policy.
  • Compact superseded expiry records or use a timing wheel at scale.
  • Add loader single-flight separately; do not hold map internals while loading.
  • Define nulls, refresh, exception caching, and close behavior before adding them.

docs.title: Evaluation rubric (10 points)
docs.text:
• 2: precise TTL boundary and injectable monotonic time;
  • 2: stale-expiry protection via identity-based conditional removal;
  • 2: thread-safe map and linearization argument;
  • 2: lifecycle and queue-growth tradeoff;
  • 2: deterministic replacement/expiry race tests.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: Given named tasks forming a directed acyclic graph, run a task only after all its dependencies succeed. Run independent tasks concurrently. If one task fails, do not run its transitive dependents. Return a future for the entire execution.

docs.title: API, invariants, and class design
docs.text:
• The graph is immutable after construction and validated before execution.
  • Names are unique; every dependency exists; cycles are rejected.
  • Each task starts at most once. RUNNING requires all direct dependencies to be SUCCEEDED.
  • Failure completes dependent futures exceptionally through composition.
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.Executor;

public final class DagScheduler {
    public record Task(String name, Set<String> dependencies, Runnable action) {
        public Task {
            java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name");
            java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(action, "action");
            dependencies = Set.copyOf(dependencies);
        }
    }

    private final Map<String, Task> tasks;
    private final Executor executor;

    public DagScheduler(List<Task> definitions, Executor executor) {
        Map<String, Task> indexed = new HashMap<>();
        for (Task task : definitions) {
            if (indexed.putIfAbsent(task.name(), task) != null)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("duplicate task: " + task.name());
        }
        for (Task task : definitions)
            for (String dependency : task.dependencies())
                if (!indexed.containsKey(dependency))
                    throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing dependency: " + dependency);
        detectCycles(indexed);
        this.tasks = Map.copyOf(indexed);
        this.executor = java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(executor, "executor");
    }

    public CompletableFuture<Void> run() {
        Map<String, CompletableFuture<Void>> futures = new HashMap<>();
        for (String name : tasks.keySet()) build(name, futures);
        return CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.values().toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new));
    }

    private CompletableFuture<Void> build(
            String name, Map<String, CompletableFuture<Void>> futures) {
        CompletableFuture<Void> existing = futures.get(name);
        if (existing != null) return existing;
        Task task = tasks.get(name);
        CompletableFuture<?>[] prerequisites = task.dependencies().stream()
                .map(dependency -> build(dependency, futures))
                .toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new);
        CompletableFuture<Void> future = CompletableFuture.allOf(prerequisites)
                .thenRunAsync(task.action(), executor);
        futures.put(name, future);
        return future;
    }

    private static void detectCycles(Map<String, Task> tasks) {
        Set<String> visiting = new HashSet<>();
        Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>();
        for (String name : tasks.keySet()) visit(name, tasks, visiting, visited);
    }

    private static void visit(String name, Map<String, Task> tasks,
                              Set<String> visiting, Set<String> visited) {
        if (visited.contains(name)) return;
        if (!visiting.add(name)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cycle at: " + name);
        for (String dependency : tasks.get(name).dependencies())
            visit(dependency, tasks, visiting, visited);
        visiting.remove(name);
        visited.add(name);
    }
}

docs.title: Races, linearization, and complexity
docs.text: run constructs its future map on one caller thread, so each task receives one stage. Completion of every prerequisite happens-before dependent stage execution through CompletableFuture. A task starts when the executor begins its action; success linearizes at normal stage completion. Validation and graph construction cost O(V + E); runtime scheduling is O(V + E) plus task work. Throughput is bounded by executor capacity and DAG width.

docs.title: Cancellation and shutdown
docs.text: Cancelling the returned allOf future does not cancel component stages, prevent pending dependents from starting, or interrupt running actions. allOf is not fail-fast: independent branches must finish before its exceptional result is ready. At-most-once is per run() invocation; calling run() twice executes two graphs. A stronger API owns handles, passes cancellation tokens, and stops admission. This class receives an executor and must not shut it down. Recursive validation/building can overflow the stack for a deep DAG; bound graph depth or use iterative topological construction before accepting untrusted graphs.

docs.title: Deterministic tests
docs.text: Use a direct executor to verify topological behavior without threads. For concurrency, make two root actions count down an entered latch and await a release latch; assert both enter before release. Make one root throw and assert its dependent never increments a counter while an independent branch completes. Test missing names, duplicate names, self-cycles, and multi-node cycles.

docs.title: Extensions and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Add task results with typed keys or a result context.
  • Add bounded concurrency, priorities, retries, and per-task timeout only after defining fairness.
  • Persist transitions for crash recovery; futures alone are in-memory orchestration.
  • Dynamic DAG mutation needs a different consistency model and cycle-validation strategy.

docs.title: Evaluation rubric (10 points)
docs.text:
• 2: validated immutable DAG and cycle detection;
  • 2: at-most-once scheduling after all dependencies;
  • 2: independent parallelism and failure propagation;
  • 2: cancellation/executor ownership caveat;
  • 2: deterministic ordering, overlap, and failure tests.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: Design an in-process event bus. Subscribers register for one exact event class. Publishing dispatches to the current subscriber snapshot without holding registry locks while user code runs. Return a future that reports handler failure.

docs.title: API and invariants
docs.text:
• Registration returns an idempotent subscription handle.
  • Exact runtime class matching avoids ambiguous hierarchy ordering.
  • One publish observes one immutable handler snapshot.
  • Removing a handler prevents future snapshots from including it; an already captured publish may still invoke it.
  • Handler order is registration order within a snapshot. Concurrent publications may overlap.
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
import java.util.concurrent.Executor;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.function.Consumer;

public final class EventBus {
    public interface Subscription extends AutoCloseable {
        @Override void close();
    }

    private static final class Handler<E> {
        private final Consumer<E> consumer;
        Handler(Consumer<E> consumer) {
            this.consumer = java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(consumer);
        }
        Consumer<E> consumer() { return consumer; }
    }
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<Class<?>, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<?>>> handlers =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Executor executor;

    public EventBus(Executor executor) { this.executor = executor; }

    public <E> Subscription subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> consumer) {
        Handler<E> handler = new Handler<>(consumer);
        CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<?>> list =
                handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, ignored -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>());
        list.add(handler);
        return new Subscription() {
            private boolean active = true;
            @Override public synchronized void close() {
                if (active) {
                    list.remove(handler);
                    active = false;
                }
            }
        };
    }

    public CompletableFuture<Void> publish(Object event) {
        if (event == null) throw new NullPointerException("event");
        List<Handler<?>> snapshot = List.copyOf(
                handlers.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()));
        return CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> deliver(snapshot, event), executor);
    }

    private static void deliver(List<Handler<?>> snapshot, Object event) {
        RuntimeException failures = null;
        for (Handler<?> handler : snapshot) {
            try {
                invoke(handler, event);
            } catch (RuntimeException failure) {
                if (failures == null) failures = new RuntimeException("event delivery failed");
                failures.addSuppressed(failure);
            }
        }
        if (failures != null) throw new CompletionException(failures);
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    private static <E> void invoke(Handler<?> raw, E event) {
        ((Handler<E>) raw).consumer().accept(event);
    }
}

Empty per-type lists are retained deliberately. A naive isEmpty followed by conditional map removal can orphan a subscriber added between those operations. Safe cleanup would use atomic per-key coordination; retaining a small empty registry entry keeps this teaching implementation clear.

Handler wrappers intentionally use identity, not record equality. Registering the same consumer twice around another handler must allow closing the second registration without removing the first and changing callback order. Subscription close serializes through actual removal so a completed duplicate close cannot return before unsubscription takes effect.

docs.title: Races, linearization, and cost
docs.text: Subscription linearizes at list.add; unsubscription at successful list removal; publish snapshot selection at List.copyOf. One executor task walks that immutable snapshot serially, so callbacks begin in registration order even on a multithreaded executor. Concurrent publications can still overlap and have no cross-publication order. Publish costs one task and O(s) callback work for s subscribers. Registration/removal copies O(s) storage, making CopyOnWriteArrayList suitable only when publishing greatly outnumbers subscription changes.

docs.title: Liveness, cancellation, and shutdown
docs.text: One stuck handler prevents later handlers in that snapshot and leaves the publish future incomplete. Runtime failures are accumulated so later handlers still run, then reported through the returned future. Apply timeouts, bulkheads, or per-subscriber queues if isolation is required. Cancelling the future does not guarantee interruption of its executor task. The bus does not own the injected executor and does not close it. Rejected execution appears as synchronous failure while constructing the stage; a production API should normalize it into the returned future.

docs.title: Deterministic tests
docs.text: Use a direct executor for order and exception tests. Use a manually queued executor to capture a delivery, unsubscribe after publish, then run it and prove snapshot semantics. Register while another snapshot is captured and verify the new handler only sees later publications. Assert registration order under a multithreaded executor and assert one failing handler completes the future exceptionally after later handlers run.

docs.title: Extensions and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Polymorphic dispatch requires a documented type order and duplicate suppression.
  • Ordering across separate publications requires a per-key serial executor or a tail-future chain; this implementation guarantees order only within each publication snapshot.
  • Weak references reduce leaks but make delivery dependent on GC.
  • Durable delivery, replay, retries, and cross-process transport require a broker, not this bus.

docs.title: Evaluation rubric (10 points)
docs.text:
• 2: explicit dispatch and unsubscribe race semantics;
  • 2: no user callback under registry coordination;
  • 2: safe snapshots and exception propagation;
  • 2: executor ownership, overload, and cancellation discussion;
  • 2: deterministic concurrent register/remove/publish tests.

docs.title: Prompt
docs.text: Crawl pages from a seed URL up to a page limit. Fetch pages concurrently, visit a normalized URL at most once, and follow only URLs accepted by a supplied policy. Support cooperative cancellation and return successfully fetched pages.

docs.title: Clarified API and scope
docs.text:
• Fetching is injected and returns page content plus discovered links.
  • URL normalization removes fragments and normalizes URI syntax; application policy decides host/scheme rules.
  • A URL is marked seen before submission, preventing duplicate in-flight fetches.
  • The page limit bounds scheduled unique URLs, not necessarily successful responses.
  • One crawl may run at a time; cancellation is terminal and later crawls are rejected.
  • This educational crawler does not implement robots.txt, politeness delays, DNS protections, persistence, HTML parsing, retries, or canonical-link semantics.
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.CancellationException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorCompletionService;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

public final class ConcurrentCrawler implements AutoCloseable {
    public record Page(URI uri, String body, List<URI> links) {
        public Page { links = List.copyOf(links); }
    }
    public interface Fetcher { Page fetch(URI uri) throws Exception; }

    private record Result(URI uri, Page page, Exception failure) {}
    private static final Result CANCEL_SIGNAL = new Result(null, null, null);

    private static final class CrawlSession {
        final BlockingQueue<Future<Result>> completed = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();
        final Future<Result> cancelSignal = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(CANCEL_SIGNAL);
        final Set<Future<Result>> tasks = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();

        void cancelTasks() {
            for (Future<Result> task : tasks) task.cancel(true);
        }
    }

    private final ExecutorService workers;
    private final Fetcher fetcher;
    private final AtomicBoolean cancelled = new AtomicBoolean();
    private final AtomicReference<CrawlSession> active = new AtomicReference<>();

    public ConcurrentCrawler(int parallelism, Fetcher fetcher) {
        if (parallelism <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("parallelism");
        this.workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(parallelism);
        this.fetcher = fetcher;
    }

    public List<Page> crawl(URI seed, int limit, Predicate<URI> allowed)
            throws InterruptedException {
        if (limit < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative limit");
        if (cancelled.get()) throw new IllegalStateException("crawler is cancelled");
        if (limit == 0) return List.of();
        CrawlSession session = new CrawlSession();
        if (!active.compareAndSet(null, session))
            throw new IllegalStateException("a crawl is already active");
        if (cancelled.get()) {
            active.compareAndSet(session, null);
            throw new IllegalStateException("crawler is cancelled");
        }
        Set<URI> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
        List<Page> pages = new ArrayList<>();
        ExecutorCompletionService<Result> completions =
                new ExecutorCompletionService<>(workers, session.completed);
        int inFlight = 0;

        try {
            URI first = normalize(seed);
            if (!cancelled.get() && allowed.test(first) && seen.add(first)
                    && submit(first, completions, session)) {
                inFlight++;
            }

            while (inFlight > 0) {
                Future<Result> completed = completions.take();
                if (completed == session.cancelSignal) break;
                session.tasks.remove(completed);
                inFlight--;
                Result result;
                try { result = completed.get(); }
                catch (CancellationException cancelledTask) { continue; }
                catch (ExecutionException impossible) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("worker wrapper failed", impossible.getCause());
                }
                if (result.failure() != null) continue;
                pages.add(result.page());
                for (URI rawLink : result.page().links()) {
                    if (seen.size() >= limit || cancelled.get()) break;
                    URI link;
                    try { link = normalize(result.uri().resolve(rawLink)); }
                    catch (IllegalArgumentException invalid) { continue; }
                    if (allowed.test(link) && seen.add(link)
                            && submit(link, completions, session)) {
                        inFlight++;
                    }
                }
            }
            return List.copyOf(pages);
        } finally {
            session.cancelTasks();
            active.compareAndSet(session, null);
        }
    }

    private boolean submit(URI uri, ExecutorCompletionService<Result> completions,
                           CrawlSession session) {
        if (cancelled.get()) return false;
        try {
            Future<Result> task = completions.submit(() -> {
                if (cancelled.get() || Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted())
                    return new Result(uri, null, new InterruptedException());
                try {
                    return new Result(uri, fetcher.fetch(uri), null);
                } catch (InterruptedException interrupted) {
                    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                    return new Result(uri, null, interrupted);
                } catch (Exception failure) {
                    return new Result(uri, null, failure);
                }
            });
            session.tasks.add(task);
            if (cancelled.get()) task.cancel(true);
            return true;
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException rejected) {
            if (cancelled.get()) return false;
            throw rejected;
        }
    }

    private static URI normalize(URI uri) {
        String raw = uri.toString();
        int fragment = raw.indexOf('#');
        return URI.create(fragment < 0 ? raw : raw.substring(0, fragment)).normalize();
    }

    public void cancel() {
        if (!cancelled.compareAndSet(false, true)) return;
        CrawlSession session = active.get();
        if (session != null) {
            session.cancelTasks();
            session.completed.offer(session.cancelSignal);
        }
        workers.shutdownNow();
    }

    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        cancel();
        if (!workers.awaitTermination(10, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("crawler did not terminate");
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Races, linearization, and complexity
docs.text:
seen.add is the deduplication linearization point and happens before submission by program order. Only the coordinator thread mutates pages and inFlight, avoiding extra locks. The loop terminates when no accepted work remains. For V scheduled pages and E discovered links, coordination is O(V + E) average with O(V) seen state; wall time approaches total fetch work divided by parallelism until remote latency, host limits, or a serial discovery frontier dominates.

There is a deliberate limit nuance: seen.size() is checked by the sole coordinator, so it cannot overshoot. Failed pages still consume budget. If workers discovered and submitted links directly, check-then-add would overshoot unless admission used an atomic counter with rollback.

docs.title: Cancellation and shutdown
docs.text:
cancel commits terminal cancellation, requests interruption of known tasks, and places a signal in the completion queue. Submission racing with cancellation checks again after registering its handle. The signal wakes a coordinator blocked in take, even if a queued task was removed by shutdownNow or a fetcher ignores interruption. It does not bound time spent in the caller-supplied allowed predicate or processing a large result; those must be short/bounded. The returned snapshot contains pages consumed by the coordinator before the signal, not every fetch that happened to finish. Worker termination still depends on cooperative, deadline-bounded fetches; close waits at most ten seconds and reports failure. Caller interruption propagates InterruptedException and cancels session tasks in finally; it does not imply those tasks have exited.

URI normalization preserves raw escapes: /a%2Fb and /a/b are different resources under RFC 3986 section 2.2. Rebuilding from decoded getPath/getQuery silently merges them and can alter query delimiters. This implementation removes literal fragments and dot segments only; default ports, unreserved escapes, redirect bases, and host policy remain explicit extensions.

docs.title: Deterministic tests
docs.text: Create a fake graph-backed fetcher. Use latches to prove two independent URLs enter fetch concurrently. Include duplicate, relative, fragment-only, cyclic, malformed, off-policy, and failing links. Count fetches per normalized URI and assert at most one. Cancel while one fetcher honors interruption and another deliberately ignores it; assert crawl still returns promptly, then release the latter for cleanup. Separately interrupt the coordinator and assert InterruptedException, not a normal partial result. Use a deadline around every test to turn deadlocks into failures.

docs.title: Extensions and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Add per-host semaphores and delayed politeness scheduling.
  • Keep bounded frontiers and define whether overload blocks, drops, or persists URLs.
  • Separate retryable failures from permanent responses and budget retries.
  • Defend against SSRF by resolving and validating IP ranges on every redirect.
  • Persist frontier and leases for crash recovery; deduplication then needs durable identity.
  • Virtual threads can simplify blocking HTTP concurrency, but host limits and memory bounds remain necessary.

docs.title: Evaluation rubric (10 points)
docs.text:
• 2: normalized atomic deduplication and explicit page-limit semantics;
  • 2: bounded worker ownership and completion-driven frontier;
  • 2: failure isolation and termination argument;
  • 2: cooperative cancellation, timeouts, and operational scope;
  • 2: deterministic graph, duplicate, concurrency, and cancellation tests.

docs.title: Track completion checklist
docs.text:
Use this as a final interview-readiness gate:

  • I define shared state and its owner before naming a lock.
  • I state safety invariants and legal state transitions.
  • I identify a linearization point for every concurrent API operation.
  • I explain the happens-before edge that publishes each result.
  • I distinguish deadlock freedom, starvation freedom, and bounded waiting.
  • I use one absolute deadline across retrying waits.
  • I preserve interruption or deliberately translate it at an API boundary.
  • I define admission during shutdown and ownership of executor termination.
  • I bound queues, maps, tasks, or explain why the caller must do so.
  • I discuss hot keys, lock granularity, fairness, and callback isolation.
  • I force key races with latches, barriers, fake clocks, and fake dependencies.
  • I use stress tests as supporting evidence, not as the correctness proof.
  • I prefer JDK primitives and keep custom logic at the domain-policy layer.
  • I can explain where the interview implementation stops and production concerns begin.

docs.title: Final interview follow-ups
docs.text:
1. Which design remains correct if a callback re-enters the component?
  2. Where can unbounded cardinality or queued work exhaust memory?
  3. How would fairness requirements alter lock or queue selection?
  4. Which cancellation requests are advisory, and which guarantee no future side effect?
  5. What state must become durable after a process crash?
  6. Which local linearization claims stop being valid in a distributed deployment?
  7. How would you instrument queue delay, lock contention, saturation, and shutdown time?
  8. Which implementation would you replace with a mature library first, and why?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A strong concurrent LLD answer starts with API semantics and invariants, not classes.
  • Token buckets serialize one strict quota; partitioning changes the quota guarantee.
  • TTL cleanup must conditionally remove the exact entry it observed.
  • DAG composition naturally propagates dependency failure but needs explicit cancellation policy.
  • Event buses need snapshot and unsubscribe semantics plus bounded handler isolation.
  • Crawlers need atomic deduplication, bounded admission, policy filtering, and cooperative fetch cancellation.
  • Educational completeness is not operational production readiness; state the boundary honestly.

docs.title: Networks for System Design Engineers
docs.text:
Networks turn local function calls into uncertain distributed interactions. Bytes cross queues, links, routing domains, translators, load balancers, kernels, and application runtimes. Each boundary can delay, duplicate, reorder, fragment, reject, or silently discard traffic. This track builds the packet-level model needed to design and operate reliable systems rather than treating "the network" as one box.

The curriculum targets experienced L5/L6 software and system design engineers. It starts at encapsulation and routing, then develops transport, naming, secure connectivity, traffic management, overload, observability, and multi-region failure reasoning.

docs.title: Competency outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the track, you should be able to:

  • trace one request from an application write to the peer process and back;
  • distinguish names, addresses, routes, connections, sockets, and application sessions;
  • calculate CIDR ranges, usable capacity, serialization delay, bandwidth-delay product, MTU budgets, queue bounds, and retry amplification;
  • explain how routing, ECMP, NAT, load balancing, TLS, TCP, UDP, and QUIC divide responsibility;
  • diagnose failures from packet captures, socket state, route state, counters, flow logs, and application telemetry;
  • separate loss, corruption, congestion, policy rejection, endpoint overload, and dependency delay;
  • design deadlines, retries, connection pools, health checks, failover, and overload controls from explicit invariants;
  • reason about asymmetric paths and partial failure across hosts, zones, regions, and providers;
  • specify an evidence plan that can disprove a networking hypothesis;
  • lead L6 tradeoffs involving blast radius, control-plane safety, capacity, cost, migration, and ownership.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You should already understand processes, threads, HTTP request/response semantics, basic Linux-style observability, binary and hexadecimal notation, powers of two, percentiles, and Little's Law. Root access and production packet capture are not prerequisites.

flowchart LR
    A[Processes and HTTP] --> B[Packet journey]
    C[Binary and powers of two] --> D[IP CIDR routing]
    B --> D
    D --> E[Transport and sockets]
    E --> F[MTU and PMTU]
    D --> G[DNS and service discovery]
    E --> H[TLS and identity]
    F --> I[Proxies and load balancing]
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I --> J[Resilience and operations]

Before Chapter 1, make these distinctions precise:

Concept Working definition Link One local delivery domain with a specific frame format and MTU. Packet A network-layer datagram routed by destination IP address. Segment A TCP protocol data unit; UDP usually calls its unit a datagram. Flow A related packet sequence, commonly identified by protocol and source/destination IP/port. Route A rule selecting a next hop and egress interface for a destination prefix. Socket An OS communication endpoint and its protocol state, not the physical connection itself. Connection Transport state between endpoints; TCP uses tuples, while QUIC can use multiple connection IDs across path changes. Session Application-level continuity, which may survive or span transport connections. Control plane Computes and distributes intended forwarding or policy state. Data plane Applies installed state to packets at line or host speed.

docs.title: The 16-chapter route
docs.text: Chapter Core question L5/L6 deliverable 01. Request and packet journey What transforms and forwards one request? Layered trace with ownership, state, queues, and evidence 02. IP, CIDR, and routing How does each hop choose where a packet goes? Address plan, route proof, ECMP and asymmetry analysis 03. Transport, sockets, and congestion How do endpoints create reliable byte streams under loss and load? TCP/UDP/QUIC boundary, capacity math, queue and lifecycle policy 04. MTU and path MTU Why do some packet sizes fail while small probes work? Encapsulation budget, PMTUD failure diagnosis, mitigation plan 05. DNS and service discovery How do names become changing endpoint sets? Cache/TTL model, authority chain, stale-state and failover policy 06. HTTP semantics and caching Which protocol semantics make retries, caching, and intermediaries correct? Method/status/cache contract and ambiguity handling 07. HTTP/2, HTTP/3, and QUIC How do multiplexing and transport choices change latency and failure coupling? Protocol choice tied to loss, concurrency, migration, and cost 08. TLS and PKI How are peers authenticated and traffic protected? Handshake trace, trust boundary, rotation, and failure evidence 09. Proxies and load balancing Where should traffic terminate and how is a backend selected? L4/L7 choice, affinity, draining, health, and overload semantics 10. Deadlines, retries, and pools How do client policies prevent ambiguous failure from becoming overload? End-to-end budget, bounded amplification, and connection capacity 11. gRPC and RPC How should service calls frame, multiplex, cancel, and report status? RPC contract, deadline propagation, streaming, and evolution 12. Realtime and media Which transport behavior fits interactive streams and sessions? Latency/loss budget, reconnect, ordering, and fanout design 13. NAT and cloud networking Which hidden virtual and translation state carries cloud flows? Tuple/state capacity, overlay path, timeout, and exhaustion analysis 14. BGP, anycast, and global routing How does traffic cross administrative domains and converge? Routing-policy, edge selection, capacity, and route-risk analysis 15. Service mesh and zero trust Where should service identity, policy, and traffic control live? Trust bootstrap, data/control-plane failure, and migration plan 16. Observability and debugging What evidence distinguishes competing network hypotheses? Layered telemetry, capture plan, and incident decision tree
