docs.title: Practical work
docs.text:
The lab and scenario routes use stable repository paths. All 16 labs are available in the lab index, and each scenario link points to a complete practice package.

Artifact Exercise Purpose Request journey evidence Lab 01: request trace Correlate application phases with bounded network inferences. Latency and throughput Lab 03: network math Check BDP, concurrency, serialization, churn, and retry calculations with units; CIDR is in Chapter 02. TCP connection pressure Lab 07: connection pool Observe pool wait, active work, throughput, and rejection. Retry amplification Lab 08: retry storm Compare synchronized retries with bounded backoff and jitter. QUIC path behavior Lab 10: QUIC migration Reason about connection identity and path migration. Load-balancer lifecycle Lab 11: load-balancer draining Verify admission stop, bounded completion, and close behavior. NAT capacity Lab 12: NAT exhaustion Calculate finite tuple state under connection churn. Global failover scenario Global realtime failover Design routing, capacity, session continuity, and recovery. Edge brownout scenario Checkout edge brownout Diagnose partial edge failure and contain retries. Identity rotation scenario Mesh certificate rotation Rotate trust without splitting service connectivity.

Safe lab boundary

Labs should prefer unprivileged inspection. Commands that create namespaces, alter routes, change MTUs, or inject loss must be marked optional and confined to a disposable VM, container, or explicitly isolated network namespace. Never apply them to a shared workstation or production host.

docs.title: How to study each chapter
docs.text:
1. Redraw the first-principles model without looking.
  2. Trace packet and state transitions in both directions.
  3. Write the invariants before selecting a product or protocol option.
  4. Recalculate every example with one changed input.
  5. For each failure, name evidence that would confirm it and evidence that would falsify it.
  6. Convert the mechanics into one system-design decision.
  7. Answer the L5 prompt in five minutes and the L6 pivot in ten.
  8. Complete exercises before opening worked solutions.

docs.title: Evidence discipline
docs.text:
Do not diagnose by symptom association alone. "Timeout" does not imply packet loss, and "retransmission" does not prove congestion. Build a time-bounded hypothesis table:

Layer Example evidence What it can establish What it cannot establish alone Application phase timers, errors, request IDs where the application waited whether the host sent a packet Socket states, queue sizes, kernel errors local transport condition remote application intent Packet headers, flags, timing, retransmissions traffic visible at one capture point what happened outside that point Host network interface drops, route and neighbor state local forwarding health every intermediate hop Network devices/cloud flow logs, ACL decisions, tunnel counters policy or path evidence within scope end-to-end application correctness Peer correlated logs and captures remote receipt and response behavior missing middle-hop evidence

docs.title: L5 and L6 bar
docs.text:
L5: Draw a coherent path, identify the controlling protocol state, calculate the relevant bound, handle the principal failure modes, and propose concrete metrics. Avoid magical network assumptions.

L6: Frame ambiguity, identify hidden shared state and blast radius, compare alternatives across failure domains, quantify overload and recovery, design safe rollout and rollback, align ownership across platform/application teams, and require evidence that distinguishes control-plane intent from data-plane reality.

Standards snapshot: TLS 1.3 is now specified by RFC 9846 (July 2026), which obsoletes RFC 8446. Older implementation documentation can still cite RFC 8446; record that historical context and check current section numbers rather than assuming an old RFC number implies a different negotiated TLS version. A full certificate handshake, resumed TLS connection, and reused HTTP connection are different evidence categories.

docs.title: Authoritative starting sources
docs.text:
• RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers
  • RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6
  • RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
  • RFC 9000: QUIC
  • RFC 9846: TLS 1.3
  • RFC 8201: Path MTU Discovery for IPv6
  • IANA Protocol Registries

Next: Request and Packet Journey

docs.title: 01. Request and Packet Journey
docs.text: An application writes bytes, not "a request across the network." Kernels and network devices wrap those bytes in protocol headers, queue them, choose next hops, transmit finite-size frames, validate them, remove headers, and deliver bytes to a peer socket. A defensible system design names those transitions and the state each transition depends on.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish application messages, transport units, IP packets, and link frames;
  • trace a request across user space, kernel space, interfaces, switches, routers, and the peer;
  • explain encapsulation and decapsulation without treating OSI layers as physical boxes;
  • identify state consulted at each step: DNS, socket, route, neighbor, forwarding, and application state;
  • calculate payload efficiency, serialization delay, packet count, and first-order latency;
  • locate queues and explain how they create delay, drops, and backpressure;
  • construct an evidence plan using application traces, socket data, packet captures, and device telemetry;
  • translate packet mechanics into timeout, retry, pooling, and observability decisions.

docs.title: 1. First-principles model
docs.text:
A network delivers bounded units over one link at a time. End-to-end communication is composed from four responsibilities:

  1. Application semantics: what the bytes mean and where one message ends.
  2. Transport: endpoint demultiplexing and, depending on protocol, reliability, ordering, flow control, and congestion control.
  3. Network: best-effort packet delivery across multiple links using IP destinations and routing state.
  4. Link: local delivery over one medium or virtual link using frames.
Application message
  -> transport header + application bytes
  -> IP header + transport unit
  -> link header + IP packet + link trailer
  -> signals/bits on one link

Each router removes the incoming link framing, processes the IP packet, and creates new framing for the outgoing link. The TCP or UDP header normally remains end to end, although NAT or a terminating proxy may rewrite or terminate transport state.

Layers are contracts, not a promise of untouched headers

Firewalls, NATs, tunnels, load balancers, offload engines, and proxies can inspect, add, remove, rewrite, or terminate protocol state. Draw the actual boundaries in the system under discussion.

docs.title: 2. Encapsulation by example
docs.text:
Assume an HTTP/1.1 client sends 900 application bytes over TCP/IPv4 on Ethernet without TCP options or VLAN tags. The simplified frame carries:

[Ethernet 14 B][IPv4 20 B][TCP 20 B][HTTP bytes 900 B][Ethernet FCS 4 B]

The frame from destination MAC through FCS is 14 + 20 + 20 + 900 + 4 = 958 B. For the classic Ethernet accounting model, add 8 byte-times for preamble/start delimiter and 12 byte-times for the interpacket gap: this frame occupies 978 byte-times, giving 900/978 = 92.02% application efficiency before acknowledgments. The gap consumes link time but is not a field inside the frame. Physical transmission also has medium-specific overhead not represented as frame payload. Ethernet's common 1500-byte MTU limits the IP packet, not the complete wire representation.

Real TCP SYNs and established packets often contain options; TLS adds records inside the TCP byte stream; HTTP/2 creates frames inside TLS; a VXLAN overlay adds an outer Ethernet/IP/UDP/VXLAN envelope. Count the headers at the boundary whose MTU or capacity you are evaluating.

Unit Scope Identifier used for delivery Typical integrity/check field Application message application protocol method, path, stream ID, message length protocol dependent TCP segment transport endpoints source/destination ports plus IPs TCP checksum UDP datagram transport endpoints source/destination ports plus IPs UDP checksum IP packet routed path destination IP prefix IPv4 header checksum; no IPv6 header checksum Ethernet frame one link destination MAC frame check sequence

Checksums have different coverage and strength. They detect classes of corruption; they do not authenticate a peer or provide application-level integrity against an attacker. TLS supplies cryptographic integrity above transport.

docs.title: 3. One request, end to end
docs.text:
Consider https://api.example.test/orders from a client to a server on another subnet. Assume DNS is already resolved and a TCP/TLS connection already exists so the trace focuses on data delivery.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Client app
    participant K as Client kernel
    participant R as Routers
    participant S as Server kernel
    participant P as Server process
    A->>K: write application bytes
    K->>K: segment, sequence, queue
    K->>R: framed IP packets
    R->>R: route, queue, forward each hop
    R->>S: destination-link frames
    S->>S: validate, reorder, acknowledge
    S->>P: readable stream bytes
    P->>S: response bytes
    S-->>K: response packets and ACKs
    K-->>A: readable response bytes

docs.title: 3.1 Before the write
docs.text:
The application may already have performed:

  • name resolution and endpoint selection;
  • a route lookup indirectly triggered by connection establishment;
  • neighbor discovery for the first-hop next hop;
  • TCP handshake, TLS handshake, and HTTP connection setup;
  • connection-pool admission and stream selection.

A warm request omits these costs. A cold request may include DNS round trips, TCP setup, TLS setup, proxy hops, certificate validation, and authentication. Always say which path a latency estimate represents.

docs.title: 3.2 The application-to-kernel boundary
docs.text:
The client serializes a request into bytes and calls a socket API. A successful write commonly means the kernel accepted some bytes into a local send buffer. It does not mean:

  • a frame reached the NIC;
  • a remote kernel acknowledged the bytes;
  • the server process read them;
  • the server committed the operation.

Blocking, nonblocking, and asynchronous APIs report acceptance differently. Partial writes are legal for stream sockets. The application or runtime must retain unwritten bytes and continue from the correct offset.

docs.title: 3.3 Transport processing
docs.text:
For TCP, the sender assigns byte sequence numbers, divides the stream according to MSS and current state, and retains unacknowledged data for possible retransmission. The amount in flight is bounded by the smaller of the receiver-advertised window and congestion-control window.

For UDP, one application send normally creates one datagram boundary. UDP does not retransmit, order, pace for congestion, or recover loss by itself. The application protocol must choose any needed behavior.

docs.title: 3.4 IP route selection
docs.text:
The host route lookup chooses an egress interface and next hop using the destination IP and policy. If the destination is off-link, the frame's destination MAC is the next-hop router, not the final server. The IP destination remains the server unless translation or tunneling changes it.

Client IP:       10.10.1.20
Default gateway: 10.10.1.1
Server IP:       10.40.8.50

First frame destination MAC = gateway MAC
IP packet destination        = 10.40.8.50

docs.title: 3.5 Neighbor resolution
docs.text: IPv4 ARP or IPv6 Neighbor Discovery maps the on-link next-hop IP to link-layer reachability information. A cache miss can queue the packet while resolution runs. Failure appears before TCP can receive any response. A stale neighbor entry can create intermittent loss during movement or failover.

docs.title: 3.6 Interface and link transmission
docs.text:
The kernel queues a packet for an interface. Offloads may let the kernel represent a larger logical buffer while hardware segments or combines packets. A packet capture at different hooks can therefore show sizes or checksums that never appeared in that form on the wire.

The interface serializes bits at a finite line rate. Switches learn or consult forwarding state and queue frames on output contention. The link validates its frame, but successful local delivery says nothing about later hops.

docs.title: 3.7 Router processing
docs.text:
At each routed hop:

  1. validate and remove incoming link framing;
  2. inspect the destination IP and policy state;
  3. decrement IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit;
  4. perform a longest-prefix route lookup;
  5. apply relevant ACL, NAT, QoS, or tunnel actions;
  6. queue the packet for an outgoing interface;
  7. create link framing suitable for the next hop.

If TTL/Hop Limit reaches zero, the router discards the packet and normally sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message. If no route exists, a node may send an unreachable indication or silently drop according to policy.

docs.title: 3.8 Destination delivery
docs.text:
The server interface and kernel validate the frame and packet, identify the transport protocol, and demultiplex using local address/port plus connection state. TCP checks sequence space, queues out-of-order bytes, acknowledges received ranges according to its rules, and exposes only an ordered byte stream to the application.

The server process may not read immediately. Scheduler delay, event-loop backlog, worker exhaustion, garbage collection, or a full downstream pool can leave bytes queued after the network has delivered them.

docs.title: 4. Packet and state flow
docs.text:
Packet flow is visible movement. State flow determines whether movement is possible.

flowchart TD
    A[Application bytes] --> B[Socket send buffer]
    B --> C[Transport packets]
    C --> D[Route and neighbor lookup]
    D --> E[Interface queue]
    E --> F[Hop forwarding queues]
    F --> G[Peer receive queue]
    G --> H[Peer application]
    I[DNS and endpoint state] -.selects.-> A
    J[Transport state] -.bounds.-> B
    K[Route policy state] -.selects.-> D
    L[Neighbor state] -.enables.-> E
    M[Application capacity] -.drains.-> G
State Owner Change trigger Failure if stale or exhausted Endpoint/DNS cache resolver and application TTL, discovery update wrong or unreachable destination Socket send/receive state endpoint kernels calls, ACKs, timers blocked writes, resets, buffer pressure Route table/FIB host and routers control-plane update wrong next hop, loop, black hole Neighbor cache each link endpoint ARP/ND exchange and timers first-hop queueing or local drop Switch forwarding state switches learning/control protocol flood, misdelivery prevention, drop Firewall/NAT flow state middlebox observed packet sequence and timeout policy drop or broken return path Server accept/request queue server stack/runtime arrivals and service completion refusal, timeout, tail-latency growth

docs.title: 5. Invariants
docs.text:
Use invariants to keep a trace honest:

  1. Layer-boundary invariant: a receiver may interpret bytes only according to the protocol and state agreed at that boundary.
  2. Next-hop invariant: an Ethernet destination identifies an on-link recipient; an IP destination identifies the routed destination before translation.
  3. Demultiplexing invariant: an arriving transport unit reaches only an endpoint whose local tuple and protocol state match it.
  4. Stream invariant: TCP preserves byte order, not application message boundaries.
  5. Buffer invariant: queued bytes occupy finite memory; sustained arrival above departure must lead to backpressure or loss.
  6. Hop-scope invariant: link-layer success is evidence for one hop, not end-to-end success.
  7. Completion invariant: transport acknowledgement is not proof of application processing or durable commit.
  8. Evidence invariant: absence at one capture point proves only that the packet was not observed there under that capture's scope and filters.

docs.title: 6.1 Serialization delay
docs.text:
Serialization delay is the time to put a unit's bits onto a link:

serialization delay (s) = size (bits) / line rate (bits/s)

A 1500-byte IP packet on a 100 Mbit/s link, ignoring additional wire overhead:

1500 B * 8 bit/B / 100,000,000 bit/s = 0.00012 s = 120 us

On 10 Gbit/s, the same calculation is 1.2 us. This is not propagation delay and not total latency.

docs.title: 6.2 Payload efficiency
docs.text:
For 1460 bytes of application data in one TCP/IPv4 packet with 20-byte IPv4 and 20-byte TCP headers:

IP-level payload efficiency = 1460 B / 1500 B = 0.9733 = 97.33%

With 40-byte IPv6 and 20-byte TCP headers under the same 1500-byte MTU, MSS is 1440 bytes and efficiency is 1440 / 1500 = 96%. TLS, HTTP, tunneling, and link overhead reduce end-to-end application efficiency further.

docs.title: 6.3 Packet count
docs.text:
For a 64 KiB = 65,536 B stream payload and MSS = 1460 B:

full segments = floor(65,536 B / 1460 B) = 44
remainder     = 65,536 B - 44 * 1460 B = 1,296 B
segments      = 45

This is a logical estimate. Segmentation offload, delayed writes, TLS record boundaries, ACK behavior, and retransmission change what captures show and what crosses each link.

docs.title: 6.4 Latency decomposition
docs.text:
one-way latency = processing + queueing + serialization + propagation
request latency = setup + outbound path + server work + inbound path

Illustrative assumption: one-way propagation is 20 ms, forwarding/serialization contributes 1 ms, server work is 8 ms, and no queueing occurs. A warm request/response is about 21 + 8 + 21 = 50 ms. Adding 30 ms of egress queueing in one direction raises it to 80 ms without changing geography or server execution.

docs.title: 7. Concrete trace: what can a timeout mean?
docs.text:
An API client times out at 500 ms. The server logs show 12 ms handler time for successful requests. Plausible paths include:

Hypothesis Packet/state story Confirming evidence Falsifying evidence Client pool wait request never reaches a socket client span has long pool phase SYN/data leaves immediately Neighbor failure packets wait/drop before gateway failed/stale neighbor state packet visible beyond first hop Path loss data or ACK disappears retransmission and capture gap no retransmission; peer receives promptly Server not accepting handshake incomplete or queued SYN retransmission, listen pressure established flow and prompt request ACK Server not reading receive queue grows peer receive queue and app backlog request consumed immediately Downstream stall server receives but handler waits server trace child span no server request correlation Response-path policy request arrives; response disappears server capture sends, client capture absent client receives bytes before deadline

The 12 ms handler metric may exclude queue time, connection setup, serialization, downstream work, or failed requests. Define timer boundaries before comparing them.

docs.title: Application evidence
docs.text:
Record phase timings rather than one total:

dns | pool_wait | connect | tls | request_write | first_byte | body_read | total

Include destination identity, protocol, connection reuse, retry attempt, deadline, and a correlation ID. Do not log secrets or full payloads.

docs.title: Socket and host evidence
docs.text:
Useful read-only evidence includes:

  • socket states and local/remote tuples;
  • send and receive queue occupancy;
  • TCP retransmission, reset, timeout, and listen-overflow counters;
  • interface errors, drops, queue drops, and link state;
  • route lookup result and neighbor state;
  • CPU scheduling, event-loop lag, and application queue depth.

docs.title: Packet evidence
docs.text:
A packet capture can establish observed sequence, timing, flags, addresses, ports, TTL/Hop Limit, ICMP, advertised windows, and retransmission patterns. Capture near both endpoints when permitted. Synchronize clocks and document capture location, filter, direction, offload context, and sampling.

Capture safely

Packet captures may contain credentials, tokens, personal data, and payloads. Follow authorization and retention policy. Prefer header-only capture, narrow filters, short duration, and isolated reproductions. The examples here do not require changing host networking.

docs.title: Common signatures
docs.text: Signature Strong possibilities Important alternative Repeated SYN, no SYN-ACK remote down, policy drop, wrong route return path failure SYN-ACK arrives, client sends reset no matching client socket, late response capture artifact or policy injection Data retransmissions and duplicate ACKs loss or reordering capture point missed packets Zero advertised receive window receiver buffer/application not draining stale or misdecoded capture Clean packet exchange, long first byte server/app/downstream delay capture taken after hidden proxy Interface drops increase local queue/ring pressure unrelated traffic on same interface ICMP Time Exceeded loop or TTL too small deliberate low-TTL probing

docs.title: 9. Design implications
docs.text:
• Budget cold and warm paths separately. Pooling removes setup from most requests but creates pool queues, stale connections, and connection storms.
  • Propagate deadlines. A server should not begin expensive work after the caller's useful deadline has expired.
  • Retry outcomes, not vague errors. A write accepted locally but timed out remotely is ambiguous. Use idempotency and reconciliation.
  • Bound every queue. Socket buffers, proxy queues, thread pools, and downstream pools trade temporary absorption for latency and memory.
  • Keep endpoint identity observable. Record resolved endpoint, selected backend, protocol, and connection reuse without exposing secrets.
  • Do not equate health checks with request success. Health may traverse a different protocol, path, payload size, or dependency set.
  • Place telemetry at ownership boundaries. Client, proxy, server kernel, and application evidence answer different questions.

docs.title: 10. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: L5 expectation L6 expectation Traces request and response through layers Identifies where overlays, proxies, NAT, and policy change the model Separates setup, network, and server latency Defines phase-level SLOs and cross-team evidence contracts Names finite queues and principal drops Quantifies overload propagation and chooses shedding boundaries Explains TCP ACK versus application success Designs idempotency and recovery for ambiguous outcomes Proposes client/server metrics and capture Builds a falsifiable multi-vantage incident plan Handles one path failure Reasons about asymmetric paths, failover, and control/data-plane disagreement

docs.title: 11. Traps
docs.text:
• Saying a request "goes down the OSI stack" without naming bytes, state, and queues.
  • Using packet, frame, segment, message, and request interchangeably.
  • Assuming the default gateway becomes the IP destination.
  • Treating a successful socket write or TCP ACK as business completion.
  • Forgetting the response path or assuming it mirrors the request path.
  • Reading an offloaded host capture as an exact wire image.
  • Attributing every retransmission to congestion; corruption, reordering, receiver behavior, and capture artifacts also matter.
  • Increasing buffers without calculating the added queueing delay.
  • Capturing broad production traffic without authorization or data controls.

docs.title: Exercise 1: calculate encapsulation
docs.text:
An Ethernet link has a 1500-byte IP MTU. TCP over IPv4 uses 20-byte IP and 32-byte TCP headers. How much application data fits in one full-sized packet? How many packets carry 10,000 bytes?

Worked solution 
effective TCP data per packet = 1500 B - 20 B - 32 B = 1448 B
full packets = floor(10,000 B / 1448 B) = 6
remainder = 10,000 B - 6 * 1448 B = 1,312 B
total data packets = 7

This excludes TLS/application framing and assumes the route really supports 1500-byte IP packets.

This is effective data length, not the SYN MSS option. Under RFC 6691 section 2, advertised MSS subtracts fixed IP/TCP headers, not options; the sender reduces actual data length for options it sends. An MSS of 1460 can coexist with 1448-byte data.

docs.title: Exercise 2: locate the destination MAC
docs.text:
A host 192.0.2.10/24 sends to 198.51.100.20 through gateway 192.0.2.1. Which address identifies the gateway in the first transmitted unit, and which identifies the final server?

Worked solution

The first Ethernet frame uses the gateway's MAC as destination. The enclosed IP packet uses 198.51.100.20 as destination. At every router, link framing changes. The IP destination remains the server unless a translator or tunnel changes the packet.

docs.title: Exercise 3: reason from two captures
docs.text:
The client capture shows request data at 10:00:00.100 and retransmission at 10:00:00.350. The server capture shows the first copy at 10:00:00.105 and emits an ACK at 10:00:00.106. The client never observes that ACK. What is established, and what remains unknown?

Worked solution

The outbound request reached the server capture point quickly, and an ACK was visible leaving that server capture point. The missing ACK lies after the server capture and before or at the client capture, subject to capture loss and clock/filter correctness. The evidence points toward the return path or client-side processing, not outbound request loss. It does not locate the exact dropping hop or prove the server application read the request.

docs.title: Exercise 4: queue delay
docs.text:
A 1 Gbit/s egress has 12 MiB queued ahead of a latency-sensitive packet. Estimate the drain time, ignoring new arrivals and framing overhead.

Worked solution 
queued bits = 12 MiB * 1,048,576 B/MiB * 8 bit/B = 100,663,296 bit
drain time = 100,663,296 bit / 1,000,000,000 bit/s
           = 0.1007 s = 100.7 ms

A large buffer can prevent a drop while violating a 50 ms latency objective. Capacity and queue policy must be evaluated together.

docs.title: Exercise 5: design an evidence plan
docs.text:
One percent of requests exceed two seconds, but server handler p99 is 40 ms. Give a minimum evidence plan.

Worked solution
  1. Verify timer boundaries and compare the same request IDs.
  2. Split client latency into DNS, pool wait, connect, TLS, write, first byte, and body.
  3. Record endpoint, protocol, reuse, attempt, and deadline.
  4. Compare proxy and server arrival timestamps, queue time, handler time, and response completion.
  5. Inspect socket queues, retransmission/reset/timeout counters, listen pressure, interface drops, and event-loop or worker queues during the same window.
  6. For an authorized narrow sample, capture headers near both endpoints or proxies with synchronized clocks.
  7. Group by zone, endpoint, connection age, payload size, and retry attempt. A size or topology correlation changes the next hypothesis.

docs.title: 02. IP, CIDR, and Routing
docs.text: IP routing is repeated local choice, not one global path reservation. Each forwarding node consults installed state, selects the most specific matching prefix, and sends the packet toward a next hop. Correct system design requires both the address arithmetic and the operational consequences of distributed, changing route state.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • use Ethernet as the architectural baseline for one-hop delivery;
  • explain ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery state and failure behavior;
  • distinguish IPv4/IPv6 addresses, prefixes, subnets, interfaces, and routes;
  • calculate network ranges and subnet plans with units and capacity margins;
  • apply longest-prefix match to a concrete route table;
  • distinguish a routing control plane, RIB, FIB, and packet data plane;
  • reason about ECMP hashing, flow distribution, asymmetry, and stateful devices;
  • diagnose route, neighbor, policy, and return-path failures from evidence;
  • turn topology mechanics into address, availability, and observability decisions.

docs.title: 1. First-principles model
docs.text:
An IP packet carries a destination address. A node compares that address against prefixes in a forwarding table. Among matching entries, the longest prefix wins because it describes the smallest, most specific destination set.

destination IP + local policy + installed forwarding state
    -> selected route
    -> next hop and egress interface
    -> on-link neighbor resolution
    -> frame transmission

The route is local. The next router repeats the decision from its own state. Forward and reverse traffic can therefore take different paths.

flowchart LR
    H[Host route lookup] --> N[Resolve next-hop neighbor]
    N --> R1[Router FIB lookup]
    R1 --> R2[Next router FIB lookup]
    R2 --> D[Destination subnet]
    C[Routing control plane] -.installs prefixes.-> R1
    C -.installs prefixes.-> R2

docs.title: 2. Ethernet as the link baseline
docs.text:
Ethernet provides frame delivery within a link-layer domain. A frame includes source and destination MAC addresses and an EtherType identifying the carried protocol. Switches forward using MAC-related state; routers forward IP packets between links.

Architecturally:

  • a MAC address is meaningful for delivery on the current link;
  • an IP address supports delivery across routed links;
  • a broadcast domain bounds Ethernet broadcast propagation;
  • a router separates IP subnets and rewrites link framing per hop;
  • VLANs create logical Ethernet segments but do not eliminate the need for routing between subnets.

For an off-subnet destination, a host sends the frame to the router's MAC while preserving the remote IP destination. This single distinction resolves many interview mistakes.

docs.title: 2.1 Switch learning baseline
docs.text:
A learning bridge observes source MAC addresses and associates them with ingress ports. For a known unicast destination, it forwards toward the learned port. Unknown unicast and broadcast frames are flooded within the applicable broadcast domain, subject to policy. Entries age; loops require prevention or a controlled fabric design.

Modern datacenters may use routed fabrics, overlays, or centrally programmed forwarding rather than one large learning domain. Ethernet remains useful as the local-delivery model, not as a claim about the whole topology.

docs.title: 3.1 IPv4 ARP
docs.text:
ARP resolves an on-link IPv4 next-hop address to a MAC address. A simplified miss is:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant H as Host
    participant L as Local link
    participant G as Next hop
    H->>L: ARP request: who has next-hop IP?
    L->>G: broadcast request
    G-->>H: ARP reply with MAC
    H->>G: queued IP packet in Ethernet frame

ARP resolves the next hop, which may be the destination host for an on-link route or a router for a remote route. Cache states and timers vary by implementation. Duplicate addresses, stale entries, suppressed replies, link isolation, or policy can prevent resolution.

docs.title: 3.2 IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
docs.text:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 messages for address resolution, router discovery, prefix information, reachability confirmation, and duplicate-address detection. It uses multicast rather than IPv4 ARP broadcast. Blocking ICMPv6 indiscriminately can break basic IPv6 operation.

Neighbor Discovery and routing remain separate:

  • routing chooses an on-link next hop;
  • ND resolves and tracks that neighbor's link-layer reachability;
  • a reachable neighbor does not prove the final destination is reachable;
  • an unresolved neighbor can stop traffic even when the route table looks correct.

docs.title: 3.3 Neighbor invariants
docs.text:
1. Resolve only addresses considered on-link by local routing state.
  2. A neighbor-cache entry has scope on one interface/link.
  3. Neighbor reachability is time-varying state, not a permanent identity fact.
  4. Gratuitous ARP or unsolicited advertisements can update caches during legitimate movement, but require security controls in hostile domains.

docs.title: 4.1 Prefix notation
docs.text:
CIDR notation writes an address and prefix length, such as 192.0.2.64/26. The first 26 bits identify the prefix; the remaining 6 bits identify addresses inside that block.

IPv4 address bits = 32
host bits          = 32 - prefix length
block size         = 2 ^ host bits addresses

For IPv6:

IPv6 address bits = 128
addresses in /64  = 2 ^ (128 - 64) = 2 ^ 64

IPv6 subnet planning should not copy IPv4 conservation habits blindly. A /64 is the standard subnet size for mechanisms that depend on 64-bit interface identifiers, including SLAAC. Plan hierarchy and route aggregation rather than counting individual host addresses.

docs.title: 4.2 Address scope and semantics
docs.text:
Family/type Example Design meaning IPv4 private-use 10.0.0.0/8 not globally routed on the public Internet; overlap is still possible IPv4 loopback 127.0.0.0/8 local host only IPv4 link-local 169.254.0.0/16 local link behavior, not general routed service addressing IPv6 global unicast commonly 2000::/3 space globally scoped unicast addressing subject to allocation/routing IPv6 link-local fe80::/10 required local-link scope; interface context matters IPv6 loopback ::1/128 local host only IPv6 unspecified ::/128 absence of an address; never a normal destination

An address assigned to an interface is not necessarily a promise of reachability. ACLs, routes, security groups, source selection, neighbor state, service binding, and return paths must all agree.

docs.title: 5.1 Find a network range
docs.text:
For 10.24.37.142/20, /20 corresponds to mask 255.255.240.0. The third-octet block size is 256 - 240 = 16. Blocks begin at 0, 16, 32, 48, and so on. 37 lies in 32-47.

network = 10.24.32.0/20
range   = 10.24.32.0 through 10.24.47.255
count   = 2 ^ (32 - 20) = 4096 addresses

Traditional IPv4 subnet terminology reserves the all-zero host address as the subnet identifier and all-one host address as directed broadcast, yielding 4094 conventional host addresses. Platform reservation rules can reserve additional addresses. /31 point-to-point semantics and /32 host routes are special cases; never apply 2^h - 2 mechanically to every context.

docs.title: 5.2 Subdivide a block
docs.text:
Split 10.40.0.0/22 into /24 blocks:

new prefix bits = 24 - 22 = 2
subnet count    = 2 ^ 2 = 4

10.40.0.0/24
10.40.1.0/24
10.40.2.0/24
10.40.3.0/24

Split it into /26 blocks:

new prefix bits = 26 - 22 = 4
subnet count    = 2 ^ 4 = 16
addresses each = 2 ^ (32 - 26) = 64

docs.title: 5.3 Size with headroom
docs.text:
Suppose a zone needs 180 workload interfaces, 30 infrastructure interfaces, and 25% growth on the combined 210:

planned interfaces = 210 * 1.25 = 262.5 -> 263

A conventional /24 has 256 total addresses and is already too small before platform reservations. A /23 has 512 total addresses. The correct choice still depends on cloud reservations, rolling deployments, surge, failure replacement, and whether each workload consumes multiple addresses.

Address capacity is deploy capacity

A subnet can exhaust during a rollout even when steady-state hosts fit. Include old and new replicas, load balancer interfaces, managed-service endpoints, node churn, and emergency headroom.

docs.title: 6. Longest-prefix match
docs.text:
Given this simplified table:

Prefix Next hop Interface 0.0.0.0/0 192.0.2.1 eth0 10.0.0.0/8 10.1.0.1 eth1 10.24.0.0/16 10.2.0.1 eth2 10.24.8.0/24 directly connected eth3 10.24.8.128/25 10.3.0.1 eth4

Selections are:

Destination Winning prefix Reason 8.8.8.8 /0 only default matches 10.9.4.5 /8 /8 is most specific match 10.24.7.5 /16 /24 does not cover third octet 7 10.24.8.40 /24 /25 covers only 128-255 10.24.8.200 /25 all broader routes match, /25 wins

Administrative preference and route metrics choose among candidate routes according to implementation/control-plane rules. Longest-prefix selection comes first for forwarding specificity; a more attractive default cannot override a matching specific route.

The table assumes usable next-hop adjacencies not shown here. Policy-routing rules select a lookup table before its longest-prefix match; a more-specific route in another VRF/table need not apply. ECMP flow affinity also assumes stable membership and hashing: reconvergence can move an existing connection's packets.

docs.title: 7. Packet and state flow: route tables, RIBs, and FIBs
docs.text:
Terms vary by implementation, but the conceptual separation is stable:

  • Routing information base (RIB): candidate routes learned from connected networks, static configuration, or routing protocols.
  • Route selection: policy chooses preferred route or next-hop set per prefix.
  • Forwarding information base (FIB): optimized installed state used to forward packets.
  • Control plane: learns, computes, validates, and distributes state.
  • Data plane: applies installed forwarding state to packets.
flowchart TD
    A[Connected and static routes] --> R[RIB]
    B[Routing protocols] --> R
    P[Import and preference policy] --> R
    R --> S[Best-route selection]
    S --> F[FIB and next-hop objects]
    F --> D[Packet forwarding]

A control plane can report intended convergence while one device, line card, host namespace, or virtual switch retains stale data-plane state. L6 diagnosis compares desired route, selected route, installed FIB, and observed packet forwarding.

docs.title: 7.1 Recursive next hops
docs.text: A route can name a next-hop IP that itself requires another route lookup to resolve an egress adjacency. Operationally, a visible prefix is usable only if its next-hop chain resolves to a valid interface/neighbor. A route shown in a control table may therefore remain inactive or fail forwarding.

docs.title: 7.2 Policy routing
docs.text: Some systems use source address, mark, interface, tenant, VRF, or other fields in addition to destination. "Show the route to X" is incomplete if the actual packet carries policy selectors. Reproduce the source, namespace, and policy context.

docs.title: 8. ECMP, hashing, and asymmetry
docs.text:
Equal-cost multipath installs multiple eligible next hops for a prefix. Implementations usually hash packet fields so packets from one flow tend to follow one path, avoiding widespread transport reordering.

Common hash inputs include some combination of:

source IP, destination IP, protocol, source port, destination port

docs.title: 8.1 Distribution is statistical
docs.text:
With N equal links and many independent, similarly sized flows, expected average flow count per link is roughly total flows divided by N. Real traffic is skewed:

  • one elephant flow usually remains on one member;
  • a small number of flows distributes unevenly;
  • correlated tuples can hash poorly;
  • member removal remaps some or many flows depending on algorithm;
  • encapsulation can hide or expose inner fields to the hash.

Four 10 Gbit/s paths do not guarantee one TCP flow 40 Gbit/s. They provide aggregate capacity across distributable flows, bounded by endpoint and path constraints.

docs.title: 8.2 Asymmetric routing
docs.text:
The reverse flow performs independent lookups and may traverse different links or devices. Asymmetry is valid IP behavior but interacts with stateful systems:

  • a firewall that sees only one direction may reject traffic;
  • NAT state created on one appliance may be absent on another;
  • captures on one path can miss the response;
  • latency and MTU can differ by direction;
  • failure detection can remove only one direction's route.

Stateful service insertion requires symmetry, synchronized/distributed state, or an architecture that does not require one box to observe both directions.

docs.title: 8.3 ECMP failure example
docs.text:
If one of eight ECMP members black-holes traffic and flow hashes are stable, approximately one eighth of sufficiently diverse new flows may fail under a simple uniform model:

expected failing-flow fraction = 1 / 8 = 12.5%

That is an expectation, not a guaranteed observed percentage. Retries with a new source port may hash to another path and appear to "fix" the request, while retries reusing a connection remain pinned to the failed path.

docs.title: 9. Routing invariants
docs.text:
1. Prefix invariant: a /p fixes the first p address bits; all remaining combinations belong to the block.
  2. Selection invariant: forwarding chooses the most specific matching installed prefix before considering equal candidates for that prefix.
  3. Hop invariant: each router chooses only the next hop from local state; no ordinary IP header guarantees the complete path.
  4. Return-path invariant: reachability is directional until the reverse path is proven.
  5. Adjacency invariant: a route that cannot resolve its next-hop adjacency cannot forward useful traffic.
  6. Aggregation invariant: advertising a summary claims reachability for the entire summary unless more specific routing or discard policy safely handles holes.
  7. Stateful-path invariant: a stateful middlebox must receive packets needed to create and use its flow state.
  8. Capacity invariant: usable subnet capacity includes platform reservations and deployment surge, not only steady-state application interfaces.

docs.title: 10. Failure signatures and observability evidence
docs.text: Failure Typical signature Evidence to collect Common confusion No matching route immediate local error or drop route lookup in exact namespace/source context remote firewall Bad more-specific route one prefix fails while aggregate works RIB/FIB entry and route provenance DNS because hostnames correlate Neighbor failure same-subnet or gateway traffic stalls neighbor state, ARP/ND exchange, interface/VLAN remote service outage Routing loop TTL/Hop Limit expires, repeating hops traceroute-style evidence, device FIBs application retry loop ECMP bad member stable subset of flows fail tuple-correlated failures, per-member counters random endpoint errors Asymmetric stateful drop one direction visible, return denied both-direction flow logs and appliance state server never responded Address overlap destination follows unintended local/private route full route/policy tables at both domains packet loss Subnet exhaustion deployments cannot allocate interfaces address manager/platform allocation errors compute quota Stale FIB control plane correct, packets wrong intended route vs installed FIB vs capture slow application propagation

docs.title: Evidence sequence
docs.text:
1. Resolve the actual destination address used by the failing request.
  2. Identify source address, namespace/VRF, interface, and policy marks.
  3. Obtain the host's route decision for that exact context.
  4. Verify next-hop neighbor state on the selected interface.
  5. Compare packet observation before and after each owned boundary.
  6. Inspect flow/ACL/NAT evidence in both directions.
  7. Compare desired control-plane route, selected route, and installed FIB.
  8. Group failures by source/destination prefix and five-tuple to expose ECMP correlation.

Read-only inspection is usually enough for diagnosis. Do not add routes, clear neighbor caches, or alter interfaces on a shared or production host merely to test a theory.

docs.title: Address plans
docs.text:
• Allocate hierarchical prefixes by region, environment, zone, and function so summaries remain meaningful.
  • Reserve growth and migration space; renumbering is a cross-system project.
  • Prevent overlap across networks that may later connect through peering, VPN, acquisition, or disaster recovery.
  • Treat IPv4 scarcity and translation as operational costs; design dual-stack behavior explicitly where used.
  • Track address utilization as a capacity SLI, not an inventory footnote.

docs.title: Routing and failure domains
docs.text:
• Prefer smaller failure domains and aggregated external announcements, while preserving specific internal steering where needed.
  • Withdraw a route only when the serving unit cannot safely handle traffic; avoid route flaps from noisy health checks.
  • Ensure failover capacity can absorb shifted traffic. Reachability without capacity is not resilience.
  • Test both directions and long-lived flows. Existing flows may retain old state while new flows use new routes.
  • Put stateful appliances in a topology with explicit symmetry or state sharing.

docs.title: ECMP-aware applications
docs.text:
• Use many connections only when concurrency and backend semantics justify them; do not multiply connections solely to game hashes.
  • Keep retries bounded and understand whether a retry reuses the same tuple/path.
  • Measure by path-relevant dimensions such as zone, interface, tunnel, source/destination prefix, and backend.
  • Plan draining for member removal so remapped traffic does not overload survivors.

docs.title: 12. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: L5 expectation L6 expectation Computes CIDR ranges and capacity correctly Creates an aggregateable plan with surge, migration, and overlap strategy Applies longest-prefix match Distinguishes desired RIB state, selected route, FIB, and observed forwarding Explains default gateway and neighbor resolution Diagnoses adjacency, policy-routing, namespace, and overlay interactions Uses ECMP for aggregate scale Quantifies skew, remapping, elephant flows, and survivor capacity Notes return-path requirements Designs stateful boundaries under asymmetry and partial convergence Suggests route and flow telemetry Defines cross-domain evidence, rollout, rollback, and ownership

docs.title: 13. Traps
docs.text:
• Treating a subnet mask as a decimal naming convention rather than fixed leading bits.
  • Using 2^(32-p)-2 for /31, /32, or provider-specific usable capacity without checking semantics.
  • Assuming private IPv4 ranges cannot overlap or cannot be routed internally.
  • Confusing the remote IP with the first-hop MAC destination.
  • Believing a route table entry proves forwarding hardware or virtual-switch state.
  • Saying ECMP "bonds bandwidth" for one flow.
  • Assuming reverse traffic follows the same path.
  • Advertising a summary without handling unreachable holes safely.
  • Fixing an apparent neighbor issue by clearing production state before collecting evidence.
  • Blocking all ICMPv6 and expecting IPv6 Neighbor Discovery to work.

docs.title: Exercise 1: range and membership
docs.text:
Find the network, final address, and total address count for 172.20.77.9/21. Does 172.20.80.1 belong?

Worked solution

/21 has mask 255.255.248.0; third-octet blocks have size 8. 77 is in the 72-79 block.

network = 172.20.72.0/21
final   = 172.20.79.255
count   = 2 ^ 11 = 2048 addresses

172.20.80.1 belongs to the next /21, so it does not match.

docs.title: Exercise 2: deployment sizing
docs.text:
A subnet must support 220 current workload interfaces, a 50% rolling surge, 24 infrastructure addresses, and 15 provider-reserved addresses. Select the smallest IPv4 prefix with enough total addresses.

Worked solution 
surged workload = 220 * 1.5 = 330
required total  = 330 + 24 + 15 = 369 addresses

A /24 has 256 total addresses and fails. A /23 has 512 and is the smallest power-of-two CIDR block that fits. Operational policy may choose a larger aggregate for future growth.

docs.title: Exercise 3: longest-prefix route
docs.text:
Routes are 10.0.0.0/8 -> A, 10.64.0.0/10 -> B, 10.80.0.0/16 -> C, and 10.80.4.0/22 -> D. Select paths for 10.80.6.7, 10.80.9.1, and 10.100.1.1.

Worked solution
  • 10.80.6.7 is inside 10.80.4.0-10.80.7.255, so /22 -> D wins.
  • 10.80.9.1 misses /22 but matches /16 -> C.
  • 10.100.1.1 is inside 10.64.0.0/10 (second octet 64-127), so /10 -> B wins over /8.

docs.title: Exercise 4: ECMP partial failure
docs.text:
Four ECMP members carry 40,000 short flows/s uniformly in expectation. One member silently drops. Estimate affected new flows and explain why retries may distort measurement.

Worked solution 
expected affected flows/s = 40,000 / 4 = 10,000 flows/s

Actual load varies with hash and flow sizes. A retry on a new connection may choose a new source port and member, masking the defect while adding traffic. A retry on the same connection remains on its established path. Measure first attempts by tuple and member-correlated evidence rather than only terminal success.

docs.title: Exercise 5: asymmetric firewall
docs.text:
Requests traverse firewall A, but route convergence sends responses through firewall B. Both keep local connection state. Predict the failure and propose three design options.

Worked solution

Firewall B may see return traffic without state created by the request and drop it. Options are:

  1. enforce symmetric routing through the same state owner;
  2. synchronize/distribute state with defined convergence and failure semantics;
  3. remove the stateful dependency from that path or use stateless policy where requirements permit.

The evidence plan compares directional flow logs, state-table entries, routes/FIBs, and endpoint captures. Merely loosening policy hides the architecture defect and may weaken security.

docs.title: 15. Authoritative sources
docs.text:
• RFC 791: Internet Protocol
  • RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6
  • RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing
  • RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol
  • RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IPv6
  • RFC 3021: Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links
  • RFC 4291: IPv6 Addressing Architecture

docs.title: 03. Transport, Sockets, and Congestion
docs.text: Transport protocols turn best-effort IP delivery into communication usable by applications. TCP offers an ordered reliable byte stream with flow and congestion control. UDP offers message-oriented datagrams with minimal transport machinery. QUIC builds secure multiplexed transport over UDP in user space. None of them defines business message boundaries or proves application success.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • model TCP as endpoint state over numbered bytes rather than a sequence of application messages;
  • explain handshake, acknowledgement, retransmission, flow control, congestion control, and teardown;
  • distinguish receiver window, congestion window, MSS, RTT, RTO, and bandwidth-delay product;
  • reason about slow start, loss, serialization, latency, and achievable throughput;
  • explain TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT, listen queues, accept queues, socket buffers, and file-descriptor limits;
  • design application framing over a stream and handle partial reads/writes;
  • choose TCP, UDP, or QUIC from application requirements and deployment constraints;
  • correlate application symptoms with socket, kernel, packet, and peer evidence;
  • establish bounded connection, buffer, queue, and retry budgets.

docs.title: 1. First-principles model
docs.text:
IP may lose, duplicate, reorder, or delay packets. A transport protocol adds endpoint behavior. TCP maintains state that maps an application byte stream onto IP packets and reconstructs the ordered stream at the peer.

Application bytes
  + endpoint identity and protocol state
  + sequence/acknowledgement state
  + retransmission timers
  + receiver capacity
  + network-capacity estimate
  = TCP's reliable ordered byte-stream service

A TCP connection is conventionally identified by protocol plus source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port. Names, processes, and users are not part of this network tuple. NAT or proxies can create different tuples on different path segments.

flowchart LR
    A[App writes stream bytes] --> S[Send buffer]
    S --> X[Sequence and segment]
    X --> N[Network]
    N --> R[Peer receive and reorder]
    R --> B[Receive buffer]
    B --> P[Peer app reads bytes]
    C[cwnd] -.network bound.-> X
    W[rwnd] -.receiver bound.-> X
    T[RTO and loss recovery] -.retransmit.-> X

docs.title: 2. Packet and state flow: TCP handshake
docs.text:
The three-way handshake establishes bidirectional sequence state and confirms both directions sufficiently to create a connection:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: SYN, seq=x
    S-->>C: SYN-ACK, seq=y, ack=x+1
    C->>S: ACK, ack=y+1
    Note over C,S: established byte-stream state

SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number. Sequence numbers count bytes, not packets. ACK value N identifies the next expected sequence position and cumulatively acknowledges the preceding contiguous sequence space. TCP sequence numbers wrap modulo 2^32, so implementations use serial-number comparisons within the valid window rather than ordinary unsigned less-than. Modern TCP may also use selective acknowledgement information to report noncontiguous received blocks.

docs.title: 2.1 Simplified active/passive states
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CLOSED
    CLOSED --> SYN_SENT: active open
    CLOSED --> LISTEN: passive open
    LISTEN --> SYN_RECEIVED: receive SYN
    SYN_SENT --> ESTABLISHED: receive SYN-ACK, send ACK
    SYN_RECEIVED --> ESTABLISHED: receive ACK
    ESTABLISHED --> FIN_WAIT_1: active close
    ESTABLISHED --> CLOSE_WAIT: receive FIN
    CLOSE_WAIT --> LAST_ACK: app closes
    FIN_WAIT_1 --> FIN_WAIT_2: FIN acknowledged
    FIN_WAIT_2 --> TIME_WAIT: receive FIN, send ACK
    LAST_ACK --> CLOSED: FIN acknowledged
    TIME_WAIT --> CLOSED: timer expires

This omits simultaneous open/close and intermediate variants, but exposes ownership: receiving a FIN moves the kernel side toward CLOSE_WAIT; only the local application closing moves it onward.

docs.title: 2.2 Handshake failure signatures
docs.text: Observation Likely boundary Alternatives to test SYN retransmits, no SYN-ACK route, policy, listener, return path capture loss, server SYN handling pressure SYN-ACK arrives, no final ACK client path/state client abort or capture point mismatch Handshake completes, immediate RST no valid socket/app policy/late tuple proxy rejection or process restart Connect latency spikes only on new connections setup path or listen pressure DNS/TLS included in timer

docs.title: 3. TCP is a byte stream: application framing
docs.text:
TCP does not preserve write boundaries. If a sender writes "ABC" then "DEF", a receiver may read "ABCDEF", "AB" then "CDEF", or other contiguous partitions. It cannot assume one read equals one message.

Common framing schemes:

Scheme Example Strength Trap Fixed length every record 64 B simple wasted space, inflexible evolution Delimiter newline-terminated record inspectable escaping and unbounded missing delimiter Length prefix 4-byte length + payload efficient binary framing malicious/invalid length allocation Self-describing protocol HTTP headers/chunks, protobuf envelope rich semantics parser complexity and limits still required

Length-prefixed receiver logic must:

  1. accumulate enough bytes for the length field;
  2. validate length against a configured maximum before allocation;
  3. accumulate exactly that payload length across any number of reads;
  4. decode one message and retain excess bytes for the next;
  5. handle EOF in a partial header or body as truncation.

Framing invariant: each accepted message consumes exactly its declared bytes under a bounded, validated grammar. Transport ordering does not make the grammar safe.

docs.title: 4. ACKs, loss, and retransmission timeout
docs.text: TCP retains unacknowledged bytes. Acknowledgements advance the send window. Loss can be inferred from acknowledgement patterns or a retransmission timer. Exact algorithms evolve; reason from principles and consult implementation evidence before claiming a specific threshold.

docs.title: 4.1 RTT estimation and RTO
docs.text:
Round-trip time varies. TCP maintains a smoothed RTT and variation estimate, then derives a retransmission timeout with a safety margin. RFC 6298 describes the standard estimator:

RTTVAR <- (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |SRTT - R'|
SRTT   <- (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R'
RTO    <- SRTT + max(G, K * RTTVAR)

where R' is a measured RTT sample, G is clock granularity, alpha = 1/8, beta = 1/4, and K = 4 in the RFC algorithm. Bounds and implementation behavior apply. Timeout retransmissions back off because repeated immediate retransmission would worsen overload.

An application deadline and TCP RTO are different clocks. The application can abandon a request before transport gives up, or wait long after the business outcome is no longer useful.

Update RTTVAR using the previous SRTT before updating SRTT. RFC 6298 initializes the first sample separately and recommends a one-second minimum computed RTO; implementation-specific lower bounds are not the formula itself. Exclude RTT samples from ambiguously retransmitted data unless timestamps resolve the ambiguity (Karn's rule).

docs.title: 4.2 Duplicate ACKs and selective acknowledgement
docs.text: If later data arrives while a gap remains, cumulative ACKs repeat the next expected sequence. This can trigger fast loss recovery before RTO. SACK-capable peers can describe received blocks so the sender retransmits missing ranges more efficiently. Reordering can produce duplicate ACK patterns without actual loss.

docs.title: 4.3 ACK is not commit
docs.text:
A TCP ACK proves reception by peer transport state according to TCP semantics. It does not prove:

  • peer application read;
  • request parsing succeeded;
  • authorization passed;
  • database committed;
  • response will arrive.

Application protocols need explicit responses, identifiers, idempotency, and reconciliation for ambiguous failures.

docs.title: 5. Flow control versus congestion control
docs.text:
These solve different capacity problems.

Mechanism Protects Signal/state Sender limit Flow control receiving endpoint and buffer advertised receive window rwnd do not outrun receiver capacity Congestion control network path congestion window cwnd, ACK/loss/ECN-derived state do not overload path estimate

Approximate outstanding-data bound:

in-flight bytes <= min(cwnd, rwnd)

Additional sender/application/socket constraints can lower actual flight size.

docs.title: 5.1 Receive window pressure
docs.text:
If the peer application stops reading, its receive buffer fills and advertised window shrinks, potentially to zero. The sender may have a successful established connection but cannot advance useful data. The root cause can be application saturation, not network congestion.

RFC 9293 section 3.8.6.1 requires zero-window probes so a lost window update cannot deadlock progress. Probe ACKs establish responsive transport state, not useful application work. Bound application deadlines and retained resources separately.

docs.title: 5.2 Congestion window
docs.text: cwnd is sender state estimating safe network flight. Congestion-control algorithms differ, but all must share path capacity responsibly. A large receiver window cannot authorize sending beyond congestion control.

docs.title: 5.3 Slow start
docs.text:
At connection start or after certain recovery conditions, the sender does not know path capacity. Slow start increases flight size rapidly as ACKs return, roughly doubling per RTT under an idealized ACK model until a threshold or congestion event changes growth.

If initial congestion window is 10 MSS, MSS is 1460 B, and no other bound applies:

initial flight = 10 * 1460 B = 14,600 B

An object of 200 KiB cannot all be sent in the first flight. Under an idealized sequence of full growth rounds, flight opportunities might be about 14.6 KB, 29.2 KB, 58.4 KB, 116.8 KB. Real ACK behavior, protocol overhead, pacing, loss, implementation, and object framing alter completion.

Connection reuse avoids repeated handshake and initial growth but can inherit stale path state, head-of-line blocking at some layers, or failure coupling. Pool decisions need both latency and resilience reasoning.

docs.title: 6. Calculations with units: latency, loss, serialization, and BDP
6.1 Propagation versus serialization
docs.text:
Propagation delay is travel time through the medium. Serialization delay is time to place bits on the link.

serialization (s) = bytes * 8 bit/B / rate (bit/s)

A 1 MiB response over a 100 Mbit/s bottleneck needs at least:

1,048,576 B * 8 / 100,000,000 bit/s = 0.0839 s = 83.9 ms

This excludes headers, contention, propagation, retransmission, and server work. A 50 ms timeout cannot succeed for that transfer over this bottleneck even with zero propagation.

docs.title: 6.2 Bandwidth-delay product
docs.text:
BDP is the amount of data needed in flight to fill a path:

BDP (bit) = bottleneck bandwidth (bit/s) * RTT (s)

For 1 Gbit/s and 80 ms RTT:

BDP = 1,000,000,000 bit/s * 0.080 s = 80,000,000 bit
    = 10,000,000 B = 10 MB decimal

To approach 1 Gbit/s for one flow, the effective flight window must be around 10 MB or more, and endpoints plus application must sustain the rate. With only a 1 MiB effective window:

window-limited throughput <= 1,048,576 B / 0.080 s
                          = 13,107,200 B/s
                          = 104.9 Mbit/s

docs.title: 6.3 Loss and throughput
docs.text: Loss can impose at least one recovery interval and reduce cwnd; repeated loss can collapse throughput even when average link utilization looks low. Small random loss is especially costly on high-BDP paths because regrowing flight takes time. Do not use one universal closed-form throughput formula as a capacity promise: congestion algorithm, RTT, loss pattern, pacing, offloads, ACK strategy, and competing flows matter.

docs.title: 6.4 Queueing
docs.text:
If arrival rate persistently exceeds service rate, queue occupancy grows until admission slows or data drops. A 20 MB queue before a 1 Gbit/s bottleneck represents:

20,000,000 B * 8 / 1,000,000,000 bit/s = 0.160 s = 160 ms

Buffering can convert loss into deadline violation. Active queue management, pacing, admission control, and bounded concurrency address different parts of this problem.

docs.title: 7. Concrete lifecycle example: teardown, TIME_WAIT, and CLOSE_WAIT
docs.text: TCP closes each byte-stream direction independently. A FIN means "I will send no more bytes"; the receiver can still send in the other direction until it closes.

docs.title: 7.1 TIME_WAIT
docs.text:
The endpoint performing the active close commonly enters TIME_WAIT after acknowledging the peer's FIN. The state allows retransmission of the final ACK and helps prevent delayed segments from an old incarnation being confused with a later connection using the same tuple.

Many TIME_WAIT sockets are not automatically a leak. They can indicate high connection churn. Risks include ephemeral-port pressure, state memory, NAT table pressure, and load balancer churn. Prefer connection reuse and measured capacity planning over unsafe timer reductions.

Approximate concurrent TIME_WAIT entries:

entries = active closes/s * TIME_WAIT duration (s)

At 5,000 active closes/s and 60 s retention:

5,000 /s * 60 s = 300,000 entries

This is a sizing estimate, not a universal OS duration or limit.

docs.title: 7.2 CLOSE_WAIT
docs.text: CLOSE_WAIT means the local TCP stack received the peer's FIN, but the local application has not closed its side. Persistent growth strongly suggests application lifecycle failure: leaked sockets, stuck cleanup, blocked handlers, or ownership confusion. Kernel tuning does not substitute for closing resources.

docs.title: 7.3 Reset versus graceful close
docs.text: FIN supports orderly EOF after preceding bytes. RST aborts connection state and can discard unread or unsent expectations. Applications must define whether EOF before a complete framed message is valid, retryable, or an ambiguous operation.

docs.title: 8. Listening, accepting, and server queues
docs.text:
A listening socket represents passive-open state. Conceptually, servers face at least two connection stages:

  1. handshakes in progress;
  2. established connections waiting for the application to accept them.

Operating systems name and implement these queues differently. The application also has worker/event-loop/request queues after accept.

flowchart LR
    S[SYN arrivals] --> H[Handshake state]
    H --> A[Completed accept queue]
    A --> P[Application accept]
    P --> R[Request parsing and work]
    R --> D[Downstream capacity]

Increasing a listen backlog can absorb a short burst but cannot repair an application that accepts or serves slower than arrivals. It adds waiting and state. Observe handshake drops, completed-queue overflow, accept rate, active connections, request queue age, and downstream saturation together.

docs.title: 8.1 Little's Law for connections
docs.text:
If a service completes 8,000 requests/s and average connection-held request time is 250 ms with one in-flight request per connection:

average in-flight requests = 8,000 request/s * 0.250 s
                           = 2,000 requests

At 70% target utilization for a relevant constrained pool:

provisioned capacity = ceil(2,000 / 0.70) = ceil(2857.143) = 2,858 slots

Tail latency and multiplexing change the relationship. Use distributions and burst tests, not only averages.

docs.title: 9.1 Buffers
docs.text:
Send buffers hold application bytes not yet fully acknowledged; receive buffers hold arrived bytes not yet consumed. Larger buffers may support high BDP and bursts but consume memory and can hide backpressure.

For 40,000 connections with an illustrative committed average of 128 KiB combined socket memory each:

memory = 40,000 * 128 KiB
       = 5,120,000 KiB
       = 4.883 GiB

Actual kernels autotune and account memory differently. Measure committed and pressured memory rather than multiplying configured maxima as if fully allocated.

docs.title: 9.2 File descriptors
docs.text:
On Unix-like systems, sockets consume file descriptors. A process limit must cover listening sockets, accepted connections, outbound connections, files, pipes, logs, and operational headroom.

FD budget >= inbound sockets + outbound sockets + non-socket FDs + surge + diagnostics reserve

If each of 20,000 inbound requests can hold one outbound connection, naive worst-case socket demand already approaches 40,000 plus overhead. Pools and multiplexing change counts but introduce queueing and per-connection stream limits.

An EMFILE-style per-process exhaustion can prevent logs, config reads, and recovery connections as well as accepts. Alert before exhaustion and preserve operational reserve.

docs.title: 10. UDP boundaries
docs.text:
UDP supplies ports, a checksum, and datagram boundaries over IP. It does not supply connection handshake, reliable delivery, ordering, duplicate suppression, flow control, congestion control, or path migration.

Use UDP directly when application semantics can tolerate loss or implement the necessary behavior, such as bounded real-time media, simple request protocols with explicit transaction IDs, or a substrate for a protocol such as QUIC.

Application responsibilities may include:

  • request/response correlation and duplicate handling;
  • authentication and anti-replay;
  • retransmission and deadline policy;
  • congestion-responsive sending;
  • fragmentation avoidance and payload bounds;
  • source spoofing/amplification defense;
  • session continuity across address changes.

One UDP send preserves one datagram boundary at the receiver if delivered. Oversized datagrams may be fragmented or dropped. A receive buffer smaller than the datagram can truncate it according to API semantics.

docs.title: 11. QUIC boundaries
docs.text:
QUIC runs over UDP and integrates transport security using TLS. It provides reliable streams, congestion control, flow control, connection IDs, and path-related mechanisms in the QUIC protocol rather than kernel TCP.

Important boundaries:

  • QUIC streams avoid transport head-of-line blocking between streams when loss affects one stream; ordered bytes within the affected stream still wait for gaps.
  • Encryption limits middlebox visibility into transport internals while exposing selected header fields needed for routing.
  • Connection IDs can support continuity across address/port changes under protocol validation; application identity and authorization remain separate.
  • QUIC still shares path capacity and must perform congestion control.
  • UDP blocking, idle timeouts, NAT state, MTU, and load-balancer connection-ID routing remain operational concerns.
  • HTTP/3 uses QUIC; QUIC itself is not the HTTP application protocol.
Requirement TCP UDP directly QUIC Reliable ordered bytes one connection stream application-defined per QUIC stream Message boundaries application framing datagram boundary application framing within streams; optional DATAGRAM extension Built-in encryption no no yes, integrated TLS Multiplexed streams application protocol, e.g. HTTP/2 application-defined transport-native streams Kernel/middlebox maturity broad broad primitive deployment path must support UDP/QUIC Address migration connection usually tuple-bound application-defined connection-ID-based protocol support

docs.title: 12. Transport invariants
docs.text:
1. Sequence invariant: TCP acknowledges byte positions, not application operations.
  2. Ordering invariant: a TCP reader sees ordered bytes or EOF/error; message boundaries require application framing.
  3. Flight invariant: useful unacknowledged flight cannot sustainably exceed receiver and congestion constraints.
  4. Queue invariant: sustained admission above completion grows queueing until backpressure, rejection, timeout, or exhaustion.
  5. Close invariant: peer FIN does not release the local application's resource ownership.
  6. Tuple/state invariant: packets must match live endpoint state; stale packets and tuple reuse require protection.
  7. Resource invariant: every accepted connection consumes bounded state, memory, descriptors, and processing opportunity.
  8. Completion invariant: transport delivery is not business commit.
  9. Congestion invariant: reliability mechanisms must not retransmit without bound into a congested path.

docs.title: 13. Failure signatures and observability evidence
docs.text: Signature Primary hypotheses Required evidence Connect timeout SYN path, listener pressure, return path, policy SYN/SYN-ACK capture, route/flow logs, listen counters Connection refused/reset no listener, explicit reject, stale pooled connection, process restart flags, listener lifecycle, deployment timeline Write blocks or EAGAIN send buffer full, peer/window/path not advancing send queue, rwnd, unacked bytes, peer receive state Zero-window episodes peer app not draining or receive pressure advertised windows, peer receive queue, event-loop/worker state Retransmission spike loss, reordering, ACK path, severe delay sequence analysis at both endpoints, interface/path counters Throughput near window/RTT bound insufficient effective window RTT, flight, cwnd, rwnd, app production/consumption rate Growing CLOSE_WAIT application does not close after peer EOF socket-to-process ownership, stack profiles, cleanup paths High TIME_WAIT active-close churn close rate, reuse policy, ephemeral ports, NAT state Accept overflow app cannot accept fast enough or burst exceeds backlog listen counters, accept rate, scheduler/event-loop delay FD exhaustion leaked/unbounded sockets or undersized process budget FD count by type, limits, connection lifecycle UDP receive drops buffer/CPU/application cannot drain, burst kernel UDP drops, socket buffer, packet rate, CPU QUIC works poorly on one path UDP policy, MTU, NAT timeout, path quality QUIC telemetry, UDP flow logs, size/path correlation

docs.title: Minimum transport telemetry
docs.text:
Record by service, zone, endpoint, and protocol:

  • connection attempts, setup latency, failures, and reuse;
  • active/idle connections and open/close rates;
  • RTT distribution, retransmitted bytes, loss/reordering indicators;
  • send/receive queue and window pressure;
  • listen/accept overflows and accept latency;
  • socket memory, file descriptors, ephemeral-port and NAT utilization where relevant;
  • application pool wait, request queue age, deadline expiry, and retry count;
  • QUIC handshake, version, stream resets, path migration, and fallback where deployed.

Kernel counters are cumulative and host-local. Use rates, resets/restarts awareness, and workload dimensions. Packet retransmission classification by analyzers is inference, not oracle truth.

docs.title: Connection lifecycle
docs.text:
• Reuse connections to amortize setup and congestion warm-up, but cap age/idle time and validate stale endpoints.
  • Drain before termination: stop new admission, allow bounded completion, then close.
  • Add jitter to connection recycling so a fleet does not reconnect simultaneously.
  • Budget client source ports, NAT state, server FDs, memory, TLS/QUIC state, and load balancer entries end to end.

docs.title: Deadlines and retries
docs.text:
• Set an end-to-end deadline from the caller's useful-work budget.
  • Allocate sub-deadlines while preserving time for cleanup and a bounded retry only when semantics permit.
  • Retry ambiguous writes only with idempotency or reconciliation.
  • Apply backoff, jitter, attempt limits, and a retry budget; congestion loss is a reason to reduce load, not multiply it.

docs.title: Framing and protection
docs.text:
• Bound message length before allocation.
  • Bound decompressed size, nesting, and parse time as well as wire bytes.
  • Treat EOF mid-message as explicit truncation.
  • Apply per-connection and global concurrency limits so one peer cannot monopolize buffers or workers.

docs.title: Protocol choice
docs.text: Choose UDP/QUIC because semantics and path support justify it, not because "UDP is faster." Choose TCP because an ordered stream matches the protocol, not because it provides exactly-once operations. Maintain fallback only if its complexity and monitoring are owned.

docs.title: 15. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: L5 expectation L6 expectation Explains handshake, stream framing, ACKs, and close Connects protocol state to ambiguous outcomes and application contracts Distinguishes rwnd and cwnd Quantifies BDP, growth, loss, and multi-tenant path fairness Sizes connection pools and FDs Creates end-to-end budgets across client, NAT/LB, server, and dependencies Recognizes TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT Separates healthy churn from leaks and designs lifecycle rollout/draining Chooses TCP/UDP/QUIC by requirements Includes deployability, middleboxes, fallback, security, and ownership Adds retries and timeouts Designs deadline propagation, retry budgets, idempotency, and overload control

docs.title: 16. Traps
docs.text:
• Treating one TCP write as one receive or one request.
  • Saying an ACK means the application processed the operation.
  • Conflating receiver flow control with network congestion control.
  • Treating RTO as the application timeout.
  • Assuming more socket buffer always improves latency.
  • Treating every TIME_WAIT socket as a leak or tuning protocol safety away first.
  • Ignoring persistent CLOSE_WAIT as a kernel cleanup problem.
  • Increasing listen backlog without fixing accept/service capacity.
  • Sizing only server FDs while a NAT, proxy, or client exhausts earlier.
  • Claiming UDP is inherently low latency without adding required reliability and congestion behavior.
  • Claiming QUIC removes all head-of-line blocking.
  • Estimating throughput from bandwidth alone while ignoring RTT, flight window, loss, and application rate.

docs.title: Exercise 1: framing across reads
docs.text:
A length-prefixed protocol uses a 4-byte unsigned length. Reads return 2 bytes, then 7 bytes, then 20 bytes. The decoded length is 10 bytes. Describe receiver state.

Worked solution

After 2 bytes, retain a partial header. After the next 7, complete the 4-byte header and hold 5 payload bytes. Validate 10 against the maximum before allocation. The final 20-byte read supplies the remaining 5 bytes for message one and 15 bytes belonging to later framing. Decode exactly 10 payload bytes and retain the 15 excess bytes. Never discard excess or assume read boundaries match messages.

docs.title: Exercise 2: BDP and window bound
docs.text:
A path offers 2 Gbit/s with 50 ms RTT. Calculate BDP. What throughput bound does a 4 MiB effective window impose?

Worked solution 
BDP = 2,000,000,000 bit/s * 0.050 s
    = 100,000,000 bit = 12,500,000 B = 12.5 MB

window throughput = 4,194,304 B / 0.050 s
                  = 83,886,080 B/s
                  = 671,088,640 bit/s
                  = 671.1 Mbit/s

Ignoring overhead and loss, the 4 MiB window limits one flow well below the 2 Gbit/s path.

docs.title: Exercise 3: socket memory budget
docs.text:
A proxy expects 80,000 established connections. Measured average charged socket memory is 96 KiB per connection. Add 30% surge. Estimate memory.

Worked solution 
surged connections = 80,000 * 1.30 = 104,000
memory = 104,000 * 96 KiB = 9,984,000 KiB
       = 9,750 MiB = 9.52 GiB

This excludes process objects, TLS/QUIC state, request buffers, allocator overhead, and kernel global structures. Validate with measured accounting under representative traffic.

docs.title: Exercise 4: diagnose close states
docs.text:
After a deploy, CLOSE_WAIT rises continuously while TIME_WAIT remains stable. What does this suggest and what evidence comes next?

Worked solution

Peers are closing, but the new application is not closing its local sockets promptly. Correlate sockets to process/connection owners, inspect stacks or async task state, review EOF/error cleanup paths, and compare peer close timing. Test cancellation and exception paths. Do not shorten TIME_WAIT; it is not the growing state.

docs.title: Exercise 5: slow start estimate
docs.text:
Using the idealized model in this chapter, initial window 10 MSS, MSS = 1460 B, how many complete growth rounds are needed before a single flight can exceed 100 KiB?

Worked solution

Flights are approximately 14,600 B, 29,200 B, 58,400 B, then 116,800 B. Since 100 KiB = 102,400 B, the fourth flight exceeds it, after three completed growth rounds following the initial flight. This is pedagogical, not a prediction of a specific implementation or transfer completion time.

docs.title: Exercise 6: protocol choice
docs.text:
A mobile collaboration client needs encrypted multiplexed streams, tolerates IP/port changes, and must avoid one lost stream blocking unrelated streams. Corporate networks may block UDP. Propose a boundary-aware design.

Worked solution

Prefer HTTP/3 over QUIC where path validation succeeds: integrated security, stream multiplexing, and connection-ID-based migration fit. Keep a measured fallback to HTTP/2 over TLS/TCP for blocked UDP. Define connection and application session identity separately, preserve request idempotency across fallback, monitor QUIC attempt/success/fallback by network, and ensure the load balancer routes connection IDs correctly. QUIC does not remove ordered waiting within one stream or application dependency ordering.

docs.text:
• RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
  • RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control
  • RFC 6298: Computing TCP's Retransmission Timer
  • RFC 7323: TCP Extensions for High Performance
  • RFC 2018: TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options
  • RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol
  • RFC 8085: UDP Usage Guidelines
