docs.title: 04. MTU and Path MTU
docs.text: MTU failures are boundary failures: an endpoint emits a packet valid for its local interface, but some later link cannot carry it under the applicable forwarding rules. Small requests may work while larger responses hang. TCP may connect successfully before data stalls. The reliable design skill is to calculate every encapsulation layer, preserve MTU feedback, and prove behavior by packet size and direction.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish link MTU, IP packet size, TCP MSS, application payload, and wire overhead;
  • explain IPv4 and IPv6 fragmentation boundaries;
  • calculate MSS and overlay/tunnel payload budgets with units;
  • explain classical PMTUD and packetization-layer PMTUD;
  • recognize ICMP filtering and PMTU black-hole signatures;
  • account for VPN, overlay, encryption, and nested-tunnel overhead;
  • select MSS clamping, endpoint MTU, tunnel MTU, or PLPMTUD mitigations deliberately;
  • build safe observability and test plans without modifying shared hosts;
  • translate MTU mechanics into platform contracts, rollout gates, and ownership.

docs.title: 1. First-principles model
docs.text:
A link MTU is the largest network-layer packet that a link can carry under its interface contract without network-layer fragmentation. A path crosses links with potentially different MTUs. The path MTU is bounded by the smallest effective link limit after considering encapsulation at each segment.

effective inner-packet budget at a tunnel boundary
    = outer link MTU - outer encapsulation overhead

advertised TCP MSS baseline
    = IP packet budget - fixed IP header - fixed TCP header
actual TCP data budget
    = IP packet budget - transmitted IP header - transmitted TCP header

The sender may know its local interface MTU but not a smaller remote bottleneck. Path MTU discovery learns or probes the path limit.

flowchart LR
    S[Sender MTU 1500] --> E[Encapsulator]
    E -->|outer packet| L[Path link MTU 1500]
    L --> D[Decapsulator]
    D --> R[Receiver]
    O[Tunnel overhead] -.reduces inner budget.-> E
    I[ICMP or probe feedback] -.updates PMTU.-> S

docs.title: 2. Vocabulary and boundaries
docs.text:
Term Boundary Meaning Link MTU one interface/link maximum IP packet accepted for ordinary transmission on that link Path MTU one directional path minimum effective MTU across the current path IPv4 total length IPv4 packet header plus IPv4 payload, maximum encoded size 65,535 B IPv6 payload length IPv6 base header field bytes after the 40-byte base header, with separate jumbogram rules TCP MSS one TCP direction maximum TCP payload a peer says it will receive in one segment Application chunk application/runtime write, record, frame, or message size; not an IP packet promise Frame size link link header/trailer plus payload according to technology Tunnel overhead encapsulation boundary outer headers added around an inner packet/frame

MSS is directional and negotiated in SYN options. It constrains TCP segment payload, not UDP datagrams and not total application messages. TCP options consume additional header space; a conservative implementation derives segment size from current path state.

Each peer independently advertises an MSS, not one shared bidirectional value. RFC 6691 subtracts fixed headers for that option; the sender separately accounts for transmitted IP/TCP options when choosing actual segment data length.

docs.title: 3.1 Ethernet MTU and TCP MSS
docs.text:
With 1500-byte IP MTU:

TCP/IPv4 MSS = 1500 B - 20 B IPv4 - 20 B TCP = 1460 B
TCP/IPv6 MSS = 1500 B - 40 B IPv6 - 20 B TCP = 1440 B

Those values assume minimum headers. Twelve bytes of TCP timestamp and padding/options would reduce actual data fitting in the same packet if not otherwise accounted for:

IPv4 TCP payload = 1500 B - 20 B - 32 B = 1448 B

docs.title: 3.2 Tunnel budget
docs.text:
Assume an illustrative IPv4 VXLAN-style outer envelope:

outer IPv4 20 B + UDP 8 B + VXLAN 8 B + inner Ethernet 14 B = 50 B

On a 1500-byte outer IP MTU, the inner frame budget under this simplified accounting is:

1500 B - 20 B - 8 B - 8 B = 1464 B for the inner Ethernet frame
1464 B - 14 B inner Ethernet = 1450 B inner IP packet

If the inner TCP uses IPv4 with minimum headers:

inner TCP MSS = 1450 B - 20 B - 20 B = 1410 B

VLAN tags, outer IPv6, encryption, integrity tags, optional headers, and provider framing can change the result. Draw the exact stack and consult the implementation contract.

docs.title: 3.3 Nested overhead
docs.text:
If an overlay is decapsulated before a VPN adds 76 B around the workload IP packet, their separate 1500-byte boundaries impose independent constraints:

VPN inner budget = 1500 B - 76 B = 1424 B
effective workload packet budget = min(1450 B, 1424 B) = 1424 B

For TCP/IPv6 with minimum headers inside:

MSS = 1424 B - 40 B - 20 B = 1364 B

The tightest boundary wins. Stacking platforms that each assumed they owned the same 50-byte margin causes hidden failure.

If the VPN wraps the still-encapsulated overlay packet, both envelopes coexist:

nested workload IP budget = 1500 - 76 VPN - 50 overlay = 1374 B
nested TCP/IPv6 data budget with fixed headers = 1374 - 40 - 20 = 1314 B

flowchart LR
    W[Workload IP up to 1374 B] --> O[Overlay adds 50 B]
    O --> V[VPN adds 76 B]
    V --> L[1500 B outer IP bottleneck]

Taking min(1450,1424) for this nested stack overstates the safe workload packet by 50 bytes. Draw the actual simultaneous headers before choosing the formula.

docs.title: 4. IPv4 fragmentation
docs.text: IPv4 supports fragmentation. Relevant header fields identify the original datagram, fragment offset, and whether more fragments follow. A router that encounters a packet larger than outgoing MTU may fragment it only when fragmentation is permitted. If the Don't Fragment flag is set, it drops the packet and should send ICMP Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed with MTU information.

docs.title: 4.1 Fragment arithmetic
docs.text:
An IPv4 packet has 20-byte header and 3980-byte payload, total 4000 B. It must cross a 1500-byte MTU link. Each fragment has a 20-byte IPv4 header. Except the final fragment, payload length must align to an 8-byte fragment-offset unit.

max payload per nonfinal fragment = floor((1500 B - 20 B) / 8 B) * 8 B
                                  = floor(1480 / 8) * 8
                                  = 1480 B

payloads = 1480 B + 1480 B + 1020 B = 3980 B
fragment sizes = 1500 B, 1500 B, 1040 B
offsets = 0, 1480/8 = 185, 2960/8 = 370

All fragments carry the identification value needed for reassembly. The first two set More Fragments; the final does not.

docs.title: 4.2 Why fragmentation is operationally costly
docs.text:
• Losing one fragment prevents reassembly of the complete original packet.
  • Every fragment consumes forwarding and reassembly work.
  • ACLs, NAT, and load balancers may lack transport headers in noninitial fragments.
  • Reassembly consumes bounded memory and timers at the destination.
  • Packet captures become harder to interpret.
  • Fragmentation can amplify packet rate and attack surface.

Avoid relying on in-path IPv4 fragmentation as a normal application strategy. Size packets to the path and preserve discovery feedback.

docs.title: 5. IPv6 fragmentation boundary
docs.text:
IPv6 routers do not fragment forwarded packets. When a router cannot forward due to MTU, it discards the packet and sends ICMPv6 Packet Too Big with the supported MTU. A source may use an IPv6 Fragment extension header when appropriate, but fragmentation occurs at the source, not an intermediate router.

IPv6 requires every link to support an MTU of at least 1280 bytes at the IPv6 layer. A link unable to carry 1280 directly must provide link-specific fragmentation/reassembly beneath IPv6. This does not mean every end-to-end path should be forced to 1280; PMTUD should discover larger usable values.

ICMPv6 is protocol machinery

Blanket ICMPv6 blocking can break Neighbor Discovery and Path MTU Discovery. Apply typed, rate-aware policy rather than treating every ICMP message as optional diagnostics.

docs.title: 6. Packet and state flow: classical Path MTU Discovery
docs.text:
Classical PMTUD sends packets that routers cannot fragment and learns from ICMP feedback:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Sender
    participant R as Small-MTU router
    participant D as Destination
    S->>R: packet larger than outgoing MTU
    R--xD: packet dropped
    R-->>S: ICMP too big with MTU
    S->>S: reduce cached path size
    S->>D: retransmit smaller packet

For IPv4, the signal is ICMP Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed. For IPv6, it is ICMPv6 Packet Too Big. Implementations cache PMTU with scope and timers because paths can change.

docs.title: 6.1 The feedback dependency
docs.text:
The control message must return to the sender and be associated with the flow. Failure can occur when:

  • an ACL blocks the ICMP type;
  • a tunnel or firewall mishandles quoted packet information;
  • NAT cannot map feedback to the originating flow;
  • rate limits suppress all useful feedback;
  • an encapsulator does not propagate the inner-path constraint;
  • anycast or asymmetric changes make cached PMTU stale;
  • the sender ignores or cannot authenticate/validate the feedback appropriately.

Security policy should validate and rate-limit control traffic, not erase required signals.

docs.title: 7. Packetization-Layer PMTUD
docs.text:
Packetization-Layer Path MTU Discovery, generalized by RFC 8899, confirms transport reachability using probes and protocol feedback rather than depending only on ICMP. It maintains a search state over candidate packet sizes, detects probe loss, and distinguishes ordinary congestion loss from repeated size-specific failure as safely as the packetization layer allows.

Conceptual state:

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Base
    Base --> Searching: base verified
    Searching --> Searching: probe succeeds
    Searching --> Confirmed: converged
    Searching --> Base: fallback required
    Confirmed --> Searching: revalidate

Revalidation includes a path change or validation-timer expiry. The fallback edge applies when the protocol requires fallback, not on every individual lost probe. Short labels keep the state transitions legible; the full protocol and its bounds remain in the surrounding explanation.

PLPMTUD does not mean "keep sending giant packets until something works." A sound implementation has:

  • a known safe base size;
  • uniquely identifiable probes or protocol confirmation;
  • bounded search and retransmission;
  • congestion-responsive behavior;
  • loss handling and fallback according to the probe state machine;
  • revalidation after path change.

TCP's Packetization Layer PMTUD specification is RFC 4821. Datagram transports and QUIC have protocol-specific considerations and probe mechanisms.

docs.title: 8. Concrete failure example: PMTU black holes
docs.text: A PMTU black hole occurs when oversized packets are dropped and usable feedback does not cause the sender to reduce size. Characteristic behavior is size dependent.

docs.title: 8.1 Typical lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Small SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK packets cross the path.
  2. TLS or other small records may also work.
  3. A larger data packet exceeds a hidden MTU after encapsulation.
  4. A router or tunnel endpoint drops it.
  5. ICMP feedback is absent, filtered, misrouted, or ignored.
  6. TCP retransmits the same-size data until a fallback or timeout.
  7. The application reports handshake success followed by body timeout.

docs.title: 8.2 Failure signatures
docs.text:
Signature PMTU interpretation Alternative to rule out Small requests work, large response stalls response direction has smaller effective PMTU server body generation/backpressure TCP connects, TLS stalls at larger records setup packets fit but record packets do not certificate/crypto CPU or protocol mismatch One VPN/region fails by payload size tunnel overhead or path differs endpoint version/config difference Repeated same-size retransmissions, no progress feedback absent or ineffective severe loss unrelated to size Lowering packet size fixes path strong MTU evidence timing/load changed simultaneously ICMP too-big visible at router but not sender return policy/NAT/control handling capture filter or wrong sender vantage UDP large datagrams fail, small succeed fragmentation/drop/size policy receiver truncation or socket buffer drop

"Ping works" is weak evidence because its payload is usually small and its treatment may differ. A large probe with the relevant no-fragment semantics is more informative, but should be run only through approved tooling and rate limits.

docs.title: 9.1 Write the entire envelope
docs.text:
For each boundary, enumerate bytes:

outer link payload budget
  - outer IP
  - UDP or tunnel transport
  - tunnel shim
  - encryption nonce/IV/header
  - authentication tag/trailer
  - optional metadata
  - encapsulated link header, if any
  = maximum inner packet/frame budget

Common sources of overhead include GRE, IP-in-IP, VXLAN, Geneve options, WireGuard/IPsec modes, service-mesh or node tunnels, and provider-specific encapsulation. Header size may vary with IPv4 versus IPv6, options, encryption mode, padding, and extension metadata.

docs.title: 9.2 Fragment before or after encapsulation
docs.text: Where fragmentation occurs matters. Fragmenting an inner IPv4 packet before encapsulation creates several inner fragments, each with outer overhead. Fragmenting an outer packet can make tunnel processing and middleboxes depend on outer fragment handling. IPv6 outer paths require source behavior rather than router fragmentation. Prefer a tunnel contract that emits packets valid for the outer path.

docs.title: 9.3 MTU ownership contract
docs.text:
For every overlay, document:

Question Required answer Outer path MTU minimum supported and how verified Maximum overhead worst case including options and encryption Advertised inner MTU value exposed to workloads TCP MSS handling endpoint calculation or controlled clamping boundary ICMP propagation how outer errors update inner sender behavior Datagram policy maximum safe UDP payload and fragmentation behavior Path change cache invalidation and reprobe behavior Telemetry owner counters, probes, alerts, and incident escalation

docs.title: 10. MSS negotiation and clamping
docs.text:
TCP peers advertise MSS in SYNs based on what they can receive. The sender combines peer MSS with local/path knowledge. If a tunnel reduces usable MTU but endpoints cannot learn it, an authorized network boundary may rewrite advertised MSS during the handshake so TCP emits smaller segments.

MSS clamping is a targeted compatibility tool, not universal PMTU repair:

  • it affects TCP, not UDP or other IP traffic;
  • it must account for direction and exact overhead;
  • too high still black-holes; too low wastes capacity and increases packet rate;
  • it can hide broken ICMP/PMTUD and complicate ownership;
  • encrypted or encapsulated locations may limit visibility;
  • path changes may require a conservative value.

Prefer correct endpoint/tunnel MTU and functional PMTUD/PLPMTUD. Use clamping where the architecture owns the boundary and cannot otherwise expose the right constraint.

docs.title: 11. Invariants
docs.text:
1. Link invariant: every emitted packet must fit the next link or invoke protocol-defined fragmentation/error behavior.
  2. Path invariant: usable packet size is bounded by the smallest effective directional path limit.
  3. Encapsulation invariant: every added outer byte reduces inner capacity unless the outer link MTU increases.
  4. MSS invariant: MSS limits TCP payload, not complete IP packet size or non-TCP datagrams.
  5. IPv6 invariant: routers do not fragment forwarded IPv6 packets.
  6. Reassembly invariant: delivery of some fragments is not delivery of the original datagram.
  7. Feedback invariant: classical PMTUD needs usable control feedback from the constraining point to the sender.
  8. Probe invariant: a failed large probe is not conclusive without controlling ordinary loss; repeated size-correlated results are stronger.
  9. Direction invariant: request and response can have different paths and PMTUs.
  10. Change invariant: cached PMTU is path state and must recover when routing changes.

docs.title: 12.1 Packet-rate cost of conservative MSS
docs.text:
A service sends 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 B of TCP payload. Compare MSS 1460 B and MSS 1360 B, ignoring retransmission and application framing:

segments at 1460 B = ceil(1,073,741,824 / 1460) = 735,440
segments at 1360 B = ceil(1,073,741,824 / 1360) = 789,517
additional segments = 54,077
increase = 54,077 / 735,440 = 7.35%

A safer smaller MSS may be correct, but it increases per-packet CPU, headers, and device work. Quantify both safety and efficiency.

docs.title: 12.2 Fragment loss amplification
docs.text:
If one datagram becomes three fragments and each fragment independently has delivery probability 0.999, complete datagram delivery probability under the simplified model is:

P(all fragments arrive) = 0.999 ^ 3 = 0.997003
P(datagram loss)        = 1 - 0.997003 = 0.002997 = 0.2997%

The independent-loss model is illustrative; real loss is often bursty and correlated. It still shows why more required pieces increase failure opportunity.

docs.title: 12.3 Goodput impact of overhead
docs.text:
With inner TCP payload 1360 B and total outer transmitted bytes of 1500 B at the evaluated boundary:

payload efficiency = 1360 / 1500 = 90.67%

At 1 Gbit/s outer serialization with no other loss:

maximum payload bit rate = 1 Gbit/s * 0.9067 = 906.7 Mbit/s

This excludes link framing and inter-frame overhead, ACKs, encryption padding variation, loss, and application headers.

docs.title: 13.1 Evidence to collect
docs.text:
• interface and tunnel MTU at both endpoints and encapsulation boundaries;
  • exact route and selected interface in each direction;
  • SYN MSS advertisements and resulting segment sizes;
  • IP length, IPv4 DF/fragment fields, IPv6 Packet Too Big, and ICMP quoted headers;
  • retransmitted ranges and whether failed packets share a size threshold;
  • tunnel encapsulation/error/drop counters;
  • firewall/NAT logs for ICMP and fragments;
  • application success/latency grouped by request and response size, path, protocol, and zone;
  • PMTU cache or transport path metrics where safely exposed;
  • changes in routing, VPN, CNI, encryption, or interface configuration.

docs.title: 13.2 Investigation sequence
docs.text:
1. Establish direction: request upload, response download, or both.
  2. Find the smallest repeatable failing size and largest repeatable successful size.
  3. Capture at sender before encapsulation and after/beyond the suspected boundary when authorized.
  4. Enumerate exact headers and calculate expected outer size.
  5. Check for ICMP too-big/fragmentation-needed at the constraining and sender sides.
  6. Compare TCP MSS and actual packet sizes; for UDP, preserve datagram boundaries in evidence.
  7. Rule out receiver truncation, application limits, rate limits, and ordinary congestion.
  8. Test a mitigation in a disposable environment or narrow canary.
  9. Validate both directions, cold/new flows, long-lived flows, failover paths, and representative payload distributions.

docs.title: 13.3 Safe experiments
docs.text: Prefer read-only inspection and application-level size sweeps. Any command that changes MTU, routing, firewall behavior, or packet loss must be optional and run only in a disposable VM, container network, or explicitly isolated namespace approved for the experiment. Record and restore state even there. Never lower a shared production interface MTU as an ad hoc test.

docs.title: 14. Failure-response matrix
docs.text:
Failure Immediate containment Durable correction Validation Tunnel inner MTU too high canary lower workload/tunnel MTU publish computed MTU contract size sweep across all paths TCP only black-holes controlled MSS clamp at owned boundary repair PMTUD and endpoint MTU SYN MSS plus large transfer ICMP blocked allow required typed feedback with safeguards policy-as-code and regression probe observe sender adjustment UDP oversized reduce protocol datagram size PLPMTUD/protocol segmentation loss by datagram size Stale PMTU after reroute reconnect/reprobe where safe correct cache/path-change handling failover test with long-lived flows Nested tunnel added pause rollout recalculate worst-case envelope and capacity canary old/new topology Fragment reassembly pressure rate-limit abusive fragments, preserve service avoid fragmentation and harden policy reassembly counters and goodput

Do not "fix" a black hole by allowing arbitrary ICMP, disabling security controls, or selecting an unexplained small MTU globally. Preserve least privilege and document the capacity cost.

docs.title: Platform contracts
docs.text:
• Publish workload MTU as an API contract of the network platform.
  • Test the worst supported path: cross-zone, VPN, encrypted overlay, failover, and provider interconnect.
  • Reserve an explicit overhead budget for future tunnel options; reject changes that exceed it or coordinate an MTU migration.
  • Expose PMTU/ICMP/tunnel drops and packet-size distributions by boundary.

docs.title: Application protocols
docs.text:
• Bound UDP datagrams below the verified safe payload or implement robust PLPMTUD and segmentation.
  • Stream large objects rather than constructing giant datagrams.
  • Make retries idempotent; a size-dependent timeout can occur after partial application progress.
  • Do not infer safe payload from a successful small health check.
  • Include representative large requests and responses in synthetic tests.

docs.title: Rollout and migration
docs.text:
An MTU change is a compatibility migration. A safe sequence is:

  1. inventory every encapsulation and path class;
  2. calculate old/new inner budgets and packet-rate cost;
  3. make receivers and intermediate paths accept the target behavior;
  4. canary senders with size-distributed traffic;
  5. monitor fragmentation, too-big feedback, retransmission, CPU, and goodput;
  6. expand by failure domain;
  7. retain a rollback value that remains compatible with already-updated nodes;
  8. test reroute while long-lived connections exist.

Increasing MTU can fail if any middle path remains smaller. Decreasing MTU is usually compatibility-safe for packet size but can raise packets/s and CPU enough to overload the fleet.

docs.title: 16. L5 and L6 expectations
docs.text: L5 expectation L6 expectation Calculates MTU/MSS and tunnel overhead Establishes a versioned cross-platform overhead budget Explains IPv4/IPv6 fragmentation difference Designs PMTUD/PLPMTUD and ICMP security policy by protocol Recognizes size-dependent black holes Builds a multi-vantage, directional, falsifiable evidence plan Suggests lower MTU or MSS clamp Chooses containment versus durable repair and quantifies packet-rate cost Tests a large payload Tests path classes, failover, long-lived flows, and size distributions Mentions tunnel overhead Owns nested-overlay changes, rollout gates, rollback, and team contracts

docs.title: 17. Traps
docs.text:
• Calling 1500 bytes the Ethernet frame size instead of the common IP MTU at that boundary.
  • Subtracting only one tunnel's overhead in a nested path.
  • Treating MSS as the maximum application message or UDP payload.
  • Assuming routers fragment IPv6.
  • Blocking all ICMP/ICMPv6 as a security default.
  • Concluding the path is healthy because a small ping or TCP handshake works.
  • Diagnosing all large-response stalls as PMTU without size-correlated evidence.
  • Clamping TCP MSS and claiming UDP is fixed.
  • Lowering MTU globally without quantifying additional packet rate and CPU.
  • Trusting a configured MTU without observing emitted outer packet size.
  • Ignoring directionality and cached state after route changes.

docs.title: Exercise 1: overlay MSS
docs.text:
An outer IPv6 path has MTU 1500 B. A tunnel adds outer IPv6 40 B, UDP 8 B, tunnel header 8 B, and inner Ethernet 14 B. The inner flow is TCP/IPv4 with 20-byte IP and TCP headers. Calculate inner IP MTU and MSS.

Worked solution 
encapsulated UDP payload budget = 1500 - 40 - 8 - 8 = 1444 B
inner IP MTU = 1444 - 14 = 1430 B
inner TCP/IPv4 MSS = 1430 - 20 - 20 = 1390 B

Any encryption tag, option, VLAN, padding, or additional metadata must also be subtracted.

docs.title: Exercise 2: IPv4 fragmentation
docs.text:
A 3000-byte IPv4 packet includes a 20-byte header and crosses a 1000-byte MTU. Compute fragment payloads, total sizes, and offsets.

Worked solution

Original payload is 3000 - 20 = 2980 B. Maximum aligned nonfinal payload is:

floor((1000 - 20) / 8) * 8 = 976 B

Payloads are 976, 976, 976, 52 B. Total fragment sizes are 996, 996, 996, 72 B. Offsets in 8-byte units are 0, 122, 244, 366. The first three have More Fragments set; the final does not.

docs.title: Exercise 3: black-hole evidence
docs.text:
Requests under 900 B work. Responses above 1380 B stall only through a VPN. TCP handshake succeeds. Give the leading hypothesis and a proof plan.

Worked solution

Leading hypothesis: response packets exceed the effective VPN path MTU and PMTU feedback does not reduce sender packetization. Prove rather than assume:

  1. sweep response sizes to establish a stable threshold;
  2. inspect server-side MSS, emitted IP sizes, DF semantics, and retransmitted ranges;
  3. calculate VPN outer size from exact headers;
  4. capture before/after encapsulation and search for fragmentation-needed/Packet Too Big feedback;
  5. compare a non-VPN path and rule out application response thresholds;
  6. canary a computed smaller endpoint/tunnel MTU or TCP MSS in isolation;
  7. test UDP separately because TCP clamping does not cover it.

docs.title: Exercise 4: packet-rate sensitivity
docs.text:
A service sends 20 Gbit/s of application payload. Reducing effective payload per packet from 1400 B to 1250 B changes approximate packet rate by how much?

Worked solution 
payload bytes/s = 20,000,000,000 / 8 = 2,500,000,000 B/s
pps at 1400 B = 2,500,000,000 / 1400 = 1,785,714 packets/s
pps at 1250 B = 2,500,000,000 / 1250 = 2,000,000 packets/s
increase = 214,286 packets/s = 12%

This payload-only estimate excludes ACKs, retransmissions, and framing. Benchmark CPU and device capacity before a fleet-wide reduction.

docs.title: Exercise 5: migration review
docs.text:
A platform team will add 24 B of optional tunnel metadata to a network whose inner MTU is already set from the previous maximum overhead. What must an L6 review require?

Worked solution

Require an exact worst-case envelope for every outer family/path, proof of remaining headroom, and packet captures from representative boundaries. If no headroom exists, version the inner-MTU contract and migrate receivers/path support before senders. Canary by failure domain with realistic size distributions and monitor ICMP too-big, fragments, retransmissions, tunnel drops, packets/s, CPU, and goodput. Test failover and long-lived flows. Define rollback that remains compatible with packets emitted by both versions, and assign ownership for endpoint configuration, tunnel behavior, and policy.

docs.title: 19. Authoritative sources
docs.text:
• RFC 8200: Internet Protocol, Version 6
  • RFC 1191: Path MTU Discovery
  • RFC 8201: Path MTU Discovery for IPv6
  • RFC 8899: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery
  • RFC 4821: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery for TCP
  • RFC 2923: TCP Problems with Path MTU Discovery
  • RFC 6691: TCP Options and Maximum Segment Size
  • RFC 6864: Updated Specification of the IPv4 ID Field

docs.title: DNS and Service Discovery
docs.text: DNS is a cached, delegated database whose answers influence later connection attempts. It is not a health oracle, a strongly consistent registry, or a traffic switch with a precise activation time.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
A stub resolver asks a recursive resolver. On a cache miss, the recursive resolver follows referrals from the root to a top-level-domain server and then to the zone's authoritative server. The authoritative server owns the answer; the recursive resolver owns cache policy within protocol and local limits.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Application
    participant R as Recursive resolver
    participant Root as Root
    participant TLD as TLD
    participant Auth as Authoritative
    A->>R: api.example.com A, AAAA
    R->>Root: query
    Root-->>R: referral to .com
    R->>TLD: query
    TLD-->>R: referral to example.com
    R->>Auth: query
    Auth-->>R: answer plus TTL
    R-->>A: cached answer

Keep four identities separate: queried name, returned address, TLS-authenticated name, and HTTP authority. See Networking for System Design for the complete request path.

The canonical Global DNS and Service Discovery case studies integrate these mechanics into complete product and control-plane designs.

docs.title: Records, delegation, and aliases
docs.text:
Item Meaning Design consequence NS plus glue delegates a child zone parent and child delegation must agree A / AAAA IPv4 / IPv6 address clients may try, reorder, or cache several answers CNAME owner name aliases another canonical name resolver follows another lookup; do not coexist with ordinary non-DNSSEC data at that owner SRV service target and port with priority and weight only useful when the application explicitly supports SRV SVCB / HTTPS service endpoint binding with priority and parameters capable clients can learn alternate endpoints, ALPN, port, and address hints before connecting SOA zone authority and negative-cache parameters serial and negative TTL affect operations

An SRV client chooses the lowest available priority and uses weights among equal-priority records. A weight is a selection hint, not a capacity guarantee. CNAME indirection separates a stable product name from provider names, but adds dependencies and cannot normally coexist with apex NS and SOA data.

SVCB and its HTTP-specific HTTPS RR use priority 0 for AliasMode and a nonzero priority for ServiceMode. ServiceMode binds a target to parameters such as alpn, port, ipv4hint, and ipv6hint; mandatory names parameters that a client must understand before using that record. HTTPS records can advertise h3 before an HTTP connection exists, unlike Alt-Svc, which is learned from an HTTP response. Address values are hints, not replacements for target-name address resolution, and the client still authenticates the original service name. Unsupported, unusable, or absent records require the protocol's defined fallback; authenticated SVCB failure must not be silently downgraded.

docs.title: Wire and cache behavior
docs.text:
DNS queries commonly start over UDP. A response may set TC=1 when truncated, prompting retry over TCP, but UDP-first is not a protocol requirement: clients may select TCP initially. General-purpose implementations must support both transports, and TCP clients should reuse persistent connections and pipeline where supported rather than paying a connection setup for every query. TCP is also used for conventional zone transfer. EDNS(0) adds an OPT pseudo-record, larger UDP payload negotiation, and extensibility. Large UDP responses fragment more easily and increase amplification risk, so deployments commonly advertise conservative sizes and must preserve DNS over TCP.

query:  ID, flags, QNAME, QTYPE, QCLASS, optional EDNS OPT
reply:  same ID, RCODE, answer, authority, additional, TTL per RRset
cache:  remaining TTL decreases; it is not reset by each cache read

Positive answers cache by TTL. An authoritative NXDOMAIN says the name does not exist; NOERROR with no requested data says the name exists but that type does not. RFC 2308 negative caching derives a bound from the SOA data. SERVFAIL is a resolution failure, not proof of absence.

An empty NOERROR answer alone is not NODATA: a referral can also have an empty answer with NS records in its authority section. Inspect SOA/NS and alias processing under RFC 2308 section 2.2 before caching absence.

DNSSEC signs DNS data and authenticates denial of existence. A validating resolver builds a chain from a configured trust anchor through DS and DNSKEY records to signed RRsets. DNSSEC authenticates data origin and integrity; it does not encrypt queries. DoT carries DNS over TLS, normally on port 853. DoH carries DNS messages over HTTPS. Both protect the resolver hop, but move policy, bootstrap, logging, and failure behavior.

dig +dnssec sets the EDNS DO bit to request DNSSEC records; it does not make dig validate the chain. An AD flag reports that the recursive resolver claims validation, so trust it only when the resolver and the path to it are trusted. For proof, use a local validator, delv with the intended trust anchors, or validator logs, and test a deliberately bogus name as a negative control.

docs.title: DNSSEC rollover sequence
docs.text:
Treat zone-signing keys (ZSKs), key-signing keys (KSKs), and the parent-published DS as separate lifecycles. For a planned ZSK rollover, publish the new DNSKEY early enough for DNSKEY caches, sign with an overlap method supported by the tooling, verify old and new validating paths, then retire old signatures and the old key only after their TTL and signature-validity windows drain. For a KSK rollover, prepublish the new KSK, arrange the parent DS change, prove the new DS -> DNSKEY -> RRset chain from independent validators, retain the old chain through parent and child cache overlap, and only then remove the old DS and KSK in the selected rollover method.

Record DNSKEY/DS TTLs, signature inception and expiry, registrar/parent publication latency, signer state, and rollback points before starting. Never remove the only parent-child trust path. Emergency rollover after compromise may shorten overlap for security, but requires explicit authority, parent coordination, continuous validation probes, and a documented availability tradeoff.

Split-horizon DNS returns different views by network, resolver, tenant, or geography. It can keep private addresses private, but means two engineers can query the same name and correctly receive different data.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every delegated zone retains at least one reachable authoritative path during change.
  2. Old endpoints remain safe for the previous TTL, resolver variance, client caches, and existing connection lifetimes.
  3. An address answer never implies endpoint health at use time.
  4. Negative and positive caches have explicit, observable expiry policy.
  5. DNSSEC changes preserve a valid trust chain; key and DS rollover order is deliberate.
  6. Discovery consumers bound retries and reject malformed, untrusted, or out-of-policy answers.

docs.title: Address selection and Happy Eyeballs
docs.text: Dual-stack clients resolve AAAA and A, order candidates by address-selection policy, and use Happy Eyeballs to avoid waiting through a broken family. RFC 8305 recommends racing connection attempts with a small delay rather than always preferring IPv6 or always firing every address simultaneously. Measure success and latency by family; otherwise an IPv6 regression hides behind successful IPv4 fallback.

docs.title: Service discovery patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Best fit Primary risk A/AAAA records coarse endpoint sets and ingress stale endpoints; no port metadata SRV clients that support service, port, priority, weight inconsistent library support registry plus client fast membership and rich metadata each client implements balancing and watches DNS-backed registry broad compatibility TTL/cache behavior limits convergence sidecar or proxy discovery centralized policy and telemetry extra hop and control-plane dependency

Separate the control plane that publishes membership from the data plane that uses the last known snapshot. During control-plane failure, prefer bounded stale-good data over deleting all endpoints. Health checks need hysteresis: instant removal on one failed probe causes flapping; slow removal sends traffic to dead instances.

docs.title: Resolver load
docs.text:
One million clients refresh a record with a 60-second TTL. With perfectly spread refreshes and no shared caches:

steady query rate = 1,000,000 / 60 = 16,667 queries/s

If all clients refresh on the minute, peak load is burst-shaped, not 16,667 QPS. Add TTL jitter where the client controls refresh and capacity-test synchronized expiry.

docs.title: Migration window
docs.text:
An old record had a 30-minute TTL. At 12:00 it changes to 30 seconds, and pooled connections can live 10 minutes.

earliest conservative removal = 12:00 + 30 min old TTL + 10 min connection drain
                              = 12:40, plus measured resolver variance

Lowering the new TTL does not rewrite old cached answers. Resolver serve-stale policies can also return expired answers during upstream failure. Inventory and bound those policies separately; TTL plus connection age is not a universal removal guarantee.

The 12:40 result assumes the old address is also removed from authoritative answers at 12:00. If only TTL changes then and cutover occurs at 12:30, a client can refresh the old answer just before cutover for another 30 seconds and open a ten-minute connection. The baseline becomes 12:40:30. Start from the last possible old-answer issuance, its TTL, and maximum connection age, not just the time a TTL configuration changed.

docs.title: Amplification
docs.text: A 90-byte UDP query that elicits a 2,700-byte response has a raw amplification factor of 2,700 / 90 = 30x. Response-rate limiting, source-address validation, minimal answers, and conservative EDNS sizes reduce abuse exposure.

docs.title: Migration playbook
docs.text:
1. Inventory authoritative zones, aliases, resolvers, cache floors, and connection maximum age.
  2. Lower TTL before the cutover and wait out the old TTL.
  3. Publish old and new targets; canary traffic and validate TLS/HTTP identity.
  4. Shift weights or records gradually while observing answers and successful connections.
  5. Keep rollback records and old capacity warm through cache and connection drain.
  6. Remove old targets, then raise TTL to the steady-state value.

For regional evacuation and capacity coupling, cross-reference Multi-Region Architecture.

docs.title: Failure matrix
docs.text: Failure User symptom Evidence Containment / recovery lame delegation intermittent SERVFAIL trace stops at an unreachable/wrong authority fix parent/child NS and glue; retain alternate authority stale positive answer connects to retired IP answer TTL and destination IP in traces restore old endpoint; wait and drain negative cache new name still absent cached NXDOMAIN, SOA negative TTL wait or query uncached authority; avoid premature publication oversized UDP blocked timeout or sporadic resolution TC, fragments, TCP retry failure reduce advertised EDNS size; allow DNS TCP DNSSEC expiry/bogus chain validating resolvers return SERVFAIL requested DNSSEC records, trusted resolver's AD flag, delv/validator result and logs restore valid signatures/DS sequence; do not disable validation globally split-view drift works internally only compare resolvers and source networks reconcile views and test each vantage point broken IPv6 connection delay before IPv4 succeeds family-specific connect timings repair IPv6; tune standards-based racing, not permanent masking discovery control-plane outage stale membership or empty pool watch age, snapshot version use bounded last-known-good state and shed safely poisoned/forged answer traffic reaches wrong host unexpected authority/address; DNSSEC validation isolate resolver, validate data, rotate affected credentials

docs.title: Evidence and diagnostics
docs.text:
These are templates, not offline lab commands. Query only an authorized test zone/resolver with bounded time and attempts; +trace contacts external authorities and a public resolver exposes query names. Do not substitute private production names. Prefer the offline DNS lab.

dig api.example.com A +trace
dig api.example.com AAAA @1.1.1.1
dig example.com SOA +noall +answer
dig signed.example DNSKEY +dnssec
delv signed.example A
dig +tcp api.example.com A
kdig +tls @resolver.example api.example.com
curl --doh-url https://resolver.example/dns-query https://api.example.com/

Capture query name/type, resolver identity, RCODE, flags (AA, AD, TC), answer set, remaining TTL, latency, retries, transport, and selected destination. Alert on SERVFAIL, validation failures, TCP fallback failures, negative-answer spikes, stale discovery snapshots, and family-specific connection regressions. Packet captures prove wire behavior; application logs prove what the runtime actually selected.

docs.title: Design choices and tradeoffs
docs.text: Choose authoritative providers by delegation safety, DNSSEC support, propagation controls, query capacity, and independent failure domains. Choose resolver ownership by privacy, policy, cache behavior, and operational evidence: not only median lookup latency. Keep steady-state TTLs long enough to absorb query bursts but short enough for the tested migration objective.

docs.title: L5 and L6 signals
docs.text: An L5 answer traces recursion, delegation and caching; distinguishes NXDOMAIN from timeout; calculates migration overlap; and chooses records, health policy, and diagnostics. An L6 answer defines fleet-wide resolver ownership, split-view governance, DNSSEC rollover, stale-data policy, regional capacity during steering, migration/rollback authority, and privacy policy for DoT/DoH.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Treating TTL as an exact global invalidation timer.
  • Assuming multiple A/AAAA records provide uniform balancing or health checks.
  • Publishing SRV records to clients that never query them.
  • Blocking TCP/53 because “DNS is UDP.”
  • Calling DoH “secure DNS” without naming the resolver trust and metadata boundary.
  • Disabling DNSSEC validation to hide an expired signature.
  • Removing an endpoint before DNS caches and pooled connections drain.

docs.title: 1. Negative answer during launch
docs.text:
A mobile app queried new.example.com ten minutes before launch and received NXDOMAIN with a 15-minute negative TTL. What happens at launch?

Worked solution

Solution: That resolver may continue returning absence for five more minutes. Publish names before use, keep negative TTL deliberate, and test through production resolvers. Repeated client queries do not force the authority to be consulted.

docs.title: 2. Dual-stack incident
docs.text:
IPv6 SYNs time out in one ISP while IPv4 works. Should the service delete AAAA globally?

Worked solution

Solution: First quantify affected paths and verify Happy Eyeballs timings. Global deletion harms healthy IPv6 paths and itself has TTL delay. Repair or selectively steer the faulty path; use a reversible, scoped mitigation only with capacity evidence.

docs.title: 3. Discovery migration
docs.text:
Design registry-to-DNS migration for 20,000 clients with five-minute pooled connections.

Worked solution

Solution: Add DNS reads in shadow mode, compare endpoint sets, publish both old and new endpoints, canary DNS-selected traffic, bound DNS cache and connection age, then shift cohorts. Keep the registry and old endpoints through the maximum DNS staleness plus five-minute drain. Roll back cohort selection, not data formats.

docs.title: HTTP Semantics and Caching
docs.text: HTTP is a message semantics shared by clients, origins, gateways, and caches. Correctness depends on method meaning, selected representation, framing, validators, and which intermediaries are allowed to reuse a response.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
request  = method + target + fields + optional content
response = status + fields + optional content
cache key is approximately scheme + authority + target URI + selecting Vary fields

HTTP semantics are independent of the transport mapping. HTTP/1.1 serializes messages onto byte streams; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 map fields and content onto frames. HTTP/2, HTTP/3, and QUIC covers those mappings.

docs.title: Methods, safety, and idempotency
docs.text:
Method Safe Idempotent Typical role GET yes yes retrieve a representation HEAD yes yes GET metadata without response content POST no no by specification process content or create subordinate resource PUT no yes replace/create state at the target URI DELETE no yes remove target mapping OPTIONS yes yes discover communication options PATCH no not inherently partial modification

Safe means the client does not request a state change; logging and billing may still occur. Idempotent means repeating the same intended request has the same intended effect, not necessarily the same response. A payment POST can become retry-safe through a stable idempotency key and stored outcome, but that is an application contract, not generic POST semantics.

docs.title: Status and fields
docs.text:
Status classes are informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx, and server error 5xx. Important distinctions include 201 created versus 202 accepted, 204 no content, 304 validator match, 400 malformed request, 401 missing/invalid authentication, 403 understood but forbidden, 404 absent or concealed, 409 state conflict, 412 failed precondition, 416 unsatisfiable range, 429 rate limiting, 502 invalid upstream response, 503 temporary unavailability, and 504 upstream timeout.

Fields are end-to-end unless defined hop-by-hop. A proxy must remove fields nominated by Connection before forwarding. Host in HTTP/1.1 and :authority in HTTP/2/3 select the origin; they are security-sensitive routing inputs. Forwarded metadata must be accepted only from trusted proxies.

docs.title: Framing and intermediaries
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 request and response framing differ. A request with Transfer-Encoding is delimited by that coding; otherwise a valid Content-Length determines its content length, and a request with neither has zero-length content. Requests are never close-delimited. Responses follow the RFC 9112 precedence rules: some statuses and methods imply no content, transfer coding or Content-Length can delimit content, and only a qualifying response with neither is delimited by connection close. Conflicting or ambiguously parsed framing can make a front end and back end disagree about request boundaries: request smuggling. Normalize once, reject ambiguous messages, and ensure every hop applies compatible RFC parsing.

flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> E[Edge cache or gateway]
    E --> P[Reverse proxy]
    P --> O[Origin]
    E -. cached representation .-> C

A forward proxy acts for clients; a reverse proxy acts for origins. Via records intermediaries. A gateway that retries, redirects, decompresses, or rewrites fields changes failure and security behavior and needs explicit ownership.

For requests, Transfer-Encoding must end in chunked; otherwise the server cannot determine message length and must return 400 and close (RFC 9112 section 6.3). Reject CL/TE ambiguity at the trust boundary rather than assuming that arbitrary transfer coding safely frames a request. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not permit HTTP/1.1 connection-specific fields; translating gateways must enforce the destination protocol, not copy a raw header list.

docs.title: Conditional requests and ranges
docs.text:
An origin can emit a strong or weak ETag and Last-Modified. If-None-Match enables cache revalidation and commonly yields 304; If-Match makes a mutation conditional and can prevent lost updates with 412. Entity tags are opaque. Strong validators support byte-range reconstruction; weak validators only establish semantic equivalence.

If-None-Match's false condition yields 304 for GET/HEAD and 412 for other methods. If-Match uses strong comparison: perform the version check and mutation atomically (for example, UPDATE ... WHERE version = expected), not a separate read/check followed by an unguarded write. A correct HTTP field cannot repair a check-then-act race in storage.

Range: bytes=... requests a partial representation. When the server honors a single satisfiable range, it returns 206 with Content-Range; a multi-range response uses multipart bodies with per-part ranges. A server can ignore Range and send the full representation. A syntactically valid but unsatisfiable range set can produce 416 Range Not Satisfiable with Content-Range: bytes */length. RFC 9110 section 14.2 permits ignoring or rejecting an invalid range specifier; do not assume every malformed or abusive range produces the same status. If-Range asks for the range only if the validator still matches, otherwise the full representation. Bound range counts and aggregate bytes to prevent amplification.

docs.title: Cache state behavior
docs.text:
freshness_lifetime = explicit max-age/s-maxage or calculated freshness
current_age        = corrected age accumulated across caches and resident time
fresh              = freshness_lifetime > current_age

Cache-Control directives include max-age, shared-cache s-maxage, no-cache (store but revalidate before reuse), no-store (do not store), private, public, must-revalidate, stale-while-revalidate, and stale-if-error. These directives have precise applicability; they are not synonyms for “disable caching.”

Vary extends the cache key with named request fields. Vary: Accept-Encoding separates compressed variants. Vary: Authorization or unbounded user-controlled fields can destroy hit rate. Vary: * prevents reuse. Responses to authenticated requests are not shared unless the response directives explicitly permit it under RFC rules; private data should normally be private, no-store where retention is unacceptable.

docs.title: Cookies and authentication
docs.text:
The presence of Cookie or Set-Cookie alone is not a general shared-cache prohibition under HTTP caching rules. Set explicit cache directives for personalized responses. Cookies are origin-server state sent in Cookie; Set-Cookie controls scope and behavior. Use Secure, HttpOnly, and an appropriate SameSite; narrow Domain and Path; rotate sessions after privilege changes. Cookie path is not a security boundary. TLS protects transit but does not correct broad cookie scope or cross-site request forgery.

Authorization carries credentials for an authentication scheme. 401 responses use WWW-Authenticate; proxy authentication uses 407. Never let an untrusted client spoof identity fields inserted by a gateway. Partition connection pools and caches when credentials, tenant, authority, or TLS policy differ.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Method contracts match side effects and retry policy.
  2. Every message has one unambiguous length at every HTTP/1 hop.
  3. Shared cache keys include every request dimension that changes the representation.
  4. Private or authenticated content is never reused across principals without an explicit safe policy.
  5. A mutation guarded by If-Match changes only the version the caller observed.
  6. Intermediaries preserve end-to-end fields and remove hop-by-hop fields correctly.

docs.title: Revalidation savings
docs.text:
At 10,000 GET/s, a 92% fresh-hit rate and 6% successful 304 revalidation leave 2% full origin responses:

full responses = 10,000 * 0.02 = 200/s
revalidations  = 10,000 * 0.06 = 600/s

The origin still processes 800 requests/s. A 304 saves body bandwidth, not all origin compute.

docs.title: Variant explosion
docs.text: Varying on 3 encodings, 8 languages, and 4 device classes creates up to 3 * 8 * 4 = 96 variants per URL. At 250 KiB each, one logical object can consume about 23.4 MiB. Normalize dimensions or move personalization out of shared-cacheable content.

docs.title: Range transfer
docs.text: A 4 GiB object is downloaded in four 1 GiB ranges. If the object changes after two ranges and the client lacks a strong validator, the assembled file can mix versions. If-Range with a strong ETag protects the invariant, at the cost of restarting with a full response after change.

docs.title: Cache poisoning and defenses
docs.text: Poisoning occurs when an attacker influences a stored representation that later victims receive. Common causes are omitted cache-key fields, trusting spoofed forwarding headers, normalization differences, caching error/reflection responses, and disagreement about authority or path. Define one canonical cache key; reject duplicate/ambiguous authority and framing; allowlist key-affecting forwarded fields; avoid caching responses that reflect unkeyed input; partition tenants; and test edge-to-origin parsing differentials.

docs.title: Failure matrix
docs.text: Failure Symptom Evidence Recovery / prevention wrong method retry duplicate side effect attempt and idempotency-key logs stable key/outcome store; retry only contracted operations stale cache old representation persists Age, cache status, validators purge carefully; revalidate; fix freshness ownership missing Vary users receive wrong encoding/language/data same cache key across differing requests add bounded Vary; purge poisoned variants variant explosion low hit rate and eviction churn cardinality by cache key normalize dimensions; separate personalized data request smuggling desync, unexplained second request raw bytes differ across proxy parsers reject CL/TE ambiguity; patch and align parsers auth leak one principal sees another's content cache HIT on authenticated request stop cache, purge, partition, set private/no-store validator misuse lost update or corrupt resumed file mismatched ETag/version strong ETag and If-Match/If-Range retrying 503 storm origin overload grows attempts exceed arrivals one retry owner, backoff/jitter, Retry-After, budget

docs.title: Evidence and diagnostics
docs.text:
Run these templates only against an authorized synthetic endpoint, adding --max-time 5; verbose/trace output can include headers and bodies. Do not test request-smuggling inputs against a shared service. A cache HIT is not by itself an authentication leak: prove which principal's representation was reused.

curl -sv https://example.com/resource -o /dev/null
curl -sI https://example.com/resource # sends HEAD; useful only when HEAD behavior is intended
curl -sD - -o /dev/null https://example.com/resource # GET response headers
curl -sD - -H 'If-None-Match: "v7"' https://example.com/resource -o /dev/null
curl -sD - -H 'Range: bytes=0-1023' https://example.com/object -o /dev/null
curl --http1.1 --trace-ascii - https://example.com/resource

Record method, normalized authority/path, status, content length, request/response bytes, upstream status, cache key hash, HIT/MISS/STALE, Age, freshness decision, validator, Vary, retry count, principal/tenant partition, and each hop's timing. Redact cookies and credentials. Compare edge and origin raw requests when parsing or poisoning is suspected.

docs.title: Design choices
docs.text:
Choice Prefer when Tradeoff explicit freshness content has a known staleness budget invalidation remains delayed to expiry validator revalidation content changes unpredictably origin request remains purge/invalidation rapid global correction is required control-plane reliability and race complexity private client cache user-specific reusable data endpoint devices retain content shared cache high reuse across principals strict keying and privacy discipline

General cache topology and stampede controls are covered in Caching; API contract design is covered in API and Data Modeling.

docs.title: L5 and L6 signals
docs.text: An L5 candidate states method/idempotency contracts, chooses validators and cache directives, calculates hit/origin load, and diagnoses framing or Vary defects. An L6 candidate standardizes gateway parsing, cache-key governance, credential boundaries, purge ownership, retry policy, incident evidence, and staged migration across heterogeneous intermediaries.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Saying no-cache means “do not store.”
  • Treating every 5xx as retryable or every POST as non-retryable.
  • Returning 200 for every domain outcome and losing intermediary semantics.
  • Keying only by path while ignoring authority, query normalization, or Vary.
  • Trusting X-Forwarded-* from the public network.
  • Using weak ETags to assemble ranges.
  • Fixing cache poisoning only by purging, without fixing key/parser behavior.

docs.title: 1. Lost update
docs.text:
Two editors fetch ETag "8" and both PUT changes. How should the API prevent overwrite?

Worked solution

Solution: Require If-Match: "8". The first successful update emits a new ETag; the second receives 412 Precondition Failed, refetches, and resolves the conflict.

docs.title: 2. Shared-cache leak
docs.text:
/profile returns Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 and varies by cookie, but omits Vary.

Worked solution

Solution: Stop shared caching and purge immediately. Make the response private, no-store unless a deliberately partitioned cache is justified. Merely adding Vary: Cookie can create unbounded variants and still needs privacy review.

docs.title: 3. Capacity during cache loss
docs.text:
Peak traffic is 40,000 GET/s, hit rate is 95%, and origin capacity is 6,000/s. Is total cache loss safe?

Worked solution

Solution: Normal origin load is 2,000/s; cache loss sends 40,000/s, 6.7 times capacity. Add admission control, stale-if-error where semantics allow, request coalescing, warmup, and a rollout that never assumes the origin can absorb full miss traffic.

docs.title: HTTP/2, HTTP/3, and QUIC
docs.text: HTTP versions preserve HTTP semantics while changing how messages share transport state. The key design question is not “which version is fastest?” but which handshake, loss, multiplexing, resource, and fallback behavior matches the path and workload.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1: HTTP messages -> ordered bytes on one TCP connection
HTTP/2:   HTTP messages -> frames -> multiplexed streams -> one TCP connection
HTTP/3:   HTTP messages -> frames -> QUIC streams -> UDP datagrams

HTTP/2 removes application-level serialization between streams, but TCP still delivers one ordered byte stream. HTTP/3 places streams directly on QUIC, so packet loss need not block unrelated streams. Both protocols still share connection-level congestion and flow-control limits.

docs.title: HTTP/1.1 connection behavior
docs.text:
Persistent connections amortize TCP and TLS handshakes. In common practice, one connection has one active request/response at a time; pipelining exists but is difficult to deploy because responses remain ordered and intermediaries vary. Parallelism therefore uses a bounded pool. Closing-delimited bodies prevent safe reuse. Idle timeouts, NAT state, server draining, and synchronized reconnects shape capacity.

At 2,000 requests/s with 50 ms mean response time, Little's Law gives 2,000 * 0.050 = 100 active requests. With one active request per connection, roughly 100 busy connections are required before burst and tail headroom. More connections do not increase throughput after the origin saturates.

docs.title: HTTP/2 wire and stream state
docs.text:
After protocol negotiation and the client connection preface, peers exchange frames. Important types include SETTINGS, HEADERS, DATA, WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, PING, and GOAWAY. Frames carry a stream identifier; stream 0 is connection control. Client-initiated streams use odd identifiers.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> idle
    idle --> open: HEADERS
    open --> halfClosedLocal: local END_STREAM
    open --> halfClosedRemote: remote END_STREAM
    halfClosedLocal --> closed: remote END_STREAM
    halfClosedRemote --> closed: local END_STREAM
    open --> closed: RST_STREAM
    halfClosedLocal --> closed: RST_STREAM
    halfClosedRemote --> closed: RST_STREAM

Frame ordering and legality depend on stream state. A stream can close while the connection remains reusable. SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS limits peer-created concurrent streams; it is not a promise of application capacity.

This diagram is the common request-stream subset, not the complete RFC 9113 state machine: reserved push states and a HEADERS frame that also carries END_STREAM are omitted. Both open and half-closed streams count toward the peer's concurrency limit. A client must respect a lower advertised limit even if its local configured cap is larger.

docs.title: HPACK
docs.text: HPACK compresses fields using static and dynamic tables. Encoder and decoder maintain synchronized connection state. Sensitive fields can be marked never-indexed, but compression still consumes memory and CPU. Bound field count, field size, compressed block size, and dynamic-table size. Cross-origin compression contexts require careful isolation because secret-dependent compression can leak information.

docs.title: Flow control and GOAWAY
docs.text:
HTTP/2 has per-stream and connection receive windows for DATA; control frames are not flow-controlled the same way. Receivers send WINDOW_UPDATE as they consume bytes. A blocked connection window stalls every data stream even if individual stream windows remain.

GOAWAY announces the last stream identifier the sender might have processed and starts graceful drain. The peer opens a replacement connection and may retry streams above that identifier if application semantics permit. A reset or missing response does not prove that an unsafe operation had no effect.

docs.title: Coalescing and TCP head-of-line blocking
docs.text:
A client may reuse one HTTP/2 connection for multiple origins when authority, certificate, DNS/address, and client policy satisfy RFC requirements. Coalescing saves handshakes but couples origins to one congestion, failure, and privacy domain. Never route solely because a certificate wildcard matches.

TCP delivers bytes in sequence. If segment 20 is lost, bytes from segment 21 onward wait even if they contain another HTTP/2 stream. This is transport head-of-line (HoL) blocking.

docs.title: QUIC transport behavior
docs.text:
QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 and exposes reliable ordered streams without exposing a reliable connection-wide byte stream. QUIC packets carry frames such as ACK, STREAM, CRYPTO, MAX_DATA, MAX_STREAM_DATA, and connection-close frames.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: Initial: ClientHello, token if available
    S-->>C: Initial/Handshake: ServerHello and TLS flight
    C->>S: Handshake completion plus application data
    S-->>C: 1-RTT HTTP/3 data
    Note over C,S: Connection state survives path change using issued CIDs

docs.title: Connection IDs and migration
docs.text:
QUIC connection IDs decouple a connection from a network 4-tuple. A client changing from Wi-Fi to cellular can validate the new path and continue. Servers issue multiple IDs and retirement rules; load balancers need routable, privacy-conscious ID design. Migration does not preserve path congestion assumptions: validate reachability and reset congestion state as required.

The connection, not one immutable wire CID, persists. RFC 9000 section 9.5 prohibits intentional reuse of a CID from multiple local addresses. Use an unused peer-issued CID for a new client path; unintentional NAT rebinding is a different case. Migration requires a confirmed handshake and compatible peer policy. Under section 9.2, a client can send to the already-known server before its new-path probe completes; the server independently validates the new client address and obeys anti-amplification. CID routing must still reach the endpoint holding connection keys and stream state; it does not make arbitrary anycast server replacement transparent. See the migration lab.

docs.title: Loss, congestion, and flow control
docs.text: QUIC acknowledges packet-number spaces and detects loss using acknowledgments and timers. Retransmission sends the lost information in new packets with new numbers. Congestion control limits aggregate sending on a path. Connection MAX_DATA and stream MAX_STREAM_DATA independently bound received application bytes; stream-count limits bound concurrency. Advertised credit must fit a finite receive-memory budget; extending credit faster than a slow application can consume bytes eventually exhausts that budget.

docs.title: Amplification and address validation
docs.text: Before validating a client's address, a server must not send more than three times the bytes it has received on that path. A 1,200-byte Initial therefore permits at most 3,600 bytes before validation. Large certificate chains can hit this limit, causing an extra round trip or Retry. Tokens let a server validate return routability while controlling replay and privacy exposure.

docs.title: 0-RTT
docs.text: With prior session state, a client may send early data before the fresh handshake completes. Early data can be replayed by an attacker; transport acceptance does not make an application action exactly once. Restrict 0-RTT to replay-safe operations, bind policy to remembered settings, and expose acceptance/rejection telemetry. TLS and PKI covers ticket and trust lifecycle.

docs.title: HTTP/3 and QPACK
docs.text: HTTP/3 maps request/response exchanges to QUIC streams and uses separate unidirectional control and QPACK streams. QPACK avoids requiring each request stream to carry the entire compression context. Dynamic-table references can still block decoding until encoder instructions arrive, so implementations bound blocked streams and table capacity. Losing one request's packets does not block unrelated stream delivery, but congestion control, CPU, connection flow control, or QPACK dependencies can still affect all work.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. HTTP meaning and retry safety remain identical across protocol versions.
  2. Stream and connection limits bound memory, CPU, and queued work.
  3. A graceful drain does not assign new work to a connection after its accepted-stream boundary.
  4. Origin coalescing occurs only when DNS, certificate, authority, and policy all authorize it.
  5. 0-RTT application data is replay-safe or rejected.
  6. QUIC path changes are validated before unrestricted sending.
  7. Every deployment retains a tested fallback path without hiding protocol-specific failures.

docs.title: Bandwidth-delay product and windows
docs.text:
A 500 Mbit/s path at 80 ms RTT needs:

BDP = 500,000,000 bit/s * 0.080 s = 40,000,000 bits = 5 MB

A 1 MiB connection window cannot fill that path if credit replenishment takes about one RTT. Raising it to 8 MiB removes this particular ceiling, not TCP congestion, stream-window, receiver, or CPU limits. Budget permitted unconsumed bytes across connections; connection credit is not necessarily preallocated RAM.

docs.title: Multiplexing capacity
docs.text: At 6,000 requests/s and 40 ms mean duration, mean concurrency is 240. If each HTTP/2 connection allows 100 concurrent streams, the arithmetic floor is three connections. Use more than the floor for draining and congestion isolation, but not hundreds without evidence.

docs.title: Handshake impact
docs.text: At 100 ms RTT, cold TCP plus a normal TLS 1.3 handshake costs roughly two RTTs before the client sends its request, or about 200 ms, absent TCP Fast Open, HelloRetryRequest, and DNS. Request/response transit and server work follow; 200 ms is not time to first response byte. QUIC combines transport establishment and TLS in one handshake progression; resumed 0-RTT may send early application data, but replay restrictions apply.

docs.title: Design choices and fallback
docs.text:
Use ALPN to negotiate HTTP/2 (h2) over TLS. HTTP/3 can be discovered from an Alt-Svc HTTP response or, for capable clients, from an RFC 9460 HTTPS DNS record whose alpn includes h3; the DNS route can expose the option before the first HTTP connection. HTTPS records can also bind an alternate target or port and provide address hints, but clients still authenticate the original origin and must reject records with unsupported mandatory parameters. Attempt QUIC over UDP while retaining a working HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 route. Race or delay fallback deliberately: waiting too long on blocked UDP hurts users; abandoning QUIC too quickly prevents recovery and masks path quality. Apply the bounded lifetime and authenticated-failure rules of the discovery mechanism, clear stale state on relevant network change or repeated failure, and compare DNS-advertised and HTTP-advertised alternatives during rollout.

Choice Strong fit Cost / risk HTTP/1.1 pool universal compatibility, simple debugging more connections and handshake churn HTTP/2 mature multiplexing on reliable low-loss networks TCP HoL and connection concentration HTTP/3 lossy/high-RTT clients, mobile path changes UDP blocking, CPU, newer tooling one multiplexed connection maximal reuse one failure/congestion domain small connection set isolation and drain headroom extra handshakes and state

docs.text: Failure Symptom Evidence Response HTTP/1 pool exhaustion queue delay before connect/use pool wait, active/idle counts bound queue; reuse; add only measured capacity HTTP/2 TCP loss all streams pause together retransmissions plus stream latency path repair; small connection set; evaluate H3 exhausted H2 window DATA stalls but control works zero windows, missing updates fix consumer; tune windows with memory budget bad GOAWAY handling failed requests during deploy last-stream ID and retry logs drain; replace connection; retry only safe work HPACK/QPACK pressure CPU/memory spike or decode errors table size, blocked streams, field bytes cap fields/table/blocked streams; reject abuse UDP blocked H3 attempt delays then H2 succeeds QUIC timeout by network quick bounded fallback; retain telemetry amplification limit handshake stalls with large cert bytes received/sent before validation shrink chain; token/Retry strategy migration routing failure connection dies on network switch connection ID/path validation logs fix LB CID routing; fall back to reconnect 0-RTT replay duplicate effect early-data and operation logs reject unsafe early data; deduplicate application command

docs.title: Evidence and diagnostics
docs.text:
curl --max-time 5 -sv --http1.1 https://example.com/
curl --max-time 5 -sv --http2 https://example.com/
curl --max-time 5 -sv --http3 https://example.com/
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -verify_hostname example.com -verify_return_error -alpn 'h2,http/1.1' </dev/null
nghttp -nv https://example.com/
# qlog is an implementation telemetry format, not a universal executable.

These are command templates for an authorized test endpoint, not the offline lab path. Check curl -V for compiled HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support. --http3 can fall back, so record the negotiated result; a successful command alone does not prove H3. OpenSSL/nghttp need an operator-enforced time limit and synthetic traffic. Skip public probing and use offline labs by default.

Capture negotiated ALPN/version, handshake/resumption time, connections per origin, active/queued streams, frame errors, GOAWAY last-stream ID, reset codes, flow-control stalls, compressed/uncompressed field bytes, TCP retransmissions, QUIC loss/PTO, congestion window, RTT, path migrations, validation state, 0-RTT acceptance, H3 attempt/fallback reason, and latency by network type. Correlate packet evidence with application request IDs; either alone is incomplete.

docs.title: L5 and L6 signals
docs.text: An L5 answer explains streams, frames, flow control, HoL, GOAWAY, QUIC migration, 0-RTT risk, capacity math, and fallback. An L6 answer defines fleet protocol policy, resource defaults, connection/coalescing isolation, abuse controls, rollout cohorts, UDP and mobile-path evidence, regional fallback capacity, and rollback ownership.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Claiming HTTP/2 eliminates HoL blocking.
  • Equating MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS with server worker capacity.
  • Retrying every stream after GOAWAY without checking the boundary and method semantics.
  • Treating QUIC as unreliable because it uses UDP.
  • Saying HTTP/3 makes loss irrelevant; congestion and connection limits remain shared.
  • Enabling 0-RTT for mutations because the request has an idempotency key without an actual deduplication store.
  • Comparing versions using only warm, lossless localhost tests.

docs.title: 1. Window sizing
docs.text:
A 1 Gbit/s inter-region path has 60 ms RTT and an HTTP/2 connection window of 2 MiB. What is the ceiling from that window?

Worked solution

Solution: BDP is 1e9 * .06 / 8 = 7.5 MB. With one RTT per credit cycle, 2 MiB / .06 s = 33.33 MiB/s = 34.95 MB/s = 279.62 Mbit/s, not 35 MiB/s. Increase carefully or use more isolated connections, while budgeting receiver memory.

docs.title: 2. Deployment drain
docs.text:
A server sends GOAWAY with last stream 101. The client had streams 99, 101, and 103.

Worked solution

Solution: Streams 99 and 101 may have been processed and require their normal outcomes. Stream 103 was not processed by that endpoint according to the boundary and may be retried on a new connection. Preserve request deadlines and idempotency contracts across other ambiguous attempts; GOAWAY does not erase effects from an earlier application retry.

docs.title: 3. H3 rollout
docs.text:
Design a safe mobile HTTP/3 rollout.

Worked solution

Solution: Advertise bounded Alt-Svc to a small cohort, keep H2 fallback, cap QUIC attempt delay, and compare handshake, p50/p99, loss, CPU, bytes, fallback, and network-change success by carrier/OS. Expand only with server and fallback headroom; withdraw the advertisement to roll back while existing alternatives age out. Coordinate HTTPS DNS records too if both discovery mechanisms are enabled; merely omitting a later Alt-Svc field does not immediately clear a previously cached alternative.
