docs.title: TLS 1.3 and Public Key Infrastructure
docs.text: TLS protects a connection only after peers agree on protocol parameters, authenticate required identities, derive fresh traffic keys, and enforce application policy. PKI makes identity scalable; it also creates lifecycle, clock, revocation, and ownership dependencies.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
DNS/address selection chooses where to connect.
SNI requests a virtual server identity at that endpoint.
Certificate validation decides whether that identity is trusted.
TLS key exchange derives connection keys.
ALPN selects the application protocol.
Authorization decides what the authenticated peer may do.

Authentication is not authorization. Encryption is not endpoint health. TLS termination is not end-to-end protection unless every later hop has an explicit protection and identity contract. See Security Architecture for the broader threat model.

docs.title: TLS 1.3 handshake
docs.text:
TLS 1.3 has three key-establishment modes: asymmetric key exchange, PSK, and PSK combined with asymmetric key exchange. The common first-connection flow below uses asymmetric key establishment and certificate-based server authentication; certificates are omitted when a PSK authenticates the handshake. A PSK can be externally provisioned or derived from an earlier connection for resumption. PSK-only mode does not provide forward secrecy for application data, while combining a PSK with fresh asymmetric key establishment does. RFC 9846 uses generic asymmetric-key-exchange language so extensions can define KEM-based groups as well as finite-field or elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: ClientHello: versions, key_share, SNI, ALPN
    S-->>C: ServerHello: selected key_share
    S-->>C: EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished
    Note over C: Validate chain, name, policy, and server proof
    C->>S: Finished
    C->>S: application data
    S-->>C: NewSessionTicket

In this illustrated mode, ephemeral asymmetric key establishment provides forward secrecy. CertificateVerify proves possession of the certificate's private key; Finished authenticates the handshake transcript. In PSK-authenticated modes, the PSK authenticates the handshake and certificate messages are omitted. After ServerHello, most handshake messages are encrypted. A HelloRetryRequest can add a round trip when the offered key shares are unsuitable. TLS alerts and transport closure are distinct failure evidence.

docs.title: PKI chain and name validation
docs.text:
A leaf certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which chains toward a locally trusted root. Servers normally send the leaf and required intermediates, not the root. Clients build and validate a path using their trust store and policy: signatures, constraints, key usage, validity interval, and revocation behavior where configured.

The Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension carries DNS or IP identities. Modern hostname verification uses SAN, not the legacy Common Name fallback. Wildcards match only constrained name patterns and do not prove tenant authorization.

SNI in ClientHello tells a shared endpoint which certificate/configuration to use; it is not application authentication and, without ECH, is generally visible on the path. ALPN negotiates protocols such as h2 or http/1.1; accepting the wrong protocol can create downgrade or routing failure.

docs.title: Termination, re-encryption, and passthrough
docs.text:
Model Strength Tradeoff edge termination, plaintext upstream simple L7 policy internal hop lacks cryptographic protection edge termination, TLS upstream L7 controls plus hop protection edge sees plaintext; two trust contexts TLS passthrough end service owns keys and end-to-end TLS load balancer has limited L7 routing/telemetry service-mesh mTLS workload identity and policy per hop certificate/control-plane/sidecar complexity

Draw every plaintext boundary. The downstream client authenticates the terminating proxy's presented server identity. The proxy then becomes a separate TLS client to the upstream and must validate its SAN and trust roots; verify=false silently removes upstream server authentication.

docs.title: Mutual TLS
docs.text:
In mTLS the server requests a client certificate and validates its chain and acceptable identity. Identity should come from a stable SAN form governed by issuance policy, not arbitrary subject strings. Map identity to authorization separately. Define behavior for missing certificates, expired credentials, unknown issuers, workload decommissioning, and emergency trust removal.

Trusting a CA means trusting every certificate it is permitted to issue. Use constrained issuers, short lifetimes, scoped trust bundles, and auditable issuance. Do not share one broad root across unrelated environments without accepting the blast radius.

docs.title: Resumption, PSKs, tickets, and 0-RTT
docs.text:
TLS 1.3 resumption uses a pre-shared key established from an earlier connection. A ticket is an opaque identity: it can reference server-side state or carry self-encrypted/authenticated state. In the latter design ticket-encryption keys are fleet secrets. Planned overlap preserves resumption; it is not mandatory to accept every still-live ticket. A server can reject tickets and require full handshakes, trading CPU for narrower exposure, especially after compromise.

RFC 9846 (July 2026) obsoletes RFC 8446 while still specifying TLS 1.3. Its section 2.2 covers PSK resumption, section 4.5.1 certificate authentication, and section 4.7.1 tickets; these section numbers differ from the older RFC. New TCP connections that resume PSKs do not prove the new certificate path. Force full handshakes for rotation canaries and separately test ticket rejection, client-identity binding, and capacity when resumption disappears.

0-RTT data lacks full replay protection. An attacker can replay the same early data to multiple nodes behind a load balancer unless the application or shared anti-replay design prevents effects. Permit only replay-safe reads or commands with robust deduplication; reject early data when policy, ticket age, ALPN, SNI, or remembered settings do not match.

docs.title: Rotation and trust overlap
docs.text:
Certificate rotation has two independent planes:

identity rotation: deploy new leaf/key -> verify serving -> retire old leaf/key
trust rotation:    distribute new root -> issue/use new chain -> remove old root

For root migration, trust both old and new roots before serving chains that require the new root. Keep dual trust through the slowest client/config propagation and rollback window, then remove old trust. Cross-signing can help path building but also makes actual client behavior less predictable; test representative trust stores.

Private-key rotation should be gradual and observable. Avoid synchronizing certificate reloads, connection closures, and ticket-key changes across the fleet. Preserve old serving capacity until new-chain handshakes succeed from every required vantage point.

docs.title: Revocation and clocks
docs.text:
CRLs list revoked certificates; OCSP answers status for a certificate. Client behavior varies on network failure, freshness, stapling, and certificate type. OCSP stapling lets the server carry a signed status response; Must-Staple is only useful when the ecosystem enforces it. Short-lived certificates reduce, but do not eliminate, the exposure window and make issuance availability more important.

Certificate validity uses wall-clock time. A fast clock can make a certificate appear expired; a slow clock can make it not yet valid or extend acceptance of retired credentials. Secure, redundant time synchronization is part of PKI reliability. Monitor offset independently from certificate expiry.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Every TLS client validates the intended peer identity against an explicit trust policy.
  2. Private keys remain scoped, access-controlled, auditable, and replaceable.
  3. Trust is added before dependents use it and removed only after old chains drain.
  4. No unsafe operation relies on TLS 0-RTT for exactly-once execution.
  5. Every plaintext hop and termination owner is documented.
  6. Certificate, trust-bundle, ticket-key, and clock lifecycles are observable before failure.
  7. TLS CPU and handshake queues remain bounded under cold-start and attack load.

docs.title: Handshake CPU
docs.text:
If one core sustains 2,500 measured full handshakes/s at the chosen cipher, key type, chain, and implementation, a cold reconnect burst of 20,000 handshakes/s needs:

raw cores = 20,000 / 2,500 = 8
at 60% target utilization = 8 / 0.60 = 13.3 -> 14 cores

This excludes application traffic and kernel/network cost. Benchmark on production hardware. Resumption hit rate helps normal load but must not be the only protection against ticket-key loss or mass reconnect.

docs.title: Certificate-chain bandwidth
docs.text: A 4 KiB chain sent on 10,000 full handshakes/s costs 40,960,000 bytes/s = 39.0625 MiB/s = 40.96 MB/s before records and packets. Removing unnecessary intermediates lowers bandwidth and can prevent QUIC amplification-limit stalls, but never omit an intermediate required by clients.

docs.title: Expiry runway
docs.text:
Assume a leaf issued at t=0 expires at t=24 h, and renewal first starts at t=8 h, leaving 16 hours. A 12-hour issuance outage ends at t=20 h; only 4 hours then remain. A further 6-hour rollout finishes at t=26 h, 2 hours after expiry, not with 2 hours to spare. Earlier renewal or a shorter outage and rollout budget is required, plus clock-skew and rollback margin.

flowchart LR
    I[Issue at 0 h] --> R[Renewal due at 8 h]
    R --> O[Issuance outage until 20 h]
    O --> E[Old leaf expires at 24 h]
    E --> L[Six-hour rollout finishes at 26 h]

Alert on minimum fleet expiry and actual oldest credential age. A periodic 8-hour job is not proof that every serving leaf is at most 8 hours old if reloads lag or prior jobs failed. Established connections may continue after leaf expiry; that masks fresh-handshake outage rather than repairing the certificate.

docs.title: Evidence and diagnostics
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -verify_hostname example.com -showcerts -verify_return_error
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -alpn 'h2,http/1.1' -status
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
openssl verify -CAfile roots.pem -untrusted intermediates.pem leaf.pem
curl -sv --cert client.pem --key client.key https://service.example/

-servername sends SNI but does not perform hostname verification; -verify_hostname checks the certificate identity. Some LibreSSL or older OpenSSL builds lack that option. In that case, use a hostname-validating client such as curl with the application trust store rather than interpreting successful chain validation as a hostname match.

From each hop record TLS version, cipher suite, SNI, selected ALPN, peer SAN/issuer/serial, chain-validation result, expiry runway, trust-bundle version, full/resumed/0-RTT mode, handshake duration, alert, ticket-key epoch, and mTLS authorization identity. Never log private keys, ticket plaintext, bearer tokens, or full sensitive certificate subject data unnecessarily.

Packet captures locate alerts and round trips; endpoint logs explain validation policy. Test from old and new trust stores, multiple client platforms, each ingress route, and a skewed-clock canary.

docs.title: Operations and migration
docs.text:
1. Inventory names, issuers, roots, key custody, termination points, client populations, and maximum connection/ticket lifetime.
  2. Canary the new leaf or trust bundle without removing the old path.
  3. Validate SAN, SNI, ALPN, chain building, mTLS mapping, resumption, and expiry from representative clients.
  4. Roll out with bounded cohorts and enough full-handshake capacity for resumption loss.
  5. Drain old connections and tickets; remove old identity or trust only after evidence shows no dependent clients.
  6. Retain a tested rollback chain and an emergency authorization-revocation path.

docs.title: L5 and L6 signals
docs.text: An L5 answer traces TLS 1.3, validates SAN/chain/SNI/ALPN, selects termination and mTLS policy, estimates handshake capacity, and designs overlap rotation. An L6 answer establishes CA and key ownership, trust-domain boundaries, issuance SLOs, revocation policy, client-compatibility evidence, ticket/0-RTT standards, clock controls, mass-reconnect capacity, staged migrations, and emergency rollback authority.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• Saying “TLS is enabled” without identifying termination and plaintext hops.
  • Trusting any certificate from a broad CA without checking SAN and usage.
  • Rotating the issuing root and leaf simultaneously without trust overlap.
  • Assuming revocation always fails closed or works uniformly.
  • Ignoring clock skew during certificate incidents.
  • Sizing for average resumed traffic rather than cold full-handshake bursts.
  • Treating mTLS identity as authorization.
  • Enabling 0-RTT because TLS accepted it.

docs.title: 1. Root migration
docs.text:
Ten thousand workloads refresh trust bundles within six hours; connections live two hours. Give the safe sequence.

Worked solution

Solution: Distribute a bundle containing old and new roots, wait beyond measured six-hour propagation, canary and then serve new-root chains, retain old trust and serving rollback through at least connection drain and straggler evidence, then remove the old root in cohorts. Do not infer completion from control-plane publication alone.

Include non-resumed handshakes in that proof. Old leaf, session, and ticket lifetimes can differ; no removal timestamp follows from just six-hour trust refresh plus two-hour connections.

docs.title: 2. Reconnect capacity
docs.text:
Fifty thousand clients reconnect over 20 seconds. Each full handshake consumes 0.4 ms of one CPU core. Estimate raw cores.

Worked solution

Solution: Arrival is 2,500 handshakes/s. CPU demand is 2,500 * 0.0004 = 1 core-second/s, so one core at 100% in the ideal benchmark. At a 50% target, reserve at least two measured-equivalent cores, then add network, application, skew, and attack headroom. Jitter reconnects because average arithmetic hides bursts.

docs.title: 3. mTLS outage
docs.text:
After a trust-bundle rollout, 8% of calls fail with unknown issuer.

Worked solution

Solution: Stop rollout and compare failing client/server bundle versions and served chains. Restore the dual-trust bundle on the affected hop before changing identities. Verify control-plane delivery and actual process reload separately; keep authorization containment available if the removed root was compromised.

In the compromise case, do not restore a known-bad trust anchor just to repair availability. Quarantine and issue safe credentials under incident authority.

docs.title: 09. Proxies and Load Balancing
docs.text:
Proxies change who opens each connection, which identity is visible at each hop, and where policy executes. Load balancing is not merely “spread requests evenly.” It must preserve trust boundaries, protocol semantics, capacity limits, locality, and safe removal while connections and requests have different lifetimes.

The canonical Global Load Balancer case study owns the complete service and control-plane design; this chapter supplies its data-path mechanics.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
• Distinguish forward, reverse, and transparent proxies by who selects them and whose traffic they represent.
  • Define trusted forwarded-header handling instead of trusting client-supplied identity.
  • Choose L4 or L7 balancing from required visibility and protocol behavior.
  • Reason about TLS termination, re-encryption, passthrough, and identity at every hop.
  • Select and test balancing algorithms under HTTP/2 and other multiplexed protocols.
  • Design active health checks, passive outlier detection, locality, affinity, draining, and retries as one system.
  • Separate gateway, ingress, service discovery, and data-plane load-balancing responsibilities.

docs.title: 1. The mechanism: one logical request, several transport legs
docs.text:
client                  edge proxy                 service proxy             instance
  |-- TCP/TLS leg A ------>|                           |                         |
  |-- HTTP request ------->|-- TCP/TLS leg B -------->|                         |
  |                        |-- forwarded request ----->|-- TCP/TLS leg C ------>|
  |                        |                           |-- application request ->|

Identity visible by default:
leg A: client address       leg B: edge address         leg C: service-proxy address

A proxy terminates one transport leg and creates another unless it performs transparent packet forwarding. Consequently, source IP, TLS peer identity, connection lifetime, congestion control, and failure scope can differ at every leg. Application code sees only what the immediate peer and an explicitly trusted identity chain provide.

docs.title: Proxy roles
docs.text:
Role Selected by Represents Common purpose Primary trust question forward proxy client or client network clients egress policy, caching, anonymity, access control may this proxy act for this client? reverse proxy service operator origin services edge termination, routing, protection, balancing which client facts may the origin accept? transparent proxy network interception/routing neither endpoint explicitly policy without client configuration, sidecar interception can interception preserve destination and protocol semantics?

A transparent proxy is transparent to configuration, not to physics. Interception still changes routing and may terminate connections. Original source and destination recovery is platform-specific; TLS remains opaque unless deliberately terminated.

docs.title: 2. Invariants
docs.text:
1. Untrusted clients cannot assert trusted hop identity. The first trusted proxy removes or overwrites identity-bearing forwarding headers received from an untrusted peer.
  2. Every hop has an authenticated peer or an explicit unauthenticated boundary. Source IP alone is not workload identity.
  3. A request uses one coherent route and policy snapshot. Mid-request configuration changes do not mix versions.
  4. Only eligible endpoints receive new work. Eligibility includes health, locality policy, protocol, capacity, deployment state, and tenant constraints.
  5. Draining removes new work before closing old work. Long-lived streams have a documented maximum drain policy.
  6. Retries do not create an unbounded second load balancer. Attempts share one deadline, retry budget, and replay-safety rule.
  7. No health mechanism can eject all capacity silently. Minimum healthy capacity, maximum ejection, and panic behavior are explicit.

docs.title: 3. Forwarded identity is a trust-chain problem
docs.text:
Common fields include standardized Forwarded, de facto X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, and X-Forwarded-Host, plus proxy-to-proxy protocols that carry connection metadata. Their presence does not make them true.

Internet client sends:
X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.7

Trusted edge receives peer 203.0.113.24 and rewrites:
Forwarded: for=203.0.113.24;proto=https;host=api.example.com

Internal proxy receives the edge as its authenticated peer and appends its hop.
Application accepts only the suffix produced by configured trusted proxies.

docs.title: Safe processing rule
docs.text:
1. Determine whether the immediate peer belongs to the configured proxy trust set and, where possible, authenticate it with mTLS.
  2. If the peer is untrusted, discard inbound forwarding identity and construct a new chain from the observed connection.
  3. If the peer is trusted, parse with strict size and element bounds; reject malformed ambiguity.
  4. Walk from the nearest hop outward only through trusted proxies. The first untrusted address is the candidate client network address, not proof of a user identity.
  5. Keep authentication and authorization tied to credentials. Use client IP mainly for network policy, abuse signals, and audit with documented NAT/privacy limits.

Host, scheme, and path normalization also cross a trust boundary. Generate redirects and absolute URLs from an allow-listed external origin, not arbitrary forwarded values. Ensure every proxy agrees whether it appends, overwrites, or rejects duplicate headers.

docs.title: 4. L4 versus L7 balancing
docs.text:
Property L4 transport balancer L7 application proxy sees addresses, ports, transport state; sometimes TLS ClientHello metadata method, authority, path, headers, status, RPC metadata routing unit flow/connection request or stream protocol coupling low high; parser and codec must match protocol TLS usually passthrough, NAT, or TCP proxy commonly terminates TLS; may re-encrypt upstream policy coarse auth, quotas, route matching, retries, transformations failure blast radius fewer parser features malformed messages, filters, and config can affect all traffic multiplexing visibility connection only individual HTTP/2 or RPC streams

L4 fits encrypted passthrough, arbitrary TCP, and very high connection rates when per-request policy is unnecessary. L7 is required for path routing, request-level telemetry, gRPC method policy, content limits, and request-aware retries. A common stack uses L4 to distribute connections across an L7 proxy fleet, then L7 to select service endpoints.

flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> L4[L4 connection balancer]
  L4 --> P1[L7 proxy A]
  L4 --> P2[L7 proxy B]
  P1 --> S1[Service instance 1]
  P1 --> S2[Service instance 2]
  P2 --> S1
  P2 --> S2

docs.title: Termination choices
docs.text:
• Edge termination: The client authenticates the edge's presented public server identity. The edge decrypts requests and separately authenticates client credentials where required; it authenticates the upstream server on the next TLS leg.
  • TLS passthrough: The balancer routes opaque connections, often using destination address or ClientHello server name. The backend owns certificates and application-layer policy.
  • Mutual TLS upstream: The proxy and service authenticate workload identities. Decide whether the service authorizes the proxy, the original principal conveyed in a signed token, or both.
  • TLS bridging: The proxy terminates one TLS session and initiates another. This is not end-to-end TLS between client and service, even though every wire hop is encrypted.

TLS termination makes plaintext available to the proxy process, memory, extensions, and observability pipeline. Minimize privileges, redact logs, bound body capture, rotate certificates, and separate certificate/config rollout from the request path. If client certificates terminate at the edge, never forward an unsigned “client certificate” header from arbitrary peers; pass a verified, integrity-protected identity assertion.

docs.title: The unit matters
docs.text:
Round robin over connections approximates round robin over work only when connections carry similar work. HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSocket, and database protocols violate that assumption: one connection may carry hundreds of concurrent streams or one long-lived hot session.

Connection-level round robin:
proxy A <- one HTTP/2 connection, 400 active streams
proxy B <- one HTTP/2 connection,   4 active streams
proxy C <- one HTTP/2 connection,   2 active streams

Connection count says 1 : 1 : 1. Work says 400 : 4 : 2.
Algorithm Useful when Failure mode round robin homogeneous short requests and endpoints ignores outstanding work and request cost weighted round robin stable known capacity ratios static weights lag degradation least connections connection work is comparable multiplexed streams and long idle sockets distort load least requests/streams proxy observes request lifecycle expensive requests still count as one power of two choices many endpoints, cheap load signal stale or incomparable load signals mislead EWMA latency latency correlates with congestion routes away from cold/new endpoints; mixes request classes random large homogeneous fleets variance at small fleet sizes consistent/rendezvous hash affinity and bounded remapping matter hot keys create hot endpoints; membership churn moves state

Use a load measure close to the constrained resource: active streams, queued work, CPU-weighted cost, or explicit endpoint utilization. Keep admission limits even with an adaptive chooser; selection cannot create capacity.

docs.title: Calculation: why stream-aware balancing matters
docs.text:
Assumption (illustrative): Four upstream HTTP/2 connections each permit 100 concurrent streams. A proxy has 300 active requests averaging 200 ms, while a second proxy has 30.

The implied completion rates are approximately 300 / 0.2 s = 1,500 requests/s and 30 / 0.2 s = 150 requests/s if service time and steady-state assumptions hold. Both may report four connections. Connection-based balancing hides a 10x work difference. Prefer request-aware distribution across the proxy fleet or open enough independently distributed connections to reduce concentration; still measure active streams and queue delay.

docs.title: Active and passive signals
docs.text:
• Active health checks test readiness when user traffic is absent. They must exercise necessary dependencies without becoming an expensive synthetic workload.
  • Passive health observes connect failures, resets, protocol errors, and latency from real attempts. It detects path-specific failures but can confuse overload with host failure.
  • Readiness answers “may this endpoint receive new work now?” Liveness answers “should the process be restarted?” Combining them can turn a dependency outage into a restart storm.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Warming
  Warming --> Healthy: readiness successes and warm-up complete
  Healthy --> Suspect: passive threshold crossed
  Suspect --> Ejected: confidence and fleet guard permit
  Suspect --> Healthy: recovery evidence
  Ejected --> Probing: ejection interval expires
  Probing --> Healthy: bounded successful probes
  Probing --> Ejected: probe fails
  Healthy --> Draining: deployment or discovery removal
  Draining --> Removed: no streams remain
  Draining --> ForcedClose: deadline with residual streams
  ForcedClose --> Removed: count disruptions and reconcile outcomes

Outlier detection requires a minimum request volume, comparison within the same request class/locality, a bounded ejection percentage, and recovery probing. Otherwise one correlated dependency failure can eject every endpoint. Evidence should include:

  • eligible, healthy, suspect, ejected, warming, and draining endpoint counts;
  • attempts, active streams, queue delay, latency, and errors by endpoint and locality;
  • ejection reason, duration, false-ejection review, and panic-mode time;
  • retry attempts per logical request and retry success versus added load;
  • connection age, stream concentration, drain duration, and forced closures.

docs.title: Locality
docs.text:
The health graph is a proposed policy, not Envoy's exact state machine. Envoy can uneject after an interval or active-check success; panic mode can select unhealthy hosts. Test those interactions and never let a capacity panic bypass authentication, revocation, or tenant policy.

Prefer same-zone or same-region endpoints only while they retain failure headroom. Define spillover in priority order and reserve cross-zone bandwidth. Strict locality reduces latency and transfer cost but may overload a partial zone; global least-load can spread every request across failure domains and increase correlated blast radius.

docs.title: Affinity
docs.text: Affinity is justified by state locality, cache reuse, or ordered sessions: not by habit. Use a stable key with consistent or rendezvous hashing and bounded remapping. Provide fallback when the target is unhealthy. Hot tenants need key splitting, per-tenant admission, or replication; hashing alone preserves the hotspot.

docs.title: Draining
docs.text:
The sequence is:

mark not eligible for new requests
        -> advertise drain / send graceful protocol signal
        -> wait for bounded in-flight work
        -> cancel or migrate according to protocol contract
        -> close transport
        -> remove endpoint

For HTTP/2 and gRPC, graceful shutdown communicates the last accepted stream before closure. For WebSockets, “wait until empty” may never complete; send an application reconnect hint, allow a grace window, then close. Preserve session epoch so a late old connection cannot overwrite state from its replacement.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text: Retry policy belongs above endpoint selection but below the logical request contract. Retry only a replay-safe operation, select a different eligible endpoint when the failure suggests endpoint scope, and stop at the shared deadline and budget. A gateway retry plus client retry plus service-mesh retry multiplies attempts; assign one layer as owner or divide an explicit total budget.

docs.title: 9. Gateway, ingress, discovery, and balancer
docs.text:
Component Scope Owns Does not inherently own service discovery service identity to endpoint set registration/watch, endpoint metadata, epochs packet forwarding or application policy load balancer one eligible endpoint per connection/request selection, health integration, locality public API lifecycle or business authorization ingress traffic entering a cluster external listeners and cluster routes organization-wide API product policy API gateway client-facing API boundary authentication integration, quotas, API routing/version policy canonical domain authorization or workflows

Products can combine these roles, but the design should not. State which control plane publishes routes and trust roots, which data plane forwards traffic, what remains available when control is down, and which component owns each retry and rate limit. See the canonical API Gateway case study for an integrated design; do not recreate that product design here.

docs.title: 10. Failure analysis and design implications
docs.text: Failure Evidence that distinguishes it Design implication one endpoint hangs endpoint queue/latency rises; peers normal passive outlier signal, per-attempt bound, different-endpoint retry if safe whole zone slows correlated locality metrics preserve remote headroom; avoid ejecting every local endpoint independently health endpoint lies probes pass while real methods fail use representative passive signals and dependency-aware readiness stale discovery endpoint epoch/age exceeds bound last-known-good policy with expiry; fail closed for revoked identity hot affinity key per-key/tenant load concentrated split key, quota tenant, replicate state, or relax affinity proxy overload downstream healthy; proxy queues and accept failures rise admission at edge; scale on streams/CPU, not connection count alone drain never completes long-lived streams remain application reconnect protocol and maximum drain time spoofed client IP forwarding chain begins at untrusted peer overwrite at first trust boundary; authenticate proxy hops retry amplification attempts/logical request rises with failure single retry owner, shared budget, fast overload rejection

docs.title: L5 expectations
docs.text:
• Draw each connection/TLS leg and state what identity each hop trusts.
  • Choose L4 versus L7 and an algorithm using the protocol’s actual work unit.
  • Define readiness, passive outliers, locality spillover, drain, and retry ownership.
  • Quantify connections, active requests/streams, bandwidth, and failover headroom.
  • Name dashboards and fault injections that would validate the design.

docs.title: L6 extensions
docs.text:
• Separate control-plane and data-plane failure domains with signed, versioned, last-known-good configuration.
  • Design multi-region locality policy, capacity reservation, and correlated-failure safeguards.
  • Establish organization-wide header trust, workload identity, retry ownership, and deprecation policy.
  • Plan algorithm rollout with shadow decisions, canaries, rollback, and fairness/cost evidence.
  • Resolve tensions among platform standardization, tenant isolation, regional sovereignty, and operational ownership.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Treating X-Forwarded-For as authenticated because a header exists.
  • Saying “least connections” for multiplexed traffic without defining active work.
  • Calling TLS bridging end-to-end encryption.
  • Using liveness checks for dependency readiness and causing restart cascades.
  • Ejecting unhealthy endpoints without a maximum-ejection or panic policy.
  • Claiming sticky sessions solve state management or hot keys.
  • Draining forever because WebSockets never become idle.
  • Allowing client, gateway, mesh, and library retries to stack.
  • Calling gateway, ingress, discovery, and load balancer synonyms.

docs.title: Exercise 1: reconstruct a trusted client address
docs.text: An application receives peer 10.2.0.8 and X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.9, 10.1.0.7. Only 10.2.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/16 are trusted proxy networks. Which address may be treated as the network client address? What changes if the immediate peer is 203.0.113.4?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

With peer 10.2.0.8, walk right-to-left through trusted hops: 10.2.0.8, then 10.1.0.7. The first untrusted address is 198.51.100.9, so it is the candidate client network address. It is not user identity. If the immediate peer is untrusted 203.0.113.4, discard the entire inbound header and use 203.0.113.4; trusting the supplied list would permit spoofing.

docs.title: Exercise 2: expose multiplexing imbalance
docs.text: Eight L7 proxies each hold 10 HTTP/2 connections. Their active stream counts are 900, 110, 105, 100, 95, 90, 85, 80. Explain why an L4 least-connections balancer cannot repair this state and propose two mitigations.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Every proxy has 10 connections, so L4 sees a tie and cannot observe the 11.25x stream difference between 900 and 80. Mitigations include distributing more independently established client connections and performing request/stream-aware selection at L7. The L7 tier should advertise or measure active work, cap concurrent streams/queued requests, and reject overload rather than depending only on selection.

docs.title: Exercise 3: design safe outlier ejection
docs.text: A 20-endpoint cluster sees five connection failures from every endpoint because a shared database is down. A rule ejects an endpoint after five failures. Repair the rule.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Classify correlated cluster/dependency failure separately from endpoint failure. Require minimum volume and comparative evidence, cap the ejected fraction, preserve a minimum probe set, and enter explicit overload/fail-fast behavior instead of ejecting all 20. Readiness may remove the cluster if it cannot serve correctly, but liveness should not restart every process solely because the database is unavailable. Record ejection and dependency evidence.

docs.title: Exercise 4: plan a long-lived drain
docs.text: A deployment has 40,000 WebSockets and must finish in ten minutes. State a safe sequence and one capacity calculation.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Stop assigning new sockets, send a reconnect hint with randomized delay, keep old and new fleets concurrently available, and close remaining old sockets after the bounded grace period with resumable session state. The average migration rate is at least 40,000 / 600 s = 66.7 reconnects/s; provision above that for randomness, retries, and normal joins. Preserve connection epochs and spread reconnects so the new fleet and authentication service do not receive a synchronized wave.

docs.title: 10. Deadlines, Retries, and Connection Pools
docs.text: Latency controls form one admission system. A timeout does not create capacity, a retry is new load, and a connection pool is a queue in front of a scarce dependency. Design them together around one absolute deadline and one logical-operation identity.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
• Distinguish connect, TLS-handshake, pool-acquisition, request, response-idle, and connection-idle limits.
  • Carry one absolute deadline through queues, attempts, backoff, and downstream calls.
  • Explain why cancellation may leave an unknown outcome.
  • Bound retries with replay safety, exponential backoff, jitter, budgets, and overload signals.
  • Place hedging, circuit breaking, and adaptive concurrency without multiplying work invisibly.
  • Define pool keys, acquisition, validation, reuse, maximum age, and shutdown behavior.
  • Apply Little’s Law while preserving its steady-state and mean-value caveats.

docs.title: 1. A timeout is local; a deadline is end-to-end
docs.text:
A timeout limits one activity for a duration. A deadline is the latest acceptable completion instant for the logical operation. Relative timeouts reset easily at every hop; an absolute deadline prevents hidden budget inflation.

absolute deadline D = 12:00:00.500

client      gateway queue      service A       pool wait      service B
 |  35 ms       20 ms             70 ms           15 ms          110 ms
 |--------------------------------------------------------------------> 250 ms spent
                                                   remaining = D - now

Each stage receives the same D, not a fresh "500 ms timeout."

Use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time enforcement inside a process. Across processes, propagate remaining duration or a deadline representation with bounded clock-skew handling. Never extend the caller’s deadline. Reserve a small response/cleanup margin instead of assigning every remaining millisecond downstream.

docs.title: 2. Name every clock
docs.text:
Limit Starts Stops Protects against Common mistake DNS resolution lookup begins usable address set blocked resolver omitted from “connect timeout” pool acquisition request asks for a lease lease obtained or rejected invisible client-side queue waiting forever before request timeout starts connect transport connect begins transport established blackholed/refused path applying once to a multi-address sequence without total bound TLS handshake TLS begins authenticated session established stalled negotiation/identity work treating TCP connect as ready-to-send request/write first write or operation starts request body accepted blocked upload/window resetting per write chunk response/header request committed response headers/result arrives silent upstream confusing it with idle timeout response idle last progress next progress stalled stream killing valid slow transfers with short whole-request timeout whole request logical operation begins terminal result excessive end-to-end latency restarting it on retry connection idle last stream/byte reuse or close unused resource retention applying it to active streams connection max age connection created retire/drain stale DNS, credentials, state concentration closing active streams abruptly

The exact APIs differ by library. Build a test matrix that proves when each timer starts, whether DNS and pool wait are included, and whether timeout interrupts I/O or only completes a caller-side future.

docs.title: 3. Core invariants
docs.text:
1. One logical operation has one immutable identity and one non-increasing deadline.
  2. No queue admits work that cannot plausibly start and finish before its deadline.
  3. Cancellation stops waiting; it does not prove the remote side stopped or rolled back.
  4. Only replay-safe operations retry automatically. Safety comes from read semantics, conditional updates, or idempotency: not HTTP method spelling alone.
  5. Total physical attempts are bounded per operation and globally.
  6. Backoff consumes the original deadline.
  7. A pool lease is released exactly once and only after successful acquisition.
  8. Pool partitioning follows security, protocol, route, and endpoint identity. Credentials or tenant state never leak across an invalid reuse boundary.
  9. Circuit and concurrency controls fail fast before queues become unbounded.

docs.title: 4. Deadline propagation and budget allocation
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  A[Receive operation and absolute deadline] --> B{Enough time for queue and service?}
  B -- no --> X[Reject deadline exceeded]
  B -- yes --> C[Acquire bounded resource]
  C --> D{Lease acquired before deadline?}
   D -- no --> Z[Release a late lease if one was obtained]
   Z --> X
  D -- yes --> E[Attempt with remaining budget]
  E --> F{Terminal result?}
  F -- yes --> G[Return and release]
  F -- retryable --> R[Release or discard attempt connection lease]
  R --> H{Replay-safe, tokens available, time remains?}
  H -- no --> Y[Return last outcome]
  H -- yes --> I[Jittered backoff within deadline]
  I --> C

Suppose a 300 ms end-to-end target reaches a service after 40 ms. Reserve 20 ms to serialize and return. At most 240 ms remains for queueing, attempts, and backoff. A fixed 200 ms timeout for each of three attempts is invalid even if the client library allows it.

A downstream deadline should be min(parent_deadline - response_margin, local_policy_deadline). Reject immediately when remaining time is below a measured minimum useful service time. This is deadline-aware admission, not a promise that execution will meet the estimate.

Release the attempt's connection or stream lease before retry backoff, discarding unusable connections, then reacquire within the remaining deadline. Holding a scarce connection while sleeping reduces recovery capacity. A separate logical-operation concurrency token may span retries to bound the number of retrying operations; it is not the same resource as a pool lease. The gRPC deadline guide also makes the application responsible for stopping spawned work after cancellation (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 5. Cancellation and unknown outcomes
docs.text:
Cancellation propagates intent. It can close a stream, reset an HTTP/2 exchange, interrupt a cooperative task, or release a caller wait. It cannot retract bytes already delivered or a transaction already committed.

caller              server                database
  |-- charge(k) ------>|                      |
  |                    |-- COMMIT charge(k) ->|
  |-- cancel/reset --->|                      |
  |<-- deadline -------|   response lost      |

Observed by caller: unknown
Actual state: may be committed
Safe next action: query/retry using the same idempotency key k

Outcomes after timeout are at least:

  • known not started: rejected before ownership or durable acceptance;
  • known failed: server returned a definitive terminal rejection;
  • known succeeded: durable result is available;
  • unknown: request may have executed but acknowledgment was lost.

For mutating operations, persist (scope, idempotency_key, request_fingerprint, state, result) atomically with the effect or ownership claim. Reuse of the key with a different fingerprint must fail. Retain results longer than the maximum legitimate retry window. “At most once” transport delivery does not solve a lost response.

docs.title: Classification before policy
docs.text:
Retry only when all are true:

  1. the failure is plausibly transient;
  2. the operation is replay-safe;
  3. another attempt has a meaningful chance of success;
  4. the absolute deadline leaves useful time;
  5. per-request and global retry tokens remain;
  6. the system is not signaling overload that retries would worsen.

Do not retry validation errors, authentication failures, terminal conflicts, exhausted quotas without a valid server hint, or writes with unknown outcomes and no stable idempotency identity. A connection failure before any request bytes were written may be safer than a reset after the complete request was sent, but libraries often cannot expose perfect evidence. Default conservatively.

docs.title: Backoff and jitter
docs.text:
For base delay b, capped exponential backoff can use cap_i = min(max_delay, b * 2^i). Full jitter samples sleep_i ~ Uniform(0, cap_i). Equal or decorrelated jitter have different distributions; choose one deliberately. Jitter desynchronizes clients but does not reduce total attempts.

Assumption (illustrative): 20,000 requests fail together. Each permits two retries with deterministic waits of 100 ms and 200 ms.

The dependency receives waves near 20,000 attempts at both boundaries. With full jitter, the first retries average roughly 20,000 / 0.1 s = 200,000 attempts/s across the first window: still large, but not concentrated at one instant. A retry budget and admission control must reduce volume; jitter alone only spreads it.

Treat Retry-After as the earliest permitted retry under the chosen server contract. If that delay exceeds the remaining deadline or policy ceiling, stop or defer the operation; do not clamp the delay downward and retry early. Rate-limit responses usually call for reduced offered load, not aggressive retries.

docs.title: Retry budgets
docs.text:
A retry budget caps retries relative to useful traffic, for example no more than 10 retry attempts per 100 initial attempts over a rolling window, with a small minimum token reserve for low traffic. Per-request attempt caps prevent one request from monopolizing the budget. Track:

amplification = physical attempts / logical operations
retry yield   = successful retries / retry attempts

Low yield plus rising amplification is evidence to stop retries. Budget at the layer that sees the whole attempt chain. If a client, gateway, and service mesh all retry twice, one logical request can produce up to 3 * 3 * 3 = 27 downstream attempts.

docs.title: Hedging
docs.text:
A hedge starts a duplicate before the original fails, often after a high percentile of historical latency. It can reduce tail latency when stragglers are independent, but always spends extra capacity.

Use hedges only for replay-safe operations, after a delay, with a tiny global hedge budget. Cancel losers cooperatively and still account for their work. Avoid hedging into the same host or shared bottleneck. Never let both winners publish distinct effects.

Assumption (illustrative): 1% of 50,000 reads/s are hedged and 60% of hedge losers continue consuming service time. The extra started load is 500 requests/s; roughly 300 requests/s continues despite cancellation. Capacity planning must include started work, not only winning responses.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
A circuit breaker rejects work for a dependency or operation class after sufficient failure evidence. It limits wasted work and gives recovery room; it does not repair the dependency.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: volume threshold and failure policy crossed
  Open --> HalfOpen: cool-down expires
  HalfOpen --> Closed: bounded probes succeed
  HalfOpen --> Open: probe fails

Partition circuits narrowly enough that one method, tenant, or locality does not suppress unrelated healthy traffic, but not so narrowly that evidence never accumulates. Use minimum sample counts and explicit handling for slow calls versus terminal application errors. Half-open probes require a strict concurrency cap.

docs.title: Adaptive concurrency
docs.text:
Fixed concurrency limits are predictable but require tuning. Adaptive limiters observe queueing or latency relative to a baseline and adjust admitted in-flight work. They need floors, ceilings, smoothing, and separate classes; otherwise traffic-mix shifts look like capacity loss and feedback loops oscillate.

The safe order is:

admission/concurrency token -> pool acquisition -> attempt -> release token and lease

Do not admit thousands of operations into a pool queue and call a 50-connection pool “backpressure.” Reject or queue a bounded number before the scarce resource.

docs.title: Pool key
docs.text:
A reusable connection belongs to a key such as:

(scheme, authority, resolved endpoint or route,
 proxy chain, TLS identity/trust config, application protocol,
 client credential scope, network namespace)

HTTP/2 connection coalescing can reuse one authenticated connection across authorities only under protocol, certificate, DNS, and client-policy conditions. Treat library support as version-sensitive and test isolation. Never key only by host name when proxy, credential, tenant, or trust context changes wire identity.

docs.title: Acquisition and reuse lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  A[Request lease] --> B{Idle reusable connection?}
  B -- yes --> C[Validate policy and state]
  B -- no --> D{Below connection cap?}
  D -- yes --> E[Resolve, connect, TLS]
  D -- no --> F[Bounded wait queue]
  F --> B
  C --> V{Validation succeeds?}
  V -- yes --> G[Use stream or connection]
  V -- no --> K[Discard failed validation connection]
  K --> B
  F -- deadline or queue cap --> X[Reject without lease]
  E -- setup failure --> X
  E --> G
  G --> H{Reusable and within age?}
  H -- yes --> I[Return idle / stream capacity]
  H -- no --> J[Drain and close]

Rules:

  • Acquisition has its own bound and is included in the whole deadline.
  • A failed acquisition does not release a lease it never obtained.
  • Validate protocol state, credential/trust generation, endpoint eligibility, idle age, and max age before reuse.
  • For multiplexed protocols, cap concurrent streams and waiting streams separately from physical connections.
  • Evict half-closed, reset, expired, or policy-stale connections; a superficial “is open” check may not detect a dead peer until use.
  • Add idle eviction jitter and connection-age jitter to avoid reconnect waves.
  • On shutdown, stop new leases, drain active work for a bounded period, then close.

Maximum age rotates stale DNS answers, certificates, credentials, and concentrated long-lived connections. It is not a substitute for explicit revocation. Age retirement should stop new streams first; immediate socket closure converts maintenance into failures.

Every acquisition loop rechecks the original deadline; failed setup/validation releases reserved connection-cap slots even when no lease was returned. The timer table's "request committed" means locally sent according to the library, not remote business commit. Timer names do not establish outcome certainty.

docs.title: 9. Little’s Law: with the mean caveat
docs.text:
For a stable system over a representative interval:

L = lambda * W

L      average number in the system
lambda average effective arrival/completion rate
W      average time in the system

Assumption (illustrative): A dependency sustains 2,000 completed requests/s and mean service time is 40 ms. Mean service concurrency is 2,000/s * 0.040 s = 80.

This does not prove that a pool of 80 meets p99 latency. Little’s Law relates long-run means under suitable stability; it does not determine a percentile, burst queue, service-time distribution, or safe utilization. At 100% utilization, variability can make queueing explode. Include queue wait in W if L includes queued requests, use observed distributions and load tests for tail sizing, and reserve failover/maintenance headroom.

If arrivals are 2,500/s while completions remain 2,000/s, the queue grows by 500/s. Over 30 seconds it adds 15,000 requests; there is no stable mean to rescue the design. Admission must match sustainable completion capacity.

docs.title: 10. Failures, evidence, and design implications
docs.text:
Symptom Evidence Likely mechanism Implication high latency before wire activity pool wait/queue age rises pool exhaustion or leaked leases bound acquisition, inspect holders, reject early timeouts but dependency completions continue cancellation count and server work after cancel caller stopped waiting only propagate cancel; design unknown outcomes and idempotency periodic synchronized spikes attempt timestamps align with backoff/connection age no jitter jitter backoff, eviction, and refresh; budget attempts circuit flaps small sample and alternating state noisy threshold minimum volume, hysteresis, bounded probes p99 rises while mean stable queue/service histogram tail variance or request-class mix isolate classes; do not size from mean alone low retry yield retry failure reasons and amplification persistent or overload failure suppress retries and shed load new deployment sees stale backend connection age and endpoint generation indefinite reuse graceful max age and discovery-aware draining 27x dependency traffic nested attempt traces retries at three layers establish one owner and total attempt budget

Instrument logical operations separately from physical attempts. Record deadline remaining at admission, pool-wait duration, connect/TLS time, time to headers, stream idle gaps, attempt number, cancellation propagation, circuit state, limiter value, active/idle connections, active streams, queue depth/age, lease duration, and outcome certainty. Keep endpoint and method dimensions bounded; use traces for individual identities.

The canonical API Gateway case study applies deadline and retry policy at an edge. The Notification System applies idempotent attempts and provider quotas. Use those integrations rather than duplicating their full designs here.

docs.title: L5 expectations
docs.text:
• Draw the complete latency budget, including pool wait, connection setup, and response margin.
  • Define retryable failures and replay safety for each operation class.
  • Quantify attempt amplification, in-flight work, queue growth, and failover headroom.
  • Specify pool keys and lifecycle for HTTP/1.1 versus multiplexed HTTP/2/gRPC.
  • Show evidence that distinguishes dependency latency, client queueing, and cancellation leakage.

docs.title: L6 extensions
docs.text:
• Establish cross-platform deadline, cancellation, idempotency, and retry-budget standards.
  • Assign retry ownership across SDK, gateway, mesh, and service boundaries.
  • Design adaptive admission with rollout guardrails, class fairness, and regional failure policy.
  • Model recovery waves from reconnect, half-open probes, failover, and cache repopulation.
  • Tie concurrency and timeout changes to SLO error budget, capacity cost, and safe rollback evidence.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Giving every hop the original relative timeout.
  • Assuming timeout or future cancellation rolled back a remote write.
  • Retrying POST blindly or refusing all retries solely because a method is POST.
  • Using exponential backoff without jitter or a global retry budget.
  • Hedging immediately and doubling every request.
  • Opening a circuit from one failure or sharing one global circuit across unrelated methods.
  • Setting a large pool queue and calling it backpressure.
  • Keying pools only by hostname and leaking trust or credentials.
  • Applying connection idle timeout to an active streaming response.
  • Using L = lambda * W to claim a p99 or a safe 100%-utilized pool size.

docs.title: Exercise 1: allocate one deadline
docs.text: A request arrives with 240 ms remaining. Return/serialization reserve is 20 ms. Pool p95 acquisition is 15 ms, one attempt normally takes 70 ms, and retry backoff would be sampled up to 40 ms. Can the policy guarantee two attempts fit? What should it do?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

The usable budget is 220 ms. Releasing the pool lease before backoff means budgeting acquisition for both attempts: 15 + 70 + 40 + 15 + 70 = 210 ms, leaving 10 ms. These are estimates, not guarantees; adding two p95 waits does not produce an end-to-end p95 bound. The policy may permit the second attempt only after recomputing remaining time and requiring enough estimated service plus response margin. Fixed per-attempt timeout caps can be useful, but each must be clamped to the remaining deadline rather than resetting 240 ms. Under rising queue/service evidence, fail fast rather than spend the final budget on a low-probability retry.

docs.title: Exercise 2: calculate nested amplification
docs.text: An SDK permits one retry, a gateway permits two, and service A permits one call retry to B. At each layer “two” means two retries after the initial attempt where stated. What is the maximum number of B attempts per client operation?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

The SDK makes at most 2 gateway attempts. Each gateway attempt makes at most 3 attempts to service A. Each A attempt makes at most 2 attempts to B. Maximum B attempts are 2 * 3 * 2 = 12. Replace this multiplication with one end-to-end attempt policy or explicit sub-budgets, and expose the logical operation identity across all attempts.

docs.title: Exercise 3: size cautiously with Little’s Law
docs.text: A dependency completes 4,000 requests/s with 25 ms mean service time and 180 ms p99. Compute mean service concurrency. Should the pool contain 100 connections?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Mean service concurrency is 4,000/s * 0.025 s = 100. That is not a safe pool recommendation. It ignores tail service time, burstiness, connection multiplexing, failures, and utilization headroom. Measure queueing and distributions under representative load, decide an admission limit from the dependency’s safe envelope, and distinguish physical connections from concurrent streams. A pool of exactly 100 non-multiplexed connections at the observed mean can run near saturation and produce unacceptable queues.

docs.title: Exercise 4: classify a timed-out payment
docs.text: The client sent the full payment request, then timed out before headers. The server does not prove whether the transaction committed. What may the client report and do?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Report an unknown or pending outcome, not failure. Query operation status or retry with the same scoped idempotency key and identical fingerprint. The server returns the stored result if committed, continues/reconciles an in-progress claim, or safely starts only if no claim exists. A new key risks a duplicate charge.

docs.title: Exercise 5: repair a pool
docs.text: A pool has no acquisition timeout, keys by hostname, keeps connections forever, and closes all sockets immediately during deployment. List four corrections.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Bound acquisition inside the absolute deadline; include route/proxy, TLS trust and client identity, protocol, and relevant credential scope in the key; apply jittered idle and maximum-age retirement with explicit revocation; and drain by stopping new leases/streams before bounded closure. Also cap waiters and streams, detect stale connections on use, and record lease ownership to find leaks.

docs.title: 13. Authoritative sources
docs.text:
• IETF, RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics and RFC 9113: HTTP/2.
  • gRPC, Deadlines, Cancellation, Retry, and Request Hedging.
  • Amazon Builders’ Library, Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter.
  • Google SRE Book, Handling Overload and Addressing Cascading Failures.
  • John D. C. Little, A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W, Operations Research, 1961.
