docs.title: 11. gRPC and RPC Systems
docs.text: RPC makes a network operation look like a procedure call, but it does not inherit local-call guarantees. gRPC combines a schema contract, generated APIs, HTTP/2 streams, metadata, deadlines, cancellation, and status. A sound design keeps those layers visible and treats retries, streaming, flow control, and compatibility as distributed-system concerns.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
• Evolve Protocol Buffer schemas without corrupting old readers or writers.
  • Choose unary, client-streaming, server-streaming, or bidirectional-streaming RPCs from interaction semantics.
  • Distinguish channel, transport connection, HTTP/2 stream, and protobuf message lifetimes.
  • Propagate deadlines and cancellation while preserving unknown-outcome semantics.
  • Design status, error details, and metadata as stable contracts.
  • Apply backpressure and message limits at every buffering boundary.
  • Define retry safety and load balancing for multiplexed connections.
  • Diagnose proxy and intermediary behavior that breaks gRPC semantics.

docs.title: 1. Keep the layers separate
docs.text:
application method:   Inventory.Reserve(ReserveRequest) -> ReserveResponse
generated RPC API:    stub, interceptor, serializer, status mapping
gRPC framing:         metadata + length-prefixed messages + trailers
HTTP/2 stream:        one RPC, ordered frames, flow-control windows
HTTP/2 connection:    many concurrent streams to one transport peer
TCP + TLS:            bytes, congestion, peer authentication
network path:         proxies, load balancers, NAT, failures

A channel is the client’s logical handle to a target. It may resolve names, maintain connectivity state, own one or more HTTP/2 connections, balance calls, and reconnect over time. It is not synonymous with one socket. One HTTP/2 connection multiplexes many RPC streams; one streaming RPC carries many protobuf messages.

At wire level, one HTTP/2 stream is one RPC attempt. A logical RPC retried by the framework can create multiple streams over its lifetime. Count both logical calls and physical attempts rather than assuming their stream counts are equal.

docs.title: 2. Service and schema contract
docs.text:
syntax = "proto3";

package inventory.v1;

service InventoryService {
  rpc GetItem(GetItemRequest) returns (Item);
  rpc Reserve(ReserveRequest) returns (ReserveResponse);
  rpc UploadAdjustments(stream Adjustment) returns (UploadSummary);
  rpc WatchStock(WatchStockRequest) returns (stream StockEvent);
  rpc Synchronize(stream SyncMessage) returns (stream SyncMessage);
}

message ReserveRequest {
  string item_id = 1;
  int32 quantity = 2;
  string idempotency_key = 3;
}

The .proto file defines wire field numbers and generated API names. Wire compatibility, source compatibility, and semantic compatibility are different:

These schema blocks are excerpts, not standalone compilable fixtures: referenced messages and ItemState are omitted. Compile a complete schema with pinned protoc/runtime versions before claiming generated-source compatibility.

  • A change can remain parseable but alter meaning for old clients.
  • Generated source can break even when the wire remains compatible.
  • Unknown fields can survive parsing/serialization in supported runtimes, but application transformations may still discard them.

docs.title: Evolution rules
docs.text:
1. Never reuse a field number, including after deletion. Mark deleted numbers and names reserved.
  2. Adding a field is usually wire-compatible when absence has a safe meaning.
  3. Do not change a field’s meaning while retaining its number.
  4. Avoid changing scalar types unless the official compatibility rules explicitly permit the pair and semantic ranges are safe.
  5. Moving fields into an existing oneof can change presence and clearing behavior; treat it as a migration.
  6. Enum consumers must tolerate unknown numeric values. Do not assume the generated UNRECOGNIZED behavior is identical across languages.
  7. Presence matters. Use explicit optional/presence-aware modeling when “not provided” differs from a scalar default.
  8. Evolve request and response semantics with mixed-version tests, not compilation alone.
message Item {
  string item_id = 1;
  reserved 2, 4;
  reserved "legacy_price", "warehouse_code";
  optional string display_name = 3;
  ItemState state = 5;
}

For a semantic migration, add a new field, have new writers populate both where safe, make readers prefer the new representation with fallback, measure old-client usage, stop old writes, and only then retire the old field. Keep its number reserved forever.

docs.title: 3. Four RPC interaction shapes
docs.text:
Shape Request messages Response messages Fits Does not imply unary 1 1 lookup, command, bounded result local-call reliability client streaming many 1 upload/aggregate with one final result resumability after disconnect server streaming 1 many watch, scan, incremental results durable replay bidirectional streaming many many independent interactive exchange globally ordered request/response pairs

In a bidirectional stream, each direction preserves its own message order. The application must define correlation, causality, completion, and concurrent-send rules. A stream is not a queue: unless the service persists messages and offsets, a disconnect can lose in-flight state.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server
  C->>S: open Synchronize(deadline, metadata)
  par client-to-server order
    C->>S: command seq=41
    C->>S: command seq=42
  and server-to-client order
    S-->>C: event seq=900
    S-->>C: ack command=41
  end
  C->>S: half-close request direction
  S-->>C: final event and OK trailers

Use explicit message IDs, sequence/offsets, epochs, and acknowledgments when recovery requires them. Half-close means one direction has ended; the other may continue according to the RPC shape and implementation.

docs.title: 4. Protocol mechanism over HTTP/2
docs.text:
gRPC commonly sends initial metadata in HTTP/2 headers, messages in DATA frames using gRPC message framing, and final status in trailers. HTTP/2 flow control operates on bytes per stream and per connection. A large or unread stream can affect shared connection capacity even though streams are logically independent.

HTTP/2 connection
  stream 1: unary GetItem      HEADERS DATA TRAILERS
  stream 3: WatchStock         HEADERS DATA DATA DATA ... TRAILERS
  stream 5: Reserve            HEADERS DATA TRAILERS

Connection window is shared; each stream also has a window.

Each gRPC message has a five-byte prefix independent of HTTP/2 DATA-frame boundaries:

byte 0:    compressed flag, 0 or 1
bytes 1-4: unsigned message length in network byte order
remaining: exactly that many serialized message bytes

A flag of 1 means the message bytes use the encoding named by grpc-encoding; compression state is not shared between messages. One message can span several DATA frames, and one DATA frame can contain several messages, so applications must parse the gRPC prefix rather than infer message boundaries from HTTP/2 frames.

An illustrative unary protobuf exchange is:

request HEADERS
  :method: POST
  :scheme: https
  :path: /inventory.v1.InventoryService/GetItem
  :authority: api.example.com
  grpc-timeout: 250m
  te: trailers
  content-type: application/grpc+proto

request DATA + END_STREAM
  00 00 00 00 07 <7 protobuf bytes>

response HEADERS
  :status: 200
  content-type: application/grpc+proto

response DATA
  00 00 00 00 12 <18 protobuf bytes>

response trailing HEADERS + END_STREAM
  grpc-status: 0

grpc-timeout is at most eight decimal digits followed by H, M, S, m, u, or n; here 250m means 250 milliseconds. Reserved pseudo-fields precede ordinary fields, te: trailers detects incompatible intermediaries, and final grpc-status is required even for success. An immediate error may use trailers-only: one terminating HEADERS block containing HTTP status, gRPC content type, grpc-status, and optional grpc-message/details, with no DATA. If a broken intermediary returns a non-gRPC HTTP response without grpc-status, the client synthesizes a gRPC status using the defined HTTP fallback mapping; that lossy fallback never overrides a valid gRPC status.

HTTP/2 multiplexing removes HTTP/1.1 application head-of-line blocking between responses, but all streams on one TCP connection still share packet-loss recovery and congestion control. One connection failure can fail many in-flight RPCs. Opening unlimited connections avoids neither overload nor fairness problems.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
1. Each accepted call uses one service/method contract version and authenticated principal.
  2. Deadlines never increase downstream.
  3. Cancellation releases local resources promptly, while durable side effects follow their idempotency contract.
  4. A stream has bounded messages, bytes, buffered elements, and lifetime or liveness policy.
  5. The producer cannot outrun the slowest required consumer without a documented drop, spill, aggregate, or disconnect policy.
  6. Retries preserve one logical operation identity and occur only when replay-safe.
  7. Load balancing uses call/stream load, not only channel or connection count.
  8. Final status and application state cannot contradict silently.

docs.title: 5. Deadlines and cancellation
docs.text:
Set a deadline at the caller and propagate remaining time through downstream RPCs. A server should check cancellation before expensive work, stop child calls, release leases, and avoid publishing a result after a cancellation-won state transition. Still, cancellation is cooperative.

flowchart TD
  A[RPC arrives with deadline] --> B{Enough useful time remains?}
  B -- no --> C[DEADLINE_EXCEEDED]
  B -- yes --> D[Acquire bounded capacity]
  D --> E[Execute and propagate child deadline]
  E --> F{Cancelled?}
  F -- yes --> G[Stop future work and release resources]
   F -- no --> H[Atomically arbitrate cancellation versus effect commit]
  H --> I[Send response and final status]

DEADLINE_EXCEEDED at the client does not prove the server did nothing. The effect may have committed while the response was delayed. Mutations need idempotency keys or a queryable operation resource. For a client-streaming upload, define whether acknowledged chunks are durable and resumable; otherwise retry starts a new upload.

Checking a cancellation flag before a later unguarded COMMIT leaves a race. If the domain promises cancellation prevents effects, arbitrate both against the same durable operation state/transaction; otherwise document best-effort cancellation and unknown outcomes.

docs.title: 6. Status, details, and metadata
docs.text:
Use gRPC status codes for transport-neutral outcome classes and typed error details for stable machine handling. Do not encode every outcome as OK plus {success:false}, and do not expose stack traces or arbitrary internal strings as contracts.

Status Typical meaning Retry posture INVALID_ARGUMENT invalid regardless of current system state do not retry unchanged FAILED_PRECONDITION system state blocks the operation caller must change state or workflow ABORTED concurrency/transaction conflict retry whole operation only if contract says so NOT_FOUND named resource absent usually terminal for that version ALREADY_EXISTS create conflicts with existing identity may query existing result RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED quota or capacity exhausted honor policy/hint; avoid amplification UNAVAILABLE transient service/path unavailable candidate for bounded safe retry DEADLINE_EXCEEDED deadline elapsed outcome may be unknown INTERNAL / DATA_LOSS invariant or integrity failure do not blindly retry mutations

Metadata carries cross-cutting context such as authentication, tracing, request identity, deadlines handled by the framework, and routing hints. Bound total metadata size and key/value cardinality. Treat received metadata as untrusted until the immediate peer and issuer are authenticated. Do not place secrets or high-cardinality payloads into routinely logged metadata. Binary metadata and ASCII metadata have different conventions; use generated/typed application messages for domain data.

Final gRPC status is normally carried in trailers. Proxies must preserve trailers; an intermediary that returns an HTTP error page or strips trailers can collapse precise statuses into UNKNOWN or UNAVAILABLE.

docs.title: 7. Backpressure and message limits
docs.text:
Flow control prevents unlimited byte transmission on one hop. It does not bound objects already decoded, application queues, fan-out to consumers, database work, or retry buffers.

network bytes -> HTTP/2 window -> gRPC decoder -> application queue -> worker -> sink
                   bounded            ?                ?             ?

Bound every ?:

  • maximum receive and send message size;
  • maximum metadata size;
  • messages and bytes buffered per stream and per connection;
  • concurrent streams per peer, tenant, and method;
  • application work queue and executor concurrency;
  • total stream duration, idle/liveness interval, and replay retention;
  • decompressed size, not only compressed wire bytes.

Read the next message only when downstream capacity exists. For server streaming, slow clients need a policy: backpressure upstream, coalesce state updates, spill durably, drop explicitly labeled lossy updates, or disconnect with a resumable cursor. Never buffer an unbounded “reliable” stream in memory.

Assumption (illustrative): 5,000 streams each buffer up to 64 messages averaging 8 KiB decoded. Payload memory alone is 5,000 * 64 * 8 KiB = 2,560,000 KiB, about 2.44 GiB, before object, queue, compression, and runtime overhead. A per-stream bound must also fit a process-wide budget.

Large unary messages delay failure recovery, monopolize windows, and require large buffers. Prefer object storage plus references for blobs, or chunked streaming with checksum, offset, idempotent chunk identity, and resumable state when the use case truly requires transfer through RPC.

docs.title: 8. Retry safety
docs.text:
Automatic retry depends on both method semantics and how far the attempt progressed. gRPC transparent retry and configured retry are implementation/spec-defined; applications must not infer that an absent response means absent execution.

The gRPC retry guide calls a call "committed" when response headers arrive and that retry mechanism stops. This is not business transaction commit. Transparent retries before application handling can occur without an explicit policy; configured maxAttempts is not a count of every internal setup operation. Propagate deadlines and measure actual attempts.

Classify methods:

GetItem:             read-only; bounded retry may be safe
Reserve(key):        mutation; retry only with durable idempotency key
UploadAdjustments:   stream; retry unsafe unless chunks/session are resumable
WatchStock(after):   stream; reconnect from durable cursor if history retained
Synchronize:         bidi; reconnect requires protocol-specific epochs and replay

Retries and hedges share the original deadline, attempt cap, and global budget. Service-config policies should be reviewed with gateway and mesh policies so attempts do not multiply. RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED and explicit pushback should reduce load. A retry after partial client-stream transmission must not silently concatenate or duplicate data.

docs.title: 9. Channels, balancing, and discovery
docs.text: Reuse channels; creating one per call defeats connection reuse and can cause handshake storms. A channel resolves a logical target into addresses and receives service configuration according to the implementation. Client-side balancing chooses endpoints directly; proxy balancing chooses a proxy connection first and may choose the backend later.

docs.title: Multiplexing trap
docs.text:
client channel -- one HTTP/2 connection --> proxy A -- 1,000 RPC streams
client channel -- one HTTP/2 connection --> proxy B --    10 RPC streams

An L4 balancer sees two connections, not 1,010 streams. Long-lived channels can pin all calls to one proxy. Mitigations include L7 request-aware proxying, client-side endpoint balancing, multiple deliberately managed connections, server load reporting, or maximum connection age with jitter. The right choice depends on trust boundaries and topology; do not churn channels per RPC.

Balance by endpoint eligibility, locality, active calls/streams, observed load, and method class. Streams may last hours, so draining must stop new calls, send graceful HTTP/2 shutdown, and bound old-stream lifetime or provide application reconnection with cursors/epochs.

The canonical API Gateway case study integrates gRPC routing, policy, and control-plane rollout. This chapter stays at protocol and client/server mechanics.

docs.title: 10. Proxy and intermediary failure modes
docs.text:
Problem Evidence Consequence Design response proxy supports HTTP/2 from client but HTTP/1.1 upstream negotiated protocols and proxy config native gRPC fails or is translated require end-to-end compatible mode; test trailers and streaming trailers stripped wire trace shows missing grpc-status status becomes ambiguous preserve HTTP/2 trailers; synthetic conformance tests idle timeout shorter than quiet stream closes at repeatable idle interval watches/bidi streams reset application keepalive/liveness within policy; resumable cursor keepalive too aggressive server sends throttling/GOAWAY; fleet sees probe load connection churn or self-induced load coordinate client/server limits and add jitter body buffering enabled memory/latency grows with stream streaming becomes store-and-forward disable buffering for streaming routes; bound proxy buffers message limit mismatch failures correlate with payload size RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED or intermediary reset publish compatible limits; chunk/reference large objects L4 connection pinning streams concentrated on few proxy sockets hotspot despite equal connection count call-aware L7/client balancing and graceful age rotation retry at multiple layers trace shows attempt tree amplification and duplicate effects one owner or explicit total budget DNS/discovery stale under long channels address generation lags control plane calls stay on retired endpoint resolver updates plus graceful connection rotation

Test the real path, including sidecars, ingress, cloud load balancers, and TLS modes. A direct local client proving streaming works does not prove production intermediaries preserve HTTP/2, trailers, cancellation, or long idle streams.

docs.title: 11. Capacity and evidence
docs.text:
Assumption (illustrative): A service receives 30,000 unary RPC/s at 50 ms mean service time and 2,000 streaming calls averaging 20 minutes. Unary mean concurrency is 30,000/s * 0.050 s = 1,500. Streaming concurrency is already 2,000, independent of unary throughput. If each stream buffers 128 KiB across all layers, streaming buffers consume about 250 MiB before connection/runtime overhead.

Mean concurrency does not establish p99 or a safe limit. Measure:

  • logical calls and physical attempts by service/method/status;
  • deadline remaining at client send and server admission;
  • queue, handler, serialization, and network durations;
  • active channels, connections, streams, and streams per connection;
  • connection age, handshake rate, resolver generation, GOAWAY/reset reasons;
  • sent/received messages and bytes, compressed and decompressed sizes;
  • flow-control stalls and application queue depth/age;
  • cancellation received, cancellation honored, and work completed afterward;
  • retry/hedge amplification and success yield;
  • status-detail parsing failures and unknown-status rate.

Avoid user IDs and call IDs as metric labels. Put them in sampled traces or controlled logs.

docs.title: L5 expectations
docs.text:
• State the proto evolution rules and demonstrate a mixed-version migration.
  • Choose an RPC shape and define ordering, completion, reconnect, and replay semantics.
  • Draw channel, connection, stream, and message boundaries.
  • Define deadline, cancellation, status, limits, backpressure, and retry safety.
  • Explain load balancing and verify every production intermediary.

docs.title: L6 extensions
docs.text:
• Govern schemas across languages with compatibility checks, ownership, deprecation evidence, and rollout sequencing.
  • Standardize deadline and attempt budgets across SDK, gateway, mesh, and services.
  • Design global discovery/locality and graceful migration for millions of long-lived channels.
  • Establish method-class admission, tenant fairness, and process-wide memory budgets for streams.
  • Plan protocol/library upgrades through conformance tests, canaries, telemetry, and rollback.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Saying RPC is “just a local function call over the network.”
  • Reusing a deleted protobuf field number.
  • Claiming every added field is semantically safe.
  • Treating bidirectional streaming as a durable ordered queue.
  • Equating a channel with one connection or a stream with one message.
  • Assuming flow control bounds application memory.
  • Mapping every domain error to INTERNAL or every failure to OK.
  • Assuming cancellation rolls back a committed mutation.
  • Retrying an entire partially consumed stream without a replay protocol.
  • Using least-connections at L4 for thousands of multiplexed calls.
  • Testing direct-to-server while ignoring production proxies and trailers.

docs.title: Exercise 1: review schema changes
docs.text: Version 1 has string state = 3. A proposal deletes it and adds State state = 3, where State is an enum. Is this safe? Provide a migration.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

It is unsafe to reinterpret field 3 from length-delimited string to varint enum and reuse the number. Keep field 3 during migration. Add the enum with explicit presence under a new number, for example optional State state_v2 = 7; make new writers populate both where mappings are exact, make new readers prefer field 7 only when present and otherwise fall back to 3, and measure old-version traffic. After retirement, reserve field number 3 and name state; never assign 3 again.

docs.title: Exercise 2: bound stream memory
docs.text: A process permits 8,000 streams. Each stream may queue 32 decoded messages averaging 16 KiB. Calculate payload memory and repair the design if the process budget for all stream queues is 1 GiB.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Payload memory is 8,000 * 32 * 16 KiB = 4,096,000 KiB, about 3.91 GiB, already nearly four times the budget before overhead. If all 8,000 streams remain possible, the average maximum payload allowance is at most 1 GiB / 8,000, about 131 KiB per stream, or roughly eight 16 KiB messages: and practical limits must be lower for overhead and unequal streams. Use process-wide byte accounting, per-stream message/byte limits, demand-driven reads, and a slow-consumer policy.

docs.title: Exercise 3: make a watch resumable
docs.text: WatchStock emits updates but has no event identity. A proxy closes idle connections during deployment. Define the minimum recovery contract.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Assign monotonic offsets or versioned cursors within a defined stock scope. The client records the last fully applied cursor and reconnects with after_cursor. The server retains replay history for a published window or returns a specific “cursor expired” status that instructs the client to fetch a snapshot and resume from its version. Updates must be idempotent by entity version. Add jittered reconnect, deadline/liveness policy, and bounded server replay.

docs.title: Exercise 4: classify a reserve timeout
docs.text: Reserve returns DEADLINE_EXCEEDED after the request was fully sent. May the client create a new request and retry?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Not with a new logical identity. The reservation may have committed. The client may query by operation identity or retry the identical request with the same scoped idempotency key and fingerprint if the server contract stores/reconciles that key atomically with the effect. The original deadline still governs automatic retry; a later user-driven status query can have its own operation deadline.

docs.title: Exercise 5: diagnose false balancing
docs.text: Four clients each create one long-lived channel through an L4 balancer to four proxies. By chance, three channels land on proxy A and one on B; C and D receive none. Each channel carries 5,000 calls/minute. What does the balancer observe, and what changes help?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

The L4 balancer observes only four long-lived connections and cannot redistribute their streams. Proxy A receives 15,000 calls/minute while B receives 5,000. Use request-aware L7 balancing, client-side balancing to service endpoints where appropriate, or a bounded set of independently distributed connections with call-aware selection. Jittered maximum connection age can eventually remix placement but is not a primary real-time load signal.

docs.title: 14. Authoritative sources
docs.text:
• Protocol Buffers, Language Guide and Updating a Message Type.
  • gRPC, Core concepts, Deadlines, Cancellation, Flow Control, and Status Codes.
  • gRPC, Metadata, Retry, and Service Config.
  • gRPC, HTTP/2 protocol mapping.
  • IETF, RFC 9113: HTTP/2.

Previous: Deadlines, Retries, and Connection Pools | Next: Real-Time Delivery and Interactive Media

docs.title: 12. Real-Time Delivery and Interactive Media
docs.text: “Real time” covers different contracts. A dashboard may tolerate seconds and replay events over one-way HTTP. Chat needs bidirectional delivery and reconnection semantics. Interactive audio and video need latency-sensitive, loss-tolerant media transport, congestion control, and relay capacity. Choose the mechanism from directionality, latency, replay, network reachability, and failure behavior.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
• Explain WebSocket upgrade, framing, masking, fragmentation, liveness, close, and replay requirements.
  • Operate Server-Sent Events (SSE) through buffering proxies and resume with Last-Event-ID.
  • Design long polling without overlap, gaps, or synchronized reconnect waves.
  • Separate WebRTC signaling from media and trace ICE, STUN, TURN, and candidate selection.
  • Explain DTLS-SRTP, RTP/RTCP, jitter buffers, NACK, and forward error correction (FEC).
  • Choose peer-to-peer, selective forwarding unit (SFU), or broadcast delivery from fan-out and latency.
  • Calculate SFU and TURN bandwidth with protocol and failure headroom.
  • Define evidence, L5/L6 depth, and common traps.

docs.title: 1. Choose the delivery contract first
docs.text:
Mechanism Direction Typical transport Server state Best fit Key limitation long polling request/response, repeated HTTP pending request + cursor broad compatibility, sparse events repeated headers and reconnect churn SSE server to client long-lived HTTP response stream subscription + replay cursor browser notifications, progress, feeds browser API is one-way; proxy buffering matters WebSocket bidirectional messages framed protocol after HTTP handshake connection/session state chat, control, collaborative updates replay and reconnect are application concerns WebRTC data/media bidirectional peer media/data ICE-selected UDP/TCP paths, secured media signaling plus media/session state interactive audio/video NAT traversal, congestion, codec, and relay complexity segmented streaming server/CDN to viewer HTTP object delivery manifests/segments massive video audiences higher latency than interactive media

The canonical Video Conferencing case study integrates SFUs, moderation, recording, and regional topology. The YouTube case study covers upload and CDN-based video playback. This chapter explains transport mechanics and does not duplicate those systems.

For application-level delivery contracts, replay, fan-out, and gateway ownership, use the canonical Realtime Updates pattern.

docs.title: 2. Shared invariants
docs.text:
1. A connection is not a durable session. Reconnect creates a new connection epoch.
  2. Delivery claims state their scope: connection-local ordering, at-most-once attempt, replayable event log, or durable consumer acknowledgment.
  3. Every buffer has byte, message, time, and ownership bounds.
  4. Slow consumers have an explicit policy: backpressure, coalesce, drop, spill, or disconnect.
  5. Liveness detects a failed path within a stated interval without making heartbeat traffic an overload source.
  6. Reconnect uses exponential backoff, jitter, admission control, and a resumable identity where continuity matters.
  7. Media packets that miss their playout deadline are useless; reliability mechanisms remain deadline-aware.
  8. Relay and SFU egress are provisioned from peak concurrent bitrate and failure scenarios, not daily averages.

docs.title: Handshake
docs.text:
A client starts an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade handshake with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, version 13, and a fresh Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server returns status 101, Upgrade: websocket, and a derived Sec-WebSocket-Accept. The accept value proves protocol participation; it is not authentication. The connection then carries WebSocket frames rather than HTTP messages. Extended CONNECT provides WebSockets over HTTP/2 when client, proxy, and server support RFC 8441.

GET /v1/chat HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Origin: https://app.example.com
Authorization: ...

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: ...

Authenticate and authorize before or immediately after upgrade. For browsers, validate Origin against an allow list; it is a browser-origin signal, not a substitute for credentials. Avoid long-lived bearer tokens in query strings because URLs leak through logs and history. Define token refresh and revocation for connections that outlive token validity.

The Authorization header illustrates a non-browser client: native browser WebSocket constructors cannot set arbitrary headers. Use a reviewed cookie/origin policy or bounded post-upgrade authentication; allow no effects before auth and expire unauthenticated sockets promptly. The sample nonce is not reusable in production. HTTP/2 extended CONNECT uses a successful 2xx, not 101/Upgrade.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
WebSocket provides text and binary messages over frames. A message may be fragmented across a first data frame and continuation frames. Control frames, close, ping, and pong, have special constraints and may appear between fragments. Client-to-server frames are masked; server-to-client frames are not. Masking is not encryption; use wss for TLS.

TCP byte stream
  [binary FIN=0][continuation FIN=0][PING][continuation FIN=1]
  <---------------- one fragmented message ---------------->

Enforce maximum frame, message, decompressed-message, and fragmentation counts. Validate UTF-8 for text. A compressed tiny wire message can expand dramatically; negotiate extensions deliberately and cap decompression. Use one logical writer or a library-supported concurrency model so fragments from different messages do not interleave incorrectly.

docs.title: Liveness and close
docs.text:
TCP can remain apparently established after a peer or path disappears. Protocol Ping/Pong measures transport-peer responsiveness. Browser JavaScript does not directly expose WebSocket control Ping/Pong, so an application heartbeat uses ordinary messages with correlation IDs. An application acknowledgment can additionally prove the handler ran; neither proves durable business processing. Choose intervals above normal jitter and coordinated with proxy/NAT idle limits. Add randomized phase so millions of clients do not ping simultaneously.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Connecting
  Connecting --> Open: handshake and auth succeed
  Open --> Suspect: pong or application ack late
  Suspect --> Open: response arrives
  Suspect --> Reconnecting: liveness deadline expires
  Open --> Closing: local or remote close
  Closing --> Closed: close handshake or timeout
  Reconnecting --> Open: new epoch and resume
  Reconnecting --> Closed: session expires

A graceful close exchanges close control frames, then closes transport. A lost path may prevent the handshake; enforce a bounded close timeout. Record close code and initiator, but do not treat every abnormal closure as server failure.

docs.title: Replay and session continuity
docs.text:
WebSocket itself offers no durable replay across reconnection. Add application envelopes:

{"stream":"room-42","epoch":8,"eventId":10421,"type":"message","payload":{}}

The client stores the last applied event ID and reconnects with a resume cursor. The server replays from a retained log, then switches atomically to live delivery so events are neither skipped between replay and subscription nor reordered. If the cursor expired, return an explicit reset requiring a snapshot plus a new cursor. Deduplicate by event ID; an acknowledgment can represent transport receipt, application apply, or durable processing: name which one.

For client commands, include command IDs and session epochs. Replayed commands must be idempotent or return their existing result. A higher connection epoch fences delayed traffic from an old connection.

Fencing requires a trusted session authority and an atomic current-epoch check at the effect sink. A client-incremented field, or a gateway check followed by an unguarded write, does not exclude an old connection's effect.

docs.title: 4. Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
SSE is a UTF-8 event stream served as text/event-stream. Fields include data, event, id, and retry; a blank line dispatches an event. Multiple data lines join with newlines. Comment lines beginning with : can act as keepalives.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 10421
event: stock
data: {"item":"A7","available":12}

: keepalive

docs.title: Flush the entire path
docs.text: Writing in application code does not prove the client received an event. Language buffers, compression, reverse proxies, and CDN buffering can hold bytes. Configure streaming routes to avoid response buffering, disable transformations that delay chunks, and test time-to-event through the production path. Keepalive comments must exceed intermediary minimum chunk behavior and remain below idle timeouts without generating excessive traffic.

docs.title: Resume with Last-Event-ID
docs.text:
When reconnecting, the browser can send Last-Event-ID from the last dispatched event. Treat it as a cursor scoped to the authenticated stream: not as authorization and not necessarily as a global sequence.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant C as Browser
  participant E as SSE endpoint
  participant L as Event log
  C->>E: GET /events
  E->>L: subscribe after cursor 10420
  E-->>C: id 10421, id 10422
  Note over C,E: path closes
  C->>E: GET /events + Last-Event-ID: 10422
  E->>L: replay after 10422, then tail
  E-->>C: id 10423 ...

Define retention and cursor-expiry behavior. If only current state matters, coalesce updates and return a fresh snapshot on expiry. If every event matters, use durable storage and application acknowledgment outside browser-native SSE where necessary. Native EventSource has constrained request customization in browsers; credential and authorization design must account for the actual client API and origin policy.

docs.title: 5. Long polling
docs.text:
The client sends GET /events?after=cursor. The server responds when an event is available or a bounded hold expires. The client immediately issues the next request with the last applied cursor.

client                         server
  |-- GET after=90 ------------->| hold
  |<-- events 91..94 -------------|
  |-- GET after=94 ------------->| hold
  |<-- 204/no events at 25 s -----|
  |-- GET after=94 ------------->|

Allow at most one outstanding poll per logical subscription unless the protocol defines ordering across overlaps. A timeout response is normal and should not advance the cursor. Bound pending polls per user/tenant and globally. Distinguish load-balancer idle timeout from application hold time; return before the shortest path timeout.

Long polling needs the same replay and deduplication semantics as WebSocket/SSE. Without a cursor, a response lost between server and client creates ambiguity. Without stable ordering scope, concurrent polls can deliver out of order.

docs.title: 6. Reconnect storms
docs.text:
A regional proxy restart, certificate rotation, mobile carrier outage, or Wi-Fi recovery can disconnect millions of clients together. Immediate reconnect turns recovery into a second outage.

bad:  1,000,000 reconnects at t = 0

good: client backoff + full jitter + server Retry-After/load hint
      admission tokens + session-resume cache protection
      staged proxy drain + randomized connection max age

Assumption (illustrative): 1.2 million clients must reconnect over ten minutes. The unavoidable average is 1,200,000 / 600 s = 2,000 handshakes/s. At 4 ms CPU per authentication/handshake, that is eight CPU-seconds per wall second before application work. Provision above 2,000/s for variance, retries, normal arrivals, and a failed zone; cap admission so queues do not grow without bound.

Clients use exponential backoff with full jitter and a maximum delay. Servers may return retry hints. If a minimum wait exceeds client policy or the useful deadline, defer or stop reconnecting under that policy instead of shortening the wait and retrying early. Preserve authenticated resume state only within bounded memory and expiry; otherwise a resume-cache stampede replaces a database stampede. Prioritize established sessions and critical control traffic over fresh optional subscriptions. Test full-fleet reconnect, not only steady-state connection count.

docs.title: 7. WebRTC: signaling is separate from media
docs.text:
WebRTC does not standardize the application signaling channel. The application uses HTTPS, WebSocket, or another mechanism to exchange session descriptions, ICE credentials/candidates, and control messages. Signaling authenticates the participant and meeting; media connectivity is negotiated separately.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
  participant A as Client A
  participant S as Signaling service
  participant T as STUN/TURN
  participant F as Peer or SFU
  A->>S: authenticate, join, capabilities
  S-->>A: session authorization and ICE servers
  A->>T: gather server-reflexive/relay candidates
  A->>S: SDP and ICE candidates
  S-->>F: authorized description/candidates
  A->>F: ICE connectivity checks
  A->>F: DTLS handshake
  A->>F: SRTP/SRTCP media and control

Session Description Protocol (SDP) communicates codecs, media sections, RTP parameters, fingerprints, and transport details. Treat it as untrusted structured input with size and count bounds. “Trickle ICE” sends candidates as discovered, reducing setup latency compared with waiting for complete gathering.

docs.title: 8. ICE, STUN, and TURN
docs.text:
Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) gathers candidate addresses, exchanges them through signaling, checks candidate pairs, nominates a working pair, and monitors consent/connectivity.

Candidate/path Learned from Meaning host local interfaces direct local address server-reflexive STUN response public mapped address observed through NAT peer-reflexive connectivity check mapped address learned during checks relay TURN allocation address on a relay that forwards packets

STUN helps discover mapped addresses and test connectivity; it is not a media relay. TURN allocates relay transport when direct paths fail or policy requires relaying. TURN improves reachability at substantial bandwidth cost and must authenticate allocations, enforce quotas, expire permissions/channels, and defend against amplification/abuse.

Preferred: client ===== direct UDP ===== peer/SFU
Fallback:  client ====> TURN relay ====> peer/SFU
                       ingress + egress billed/carried by relay

ICE candidate priority prefers useful paths but actual selection also reflects checks and policy. Enterprise networks may force TURN over TCP or TLS; this increases reachability but TCP retransmission can conflict with media’s playout deadlines. Observe selected candidate type and transport rather than assuming most sessions are direct.

docs.title: 9. DTLS-SRTP, RTP, and RTCP
docs.text:
WebRTC media is protected with SRTP. DTLS authenticates the negotiated endpoint fingerprint and derives/export keys for SRTP according to the DTLS-SRTP profile. This provides transport security per peer connection. In an SFU topology, ordinary hop-by-hop SRTP terminates at the SFU; end-to-end frame encryption above SRTP is a separate design with tradeoffs for recording, moderation, and transcoding.

RTP carries timestamped media packets with sequence numbers and synchronization source identifiers. Sequence numbers help detect loss and reorder packets; timestamps drive playout timing rather than serving as wall-clock timestamps. RTCP carries reception reports, sender timing, feedback, and control information used for synchronization and congestion/quality adaptation.

encoder -> RTP packets -> network jitter/loss -> jitter buffer -> decoder -> playout
               ^                 |                    |
               |---- RTCP feedback / NACK ------------|

docs.title: Jitter buffer
docs.text: The receiver delays playout to absorb packet arrival variation. A larger buffer hides more jitter but adds interactive latency. Adapt within bounds from observed delay variation. Audio continuity usually takes priority over high video quality. Drop packets arriving after their playout deadline.

docs.title: NACK and retransmission
docs.text: Negative acknowledgment (NACK) asks for recent missing RTP packets. Retransmission helps only if round-trip time plus processing leaves time before playout. Senders/SFUs need a bounded recent-packet cache. During burst loss, unlimited NACKs can add congestion; deduplicate and rate-limit feedback.

docs.title: FEC
docs.text: Forward error correction sends redundant information so some loss can be recovered without a round trip. It consumes bandwidth even when no loss occurs but helps when RTT is too high for retransmission or loss is bursty within the code’s capability. Adapt FEC to path and media priority; combining aggressive retransmission and FEC can worsen congestion.

docs.title: Congestion and quality adaptation
docs.text: Estimate available bitrate from loss, delay, and transport feedback. Preserve audio, then screen-share legibility, then prioritized video. Use simulcast or scalable coding so an SFU can forward an appropriate layer without transcoding every stream. Apply hysteresis to avoid layer oscillation, coalesce keyframe requests, and shed low-priority video before queues create seconds of latency.

docs.title: 10. Topologies: mesh, SFU, and broadcast
docs.text:
Topology Publisher upload Server work Receiver download Fit peer mesh one encoded stream per peer, roughly O(N) signaling/relay only O(N) very small calls with reachable peers SFU one or several simulcast layers forwards selected packets, often no decode selected participant layers interactive multiparty meetings MCU/compositor usually one stream decodes/mixes/encodes one composed stream constrained clients, recording, legacy interop CDN broadcast one ingest transcode/package/cache adaptive segments huge audiences accepting added latency

For N users in a full mesh, there are N*(N-1)/2 peer relationships and each user sends to N-1 peers. At 10 participants and 1.5 Mbps per outgoing encode, each publisher may need 13.5 Mbps: often impractical. An SFU lets a publisher send a bounded simulcast ladder once and moves fan-out to server egress.

The SFU is primarily an egress and packet-processing system. It needs per-receiver congestion decisions, packet caches, subscription state, and failure headroom. Do not size it from participant count alone.

docs.title: SFU egress
docs.text:
Assumption (illustrative): 20,000 concurrent participants each receive 2.2 Mbps of selected video/audio on average. Protocol, retransmission, and FEC add 20%. Normal SFU egress is 20,000 * 2.2 Mbps * 1.2 = 52.8 Gbps. With 30% evacuation headroom, provision at least 52.8 / 0.7 = 75.4 Gbps of usable fleet egress before additional maintenance and regional risk margins.

Dividing by a nominal NIC rate is insufficient. Measure packets/s, encryption, forwarding-table lookups, kernel/network overhead, burst behavior, and safe sustained utilization. Reserve inter-SFU and recording traffic separately.

docs.title: TURN relay
docs.text:
TURN sizing counts both sides of relayed traffic at the relay.

Here each relayed user has one client-to-SFU allocation. Do not count both ends of one peer-to-peer leg again as independent traffic. RX+TX is processing load, not automatically billed egress or one direction's NIC capacity; check each full-duplex direction separately.

Assumption (illustrative): 100,000 concurrent media sessions send 1.0 Mbps and receive 2.5 Mbps per user. Twelve percent require TURN. Each relayed payload byte crosses the relay boundary twice: once entering TURN and once leaving it. Aggregate relay-interface throughput is therefore 100,000 * 0.12 * (1.0 + 2.5) Mbps * 2 = 84 Gbps. Adding 20% protocol/retransmission overhead gives 100.8 Gbps. Surviving loss of one of three equal failure domains without overload requires each remaining domain to carry at least half of 100.8 Gbps, or 50.4 Gbps usable, plus maintenance margin.

Do not confuse user media bitrate with aggregate relay-interface throughput: summing user send and receive counts both media directions, while multiplying by two counts the ingress and egress traversal of each direction at TURN. If a capacity metric deliberately measures only one interface or one traffic direction, name that scope and do not apply the aggregate factor again. Draw byte direction explicitly and count every relay interface once. Track allocation count, selected transport, ingress/egress bitrate, packets/s, allocation failures, abuse drops, and cost by region.

docs.title: 12. Failures, evidence, and implications
docs.text:
Failure Evidence Design implication proxy buffers SSE server write time is low; client event delay is periodic/large disable buffering/compression that delays flush; production-path test WebSocket half-open missing pong/application ack while socket appears open liveness deadline and bounded reconnect replay gap cursor jumps or retention expired atomic replay-to-live handoff; snapshot/reset contract slow consumer per-session queue bytes/age rise coalesce, drop, spill, or disconnect before process OOM reconnect storm handshake/auth rate spikes after fleet event jitter, retry hints, admission, staged drain, resume-cache protection ICE direct failure relay candidate selected; check-pair failure reasons regional TURN capacity and enterprise-network testing media freezes but signaling healthy RTP gap, jitter-buffer/NACK metrics separate signaling from media health and recovery audio degrades under video load queue delay/loss by media type prioritize audio and shed video layers NACK storm feedback and retransmit rate rise with loss deadline-aware bounded packet cache and feedback suppression SFU zone loss subscription migration and remaining egress jump reserve evacuation bandwidth and reconnect gradually TURN bill spike relay ratio/bitrate shifts by region/client version investigate path regression; quotas and routing policy

Evidence must join control and media timelines: signaling state/epoch, ICE gathering/check duration, selected candidate pair and transport, DTLS setup, time to first audio/video, RTP loss/reorder/jitter, RTCP feedback, NACK/FEC/retransmit rate, jitter-buffer delay, encode bitrate/layers, SFU ingress/egress, slow-consumer drops, reconnect attempts, and close reasons. Protect privacy: do not log raw SDP, IP candidates, meeting content, or tokens without strict need and handling.

The Notification System case study covers durable multi-channel fan-out; use it when “real time” actually means eventually delivered alerts rather than a live socket.

docs.title: L5 expectations
docs.text:
• Choose WebSocket, SSE, long polling, WebRTC, or segmented delivery from a stated contract.
  • Define connection/session identity, ordering scope, replay cursor, slow-consumer policy, and liveness.
  • Trace signaling, ICE, STUN/TURN, DTLS-SRTP, RTP/RTCP, and media feedback.
  • Quantify concurrent sessions, buffer memory, handshake recovery rate, SFU egress, and TURN relay load.
  • Describe production-path evidence and failure injection for reconnect, loss, jitter, relay fallback, and zone loss.

docs.title: L6 extensions
docs.text:
• Design multi-region session placement, SFU cascading, TURN sovereignty, and evacuation capacity.
  • Establish fleet-wide reconnect control across clients, DNS, edge, auth, signaling, and media tiers.
  • Govern codecs, protocol changes, browser/client-version compatibility, privacy, and deprecation.
  • Balance quality, cost, fairness, accessibility, moderation, recording, and end-to-end encryption.
  • Build closed-loop capacity policy from relay ratio, media quality, regional egress, and failure forecasts with canary/rollback controls.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Saying WebSocket guarantees replay or exactly-once delivery.
  • Treating the WebSocket accept key or browser Origin as authentication.
  • Ignoring fragmentation, decompression limits, and slow consumers.
  • Assuming an SSE write() flushed through every proxy.
  • Advancing a long-poll cursor on timeout or allowing overlapping unordered polls.
  • Reconnecting every client immediately after failure.
  • Saying STUN relays media or TURN only helps discovery.
  • Calling signaling the WebRTC media path.
  • Claiming DTLS-SRTP through an SFU is automatically end-to-end encryption among users.
  • Retrying media packets after their playout deadline.
  • Sizing an SFU by CPU or participants while ignoring egress and packets/s.
  • Calculating TURN from average users without relay ratio, both relay directions, overhead, locality, and failover.

docs.title: Exercise 1: design WebSocket replay
docs.text: A chat client applies event 500, loses the connection while event 501 may be in flight, and reconnects. Specify the protocol behavior.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

The client reconnects with room scope, authenticated session identity, a higher connection epoch, and after_event_id=500. The server reads a durable ordered log after 500 and atomically bridges replay to live subscription. If 501 had reached the old connection but was not applied, it is delivered again and deduplicated by event ID. If retention expired, the server returns an explicit snapshot/reset response. Client commands use separate idempotent command IDs; the new epoch fences delayed old-socket commands.

docs.title: Exercise 2: diagnose delayed SSE
docs.text: The application emits one 200-byte SSE event each second, but clients receive 20 events every 20 seconds. Server timestamps show prompt writes. What evidence and changes do you seek?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Compare timestamps/bytes at application, sidecar, ingress, CDN, and client; inspect response buffering, compression, minimum chunking, caching, HTTP version, and idle policies. Configure text/event-stream routes for streaming and no inappropriate buffering/transformation, flush complete events, and use bounded comment keepalives if needed. Validate through the real production path; increasing application write frequency alone does not fix downstream buffering.

docs.title: Exercise 3: bound reconnect recovery
docs.text: Three million clients disconnect. Authentication safely handles 5,000 reconnects/s while preserving normal traffic. What is the fastest theoretical recovery and what policy is required?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

At the full safe reconnect allocation, 3,000,000 / 5,000 = 600 s, or ten minutes. Actual recovery needs longer for failed attempts, variance, and normal joins. Enforce server admission near the safe rate, return retry hints, and have clients use exponential backoff with full jitter. Staged drains and randomized connection age prevent recurrence. Measure queue age and reject rather than allowing millions of blocked handshakes.

docs.title: Exercise 4: calculate TURN capacity
docs.text: There are 60,000 concurrent users. Each sends 0.8 Mbps and receives 2.0 Mbps. Fifteen percent use TURN, and overhead is 25%. Calculate aggregate relay throughput using this model.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

Relayed users are 60,000 * 0.15 = 9,000. Per-user media is 0.8 + 2.0 = 2.8 Mbps; each byte enters and exits TURN, so aggregate relay-interface traffic is 2.8 * 2 = 5.6 Mbps per relayed user. Base throughput is 9,000 * 5.6 = 50.4 Gbps; with 25% overhead, 50.4 * 1.25 = 63 Gbps. Add regional imbalance, safe NIC/packets-per-second limits, maintenance, and failure-domain headroom before provisioning.

docs.title: Exercise 5: choose NACK or FEC
docs.text: A mobile audio path has 180 ms RTT and a 60 ms remaining playout margin when loss is detected. Should the receiver depend on retransmission?

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

No. A NACK round trip cannot return the packet inside a 60 ms margin on a 180 ms RTT path. Prefer bounded FEC/redundancy appropriate to the codec and path, conceal loss, and adapt bitrate. NACK can still help paths with enough playout margin; both mechanisms must avoid adding congestion and prioritize audio continuity.

docs.title: Exercise 6: compare mesh and SFU
docs.text: Eight participants each send 1.2 Mbps video. Estimate each user’s upload in a full mesh and compare it with sending a 2.4 Mbps simulcast ladder to an SFU.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Open after your attempt

In full mesh, each user sends seven copies: 7 * 1.2 = 8.4 Mbps upload, before overhead. With the assumed SFU ladder, upload is about 2.4 Mbps regardless of participant count, while SFU egress carries selected copies to receivers. The SFU improves client uplink scaling but transfers cost and failure responsibility to server egress, packet processing, and regional capacity.

docs.text:

  • WHATWG, HTML Living Standard: Server-sent events.
  • IETF, RFC 8825: Overview: Real-Time Protocols for Browser-Based Applications and RFC 8835: Transports for WebRTC.
  • IETF, RFC 8445: Interactive Connectivity Establishment, RFC 8489: STUN, and RFC 8656: TURN.

docs.title: 13. NAT and Cloud Networking
docs.text: The stateful NAT/NAPT commonly used for cloud egress is a tuple-rewrite system, not a synonym for security. Stateless algorithmic translation also exists: SIIT translates IPv4 and IPv6 headers without per-flow mappings, while NPTv6 translates IPv6 prefixes without transport-port state. This chapter focuses on stateful SNAT, DNAT, port allocation, and conntrack; cloud networking adds routes, virtual firewalls, gateways, and provider-managed failure domains around that state. At L5, design the packet path and size its finite tables. At L6, standardize address ownership, egress identity, isolation, evidence, and recovery across accounts and regions.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • trace SNAT, DNAT, conntrack, routing, and filtering for both directions of a flow;
  • calculate port and translation capacity under connection churn;
  • distinguish public/private subnets, security groups, NACLs, and host firewalls;
  • design transit, hybrid, overlapping-address, hairpin, and asymmetric paths; and
  • prove cloud-egress behavior and recovery with packet, flow-log, and gateway evidence.

docs.title: 1. Start with the tuple
docs.text:
A transport flow is commonly identified by:

(protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port)

For outbound TCP, SNAT changes the source. For inbound publishing, DNAT changes the destination. Port address translation may change a port so many private flows share one public address.

Before SNAT: TCP 10.20.4.17:49152 -> 198.51.100.40:443
After SNAT:  TCP 203.0.113.8:62001 -> 198.51.100.40:443

Return packet received by NAT:
             TCP 198.51.100.40:443 -> 203.0.113.8:62001
Reverse map:
             TCP 198.51.100.40:443 -> 10.20.4.17:49152

The translator records enough state to reverse the transformation. A packet that misses that state is not the same flow, even if an operator believes it is a reply.

docs.title: SNAT and DNAT are independent decisions
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Private client<br/>10.20.4.17:49152] -->|original tuple| N[NAT gateway<br/>conntrack]
    N -->|SNAT<br/>203.0.113.8:62001| I[Internet server<br/>198.51.100.40:443]
    I -->|reply tuple| N
    N -->|reverse translation| C
    P[Public client] -->|203.0.113.10:443| D[DNAT or public LB]
    D -->|10.20.8.25:8443| S[Private service]

DNAT makes an internal target reachable; it does not by itself authenticate the caller. SNAT hides private addressing from the destination; it does not make a malicious connection safe. Routing establishes a possible path. Stateful and stateless policy then decides whether packets may traverse it. Application authorization remains separate; see Security Architecture.

docs.title: 2. Conntrack is finite distributed state
docs.text:
Linux netfilter connection tracking classifies packets into states such as NEW, ESTABLISHED, RELATED, and INVALID. NAT normally selects a mapping on the first packet and applies it to later packets in that tracked flow. Managed gateways implement equivalent behavior, although their exact allocation and limits are provider-specific.

Important resource dimensions include:

  • active conntrack entries;
  • mappings per public source address and destination tuple;
  • ephemeral source ports;
  • packet and byte throughput;
  • new-flow allocation rate;
  • idle and closing-state retention; and
  • per-destination concentration.

TCP TIME_WAIT belongs to an endpoint that actively closed a connection; a gateway can have different translation-retention rules. Do not infer gateway capacity from host TIME_WAIT counts alone. Both can limit churn, but they are different state machines.

docs.title: Port arithmetic
docs.text:
Assume one egress IP has 55,000 usable translated ports for one destination (IP, port, protocol). If mappings remain unavailable for an average of 70 seconds, an idealized steady-state churn ceiling is:

new-flow ceiling = usable ports / occupancy time
                 = 55,000 / 70
                 = 786 new flows/s

At 4,000 new connections/s to that destination:

required simultaneous mappings = 4,000 * 70 = 280,000
minimum egress IPs by ports      = ceil(280,000 / 55,000) = 6

Six is only a port-space floor. Add headroom for skew, retries, health checks, deployment reconnects, provider reservations, and failure of one gateway or address. If N+1 requires losing one of eight equal egress addresses, normal utilization should remain below 7/8 = 87.5% before skew; an operational target may be materially lower.

The 55,000 ports and 70 seconds are fixture inputs, not universal cloud quotas or TCP timers. A mean occupancy calculation is an arithmetic ceiling, not a conservative tail guarantee; skew can exhaust one allocation pool earlier.

Destination diversity can allow reuse of the same source port in distinct five-tuples. Provider allocation rules vary, so validate with the exact gateway and workload. The most effective fix is often persistent connection reuse or multiplexing, not an ever-larger NAT fleet.

docs.title: 3. Packet-processing order matters
docs.text:
A useful conceptual path is:

ingress interface
  -> destination translation
  -> route lookup
  -> stateful/stateless policy
  -> source translation
  -> egress interface

Implementations differ in hook order and optimization. Diagnose against the platform's documented datapath rather than memorizing one universal chain.

For every failed flow, write a two-row packet ledger:

Direction Tuple at source Tuple at gateway/public boundary Expected route and policy request 10.20.4.17:49152 -> 198.51.100.40:443 203.0.113.8:62001 -> 198.51.100.40:443 default route to NAT; outbound permitted response 198.51.100.40:443 -> 203.0.113.8:62001 198.51.100.40:443 -> 10.20.4.17:49152 same stateful device; return route to subnet

This reveals wrong assumptions about which address a firewall, allowlist, log, or peer actually observes.

docs.title: 4. Public and private are routing properties
docs.text:
A subnet is not private because its instances lack public DNS names. In common cloud designs:

  • a public subnet has a route to an internet gateway, and a workload also needs a usable public address or public front end;
  • a private subnet has no direct internet-gateway path for workload addresses;
  • an egress subnet hosts NAT, proxies, or firewalls through which private workloads reach external destinations; and
  • an isolated subnet has no general internet route in either direction.
flowchart TB
    Internet((Internet)) --> IGW[Internet gateway]
    IGW --> ALB[Public load balancer]
    ALB --> App[Private application subnets]
    App --> DB[(Isolated data subnets)]
    App --> NAT[NAT or egress proxy]
    NAT --> IGW
    App --> EP[Private service endpoints]
    Corp[Corporate network] --> TGW[Transit hub]
    TGW --> App

Route tables choose next hops by longest-prefix match. A default route is less specific than a private endpoint, peering prefix, or propagated hybrid route. Record both the selected route and the alternatives; “the route table looks right” is not evidence that the expected route won.

docs.title: 5. Layered filtering without false confidence
docs.text:
Control Typical state Scope Frequent failure security group stateful interface/workload correct request rule but wrong group attachment network ACL stateless subnet boundary request allowed, ephemeral return ports denied host firewall implementation-dependent operating system cloud policy allows flow but local chain drops it managed firewall/proxy often stateful and L7-capable centralized path asymmetric return misses state; TLS identity unavailable application authorization request-aware API/resource network reachability mistaken for permission

Stateful policy usually permits return traffic for an admitted flow. Stateless policy needs explicit rules for both directions. For a client connecting to destination port 443, the response's destination is the client's ephemeral port, not 443. Avoid opening 0-65535 reflexively: derive the actual client port range, direction, protocol, and subnet boundaries.

This table uses AWS-style security-group/NACL semantics, not a universal mapping to Azure NSGs or Google Cloud firewall policies. A post-SNAT boundary can see a translated port range instead of the original client's ephemeral range.

Security groups and NACLs cannot compensate for an unintended route, a public address on the wrong workload, or a proxy that can reach every tenant. Use independent controls, but assign a test and owner to each one.

docs.title: 6. Transit and hybrid routing
docs.text: A transit hub reduces a full mesh, but centralization introduces route-policy and throughput blast radius. Separate route domains for production, non-production, shared services, inspection, and partners. Propagate only intended prefixes; do not turn every attachment into universal reachability.

docs.title: Overlapping address space
docs.text:
Two networks that both own 10.20.0.0/16 cannot be unambiguously routed through one ordinary IP forwarding domain. Options are:

  1. renumber one side: the cleanest long-term answer;
  2. expose services through load balancers, proxies, or private service endpoints instead of routing whole networks;
  3. translate one or both sides into non-overlapping ranges and maintain identity outside the translated address; or
  4. isolate them in distinct routing domains and join only through application gateways.

Translation solves address ambiguity, not service identity, audit attribution, DNS views, or policy lifecycle. A translated partner source may collapse many principals into one address.

docs.title: Hybrid route ownership
docs.text:
For VPN or dedicated circuits, define:

  • which side originates each prefix;
  • whether static and dynamic routes coexist and which wins;
  • maximum accepted prefixes and explicit filters;
  • primary/backup preference and equal-cost behavior;
  • bidirectional maximum transmission unit (MTU) and fragmentation behavior; and
  • what evidence proves failover and failback.

A broad on-premises route can accidentally attract cloud-to-cloud traffic. A more-specific stale route can black-hole one subnet while aggregate probes remain green.

docs.title: 7. Hairpins and asymmetry
docs.text:
A hairpin occurs when traffic exits toward a public or shared front door and returns to a target near its source. It may incur two translations, extra zones, inspection cost, source-identity loss, or unsupported same-interface forwarding.

Bad surprise:
app A -> public service name -> internet/NAT/LB -> app B in same VPC

Often preferable:
app A -> private service name -> private LB/endpoint -> app B

Split-horizon DNS can expose private and public answers, but now DNS view is part of correctness. Test from every resolver domain.

Stateful middleboxes require flow symmetry:

request:  client -> firewall A -> server
response: server -> firewall B -> client   # B has no state: drop/reset

Asymmetry can result from equal-cost routing, a changed default route, multiple VPNs, zone-specific appliances, or failover during long-lived connections. Either preserve affinity to the same stateful device, synchronize state where explicitly supported, or remove that device from the stateful path. Do not assume route symmetry merely because both endpoints are reachable.

docs.title: 8. Cloud egress architecture
docs.text:
Choose deliberately among:

Pattern Strength Cost and risk NAT per zone avoids cross-zone dependency; scalable failure domains more gateways and public IPs; destination allowlists grow centralized NAT/firewall common policy and stable egress identity transit cost, hairpins, large blast radius, scaling complexity explicit forward proxy domain/user policy and richer logs application compatibility, TLS policy, proxy outage private service endpoint avoids public path and often NAT provider/service coverage, endpoint and DNS complexity no default egress strongest exfiltration reduction dependency inventory and update paths required

Include processing charges, cross-zone bytes, transit bytes, firewall bytes, log ingestion, and failure traffic. The Cost Engineering chapter provides the broader model.

At L6, assign egress identities by trust domain rather than sharing one organization-wide public IP. A compromised development workload must not inherit a production partner allowlist. Maintain a destination inventory, expiry for exceptions, emergency deny capability, and controlled DNS because a domain allowlist ultimately resolves to addresses.

docs.title: 9. Failure evidence and recovery
docs.text:
Failure Evidence that distinguishes it Recovery and proof port exhaustion gateway allocation errors; active mappings near limit; old connections work while new ones fail reduce churn, add source capacity; prove new-flow success and falling utilization conntrack saturation kernel/gateway insertion drops, INVALID packets, table occupancy shed or scale; prove insert failures cease under peak replay missing return route request seen at target, no response at source boundary; flow logs differ by direction repair route propagation; capture both directions NACL return denial reject log on ephemeral destination port narrow corrective rule; synthetic handshake from affected subnet asymmetric firewall path request and response observed on different appliances; state miss restore symmetric route/affinity; prove long-lived and new flows stale partner allowlist peer sees unexpected translated source IP restore approved egress identity; peer log plus local tuple evidence zonal NAT loss one zone's new outbound flows fail; other zones healthy fail locally or controlled reroute; verify capacity and cross-zone cost MTU/PMTUD failure handshake works, larger payload stalls; ICMP too-big absent correct MTU or permit PMTUD; test increasing payload sizes

Recovery is not “the graph is green.” Capture the failed tuple, change identifier, restored request rate, allocation headroom, reject count, path/zone distribution, and rollback readiness. Follow the recovery discipline in Reliability Engineering.

docs.title: 10. Design review checklist
docs.text:
• Draw forward and reverse tuples before and after every translation.
  • Name every route table, longest-prefix winner, and stateful hop.
  • Calculate ports, conntrack entries, new flows/s, throughput, and N+1 headroom.
  • Keep NAT, routing, network filtering, workload identity, and authorization distinct.
  • Test ephemeral return ports for every stateless boundary.
  • Eliminate or justify hairpins and cross-zone egress.
  • Resolve overlapping ranges with an explicit identity and DNS plan.
  • Prove hybrid failover, route withdrawal, MTU, and asymmetric-flow behavior.
  • Partition egress identities by trust domain and audit destination exceptions.
  • Price normal traffic, retries, failover, transit, processing, and telemetry.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Size an egress pool
docs.text:
A worker fleet opens 9,000 TLS connections/s to one vendor endpoint. Connections are not reused. A mapping occupies a port for 50 seconds, each egress IP provides 60,000 usable ports for that destination, and the design must survive one egress IP failure while staying below 70% port utilization. How many IPs are required?

Worked solution

Solution: Required mappings are 9,000 * 50 = 450,000. One IP's operating capacity is 60,000 * 0.70 = 42,000. After one failure, N - 1 IPs must provide capacity: ceil(450,000 / 42,000) = 11, so N = 12. This is a port bound only. Verify gateway new-flow and throughput limits. Connection reuse would reduce both risk and cost.

Twelve addresses do not imply one gateway supports twelve: for example, the checked AWS NAT gateway limit is up to eight IPv4 addresses and public-address quota increases can be required. Distribute capacity across supported gateways and separately test loss of a whole gateway, not just one source address.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Diagnose a one-way flow
docs.text:
Flow logs show an accepted SYN from 10.1.2.8:53000 to 10.50.4.9:443. The server capture shows SYN arrival and SYN-ACK departure. The client never receives it. Two VPN attachments advertise 10.1.0.0/16; the return route changed during maintenance.

Worked solution

Solution: The application and inbound policy are not the first suspects because the server received the SYN and emitted a SYN-ACK. Correlate the response tuple at each boundary and inspect the selected return route. The likely failure is asymmetric return through an attachment without matching state or reachability. Restore deterministic preference, withdraw the unintended advertisement, then prove request and response traverse the intended attachment for new and long-lived flows.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Design partner connectivity with overlap
docs.text:
Both the company and a partner use 10.20.0.0/16. The partner needs two HTTPS APIs, not general network access.

Worked solution

Solution: Do not route both full ranges into one table. Publish the two APIs through narrowly scoped private endpoints or application proxies with non-overlapping endpoint addresses. Authenticate partner workloads independently of source IP, authorize only the required APIs, and log original identity. If translation is unavoidable, allocate explicit translated ranges in both directions and test DNS, callbacks, logs, and policy against translated tuples. Plan renumbering if the relationship expands.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• NAT consumes tuple state, ports, allocation rate, bytes, and operational attention.
  • Public/private classification follows addresses and routes, not subnet names.
  • Stateful and stateless filters fail differently; neither replaces application authorization.
  • Hybrid transit needs prefix ownership, filtering, symmetry, MTU, and failover proof.
  • Egress identity is a security and partner contract as well as a networking detail.
  • Recovery evidence must show the restored bidirectional packet path and remaining headroom.
