docs.title: 14. BGP, Anycast, and Global Routing
docs.text: Global routing is a policy system under delayed, partial information. BGP exchanges reachability between autonomous systems; it does not understand application correctness or choose the mathematically shortest geographic path. Anycast, DNS steering, and CDNs build different control loops on top of that reality.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • explain ASes, eBGP/iBGP, route advertisements, attributes, import/export policy, and convergence;
  • reason about leaks, hijacks, route-origin validation, and the limits of RPKI;
  • model anycast catchments, withdrawal, state, and evacuation headroom;
  • combine DNS, anycast, CDN, and application failover without conflicting controllers; and
  • demand evidence for routing changes and global recovery.

docs.title: 1. Autonomous systems and reachability
docs.text:
An autonomous system (AS) is a network or group of networks under one routing policy, identified by an autonomous system number (ASN). BGP speakers advertise IP prefixes plus path attributes. External BGP (eBGP) exchanges routes between ASes. Internal BGP (iBGP) distributes externally learned and internal reachability inside an AS, commonly with route reflectors at scale.

flowchart LR
    U[Client network<br/>AS 64510] --> T[Transit<br/>AS 64520]
    T --> E1[Edge A<br/>AS 64530]
    T --> E2[Edge B<br/>AS 64530]
    E1 --> R1[Region A]
    E2 --> R2[Region B]

Conceptually, an update says: “I can reach this prefix through this path, with these attributes.” Each neighbor applies import policy, selects a best path using its implementation and policy, installs eligible routes, and applies export policy before advertising onward.

receive routes -> reject/filter -> modify attributes -> select best
               -> install/resolve next hop -> export selected/eligible routes

BGP is path-vector, not link-state. The AS_PATH helps detect loops and expresses traversed ASes, but operators can prepend ASNs and apply local policy. Reachability is economic and administrative, not simply geographic.

docs.title: 2. Attributes and policy
docs.text:
Exact selection order varies by implementation. The following attributes are core reasoning tools:

Attribute Scope and purpose Operational implication LOCAL_PREF internal preference within an AS; higher commonly preferred primary policy lever for outbound path choice AS_PATH sequence of ASes; shorter often preferred after local policy prepending is a hint, not a guarantee ORIGIN route-origin mechanism (IGP, EGP, incomplete) usually late in selection; not origin authorization MED suggestion to a neighboring AS about entry point; lower commonly preferred comparison and propagation rules vary NEXT_HOP address used to resolve forwarding a valid BGP route can fail if next hop is unreachable communities policy labels interpreted by agreement semantics are provider-specific unless standardized

The selection that matters to your service can happen several ASes away. Changing MED at one provider may do nothing for clients whose networks prefer another transit. AS-path prepending can be outweighed by customer routes, local preference, paid peering, or more-specific prefixes.

docs.title: Prefix specificity dominates many intentions
docs.text: Forwarding uses longest-prefix match. If one site announces 203.0.113.0/24 and another leaks 203.0.113.0/25, networks accepting both usually forward the first half to the /25, regardless of the aggregate's BGP attributes. Filters and global routing norms constrain acceptable prefix lengths, but never rely on “our normal route should be preferred” as protection.

docs.title: Policy as code
docs.text:
For every peering session define:

  • expected neighbor ASN and authenticated session protections where available;
  • accepted prefix allowlist or maximum prefix length/count;
  • origin and AS-path constraints;
  • communities set, accepted, stripped, or acted upon;
  • default-route policy;
  • maximum-prefix shutdown behavior; and
  • change, canary, rollback, and out-of-band access.

Generate and test policy from an authoritative prefix/ASN inventory. A syntactically valid route map can still export the full internet table or an internal prefix.

docs.title: 3. Convergence is not one timer
docs.text:
A route change propagates hop by hop. Each router processes updates, selects a path, updates forwarding state, and advertises according to policy. Some networks never receive or accept the change. Existing flows may survive, reset, or move depending on topology and state.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Edge site
    participant P as Transit/peer
    participant R as Client AS router
    participant C as Client
    participant N as Surviving site
    S->>P: Withdraw prefix
    P->>P: Recompute and update forwarding
    P->>R: Propagate withdrawal or alternate path
    R->>R: Apply local policy
    C->>R: Next packet
    R->>N: Forward next packet via selected alternate
    N-->>C: Response if connection and service state permit

Measure at least:

Tdetect + Tdecision + Texport + Tpropagation + Tremote decision + Ttraffic shift

BGP session timers are only part of Tdetect. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection can detect some forwarding failures quickly, but aggressive timers can create false churn. Route flap damping can delay recovery and is not a universal answer. Application drain, DNS cache age, connection lifetimes, and load-balancer health add independent timelines.

docs.title: 4. Leaks, hijacks, and RPKI
docs.text:
A route leak propagates legitimate reachability beyond its intended policy scope: for example, a customer accidentally announces provider-learned routes to another provider. A prefix hijack originates or propagates unauthorized reachability, accidentally or maliciously. Both can attract, intercept, or black-hole traffic.

Defenses are layered:

  1. strict import/export prefix and path filters;
  2. maximum-prefix limits;
  3. Internet Routing Registry data used carefully;
  4. RPKI Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) and Route Origin Validation (ROV);
  5. route monitoring from independent vantage points; and
  6. rehearsed withdrawal, deaggregation where accepted and safe, provider escalation, and customer communication.

RFC 9234 adds negotiated BGP Roles for eBGP relationships and the transitive Only-to-Customer (OTC) attribute. Role pairs let peers detect incompatible relationship configuration during session establishment. OTC marks routes so compliant ASes can reject propagation that violates the customer-to-provider/peer export model and can detect several route-leak classes. It complements rather than replaces prefix/path filters and RPKI: deployment is incremental, both parties must configure compatible roles for negotiation, legacy neighbors may not set or enforce OTC, and incorrect business-relationship configuration can reject legitimate routes. Define fail-closed or exception behavior per neighbor and monitor role mismatch and OTC rejection explicitly.

RPKI origin validation classifies a route as commonly Valid, Invalid, or NotFound by checking whether a ROA authorizes the origin ASN and prefix length. It has important limits:

  • it validates route origin, not the entire AS path;
  • NotFound is not proof of legitimacy;
  • coverage and enforcement are incomplete;
  • stale or incorrect ROAs can invalidate the owner's route;
  • max-length choices can authorize more-specific announcements more broadly than intended; and
  • it does not prove that the application at the routed address is authentic.

TLS remains necessary even when routing is valid. BGPsec aims at path validation but deployment is not universal. ASPA is intended to help detect some route leaks; treat deployment status as an evolving ecosystem property, not a completed control.

docs.title: 5. Anycast mechanics and catchments
docs.text:
With anycast, multiple sites originate the same service prefix. A client's catchment is the set of sources whose routing policy currently sends traffic to one site. Catchments depend on peering, transit policy, failures, and route propagation; they do not form stable geographic circles.

flowchart TD
    A[One anycast service prefix] --> P1[PoP A announcement]
    A --> P2[PoP B announcement]
    A --> P3[PoP C announcement]
    C1[Client AS group 1] -->|policy-selected path| P1
    C2[Client AS group 2] -->|policy-selected path| P2
    C3[Client AS group 3] -->|policy-selected path| P3
    P1 --> O1[Regional service]
    P2 --> O2[Regional service]
    P3 --> O3[Regional service]

Anycast works well for stateless or rapidly reconstructable edge functions such as authoritative DNS, recursive DNS, DDoS absorption, and CDN ingress. Stateful transports need care. A route change can send subsequent packets to another site that lacks connection, QUIC, NAT, or TLS-session state. QUIC connection IDs can support migration only when the implementation, routing, keys, and server state are designed for it; anycast alone does not provide migration.

docs.title: Health must control advertisements safely
docs.text:
Do not connect one flaky process health check directly to global route withdrawal. Use layered gates:

instance health -> local pool eligibility -> site capacity/readiness
                -> advertisement policy -> external traffic evidence

Apply hysteresis, minimum hold times, quorum or aggregate site health, manual override, and fail-safe behavior. Preserve out-of-band management when the service prefix is withdrawn.

docs.title: 6. Catchment and evacuation calculations
docs.text:
Suppose normal peak demand is:

Site Normal peak Tested safe capacity A 800k req/s 1.20M req/s B 600k req/s 1.05M req/s C 400k req/s 0.80M req/s

Tests show that withdrawing A shifts 55% of A to B, 35% to C, and 10% to an external fallback.

B after withdrawal = 600k + 0.55 * 800k = 1.04M req/s
C after withdrawal = 400k + 0.35 * 800k = 680k req/s

B is below its tested ceiling by only 10k req/s, less than 1% headroom. The design is not robust to forecast error, retry amplification, uneven object mix, or loss of a B cluster. Either add B capacity, alter catchments/overflow policy, shed optional traffic, or stage A's withdrawal while observing external traffic.

Do not assume proportional redistribution. Measure with controlled announcements and independent vantage points. Capture request rate, bandwidth, connection rate, cache misses, TLS handshakes, origin load, latency, errors, and per-client-AS movement.

docs.title: 7. DNS steering, anycast, CDN, and global failover
docs.text:
These mechanisms operate at different scopes:

Mechanism Decision granularity State/staleness Best use BGP anycast destination prefix and network policy routing convergence nearest-policy edge ingress, DDoS distribution authoritative DNS name lookup recursive/client TTL caches coarse region/provider steering CDN request mapping request/connection at edge provider mapping and cache state content delivery and origin shielding L4/L7 load balancer connection/request local health and affinity site/region pool selection application routing operation/key/tenant business state home-region and correctness decisions 
flowchart LR
    U[User] --> DNS[DNS chooses provider or service IP]
    DNS -. returned address constrains destination .-> AC
    U --> AC[Anycast catchment chooses edge]
    AC --> CDN[CDN or edge policy]
    CDN --> RG[Regional gateway]
    RG --> APP[Application chooses data home]

Assign one owner to each decision. If DNS shifts users west while the CDN independently shifts origin east and the application redirects writes west, control loops can oscillate or create transoceanic hairpins.

DNS failover is bounded by cached records and resolver behavior. Anycast withdrawal can move traffic faster for many networks but with less precise destination control. A CDN can keep serving cached objects during origin failure while dynamic requests fail. Global failover must therefore define behavior per operation, not only per hostname; see Multi-Region Architecture.

docs.title: 8. Withdrawal and failback procedure
docs.text:
1. Establish baseline: route visibility, catchment request/byte/connection mix, downstream headroom, cache state, and error budget.
  2. Prepare survivors: prewarm safe cache/state, reserve autoscaling quota, lower optional traffic, and verify origin/dependency capacity.
  3. Canary policy: use a community, one peer, or a less-preferred advertisement to shift a bounded catchment where supported.
  4. Observe externally: route collectors, RIPE Atlas-style probes, DNS checks, synthetic transactions, client-AS telemetry, and service signals.
  5. Withdraw in stages: avoid taking multiple peers/sites at once unless security requires immediate withdrawal.
  6. Prove recovery: user success, not merely route absence; surviving sites must remain within tested envelopes.
  7. Fail back slowly: restore announcement preference in stages. Cold caches and synchronized reconnection can overload the recovered site.

Security incidents may require immediate full withdrawal despite availability risk. Pre-authorize who can make that tradeoff. The Reliability Engineering chapter covers recovery ownership and degraded modes.

docs.title: 9. Failure evidence
docs.text:
Symptom Evidence to collect Likely classes one ISP/ASN cannot connect looking-glass path, route visibility, traceroute boundary, client-AS errors missing propagation, import filter, RPKI invalid, provider fault latency jumps for one geography edge site ID, client ASN, route path, DNS answer catchment shift, DNS steering, peering congestion all traffic leaves a healthy site local BGP session/advertisement, upstream received routes, ROV state export error, peer rejection, invalid ROA site withdrawal overloads neighbor measured redistribution, connection/TLS/cache-miss rates insufficient evacuation headroom TCP resets during route change five-tuples and site IDs before/after, connection-state locality stateful anycast path change valid route but wrong service TLS certificate/name, HTTP authority, destination ownership misbound VIP, stale config, hijack beyond origin validation intermittent global oscillation timelines of DNS, BGP, CDN, autoscaling controllers competing health loops or insufficient hysteresis

Route collectors show control-plane views, not guaranteed packet delivery. Traceroute shows selected ICMP/TTL-expiry behavior, not necessarily the application path. Combine control-plane, data-plane, and user-journey evidence.

docs.title: 10. Design review checklist
docs.text:
• Inventory prefixes, ASNs, owners, peers, ROAs, and maximum lengths.
  • Specify import/export policy and maximum-prefix behavior per session.
  • Separate routing reachability from application and capacity health.
  • Measure catchments by request, bytes, connection churn, client ASN, and workload type.
  • Calculate each withdrawal scenario with non-proportional redistribution and retries.
  • Keep every survivor inside a tested safe envelope with degradation policy.
  • Define which controller owns BGP, DNS, CDN, regional, and application decisions.
  • Test stale DNS, route rejection, invalid ROA, site withdrawal, and cold-cache failback.
  • Use independent external route and transaction evidence.
  • Preserve emergency authority and out-of-band access.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Test an AS-path-prepend proposal
docs.text:
A team wants to prepend its ASN three times at Site A so all traffic moves to Site B. Is the claim valid?

Worked solution

Solution: No. Remote ASes first apply local policy; some may prefer customer or peering routes regardless of path length, and some may not receive both routes. Define the target catchments, canary the prepend by peer/community, and measure external route selection plus actual traffic. If deterministic evacuation is required, staged withdrawal is stronger but has greater blast radius.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Validate failover capacity
docs.text:
Site X serves 500k req/s. On withdrawal, 70% moves to Y and 30% to Z. Y normally serves 900k with a tested ceiling of 1.30M; Z serves 300k with a ceiling of 700k. Retries can add 10% to shifted traffic. Is failover safe?

Worked solution

Solution: Y receives 500k * 0.70 * 1.10 = 385k, reaching 1.285M, only 15k below its ceiling. Z receives 165k, reaching 465k. Y has about 1.2% headroom and is unsafe against ordinary skew. Add capacity or shed/redirect enough load before withdrawal, then verify with measured catchments.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Explain an RPKI incident
docs.text:
After adding a ROA for 203.0.113.0/24 with origin AS 64530 and maximum length /24, a disaster procedure announces two /25s from AS 64530. Some networks lose reachability.

Worked solution

Solution: The /25 announcements are RPKI Invalid because the ROA's maximum length is /24, even though the origin ASN matches. Prefer keeping the authorized aggregate strategy if operationally viable. If more-specific emergency announcements are truly required, change the ROA through a reviewed procedure before the event and understand that broader max length increases authorization scope. Verify propagation from ROV-enforcing and non-enforcing networks.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Choose steering layers
docs.text:
A payments API needs stable regional data ownership; static assets need low-latency global delivery.

Worked solution

Solution: Use CDN/anycast edge ingress for static assets, with cache and origin shielding. Use DNS or edge routing for coarse API region selection, but let application routing enforce account/home-region write correctness. Do not let BGP movement silently change the data owner. Document independent failure behavior and the handoff between edge and application policy.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• BGP distributes policy-qualified reachability, not geographic truth or application health.
  • More-specific prefixes and remote local preference can override intended traffic engineering.
  • RPKI origin validation is valuable but does not validate the whole AS path or service identity.
  • Anycast catchments are measured external outcomes, not circles drawn around PoPs.
  • Withdrawal is a capacity event; failback is a cold-cache and reconnection event.
  • Combine DNS, CDN, routing, and application controls only with explicit ownership and evidence.

docs.text:

docs.title: 15. Service Mesh and Zero Trust
docs.text: A service mesh moves selected traffic policy into a shared data plane. Zero trust removes implicit trust based on network location and requires continuously evaluated identity, device/workload state, policy, and context. They overlap, but neither implies the other: a mesh can encrypt traffic while authorizing everything, and a system can apply zero-trust principles without a mesh.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • separate north-south gateways from east-west service communication;
  • compare sidecar and ambient or node-level data planes;
  • explain desired configuration, discovery, xDS-like distribution, and stale-state behavior;
  • design workload identity, mTLS, authorization, retries, telemetry, and certificate rotation;
  • evaluate control-plane outage, bypass, cost, and multi-tenant isolation; and
  • prove policy and recovery at workload, proxy, and application boundaries.

docs.title: 1. Define the boundaries first
docs.text:
North-south traffic crosses a system boundary: user to edge, partner to API, or workload to the public internet. East-west traffic moves between internal services. The labels describe trust and operational boundaries, not compass directions.

flowchart LR
    U[User or partner] --> G[North-south gateway]
    G --> A[Service A]
    A --> B[Service B]
    B --> D[(Database)]
    A --> E[Egress gateway]
    E --> X[External API]
    CP[Mesh control plane] -. desired config .-> G
    CP -. desired config .-> A
    CP -. desired config .-> B

An ingress gateway commonly terminates public TLS, validates user credentials, applies coarse policy, and routes HTTP. East-west policy authenticates workload identities and authorizes service-to-service actions. An egress gateway can constrain external destinations and provide audit or stable egress identity, but it becomes a stateful capacity and availability dependency.

Draw every bypass path: host networking, loopback, direct pod IP, node port, unmanaged workload, UDP protocol, external load balancer, debug container, and cloud metadata endpoint. A policy enforced only in the proxy is not enforced on traffic that avoids the proxy.

docs.title: Sidecar
docs.text:
A sidecar proxy runs beside each workload instance, usually sharing its network namespace or receiving redirected traffic.

pod A                                  pod B
+-------------+                       +-------------+
| app -> proxy| === authenticated ==> |proxy -> app |
+-------------+                       +-------------+

Strengths: per-workload policy boundary, mature L7 controls, local telemetry, independent rollout by workload. Costs: one proxy per workload, CPU/memory overhead, connection and file-descriptor duplication, startup ordering, version skew, and difficult transparent interception.

docs.title: Ambient or node-level
docs.text:
Ambient designs move secure L4 transport into a shared node or network-layer component and add optional L7 waypoint proxies where policy requires them.

flowchart LR
    A[Workload A] --> ZA[Node secure tunnel A]
    ZA --> W[Optional L7 waypoint]
    W --> ZB[Node secure tunnel B]
    ZB --> B[Workload B]

Strengths: lower per-pod overhead, fewer injected containers, infrastructure-managed upgrades. Costs: a larger shared blast radius, identity attribution at the shared layer, node interception complexity, and possible extra waypoint hops for L7 policy.

Neither architecture is universally cheaper. Benchmark actual requests/s, connection count, payload sizes, TLS handshakes, filter chains, telemetry sampling, and node density. Include cross-zone hops and gateway processing in the Cost Engineering model.

docs.title: 3. Desired state is not observed state
docs.text:
Most meshes separate:

  • a control plane, which accepts intent, validates and compiles policy, discovers endpoints, and distributes desired configuration; and
  • a data plane, which serves traffic from locally held configuration and credentials.

An xDS-like protocol streams versioned listeners, routes, clusters/endpoints, secrets, and related resources. The important concepts are generic: version, nonce or acknowledgement, dependency ordering, rejection detail, and eventual convergence.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Operator or API
    participant C as Control plane
    participant P as Proxy
    participant W as Workload
    O->>C: Submit desired policy version 42
    C->>C: Validate and compile
    C->>P: Push snapshot or delta 42
    P->>P: Validate dependencies
    P-->>C: ACK 42 or NACK with error
    P->>W: Serve using accepted state

Track at least four versions:

authored -> accepted by API -> compiled/distributed -> active in each data plane

An API success proves only acceptance, not fleet activation. A control-plane dashboard showing version 42 does not prove that a disconnected proxy left on version 39 is safe. Define convergence SLOs and maximum permissible staleness for routes, authorization, revocation, and trust bundles separately.

docs.title: Discovery is routing input
docs.text:
Discovery maps a service identity to endpoints and metadata such as zone, health, protocol, and subset. Stale discovery can keep terminated endpoints, omit new capacity, or mislabel a tenant. Define:

  • source of truth and readiness semantics;
  • endpoint removal and drain ordering;
  • locality preference and spillover;
  • outlier ejection and minimum healthy capacity;
  • stale-cache behavior during control-plane loss; and
  • whether application DNS and mesh discovery can disagree.

Outlier ejection is not a substitute for capacity management. If 20% of endpoints are slow because the dependency is overloaded, ejecting them can overload the remainder.

docs.title: 4. Workload identity and mTLS
docs.text:
IP addresses identify interfaces and routes, not durable principals. A workload identity should bind an authenticated workload to a trust domain and service account or equivalent principal. SPIFFE defines URI-form identities such as:

spiffe://prod.example/payments/settlement-worker

The identity issuer must attest workload properties before issuing short-lived credentials. The mesh then uses mutual TLS (mTLS): both peers authenticate, traffic is encrypted in transit, and the receiving policy can authorize the authenticated source.

identity issuance:
node/workload evidence -> attestor -> identity document + private key

request:
source proxy presents identity -> destination validates trust chain/name
destination presents identity -> source validates expected service

mTLS answers “which certified workload is at the other end?” It does not answer “may it refund order 123?” Authorization must evaluate source identity, destination, operation, tenant, and request context. Keep end-user identity distinct from proxy workload identity; propagate user claims through a constrained, integrity-protected mechanism rather than trusting arbitrary headers.

See Security Architecture for threat modeling, authentication, and key ownership.

docs.title: 5. Authorization: default deny with explicit ownership
docs.text:
A useful policy model is:

allow if
  authenticated source in approved trust domain
  AND destination workload matches policy target
  AND method/path or RPC is allowed
  AND tenant/context constraints pass
  AND no higher-priority deny applies

Prefer stable identities and named operations over IP ranges. Separate platform guardrails from application-owned grants:

Layer Example Owner organization deny unknown trust domains security/platform environment production cannot receive from development platform service checkout may call payment authorization destination team resource caller may mutate this merchant's order application/data layer

L7 mesh policy sees only what the proxy parses. End-to-end encrypted, custom, tunneled, or unsupported protocols may expose only L4 identity. If the destination application alone knows resource ownership, keep that authorization there.

docs.title: Safe rollout
docs.text:
1. Inventory observed flows, including jobs, probes, failover, and break-glass paths.
  2. Create policy in audit/dry-run mode where available.
  3. Investigate denied flows; do not automatically permit every observed flow.
  4. Enforce on a canary subset.
  5. Compare user success, authorization denies, and bypass probes.
  6. Expand with an immediate rollback that does not require the failed control plane.

Observed traffic includes compromise and accidental dependencies. It is evidence, not the policy specification.

docs.title: 6. Certificate and trust-bundle rotation
docs.text:
Short-lived credentials reduce exposure but increase dependence on issuance and time. Let certificate lifetime be L, renewal begin after fraction r, and maximum issuer outage tolerance before expiry be approximately:

renewal reserve = L * (1 - r)

For a 24-hour certificate renewed at 50% lifetime, nominal reserve is 12 hours. Clock skew, retry delay, rollout lag, and already-failed renewals reduce it. Monitor remaining lifetime distribution, issuance success, and signer availability.

Rotate roots with overlap:

1. distribute trust bundle containing old + new roots
2. prove receivers accept credentials from both
3. issue leaf credentials from new root
4. prove fleet adoption and drain old sessions
5. remove old root only after maximum leaf/connection lifetime and rollback window

Rotating issuer and trust bundle simultaneously can partition the fleet. A control-plane outage during rotation must have an explicit policy: continue with cached, unexpired material; fail closed after expiry; and preserve a narrowly controlled recovery path.

Leaf expiry is checked during certificate validation; it does not automatically terminate live TLS sessions or all resumption tickets. Force non-resumed canaries and govern session/ticket age and invalidation separately. A no-effects-after- expiry policy needs request/effect-boundary enforcement, not just TLS sockets.

docs.title: 7. Retries, deadlines, and traffic policy
docs.text:
A mesh can standardize connect timeouts, circuit breaking, load balancing, and retries, but it cannot infer business idempotency. Default retries at a proxy can repeat non-idempotent application actions or multiply application retries.

If a client makes 2 attempts, the ingress makes 2, service A makes 3, and its sidecar makes 2:

maximum dependency attempts = 2 * 2 * 3 * 2 = 24

Choose one retry owner per call boundary, propagate an end-to-end deadline, restrict retries to transient failures and replay-safe operations, and cap retry traffic with a budget. Account for per-try timeout plus connection acquisition and response reserve. See Deadlines, Retries, and Pools.

Traffic splitting also needs denominator clarity. A 1% canary by requests may receive more than 1% of CPU if requests are larger or long-lived. Hash-based splits can stick tenants to one version. Track requests, bytes, concurrent streams, tenant distribution, and outcomes.

docs.title: 8. Telemetry without accidental explosion
docs.text:
The mesh can emit transport and request signals without application changes:

  • connection attempts, resets, handshake failures, and certificate identity;
  • request rate, response codes, latency, retries, and upstream endpoint;
  • policy allow/deny decisions and active config version; and
  • bytes, protocol, source/destination workload, zone, and route.

It cannot know whether a 200 response violated a business invariant or whether a timeout happened after a durable commit. Application telemetry remains necessary.

High-cardinality labels, source workload, destination, route, response code, zone, tenant, certificate, and version, multiply. At 2,000 sources, 500 destinations, 20 routes, 10 status classes, and 3 zones, the theoretical space is:

2,000 * 500 * 20 * 10 * 3 = 600,000,000 series

Do not pre-aggregate every combination. Keep bounded service-level metrics, sampled traces, short-retention structured access logs, and targeted debug capture. Redact credentials and sensitive headers. Link mesh cost to Cost Engineering.

docs.title: 9. Control-plane outage and stale state
docs.text:
A robust data plane continues serving with its last accepted configuration during a temporary control-plane outage. That improves availability but delays endpoint changes, revocation, routes, and trust updates.

This depends on resource validity and policy: Envoy resource TTLs can expire while disconnected. A NACK reports at least one invalid resource; it does not prove that every resource in the response was rejected. Likewise, an ACK records validation and intent to apply, not successful activation. Inspect each resource's accepted, active, warming, and expired state instead of treating one response version as an atomic fleet-wide configuration.

Define per-resource failure posture:

Resource Cached operation Staleness risk Expiry response route/listener continue accepted version stale destination or policy reject unknown config; preserve known routes if safe endpoints use last set with local health dead endpoint, missing capacity eject locally; avoid inventing endpoints authorization continue accepted policy delayed revocation high-risk deny may need independent emergency path leaf certificate use until expiry issuance outage alert before reserve consumed; fail closed at expiry trust bundle retain validated bundle cannot trust newly rotated issuer overlap roots; block unsafe single-step rotation

The control plane itself needs multi-zone deployment, durable desired state, admission validation, backpressure, bounded fan-out, versioned rollback, and tenant/resource quotas. A bad global policy can be more dangerous than control-plane unavailability.

docs.title: 10. Bypass and multi-tenancy
docs.text:
Zero-trust claims fail if traffic can bypass enforcement. Test, do not assume:

  • direct workload IP and localhost paths;
  • host-networked or privileged workloads;
  • DNS changes and alternate ports/protocols;
  • egress through unmanaged nodes or NAT;
  • control-plane/admin APIs;
  • packet redirection failure after restart; and
  • namespace or service-account impersonation.

In multi-tenant platforms, protect both data plane and control plane:

  • namespace policy objects and prevent cross-tenant references;
  • validate that a tenant cannot select another tenant's workloads;
  • partition certificate names and private-key access;
  • quota routes, endpoints, filters, telemetry, and config churn;
  • avoid shared gateway connection pools when credentials or tenant context differ; and
  • test noisy-neighbor CPU, memory, connection, and config-push effects.

See Multi-Tenant Isolation for cell and control-plane boundaries.

docs.title: 11. Failure evidence and recovery
docs.text:
Failure Distinguishing evidence Recovery proof proxy config rejected NACK/error, active version behind desired, dependency detail accepted version equal across canary; expected route works mTLS trust break handshake alert, presented identity, chain/root version, clock both directions authenticate with rotated bundle authorization regression deny decision with source/destination/policy rule; app not reached intended flow succeeds; forbidden fixture still fails stale discovery proxy endpoint dump differs from registry; calls to terminated IP stale endpoint absent; new endpoint receives bounded traffic retry amplification attempt count in trace exceeds request count; retry response flags one owner and bounded ratio under injected fault control-plane outage streams disconnected while data path continues on known version existing routes meet SLO; reconnect converges without surge transparent-capture bypass packet capture reaches app without proxy identity/log bypass probe blocked at independent network/app control noisy tenant proxy/gateway resource and config fan-out dominated by tenant quota isolates healthy tenants under repeated test

Recovery needs a positive and negative proof. Show that the required call works and a forbidden call remains denied. Also record desired/active versions, identity chain, retry count, and latency/capacity after recovery.

docs.title: 12. Design review checklist
docs.text:
• Mark north-south, east-west, egress, admin, and bypass paths.
  • Choose sidecar, ambient, gateway, or no mesh per protocol and boundary.
  • Record authored, accepted, distributed, and active config versions.
  • Define stale behavior and convergence SLO per resource type.
  • Bind mTLS credentials to attested workload identity, not mutable IP.
  • Keep workload authentication, end-user identity, and resource authorization distinct.
  • Assign one retry owner and propagate deadlines.
  • Rotate roots with trust overlap and measurable fleet adoption.
  • Bound telemetry cardinality and redact sensitive fields.
  • Test control-plane outage, config rejection, bypass, noisy tenant, and rollback.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Control-plane outage during deployment
docs.text:
The control plane becomes unavailable after 60% of proxies activate route version 18. Version 18 sends 5% of traffic to a new service version. What should the system do?

Worked solution

Solution: Do not claim a coherent fleet state. Freeze further rollout and inspect whether mixed versions preserve correctness. Data planes should continue with their last accepted state if safe. If the canary is harmful, use a preplanned rollback path that remains available without the failed control plane; otherwise hold and restore control-plane quorum. Prove per-proxy active versions, canary traffic distribution, user outcomes, and no retry/connection surge when streams reconnect.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Calculate rotation reserve
docs.text:
Leaf certificates last 12 hours and renewal starts at 60% of lifetime. Issuance is unavailable for 4 hours. Ignoring skew, do all certificates survive?

Worked solution

Solution: Renewal starts after 12 * 0.60 = 7.2 hours, leaving 4.8 hours nominal reserve. Certificates that had just reached renewal should survive a 4-hour outage, but those with prior failures or skew may not. Alert on remaining lifetime, not average age, and validate the minimum across the fleet. Preserve cached unexpired credentials; fail closed after expiry.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Stop retry multiplication
docs.text:
An application retries twice and its sidecar retries twice, while the ingress retries once after the original attempt. How many downstream attempts can one user request create?

Worked solution

Solution: Interpreting “retries twice” as three application attempts, sidecar three attempts, and ingress two attempts gives 3 * 3 * 2 = 18. Disable implicit retries at layers that do not know idempotency, choose one owner, propagate the remaining deadline, and enforce a retry budget. Verify attempt counts in traces during a forced transient failure.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Prove zero-trust enforcement
docs.text:
A policy allows checkout to call payments and denies all others. What constitutes proof?

Worked solution

Solution: Show an authenticated checkout identity completing the intended operation, an authenticated unrelated identity denied with the matching rule, an unauthenticated/bypass fixture denied before the application effect, and application resource authorization rejecting a checkout identity for an unauthorized tenant. Include active policy versions and destination logs. Reachability success alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• A mesh is a policy delivery and enforcement system, not automatic zero trust.
  • Desired configuration, accepted configuration, and fleet-active state are different facts.
  • mTLS authenticates workloads; application authorization still protects resources and tenants.
  • Data planes should survive bounded control-plane loss without accepting unknown state.
  • Retries, telemetry, gateways, and proxies consume finite capacity and can amplify failures.
  • Every enforcement claim needs a tested bypass path and a negative authorization proof.

docs.text:

docs.title: 16. Network Observability and Debugging
docs.text: Network debugging is evidence-driven boundary isolation. “The network is slow” is not a diagnosis: name resolution, route selection, packet filtering, socket queues, transport loss, TLS policy, proxies, application queues, and downstream work expose different evidence. Work from the user symptom toward the narrowest failing boundary, one hypothesis at a time.

docs.title: Learning goals
docs.text:
After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • run a layered DNS-to-application troubleshooting method;
  • interpret dig, curl, openssl, ss, tcpdump, and mtr within their limits;
  • combine metrics, traces, flow logs, socket state, and packet captures;
  • distinguish connect, TLS, HTTP, routing, MTU, saturation, and dependency failures;
  • command an incident with safe rollout, rollback, and recovery proof; and
  • design fixture-based alternatives when production shell or packet access is unavailable.

docs.title: 1. Define the failed contract
docs.text:
Before opening a dashboard, capture:

who:       client population, ASN/network, zone, workload, tenant
what:      operation, hostname, method, protocol, payload size
when:      first/last seen, continuous or intermittent, deployment timeline
expected:  SLI and threshold
observed:  error, phase duration, status, affected fraction
scope:     one host/zone/region/version/path or global

Use one correlation bundle when possible:

timestamp + request/trace ID + client/source + hostname
+ resolved address + destination port + region/zone + deployment version

Compare a failing request with a known-good control that differs by one dimension. Aggregate graphs establish scope; one trace or packet path explains mechanism.

docs.title: 2. The layered method
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S[Reproduce exact symptom] --> D{DNS answer correct?}
    D -- no --> DE[Inspect resolver, authority, TTL, DNSSEC]
    D -- yes --> R{Route and policy permit path?}
    R -- no --> RE[Inspect route, flow logs, ACL, NAT, firewall]
    R -- yes --> T{Transport established?}
    T -- no --> TE[Inspect SYN path, loss, MTU, sockets, capacity]
    T -- yes --> L{TLS established and identity valid?}
    L -- no --> LE[Inspect SNI, chain, trust, time, policy]
    L -- yes --> H{HTTP response valid and timely?}
    H -- no --> HE[Inspect proxy route, queue, retry, upstream]
    H -- yes --> A[Validate application/business outcome]

The layers are not a rigid OSI checklist. A proxy can terminate TCP/TLS and open a different upstream flow. Repeat the method for each hop and record where identity, protocol, tuple, deadline, and ownership change.

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
1. User journey: did the intended operation succeed within contract?
  2. Application/proxy: what route, upstream, code, deadline, and retry state were used?
  3. TLS: which name, certificate chain, version, alert, and peer identity?
  4. Transport/socket: did connection setup complete; were there retransmissions, resets, queueing, or exhaustion?
  5. Packet/flow: where was the tuple accepted, rejected, translated, or lost?
  6. Routing/DNS control plane: which answer and route should have produced that data path?

Start at the cheapest decisive evidence. Escalate capture depth only when the current layer cannot distinguish hypotheses.

Commands below are templates for authorized test endpoints/namespaces, not localhost fixtures. Documentation addresses require an approved substitution. Prefer the bounded labs; do not elevate privileges or send production payloads merely to reproduce a template.

docs.title: 3. DNS evidence
docs.text:
dig can query a chosen resolver or authoritative server and show answer, TTL, response code, flags, and delegation. It does not prove which resolver an application used, whether the application cached an older answer, or whether connecting to the address succeeds.

dig api.example.com A
dig api.example.com AAAA
dig @resolver.example api.example.com A +dnssec
dig +trace api.example.com

Record:

  • queried name, type, resolver address, response code, and flags;
  • answer/CNAME chain and TTLs;
  • authoritative serial and delegation when relevant;
  • positive versus negative caching;
  • DNSSEC validation status where enabled; and
  • application/runtime cache and search-domain behavior.

Fixture alternative without production DNS access:

fixture fields:
queried_at, resolver, qname, qtype, rcode, answers[], ttl[], flags[], transport

Replay the fixture through the same parser/decision logic. For integration tests, run an isolated authoritative DNS container with scripted stale, NXDOMAIN, delayed, truncated, and split-horizon answers.

docs.title: Common DNS traps
docs.text:
• Testing the apex while the application requests a CNAME target or different hostname.
  • Ignoring AAAA when clients prefer IPv6 and its path is broken.
  • Lowering a TTL after old high-TTL answers are already cached.
  • Treating NXDOMAIN and empty successful answers as equivalent.
  • Using /etc/hosts or curl --resolve and then claiming resolver behavior works.

docs.title: 4. Routes, filtering, and flow logs
docs.text:
A route lookup should answer which source, destination, table, rule, interface, and next hop the host selects. Platform route tables and transit policy may add more hops.

ip route get 198.51.100.40 from 10.20.4.17

On systems without ip, use the platform-native route inspection command or an exported route fixture. Capture the effective route, not only intended configuration.

Cloud flow logs usually summarize accepted/rejected tuples at selected interfaces or boundaries. They are not packet captures: sampling, aggregation, delayed delivery, and provider fields vary. A missing record may mean no packet reached the capture boundary, logging was disabled, the record was sampled out, or filters excluded it.

Build a boundary ledger:

Boundary Request tuple/status Response tuple/status Clock/source client interface emitted received or absent pcap/socket subnet/interface policy accept/reject accept/reject flow log NAT/firewall pre/post translation reverse state gateway metrics/log server interface received emitted pcap/socket

If the server sees the SYN and sends SYN-ACK but the client sees no SYN-ACK, do not debug HTTP. Isolate return routing, stateless return rules, NAT state, or asymmetric middleboxes; see NAT and Cloud Networking.

docs.title: 5. Socket and TCP evidence
docs.text:
ss shows local socket state and queue information. Exact options and exposed TCP diagnostics depend on privileges and kernel.

ss -s
ss -tanp
ss -ti dst 198.51.100.40

Interpret patterns rather than one count:

Observation Hypotheses Next evidence many SYN-SENT destination/filter loss, wrong route, listener absent captures at both ends; flow logs many SYN-RECV client return path loss, accept pressure, SYN flood server queues, SYN-ACK capture, backlog counters accept queue full application not accepting fast enough listener backlog, CPU/thread profile send queue persists receiver/window/path congestion TCP info, receiver state, pcap ACK/window receive queue persists application not reading app thread/GC/CPU evidence high TIME-WAIT connection churn at active closer connection reuse, port range, NAT metrics resets explicit endpoint/middlebox termination packet flags, process logs, timing

docs.title: Handshake interpretation
docs.text:
client                       server
SYN ------------------------>
    <---------------- SYN,ACK
ACK ------------------------>
  • Repeated SYN with no SYN-ACK: request or return path, filter, listener, or overload.
  • SYN-ACK visible at server but not client: return path/filter/middlebox.
  • ACK followed by immediate RST: wrong listener/protocol, application close, or middlebox policy.
  • Handshake succeeds but payload stalls: TLS/application, receive window, PMTU, or downstream queue.

TCP retransmission is evidence of missing acknowledgement, not proof of physical packet loss. Reordering, capture loss, asymmetric observation, delayed ACK, or receiver pressure can mislead. Capture both boundaries and use sequence/acknowledgement numbers.

docs.title: 6. TLS evidence
docs.text:
Use openssl s_client to inspect a handshake explicitly:

openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.20:443 \
  -servername api.example.com -verify_hostname api.example.com \
  -showcerts -verify_return_error

Record SNI, destination address, negotiated TLS version/cipher, ALPN, certificate subject/SAN, issuer chain, validity, verification result, and alert. -servername supplies SNI so shared endpoints select the intended certificate and route; it does not verify that the certificate matches that name. -verify_hostname performs that identity check. If the installed s_client lacks this option, use a hostname-validating client such as curl --resolve with the application trust store rather than treating chain validation alone as success.

Test the actual trust store and client-certificate behavior used by the application. A shell OpenSSL build may trust a different root bundle. For mTLS, capture which client identity was presented and what destination policy authorized it; see Service Mesh and Zero Trust.

Failure distinctions:

Error Likely evidence hostname mismatch SAN lacks requested SNI/hostname unknown CA incomplete chain or trust bundle lacks issuer expired/not yet valid certificate validity versus both endpoint clocks no shared protocol/cipher offered/selected versions and policy handshake timeout TCP established but TLS records/response absent mTLS rejection server requests client cert; identity or chain rejected

Do not use -k or disabled verification as a fix. It is a diagnostic comparison only, and the insecure result must not be used as recovery proof.

docs.title: 7. HTTP and proxy evidence with curl
docs.text:
curl can expose phase timings and force one variable while preserving hostname identity:

curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error \
  --connect-timeout 2 --max-time 8 \
  --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.20 \
  -o /dev/null \
  -w 'code=%{http_code} ip=%{remote_ip} dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} first_byte=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' \
  https://api.example.com/health/ready

Interpret cumulative timestamps correctly:

DNS phase       = time_namelookup
TCP after DNS   = time_connect - time_namelookup
TLS after TCP   = time_appconnect - time_connect
TTFB after TLS  = time_starttransfer - time_appconnect
body transfer   = time_total - time_starttransfer

For example:

dns=0.030 connect=0.090 tls=0.180 first_byte=0.780 total=0.800 seconds

TCP increment  = 0.060 s
TLS increment  = 0.090 s
server/proxy   = 0.600 s
body transfer  = 0.020 s

The dominant phase is after TLS and before first byte. Investigate proxy queue, upstream calls, retries, and application work before changing DNS.

The 600 ms includes request transmission and path transit, not just server CPU. These differences assume fresh direct TLS-over-TCP without redirects; reuse, proxy CONNECT, and QUIC need different interpretation. The 30 ms DNS fixture models normal resolution, not the preceding --resolve bypass command.

--resolve bypasses normal DNS lookup while retaining URL hostname for SNI and HTTP authority. That makes it a useful A/B test, not proof that DNS is healthy. A health endpoint can also bypass the failing dependency or tenant path; replay a safe representative transaction when possible.

Fixture alternative:

{
  "url_host": "api.example.com",
  "remote_ip": "203.0.113.20",
  "status": 504,
  "dns_ms": 30,
  "connect_ms": 60,
  "tls_ms": 90,
  "ttfb_after_tls_ms": 600,
  "total_ms": 800,
  "trace_id": "fixture-7"
}

Use deterministic proxy/application fixtures to teach classification without contacting production.

docs.title: tcpdump
docs.text:
Capture narrowly to reduce sensitive data and volume:

timeout 30s tcpdump -i any -nn -c 200 -s 128 -w incident.pcap \
  'host 198.51.100.40 and tcp port 443'

-nn avoids reverse lookups and service-name conversion. A short snap length can retain headers while limiting payload, but VLAN, IPv6 extension, encapsulation, and TLS metadata may require more. Obtain authorization, set duration/size limits, protect the file, and delete it under retention policy. Packet captures can contain credentials or personal data.

This form requires GNU timeout and Linux's any interface. Otherwise use an approved platform wrapper or skip capture. Run in a new restricted disposable directory with umask 077 to avoid overwriting an existing capture. Packet count alone does not bound time on an idle interface. Snaplen 128 can retain payload and is not a privacy guarantee.

Capture can lie through:

  • NIC offloads that coalesce or segment packets differently from the wire;
  • dropped capture packets under CPU pressure;
  • the any pseudo-interface's link-layer differences;
  • clock skew between hosts;
  • asymmetric routing; and
  • capture at the wrong side of NAT, proxy, or tunnel.

Record interface, namespace, pre/post-NAT location, filter, snap length, drop count, clock source, and tool version.

docs.title: mtr and traceroute boundaries
docs.text:
mtr repeatedly sends probes with increasing TTL/hop-limit and combines latency/loss statistics. Routers may deprioritize, rate-limit, or block probe responses while forwarding application traffic normally. Different protocols and ECMP hashes can take different paths. Loss at an intermediate hop that does not continue at later hops is not evidence of forwarding loss.

mtr --report --report-cycles 50 --tcp --port 443 api.example.com

Use a protocol/port close to the application where legal, compare both directions if possible, and correlate the last common healthy boundary with packet/flow evidence. Never identify an intermediate router as root cause from one mtr output alone.

Fixture alternatives include saved pcap files, sanitized flow-log rows, route-table snapshots, socket-state dumps, and deterministic network namespaces with injected delay/loss. These are preferable for exercises and CI because they are repeatable and avoid production access.

docs.title: 9. Metrics, traces, logs, and pcap together
docs.text:
Each evidence type answers different questions:

Evidence Strength Blind spot metrics scope, rate, percentiles, saturation aggregation hides individual path and causality distributed traces per-request hop timing and retries sampling, missing propagation, work after timeout structured logs decisions, errors, config/version context volume, clock/order, missing events flow logs tuple, accept/reject, bytes at cloud boundary not packets; delayed/aggregated/sampled socket state endpoint queues and TCP state local view only pcap packet-level sequence and timing at capture point privacy, volume, capture artifacts, one boundary

Correlate by stable request/trace ID where possible and by bounded timestamp, tuple, connection ID, proxy upstream, and deployment version otherwise.

docs.title: USE and RED at network boundaries
docs.text:
For resources, inspect utilization, saturation, and errors (USE): NIC bytes/packets, conntrack occupancy, NAT ports, socket queues, CPU, drops, gateway limits. For request paths, inspect rate, errors, and duration (RED) by route, status, zone, and version. Histograms must use compatible buckets and units; averages hide tails.

Avoid unbounded source-IP, URL, tenant, or trace-ID metric labels. Keep high-cardinality context in sampled traces or indexed logs. Observability itself has ingestion and incident-query failure modes; see Cost Engineering.

docs.title: 10. Symptom matrix
docs.text: Symptom First discriminating checks Common causes NXDOMAIN resolver, qname/type, authority, negative TTL wrong name/view, stale delegation, negative cache connect timeout SYN at source/destination, route, flow rejects route/filter, no listener, NAT exhaustion, black hole connection refused RST source, listener/socket closed port, wrong target, process restart intermittent connect failures destination/zone/IP split, NAT and conntrack one bad target/path, port exhaustion, asymmetric ECMP TLS alert SNI, chain, time, ALPN, client identity expiry, trust rotation, hostname, mTLS policy fast 503 response issuer and route/upstream state no healthy upstream, admission rejection, deployment slow 504 proxy timeout, trace attempt timeline downstream deadline, queue, retries, stale endpoint high TTFB, low connect/TLS proxy/app queue and dependencies saturation, lock/GC, slow dependency small requests work, large stall PMTU, ICMP, MSS, packet sizes PMTUD black hole, proxy/body limits one ISP/geography fails DNS answer, client ASN, route visibility BGP propagation/filter/catchment recovery causes second spike connection/TLS/cache-miss/retry rates synchronized reconnect, cold cache, retry storm

docs.title: 11. Incident command and hypothesis control
docs.text:
Use explicit roles:

  • incident commander: owns objective, priority, risk, decisions, and cadence;
  • operations lead: executes approved mitigations and records change IDs;
  • investigation lead: maintains hypotheses and requests evidence;
  • communications lead: updates stakeholders with impact and uncertainty; and
  • scribe: records timeline, observations, commands, and recovery proof.

Keep a hypothesis table:

Hypothesis Prediction Evidence Status Next safe test DNS serves old IP failures correlate with resolver/answer answer + remote IP open/rejected query affected resolver NAT ports exhausted new connections fail; reused survive allocation metric open/rejected canary extra IP/reuse bad release errors correlate with version trace + deployment open/rejected remove canary

Do not run multiple uncontrolled changes. Timestamp every action. Preserve pre-change evidence when safe. Announce uncertainty rather than turning a plausible story into fact.

docs.title: Mitigation selection
docs.text:
Prefer the smallest reversible action that protects the user journey:

  1. stop a harmful rollout;
  2. shed optional load or disable amplification;
  3. drain a bounded target/path;
  4. restore last-known-good policy/configuration;
  5. fail over only after proving destination headroom; and
  6. make invasive network or trust changes with explicit security review.

Use the Reliability Engineering framework for degraded modes and error-budget decisions. Global path changes require the headroom and withdrawal analysis in BGP, Anycast, and Global Routing.

docs.title: 12. Rollout and recovery proof
docs.text:
A safe network-related rollout defines:

scope -> canary -> observation window -> success guardrails
      -> automatic stop -> rollback path -> fleet convergence proof

Segment outcomes by version, zone, route, destination, protocol, and client cohort. Fleet averages can hide a dead zone or one stale proxy.

Recovery proof should include:

  • the original representative user operation succeeds;
  • error and latency return inside SLO for a sustained window;
  • DNS, route, proxy, and policy versions match intended state;
  • connection, retry, TLS-handshake, cache-miss, and queue rates stabilize;
  • NAT/conntrack/socket/resource headroom remains under peak replay;
  • forbidden paths and security controls still fail as intended;
  • no delayed queue, replay, or failback wave is accumulating; and
  • rollback remains available until the observation window completes.

“Pods are healthy” and “ping works” do not meet this bar. Recovery closes the causal chain from user contract through each changed boundary.

docs.title: 13. Troubleshooting checklist
docs.text:
• Preserve the exact hostname, tuple, timestamp, trace ID, client cohort, and version.
  • Compare one failing and one controlled-good request.
  • Resolve cumulative timings into DNS, connect, TLS, TTFB, and transfer increments.
  • Repeat the layered method at every proxy or translation hop.
  • Record both directions and both sides of stateful boundaries.
  • State tool limitations before drawing conclusions.
  • Bound and protect packet captures and sensitive diagnostics.
  • Change one variable at a time and log the result.
  • Prove user recovery, capacity headroom, and negative security behavior.
  • Keep monitoring through failback, cache warming, and connection drain.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Classify phase timings
docs.text:
curl reports time_namelookup=0.120, time_connect=0.170, time_appconnect=0.260, time_starttransfer=1.060, and time_total=1.080 seconds. Calculate the phases and select the first investigation boundary.

Worked solution

Solution: DNS is 120 ms; TCP after DNS is 170 - 120 = 50 ms; TLS after TCP is 260 - 170 = 90 ms; time from completed TLS to first byte is 1,060 - 260 = 800 ms; body transfer is 20 ms. The dominant phase is proxy/application/upstream processing before first byte. Inspect route selection, queue time, retry timeline, and downstream spans. DNS is nontrivial but does not explain most latency.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Interpret an mtr result
docs.text:
Hop 5 shows 60% probe loss, but hops 6 through 12 and the destination show 0% loss with stable latency. Is hop 5 dropping application packets?

Worked solution

Solution: The evidence does not support that conclusion. Hop 5 likely rate-limits or deprioritizes TTL-expired probe responses while forwarding packets. Test the application protocol, destination loss, and packet/flow evidence. Only loss that persists downstream and correlates with the affected flow is meaningful.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Isolate a TLS failure
docs.text:
Connecting by IP succeeds with certificate verification disabled. Connecting to the hostname fails with certificate verify failed. What next?

Worked solution

Solution: Do not declare the network fixed or ship disabled verification. Repeat with the correct SNI and application trust bundle. Inspect SAN, chain completeness, issuer, validity, clock, and destination IP. Compare a known-good client. Recovery requires verified hostname authentication and, if applicable, client identity: not merely encrypted bytes.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Prove NAT recovery
docs.text:
After adding two egress IPs, new connection errors disappear for five minutes. What additional proof is required?

Worked solution

Solution: Show allocation failures remain zero through representative peak and reconnect churn, per-IP port utilization is balanced with N+1 headroom, conntrack and gateway throughput are below tested limits, vendor logs observe approved source IPs, reused and new connections succeed, and retry rate has normalized. Keep rollback and observe beyond old mapping lifetimes.

docs.title: Exercise 5: Debug “small works, large hangs”
docs.text:
TCP and TLS complete. A 200-byte request succeeds, while a 4 KiB request stalls after initial packets. What hypothesis and evidence come first?

Worked solution

Solution: Suspect PMTU/MSS or a size policy before DNS. Capture packet sizes, acknowledgements, retransmissions, ICMP Packet Too Big/fragmentation-needed messages, negotiated MSS, and proxy body-limit logs at both boundaries. Reproduce with increasing fixture sizes. Correct the MTU/PMTUD path or policy, then prove both small and large representative payloads.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Define the failed user contract and preserve one correlation bundle before changing anything.
  • Isolate DNS, route, transport, TLS, HTTP, and application boundaries with discriminating evidence.
  • Every tool has a viewpoint and blind spot; no single command proves end-to-end health.
  • Pair aggregate metrics with request traces and boundary-level packet or flow evidence.
  • Incident command controls hypotheses, risky changes, and communication under uncertainty.
  • Recovery proof includes sustained user success, remaining headroom, converged state, and intact security controls.

docs.title: Network Calculations Workbook
docs.text: Use this workbook to turn network claims into testable capacity and latency decisions. Every problem carries units, states its simplifying assumptions, and ends with an operational implication.

docs.title: Working conventions
docs.text:
• Network rates use decimal units: 1 Mbps = 1,000,000 bit/s and 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes.
  • Address sizes use powers of two.
  • Unless stated otherwise, RTT includes the round trip but not application work.
  • Little's Law uses mean arrival rate and mean time in system. A p99 latency is not a valid substitute for the mean.
  • Protocol overhead is workload- and path-dependent. Treat each supplied percentage as a fixture, not a universal constant.
  • Round only after completing the calculation.

docs.title: Formula sheet
docs.text: Topic Formula IPv4 addresses in prefix 2^(32 - prefix_length) IPv6 addresses in prefix 2^(128 - prefix_length) Serialization delay bits / link_rate_bit_per_s One-way propagation delay distance_km / propagation_km_per_s Bandwidth-delay product rate_bit_per_s * RTT_s Window-limited throughput window_bytes / RTT_s Little's Law mean_in_flight = mean_rate * mean_time_in_system Retry amplification product of attempts at each retrying layer Goodput useful_payload / elapsed_time Wire efficiency useful_bytes / wire_bytes NAT churn ceiling usable_source_ports / non_reuse_seconds per source/destination tuple TLS cores handshakes_per_s * CPU_seconds_per_handshake Cross-zone cost billable_bytes * price_per_GB

docs.title: Problem 1: Count a subnet
docs.text:
A service receives 10.42.16.0/20. How many IPv4 addresses exist? How many /24 blocks fit inside it?

Worked solution

Solution. The host width is 32 - 20 = 12 bits, so the prefix contains 2^12 = 4,096 addresses. Moving from /20 to /24 adds 4 prefix bits, so 2^4 = 16 /24 blocks fit. The arithmetic counts all addresses; platform reservations determine usable host count.

docs.title: Problem 2: Find the containing network
docs.text:
Which /26 contains 192.0.2.141, and what is its address range?

Worked solution

Solution. A /26 has blocks of 2^(32 - 26) = 64 addresses. The fourth-octet boundaries are 0, 64, 128, and 192. Address 141 is in 192.0.2.128/26, covering 192.0.2.128 through 192.0.2.191. Do not automatically subtract two addresses when estimating a cloud subnet; reservation rules vary.

docs.title: Problem 3: Split failure domains
docs.text:
Split 10.8.0.0/21 evenly across four zones. Give each resulting prefix.

Worked solution

Solution. Four equal pieces require 2 more prefix bits: /21 + 2 = /23. The subnets are 10.8.0.0/23, 10.8.2.0/23, 10.8.4.0/23, and 10.8.6.0/23. Each contains 512 addresses. Equal address space does not imply equal workload; capacity still needs per-zone headroom.

docs.title: Problem 4: Summarize routes
docs.text:
Can 172.16.8.0/24, 172.16.9.0/24, 172.16.10.0/24, and 172.16.11.0/24 be represented by one prefix?

Worked solution

Solution. Four contiguous /24 blocks can form a /22 only when aligned on a multiple-of-four third octet. Eight is aligned, so the summary is 172.16.8.0/22, covering third octets 8 through 11. Announcing 172.16.8.0/21 would also include 12 through 15 and could black-hole unrelated traffic.

docs.title: Problem 5: Size dual-stack growth
docs.text:
A zone needs 1,500 IPv4 interface addresses now and 40 percent growth. The platform reserves 5 addresses per subnet. Is a /21 sufficient?

Worked solution

Solution. Required interfaces are 1,500 * 1.40 = 2,100. A /21 contains 2,048 addresses and 2,043 after the fixture's reservations, so it is insufficient. A /20 contains 4,096, or 4,091 after reservations. Choose /20, then test whether blast-radius policy favors several smaller subnets instead.

docs.title: Problem 6: IPv6 hierarchy
docs.text:
A company receives 2001:db8:1200::/40 and assigns one /48 per region. How many region prefixes are available, and how many /64 subnets fit in each region?

Worked solution

Solution. Region selection has 48 - 40 = 8 bits, giving 2^8 = 256 /48 prefixes. Each /48 has 64 - 48 = 16 subnet bits, giving 65,536 /64 subnets. The large count is for hierarchy and stable allocation, not permission to ignore route aggregation.

docs.title: Problem 7: Serialize an object
docs.text:
How long does a 1.5 MB response take to serialize onto a 100 Mbps link, ignoring overhead and contention?

Worked solution

Solution. 1.5 MB * 8 = 12 Mbit; 12 Mbit / 100 Mbit/s = 0.12 s = 120 ms. This delay is paid at a bottleneck link even if propagation is near zero.

docs.title: Problem 8: Compare packet and object serialization
docs.text:
A 1,500-byte packet and a 10 MB object traverse a 1 Gbps egress link. Find each serialization time.

Worked solution

Solution. Packet: 1,500 * 8 / 1e9 = 0.000012 s = 12 us. Object: 10,000,000 * 8 / 1e9 = 0.08 s = 80 ms. Packet latency can look excellent while large-response completion remains bandwidth-bound.

docs.title: Problem 9: Estimate propagation floor
docs.text:
Two sites are 6,000 route-km apart. Use a fiber propagation speed of 200,000 km/s. What is the propagation-only RTT?

Worked solution

Solution. One way is 6,000 / 200,000 = 0.03 s = 30 ms; RTT is 60 ms. Routers, queuing, path inflation, serialization, and processing make observed RTT higher. A 20 ms cross-site SLO is physically inconsistent with this fixture.

docs.title: Problem 10: Calculate BDP
docs.text:
A 2 Gbps path has an 80 ms RTT. How much data must be in flight to fill it?

Worked solution

Solution. 2e9 bit/s * 0.080 s = 160 Mbit = 20 MB. Flow and congestion windows must jointly permit about 20 MB in flight. More server threads cannot overcome a 4 MB transport window.

docs.title: Problem 11: Find a window-limited ceiling
docs.text:
A flow has a 3 MB effective window and 75 ms RTT. What is its maximum throughput before loss and overhead?

Worked solution

Solution. 3,000,000 bytes / 0.075 s = 40 MB/s = 320 Mbps. On a 1 Gbps link, this flow can use at most 32 percent of capacity under the simplified fixture.

docs.title: Problem 12: Parallel flows and fairness
docs.text:
Four independent flows each have the 3 MB window from Problem 11 over the same 1 Gbps bottleneck. What aggregate does the window math suggest, and what is the actual ceiling?

Worked solution

Solution. Window math suggests 4 * 320 = 1,280 Mbps, but the shared link caps aggregate wire throughput at 1,000 Mbps before overhead. The flows now compete through congestion control. Adding connections can consume a larger share of a shared bottleneck; it does not create capacity.

docs.title: Problem 13: Fresh HTTPS request latency
docs.text:
DNS is warm. RTT is 45 ms, TCP setup costs 1 RTT, TLS 1.3 costs 1 RTT after TCP, server work is 30 ms, and the response returns in one final RTT. Estimate completion time.

Worked solution

Solution. 3 * 45 + 30 = 165 ms. A warm connection removes the first two RTTs and gives roughly 45 + 30 = 75 ms. This simplified serial model does not include TCP/TLS implementation overlap.

docs.title: Problem 14: QUIC handshake comparison
docs.text:
For the same 45 ms path, assume a fresh QUIC connection can authenticate and become ready for request data in 1 RTT, followed by server work and one response RTT. Compare with Problem 13.

Worked solution

Solution. QUIC completion is 2 * 45 + 30 = 120 ms, 45 ms lower than the fixture's fresh TCP plus TLS path. This is not a universal HTTP/3 gain: resumed connections, 0-RTT replay constraints, packet loss, and implementation CPU change the result.

docs.title: Problem 15: Wire efficiency
docs.text:
A batch sends 1,000 records. Each useful record is 900 bytes. Per-record framing is 36 bytes, and the batch adds 4,000 bytes of transport/TLS/IP overhead. Find wire bytes and efficiency.

Worked solution

Solution. Useful data is 1,000 * 900 = 900,000 bytes. Framing is 36,000 bytes, so wire data is 900,000 + 36,000 + 4,000 = 940,000 bytes. Efficiency is 900,000 / 940,000 = 95.74 percent. The 4.26 percent overhead must appear in bandwidth and cost estimates.

docs.title: Problem 16: Goodput under retransmission
docs.text:
A transfer delivers 400 MB of useful data in 10 seconds. The sender puts 460 MB on the wire because of headers and retransmissions. Find useful goodput, wire rate, and efficiency.

Worked solution

Solution. Goodput is 400 MB / 10 s = 40 MB/s = 320 Mbps. Wire rate is 460 MB / 10 s = 46 MB/s = 368 Mbps. Efficiency is 400 / 460 = 86.96 percent. Actual egress is 15 percent higher than an estimate based only on application bytes; equivalently, that estimate is 13.04 percent below actual egress.

docs.title: Problem 17: Small-message overhead
docs.text:
A telemetry sample has 80 useful bytes and incurs 70 bytes of combined framing. At 100,000 samples/s, compare useful and wire bandwidth.

Worked solution

Solution. Useful rate is 80 * 100,000 = 8 MB/s = 64 Mbps. Wire rate is 150 * 100,000 = 15 MB/s = 120 Mbps. Efficiency is only 80 / 150 = 53.33 percent. Batching can save bandwidth if its latency and failure coupling are acceptable.

docs.title: Problem 18: NAT churn ceiling
docs.text:
A NAT has 28,000 usable source ports for one source IP and destination tuple. Closed mappings cannot be reused for 60 seconds. What is the rough sustainable new-connection rate?

Worked solution

Solution. 28,000 / 60 = 466.7 connections/s is an idealized ceiling when active connection lifetime is negligible. Add mean active lifetime to the 60-second non-reuse period for a more realistic bound. A workload opening 900 connections/s to that tuple will eventually exhaust ports even if active concurrency appears low. Reuse connections or add independently usable source addresses.

docs.title: Problem 19: Add source addresses
docs.text:
How many equivalent source IPs are needed for 3,000 new connections/s under Problem 18's assumptions, with 25 percent headroom?

Worked solution

Solution. Define 25 percent headroom as 25 percent installed capacity unused: required ceiling is 3,000 / 0.75 = 4,000/s. ceil(4,000 / (28,000 / 60)) = ceil(8.5714) = 9 source IPs. Adding 25 percent to load is a different policy, although rounding also gives nine here. Validate allocation skew and destination sharing.

docs.title: Problem 20: Conntrack occupancy
docs.text:
A gateway sees 12,000 new flows/s. Mean tracked lifetime is 40 seconds, including closing states. Estimate mean conntrack occupancy. If the table limit is 600,000, what utilization does the mean imply?

Worked solution

Solution. Little's Law gives 12,000 * 40 = 480,000 entries. Mean utilization is 480,000 / 600,000 = 80 percent. Burst and lifetime tails can still overflow the table, so 80 percent mean is not safe proof.

docs.title: Problem 21: Time to exhaustion
docs.text:
A conntrack table has 100,000 free entries. During an incident, arrivals exceed expirations by 8,000 entries/s. How long until the table fills if nothing changes?

Worked solution

Solution. 100,000 / 8,000 = 12.5 seconds. Autoscaling in minutes cannot help the immediate gateway. Shed new flows, stop retry amplification, or redirect only to known spare capacity.

docs.title: Problem 22: TLS handshake CPU
docs.text:
A full TLS handshake consumes 1.2 ms of CPU on the server. Traffic creates 8,000 full handshakes/s. How many continuously busy CPU cores does handshake work require?

Worked solution

Solution. 8,000 * 0.0012 CPU-s = 9.6 cores. At a 60 percent CPU policy ceiling, provision at least 9.6 / 0.60 = 16 cores solely for handshake work under this fixture, before application and kernel costs.

docs.title: Problem 23: Resumption mix
docs.text:
Full handshakes cost 1.2 ms CPU, resumed handshakes cost 0.25 ms, and the server receives 10,000 handshakes/s with an 80 percent resumption hit rate. Find total handshake cores.

Worked solution

Solution. Full rate is 2,000/s and resumed rate is 8,000/s. CPU is 2,000 * 0.0012 + 8,000 * 0.00025 = 2.4 + 2.0 = 4.4 cores. Losing the resumption cache would raise this to 12 cores, so cache health is capacity evidence, not a minor optimization.

docs.title: Problem 24: Pool concurrency from the mean
docs.text:
A service makes 18,000 dependency calls/s. Mean dependency time is 22 ms. Estimate mean useful concurrency.

Worked solution

Solution. 18,000/s * 0.022 s = 396 calls in flight. Begin load testing near this concurrency with bounded acquisition, burst allowance, and a downstream ceiling. Do not calculate pool occupancy with the 180 ms p99; Little's Law requires the mean time.

docs.title: Problem 25: Why p99 is not the mean
docs.text:
Problem 24 has p99 latency 180 ms. A team sizes the pool as 18,000 * 0.180 = 3,240. What is wrong with that conclusion?

Worked solution

Solution. The multiplication is arithmetically correct but semantically wrong: 3,240 would be the mean concurrency only if 180 ms were the mean time. The measured mean predicts 396. The p99 still matters for acquisition deadlines, tail risk, and burst tests, but using it in Little's Law can inflate the pool and overload the dependency.

docs.title: Problem 26: Queue fill time
docs.text:
A pool serves 14,000 calls/s while arrivals spike to 19,000/s. Its waiting queue holds 7,500 calls. How quickly does it fill?

Worked solution

Solution. Net growth is 19,000 - 14,000 = 5,000 calls/s. Fill time is 7,500 / 5,000 = 1.5 seconds. A 30-second autoscaling response arrives too late; admission control and early shedding are required.

docs.title: Problem 27: Layered retry amplification
docs.text:
A mobile client makes up to 3 attempts, an edge makes up to 2, and a service library makes up to 2. How many dependency attempts can one logical operation produce?

Worked solution

Solution. 3 * 2 * 2 = 12 attempts. At 5,000 logical operations/s, the theoretical attempted rate is 60,000/s. Assign one retry owner and a shared attempt/deadline budget.

docs.title: Problem 28: Retry load during failure
docs.text:
Normal traffic is 20,000 operations/s. Thirty percent receive a retryable error and each affected operation makes one retry. Ignore retry success and latency. What attempted rate reaches the dependency?

Worked solution

Solution. Original rate is 20,000/s. Retry rate is 20,000 * 0.30 = 6,000/s, so attempted rate is 26,000/s, a 30 percent increase exactly when capacity is impaired. A retry budget capped at 5 percent of normal traffic would permit only 1,000 retries/s.

docs.title: 6. DNS, failover, TURN, anycast, and cost
Problem 29: DNS migration hold time
docs.text:
The old DNS TTL was 20 minutes. At 12:00 the team lowers it to 30 seconds. When is the earliest well-behaved cache that fetched just before 12:00 expected to expire the old value?

Worked solution

Solution. Near 12:20, because the cache retains the TTL attached to the answer it already has. The new 30-second TTL affects later answers. Expiration does not guarantee removal from all responses: a resolver's serve-stale policy can extend use during failures. Endpoint removal must also wait for connection drain and account for resolver floors and client caches.

docs.title: Problem 30: Load-balancer failover headroom
docs.text:
Three zones each receive 10,000 requests/s and have a tested safe ceiling of 16,000/s. Can the system lose one zone without shedding?

Worked solution

Solution. After one-zone loss, 30,000/s spreads across two zones, or 15,000/s each under perfect balance. That is below 16,000/s with only 1,000 / 16,000 = 6.25 percent remaining headroom. It passes steady arithmetic but is operationally fragile under skew, retries, or cold caches. A policy requiring 20 percent post-failover headroom would cap each survivor at 12,800/s and fail this design.

docs.title: Problem 31: Drain duration
docs.text:
A target has 24,000 established connections. Clients naturally close 300 connections/s, while 40 new connections/s still arrive because one discovery cache is stale. Estimate net drain time if rates remain constant.

Worked solution

Solution. Net drain is 300 - 40 = 260 connections/s. Time is 24,000 / 260 = 92.3 seconds. If long-lived connections do not follow the mean, enforce a maximum drain deadline and close them in bounded batches with reconnect jitter.

docs.title: Problem 32: TURN relay capacity
docs.text:
During a video event, 18,000 calls require TURN. Each call has two directions with an average 1.2 Mbps media rate per direction. Add 15 percent protocol and safety overhead. What relay bandwidth is required?

Worked solution

Solution. Each call contributes 2 * 1.2 Mbps = 2.4 Mbps to relay ingress and the same amount to relay egress because every relayed media bit enters and leaves the relay. Per direction, load is 18,000 * 2.4 Mbps = 43.2 Gbps; with overhead, each direction requires 43.2 * 1.15 = 49.68 Gbps. The relay therefore needs at least 49.68 Gbps ingress and 49.68 Gbps egress, or 99.36 Gbps aggregate RX plus TX processing if a platform reports their sum. Confirm whether NIC and provider limits are full-duplex, per direction, or aggregate and whether billing counts ingress, egress, or both.

docs.title: Problem 33: Anycast catchment shift
docs.text:
An anycast site normally serves 220 Gbps. On withdrawal, 55 percent shifts to site B, 30 percent to C, and 15 percent to D. Current loads and safe ceilings are B 500/650, C 300/390, and D 140/210 Gbps. Which site overloads?

Worked solution
