Solution. Shifted loads are B 121, C 66, and D 33 Gbps. New totals are B 621, C 366, and D 173 Gbps. None exceeds its ceiling, but remaining headroom is B 29, C 24, and D 37 Gbps. B has only 4.46 percent ceiling headroom and is the first concern under route variance or retries.

docs.title: Problem 34: Cross-zone service cost
docs.text:
A service sends 75,000 responses/s averaging 32 KB. Forty percent cross a zone boundary. Assume one billable transfer direction and $0.01/GB, with decimal units. Estimate daily cross-zone bytes and cost.

Worked solution

Solution. Total response rate is 75,000 * 32,000 = 2.4 GB/s. Cross-zone rate is 2.4 * 0.40 = 0.96 GB/s. Daily transfer is 0.96 * 86,400 = 82,944 GB; cost is $829.44/day, or about $24,883 per 30-day month. Include requests, replicas, retries, and bidirectional billing when they apply.

docs.title: Problem 35: Locality versus resilience
docs.text:
Changing routing lowers cross-zone traffic in Problem 34 from 40 percent to 10 percent, but requires 12 extra instances at $180 each per month. What is the simple monthly delta?

Worked solution

Solution. Avoided transfer is 75 percent of $24,883, or about $18,662/month. Extra compute costs 12 * $180 = $2,160/month. Simple net savings are about $16,502/month. The decision still needs zone-failure tests: strict locality can strand capacity or amplify a zonal outage.

docs.title: Problem 36: Combined incident budget
docs.text:
A service has a 700 ms deadline and 80 ms response reserve. A fresh connection costs 2 RTTs before a request can start. RTT is 90 ms, and mean server work is 250 ms. How much budget remains for queueing and one backoff? Can a 250 ms retry fit sequentially?

Worked solution

Solution. Assume symmetric transit: after setup the request still needs 90/2 = 45 ms to reach the server. The 80 ms response reserve covers 45 ms return transit and 35 ms other return work. Usable budget is 620 ms; setup, outbound transit and service consume 180 + 45 + 250 = 475 ms, leaving 145 ms, not 190 ms. Another 250 ms service attempt cannot fit even on a reused connection. These means are not guarantees; report unknown/pending for ambiguous effects, not an unconditional retry signal.

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text:
• I wrote units beside every input and intermediate result.
  • I separated useful bytes from wire bytes.
  • I separated propagation, serialization, setup, queueing, and service time.
  • I used mean time, not p99, in Little's Law.
  • I identified the tuple or scope behind every NAT limit.
  • I converted retry policy into attempted dependency load.
  • I modeled stale DNS and long-lived connections during change.
  • I checked post-failover headroom, not only normal utilization.
  • I included TURN and cross-zone traffic in network cost.
  • I tied each result to a design, alert, test, or rollout gate.

docs.title: Network Failure Cards
docs.text:
Use one card at a time during incident drills. Begin with discriminating evidence, not a preferred diagnosis. Calculations are order-of-magnitude fixtures; replace them with measured values before acting in production. For every observation, record vantage point, time window, clock source, sampling or drop behavior, relevant counter semantics, and at least one fact the evidence cannot establish.

These cards are answer-bearing facilitator references, not executable faults or blind prompts. Disclose symptoms first during a blind drill. Never restore compromised trust or unsafe policy merely because a card says "restore prior". Expiry does not automatically terminate live TLS sessions; include non-resumed handshakes in recovery proof. Primary mechanisms are in RFC 9293, RFC 9846, RFC 9000, and RFC 2308; numbers below are fixtures.

docs.title: Card 1: DNS answers remain stale
docs.text:
Symptoms: Traffic continues to a retired address after a record change. Failures vary by client network or recursive resolver.

Discriminators: Compare authoritative answers, recursive-cache answers, and client connection destinations. Check the old TTL and existing connection age.

Evidence: Timestamped dig-equivalent captures from several resolvers, DNS change audit, per-address connection counts, oldest live connection.

False conclusions: "The 30-second TTL guarantees migration in 30 seconds." "All remaining traffic is malicious."

Safe mitigation: Restore the old endpoint if safe, publish overlapping answers, and drain only after old TTL and connection lifetimes decay.

Rollback: Restore the prior answer set and weights; verify both authoritative and recursive views.

Owner: DNS control-plane owner with endpoint owner as incident co-owner.

Calculation: If the previous TTL was 1,800 s and changed at 12:00, a cache refreshed at 11:59:59 may retain the answer until nearly 12:29:59.

docs.title: Card 2: Resolver or authoritative DNS failure
docs.text:
Symptoms: Name-resolution latency and SERVFAIL rise while direct-address probes remain healthy.

Discriminators: Separate stub, recursive, delegation, DNSSEC, and authoritative failures. Compare cached and uncached names.

Evidence: Resolution phase timing, response codes, recursion path, DNSSEC validation result, cache hit rate.

False conclusions: "The application is down because requests never arrived." "Increasing application replicas will help."

Safe mitigation: Fail over to a validated recursive or authoritative path, preserve negative-cache semantics, and reduce nonessential lookup churn.

Rollback: Return traffic gradually to the repaired resolver while comparing answer parity and latency.

Owner: DNS platform owner; security owner joins for DNSSEC or suspicious answer changes.

Calculation: At 50,000 requests/s and a drop from 95 to 60 percent cache hits, upstream DNS load rises from 2,500 to 20,000 queries/s, an 8x increase.

docs.title: Card 3: Path packet loss
docs.text:
Symptoms: Tail latency and retransmissions rise before total request errors; large transfers degrade more than small probes.

Discriminators: Break down by path, protocol, packet size, zone, and destination. Compare TCP retransmissions or QUIC loss with server queue time.

Evidence: Loss and retransmission counters, RTT distribution, congestion window, interface drops, path traces.

False conclusions: "CPU is low, so capacity is fine." "A successful ping proves the path is healthy."

Safe mitigation: Stop retry amplification, shift only to proven spare paths, and lower admission to protect useful goodput.

Rollback: Restore routing after loss and goodput remain stable through a full observation window.

Owner: Network path owner with service owner controlling retries and admission.

Calculation: With framing excluded, 400 MB delivered plus 60 MB retransmitted yields 400 / 460 = 86.96 percent payload transmission efficiency. Actual wire efficiency is lower after headers and other traffic are included.

docs.title: Card 4: MTU or PMTU black hole
docs.text:
Symptoms: Small requests work, larger TLS records or responses stall, and connection setup may succeed.

Discriminators: Test deterministic payload sizes with and without fragmentation-related behavior. Compare IPv4 and IPv6 paths and tunnel overhead.

Evidence: Packet-size threshold, ICMP Packet Too Big visibility, retransmission pattern, interface and tunnel MTUs.

False conclusions: "TLS is broken because the stall begins after ClientHello." "The database is slow because large responses time out."

Safe mitigation: Restore PMTU signaling or apply a validated MSS clamp for TCP at the correct boundary. An MSS clamp does not fix UDP/QUIC packet sizing. Avoid globally shrinking MTU without evidence.

Rollback: Remove the temporary clamp after end-to-end probes pass at expected sizes.

Owner: Network/tunnel owner; host networking owner validates endpoint MTU.

Calculation: A 1,500-byte underlay with 70 bytes of tunnel overhead leaves 1,430 bytes before inner-protocol headers.

docs.title: Card 5: NAT source-port exhaustion
docs.text:
Symptoms: New outbound connections fail while established ones continue; failures concentrate on a destination tuple.

Discriminators: Compare active translations, allocation failures, new-connection rate, reuse lifetime, and connection-pool reuse.

Evidence: NAT table occupancy, ephemeral-port range, destination tuple cardinality, TIME_WAIT or mapping lifetime.

False conclusions: "The remote service is refusing all traffic." "Low active requests mean ports cannot be exhausted."

Safe mitigation: Reuse connections, reduce churn and retries, add source addresses or validated NAT capacity.

Rollback: Remove emergency source capacity only after churn and allocation-failure alerts remain normal.

Owner: Egress/network owner with client-library owner.

Calculation: 28,000 ports / 60 s = 467 new connections/s per source/destination tuple is an idealized ceiling with negligible active lifetime. Include active lifetime as well as the non-reuse interval when estimating actual port occupancy.

docs.title: Card 6: Conntrack table saturation
docs.text:
Symptoms: New flows drop across otherwise unrelated services; existing flows can remain healthy.

Discriminators: Compare table occupancy and insert failures with NIC, CPU, and application errors. Inspect flow lifetime by state.

Evidence: Entries by protocol/state, insert/drop counters, arrival and expiry rates, configured limit.

False conclusions: "Every affected service failed simultaneously." "Raising the table limit alone removes the cause."

Safe mitigation: Shed new flows, stop retries, expire only states proven safe, and add capacity after memory impact is understood.

Rollback: Restore normal admission and limits gradually while checking occupancy slope.

Owner: Host or gateway networking owner.

Calculation: With 100,000 free entries and net growth of 8,000/s, exhaustion arrives in 12.5 seconds.

docs.title: Card 7: TLS certificate expiry or name mismatch
docs.text:
Symptoms: Handshakes fail before HTTP; failures may depend on SNI, client trust store, or clock.

Discriminators: Validate chain, hostname, validity, client clock, signature policy, and served certificate by endpoint.

Evidence: Sanitized handshake error, certificate fingerprint and validity, SNI, endpoint, trust-bundle version.

False conclusions: "The network is blocked because no HTTP status appears." "Disabling verification is a mitigation."

Safe mitigation: Serve the approved overlapping certificate and verify canaries across client populations. Never bypass verification.

Rollback: Re-select the prior still-valid certificate and trust bundle if the new material is wrong.

Owner: Certificate automation owner and service identity owner.

Calculation: If rotation starts 48 hours before expiry but global convergence p99 is 60 hours, policy is short by at least 12 hours plus safety margin.

docs.title: Card 8: TLS handshake CPU storm
docs.text:
Symptoms: Handshake latency and edge CPU rise; established connections perform better than new ones.

Discriminators: Compare full versus resumed handshake rate, reconnect events, accept queue, and application CPU.

Evidence: Handshakes/s by type, resumption hit rate, CPU per handshake, connection-age distribution.

False conclusions: "TLS traffic volume is unchanged, so TLS cannot be the cause." "Adding retries helps handshakes complete."

Safe mitigation: Restore resumption, slow reconnects with jitter, preserve warm connections, and shed unauthenticated excess early.

Rollback: Remove temporary admission limits after resumption and CPU headroom recover.

Owner: Edge/TLS owner with client connection-policy owner.

Calculation: 8,000 handshakes/s * 1.2 ms = 9.6 busy CPU cores before safety margin.

docs.title: Card 9: Load-balancer target fails without draining
docs.text:
Symptoms: Resets spike during deployment or removal; long requests fail despite healthy replacement targets.

Discriminators: Compare connection close reason, target lifecycle state, in-flight requests, and termination timing.

Evidence: Target state timeline, accepted/new/in-flight connections, reset source, deployment audit.

False conclusions: "Passing health checks makes immediate termination safe." "Connection count equals request count under HTTP/2."

Safe mitigation: Stop new assignments, keep target alive through bounded drain, then terminate residual work according to protocol policy.

Rollback: Re-enable the target only if its binary and dependencies are still safe; otherwise pause rollout.

Owner: Load-balancer platform owner and workload deployment owner.

Calculation: 24,000 connections / 300 closes/s = 80 s minimum drain without stale new assignments or long-lived outliers.

docs.title: Card 10: Health-check false positive or false negative
docs.text:
Symptoms: Healthy targets are ejected, or unhealthy targets keep receiving production traffic.

Discriminators: Compare probe path with real request dependencies, thresholds, interval, timeout, and source network.

Evidence: Raw probe outcomes, application SLI by target, ejection reason, dependency state.

False conclusions: "The health endpoint returned 200, so all traffic is safe." "One timeout proves the target is dead."

Safe mitigation: Use thresholded state changes, bounded outlier ejection, and a probe that checks only traffic-critical readiness.

Rollback: Restore the last validated policy and cap simultaneous ejections.

Owner: Service owner defines readiness; load-balancer owner implements policy.

Calculation: With 3 failures required at 5-second intervals, detection is roughly 10 seconds after the first failed probe. From an arbitrary failure onset it is roughly 10-15 seconds, plus relevant probe duration and propagation, depending on whether intervals are measured between probe starts or completions.

docs.title: Card 11: Proxy connection-pool saturation
docs.text:
Symptoms: Pool-acquisition time rises, upstream service time stays flat, and proxy queues grow.

Discriminators: Separate queue time from connect and service time. Check per-destination pool keys and multiplexed stream limits.

Evidence: In-use/idle/pending counts, acquisition timeout, upstream latency, requests per connection.

False conclusions: "The upstream is slow because end-to-end latency rose." "An unbounded pool fixes saturation."

Safe mitigation: Bound and shed the queue, fix skewed pool keys, and increase concurrency only within measured upstream capacity.

Rollback: Restore the prior pool limit if upstream saturation or error rate increases.

Owner: Proxy/client-platform owner with dependency owner approving capacity.

Calculation: At 18,000 calls/s and 22 ms mean time, mean active calls are 18,000 * 0.022 = 396.

docs.title: Card 12: Layered retry storm
docs.text:
Symptoms: Attempted load grows while logical traffic is stable; recovery slows after a transient fault.

Discriminators: Correlate stable operation IDs across client, gateway, service, and dependency attempts.

Evidence: Attempts per logical operation, retry reason, backoff, deadline remaining, per-layer retry config.

False conclusions: "Each layer only retries once, so amplification is small." "Retries improve availability regardless of capacity."

Safe mitigation: Select one retry owner, enforce a shared budget, add jitter, and shed work with insufficient deadline.

Rollback: Re-enable retries in a canary only after dependency headroom and attempt ratios recover.

Owner: End-to-end API owner; each platform owner removes hidden retry layers.

Calculation: Three client attempts, two gateway attempts, and two library attempts produce up to 3 * 2 * 2 = 12 dependency attempts.

docs.title: Card 13: HTTP/2 connection concentration
docs.text:
Symptoms: One connection loss or congestion event affects many streams; target load is uneven despite few connections.

Discriminators: Compare streams and outstanding work per connection, not only connection count. Identify stream limits and connection age.

Evidence: Active streams/connection, queued streams, resets, per-connection RTT and loss, target work.

False conclusions: "Least connections means least work." "One multiplexed connection is always most efficient."

Safe mitigation: Use a small bounded set of connections, cap concurrent streams, and balance by outstanding work or measured load.

Rollback: Return to the prior connection count if handshakes, target skew, or NAT churn worsen.

Owner: HTTP client/proxy owner.

Calculation: Losing one connection carrying 800 of 1,000 active streams disrupts 80 percent of work even if nine idle connections survive.

docs.title: Card 14: QUIC or UDP path impairment
docs.text:
Symptoms: HTTP/3 handshake or throughput fails on selected networks while HTTP/2 fallback works.

Discriminators: Break down by ASN, device, UDP reachability, QUIC version, RTT, and loss; compare fallback success.

Evidence: QUIC handshake phase, UDP timeout, version negotiation, fallback latency, path MTU and loss.

False conclusions: "QUIC is globally broken." "Fallback success means the incident has no user impact."

Safe mitigation: Use bounded, remembered fallback and reduce HTTP/3 exposure for affected cohorts without disabling it globally.

Rollback: Restore cohort rollout after path-specific canaries meet handshake and goodput gates.

Owner: Edge transport owner; client owner controls fallback behavior.

Calculation: A failed 300 ms QUIC attempt before a 165 ms TCP/TLS path yields at least 465 ms, not the 165 ms fallback alone.

docs.title: Card 15: Anycast site withdrawal overloads neighbors
docs.text:
Symptoms: A withdrawn site recovers locally while latency and errors rise in neighboring catchments.

Discriminators: Map route withdrawals to shifted traffic and post-shift headroom at every receiving site.

Evidence: BGP announcements, traffic by site/ASN, capacity ceilings, cache warmth, retry rates.

False conclusions: "Withdrawal removes load from the system." "Traffic shifts evenly."

Safe mitigation: Stage withdrawal, cap advertised scope where possible, prewarm receivers, and shed noncritical traffic before ceilings.

Rollback: Re-announce only if the original site is safe and route flapping risk is controlled.

Owner: Global traffic owner with receiving-site owners holding veto over capacity.

Calculation: A 220 Gbps withdrawal shifting 55 percent to site B adds 121 Gbps there.

docs.title: Card 16: BGP route leak or hijack signal
docs.text:
Symptoms: Reachability or latency changes by Internet origin; an unexpected origin AS or path appears.

Discriminators: Compare control-plane collectors, configured origins, route-object/RPKI state, and data-plane probes.

Evidence: Prefix, origin AS, AS path, first-seen time, RPKI validation, affected catchments.

False conclusions: "Application health checks prove routing integrity." "One looking glass represents the whole Internet."

Safe mitigation: Apply validated prefix filters, coordinate upstream withdrawal or correction, and communicate affected scope. Do not improvise broader announcements.

Rollback: Remove emergency routing changes in stages after global collectors and probes converge.

Owner: Network routing owner and security incident owner.

Calculation: If 35 percent of 80,000 requests/s follow the bad route, up to 28,000 requests/s are exposed before retries.

docs.title: Card 17: WebSocket reconnect storm
docs.text:
Symptoms: A brief edge event becomes sustained handshake, authentication, and subscription load.

Discriminators: Compare reconnect attempts, unique clients, backoff distributions, session-resume success, and downstream replay.

Evidence: Attempts/client, reconnect delay histogram, TLS CPU, auth QPS, subscription restore size.

False conclusions: "Traffic is organic growth." "Immediate reconnect minimizes downtime for everyone."

Safe mitigation: Issue randomized retry guidance, cap reconnect admission, resume from durable cursor, and degrade noncritical subscriptions.

Rollback: Relax admission slowly after connection-age distribution and downstream queues normalize.

Owner: Realtime platform owner with client SDK owner.

Calculation: One million clients reconnecting uniformly over 5 seconds create 200,000 attempts/s; spreading over 120 seconds lowers the mean to about 8,333/s.

docs.title: Card 18: Service-mesh sidecar saturation
docs.text:
Symptoms: Service latency rises with sidecar CPU, pending requests, or connection limits while application work stays stable.

Discriminators: Separate application and proxy timing. Compare sidecar policy/config version and per-cluster pools.

Evidence: Downstream/upstream request timing, proxy CPU/memory, pending overflow, config distribution state.

False conclusions: "The application must scale because the pod is slow." "A transparent proxy has no independent capacity ceiling."

Safe mitigation: Shed at ingress, reduce expensive filters where policy permits, restore known-good config, and scale proxy capacity with measured limits.

Rollback: Reapply the previous signed config snapshot and verify policy plus traffic behavior.

Owner: Mesh platform owner; service owner controls workload admission.

Calculation: At 25,000 requests/s and 0.08 ms proxy CPU per request per direction, two directions consume 25,000 * 0.00008 * 2 = 4 cores.

docs.title: Card 19: mTLS trust-bundle split
docs.text:
Symptoms: Calls fail only for selected workload versions or directions during certificate rotation.

Discriminators: Compare presented issuer, trust-bundle version, certificate epoch, SNI/SAN, and clock on both peers.

Evidence: Non-secret fingerprints, issuer/subject/SAN, bundle hashes, rollout cohort, handshake error.

False conclusions: "The new certificate is valid, so every peer trusts it." "Restarting all workloads is the safest repair."

Safe mitigation: Restore dual trust before changing identity, pause issuance rollout, and canary every communication direction.

Rollback: Reissue or select the prior still-valid identity while retaining both trusted roots through overlap.

Owner: Identity platform owner with each service owner validating policy.

Calculation: A 24-hour certificate with 6-hour worst-case rollout and 4-hour rollback window has only 14 hours left before any added safety margin.

docs.title: Card 20: Cross-zone dependency amplification
docs.text:
Symptoms: Network cost and inter-zone bandwidth rise without matching logical traffic growth; zone impairment affects otherwise local calls.

Discriminators: Map request and response bytes by source/destination zone, retry count, and replica placement.

Evidence: Flow logs, topology labels, logical versus attempted QPS, response-size distribution, billing dimensions.

False conclusions: "Round robin is cost-neutral." "Strict locality is always safer."

Safe mitigation: Prefer locality with bounded spillover, preserve zonal failover headroom, and stop retries that duplicate large responses.

Rollback: Restore broader balancing if local queues or zonal error budgets degrade.

Owner: Service owner and traffic platform owner; finance provides billing validation.

Calculation: 0.96 GB/s * 86,400 s * $0.01/GB = $829.44/day for one billed direction.

docs.title: Card-use checklist
docs.text:
• Identify the failure boundary before changing capacity or routing.
  • Capture a timestamped baseline and one discriminator.
  • Record evidence vantage, interval, clock, sampling/drop behavior, counter semantics, and one explicit limitation.
  • Quantify time to exhaustion or post-failover headroom.
  • Assign one incident owner and one rollback authority.
  • Prefer reversible, scoped mitigation over fleet-wide changes.
  • Verify recovery using user, transport, and capacity evidence.

docs.title: Network Design L5/L6 Rubric
docs.text: Score observable evidence, not vocabulary. The rubric totals 100 points. An answer can be technically broad and still be capped by an unsafe omission.

docs.title: Score bands
docs.text:
Score Interpretation 0-49 Below L5: fragmented, unquantified, or operationally unsafe 50-64 Developing L5: plausible path with material gaps 65-79 L5: independently coherent, quantified, and recoverable 80-89 Strong L5 / emerging L6: handles ambiguity and evolution but lacks consistent policy depth 90-100 L6: shapes cross-team policy, failure domains, migration, economics, and evidence

An L5 pass requires at least 65 points and every L5 gate below. An L6 pass requires at least 90 points, every L5 gate, every L6 gate, and no cap.

docs.title: 1. Scope, contracts, and assumptions - 10 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Names components without user latency, availability, geography, payload, or protocol constraints. 3-5 Clarifies main traffic and SLOs but leaves important exclusions or assumptions implicit. 6-8 L5: states workload, latency, availability, geography, payload, streaming, privacy, and failure contract; marks assumptions. 9-10 L6: resolves ambiguous product tradeoffs, separates mandatory from degradable traffic, and defines how assumptions will be retired.

docs.title: 2. End-to-end protocol trace - 12 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-3 Treats the network as a single hop. 4-6 Mentions DNS, TLS, and load balancing but misses queues, identities, or connection reuse. 7-10 L5: traces resolution, address choice, transport, TLS identity, HTTP, every proxy/queue, application work, and response path. 11-12 L6: separates control and data planes, trust and routing identities, state lifetimes, and correlated failure boundaries.

docs.title: 3. Quantitative reasoning - 15 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-4 Uses adjectives or incorrect units instead of calculations. 5-8 Calculates traffic or latency but does not connect numbers to limits. 9-12 L5: correctly estimates RTT budget, serialization, bandwidth/BDP, mean concurrency, pool/queue behavior, and retry load. 13-15 L6: models skew, overhead, tails without abusing Little's Law, failure headroom, cost, and sensitivity to uncertain inputs.

docs.title: 4. Protocol and topology choices - 10 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Selects HTTP/3, a CDN, anycast, or a mesh as a slogan. 3-5 Makes plausible choices but lacks workload evidence or alternatives. 6-8 L5: compares HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, L4/L7 balancing, locality, and connection reuse against workload and failure needs. 9-10 L6: defines cohorting, compatibility, standards, exception policy, and evidence-based retirement of alternatives.

docs.title: 5. Capacity, overload, and efficiency - 12 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-3 Uses unbounded queues/pools or assumes scaling creates downstream capacity. 4-6 Adds limits but does not quantify them or define shedding. 7-10 L5: bounds streams, pools, queues, payloads, NAT/conntrack, TLS CPU, and retry attempts; identifies the bottleneck. 11-12 L6: reserves control/recovery capacity, defines fairness and degraded modes, and links utilization policy to measured envelopes.

docs.title: 6. Failure diagnosis and recovery - 14 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-4 Lists failures with generic retries or failover. 5-8 Handles common failures but lacks discriminators, rollback, or unknown-outcome semantics. 9-11 L5: diagnoses DNS, loss, TLS, NAT, LB, retry, and partial-path failures with evidence; supplies safe mitigation and rollback. 12-14 L6: reasons about correlated failures, catchment shifts, recovery storms, blast radius, rollback authority, and reconciliation.

docs.title: 7. Change, migration, and compatibility - 10 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-2 Proposes a flag day. 3-5 Mentions canary or rollback without state overlap or gates. 6-8 L5: uses overlap, version compatibility, staged rollout, drain, measurable gates, and tested rollback. 9-10 L6: defines migration epochs, stale-client policy, trust/identity overlap, ownership, and criteria to remove the old path.

docs.title: 8. Security and identity - 7 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-1 Equates encryption with authorization or suggests bypassing verification. 2-3 Uses TLS/mTLS but leaves identity, trust, or rotation vague. 4-5 L5: defines authenticated names/workloads, termination points, least privilege, certificate validation, and overlap rotation. 6-7 L6: defines fleet trust policy, emergency rotation, revocation limits, audit evidence, and organizational authority.

docs.title: 9. Observability and validation - 6 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0-1 Watches only aggregate latency or CPU. 2-3 Names useful metrics but not decision gates. 4-5 L5: separates DNS, connect, TLS, queue, service, transfer, attempts, loss, and saturation; defines a deterministic test. 6 L6: sets fleet-level SLOs, cardinality/retention policy, cross-domain correlation, and evidence owners.

docs.title: 10. Economics and ownership - 4 points
docs.text: Points Anchor 0 Ignores cost and ownership. 1-2 Mentions egress or teams without a decision model. 3 L5: identifies bandwidth, TURN, cross-zone, proxy, and operational cost drivers plus component owners. 4 L6: defines cost attribution, capacity commitments, escalation boundaries, and who can approve or roll back global policy.

docs.title: L5 gates
docs.text:
All are required for an L5 pass:

  • Draws or narrates the request path from DNS through response transfer.
  • Performs at least three correct calculations, including one latency and one capacity/concurrency calculation.
  • Uses mean latency for Little's Law and treats p99 separately.
  • Defines bounded pools/queues and one end-to-end deadline/retry owner.
  • Handles stale DNS, connection draining, and one transport/security failure with evidence and rollback.
  • States TLS identity and termination behavior.
  • Gives measurable rollout or incident exit criteria.

docs.title: L6 gates
docs.text:
All are required for an L6 pass:

  • Satisfies every L5 gate without interviewer repair.
  • Quantifies a correlated failure or evacuation, including receiver headroom.
  • Defines a staged migration with compatibility, overlap, rollback authority, and old-path removal criteria.
  • Establishes a fleet policy for identity, deadlines/retries, or protocol rollout and a governed exception path.
  • Connects topology to cost and organizational ownership.
  • Names evidence that can falsify the chosen design and who owns collecting it.

docs.title: Safety and completeness caps
docs.text:
Apply the lowest applicable cap after adding dimension points.

Cap Condition 39 Suggests disabling certificate or hostname verification, accepting replay-unsafe 0-RTT writes, or making an unbounded retry/queue policy. 49 Cannot trace a request or does not define an end-to-end deadline and overload behavior. 59 No correct capacity or latency calculation, or uses p99 as the mean in Little's Law without correction. 64 No rollback for routing, certificate, protocol, or load-balancer change. 79 No migration/compatibility path, no correlated-failure analysis, or no ownership boundaries. 89 No fleet-level policy, exception governance, economics, or evidence to retire assumptions.

docs.title: Evidence quality modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers cannot raise a score above 100 or override gates/caps.

Compute final = min(applicable_cap, max(0, min(100, raw + modifiers))), using 100 when no cap applies. Apply each modifier once; record its evidence separately and avoid double-counting the same strength. A score band describes numeric performance only: unmet L5/L6 gates still prevent that level. These are course calibration heuristics, not validated hiring thresholds, and are not directly interchangeable with a scenario's normalized 40-point scale.

Adjustment Evidence +2 Uses a compact, correct diagram that exposes queues, trust, and failure domains. +2 Tests a sensitivity range and changes a design decision based on the result. +1 Separates logical operations, attempts, connections, streams, and bytes. -2 Gives precise-looking constants without source, fixture, or measurement plan. -3 Claims DNS TTL, health checks, anycast, or exactly-once transport provides stronger guarantees than it does. -3 Uses aggregate success to dismiss cohort-, zone-, path-, or version-specific failure.

docs.title: Interview scoring sheet
docs.text: Dimension Maximum Score Evidence Scope and assumptions 10 End-to-end trace 12 Quantitative reasoning 15 Protocol and topology 10 Capacity and overload 12 Failure and recovery 14 Change and migration 10 Security and identity 7 Observability 6 Economics and ownership 4 Raw total 100 Modifier Applicable cap Final score 100

docs.title: 62: Developing L5
docs.text: The candidate chooses HTTP/2, calculates bandwidth and a connection pool, and handles target health. They define an end-to-end deadline and bounded retries and queues, but leave retry ownership ambiguous across layers and do not quantify NAT churn or give a safe certificate-rotation rollback. The design is plausible but needs interviewer repair and misses L5 gates. If they omit the deadline or overload behavior entirely, apply cap 49 rather than awarding 62.

docs.title: 74: L5
docs.text: The candidate traces DNS through two proxies and the response path, including TLS identity and termination. They budget RTT and serialization, size mean concurrency correctly, bound queues, and assign one retry owner. They handle stale DNS, connection draining, and a TLS failure with discriminating evidence and rollback, and give measurable rollout and incident-exit criteria. They do not deeply model catchment shifts, fleet policy, or cross-team migration. This satisfies every L5 gate and is independently coherent L5 work.

docs.title: 86: Strong L5 / emerging L6
docs.text: The candidate adds zonal failover headroom, protocol cohorts, trust overlap, cost estimates, and receiving-team gates. They still leave exception governance and evidence ownership incomplete, so the answer does not clear the L6 gates.

docs.title: 94: L6
docs.text:
The candidate exposes hidden identity and state-lifetime constraints, quantifies normal and evacuation capacity, defines compatibility epochs and rollback authority, and establishes fleet retry and mTLS policy with exceptions. Cost attribution and telemetry owners make the design governable after the interview.

These short sketches illustrate bands, not complete scored transcripts. To reproduce the illustrative numbers with zero modifiers, dimension vectors 1-10 can be [7,8,9,7,7,8,3,5,5,3]=62, [8,9,11,8,9,10,7,5,4,3]=74, [9,10,13,9,10,12,9,6,5,3]=86, and [10,12,14,9,11,13,9,6,6,4]=94. A real score needs evidence for each dimension; do not infer unstated L5/L6 gates from these vectors.

docs.title: Reviewer checklist
docs.text:
• Score only evidence stated or drawn by the candidate.
  • Record one sentence for every nonzero dimension.
  • Apply gates before assigning the level.
  • Apply the lowest safety/completeness cap.
  • Do not award L6 for breadth without migration, policy, failure isolation, cost, and ownership.
  • Recalibrate periodically using the same sample answers across interviewers.

docs.title: Network Evidence Labs
docs.text:
These labs turn network claims into reproducible evidence. Labs 1-8 use localhost, Python 3, and common command-line tools. Labs 9-16 are available offline reasoning and standard-library simulation labs. None requires public endpoints, root access, or Docker.

Start with Networking for System Design for the protocol model behind the exercises.

docs.title: Working method
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Q[Question] --> H[Hypothesis]
    H --> B[Baseline]
    B --> F[Inject one fault]
    F --> O[Observe]
    O --> C[Calculate]
    C --> L[State limits]
    L --> R[Recover and verify]

For every run, preserve the distinction between:

  • Observation: what a command, trace, or counter directly shows.
  • Inference: the explanation most consistent with those observations.
  • Unknown: what the available vantage point cannot establish.
  • Decision: the operational or design action justified by the evidence.

One successful request proves reachability for one path at one time. It does not prove DNS convergence, fleet health, certificate correctness for every name, tail latency, or absence of retries.

docs.title: Common evidence package
docs.text:
Create one text or Markdown record per lab. Copy this header before running commands:

Lab:
Run ID:
Start time and timezone:
End time and timezone:
Host and OS:
Python version:
Commands and options:
Fixture or input version:
Baseline observation:
Injected fault:
Fault observation:
Calculations with units:
Recovery observation:
Evidence limitations:
Conclusion:

Use a unique run ID such as netlab-20260906-143000. Keep raw output unchanged, then add interpretation below it. Record stderr as well as stdout. Redact credentials, cookies, tokens, internal names, and personal data before sharing. Do not collect packet payloads or production traffic without authorization.

docs.title: Minimum acceptance standard
docs.text:
An evidence package is complete when it contains:

  1. the exact input and command;
  2. a healthy baseline;
  3. one controlled failure;
  4. timestamps or durations with units;
  5. expected versus actual behavior;
  6. a recovery check, not only a cleanup command;
  7. at least one limitation or competing explanation; and
  8. a conclusion no broader than the evidence.

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
• Bind test servers to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0.
  • Use ports in the unprivileged range. Change a port if it is already occupied.
  • Run load only against the supplied localhost fixture.
  • Keep request counts and concurrency at the values in the lab.
  • Never paste secrets into command history or evidence files.
  • Treat tcpdump, firewall changes, traffic shaping, namespace changes, and packet injection as privileged enhancements. Skip them unless you have explicit authorization on a disposable host.
  • Stop background processes and verify their ports are closed.

docs.title: Lab map
docs.text: Lab Core question Evidence artifact Status 01. Request trace Where did request time go? phase timeline and bounded conclusion Available 02. Command evidence What does each diagnostic command actually prove? observation/inference matrix Available 03. Network math Are units and capacity assumptions coherent? checked calculations and sensitivity table Available 04. Proxy headers Which identity can an application trust through a proxy? header transformations and trust policy Available 05. DNS failure How do stale and negative answers affect recovery? cache timeline and migration rule Available 06. TLS handshake Which handshake phase failed, and what identity was checked? handshake interpretation and latency budget Available 07. Connection pool When does a pool become a queue? concurrency, wait-time, and throughput evidence Available 08. Retry storm How does retry policy amplify an outage? attempt amplification and recovery comparison Available 09. HTTP/2 multiplexing When do streams share transport loss and connection state? multiplexing and loss comparison Available 10. QUIC migration How does a connection survive an address change? connection identity and migration analysis Available 11. Load-balancer draining What should stop, drain, or close during removal? lifecycle timeline and invariants Available 12. NAT exhaustion How does connection churn exhaust finite tuples? tuple-capacity and churn calculation Available 13. BGP anycast Can a catchment shift safely during route change? capacity and route-risk analysis Available 14. WebSocket reconnect How does reconnect synchronization amplify failure? reconnect envelope and containment plan Available 15. Service mesh What happens when mesh data-plane state fails? boundary evidence and degraded behavior Available 16. mTLS rotation Can trust and identity rotate without a flag day? staged rollout and rollback proof Available

docs.title: Suggested progression
docs.text:
• Evidence first: Labs 1-2 teach disciplined capture and cautious claims.
  • Quantify: Lab 3 makes units, latency, throughput, and concurrency explicit.
  • Trust and discovery: Labs 4-6 cover proxy identity, DNS state, and TLS identity.
  • Capacity and recovery: Labs 7-8 expose queueing and retry amplification.
  • Fleet behavior: Labs 9-16 extend the same method to multiplexing, migration, draining, finite state, routing, reconnects, mesh failure, and trust rotation.

Run each lab blind first: record predictions and evidence before opening its closed answer key. Then change one input and predict the result before running again. Collapsed answers are a study aid, not secure exam isolation.

docs.title: Fixture Regression
docs.text: From the repository root, run python3 docs/networks/labs/verify.py. The runner extracts the actual inline Python programs, checks bounded loopback fixtures, and exercises deterministic calculations. It does not contact public endpoints, change routing, or require root. It is a regression check, not evidence that the offline HTTP/2, QUIC, BGP, mesh, or certificate models implement those protocols. Enhanced OpenSSL and real-protocol exercises remain separate manual paths.

docs.title: Lab 01: Trace One Request End to End
docs.text: Lab index | Next: Command Evidence

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Build a phase timeline for one HTTP request and separate measured time from inferred DNS, connect, server, and transfer time. Explain why a warm localhost trace cannot predict a production p99.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: Use only 127.0.0.1. The fixture serves synthetic text and handles a few requests. Do not replace the URL with a production endpoint. No root access, Docker, or public network is needed.

docs.title: Supplied fixture transcript
docs.text:
$ curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sS -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} first_byte=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' 'http://127.0.0.1:18081/?delay_ms=120'
code=200 dns=0.000025 connect=0.000142 first_byte=0.121031 total=0.121118

$ curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sS 'http://127.0.0.1:18081/?delay_ms=0'
request_id=2 delay_ms=0 body_bytes=2048

Treat these numbers as supplied data if curl is unavailable.

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Start the server in terminal A:

python3 - <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlparse
import threading, time

count = 0
lock = threading.Lock()
class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        global count
        q = parse_qs(urlparse(self.path).query)
        try:
            delay = max(0, min(int(q.get("delay_ms", ["0"])[0]), 1000))
        except ValueError:
            self.send_error(400, "delay_ms must be an integer"); return
        with lock:
            count += 1
            request_id = count
        time.sleep(delay / 1000)
        prefix = f"request_id={request_id} delay_ms={delay} body_bytes=2048\n".encode()
        body = prefix + b"x" * (2048 - len(prefix))
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)
    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        print(time.strftime("%H:%M:%S"), fmt % args, flush=True)

with ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 18081), Handler) as server:
    server.serve_forever()
PY

In terminal B, use curl if present:

curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sS -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} first_byte=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' 'http://127.0.0.1:18081/?delay_ms=120'

Pure Python alternative:

python3 - <<'PY'
import http.client, time
t0 = time.perf_counter()
c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 18081, timeout=2)
t1 = time.perf_counter(); c.request("GET", "/?delay_ms=120")
r = c.getresponse(); t2 = time.perf_counter(); body = r.read(); t3 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"setup_object_ms={(t1-t0)*1000:.3f}")
print(f"request_to_headers_ms={(t2-t1)*1000:.3f}")
print(f"body_read_ms={(t3-t2)*1000:.3f} status={r.status} bytes={len(body)}")
c.close()
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text: curl -v exposes request and response headers. curl --trace-time --trace-ascii - adds event timestamps but may reveal sensitive headers. A packet capture is not needed; if authorized on a disposable host, capture only loopback metadata and avoid payload retention.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Record tool versions and run ID.
  2. Run delays of 0, 40, and 120 ms three times each.
  3. Compute connect - dns, first_byte - connect, and total - first_byte for the supplied trace.
  4. Label each result as direct measurement or derived value.
  5. Predict a 300 ms delay, inject it, and compare actual first-byte time.
  6. Stop the server, repeat one request, and preserve the failure.
  7. Restart the server and prove recovery with a 200 response.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text:
• The configured server delay mostly appears between connection completion and first byte.
  • DNS time is near zero because the request uses a numeric loopback address.
  • Body transfer is small and local, so it is usually much shorter than server delay.
  • After shutdown, connection establishment fails; there is no HTTP status.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text: Subtract adjacent cumulative curl timestamps to obtain non-overlapping DNS, connect, post-connect, and body-transfer phases. Keep the result in seconds until the final conversion to milliseconds.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: First inject latency with delay_ms=300. Then stop terminal A with Ctrl-C to inject refusal. Keep these failure classes separate: a slow HTTP response proves a connection and server existed; refusal means the HTTP exchange never began.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
Loopback removes real resolver, router, congestion, packet-loss, proxy, and TLS behavior. A single process timestamp does not isolate server queue from server work. Three samples do not estimate p99. Curl's phase clocks are cumulative and tool-specific.

The Python object's construction does not connect: request() lazily opens the connection. Its request-to-headers timer includes that setup. Curl's time_starttransfer measures time to the first response byte, not completion of all response headers. Do not equate the two measurements exactly.

Source: curl write-out timing variables and Python HTTPConnection.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Press Ctrl-C in terminal A. Verify cleanup:

python3 - <<'PY'
import socket
s = socket.socket(); s.settimeout(0.2)
error = s.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", 18081))
print("connected" if error == 0 else f"not-connected errno={error}")
s.close()
PY

A nonzero result proves only that this probe did not connect. Record the errno; connection refusal is stronger evidence of no listener than a timeout or another socket error.

Answer key 
connect phase = 0.000142 - 0.000025 = 0.000117 s = 0.117 ms
post-connect to first byte = 0.121031 - 0.000142 = 0.120889 s = 120.889 ms
body transfer = 0.121118 - 0.121031 = 0.000087 s = 0.087 ms
unaccounted labels do not imply separate clocks; curl timestamps are cumulative

The 120 ms fixture delay dominates post-connect time. The trace supports: "For this request from this client process, connection setup completed quickly and the first response byte arrived about 121 ms after start." It does not support: "the network added 121 ms" or "the service p99 is 121 ms." The stopped-server result should be recorded as a connection failure with no HTTP response.

docs.title: L5 extension
docs.text: Draw the production path and assign an owner, timeout, metric, and request identifier to DNS, connect, TLS, proxy queue, service queue, work, and transfer.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Define an organization-wide phase-timing schema. Address clock source, sampling, high-cardinality IDs, proxy spans, privacy, protocol changes, and how teams distinguish client abandonment from completed side effects.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Captured baseline and two injected failures
  • Calculated non-overlapping phase differences with units
  • Distinguished measurement from inference
  • Proved recovery after restart
  • Recorded at least three evidence limitations
  • Stopped the localhost server

docs.title: Lab 02: Turn Commands into Defensible Evidence
docs.text: Previous: Request Trace | Lab index | Next: Network Math

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Create an evidence matrix that states what a command observed, what it did not observe, and which follow-up would discriminate between competing explanations.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: Probe only the supplied localhost service. Do not scan address ranges, production ports, or systems you do not own. Verbose HTTP output can contain credentials; this fixture has none.

docs.title: Supplied fixture transcript
docs.text:
$ python3 probe.py
resolve host=localhost addresses=['127.0.0.1', '::1']
connect address=127.0.0.1 port=18082 result=ok elapsed_ms=0.18
http status=204 server_header=EvidenceFixture/1 elapsed_ms=0.71

$ python3 probe.py --port 18083
resolve host=localhost addresses=['127.0.0.1', '::1']
connect address=127.0.0.1 port=18083 result=ConnectionRefusedError elapsed_ms=0.09

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Start a small service in terminal A:

python3 - <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    server_version = "EvidenceFixture/1"
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(204); self.end_headers()
    def log_message(self, *args): pass
with HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 18082), H) as server:
    server.serve_forever()
PY

Run the layered probe in terminal B:

python3 - <<'PY'
import http.client, socket, time
host, port = "localhost", 18082
rows = socket.getaddrinfo(host, port, type=socket.SOCK_STREAM)
print("resolve", sorted({r[4][0] for r in rows}))
t = time.perf_counter(); s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port), 1)
print(f"connect=ok elapsed_ms={(time.perf_counter()-t)*1000:.2f}"); s.close()
t = time.perf_counter(); c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", port, timeout=1)
c.request("GET", "/"); r = c.getresponse(); r.read()
print(f"http_status={r.status} server={r.getheader('Server')} elapsed_ms={(time.perf_counter()-t)*1000:.2f}")
c.close()
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text:
Use whichever commands exist on your OS:

curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sv -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:18082/
getent hosts localhost
lsof -nP -iTCP:18082
ss -ltn
netstat -an

Command absence is not a network failure. Record the tool as unavailable and use the Python path.

dig and nslookup normally query a DNS server, which may be outside this host; they are not substitutes for the OS resolver/hosts-file observation. Skip them in this loopback-only exercise. The supplied probe.py transcript is illustrative, not a shipped file: change port in the inline Python probe for the wrong-port test. Verify 18083 is unused first; another lab uses that port.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Capture the healthy resolve, connect, and HTTP observations separately.
  2. Build columns for command, vantage point, direct observation, inference, unknown, and next test.
  3. Compare localhost resolution with the explicit 127.0.0.1 connection.
  4. Probe unused port 18083 and classify the failure layer.
  5. Stop the server and rerun the same probe against 18082.
  6. Restart and verify a 204 response.
  7. Write one conclusion that does not overclaim.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: Evidence Supports Does not prove getaddrinfo returns addresses local resolver produced candidates either candidate accepts connections TCP connect succeeds one address/port accepted a connection HTTP correctness or future availability HTTP 204 arrives one HTTP exchange completed response body correctness or fleet health connection refused target stack rejected/no listener for that tuple firewall state elsewhere or why listener is absent

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
For repeated probes, calculate success rate and simple range:

success rate = successful probes / total probes
latency range = maximum elapsed_ms - minimum elapsed_ms

Do not substitute the sample counts until after recording the formula and units. Five probes are far too few to estimate an availability SLO.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Use port 18083 for a controlled wrong-port failure. Then stop the server for a second refusal with the intended port. Do not use firewall rules to simulate timeout; that is a privileged and host-wide change.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
Local resolver behavior may come from files or OS caches rather than DNS. Refusal is different from timeout. The Server header is application-provided and not authenticated. Listener tools show one host's socket state, not a remote path.

Source: Python socket resolution and connection APIs.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Press Ctrl-C in terminal A. Confirm port 18082 rejects a connection with socket.connect_ex as shown in Lab 01.

Answer key

A sample with four successes in five probes has an observed success rate of 4 / 5 = 80%; it is not an availability estimate.

A defensible conclusion is: "From this process, the local resolver returned loopback candidates; TCP to IPv4 loopback port 18082 succeeded; one HTTP request returned 204. Port 18083 refused the connection. This does not test IPv6, TLS, a proxy, or any non-local path." A useful next test for IPv6 is a server explicitly bound to ::1, not an assumption based on the resolver list.

docs.title: L5 extension
docs.text: Given 502, 503, timeout, reset, and DNS failure examples, define the smallest command sequence that distinguishes proxy-generated failure from upstream refusal or slow response.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Design a safe diagnostic standard for a fleet: approved probes, output schema, redaction, retention, sampling, time synchronization, ownership, and rules preventing an incident probe from becoming load.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Captured resolver, TCP, and HTTP evidence separately
  • Built the six-column evidence matrix
  • Distinguished refusal from timeout
  • Included calculations with sample-size caveat
  • Verified recovery and cleanup
  • Wrote a bounded conclusion

docs.title: Lab 03: Check Network Math with Units
docs.text: Previous: Command Evidence | Lab index | Next: Proxy Headers

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Calculate bandwidth-delay product, useful concurrency, transfer time, connection churn, and retry amplification while preserving units and assumptions.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: This lab uses supplied data and a localhost timing fixture. It creates no meaningful load: one 1 MiB transfer at a time. Do not extrapolate results to a real link without measuring protocol overhead and bottlenecks.

docs.title: Supplied fixture data
docs.text:
Path capacity:             1 Gbit/s decimal
Round-trip time:           80 ms
Request rate:              8,000 request/s
Mean time in dependency:   25 ms/request
Payload:                   10 MB decimal
Usable ephemeral ports:    28,000 ports/source-address/destination-tuple
Tuple hold/reuse interval: 60 s
Retry layers:              client 3 attempts, gateway 2, service 2

Calculate from the supplied values before opening the answer key.

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Run a bounded local transfer; this measures host software and loopback, not link capacity:

python3 - <<'PY'
import socket, time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
SIZE = 1024 * 1024
RECEIVER_DELAY = 0.0
def receive(listener):
    c, _ = listener.accept()
    with c:
        c.settimeout(2)
        time.sleep(RECEIVER_DELAY)
        left = SIZE
        while left:
            data = c.recv(min(65536, left))
            if not data:
                raise RuntimeError(f"short transfer: {left} bytes missing")
            left -= len(data)
        return time.perf_counter()
with socket.socket() as listener:
    listener.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    listener.bind(("127.0.0.1", 18083)); listener.listen(1); listener.settimeout(2)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:
        received = executor.submit(receive, listener)
        with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 18083), timeout=2) as c:
            payload = b"x" * SIZE
            t = time.perf_counter(); c.sendall(payload)
            sender_dt = time.perf_counter() - t
            c.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR)
        receiver_dt = received.result(timeout=3) - t
print(f"bytes={SIZE} sender_seconds={sender_dt:.6f} receiver_seconds={receiver_dt:.6f}")
print(f"receiver_Mbit_s={SIZE*8/receiver_dt/1e6:.1f}")
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text: If installed, iperf3 can measure controlled throughput between machines you own. Use explicit duration and rate limits. OS socket tools can show buffers, but defaults are not proof of the effective congestion or flow-control window.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Normalize every supplied value to bits, bytes, seconds, or requests.
  2. Calculate BDP as rate times RTT.
  3. Use Little's Law to calculate mean useful concurrency.
  4. Calculate ideal serialization time for the payload at path capacity.
  5. Calculate the rough new-connection churn ceiling.
  6. Calculate layered retry amplification.
  7. Run the local transfer and explain why its rate can exceed a physical NIC rate.
  8. Inject a 40 ms receiver delay before reading and compare elapsed time.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: The formulas are dimensionally consistent only after conversion. Loopback can report very high throughput because bytes do not traverse the external path. Receiver delay raises receiver completion time; sender completion may precede the receiver consuming buffered bytes.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Normalize all values to base units, then apply BDP, Little's Law, serialization, churn, and retry-product formulas. Keep decimal MB distinct from binary MiB.

Actual transfer time also includes protocol framing, acknowledgments, contention, flow and congestion windows, application reads, and loss.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Set RECEIVER_DELAY = 0.040. Predict whether measured sender completion changes on your OS. A small send may fit buffers, so sender completion might precede receiver work; that is itself evidence about what sendall measures. Both clocks use the same process monotonic timer; the receiver result proves application reads, not durable storage.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
Average latency gives average concurrency, not a safe pool bound. BDP does not predict application throughput alone. Port reuse rules vary. Retry multiplication is a ceiling only if every layer exhausts attempts. Decimal MB and binary MiB differ.

Source: Python socket sendall and timeouts. Binding happens before starting the worker so an occupied port fails promptly; worker exceptions are propagated rather than silently abandoning a readiness wait.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
The script closes both sockets and exits. If interrupted, rerun after the OS releases port 18083 or choose another unprivileged port.

Answer key 
BDP = 1,000,000,000 bit/s * 0.080 s
    = 80,000,000 bit = 10,000,000 byte = 10 MB decimal

mean concurrency = 8,000 request/s * 0.025 s/request = 200 requests

ideal transfer time = (10,000,000 byte * 8 bit/byte) / 1,000,000,000 bit/s
                    = 0.080 s = 80 ms

churn ceiling = 28,000 ports / 60 s = 466.7 new connections/s

attempt ceiling = 3 * 2 * 2 = 12 dependency attempts/original request

The checked results are 10 MB BDP, 200 mean in-flight requests, 80 ms ideal serialization, about 467 new connections/s, and 12 maximum dependency attempts. A design answer must add headroom and measured distributions rather than turning any of these means or ceilings into a production limit.

docs.title: L5 extension
docs.text: Size a starting pool for 12,000 request/s at 20 ms mean and 80 ms p99. Explain why neither 240 nor 960 is automatically the right permit count, and define the load test needed.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Create a capacity worksheet for normal load, one-zone loss, synchronized reconnect, and retries. Include per-source port space, TLS CPU, accept queues, downstream limits, and rollback triggers.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Carried units through all five calculations
  • Distinguished decimal MB from MiB
  • Ran and interpreted the localhost transfer
  • Injected receiver delay and predicted the result
  • Named at least four omitted real-path factors
  • Kept conclusions within measured scope

docs.title: Lab 04: Trace and Trust Proxy Headers
docs.text: Previous: Network Math | Lab index | Next: DNS Failure

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Observe how a reverse proxy rewrites forwarding headers, demonstrate header spoofing, and define a trust policy based on the immediate peer rather than header presence.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: Both listeners bind to 127.0.0.1. The proxy forwards only to the supplied origin. Do not use this fixture as a production proxy or send credentials through it.

docs.title: Supplied fixture transcript
docs.text:
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18084/demo
peer=127.0.0.1
host=127.0.0.1:18084
x-forwarded-for=127.0.0.1
x-forwarded-proto=http
x-request-id=req-0001

$ curl -s -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9' http://127.0.0.1:18084/demo
x-forwarded-for=127.0.0.1

The fixture intentionally replaces, rather than appends to, untrusted inbound forwarding headers.

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Run the origin and proxy together in terminal A:

python3 - <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
import http.client
import threading

class Origin(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        values = {
            "peer": self.client_address[0],
            "host": self.headers.get("Host", ""),
            "x-forwarded-for": self.headers.get("X-Forwarded-For", ""),
            "x-forwarded-proto": self.headers.get("X-Forwarded-Proto", ""),
            "x-request-id": self.headers.get("X-Request-Id", ""),
        }
        body = "".join(f"{k}={v}\n" for k, v in values.items()).encode()
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body)
    def log_message(self, *args): pass

class Proxy(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    counter = 0
    lock = threading.Lock()
    def do_GET(self):
        if not self.path.startswith("/") or self.path.startswith("//"):
            self.send_error(400, "origin-form path required"); return
        with Proxy.lock:
            Proxy.counter += 1
            request_id = Proxy.counter
        headers = {
            "Host": self.headers.get("Host", ""),
            "X-Forwarded-For": self.client_address[0],
            "X-Forwarded-Proto": "http",
            "X-Request-Id": f"req-{request_id:04d}",
        }
        c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 18085, timeout=2)
        try:
            c.request("GET", self.path, headers=headers)
            r = c.getresponse(); body = r.read(); status = r.status
        except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException):
            self.send_error(502, "local origin unavailable"); return
        finally:
            c.close()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))); self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)
    def log_message(self, *args): pass

with ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 18085), Origin) as origin:
    with ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 18084), Proxy) as proxy:
        threading.Thread(target=origin.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
        try:
            proxy.serve_forever()
        finally:
            origin.shutdown()
PY

In terminal B:

curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sS http://127.0.0.1:18084/demo
curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sS -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9' -H 'X-Request-Id: forged' http://127.0.0.1:18084/demo
curl --noproxy '*' --max-time 2 -sS http://127.0.0.1:18085/direct

If curl is unavailable, use http.client.HTTPConnection as in Lab 01. Do not use an environment-configured forward proxy for these loopback probes.

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text: Use curl -v to display both hops separately by calling proxy and origin. Production proxies may support standardized Forwarded, PROXY protocol, or signed identity metadata; enable none merely because a header exists.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Draw client -> proxy -> origin and mark TCP peer identity at each hop.
  2. Capture normal proxy output.
  3. Send forged forwarding and request-ID headers.
  4. Call the origin directly and compare missing headers.
  5. Change the fixture temporarily so the proxy preserves the inbound X-Forwarded-For; demonstrate the spoof.
  6. Restore replacement behavior and verify it.
  7. Write an allowlist and direct-origin isolation policy.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: The origin's immediate peer is the proxy in both proxied requests. Header values are strings supplied by the proxy, not properties of TCP. Direct origin access bypasses proxy normalization. A safe origin trusts forwarding metadata only when the immediate peer is an authenticated, authorized proxy and direct access is blocked in the real deployment.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Let n count header addresses only and p count trusted proxy hops, including the immediate TCP peer. With one appended predecessor address per proxy, the zero-based candidate index is n - p, not n - p - 1: the last proxy is the socket peer and does not append itself. Require n >= p >= 1 and verify the trusted suffix right-to-left. Ignore any untrusted prefix; reject malformed or unexpectedly short chains. If paths have different trusted hop counts, a fixed index is unsafe; use the actual authenticated peer chain.

flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> E[Trusted edge replaces forged header]
    E --> P[Trusted inner proxy appends edge address]
    P --> O[Origin sees inner proxy as socket peer]
    O --> V[Walk header from right to left across trusted hops]

This follows RFC 7239 sections 5.2, 7.5, and 8.1 for predecessor ordering and integrity; X-Forwarded-For itself is not the standardized Forwarded syntax. The fixture uses a fixed HTTPConnection, so proxy environment variables, redirects, and request authority cannot change the upstream destination. The reflected Host is still untrusted application input.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Replace the proxy assignment with the inbound header value, rerun the forged request, and record that the origin reports 203.0.113.9. This is a controlled identity-integrity failure, not evidence that the address belongs to the caller.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text: All peers share loopback, so the lab demonstrates trust logic rather than real client addressing. It does not cover TLS client identity, PROXY protocol, IPv6 normalization, multiple proxy vendors, or header parsing ambiguities.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Press Ctrl-C in terminal A. Verify both ports 18084 and 18085 are closed. Restore any temporary fixture edit before recording the final result.

Answer key

For n=3 and p=2, the candidate client index is 3 - 2 = 1. For example, [forged, client, edge] plus socket peer inner-proxy yields client, never forged. With only [client, edge], n=2, p=2 yields index 0.

Trust is established by the connection peer and deployment policy, then applied to normalized metadata. The edge must remove or replace client-supplied identity headers. Each additional trusted proxy must use one documented append rule. The origin should be reachable only from trusted proxies and should reject forwarding metadata from other peers.

docs.title: L5 extension
docs.text: Specify trusted hops, parsing direction, maximum chain length, IPv4/IPv6 normalization, request-ID ownership, and tests for direct access and duplicate headers.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Design a fleet migration from vendor-specific forwarding headers to one identity envelope. Include cryptographic or mTLS binding, mixed-version behavior, audit fields, privacy retention, canaries, and rollback.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Captured normal, forged, and direct-origin cases
  • Marked immediate peer versus claimed client identity
  • Demonstrated and repaired spoof acceptance
  • Completed the trusted-hop calculation
  • Defined origin isolation and malformed-chain behavior
  • Closed both listeners

docs.title: Lab 05: Model DNS Cache Failure and Recovery
docs.text: Previous: Proxy Headers | Lab index | Next: TLS Handshake

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Explain positive caching, negative caching, stale addresses, and safe endpoint migration using a deterministic offline resolver model.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: Do not edit /etc/hosts, flush system caches, or query public resolvers. The portable path is an in-process model that opens no sockets. The separate OS observation resolves only localhost.

docs.title: Supplied fixture data
docs.text:
t=0s    cache miss; authority returns 127.0.0.1 with TTL 30s
t=10s   authority changes answer to 127.0.0.2
t=20s   client uses cached 127.0.0.1; old endpoint still serves
t=31s   cache expires; client obtains 127.0.0.2
t=35s   an independent empty cache receives NXDOMAIN with negative TTL 20s
t=40s   authority restores 127.0.0.2, but that cache retains NXDOMAIN
t=56s   the negative cache expires; resolution succeeds

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Run the deterministic cache model:

python3 - <<'PY'
events = [(0, "A", "127.0.0.1", 30), (10, "A", "127.0.0.2", 30),
          (35, "NX", None, 20), (40, "A", "127.0.0.2", 30)]
def authority(t):
    return max((e for e in events if e[0] <= t), key=lambda e: e[0])
def resolve(cache, t):
    if cache.get("answer") and t < cache["expiry"]:
        kind, value = cache["answer"]
        return "cache", kind, value, cache["expiry"] - t
    _, kind, value, ttl = authority(t)
    cache.update(answer=(kind, value), expiry=t + ttl)
    return "authority", kind, value, ttl

positive_cache = {}
for t in (0, 10, 20, 31):
    print(f"positive t={t:02d}", resolve(positive_cache, t))

negative_cache = {}
for t in (35, 40, 54, 56):
    print(f"negative t={t:02d}", resolve(negative_cache, t))
PY

For a real localhost resolution observation:

python3 - <<'PY'
import socket
for row in socket.getaddrinfo("localhost", 80, type=socket.SOCK_STREAM):
    print(row[0].name, row[4][0])
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text: Local OS tools include getent hosts localhost and macOS dscacheutil -q host -a name localhost. Their output reflects different APIs and caches. dig and nslookup may query an external configured resolver; skip them under this lab's no-public-query boundary. Do not treat disagreement as corruption until you identify each vantage point.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Predict every model result before execution.
  2. Identify the positive-cache stale interval after the authority change.
  3. Identify the negative-cache recovery delay.
  4. Start any earlier HTTP fixture on 127.0.0.1 and show that resolution success is separate from service reachability.
  5. Inject early removal: declare the old endpoint unavailable at t=15.
  6. Write a migration sequence that respects the previous TTL and pooled connections.
  7. Record which parts are simulated and which are observed from the OS resolver.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: The cache continues returning the old positive answer until expiry. Restoring an authoritative answer does not immediately remove a cached negative answer. A DNS answer is an address candidate, not a health guarantee.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Calculate each stale window as cache expiry minus the authority-change time. Planned overlap must cover at least the previous positive TTL plus connection drain allowance.

If the old TTL was 1,800 seconds before being lowered, wait for that old TTL to age out before relying on the lower value.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Mark 127.0.0.1 unavailable at t=15 while clients may cache it through t=30. Then inject NXDOMAIN at t=35 and restore at t=40. Explain why adding retries against the same cached answer does not repair either failure.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
The model simplifies authority selection, referral caching, TTL floors, stale serving, search domains, Happy Eyeballs, and application-specific DNS caches. Loopback aliases vary by OS. It does not prove a particular recursive resolver's behavior.

RFC 2308 section 5 derives the negative TTL from min(SOA TTL, SOA.MINIMUM), not the restored A record's TTL. NXDOMAIN is keyed by name/class; NODATA also includes query type. The fixture models one name/type only. Its overlap formula is a planning lower bound, not a recovery guarantee for stale-serving or noncompliant clients.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
The model exits without changing host state. Stop any localhost HTTP fixture you started. No cache flush is required or recommended.

Answer key 
positive stale window after change at t=10 = expiry t=30 - t=10 = 20 s
negative recovery delay after restore at t=40 = expiry t=55 - t=40 = 15 s
minimum planned overlap >= previous positive TTL + connection drain allowance

Clients can use 127.0.0.1 for 20 seconds after the authority changes. Early removal at t=15 creates a 15-second stale-answer failure interval. NXDOMAIN restored at t=40 can remain visible until t=55. Safe migration lowers TTL in advance, waits for the previous TTL, publishes overlapping healthy endpoints, observes old traffic and connection drain, then removes the old endpoint with rollback capacity intact.

docs.title: L5 extension
docs.text: Design client behavior for multiple A/AAAA answers: address racing, per-address failure memory, overall deadline, refresh, and connection-pool rotation.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Define a cross-region DNS evacuation policy with resolver diversity, TTL history, stale-serving assumptions, catchment capacity, certificate overlap, staged withdrawal, and abort signals.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Predicted and ran the cache timeline
  • Calculated positive and negative stale windows
  • Separated resolution from endpoint health
  • Injected early removal and NXDOMAIN
  • Wrote an overlap-and-drain migration sequence
  • Made no host resolver changes

docs.title: Lab 06: Diagnose a TLS Handshake
docs.text: Previous: DNS Failure | Lab index | Next: Connection Pool

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Map a TLS transcript to transport setup, certificate identity, trust validation, and application data. Distinguish a TLS failure from DNS, TCP, and HTTP failure.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: The base exercise is offline transcript analysis plus localhost TCP. The enhanced TLS server uses a temporary self-signed certificate on loopback. Never disable certificate verification in production. No public endpoint or root access is required.

docs.title: Supplied fixture transcript
docs.text:
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 CN = localhost
verify error:num=18:self-signed certificate
---
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN = localhost
   i:CN = localhost
---
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Verification error: self-signed certificate
Verify return code: 18 (self-signed certificate)

Second fixture:

TCP connect: success
TLS version: TLSv1.3
Certificate SAN: DNS:service.test
Requested server name: localhost
Result: hostname mismatch
HTTP status: not available; no authenticated TLS channel was established

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Observe that TCP success does not imply TLS success:

python3 - <<'PY'
import socket, ssl
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
def plain_server(listener):
    c, _ = listener.accept()
    with c:
        c.settimeout(2)
        c.recv(16384)  # Consume the ClientHello before replying with plaintext.
        c.sendall(b"not tls\n")
with socket.socket() as listener:
    listener.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    listener.bind(("127.0.0.1", 18086)); listener.listen(1); listener.settimeout(2)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:
        peer = executor.submit(plain_server, listener)
        with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 18086), 1) as raw:
            try:
                with ssl.create_default_context().wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname="localhost"):
                    raise RuntimeError("unexpected TLS success")
            except ssl.SSLError as e:
                print(type(e).__name__, str(e).split("\n")[0])
        peer.result(timeout=3)
PY

This failure occurs after TCP connect when the peer sends bytes that are not a TLS record.

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text:
Use OpenSSL 1.1.1+ or 3.x with req -addext support; the system openssl on macOS may instead be an incompatible LibreSSL version. Record openssl version and use offline transcripts if the flags are unavailable. Create a disposable local certificate and server:

(
umask 077
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/netlab-tls.XXXXXX") || exit 1
cleanup() { rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"; }
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'exit 129' HUP
trap 'exit 130' INT
trap 'exit 143' TERM
printf 'Lab directory: %s\n' "$tmpdir"
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 \
  -keyout "$tmpdir/key.pem" -out "$tmpdir/cert.pem" \
  -subj '/CN=localhost' -addext 'subjectAltName=DNS:localhost' || exit 1
openssl s_server -quiet -accept 127.0.0.1:18086 \
  -cert "$tmpdir/cert.pem" -key "$tmpdir/key.pem" -www
)

In another terminal, set tmpdir to the printed directory, then first use the default trust store and explicitly trust only the temporary certificate:

tmpdir='/replace/with/printed/lab/directory'
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:18086 -servername localhost -verify_return_error </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:18086 -servername localhost \
  -CAfile "$tmpdir/cert.pem" -verify_hostname localhost -verify_return_error </dev/null

The certificate is for this lab only.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Annotate the supplied transcript: TCP, certificate chain, negotiated protocol/cipher, verification result.
  2. State separately whether encryption was negotiated and whether identity was trusted.
  3. Run the plain-server failure and classify it.
  4. If OpenSSL exists, run both trust cases.
  5. Inject a hostname mismatch by verifying wrong.test.
  6. Calculate fresh TCP plus TLS latency for 40 ms RTT.
  7. Recover by restoring localhost and explicit lab CA trust.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: A TLS session can negotiate encryption while certificate verification still fails. A plaintext peer causes a protocol error after TCP success. Hostname and chain validation are separate checks. No HTTP status exists when TLS fails before application data.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Ignoring DNS, server work, and implementation overlap:

Add the approximate TCP and TLS handshake RTT costs, then substitute the fixture RTT. Keep this protocol estimate separate from measured elapsed time.

Resumption can reduce work, while loss and certificate processing increase elapsed time. Do not add this fixed estimate to every pooled request.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Use three distinct faults: plaintext on a TLS port, untrusted self-signed issuer, and wrong hostname. Preserve each exact error; they require different repairs.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
