OpenSSL output is implementation-specific. A self-signed local certificate does not model intermediates, revocation, OCSP, clock skew, SNI routing, mTLS, resumption, or TLS offload. Handshake RTT counts are protocol approximations, not latency measurements.

Sources: TLS 1.3 authentication, RFC 9846 section 4.5 and OpenSSL s_client verification options. SNI chooses a server name for routing; it does not enable hostname verification. The first transcript illustrates diagnostic s_client behavior that can continue after a verification error. A verifying application must fail closed.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Stop openssl s_server with Ctrl-C. The terminal-A trap removes only its randomly created directory. Verify port 18086 is closed and the printed directory no longer exists.

Answer key 
TCP handshake = about 1 RTT
TLS 1.3 fresh handshake = about 1 RTT after TCP
at RTT 40 ms: setup before request data is about 2 * 40 ms = 80 ms

The first supplied transcript shows TCP success and TLS 1.3 negotiation, but verification fails because the issuer is not trusted. The second shows a name mismatch even though protocol negotiation succeeds. Neither case yields authenticated HTTP. Recovery must fix the specific trust or name condition; -k-style verification bypass is not a repair.

docs.title: L5 extension
docs.text: Write a certificate rotation plan covering SANs, SNI, chain overlap, trust-bundle rollout order, session lifetime, expiry alerting, canary verification, and rollback.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Design fleet-wide workload identity and TLS policy: issuance, short-lived credentials, revocation limits, trust-domain federation, mixed-version migration, observability without secret capture, and emergency authority.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• Annotated both supplied transcripts
  • Separated encryption, chain trust, and hostname checks
  • Ran the localhost non-TLS failure
  • Calculated handshake RTT budget with assumptions
  • Injected at least two distinct TLS failures
  • Removed temporary keys and stopped the listener

docs.title: Lab 07: Bound a Connection Pool and Its Queue
docs.text: Previous: TLS Handshake | Lab index | Next: Retry Storm

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Measure active work, pool-acquisition wait, throughput, and rejection while a bounded client calls a slow localhost service. Explain why a larger pool can move a bottleneck rather than remove it.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: The script binds to 127.0.0.1, makes at most 40 requests, and caps concurrency at 16. Do not point it at another host. It models permits around short-lived connections; production pools also manage reuse, idle state, protocol streams, and TLS context.

docs.title: Supplied fixture transcript
docs.text:
requests=40 batches=16,16,8 service_ms=100 pool=4 acquire_timeout_ms=50
ok=12 rejected=28
accepted_acquire_ms median=0.0
rejected_acquire_ms median=50.1

requests=40 batches=16,16,8 service_ms=100 pool=16 acquire_timeout_ms=50
ok=40 rejected=0
accepted_acquire_ms median=0.0

This transcript is an illustrative three-batch outcome, not a deterministic oracle. Barriers align release, not OS scheduling; late workers can acquire permits after early work completes. Counts and times remain host-dependent. The second run is not automatically better: the local listener and scheduler now absorb more simultaneous work.

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Run this self-contained experiment:

python3 - <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import http.client, statistics, threading, time

REQUESTS, WORKERS, POOL, SERVICE_MS, ACQUIRE_MS = 40, 16, 4, 100, 50
if not (REQUESTS == 40 and WORKERS == 16 and 1 <= POOL <= 16
        and 0 < SERVICE_MS <= 300 and 0 < ACQUIRE_MS <= 1000):
    raise ValueError("keep the bounded fixture workload")
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        time.sleep(SERVICE_MS / 1000)
        body = b"ok\n"; self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body)
    def log_message(self, *args): pass
class Server(ThreadingHTTPServer):
    request_queue_size = WORKERS
server = Server(("127.0.0.1", 18087), H)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
permits = threading.BoundedSemaphore(POOL); lock = threading.Lock(); rows = []
def call(i, barrier):
    barrier.wait(timeout=5)
    start = time.perf_counter(); got = permits.acquire(timeout=ACQUIRE_MS / 1000)
    acquired = time.perf_counter()
    if not got:
        row = ("rejected", (acquired-start)*1000, 0)
    else:
        c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 18087, timeout=1)
        try:
            c.request("GET", "/"); r = c.getresponse(); r.read()
            outcome = "ok" if r.status == 200 else "http_error"
        except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException):
            outcome = "transport_error"
        finally:
            c.close(); permits.release()
        row = (outcome, (acquired-start)*1000, (time.perf_counter()-acquired)*1000)
    with lock: rows.append(row)
def run_batch(first, size):
    barrier = threading.Barrier(size)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=size) as ex:
        list(ex.map(lambda i: call(i, barrier), range(first, first + size)))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
first = 0
try:
    for size in (WORKERS, WORKERS, REQUESTS - 2 * WORKERS):
        run_batch(first, size); first += size
    wall = time.perf_counter() - t0
finally:
    server.shutdown(); server.server_close()
ok = [r for r in rows if r[0] == "ok"]
rejected = sum(r[0] == "rejected" for r in rows)
errors = len(rows) - len(ok) - rejected
print(f"ok={len(ok)} rejected={rejected} errors={errors} wall_ms={wall*1000:.1f} throughput_ok_s={len(ok)/wall:.1f}")
accepted_wait = [r[1] for r in ok]
rejected_wait = [r[1] for r in rows if r[0] == "rejected"]
if accepted_wait:
    print(f"accepted_acquire_ms_median={statistics.median(accepted_wait):.1f} accepted_acquire_ms_max={max(accepted_wait):.1f}")
if rejected_wait:
    print(f"rejected_acquire_ms_median={statistics.median(rejected_wait):.1f} rejected_acquire_ms_max={max(rejected_wait):.1f}")
if ok:
    print(f"request_ms_median={statistics.median(r[2] for r in ok):.1f} request_ms_max={max(r[2] for r in ok):.1f}")
PY

Change only the constants at the top between runs.

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text: While the script runs, lsof -nP -iTCP:18087, ss -tan, or netstat -an can sample socket states. Sampling may miss short connections. A production client library's pool metrics are preferable to inferring ownership from OS sockets.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Predict useful mean concurrency for 40 request/s and 100 ms service time.
  2. Run POOL=4, then POOL=8, holding all other values fixed.
  3. Record successful, rejected, wall time, acquisition wait, and request time.
  4. Separate time waiting for a permit from time using the dependency.
  5. Increase SERVICE_MS to 300 without changing acquisition timeout.
  6. Inject an unbounded-wait policy by changing acquire(timeout=...) to acquire(); compare user-visible wait.
  7. Restore bounded acquisition and prove the script exits with the port closed.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: A pool's ideal steady throughput is its permit count divided by mean service time. Bursty arrival causes permit waits and rejections. Increasing service time cuts capacity. Removing the acquisition timeout converts rejection into hidden queueing and longer latency.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
useful mean concurrency = arrival rate * mean service time
ideal pool throughput ceiling = permits / mean service time
observed successful throughput = successful requests / wall seconds

These estimates ignore burst shape, client and server overhead, variance, connection setup, and downstream saturation.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Use SERVICE_MS=300 as dependency slowness. Then remove the acquisition timeout as a queue-policy failure. Do not raise workers or pool above the stated caps.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
The fixture opens one connection per accepted request, so it models concurrency permits more directly than reuse. Python threads, loopback, and a toy HTTP server do not model production HTTP/2 streams, NAT, TLS, fair queueing, or multiple destinations. Median service time cannot size a p99-safe pool.

Source: Python socketserver lifecycle and request queue. The listener backlog is set explicitly so an OS-dependent small default is less likely to dominate the pool experiment. Transport errors are not permit rejections; report them separately. The 40 request/s calculation is a hypothetical steady arrival rate, not the offered rate of these synchronized batches.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
The script shuts down the server. If interrupted, stop the Python process and verify port 18087 is closed before rerunning.

Answer key 
useful mean concurrency = 40 request/s * 0.100 s = 4 requests
ideal pool throughput ceiling = 4 / 0.100 s = 40 request/s
with 300 ms service time = 4 / 0.300 s = 13.3 request/s

Little's Law gives mean concurrency four at 40 request/s and 100 ms. A bounded pool near four exposes overload through short acquisition failures. At 300 ms its ideal ceiling falls to about 13.3 request/s. An unbounded acquisition wait may increase completion count in a finite test but violates a latency budget and retains queued work after callers no longer benefit.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Define fleet-wide connection governance for reconnect storms, DNS and certificate rotation, tenant isolation, NAT capacity, zone evacuation, and safe defaults that libraries cannot silently override.

  • Separated acquisition wait from request time
  • Injected service slowness and unbounded waiting
  • Explained why more permits may move the queue
  • Verified the listener closed

docs.title: Lab 08: Contain a Retry Storm
docs.text: Previous: Connection Pool | Lab index | Next: HTTP/2 Multiplexing

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Measure retry amplification during a controlled localhost failure, then compare synchronized retries with bounded exponential backoff and jitter.

docs.title: Safety boundary
docs.text: The fixture accepts only loopback traffic. Keep CLIENTS <= 20, ATTEMPTS <= 4, and the supplied delays. Never use this client against an external or production service. The experiment demonstrates shape and amplification, not production capacity.

docs.title: Supplied fixture transcript
docs.text:
policy=immediate clients=20 max_attempts=4 fail_for_ms=250
attempts=80 successes=0 failures=80 amplification=4.00
attempt_buckets_100ms={0: 40, 1: 40}

policy=jittered clients=20 max_attempts=4 fail_for_ms=250 retry_budget=20
attempts=40 successes=0 failures=40 amplification=2.00
attempt_buckets_100ms={0: 40}

These are illustrative outputs, not measured benchmarks or fixed assertions. Exact counts vary with scheduling and jitter. With the shared budget, all 20 tokens can be spent on first retries before the outage ends; lower amplification does not guarantee success. Preserve your actual run.

docs.title: Portable localhost path
docs.text:
Run the immediate-retry baseline. Then select POLICY = "backoff", "jitter", or "budget" for complete improved paths in the same fixture:

python3 - <<'PY'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import http.client, random, threading, time

CLIENTS, ATTEMPTS, FAIL_MS = 20, 4, 250
POLICY, FAILURE_CODE, DEADLINE_S = "immediate", 503, 2.0
if not (1 <= CLIENTS <= 20 and 1 <= ATTEMPTS <= 4 and 0 <= FAIL_MS <= 250):
    raise ValueError("keep the bounded fixture workload")
if POLICY not in {"immediate", "backoff", "jitter", "budget"}:
    raise ValueError("unknown policy")
started = 0.0; lock = threading.Lock(); events = []
retry_budget = threading.BoundedSemaphore(20)
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000
        code = FAILURE_CODE if elapsed < FAIL_MS else 200
        with lock: events.append((time.perf_counter() - started, code))
        self.send_response(code); self.send_header("Content-Length", "0"); self.end_headers()
    def log_message(self, *args): pass
class Server(ThreadingHTTPServer):
    request_queue_size = CLIENTS
server = Server(("127.0.0.1", 18088), H)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
def start_clock():
    global started
    started = time.perf_counter()
barrier = threading.Barrier(CLIENTS, action=start_clock)
def client(i):
    rng = random.Random(i)
    barrier.wait(timeout=5)
    deadline = started + DEADLINE_S
    made = 0
    for attempt in range(ATTEMPTS):
        if attempt:
            delay = 0.0 if POLICY == "immediate" else 0.050 * (2 ** (attempt - 1))
            if POLICY in {"jitter", "budget"}:
                delay = rng.uniform(0, delay)
            if time.perf_counter() + delay >= deadline:
                return (False, made, "deadline")
            time.sleep(delay)
        remaining = deadline - time.perf_counter()
        if remaining <= 0:
            return (False, made, "deadline")
        if attempt and POLICY == "budget" and not retry_budget.acquire(blocking=False):
            return (False, made, "budget_denied")
        # Tokens count extra attempts and are deliberately never released.
        c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 18088, timeout=min(1, remaining))
        made += 1
        try:
            c.request("GET", "/"); r = c.getresponse(); r.read(); code = r.status
        except (OSError, http.client.HTTPException):
            return (False, made, "transport_error")
        finally:
            c.close()
        if code == 200:
            return (True, made, "ok")
        if code != 503:
            return (False, made, "non_retryable")
    return (False, made, "attempt_limit")
try:
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=CLIENTS) as ex:
        results = list(ex.map(client, range(CLIENTS)))
finally:
    server.shutdown(); server.server_close()
buckets = {}
for t, code in events: buckets[int(t * 10)] = buckets.get(int(t * 10), 0) + 1
attempts = sum(r[1] for r in results)
print(f"attempts={attempts} observed_server_attempts={len(events)} successes={sum(r[0] for r in results)} amplification={attempts/CLIENTS:.2f}")
print("outcomes=", {reason: sum(r[2] == reason for r in results) for reason in sorted({r[2] for r in results})})
print("attempt_buckets_100ms=", buckets)
PY

budget combines full jitter with 20 shared extra-attempt tokens. No sleep is performed after the last attempt, and 400 is non-retryable. Random draws are seeded per client for repeatability, but scheduling and budget winners are not deterministic. A bounded policy can exhaust all attempts before recovery; a later healthy probe is a separate recovery observation, not a guaranteed retry success.

docs.title: Optional enhanced commands
docs.text: Plot bucket counts with a spreadsheet or local Python installation containing matplotlib. OS connection-state commands can show churn but are samples, not complete attempt counts. No traffic shaping or firewall manipulation is required.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Predict the no-success attempt ceiling.
  2. Run immediate retries and record attempts per 100 ms bucket.
  3. Calculate amplification and unsuccessful-work ratio.
  4. Add deterministic exponential backoff without jitter; compare bucket alignment.
  5. Add full jitter and rerun at least three times.
  6. Add the shared budget of 20 retries and record denied retries separately.
  7. Inject a non-retryable 400 response and ensure clients stop after one attempt.
  8. Restore the 503-then-200 fixture. Record whether any retry observed recovery; if none did, run with FAIL_MS=0 to verify the healthy path separately.

docs.title: Expected observations
docs.text: Immediate retries cluster near the initial failure and may finish before recovery. Backoff spreads attempts in time; identical backoff can still synchronize clients. Jitter reduces alignment. A retry budget bounds extra work. A 400 should not be retried by this policy.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
maximum attempts = clients * attempts/client
amplification = total dependency attempts / original client operations
unsuccessful-work ratio = non-200 attempts / total attempts

maximum dependency amplification = product of each layer's attempt limit

A shared retry budget caps extra work in addition to each client's initial attempt.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: The server returns 503 for its first 250 ms. Change 503 to 400 for the classification fault. To model slow failure, sleep 100 ms before each 503 and observe how attempts consume both time and concurrency. Keep the same client caps.

docs.title: Evidence limitations
docs.text:
The server does not overload as request rate rises, so it understates positive feedback. Thread scheduling affects buckets. HTTP 503 is not always safe to retry; method replay safety, idempotency, Retry-After, deadlines, and side-effect ambiguity matter. A semaphore budget in one process is not a fleet-wide budget.

Sources: RFC 9110 section 9.2.2 and Python socketserver lifecycle. Only this synthetic GET retries 503. Transport errors stop rather than being silently classified as HTTP failures. Socket timeouts bound individual blocking operations, not a strict end-to-end deadline: this fixture checks its monotonic budget before each attempt, but a production client needs cancellation across all I/O phases. No arbitrary or streaming peer is modeled here.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Each script calls shutdown() and closes port 18088. If interrupted, stop the process. Confirm the port is closed and no temporary files remain.

Answer key 
maximum attempts = 20 clients * 4 attempts/client = 80 attempts
maximum dependency amplification for limits 3, 2, and 2 = 3 * 2 * 2 = 12
20 retry tokens + 20 initial attempts = 40 attempts, or amplification 2.0

The immediate ceiling is 80 attempts and amplification 4.0. If all attempts occur during the 250 ms outage, none helps. Exponential backoff creates recovery opportunities, jitter avoids coordinated waves, and the shared budget limits added pressure. Correct policy also requires one retry owner, an end-to-end deadline, retryable error classes, replay-safe operations, and admission control.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Explain when HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces connection and queue cost, when TCP loss couples independent streams, and why connection count is a poor load signal. Produce a bounded connection and stream policy from deterministic evidence.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: This lab is offline. It opens no sockets and changes no host settings. Use only the inline fixture and the optional standard-library simulation. Do not run packet-loss commands against a shared host.

docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
Six requests are already deliverable to the server at the model's t=0. Service time starts then, subject to the H1 queues. Ignore handshake, transit, and response serialization; these are server-relative completion times, not client end-to-end latency on a 50 ms RTT path.

Request Service time HTTP/1.1 connection HTTP/2 stream A 20 ms c1 1 B 80 ms c2 3 C 30 ms c1 5 D 10 ms c2 7 E 40 ms c1 9 F 20 ms c2 11

Rules:

  • HTTP/1.1 uses two connections and one active request per connection. Each connection processes its assigned requests in table order.
  • HTTP/2 uses one established TCP connection. All six streams begin together.
  • Without loss, response completion equals queue delay plus service time.
  • In the loss run, a gap in the response TCP byte stream exists from 15 through 65 ms. Every response completing after 15 ms needs bytes after that gap. Application work continues during recovery. Delivery completion is therefore max(service_time, 65) for these responses, not service_time + 50.
  • This fixture isolates scheduling. It does not model congestion-control growth or header compression.

docs.title: Portable simulation or reasoning
docs.text:
Reason directly from the rules, or run this Python 3 simulation from any directory:

python3 - <<'PY'
requests = [('A',20,'c1'),('B',80,'c2'),('C',30,'c1'),
            ('D',10,'c2'),('E',40,'c1'),('F',20,'c2')]
clock = {'c1': 0, 'c2': 0}
for name, service, conn in requests:
    clock[conn] += service
    print('h1', name, clock[conn])
for name, service, _ in requests:
    print('h2-clean', name, service)
    print('h2-loss ', name, max(service, 65) if service > 15 else service)
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced path
docs.text: On an isolated loopback-only environment, compare an HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2-capable local server with six fixed-delay handlers. Capture connection IDs, stream IDs, and completion times. If you inject loss, do so only inside a disposable network namespace or container and record the exact command and cleanup. The fixture remains the grading source.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Calculate completion time for each HTTP/1.1 request.
  2. Calculate each HTTP/2 completion with and without the loss event.
  3. Compare p50 and maximum completion qualitatively; do not infer production p99 from six samples.
  4. Explain which benefit comes from multiplexing and which failure comes from the shared TCP delivery order.
  5. Propose a client policy for a destination handling 1,200 concurrent requests: number of connections, maximum streams per connection, acquisition deadline, and load signal.
  6. Name two measurements that would justify HTTP/3 for this path.

docs.title: Expected evidence
docs.text:
• A table with all 18 completion values: six H1, six clean H2, and six loss H2.
  • A statement that H2 avoids application-level serialization across requests but does not remove transport-level coupling under TCP loss.
  • A policy that uses bounded streams and outstanding work, not only least connections.
  • A falsifiable HTTP/3 hypothesis tied to RTT, loss, handshake, and goodput.
flowchart LR
    W[Independent application work continues] --> R[Response bytes ready]
    R --> G[TCP gap blocks later byte delivery]
    G --> F[Gap recovered at 65 ms]
    F --> D[Deliver ready responses]
    W --> L[Work finishing after 65 ms is not delayed by this gap]

Sources: RFC 9113 sections 5.1.2 and 5.2 and TCP ordered delivery, RFC 9293 section 3. This is a delivery gate, not a TCP loss-recovery implementation. Real losses can also reduce the shared congestion window and affect later work. A 300-stream client cap is usable only if the server's SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS allows it; four connections with a peer cap of 100 permit only 400 concurrent streams, leaving 800 requests to queue within a deadline or be rejected.

docs.title: Calculation checkpoint
docs.text: HTTP/1.1 completion times are cumulative per connection. For c1, request C cannot start until A finishes. Apply the fixture's loss delay only to clean H2 completions that cross the loss point. For the policy calculation, divide active requests by connections and express one-connection loss as a fraction of total active work.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text:
Apply the fixture's synthetic loss at 15 ms. Then inject a connection reset at 25 ms and answer:

  • Which streams become uncertain or failed?
  • Which operations are safe to retry?
  • How does a stable idempotency key prevent duplicate effects?
  • Would opening one connection per request improve reliability enough to justify handshake, NAT, and CPU cost?

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: No cleanup is required for fixture reasoning or the Python simulation. If you used the enhanced path, remove its disposable namespace/container and confirm no traffic-control rule remains.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

HTTP/1.1 completions are A 20, B 80, C 50, D 90, E 90, and F 110 ms. Clean HTTP/2 completions are A 20, B 80, C 30, D 10, E 40, and F 20 ms. Under the fixture loss rule they are A 65, B 80, C 65, D 10, E 65, and F 65 ms. B's application work finishes after recovery, so this isolated gap adds no delay to B.

For 1,200 requests over 4 equally loaded connections, the cap is 300 streams per connection and loss of one maximally loaded connection disrupts 25 percent of active work.

Multiplexing removes the two per-connection request queues, so D finishes in 10 ms rather than waiting behind B. TCP loss then delays bytes for all streams whose completion crosses the loss point. A small bounded connection set limits that coupling without returning to one connection per request. For 1,200 concurrent requests, a defensible starting experiment is 4 connections with at most 300 streams each, a short acquisition deadline, and balancing by outstanding requests or bytes. Production values require load, loss, CPU, and target-skew measurements.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Reason about a QUIC connection surviving a client address change, distinguish connection identity from the network tuple, and design a safe HTTP/3 fallback and rollout policy.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The default exercise is an offline state-machine simulation. It sends no UDP traffic and changes no routes. Do not change Wi-Fi, VPN, firewall, or production edge policy for this lab.

docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
One client has logical connection conn-1, initially using destination connection ID cid-7, and sends requests with stable operation IDs. The handshake is confirmed, active migration is allowed, and the server has supplied unused cid-8 mapped to the same connection state for the new client path.

t_ms  event
0     path P1 validated: 10.0.0.8:53000 -> 203.0.113.10:443, RTT 40 ms
20    request op-1 sent on stream 0
65    response op-1 received
100   client address changes to 198.51.100.24:61000
105   request op-2 queued; P2 is not yet validated
110   PATH_CHALLENGE sent on P2 using unused destination CID cid-8
150   matching PATH_RESPONSE received; client validates P2, probe elapsed 40 ms
155   request op-2 sent on P2 using cid-8; server validates new client address independently
240   response op-2 received
300   P1 retired

Rules:

  • The server routes packets by connection ID, not solely by the four-tuple.
  • The client conservatively waits for its P2 probe before sending application data. This is a fixture policy, not a QUIC-wide prohibition on data before validation. Client and server validation are separate directional checks.
  • Anti-amplification permits at most 3 times the bytes received on an unvalidated server path.
  • In fallback scenario F, UDP receives no response for 300 ms; fresh TCP plus TLS then costs 2 RTTs on a 70 ms path before request transmission.
  • op-2 is idempotent. A transport timeout does not prove whether the server applied it.

docs.title: Portable simulation or reasoning
docs.text:
Trace the state machine manually or run:

python3 - <<'PY'
events = [(0,'P1','validated'),(100,'P2','candidate'),
          (110,'P2','challenge-sent'),(150,'P2','validated'),
          (300,'P1','retired')]
state = {}
for t, path, value in events:
    state[path] = value
    allowed = [p for p, s in state.items() if s == 'validated']
    print(t, path, value, 'data_paths=' + ','.join(allowed))
print('fallback_ready_ms', 300 + 2 * 70)
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced path
docs.text: Use a loopback-only QUIC demo that exposes connection IDs and path-validation events. Move between two addresses inside a disposable namespace, not between real corporate networks. Capture only synthetic identifiers; never publish tokens or packet captures containing credentials.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Draw the P1/P2 state transitions and mark when each can carry application data.
  2. Explain how cid-7 and cid-8 map to the same connection state even though the client tuple changes.
  3. Calculate how many bytes the server may send on an unvalidated path after receiving 1,250 bytes there.
  4. Calculate fallback readiness in scenario F and its user-latency penalty.
  5. Define retry behavior if the response to op-2 is lost after server commit.
  6. Propose rollout and rollback gates by client network, handshake success, migration success, CPU, and goodput.

docs.title: Expected evidence
docs.text:
• A state trace with candidate, validating, validated, and retired path states.
  • Explicit separation of connection ID, address tuple, TLS identity, and application operation ID.
  • Correct anti-amplification and fallback calculations.
  • A fallback policy that avoids repeatedly paying a known-bad UDP timeout.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client on P2
    participant S as Server retaining conn-1
    C->>S: PATH_CHALLENGE using unused cid-8
    S->>C: Matching PATH_RESPONSE
    Note over C: Client probe succeeds
    C->>S: op-2 on same connection with new CID
    S->>C: Independent PATH_CHALLENGE for client address
    C->>S: Matching PATH_RESPONSE
    Note over S: Lift path anti-amplification limit after validation

RFC 9000 sections 8.2, 9.2, and 9.5 allow client migration without first validating the already-known server address, but prohibit intentional CID reuse from multiple local addresses. NAT rebinding can change the observed tuple without the client knowing; that case is different. A CID routes to retained cryptographic/transport state; it does not reconstruct that state at an unrelated anycast server.

docs.title: Calculation checkpoint
docs.text: Multiply bytes received on the unvalidated server path by the anti-amplification factor. For fallback readiness, add the UDP wait to the TCP and TLS RTT costs; application work and response transit remain outside that result.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text:
At 140 ms, drop the P2 validation response and make P1 unreachable. Decide:

  • whether queued application data may use P2;
  • when fallback should begin;
  • how to avoid duplicate op-2 effects;
  • which counters distinguish blocked UDP, validation loss, and server overload.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: The default path creates nothing. For an enhanced namespace or container, remove both addresses, routes, packet-capture files, and the disposable environment.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

P1 starts validated and can carry data until retirement or failure. P2 moves from candidate to challenge-sent to client-validated at 150 ms; only then does the fixture permit op-2 to leave. Logical connection conn-1 persists while its destination CID changes from cid-7 to cid-8. The 110-to-150 probe interval is 40 ms, not 80 ms. TLS authenticates the peer and op-2 identifies the application effect; none of these identities substitutes for the others.

The anti-amplification total is 3,750 bytes on that unvalidated server path; subtract bytes already sent there to get remaining allowance. It includes validation/control traffic, not just response payload. Fallback transport is ready at 440 ms, a 300 ms penalty versus starting TCP/TLS immediately, excluding request/response time. A client should remember path-specific UDP failure for a bounded period rather than paying that wait repeatedly. If op-2 becomes unknown, retry with the same operation ID under a server-side atomic deduplication and stored-outcome contract; a stable ID alone does not implement that contract.

anti-amplification limit = 3 * 1,250 bytes = 3,750 bytes
fallback ready = 300 ms + 2 * 70 ms = 440 ms

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Design target removal that stops new assignments, preserves bounded in-flight work, handles long-lived connections, and has explicit rollback and completion criteria.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: This lab uses a deterministic offline event stream. Do not deregister real targets or shorten production termination grace periods. The optional path must use a disposable local environment.

docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
At t=0, target old-a enters draining.

initial established connections                 12000
ordinary connection closes per second             180
stale-discovery new connections per second         20
HTTP requests in flight at t=0                    600
request completions per second                    150
long-lived WebSocket connections                  900
WebSocket natural closes per second                 5
forced-drain signal starts                        120 s
final termination deadline                        150 s
replacement target safe spare request capacity   2200 requests/s
traffic previously assigned to old-a             1800 requests/s

Rules:

  • The load balancer immediately stops assigning new traffic, but stale clients account for the 20 new connections/s.
  • Ordinary connections drain at the net rate implied above.
  • The fluid model clamps ordinary occupancy at zero. In the real deployment, stale arrivals do not cease merely because that counter reaches zero: reject new connections/work on the draining target and verify convergence before claiming quiescence. The 69.4-second value is an estimate, not that proof.
  • In-flight HTTP requests complete at the stated rate and receive no new work.
  • WebSockets are included in the initial connection count but have their own close rate.
  • The 15 percent receiver gate applies to the 2,200 requests/s spare budget reserved for this migration. Existing receiver traffic is already accounted for when computing that budget; this is not whole-target utilization.
  • At 120 seconds, remaining connections receive a reconnect signal and then close in equal batches before final termination at 150 seconds.

docs.title: Portable simulation or reasoning
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
ordinary = 12000 - 900
websockets = 900
for t in range(0, 121, 10):

docs.title: Expected evidence
docs.text:
• A timeline of serving -> draining -> quiescent -> terminated, including a reversible point.
  • Separate counts for connections, HTTP requests, and WebSockets.
  • A capacity check on the receiver before removal.
  • Exit criteria based on new assignments, in-flight work, connection age, resets, and replacement saturation.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Serving
    Serving --> Draining: stop new assignments
    Draining --> Serving: rollback before termination
    Draining --> Quiescent: admission fenced and requests and sessions clear
    Draining --> ForcedClose: hard deadline with residuals
    ForcedClose --> Terminated: count disruptions and reconcile outcomes
    Quiescent --> Terminated: grace expires and checks pass
    Terminated --> [*]

RFC 9113 section 6.8 defines the HTTP/2 drain boundary: a received GOAWAY forbids new streams, while streams at or below Last-Stream-ID might have been processed. A timeout or forced close does not make their application effects safe to repeat. Stop assignment at the LB and admission on retained connections; neither action alone covers the other path.

docs.title: Calculation checkpoint
docs.text: Calculate HTTP drain from in-flight work divided by completion rate. Calculate ordinary connections separately using their net close rate, and calculate the WebSocket residual at forced-drain start. Apply the receiver gate to remaining safe capacity as a percentage of its safe ceiling.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: At 30 seconds, replacement capacity falls from 2,200 to 1,700 requests/s. Choose between rollback, shedding, or continuing drain. State what makes rollback unsafe and how you prevent oscillation between target states.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: The simulation creates no state. Stop local proxies and servers from the enhanced path, remove temporary configs, and verify no listener remains.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

HTTP work is clear after about 4 seconds, but connection count is not: ordinary connections take about 69.4 seconds and 300 WebSockets remain when forced drain starts. The receiving target initially has 18.18 percent headroom. If it drops to 1,700 requests/s, shifted demand exceeds safe capacity by 100 requests/s before retries, so pause removal and either restore old-a while it remains safe or shed lower-priority work.

HTTP drain = 600 / 150 = 4 seconds
ordinary drain = (12,000 - 900) / (180 - 20) = 69.4 seconds
WebSockets at forced-drain start = 900 - 5 * 120 = 300
spare-budget utilization = 1,800 / 2,200 = 81.82 percent
remaining spare-budget headroom = 18.18 percent

At 120 seconds, notify the 300 residual WebSockets and clear them across 30 seconds at an average total of 10 closes/s, including natural closes, with client reconnect jitter. Do not add another 5/s of natural closes to that same population without recomputing it. Graceful quiescence requires no new admission, zero in-flight requests, and zero live sessions. At the hard deadline, residual forced closures are a separately counted disruption, not successful draining. Rollback is available only before destructive termination and only if the old target remains correct and compatible.

docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
source public IPs                                      2
usable ports per source/destination tuple          28000
mapping non-reuse lifetime                             60 s
baseline new connections to one destination           600/s
incident new connections to that destination         1400/s
connection reuse before incident                        92 percent
connection reuse during incident                        45 percent
conntrack table limit                               500000
conntrack occupied at incident start                410000
new tracked flows across all destinations            16000/s
expiring tracked flows                               10000/s

At t=20 s, a retrying client opens another 400 connections/s to the hot destination unless mitigated.

Treat the NAT and conntrack projections as independent offered-demand models. Once either starts rejecting traffic, admitted-flow slopes can change. The 60-second non-reuse lifetime is synthetic, not a TCP TIME_WAIT constant or a universal NAT idle timeout. RFC 5382 section 5 distinguishes established and transitory TCP state with different requirements. The port-demand model neglects active connection lifetime. Its calculated churn ceiling is optimistic; add active lifetime to the hold interval when it matters.

docs.title: Calculation checkpoint
docs.text: Calculate tuple churn as total usable mappings divided by non-reuse lifetime. For each arrival rate, compare rate times lifetime with available mappings. Calculate conntrack exhaustion from free entries divided by net growth.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: Assume an operator doubles conntrack capacity at 10 seconds but does not change connection churn. Calculate the extra time gained if net growth remains 6,000/s, and explain what new resource or downstream failure may appear.

docs.title: Cleanup

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab 
tuple churn ceiling = 2 * 28,000 / 60 = 933.3 connections/s
mapping demand = 36,000 at 600/s; 84,000 at 1,400/s; 108,000 at 1,800/s
available mappings = 56,000
conntrack exhaustion = (500,000 - 410,000) / (16,000 - 10,000) = 15 seconds

The NAT tuple ceiling is about 933 new connections/s, so baseline fits and incident demand does not. New connections fail while established reused connections bypass fresh allocation. Conntrack independently reaches its 500,000 limit in 15 seconds.

Doubling the conntrack limit at 10 seconds sets the new ceiling to 1,000,000. Occupancy then is about 470,000, leaving 530,000 entries, or about 88.3 more seconds at 6,000/s. It delays failure but increases memory use and does not fix NAT tuple exhaustion or downstream load. First suppress retries and restore pooling, then add validated source capacity if necessary. Exit only when allocation failures are zero, occupancy has negative or stable slope below policy, and logical-to-attempt ratio is normal.

The new exhaustion timestamp is t=98.33 s, so the time gained over the original t=15 s failure is 83.33 s, not 88.33 s. The later retry injection does not alter this calculation only because the question explicitly holds net growth at 6,000/s. Steady mapping demand alone cannot establish NAT time-to-exhaustion: that also needs incident-start occupancy and the ages of existing mappings.

docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
All five sites announce 203.0.113.0/24. Site A must be withdrawn for maintenance.

Site Current load Safe ceiling Share of A after withdrawal A 240 Gbps 300 Gbps - B 500 Gbps 680 Gbps 50 percent C 330 Gbps 450 Gbps 30 percent D 170 Gbps 280 Gbps 15 percent E 90 Gbps 180 Gbps 5 percent

Synthetic collector snapshots:

collector  prefix          best_origin  path             observed_rtt_ms
east-1     203.0.113.0/24  AS64510      64501 64510      18
central-1  203.0.113.0/24  AS64510      64502 64510      31
west-1     203.0.113.0/24  AS64510      64503 64510      22

unexpected candidate during drill:
east-1     203.0.113.0/25  AS64599      64501 64599      42

Rules:

  • The shift shares are measured estimates, not BGP guarantees.
  • A receiving site must retain 15 percent of safe ceiling after the shift.
  • An accepted, installed /25 wins forwarding longest-prefix selection for addresses it covers, regardless of the /24 path length. Many Internet peers filter IPv4 prefixes longer than /24; a collector observation alone does not establish installation or global propagation.
  • Application health does not directly withdraw the route in this fixture; a route controller requires explicit evidence and approval.

docs.title: Portable simulation or reasoning
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
a = 240
sites = {'B': (500,680,.50), 'C': (330,450,.30),
         'D': (170,280,.15), 'E': (90,180,.05)}
for name, (current, ceiling, share) in sites.items():
    shifted = a * share
    total = current + shifted
    remaining = ceiling - total
    print(name, shifted, total, round(100 * remaining / ceiling, 2))
PY

The dashed arrows represent predicted traffic redistribution, not BGP forwarding traffic through A to the other sites. "10 percent scoped withdrawal" below means withdrawing selected sessions/sites whose measured catchment is about 10 percent; BGP has no withdraw-exactly-10-percent-of-clients operation. RFC 4786 section 4.4 describes service availability coupling and routing policy; the shares and headroom threshold here are exercise assumptions, not protocol guarantees.

docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Shifted loads are B 120, C 72, D 36, and E 12 Gbps. Post-shift totals are B 620, C 402, D 206, and E 102 Gbps. Remaining headroom as a share of ceiling is B 8.82 percent, C 10.67 percent, D 26.43 percent, and E 43.33 percent. B and C fail the 15 percent gate.

If accepted and installed, the /25 is more specific than the intended /24, so matching addresses prefer it even with a less attractive AS path. Pause the drill, validate authorization/RPKI and configured origins, compare several collectors, and test the data plane. Origin validation does not validate the entire AS path or exclude a route leak by an authorized origin. Reannouncing the less-specific /24 alone cannot override an installed /25; removal/filtering of an unauthorized route needs the routing/security owner. docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
disconnected clients                              1200000
naive fixed reconnect delay                             5 s
jittered reconnect window                             180 s
edge reconnect admission ceiling                     12000/s
full TLS CPU per handshake                            1.0 ms
resumed TLS CPU per handshake                         0.2 ms
resumption hit rate                                    75 percent

Client fixture:

client cohort  count    durable_cursor  reconnect_window
A              600000   yes             180 s
B              360000   yes              60 s
C              240000   no                5 s fixed

Rules:

  • Uniform jitter means only average arrival rate is calculated; real buckets still vary.
  • A resumed session authenticates again but uses the lower TLS CPU fixture.
  • Clients with a durable cursor request events after the last acknowledged sequence.
  • Clients without a cursor receive a fresh snapshot capped at 100 objects; they do not request unbounded history.
  • A and B jitter uniformly from t=0 across their respective windows. C waits exactly 5 seconds, then all 240,000 clients attempt together. Use the one-second bucket [5,6) to estimate its spike; 240000 / 5 is not its arrival rate.

docs.text:
Divide only uniformly jittered cohorts by window length. Put the fixed-delay cohort into a declared measurement bucket and add the background arrivals in that bucket. Apply TLS cost to offered or admitted attempts explicitly; those denominators differ when admission rejects work. Separate replay events from snapshot objects and repeat after moving all clients to the common pacing window.

flowchart LR
    A[Attempt spike after fixed delay] --> T[TLS work if admitted before HTTP gate]
    T --> G[Authentication admission]
    G --> C{Durable cursor available}
    C -->|Yes| R[Bounded event replay]
    C -->|No| S[Bounded snapshot]
    G -->|Rejected| J[Jitter and server retry guidance]
    J --> P[Paced retry attempts]

RFC 6455 section 7.2.3 recommends a randomized initial reconnect delay and increasing backoff after abnormal closure. A fixed delay merely moves the synchronized burst. Admission after TLS does not protect handshake CPU; identify the actual gate placement.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: At 60 seconds, resumption hit rate falls from 75 to 20 percent while 300,000 clients remain disconnected. Pace those clients uniformly over the remaining 120 seconds. docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab 
A = 600,000 / 180 = 3,333.3/s
B = 360,000 / 60 = 6,000/s
C = 240,000 attempts in the [5,6) one-second bucket
spike bucket = 240,000 + 3,333.3 + 6,000 = 249,333.3 attempts/s
weighted TLS CPU = 0.75 * 0.2 + 0.25 * 1.0 = 0.4 ms/reconnect
offered TLS demand = 249,333.3 * 0.4 ms / 1000 = 99.73 cores
A/B replay demand = 9,333.3 * 40 = 373,333 events/s
C snapshot upper bound = 240,000 * 100 = 24,000,000 objects
counterfactual all-cursor spike replay = 249,333.3 * 40 = 9,973,333 events/s
all clients over 180 s = 6,666.7/s, 2.67 TLS cores, 266,667 events/s

The spike bucket contains about 249,333 offered reconnects, not a steady 57,333/s. Finer buckets can reveal a much sharper burst. During the first 60 seconds outside the spike, A/B average 9,333/s; after B's window ends, A averages 3,333/s until 180 seconds. Move all cohorts to the 180-second jitter policy, honor server retry guidance, and admit fairly. Its 6,667/s is still an average, not a hard bound or proof that every bucket fits.

Actual A/B replay demand is below the event ceiling; C instead exercises a snapshot path whose object-processing capacity is unspecified. The 9,973,333 events/s spike is a counterfactual if C also resumed 40 events, not observed replay. At 20 percent resumption, weighted CPU is 0.2 * 0.2 + 0.8 * 1.0 = 0.84 ms per handshake. Pacing the remaining 300,000 clients over 120 seconds yields 2,500 reconnects/s and 2.1 TLS cores. Disabling safe resumption raises that to 2.5 cores. Verify resumption-cache health and retain cursor/snapshot caps. These CPU demands need an actual available-core budget before declaring overload or sufficient headroom.

Weight unaffected and reset-affected attempt counts to obtain attempts per logical request. Multiply by logical rate for dependency load and by per-attempt CPU for each proxy direction. Divide queue capacity by arrival rate above the tested dependency ceiling.

Use free queue slots for an incident snapshot. A 7,600-entry queue with only 400 slots free has much less intervention time than an empty 8,000-entry queue. queue fill from empty = 8,000 / (30,000 - 25,000) = 1.6 seconds
remaining at snapshot = (8,000 - 7,600) / 5,000 = 0.08 seconds

The unchanged 18 ms application time and rising proxy queue, attempts, and CPU support the proxy/retry hypothesis, but do not exclude sampling bias or a concurrent dependency fault. Under the fixture rules, retries raise inventory to 30,000 attempts/s and fill an empty queue in 1.6 seconds; from the observed 7,600 occupancy only 80 ms remain at that slope. Automated admission/retry controls must act faster than a human rollback. Both proxy CPU estimates remain below their 3-core budgets, so dependency capacity is the modeled bottleneck.

Pause rollout, disable or reduce retries through a compatible pre-positioned config, shed insufficient-deadline work, and restore v41 while it remains accepted. Do not restart proxies when the control plane is unavailable unless the bootstrap behavior and cached config are proven; a restart may lose the last good state. Reads may receive one budgeted retry for specific transient failures. Writes require idempotency and a single retry owner, and unknown outcomes must reconcile rather than receive new identities.

docs.title: L5-L6 extension
docs.text:
L5: Calculate attempt and proxy capacity, isolate proxy versus application latency, bound retries/queues, and execute a compatible rollback.

L6: Define fleet config epochs, signed last-known-good distribution, control-plane outage behavior, service-owner intent APIs, exception governance, proxy capacity policy, and cross-team rollback authority.

docs.title: Lab 16: mTLS Certificate and Trust Rotation
Outcome
docs.text: Plan a no-flag-day mTLS rotation that separates identity issuance from trust distribution, proves every call direction, preserves rollback, and handles short-lived certificates safely.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: All certificates, names, hashes, and times are synthetic. Do not copy production private keys, trust bundles, or certificate dumps into the exercise. Never disable peer or hostname/workload-identity verification as a workaround.

docs.title: Inline deterministic fixture
docs.text:
Two roots and two identity epochs are involved:

R1 trusted by current fleet
R2 new root
C1 identity certificate issued by R1
C2 identity certificate issued by R2
certificate lifetime                           24 h
renewal begins                                  8 h before expiry
trust-bundle rollout p99                        5 h
identity rollout p99                            3 h
rollback decision and execution reserve         4 h
clock-skew allowance                            5 min

Current snapshots at 12:00 UTC:

Cohort Fleet share Trust bundle Presented identity A 55 percent R1 + R2 C1 B 25 percent R1 only C1 C 15 percent R1 + R2 C2 D 5 percent R2 only C2

Validation rule: one-sided validation succeeds only if the verifier trusts the peer's issuer and its workload identity matches policy. A fresh mTLS handshake requires both caller validation of the server and server validation of the caller. Assume valid dates, key usage, chains, and identity names; request authorization remains a separate check.

docs.title: Portable simulation or reasoning
docs.text:
python3 - <<'PY'
cohorts = {
 'A': ({'R1','R2'}, 'R1'),
 'B': ({'R1'}, 'R1'),
 'C': ({'R1','R2'}, 'R2'),
 'D': ({'R2'}, 'R2'),
}
for caller, (trust, caller_issuer) in cohorts.items():
    for peer, (peer_trust, issuer) in cohorts.items():
        validates_peer = issuer in trust
        peer_validates_caller = caller_issuer in peer_trust
        print(caller + '->' + peer,
              'validates_peer=' + str(validates_peer),
              'mtls=' + ('PASS' if validates_peer and peer_validates_caller else 'FAIL'))
PY

docs.title: Optional enhanced path
docs.text: Generate disposable local roots and leaf certificates with an offline certificate tool, using only names such as client.test and server.test. Validate the four trust combinations on loopback. Protect private files with restrictive permissions and delete them during cleanup. The fixture matrix remains authoritative.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Build both the 4 by 4 one-sided validation matrix and the fresh mTLS matrix.
  2. Identify the unsafe cohorts and the order violation that created them.
  3. Calculate whether an 8-hour renewal lead covers trust rollout p99 plus identity rollout p99 plus rollback reserve.
  4. Design the expand/migrate/contract sequence for R1 to R2.
  5. Define canaries for every call direction and evidence that excludes secrets.
  6. Define emergency rollback if C2 causes failures after 40 percent identity rollout.
  7. State when R1 can be removed and who has authority to approve removal.

docs.title: Expected evidence
docs.text:
• A directional compatibility matrix, not only a list of trusted roots.
  • Explicit sequence: distribute dual trust, prove convergence, issue/select C2, prove adoption, then remove C1/R1 after overlap.
  • Timing math that includes rollback and clock skew.
  • Fingerprint, issuer, identity, bundle version, and handshake-result evidence without private material.
flowchart LR
    T1[Trust R1] --> TD[Trust R1 and R2]
    TD --> G[Prove effective dual trust in every eligible cohort]
    G --> I2[Present C2 issued by R2]
    I2 --> V[Validate all call directions]
    V --> T2[Remove R1 only after old identity and rollback gates]
    I2 -. rollback while C1 valid and R1 trusted .-> TD

docs.title: Calculation checkpoint
docs.text:
For every caller/peer pair, test whether the peer issuer appears in the caller's bundle. Add sequential trust rollout, identity rollout, rollback reserve, and clock allowance before comparing the result with renewal lead. Do not assume parallel rollout before compatibility has been proven.

RFC 9846 sections 4.4.2 and 4.5.1 separate the server certificate from the requested client certificate. The one-sided matrix is useful diagnostic evidence, but not an mTLS success matrix. Also, adding rollout p99 values is a planning estimate, not a proven p99 bound for their sum: correlation and tails matter. Root rollover need not occur on each routine leaf renewal; this exercise intentionally schedules both together.

docs.title: Failure injection
docs.text: At 14:00, a policy bug rejects the workload identity in C2 even when R2 is trusted. Forty percent of workloads now present C2. Define immediate containment, rollback identity selection, evidence to distinguish trust failure from identity-policy failure, and treatment of already-issued C2 certificates.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: The standard simulation creates nothing. If you generated local material, stop test processes, delete leaf private keys, roots, and temporary trust stores, and verify no environment variable still points to them. Ordinary deletion may not securely erase data on copy-on-write filesystems or SSDs; use an approved encrypted ephemeral workspace when secure erasure is required.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Open after completing the lab

Rows for callers A and C are all PASS. Caller B passes A and B but fails C and D. Caller D fails A and B but passes C and D. B lacks R2 too late in the rollout, while D removed R1 too early. Restore dual trust to every cohort before expanding C2.

Those rows describe one-sided issuer validation only. Requiring both directions gives this fresh mTLS matrix:

Caller / server A B C D A PASS PASS PASS FAIL B PASS PASS FAIL FAIL C PASS FAIL PASS PASS D FAIL FAIL PASS PASS

For example, A trusts D's R2 identity, but D rejects A's R1 client identity. Ten of sixteen ordered pairs pass, not twelve. Assuming uniform random pair selection is not the same as weighting by the fleet shares, and neither establishes actual traffic success without a call graph.

required lead = 5 h + 3 h + 4 h + 5 min = 12 h 5 min
shortfall = 12 h 5 min - 8 h = 4 h 5 min

An 8-hour renewal lead cannot cover the fixture's 12 hours plus 5 minutes. Start earlier or shorten measured rollout while preserving the 4-hour rollback reserve. During the injected identity-policy failure, pause C2 selection and switch affected workloads back to still-valid C1; keep R1 and R2 trusted. Compare "unknown issuer" with identity/SAN policy errors and certificate fingerprints. Remove R1 only after no valid C1 remains in use, all directions pass, stale workloads and rollback windows expire, and the identity owner approves the irreversible contract step.

docs.title: L5-L6 extension
docs.text:
L5: Produce the directional matrix, calculate overlap timing, execute trust-before-identity rotation, and preserve rollback without disabling verification.

L6: Define fleet certificate epochs, issuer compromise response, revocation limitations, maximum stale-workload policy, audit ownership, multi-mesh interoperability, exception governance, and authority for irreversible trust contraction.

docs.title: Completion checklist
docs.text:
• I tested trust compatibility in both call directions.
  • I distributed trust before presenting the new issuer.
  • I included rollout, rollback, and clock skew in timing.
  • I separated issuer trust from workload-identity policy.
  • I defined irreversible root-removal gates and authority.

docs.title: Practice rules
docs.text:
• State assumptions before calculating.
  • Trace one request across every network hop and queue.
  • Separate observations, hypotheses, and verified causes.
  • Give every retry, timeout, and queue an owner and a bound.
  • Prefer a reversible containment action over an elegant redesign during an incident.

Start the prompt

docs.title: Hidden-Defect Design Review
docs.text: Practice home | Rubric | Failure lab

docs.title: Review task
docs.text: You are the release reviewer for the proposed checkout edge. Spend 15 minutes finding defects. For each, give severity, a concrete failure sequence, the violated invariant, and the smallest safe correction. Do not redesign unrelated systems.

docs.title: Proposed design
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    M[Mobile] -. lookup .-> D[DNS TTL 300s]
    D -. answer .-> M
    M --> E[TLS edge]
    E --> X[Proxy]
    X --> C[80 checkout instances]
    C --> P[Payment]

The DNS deploy controller replaces the edge address and immediately terminates the old edge after the authoritative record changes. Mobile resolvers should honor the 300-second TTL. TLS ends at the edge; origin traffic is plain HTTP. The edge appends X-Forwarded-Proto: https but preserves a client-supplied value when already present. The proxy uses that header to issue canonical redirects and decide whether secure cookies are required.

The mobile client, edge, proxy, and checkout payment client each use max_attempts=2, including the initial attempt, on reset, 502, 503, or timeout. Each attempt has a three-second timeout. Checkout creates a fresh payment request ID per attempt. The proxy queue is unbounded because average CPU is low. Each checkout instance has 16 workers and four outbound payment connections. Autoscaling uses CPU above 70 percent for five minutes.

During deployment, checkout readiness becomes false and the process sleeps ten seconds before exit. The proxy health interval is 15 seconds. Existing HTTP/2 streams may continue on pooled connections. The longest checkout timeout is three seconds. Dashboards aggregate all edges and checkout instances into regional p99 latency and CPU.

Payment connections allow four H2 streams each. The sketch's DNS arrows denote lookup, not transit of checkout HTTP through a DNS server.

docs.title: Defect worksheet
docs.text: ID Defect Severity Failure sequence Violated invariant Smallest safe correction Block release? D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6 D7 D8

docs.title: Adversarial probes
docs.text:
1. A resolver returns the old edge address four minutes after the record change. What serves it?
  2. A client sends X-Forwarded-Proto: http over HTTPS. Which value reaches checkout?
  3. Payment mean latency rises from 180 ms to 900 ms at 8,000 requests/s. Which resource fills first?
  4. The client times out while inner retries continue. How many payment attempts can one tap create?
  5. CPU remains at 45 percent while all outbound connections are busy. Will autoscaling react?
  6. A pod starts draining just before the next proxy health check. Can it exit before removal propagates?
  7. A long-lived HTTP/2 connection sends a new stream after readiness withdrawal. Is it admitted?
  8. A dashboard reports acceptable p99 for successful requests while 20 percent of clients use an unhealthy old edge. Which failed requests are missing from that denominator?

docs.title: Severity guide
docs.text:
• Critical: plausible duplicate payment, trust-boundary bypass, or unrecoverable operation ambiguity.
  • High: broad deadline failure, lost in-flight work, retry storm, or deployment outage.
  • Medium: bounded cohort outage, misleading telemetry, or inefficient recovery with a safe fallback.
  • Low: maintainability or cost concern without immediate safety impact.

docs.title: Stop line
docs.text:
Write your release decision before opening the reviewer key.

Reviewer key: expected hidden defects
  1. Stale DNS has no overlap window. Recursive resolvers, device caches, and active connections may outlive the authoritative update. Keep the old edge healthy for at least measured cache and connection age, publish before cutover, and verify traffic has drained.
  2. Forwarded scheme is not canonical. Preserving client input lets an untrusted value influence redirects, cookies, callback URLs, and policy. Strip forwarding headers at the trust boundary and write one canonical value; authenticate edge-to-origin traffic.
  3. The checkout and outbound pools are undersized for latency sensitivity. Offered 8,000/s at 900 ms requires 7,200 in flight, versus 1,280 workers and 1,280 payment permits on 320 connections. This is required capacity, not measured occupancy. Bound admission and protect dependency dispatch.
  4. Layered retries multiply attempts and exceed the user deadline. Four named layers with two total attempts each can produce 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 = 16 payment calls. Assign one retry owner, use an absolute deadline, and enforce a global retry budget.
  5. Fresh payment identity makes retry unsafe. A timeout does not prove non-execution. Persist one checkout operation and payment idempotency key across attempts; return the canonical state.
  6. Unbounded queueing hides overload. Work can wait beyond the client deadline while consuming memory and connections. Bound queue age and length; shed before useful completion becomes impossible.
  7. CPU-only autoscaling misses wait saturation. Outbound pool occupancy, queue age, remaining deadline, payment latency, and concurrency should drive protection and scaling.
  8. Drain timing is internally inconsistent. The ten-second sleep is shorter than a 15-second health interval and does not account for propagation or active streams. Withdraw readiness, confirm route removal, stop new streams, wait for active work to reach zero or a bounded deadline, then terminate.
  9. Long-lived connections bypass endpoint withdrawal unless handled. Send drain signals such as connection close or GOAWAY as appropriate and reject new work after the drain barrier.
  10. Regional aggregates hide cohorts. Slice by DNS answer, edge endpoint and generation, connection age, proxy, instance, zone, app version, and retry count.
  11. Plain origin HTTP weakens the trust claim. A protected network may reduce risk but does not authenticate the edge. Prefer mTLS or an equivalent authenticated encrypted origin channel for forwarded identity.
  12. Timeouts are not nested. Independent three-second timers can exceed the four-second mobile deadline. Propagate the absolute deadline and reserve response time.

docs.text:
1. Block because:
  2. Minimum resubmission evidence:
  3. Can defer safely:

docs.title: Annotated Exemplars
docs.text:
Practice home | Rubric | Design review

These fragments calibrate visible evidence. They are not scripts or complete reference designs. Scores follow dimensions A through J in the rubric.

Section headings retain the original target bands for stable links; the revised scores below grade only stated evidence. Missing trust, tests, calculations, or ownership cannot receive credit merely because the target heading names L5/L6. Physical payment connections permit four H2 streams each in this fixture: 320 connections mean 1,280 call permits, not 320 concurrent calls. All demand calculations describe hypothetical required capacity, not observed occupancy.

docs.title: 1. Unsafe fragment
docs.text: CPU is only 55 percent, so I would add more proxy retries and increase every queue. DNS should converge eventually. The edge can pass through X-Forwarded-Proto, and checkout can trust it. Mobile, edge, proxy, and payment client each use max_attempts=2, including the initial attempt, on a 502. If payment times out, the next checkout attempt creates a new payment request. During deployment, wait ten seconds and kill the old instances. Autoscaling should solve the rest.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Notices retries, DNS, and deployment Names relevant areas without defining safe contracts Larger queues despite a fixed deadline Converts overload into expired work Trusts inbound forwarded metadata Permits spoofing and wrong scheme decisions Independent retries Two total attempts at four named layers can create up to 16 payment calls New payment identity after timeout Can duplicate the irreversible effect; critical cap applies Fixed drain sleep Does not prove route withdrawal or active-work completion

Calibration: below L5. The response amplifies the incident and leaves payment safety undefined.

Score: A1 B0 C1 D0 E0 F0 G0 H0 I0 J0 = 2/40, cap 17 does not raise it.

Upgrade evidence: one operation identity, one retry owner, an end-to-end deadline, bounded admission, trusted-header rewriting, and measured drain completion.

docs.title: 2. Weak L5
docs.text: I would add request IDs and traces from the edge through payment. At 8,000 requests/s and about 250 ms, we need roughly 2,000 concurrent requests, so 80 instances need 25 each. The proxy gets a two-second timeout and max_attempts=2, including the initial attempt, on connection failure. I would autoscale checkout at 70 percent CPU, use health checks, and lower the DNS TTL during deployments. Dashboards show p50, p95, and p99 by service.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Uses Little's Law with units Useful estimate, but the assumed time omits the observed slowdown Adds correlation and percentiles Missing queue, endpoint, attempt, and cohort dimensions One proxy retry Does not coordinate with client retries or prove payment safety CPU autoscaling Misses connection-pool and dependency-wait saturation Health checks and lower TTL No TTL overlap, connection drain, or active-request exit condition

Calibration: below L5 on this fragment. It contains no TLS trust mechanism, stable payment identity, security tests, or enforceable end-to-end budget.

Score: A1 B2 C1 D0 E1 F1 G1 H1 I0 J1 = 9/40. The deployment comments name a concern, not a compatibility or ownership plan.

Upgrade evidence: latency sensitivity, outbound-pool sizing, attempt counts, absolute deadlines, trusted forwarding rules, and an ordered drain protocol.

docs.title: 3. Strong L5
docs.text:
I treat 4.0 seconds as one budget and propagate an absolute deadline. I reserve 300 ms for the response, cap proxy queueing at 100 ms, and do not start payment unless its 2.2-second budget plus response reserve remains. One checkout operation ID survives all retries and becomes the payment idempotency key. The mobile client owns one bounded retry only before a payment attempt is acknowledged; edge, proxy, and checkout do not independently retry writes.

Baseline mean service time of 240 ms at 4,000 requests/s requires about 960 in flight. If payment raises mean service time to 900 ms at 8,000 requests/s, demand becomes 7,200. The current 1,280 checkout-worker slots and 320 outbound connections cannot absorb that case. I cap payment concurrency below its tested saturation point, shed before queue age reaches 100 ms, and return a stable processing result for an accepted operation. I split traces by resolver answer, edge endpoint, connection age, proxy, checkout instance, zone, and attempt count. A drain first removes readiness, waits for routing and connection withdrawal, then waits on active requests before termination.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Allocates one deadline and names retry ownership Prevents timeout stacking and amplification Stable operation identity Supports provider deduplication; serialized dispatch and unknown-outcome handling are still needed Calculates 960 and 7,200 in-flight sensitivity cases Explains why moderate CPU does not disprove saturation Compares demand to workers and outbound connections Converts estimates into containment Defines cohort telemetry and ordered drain Supports diagnosis and safe rollout Omits detailed proxy trust and migration Leaves two areas shallow

Calibration: borderline L5 on stated evidence. Trust and security/test mechanisms are absent. "Before acknowledgement" is not a safe-retry boundary: a lost acknowledgement can follow a charge. Restrict client retries to known pre-admission rejection, or use the same key and serialized operation owner with status reconciliation after an ambiguous attempt.

Score: A3 B4 C3 D0 E3 F4 G3 H3 I0 J1 = 24/40.

docs.title: 4. Borderline L6
docs.text:
I would make edge generations explicit. A new edge or checkout generation warms connections, passes synthetic checkout and header-contract tests, then receives 1, 5, 25, and 100 percent cohorts. Old addresses remain routable for at least the maximum observed resolver cache plus connection age. Trusted edge proxies delete inbound forwarding headers and write canonical scheme, host, client chain, request ID, and deadline. Origin mTLS authenticates the edge.

Admission is hierarchical: edge token budgets protect the region, proxies use short pending queues, checkout uses adaptive concurrency around payment latency, and payment reserves capacity for status resolution. Promotion pauses on endpoint-specific error rate, deadline exhaustion, pool wait, retry amplification, or drain-reset thresholds. Rollback stops new cohorts but preserves operation generation and idempotency. Regional failover uses one write home for an operation and never shifts an ambiguous payment attempt.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Versioned rollout and compatibility overlap Handles cached network state during migration Canonical forwarded metadata and mTLS Defines the trust boundary precisely Hierarchical admission and recovery reserve Protects useful work during dependency slowdown Operation ownership across rollback and regions Preserves payment safety Named promotion gates Makes rollout reversible Missing cost quantities and accountable decision owners Leadership execution remains incomplete

Calibration: borderline L5 on this fragment. It supplies no workload calculation for B and no quantified retry budget to justify E4. It is a good migration fragment, not evidence of every omitted competency.

Score: A3 B0 C4 D4 E2 F3 G3 H3 I2 J3 = 27/40.

docs.title: 5. Strong L6
docs.text:
The customer contract is one checkout operation, one bounded deadline, and no duplicate payment effect. I establish a hop contract: DNS publishes versioned endpoints with measured cache overlap; the TLS edge authenticates clients and the origin, overwrites forwarding metadata, and creates a trace ID; the proxy performs bounded admission but never retries payment writes; checkout owns durable operation state and one stable payment key. An atomic claim selects one dispatcher; an unresolved call blocks takeover until reconciliation proves it finished. Every hop receives an absolute deadline and records queue, connect, handshake, service, and dependency time.

Capacity is latency-sensitive. 4,000/s * 0.24 s = 960 baseline in flight. 8,000/s * 0.90 s = 7,200 during slowdown, before retries. With 80 instances, 16 workers each provide 1,280 slots and four payment connections each provide 320 connections with four streams apiece, or 1,280 call permits, so the current system must shed and protect payment rather than queue thousands of requests. A 2x client, 2x edge, 2x proxy, and 2x service retry policy has a theoretical 16x payment amplification; I remove all but the client retry for pre-admission failures and a checkout-owned retry proven safe by the same payment key and remaining budget.

Migration first instruments the existing path, then enforces header and identity contracts, then introduces bounded admission, then moves DNS and edge generations with overlap, and finally replaces fixed drain sleeps with readiness withdrawal plus active-request completion. Each stage uses synthetic probes and cohort gates. The mobile, edge, checkout, payments, and SRE owners have named stop authority. We page on endpoint-specific handshake and 5xx rates, queue age, pool wait, remaining deadline, physical attempts per operation, payment latency, and drain resets. A second region serves reads and cold standby endpoints; operation writes stay home, and failover fences the prior generation at an enforced egress or provider boundary and resolves outstanding calls before dispatch transfers. A database flag alone cannot stop a partitioned caller. We revisit active-active only if the payment API supplies globally enforced idempotency and the business accepts the consistency and cost model.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Defines invariants and every hop contract Complete end-to-end authority model Quantifies normal, sensitivity, and 16x amplification Links arithmetic to controls Chooses safe retries and bounded overload Preserves payment and deadline correctness Gives staged migration with compatibility and gates Credible execution plan Names operational slices and decision owners Supports cross-team operation Gives regional losing conditions and revisit trigger Demonstrates reversible L6 judgment

Calibration: strong L6.

Score: A4 B4 C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 H4 I3 J3 = 38/40. Security negative-test details and quantitative cost evidence remain incomplete, so this is not 40/40.

docs.title: Self-comparison questions
docs.text:
1. Did your calculation include dependency latency and physical retry attempts?
  2. Could you explain every millisecond of the deadline from trace evidence?
  3. Did you define who may create or overwrite forwarded metadata?
  4. Can an endpoint leave service without invalidating cached addresses or live connections?
  5. Does migration preserve request identity and payment ownership through rollback?

Continue to the hidden-defect review.

docs.title: Failure Lab: Checkout Works, Except When It Does Not
docs.text: Practice home | Design review | Migration

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: Diagnose the brownout from supplied evidence. Build a causal graph, distinguish triggers from amplifiers and latent defects, choose safe containment, and define recovery proof. Do not assume one root cause explains every failed cohort.

docs.title: Architecture context
docs.text:
The mobile client resolves DNS, then sends checkout traffic through the TLS edge, proxy, 80-instance checkout pool, and payment dependency. The mobile deadline is 4.0 seconds. Deployments replace edge endpoints and roll checkout instances. The current system permits retries in several layers.

DNS is lookup before HTTP, not a forwarding hop. This is an offline synthetic incident: never inject real charges. Each payment connection permits four H2 streams. Offered attempts at payment-client ingress include queued/rejected attempts and are distinct from provider dispatch/completion counters.

docs.title: Incident timeline
docs.text:
All times are UTC on 2026-09-03.

Time Event 13:55 Promotion traffic begins rising from 4,100 to 7,700 requests/s. 13:58 DNS changes checkout from edge 203.0.113.10 to 203.0.113.44; advertised TTL is 300 s. 14:00 New edge generation e207 reaches 100 percent of authoritative answers. 14:01 Payment mean latency rises from 180 ms to 880 ms; p99 reaches 2.1 s. 14:02 Checkout outbound connection wait p99 exceeds 1.4 s; CPU remains 47 percent. 14:03 Edge and proxy retry rates rise after upstream resets and timeouts. 14:04 Checkout generation c511 begins a rolling replacement of c510. 14:05 Old edge 203.0.113.10 is terminated. About 17 percent of requests still target it. 14:06 Redirect responses and missing secure session cookies increase on edge e207. 14:07 First c510 processes exit ten seconds after readiness withdrawal. Proxy health interval is 15 s. 14:08 Payment-client ingress reports offered attempts 2.7 times logical checkout volume. 14:10 Regional checkout p99 is 3.2 s; endpoint-level p99 ranges from 900 ms to timeout. 14:12 Support reports failed screens followed by completed card charges. 14:15 On-call pauses the rollout but leaves retry settings unchanged. 14:19 Traffic falls to 6,100 requests/s; error rate improves but remains above SLO.

docs.title: Supplied fixture evidence
docs.text: Treat the following as authoritative observations for the exercise. You may request additional derived views from the interviewer.

docs.title: Traffic and resource metrics
docs.text:
Metric Baseline Incident peak Checkout logical operations/s 4,000 7,700 Edge upstream attempts/s 4,080 15,600 Offered payment-client attempts/s 3,920 20,900 Sampled admitted checkout mean service time 240 ms 930 ms Checkout worker slots 1,280 1,280 Checkout active workers 860 1,274 Payment connection limit 320 320 Streams per connection / total call permits 4 / 1,280 4 / 1,280 Payment pool wait p99 18 ms 1,460 ms Proxy pending requests 140 11,800 Proxy queue age p99 12 ms 2,280 ms Checkout CPU 51 percent 47 percent Mobile deadline exceeded 0.3 percent 18.6 percent

The latency histogram covers admitted requests with a completed server response. Mobile deadline-exceeded rates also include requests that never reach a healthy edge. These denominators differ: the regional 3.2-second p99 does not describe all user attempts and cannot erase the 18.6 percent deadline-exceeded rate.

docs.title: DNS and edge cohorts
docs.text:
Offered logical rate times sampled service time estimates required concurrency to serve that load, not observed occupancy during unstable overload. Baseline payment demand 3920 * .180 = 705.6 fits 1,280 permits; it could not fit a mistaken 320 non-multiplexed-call model. At incident latency, actual provider dispatch is capped by permits and need not match the offered client-attempt counter.

docs.title: 1. Build a causal graph
docs.text:
Include all independent defect paths. Label trigger, amplifier, latent defect, symptom, and customer or payment harm.
