docs.title: 2. Perform the calculations
docs.text:
Calculate and interpret:

  1. Baseline in-flight demand at 4,000/s and 240 ms.
  2. Incident in-flight demand at 7,700/s and 930 ms.
  3. Per-instance demand across 80 instances, assuming perfect balance.
  4. Maximum physical payment calls from the configured retry layers.
  5. Explain why resolver cache age does not establish a fixed safe overlap, and define the observed-use gate for retiring the old edge.
  6. The gap between payment request rate and logical checkout operation rate.

docs.title: 3. Rank hypotheses
docs.text: Rank Hypothesis Supporting evidence Disconfirming evidence Next query 1 2 3 4

docs.title: 4. Choose immediate actions
docs.text:
For each action, state the customer and payment safety risk.

  • New checkout admission:
  • Retry policy:
  • Payment concurrency:
  • DNS and old edge:
  • Checkout rollout and drain:
  • Header handling:
  • Customer status response:

docs.title: 5. Define deterministic recovery
docs.text:
Explain how to:

  • identify operations with multiple payment request IDs;
  • query payment by stable merchant reference;
  • return a canonical checkout result;
  • reconcile duplicate provider effects without issuing blind compensations;
  • replay or notify customers safely;
  • prove queues, pools, endpoints, and old generations are drained.

docs.title: 6. Define exit criteria
docs.text: Include endpoint-specific connect success, forwarded-scheme correctness, queue age, pool wait, attempts per operation, duplicate-effect reconciliation, active requests at termination, and SLO recovery over a fixed window.

docs.title: Stop line
docs.text:
Complete the tasks before opening the diagnosis.

Facilitator diagnosis and calculation key

This is a multi-cause brownout.

  1. Name-resolution path: the old edge is terminated about 422 seconds after publication begins, yet at 14:05, 17 percent still targets the dead address. One resolver family's observed cache age p99 is 412 seconds, but cache age is not remaining TTL and cannot establish a fixed safe overlap. Advertised TTL is not proof of client eviction. Keep the old edge serving until endpoint-specific requests and old connections remain below an explicit threshold for a full drain and rollback observation window.
  2. Forwarded-scheme path: edge e207 preserves untrusted inbound metadata and appends https. The origin parser selects the first value, generates an HTTP redirect, and loses the secure cookie on that redirected request. The mobile client retries, adding traffic and user-visible loops.
  3. Dependency and capacity path: offered-load requirements are 960 and 7,161, not measured occupancies. There are 1,280 workers and 1,280 payment permits on 320 physical H2 connections. Serving 7,700 calls/s at 880 ms needs 6,776 payment permits before retries; queues and acquisition failures expose that deficit.
  4. Retry path: four two-attempt layers permit up to 16 calls per operation. 20900/7700=2.71 is offered client-attempt amplification, not provider dispatch. Different UUIDs defeat deduplication; the independent provider sample proves two effects for co_771.
  5. Drain path: a process exits at 14:07:20 while the proxy can regard it healthy until 14:07:23. A long-lived connection starts a stream after readiness withdrawal, and seven requests remain active at exit. The fixed sleep is not a drain protocol.

Immediate containment should disable inner write retries, preserve or derive one stable payment key per checkout operation, cap new admission, apply a payment concurrency limit, and reserve capacity for status resolution. Restore the old edge or route its address until stale traffic and connections reach zero. Pause checkout termination, extend grace, withdraw routes, stop new streams, and wait on active work. Strip all inbound forwarding headers at the trusted edge and set one canonical scheme. If safe identity cannot be guaranteed for new payment writes, reject them rather than guess.

Recovery groups operations by checkout operation and merchant reference, queries the payment authority, records every provider effect, and chooses one canonical checkout outcome. Duplicate financial effects require provider-supported idempotent void or refund under controlled reconciliation; do not issue a blind compensation. Exit only after cohort metrics remain within thresholds and every ambiguous operation is resolved or quarantined with an owner.

docs.title: Prevention tests
docs.text:
• Resolver simulation that ignores or extends advertised TTL within observed behavior.
  • Header-spoofing matrix for absent, single, repeated, and comma-separated forwarding values.
  • Load test at 8,000/s with payment mean latency at 900 ms and constrained connections.
  • Retry-tree assertion that counts physical calls per logical operation.
  • Drain test with old health state, long-lived HTTP/2 connections, and active work.
  • Payment simulator that records operation keys without moving real money.

Continue to the migration exercise.

docs.title: Progressive Hints
docs.text:
Practice home | Prompt | Workbook

Open one hint at a time. The summaries reveal only the direction; opening a hint spends interview signal.

Hint 1: Treat the path as one deadline

List every place a request can wait. Local timeouts that each fit inside four seconds can still add up to more than four seconds. Carry an absolute deadline or a decreasing remaining budget.

Checkpoint: Can a downstream call start when too little time remains to return a useful result?

Hint 2: Calculate concurrency, not only QPS

Use Little's Law. At a fixed arrival rate, a slower dependency increases in-flight work even when CPU stays flat. Compare that demand with worker and outbound-connection limits.

Checkpoint: Which finite resource fills first when payment latency rises?

Hint 3: Count physical attempts

One user action can become several network requests when the client, edge, proxy, and service each retry. Write the maximum attempt tree and assign one retry owner for each failure class.

Checkpoint: Does any inner layer retry a request after an outer layer has already abandoned it?

Hint 4: Separate reachability from freshness

An address can remain cached after traffic management changes. Consider TTLs, resolver behavior, connection reuse, health withdrawal, and overlap between old and new endpoints.

Checkpoint: Can a valid client cache outlive the endpoint's serving window?

Hint 5: Define the proxy trust boundary

Forwarded metadata is safe only when trusted proxies overwrite untrusted inbound values. Identify the authoritative scheme after TLS termination and how redirects, secure cookies, callback URLs, and policy checks consume it.

Checkpoint: Could an attacker or configuration error make checkout believe an HTTPS request arrived over HTTP?

Hint 6: Bound waiting before execution

Large queues hide saturation and consume deadlines. Prefer explicit admission limits, short bounded queues, fair shedding, and capacity reserved for status or recovery work.

Checkpoint: Does accepted work still have enough budget to finish before it begins execution?

Hint 7: Drain is a protocol

Removing an instance requires an ordered sequence across routing, readiness, persistent connections, active requests, and process termination. One fixed sleep rarely proves completion.

Checkpoint: What measurable condition permits termination?

Hint 8: Diagnose with distributions and cohorts

Split data by resolver answer, edge endpoint, connection age, proxy, checkout instance, zone, app version, deployment generation, and payment outcome. Aggregates can hide two populations.

Checkpoint: Which cohort succeeds while another fails?

Hint 9: Protect the dependency during recovery

When payment slows, unbounded retries and connection growth increase its load. Use a concurrency limiter, retry budget, jitter, and degraded response. Preserve stable operation identity across safe retries.

Checkpoint: Can containment reduce offered load without creating a second charge attempt?

Hint 10: L6 evidence

Define rollout generations, compatibility overlap, promotion gates, rollback semantics, control owners, cost sensitivity, and a regional policy. Connect every architecture split to measured evidence.

Checkpoint: Could another team migrate and operate the path without guessing your safety conditions?

After scoring the first pass, continue to the rubric.

docs.title: Branching Interviewer Packet
docs.text:
Practice home | Rubric | Exemplars

This file contains disclosures, fixture keys, probes, and calibration material. Keep it closed until the candidate finishes the blind first pass.

docs.title: Interview objective
docs.text: Assess whether the candidate can reason across network layers without losing the end-to-end customer and payment contracts. Reward quantified concurrency, explicit trust, bounded retries, discriminating telemetry, safe containment, and reversible migration.

docs.title: Mode selection
docs.text: Mode Use when Required evidence Optional branch 15 minutes Screen or warm-up Scope, path, concurrency, deadline, one failure Retry tree 30 minutes Standard L5 loop Safe core, trust contract, pools, telemetry, containment DNS or drain 45 minutes Deep L5 or emerging L6 Full diagnosis, overload, deployment, tests, tradeoffs Multi-cause incident 60 minutes Dedicated L6 exercise Full design, migration, regional posture, ownership Leadership branch

docs.title: Opening script
docs.text:
Design and diagnose a mobile checkout path through DNS, a TLS edge, a proxy, a checkout pool, and payment. Some users see latency, gateway errors, and duplicate-looking attempts during peaks and deployments. Start with scope, invariants, and a request trace. Ask for evidence as you need it.

Do not name the injected defects. Let the candidate choose what to measure before disclosing fixture evidence.

docs.title: Assumptions available on request
docs.text: Candidate asks about Disclosure Signal to observe Payment semantics Payment accepts an idempotency key and supports status lookup by merchant reference. A timeout can follow execution. Preserves one stable operation identity Client behavior Mobile uses max_attempts=2, including the initial attempt, on timeout or selected gateway errors; versions remain active for 90 days. Includes client in attempt and compatibility models DNS Authoritative TTL is 300 seconds; actual resolver behavior must be measured. Separates advertised policy from observed cache state TLS Public TLS ends at the edge. The candidate chooses and defends origin protection. Defines the trust boundary Proxy Persistent HTTP/2 upstream connections are used. Considers new streams during drain Checkout pool 80 instances, 16 workers and 4 payment connections each; 4 H2 streams/connection give 1,280 call permits. Distinguishes physical connections, permits, offered demand and dispatch Traffic Use prompt values; promotion peak is 8,000/s. Calculates sensitivity rather than hand-waving Regions One active region is sufficient initially; discuss recovery in longer modes. Avoids premature active-active writes Existing rollout Edge addresses and checkout instances change during deployment. Defines overlap and drain generations

docs.title: Fixture disclosure ladder
docs.text:
Disclose only after the candidate asks a discriminating question. Give one row or block at a time from failure-lab.md.

Candidate asks for First disclosure Follow-up if they interpret it CPU and saturation CPU 47 percent; payment pool wait p99 1,460 ms Worker occupancy 1,274/1,280 and connection limit 320 Request amplification Edge attempts 15,600/s for 7,700 logical operations/s Payment-client ingress offers 20,900/s including queued/rejected attempts; provider dispatch is separate Endpoint cohorts 17 percent still targets old address at 14:05 Resolver cache p99 is 412 s for one family Redirect or cookie failures Show the two header samples State that origin selects the first forwarded value Deployment resets Show pod timestamps Reveal seven active requests at exit and the 15-second health interval Payment duplicates Show co_771 record Confirm two provider effects under different payment UUIDs Aggregate versus cohort latency Regional p99 3.2 s Endpoint p99 ranges from 900 ms to timeout

docs.title: Minute 5
docs.text:
Look for the customer deadline, one-operation invariant, and the full hop path. If absent, ask:

Which facts and timing guarantees must survive a transport retry?

docs.title: Minute 12
docs.text:
Look for Little's Law and a dependency-latency sensitivity. If absent, ask:

What happens to in-flight work if QPS stays fixed but payment time grows fivefold?

docs.title: Minute 20
docs.text: Look for one retry owner, stable payment identity, and forwarded-header trust. If absent, choose the retry or trust recovery branch.

docs.title: Minute 30
docs.text:
Look for bounded queues, payment concurrency, cohort telemetry, and immediate containment. Ask:

Which action reduces harm in the next five minutes, and what new risk can it create?

docs.title: Minute 45
docs.text:
Look for endpoint overlap, measurable drain, fault tests, and rollback. Ask:

What evidence proves an old endpoint and process generation can be retired?

docs.title: Minute 55
docs.text:
Look for migration generations, regional fencing, owners, and cost tradeoffs. Ask:

A rollback changes routing while payment outcomes remain unresolved. Which generation owns those operations?

docs.title: Branching guide
docs.text: Choose one branch based on the candidate's current model. Do not ask every branch.

docs.title: Branch A: Candidate follows aggregate CPU
docs.text:
1. CPU falls while latency and errors rise. Name three finite resources that can still saturate.
  2. Which wait-time metrics distinguish queue, worker, connection, and dependency pressure?
  3. Calculate in-flight demand at 7,700/s and 930 ms.
  4. Which limiter should react before autoscaling can help?

Strong evidence: calculates 7,161 in flight, identifies 1,280 workers and 320 payment connections, and sheds before queue age consumes the deadline.

Require the candidate to label 7,161 as required concurrency at offered load, not measured occupancy under overload. The 320 H2 connections provide 1,280 permits. Do not infer provider QPS from client acquisition attempts. A stable payment key protects effects; separately probe serialized dispatch and unknown takeover.

docs.title: Branch B: Candidate misses retry amplification
docs.text:
1. Draw one logical operation and every physical attempt.
  2. If four layers each permit two attempts, what is the theoretical maximum?
  3. Which layer should own a payment-write retry?
  4. What identity and remaining-time conditions make it safe?

Strong evidence: derives 16 possible payment calls, disables independent inner retries, uses a stable payment key, and applies a global attempt and deadline budget.

docs.title: Branch C: Candidate diagnoses payment only
docs.text:
1. Why do some clients fail before reaching checkout?
  2. Which cohorts would reveal endpoint and redirect defects?
  3. Can one payment slowdown explain connection refusal and missing secure cookies?
  4. Build a causal graph with independent branches.

Strong evidence: recognizes stale endpoint reachability and forwarded-scheme failure as independent defects amplified by retries.

docs.title: Branch D: Candidate handles DNS shallowly
docs.text:
1. Is an advertised TTL a client-side deletion guarantee?
  2. How do recursive caches, device caches, and persistent connections affect overlap?
  3. When may the old address stop serving?
  4. Which metric proves retirement rather than merely record publication?

Strong evidence: uses observed cache and connection-age distributions, overlapping generations, endpoint-specific traffic, and a zero-use retirement gate.

docs.title: Branch E: Candidate handles forwarding shallowly
docs.text:
1. Who may set X-Forwarded-Proto?
  2. What should the trusted edge do with client-supplied copies?
  3. Which behaviors depend on canonical scheme?
  4. How is the edge authenticated to the origin?

Strong evidence: strips and overwrites metadata, defines parser behavior, names redirects and secure cookies, and protects origin transport with mTLS or equivalent authentication.

docs.title: Branch F: Candidate says readiness solves drain
docs.text:
1. How long can routing state remain positive after readiness changes?
  2. Can a persistent connection open a new stream?
  3. What happens to active requests at process exit?
  4. What exact exit condition replaces a fixed sleep?

Strong evidence: orders readiness withdrawal, route confirmation, connection drain, new-work rejection, active-work completion, and bounded termination.

docs.title: Branch G: Candidate is incident-strong
docs.text:
1. Rank containment actions by reversibility and safety.
  2. How do you reconcile multiple provider effects without blind refunds?
  3. Which exit criteria prove every defect path is closed?
  4. Who may reopen admission?

Strong evidence: reduces amplification first, preserves identity and evidence, uses provider-authoritative reconciliation, defines cohort thresholds, and names decision authority.

docs.title: Branch H: Candidate is migration-strong
docs.text:
1. Which contract should move first and why?
  2. How do old clients coexist with a new deadline and operation-ID contract?
  3. What does rollback mean for accepted operations?
  4. When can an old edge address and forwarding parser be deleted?

Strong evidence: uses processing generations, compatibility adapters, staged gates, immutable operation ownership, and measured no-use windows.

docs.title: Branch I: Candidate proposes active-active regions
docs.text:
1. Two regions retry one ambiguous payment with different keys. What prevents two effects?
  2. Which region owns an accepted operation after failover starts?
  3. How is the prior writer fenced?
  4. Which evidence would justify active-active writes?

Strong evidence: converges on home-region operation ownership, stable keys, fenced promotion, and safe status-read degradation.

docs.title: Evidence capture
docs.text:
Capture exact candidate statements and whether they were independent, prompted, or supplied.

Topic Independent evidence Prompt used Risk or contradiction Invariants and SLO Calculation Trust boundary Retry identity Admission and pools Diagnosis Drain and recovery Tests and security Migration and regions Ownership and tradeoffs

docs.title: Mode-aware scoring
docs.text:
Use the rubric normalization formula. A hint or fixture does not erase evidence, but note how much structure the interviewer supplied. Do not score omitted dimensions outside the selected mode.

Mode Strong completion anchor 15 minutes Correct path, invariant, concurrency estimate, deadline, and one safe failure trace 30 minutes Adds retry and trust contracts, bounded pools, cohort telemetry, and containment 45 minutes Adds multi-cause diagnosis, deployment lifecycle, recovery proof, and fault tests 60 minutes Adds staged migration, rollback ownership, regional fencing, and cost judgment

docs.title: Weak L5
docs.text: Draws the components but relies on CPU, autoscaling, larger queues, or generic retries. Needs interviewer help to discover the controlling resource or payment risk.

docs.title: Borderline L5
docs.text: Finds the main bottleneck and gives a plausible path, but leaves one important trust, retry, deadline, or drain boundary implicit after probing.

docs.title: Strong L5
docs.text: Independently quantifies concurrency, coordinates retries and deadlines, defines trusted forwarding, bounds overload, and uses cohort evidence to contain and recover.

docs.title: Borderline L6
docs.text: Adds migration generations, regional posture, and operational gates, but ownership, cost, or compatibility execution remains incomplete.

docs.title: Strong L6
docs.text: Shapes the cross-team contract, diagnoses interacting failures, protects payment during containment, and leads a measured, reversible migration with explicit decision rights.

docs.title: Calibrated debrief
docs.text:
Deliver four points in under three minutes:

  1. Strength: cite one exact decision and its effect.
  2. Highest-risk gap: give a concrete failure sequence.
  3. Mode evidence: report subtotal/available -> normalized/40 (mode) and any cap.
  4. Next action: name one artifact or experiment that closes the gap.

Example:

You calculated the payment-latency sensitivity and tied it to outbound-pool wait, so your containment protects the dependency rather than scaling on CPU. The main gap is retry identity: the proxy retry can still create a new payment key after an ambiguous timeout. Your score is 23/28 -> 33/40 in 30-minute mode, capped at 17 because that sequence can duplicate payment. To close it, write the create-operation protocol, operation record, retry owner, and timeout trace with one stable provider key; do not derive the key heuristically.

docs.title: Interviewer anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Do not reveal defect names before the candidate asks for evidence.
  • Do not treat one root cause as sufficient for a multi-cause brownout.
  • Do not award credit for CDN, service mesh, or circuit breaker names without contracts and bounds.
  • Do not assume low CPU means spare request capacity.
  • Do not encourage a blind retry or refund during ambiguous payment state.
  • Do not penalize omitted migration or regional detail outside the selected mode.
  • Do not compare normalized scores without retaining the mode label.

After debrief, direct the candidate to the annotated exemplars, failure diagnosis, and migration.

docs.title: Migration: Fragile Checkout Path to a Robust Edge
docs.text: Practice home | Failure lab | Interviewer packet

docs.title: Starting point
docs.text:
The current path has mutable DNS endpoints, inconsistent forwarding rules, independent retries, fixed-size checkout and payment pools, CPU-only scaling, and time-based termination. Mobile clients and resolvers retain network state longer than one deployment.

The service cannot stop for a big-bang replacement. Existing checkout operations must keep their payment identity and processing generation through retries, rollout, rollback, and regional recovery.

docs.title: Target properties
docs.text:
• Versioned edge endpoints with measured compatibility overlap.
  • TLS at the public edge and authenticated encrypted origin transport.
  • Canonical forwarded metadata written only by trusted proxies.
  • One absolute request deadline and one bounded retry policy.
  • Durable checkout operation identity, established before payment, reused as the payment idempotency key.
  • Bounded queues, dependency-aware concurrency, and explicit load shedding.
  • Endpoint lifecycle driven by readiness, route withdrawal, connection drain, and active-work completion.
  • Hop-level traces and cohort metrics.
  • Single-owner payment writes with fenced regional failover.

docs.title: Candidate tasks
docs.text:
1. Order the risks by customer and payment harm.
  2. Define compatibility contracts for mobile clients, resolvers, edge generations, headers, deadlines, and operation IDs.
  3. Produce stages with entry, observation, promotion, and rollback gates.
  4. Preserve in-flight ownership when feature flags or traffic generations change.
  5. Prove the new admission and retry behavior under payment slowdown.
  6. Remove old endpoints and legacy headers only after usage reaches a measured exit condition.

docs.title: Required control plane
docs.text: Every accepted checkout records a stable operation ID and processing generation. Retries follow that record rather than the current traffic flag. Endpoint generations have explicit states: WARMING, SERVING, DRAINING, and RETIRED. A generation may be retired only after address, connection, and active-operation evidence reaches its exit threshold.

docs.title: Migration worksheet
docs.text: Stage Authority and generation Shadow or comparison Promotion gate Rollback behavior 0. Baseline evidence 1. Identity and trace contract 2. Trusted edge contract 3. Deadline and retry control 4. Admission and pool control 5. Versioned endpoint lifecycle 6. Regional recovery 7. Legacy retirement

docs.title: Stop line
docs.text:
Draft the migration before opening the reference plan.

Reference migration and facilitator notes

After completing the exercise, use the branching interviewer guide.

docs.title: Target architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    M[Mobile clients] -. lookup .-> D[Versioned DNS]
    D -. answer .-> M
    M --> E[TLS edge and admission]
    E -->|mTLS, canonical headers, deadline| X[Bounded proxy]
    X --> C[Checkout operation owner]
    C -->|stable key, concurrency limit| P[Payment]
    C --> S[(Operation store)]
    O[Observability] --- E
    O --- X
    O --- C

docs.title: Stage 0: Baseline evidence
docs.text:
Instrument the existing path without changing authority. Record one correlation ID across DNS answer when available, edge endpoint, connection age, proxy, checkout generation, operation ID, physical attempt, and payment key. Measure cache age, handshake failures, forwarded-header variants, queue age, pool wait, retries, resets during drain, and provider effects per operation.

Gate: normal peak and one controlled payment-slowdown window are represented; dashboards expose mixed endpoint and app-version cohorts.

docs.title: Stage 1: Identity and trace contract
docs.text:
At first trusted ingress, create or validate a bounded request ID. Before any payment attempt, execute an idempotent create-operation protocol: use a stable merchant or order identifier when one already exists, otherwise persist a new opaque operation ID and return it to the client before payment can begin. Persist the operation ID, request hash, processing generation, canonical state, and payment idempotency key. A retry of create-operation returns the same record. Old clients that cannot retain the returned ID must use a compatibility adapter backed by a stable order identifier; never derive a payment key heuristically from payload contents, timing, or a deduplication window. If no collision-safe identity exists, reject payment initiation rather than guess.

Rollback: stop assigning new operations to the wrapper. Existing operations retain their generation and key. Never create a fresh payment identity because traffic moved backward.

An atomic operation claim authorizes one dispatcher; a stable provider key alone does not serialize concurrent calls. Unknown outcomes require reconciliation, not concurrent takeover. Create-operation needs a stable client/order key even when the server first assigns an opaque operation ID: returning it before dispatch does not prove the client received the reply.

docs.title: Stage 2: Trusted edge contract
docs.text:
Deploy edge generation E2 in shadow and synthetic modes. Strip inbound forwarding headers, then set canonical scheme, authority, client chain, trace context, and signed or authenticated origin identity. Add mTLS from edge to proxy or an equivalent authenticated encrypted channel. Compare redirect, cookie, callback URL, and policy decisions between generations.

Gate: spoofing tests pass; no unexpected redirect or secure-cookie delta; origin accepts metadata only from authenticated edge identities.

docs.title: Stage 3: Deadline and retry control
docs.text:
Introduce an absolute deadline header on trusted internal hops. Old clients still receive server-side budgets. Disable inner write retries first, then enable one checkout-owned retry only for proven-safe transport conditions, with the same payment key, jitter, remaining budget, and a global attempt token. Return a stable processing response when an accepted payment outcome is unresolved.

Gate: physical calls per operation remain within budget during reset, timeout, and late-response tests; no call begins without response reserve.

docs.title: Stage 4: Admission and pool control
docs.text:
Add short bounded proxy queues, checkout concurrency limits, and payment-specific adaptive concurrency. Scale on admitted concurrency, queue age, pool wait, payment latency, and deadline exhaustion rather than CPU alone. Reserve capacity for status and reconciliation. Test the 4,000/s baseline and 8,000/s sensitivity with 900 ms payment latency.

Gate: queues remain bounded, accepted work meets its deadline target, payment offered load stays within contract, and shedding is fair and observable.

docs.title: Stage 5: Versioned endpoint lifecycle
docs.text:
Publish new endpoints before shifting traffic. Warm TLS, origin connections, caches, and health. Move cohorts through 1, 5, 25, and 100 percent. Keep old endpoints serving for more than the measured resolver cache and connection-age window. To remove checkout instances: mark not ready, confirm route withdrawal, send the protocol-appropriate drain signal, reject new streams, wait for active operations to finish or reach their owned recovery state, then terminate.

Gate: zero requests reach a retired endpoint, active work at exit is zero, drain reset rate is within budget, and rollback has been rehearsed.

docs.title: Stage 6: Regional recovery
docs.text:
Keep each accepted checkout operation in one home region. Replicate operation evidence and serve safe status reads from a secondary region. Promotion requires fencing the prior writer generation and deciding how in-flight payment operations finish. Never replay an ambiguous operation in a new region with a new key.

Gate: a game day proves stale-writer rejection, operation lookup, dependency credential readiness, and RPO/RTO targets without duplicate effects.

A database generation flag does not fence a partitioned worker's external API call. Before transferring dispatch, stop/fence that caller at an enforced egress or provider boundary and resolve outstanding calls. If strict no-concurrent-call proof is unavailable, pause new payment dispatch; global key deduplication can protect effects but is not proof that calls did not overlap.

docs.title: Stage 7: Legacy retirement
docs.text: Inventory mobile versions, resolver cohorts, edge addresses, forwarding variants, retry paths, dashboards, and manual runbooks. Remove one compatibility path at a time after no-use and fault-recovery windows. Archive generation mappings and operation evidence for the required retry and dispute horizon.

docs.title: Promotion scorecard
docs.text: Gate Example threshold Stop authority Payment effects per operation No unexplained value above 1 Payments on-call Physical attempt amplification p99 at or below approved budget Checkout owner Queue age p99 below admission budget Edge SRE Header correctness 100 percent canonical in canary Security owner Endpoint retirement Zero traffic after retirement Network owner Active work at process exit Zero, except recorded recoverable operations Checkout owner SLO regression Within approved canary error budget Incident commander

docs.title: Cost and reversal triggers
docs.text:
• More edge overlap increases address, certificate, and egress cost but protects cached clients.
  • More checkout instances do not fix a hard payment concurrency limit; scale only after dependency budgets are enforced.
  • mTLS adds certificate and handshake operations; revisit termination placement if measured latency or ownership cost exceeds the security benefit, not to bypass authentication.
  • A managed global edge may replace bespoke DNS control when it can expose endpoint cohorts, drain state, and origin trust evidence.
  • Active-active payment writes remain rejected until the provider and checkout authority can enforce global idempotency and fence stale writers.

docs.title: Candidate Prompt: Checkout Edge Brownout
docs.text: Practice home | Workbook | Hints

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A commerce company serves mobile checkout through this path:

flowchart LR
    M[Mobile app] -. lookup .-> D[DNS]
    D -. answer .-> M
    M --> E[TLS edge]
    E --> X[Reverse proxy]
    X --> C[Checkout pool]
    C --> P[Payment dependency]

Customers intermittently see slow checkout, gateway errors, and duplicate-looking attempts during traffic peaks and deployments. Aggregate CPU remains below 55 percent. The incident appears as a brownout: some requests succeed while neighboring requests fail or exceed the user deadline.

Design a reliable request path and explain how you would diagnose and contain the current incident. Treat payment as an external dependency with an idempotent charge API. Do not redesign card networks, order storage, catalog, or fraud systems.

docs.title: Starting scale
docs.text:
• 4,000 checkout requests/s at normal peak.
  • Promotion peak can reach 8,000 requests/s for 20 minutes.
  • Mobile clients allow 4.0 seconds before showing an unsuccessful attempt.
  • End-to-end checkout target: p99 below 2.5 seconds during normal peak.
  • Successful checkout availability target: 99.95 percent per 30 days.
  • A checkout request averages 6 KiB inbound and 4 KiB outbound, excluding TLS overhead.
  • The checkout pool has 80 instances in two zones.
  • Each successful checkout makes one payment call.
  • Mobile versions remain active for 90 days.

You may challenge any value. Label changed assumptions and explain the design consequence.

The legacy payment connection supports four concurrent HTTP/2 streams. Count connections separately from call permits. The UI's four-second timeout means it stopped waiting, not a failed charge. Provider idempotency prevents duplicate effects, not concurrent calls; requirement 4 also needs an operation dispatcher.

docs.title: Required behavior
docs.text:
1. Resolve and reach a healthy edge endpoint.
  2. Preserve the original request scheme and client identity across trusted hops.
  3. Admit work without allowing queues to consume the user deadline.
  4. Call payment at most once concurrently for one checkout operation.
  5. Return a stable result when clients or infrastructure retry.
  6. Drain instances without routing new work to them or terminating active work early.
  7. Expose enough hop-level evidence to distinguish routing, handshake, queueing, application, and dependency delay.
  8. Degrade safely when payment slows or the checkout pool saturates.

docs.title: Questions your design must answer
docs.text:
• What outcome and timing invariants matter to the customer and merchant?
  • How is one logical checkout identified across client, proxy, service, and payment attempts?
  • How do you divide the 4.0-second client deadline across hops and retries?
  • What limits concurrency at the edge, proxy, checkout pool, and payment dependency?
  • How many concurrent checkout requests must the pool support at normal and promotion peak?
  • Which headers are trusted, overwritten, and forwarded?
  • How do DNS records, connection reuse, and endpoint health interact during changes?
  • What is the retry budget, and which layer owns each retry?
  • What happens when payment latency rises while checkout CPU remains moderate?
  • What is the safe sequence for adding and removing checkout instances?
  • Which metrics and traces prove where time was spent?
  • How would you migrate without a big-bang edge replacement?

docs.title: 15-minute mode
docs.text:
By minute 3, state scope, SLOs, and three invariants. By minute 7, draw the request path and trust boundaries. By minute 11, calculate required concurrency. Use the final 4 minutes for one timeout trace and immediate containment.

Expected artifact: one page or board containing assumptions, a hop diagram, one capacity equation, a deadline budget, and one failure sequence.

docs.title: 30-minute mode
docs.text:
Complete the 15-minute artifact, then add:

  • request identity and idempotency behavior;
  • proxy header and TLS contracts;
  • queue, connection-pool, and admission limits;
  • retry ownership and backoff;
  • hop-level SLIs and one fault test.

Use the final 5 minutes to summarize detection, containment, and recovery.

docs.title: 45-minute mode
docs.text:
Complete the 30-minute artifact, then add:

  • overload and degraded-mode policy;
  • endpoint lifecycle and drain protocol;
  • zone and dependency failure behavior;
  • dashboards, alerts, rollback gates, and reconciliation;
  • two design alternatives and revisit triggers.

Use the final 6 minutes for adversarial review.

docs.title: 60-minute mode
docs.text:
Complete the 45-minute artifact, then add:

  • phased migration from the current path;
  • compatibility for old mobile clients and cached network state;
  • regional ownership and failover posture;
  • capacity and cost sensitivity;
  • team ownership and incident decision rights.

Use the final 8 minutes for follow-ups and an executive summary.

docs.title: Deliverable format
docs.text:
Present in this order:

  1. scope, requirements, SLOs, and invariants;
  2. workload and concurrency estimates;
  3. request, header, timeout, retry, and idempotency contracts;
  4. architecture and trust boundaries;
  5. normal and failure traces;
  6. overload, recovery, and deployment behavior;
  7. security, observability, and tests;
  8. tradeoffs, regions, and migration.

docs.title: Candidate stop point
docs.text: Do not read the rubric, exemplars, design review, failure lab, migration, or interviewer packet until your first pass is complete.

docs.title: Evidence Rubric
docs.text:
Practice home | Exemplars | Interviewer packet

Score demonstrated evidence, not product names. Give credit only when the candidate connects a mechanism to a boundary, failure, calculation, or operator action.

docs.title: Scoring model
docs.text:
Each dimension receives 0 to 4 points.

Score Evidence standard 0 Missing, contradictory, or unsafe 1 Names a concern but provides no enforceable mechanism 2 Coherent normal path with material gaps under load or failure 3 Correct mechanism, explicit bound, and important failure behavior 4 Level 3 plus quantified sensitivity, operational proof, or evolution judgment

Critical caps override totals.

docs.title: A. Framing, SLOs, and invariants
docs.text:
• Defines checkout success, client deadline, availability, exclusions, and degraded behavior.
  • Protects one logical checkout and one payment operation across transport retries.
  • Prioritizes bounded latency and payment safety over accepting unlimited work.

docs.title: B. Capacity and workload reasoning
docs.text:
• Calculates in-flight demand from arrival rate and service time with units.
  • Includes normal peak, promotion peak, retry amplification, bandwidth, and a dependency-latency sensitivity.
  • Converts the estimate into pool, connection, queue, and headroom decisions.

docs.title: C. End-to-end architecture and contracts
docs.text:
• Traces mobile, DNS, TLS edge, proxy, checkout, and payment boundaries.
  • Defines request identity, absolute deadline, payment idempotency, response semantics, and authority.
  • Distinguishes endpoint discovery, connection reuse, health, and application readiness.

docs.title: D. TLS, proxy, and trust correctness
docs.text:
• Terminates TLS deliberately and protects trust between edge and origin.
  • Overwrites untrusted forwarded metadata and defines scheme, host, client identity, and trace handling.
  • Connects scheme correctness to redirects, secure cookies, URL generation, and policy.

docs.title: E. Timeouts, retries, and duplicate control
docs.text:
• Allocates one end-to-end deadline and reserves response time.
  • Assigns retry ownership, bounded attempts, backoff, jitter, and a retry budget.
  • Prevents layered amplification and keeps the payment operation identity stable.

docs.title: F. Admission, pools, and backpressure
docs.text:
• Sizes worker and outbound-connection concurrency against latency sensitivity.
  • Uses bounded queues and load shedding before useful deadlines expire.
  • Isolates or reserves capacity for recovery and status work.

docs.title: G. Failure diagnosis and observability
docs.text:
• Separates observations, hypotheses, and causes; asks discriminating questions.
  • Uses hop latency, queue time, connection age, endpoint, instance, zone, client version, and attempt count.
  • Defines actionable alerts, trace correlation, and dashboards that expose mixed cohorts.

docs.title: H. Endpoint lifecycle and resilience
docs.text:
• Coordinates registration, readiness, health withdrawal, connection draining, active-work completion, and termination.
  • Handles zone loss, cached endpoint state, and dependency degradation.
  • Gives detection, containment, recovery, rollback, and measurable exit criteria.

docs.title: I. Security, privacy, and verification
docs.text:
• Covers TLS validation, header spoofing, secrets, least trust, log redaction, and abuse limits.
  • Defines deterministic, load, compatibility, and fault-injection tests.
  • Makes pass conditions observable and avoids real payment effects in destructive tests.

docs.title: J. Tradeoffs, migration, and ownership
docs.text:
• Starts with the simplest robust edge and names rejected alternatives.
  • Gives compatibility overlap, rollout generations, promotion gates, rollback, and decommission criteria.
  • Defines regional posture, cost drivers, team ownership, and revisit triggers.

Maximum: 40 points.

docs.title: Critical caps
docs.text:
Apply the lowest relevant cap after normalization.

Defect Maximum outcome Allows independent retries at multiple layers for payment writes without stable operation identity 17/40; below L5 Treats a timeout as proof that payment did not execute 17/40; below L5 Uses untrusted forwarded headers for security or URL decisions 17/40; below L5 Uses unbounded queues or concurrency as the primary overload response 17/40; below L5 Removes endpoints before health withdrawal and active-request drain 27/40; borderline L5 Diagnoses only from aggregate CPU and end-to-end latency 27/40; borderline L5 At 60 minutes, has no credible migration, rollback, or operational ownership 32/40; strong L5

docs.title: Level calibration
docs.text:
Outcome Normalized total Required pattern Weak L5 18-23 Basic path works, but retry, trust, saturation, or recovery gaps remain Borderline L5 24-27 Coherent diagnosis and design with one important boundary still weak Strong L5 28-32 Quantified, bounded, observable path with credible failure handling Borderline L6 33-35 Strong L5 plus evolution and cross-team judgment with one leadership gap Strong L6 36-40 Shapes risk, proves operations, and leads a reversible migration across owners

A normalized score below 18 is below the target band. Totals never override a critical cap.

docs.title: Mode normalization
docs.text:
Score only the listed dimensions, then calculate normalized = subtotal / available points * 40. Round to the nearest whole point. Apply critical caps afterward.

Use round-half-up, floor(40 * subtotal / available + 0.5), for reproducibility. A required dimension without evidence earns zero, not removal from the denominator. Short-mode numeric bands do not establish unassessed migration or leadership; these are educational bands, not validated hiring predictions.

Mode Scored dimensions Available points Evidence required outside the dimensions 15 minutes A-E 20 One concurrency calculation and one failure trace 30 minutes A-G 28 One actionable containment and one fault test 45 minutes A-I 36 Deployment recovery and a revisit trigger 60 minutes A-J 40 Migration gates, ownership, and regional judgment

Record scores as subtotal/available -> normalized/40 (mode). Normalization compares performance within a mode; it does not imply that omitted dimensions were demonstrated.

Example: 22/28 -> 31/40 (30-minute mode) is strong L5 evidence for that mode, not proof of 60-minute migration depth.

docs.title: Debrief rule
docs.text: Give feedback in this order: one demonstrated strength, one highest-risk failure sequence, the exact evidence needed to close it, and one stretch question.

docs.title: Global Realtime Failover Practice Pack
docs.text: Design and operate a global presence and update platform reached through anycast edges, regional gateways, WebSocket, and WebTransport over HTTP/3. This is a blind-first L5/L6 exercise. Attempt the prompt before opening solution or facilitator material.

docs.title: Recommended order

  6. Find defects in the adversarial design review.
  7. Diagnose and recover from the failure lab.
  8. Plan the regional WebSocket migration.
  9. Run a mock interview with the branching interviewer packet.

docs.text: During an assessment, expose only prompt.md and a blank workbook.md. Stop at every explicit stop line. Keep hints, scoring anchors, fixture interpretation, exemplars, expected defects, recovery guidance, migration reference, and interviewer branches hidden until the stated reveal point.

docs.title: Practice rules
docs.text:
Protocol snapshot (2026-09-19): the IETF WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 document is active Internet-Draft draft-ietf-webtrans-http3-16, not a published RFC. Pin client/server draft and browser compatibility; QUIC is separately specified by RFC 9000. Reconnect guidance follows RFC 6455 section 7.2.3, and anycast operational limits follow RFC 4786.

  • State protocol semantics and failure boundaries before naming products.
  • Distinguish control-plane reachability, transport establishment, session admission, and application health.
  • Treat reconnects, authentication, resumption, and replay as load.
  • Attach every recovery action to a safety check and rollback trigger.

docs.title: Adversarial Design Review
docs.text: Practice home | Rubric | Failure lab

docs.title: Review task
docs.text: Spend 12 minutes finding defects, 8 minutes ranking them, and 5 minutes writing release blockers. For each defect, give a concrete failure sequence and the smallest safe correction. Do not replace the whole design.

docs.title: Proposed design
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Mobile clients] --> A[Anycast VIP]
    A --> E[Edge proxy]
    E --> G[Regional gateways]
    G --> R[(Regional Redis)]
    G --> P[Presence service]
    G --> U[Update stream]
    G --> N[Site NAT]
    N --> D[Identity dependency public endpoint]

Each site advertises the same prefix while its edge proxy responds to a local TCP probe. The proxy forwards WebSocket and WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 sessions to regional gateways. A gateway stores account_id -> socket_id in regional Redis with a 60-second TTL. Heartbeats refresh it. On disconnect, every mobile client reconnects after five seconds to the same anycast hostname.

The fixture's identity dependency uses a public endpoint through the site NAT; private regional service traffic would not inherently traverse NAT.

The client sends its last received timestamp. The new gateway reads updates newer than that timestamp from a replicated stream, sends them, and then consumes live updates. Duplicate timestamps are discarded. WebTransport uses QUIC connection migration, so the proposal assumes mobile address changes do not require reconnect. After three QUIC timeouts the client races WebSocket and WebTransport and keeps the first.

If gateway errors exceed 50%, autoscaling adds gateways. If the site remains unhealthy for two minutes, the on-call manually withdraws BGP. The proposal claims all sessions fit after either site or region loss because each site normally runs below 80%. Gateways open a fresh TLS connection to the regional identity service for every authentication and use eight NAT addresses. During recovery, operations readvertise the full prefix and remove reconnect rate limits so users return quickly.

docs.title: Defect worksheet
docs.text: ID Defect Severity Failure sequence Violated invariant Smallest safe correction Release blocker? D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6 D7 D8 D9 D10

docs.title: Adversarial probes
docs.text:
1. The edge TCP probe succeeds while the gateway dependency fails. Where do new clients go?
  2. Four million clients lose the site at once. What rate does five-second retry create?
  3. What proves that 80% normal utilization is safe under one-site N-1 or full-region N-2 plus handshakes and replay?
  4. Two updates share a timestamp, and replication reorders them. Which one is discarded?
  5. A handset changes address and QUIC path validation fails. What happens before three timeouts?
  6. A network blocks UDP. What does racing both protocols do during a mass reconnect?
  7. How many concurrent identity connections fit through the stated NAT pool?
  8. Regional Redis is lost after old and new gateways both accept the same account. Which connection wins?
  9. BGP converges slowly for one carrier. How does that carrier escape the stale route?
  10. Full readvertisement exposes a latent gateway defect. What limits the second incident?

docs.title: Severity guide
docs.text:
• Critical: widespread black hole, silent update loss, uncontrolled overload, or unsafe session takeover.
  • High: major outage amplification, capacity claim without proof, or recovery likely to relapse.
  • Medium: bounded contradiction or weak isolation with a known repair path.
  • Low: maintainability or efficiency issue without immediate correctness impact.

docs.title: Reviewer key
docs.text:
Reveal expected defect families
  1. Probe does not cover the serving chain. A healthy edge keeps advertising while gateways or dependencies fail. Stop admission quickly and combine local dependency plus outside-in evidence under a damped route controller.
  2. Manual withdrawal is too slow and convergence is unbounded. Add controlled automated withdrawal and a region-specific recovery endpoint or endpoint set for stale-route escape.
  3. Fixed retry synchronizes the fleet. Four million clients at five seconds can create 800,000 attempts/s. Use full jitter, server retry windows, and server-side admission.
  4. The capacity statement is false. One-site N-1 reaches 4.8 million sessions/site against 5.2 million tested, leaving only 7.7% before connection churn, replay, and imbalance. Full-region N-2 reaches 6.0 million/site, exceeding the tested ceiling by 0.8 million/site, so it requires explicit degraded priority admission or additional proven capacity.
  5. Timestamp is not a stable ordered cursor. Equal timestamps and cross-region reorder can lose updates. Use an owner-scoped monotonic sequence and explicit retention-gap response.
  6. QUIC mobility is not guaranteed. Bound path validation and resume over a new connection. Classify UDP failure and pace fallback.
  7. Protocol racing amplifies the storm. Bound happy-eyeballs style racing, cancel the loser, cache temporary network capability, and retry probes with jitter.
  8. Regional socket mapping is not session authority. TTL loss, replication lag, and concurrent connects need a logical session generation, replacement rule, and durable or reconstructable cursor boundary.
  9. Per-auth fresh outbound connections waste NAT mappings. The stated pool has about 440,000 mappings before safety margin. Reuse pools, bound timeouts, isolate destinations, and monitor allocation states.
  10. Autoscaling does not repair dependency or NAT saturation. It can increase connection attempts and outbound mappings. Scale only against the actual constrained resource.
  11. Error percentage hides the denominator and stage. Track route reachability and each handshake stage by site, network, transport, and client version.
  12. Full readvertisement and removing limits can relapse. Canary admission, preserve rate limits, verify all guardrails, and abort on regression.

The 800,000/s figure is a five-second cycle mean. An aligned cohort produces 4 million attempts in the burst itself; admission must be sized by explicit bucket/envelope, not that mean. No client hint can pace an old SDK that ignores it: retain server-side rejection and protect pre-auth handshake resources.

docs.title: Five Scored Exemplars
docs.text:
Practice home | Rubric | Design review

These are calibrated answer fragments, not complete reference designs. Scores use all ten rubric dimensions and therefore do not substitute for scoring visible candidate evidence.

Read all 800,000/s and 32x reconnect figures as five-second cycle averages. Exact synchronization produces 4 million attempts in a burst; a one-second bucket is 160x the normal 25,000/s, before gating. In the L6 fragment, session generation is safe only with atomic installed-generation checks and a fenced authority handoff, as detailed in the migration exercise; a monotonically increasing field alone does not implement exclusion.

docs.title: Exemplar 1: Unsafe component sketch
docs.text: Put global anycast in front of six WebSocket clusters. Anycast detects a failed region and sends all users to the nearest healthy region. WebTransport over HTTP/3 and QUIC keeps sessions alive when phones change networks. If a socket closes, every client retries after five seconds. Kafka provides exactly-once updates. Autoscaling adds gateways during failover, and NAT can be increased if needed.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Names anycast, WebSocket, QUIC, streaming, and autoscaling Components have no authority or failure mechanism Equates anycast with application health Unhealthy advertising site remains a black hole; cap applies Guarantees QUIC mobility Ignores path-validation and UDP failure; cap applies Fixed-delay retry Creates synchronized reconnect load; cap applies Exactly-once transport claim No update identity, cursor, or gap recovery Defers capacity and NAT Does not test one-site N-1 or full-region N-2 feasibility

Raw score: A1 B0 C1 D0 E0 F0 G0 H0 I0 J0 = 2/40; normalized 2/40.

Final calibration: 2/40, below L5. Multiple critical caps apply.

docs.title: Exemplar 2: Developing design
docs.text: Gateways keep session state in Redis and clients reconnect to another region if health checks fail. Updates carry sequence numbers, and the client asks for messages after its last number. We use exponential backoff to ten seconds. Each region runs at 70% utilization so another region can take traffic. WebTransport over HTTP/3 falls back to WebSocket when it fails. Dashboards track connection count, latency, and errors.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Logical resume and sequence direction Scope, token security, retention gap, and concurrent connection behavior are absent Some backoff and transport fallback No jitter, admission, deadline, or fallback-loop control Percentage headroom claim Contradicts supplied per-site limit and ignores handshakes/replay Generic health check Does not connect gateway dependency health to route withdrawal Generic dashboard Cannot localize route, handshake stage, NAT, or cohort

Raw score: A2 B1 C2 D1 E2 F1 G2 H0 I1 J0 = 12/40; normalized 12/40.

Final calibration: 12/40, fragmented. The full-region failover claim triggers a 27/40 cap but does not change the lower arithmetic result.

docs.title: Exemplar 3: Developing with sound mechanisms
docs.text: A session ID is separate from a connection ID. The client reconnects with an expiring signed resume token and last account sequence. A gateway atomically replaces the old connection, replays retained updates, and sends FULL_SYNC_REQUIRED if the cursor is too old. Clients use exponential full jitter and honor Retry-After; gateways limit handshakes and preserve established traffic. Site health combines edge and gateway probes and can withdraw BGP after a drain period. QUIC gets a bounded path-validation attempt, then the client opens WebSocket. We alert on handshake failure and session count.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Good identity and replay boundary Presence semantics and cross-region cursor authority remain vague Jitter plus admission No quantitative retry budget or fairness between auth, replay, and new work Drain/withdraw direction No external probe, convergence behavior, false-positive defense, or canary return Transport fallback No UDP-memory expiry or fallback pacing details Missing supplied arithmetic and NAT Cannot establish feasible failure posture; NAT cap applies

Raw score: A3 B0 C3 D2 E3 F3 G3 H0 I2 J0 = 19/40; normalized 19/40.

Final calibration: 19/40, below L5. No supplied calculation or migration/test evidence supports B/J points; the NAT cap does not raise this raw result.

docs.title: Exemplar 4: Strong L5
docs.text:
At peak, each site holds 4 million sessions. Losing one site would place 4.8 million on each survivor, below the 5.2 million tested connection ceiling but leaving only 400,000 connections, or 7.7%, of margin before handshake and replay work. Losing a full two-site region would require 6.0 million per survivor, 0.8 million above the tested ceiling, so critical established cohorts retain capacity while lower-priority reconnect and replay work is deferred or rejected. Presence generates 800,000 heartbeats/s globally. Four million disconnected clients on a five-second fixed retry would generate 800,000 attempts/s, 32 times normal handshakes, so the client uses exponential full jitter and server retry hints while each site reserves separate budgets for established traffic, handshakes, auth, and replay.

The edge stops new admissions when gateway health fails and a route controller withdraws only after local plus external evidence; clients also rotate to a region-specific recovery endpoint because convergence is not bounded. Logical sessions carry a signed, short-lived resume token and account cursor. Updates use account-scoped sequence numbers; old/duplicate sequences are ignored, gaps are replayed, and an expired cursor requires full sync. WebTransport's QUIC path validation has a deadline; failure creates a new transport connection for the same logical session, first over paced WebTransport and then WebSocket when UDP failure is classified. NAT allocation, handshake stages, resume outcomes, route observations, and update gaps are broken down by site, network, transport, and client version.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
Evidence Assessment Correct supplied calculations and implications Recognizes that one-site margin is thin and full-region capacity requires degradation Route withdrawal plus recovery endpoint Contains stale advertisements without claiming immediate convergence Session/cursor and gap contract Safe bounded replay semantics Transport-aware mobility and fallback Gives deadlines and avoids guaranteed migration claim Layered telemetry Supports diagnosis by site, network, transport, and version Missing migration stages and detailed NAT sizing response Limits L6 breadth

Raw score: A3 B4 C3 D3 E3 F4 G3 H2 I3 J0 = 28/40; normalized 28/40. No migration, compatibility, rollback, decommission, or test evidence is visible for dimension J.

Final calibration: 28/40, meets L5.

docs.title: Exemplar 5: Meets L6
docs.text:
I will separate four authorities: the route controller owns advertisements, the gateway admission plane owns new connection budgets, the session directory owns a lease and monotonically increasing connection generation, and the account update log owns replay sequence. None proves another healthy. Local dependency probes can stop admission immediately; withdrawal requires independent edge-to-gateway and outside-in evidence with dampening. A region-specific signed recovery endpoint limits exposure while BGP converges. Readvertisement starts with a narrow canary and aborts on handshake-stage, NAT, or resume regression.

Capacity policy is explicit. Normal load is 4 million sessions/site; one-site N-1 is 4.8 million, leaving 7.7% connection margin. Full-region N-2 is 6.0 million/site, exceeding the tested ceiling by 0.8 million/site, so it invokes measured priority admission rather than a false all-session guarantee. Even one-site loss is not adequate for an uncontrolled event because four million clients at five seconds produce 800,000 attempts/s versus 25,000/s normally. We reserve capacity for established writes and heartbeats, cap reconnect/auth/replay independently, return randomized retry windows, and admit priority cohorts when the connection or NAT budget is exhausted. Eight NAT addresses provide about 440,000 mappings/site; destination and connection-reuse assumptions determine safety, so we alarm before 70/85/95% allocation and fail closed for optional dependencies while preserving route control and authentication. We test drain time from the admitted reconnect rate rather than promise instant recovery.

The session token binds account, device, expiry, last connection generation, cursor scope, and allowed region; replay never trusts a client cursor beyond server acknowledgement. Account sequences are monotonic at their owner. Duplicates are harmless, out-of-order updates buffer within a bound, and retention loss returns FULL_SYNC_REQUIRED. WebTransport over HTTP/3 uses QUIC path validation under a deadline; on failure, a new WebTransport or WebSocket connection resumes the same logical session. UDP fallback is cached briefly by network fingerprint and probed later with jitter, avoiding permanent downgrade and dual-protocol storms.

Migration adds identities and cursor acknowledgements to regional WebSockets, shadows a global directory and replay log, enables signed resume for stable cohorts, then adds WebTransport over HTTP/3 and anycast independently. Every in-flight session records a protocol generation. Gates cover gap rate, duplicate rate, reconnect p95, NAT high-water mark, cross-region resume success, route-withdraw game days, one-site N-1 soak, and full-region N-2 degraded admission. Rollback stops new cohorts but honors existing generation and cursor authority. Networking owns route automation, realtime owns sessions/replay, mobile owns retry/fallback, identity owns token revocation, and SRE owns capacity gates.

docs.title: Failure Lab: Advertising Black Hole and Reconnect Storm
docs.text: Practice home | Design review | Migration

docs.title: Incident brief
docs.text:
At 14:00 UTC, site SFO-1 loses connectivity from its gateways to the identity and session dependencies. Its edge process and BGP speaker remain healthy, so the anycast prefix is still advertised. Mobile clients repeatedly fail authentication or lose application heartbeats. Many change from Wi-Fi to cellular. QUIC path validation fails on several carrier paths. Clients retry every five seconds.

Your priorities are:

  1. stop routing clients into a serving-path black hole;
  2. protect established sessions and healthy sites;
  3. prevent reconnect, authentication, replay, and NAT collapse;
  4. restore bounded service under insufficient failover headroom;
  5. recover the site without a second storm and repair session evidence.

docs.title: Fixture A: Route evidence
docs.text:
These are offline synthetic observations, not a live fault harness. Use no real route changes, traffic generators, production tokens or customer data. Route collectors measure visibility; outside-in establishment includes auth/session admission, unlike the local TCP-only probe.

Time SFO-1 BGP collectors seeing prefix Outside-in session establishment success Edge TCP probe Gateway dependency success Client app-heartbeat timeout 13:58 96% 99.7% 99.9% 99.8% 0.3% 14:00 96% 62% 99.9% 41% 8% 14:02 95% 11% 99.8% 3% 47% 14:05 94% 8% 99.8% 2% 71%

docs.title: Fixture B: Handshake and path evidence
docs.text:
Time TCP connect p95 TLS success WebSocket upgrade success QUIC handshake success QUIC path-validation failure Auth success 13:58 90 ms 99.8% 99.7% 98.9% 0.6% 99.8% 14:01 94 ms 99.7% 96% 94% 11% 43% 14:03 101 ms 99.5% 81% 68% 38% 9% 14:06 170 ms 97% 52% 41% 55% 6%

Carrier C-17 still routes 82% of attempts to SFO-1. UDP success for C-17 fell to 23%; TCP remains 91% reachable.

Stage percentages use attempts reaching each respective stage, not one shared end-to-end denominator. Do not multiply these unrelated time/cohort samples into a session-availability estimate.

docs.title: Fixture C: Reconnect and capacity evidence
docs.text:
Time Disconnected clients Attempts/s Offered handshake demand/s Resume requests/s Replay reads/s Sessions/surviving site 13:58 80k 25k 25k 9k 45k 4.0M 14:01 1.2M 210k 88k 71k 480k 4.12M 14:03 3.1M 610k 130k 112k 1.1M 4.43M 14:06 4.0M 790k 145k 126k 1.8M 4.76M

The client retry delay is exactly five seconds. Offered handshake demand/s is global demand presented before per-site admission and is not successful admission. After one-site loss, the five surviving sites have aggregate tested handshake capacity of 5 * 18,000 = 90,000/s; offered demand above that value is an explicit capacity breach that must be shed or delayed. Each surviving site has a tested limit of 5.2 million sessions. Gateway CPU is 58%, but auth queues and replay storage are saturated.

Rates are cycle-window observations. Four million exactly synchronized clients produce4 million attempts at once every 5 seconds: 800,000/s is the cycle mean, not peak. A one-second bucket containing the burst averages 4 million/s. Session counts include retained old/half-open server entries and replacement overlap; they are not disjoint healthy users to add to disconnected-client counts. Resume requests may use previously established transports, so these counters are not one same-window handshake conversion funnel. Global demand above 90,000/s exceeds surviving capacity if redirected there; per-site routing and admission evidence is still needed to locate actual overload.

docs.title: Candidate tasks
docs.text: Fixture D is the worst-affected survivor's hot identity-destination pool, not global NAT totals. Its "TIME_WAIT or equivalent" is gateway retained/closing state, not host TCP TIME_WAIT. The 440,000 limit assumes eight usable addresses for that destination and provider quotas already approved.

docs.title: Phase 1: First five minutes
docs.text:
Select and order actions. For each, predict one signal and state one safety check.

  • Add gateway replicas in every site.
  • Stop new admission at SFO-1.
  • Withdraw or de-preference the SFO-1 advertisement through the controlled route mechanism.
  • Publish randomized retry windows and enforce handshake admission.
  • Disable all established sessions globally.
  • Reserve healthy-site capacity for established traffic and critical reconnect cohorts.
  • Reduce fresh outbound identity connections and protect the shared pool.
  • Force every client to race QUIC and WebSocket.
  • Activate a region-specific recovery endpoint for networks pinned to the stale route.
Order Action Expected signal Safety check 1 2 3 4 5

docs.title: Phase 2: Diagnose
docs.text:
Complete the causal chain:

gateway dependency failure
  -> site remains __________________
  -> clients fail at ______________
  -> fixed delay creates ___________
  -> auth connections consume ______
  -> replay and admission __________
  -> healthy-site headroom _________

Answer:

  1. Why do successful TCP and edge probes not clear the site?
  2. Why does 58% gateway CPU not prove spare capacity?
  3. Which evidence distinguishes UDP/path failure from application failure?
  4. What does 790k attempts/s imply relative to normal handshakes?
  5. Why can adding gateways worsen NAT pressure?
  6. Which clients receive degraded admission when failover headroom is insufficient?

docs.title: Phase 3: Calculate
docs.text:
1. Sessions/site before failure.
  2. Even one-site N-1 sessions per surviving site and percentage margin below the tested limit.
  3. Full-region N-2 sessions per surviving site and deficit above the tested limit.
  4. Attempts/s from four million clients retrying every five seconds.
  5. Amplification relative to 25,000 normal global handshakes/s.
  6. Maximum stated NAT mappings/site and remaining mappings at 14:03.
  7. Minimum drain time for four million reconnects if the five surviving sites each admit 12,000 reconnects/s and no new disconnects occur.

docs.title: Phase 4: Recovery plan
docs.text:
Define gates for:

Step Entry evidence Traffic limit Abort trigger Completion proof Dependency repair Internal gateway canary Narrow external canary Route readvertisement Reconnect-budget increase Replay drain Normal admission

docs.title: Phase 5: Evidence repair
docs.text:
Explain how to resolve:

  • sessions accepted by two gateways;
  • presence that became stale during the outage;
  • client cursors beyond or behind server acknowledgement;
  • replay requests outside retention;
  • updates delivered twice or observed with a sequence gap.

docs.title: Facilitator diagnosis and calculation key
docs.text:
Reveal after the stop line

The initiating fault is a serving-chain dependency failure hidden by a shallow route-health check. Continued advertisement traps clients. Fixed five-second retries synchronize four million devices, saturating auth and replay before gateway CPU. Fresh outbound auth connections exhaust NAT mappings and form a positive feedback loop. QUIC path failure on C-17 is a separate transport impairment; uncontrolled protocol racing would amplify load. Surviving sites approach a connection limit that leaves too little churn and replay margin, so recovery requires explicit degraded admission.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
• Normal sessions/site: 24M / 6 = 4.0M.
  • Even one-site N-1 load: 24M / 5 = 4.8M sessions/site.
  • Remaining connection margin: 5.2M - 4.8M = 0.4M, or 0.4 / 5.2 = 7.7% of tested capacity.
  • Full-region N-2 load: 24M / 4 = 6.0M sessions/site, exceeding the tested limit by 6.0M - 5.2M = 0.8M, or 15.4% of tested capacity. Full admission is impossible under the supplied limits, so established critical cohorts take priority while lower-priority reconnect and replay work is deferred or rejected.
  • Fixed-delay cycle-mean attempts: 4M / 5 s = 800,000/s; a synchronized one-second burst bucket sees 4 million/s, not 800,000/s.
  • Cycle-mean offered-attempt ratio to normal handshakes: 32x. This is not a count of successfully admitted TLS handshakes or a per-operation retry factor.
  • At 14:06, offered handshake demand is 145,000/s, which is 1.61 times the five survivors' aggregate tested 90,000/s; it is demand to shed, not admitted success.
  • NAT capacity: 8 * 55,000 = 440,000 mappings/site.
  • Mapping margin at 14:03: 440,000 - 401,000 = 39,000, or 8.9% before a safety reserve.
  • Drain capacity: 5 * 12,000 = 60,000 reconnects/s; ideal lower bound is 4M / 60,000 = 66.7 seconds. Real drain is longer because new disconnects, retries, auth, replay, imbalance, and safety reserves consume capacity.

docs.title: Safe containment order
docs.text: Stop SFO-1 admission, trigger controlled withdrawal/de-preference, and offer the recovery endpoint to networks stuck on stale routes. Simultaneously enforce randomized retry windows and per-stage admission. Preserve established healthy sessions and reserve capacity for critical cohorts. Reuse or shed optional outbound identity work before NAT exhaustion. Do not solve the incident by indiscriminately adding gateways or racing transports.

docs.title: Recovery posture
docs.text: Repair dependencies and prove them through internal traffic first. Add narrow external canaries while the broad route remains withdrawn. Increase advertisement and reconnect budgets in steps. Abort on route-specific connect failure, auth saturation, NAT high-water mark, resume failure, replay lag, update gap, or headroom breach. Restore optional cohorts last. Reconcile session generations and cursors; emit conservative presence changes; request full sync for cursors outside retained proof.

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
• Failed-site admissions reach zero or a declared canary rate.
  • Reconnect attempts become distributed and admitted work remains within budget.
  • NAT allocation and auth latency return below recovery gates.
  • Established healthy traffic retains its objective.
  • No silent cursor gap is accepted.
  • Site traffic returns through staged evidence, not a full-route flip.

Next: Migration exercise

docs.title: Hidden Hint Ladder
docs.text:
Keep this file hidden during the initial attempt. Open one rung at a time, then return to the workbook for at least five minutes.

Rung 1: Separate failure layers

Write independent states for route reachability, edge process health, gateway dependency health, transport establishment, authentication, session admission, and application liveness. Success at an earlier layer does not prove success at a later one.

Rung 2: Name advertisement authority

Anycast chooses a network path; it does not inspect application semantics. Decide which local and external signals can drain admission or withdraw an advertisement, how false positives are limited, and what happens while routing converges.

Rung 3: Split session from connection

A logical session can outlive one TCP or QUIC connection. Give connections unique identities while a resumable session carries authentication context, an expiry, and a delivery cursor. Define when a new connection replaces an old one.

Rung 4: Bound replay semantics

Sequence updates inside a declared scope. Advance a cursor monotonically, tolerate redelivery, detect a gap outside retention, and require a full state sync rather than silently skipping it.

Rung 5: Treat mobility as transport work

WebTransport runs over HTTP/3 and QUIC and may validate a new network path without a fresh logical session, but validation can time out or be blocked. Specify a deadline, then establish a new transport connection and resume the same application session. For UDP failure, use a paced WebSocket fallback rather than racing every transport indefinitely.

Rung 6: Break synchronization

Fixed delay preserves a herd. Consider exponential backoff with full jitter, server retry hints, per-device randomness, attempt caps, and a stable minimum. Admission must protect authentication, session creation, replay, and healthy established traffic separately.

Rung 7: Calculate N-1 before claiming failover

Calculate both one-site loss, 24M / 5 = 4.8M, and full-region loss, 24M / 4 = 6.0M, against the 5.2M tested connection limit. Then add handshake and replay work; connection count alone is not the failover budget. Region loss has a 0.8M-session deficit per survivor, so define a product-aware degraded admission policy instead of pretending every client moves instantly.

Rung 8: Inspect NAT as a finite state table

Outbound regional calls can consume source-port mappings even when CPU is low. Estimate mappings, connection reuse, timeout states, destination tuples, and monitoring. Reduce dependency fan-out and preserve essential control traffic before exhaustion.

Rung 9: Use evidence by stage

Correlate route collectors and external probes with edge accepts, TCP/TLS/QUIC stages, WebSocket upgrades, auth outcomes, reconnect cohorts, NAT allocation, resume results, and delivery gaps. A global success rate can hide one carrier-to-site failure.

Rung 10: Recover gradually

First stop sending clients into a black hole and cap the retry load. Preserve established sessions where safe. Restore a site with canary routes or limited admission, then increase traffic only while handshakes, NAT, replay, update latency, and headroom remain within gates.

docs.title: Final synthesis check
docs.text:
Can the design explain all six without hand-waving?

  • A healthy BGP speaker in front of a failed gateway dependency.
  • A handset changing address while a QUIC session is active.
  • UDP blocked after the client caches WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 preference.
  • Four million clients retrying every five seconds.
  • A NAT table near exhaustion while CPU remains low.
  • Surviving sites retaining 7.7% connection margin after one-site loss but exceeding the tested limit by 0.8M/site after full-region loss.

docs.text:
Practice home | Prompt | Rubric

Keep this file hidden from the candidate. Give only prompt.md and a blank workbook.md.
