docs.text:
Mode Candidate-led design Injected branch Close/feedback 20-minute incident drill 4 min 13 min 3 min 35-minute L5 screen 25 min 7 min 3 min 50-minute standard 32 min 13 min 5 min 70-minute L6 deep dive 38 min 24 min 8 min

Score only dimensions exposed by the mode. Use the normalization and confidence rules in the rubric.

Required dimensions without candidate evidence score zero; do not improve the score by omitting them. Report unassessed interviewer omissions as incomplete. For fixed five-second retries, require both 800,000/s cycle mean and the 4 million aligned burst, not an 800,000/s peak claim. The warm 3-second objective is not a mass-failover guarantee, and offered attempts are not successful handshakes.

docs.title: Opening script
docs.text:
Design the global realtime platform described in the prompt. Start by defining the client-visible contract and your assumptions. You own the discussion. I will answer clarification questions and inject one or more failures.

Do not volunteer solution nouns, fixture implications, or arithmetic.

docs.title: Canonical clarifications
docs.text:
Provide only when asked:

  • Anycast is BGP-based and can converge differently by network.
  • The current route check proves only that the edge accepts TCP.
  • A route controller can drain admission, de-preference, or withdraw a site.
  • Account access tokens are region-valid; resume tokens are a design choice.
  • Update producers redeliver, and regional replication can reorder.
  • Presence may be conservatively unknown during ambiguity.
  • Clients include old versions with fixed five-second retry.
  • Some networks block UDP; QUIC path validation can fail after address change.
  • Eight NAT addresses/site each offer about 55,000 usable mappings under the stated operating assumption.
  • One-site loss spreads 24M sessions across five sites, or 4.8M/site; full two-site region loss spreads them across four sites, or 6.0M/site against a 5.2M tested ceiling.
  • Product accepts priority cohort admission during a capacity emergency if the policy is explicit and measured.

docs.title: Branching map
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Candidate defines contract] -->|Clear| B[Ask for N-1 and N-2 math]
    A -->|Vague| C[Ask what connected and resumed mean]
    C --> B
    B -->|Calculates coupled load| D[Inject unhealthy advertising site]
    B -->|Uses utilization only| E[Reveal tested limits]
    E --> D
    D -->|Separates route and app health| F[Inject stale carrier route]
    D -->|Assumes automatic failover| G[Reveal edge probe remains green]
    G --> F
    F --> H[Inject mobile address change]
    H -->|Bounds QUIC validation| I[Inject UDP blocking]
    H -->|Claims transparent migration| J[Reveal path validation failure]
    J --> I
    I --> K[Inject fixed-delay reconnects]
    K -->|Controls herd| L[Choose NAT, replay, or migration]
    K -->|Adds gateways only| M[Reveal NAT allocation failures]
    M --> L

docs.title: Branch A: Contract and state
docs.text:
Probe: What persists across a transport disconnect, and what exactly does resume guarantee?

  • If session equals socket, move the client between Wi-Fi and cellular.
  • If the client cursor is trusted, submit a cursor beyond server acknowledgement.
  • If replay is unlimited, exceed ten minutes and 2,000 updates.
  • Strong L5 evidence: separate session/connection IDs, signed expiry, scoped cursor, dedupe, explicit full sync.
  • L6 follow-up: concurrent replacement generations, owner authority, revocation, replay/fresh interleaving, repair.

docs.title: Branch B: Capacity and headroom
docs.text:
Probe: Show whether one lost site can fail over safely.

  • If candidate cites average utilization, provide tested connection and handshake limits.
  • If only connections are calculated, add four million reconnects and replay.
  • Strong L5 evidence: 4.8 million sessions/survivor and 7.7% margin for one-site loss; 6.0 million/site and a 0.8 million/site deficit for full-region loss; 800,000 attempts/s fixed-delay rate; 32x normal.
  • L6 follow-up: explicit full-region degraded policy, capacity-removal plan, imbalance, cohort admission, separate budgets, drain-time model, and separate N-1/N-2 game-day thresholds.

docs.title: Branch C: Unhealthy site still advertising
docs.text:
Probe: The edge TCP probe is green, gateway dependency success is 2%, and the site still advertises. What happens now?

  • If withdrawal is immediate from one metric, inject a false dependency alarm.
  • If withdrawal is manual, ask about four million fixed-delay clients during two minutes.
  • If BGP is treated as bounded, reveal carrier C-17 retains the route.
  • Strong L5 evidence: admission drain, serving-chain health, controlled withdrawal, outside-in proof, recovery endpoint.
  • L6 follow-up: dampening, quorum/authority, false-positive policy, route collectors, canary readvertisement.

docs.title: Branch D: Mobility and transport
docs.text:
Probe: A handset has a WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 session and changes address. QUIC path validation fails, and its network blocks UDP.

  • If migration is guaranteed, ask for the timeout path.
  • If both transports race forever, inject a reconnect storm.
  • If fallback is permanent, ask how a transient UDP block recovers.
  • Strong L5 evidence: distinguishes WebTransport application streams from HTTP/3 and QUIC transport state, bounds validation, creates a new connection with logical resume, uses paced WebSocket fallback, and cancels the loser.
  • L6 follow-up: network-scoped capability memory, anti-downgrade/security, battery cost, version rollout.

docs.title: Branch E: Reconnect and NAT
docs.text:
Probe: Four million clients retry exactly every five seconds. Auth creates one fresh outbound TLS connection per attempt through the stated NAT pool.

  • If candidate only adds gateways, reveal 401,000/440,000 mappings and 4,200 allocation failures/s.
  • If client change is the only control, retain an old-client cohort.
  • If all reconnects are admitted, ask what happens to established updates.
  • Strong L5 evidence: server admission, randomized retry windows, client full jitter, pool reuse, per-stage budgets.
  • L6 follow-up: cohort priority, destination-specific NAT states, reserve borrowing, overload API, staged release.

docs.title: Branch F: Update and presence repair
docs.text:
Probe: An old and a new gateway both believe they own the account; cross-region replay arrives out of order.

  • If last write wins, ask whether an old connection may advance the cursor.
  • If timestamps order updates, provide equal timestamps.
  • If presence flips offline immediately, inject a sleeping handset and delayed heartbeat.
  • Strong L5 evidence: session generation, owner-scoped sequence, contiguous acknowledgement, dedupe, gap/full sync, grace.
  • L6 follow-up: authority failover, conservative unknown, conflict reconciliation, customer-visible versioning.

docs.title: Deep-dive selection
docs.text:
Choose the weakest consequential branch. If core areas are sound, select a stretch branch.

Observed gap or strength Next action Weak routing model Route fixture A in failure lab Weak transport model Handshake fixture B Weak overload model Reconnect fixture C Weak dependency model NAT fixture D Strong local design Cross-region cursor ownership Strong operations Staged site recovery Strong architecture Migration authority cutover

docs.title: Incident reveal protocol
docs.text:
Read only this first:

One site has 2% gateway dependency success but remains advertised. Edge TCP probes are green. Clients reconnect every five seconds, and healthy-site auth latency is rising.

Reveal fixture rows only when the candidate asks for the corresponding evidence. Do not interpret them. Evaluate containment order before root-cause completeness.

Stop condition: if the candidate remains at component level after two probes, ask for the first three incident actions and preserve five minutes for summary and feedback.

docs.title: Expected level signals
docs.text: Level Observable behavior Below L5 Infers application health from anycast, assumes transparent QUIC migration, or leaves reconnects uncontrolled L5 borderline Coherent sessions and failover, but omits one consequential capacity or repair boundary Meets L5 Calculates one-site N-1 and full-region N-2, defines degraded admission, separates failure layers, bounds reconnect/replay, handles gaps, and gives operable telemetry Strong L5 Integrates route, transport, session, NAT, and recovery tradeoffs with explicit degraded behavior L6 Shapes authorities, policy, staged migration, organizational ownership, game-day proof, and residual risk

docs.title: Red flags
docs.text:
• “Anycast detects unhealthy applications.”
  • “HTTP/3 alone is the realtime session protocol” or “QUIC always survives network changes.”
  • Fixed or immediate retry without jitter and admission.
  • Autoscaling as the answer to dependency or NAT saturation.
  • Timestamp-only update ordering.
  • Trusting a client cursor beyond server acknowledgement.
  • Full-route readvertisement with rate limits removed.
  • N-1 or N-2 claim based only on average CPU or connection percentage.
  • Metrics aggregated globally without site/network/transport dimensions.

docs.title: Positive signals
docs.text:
• Candidate asks what each probe proves.
  • Calculations change admission or failover policy.
  • Established traffic, new handshakes, auth, resume, and replay have separate budgets.
  • Candidate represents unknown presence and unrecoverable replay gaps honestly.
  • Recovery has canaries and abort gates.
  • Migration keeps one authority and stable protocol generation.

docs.title: Closing probes
docs.text:
1. Which single action stops the largest feedback loop, and what could make it unsafe?
  2. Which capacity limit invalidates full-region all-session failover, and what degraded policy follows?
  3. Which evidence proves a route problem rather than a QUIC problem?
  4. What must remain authoritative through rollback?
  5. What game day would you require before automating withdrawal?

docs.title: Feedback format
docs.text:
1. Strongest evidence: decision, mechanism, and protected requirement.
  2. Highest-risk gap: concrete failure sequence and applicable rubric cap.
  3. Next practice target: one dimension, one calculation, and one branch.

docs.title: Migration Exercise: Regional WebSockets to Global Resumable Sessions
docs.text: Practice home | Failure lab | Interviewer packet

docs.title: Legacy platform
docs.text:
Mobile clients resolve a geography-specific hostname and open a WebSocket to one regional gateway cluster. The gateway owns the socket and stores presence in a regional cache. Update workers publish directly to the region selected in the account profile.

flowchart LR
    C[Mobile client] -. lookup .-> D[Regional DNS]
    D -. answer .-> C
    C --> G[Regional WebSocket gateway]
    G --> P[(Regional presence cache)]
    U[Update producer] --> Q[Regional update queue]
    Q --> G

Known constraints:

  • A reconnect creates a new socket identity and loses the old delivery position.
  • Clients retry every five seconds; old versions cannot be upgraded immediately.
  • Regional caches use different session and presence schemas.
  • Updates have producer IDs but no common account-scoped delivery sequence.
  • Region changes can duplicate, reorder, or miss updates.
  • WebSocket is supported by all current clients; WebTransport over HTTP/3 is not.
  • Some networks block UDP, and mobile addresses change frequently.
  • The edge supports anycast, but route withdrawal is manual and checks only edge health.
  • Gateways make per-request outbound identity calls through finite IPv4 NAT.
  • Peak traffic cannot be stopped for a big-bang cutover.

docs.title: Target capability
docs.text:
Evolve to a global entry plane with controlled anycast, WebSocket and WebTransport over HTTP/3, logical resumable sessions, explicit update cursors, bounded replay, conservative presence, transport-aware fallback, one-site N-1 gates, and a full-region N-2 degraded-admission policy.

The target diagram is not a migration plan. Define authority at every stage, behavior for old clients, stable cohort assignment, in-flight ownership, shadow proof, rollback, and deletion criteria.

docs.title: Candidate tasks
docs.text:
1. Identify the first three risks to reduce and justify their order.
  2. Introduce stable identities and update sequencing without breaking regional clients.
  3. Define a compatibility envelope and protocol-generation field.
  4. Separate DNS/anycast rollout from session-resumption and WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 rollout.
  5. Shadow global session and replay state before making either authoritative.
  6. Migrate presence without inventing false offline/online transitions.
  7. Prove route withdrawal, reconnect control, NAT safety, one-site N-1 capacity, and full-region N-2 degraded admission.
  8. Define cohort promotion, rollback, and old-client containment.
  9. Retire regional authority only after proving no producer, client, or repair path depends on it.

docs.title: Stage 0: Baseline and instrument
docs.text:
Add bounded-cardinality measurements for DNS/route destination, TCP, TLS, WebSocket upgrade, QUIC, auth, session establishment, reconnect interval, NAT allocation, presence age, duplicate update, suspected gap, and regional queue delay. Build outside-in probes by network and site. Rehearse one manual site drain and measure convergence and reconnect amplification.

Gate: normal peaks and one controlled drain have complete stage telemetry; the team can account for update loss uncertainty rather than report only socket availability.

docs.title: Stage 1: Stable update identity
docs.text:
Wrap producer updates in an immutable envelope with event ID, account, producer identity, source version, and payload reference. At an account owner, assign a monotonic delivery sequence. Legacy regions still receive updates through compatibility consumers. They may ignore sequence for presentation, but clients capable of acknowledgement return the highest contiguous sequence.

Gate: duplicate IDs, per-account sequence gaps, replication reorder, and producer omissions are measured; full-sync source can reconstruct current account state.

docs.title: Stage 2: Logical session envelope
docs.text:
Introduce a logical session ID distinct from socket ID. Record protocol generation, client capabilities, account/device, expiry, connection generation, and cursor scope. Regional gateways remain authority but issue a signed resume envelope to capable clients. Old clients retain reconnect-as-new behavior and receive server-side admission pacing.

Rollback: stop issuing new envelopes. Existing signed envelopes remain interpretable until expiry; do not reinterpret them through a different generation.

docs.title: Stage 3: Shadow global directory and replay
docs.text:
Mirror regional connection transitions and cursor acknowledgements to a global directory and bounded replay log. Do not use the shadow to route or replace sessions. Compare current connection generation, cursor, duplicate deliveries, replay availability, and presence age by cohort. Inject delayed and reordered mirrors.

Gate: unexplained ownership conflicts and silent gaps are zero in the approved window; known lag remains inside the resumption objective under regional stream loss.

docs.title: Stage 4: Move resumption authority
docs.text:
For a small capable-client cohort, make the global session generation authoritative. A new connection conditionally advances generation; old connections cannot advance the cursor. Resume replays after the server-acknowledged contiguous cursor, not an arbitrary client claim. If retention is insufficient, return FULL_SYNC_REQUIRED. Regional WebSocket remains the transport.

A full sync must bridge back to live updates without a second gap. Return a snapshot tied to an account-log watermark, retain or buffer subsequent updates, and replay strictly after that watermark before joining the live tail. If the snapshot finishes after its bridge history has expired, restart within a bounded budget or return an explicit unavailable state. A fresh snapshot alone does not prove continuity.

Rollback: stop assigning new cohorts. Existing sessions finish under their recorded generation. Route reads through a compatibility projection; never lower an authoritative generation or cursor.

Shadow parity before cutover is insufficient. For each bounded cohort, fence regional generation grants and cursor/presence mutations, record the final committed watermark, apply that prefix to the new authority, and verify it before enabling global grants. The effect sinks must atomically compare the installed current generation, not merely observe an increasing number later. If catch-up fails after fencing, hold admission or perform a verified reverse handoff; do not reactivate the old writer by flipping routing alone.

docs.title: Stage 5: Global entry and route control
docs.text:
Add the anycast endpoint independently of WebTransport over HTTP/3. Start with one network and small geography cohorts while keeping regional recovery endpoints. Route health includes gateway dependencies and outside-in probes. Local admission drain precedes damped withdrawal. Test stale advertisements, partial convergence, false health alarms, and narrow canary readvertisement.

Pre-distribute the regional recovery set over an authenticated configuration channel with bounded validity. A client trapped behind a failed route cannot rely on fetching its escape endpoint through that same route. Validate the recovery origin/TLS identity and permitted region; never follow an arbitrary unsigned failure hint to a new authentication endpoint. Old clients that cannot use recovery hints still need server-side protection and their supported DNS/endpoint compatibility path.

Gate: route-to-site mapping, establishment SLO, reconnect amplification, NAT, replay, and healthy-site headroom remain within explicit thresholds during one-site N-1 game days; full-region N-2 game days must enforce and verify the declared degraded-admission policy.

docs.title: Stage 6: Add WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 cohorts
docs.text:
Advertise WebTransport over HTTP/3 only to capable cohorts. Its bidirectional streams carry the same versioned application-session framing and cursor contract as WebSocket; HTTP/3 by itself is not the session protocol. Bound QUIC path validation; on failure establish a new WebTransport connection or fall back to WebSocket while resuming the same logical session. Use paced transport fallback, cancel losing attempts, and retain a short-lived network-specific UDP outcome. Compare WebTransport and WebSocket by network, client version, handshake stage, battery cost, resume success, and update latency.

Rollback: stop WebTransport advertisement for new connections. Existing sessions may drain; WebSocket fallback resumes the same logical session and does not fork authority.

Pin the negotiated WebTransport draft/browser behavior; as of 2026-09-19 the IETF HTTP/3 mapping is draft 16, not a published RFC. HTTP/3 support alone does not prove extended-CONNECT/WebTransport interoperability. QUIC migration must still reach retained connection state and use protocol-correct issued CIDs.

docs.title: Stage 7: Move presence authority
docs.text:
Derive presence from logical session leases and connection generations. During shadowing, compare regional and global freshness without emitting customer-visible transitions from both. At cutover, one authority emits versioned presence changes. Use grace periods for sleeping clients and conservative unknown when evidence is ambiguous.

Gate: false offline/online oscillation, stale presence age, and ownership conflicts remain within product-approved bounds across mobility and failover tests.

docs.title: Stage 8: Retire regional paths
docs.text:
Inventory old clients, direct regional DNS users, producers, queue consumers, dashboards, support tools, and repair scripts. Keep regional endpoints as controlled fallback until the minimum supported client horizon passes. Remove direct update fan-out, regional cursor authority, and mutable presence writes in separate releases. Archive protocol-generation interpretation and incident evidence.

Exit: no authoritative regional writer remains, rollback no longer depends on deleted state, restore tests include directory/replay/route control, and decommission approval covers mobile, realtime, networking, identity, SRE, and support owners.

docs.text:
flowchart LR

    B --> C[Logical session compatibility]

docs.title: Migration traps
docs.text:
• Enabling anycast, resumption, new sequencing, and WebTransport over HTTP/3 in one cohort.
  • Dual-writing cursor authority and resolving by last write.
  • Moving an in-flight retry because a feature flag changed.
  • Treating socket count parity as proof of update correctness.
  • Backfilling cursors from timestamps as though order were unambiguous.
  • Disabling rate limits during rollback or recovery.
  • Retiring regional endpoints before old fixed-retry clients age out.

docs.title: Candidate brief
docs.text:
Design a global realtime platform for mobile clients:

mobile client -> WebSocket over TLS or WebTransport over HTTP/3
              -> anycast edge -> regional gateway -> presence/update service

Clients maintain long-lived sessions, publish presence heartbeats, and receive ordered account-scoped updates. They move between Wi-Fi and cellular networks, change IP addresses, sleep, wake, and retry after disconnects. A client may use WebSocket over TCP/TLS or WebTransport over HTTP/3 and QUIC. WebTransport provides the bidirectional application streams; HTTP/3 alone is not treated as a realtime session protocol.

The platform must survive an edge site becoming unhealthy without exceeding tested steady-state connection capacity. A full two-site region loss must preserve established critical traffic and may use an explicit degraded, priority-based admission contract rather than promising every session immediate admission. Include a site that continues advertising its anycast prefix. Explain normal operation, degradation, failover, reconnection, resumption, overload behavior, and incident recovery.

docs.title: Initial scale and objectives
docs.text:
Use these values unless you replace them with explicit assumptions:

Dimension Value Registered devices 300 million Peak concurrent sessions 24 million Regions/sites 6 sites across 3 regions Normal session distribution 4 million/site Presence heartbeat interval 30 seconds while active Peak delivered updates 1.2 million/s globally Normal new handshakes 25,000/s globally Warm reconnect target p95 under 3 seconds Update target p99 under 1 second when connected Replay retention 10 minutes or 2,000 updates/account, whichever comes first Availability objective 99.99% monthly for session establishment and update delivery Per-site tested limit 5.2 million sessions and 18,000 handshakes/s Regional egress NAT 8 public IPv4 addresses/site; about 55,000 usable mappings/address

docs.title: Required semantics
docs.text:
The three-second warm-reconnect objective is for isolated reconnects under normal admitted load. It is not a mass-evacuation guarantee: even five sites at 18,000 handshakes/s need at least 44.4 seconds for 4 million handshakes before other work. Define incident/degraded SLO accounting without silently excluding rejected sessions from the availability denominator. NAT's 55,000/address fixture applies to the hot identity destination tuple, not all possible destination tuples.

  • Define when a session is connected, resumed, replaced, or expired.
  • Define ordering, duplication, and gap behavior for delivered updates.
  • Make presence freshness and offline transitions explicit.
  • Do not assume anycast routing follows application health automatically.
  • Do not assume a WebSocket or QUIC connection survives every address change.
  • Do not claim exactly-once delivery without proving the complete boundary.

docs.title: What to deliver
docs.text:
1. Clarify guarantees, non-goals, trust boundaries, and SLO measurement points.
  2. Estimate steady-state, one-site-loss, and full-region-loss capacity, including the degraded N-2 policy.
  3. Define client, session, connection, presence, cursor, and update identities.
  4. Specify connection, authentication, heartbeat, resume, replay, and replacement interfaces.
  5. Draw the route, transport, gateway, session, presence, update, and storage architecture.
  6. Explain anycast advertisements, health authority, draining, route convergence, and regional ownership.
  7. Handle WebSocket and WebTransport-over-HTTP/3 establishment, address changes, QUIC path validation failure, application-session resumption, and transport fallback.
  8. Prevent a fixed-delay reconnect storm and bound authentication, replay, and session-admission work.
  9. Account for regional egress NAT pressure, thin one-site N-1 headroom, and the full-region N-2 deficit.
  10. Define observability using route, handshake, NAT, reconnect, session, and update evidence.
  11. Give incident containment, recovery, rollback, and verification steps.
  12. Outline migration from regional WebSockets to a global resumable platform.

docs.title: 35-minute L5 screen
docs.text: Time Focus 0-5 min Contract, SLOs, assumptions 5-9 min Capacity, one-site N-1, and regional N-2 estimate 9-19 min Interfaces, session model, baseline architecture 19-28 min Failover, reconnect, resumption, transport behavior 28-33 min Overload, NAT, telemetry 33-35 min Risks and summary

docs.title: 50-minute standard
docs.text: Use the L5 flow, then spend 15 minutes on an unhealthy site that still advertises, a mobile address change, and a reconnect burst.

docs.title: 70-minute L6 deep dive
docs.text: Time Focus 0-10 min Product contract, invariants, error budget, assumptions 10-24 min Estimates, authority, data/session model, architecture 24-39 min Anycast failure and regional/session ownership 39-51 min WebTransport/QUIC migration, fallback, replay, reconnect control 51-62 min N-1/N-2 capacity, NAT, incident recovery, observability 62-70 min Migration, game-day proof, executive summary

docs.title: 20-minute incident drill
docs.text: Start with: one site is unhealthy but still advertising; clients reconnect every five seconds; QUIC path validation fails after address changes. State the first five actions, expected signals, rollback triggers, and residual risk.

docs.title: Finish condition
docs.text:
The design is complete when another engineer can explain: who withdraws a route, what a client does at each failure layer, how a session resumes without silent gaps, which capacity saturates first, and how operators recover without causing a second storm.

docs.title: Mode-Normalized Evidence Rubric
docs.text: Keep this file hidden until the candidate reaches the workbook stop line. Score demonstrated mechanisms, calculations, failure responses, and tradeoffs. Product names alone earn no credit.

docs.title: Base scoring
docs.text:
Each of ten dimensions receives 0-4 points.

Score Evidence standard 0 Missing, contradicted, or unsafe 1 Names the concern without a workable mechanism 2 Coherent happy path with consequential gaps 3 Correct mechanism, tradeoff, primary failure, and metric 4 Quantified, testable, repairable, and explicit about authority and limits

docs.title: A. Contract and invariants
docs.text: Defines connected, presence freshness, ordering scope, duplicate/gap semantics, replacement, resumption, and SLO boundaries. L6 evidence maps invariants to authority, enforcement, and repair.

docs.title: B. Capacity and headroom
docs.text: Calculates sessions/site, heartbeats, handshakes, reconnect amplification, replay work, NAT mappings, one-site N-1 capacity, and full-region N-2 capacity. L6 evidence identifies the 6.0M-versus-5.2M regional-loss deficit, coupled bottlenecks, degraded admission policy, and recovery drain time.

docs.title: C. Identity, state, and interfaces
docs.text: Separates device, logical session, transport connection, presence lease, update identity, and cursor. Defines secure resume, expiry, revocation, replacement, and full-sync behavior. L6 evidence handles concurrent old/new connections and cross-region ownership.

docs.title: D. Routing and site health
docs.text: Separates anycast advertisement from application health. Defines drain/withdraw authority, external probes, dependency health, convergence limits, and stale-route containment. L6 evidence addresses false withdrawal, route oscillation, and canary readvertisement.

docs.title: E. Transport and mobility
docs.text: Distinguishes TCP, TLS, WebSocket, WebTransport/HTTP/3 establishment, QUIC handshake, path validation, and application heartbeat failures. Defines application-session semantics, address-change handling, deadlines, UDP fallback, and half-open cleanup. L6 evidence avoids uncontrolled protocol racing and measures path-specific outcomes.

docs.title: F. Reconnect and overload control
docs.text: Uses exponential backoff with jitter, server hints, admission budgets, and fairness between established, new, resumed, and replay traffic. L6 evidence models synchronized cohorts, retry amplification, load shedding, and gradual release.

docs.title: G. Delivery, replay, and presence correctness
docs.text: Defines scoped sequence/cursor behavior, deduplication, retention gaps, full sync, monotonic cursor advance, and conservative presence expiry. L6 evidence handles cross-region reorder, replay/fresh interleaving, and reconciliation.

docs.title: H. NAT and dependency resilience
docs.text: Treats NAT mappings and outbound pools as finite capacity. Uses connection reuse, timeouts, dependency isolation, destination-aware metrics, and reserved control capacity. L6 evidence includes port-state sensitivity and a no-NAT or scaled-egress evolution path.

docs.title: I. Incident recovery and observability
docs.text: Uses route, edge, handshake-stage, auth, reconnect, resume, NAT, presence, update, and headroom evidence. Orders containment, canary recovery, rollback, and customer communication. L6 evidence ties every action to expected signal and abort gate.

docs.title: J. Migration, testing, and judgment
docs.text: Provides compatible client rollout, stable cohort/generation, shadow comparison, rollback, decommissioning, and route/transport/failover tests. L6 evidence assigns owners, automates proof, rejects unsafe alternatives, and states residual risk.

docs.title: Critical caps
docs.text: Defect Maximum normalized result Assumes anycast automatically stops sending traffic to an unhealthy application 23/40; below L5 Keeps fixed-delay reconnects or admits them without a server-side budget 23/40; below L5 Claims all sessions survive full-region loss despite the 6.0M/site demand exceeding the 5.2M tested limit 27/40; L5 borderline Cannot detect or recover an update gap outside replay retention 27/40; L5 borderline Treats QUIC connection migration as guaranteed across address changes 27/40; L5 borderline Omits NAT despite the stated finite mapping limit 32/40; strong L5 maximum Has no safe route-withdrawal or traffic-drain mechanism 23/40; below L5

docs.title: Mode normalization
docs.text:
Not every timed mode exposes all ten dimensions. Mark each dimension S (scored), N/O (not observed), or C (cap-triggering evidence). Do not score an unobserved area as zero.

N/O is for an area excluded by the selected mode, not a required competency the candidate omitted. Missing required evidence earns zero. If the interviewer did not allow a required area to be assessed, report the assessment incomplete rather than normalizing it away. Select optional scored dimensions before the attempt, and track a cap flag separately from whether a dimension is scored.

  1. Add points for scored dimensions.
  2. Compute normalized = floor(40 * earned / (4 * scored dimensions) + 0.5) (round-half-up).
  3. Apply any critical cap after normalization.
  4. Record confidence: high for 9-10 scored dimensions, medium for 7-8, low for 5-6. Do not make a level decision below five dimensions.
Mode Required scored dimensions Optional dimensions 20-minute incident drill D, E, F, H, I A, B, C, G, J 35-minute L5 A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I J 50-minute standard A-I J 70-minute L6 A-J None

docs.title: Worked normalization example
docs.text: A 35-minute attempt scores 3,3,3,2,3,3,2,3,3 across its nine required dimensions: 25 / 36, normalized to 28/40. If it also claims automatic anycast health failover, the critical cap lowers the final result to 23/40.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Normalized score, out of 40 Interpretation 0-15 Fragmented or unsafe 16-23 Developing; below L5 24-27 L5 borderline 28-33 Meets L5 34-37 Strong L5 / emerging L6 38-40 Meets L6

L6 requires the 70-minute mode, all 10 required dimensions assessed, no critical cap, and evidence across routing authority, overload, recovery and migration. A short mode can show signals, not the full L6 result. These bands are course heuristics, not empirically validated hiring thresholds.

docs.title: Adversarial Design Review
docs.text: Practice home | Rubric | Failure lab

docs.title: Review task
docs.text:
Act as the release approver. Find correctness, availability, security, protocol, observability, and governance defects. For each defect, give evidence, consequence, smallest safe repair, and release severity.

Do not accept a component name or dashboard as a repair. Require a gate that an operator can evaluate.

docs.title: Proposed design
docs.text:
The platform team proposes this seven-step plan:

  1. Configure the new CA as the issuer for all inventory server proxies at 09:00.
  2. Push the new root to client proxies afterward; the control-plane deployment status is the completion signal.
  3. Leave database authorization unchanged because mTLS already allows only trusted services.
  4. Restart every proxy after five seconds so no connection can retain an old certificate.
  5. Let the application SDK keep max_attempts=2, the client proxy keep max_attempts=3, and the inventory client keep max_attempts=2, all including the initial attempt, to mask brief errors.
  6. Watch aggregate 5xx rate and CPU for ten minutes. Roll forward if both remain under their normal alert thresholds.
  7. Delete the old root and signing key when the dashboard is green.
flowchart TD
    NS[Enable new server issuer] --> CT[Push new client trust]
    CT --> R[Restart all proxies]
    R --> M[Watch aggregate 5xx and CPU]
    M --> D[Delete old CA]

docs.title: Defect worksheet
docs.text: ID Defect Evidence in proposal Consequence Repair Severity 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

docs.title: Adversarial probes
docs.text:
1. A disconnected client proxy retains old-only trust. What happens on its next fresh connection?
  2. A healthy 40-minute-old HTTP/2 connection carries canary traffic. What did the canary prove?
  3. A trusted analytics identity calls the inventory write route. Which control denies it?
  4. A five-second deadline expires with 2,000 active streams. What frames and client outcomes follow?
  5. All three retry layers activate. What is the maximum dependency attempt count?
  6. TLS handshakes succeed, PING receives ACK, but DATA does not progress. Which evidence do you inspect?
  7. One zone cannot reach the control plane. Is old-root deletion still allowed?
  8. The old CA is suspected compromised. Which routine safety assumption no longer holds?

docs.title: Severity guide
docs.text: Severity Meaning Release action Blocker Can break trust compatibility, bypass authorization, or make rollback impossible Reject release High Can create broad outage, retry storm, or unobservable mixed state Pause until repaired and tested Medium Weakens diagnosis, capacity margin, or auditability Require owner and dated correction Low Improves clarity or efficiency without changing immediate safety Track after release

docs.title: Reviewer answer key
docs.text:
Open after recording defects and a release decision
  1. Issuer changes before receiver trust expands - Blocker. New-issued server chains fail at old-only clients. Distribute and activate {old,new} trust first, then prove fresh connections from every eligible cohort.
  2. Desired state is treated as active state - High. Deployment success does not prove proxy acknowledgement, activation, or data-plane behavior. Gate on active resource version, trust digest, issuer inventory, and fresh probes.
  3. Identity is equated with authorization - Blocker. Trusting a certificate issuer authenticates an identity; route and database policy must still authorize that identity and action. Add positive and negative policy tests and monitor denials separately.
  4. The plan ignores stale sidecars - Blocker. A disconnected old-only client can fail after server issuance changes and can reconnect after old trust removal. Quarantine, update, replace, or expire explicit exceptions before cleanup.
  5. Existing HTTP/2 connections can hide incompatibility - High. Traffic on an established session performs no fresh TLS handshake. Canary with forced fresh connections while retaining enough steady traffic to observe normal behavior.
  6. Five-second mass restart is not a graceful drain - High. Active streams reset and all peers reconnect together. Send GOAWAY, stop new streams, wait a capacity-derived interval, account for forced closes, and rate-limit reconnects.
  7. Retries are uncoordinated - High. SDK, mesh, and dependency retries multiply load during the failure. Propagate deadlines, choose retry owners, cap total attempts, add jitter, and disable retries under overload.
  8. Aggregate metrics hide cohort failures - High. Split handshake and request results by source zone, proxy/config version, trust digest, presented issuer, and connection age.
  9. 5xx and CPU cannot separate failure classes - Medium. Add TLS alerts, authorization outcomes, resets, GOAWAY, active streams, connection/stream windows, retry tax, and config convergence.
  10. Ten minutes has no relation to traffic cycles or certificate lifetime - Medium. Use stated peak-window, stale-age, and maximum-old-credential criteria.
  11. Old CA deletion is premature and irreversible - Blocker. Stop routine old issuance before retirement, retain protected rollback material while policy permits, then remove old trust only after inventory and fresh-path proof. Disabling issuance, destroying a private key, and removing a public trust anchor are different actions; the migration plan retains key material until its final destruction gate.
  12. Compromise is conflated with routine rotation - High. A compromised old root may require rapid distrust and accepted availability loss. Maintain a separate emergency playbook.
  13. No zone sequencing or failure-budget gate - High. Canary one cohort and one zone, preserve one healthy zone, and stop before consuming the rollout error budget.
  14. No named decision rights - Medium. Define who can promote, pause, rollback, quarantine, revoke, and approve final deletion.

docs.title: Release decision
docs.text:
Reject. Blockers 1, 3, 4, and 11 make the plan unsafe. Approval requires a dual-trust sequence, active-state proof, independent authorization, stale-fleet closure, graceful drain, bounded retries, and reversible cleanup.

Source checks: RFC 9846 certificate authentication, RFC 9113 GOAWAY and flow control, and Envoy xDS sequencing. The deliberately defective diagram is the proposal under review, not a recommended sequence.

docs.title: Five Scored Exemplars
docs.text:
Practice home | Rubric | Migration

Read only after completing a blind attempt. Scores use rubric dimensions A through J and grade only visible evidence.

docs.title: 1. Unsafe: arithmetic cannot rescue the sequence
docs.text: Push new certificates to inventory servers, restart them, and then update clients with the new root. If calls fail, temporarily disable verification and let each layer retry. A trusted service certificate proves the caller is allowed. Restart all connections after deployment so no old certificate remains.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
The plan presents new-issued credentials before clients trust them, equates identity with authorization, permits fail-open verification, and creates synchronized reconnect and retry load. It does not distinguish desired config from active state or a handshake from an HTTP/2 stream.

A B C D E F G H I J Total Cap Outcome 1 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 0 6/40 17, not reached Below target

docs.title: 2. Weak L5: safe overlap, shallow protocol proof
docs.text: Add both roots to receiver roles on both sides, wait for the control plane to report success, rotate server certificates by zone, then rotate clients. Do not remove the old root while an old-issued or disconnected peer can still reconnect; hold if that cannot be proven. Monitor TLS errors and latency. Roll back the issuer if errors rise. Keep authorization policy unchanged. Retry failed reads with backoff.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
The intended trust-before-issuer direction, unchanged authorization policy, and retirement hold are sound. However, acknowledgement is treated as active-state proof, reused connections can hide fresh-handshake failure, drain behavior is absent, and retry ownership is vague. Award 20 only if the missing proof remains a hold, not permission to issue incompatible credentials. If the candidate continues before eligible peers have active compatible trust, cap at 17.

A B C D E F G H I J Total Outcome 3 3 2 3 1 2 2 2 2 0 20/40 Weak L5

Dimension I remains at 2 because the answer has a rollout and issuer rollback direction but no enforceable stale-workload quarantine, exception expiry, or old-CA removal proof. In both first examples J is zero: no cross-team leadership or tradeoff evidence was stated.

docs.title: 3. Strong L5: defensible execution plan
docs.text: Inventory active trust digests and issuers first. Expand receivers to {old,new} and prove compatible active trust for every eligible peer before changing any issuer; quarantine incompatible paths including reconnects. Also require 99.99% fresh, non-resumed probe success by zone as an operational signal, not a waiver of known incompatibility. Rotate server and client credentials in bounded cohorts. A valid identity still passes the existing route and database authorization checks. For each cohort, send GOAWAY, stop new streams, allow up to 60 seconds for active streams, and shape reconnects. Keep old signing and dual trust until no old-issued certificate or stale proxy can serve. One mesh retry owner gets at most two total attempts inside the propagated deadline; applications do not retry mesh failures independently. Split TLS, authz, reset, flow-control, and retry metrics by issuer pair and config version.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
This answer separates identity from authorization, validates fresh handshakes, gives a graceful connection transition, and controls retries. It is operationally credible but leaves diagnosis and rollback detail incomplete. J is zero because no leadership evidence is stated; keeping rollback material without specifying its restoration is only partial I evidence.

A B C D E F G H I J Total Outcome 3 3 3 4 3 3 3 3 2 0 27/40 Borderline L5 on stated evidence

The section title describes the intended target, not a waiver of visible-evidence scoring. To reach strong L5, state the compatible credential restoration, fresh-path rollback gate, and component ownership; do not infer them from tool names or retained signing material.

docs.title: 4. Borderline L6: strong operations, incomplete governance
docs.text: Use a dual-trust state machine with signed rollout manifests. Compare desired version, proxy acknowledgement, active trust digest, active issuer, and fresh-probe result. Promote one zone only after error, latency, forced-close, retry-tax, and stale-fleet gates hold for two peak windows. Existing HTTP/2 sessions are not proof, so canaries force reconnects. Drains use GOAWAY and a capacity-derived deadline. At the prompt limits, naive independent retries permit 2 * 3 * 2 * 2 = 24 database attempts per original request: two SDK attempts, three mesh attempts, two database operations, and two attempts per operation. Central policy allows two inventory attempts and one attempt for each of two database operations, for at most four database attempts, subject to a 10% retry budget. Quarantine stale workloads from new traffic and retain old trust while exceptions remain. Rollback changes issuance first and preserves dual trust.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
The answer quantifies amplification, joins control-plane and data-plane evidence, and handles HTTP/2 correctly. It does not name who owns stale exceptions, who may pause the rollout, how old-CA removal is audited, or how emergency compromise changes the sequence.

A B C D E F G H I J Total Outcome 4 4 4 4 4 3 4 3 2 0 32/40 Strong L5 in 50-minute mode; L6 target not reached

In 70-minute mode, cap 32 also applies because detailed cross-team ownership and completion governance are absent. J is zero rather than assumed leadership; the raw score is already 32. Always record the mode. The section's borderline-L6 target requires additional visible evidence.

docs.title: 5. Strong L6: quantified and governable
docs.text:
Security owns CA state and revocation; platform owns bundle and issuer distribution; service and database teams own fresh-path canaries and capacity; incident command owns pause and rollback. Stage 0 inventories active issuer, trust digest, config age, and authorization policy. Stage 1 distributes {old,new} trust and proves active adoption with fresh TLS connections, including one-zone-unavailable and stale-sidecar cohorts. Stage 2 rotates servers in 1%, zone, then fleet cohorts; stage 3 rotates clients; stage 4 holds dual trust beyond the maximum certificate lifetime or proves every old credential revoked and unreachable; stage 5 removes old trust. Each gate uses two peak windows with less than 0.01% rotation-attributed handshake failure, no authorization-policy drift, forced closes below 0.1%, and retry tax below 10%.

For 10,000 live connections drained over 600 seconds, the mean reconnect rate is 10,000 / 600 = 16.7/s. At 150 ms per handshake, expected concurrent handshakes are about 16.7 * 0.15 = 2.5; I capacity-test at 5x for burst and zone skew. We preserve GOAWAY and frame telemetry because a zero-window DATA stall is not a certificate error. The retry policy allows at most two end-to-end inventory attempts and propagates the remaining deadline; overload disables retries before admitting more primary traffic. A stale proxy is removed from service and gets a time-bound owner exception, never broader authorization. Rollback stops new issuance, restores old-issued credentials where safe, keeps dual trust, and reopens traffic by verified cohort. Old-root deletion needs signed inventories, zero old-issued fresh handshakes, expired exceptions, a rollback drill, and joint security/platform approval. A compromised old CA uses a separate emergency plan that accepts controlled availability loss rather than trusting a known-bad root.

docs.title: Annotation
docs.text:
The answer provides invariants, ordered set transitions, fresh-path proof, calculations, overload policy, separate authn/authz controls, rollback, completion evidence, and decision rights. The one shallow area is detailed analysis of database-proxy-specific policy behavior.

A B C D E F G H I J Total Outcome 4 3 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 39/40 Strong L6

docs.title: Mode-normalized examples
docs.text:
Attempt Mode Raw evidence Calculation Reported result Safe short answer scores 16 across A-E 20 min 16/20 floor(16 / 20 * 40 + 0.5) 32/40, strong L5 numeric band for this mode; omitted competencies unassessed Same answer submitted in 50-minute mode 50 min 16/40 No omitted dimensions 16/40, below target Strong plan scores 27 across A-H 35 min 27/32 floor(27 / 32 * 40 + 0.5) 34/40, borderline L6 numeric band only; L6 leadership not assessed

Normalization never bypasses a safety cap.

All five A-J row totals are raw 40-point examples before mode-specific caps. For the strong L6 example, 150 ms is an assumed mean handshake duration; 5x testing is a stress hypothesis, not a quantified failure guarantee. Fresh probes must exercise certificate authentication rather than only resumed PSKs; old session/ticket lifetimes also enter retirement proof. These details follow RFC 9846 sections 2.2 and 4.7.1 and the migration gates, not a promise that certificate expiry terminates existing sessions.

docs.title: Self-comparison
docs.text:
1. Did your sequence maintain trust compatibility for every fresh connection?
  2. Did you prove active data-plane state rather than desired control-plane state?
  3. Did your test create fresh HTTP/2 connections?
  4. Did you separate identity authentication from request authorization?
  5. Did you calculate attempts and reconnect load?
  6. Did you define a reversible overlap and auditable old-CA removal gate?

docs.title: Failure Lab: The Rotation That Failed Twice
docs.text: Practice home | Workbook | Migration

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: Diagnose a partial outage during CA rotation. Build a causal graph from fixtures, separate concurrent failure modes, choose immediate actions, and define safe recovery. Do not assume every timeout has one cause.

docs.title: Architecture context
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    API[API app] --> CP[Client proxy]
    CP -->|mTLS HTTP/2| SP[Server proxy]
    SP --> INV[Inventory app]
    INV -->|mTLS HTTP/2| DP[DB proxy]
    DP --> DB[(DB)]
    CTRL[Control plane] -. trust, issuer, config, policy .-> CP
    CTRL -. trust, issuer, config, policy .-> SP
    CTRL -. trust, issuer, config, policy .-> DP

All timestamps are UTC on 2026-09-06. These are offline synthetic transcripts, not captured production traffic or an executable mesh. Do not inject these faults into a shared cluster. Configuration and certificate metadata exclude private keys and credentials.

docs.title: Incident timeline
docs.text: Time Event 09:00 Control plane begins trust bundle version 41 rollout 09:06 Rollout reports 89% client proxies acknowledged version 41 09:08 Inventory server issuer switches from ca-old to ca-new 09:09 Fresh TLS handshake failures appear in zone z2; aggregate success remains high 09:11 Operator requests a five-second connection drain fleet-wide; some disconnected proxies miss the command 09:12 Resets, reconnects, and retries spike across all zones 09:14 Database latency rises although database CPU remains at 42% 09:17 Inventory p99 reaches 4.8 seconds; 18% of requests fail 09:20 Rotation is paused; no configuration is rolled back 09:23 Old HTTP/2 cohorts on proxies that missed the drain still show successful inventory calls

docs.title: Fixture A: trust inventory
docs.text:
Snapshot at 09:08:30:

Proxy cohort Count Active trust roots Last control-plane contact API client z1-v41 790 ca-old,ca-new under 30 s API client z2-v40 264 ca-old 2 h to 19 h API client z3-v41 1,346 ca-old,ca-new under 30 s Inventory server 240 ca-old,ca-new under 30 s Database proxy 180 ca-old,ca-new under 45 s

docs.title: Fixture B: issuer inventory
docs.text: Time Endpoint cohort Presented leaf issuer Leaf expiry 09:07 Inventory server ca-old 2026-09-07 09:07 09:08 Inventory server ca-new 2026-09-07 09:08 09:08 API client mixed: 93% ca-old, 7% ca-new within 24 h 09:08 Database proxy ca-old within 24 h

docs.text:
proxy=api-z2-117 desired=41 acked=40 active=40 trust_sha=7f-old issuer=ca-old stale_for=11h
proxy=api-z1-044 desired=41 acked=41 active=41 trust_sha=91-dual issuer=ca-old stale_for=0s
