proxy=db-z2-019 desired=63 acked=63 active=63 trust_sha=91-dual issuer=ca-old stale_for=3s

The rollout dashboard counts a proxy as complete when the distributor accepts the desired version. It does not query the proxy's active version.

docs.title: Fixture D: fresh TLS and authorization records
docs.text:
09:09:03 conn=f912 src=api-z2-117 dst=inv-z2-008 tls=fail alert=unknown_ca peer_issuer=ca-new
09:09:04 conn=f913 src=api-z1-044 dst=inv-z2-008 tls=ok peer_issuer=ca-new peer_id=inventory
09:09:04 conn=f913 request=r101 authz=deny principal=spiffe://prod/analytics action=inventory.write status=403
09:09:05 conn=f914 src=api-z1-044 dst=inv-z2-008 tls=ok peer_issuer=ca-new peer_id=inventory

The 403 record proves successful authentication for that connection and a separate authorization denial. It is not a CA-rotation failure.

docs.title: Fixture E: HTTP/2 frame trace
docs.text:
Connection db-c771 was established at 08:51 with valid ca-old credentials and remains cryptographically valid.

09:13:40.010 stream=301 HEADERS end_stream=0
09:13:40.011 stream=301 DATA_total bytes=65535 frames=4 conn_send_window=0
09:13:40.050 type=PING ack=0
09:13:40.052 type=PING ack=1
09:13:41.000 stream=303 HEADERS end_stream=0
09:13:44.900 stream=301 DATA blocked_ms=4889 conn_send_window=0
09:13:44.901 stream=303 DATA blocked_ms=3901 conn_send_window=0
09:13:45.000 type=WINDOW_UPDATE observed=none duration_ms=4990

The trace aggregates four DATA frames, each at most the default 16,384-byte frame payload; it is not one oversized frame. It shows connection liveness but no DATA progress after the connection-level send window reaches zero. PING and HEADERS are not DATA flow-controlled. The missing update alone does not establish whether the receiver stopped consuming, a proxy bug withheld updates, or the trace vantage point missed them.

docs.title: Fixture F: GOAWAY and drain records
docs.text:
09:11:00.000 conn=inv-c441 active_streams=187 action=GOAWAY last_stream_id=781 drain_deadline_ms=5000
09:11:05.001 conn=inv-c441 active_streams=63 action=force_close
09:11:05.002 conn=inv-c441 rst_streams=63 reason=connection_termination
09:11:05.020 cohort=all reconnect_rate_s=1840 handshake_p99_ms=920

Before the drain, the fleet had 18,000 established API-to-inventory connections. A planned reconnect capacity test sustained 300 handshakes/s with p99 below 250 ms.

docs.title: Fixture G: layered retry trace
docs.text:
root_request=u77 sdk_attempts=2
sdk=1 mesh_attempts=3 db_operations_per_inventory_attempt=2 db_attempts_per_operation=2
sdk=2 mesh_attempts=3 db_operations_per_inventory_attempt=2 db_attempts_per_operation=2
root_request=u77 inventory_attempts=6 database_attempts=24 final=deadline_exceeded

At 12,000 original requests/s, primary inventory traffic normally causes 24,000 database operations/s before retries.

docs.title: Fixture H: aggregate signals
docs.text:
Window Fresh TLS failure (% of fleet fresh attempts) Reused-connection success Authorization deny Forced stream reset Retry tax DB CPU 09:00-09:08 0.00% 99.97% 0.04% 0.00% 3% 41% 09:09-09:11 10.8%, attributed to z2-v40 99.94% 0.05% 0.00% 21% 41% 09:12-09:17 7.1%, attributed to z2-v40 81.6% 0.05% 6.4% 286% 42%

These are fleet-attempt denominators, not success fractions within the old-only cohort: fresh calls from that cohort to new-only-issued servers fail trust validation. For this pack, retry tax = retry inventory attempts / primary inventory attempts, including failed primaries, within the same window. It is not the fraction of all attempts that failed or an SLO error fraction.

docs.title: 1. Build a causal graph
docs.text:
Connect only claims supported by fixtures. Include at least two independent causes.

flowchart TD
    A[Observed symptom] --> B[Candidate cause]
    B --> C[Evidence]
    B --> D[Safe action]

docs.title: 2. Rank hypotheses
docs.text: Rank Hypothesis Supporting fixtures Disconfirming fixtures Next query 1 2 3

docs.title: 3. Calculate impact
docs.text:
1. Maximum inventory attempts per original request.
  2. Maximum database operation attempts per original request.
  3. Maximum attempted inventory calls/s and database operations/s at 12,000 requests/s.
  4. Mean reconnect rate required to drain 18,000 connections in 5 seconds and in 10 minutes.
  5. For a hypothetical constant 18% failure lasting 14 minutes, calculate equivalent full-outage minutes and compare with a 99.95% 30-day error budget. The timeline does not supply enough interval data to claim this as the incident's actual budget consumption.

docs.title: 4. Choose immediate actions
docs.text: Order actions for the first 15 minutes. State what to pause, what to restore, what not to disable, how to shed load, and which traffic to quarantine.

docs.title: 5. Define recovery and exit criteria
docs.text: Specify the evidence required to resume issuance, complete draining, clear stale cohorts, fix frame progress, re-enable bounded retries, and close the incident.

docs.title: Facilitator diagnosis
docs.text:
Open after committing to hypotheses, calculations, and recovery actions

There are four interacting faults and one correctly functioning control:

  1. Trust/issuer incompatibility. New-issued inventory server credentials appeared while 264 z2 clients still trusted only ca-old. Fresh handshakes from that cohort failed with unknown_ca.
  2. Long-lived connection masking. Old HTTP/2 connections remained successful because they did not perform new handshakes. Aggregate success hid the fresh-path failure.
  3. Unsafe drain. A five-second fleet-wide deadline forced 63 streams closed on one sampled connection and drove 1,840 reconnects/s against tested capacity of 300/s.
  4. Retry amplification and a separate flow-control stall. Layered retries amplified one request into 6 inventory and 24 database attempts. Connection db-c771 was alive and authenticated, but its connection window reached zero without WINDOW_UPDATE, so certificate rollback alone could not restore DATA progress.
  5. Authorization worked. The analytics principal authenticated and then received 403. Do not weaken policy or classify that denial as a trust failure.

docs.title: Worked calculations
docs.text:
Inventory attempts/request = 2 SDK attempts * 3 mesh attempts = 6
Database attempts/request = 6 * 2 operations * 2 attempts = 24
Inventory attempts/s = 12,000 * 6 = 72,000
Database operation attempts/s = 12,000 * 24 = 288,000

Reconnects/s over 5 s = 18,000 / 5 = 3,600/s
Reconnects/s over 10 min = 18,000 / 600 = 30/s

30-day minutes = 30 * 24 * 60 = 43,200
99.95% error budget = 43,200 * 0.0005 = 21.6 full-outage minutes
Hypothetical equivalent outage = 14 min * 0.18 = 2.52 min
Hypothetical budget consumed = 2.52 / 21.6 = 11.7%

This is a constant-volume sensitivity calculation, not the actual request-based SLO consumption. Time-equivalent outage is sum(duration * failure fraction); request-based consumption is failed eligible requests / (0.0005 * total eligible requests in the 30-day window). Unequal traffic across intervals makes the two different. Layered retries produce up to 24 DB attempts versus a two-operation baseline, so database attempt amplification is 12x, not 24x.

The 5-second mean of 3,600 reconnects/s is already 12x tested capacity; the observed 1,840/s can still overload handshakes. At 10 minutes, 30/s leaves 10x mean headroom below the 300/s tested limit, though zone skew and burst behavior still require measurement.

docs.title: Immediate response
docs.text:
1. Stop new-CA issuance and the global drain; keep dual trust installed.
  2. Route new traffic away from stale z2-v40 clients and preserve healthy established sessions temporarily.
  3. Restore old-issued inventory credentials by verified cohort if fresh-connect availability requires it.
  4. Disable optional retries first, enforce propagated deadlines, and shed excess traffic before primary work.
  5. Inspect receiver consumption, both flow-control windows, and version-split traces for the database path. No supplied fixture proves a bad proxy version. Roll one back only with supporting cohort evidence and compatibility checks; otherwise isolate stalled work or shift to a verified healthy path under replay-safety and capacity limits. Verify resumed DATA progress.
  6. Do not disable certificate verification or broaden authorization.
  7. Resume only after active-state inventory and forced-fresh probes pass by cohort.

docs.title: Prevention review
docs.text:
• Gate issuer changes on active dual-trust proof, not distributor acceptance.
  • Include disconnected and stale proxies in a quarantine or replacement workflow.
  • Probe fresh and reused connections separately.
  • Derive drain duration from connections, active streams, handshake latency, and tested reconnect capacity.
  • Keep frame-level progress signals for HTTP/2 dependencies.
  • Enforce one end-to-end retry budget and alert on retry tax.
  • Preserve independent authorization tests throughout security migrations.

Sources: RFC 9113 sections 4.2, 5.2, and 6.8, RFC 9846 section 4.5.1, and Envoy xDS eventual consistency. The offline mTLS lab checks a two-sided compatibility matrix; it does not execute this incident or establish its cause.

docs.title: Progressive Hints
docs.text:
Practice home | Prompt | Workbook

Open one level at a time. Each level spends interview signal and reveals part of the reasoning path.

Hint 1: Separate three security decisions

A certificate chain can authenticate a peer and expose an identity. It does not prove that the identity may call an inventory method or access a database resource. Write separate invariants for trust-chain validation, identity mapping, and authorization policy.

Checkpoint: Can a validly authenticated but unauthorized workload still be denied?

Hint 2: Draw both planes

The control plane distributes desired trust, credentials, listeners, and policy. A data-plane proxy activates a particular version and applies it to handshakes and requests. Desired state is not proof of active state.

Checkpoint: What evidence shows each proxy acknowledged and activated the intended version?

Hint 3: Think like a set transition

Represent accepted trust anchors as a trust set and presented credentials as a certificate chain. During an overlap, every presented chain must validate to an approved anchor in the receiver's active trust set, subject to identity, validity, key-usage, algorithm, and policy constraints.

Checkpoint: Which set must expand before the issuer choice changes?

Hint 4: Existing HTTP/2 is not a new handshake

A live connection can continue carrying streams under the credential negotiated when the connection was established. Success on that connection does not prove that a fresh connection can authenticate.

Checkpoint: Does the canary force a new connection and a full certificate handshake rather than only TLS PSK resumption? RFC 9846 section 2.2 permits resumption without a new certificate exchange. Keep existing-session, resumed-session, and full-handshake evidence separate.

Hint 5: Drain is a protocol operation

Use graceful retirement: stop admitting new work to an old connection, signal the peer, let eligible streams finish, and enforce a bounded deadline. A short global close can convert a safe trust change into resets and synchronized reconnects.

Checkpoint: How are GOAWAY, active streams, deadline, and forced close observed separately?

Hint 6: Do not call every timeout a certificate failure

TLS failures occur before HTTP/2 request processing. HTTP/2 flow-control stalls can leave a valid connection open while DATA progress stops. Compare handshake errors, frame progress, connection windows, stream windows, and application latency.

Checkpoint: What observation would disprove a trust-chain hypothesis?

Hint 7: Multiply retry layers before adding capacity

Independent retry counts can multiply. Assign one end-to-end attempt budget, one retry owner per hop, deadline propagation, backoff with jitter, and a retry budget. This pack defines retry tax relative to all primary inventory attempts in the same window; a successful-traffic-based budget is a possible different policy, not an interchangeable denominator.

Checkpoint: What is the maximum inventory and database load from one original call?

Hint 8: Stale is a state, not a surprise

Track last acknowledged config, active resource version, certificate issuer, trust-bundle digest, and last control-plane contact. Exclude stale instances from canaries and new traffic, but do not remove old trust while they can still serve or reconnect.

Checkpoint: Is stale-fleet handling fail-open, fail-closed, or explicitly quarantined?

Hint 9: Rollback has a point of no easy return

Retain dual trust and old signing capability until new issuance, fresh-connection tests, fleet convergence, and rollback drills pass. Removing old trust is a later cleanup, not the first sign of success.

Checkpoint: Which stage is reversible by configuration alone?

Hint 10: L6 evidence

Define cohort gates, zone failure budget, stale-workload ownership, certificate inventory, control-plane lag SLO, data-plane probes, retry tax, audit trail, and an exception expiry process. State which team may pause, rollback, quarantine, and revoke.

Checkpoint: Can teams execute and audit the migration without relying on the original designer?

After the attempt, continue to the evidence rubric.

docs.title: Interviewer Packet
docs.text:
Practice home | Rubric | Exemplars | Failure lab

Keep this file closed to candidates during the blind phase.

docs.title: Interview objective
docs.text: Evaluate whether the candidate can reason from mTLS and HTTP/2 properties, preserve authorization independently from identity, separate control-plane intent from data-plane fact, diagnose mixed evidence, and lead a reversible migration under load.

docs.title: Mode selection
docs.text: Mode Use when Required evidence Optional extension 20 min Focused screen Invariants, plane split, safe sequence, one rollback Fresh versus reused connection 35 min Standard L5 Add drain, retries, observability, gates Stale cohort 50 min Deep L5/L6 Add fixtures, calculations, flow control, migration Zone loss 70 min Staff calibration Add ownership, compromise policy, governance, alternatives Executive debrief

docs.title: Opening script
docs.text:
"Design a zero-downtime CA rotation for the path in the prompt. Start by stating invariants and boundaries. You may ask for details. I will provide incident evidence only when you request a relevant category. Keep identity authentication separate from request authorization."

Do not mention the unsafe rollout order, stale cohort, connection masking, short drain, retry multiplication, or flow-control stall in the opening.

docs.title: Assumptions available on request
docs.text: Candidate asks about Disclosure Signal to observe Certificate model Proxies receive trust bundles and short-lived workload leaves from the mesh control plane Separates root trust, issuer choice, and leaf identity mTLS direction Both peers authenticate; inventory and database paths have independent policy Expands receiver trust on both sides Configuration status Distributor success does not guarantee proxy activation Requests active version and rejection evidence Connections HTTP/2 sessions can last 45 minutes Requires fresh-connect probes Streams Long requests exist; active stream duration p99 is 38 seconds Derives drain deadline rather than guessing Retries SDK max_attempts=2; client proxy max_attempts=3; DB client max_attempts=2; each count includes the initial attempt Calculates 6 inventory and 24 DB attempts maximum Staleness 264 of all 2,400 API client sidecars, or 11%, missed the bundle; all belong to z2-v40 Quarantines and blocks old-root removal Authorization Policy maps workload identity and action; it is not encoded by root trust alone Preserves negative tests Failure symptoms TLS errors cluster by client config version; some authenticated DB streams also stall Looks for multiple causes Compromise The planned case is expiry, not compromise Keeps overlap; can articulate emergency exception

docs.title: Minute 5
docs.text:
Look for scope, zero-downtime definition, trust compatibility, least privilege, and explicit identity-versus-authorization separation.

If absent, ask: "What does validating a certificate prove, and what does it not prove?"

docs.title: Minute 12
docs.text:
Look for control-plane desired/active distinction, data-plane handshakes, and trust expansion before issuer change.

If absent, ask: "Can a successful config push prove a fresh connection will work?"

docs.title: Minute 22
docs.text:
Look for dual trust, credential cohorts only after all receiver trust is active, fresh non-resumed canaries, and rollback. Server-before-client issuance is this pack's operational choice, not a TLS requirement once every receiver has dual trust; accept an equivalently safe alternate order.

If absent, ask: "What happens to an old-only client when the server presents a new-issued leaf?"

docs.title: Minute 35
docs.text:
Look for GOAWAY, active-stream completion, drain capacity, reconnect shaping, and one retry budget.

If absent, disclose the 45-minute connection lifetime and retry counts.

docs.title: Minute 50
docs.text:
Look for evidence joins across trust, issuer, config, TLS, frames, GOAWAY, retry traces, and authorization.

If absent, provide Fixture E from the failure lab and ask what it disproves.

docs.title: Minute 65
docs.text: Look for ownership, stale exception expiry, audit proof, completion criteria, rejected alternatives, and emergency-compromise policy.

docs.title: Branch A: Candidate rotates servers before expanding trust
docs.text:
Ask: "A client is disconnected and trusts only the old CA. The server reconnect presents a new-issued leaf. Walk the handshake."

  • Strong recovery: identifies unknown_ca, pauses issuance, restores compatible server credentials if needed, distributes dual trust, and proves active state.
  • Weak recovery: adds retries or disables verification.
  • Apply the 17-point safety cap if the final design remains unsafe.

docs.title: Branch B: Candidate says dual trust solves everything
docs.text:
Ask: "A certificate from a trusted CA identifies an analytics workload calling inventory.write. Should the call pass?"

  • Strong: authentication succeeds; separate authorization denies the action.
  • Weak: any trusted certificate is accepted.
  • Apply the identity-equals-authorization cap if uncorrected.

docs.title: Branch C: Candidate trusts rollout status
docs.text:
Reveal Fixture C from the failure lab.

Ask: "Which field is authority for active proxy behavior, and what data-plane proof remains necessary?"

  • Strong: uses active version/digest plus fresh handshake probes.
  • L6: redesigns readiness and rollout accounting so desired, acked, active, and observed states remain separate.

docs.title: Branch D: Candidate overlooks long-lived HTTP/2
docs.text:
Ask: "Your canary sent 10,000 successful requests over one 40-minute-old connection. What did it prove?"

  • Strong: only the established session and request path; it did not test the new chain.
  • Follow-up: request a fresh/reused probe matrix and graceful drain plan.

docs.title: Branch E: Candidate proposes a short restart
docs.text:
Reveal Fixture F.

Ask: "Calculate reconnect demand and explain the 63 resets."

  • Strong: computes 3,600/s mean for five seconds, compares with 300/s tested capacity, then proposes GOAWAY, stream-aware deadline, and shaping.
  • L6: reserves zone capacity and defines overload ordering.

docs.title: Branch F: Candidate calls every timeout TLS failure
docs.text:
Reveal Fixture E.

Ask: "PING is acknowledged but DATA is blocked. What hypothesis fits, and what evidence would confirm it?"

  • Strong: connection-level flow-control stall; inspect WINDOW_UPDATE, windows, reader progress, proxy version, and downstream consumption.
  • Weak: rotate certificates again or increase timeout.

docs.title: Branch G: Candidate says retries will hide the event
docs.text:
Reveal Fixture G.

Ask: "Show the attempt tree and choose retry owners."

  • Strong: computes 6 inventory and 24 DB attempts; removes independent retries, propagates deadlines, adds jitter and retry budgets.
  • L6: sheds retries before primary traffic and quantifies retry tax.

docs.title: Branch H: Candidate handles stale workloads well
docs.text:
Ask: "Eight percent cannot receive config for seven days; leaves expire in 24 hours. Do you wait, fail open, or isolate?"

  • Strong: removes them from service, replaces or repairs them, gives exceptions an owner and expiry, and blocks old-root removal until proof.
  • L6: distinguishes availability policy from a compromised-root emergency.

docs.title: Branch I: Candidate is migration strong
docs.text:
Ask: "Where is the point of no easy return? What evidence permits destruction of old signing material?"

  • Strong: old-trust removal and key destruction follow zero old use, fresh matrices, expired exceptions, rollback drill, and joint approval.
  • L6: distinguishes disabling routine issuance, retaining protected rollback, revocation, trust removal, and key destruction.

docs.title: Branch J: Candidate is technically strong but organizationally vague
docs.text:
Ask: "Security wants immediate removal, platform sees config lag, and inventory owns the SLO. Who decides?"

  • Strong L6: preassigns pause and rollback authority, uses explicit gates, records risk acceptance, and gives security final CA-retirement approval.

docs.title: Evidence notes
docs.text:
Capture exact statements, not impressions.

Area Evidence heard Contradiction Follow-up used Score Invariants Identity/access Planes/config Sequence HTTP/2/drain Diagnosis Retries/overload Observability Migration/rollback Leadership

docs.title: Below target
docs.text: Changes issuers before trust, removes old trust too early, weakens verification, or treats trusted identity as authorization. Uses retries and restarts as the main recovery.

docs.title: Weak L5
docs.text: Finds dual trust but misses fresh-connection proof, graceful drain, active-state evidence, or retry multiplication.

docs.title: Borderline L5
docs.text: Safe sequence and rollback exist. Diagnosis or stale-fleet policy remains shallow, and calculations need interviewer prompting.

docs.title: Strong L5
docs.text: Runs a safe end-to-end migration, separates both planes and security decisions, handles HTTP/2 lifecycle, bounds retries, and gives actionable evidence.

docs.title: Borderline L6
docs.text: Adds quantified gates, mixed-failure diagnosis, cohort governance, and completion proof, but leaves one material ownership or emergency-policy gap.

docs.title: Strong L6
docs.text: Shapes requirements, distinguishes routine and compromise paths, quantifies reconnect and retry risk, assigns decision rights, and makes removal auditable and reversible until the declared boundary.

docs.title: Scoring procedure
docs.text:
1. Select the mode before the interview.
  2. Score only dimensions available in that mode.
  3. Record exact evidence and contradictions.
  4. Normalize using the rubric formula.
  5. Apply the lowest safety cap.
  6. Report mode, subtotal/available -> normalized/40, cap, and level.

Example: 35 min, 26/32 -> 33/40 (round-half-up), no cap, borderline L6 numeric band for mode; I/J unassessed, no L6 leadership conclusion.

The fixtures are synthetic disclosure cards, not an executable mesh. Read the RFC 9113 flow-control and GOAWAY rules before treating PING, WINDOW_UPDATE absence, or a reset as causal proof. Ask for receiver consumption/version evidence before accepting a proxy-version rollback; the supplied trace does not identify a defective version.

docs.title: Debrief script
docs.text:
1. "Your strongest demonstrated evidence was..."
  2. "The highest-risk gap was..."
  3. "To close it, I needed to see..."
  4. "A next-level exercise is..."

Do not reveal fixture answers before the candidate commits to a hypothesis. Reward corrections when new evidence appears, but distinguish independent discovery from interviewer-led repair.

docs.title: Interviewer anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Leading with the unsafe server-first event instead of allowing sequence discovery.
  • Calling a control-plane acknowledgement proof of data-plane activation.
  • Treating every 403, reset, or timeout as a certificate symptom.
  • Rewarding product names without protocol behavior.
  • Penalizing a candidate for choosing controlled unavailability during confirmed CA compromise.
  • Comparing normalized scores without stating the mode.

docs.title: Dual-Trust Staged Migration and Rollback
docs.text: Practice home | Failure lab | Interviewer packet

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Move every eligible mesh path from ca-old to ca-new without presenting an untrusted chain, broadening authorization, or losing rollback. This is a routine planned rotation. A known CA compromise requires the separate emergency rule below.

docs.title: Core invariant
docs.text:
For every fresh mTLS connection in either direction:

presented_chain validates to an approved anchor in receiver_active_trust_set
and authenticated_identity maps to the expected workload
and authorization_policy permits the requested action

Chain validation establishes that a credential reaches an approved trust anchor under validity, key-usage, algorithm, and policy constraints. Identity mapping says which workload the certificate represents. Authorization independently decides what that workload may do.

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldOnly
    OldOnly --> DualTrustOldIssue: activate old+new trust
    DualTrustOldIssue --> DualTrustServerNew: prove fresh paths, rotate servers
    DualTrustServerNew --> DualTrustAllNew: rotate client credentials
    DualTrustAllNew --> RetirementGate: stop old issue and close stale and resumption paths
    RetirementGate --> NewOnly: approve old trust removal
    RetirementGate --> DualTrustAllNew: gate fails or rollback needed
    DualTrustServerNew --> DualTrustOldIssue: stop new issue, restore server credentials
    DualTrustAllNew --> DualTrustServerNew: stop client issue, restore client credentials
    DualTrustOldIssue --> OldOnly: remove unused new trust
    NewOnly --> [*]

Do not jump from OldOnly to a new-issued credential. Do not enter NewOnly while any serving or reconnecting peer can present ca-old.

docs.title: Roles and decision rights
docs.text: Role Owns May pause May rollback Completion approval Security PKI Roots, intermediates, signing, revocation, audit Any trust anomaly Issuer/signing state Required Mesh platform Bundle and credential distribution, proxy readiness, drain Config or handshake gate Bundle/issuer config Required API and inventory teams Fresh-path probes, deadlines, retry policy, capacity SLO or functional gate Workload cohort Consulted Database platform DB-proxy identity, policy, flow-control health DB path gate DB-proxy cohort Required for DB path Incident commander Cross-team execution and communications Any unsafe condition Coordinates Records decision

docs.title: Stage 0: establish baseline and rollback assets
docs.text:
Inventory every proxy by zone, workload identity, active config version, trust-bundle digest, leaf issuer, leaf expiry, proxy version, and last control-plane contact. Capture authorization policy hashes and positive/negative test results.

Required before change:

  • old signing path and old-issued rollback credentials remain usable;
  • ca-new chain and identity mapping pass offline validation;
  • fresh and reused HTTP/2 probes are distinguishable;
  • retry budgets and reconnect admission controls are enabled;
  • per-cohort dashboards and an audit manifest exist;
  • stale sidecars have an owner, deadline, and quarantine route.

docs.title: Stage 1: expand trust everywhere
docs.text:
Distribute {ca-old,ca-new} to API client proxies, inventory server proxies, inventory clients, and database proxies. Because mTLS authenticates both peers, all receiver roles need compatible trust before either side presents a new-issued certificate.

Promotion gate per cohort:

  • desired, acknowledged, and active versions match;
  • active trust digest equals the approved dual bundle;
  • configuration rejection is zero;
  • fresh connections validate both old-issued and new-issued test peers;
  • unauthorized identities remain denied;
  • disconnected proxies are excluded from incompatible call paths, including fresh reconnects, and any retained compatible island has an owner and expiry. Merely recording an exception does not make old-only trust compatible.

Hold for two representative peak windows and one control-plane interruption test.

docs.title: Stage 2: rotate server credentials before client credentials
docs.text:
After Stage 1 is proven, rotate inventory server proxies and database server-facing endpoints to ca-new in this order:

  1. 1% canary in one zone;
  2. remaining canary zone;
  3. second zone;
  4. final zone while one previously proven zone remains available.

Each canary must force a fresh, non-resumed TLS certificate handshake. A new TCP connection with TLS PSK resumption can still bypass a new certificate exchange. Reused HTTP/2 and resumed TLS success are tracked separately and do not satisfy the issuer gate.

Graceful connection replacement:

  1. stop assigning new streams to the retiring connection;
  2. send GOAWAY with the highest peer-initiated stream identifier that was or might be processed, not just the last completed stream;
  3. let eligible streams finish until the calculated deadline;
  4. reconnect under a token-bucket limit with jitter;
  5. count forced closes; streams above the final Last-Stream-ID were not processed on that connection and can be retried within budget. Streams at or below it have uncertain outcomes unless separately proven; require replay-safe semantics or reconciliation rather than assuming no effect.

Suggested gate values for the exercise, not universal thresholds:

Signal Promotion gate Rotation-attributed fresh TLS failure under 0.01% for two peak windows Authorization policy drift zero Forced stream closes under 0.1% of drained streams Retry tax retry inventory attempts / all primary inventory attempts under 10% in the same window p99 latency under 300 ms, or approved error-budget exception Stale serving proxies zero in promoted cohort

docs.title: Stage 3: rotate client credentials
docs.text:
Rotate API client and inventory-to-database client credentials by the same cohort and zone strategy. Server-side dual trust already accepts both issuers. Verify expected client identities and negative authorization tests at both boundaries.

Do not use a shared wildcard identity to simplify migration. Preserve workload identity granularity and policy bindings.

docs.title: Stage 4: stop old issuance and observe
docs.text:
Disable routine ca-old issuance but retain protected rollback capability. Continue dual trust while:

  • old-issued certificate count falls to zero or all remaining exceptions expire;
  • no fresh connection presents an old-issued leaf;
  • certificate lifetime plus clock-skew policy has elapsed, unless revocation proof is stronger;
  • every zone has passed cold-start, reconnect, control-plane-loss, and one-zone-unavailable tests;
  • drain and retry metrics remain within gates;
  • old-root rollback has been rehearsed before final destruction.

Start the old-leaf expiry clock at the last old issuance, including emergency rollback issuance, not at rollout start. Terminate or reauthenticate old sessions and invalidate or age out associated resumption credentials according to the implementation's identity binding. Leaf expiry does not automatically close established TLS connections or invalidate every session ticket. Audit these separate lifetimes before removing the old trust path.

docs.title: Stage 5: remove old trust and retire the CA
docs.text:
Remove ca-old from a 1% receiver canary, force fresh connections to all required peer types, and repeat the zone sequence. Revoke or destroy old signing material only after the removal proves stable and the retention policy permits it.

Completion evidence:

  • signed inventory shows no eligible old-issued credential;
  • active trust digests are ca-new only;
  • fresh handshake matrix passes for every allowed identity pair;
  • negative authorization matrix still denies forbidden actions;
  • no valid stale exception remains;
  • rollback and incident records are archived;
  • security and platform owners approve retirement.

docs.title: Retry amplification
docs.text:
Without coordination:

Inventory attempts/request = 2 SDK attempts * 3 proxy attempts = 6
Database attempts/request = 6 * 2 DB operations * 2 attempts = 24
At 12,000 requests/s:
inventory attempts = 72,000/s
database operation attempts = 288,000/s

A safer policy allows at most two end-to-end inventory attempts, no independent SDK retry for mesh-generated failures, and one attempt for each database operation unless the operation is idempotent, budget remains, and the retry stays inside the propagated deadline. That bounds the normal exercise case at four database operation attempts per original request.

docs.title: Drain sizing
docs.text:
For 18,000 connections over 10 minutes:

mean reconnect rate = 18,000 / 600 = 30/s
assumed measured mean handshake latency = 150 ms
mean in-flight handshakes = 30 * 0.15 = 4.5
250 ms tail-latency sensitivity = 30 * 0.25 = 7.5 (not mean or p99 concurrency)

Capacity-test at least 5x the mean for burst and zone skew. Use measured active-stream duration to select the drain deadline; the mean alone does not protect long streams.

Sources: RFC 9113 section 6.8, RFC 9846 sections 2.2 and 4.7.1, and Envoy xDS sequencing and resource TTL. The 150 ms mean and 5x factor are exercise assumptions to validate, not protocol guarantees. Resource TTL expiry can also change behavior during a control-plane outage even if no new update arrives.

docs.title: Rollback matrix
docs.text:
Current stage Trigger First action Credential action Trust action Traffic action Stage 1 Config rejection or authz drift Pause bundle rollout Keep old issuance Restore old-only only after no new-issued test peer remains Remove failed cohort from canary Stage 2 Fresh handshake or drain gate fails Stop new server issuance and drains Restore old-issued server credentials by cohort Keep dual trust Route away from affected cohort Stage 3 Client authn/authz gate fails Stop client rotation Restore old-issued clients Keep dual trust Quarantine failed client cohort Stage 4 Old peer reappears Reopen exception investigation Reissue old only if availability requires and risk permits Keep dual trust Remove stale peer from service Stage 5 canary New-only receiver rejects valid peer Stop old-trust removal Keep new issuance; restore old credential only if needed Restore dual trust to canary Reopen through verified cohort

Rollback does not mean removing ca-new immediately. Dual trust is the compatibility bridge. First stop the incompatible issuer change, then restore credentials or traffic by verified cohort.

docs.title: Emergency compromise rule
docs.text: If ca-old is known or strongly suspected to be compromised, preserving its trust for availability may be unsafe. Security and incident command can choose rapid distrust, credential revocation, quarantine, and controlled outage. Record the different invariant: reject potentially forged identity even if availability falls. Do not silently reuse the routine-rotation gates.

docs.title: Candidate challenge
docs.text: Change one assumption: 8% of sidecars cannot reconnect to the control plane for seven days, while old certificates expire in 24 hours. Propose a policy that preserves identity assurance, limits outage scope, gives each exception an owner and expiry, and still reaches old-CA retirement.

docs.title: Candidate Prompt: Mesh Certificate Rotation
docs.text: Practice home | Workbook | Hints

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your company runs an inventory request path through a service mesh:

flowchart LR
    API[API application] --> CP[API client proxy]
    CP --> SP[Inventory server proxy]
    SP --> INV[Inventory application]
    INV --> DP[Database proxy]
    DP --> DB[(Inventory database)]

Proxy-to-proxy and inventory-to-database-proxy traffic uses mTLS and HTTP/2. A control plane distributes workload certificates, trust bundles, listener configuration, and policy. Proxies enforce those artifacts on the data plane.

The current root certificate authority must be retired. Design the rotation and the operating model that keeps requests available, preserves peer identity, and prevents unintended access. Then explain how you would investigate a partial failure during rollout.

docs.title: Starting facts
docs.text:
• Peak API traffic is 12,000 requests per second.
  • One API request makes one inventory call and two database operations.
  • The API client proxy uses max_attempts=3, including the initial attempt, for eligible inventory calls.
  • The inventory client uses max_attempts=2, including the initial attempt, for an eligible database operation.
  • The application SDK uses max_attempts=2, including the initial attempt, for an eligible API call.
  • HTTP/2 connections can remain open for 45 minutes.
  • There are 2,400 application sidecars and 180 database proxies across three zones.
  • For inventory accounting, the 2,400 are API client sidecars; inventory adds 240 server sidecars. Do not count these as the same fleet population.
  • The availability SLO is 99.95% over 30 days; the p99 latency objective is 300 ms.
  • The rotation must tolerate an unavailable zone and a slow configuration distributor.
  • Some sidecars can miss updates while disconnected.

These are design assumptions, not measured benchmarks. Challenge them if necessary and state the consequence.

The database proxy exposes a synthetic HTTP/2 RPC interface, not a claim that native database wire protocols use HTTP/2. Interpret the availability SLO as successful eligible requests divided by eligible requests over the window; state how rejections, authorization denials, and client cancellations enter it. No request in the fixture is declared safe to replay merely because it uses RPC.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Rotate from the old CA to a new CA without a planned outage.
  2. Detect and quarantine stale workloads without silently broadening access.
  3. Preserve authenticated workload identity through the transition.
  4. Keep authorization policy explicit and independently testable.
  5. Bound retries, connection churn, and recovery load.
  6. Support rollback until the new trust path is proven.
  7. Produce evidence that the old CA can be removed safely.
  8. Define ownership across security, platform, service, database, and incident teams.

docs.title: Questions your design must answer
docs.text:
• What must always be true during trust-bundle and certificate changes?
  • Which steps belong to the control plane, and which effects occur on the data plane?
  • In what order do you change trust, issuers, and workloads?
  • How do existing and new HTTP/2 connections behave at each stage?
  • How do you drain connections without cutting off active streams?
  • What proves that each proxy received and activated the intended configuration?
  • What signals distinguish trust failure, authorization denial, transport reset, and flow-control delay?
  • How many downstream attempts can one user request create?
  • How do you stop retry amplification during reconnect storms?
  • What are the abort, rollback, and final old-CA removal gates?
  • How do you handle workloads that remain stale beyond the rollout deadline?

docs.title: 20-minute mode
docs.text: By minute 4, state scope and four invariants. By minute 9, draw control and data planes. By minute 14, give a staged rotation. Use the final 6 minutes for one failure diagnosis and rollback decision.

docs.title: 35-minute mode
docs.text: Complete the 20-minute artifact, then add connection lifecycle, trust/config telemetry, an end-to-end retry budget, and promotion gates.

docs.title: 50-minute mode
docs.text: Complete the 35-minute artifact, then quantify retry amplification and drain capacity. Diagnose a mixed-fleet incident using evidence categories rather than symptoms alone.

docs.title: 70-minute mode
docs.text: Complete the 50-minute artifact, then add a stale-fleet quarantine policy, zone sequencing, ownership, audit evidence, rejected alternatives, and reversal conditions.

docs.title: Deliverable format
docs.text:
Present in this order:

  1. scope, assumptions, and exclusions;
  2. invariants and SLO impact;
  3. identity, authentication, and authorization boundaries;
  4. control-plane and data-plane model;
  5. staged rollout and connection lifecycle;
  6. failure diagnosis and mitigation;
  7. calculations, overload controls, and observability;
  8. rollback, completion proof, and ownership.

docs.title: Candidate stop point
docs.text: Do not read the rubric, exemplars, design review, failure lab, migration exercise, or interviewer packet until your first pass is complete.

docs.title: Evidence Rubric
docs.text:
Practice home | Exemplars | Interviewer packet

Score visible evidence, not terminology. Naming mTLS, xDS, GOAWAY, or retries earns no credit without a mechanism, boundary, and failure behavior.

docs.title: Scoring model
docs.text:
Each dimension receives 0 to 4 points.

Score Evidence standard 0 Missing, contradictory, or unsafe 1 Names the concern without an enforceable mechanism 2 Coherent happy path with a material failure or proof gap 3 Correct mechanism, boundary, evidence, and recovery behavior 4 Level 3 plus calculation, operational gate, rejected alternative, or evolution judgment

Safety caps override arithmetic totals.

docs.title: A. Framing and invariants
docs.text:
• Defines zero-downtime, peer-authentication, authorization, rollback, and old-CA retirement goals.
  • States that every presented chain must terminate in an active trusted root for the receiving peer.
  • Preserves least privilege and avoids broad fail-open trust or authorization.

docs.title: B. Identity, trust, and authorization
docs.text:
• Separates certificate-chain authentication, workload identity mapping, and request authorization.
  • Defines expected identities at API-to-inventory and inventory-to-database boundaries.
  • Tests negative access during and after rotation; a trusted identity is not automatically authorized.

docs.title: C. Control-plane and data-plane reasoning
docs.text:
• Separates desired configuration distribution from active proxy state and live traffic effects.
  • Tracks version, acknowledgement or rejection, trust digest, issuer, freshness, and proxy readiness.
  • Handles slow distribution and disconnected sidecars without assuming fleet convergence.

docs.title: D. Safe trust and issuer sequence
docs.text:
• Expands trust to old plus new before presenting new-issued certificates.
  • Proves dual trust on fresh connections, changes issuers by cohort, and removes old trust last.
  • Retains a reversible overlap and defines revocation or emergency-compromise exceptions.

docs.title: E. HTTP/2 lifecycle and drain
docs.text:
• Distinguishes existing connections from fresh TLS handshakes.
  • Uses graceful GOAWAY, stream completion, bounded drain, reconnect shaping, and forced-close accounting.
  • Tests fresh connections so long-lived old sessions cannot mask an invalid rollout.

docs.title: F. Evidence-based diagnosis
docs.text:
• Correlates trust bundle, presented issuer, active config, TLS result, HTTP/2 frames, GOAWAY, and retry records.
  • Distinguishes TLS handshake failure, authorization denial, reset, upstream timeout, and flow-control stall.
  • Ranks hypotheses with supporting and disconfirming evidence before remediation.

docs.title: G. Retry, deadline, and overload control
docs.text:
• Calculates cross-layer attempt amplification.
  • Assigns one retry owner per boundary under a propagated end-to-end deadline.
  • Uses retry budgets, exponential backoff with jitter, admission control, and reconnect rate limits.

docs.title: H. Observability and validation
docs.text:
• Defines fresh-connection probes, certificate and trust inventory, config convergence, authn/authz outcomes, frame progress, drain health, and retry tax.
  • Splits signals by zone, proxy version, issuer pair, trust digest, response code, and cohort.
  • Gives actionable gates, windows, and owner responses rather than dashboard names alone.

docs.title: I. Migration, rollback, and stale fleet
docs.text:
• Uses canary, cohort, zone, and dependency-aware promotion.
  • Quarantines or replaces stale workloads through an explicit policy and exception expiry.
  • Keeps rollback viable, defines the point of no easy return, and proves old-CA removal readiness.

docs.title: J. L6 leadership and tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Assigns security, platform, service, database, and incident responsibilities.
  • Quantifies risk and capacity, records decisions, and defines pause authority and audit evidence.
  • Rejects alternatives with reversal conditions and addresses compromise response separately from routine rotation.

Maximum: 40 points.

docs.title: Safety caps
docs.text:
Apply the lowest relevant cap after normalization.

Defect Maximum outcome Presents new-issued server credentials before all eligible clients trust the new CA 17/40; below L5 Removes old trust before old-issued peers and stale reconnectors are eliminated 17/40; below L5 Treats possession of any trusted certificate as sufficient authorization 17/40; below L5 Disables certificate verification or broadens authorization to recover availability 17/40; below L5 Validates only reused HTTP/2 connections and claims rotation success 23/40; weak L5 Allows independent layered retries without a shared attempt or deadline budget 23/40; weak L5 Closes all HTTP/2 connections at once with no graceful drain or reconnect shaping 23/40; weak L5 Has a safe single-zone sequence but no stale-fleet or rollback treatment in 50/70-minute mode 27/40; borderline L5 Strong technical plan but no cross-team ownership or completion proof in 70-minute mode 32/40; strong L5

docs.title: Level calibration
docs.text:
Outcome Typical normalized total Required pattern Below target 0-17 A central trust, authorization, or availability defect remains Weak L5 18-23 Basic sequence works, but connection, retry, evidence, or recovery gaps are significant Borderline L5 24-27 Safe core with shallow diagnosis, migration, or overload control Strong L5 28-32 End-to-end safe rotation with credible evidence, drain, retries, and rollback Borderline L6 33-35 Strong L5 plus operational and organizational judgment, with one material leadership gap Strong L6 36-40 Shapes risk, quantifies limits, governs migration, and makes reversible cross-team decisions

Totals do not override safety caps.

docs.title: Evidence capture sheet
docs.text:
Dimension Score Exact evidence Missing proof or contradiction A. Framing/invariants B. Identity/access C. Planes/config D. Trust/issuer sequence E. HTTP/2/drain F. Diagnosis G. Retries/overload H. Observability I. Migration/rollback J. Leadership/tradeoffs

Safety cap applied:

Final level:

docs.title: Mode normalization
docs.text:
Score only the listed dimensions. Normalize with:

normalized = floor(subtotal / available_points * 40 + 0.5)

Use round-half-up for these nonnegative scores, not a language's unspecified round behavior: 26/32 * 40 = 32.5 becomes 33, including in Python where built-in round(32.5) would give 32. Apply safety caps afterward.

Mode Scored dimensions Available points Required evidence outside the scored set 20 minutes A-E 20 One evidence-based failure decision 35 minutes A-H 32 Rollback boundary stated even though I is not scored 50 minutes A-J 40 Calculations and stale-fleet handling required 70 minutes A-J 40 Strong L6 requires ownership, governance, and reversal conditions

Record subtotal/available -> normalized/40, the mode, and any cap. Normalization compares performance within an assigned mode; it does not fabricate evidence for omitted dimensions.

Report the numerical band as mode-local, separately from demonstrated level. A 20/35-minute score cannot establish L6 migration/leadership competencies I/J that were not assessed. Keep those unassessed rather than treating normalized points as evidence. These bands are educational calibration, not validated hiring predictions; they are distinct from the track's 100-point rubric.

Protocol checks behind safety gates: RFC 9846 certificate authentication and RFC 9113 GOAWAY. An eligible peer must be compatible; an aggregate 99.99% probe target cannot waive a known old-only trust island. Quarantine must actually prevent that incompatible path, including reconnects, not merely register an exception.

docs.title: Debrief rule
docs.text: Give one demonstrated strength, the highest-risk gap, the exact evidence needed to close it, and one stretch question. Never average away a trust or authorization safety defect.

docs.title: Pattern: Distributed Coordination
docs.text:
Distributed coordination lets unreliable processes agree on small, high-value control decisions: who owns a role, whether a version still matches, which member is next, or when temporary ownership has ended. It is not a bulk data store or a substitute for designing idempotent work. Keep coordinated state small, operations bounded, and the failure contract visible to callers.

ZooKeeper and etcd are examples of systems that can expose these ideas. The pattern does not depend on either product's API or naming.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use coordination for service membership, leader election, distributed locks, shard assignment, configuration pointers, and generation allocation when participants need one ordered authority. Prefer a database conditional update when all contenders already share that database and the scale is modest. Prefer a work queue, partition ownership protocol, optimistic transaction, or idempotent operation when exclusive ownership is unnecessary.

Do not place large values, high-volume event streams, arbitrary queries, or one key per end-user action in the coordination plane. A slow or unavailable coordination quorum must not sit on every application data request unless that availability tradeoff is intentional.

docs.title: Minimal model
docs.text:
Organize keys in bounded namespaces so ownership, ACLs, quotas, and operational blast radius are explicit. A record contains a value, creation revision, modification revision, and optional attachment to a session. Every committed mutation receives an ordered revision within its documented scope; callers must not compare revisions from unrelated shards as though they were global.

Record(namespace, key, value, create_revision, modify_revision, session_id?)
Session(session_id, generation, ttl, expires_at, state)
Change(revision, key, type, value_hash)

The core mutation is compare-and-swap (CAS): apply a transaction only if predicates such as key absent, modify_revision = 42, value = X, or session generation = 7 still hold. The comparison and writes share one serialization point. Reads used to make ownership decisions are linearizable; explicitly stale reads are acceptable only for displays, hints, or caches.

flowchart LR
    C[Client operation] --> G[Namespace and quota gate]
    G --> L[Shard leader]
    L --> Q[Consensus quorum]
    Q --> R[(Revisioned records)]
    R --> W[Bounded watch fanout]
    W --> C

docs.title: Sessions and ephemeral ownership
docs.text:
A session represents liveness for one client generation. Ephemeral records attached to it are eligible for removal after the authority commits session expiry. They are useful for membership and ownership hints because cleanup does not rely on a crashed client. A replacement process must create a higher generation or a new session; delayed heartbeats from the former process cannot revive it.

Expiry timers are hints, not decisions. When a timer fires, the leader rechecks session ID, generation, and deadline, then commits expiry through consensus before deleting attached records or transferring ownership. Use authority time with a stated clock-uncertainty policy. Clients renew early with jitter and must stop ownership-dependent work when renewal confidence is lost.

Batching amortizes lease traffic. In an illustrative implementation that durably records every renewal, suppose 300,000 ephemeral resources renew every 10 seconds: one lease per resource creates 300,000 / 10 = 30,000 renewal writes/s. If each session owns 100 resources, only 3,000 sessions renew, producing 3,000 / 10 = 300 renewal writes/s. This counts the proposed design's renewal records, not a benchmark or a claim that etcd commits a consensus write for every keepalive. The 100x reduction comes with correlated failure: one expired session releases 100 resources at once. Cap resources per session, stagger renewals, and reserve quorum capacity for established renewals and expiry cleanup.

docs.title: Watches are advisory
docs.text:
A durable watch consumer must tolerate replay across reconnects and crashes; delivery guarantees on one stream are product-specific. It may disconnect, lag, or encounter compacted history. Establish snapshot and watch without a gap by taking a consistent snapshot at revision R and watching strictly after R, with sufficient retained history. A paginated snapshot must use the same revision for every page, not a fresh latest read per page.

Checkpoint only a completely applied revision. One transaction can change several keys at revision 901: applying the first event and saving 901 before the second event commits would lose the second on restart at 902. Apply the revision's events and cursor atomically when possible; otherwise use replay-safe effects and checkpoint only after all events complete. Do not discard a second key merely because its revision equals the first key's revision. When history has compacted, rebuild from a fresh consistent snapshot.

Vendor (etcd 3.6, accessed 2026-09-08): API guarantees, Watch APIs and Revision specifies unique events on a watch, complete revisions in event lists, and resumability within retained history. That is not an exactly-once guarantee for a consumer's external effects. Its watch is not linearizable, and its guarantees must not be assumed for ZooKeeper watches or arbitrary streaming APIs.

Never treat a watch notification as an ownership grant. A key deleted event means contenders may attempt CAS; it does not authorize all observers to act. Bound server and client queues, coalesce replaceable state, limit watched prefixes, and return an explicit reset/compacted response rather than retaining unbounded history for a slow consumer.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Coordination authority
    C->>A: snapshot prefix
    A-->>C: records at revision 900
    C->>A: watch after revision 900
    A-->>C: revision 901
    A-->>C: revision 902
    Note over C,A: connection breaks and history compacts
    C->>A: watch after revision 902
    A-->>C: compacted, snapshot required
    C->>A: snapshot prefix

docs.title: Leader election recipe
docs.text:
Create an ephemeral candidacy record tied to the caller's session. Choose the eligible candidate with the smallest creation revision. A candidate reads the current winner and watches the relevant predecessor or election generation; after any notification or reconnect, it re-reads authoritative state before declaring leadership. Session loss ends eligibility.

Specify a deterministic tie-breaker such as (create_revision, candidate_id), or restrict creation to one candidate per transaction. In etcd, multiple keys changed by one transaction share a revision, so revision alone need not uniquely rank candidates. Distinguish a newly granted lease from a confirmed downstream fence; neither a watch nor election position bypasses the protected resource's guard.

Leadership must carry a monotonically increasing term or fencing token allocated by the coordination authority. Every external side effect includes that token, and the protected resource atomically rejects operations older than the highest token it has accepted. This maximum-seen scheme rejects the former leader only after the sink observes the newer token. For transfer-time revocation, install the new token at the sink before declaring the handoff complete; the engineering authority chapter traces that protocol. Election alone does not stop a paused former leader.

docs.title: Fair lock queue recipe
docs.text:
For a contended lock, each waiter creates an ephemeral sequential queue entry. The lowest live sequence may acquire through CAS. Every other waiter watches only its immediate predecessor, not the lock root; predecessor deletion wakes one successor rather than every contender. After wakeup, reconnect, or timeout, the waiter lists enough queue state to verify its position and session before acting.

flowchart TD
    J[Create ephemeral sequential waiter] --> P{Lowest live sequence?}
    P -- yes --> A[CAS ownership and allocate fence]
    P -- no --> W[Watch immediate predecessor]
    W --> R[Notification or reconnect]
    R --> P
    A --> X[Call protected resource with fence]
    X --> V{Fence current?}
    V -- yes --> E[Apply operation]
    V -- no --> D[Reject stale owner]

Cancellation and ownership transfer are revisioned state transitions. If they race, the committed order decides whether the client acquired and must release, or cancellation won. Bound queue length and wait duration. Strict FIFO can reduce throughput when the head is slow; document whether ineligible or unconfirmed heads may be skipped.

docs.title: Resource fencing is mandatory
docs.text:
A lease or ephemeral node only controls records inside the coordination service. It cannot retract a process that paused, lost its session, and later resumes with buffered credentials or network requests. Therefore any lock or leadership used to protect an external database, object store, scheduler, device, or API must issue a monotonically increasing fencing token, and that resource must atomically reject stale tokens.

A random lease ID proves identity but not order. Wall-clock timestamps are unsafe ordering tokens under skew. A consensus term may be insufficient if tokens reset across restore or shard movement. Persist the token high-watermark and migration epoch so newly issued tokens compare above every token that could have escaped before failover. If the protected resource cannot enforce fencing, describe the guarantee as best effort and do not use it for destructive or non-idempotent work.

docs.title: Quorum loss and recovery
docs.text:
When the authority loses quorum, it cannot create sessions, renew ownership, complete CAS, elect leaders, or grant locks. Minority replicas must not trade consistency for availability. Clients may continue work only within an application-specific safety window and only when external fencing still makes stale operations rejectable; the conservative default is to stop before lease confidence expires.

After quorum recovery, sessions whose expiry was not safely extended are treated as lost and clients establish new generations. Reconciliation removes orphaned ephemeral records, verifies token monotonicity, and checks watch consumers against a fresh snapshot. Restore into an isolated cluster, preserve revision and fencing high-watermarks, assign a new cluster epoch, and prevent promotion until stale authorities are fenced.

docs.title: Scale and operational limits
docs.text:
Shard by namespace or stable key while keeping each CAS transaction, lock queue, and election in one consensus group. Hot keys remain serialized and cannot be scaled by adding replicas. Publish limits for key/value size, transaction operations and bytes, sessions, ephemeral records per session, watches per client and prefix, watch backlog, queue length, TTL range, and operations per tenant.

Reserve capacity for session renewals, releases, and cleanup ahead of new acquisitions and broad watches. Apply jitter to heartbeats and reconnects, return retry windows during overload, and isolate high-churn namespaces. Measure proposal-to-commit latency, quorum state, session renewal margin, expiry batches, CAS conflicts, watch lag/resets, queue depth, election churn, hot keys, rejected stale fences, and revision/compaction distance.

Test process pauses, delayed packets, duplicate requests, expiry-renew races, predecessor cancellation, leader partitions, clock uncertainty, compaction during reconnect, restore, and shard movement. Model-check election and lock transitions; integration tests must prove protected resources reject stale fencing tokens.

docs.title: Pattern mappings
docs.text:
Service discovery maps instance registration to ephemeral ownership, registry versions to revisions, and endpoint propagation to advisory watches. Its health aggregation, DNS behavior, stale-cache policy, and locality-aware load balancing remain discovery-specific.

Distributed locking maps sessions, CAS, revisioned predecessor queues, and expiry onto exclusive ownership. It adds lock-specific fairness, reentrancy choices, contention controls, and mandatory protected-resource fencing.

A general distributed key-value store can provide linearizable CAS and ordered revisions, but coordination additionally requires carefully specified session expiry, ephemeral cleanup, watch recovery, queue recipes, fencing continuity, and strict operational limits.

docs.title: Interview checklist
docs.text:
• What is the revision and linearizability scope?
  • Which state is durable, and which state is session-owned and ephemeral?
  • How does a client recover a watch after compaction?
  • Does each waiter watch one predecessor or create a broadcast herd?
  • What happens to renewals and elections during quorum loss?
  • Which external resource validates fencing tokens, and how does it persist the high-watermark?
  • Which limits prevent one namespace, session, watch, or hot key from exhausting the quorum?

docs.title: Handoff exercise
docs.text:
Owner A holds token 41. The authority grants token 42 to B, but B has not yet contacted the protected store. The store's highest recorded token is still 41. Must the store reject A's next write?

Check which authority the store can observe

No. A maximum-seen guard can accept 41 while 41 is still its highest token. If the promised handoff must revoke A before B begins work, install 42 at the protected store and obtain a durable acknowledgment before declaring takeover complete. If the installation times out, the authority must preserve the uncertain handoff state and retry or query it safely. Issuing a larger number in a separate coordination service does not atomically update the external store.

docs.title: Pattern: Feed Generation
docs.text: Feed generation combines eligibility, retrieval, ranking, and pagination under extreme graph skew. In a network of 100 million users, ordinary creators may have hundreds of followers while one celebrity has 50 million. One universal strategy either amplifies writes catastrophically or makes reads perform unbounded work.

docs.title: Choosing push, pull, or hybrid
docs.text:
Use fan-out-on-write for bounded follower sets and latency-sensitive reads; use fan-out-on-read for high-fan-out publishers or rapidly changing ranking; use hybrid for a skewed social graph. Avoid universal push when one post creates millions of writes and universal pull when users follow thousands of sources.

Model Read cost Write cost Main risk push low followers per post celebrity amplification pull followed sources low expensive merge at read hybrid bounded merge bounded push dual-path consistency

Canonical post storage owns bodies, author, visibility, and deletion. Inbox rows are pointers such as (user_id, post_id, candidate_time, reason, source_version), never duplicated post bodies. Reads recheck blocks, audience, deletion, and current post state because materialized eligibility can become stale.

flowchart LR
    P[Publish] --> D[(Canonical posts)]
    D --> Q[(Fan-out log)]
    Q --> F[Fan-out workers]
    F --> I[(User inboxes)]
    R[Feed read] --> I
    R --> H[Pull-author post lists]
    I --> M[K-way merge and dedupe]
    H --> M
    M --> V[Policy and ranking]

docs.title: Worked fan-out threshold
docs.text:
The threshold should come from capacity and latency rather than a label such as "celebrity." Let:

F = follower count
p = expected posts per publisher per second
cw = cost of one inbox insertion
q = follower feed reads per second attributable to this publisher
cr = cost to retrieve and merge one pull candidate

Push work per second is F*p*cw; pull work is approximately q*cr, adjusted for cache hits and the number of posts fetched. Push when its work fits both the per-post completion SLO and reserved worker capacity:

F <= min(workerWriteBudget / (p*cw), completionSLO * effectiveWritesPerSecond)

Suppose workers sustain 200,000 inserts/s for this tenant, a post must fan out in 30 seconds, and 25% headroom is reserved. The per-post threshold is 200,000 * 0.75 * 30 = 4.5 million followers. If a creator posts four times during that interval, divide the threshold by four: about 1.125 million. A global threshold is still crude; include publisher rate, follower activity, inbox write cost, cacheability, and regional placement.

Economic comparison can lower it further. If a 500,000-follower creator posts twice/day, push performs one million inserts/day. If only 2% of followers open the app and a cached author timeline serves those reads, pull may be cheaper. Conversely, a highly active follower base may favor push. Recalculate from rolling estimates with hysteresis: enter pull mode above 1.2 million effective followers, return to push below 800,000 for seven days. This prevents oscillation.

flowchart TD
    S[Publisher statistics] --> C[Estimate push and pull cost]
    C --> B{Push within budget and SLO?}
    B -->|yes| P[Push mode]
    B -->|no| L[Pull mode]
    P --> H{Upper threshold crossed?}
    L --> J{Lower threshold sustained?}
    H -->|yes| L
    J -->|yes| P
    H -->|no| KeepPush[Keep push mode]
    J -->|no| KeepPull[Keep pull mode]

Fan-out work is idempotent on (user_id, post_id). Partition jobs into follower-page ranges so retries do not restart 50 million writes. Prioritize active recipients; inactive users can be filled lazily or rely on pull. Record high-water marks per job and expose completion lag.

docs.title: K-way merge
docs.text:
Pull mode reads each followed source as a list sorted by (candidate_time desc, post_id desc). A K-way merge avoids loading and sorting every post:

select at most sourceBudget sources using the retrieval policy
fetch first pages within fetchBudget and deadline
heapify first available items ordered by (time, postId)
popped = 0
while heap not empty and output.size < candidateBudget:
  if popped == popBudget or deadline elapsed: break
  item = heap.pop()
  popped += 1
  if unseen(item.postId): output.add(item)
  advance within the already fetched source page
  fetch another page only if fetchBudget and deadline permit
  push next available item, if any
return output and source positions with omitted-source status

With K sources and P popped entries, heap work is O(K + P log K) with heapify, plus source fetches. P may exceed the N unique emitted candidates because of duplicates. Bound both popped entries and fetches, not only output size. Batch source reads and apply deadlines; one slow author list must not hold the entire feed. Overfetch because policy and ranking discard candidates: if historical pass-through is 40% and the page needs 20, start near ceil(20/0.4)=50, plus safety margin, then perform at most one bounded refill.

Hybrid reads merge the materialized inbox with pull-author timelines using the same heap. A post can appear through both paths during migration, so deduplicate by canonical post ID before ranking. Candidate time must have one defined meaning, such as publish time; mixing fan-out insertion time with publish time causes retries to reorder old posts.

docs.title: Ranking and cursor semantics
docs.text:
Retrieval answers "what might be eligible"; policy answers "what may be shown"; ranking answers "in what order." Cheap hard filters run before expensive model inference. The ranker may use affinity, freshness, quality, and diversity, but it should retain a stable unique tie-breaker.

Offset pagination is unstable as new posts arrive. Use an opaque authenticated cursor:

{
  "session":"f-91",
  "snapshot_time":"2026-09-06T10:00:00Z",
  "ranker":"r42",
  "last_score":0.781,
  "last_post_id":"p882",
  "source_positions":{"inbox":"i77","author-9":"a12"},
  "expires_at":"2026-09-06T10:15:00Z"
}

A snapshot-like feed excludes candidates newer than snapshot_time and stores a short-lived candidate-session list or enough source positions to reproduce traversal. It gives stable pages but delays new content. A best-effort feed uses (score, post_id) search-after and can change as features update; document that duplicates are deduplicated client-side or server-side. Never expose raw cursor fields for modification: encode and authenticate them, cap size, and expire them.

Ranking-version changes invalidate score-based continuation. Either pin the session to r42, preserve its candidate order briefly, or return an explicit expired-cursor response that restarts the feed. For ads or compliance insertions, use separate placement state so organic cursor movement remains explainable.

Pinning the ranker version alone does not freeze scores if features change. Preserve the candidate order or feature snapshot as well. Elasticsearch's PIT and search-after contract stabilizes index state, not an external reranker's live features. Recheck current authorization on every page even when the ranking snapshot is old (accessed 2026-09-08).

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Feed API
    participant I as Inbox
    participant P as Pull timelines
    participant R as Ranker
    C->>A: page(cursor)
    A->>I: candidates after inbox position
    A->>P: candidates after source positions
    A->>A: K-way merge and dedupe
    A->>R: bounded eligible candidates
    R-->>A: stable scored page
    A-->>C: posts and authenticated cursor

docs.title: Hybrid migration
docs.text:
Mode changes require an overlap protocol. For push-to-pull, record cutover publish sequence T. Keep fan-out for posts through T; route posts after T only to the pull timeline. Until the through-T fan-out watermark is complete, readers also pull the uncovered pre-T interval and deduplicate. After that, combine inbox through T with pull after T. Keep the old inbox history until its product retention and all dependent cursors expire, or serve the same history from pull before cleanup.

For pull-to-push, record T, start fan-out after T, and backfill a bounded history if the product requires it. During backfill, readers continue pulling posts through T and read inbox entries after T. They also pull the post-T interval above the verified fan-out watermark, because newly published posts may not yet be materialized. Deduplicate that overlap by post ID. Verify backfill coverage, sampled IDs, and live fan-out progress before ending migration overlap; retain the ordinary lag fallback for future delayed jobs. A mode field without an epoch is unsafe because cached readers and delayed jobs disagree; store (mode, epoch, cutover_sequence).

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Push
    Push --> PushToPull: threshold crossed at T
    PushToPull --> Pull: jobs and cursors before T drained
    Pull --> PullToPush: lower threshold sustained at T2
    PullToPush --> Push: backfill verified and overlap elapsed

Follow and unfollow changes have similar temporal semantics. An unfollow or block must take effect at read time immediately, while asynchronous cleanup removes old pointers. A new follow can expose only future posts or a bounded backfill according to product policy. Relationship versions prevent delayed fan-out from recreating entries after an unfollow.

docs.title: Deletion, privacy, and cache behavior
docs.text:
Deleting a post atomically writes a canonical tombstone and an outbox intent for invalidation. A relay may deliver that intent more than once, so consumers invalidate idempotently. Feed reads filter it immediately even if millions of inbox pointers remain. Cleanup is idempotent and low priority after visibility is blocked. Account blocks and audience changes use the same defense: authoritative checks or a fresh policy cache precede response serialization.

Cache candidate IDs, not fully authorized responses, unless the key includes viewer identity and policy version. Celebrity pull timelines cache well; personalized final pages often do not. Prevent cache stampedes with request coalescing, soft TTL, jitter, and stale-while-revalidate only when policy permits. Never serve stale content after a block merely to protect latency.

docs.title: Failure semantics and operations
docs.text:
Failure Behavior fan-out worker retries idempotent (user, post) insertion and range checkpoint fan-out lags direct-author fallback or explicit freshness degradation post is deleted canonical tombstone filters reads; cleanup follows asynchronously follow or block races relationship version controls eligibility celebrity spike pull path, coalesced cache, bounded candidates, and admission control one source times out deadline and documented partial-source behavior ranker unavailable approved deterministic fallback, not random order

For fan-out lag, inspect publish-log age by partition, worker throughput, inbox throttling, and hot publishers. Stop low-value backfills, prioritize recent posts for active users, and activate pull fallback at a known source sequence. Do not blindly add workers when the inbox store is saturated. For inbox-store loss, rebuild from canonical posts, graph history, relationship versions, and deletion tombstones; shadow-read rebuilt buckets before routing traffic.

For a ranker incident, pin or disable the failing model version and use a deterministic recency-plus-quality fallback. Preserve cursor compatibility or expire affected sessions explicitly. For a celebrity event, prewarm the author timeline, increase cache TTL within freshness bounds, coalesce misses, and cap per-viewer candidates before shedding optional enrichment.

Monitor feed freshness, publish-to-inbox completion, fan-out amplification, writes per publisher, active-recipient ratio, pull sources per read, heap candidates, candidate-to-served ratio, policy rejection, deduplication rate, hot publisher QPS, cache hit and age, ranking latency, cursor expiry, and rebuild divergence.

Capacity planning should model peak work by path rather than average feed QPS. For push, multiply peak publications by effective followers, replication factor, index overhead, and retry allowance; reserve enough queue retention to survive the longest planned inbox outage. For pull, multiply peak reads by pull publishers consulted, pages fetched per publisher, and overfetch ratio. Then budget ranker calls and canonical policy lookups separately. Load tests must preserve the heavy-tailed follower graph: uniformly generated publishers hide celebrity partitions, cache stampedes, and oversized fan-out jobs. Exercise a publish burst while one inbox shard is throttled, confirm queues stay within retention, and verify that fallback begins at an explicit sequence without duplicate or missing candidates.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Derive fan-out mode from write capacity, activity, publication rate, and cache economics.
  • Store pointers and keep posts, relationships, and policy canonical.
  • Bound K-way merge sources, candidates, refills, and deadlines.
  • Define snapshot or best-effort pagination and ranker-version behavior.
  • Migrate modes with sequence cutovers, overlap, deduplication, and hysteresis.
  • Make deletion and blocks effective before asynchronous cleanup.
  • Preserve canonical data and tombstones sufficient to rebuild inboxes.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• How is the fan-out threshold calculated and adapted?
  • Why is K-way merge preferable to concatenating and sorting all posts?
  • How are deletes and blocks enforced before cleanup completes?
  • What consistency does the cursor provide as ranking changes?
  • How does a publisher migrate between push and pull without gaps?
  • Can inboxes be rebuilt, and from which canonical data?

docs.title: Pattern: Handling Contention
docs.text: Contention appears when concurrent operations coordinate on the same logical resource. More replicas do not solve a hot lock because the invariant still needs one authoritative decision. A concert onsale illustrates the problem: 50,000 users attempt to buy 1,000 seats in one minute, and thousands may select the same front-row seat. The design must preserve "no oversell" while bounding retries, queueing, and unfair advantage.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use optimistic concurrency when conflicts are rare, pessimistic locks for short high-conflict transactions, serialization for a very hot key, and escrow when divisible rights can be partitioned. Avoid distributed locks when a database constraint suffices. Avoid adding a queue if users require immediate decisions but queue delay has no bound; admission control must accompany serialization.

Mechanism Fits Loses when compare-and-set/version rare conflicts retry storms under high conflict row lock short local transaction lock convoy and deadlock unique constraint uniqueness cannot express richer policy alone single-key command queue hot key, ordered decisions one-key throughput ceiling escrow/reservation pools divisible finite capacity rights become stranded waiting room demand far above capacity fairness and token operations become product-critical

docs.title: State the invariant and owner
docs.text:
For assigned seating, a database unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) is the final defense: at most one live claim owns a seat. For general admission, the invariant is sold + active_holds <= capacity. Place that check and mutation in one transactional owner. Caches, queue positions, and availability counters are hints; none may authorize the final sale independently.

Make hold lifecycle explicit: AVAILABLE -> HELD -> SOLD, with HELD -> AVAILABLE on expiry. Use server or database time and store an absolute expiry. A payment response arriving after expiry is not automatically failure; it is a late outcome requiring an explicit policy such as honor from a grace pool, reacquire capacity, or refund.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Available
    Available --> Held: conditional claim
    Held --> Sold: payment confirmed before deadline
    Held --> Available: server-time expiry
    Held --> Reconciling: payment outcome unknown
    Reconciling --> Sold: verified success and capacity honored
    Reconciling --> Available: verified failure
    Reconciling --> Refunding: late success cannot be honored

docs.title: Queueing explains collapse
docs.text:
Contention is often a queueing problem disguised as a database problem. If one reservation owner makes 2,000 decisions/s and 20,000 commands/s arrive, backlog grows by 18,000/s. In ten seconds, 180,000 requests wait. Faster retries add work without adding decision capacity.
