Utilization near 100% produces nonlinear waiting time. For an illustrative M/M/1 queue with service rate mu = 2,000/s, arrival rate lambda = 1,800/s, utilization is rho = 0.9; expected time in system is 1 / (mu - lambda) = 5 ms. At 1,980/s, rho = 0.99 and expected time rises to 50 ms. Real arrivals and service times need not follow M/M/1 assumptions. Pauses and burst correlation can make tails much worse, while less-variable service can reduce waiting; use the model to identify pressure, not predict a universal percentile. Operate below saturation and reject excess work before it consumes the constrained tier.

Little's Law, L = lambda * W, relates stable mean occupancy to mean residence time, not p99. At 2,000 completions/s and a 250 ms mean, average occupancy is 500 requests. If 20,000 requests are concurrently in that stage at the same completion rate, mean residence is 10 seconds. Admission bounds still need burst and tail tests; a percentile target is not a substitute for the mean.

docs.title: Conflict amplification
docs.text:
Optimistic concurrency reads version v, computes an update, then executes UPDATE ... WHERE version = v. This is efficient when collisions are uncommon. Under a flash crowd, losers re-read and retry, creating conflict amplification: physical attempts divided by successful logical operations.

Suppose 1,000 clients race for one remaining seat. One succeeds and 999 fail. If every loser retries three times without learning the seat is gone, the database sees about 3,997 writes or conditional attempts for one success. Amplification is nearly 4,000x. Exponential backoff only spreads waste; it does not create another seat. Return a definitive 409 unavailable and prohibit retries for terminal conflicts.

For a counter with 100 units, bounded retry can help while inventory remains. Use jitter and a retry budget, for example at most two retries within 150 ms. Re-read authoritative state before each retry. Stop immediately on sold out, deadline expiry, or admission-token invalidity. Track attempts per success; rising amplification is an early overload signal.

flowchart TD
    R[Command arrives] --> A{Valid admission token?}
    A -- no --> X[Reject before database]
    A -- yes --> C{Conflict rate below threshold?}
    C -- yes --> O[CAS with bounded retry]
    C -- no --> Q[Route to keyed serializer]
    O --> S{Succeeded?}
    S -- yes --> H[Return durable hold]
    S -- terminal conflict --> U[Return unavailable]
    S -- transient and budget remains --> O
    Q --> S

docs.title: Locks, serialization, and fencing
docs.text:
A row lock works when the transaction is short and entirely inside one database. Acquire locks in a stable order to reduce deadlocks, do not call payment while holding the lock, and set a lock timeout shorter than the request deadline. Pessimistic locking converts repeated conflicts into waiting, but a convoy can still exhaust connection pools.

A keyed command queue gives one logical owner ordered access to an event, section, or inventory bucket. Persist commands before processing so owner failure does not lose accepted requests. The owner can batch compatible operations, answer immediately when sold out, and publish authoritative results. This simplifies contention but does not exceed one owner's throughput for that key.

Ownership must be fenced. A lease alone is unsafe: owner A can pause past expiry, owner B can acquire the lease, and A can resume and write. Assign a monotonically increasing fencing token on acquisition. Every protected write includes the token, and storage rejects a token lower than the latest accepted value.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Owner A token 41
    participant L as Lease service
    participant B as Owner B token 42
    participant D as Inventory store
    A->>L: acquire event owner
    L-->>A: token 41
    A--xA: long pause
    B->>L: acquire after expiry
    L-->>B: token 42
    B->>D: claim with token 42
    D-->>B: accepted
    A->>D: stale claim with token 41
    D-->>A: rejected as fenced

The token must be checked by the resource being protected. A distributed lock that issues tokens but a database that ignores them does not prevent stale writes. Database transaction isolation and constraints remain the final correctness boundary.

With maximum-seen fencing, token 41 may still be accepted before token 42 reaches storage. If takeover must revoke the old worker immediately, install 42 before reporting takeover complete. etcd's atomic KV guarantees do not extend an atomic transaction to an external inventory store (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Escrow and preallocated rights
docs.text:
Escrow turns one global counter into independently spendable rights. For 10,000 general-admission tickets and 10 reservation partitions, allocate 1,000 rights to each. A partition can create a hold locally only while its balance remains positive. The global invariant holds because total rights never exceeds capacity.

Rights can become stranded: partition A has 400 idle rights while partition B is sold out. Rebalance using a durable transfer protocol. First freeze or decrement rights at the donor, creating transfer ID T; only then credit the receiver idempotently. Never credit before the debit commits. Periodically reconcile available rights + active holds + sold + rights in transfer = capacity.

Choose pool size from skew and transfer latency. If a busy partition consumes 200 rights/s and redistribution takes five seconds, retain at least 1,000 rights of local headroom to avoid stalling. Small pools balance efficiently but transfer frequently; large pools reduce coordination but strand more capacity. A central reserve of perhaps 10% can absorb skew without clawing rights back from every partition.

Escrow fits divisible capacity, not assigned seat A10. Assigned resources can instead be partitioned by section, while the unique seat claim remains authoritative.

docs.title: Virtual waiting room
docs.text:
When demand exceeds reservation capacity by an order of magnitude, place a waiting room before expensive authentication, catalog fan-out, and database work. It controls admission rate rather than merely displaying a queue.

  1. On arrival, create a durable or verifiable queue entry bound to account, event, and device risk signals.
  2. Apply the declared fairness policy: FIFO by trusted arrival, randomized batches, or explicit priority windows.
  3. Admit at a rate derived from reservation completion and error signals, not a fixed optimistic number.
  4. Issue a short-lived signed token containing event, account, admission epoch, expiry, and nonce.
  5. At the reservation gateway, verify signature and claims, enforce per-account concurrency, and consume or rate-limit the nonce.

If the reservation tier safely completes 1,500 commands/s, start admission below that, perhaps 1,200/s, and adjust slowly. With 50,000 arrivals and 1,200/s admission, draining the initial crowd takes roughly 42 seconds before accounting for think time. Show an interval, not a false exact rank, when users may abandon or entries may be weighted.

Fairness is a product policy, not an implementation detail. Strict global FIFO requires a trusted total order and creates pressure around clock accuracy and geographic latency. Randomized admission can reduce latency advantage but feels less predictable. Priority access must be explicit and auditable. Bind tokens to identity and enforce quotas so bots cannot open thousands of queue positions.

docs.title: Reservation algorithm
docs.text:
For assigned seating, process this durable command:

  1. Validate admission token, account limit, show state, and idempotency key.
  2. Read an existing result by (account_id, operation, idempotency_key) and compare its canonical request hash. Return the saved result only for the same request; reject key reuse with different seats or show.
  3. Begin a short transaction. Evaluate expiry using authoritative decision time after acquiring any required ownership lock, not a stale timestamp captured before waiting.
  4. Insert a hold with unique (show_id, seat_id) and expiry, or conditionally change an expired hold.
  5. Insert the idempotency result under a uniqueness constraint and the outbox event in the same transaction. If a concurrent identical request wins the key, roll back this entire attempt and return its committed result; the preliminary read in step 2 is only a fast path.
  6. Commit, then return the hold ID and server deadline.

Never call the payment provider inside this transaction. Payment uses the hold ID and its own idempotency key. A reconciler queries unknown provider outcomes and applies a conditional state transition based on hold version and policy.

docs.title: Failures and overload
docs.text:
Failure Rule response lost after claim same idempotency key returns the existing hold payment succeeds after hold expiry compensate/refund or honor from a reserved grace pool owner crashes durable commands replay; fenced successor owns a higher epoch waiting room overload shed before the reservation tier and preserve existing admitted users clock disagreement database or authoritative server time controls expiry escrow receiver retries transfer transfer ID makes credit idempotent database slows lower admission rate; do not allow client retries to multiply load

Reserve capacity for expiration, reconciliation, and payment callbacks; accepting holds at 100% database capacity can prevent holds from completing or releasing. Under severe overload, prioritize already-issued holds and payment finalization over new browsing and claims. Return stable outcomes: 409 for unavailable inventory, 429 for account or admission limits, and 503 when authoritative decisions cannot safely be made.

docs.title: Migration path
docs.text:
1. Begin with a transactional unique constraint or conditional counter.
  2. Add idempotency, short transactions, and bounded retries.
  3. Instrument conflict amplification, lock wait, and sold-out attempts.
  4. Add per-event admission and waiting-room tokens before a known onsale.
  5. Serialize exceptionally hot keys or allocate escrow rights where capacity is divisible.
  6. Introduce fencing before moving ownership dynamically.

Migrate gradually. Shadow a waiting-room decision without enforcing it, validate admission rates, then enable it for a small event. When moving from a global counter to escrow, initialize rights from an authoritative snapshot, pause allocations briefly or replay changes after a watermark, verify conservation, and only then let partitions spend rights. Keep a kill switch that stops new holds while allowing payment completion.

docs.title: Observability and verification
docs.text:
Measure arrival, admission, success, and rejection rates separately; queue age; lock wait; deadlocks; CAS attempts per success; hot-key distribution; active holds; expiry lag; escrow rights by partition; fencing rejections; payment unknowns; and waiting-room token abuse. Alert on growing attempt amplification and oldest command age before the database saturates.

Test response loss after commit, lease expiry during a pause, duplicate escrow transfer, late payment success, database clock boundaries, and owner failover under load. Continuously verify conservation equations and unique constraints. Reconciliation is a safety net, not permission to weaken the write path.

docs.title: L5 and L6 guidance
docs.text:
An L5 design should state the invariant, choose the authoritative owner, compare optimistic and pessimistic approaches based on expected conflict, define idempotency and hold expiry, and calculate the admitted rate and queue bound. It should explain why retries stop on terminal conflicts and why payment stays outside the seat-lock transaction.

An L6 design should model conflict amplification and degraded capacity, define fairness as product policy, fence dynamic owners, and show conservation for escrow transfers. It should prioritize in-flight customers during overload, specify migration and rollback controls, and connect admission rate to live queue age and database health. Senior judgment appears in reducing the scope of coordination instead of hiding it behind more replicas.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• What invariant prevents oversell at the final write?
  • Why does optimistic retry collapse at extreme contention?
  • Is strict FIFO required, and what does it cost?
  • How are payment and hold expiry reconciled?
  • Where is a fencing token enforced?
  • How do escrow transfers preserve total capacity?

docs.title: Pattern: Large Blob Storage
docs.text: Large blobs have different economics and access paths from metadata. A video platform that ingests 2 PB/day, serves originals and renditions globally, and supports resumable upload and deletion cannot treat a 20 GB video like a database row. Bytes need a throughput-oriented object store; ownership, lifecycle, authorization, and processing state need a transactional metadata system.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use object storage for large, mostly immutable bytes, a metadata database for ownership and state, and a CDN for repeated delivery. Avoid storing blobs in relational rows at scale, proxying all bytes through application servers, and treating a public URL as authorization. A database BLOB can still be reasonable for small objects when atomicity matters more than independent scaling.

Choice Benefit Tradeoff direct signed upload removes API bandwidth bottleneck client protocol and abandoned parts multipart upload resumable, parallel chunks manifest and cleanup content hash integrity and optional deduplication hashing cost and privacy risk from global deduplication CDN edge latency and origin egress reduction invalidation and signed access storage tiers lower retention cost restore delay and retrieval fees erasure coding lower durable-storage overhead than replication more reads and CPU during repair

docs.title: Baseline architecture
docs.text:
1. The metadata API creates an upload record but does not carry the bytes.
  2. It issues scoped multipart URLs for one object key and a short expiry.
  3. The client uploads parts directly and records each part checksum and returned tag.
  4. Finalization verifies the manifest, total size, and root checksum before accepting the asset for processing. Publication waits for the required processing checks to succeed.
  5. A durable event starts malware scanning, media probing, and rendition generation.
  6. Immutable, versioned objects are delivered through a CDN.
  7. Lifecycle and deletion workers reconcile metadata with physical storage.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Metadata API
    participant O as Object store
    participant W as Processor
    C->>A: create upload(size, root checksum)
    A-->>C: upload ID and signed part URLs
    loop Every part
        C->>O: PUT part with checksum
        O-->>C: part tag
    end
    C->>A: finalize(upload ID, manifest)
    A->>O: complete and verify object
    A->>W: durable processing event
    W->>O: write immutable renditions

Metadata states are PENDING_UPLOAD -> FINALIZING -> PROCESSING -> READY | FAILED, followed by DELETING -> DELETED when eligible. Only READY is visible. Object keys must be access-controlled; unguessability alone is not authorization. Signed URLs are short-lived and scoped to a method, object, content length where supported, and optionally checksum.

docs.title: Worked multipart upload
docs.text:
Choose part size from object size, object-store part-count limits, retry cost, memory, and desired concurrency. Suppose a 20 GiB file uses 64 MiB parts:

parts = ceil(20 * 1024 MiB / 64 MiB) = 320
parallelism = 8
ideal upload time at 400 Mbit/s = 20 * 2^30 B * 8 / 400,000,000 bit/s
                               = about 429.5 s

The client persists {upload_id, object_key, part_size, completed_parts} locally. Each worker reads one part, calculates SHA-256 while streaming, and sends part_number, Content-Length, and checksum. It retries only failed parts with exponential backoff and jitter. A resume call lists server-accepted parts and compares both length and checksum rather than trusting local state.

Finalization is a business-level idempotent operation:

finalize(uploadId, expectedVersion):
  short transaction: validate tenant, manifest hash and expectedVersion
  if already finalized with same manifest: return existing assetId
  CAS PENDING_UPLOAD to FINALIZING; persist manifest and object key
  outside transaction: reconcile existing completed object first
  if not already completed:
    paginate listParts for verification against saved part receipts
    require verified size and part checksums match declared manifest
    completeMultipartUpload(saved manifest, conditional create)
  verify completed object version, checksum and size
  transaction: CAS FINALIZING to PROCESSING; append AssetCreated once
  return assetId

The object store may expose a multipart ETag that is not the SHA-256 of the complete object. Never infer integrity from an undocumented ETag format. Store an explicit whole-object checksum or a checksum tree root.

S3's multipart contract says completed parts no longer exist, listings are paginated, and the completion manifest should come from saved upload receipts, not a listing. If completion succeeds but its response is lost, reconcile the exact immutable object and upload metadata before retrying; absence of the upload ID is not proof of failure. FINALIZING recovery must be leased/fenced, and no database row lock spans remote I/O (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Checksum tree
docs.text:
A checksum tree verifies parts independently and permits parallel recomputation. For a new protocol, separate leaf and parent domains: hash each part as SHA256(0x00 || part_bytes) and each parent as SHA256(0x01 || left_hash || right_hash), duplicating or promoting the final unpaired leaf according to one documented convention. The client sends leaf hashes and the root; the service stores the root in canonical metadata.

flowchart BT
    P1[Part 1 hash] --> H12[Hash 1 and 2]
    P2[Part 2 hash] --> H12
    P3[Part 3 hash] --> H34[Hash 3 and 4]
    P4[Part 4 hash] --> H34
    H12 --> R[Root checksum]
    H34 --> R

For four 64 MiB parts with hashes h1..h4, compute a = H(0x01 || h1 || h2), b = H(0x01 || h3 || h4), and root = H(0x01 || a || b). During repair, a mismatching root triggers comparison down the tree to identify the corrupt part without rereading healthy replicas. Bind tree metadata to algorithm, part size, object length, and leaf count; otherwise two implementations can calculate incompatible roots.

Encryption must not invalidate the integrity model. Transport checksums protect upload transit. A plaintext content hash detects logical equality but exposes confirmation attacks when used for cross-tenant deduplication. A ciphertext checksum verifies stored bytes. A safe default is per-tenant deduplication, server-side encryption with a key reference in metadata, and separate plaintext and ciphertext integrity fields where the threat model permits them.

docs.title: Range reads and media delivery
docs.text:
Large-object clients should not fetch an entire object to seek or resume. A download endpoint validates authorization, resolves the immutable version, and either redirects to a signed CDN URL or serves a signed origin request. It supports Range: bytes=start-end, returns 206 Partial Content, Content-Range, Accept-Ranges: bytes, and a stable ETag. An unsatisfiable range returns 416 with the object length.

For a 10 GiB object and Range: bytes=1048576-2097151, return exactly 1 MiB. Cap the number of ranges and reject pathological multi-range requests that amplify origin work. If compression changes byte offsets, store a precompressed representation as a separate immutable object rather than applying dynamic compression to arbitrary ranges. Clients send a strong version validator in If-Range. A mismatch makes the server return the full representation instead of the requested partial range; the client must restart or replace its download, never append that 200 body to old bytes.

flowchart LR
    C[Authorized client] --> E[CDN edge]
    E -->|cache hit range| C
    E -->|cache miss| S[Signed origin request]
    S --> O[(Immutable object)]
    O --> S
    S --> E
    M[Metadata API] -->|short-lived signed URL| C

Use versioned paths such as /asset/{asset_id}/rendition/{version} so normal publication never requires purge. The CDN cache key must include the rendition identity and every representation-changing dimension, but not incidental authorization query parameters. Signed cookies suit many segments under one entitlement; signed URLs suit one object. Keep origin private so bypassing the CDN does not bypass access control. Track byte hit ratio in addition to request hit ratio because a few large misses dominate egress.

Validate authorization before every cache hit if immediate revocation is promised. Merely stopping issuance of signed URLs leaves existing bearer URLs usable until expiry. Otherwise state that revocation is bounded by token lifetime and cache policy; purge alone is not proof that every edge has stopped serving bytes.

docs.title: Erasure coding and durability
docs.text:
Three full replicas cost 3x raw capacity and make reads and repair simple. A Reed-Solomon 10+4 layout splits data into ten data shards and four parity shards, stores them across distinct failure domains, and reconstructs the object from any ten shards. Its raw overhead is 14/10 = 1.4x, excluding metadata and temporary repair space.

For a 1 GiB stripe group, each shard is roughly 102.4 MiB. Loss of up to four shards remains recoverable, but degraded reads fetch more fragments and consume decode CPU. Durability depends on independent placement and repair time, not merely parity count. Never place all fragments in one rack or power domain. A placement policy should select region, zone, rack, then host; a repair controller should rate-limit reconstruction so a zone loss does not collapse foreground traffic.

Use replication for hot small objects, write-heavy staging, or low-latency reads. Convert sealed, colder objects to erasure coding asynchronously. During conversion, write and verify the coded generation, atomically switch the metadata generation, then garbage-collect replicas. Keep enough free capacity for the largest credible rebuild. Scrub stored checksums continuously, prioritize repairs by remaining fault tolerance, and test loss of an entire placement domain.

docs.title: Deletion lifecycle
docs.text:
Deletion is a distributed workflow, not one DELETE call. Define the user-visible guarantee separately from physical erasure and backup expiry.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> READY
    READY --> DELETING: authorized delete
    DELETING --> HIDDEN: tombstone committed
    HIDDEN --> PURGING: retention hold cleared
    PURGING --> DELETED: all objects confirmed absent
    note right of PURGING
      Retry incomplete purges in this state.
    end note
    DELETED --> [*]

An authorized delete transaction writes a tombstone and outbox record. Reads reject the asset immediately, CDN tokens stop being issued, and policy filters block any stale index or inbox entry. The purge worker enumerates the original, every rendition, incomplete multipart upload, replica or erasure generation, CDN key, and derived analysis artifact from an asset manifest. Deletes are idempotent: absence counts as success. It records per-location evidence and retries transient failures.

Legal holds pause physical purge without restoring visibility. Versioned object stores require deleting every version and delete marker, not only the current version. Replication queues can resurrect data if a stale create arrives after delete, so both events carry monotonically increasing asset versions and destinations retain tombstones through maximum replay age. Backups expire by documented retention; the product should say "unavailable immediately, purged from active storage within 24 hours, expired from backups within 30 days" only when entitlement checks enforce that visibility boundary, rather than promise instantaneous physical destruction.

A daily reconciler starts from both directions. Metadata-to-storage checks that every READY asset has its declared generation. Storage-to-metadata inventory finds unreferenced objects older than a safety delay. It quarantines before deleting when ownership is ambiguous. Report deletion age by stage and page on records beyond the contractual deadline.

docs.title: Failure semantics and operations
docs.text:
Failure Recovery interrupted part upload list verified parts and resume; expire and abort abandoned uploads finalize response lost idempotent finalize returns the same asset processor retry deterministic rendition key and conditional create prevent duplicates metadata committed but blob absent hide asset, mark failed, and reconcile from the outbox corrupt shard checksum identifies it; rebuild from surviving fragments into a new placement CDN serves deleted content deny at entitlement layer, purge as defense in depth, rotate signing key only for broad compromise regional store unavailable fail or route according to explicit residency policy; never silently cross a boundary delete partially completes tombstone remains authoritative while asynchronous retries continue

Operational procedures should be rehearsed. For upload failures, inspect completion latency, object-store error codes, and abandoned-part bytes; disable only the unhealthy region and preserve upload IDs if recovery is possible. For corruption, freeze lifecycle transitions, identify affected generations from checksum alarms, reconstruct to new keys, verify roots, and conditionally switch metadata. For a signing-key leak, revoke the key identifier, shorten cache authorization, issue a replacement, and audit object access; renaming every object is usually unnecessary.

Keep checksum algorithm and root, size, sniffed MIME type, encryption key reference, owner, retention class, object version, placement generation, and processing lineage in metadata. Scan untrusted content before publication. Measure orphan bytes, checksum failures, finalize latency, processing age, repair backlog, CDN byte hit ratio, origin egress, storage overhead, incomplete upload age, and deletion completion age.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Define maximum object size, part limits, retry budget, and finalization idempotency.
  • Distinguish transport, plaintext, ciphertext, and tree checksums.
  • Make object names immutable and CDN authorization explicit.
  • Specify byte-range behavior, version validators, and abuse limits.
  • Choose replication or erasure coding from latency, repair, and failure-domain requirements.
  • Inventory every derivative and version in deletion scope.
  • Test reconciliation, restore, corruption repair, regional isolation, and expired credentials.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• Why are metadata and bytes separate sources with different semantics?
  • How is an upload resumed and finalized exactly once at the business level?
  • How does the checksum tree isolate a corrupt part?
  • When does 10+4 erasure coding lose to three replicas?
  • What does deletion guarantee while backups still retain bytes?
  • How do range requests and signed CDN access prevent cross-tenant exposure?

docs.title: Pattern: Long-Running Tasks
docs.text: Long-running work outlives an HTTP request and requires durable acceptance, progress, cancellation, retry, and result retention. Exporting a tenant's 2 TB audit history may take hours, cross deployments, and use substantial database, network, CPU, and object-storage capacity. The API should expose a job resource, while a scheduler and leased workers execute bounded, restartable units.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use a job resource and durable queue when work exceeds request deadlines, needs scheduling, or consumes constrained workers. Keep fast operations synchronous when the immediate result simplifies clients. A queue is not capacity: without quotas and fair scheduling, it only converts overload into a growing delay and storage problem.

Concern Contract creation POST /exports with idempotency key returns 202 and job ID status state, phase, processed/estimated units, timestamps, stable error code cancellation requested versus actually stopped result signed short-lived URL and retention timestamp retry immutable chunks, durable checkpoint, and attempt budget

docs.title: Job state and durable acceptance
docs.text:
Persist the job before returning 202. In the same transaction, insert an outbox row that will make the job schedulable. This avoids losing an accepted job if the API crashes before publishing. Repeated creation with the same tenant-scoped idempotency key returns the same job and request fingerprint; reject reuse with materially different parameters.

A useful lifecycle distinguishes intent from reality: QUEUED, RUNNING, CANCEL_REQUESTED, CANCELLED, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, and possibly DELETING. Store state_version so completion and cancellation use conditional transitions. Terminal state must follow one deterministic rule when they race.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Queued
    Queued --> Running: lease acquired
    Queued --> Cancelled: cancellation accepted
    Running --> Running: checkpoint committed
    Running --> CancelRequested: cancellation requested
    CancelRequested --> Cancelled: workers stop and cleanup completes
    Running --> Succeeded: manifest committed
    Running --> Failed: attempt budget exhausted
    Succeeded --> Deleting: retention expires
    Deleting --> [*]: objects removed

Return cancellation as a request, not a claim that execution instantly stopped. If completion commits before cancellation, the job is SUCCEEDED; if cancellation changes the version first, workers cannot publish the result and clean up temporary output. Document this policy so clients do not infer stronger semantics.

docs.title: Architecture and leases
docs.text:
Separate API, scheduler, and workers. The scheduler chooses eligible jobs under priority, tenant quota, and resource capacity. A worker leases a job or chunk for a short interval and heartbeats while progressing. Lease acquisition returns a monotonically increasing fencing token. Every checkpoint and terminal write includes job version and token; stale workers are rejected.

Lease token 12 prevents a paused worker whose lease expired from overwriting progress produced by token 13. The storage layer, not merely the scheduler, must enforce the token. Set lease duration above normal heartbeat jitter but below acceptable recovery time. For a 60-second lease, a heartbeat every 15 seconds allows several missed heartbeats while bounding takeover delay.

flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> API[Job API]
    API --> D[(Job DB and outbox)]
    D --> S[Fair scheduler]
    S --> Q[(Ready queues)]
    Q --> W[Leased workers]
    W --> O[(Object storage)]
    W --> D
    D --> M[Manifest publisher]
    M --> O
    C --> API

docs.title: Worked 2 TB export plan
docs.text:
Define whether 2 TB means source bytes scanned or final bytes produced. Assume 2 TiB of source rows, stable snapshot semantics, 4:1 output compression, and 512 MiB uncompressed chunks. The export contains 2 TiB / 512 MiB = 4,096 chunks and produces about 512 GiB compressed.

Choose chunks by stable key ranges, not page offsets. Offset pagination becomes slower and can duplicate or skip rows as data changes. Capture a database snapshot timestamp or high watermark, then split (tenant_id, event_time, event_id) into non-overlapping ranges. Each query includes the snapshot boundary and range endpoints. If the source cannot retain a six-hour snapshot, export from an immutable lake partition or change-log-backed snapshot rather than holding one database transaction open.

Suppose each worker can scan 80 MiB/s but tenant read policy caps aggregate source load at 1 GiB/s. The lower bound to scan 2 TiB is about 2,097,152 MiB / 1,024 MiB/s = 2,048 seconds, or 34 minutes. Thirteen workers would nominally reach the cap at 1,040 MiB/s, so schedule at most 12 to leave headroom. With per-worker startup, skew, retries, and finalization, a realistic target may be 50 to 60 minutes.

At 12 workers, each processes about 341 chunks. A 512 MiB chunk takes roughly 6.4 seconds at 80 MiB/s, which is short enough for recovery but creates 4,096 object commits. A 4 GiB chunk would reduce object count to 512 but repeat up to about 51.2 seconds of scanning after failure at this rate, plus encoding and upload work. It also reduces the number of independently schedulable units. Tune chunk size against query overhead, retry cost, and object-store limits.

Use attempt-scoped immutable keys such as exports/{job_id}/generation-{generation}/range-{range_id}/attempt-{attempt_id}. Upload with conditional create or pin the returned object version; verify checksum and row count, then commit a checkpoint referencing those exact bytes. A stale worker must not overwrite an already checkpointed object merely because it knows a deterministic key. Publish the final manifest only after all expected ranges are durably complete. Clients see no partial export as successful.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant S as Scheduler
    participant W as Worker token 13
    participant DB as Snapshot source
    participant O as Object storage
    participant J as Job store
    S->>W: range 2048, snapshot T, token 13
    W->>DB: scan bounded key range at T
    DB-->>W: rows
    W->>O: create immutable attempt chunk and checksum
    W->>J: commit checkpoint(range, checksum, token 13)
    J-->>W: accepted
    W-->>S: range complete

docs.title: Checkpoint algorithm
docs.text:
A checkpoint should describe completed immutable work, not an opaque byte percentage. For every range store range ID and boundaries, snapshot watermark, generation, output key, checksum, row count, byte count, fencing token, attempt count, and completion time.

The chunk algorithm is:

  1. Acquire a lease for an uncompleted range and receive fencing token f.
  2. Recheck job state; stop if cancellation is requested.
  3. Read only that range at the job snapshot watermark.
  4. Encode and upload using an immutable, attempt-scoped key for the current generation.
  5. Verify object length/checksum, then conditionally insert checkpoint with token f.
  6. If another valid checkpoint exists, discard or lifecycle-delete duplicate output.
  7. Heartbeat job progress and request another range.
  8. When every expected range is checkpointed, build a manifest from checkpoint rows and conditionally transition the job to SUCCEEDED.

Database checkpoint and object upload cannot share a transaction. Immutable attempt keys, checksums, fenced checkpoint publication, and reconciliation close the gap. A crash after upload but before checkpoint leaves an orphan that a retry can verify/reuse or a sweeper can delete. A crash after checkpoint is safe only while the referenced version remains immutable and retained. S3 multipart documentation describes conditional completion to prevent overwrites; job-store fencing alone cannot protect mutable object keys (accessed 2026-09-08).

Progress can be completed_source_bytes / estimated_source_bytes, but call it an estimate. Also report exact completed ranges and current phase such as snapshotting, scanning, manifesting, or cleanup. Percentages may move slowly under skew and should never regress merely because the estimate changes; expose revised total separately.

docs.title: Fair scheduling
docs.text:
FIFO alone lets one tenant's 1,000 exports monopolize workers. Strict priority alone can starve low-priority jobs. Apply hierarchical scheduling: first enforce global resource capacity, then tenant concurrency and byte-rate quotas, then choose among eligible tenants with weighted deficit round robin (WDRR).

For each tenant maintain a deficit counter. On each scheduling round, add weight * quantum; dispatch a chunk whose estimated cost fits the deficit, subtract its cost, and skip tenants at their concurrency limit. Measuring cost in estimated source bytes is fairer than counting jobs because a 2 TB export and 10 MB export are not equivalent. Age jobs gradually or reserve 10% of slots for the oldest low-priority work to prevent starvation.

Example: tenants A, B, and C have weights 4, 2, and 1 with a 512 MiB quantum. Over a saturated interval they receive roughly 4:2:1 scan bytes, subject to source-specific caps. If A reaches its 1 GiB/s database quota, unused worker capacity flows to B and C. Reserve separate pools when tasks consume incompatible resources, such as database-heavy exports versus CPU-heavy rendering.

Backfill small jobs into capacity gaps without allowing them to delay an already-admitted deadline class. Scheduling policy is externally meaningful; document whether paid priority changes queue order and report queue age by class.

docs.title: Speculative execution for stragglers
docs.text:
Parallel jobs often finish at the speed of the slowest range. A skewed shard, noisy worker, or unusually expensive encoding workload can become a straggler. Speculative execution starts a duplicate attempt only when spare capacity exists and evidence indicates abnormal slowness.

After enough chunks establish a baseline, compute duration normalized by bytes. If a running chunk exceeds, for example, p95 completed duration by 1.5x and is not close to completion, register a second authorized attempt ID under the same current range generation. Do not advance an exclusive fencing epoch while claiming both attempts remain eligible. The first checkpoint from an authorized attempt in the current generation wins atomically; cancellation or takeover invalidates that generation. The loser deletes only its own unreferenced output. Cap speculation at, for example, 5% of workers and disable it during overload.

Suppose 4,095 chunks finish in 40 minutes but one skewed chunk takes another 30 minutes. A speculative copy that finishes in eight minutes reduces completion by 22 minutes. Conversely, duplicating every chunk doubles source load and worsens all jobs. Speculation is tail optimization, not baseline capacity.

Fencing remains necessary: attempts may continue after cancellation or lease loss. Deterministic finalization ensures only one output appears in the manifest even if duplicate objects temporarily exist.

docs.title: Cooperative cancellation
docs.text:
Cancellation flows from job to scheduler to workers. The API conditionally changes RUNNING to CANCEL_REQUESTED; the scheduler stops assigning ranges; workers check the flag between bounded reads, during multipart upload boundaries, and before checkpoint. Long database queries should have query IDs or cancellation handles, but cancellation may not be instantaneous or guaranteed by every dependency.

Bound cancellation latency through work granularity. If a worker checks every 512 MiB and scans at 80 MiB/s, normal detection is under 6.4 seconds plus query cancellation. A single 100 GiB query could ignore cancellation for 21 minutes. Break reads into pages within chunks while keeping chunk output atomic.

On cancellation, abort multipart uploads, delete unreferenced generation objects, release snapshot leases, and preserve an audit record. Cleanup itself can retry durably. Return CANCEL_REQUESTED until workers and cleanup acknowledge; only then report CANCELLED. For irreversible side effects, describe cancellation as "stop future work" rather than rollback.

docs.title: Failure and overload semantics
docs.text:
Failure Outcome API dies after job commit outbox eventually makes the job schedulable worker dies lease expires; another worker resumes uncheckpointed range stale worker resumes fencing token rejects checkpoint and terminal writes cancellation races completion conditional state transition chooses one terminal result progress event is lost status derives from durable checkpoints object upload succeeds before crash retry verifies/reuses object or sweeper deletes orphan poison input bounded retries, stable failure code, diagnostic reference tenant floods queue tenant admission, byte quota, concurrency cap, and fair scheduler

Admission should bound queued cost, not only job count. Ten queued 2 TB exports represent more work than 10,000 tiny reports. Estimate source bytes and reject, defer, or require a scheduled window when tenant queued-byte budget is exceeded. If estimates are unavailable, use conservative limits and refine after sampling.

During source database degradation, lower export concurrency before transactional traffic is affected. Pause low-priority ranges, but keep leases and heartbeats cheap. Under object-store errors, stop scanning if buffered output is bounded; do not accumulate unbounded local temporary files. Autoscale on oldest eligible queue age and resource headroom, not raw queue length alone.

Poison chunks should not retry forever. After perhaps five attempts across distinct workers, mark the range failed and either fail the job or enter operator review, according to whether partial output has value. Stable error codes let clients distinguish invalid input from temporary capacity.

docs.title: Result publication, security, and retention
docs.text:
The final manifest lists snapshot watermark, schema version, ordered chunk keys, checksums, counts, and total bytes. Write it to a temporary key, then atomically expose a final manifest reference in the job transaction. A signed URL should be short-lived and authorized when issued; knowledge of job ID alone must not grant access.

Encryption, tenant isolation, and deletion apply to chunks, manifests, checkpoints, local spill files, and logs. Retention starts from successful publication, not job creation. A deletion workflow removes objects and manifest, records completion, and retries partial cleanup. Object lifecycle rules provide defense in depth but should not be the only evidence of deletion.

docs.title: Migration and evolution
docs.text:
1. Begin with a persisted job and local background pool whose restart scan rediscovers queued or abandoned jobs. An in-memory submission alone cannot satisfy durable acceptance.
  2. Add transactional outbox and durable queue so accepted jobs cannot disappear.
  3. Separate scheduler and workers; lease with fencing and heartbeat.
  4. Split jobs into immutable ranges with checkpoints and a final manifest.
  5. Add tenant quotas, WDRR fairness, cancellation cleanup, and queue-age autoscaling.
  6. Add bounded speculation, multi-region recovery, and cost-aware placement only after measuring stragglers.

To migrate an old monolithic export, create new jobs with chunk-plan version 2 while existing version-1 jobs drain. Persist algorithm version and snapshot semantics on each job. Do not reinterpret old checkpoints with new range boundaries. If a v1 job must migrate, create a new generation, map only provably complete ranges, validate counts/checksums, and retain old output until v2 succeeds.

Schema evolution follows the same rule. Record output schema version in the job and manifest. In-flight jobs finish with their original schema unless a tested transformer exists. Canary new chunking and encoding by tenant, compare source row counts and checksums, then expand. Rollback means routing new jobs to the old planner; already-published manifests remain immutable.

docs.title: Observability and verification
docs.text:
Measure creation and completion rates; queue age and estimated bytes by tenant/priority; scheduler fairness share; active leases; heartbeat misses; lease steals; checkpoint rate; range duration distribution; speculative wins and wasted bytes; cancellation latency; source read throughput; object upload failures; orphan bytes; result age; and cost per job. Avoid high-cardinality job IDs in metric labels; use traces and searchable logs for individual jobs.

Test crashes after each boundary: job commit, lease, upload, checkpoint, and manifest write. Test stale-worker fencing, duplicate creation, snapshot consistency during concurrent writes, skewed ranges, cancellation during query and upload, speculation races, scheduler starvation, source throttling, and lifecycle deletion. Restore from checkpoints in a different worker fleet to prove they are sufficient.

For the 2 TB example, verify conservation: sum of manifest row counts equals snapshot query count, key ranges neither overlap nor leave gaps, all object checksums match, and no object from an older generation enters the final manifest.

docs.title: L5 and L6 guidance
docs.text:
An L5 design should expose a durable job API, calculate chunk count and worker throughput, explain leases and fencing, define checkpoint and manifest atomicity, and give precise cancellation semantics. It should include tenant concurrency limits and recovery from worker death.

An L6 design should schedule by cost rather than job count, protect transactional dependencies under overload, quantify catch-up and snapshot retention, and use speculation only from measured tail behavior. It should define migration across planner/schema versions, result deletion, degraded modes, and fairness policy. Senior judgment appears in choosing bounded work units and explicit state transitions so every crash becomes replayable rather than mysterious.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• What exactly does cancellation guarantee?
  • How is stale-worker output fenced?
  • Can a 2 TB job resume without repeating completed work?
  • How are fairness and priority enforced under overload?
  • What snapshot semantics keep chunks mutually consistent?
  • When does speculative execution help, and when does it amplify load?

docs.title: Pattern: Multi-Step Workflows
docs.text: A workflow coordinates durable state transitions across services without pretending they share one transaction. Checkout may reserve inventory, authorize payment, create shipment, and confirm an order. Each service can fail independently, responses can be lost, and the process may take longer than one request or deployment. Correctness comes from durable state, idempotent commands, explicit uncertainty, and reconciliation.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use a saga when steps cross ownership boundaries, failures need compensation, and progress must survive restarts. Keep operations in one database transaction when they share a storage boundary and require atomicity. Avoid automating an irreversible ambiguous step unless the business defines how to investigate or compensate it.

Style Strength Cost orchestration visible state, timers, and central policy coordinator dependency and coupling to flow choreography loose producer coupling emergent cycles and poor end-to-end visibility database transaction strongest local atomicity limited to one storage boundary manual case handles ambiguous irreversible failure delay and operational expense

docs.title: Model business states, not call order
docs.text:
paymentService.authorize() followed by inventoryService.reserve() is a call chain, not a durable workflow. A workflow instance stores its identity, definition version, current state, state version, business references, step attempts, deadlines, and terminal outcome. States should communicate business truth: RESERVING, PAYMENT_UNKNOWN, COMPENSATING, or REVIEW, rather than generic STEP_3.

Identify the point of no return. Before shipment handoff, payment authorization and inventory holds may be reversible. After a carrier accepts a parcel, "cancel" may mean intercept, return, or refund rather than rollback. Compensation is a new business action with its own failures and audit trail; it does not erase history.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Reserving
    Reserving --> Authorizing: inventory reserved
    Reserving --> Failed: unavailable
    Authorizing --> Confirming: payment authorized
    Authorizing --> Releasing: payment failed
    Authorizing --> PaymentUnknown: timeout
    PaymentUnknown --> Confirming: reconciliation finds success
    PaymentUnknown --> Releasing: reconciliation finds failure
    Confirming --> Completed: order confirmed
    Confirming --> Review: ambiguous shipment result
    Releasing --> Failed: inventory released

docs.title: Durable transition algorithm
docs.text:
Process every event or timer with a transactional compare-and-set on workflow version:

  1. Load the workflow and inbox entry by event ID.
  2. If the event was already consumed, return its recorded result.
  3. Validate that the event is legal in the current state and definition version.
  4. Compute the next state, attempt record, commands, and timers deterministically.
  5. In one local transaction, update state and increment state_version, insert inbox deduplication, append outbox commands, and create or cancel timer rows.
  6. Commit before acknowledging the incoming event.
  7. Let independent relays publish outbox commands and timer notifications at least once.

Use UPDATE workflow SET state=?, state_version=v+1 WHERE id=? AND state_version=v. If zero rows change, another handler won; reload and decide whether the event is now duplicate, stale, or still applicable. Do not hold the transaction open while calling another service.

For example, workflow 891 in AUTHORIZING at version 7 receives PaymentAuthorized(command-42). Its transaction writes state CONFIRMING, version 8, inbox event pay-event-9, outbox ConfirmOrder(command-43), and a confirmation deadline. A crash after commit but before broker acknowledgment redelivers pay-event-9; the inbox turns it into a no-op.

flowchart TD
    E[Event or due timer] --> L[Load workflow and inbox]
    L --> D{Event already consumed?}
    D -- yes --> N[Return recorded result]
    D -- no --> V{Legal for state and version?}
    V -- no --> Q[Quarantine or ignore stale event]
    V -- yes --> C[Compute transition]
    C --> T[Transaction: state + inbox + outbox + timers]
    T --> P[Relay publishes command]
    P --> X[Remote service executes idempotently]

docs.title: Transactional outbox and inbox
docs.text:
The dual-write problem appears if an orchestrator commits state and separately publishes a command. A crash between operations either loses the command or sends it while state remains old. An outbox solves this within one database: business state and an unpublished message commit atomically. A relay polls or streams rows, publishes, then marks progress.

Publication is at least once. If the relay publishes and crashes before marking the row, it publishes again. Therefore the receiver needs an inbox or operation table keyed by stable command ID. The receiver transactionally records the ID with its business mutation and returns the original result on duplicate delivery.

Retention needs care. Do not delete inbox records before the maximum retry and replay horizon unless another permanent business key prevents repetition. Archive outbox rows after broker retention and reconciliation requirements are met. Monitor oldest unpublished row; a healthy orchestrator with a stuck relay still makes no progress.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as Orchestrator DB
    participant R as Outbox relay
    participant B as Broker
    participant P as Payment service
    O->>O: commit state and command-42
    R->>O: read unpublished command-42
    R->>B: publish command-42
    B->>P: deliver command-42
    P->>P: commit inbox and durable authorization intent
    Note over P: external provider call uses stable key after commit
    P-->>B: ack
    R--xR: crash before marking publish
    R->>B: republish command-42
    B->>P: redeliver command-42
    P-->>B: acknowledge existing pending intent
    Note over P: pending intent is not payment success

docs.title: Timers that survive restarts
docs.text:
In-memory sleep and process schedulers lose deadlines during restarts. Store each timer with workflow ID, timer type, due time, expected state/version, and unique timer ID. A scheduler scans due ranges, leases timers, and emits them at least once. The transition handler decides whether a late or duplicate timer still applies.

Partition timers by due-time bucket plus hash of workflow ID. A single ordered index on due_at can become a hot range. For 20 million active payment deadlines spread over 15 minutes, average expiry is about 22,222/s. If the scheduler handles 5,000 timers/s per shard, at least five shards are needed, plus failure headroom. Scan slightly ahead into bounded batches but do not mark a timer complete until its event is durably accepted.

Timer correctness cannot depend on exact firing time. A five-minute deadline means the transition becomes eligible after authoritative time reaches the deadline. The handler compares stored deadline and current database/server time. A delayed timer should still fire; an early or stale timer should not transition the workflow. If an early notification arrives while its timer is still valid, retain or re-arm the durable timer for its due time. Consuming the sole notification as a no-op would otherwise lose the deadline. Cancellation can be represented by status or superseded version rather than requiring race-free physical deletion.

docs.title: Unknown outcomes and late success
docs.text:
A timeout says the caller does not know the outcome; it does not prove failure. Retrying payment with the same provider idempotency key is safe only within the provider's contract. Stripe may prune keys after at least 24 hours, making reuse a new request. Without a valid deduplication guarantee, a negative merchant-reference lookup does not rule out an in-flight or not-yet-visible charge. Record PAYMENT_UNKNOWN, reconcile, and escalate rather than treating absence as permission to charge again (accessed 2026-09-08).

Consider a 10-second client timeout, a two-minute inventory hold, and a payment provider that answers after 130 seconds. By then the hold expired. The workflow needs an ordered policy:

  1. Query whether inventory can be reacquired or whether a small grace allocation exists.
  2. If capacity can be honored, reserve idempotently and continue confirmation.
  3. Otherwise create an idempotent refund or void command.
  4. Keep the order in REFUNDING until provider confirmation; do not label it FAILED while money remains captured.
  5. Escalate to REVIEW after bounded automated attempts.

Late success events carry original command ID and provider reference. The transition table defines their meaning in every reachable state. Ignoring an event merely because the workflow moved on can lose money. Reconciliation should periodically compare local records to provider settlements and inventory ownership, independent of normal event flow.

docs.title: Retry and compensation policy
docs.text:
Classify errors as terminal business failure, transient technical failure, unknown outcome, or invariant violation. Retry transient operations with exponential backoff, full jitter, and a deadline. Keep attempt count and next-attempt time durable. Do not retry card declines or unavailable inventory. Do not execute compensation merely because a request timed out.

Compensations run in reverse dependency order when required, but parallelize independent actions. Each compensation has a command ID, idempotency contract, retry budget, and terminal escalation. A failed inventory release may be retried for hours; a failed refund may require immediate operations visibility. The original workflow terminal state should distinguish FAILED_COMPENSATED, FAILED_COMPENSATION_PENDING, and REVIEW where product semantics warrant it.

docs.title: Quantitative capacity example
docs.text:
Suppose checkout peaks at 8,000 workflows/s. Each successful workflow performs four durable transitions, two timer writes/cancellations, and four outbox inserts. That is roughly 32,000 state transitions/s and 32,000 outbox rows/s, not 8,000 writes/s. If 5% of payment calls become unknown and each causes two reconciliation attempts, add 8,000 * 0.05 * 2 = 800 commands/s plus timer traffic.

At an average 1.5 KiB across state, inbox, and outbox writes per transition, 32,000 transitions/s produce 49.152 MB/s (46.875 MiB/s) logical database writes before indexes, WAL, replication, and compaction. Partition by order_id for local workflow ordering. Provision the relay for catch-up: after a ten-minute outage at 32,000 outbox rows/s, backlog is 19.2 million messages. A relay that resumes at only the normal rate never catches up; at 64,000/s it needs another ten minutes while new traffic continues.

Little's Law also sizes active workflow state. At 8,000 starts/s and a 30-second average completion, about 240,000 workflows are active. A payment incident that raises average completion to ten minutes creates 4.8 million active instances and many due timers, even if start rate is unchanged.

docs.title: Failures and overload
docs.text:
Failure Recovery request times out query step by idempotency key before retry duplicate event inbox or event ID suppresses repeated transition compensation fails retry independently, then operator queue event arrives out of order validate expected workflow state and version orchestrator restarts scan durable timers and resume instances irreconcilable outcome enter REVIEW; never report false success outbox relay stalls state remains durable; alert on outbox age and catch up stale workflow worker conditional state version rejects its transition

During overload, protect transitions that reduce liability: payment result ingestion, refunds, hold releases, and reconciliation should outrank new starts. Apply per-tenant admission before creating workflows. Bound concurrent calls to each dependency with separate pools or bulkheads. If payment is degraded, stop admitting checkouts before millions enter PAYMENT_UNKNOWN.

Expose accepted, pending, completed, failed, compensating, refunding, and review states honestly. A 202 means accepted for processing, not purchased. Provide stable status and safe client retry semantics.

docs.title: Workflow version migration
docs.text:
Persist definition_version on every instance. New workflows use version 3 while running version-2 instances continue with version-2 transition logic. This is safest when old logic can remain deployed until its instances drain.

When migration is necessary, define an explicit mapping from each old state and data shape to a valid new state. Run migration as a conditional transition: read version and state, transform data, update definition and state version atomically, and record a migration event. Timers and pending commands require mapping too. Never reinterpret an already-issued command under new semantics.

Use counts by definition and state to estimate drain time. If 2 million workflows run v2 and 99.9% finish within 24 hours, wait before migrating the remaining 0.1%; those 2,000 exceptional instances deserve a reviewed migration rather than a broad risky rewrite. Canary new definitions by tenant or percentage, compare transition and compensation rates, and retain rollback for workflows that have not crossed an incompatible point of no return.

Schema changes should be additive through the maximum workflow lifetime. Readers supply defaults for old payloads; writers include schema version. Avoid deleting an event field while delayed messages containing the old shape can still arrive.

docs.title: Evolution path
docs.text:
1. Keep order-local changes in one service and database transaction.
  2. Add idempotent remote command IDs and persist workflow state.
  3. Replace fragile call chains with durable transitions, outbox/inbox, and timers.
  4. Add unknown-outcome states and independent reconciliation.
  5. Partition by order_id, introduce priority and dependency bulkheads, and test catch-up.
  6. Version workflow definitions so in-flight instances finish or migrate explicitly.

Migrate from synchronous checkout by first recording shadow workflow state around the existing path. Move one remote step at a time behind an outbox. Preserve the old response contract until status polling or callbacks are available. Reconcile old and new paths before increasing traffic.

docs.title: Observability and verification
docs.text:
Measure starts and completions; active and oldest age by state and definition; transition conflicts; timer lateness; outbox age; inbox duplicates; retry and unknown-outcome rates; compensation and refund backlog; dependency latency; and reconciliation mismatches. Attach workflow ID, command ID, and provider reference to traces without exposing sensitive data.

Test a crash before and after every transaction boundary, response loss after remote success, duplicate and reordered events, late timers, late payment success, compensation failure, relay outage and catch-up, and mixed workflow versions. Model-based tests can generate event permutations and verify that impossible states such as COMPLETED without durable payment never occur.

docs.title: L5 and L6 guidance
docs.text:
An L5 design should identify service boundaries and the point of no return, draw explicit states, define idempotency and unknown outcomes, and explain atomic state-plus-outbox transitions. It should show durable timers, compensation semantics, and user-visible status.

An L6 design should quantify active instances and catch-up capacity, prioritize liability-reducing work under overload, design provider reconciliation, and migrate long-lived workflow versions safely. It should challenge whether every step belongs in the saga and define operational ownership for REVIEW. Senior design treats late success and old-version execution as normal states, not edge cases.

For bounded model planning, typed tools, principal-bound capabilities, durable agent replay, memory, and human approval, continue with the Applied AI Systems track.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• Which step is the point of no return?
  • What does each compensation mean to the business?
  • How are unknown outcomes distinguished from failures?
  • How are timers persisted and deduplicated?
  • What happens when payment succeeds after inventory expiry?
  • How are running workflows migrated to a new definition?

docs.title: Pattern: Probabilistic Data Structures
docs.text: Probabilistic data structures trade exact answers for bounded memory or work. Start exact, identify the resource that fails, and choose a sketch only when its error direction is safe for the decision. Keep canonical events or records whenever an exact rebuild, appeal, deletion, audit, or model comparison may be required.

docs.title: Exact-first selection
docs.text:
Ask three questions before choosing a structure:

  1. Could an exact set, counter map, heap, histogram, or sampled exact computation meet the measured envelope?
  2. Which error is tolerable: false positive, overcount, missed candidate, cardinality error, or rank error?
  3. Is the answer advisory, or can it deny service, move money, enforce policy, or delete data?
Need Exact first Approximate choice Error direction Safe use membership hash set or indexed lookup Bloom filter may say present for an absent item; no false negatives after successful insert under stated assumptions skip expensive negative lookups, then verify positives when a false positive could suppress required work point frequency counter map Count-Min Sketch (CMS) overestimates in a non-negative stream telemetry, candidate generation, conservative admission with an exact verification boundary frequent items exact counters plus heap Space-Saving tracked counts are overestimates; low-frequency items can be absent bounded heavy-hitter candidate discovery followed by exact rescoring distinct count exact set HyperLogLog (HLL) statistical error in either direction after estimator corrections dashboards, planning, and mergeable aggregate features quantile sorted samples or exact histogram KLL or another quantile sketch bounded rank error, not bounded value error latency and distribution summaries whose rank tolerance is explicit

Do not choose by name recognition. A Bloom filter does not count, CMS does not enumerate all keys, HLL does not answer membership, and a quantile sketch cannot reconstruct arbitrary values. Space-Saving retains candidate identities; CMS needs a separate candidate source.

flowchart TD
    Q[Required query] --> E{Exact fits measured envelope?}
    E -->|Yes| X[Use exact structure]
    E -->|No| D{Acceptable error}
    D -->|False positives| B[Bloom filter]
    D -->|Frequency overestimate| C[Count-Min Sketch]
    D -->|Heavy-hitter candidate miss| S[Space-Saving]
    D -->|Cardinality error| H[HyperLogLog]
    D -->|Rank error| K[Quantile sketch]
    B --> A{Authoritative action?}
    C --> A
    S --> A
    H --> A
    K --> A
    A -->|Yes| V[Verify against exact state]
    A -->|No| M[Publish error contract]

docs.title: Bloom filters: size from downstream cost
docs.text:
A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits with k hash positions. Insert sets all positions; query returns "possibly present" only when all are set. With n expected inserted items and desired false-positive probability p, near-optimal sizing is:

m = ceil(-n * ln(p) / (ln(2)^2)) bits
k = round((m / n) * ln(2)) hash probes
p ~= (1 - exp(-k*n/m))^k

For one billion URLs and p=0.001, m is about 14.38 billion bits, or 1.80 GB, and k is about 10. Capacity is part of correctness: inserting two billion URLs into a filter sized for one billion raises the false-positive rate sharply. For the same 14.38 billion bits and ten probes, doubling distinct inserted keys makes the estimate (1-exp(-10*2/14.38))^10, about 5.7%, instead of 0.1%. Track distinct insertions or estimate occupancy and rotate or rebuild before exceeding the design point; repeated insertion of the same key does not consume new capacity like a distinct key.

Choose p from total cost, not a fashionable percentage. If 200,000 absent keys/s reach the filter, p=0.001 sends about 200 unnecessary authoritative reads/s downstream. If each read consumes 3 ms of backend CPU, false positives cost roughly 200 * 0.003 = 0.6 CPU-seconds/s plus I/O and tail-latency interference. Lowering p to 0.0001 needs about 19.17 billion bits, or 2.40 GB, and about 13 probes, but reduces false reads to 20/s. The extra 0.60 GB and hash work are justified only if avoiding about 180 reads/s is worth more.

The rate p is conditional on an absent key; it is not the fraction of positive answers that are wrong. With 99% absent queries and p=0.001, false positives comprise 0.99*0.001 / (0.01 + 0.99*0.001) = 9.0% of positive answers. Redis's Bloom sizing section verifies the bits/item formula; library probe rounding can differ from this near-optimal theoretical calculation (accessed 2026-09-08).

false positive reads/s = negative queries/s * p
downstream CPU-s/s = false positive reads/s * CPU seconds/read
total cost(p) = filter memory + filter CPU + false-positive downstream cost

Standard Bloom filters cannot delete: clearing one bit can create false negatives for other keys. A counting Bloom filter replaces bits with counters but costs more memory and requires correct balanced updates; counter overflow and missed deletes break its guarantee. For time retention, use immutable time-sliced filters and expire whole slices, or rebuild from canonical state. A negative answer is authoritative only if every relevant successful write reached the filter, the queried generation covers the data, and corruption or concurrent publication cannot omit bits.

docs.title: Count-Min Sketch: bounded overcount
docs.text:
CMS stores d rows of w non-negative counters using independent hash functions. Update increments one counter in each row; query returns their minimum. Collisions can only increase a result in the cash-register model, so estimate(x) >= true_count(x).

w = ceil(e / epsilon)
d = ceil(ln(1 / delta))
estimate(x) <= true_count(x) + epsilon*N with probability at least 1-delta

The probability statement applies to a fixed queried key under the hash assumptions. It is not automatically a simultaneous guarantee for every query; choose a smaller per-key failure probability or use the appropriate uniform bound when many decisions must hold together. Here N is total positive count added to the sketch. With epsilon=0.001 and delta=0.01, w=2,719, d=5, and four-byte counters consume about 53 KiB. The additive error can still dwarf a rare key when N is huge. Size from the smallest frequency difference the product must distinguish, not from memory alone.

CMS arrays merge by element-wise addition only when width, depth, hash algorithm, seeds, counter semantics, and epoch match. Watch counter saturation. Ordinary negative updates can invalidate one-sided guarantees; use an algorithm designed for the relevant turnstile model or recompute from retained deltas. CMS can test the frequency of a supplied key but cannot list candidate keys, so pair it with sampled identities, a bounded heap, or Space-Saving.

docs.title: Space-Saving: heavy-hitter candidates
docs.text:
Space-Saving keeps at most s (item, count, error) entries. Increment a tracked item directly. For an untracked item when full, replace the minimum-count entry and initialize the new item's count to the old minimum plus the update; that inherited minimum is its error bound. Reported counts therefore overestimate true counts by no more than the stored error for that entry.

Any item with frequency greater than N/s is guaranteed to be represented under the standard unit-increment algorithm, but a product top-K can contain much smaller or weighted frequencies. Pick candidate count M through replay against exact data, not from the theorem alone. Union candidates from every partition, then fetch exact counts for the union. Taking only each partition's top K can miss a globally frequent item that ranks just below K in many partitions.

Distributed Space-Saving variants have merge details that affect guarantees. The safest applied design treats local summaries as candidate generators and performs exact final scoring from retained buckets. For weighted updates, deletions, or decayed scores, use a structure with documented support and validate against the actual stream distribution.

docs.title: HyperLogLog: distinct counts
docs.text:
HLL hashes each item, uses p bits to select one of m=2^p registers, and records a leading-zero rank. Its relative standard error is approximately:

RSE ~= 1.04 / sqrt(m)

At p=14, m=16,384, the RSE is about 0.81%. The estimate may be above or below truth; implementation-specific small- and large-range corrections matter. Compare confidence bands rather than treating 1,003,000 as exact.

HLLs with identical precision and hash semantics merge by register-wise maximum. Folding a higher-precision sketch to lower precision may be supported, but increasing precision after collection cannot recover discarded information. HLL does not support arbitrary deletion. Use time-bucketed HLLs for expiring windows and merge the still-live buckets; because register-wise maximum has no inverse, sliding-window subtraction is not available. Rebuild when deletion, privacy erasure, or corrected identity semantics require it.

docs.title: Quantile sketches: rank is not value
docs.text:
A quantile sketch answers questions such as p99 without storing every observation. For N values, a rank-error guarantee of epsilon means the returned value's true rank is within roughly epsilon*N positions of the requested rank. It does not bound numeric error. If latency jumps from 20 ms to 20 seconds across adjacent ranks, a small rank error can still produce a large value difference.

KLL-style sketches offer compact mergeable summaries with rank-error guarantees. Some tail-oriented sketches provide strong practical relative accuracy but different or empirical guarantees. Record algorithm, parameters, library version, value mapping, and merge rules rather than calling every summary a "percentile sketch." Never average p99 values across hosts; merge compatible sketches or aggregate the original histogram buckets.

Deletion is generally not an inverse merge. Window quantiles need time-bucketed sketches, an algorithm built for sliding windows, or recomputation. Preserve negative values, infinities, and overflow behavior deliberately, and test adversarial distributions with repeated values and extreme tails.

docs.title: Merge, deletion, and lifecycle contract
docs.text:
Every stored sketch needs metadata and an owner:

SketchEnvelope(type, algorithm_version, parameters, hash_id, seed_id,
               epoch, window_start, window_end, item_count, checksum, payload)

Reject incompatible merges instead of silently producing a number. Seeds may be secret when adversaries can choose keys to force collisions; rotate them through a versioned rebuild, not in place. Checksums detect damaged payloads but do not prove semantic compatibility.

Use a generation lifecycle:

  1. Build a new generation from canonical records or dual-write it from a recorded offset.
  2. Compare it with exact samples and the current generation.
  3. Publish the generation and parameters atomically.
  4. Keep the prior generation through rollback and maximum reader lifetime.
  5. Delete it only after retention, erasure, and replay obligations permit.

Time-sliced sketches make expiry and partial rebuild practical. They add query-time merge work and boundary approximation. Choose slice width from freshness, retention, state count, and rebuild cost. Do not mutate a historical sketch after publishing it without a revision protocol.

docs.title: Authority safety
docs.text:
Approximation is safest for acceleration, observability, and candidate discovery. Put exact verification before irreversible or rights-affecting actions:

Approximate signal Unsafe direct action Safe boundary Bloom says seen discard a newly discovered URL or payment event consult durable seen state, or allow only a documented low-value coverage tradeoff CMS says quota exceeded permanently ban an account verify exact bounded-window usage Space-Saving omits item declare item ineligible use omission only to reduce ranking candidates and measure recall HLL reports unique users issue exact invoices bill from canonical usage records quantile sketch reports SLO breach delete raw evidence retain evidence and use the sketch for alerting

When exact verification is too expensive, disclose the policy error budget, provide an appeal or reconciliation path, and cap harm. Security filters often prefer false positives while fraud review verifies them; coverage systems may prefer false negatives differently. "Approximately correct" is not a complete safety argument.

docs.title: Validation and observability
docs.text:
Validate before rollout and continuously:

  1. Replay representative and adversarial distributions into both exact and approximate implementations.
  2. Measure observed false-positive rate, frequency overcount, heavy-hitter recall@K, cardinality relative error, or quantile rank error as applicable.
  3. Test empty, tiny, saturated, highly skewed, repeated-value, and hash-adversarial inputs.
  4. Verify serialization round trips, incompatible-merge rejection, cross-language hashes, restart restore, and old-generation rollback.
  5. Shadow decisions and compare downstream cost and product harm before allowing the sketch onto a decision path.

Monitor inserted count versus design capacity, fill ratio or register distribution, saturated counters, update/query rate, bytes, merge rejection, sketch age, exact-sample divergence, candidate recall, rebuild duration, and false-positive downstream QPS. Alert on the user-visible error contract, not merely sketch health.

docs.title: Interview traps
docs.text:
• Starting with a sketch before showing why exact state fails.
  • Saying "Bloom filters are accurate" without naming false-positive probability, expected insertions, and downstream behavior.
  • Claiming CMS undercounts in a positive-update stream or using it to enumerate keys.
  • Using local top-K as global top-K without candidate oversampling and exact union scoring.
  • Treating HLL error as one-sided or trying to subtract one HLL from another.
  • Treating quantile rank error as milliseconds of value error or averaging host percentiles.
  • Merging structures with different seeds, dimensions, precision, epochs, or algorithm versions.
  • Clearing Bloom bits or applying negative CMS updates without a deletion-capable design.
  • Letting an approximation deny, charge, delete, or suppress without an explicit authority boundary.
  • Keeping no canonical data, exact sample, rebuild path, or rollout metric.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Prove the exact design misses a measured memory, latency, bandwidth, or cost envelope.
  • State error direction, bound, confidence, and product consequence.
  • Size from expected cardinality or stream mass and downstream cost.
  • Version parameters, hashes, seeds, serialization, windows, and generations.
  • Define compatible merge, deletion, expiry, rebuild, and corruption behavior.
  • Put exact verification before high-impact actions.
  • Validate on replayed production-like data and continuously sample exact answers.
  • Preserve canonical inputs for correction, audit, and migration when required.

docs.title: Pattern: Proximity Search
docs.text: Proximity search finds candidates near a point, then applies exact distance and business filters. Consider finding available drivers within 3 km at 20,000 queries/s while one million drivers update location every four seconds. A spatial index narrows the search; it does not make location, availability, or assignment authoritative.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use spatial cells for rapidly changing points and radius queries, an R-tree or geospatial database for moderate precise datasets, and a search engine for geo plus rich filters. Avoid calculating distance to every object. Avoid exposing exact sensitive coordinates when a coarse cell, ETA, or distance band satisfies the product need.

Index Strength Weakness geohash or grid simple prefix and cell routing boundaries and latitude distortion S2 or H3 hierarchical globe coverage library and indexing complexity R-tree precise rectangles and ranges distributed high-update scaling search geo index filters plus geo ranking projection lag

docs.title: Candidate architecture
docs.text:
Every location event carries entity ID, sequence, event time, coordinates, accuracy, and expiry. The updater maps it to a cell and conditionally replaces older membership. The query planner covers a radius with cells, retrieves a bounded candidate set, computes exact distance, rejects stale or inaccurate points, checks canonical availability, and ranks by ETA or business score.

flowchart LR
    L[Location updates] --> U[Versioned cell updater]
    U --> C[(Cell membership index)]
    R[Rider query] --> N[Cell cover and ring planner]
    N --> C
    C --> V[Freshness and Haversine filter]
    V --> A[Canonical availability]
    A --> K[Rank top K by ETA]

A move between cells cannot be one atomic write in many stores. Write the new membership with sequence s, then remove the old membership conditionally if its sequence is below or equal to s. Query results carry sequence; deduplicate by driver ID and retain the newest. TTL removes ghosts after missed cleanup. Final assignment uses a conditional transition such as AVAILABLE -> RESERVED, so two riders cannot win the same driver.
