Deduplication only works for copies actually returned by this query. A stale old-cell copy can be the only copy in the radius while the driver has moved outside it. Hydrate the latest canonical location/version before eligibility and reject a mismatched cell sequence. Keep per-entity incarnation plus sequence across device restarts, and use durable move intent or periodic repair so a lost new-cell write is not treated as completed movement.

docs.title: Choosing cell resolution
docs.text:
Cell size controls two opposing costs. Coarse cells require fewer index reads but return many false positives. Fine cells reduce candidates per cell but require many cells to cover one radius and create more move updates. Choose resolution from density and radius, then validate with production geography.

For a square approximation with side s and query radius r, covered cells are roughly:

cells read ~= (2r / s + 2)^2
candidates ~= density * covered area

Suppose an urban area has 300 active drivers per square kilometre and r=3 km. With s=1 km, a conservative 8 x 8 cover reads 64 cells and may inspect 64 * 300 = 19,200 memberships before exact filtering. With s=0.25 km, an approximate 26 x 26 cover reads 676 cells, but each averages only 18.75 drivers, or about 12,675 candidates. The latter reduces false positives but multiplies storage calls. Batching cell reads and applying an explicit candidate budget may make an intermediate resolution best. A budget cutoff can sacrifice recall; exact nearest-K requires the stopping proof below.

Hierarchical systems express resolution as levels rather than metres. Do not assume every cell has identical shape or area. Measure area by latitude, compact neighbouring cells where supported, and cap both cells and candidates. Select a default level so a normal-radius query covers tens, not thousands, of cells, then adapt in dense areas.

flowchart TD
    Q[Radius and local density] --> R{Estimated candidates}
    R -->|too many| F[Use finer child cells]
    R -->|too few| C[Use coarser cells or more rings]
    R -->|within budget| K[Keep current resolution]
    F --> B[Apply cell and candidate caps]
    C --> B
    K --> B

docs.title: Ring expansion without boundary misses
docs.text:
Never query only the origin cell. A rider one metre from a cell edge may have a driver two metres away in a neighbouring cell. Start with the origin cell and its immediate neighbours, then expand rings. Cell coverage must contain the radius circle, so it intentionally overfetches.

target = 20 eligible drivers
candidateCap = 500
for ring = 0..maxRing:
  cells = cellsInRing(originCell, ring) minus alreadyRead
  batch = read cells within remaining cell, byte and candidate budgets
  candidates += batch
  if any cells or rows omitted: mark budgetLimited
  exact = validateAndSort(candidates)
  if not budgetLimited and exact has target:
    if distanceToUnreadBoundary > distance(exact[target - 1]): break
  if candidates.size >= candidateCap: break
return first target of exact, together with coverage status

Stopping merely after finding 20 candidates is wrong: an unread neighbouring cell may contain a closer driver. The boundary test stops only when the nearest possible point in every unread cell is farther than the current Kth exact result. If that lower bound is hard to compute, cover the complete requested radius before returning. For dispatch systems, rank by ETA after geometric filtering because road networks, one-way streets, and bridges make straight-line distance an imperfect proxy.

If candidateCap or maxRing stops the search before that proof, label the result budget-limited, not exact nearest K. The distance lower bound proves only geometric order, not ETA order. An ETA guarantee needs a valid travel-time bound or evaluation of all eligible candidates in the requested scope.

docs.title: Exact Haversine distance
docs.text:
"Exact" here means the spherical distance calculation after coarse cell filtering, not an exact Earth geodesic or GPS position. PostGIS ST_Distance explicitly distinguishes planar geometry units, spherical distance, and geography's default spheroidal meters (accessed 2026-09-08).

For latitude and longitude in radians:

dLat = lat2 - lat1
dLon = lon2 - lon1
a = sin^2(dLat/2) + cos(lat1)*cos(lat2)*sin^2(dLon/2)
c = 2*atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1-a))
distance = 6371.0088 km * c

From (12.9716, 77.5946) to (12.9816, 77.6046), dLat and dLon are each about 0.0001745 radians. Substitution yields about 1.55 km. Use double precision, clamp a into [0,1] against floating-point drift, and normalize longitude differences. For short distances an equirectangular approximation can rank cheaply, followed by Haversine for the final boundary. For navigation or legal geofences, use an ellipsoidal/geodesic library rather than a spherical approximation.

A bounding box is an efficient prefilter: latitude delta is approximately r/111.32 km; longitude delta is r/(111.32*cos(latitude)). Near poles, longitude becomes unstable, reinforcing the value of globe-aware cells.

docs.title: Dense-cell splitting
docs.text:
A stadium release can put 30,000 drivers and requests in one parent cell. A single partition then becomes hot even if the global load is modest. Track membership count, update QPS, query QPS, and response bytes per cell. When any exceeds a sustained threshold, create child cells one level finer.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ParentOnly
    ParentOnly --> DualWrite: split threshold sustained
    DualWrite --> ChildReads: backfill and verify counts
    ChildReads --> ChildrenOnly: old membership TTL elapsed
    ChildrenOnly --> DualWrite: merge threshold sustained
    DualWrite --> ParentOnly: parent rebuilt and verified

During split, publish routing metadata version v2, dual-write updates to parent and child, backfill current parent entries into children, and have readers query both while deduplicating by ID and sequence. Once all writers observe v2, backfill is verified, and the maximum old-entry TTL passes, read children only. Merging sparse children reverses this process. Add hysteresis: split above 10,000 members for ten minutes, but merge only below 2,000 for an hour. Without it, traffic near one threshold causes continual repartitioning.

Splitting by spatial child alone may not solve a hotspot where all points occupy one venue. Salt the leaf cell into buckets by entity hash, batch reads across salts, cache short-lived candidate snapshots, and enforce admission control. Salting distributes storage load but does not reduce total candidates, so exact filtering and budgets still matter.

docs.title: Antimeridian and polar correctness
docs.text:
The interval from longitude 179.8 to -179.8 crosses the antimeridian and spans 0.4 degrees, not 359.6. Normalize longitude into a consistent range and split a crossing box:

[179.8, 180] union [-180, -179.8]
normalizedDelta = ((lon2 - lon1 + 540) mod 360) - 180

Do not compare numeric minimum and maximum longitudes without crossing metadata. Cell libraries designed on a sphere usually provide cover operations that handle this; use those APIs rather than hand-built prefix arithmetic. Test points on both sides of 180, cell edges, corners, poles, and exactly on a radius boundary. Near a pole, all longitudes converge and a conventional rectangular grid can touch many cells. Cap resolution and use S2/H3-style topology or a polar-aware index.

docs.title: Freshness, privacy, and semantics
docs.text:
A point with high GPS error should not be treated as exact. One policy accepts only updates newer than 15 seconds and accuracy radius below 100 metres; another expands candidate distance by reported accuracy but marks confidence. Use server receive time for TTL while retaining event time for movement logic, because a bad device clock must not create immortal membership. Sequence numbers prevent delayed updates from moving a driver backward.

Store only the retention necessary for dispatch. Encrypt precise history, separate current-location access from historical analytics, audit purpose-bound reads, and return coarse positions to users until matching policy permits disclosure. Rate-limit entity tracking queries and prevent enumeration through cell APIs.

docs.title: Failure semantics and runbooks
docs.text:
Failure Behavior location update lost TTL removes stale membership; the next update repairs it new cell written but old cell remains latest canonical location check rejects stale membership; deduplication and TTL clean overlap cell partition becomes hot adaptive children, salting, coalescing, and quotas index unavailable return explicitly degraded static results or no match, never invented precision candidate accepts elsewhere canonical conditional assignment resolves the race routing version is mixed dual-read and deduplicate until convergence

For stale-location alarms, compare producer rate, broker lag, updater rejection, and index write latency. If ingestion is delayed, shorten eligibility age rather than dispatch stale drivers and surface reduced supply. For a hot cell, identify whether reads, writes, or candidate bytes dominate; activate pre-created child routing, add salt partitions, and lower maximum rings before broad shedding. For index corruption, rebuild memberships from the latest compacted location stream, preserve sequence guards, shadow-query counts, then switch routing metadata.

If one region fails, do not silently search a remote region whose latency causes stale assignments. Fence the failed writer generation, restore from the compacted stream or latest snapshot plus replay, and allow traffic only after update-age and count checks pass. Reconciliation samples active entities from canonical availability and verifies exactly one current cell membership at the newest sequence.

Monitor update age, rejected stale sequences, membership TTL expiry, cells and candidates scanned per query, ring expansions, exact-filter rejection, false-positive rate, Kth-result distance, cell and salt skew, split state age, query latency, degraded responses, and assignment conflicts.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Select cell resolution from measured density, radius, and storage-call budgets.
  • Cover boundaries and stop rings only with a valid lower-bound condition.
  • Apply Haversine after spatial prefiltering and ETA after geometric distance.
  • Version moves, deduplicate query results, and expire ghosts.
  • Split and merge dense cells with dual-read/write, verification, and hysteresis.
  • Test antimeridian, poles, edges, inaccurate GPS, and delayed events.
  • Keep assignment canonical and location access purpose-bound.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• How do you avoid missing objects across cell boundaries?
  • What controls the tradeoff between cell size and candidate count?
  • When can ring expansion safely stop?
  • How do dense-cell splitting and salting differ?
  • How are antimeridian queries represented?
  • Why must final driver assignment be canonical and conditional?

docs.title: Pattern: Realtime Updates
docs.text:
Realtime delivery means bounded end-to-end freshness, not merely using WebSockets. An order-tracking system targeting p99 visibility below two seconds for 5 million connected clients must manage millions of long-lived sessions, route updates to the right gateways, recover missed history, and survive reconnect storms. The canonical service still owns order state; the realtime tier delivers a low-latency view of it.

This page owns the application delivery pattern. Use Realtime and Media for transport behavior, congestion, connection migration, and packet-path evidence.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use WebSockets for frequent bidirectional traffic, server-sent events (SSE) for server-to-browser streams, and long polling for simple low-rate compatibility. Use mobile push to wake an application, then fetch canonical state. Avoid persistent connections for rare updates where polling or push costs less and has a simpler operational model.

Transport Strength Weakness WebSocket bidirectional and low per-message overhead connection state and proxy complexity SSE simple ordered server stream with HTTP semantics browser-to-server traffic uses separate HTTP long poll broad compatibility request churn and latency mobile push power-efficient wakeup provider delay and no strict delivery

Polling cost is explicit. With N clients polling every T seconds, origin load is N / T requests/s, average detection delay is about T / 2, and worst-case detection delay is nearly T plus request latency. Five million clients polling every 10 seconds produce 500,000 requests/s for roughly five-second average freshness, even when nothing changes. Conditional requests with ETag reduce response bytes, not request rate; add jitter so intervals do not align.

Long polling holds a request until an update or timeout, then reconnects immediately. With five million clients and a 30-second timeout, a quiet system still completes about 5,000,000 / 30 = 166,667 timeout requests/s and holds roughly five million concurrent requests. Changes add early completions, so size connection state, TLS handshakes, and retry admission separately. Long polling improves quiet-period latency but is not a way to avoid connection capacity.

docs.title: Streaming compatibility details
docs.text:
For SSE, emit Content-Type: text/event-stream, an id for resumable events, periodic comment heartbeats, and optionally a retry hint. Browsers reconnect with Last-Event-ID; the server maps it to a retained cursor or returns an explicit resync event. Disable response buffering and delayed compression at reverse proxies, flush complete events promptly, and set proxy/LB idle timeouts above the heartbeat interval. HTTP/1.1 browser per-origin connection limits can constrain many tabs; HTTP/2 multiplexing helps only when every intermediary preserves streaming semantics.

Load balancers must support long response lifetimes, SSE chunk flushing, and WebSocket upgrade where used. Connection affinity may improve cache locality, but correctness cannot depend on it: reconnect can land on any healthy gateway and recover from a cursor. Drain connections deliberately rather than resetting them at deployment, and test the actual CDN, ingress, WAF, and LB path for idle timeout, buffering, maximum connection age, and graceful close behavior.

WebRTC belongs at the peer-to-peer media or data boundary, not as the default server-to-millions update channel. It still needs signaling, NAT traversal through ICE/STUN, and often TURN relay capacity; transport reliability and ordering depend on channel configuration. Use it when direct low-latency peer exchange justifies that machinery, while keeping authoritative state changes and resumable notifications on the server delivery path.

docs.title: Define the delivery contract
docs.text:
Decide whether clients require every event or only the latest state. Location dots can usually be coalesced; audit events cannot. Define ordering scope, replay retention, duplicate handling, maximum tolerated staleness, and what happens beyond retention. "Exactly once over a socket" is not a useful promise: a connection can break after the server sends but before the client processes. Prefer at-least-once delivery with stable event IDs, entity versions, and client-side deduplication.

Each event should contain event_id, entity key, monotonically increasing entity version or partition sequence, event time, and payload/schema version. On reconnect, the client sends its last durable cursor. The service replays retained events or responds resync_required; the client fetches a canonical snapshot and starts from the snapshot watermark.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant R as Replay service
    participant S as Canonical API
    C->>G: connect(token, cursor=814)
    G->>R: read after 814
    alt cursor retained
        R-->>G: events 815..829
        G-->>C: ordered replay then live stream
    else cursor expired
        R-->>G: resync required
        G-->>C: resync_required
        C->>S: GET snapshot
        S-->>C: state at watermark 829
        C->>G: resume after 829
    end

docs.title: Capacity: memory, file descriptors, and network
docs.text:
Persistent connections shift cost from requests per second to concurrent state. Estimate the complete per-connection footprint: socket buffers, TLS state, protocol parser, authentication identity, subscriptions, pending outbound messages, and runtime object overhead.

Suppose a gateway keeps 12 KiB of application and runtime state, 16 KiB of effective kernel socket buffers, and 4 KiB of TLS state per connection: 32 KiB total. At 100,000 connections, that is 3.277 GB (3.052 GiB) before fragmentation, code, caches, and safety margin. On a 16 GiB host, assigning 8 GiB to connections yields 262,144 theoretical sessions, but CPU, network, GC, and full-buffer tests may lower the safe limit to 100,000. Five million clients need 50 gateways without failure reserve. Three balanced zones need at least 75 gateways so the 50 survivors can carry all clients after one-zone loss; rollout and skew require additional reserve.

Every socket consumes a file descriptor. A host serving 100,000 clients also needs descriptors for listeners, pub/sub connections, logs, and temporary files. Set OS and process limits above the engineered maximum, for example 150,000 rather than exactly 100,000, and monitor usage. Validate ephemeral port and NAT limits on outbound fan-out links; they differ from inbound descriptor limits.

Network can dominate. At one 300-byte update every 20 seconds for 5 million clients, payload traffic is 75 MB/s, before framing, TLS, retransmission, and fan-out duplication. If a popular event fans one 500-byte update to 1 million subscribers, the egress is 500 MB for one logical event. Coalesce state updates, compress only when CPU savings justify it, and isolate celebrity topics.

docs.title: Heartbeats and liveness
docs.text:
Connections can become half-open after network or device failure. Heartbeats detect dead peers and keep load balancers or NAT mappings active. Their interval must be below infrastructure idle timeouts but not so aggressive that heartbeat traffic becomes the workload.

For 5 million clients with a 30-second heartbeat, average heartbeat arrival is about 5,000,000 / 30 = 166,667/s; request and response frames may double that. At 40 bytes per frame, raw heartbeat egress alone is roughly 6.7 MB/s, but syscall and TLS costs matter more than bytes. A 60-second interval halves processing but detects dead clients more slowly. Add per-client jitter so every connection does not ping on the same second.

Treat transport liveness and application freshness separately. A healthy WebSocket can carry stale data if the upstream router is lagging. Publish stream watermarks or occasional version markers so clients and operators can distinguish a live socket from a current view.

flowchart TD
    S[Order service] --> O[(Outbox and durable log)]
    O --> F[Partitioned fan-out routers]
    F --> G1[Gateway zone A]
    F --> G2[Gateway zone B]
    G1 --> C1[Clients in zone A]
    G2 --> C2[Clients in zone B]
    C1 -. cursor and heartbeat .-> G1
    G1 --> P[(Ephemeral presence leases)]
    G2 --> P
    subgraph Source[Hop 1: source to gateways]
      S
      O
      F
    end
    subgraph ZoneA[Hop 2: gateway to clients in A]
      G1
      C1
    end
    subgraph ZoneB[Hop 2: gateway to clients in B]
      G2
      C2
    end

Treat these as two independent delivery hops. Hop 1 moves a committed source change through an outbox/log and routing layer to the responsible gateway; its cursor, partition ordering, retry, and lag are server-side concerns. Hop 2 moves gateway output over SSE, WebSocket, or long polling to a client; it has separate buffering, acknowledgement, disconnect, and device-network behavior. Budget freshness as source commit + publish/log lag + routing lag + gateway queue + network/client apply, and instrument each term. A gateway receiving an event does not prove that a client received or applied it.

docs.title: Routing and subscriptions
docs.text:
At small scale, one gateway stores subscriptions in memory. At scale, route by stable user or tenant key so a router can compute the gateway shard without a global lookup for every event. If clients can land anywhere, maintain short-lived user -> gateway leases and accept that lease state is eventually consistent. Duplicate delivery during movement is safer than dropped delivery.

Strategy Best fit Cost and failure behavior deterministic routing stable ownership such as one user mapped to a gateway shard no subscription lookup on each event, but placement changes require epochs, forwarding, or dual delivery during movement subscription pub/sub dynamic many-to-many topics and clients landing on arbitrary gateways flexible fan-out, but subscription cardinality, broker amplification, authorization updates, and stale subscribe/unsubscribe races must be bounded

A hybrid is common: partition source events deterministically by tenant or entity, then use a bounded subscription index near the gateway for final fan-out. Deterministic routing answers where to send; pub/sub answers who currently wants it. Neither replaces durable replay, and neither should make transient presence the canonical business state.

Do not create one pub/sub topic per arbitrary entity if the broker cannot support that cardinality. Partition events by entity key, let fan-out routers consume partitions, and maintain subscription indexes near gateways. For one user subscribing to 100,000 entities, apply product limits, use aggregate topics, or deliver a filtered snapshot stream; a giant per-session hash set consumes memory and makes authorization revocation expensive.

Authenticate the connection and authorize every subscription against current membership. Tokens valid at connect time do not handle later removal from an organization. Propagate revocation events, use short authorization cache TTLs, and recheck sensitive subscriptions. Presence is ephemeral derived state represented by a lease, not durable truth.

docs.title: Backpressure and slow clients
docs.text:
Never allow an unbounded per-connection queue. A disconnected radio, background browser tab, or slow consumer can turn small updates into gigabytes of gateway memory. Classify streams:

  • For state streams, replace queued version 40 with version 41 and count it as coalesced.
  • For event streams, retain a small bounded window and disconnect with a resumable cursor when full.
  • For priority messages, reserve queue space so heartbeats or control frames are not trapped behind bulk data.

Suppose the cap is 64 KiB per session. Across 100,000 connections, a completely full set is 6.554 GB (6.104 GiB), which may exceed the normal connection footprint. Set both per-session and process-wide limits. When the gateway reaches a global high-water mark, stop accepting connections, coalesce aggressively, and shed low-priority streams before health collapses.

End-to-end backpressure usually cannot pause a canonical order service merely because one browser is slow. The durable log decouples production, while gateway policy disconnects lagging consumers and lets them replay or resync later.

docs.title: Reconnect storms
docs.text:
A gateway or zone failure can disconnect hundreds of thousands of clients at once. Immediate retries overwhelm DNS, TLS termination, authentication, replay, and the surviving gateways. Exponential backoff without jitter still synchronizes clients into waves.

Use full jitter. For attempt n, choose a random delay uniformly between zero and min(cap, base * 2^n). With base 500 ms and cap 30 seconds, later retries spread over a 30-second window. Treat a server retry_after hint as a minimum wait and add jitter after it, cap attempts while applications are backgrounded, and reset the attempt counter only after a stable connection period.

If 500,000 clients reconnect over one second and a gateway fleet can safely establish 20,000 TLS sessions/s, backlog begins at 480,000. Spreading retries uniformly over 60 seconds lowers average attempts to about 8,333/s. Capacity admission should issue temporary rejection before allocating expensive session state. Resume tokens can avoid repeated full authorization where security policy permits, but they must expire and remain revocable.

flowchart TD
    D[Connection lost] --> J[Full-jitter backoff]
    J --> A{Admission capacity?}
    A -- no --> H[Receive retry_after and back off]
    A -- yes --> T[Authenticate or validate resume token]
    T --> R{Cursor retained?}
    R -- yes --> P[Replay bounded gap]
    R -- no --> S[Fetch canonical snapshot]
    P --> L[Enter live stream]
    S --> L

docs.title: Replay correctness
docs.text:
Persist events before fan-out using a transactional outbox or change log. A relay may publish duplicates if it crashes after publish but before marking an outbox row sent. Consumers and clients therefore apply events by ID or monotonic version.

The replay-to-live handoff needs a gap-free boundary: subscribe and buffer live events, replay through a captured watermark W, discard buffered duplicates through W, then drain later events in order. If the live buffer overflows, restart or resync rather than silently skip. PostgreSQL exported snapshots illustrate how a snapshot must be tied to its subsequent change stream; two independent reads of "current" are not that boundary (accessed 2026-09-08).

For entity state, accept version v only if it is newer than current; if versions jump from 10 to 14, either apply a self-contained state event or fetch a snapshot. For a complete event history, a partition cursor is more appropriate. Do not compare cursors from different partitions as though they form one global order.

Size replay retention from outage objectives. At 50,000 events/s and 400 bytes each, one hour is 72 GB raw; with replication factor 3, 216 GB. A six-hour replay window needs roughly 1.3 TB before overhead. If clients commonly stay offline for days, canonical snapshot recovery is more economical than retaining every realtime event for every client.

Prevent replay from starving live traffic. Give replay a bandwidth quota, limit concurrent replays per gateway, and force snapshot resync for gaps above a threshold. During a regional recovery, snapshot services also need admission controls.

docs.title: Gateway draining and deployments
docs.text:
Rolling deployment must not resemble a fleet failure. Mark a gateway draining: remove it from new-connection load balancing, keep existing sessions, and advertise a randomized reconnect window. After a grace period, send a reconnect control frame containing a resume cursor and optional destination hint. Close sessions gradually, with a hard deadline for the remainder.

For 100,000 sessions and a ten-minute drain, move about 167 sessions/s from one gateway. Across multiple simultaneous drains, ensure destination headroom. Deploy by small batches and stop if reconnect latency, replay lag, or rejection rises. Connection age should not pin an old binary forever; enforce a maximum drain deadline while preserving resumability.

Schema changes need mixed-version support. Add fields compatibly, carry payload version, and keep old event readers during the maximum connection and replay window. For an incompatible change, dual-publish or translate at gateways until old clients fall below an explicit threshold.

docs.title: Failures and overload
docs.text:
Failure Behavior connection drops reconnect with full jitter and resume cursor duplicate or out-of-order event ignore duplicate ID or non-newer entity version gateway dies clients reconnect elsewhere; ephemeral lease expires slow client bounded buffer, state coalescing, then resumable disconnect pub/sub loss durable replay or explicit snapshot resync replay tier overload quota replay and prefer snapshots for large gaps zone loss reserve cross-zone capacity and rate-limit handshakes

Under overload, protect established healthy sessions from new handshakes because TLS and authentication are expensive. Preserve control frames and high-priority updates, coalesce replaceable state, and reject optional subscriptions. Never claim a client is current based only on socket health.

docs.title: Evolution path
docs.text:
1. Poll canonical status with ETag, jitter, and backoff.
  2. Add one gateway with in-process subscriptions for measured latency needs.
  3. Persist source changes in an outbox and support versioned reconnect.
  4. Externalize routing with leases or deterministic gateway shards and a pub/sub backbone.
  5. Add durable replay, snapshot fallback, gateway draining, and reconnect admission.
  6. Partition by tenant/user, isolate celebrity topics, and test zone-loss capacity.

Keep polling as a fallback during rollout. Shadow realtime delivery against canonical versions, then enable it by client cohort. A transport migration from SSE to WebSocket can run both from the same event contract; avoid coupling domain events to one wire protocol.

docs.title: Observability and verification
docs.text:
Measure connected sessions, descriptors, memory per connection, handshake rate and latency, heartbeat misses, server delivery lag from source commit to client send, replay gap, replay bytes, dropped/coalesced messages, reconnect attempt distribution, authorization failures, and slow-consumer disconnects. For the p99 visibility SLO, sample client acknowledgments after application or rendering and account for client clock error. Report the population and missing acknowledgments explicitly; server send time alone cannot establish visibility. Break metrics down by gateway, zone, client version, and tenant without creating unbounded labels.

Load tests must hold realistic connection durations, not merely establish sockets. Test half-open peers, a 100,000-client reconnect, replay during live load, subscription revocation, gateway drain, broker interruption, and snapshot fallback. Verify file-descriptor limits and memory under full outbound buffers.

docs.title: L5 and L6 guidance
docs.text:
An L5 design should choose transport from traffic direction and frequency, calculate gateway count from connection memory and descriptors, define heartbeat and slow-client policy, and explain cursor-based recovery. It should distinguish canonical state from delivery infrastructure and account for reconnect jitter.

An L6 design should model zone-loss and handshake capacity, separate state coalescing from event replay, establish replay-versus-snapshot thresholds, and design gradual draining and schema migration. It should specify overload priorities, authorization revocation, and operational signals that prove freshness. The senior move is to treat reconnect and replay as primary traffic modes, not rare exceptions.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• Is every event required, or only the latest state?
  • How does a client recover a missed interval?
  • Where is subscription authorization rechecked?
  • What happens when one user subscribes to 100,000 entities?
  • How many connections fit per host after memory, descriptors, and failover headroom?
  • How does a deployment drain gateways without creating a reconnect storm?

docs.title: Pattern: Scaling Reads
docs.text: Read scaling reduces latency or canonical-store load while preserving an explicit freshness contract. Example: a product catalog grows from 500 to 80,000 peak reads/s; prices may be 30 seconds stale in browsing but never at checkout.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use replicas, caches, and projections after query plans and indexes are sound and measured reads exceed capacity. Avoid blind routing to asynchronous replicas when strict read-after-write is required; use a compatible replay-position check and fresh snapshot, caches for low-reuse data, and search projections for correctness decisions.

Technique Best trigger Tradeoff query/index tuning scans or excessive rows write/index cost read replica read-heavy canonical queries lag and failover semantics cache/CDN repeated keys or static bytes invalidation and stampede denormalized projection expensive stable access path lag and rebuild shard one cluster's storage/IO limit routing and cross-shard queries

docs.title: Baseline to scaled
docs.text:
1. One database with access-path indexes and bounded cursor pagination.
  2. Add replicas for stale-safe reads; primary or version-aware reads for sessions.
  3. Add cache-aside for hot products and CDN for images.
  4. Build search/list projections from an outbox stream.
  5. Partition canonical data only when a measured hard limit remains.
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> E[Edge/CDN]
    E --> API[Catalog API]
    API --> K[(Cache)]
    API --> R[(Read replicas)]
    API --> P[(Primary)]
    P --> O[Outbox]
    O --> X[(Search projection)]

Checkout reads price and stock from canonical storage; browse reads cache/search and displays as_of. A write response can carry version 74; subsequent reads route to a replica only after it reaches 74.

docs.title: Failure semantics
docs.text:
Failure Behavior cache outage bounded origin bypass, then shed browse traffic replica lag route version-sensitive reads to primary projection lag browsing may be stale; publish lag and preserve checkout correctness primary overload reserve capacity for writes; reject optional strong reads fan-out partial result fail or mark partial explicitly; never silently omit

Use TTL jitter and request coalescing for stampedes. Monitor hit rate per endpoint, replica replay delay, result age, origin QPS, rows scanned, and hottest keys.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• Which reads require read-your-writes, and how does the client communicate that?
  • What happens to the database when the cache is cold?
  • Why is a projection safe for browse but unsafe for checkout?
  • At what measured threshold would you shard rather than add replicas?

docs.title: Workload and correctness contract
docs.text:
Use one concrete catalog throughout the progression. Peak traffic grows from 500 to 80,000 read requests/s. A request returns 4 KB at the API boundary. Traffic is 55% product detail, 30% category/list pages, 10% search, and 5% checkout validation. The primary database safely sustains 8,000 simple reads/s while preserving write headroom. Browsing may show product text for five minutes and price for 30 seconds; checkout must read authoritative price and available stock. A seller expects read-your-writes in the administration session.

These are different read products. Product detail has high key reuse and suits caching. Category and search are multi-row ranking queries and suit projections. Checkout is low-volume but correctness-sensitive and stays on canonical storage. Administration carries a minimum version from the write response and uses only a replica that has replayed through that version.

Before adding infrastructure, measure request rate by endpoint, key popularity, response bytes, rows examined, database CPU and I/O, connection wait, and p50/p95/p99 latency. A high global hit rate can conceal one expensive zero-hit query.

flowchart TD
    R[Read request] --> T{Read contract}
    T -->|Static asset| E[CDN]
    T -->|Stale-safe repeated key| C[Cache-aside]
    T -->|Browse or search| X[Derived projection]
    T -->|Read-your-writes| V[Version-aware replica route]
    T -->|Price or stock decision| P[Canonical primary]

docs.title: Stage 1: 500 RPS on one database
docs.text:
At 500 RPS, one indexed database is the smallest correct design. If average query time is 8 ms, reads consume about four concurrent query slots by Little's Law: 500 * 0.008 = 4. That does not imply only four connections are needed because bursts and tail latency need headroom, but it shows that sharding would be premature.

Use covering or selective indexes derived from access paths, not an index on every field. Inspect query plans and cap rows examined. Cursor pagination over immutable (created_at, product_id) avoids deep offset scans; a mutable updated_at can move rows across the cursor and cause omissions or repeats. Use a snapshot if the query must order by changing fields. Select only needed columns and batch related key lookups to eliminate application-level N+1 queries.

Elasticsearch pagination similarly requires unchanged query/sort and a point-in-time context to stabilize index state. A version-aware replica read solves freshness, not stable pagination across multiple reads (accessed 2026-09-08).

Reserve database capacity for writes and operational work. If the safe total is 8,000 reads/s, do not plan steady state at 7,950. A slow query, backfill, or failover will consume the remaining margin. At this stage, a cache may reduce latency, but it is not needed for capacity and adds invalidation failure modes.

docs.title: Stage 2: 5,000 RPS with read replicas
docs.text:
At 5,000 RPS the primary still fits numerically, but mixing browse reads with writes increases lock, buffer-cache, and failover risk. Add two asynchronous read replicas and route stale-safe detail reads across them. Keep checkout, writes, and version-sensitive administration on the primary unless a replica proves sufficiently fresh.

Assume each replica has a safe limit of 4,000 reads/s. At 5,000 browse RPS, two replicas average 2,500 each, leaving useful headroom and allowing one replica to be removed without immediate overload only if optional reads can be shed. If N-1 service is mandatory with no shedding, each must safely carry all 5,000.

Replication does not increase write capacity. Every index update and log record still originates on the primary, and replicas must replay it. A long-running replica query can delay cleanup or replay depending on the database. Monitor replay bytes, apply delay, oldest transaction, and query cancellation, not just replica CPU.

docs.title: Lag-aware routing
docs.text:
A write response returns commit position 9,240. The client includes X-Min-Version: 9240 on the next read. Replica R1 is at 9,238 and R2 is at 9,245, so route to R2. If neither reaches 9,240 within the read deadline, use the primary or return an explicit pending result according to the endpoint contract. Wall-clock "lag below one second" cannot guarantee a particular write is visible.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant API as Catalog API
    participant P as Primary
    participant R as Replica router
    participant R2 as Replica 2
    C->>API: update product
    API->>P: commit
    P-->>API: commit version 9240
    API-->>C: success, min-version 9240
    C->>API: read with min-version 9240
    API->>R: choose replica at or beyond 9240
    R-->>API: R2 replayed through 9245
    API->>R2: read using fresh snapshot after replay check
    R2-->>API: product value, snapshot includes write 9240
    API-->>C: product value

Route ordinary reads using load, health, and lag. Remove a replica before it becomes dangerously stale; otherwise it returns fast but wrong-enough data and accumulates more work. Do not retry a timed-out replica against every other replica without a shared deadline and attempt budget.

docs.title: Stage 3: 20,000 RPS with cache and CDN
docs.text:
At 20,000 RPS, replicas alone require more database instances and repeat the same popular lookups. Add cache-aside for product detail and CDN caching for immutable images and public static responses. Cache derived values with a version and bounded TTL. Invalidate after canonical commit through an outbox event; TTL limits the effect of lost invalidations but does not make checkout safe.

For this sensitivity example, assume 95% of 20,000 requests are cache-eligible, including repeated category and search result pages, and eligible reads achieve an 80% hit rate. This is an optimistic workload assumption to measure by endpoint, not a property of every browse query. Cache keys must include query, locale, tenant/policy scope, and representation version where those affect results. Origin load is:

ineligible = 20,000 * 0.05 = 1,000 RPS
eligible misses = 20,000 * 0.95 * 0.20 = 3,800 RPS
total origin = 4,800 RPS

The result fits the 8,000 RPS database envelope but leaves only 3,200 RPS of margin. A statement such as "the cache has 80% hit rate" is not enough; calculate which endpoints are eligible and where misses land.

docs.title: Hit-rate sensitivity
docs.text:
At 80,000 RPS with 95% eligibility, origin demand changes sharply:

Eligible hit rate Eligible misses Ineligible reads Total origin RPS 99% 760 4,000 4,760 95% 3,800 4,000 7,800 90% 7,600 4,000 11,600 80% 15,200 4,000 19,200 0% 76,000 4,000 80,000

A five-point fall from 95% to 90% adds 3,800 origin RPS and exceeds one 8,000-RPS database limit. Capacity planning must use degraded hit rates, not the best weekly average. Segment hit rate by endpoint, region, tenant, response status, and key cohort.

Use per-key request coalescing so 2,000 simultaneous misses for one product produce one loader request rather than 2,000. Bound waiters and loader time. Add TTL jitter to avoid synchronized expiry. Negative-cache missing IDs briefly, but never let a transient database error become a long-lived "not found." Hot keys can use process-local near caches, while admission prevents one-hit keys from evicting reusable entries.

docs.title: Stage 4: 40,000 RPS with projections
docs.text:
Category pages and search perform joins, filters, and ranking that a key cache cannot efficiently answer. Build read-optimized projections from the canonical outbox stream. A category document may contain product IDs, display price, title, image reference, rank inputs, source versions, and as_of. Search can tolerate bounded lag; checkout validates selected IDs against canonical state.

Projection consumers process at least once, update idempotently by entity version, and checkpoint after state is committed. Rebuild into a new index from a snapshot plus change log, compare counts and sampled queries, catch up, then atomically switch an alias. Destroying the serving index before rebuild turns maintenance into downtime.

Projection fan-out can still hurt tails. Suppose a list request contacts 20 shards and each shard independently meets its 40 ms target 99% of the time. The chance all finish within 40 ms is 0.99^20, about 81.8%; roughly 18.2% of aggregate requests encounter at least one shard's one-percent tail. For 100 shards, all-fast probability falls to about 36.6%.

flowchart LR
    Q[Category query] --> S1[Shard 1]
    Q --> S2[Shard 2]
    Q --> S3[Shard 3]
    Q --> SN[Shard N]
    S1 --> M[Bounded top-K merge]
    S2 --> M
    S3 --> M
    SN --> M
    M --> O[Result or explicit partial status]

Reduce fan-out with tenant, category, locale, or time routing. Request only local top K rather than full result sets, enforce one aggregate deadline, cancel outstanding shard work, and avoid retrying every slow shard. If partial results are product-acceptable, mark them and include a continuation or missing-scope token; never silently omit results.

docs.title: Stage 5: 80,000 RPS and the decision to shard
docs.text:
At 80,000 RPS with a 95% eligible hit rate, origin demand is about 7,800 RPS, already near the primary's safe read limit. In practice, several read replicas handle browse misses, while the primary retains checkout and write headroom. For example, route 4,000 correctness-sensitive RPS to the primary and spread 3,800 stale-safe misses across three replicas. A replica loss raises the survivors from about 1,267 to 1,900 RPS each, still below their 4,000-RPS limits.

Do not shard solely because request traffic reached 80,000 RPS; cache and projections may absorb it. Shard canonical storage when measured data size, write rate, working-set I/O, maintenance duration, or single-cluster recovery time crosses a hard limit. Partition by a key that preserves dominant operations, and keep checkout invariants local. Sharding adds routing, rebalancing, fan-out, cross-shard transaction, and backup complexity.

The serving topology is now layered, but correctness remains simple: canonical state owns price and stock; replicas are delayed copies; cache and search are derived. Every endpoint has one declared source and fallback policy.

flowchart TD
    C[80k RPS clients] --> CDN[CDN and edge cache]
    CDN --> A[Regional API admission]
    A --> K[(Distributed plus near cache)]
    A --> X[(Search and list projection)]
    A --> RR[Lag-aware replica router]
    RR --> R1[(Replica 1)]
    RR --> R2[(Replica 2)]
    RR --> R3[(Replica 3)]
    A --> P[(Canonical primary)]
    P --> O[Transactional outbox]
    O --> K
    O --> X

docs.title: Cache-loss overload
docs.text:
A complete cache loss at 80,000 RPS would direct as many as 80,000 reads/s toward stores designed for a small fraction of that. "Fall back to the database" is therefore not a valid unbounded policy. Protect the origin with a fixed miss budget below its safe limit.

  1. Detect cache failure separately from a normal miss; stop repeated connection waits quickly.
  2. Admit checkout and read-your-writes traffic first. Reserve primary connections for writes and correctness reads.
  3. Permit only a bounded rate of browse misses to the origin. Shed excess with fast 429/503 responses or serve explicitly bounded stale entries from a regional or process cache.
  4. Coalesce loaders and warm only the highest-value keys. Do not scan the entire catalog into cache.
  5. Ramp cache traffic while watching origin CPU, connections, replica lag, and cache eviction. A warmup that admits one-hit keys can evict the hot set continuously.

If origin safe capacity is 8,000 RPS and 4,000 is reserved for mandatory traffic, only 4,000 RPS remains for warmup and optional misses. At an average 4 KB value, 4,000 unique fills/s loads about 16 MB/s before protocol overhead. Popularity-aware warmup yields more saved requests per origin read than uniform preloading.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Warm
    Warm --> CacheImpaired: errors or hit-rate collapse
    CacheImpaired --> OriginProtected: enforce miss budget
    OriginProtected --> Warming: cache service stable
    Warming --> Warm: hot-set hit rate passes guardrail
    Warming --> OriginProtected: origin or eviction saturates

docs.title: Safe rollout plan
docs.text:
Roll out each layer independently. For replicas, shadow a sample of primary reads and compare versions and results before serving users. Start with stale-safe endpoints, then add version-token routing. For cache, canary one percent of keys or traffic, verify hit rate, value age, invalidation delay, and origin load, then increase gradually. Hash by key rather than request when comparing behavior so one key does not oscillate between policies.

For a projection, dual-read in shadow mode and compare top results, counts, and age. Because ranking may legitimately differ, define comparison tolerances rather than demanding byte equality. Cut over one region or tenant cohort and keep the old index consuming updates and deletions throughout the rollback window. Immediate alias rollback is safe only to a sufficiently current, compatible index; otherwise catch it up and verify before switching.

Every rollout has automatic guardrails: user error and p99, origin RPS, write latency, replica lag, cache timeout rate, projection age, and correctness mismatch. Pause backfills and warmups before they compete with foreground work. Rollback must not depend on the new layer being healthy.

docs.title: Failure and observability matrix
docs.text:
Signal Why it matters Protective action hit rate by endpoint predicts origin demand enforce endpoint miss budgets cache timeout, not just miss consumes request deadline fail fast and isolate clients replica position and replay rate controls freshness and catch-up remove stale replica from routing primary connection wait early saturation signal shed optional strong reads projection event age user-visible staleness mark stale or route limited fallback fan-out width and slowest shard drives tail latency narrow routing and cancel stragglers rows examined per result catches query regressions halt rollout and fix access path hot-key share reveals skew hidden by averages near-cache or isolate key

Test cache blackhole and cold restart, one and all replica losses, replica lag spikes, projection rebuild, partial shard timeout, invalidation loss, and primary failover. Verify not only that requests return, but that checkout remains correct, origin stays below its limit, stale results expose their contract, and the system returns to normal without another overload wave.

docs.title: Interview close
docs.text: The progression is requirement-driven: optimize one database at 500 RPS; isolate stale-safe reads on replicas near 5,000; cache repeated keys around 20,000; move list and search work to replayable projections around 40,000; and at 80,000 use all layers while sharding only for a measured canonical-store limit. Quantify hit-rate sensitivity and N-1 replica capacity, route sessions by version, and treat cache loss as an overload event. The strongest answer explains which reads may be stale, which source remains canonical, and how every acceleration layer fails safely.

docs.title: Pattern: Scaling Writes
docs.text: Write scaling is constrained by coordination, durable I/O, indexes, replication, and hot keys. Adding application servers does not make a storage engine flush disks faster or let two leaders safely assign the same sequence number. Consider telemetry ingestion growing from 2,000 to 500,000 events/s while preserving per-device ordering and acknowledging only data that can survive one node loss. The design must define what an acknowledgment means, where ordering applies, and how much delayed visibility is acceptable.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use batching for amortizable independent records, partitioning for key-local operations, and durable logs for buffering and replay. Avoid asynchronous acknowledgment when the caller needs the committed result, sharding before removing unnecessary indexes, and random sharding when reads need key locality. First reduce work per logical write; then add parallelism.

Technique Gain Cost batch/append amortized fsync and network queueing delay and partial outcomes remove synchronous derived writes shorter critical path projection lag partition by entity parallel writes, local ordering skew and rebalancing durable ingestion log absorbs bursts backlog and duplicate delivery preallocated rights local constrained writes allocation and rebalance complexity

docs.title: Start with the write contract
docs.text:
Separate four milestones that teams often call "written": accepted by a process, appended to a leader, replicated durably, and visible in query projections. A response after a quorum log append means durably accepted, not necessarily queryable. Return an ingestion ID and publish a visibility SLO such as p99 under 10 seconds. If a balance update must be read-your-write consistent, route that operation to the authoritative store rather than weakening language around eventual visibility.

Ordering should also be scoped. Global ordering forces all traffic through one sequencer. Per-device ordering requires records for one device_id to reach one ordering authority and carry a monotonic sequence within a producer epoch. The authority must reject duplicates, detect gaps, and define how rebooted devices obtain a new epoch. Partition placement alone orders arrival, not the intended order of concurrent or retried sends. Independent devices can proceed in parallel. Idempotency keys must identify the logical event, not an individual attempt, so a timed-out producer can safely retry.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant P as Producer
    participant L as Partition leader
    participant F1 as Follower 1
    participant F2 as Follower 2
    participant W as Batch writer
    P->>L: append(event_id, device_id, epoch, seq)
    L->>L: durably append own log copy
    par replicate
        L->>F1: log bytes
        L->>F2: log bytes
    end
    F1-->>L: durable offset
    L->>L: establish commit under current-term rules
    L-->>P: accepted at committed offset
    L-->>W: committed records
    W->>W: deduplicate and batch

docs.title: Fsync, batching, and group commit
docs.text:
An fsync asks the operating system and storage device to make prior writes durable. If each event causes one 0.8 ms flush, a single serial log can perform at most about 1 / 0.0008 = 1,250 flushes/s, regardless of spare CPU. Group commit turns many logical events into one durable flush. With a 5 ms batch window and 2,500 events arriving in that window, one flush amortizes its latency across all 2,500 acknowledgments.

Use two batch triggers: maximum records or bytes, and maximum age. A writer can collect up to 4,000 records or 5 ms, append one contiguous block, flush, then resolve each record's promise. The age trigger bounds quiet-period latency; the size trigger bounds memory and request size during bursts. Never leave a partially filled batch waiting indefinitely.

docs.title: Worked ingestion budget
docs.text:
Assume 500,000 events/s, each 600 bytes after encoding. Raw ingress is 300 MB/s. With replication factor 3, the log writes roughly 900 MB/s across brokers before overhead. Across 20 balanced partitions, each receives 25,000 events/s and 15 MB/s. A 5 ms partition-local window collects about 125 records, so each partition produces about 200 batches/s and the fleet 4,000. Collecting 2,500 records per partition instead takes about 100 ms, not 5 ms. If network plus quorum flush p99 is 12 ms, the 5 ms collection design budgets approximately 17 ms plus queueing; validate the end-to-end percentile.

PostgreSQL's WAL description confirms that one flush may commit multiple transactions. It does not imply one global batch across independent partition logs. Measure flush coalescing and batch occupancy per log (accessed 2026-09-08).

This calculation exposes the real bottleneck. A cluster with aggregate disk bandwidth below 900 MB/s cannot meet the target just by increasing batch size. Provision headroom for compaction, recovery, and one-node loss; at 60% steady-state utilization, required aggregate sequential write capacity is about 900 / 0.60 = 1.5 GB/s.

Batch results require per-item semantics. Validation failures can be rejected before append. Once a mixed batch is durably appended, downstream storage may partially succeed. Persist event IDs and report ingestion acceptance independently from projection status rather than pretending the entire end-to-end batch is atomic.

docs.title: Replication and acknowledgments
docs.text:
Replication factor and acknowledgment policy determine durability and availability. Leader-only acknowledgment is fast but may lose acknowledged writes if the leader dies before replication. Quorum acknowledgment waits for enough replicas that one failure cannot erase the committed prefix. Requiring every replica makes a slow or unavailable replica block progress. It can increase the number of durable copies at acceptance, so evaluate that added protection against the named failure model rather than assuming it is free or always necessary.

The leader must fence stale leaders using a term or epoch. Followers reject stale terms and update leadership state according to the protocol, and a new leader commits only after satisfying the consensus protocol's quorum rules. Client retries still produce duplicates when the response is lost, so consensus does not remove the need for application idempotency.

flowchart LR
    D[Devices] --> A[Admission and validation]
    A --> L[(Replicated partitioned log)]
    L --> W1[Batch writer]
    L --> W2[Realtime projection]
    W1 --> S[(Sharded store)]
    W2 --> C[(Current-state cache)]
    S --> O[Outbox for derived work]
    O --> I[Index and notification workers]

During a follower outage, continue only if the in-sync replica policy still satisfies the promised failure tolerance. Otherwise reject or pause rather than silently downgrade durability. Track replica lag in bytes and time. A replica 100 GB behind can consume enough disk and network during catch-up to destabilize healthy traffic, so throttle recovery and reserve bandwidth for it.

docs.title: Write amplification
docs.text:
One 600-byte event rarely costs only 600 bytes. Define write amplification as physical bytes written across the system divided by logical bytes accepted. Sources include replication, write-ahead logs, database pages, secondary indexes, compaction, outbox rows, and projections.

For 300 MB/s logical ingress, suppose log replication contributes 3x, an LSM database averages 4x compaction amplification on each projection byte, and two projections each store 40% of the source payload. The log writes 900 MB/s. Projection logical traffic is 300 * 0.8 = 240 MB/s; with WAL plus compaction approximated at 5x, one copy writes 1.2 GB/s. Total with single-copy rebuildable projections is 2.1 GB/s, or 7x; with three projection copies it is 0.9 + 1.2*3 = 4.5 GB/s, or 15x, before backups. Removing an index storing 20% of source size at 5x saves 300 MB/s per copy.

Measure amplification rather than assuming it. Compression lowers bytes but costs CPU. LSM compaction improves append throughput but creates background I/O and tail-latency spikes. B-tree updates may perform random page writes and page splits. Select storage around workload and SLO, not a generic claim that one engine is always faster.

Move search indexes, analytics, and notifications behind an outbox or committed log when they need not participate in the primary invariant. Keep uniqueness and balance constraints in the authoritative transaction. The outbox row and business mutation commit atomically; a relay publishes at least once, and consumers deduplicate by event ID.

docs.title: Partitioning and hot keys
docs.text:
Hash partitioning distributes ordinary keys well, but traffic distribution matters more than key count. If one device emits 10% of 500,000 events/s, its 50,000 ordered writes/s still land on one partition. First determine whether that device truly needs one ordered stream. If ordering is only per sensor channel, partition by (device_id, channel_id). If strict per-device order is required, one owner must serialize the stream; optimize that path or impose a producer quota.

Ordered epochs can split a hot entity only at explicit boundaries. A coordinator closes epoch 41 at sequence 8,000, assigns epoch 42 to another partition, and records the handoff durably. Readers concatenate closed epochs in order. Never hash individual events randomly and hope timestamps reconstruct causality.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Stable
    Stable --> Copying: create target shard
    Copying --> CatchingUp: bulk snapshot complete
    CatchingUp --> DualRead: replay reaches watermark
    DualRead --> Cutover: fence source and replay final position
    Cutover --> Stable: routing epoch advanced
    Copying --> Aborted: validation or capacity failure
    CatchingUp --> Aborted: lag exceeds limit

docs.title: Repartitioning without losing writes
docs.text:
Consistent hashing reduces movement when adding shards, but movement is still a production operation. Use versioned routing and an explicit migration state machine:

  1. Create target partitions and reserve capacity.
  2. Copy an immutable snapshot from source at watermark W.
  3. Stream changes after W to the target using event IDs and source sequence numbers.
  4. When lag is small, shadow-read or checksum ranges and compare counts and hashes.
  5. Gate and drain source writes, durably fence the old owner, record its final committed position, and verify target replay through it. Install the new epoch at the write guard before advancing routing and enabling target writes.
  6. Keep source data fenced through a rollback window. After target writes begin, rollback must gate and fence the target, reverse-replay its accepted tail to the old replica set, verify a final watermark, and grant a fresh epoch. A frozen source copy alone is not a safe rollback target. Delete retired copies only after that window.

Dual writing from an application to old and new shards creates an atomicity gap. Prefer one authoritative write plus change-data capture. If dual writes are unavoidable, record repairable intent and continuously reconcile. During cutover, requests carrying a stale routing epoch receive a redirect or retryable error; they must not commit to the retired owner.

Migration traffic competes with foreground writes. Rate-limit snapshot scans, cap catch-up bandwidth, and pause movement when fsync p99 or replica lag crosses a threshold. Move small ranges first and avoid migrating many hot partitions simultaneously.

docs.title: Overload and failure semantics
docs.text:
Backpressure must propagate before memory queues fill. Admission should enforce global capacity, per-tenant rates, and bounded outstanding bytes. A token bucket allows a documented burst while protecting sustained capacity. If persistence can drain 450,000 events/s and arrivals remain at 500,000/s, backlog grows by 50,000 events/s: 180 million events per hour. At 600 bytes, that is 108 GB/hour before replication. A six-hour retention buffer only postpones failure unless operators add capacity or shed load.

Failure Outcome timeout before log acknowledgment outcome unknown; retry the same event ID worker crashes after database commit redelivery; event ID deduplicates shard unavailable affected partitions pause; queue age grows tenant burst tenant quota rejects with a retry hint backlog approaches retention reject before accepting data that cannot be retained disk full stop leaders or affected partitions; never acknowledge volatile-only writes stale routing client fence by routing epoch and refresh ownership

Use 429 for quota rejection and 503 for unavailable durable capacity, with bounded Retry-After guidance. Prefer shedding low-priority telemetry over violating high-priority audit durability. If product policy permits sampling, label sampled data explicitly and perform it before acknowledgment.

docs.title: Evolution path
docs.text:
1. Begin with one transactional store and conditional writes for invariants.
  2. Batch noninteractive inserts and remove unnecessary synchronous indexes.
  3. Put notifications and projections behind a transactional outbox.
  4. Add a replicated ingestion log when bursts exceed database capacity.
  5. Partition log and storage by the narrowest key that preserves required ordering.
  6. Add per-tenant admission, online repartitioning, and automated skew detection.

Each step should solve a measured limit. A log adds operational cost and eventual consistency; it is not automatically an improvement at 2,000 writes/s. Before sharding, load-test the current store with realistic index count, durability settings, record sizes, and skew.

docs.title: Observability and verification
docs.text:
Monitor accepted, committed, and projected rates separately; oldest unprojected event age; batch fill ratio; batch wait; fsync p50/p99; quorum latency; replica lag; partition skew; duplicate rate; disk utilization; compaction debt; and physical bytes per logical byte. Alert on leading indicators such as rising queue age and fsync latency, not only dropped writes.

Test crash points: before append, after leader flush but before response, after projection commit but before offset commit, and during routing cutover. Verify that retries neither lose events nor repeat external effects. Run a node-loss capacity test at target load, because a cluster that works only with every replica healthy has no usable failure margin.

docs.title: L5 and L6 guidance
docs.text:
An L5 design should quantify average and peak logical throughput, choose an acknowledgment boundary, define ordering and idempotency scope, estimate batch and partition counts, and explain one safe failure path. It should distinguish durable acceptance from query visibility and identify the final invariant-enforcing write.

An L6 design should model amplification and degraded-mode capacity, challenge whether ordering can be narrowed, and describe repartitioning as a versioned online protocol rather than "add shards." It should set overload priorities, recovery bandwidth, migration abort thresholds, and observability tied to error budgets. The key senior judgment is knowing which work stays synchronous for correctness and which work can become replayable asynchronous state.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• What exactly does the producer acknowledgment guarantee?
  • Which ordering scope is required, and what parallelism does it permit?
  • How do retries avoid duplicate external effects?
  • How would one device producing 10% of writes be isolated?
  • What is the estimated physical write rate after replication and compaction?
  • How are stale writers fenced during a shard cutover?

docs.title: Pattern: Search and Indexing
docs.text: Search indexes are read-optimized projections, not usually canonical state. A marketplace may require listings searchable by text, category, price, and availability within 30 seconds of an update. The database remains authoritative for purchase and policy decisions; the index makes broad candidate retrieval and ranking affordable.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use a search engine for relevance, inverted indexes, filters, aggregations, and approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval. Avoid it for transactional constraints, authoritative inventory, or simple primary-key lookups. Indexed SQL and database full-text search may be enough at modest scale and remove an entire consistency boundary.

Here, "search index" means a derived candidate-retrieval projection. A database B+ tree is an access path maintained with canonical rows and has different page, MVCC, and transaction semantics; see Database Indexing and Relational Databases.

Need Index structure Cost term search inverted index analysis and update amplification exact filter keyword, bitmap, or postings cardinality-dependent memory numeric range sorted or BKD structure indexing overhead prefix/autocomplete edge n-gram or FST index growth semantic similarity vector ANN approximate results and compute

docs.title: Projection architecture
docs.text:
The write transaction updates canonical data and appends an outbox event. An indexer consumes events, loads any required canonical fields, analyzes text, and upserts only if the incoming entity version is newer. Queries retrieve candidates, apply policy filters, optionally rerank, and validate correctness-sensitive fields against their source.

flowchart LR
    W[Listing API] --> D[(Canonical DB and outbox)]
    D --> I[Index pipeline]
    I --> X[(Versioned search index)]
    Q[Search API] --> X
    X --> R[Candidate reranker]
    R --> P[Policy and availability validation]
    P --> Q

Partition by a stable routing key when queries naturally include one, and replicate shards for throughput and availability. Separate indexing capacity from query capacity where the engine permits it. Use cursor pagination over a point-in-time snapshot and a stable sort tuple such as (score, listing_id). Deep offsets make every shard retain and sort discarded hits, and live updates cause duplicates or omissions.

docs.title: Preserve relationships inside arrays
docs.text:
A projection can be fresh and still answer the wrong question. Consider a listing with two offers:

{"offers": [{"seller": "north", "price": 120}, {"seller": "south", "price": 70}]}

The query "seller north with price below 100" should not match. If indexing turns this into independent arrays of sellers and prices, it can combine north from the first offer with 70 from the second. The requirement is a conjunction on one offer, not two independent existential matches on the listing.

Vendor (Elasticsearch current reference, accessed 2026-09-19): An ordinary object array loses those associations. A nested mapping stores each array element as a separate hidden document, and both predicates must occur inside the same nested query. A listing with two offers creates three Lucene documents: two children and the root. This increases indexing and query cost. See the official nested mapping reference.

Model Correct query boundary Tradeoff one search document per offer seller and price on that document listing fields duplicate; group results explicitly listing with nested offers both predicates in one nested scope child/root expansion and more expensive updates independent arrays only independent membership tests cannot preserve the seller-price relationship

Test the example above as a negative case and seller south AND price < 100 as a positive case. For facets, state whether counts represent matching offers or distinct listings; those are different metrics even when the query is correct. Keep checkout validation in the canonical store regardless of the chosen search representation.

docs.title: Analyzer: text to searchable terms
docs.text:
An analyzer must be identical in meaning at index and query time, although query analysis may omit expansion that is useful only during indexing. Consider the title Women's Running Shoes, Size 8:

Unicode normalization: Women's Running Shoes, Size 8
lowercase:             women's running shoes, size 8
tokenize:              [women's, running, shoes, size, 8]
possessive handling:   [women, running, shoes, size, 8]
stemming:              [women, run, shoe, size, 8]

Do not blindly remove stop words: a query for the band "The Who" can lose both meaningful tokens with an aggressive English stop list. Preserve token positions for phrase queries and offsets for highlighting. Use language-specific analyzers; stemming English text with rules intended for another language damages recall. Synonyms require direction and timing: mapping sneakers => sneakers, shoes at query time is easy to update, while index-time expansion increases postings and requires reindexing.

Keep exact and analyzed fields separate. brand.keyword = "New Balance" supports filtering and aggregation; brand.text supports lexical matching. Normalize keyword values deliberately for case, whitespace, and Unicode. Never change an analyzer in place and assume old tokens follow the new rules; create a versioned index.

docs.title: Inverted lists
docs.text:
An inverted index maps each term to an ordered postings list. For three documents:

D1: red running shoe
D2: blue trail shoe
D3: red trail jacket

red     -> [(D1, tf=1, pos=[0]), (D3, tf=1, pos=[0])]
trail   -> [(D2, tf=1, pos=[1]), (D3, tf=1, pos=[1])]
shoe    -> [(D1, tf=1, pos=[2]), (D2, tf=1, pos=[2])]

For red AND shoe, intersect the sorted document IDs for red and shoe, producing D1. Skip pointers and block metadata jump over ranges that cannot match. Phrase trail shoe additionally checks adjacent positions. Filters can intersect bitmaps or postings before expensive scoring. Compression commonly stores document-ID deltas rather than full IDs. Dense postings have small gaps; sparse terms can have large gaps, so compression effectiveness depends on the distribution.

Indexing is write amplification: one document creates entries in many term, numeric, facet, and vector structures. A document update is commonly represented as a deletion marker plus a newly indexed version. This is why frequent counters and rapidly changing inventory should often remain outside the text index or update through a narrower structure.

docs.title: Worked BM25 scoring
docs.text:
BM25 rewards term frequency, penalizes common terms, and normalizes document length. One common form is:

IDF(q) = ln(1 + (N - df(q) + 0.5) / (df(q) + 0.5))
score(D,q) = IDF(q) * tf*(k1+1) / (tf + k1*(1-b+b*dl/avgdl))

Suppose N=1,000,000, df(shoe)=10,000, tf=3, document length dl=120, average length avgdl=100, k1=1.2, and b=0.75. Then IDF is approximately ln(1 + 990000.5/10000.5) = 4.60. The length term is 1.2 * (0.25 + 0.75*1.2) = 1.38; term saturation is 3*2.2/(3+1.38) = 1.51. The contribution is about 6.95.

A tenfold repeat does not yield a tenfold score because term frequency saturates. Longer documents receive a penalty, but tuning b changes its strength. Combine field scores carefully: title matches may receive a boost, while category and stock are filters. Offline judgments should measure NDCG or recall at K; online experiments should monitor conversion, abandonment, latency, and harmful-result rates. Do not tune solely to clicks because position bias reinforces the existing ranker.

docs.title: Distributed shard top-K
docs.text:
With six shards and a requested top 20, the coordinator asks every shard for local candidates, then merges them. Returning exactly 20 per shard is sufficient for the global top 20 only when all shards use comparable final scores and no later reranker can promote omitted documents. In practice request K + margin, such as 100, to accommodate policy filtering and reranking.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Coordinator
    participant S1 as Shard 1
    participant S2 as Shard 2
    participant SN as Shard N
    C->>S1: query and local top 100
    C->>S2: query and local top 100
    C->>SN: query and local top 100
    S1-->>C: scored candidates
    S2-->>C: scored candidates
    SN-->>C: scored candidates
    C->>C: heap merge, filter, rerank
    C-->>C: top 20 of retrieved candidates

The merge maintains a min-heap of size K; processing S*M candidates costs O(S*M*log K). If shard statistics differ, IDF and scores may not be comparable. A distributed-frequency prequery improves accuracy but adds a round trip; global term statistics or stable routing can be alternatives. Shard timeouts need a product policy. Commerce usually fails explicitly rather than silently hiding inventory; exploratory search may return labeled partial results.

Use search_after with the last stable tuple and a point-in-time identifier:

{"pit":"p17","after":[6.95,"listing-842"],"ranking_version":"r12"}

The tie-breaker must be unique and ordering must be deterministic. Encode, authenticate, and expire cursors; clients must not alter shard state or ranking versions.

Elasticsearch pagination requires the same query and sort, the complete last-hit sort tuple, and the latest returned PIT ID. Keep index-native sort separate from external reranking: a bounded candidate margin does not prove globally exact reranked top-K, and an external score cannot be used as native search_after without a materialized ordering (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Immutable segments and merge
docs.text:
Search engines commonly buffer documents, flush immutable segments, and expose them after refresh. Deletes are tombstones until merge rewrites surviving documents. Many tiny segments increase file handles, duplicated dictionaries, and query fan-out. Large merges reclaim space and improve reads but consume disk bandwidth, CPU, and temporary capacity.

flowchart TD
    B[In-memory buffer] --> S1[Small segment]
    U[Updates and delete markers] --> S2[Small segment]
    S1 --> M[Background merge]
    S2 --> M
    S3[Older segment] --> M
    M --> L[Large compact segment]
    L --> Q[Search readers]

A tiered merge policy groups similarly sized segments to avoid repeatedly rewriting one huge segment. If ten 1 GB segments merge, budget more than 10 GB of temporary free space plus concurrent writes. Throttle merges before they saturate query disks; if indexing backlog grows, add capacity or reduce refresh frequency rather than disabling durability. During incident response, inspect segment count, merge queue, disk latency, heap pressure, and rejected writes together.

docs.title: Vector retrieval: HNSW versus IVF
docs.text:
HNSW builds a multilayer proximity graph. A query descends sparse upper layers, then explores neighbors at the base layer. It usually offers high recall and low latency, but graph edges consume substantial memory and updates/deletes can be expensive. efSearch controls candidates explored: increasing it improves recall and latency cost. M controls graph degree and affects memory and build quality.

IVF trains centroids, assigns vectors to coarse lists, and searches only the nearest nprobe lists. Product quantization can compress vectors further. IVF is attractive for very large, batch-oriented corpora and memory constraints, but needs representative training and suffers when distribution drifts. Higher nprobe improves recall at greater compute cost.

Property HNSW IVF or IVF-PQ training none for basic HNSW centroid and optional codebook training memory high graph overhead lower with quantization updates convenient inserts, costly cleanup often best with batch rebuilds tuning M, construction/search breadth list count, nprobe, quantization fit high-recall interactive search billion-scale or compressed retrieval

Measure recall against an exact-search sample using production embeddings and filters. Applying a selective filter after ANN can leave too few hits; prefilter where supported, route by filter, or overfetch with a bounded retry. Version the embedding model in every vector record. Vectors from different model spaces are not comparable.

docs.title: Zero-downtime migration
docs.text:
Create listings_v2 rather than mutate v1. Record source snapshot version T0, bulk-load that snapshot, and continue capturing changes. Replay events newer than T0 with entity-version guards until lag approaches zero. Dual-write only if its failure semantics are understood; an outbox replay is easier to repair.

Shadow a sample of queries to both indexes. Compare error rate, latency, result overlap, policy violations, zero-result rate, and judged relevance rather than requiring identical ranking. Then canary a small read percentage, increase gradually, and atomically switch the alias. Keep feeding canonical updates and tombstones to v1 during the rollback window, or catch it up and verify before alias rollback. A frozen old index is not a fresh rollback target. Delete v1 only after retention and rollback criteria pass.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> BulkLoad
    BulkLoad --> CatchUp: snapshot T0 complete
    CatchUp --> Shadow: replay lag bounded
    Shadow --> Canary: quality gates pass
    Canary --> Active: increase traffic
    Canary --> RolledBack: regression
    Active --> Retired: rollback window elapsed

Deletes are the dangerous migration case. A snapshot can contain a listing deleted after T0; replay must include tombstones, and stale versions must never resurrect it. Store a tombstone through the maximum event replay and migration duration.

docs.title: Failure semantics and operations
docs.text:
Failure Behavior duplicate indexing event upsert only if entity version is newer events arrive out of order version guard rejects stale update and delete index corruption build a new version, validate, and switch the alias pipeline lag expose freshness and alert against the 30-second SLO shard timeout follow an explicit partial-result policy merge storm throttle merge/indexing, preserve query headroom, add temporary capacity ANN recall regression compare exact sample, inspect model/version and parameter drift, roll back alias

For lag, identify whether the bottleneck is source capture, transform, bulk rejection, or refresh. Preserve offsets, scale the constrained stage, and prioritize tombstones and policy updates. For disk pressure, stop allocation to the node, reduce replicas only if durability permits, throttle ingestion, and relocate shards; never delete segment files manually.
