For suspected corruption, remove the replica from routing, verify another copy, rebuild from canonical data, and compare document counts and sampled fields.

Monitor source-to-index version age, event backlog, rejected writes, refresh and merge time, segment count, disk watermark, shard skew, p95/p99 query latency, timeout and partial-result rate, zero-result rate, BM25 and ANN candidate counts, exact-sample recall, index-to-source mismatch, and deletion age.

For embedding compatibility, hybrid retrieval, reranking, RAG grounding, and stage-specific evaluation, continue with the Applied AI Systems track.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Specify analyzers, exact fields, token positions, and schema versions.
  • Explain candidate generation, BM25 tuning, filters, and final ranking separately.
  • Bound distributed top-K work and define pagination consistency.
  • Capacity-plan segments, merges, temporary disk, replicas, and rebuild time.
  • Select HNSW or IVF using measured recall, memory, updates, and latency.
  • Reindex from a snapshot plus ordered replay with tombstones and rollback.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• Which fields are filters versus ranking signals?
  • How are out-of-order updates prevented from resurrecting deleted listings?
  • Why can shard-local scores be incomparable, and how is global top-K merged?
  • How do HNSW and IVF differ operationally?
  • How do pagination results remain stable during updates?
  • What is the zero-downtime reindex and rollback plan?

docs.title: Pattern: Streaming Aggregation
docs.text: Streaming aggregation incrementally computes results over event time. A payment dashboard may need success rate per merchant in one-minute windows within ten seconds while handling duplicates and events up to five minutes late. The design must define time, completeness, correction, durability, and approximation rather than merely selecting a stream processor.

docs.title: When to use and avoid
docs.text:
Use streaming when freshness matters and incremental computation is cheaper than rescanning. Use batch when hours-old results suffice, corrections dominate, or operational simplicity wins. Keep immutable raw events so every projection can be rebuilt after code, schema, or policy errors.

Window Use Caveat tumbling fixed non-overlapping reports boundary effects hopping rolling metrics at fixed steps one event updates several windows sliding continuously changing recent interval greater compute and state session activity separated by an inactivity gap late events can merge sessions 
flowchart LR
    E[Timestamped events] --> L[(Partitioned durable log)]
    L --> A[Keyed event-time operators]
    A --> S[(Checkpointed state)]
    A --> O[(Revisioned aggregate sink)]
    L --> B[Batch recomputation]
    B --> O
    A --> C[(Late correction stream)]

An event contains event_id, merchant, outcome, amount, event time, producer version, and ingestion time. Partition by merchant so one task owns a merchant's ordinary state. Salt exceptional hot merchants into deterministic subkeys and combine partial aggregates downstream.

docs.title: From logical operators to physical subtasks
docs.text:
A logical plan says what happens: read, validate, assign timestamps, key, aggregate, and publish. A physical plan says how many concurrent subtasks execute each operator, where records cross the network, and which subtask owns each state entry. Do not draw one logical box and assume it is one process.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Logical[Logical dataflow]
        LS[Source] --> LV[Validate]
        LV --> LK[Key by merchant]
        LK --> LA[Window aggregate]
        LA --> LO[Revisioned sink]
    end
    subgraph Physical[Example physical execution]
        S0[Source 0] --> V0[Validate 0]
        S1[Source 1] --> V1[Validate 1]
        V0 -->|keyed shuffle| A0[Aggregate 0]
        V0 -->|keyed shuffle| A1[Aggregate 1]
        V1 -->|keyed shuffle| A0
        V1 -->|keyed shuffle| A1
        A0 --> O0[Sink 0]
        A1 --> O1[Sink 1]
    end

For a partitioned-log source with one active reader per partition, useful source parallelism is bounded by readable input partitions. Stateless validation can chain to source subtasks when CPU and failure isolation allow it. keyBy(merchant) is a shuffle boundary: every record for one key maps to one key group, and exactly one active aggregate subtask owns that key group's state. This ownership, not the machine that first received the event, provides per-key serialization.

Choose more stable key groups than current workers, for example 4,096 key groups mapped across 128 aggregate subtasks. Rescaling then moves key groups rather than changing the hash of every key. The mapping and hash function are durable job metadata; changing either without migration can make restored state unreachable. A salted hot key creates several independently owned partials and therefore requires a second keyed shuffle to combine them.

flowchart TD
    K[Event key] --> H[Stable hash to key group]
    H --> G0[Key groups 0 to 1023]
    H --> G1[Key groups 1024 to 2047]
    H --> G2[Key groups 2048 to 3071]
    H --> G3[Key groups 3072 to 4095]
    G0 --> T0[Subtask owner]
    G1 --> T1[Subtask owner]
    G2 --> T2[Subtask owner]
    G3 --> T3[Subtask owner]
    T0 --> L0[(Local state)]
    T1 --> L1[(Local state)]
    T2 --> L2[(Local state)]
    T3 --> L3[(Local state)]

Local state makes each update cheap but is not the durable authority. A subtask may keep indexes, windows, and timers in memory plus local disk; completed checkpoints copy a consistent recoverable form to failure-independent durable storage. Losing a worker discards its local copy, restores its assigned key groups from a completed checkpoint, and replays source records. Replicated local disks can shorten recovery, but they do not replace a checkpoint that binds state to source positions.

docs.title: Timestamped window assignment
docs.text:
Event time represents when the business action happened; processing time represents when the processor observed it. A delayed mobile event at 12:01:12 received at 12:04:00 belongs to its event-time window, not the current processing-time window.

For a tumbling window of size W, assign timestamp t to:

start = floor(t / W) * W
end = start + W

With W=60 seconds, events at 12:01:00.000 through 12:01:59.999 belong to [12:01, 12:02). Half-open intervals prevent an event exactly at 12:02 from entering two windows.

A hopping window has size W and slide S. With a ten-minute window sliding every minute, each event contributes to ten starts. Compute the latest aligned start floor(t/S)*S, then enumerate starts latest, latest-S, ... while start > t-W. This write amplification must be included in state and CPU estimates.

Session windows track intervals per key and merge events separated by no more than gap G. With last/first event spans [10:00,10:05] and [10:12,10:15] and G=5m, the seven-minute gap initially keeps them separate. A late event at 10:09 is four minutes after 10:05 and three minutes before 10:12, connecting them. The processor must replace the two old session results with one merged revision if their state is still retained.

docs.title: Watermarks and late data
docs.text:
A watermark is a lower-bound policy for expected future event timestamps, not proof that no older event will arrive. A simple bounded-out-of-orderness watermark per partition is:

partitionWatermark = maxEventTimeObserved - outOfOrderBound
operatorWatermark = min(active partition watermarks)

If the maximum observed timestamp is 12:10 and allowed disorder is five minutes, the partition watermark is 12:05. Windows ending at or before 12:05 can emit an on-time result. Taking the minimum prevents a fast partition from closing state needed by a slower one.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant P1 as Partition 1
    participant P2 as Partition 2
    participant O as Window operator
    participant S as Revisioned sink
    P1->>O: max event time 12:10, watermark 12:05
    P2->>O: max event time 12:08, watermark 12:03
    O->>O: operator watermark is 12:03
    O->>S: close windows ending at or before 12:03
    P2->>O: late event for 12:02 window
    O->>S: upsert higher revision or retract and replace

Idle partitions would freeze the minimum forever. Mark a partition idle only after a configured no-data period and broker health check; when it resumes, process its older records through the late-data policy. Never advance watermarks from wall clock alone while input is backlogged.

Define two lateness bounds. Allowed lateness keeps closed-window state available for immediate revision, perhaps five minutes. Beyond that, route events to a correction topic and periodic recomputation rather than dropping silently. Track lateness distributions to choose bounds from evidence. Financial totals may accept corrections for days; an alerting chart may freeze after minutes.

The out-of-order bound delays the watermark; allowed lateness separately extends state retention after the on-time firing. Flink 1.20 windows distinguishes these controls and defaults allowed lateness to zero. Its time-window timers use the largest included timestamp (end - 1 ms), so test exact boundaries against engine granularity rather than copying continuous-time inequalities literally (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Retractions and revisioned output
docs.text:
An append-only sink cannot correct an already emitted aggregate without encoding change. Use either upsert revisions or changelog records. For an upsert key (merchant, window_start), store {count, successes, amount, revision} and conditionally apply only a larger revision.

For a changelog, emit -old then +new. Suppose a closed window reported 8 successes / 10 attempts. A late successful payment changes it to 9/11:

RETRACT merchant=M1 window=12:01 revision=4 successes=8 attempts=10
UPSERT  merchant=M1 window=12:01 revision=5 successes=9 attempts=11

Consumers applying signed deltas must deduplicate each change leg and apply the pair atomically if transient totals cannot be exposed. A consumer of full-value upserts may instead replace the value conditionally by revision. Merely giving both delta records a revision does not prevent a crash between them from leaving an incorrect total. Ratios are derived from mergeable components; never average per-partition success percentages. Correct combination is sum(successes)/sum(attempts).

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Open
    Open --> OnTimeEmitted: watermark passes window end
    OnTimeEmitted --> Revised: event within allowed lateness
    Revised --> Revised: another accepted late event
    OnTimeEmitted --> Final: cleanup watermark passes
    Revised --> Final: cleanup watermark passes
    Final --> Correction: very late event

State expires only after window_end + allowed_lateness and sink durability. Early cleanup makes a legal late event impossible to apply. Very-late correction can write a higher namespace or revision from batch; establish precedence so replaying old stream output cannot overwrite corrected values.

docs.title: Checkpoints and replay
docs.text:
A checkpoint captures operator state, source offsets, timers, and relevant metadata at a consistent barrier. In aligned checkpointing, barriers flow through every input; an operator temporarily waits for all inputs before snapshotting. Unaligned checkpoints include in-flight buffers and can finish during backpressure but produce larger state.

flowchart TD
    C[Coordinator starts checkpoint 42] --> P[Sources persist offsets]
    P --> B[Barriers cross partitions]
    B --> O[Operators snapshot keyed state and timers]
    O --> D[(Durable checkpoint storage)]
    D --> K[Checkpoint acknowledged]
    K --> T[Commit transactional or revisioned sink effects]

After a crash, restore the latest completed checkpoint, seek each source to captured offsets, and replay. Any sink write made after that snapshot may repeat. Engine-level "exactly once" does not automatically cover arbitrary HTTP or database sinks. Use a transactional sink coordinated with checkpoints, or revisioned idempotent keys with the replay conditions below. A payment-window upsert such as (window_key, revision) rejects lower or duplicate revisions but needs deterministic revision identity to make replay harmless.

A locally incremented revision alone is insufficient if replay can assign that same revision to different aggregate contents. Require deterministic per-key replay including timer order, or coordinate sink commit with checkpoints. A new attempt epoch fences old writers but must not publish incomplete restored totals over a later accepted result. Batch corrections need their own authority/cutoff so old stream output cannot win by accidental counter size.

Checkpoint interval trades recovery point and overhead. If state is 500 GB, incremental checkpoints every 30 seconds may be practical only when changes are small and durable storage supports throughput. Measure duration, alignment delay, bytes, failure rate, and restore time. Retain several known-good checkpoints because a completed snapshot can encode a logic-corrupted state. Periodically restore one in an isolated environment.

Separate steady-state checkpoint bandwidth from full recovery bandwidth. If 2.4 TB of owned state changes at 2% per minute, incremental snapshots write about 2.4 TB * 0.02 / 60 = 0.8 GB/s before compression and storage amplification. If the recovery objective is 20 minutes, a full restore needs at least 2.4 TB / 1,200 s = 2 GB/s of useful read bandwidth, plus replay and state-index rebuild. A storage service that handles incremental writes but throttles a fleet-wide restore does not meet that objective.

Deployment state compatibility matters. Assign stable operator identifiers; changing them can orphan savepoint state. For risky logic changes, start a parallel projection from a source offset, compare results, then switch sink aliases instead of mutating irreplaceable state.

docs.title: Parallelism, failure headroom, and rescaling
docs.text:
Measure a subtask's sustainable rate with realistic key skew, window overlap, serialization, checkpointing, and sink latency. Let lambda_peak be peak input rate, r_safe the measured sustainable rate per subtask at the chosen latency/utilization target, and f_survive the fraction of workers remaining after the planned failure. Then:

required parallelism = ceil(lambda_peak / (r_safe * f_survive))

Suppose peak input is 1.2 million events/s, a benchmarked aggregate subtask safely sustains 18,000 events/s, and the fleet must survive losing one of three equal zones. f_survive=2/3, so the minimum is ceil(1,200,000 / (18,000 * 2/3)) = 100 subtasks. Choose 108 to distribute 36 per zone. Normal load is about 11,111 events/s per subtask; after one-zone loss it is 16,667, still below the measured 18,000 limit. This arithmetic is invalid if a hot key cannot be split or the sink saturates first.

Rescaling has its own temporary capacity budget. Moving 900 GB of key-group state through an effective 3 GB/s transfer path has a lower bound of five minutes. At 1.2 million events/s and 300 bytes/event, five minutes can add 108 GB of replay or buffered input, before replication. Confirm source retention, network headroom, local free disk, checkpoint timeout, and downstream catch-up capacity before starting.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Control plane
    participant O as Old owners
    participant D as Durable checkpoint
    participant N as New owners
    participant L as Source log
    C->>O: stop at consistent checkpoint
    O->>D: snapshot key groups and offsets
    C->>N: assign key groups under new parallelism
    D->>N: restore assigned state
    N->>L: resume captured offsets
    L->>N: replay while live input remains durable
    N-->>C: healthy and caught up

Prefer a coordinated stop-and-restore when duplicate ownership would violate correctness. Online migration requires epoch-fenced ownership and dual-read or dual-write rules; it is not merely adding workers. Autoscaling is also bounded by input partitions, available key groups, state movement time, and the time until backlog exhausts retention.

docs.title: Worked HyperLogLog example
docs.text:
Exact unique-user sets can dominate memory. HyperLogLog (HLL) hashes each user, uses the first p bits to select one of m=2^p registers, and stores the maximum observed position of the first one bit in the remaining hash. Many leading zeros imply a rarer hash and therefore larger cardinality.

For a tiny teaching example with p=2, there are four registers. Suppose hashes produce:

bucket 00 remainder 001... => rank 3, register[0] = 3
bucket 01 remainder 1...   => rank 1, register[1] = 1
bucket 00 remainder 0001...=> rank 4, register[0] = 4
bucket 10 remainder 01...  => rank 2, register[2] = 2
registers = [4, 1, 2, 0]

The estimator uses a bias-corrected harmonic mean of 2^-register. Real systems use thousands of registers and small-range corrections; the toy estimate is not accurate. Relative standard error is approximately 1.04/sqrt(m). With p=14, m=16,384, error is about 0.81%, and one-byte registers require roughly 16 KiB per sketch. HLLs merge by register-wise maximum, making per-partition partials easy to combine. They do not support exact deletion: use time-bucketed sketches or recompute when retractions matter. See Probabilistic Data Structures for exact-first selection and lifecycle rules.

docs.title: Worked Count-Min Sketch example
docs.text:
A Count-Min Sketch (CMS) estimates frequencies using d hash rows and w counters per row. Increment one counter in every row. Query returns the minimum, because collisions only overcount.

width w = ceil(e / epsilon)
depth d = ceil(ln(1 / delta))

For additive error at most epsilon*N with probability 1-delta, choose epsilon=0.001, delta=0.01: w=2719, d=5, or about 13,595 counters. With four-byte counters that is about 53 KiB.

Toy rows of width five might hash apple to columns [1,3] and pear to [1,4]. After three apples and two pears, row one's shared counter is five; row two has apple at three and pear at two. Querying apple takes min(5,3)=3, recovering its count despite one collision. In general CMS can overestimate. Conservative update increments only counters equal to the current minimum and reduces overcount for skewed streams.

Ordinary CMS supports element-wise addition and merge when dimensions and hash seeds match. Do not assume conservative-update arrays are equivalent to processing the combined stream with conservative update; use documented merge guarantees for that variant. Standard CMS does not safely handle arbitrary negative updates without assumptions; a turnstile sketch or exact correction store may be required. Use it for heavy-hitter candidates, then verify candidates against exact storage when decisions have financial or abuse impact.

docs.title: Hot keys and state sizing
docs.text:
One merchant may generate 30% of events, defeating key partitioning. Salt it to (merchant, hash(event_id) mod 32), aggregate partial counts, sums, HLL registers, or CMS arrays, then combine by unsalted key. All components must be associative and mergeable. Average, percentile, and ratio need mergeable state: sum plus count, a quantile sketch, and numerator plus denominator respectively.

Estimate state before deployment:

state ~= activeKeys * overlappingWindows * bytesPerAccumulator

One million merchants, ten hopping windows, and a 200-byte accumulator imply roughly 2 GB before framework and storage overhead; an HLL per window at 16 KiB would imply 163.84 GB (about 152.6 GiB). Use lower precision, fewer windows, sparse representation, or two-stage aggregation.

docs.title: Failure semantics and runbooks
docs.text:
Failure Recovery duplicate event deduplicate by event ID within retention or use idempotent source semantics processor crash restore a completed checkpoint and replay offsets sink succeeds before checkpoint transactional commit or revisioned idempotent upsert event is late revise within policy; route very-late data to correction hot key salt into mergeable partial aggregates state exceeds disk expire by watermark, add partitions, or use a disclosed approximation bad deployment stop output, restore prior job/savepoint, replay or rebuild a new projection

When watermark lag grows, compare broker lag, partition idleness, timestamp validity, backpressure, and one hot key. Quarantine producers emitting future timestamps because they can advance a naive watermark and close valid windows early. When checkpoints fail, preserve the last good snapshot, inspect storage latency and alignment, reduce concurrent heavy operations, and scale state bandwidth; do not restart repeatedly until retention deletes replayable input.

For incorrect aggregates, freeze consumer-visible alias or mark results stale, identify affected code version and time range, run batch recomputation from immutable events, write higher revisions, and compare stream versus batch samples before reopening. Keep raw-log retention longer than maximum detection plus rebuild time.

Monitor input/output rate, broker and event-time lag, watermark by partition, late-event histogram, retractions, correction backlog, duplicate rate, checkpoint duration/bytes/failures, restore tests, state bytes, hot partitions, sink conflicts, HLL/CMS parameters, and batch-versus-stream divergence.

docs.title: Design checklist
docs.text:
• Define event timestamp, half-open windows, watermark, allowed lateness, and finality.
  • Specify revision or retraction semantics for every downstream consumer.
  • Coordinate checkpoints with source offsets and idempotent sink effects.
  • Distinguish logical operators, physical subtasks, keyed shuffle boundaries, and state owners.
  • Calculate normal, failure, and rescaling capacity from measured rates and restore bandwidth.
  • Size state from keys, overlapping windows, accumulator bytes, and retention.
  • Salt hot keys only with correctly mergeable accumulators.
  • Publish HLL/CMS error bounds and retain an exact validation path.
  • Preserve raw events and regularly rehearse checkpoint restore and batch rebuild.

docs.title: Interview prompts
docs.text:
• Is time processing time or event time, and why?
  • What exactly does a watermark guarantee?
  • How is a late event retracted or revisioned downstream?
  • How are sink writes safe across checkpoint replay?
  • When should HLL or CMS replace exact state, and what errors result?
  • How can every aggregate be rebuilt after a logic bug?

docs.title: Deliberate Practice System
docs.text: This practice track turns course knowledge into observable system design skill. Every activity works with paper, a text editor, a timer, and the supplied scoring keys. No service, simulator, or backend is required.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
For executable mechanism-level evidence, add the eight engineering fault labs, engineering assessment, and Atlas longitudinal capstone. These are optional Python-based extensions to this track's paper-first exercises. Use the registry to find prerequisites and explicit coverage gaps.

flowchart LR
    D[Entry diagnostic] --> S[Score evidence]
    S --> R[Route weak skills]
    R --> P[Progressive drills]
    P --> F[Failure or migration lab]
    F --> M[Timed mock]
    M --> C[Review and schedule retry]
    C --> P
  1. Read the competency model.
  2. Take the 75-minute entry diagnostic without notes.
  3. Record evidence in the learner scorecard.
  4. Use the diagnostic route to select progressive drills.
  5. Add one failure lab or migration lab each week.
  6. Retain decisions with spaced repetition.
  7. Run paired mocks with interviewer mode.

docs.title: Scenario packs
docs.text:
Choose one pack and open only its candidate prompt and workbook until the timer ends:

Scenario Candidate start Primary emphasis Payment orchestration Start prompt Irreversible effects and financial authority Notification platform Start prompt Policy, fairness, and provider uncertainty Distributed job scheduler Start prompt Time, leases, worker fit, and regional ownership

Open each pack overview, hints, rubric, exemplars, labs, and interviewer material only after the first attempt.

A blind attempt uses only prompt and workbook until time expires. If blocked, freeze that artifact before opening a hint and label the continuation assisted; never merge the repaired answer into the original score. Hidden HTML sections are a convenience, not access control: source view and site search can reveal them. Evaluators should provide a prompt/workbook-only copy for a measured session.

docs.title: Practice modes
docs.text: Mode Time Output Use when Micro drill 3-8 min One calculation, decision, or trace Building fluency Focus lab 15-25 min Failure or migration artifact Fixing a narrow gap Integrated design 45 min End-to-end design and summary Combining skills Diagnostic or mock 75 min Design, challenge responses, scorecard Measuring readiness

docs.title: Evidence loop
docs.text:
For each attempt, preserve only four artifacts:

  • the prompt and assumptions;
  • the design or decision record;
  • the evaluator's observed evidence and score;
  • one retry objective with a due date.

An explanation counts only when it changes a design, predicts behavior, or defends a tradeoff. Vocabulary without application does not count.

docs.title: Course connections
docs.text:
• Use the delivery framework for interview structure.
  • Use estimation when a number must change a choice.
  • Review API and data modeling, consistency, and reliability after related misses.
  • Practice scale mechanisms through scaling reads, scaling writes, and handling contention.
  • Select domain cases from the study plans.

docs.title: Weekly minimum
docs.text:
• Two micro-drill sessions.
  • One Design-Break-Recover lab.
  • One 45-minute design or paired mock.
  • One scored retry of a previous weakness.
  • Daily due cards from the spaced repetition deck.

Do not average away a critical invariant violation. A design that can double charge, oversell, lose acknowledged data, or expose unauthorized data must be repaired before increasing difficulty.

docs.title: Evidence-Based Competency Model
docs.text: Use the same 0-4 scale for every skill. Score the strongest level fully supported by the artifact or spoken answer. Intent, confidence, and diagram polish are not evidence.

docs.title: Universal scale
docs.text:
Level Observable evidence 0 Omits the skill, contradicts requirements, or creates a critical correctness risk. 1 Names a relevant concept but cannot apply it to the prompt. Decisions are generic or reactive. 2 Applies the skill correctly to the main path and connects it to a stated requirement. Important edges remain untested. 3 Quantifies or traces the decision, handles credible failures, compares an alternative, and names validation signals. This is the L5 anchor. 4 Exposes hidden constraints, designs safe evolution and ownership boundaries, and reasons across failure domains, cost, and policy. This is the L6 anchor.

Evidence rule

Award a level only when all lower-level behavior is also present. Record a quote, calculation, diagram element, or artifact cell that supports the score.

docs.title: Competencies and anchors
docs.text: Competency Level 3: L5 anchor Level 4: L6 anchor Framing Prioritizes users, use cases, exclusions, invariants, and measurable SLOs in five minutes. Finds policy, tenant, regulatory, or organizational constraints that reverse choices. Estimation Computes peak load, storage, amplification, skew, and failure headroom; each changes a decision. Models uncertainty, cost drivers, regional loss, and the measurement plan that replaces assumptions. API and data model Aligns contracts, identifiers, state transitions, indexes, pagination, and access patterns. Defines compatibility, ownership, retention, privacy deletion, and cross-boundary semantics. Baseline architecture Presents the smallest correct end-to-end path and traces acknowledgment meaning. Separates control and data planes or teams only when isolation and evolution justify it. Scale and contention Locates the limiting resource and uses a fitting partition, cache, or asynchronous mechanism. Handles hot-key skew, overload isolation, capacity economics, and explicit redesign triggers. Consistency Assigns operation-specific guarantees and makes retries and duplicate effects safe. Defines reconciliation, fencing, conflict policy, and guarantees during migration or regional failover. Reliability Covers deadlines, bounded retries, degradation, recovery, and evidence of recovery. Connects blast radius, RTO/RPO, regional strategy, game days, and ownership. Operations Names SLIs, alerts, queue/capacity signals, rollout gates, and runbook actions. Defines error-budget policy, safe automation, cost accountability, and cross-team escalation. Tradeoffs Compares realistic alternatives against requirements and rejects unnecessary complexity. Frames reversible versus irreversible decisions and stages investment across growth horizons. Communication Maintains a structured narrative, checks alignment, and closes with risks and recommendation. Reframes under new evidence, resolves stakeholder conflict, and communicates uncertainty precisely.

docs.title: Critical gates
docs.text:
A total score never compensates for these failures:

  • broken domain invariant;
  • acknowledgment before promised durability;
  • unsafe retry of a non-idempotent effect;
  • unauthorized access or unbounded sensitive-data exposure;
  • no recovery path for canonical state;
  • migration with no compatibility window or rollback boundary.

Cap overall readiness at level 1 if a critical gate remains after one interviewer prompt. Cap at level 2 if the candidate repairs it only after direct instruction.

These are readiness ceilings on the universal evidence scale, not replacements for a numeric total. Keep raw /40, unresolved gates, hint-assisted repairs, and readiness separately. Scenario packs use their own dimensions and numeric caps; do not convert their totals into these ten competencies without rescoring actual evidence. Apply dimension hint limits first, then the lowest applicable total cap. Neutral probes supply no mechanism; directional probes cap the affected evidence at 3, and direct repair instruction at 2.

docs.title: Readiness rules
docs.text:
Score all ten competencies, maximum 40.

Target Readiness evidence Developing Below 22, or any critical gate failed L5 practice-ready 22-27, no critical gate, framing and baseline at least 2 L5 interview-ready 28+, at least seven competencies at 3+, no score below 2, repeated across three prompts L6 practice-ready L5 interview-ready plus at least three level-4 competencies L6 interview-ready L5 interview-ready plus 34+, at least six level-4 competencies including evolution and reliability evidence, repeated across three domains

These are course calibration labels, not guarantees of hiring level or a substitute for an employer-specific rubric. Use repeated evidence, not one exceptional attempt. Compare this model with the course's shorter interview scorecard, then capture attempts in the learner scorecard.

docs.title: 75-Minute Entry Diagnostic
docs.text: This diagnostic samples framing, quantitative reasoning, architecture, failure recovery, evolution, and communication. Take it closed-book. Use paper or one local text file. The evaluator may be another person or the learner after a 30-minute break.

docs.title: Candidate prompt
docs.text:
Design a multi-tenant notification platform for product teams. A producer submits email, push, or SMS notifications to one user or to an audience. The platform selects a permitted channel, renders a versioned template, calls external providers, and exposes delivery status.

Assume:

  • 40 million notifications/day; normal peak is 8,000 requests/s and a product launch can produce 40,000 requests/s for ten minutes;
  • payload metadata averages 1 KB; rendered bodies average 4 KB and are retained for 30 days;
  • a tenant may send 5 million notifications in one campaign;
  • API acceptance p99 is under 300 ms with 99.95% monthly availability;
  • an accepted request must not disappear; duplicate provider delivery is undesirable but providers can time out after accepting;
  • user consent and tenant quotas must be enforced;
  • delivery status may lag by one minute;
  • start in one region across three zones; describe a credible path to a second region.

You may clarify details. State assumptions when no evaluator is present.

docs.title: Candidate timeline
docs.text: Time Task Required artifact 0-7 min Clarify and frame Prioritized requirements, exclusions, invariants, SLOs 7-15 min Estimate Peak, campaign skew, storage, concurrency or bandwidth, headroom 15-25 min Contracts API, identifiers, state machine, core records 25-42 min Baseline and scale Diagram plus accepted-notification trace 42-55 min Break and recover Three failure traces, overload policy, recovery evidence 55-65 min Evolution Second-region and schema/provider migration plan 65-71 min Evaluator changes Respond to two challenge cards 71-75 min Close Recommendation, top risks, validation metrics

docs.title: Challenge cards
docs.text:
The evaluator chooses two. A solo learner reveals them only at minute 65.

Reveal challenge cards at minute 65
  1. One provider's p99 rises from 400 ms to 20 seconds while returning intermittent success.
  2. A celebrity campaign sends 80% of the launch traffic to one tenant and one template.
  3. Legal requires a tenant-specific data residency boundary in the new region.
  4. A template schema change must roll out while old producers continue for 60 days.
  5. A zone fails during the 40,000 requests/s launch spike.
  6. A provider callback arrives before the worker records its attempt result.

docs.title: Candidate stop line
docs.text:
Do not open the evaluator material until the attempt and 30-minute self-review break are complete.

Evaluator rubric, reference outline, and worked scoring

docs.title: Answer rubric
docs.text:
Score each dimension 0-4 using the competency scale. Multiply by the weight.

Dimension Weight Full-credit evidence Framing and invariants 2 Separates acceptance from delivery; states consent, tenant isolation, durable acceptance, and duplicate-effect expectations. Quantitative reasoning 2 Calculates useful values and recognizes the 5x spike plus tenant/template skew. API and state 2 Uses request/idempotency IDs, stable status semantics, template version, tenant scope, and pagination. Baseline design 3 Keeps acceptance short, durably records work, processes asynchronously, and traces provider interaction. Scale and isolation 2 Uses bounded partitions/queues, fair admission, quotas, and hot-tenant isolation without claiming queues create capacity. Consistency and duplicates 3 Makes acceptance idempotent, defines attempt identity, handles ambiguous provider outcomes, and reconciles callbacks. Failure and recovery 3 Defines deadlines, retry budgets, poison handling, rebuild/replay, zone loss behavior, and recovery evidence. Evolution and migration 2 Provides compatibility, staged traffic, data movement, rollback, and decommission gates. Operations and security 2 Covers consent authorization, secrets, audit, SLIs, alerts, and capacity/lag signals. Communication 1 Structured, requirement-led, responsive, and closes with risks and triggers.

Maximum weighted points: 4 * 22 = 88.

docs.title: Critical checks
docs.text:
Mark the attempt unsafe regardless of total if it:

  • acknowledges before durable storage without stating the loss tradeoff;
  • retries provider calls indefinitely or promises exactly-once delivery;
  • permits cross-tenant reads or bypasses consent;
  • has no overload behavior at 40,000 requests/s;
  • proposes active-active writes without conflict, fencing, or ownership semantics.

docs.title: Reference answer outline
docs.text: This is a scoring key, not a required architecture.

docs.title: Contract and useful estimates
docs.text:
• For these estimates, daily volume and send-rate figures mean expanded recipient notifications. If they instead count audience API commands, multiply by measured audience size before sizing workers or storage.
  • Invariants: every accepted command has durable status; tenant A cannot access tenant B; no new dispatch authorized after an opt-out wins the policy/dispatch serialization boundary; repeated command ID returns the original logical result.
  • Delivery is at-least-once processing with idempotent local effects. Provider ambiguity prevents a universal exactly-once claim.
  • Average intake is 40,000,000 / 86,400 = 463/s; normal peak is already 17x average and launch peak is 5x normal peak.
  • One 5-million campaign over ten minutes averages 8,333 notifications/s before retries and channel fan-out.
  • Thirty-day logical body storage is about 40M * 4 KB * 30 = 4.8 TB; 1 KB metadata adds about 1.2 TB if retained for the same 30 days, before indexes and replicas.
  • If mean provider occupancy is 500 ms at 8,000 sends/s, Little's Law gives about 4,000 in-flight calls. If that mean rises to 20 seconds, concurrency would become 160,000, so workers need strict per-provider limits. The challenge supplies p99, not mean; do not substitute that percentile into Little's Law as a measured average.

docs.title: Contracts and records
docs.text:
POST /v1/tenants/{tenantId}/notifications
Idempotency-Key: command-id
{recipient|audience, templateId, templateVersion, variables, channelPolicy}

202 {notificationId, status: ACCEPTED}
GET /v1/tenants/{tenantId}/notifications/{notificationId}
GET /v1/tenants/{tenantId}/notifications?cursor=...&status=...

Core records: notification command, recipient expansion or campaign cursor, immutable template version, consent snapshot/reference, delivery attempt, provider receipt, status event, and audit record. State might progress from ACCEPTED to ELIGIBLE to DISPATCHING to DELIVERED, FAILED, or SUPPRESSED; callback ordering requires monotonic transition rules rather than arrival-order overwrites.

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Producer] --> A[Admission API]
    A --> D[(Canonical store)]
    D --> O[Outbox relay]
    O --> Q[Partitioned work log]
    Q --> W[Channel workers]
    W --> V[External providers]
    V --> C[Callback API]
    C --> D
    D --> S[Status API]

The API authenticates tenant scope, checks quota and a fast consent policy, validates a pinned template version, and atomically stores the command plus outbox record. Acceptance means this transaction committed across the required zone durability boundary. Expansion is chunked and resumable. Work partitions preserve only the ordering scope actually needed; tenant-aware admission and weighted scheduling prevent one campaign from consuming all capacity.

An opt-out cannot recall a request already handed to a provider. Serialize the final consent decision with dispatch authorization and state this boundary in the user contract. Workers claim an attempt with a stable attempt ID, recheck current consent when policy requires it, apply per-provider concurrency and retry budgets, and send the attempt ID when the provider supports idempotency. A timeout produces UNKNOWN, not immediate blind retry. Callback and poll-based reconciliation converge state. Status projections may lag and can rebuild from durable events.

docs.title: Failure and evolution
docs.text:
• Provider slowdown: open per-provider circuit, stop creating unbounded in-flight work, route only when policy permits, delay low-priority traffic, and expose age by tenant/channel.
  • Zone loss at launch: capacity must sustain core traffic after loss or admission must reject/defer by priority. Queue age and accepted-to-dispatched SLO show recovery.
  • Poison template: bounded retries, quarantine by template version, preserve unrelated partitions, repair, and replay.
  • Region two: begin with disaster-recovery replication and fenced failover. Assign tenant home regions for writes if residency applies. Replicate only allowed data, shadow status reads, canary tenants, prove lag/RPO, then increase traffic. Roll back routing before removing old copies.
  • Schema/template change: readers accept old and new; writers initially emit old, then dual-read or dual-write only with a reconciliation artifact; backfill with checkpoints; switch reads; retain rollback; decommission after old-producer and discrepancy gates pass.

docs.title: Worked evaluator notes
docs.text:
Example notes for a plausible candidate answer:

Observation Score implication "Acceptance means the database transaction committed; delivery is later." Baseline and framing at least 2. Calculates average QPS and storage but ignores campaign concentration and zone-loss capacity. Estimation 2, not 3. Uses idempotency key for API but says a queue gives exactly-once provider delivery. Consistency 1; ask about timeout after provider acceptance. On a directional challenge, changes timeout retry to an UNKNOWN attempt plus provider query/callback reconciliation. Consistency is 2 here because key lifetime and safe replay remain unexplained; a directional probe alone permits up to 3, unlike direct repair instruction. Adds per-tenant admission and weighted scheduling after seeing skew. Scale 2; level 3 needs thresholds and saturation signals. Says "multi-region database" with no write ownership or rollback. Evolution 1 and critical follow-up required. Names queue age, provider unknown-attempt age, suppression count, and acceptance errors. Operations 3 if alerts and actions are connected.

docs.title: Worked weighted-score audit
docs.text:
Dimension Raw score Weight Weighted points Framing and invariants 3 2 6 Quantitative reasoning 2 2 4 API and state 2 2 4 Baseline design 3 3 9 Scale and isolation 2 2 4 Consistency and duplicates 2 3 6 Failure and recovery 2 3 6 Evolution and migration 1 2 2 Operations and security 3 2 6 Communication 2 1 2 Total 22 49/88

Diagnostic bands describe one attempt; they do not replace the repeated-domain readiness rules in the competency model.

Weighted total Diagnostic interpretation 0-43 Developing; weighted average is below level 2 or a critical gate remains 44-65 Coherent baseline with material depth gaps 66-76 L5-depth evidence, subject to per-dimension and critical-gate checks 77-88 L6-depth evidence, subject to level-4 distribution and critical-gate checks

Worked result: 49/88 raw. The notes do not show a repair for regional write ownership and rollback, so the evolution critical gate remains unresolved and readiness is blocked. Do not invent a successful follow-up. Route to ambiguity drills, failure card F1 with constraint C2, and migration labs M1-M2 before another full mock.

docs.title: Study routing
docs.text:
Finding First route Proof before retest Framing below 2 Delivery framework, drills R1-R4 and P1 Produce a five-minute contract with three decision-changing questions. Estimation below 2 Estimation, drills C1-C10 Complete eight calculations with units and a design consequence. API/data below 2 API and data modeling, drills R5-R6 and I2 Trace identifiers and state transitions through one retry. Scale below 2 Scaling writes and contention, drills D3-D6 Identify limiting resource, skew, saturation metric, and overload action. Consistency below 2 Consistency, failure cards F1-F3 Resolve three ambiguous outcomes without exactly-once claims. Reliability below 2 Reliability, all failure decks Complete Design-Break-Recover tables with recovery evidence. Evolution below 2 Migration labs Submit compatibility matrix, rollout gates, and rollback trigger twice. Communication below 2 Pressure drills P1-P10 and interviewer mode Give a five-minute summary with recommendation, risk, and trigger.

Retake after at least seven days using the same prompt only if you keep the challenge cards hidden. Otherwise use a new case and the same rubric.

docs.title: Design-Break-Recover Failure Labs
docs.text:
For runnable complements, use the engineering fault fixtures and correctness-methods guide. Their independent oracles, broken/fixed paths, deterministic cuts, and explicit simulation limits can strengthen the evidence recorded for the tabletop labs below.

Each lab uses a reusable deck. Draw one card from each column, apply it to any course case study, and produce the six-part artifact below. Start with reliability engineering if failure semantics are unfamiliar.

docs.title: Design - 5 minutes
docs.text: Record the invariant, normal request trace, acknowledgment boundary, dependencies, capacity assumption, and top three SLIs.

docs.title: Break - 5 minutes
docs.text: Apply a fault card plus a stress modifier. Trace what each actor knows. Do not jump directly to a solution.

docs.title: Recover - 8 minutes
docs.text:
Define containment, degraded behavior, retry ownership, repair/replay, proof of convergence, and one prevention change.

flowchart LR
    D[Design contract] --> B[Inject fault]
    B --> O[Observe outcomes]
    O --> C[Contain blast radius]
    C --> R[Repair or replay]
    R --> E[Prove convergence]
    E --> L[Change design or runbook]

docs.title: Fault cards
docs.text:
Card Fault F1 Caller times out after the server commits. F2 Server dies before durable acceptance. F3 Queue redelivers a message after worker completion. F4 Dependency latency rises 30x but does not fully fail. F5 One database replica returns stale data. F6 A poison event always crashes one consumer path. F7 Cache fleet loses 80% of capacity. F8 One zone disappears without clean shutdown. F9 Clock skew reaches 90 seconds on some workers. F10 Credentials expire during a long-running workflow. F11 A partial network partition isolates the old leader. F12 A backfill writes malformed records to 0.5% of rows. N1 DNS caches retain a stale endpoint after traffic has moved. N2 PMTU discovery fails, so handshakes work but larger payloads disappear. N3 NAT or conntrack tuple state exhausts during connection churn. N4 A route or anycast catchment shifts traffic onto an under-capacity path. N5 Certificate trust rotates before every verifier accepts the new root. N6 Reconnects and retries synchronize after an edge brownout.

The complete diagnosis, containment, evidence, and recovery prompts are in the Network Failure Cards.

docs.title: Stress modifiers
docs.text: Card Modifier S1 Traffic is at launch peak. S2 One tenant contributes 70% of demand. S3 Retries have no jitter in the current client. S4 A deployment is halfway complete. S5 Observability is delayed by five minutes. S6 A second dependency is at 80% capacity. S7 The on-call cannot manually inspect individual records. S8 The event log can replay only seven days.

docs.title: Constraint cards
docs.text: Card Constraint C1 No acknowledged canonical data may be lost. C2 Duplicate external effects can create financial loss. C3 Reads may be stale for 60 seconds. C4 Recovery must finish within 15 minutes. C5 One tenant must not affect another. C6 No cross-region personal-data copy is allowed. C7 New infrastructure cannot be added during the incident. C8 The system must remain read-only during repair.

docs.title: Failure artifact
docs.text:
Copy and complete:

Field Response System and cards Protected invariant/SLO Last definitely durable step Ambiguous states Immediate containment Degraded user contract Retry owner, bound, and budget Repair/replay procedure Convergence query or metric Rollback/abort trigger Prevention change and owner

docs.title: Scoring key: 0-12
docs.text:
Award 0, 1, or 2 for each:

  1. Causality: traces the fault instead of listing components.
  2. Correctness: protects the stated invariant and labels unknown outcomes.
  3. Containment: bounds retries, queues, concurrency, and tenant blast radius.
  4. Recovery: distinguishes restart, replay, reconciliation, and rebuild.
  5. Evidence: proves convergence with a durable query or actionable metric.
  6. Learning: changes a design, capacity policy, alert, test, or runbook.

Pass at 9+, with no zero in correctness or recovery.

docs.title: Worked lab
docs.text:
System: payment creation. Cards: F1, S3, C2.

  • Design: command ID is unique per merchant order; one transaction records payment intent and outbox. Provider charge is an external effect.
  • Break: provider accepts the charge, worker times out, and synchronized retries begin. Local state is UNKNOWN; another charge could violate the constraint.
  • Contain: stop retries for that attempt ID, cap provider concurrency, and preserve unrelated provider traffic.
  • Recover: query provider by merchant/attempt ID or consume callback; reconcile to charged or failed only with evidence. A transient not-found response is not proof that a delayed original call cannot still commit. Retry only within a documented same-key deduplication window, or after the provider has conclusively fenced/terminated the old operation with no effect; otherwise quarantine unknown work.
  • Evidence: reconcile the expected durable attempt set against provider receipts and ledger entries. Every aged UNKNOWN has either authoritative resolution or an explicitly owned quarantine case; deleting unknown records to make an age metric zero is not recovery. Unexplained ledger/provider discrepancies must be zero.
  • Prevention: provider-specific ambiguity state, jittered retry budget, reconciliation SLO, and a game-day test.

Use the payment system, job scheduler, or notification system for varied semantics.

docs.title: Interviewer Mode
docs.text: This protocol creates consistent mocks without requiring an expert interviewer. The interviewer controls ambiguity and pressure but does not steer toward a favorite architecture.

docs.title: Roles and materials
docs.text:
Candidate: timer view, blank paper/editor, prompt only. Interviewer: prompt, follow-up tree, scorecard, and private constraint cards. Observer, optional: captures quotes and timing but never intervenes.

Both agree on target level, duration, and whether this is assisted practice or a blind measured attempt. For measured attempts use the hint effects below; record assisted attempts separately. Use the competency model and learner scorecard.

docs.title: 60-minute protocol
docs.text:
Time Interviewer action Candidate evidence 0-3 Read prompt; answer only asked clarifications Initial prioritization 3-10 Let candidate frame; reveal scale facts when requested Requirements, invariants, SLOs 10-20 Challenge one assumption or number Estimates, contracts, data model 20-35 Ask for end-to-end trace; interrupt vague arrows Smallest correct architecture 35-45 Inject one failure and one skew/overload change Failure semantics and adaptation 45-53 For L6, inject evolution or ownership constraint Migration, policy, cost, boundaries 53-57 Ask candidate to choose and defend one tradeoff Decision quality 57-60 Request concise summary Recommendation, risk, trigger

For a 45-minute mock, use framing 7, estimates/contracts 8, baseline 12, failure/overload 10, tradeoff 4, and close 4 minutes. For a 75-minute mock, use the entry diagnostic timeline, or extend this 60-minute protocol by ten minutes of migration artifacts and five minutes of failure tracing. Feedback is additional, not deducted from candidate time.

docs.title: Candidate protocol
docs.text:
• Clarify only facts that can alter a decision; state defaults for unanswered details.
  • Keep a visible contract: requirements, invariants, SLOs, scale, exclusions.
  • Narrate why each component exists and what acknowledgment means.
  • When challenged, restate the changed constraint before changing the design.
  • Label uncertainty. Do not bluff benchmarks or guarantees.
  • Close with recommendation, largest residual risk, and first redesign trigger.

docs.title: Interviewer protocol
docs.text:
• Answer clarification questions consistently. If a fact is not on the card, say "choose a reasonable assumption."
  • Wait through productive silence. Do not rescue the candidate before the agreed hint threshold.
  • Ask for observable behavior: "What does the caller know now?" beats "Would you use Kafka?"
  • Change one variable at a time unless testing explicit pressure recovery.
  • Record exact evidence during the attempt; assign scores afterward.
  • Accept multiple architectures when they satisfy the contract.

docs.title: Hint policy
docs.text: Hint Example Score effect Neutral probe "What does accepted mean?" None; tests completeness. Directional probe "Could the provider have succeeded before timeout?" Dimension cannot exceed 3 from this evidence alone. Repair instruction "Add an idempotency record and reconciliation." Dimension cannot exceed 2.

docs.title: Framing tree
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Candidate receives prompt] --> B{States invariant and SLO?}
    B -->|yes| C[Change one requirement]
    B -->|no| D[Ask what must never happen]
    D --> E{Can derive mechanism?}
    E -->|yes| C
    E -->|no| F[Record framing gap]
    C --> G[Ask which design choice changes]

Suggested branches:

  • If every requirement is "high," ask for a percentage, window, and operation.
  • If scope expands without limit, ask what can be excluded for version one.
  • If the candidate asks many low-value questions, ask which answer would reverse a choice.

docs.title: Scale and skew tree
docs.text:
1. Ask for peak QPS and limiting resource.
  2. If only averages appear, reveal that one key has 40% of traffic.
  3. If response is "add shards," ask where that key maps.
  4. If a fitting mechanism appears, remove one zone and ask for utilization.
  5. If capacity is exceeded, ask which work is rejected, delayed, or degraded first.

docs.title: Ambiguous outcome tree
docs.text:
1. State: "The dependency accepted the request, but the response was lost."
  2. Ask what caller and server know.
  3. If candidate retries, ask whether the effect is safe to repeat.
  4. If candidate claims exactly once, ask for the atomic boundary across both systems.
  5. Look for stable identity, unknown state, bounded retry, query/callback reconciliation, and evidence.

docs.title: Migration tree
docs.text:
1. Require old and new versions to coexist.
  2. Ask which version deploys first and why.
  3. Inject 0.5% disagreement during shadowing.
  4. Ask for abort threshold, correction owner, and source of truth.
  5. Ask what rollback remains possible after backfill or write cutover.
  6. Ask for the decommission gate.

docs.title: L6 ownership tree
docs.text:
1. State that two teams own adjacent components with different on-call rotations.
  2. Ask who owns the end-to-end SLO and reconciliation.
  3. Add a tenant residency or cost constraint.
  4. Ask whether a control/data-plane split helps and how stale control state behaves.
  5. Ask what complexity can be postponed and which metric reopens the decision.

docs.title: Feedback protocol: 10 minutes
docs.text:
1. Candidate self-assesses first: strongest decision, critical miss, one retry objective.
  2. Interviewer gives two evidence-backed strengths and the highest-risk gap.
  3. Compare one pivotal decision, not entire architectures.
  4. Agree on one drill/lab and a retry within 48 hours.
  5. Do not debate the total until critical gates are resolved.

Avoid personality labels. Replace "weak at scale" with "used average QPS after being given 40% hot-key concentration and did not revise the partition plan."

docs.title: Learner Scorecard
docs.text: Copy this file section for every diagnostic, drill set, lab, or mock. Score after the attempt. Use the 0-4 definitions in the competency model.

docs.title: Attempt record
docs.text: Field Entry Learner Date Prompt/system Practice mode and duration Target level L5 / L6 Interviewer or self-review Constraints/challenge cards Prior retry objective Rubric and mode; raw subtotal/available Hints supplied and affected dimensions Normalized total, lowest cap, final result

docs.title: Critical gates
docs.text:
Gate Pass/fail Evidence Domain invariant protected Acknowledgment matches durability Retries cannot repeat unsafe effects without control Authorization, tenant, and sensitive-data boundaries hold Canonical state has a recovery path Migration has compatibility and rollback boundaries, if applicable

Any unresolved failure blocks readiness regardless of total.

docs.title: Competency evidence
docs.text: Competency 0-4 Exact evidence from the attempt Next-level evidence needed Framing Estimation API and data model Baseline architecture Scale and contention Consistency Reliability Operations Tradeoffs Communication Total /40

docs.title: L5 anchor
docs.text:
• Total is at least 28/40 on the competency model, not a normalized scenario screen.
  • Seven or more competencies scored 3+.
  • No competency scored below 2.
  • No critical gate failed.
  • Numbers changed at least one choice.
  • One success and one failure were traced end to end.
  • The close included a recommendation, risk, and trigger.

docs.title: L6 anchor
docs.text:
• Total is at least 34/40 on the competency model.
  • L5 anchor is satisfied.
  • Six or more competencies scored 4.
  • Evolution includes compatibility, reconciliation, rollback, and decommission.
  • Failure strategy covers isolation, RTO/RPO, and ownership.
  • Hidden policy, cost, or organizational constraints changed the design.
  • Complexity is staged with measurable adoption triggers.

Readiness requires the relevant anchor across three prompts from different domains, not one attempt.

docs.title: Decision log
docs.text: Decision Requirement/evidence Alternative rejected Failure/cost accepted Metric that reopens it

docs.title: Timing and delivery
docs.text: Checkpoint Planned Actual Adjustment Contract complete Estimates complete Baseline trace complete Failure/evolution deep dive started Summary started

docs.title: Feedback and retry
docs.text:
Best decision:

Highest-risk miss:

Unjustified complexity to remove:

Interviewer hint required:

Single retry objective:

Assigned practice: drill / failure lab / migration lab / spaced repetition card

Retry date, within 48 hours:

Proof of improvement: State the observable behavior that must appear on the retry.

docs.title: Trend ledger
docs.text:
Date Prompt/domain Total /40 Critical gate Lowest competency Retry result

Use the trend to choose work, not to chase a smooth average. A recurring score of 1 or a repeated critical failure gets the next practice slot even if the total rises.

docs.title: Migration Labs
docs.text:
For mechanism-level preparation, read brownfield migrations, run the shard-movement fixture, and carry the same authority and rollback obligations through Atlas stages 5-6.

A migration is a distributed protocol across versions, data, traffic, and operators. These labs require artifacts that make compatibility and rollback testable. They work entirely on paper.

docs.title: Compatibility matrix
docs.text: Writer/Caller Old reader/server New reader/server Required behavior Old New

docs.title: Rollout ledger
docs.text: Phase Change Entry gate Success signal Abort trigger Rollback action 0 Baseline measurement 1 Compatibility deployment 2 Shadow or dual path 3 Canary traffic 4 Majority traffic/backfill 5 Read/source switch 6 Decommission

docs.title: Reconciliation contract
docs.text: Define identity, source of truth, comparison window, tolerated difference, correction owner, rate limit, checkpoint, and evidence that reconciliation completed.

docs.title: M1: Add a required API field
docs.text:
An order API adds fulfillmentMode, required by the new business flow. Old mobile clients remain active for 90 days.

Deliver: request/response compatibility matrix, default semantics, telemetry by client version, rollout ledger, and removal gate.

docs.title: M2: Split one database table
docs.text:
Move customer profile preferences from customer into a separately owned preferences store without downtime.

Deliver: source-of-truth timeline, dual-read/write decision, backfill checkpoint, conflict rule, discrepancy query, rollback boundary, and deletion order.

docs.title: M3: Repartition a hot event stream
docs.text:
Increase a stream from 64 to 256 partitions while consumers currently depend on per-account ordering.

Deliver: key/ordering analysis, producer and consumer compatibility, cutover protocol, duplicate/gap detection, lag gates, and rollback.

docs.title: M4: Move writes to a second region
docs.text:
Tenants have home regions. Reads are already global; writes currently occur in region A.

Deliver: RTO/RPO, tenant routing state, replication/lag gate, fencing token, dependency checklist, canary cohort, rollback/failback sequence, and residency matrix.

docs.title: M5: Replace a cache technology
docs.text:
The new cache has different TTL precision, eviction behavior, and maximum item size.

Deliver: semantic compatibility table, shadow comparison, cold-start capacity plan, canary, fallback path, and cache deletion gate.

docs.title: M6: Change an event schema
docs.text:
Rename userId to structured subject, and some consumers replay 30-day-old events.

Deliver: schema compatibility matrix, producer sequence, consumer inventory, replay test, unknown-field policy, rollback, and deprecation gate.

Post-attempt migration keys
  • M1: Old requests remain valid or fail intentionally by documented version; new servers deploy before new clients; the default cannot silently violate an invariant; rollback does not depend on recalling clients; removal waits for usage and policy gates.
  • M2: Deploy tolerant readers; establish change capture or an outbox; backfill by stable key with rate limits; reconcile; shadow reads; switch a read canary; expand reads; keep old storage authoritative for writes until source writes are fenced and the target has replayed through a verified final watermark; activate the new writer; retain a reverse-replay or forward-repair rollback path; remove only after the observation window. Dual writes without atomicity need explicit repair.
  • M3: Preserve account key ownership; version destinations; consume old and new with deduplication or define a fenced epoch; record cutover offsets; prevent concurrent owners; compare counts/checksums; retire old stream after retention and replay gates.
  • M4: Assign one write owner per tenant; replicate allowed data; test shadow reads; pre-provision dependencies; move internal tenants first; fence A before promoting B; route and monitor errors/lag/conflicts. After B has accepted writes, failback requires draining/fencing B, catching A up through a verified watermark, granting A a higher epoch, and only then routing. Schema compatibility alone cannot make stale A authoritative.
  • M5: Treat canonical storage as truth; compare hit/miss and value semantics, not only bytes; warm selectively; protect origin with admission; retain old cache until origin load and correctness pass; tolerate dual cache misses.
  • M6: Add subject while retaining userId; deploy consumers that read both with defined precedence; emit both; backfill only if stored data requires it; stop the old field after all live and replay consumers prove compatibility; never reuse the old field number or name incompatibly.

docs.title: Migration scoring: 0-16
docs.text:
Award 0-2 for each:

  • invariant and source of truth;
  • backward and forward compatibility;
  • measurable phase gates;
  • traffic/data isolation and canary scope;
  • backfill/checkpoint safety;
  • reconciliation and discrepancy repair;
  • rollback while versions coexist;
  • decommission evidence and ownership.

Pass at 12+, with no zero in compatibility, source of truth, or rollback. For deeper patterns, review multi-step workflows, messaging and streams, and multi-region architecture.

docs.title: Progressive Drill Bank
docs.text: Use a timer and answer before opening the key. Record correct, partial, or miss, plus one sentence of evidence. The 50 prompts progress from retrieval to interview pressure.

docs.title: Recall: 10 prompts, 3 minutes each
docs.text: ID Prompt R1 Distinguish an invariant from an SLO. R2 What does an API acknowledgment need to define? R3 Name five boundary contract fields. R4 Why is "high availability" incomplete? R5 What makes cursor pagination safer than offsets under inserts? R6 Name the minimum idempotency record. R7 Why does adding replicas not fix a hot write lock? R8 What is recovery evidence? R9 Distinguish control plane and data plane. R10 When is a queue not backpressure? Recall answer key ID Answer key R1 Invariant must always hold; SLO is a measured target over a scope/window with an error budget. R2 Whether work is validated, buffered, durably committed, replicated, or completed. R3 Input/output, deadline, identity/idempotency, durable state, retry owner, overload response; any five. R4 It lacks operation, percentage, window, geography, and failure scope. R5 Cursor resumes from stable sort keys; offsets shift as rows change. R6 Scoped key, canonical request hash, status/result, and retention/expiry. R7 Replicas add read capacity; serialized ownership remains the write bottleneck. R8 A metric or durable fact proving state converged, such as zero unpublished outbox rows and bounded lag. R9 Control plane configures/orchestrates; data plane serves workload. They need explicit propagation and failure boundaries. R10 When producers can enqueue without a bound; it delays overload and grows age/storage rather than limiting demand.

docs.title: Calculation: 10 prompts, 5 minutes each
docs.text:
Show units and one design consequence.

ID Prompt C1 86.4M writes/day, peak factor 6. Find average and peak QPS. C2 12K requests/s with 250 ms mean time in the system at steady state. Find mean in-flight work. C3 Three equal zones run at 70%. One fails. Survivor utilization? C4 20K QPS, 2 KB response. Egress? C5 10M objects/day, 1.5 KB, 90 days, 3 replicas, 30% indexes. C6 A lock is held 8 ms per operation. Max serial throughput? C7 Cache hit rate falls from 95% to 80% at 50K reads/s. Origin change? C8 5K events/s, fan-out 200, two writes per delivery. Work rate? C9 99.95% availability over 30 days. Approximate error budget? C10 30K calls/s; 10% of original calls time out and each makes two retries. Load if all retries fire? Calculation scoring key ID Scoring key C1 1,000/s and 6,000/s; size peak path for at least peak plus failure headroom. C2 12,000 * 0.25 = 3,000; bound concurrency/queues accordingly. C3 70% * 3/2 = 105%; unsafe without shedding or more headroom. C4 40 MB/s before protocol overhead; check network and downstream fan-out. C5 About 5.27 TB: 10M * 1.5 KB * 90 * 3 * 1.3; separate assumptions. C6 About 125 operations/s; optimize lock scope or partition ownership. C7 2.5K to 10K reads/s, 4x origin load. C8 2M writes/s; fan-out dominates ingress. C9 21.6 minutes; define which failures count. C10 36K calls/s: 30K + (30K * 10% * 2); 20% amplification before secondary effects.

Full credit requires correct method, units, and a consequence. Partial credit for correct arithmetic without consequence.

docs.title: Decision: 10 prompts, 6 minutes each
docs.text:
Score 0-2: 1 for a requirement-led choice, 1 for a credible rejected alternative or trigger.

ID Prompt D1 Payment creation needs no duplicate charge after client timeout. D2 Feed reads are huge; celebrity updates create massive fan-out. D3 One inventory SKU receives 40% of writes. D4 Search may lag 30 seconds but checkout must use current stock. D5 A task can run for hours and workers restart. D6 Global profile reads, rare writes, 5-minute staleness allowed. D7 Per-tenant rate limits must change in seconds without blocking requests on config storage. D8 Audit records must survive account deletion, while personal data must be erased. D9 Queue lag grows although CPU is low. D10 Choose SQL or distributed KV for reservations. Decision answer key ID Strong key D1 Transactional command record/idempotency key; provider idempotency or unknown-state reconciliation. D2 Hybrid push/pull based on follower distribution; avoid universal fan-out-on-write. D3 Conditional claims or serialized/key-split ownership; generic hash sharding alone keeps one hot key. D4 Search projection for discovery; canonical inventory check for checkout. D5 Durable state machine, lease/heartbeat, checkpoints, idempotent steps, cancellation. D6 Regional caches/replicas with asynchronous propagation; single write authority is likely sufficient. D7 Versioned control-plane config pushed/cached in data plane with safe stale behavior. D8 Separate immutable minimal audit facts from deletable/tokenized personal data and define legal policy. D9 Inspect dependency latency, partitions, lock/contention, poison messages, and concurrency caps before adding CPU. D10 Start from transaction/invariant and access key; SQL baseline unless measured scale/partition-local model requires KV.

docs.title: Integration: 10 prompts, 10 minutes each
docs.text:
Before starting, deliver contract/API, authoritative state, success trace, duplicate/failure trace, capacity/overload behavior, and validation evidence where relevant. Afterward score one point per comma-separated key element in the hidden row, recording earned/available for that prompt; denominators differ. A critical contradiction blocks full credit regardless of element count. Never reveal the key merely to learn what artifact to produce.

ID Prompt I1 Design URL creation and redirect. I2 Trace an order command whose response is lost after commit. I3 Design a five-minute seat hold. I4 Design a large file upload. I5 Design notification fan-out for a 10M-user campaign. I6 Design a distributed rate limiter. I7 Design top-K trending per hour. I8 Design a regional failover for a write service. I9 Evolve synchronous report generation to async. I10 Trace deletion through source, cache, search, backups, and analytics. Integration scoring key ID Scoring key I1 API/idempotency, key generation, durable mapping, cache, abuse controls, deletion/expiry, hot-key metric. I2 Command ID, atomic result record, unknown outcome, retry reads same result, downstream outbox. I3 Capacity invariant, conditional transaction, expiry ownership, payment race, reconciliation, availability projection. I4 Initiation, chunk IDs, object storage, checksum, completion manifest, retries, cleanup, scan state. I5 Chunked cursor, quotas/fairness, consent, template version, attempts, provider limits, status lag. I6 Scope/key, algorithm, time semantics, partitioning, failure mode, config propagation, observability. I7 Event time/window, duplicates, partition/local aggregation, merge, late events, query serving, correction policy. I8 RTO/RPO, replication, lag gate, fencing, routing, dependency readiness, rollback/failback. I9 Compatibility contract, job state/API, dual path or adapter, canary, cancellation, rollback, retirement metric. I10 Scope/identity, tombstone or workflow, propagation, proof, retry, legal retention, restore behavior.

docs.title: Pressure: 10 prompts, 4 minutes each
docs.text:
Answer aloud. Score 0-2: direct answer and defended tradeoff.

ID Interviewer challenge P1 "Why not use Kafka for everything?" P2 "Traffic grows 10x tomorrow." P3 "Make it exactly once." P4 "The database is down." P5 "We need active-active globally." P6 "Your estimate is wrong by 5x." P7 "Remove one component." P8 "A VIP tenant cannot be throttled." P9 "Ship the schema change today." P10 "Summarize your design in 60 seconds." Pressure scoring key ID Strong response must include P1 Specific need it solves, costs it adds, and simpler baseline. P2 Recompute limiting resource, immediate protection, then targeted evolution. P3 Define observable effect; use atomicity/idempotency/reconciliation; reject blanket guarantee. P4 What callers know, admission/degradation, durability boundary, recovery evidence. P5 Ask latency/RTO/residency need; define ownership/conflicts and complexity. P6 Identify sensitive choice, safe envelope, measurement, and trigger. P7 Choose least justified component and describe changed tradeoff. P8 Isolation/reserved capacity without allowing shared-fleet collapse; explicit policy. P9 Compatibility first, canary, discrepancy gate, rollback, deferred cleanup. P10 Contract, core path, key decision, failure behavior, largest risk/trigger.

docs.title: Progression rule
docs.text: Advance within a category after 8 of 10 prompts are fully correct on two sessions at least 48 hours apart. If below 6, review the linked foundation and retry missed prompts with changed numbers or constraints. Mix categories only after recall and calculation are stable.

docs.title: Decision-Based Spaced Repetition
docs.text: Do not memorize component definitions. Rehearse the cue that activates a decision, the evidence needed, the tradeoff, and the failure mode.

docs.title: Card format
docs.text:
Front: [Situation and constraint] What do you decide, and what evidence could reverse it?
Back: [Decision] [Reason] [Rejected alternative] [Failure mode] [Metric/trigger]

Rate each answer:

  • Again (0): wrong, unsafe, or no reason;
  • Hard (1): correct after hesitation, missing tradeoff or trigger;
  • Good (2): direct, requirement-led, includes failure and signal;
  • Easy (3): good answer plus a valid alternative under changed assumptions.

docs.title: Starter deck fronts
docs.text: ID Front SR1 Response lost after commit. Client retries. SR2 Read-heavy data may be 60 seconds stale. SR3 One key owns 30% of writes. SR4 Work exceeds request latency but must not disappear. SR5 External provider times out after possible effect. SR6 Three zones at 70%, one fails. SR7 Search and checkout disagree on inventory. SR8 Need cross-service atomic workflow. SR9 Queue lag grows while CPU is low. SR10 New required event field. SR11 Region failover for writes. SR12 Cache fails during peak. SR13 Tenant sends 80% of traffic. SR14 Asked for exactly once. SR15 Delete user data across projections. SR16 Choose SQL versus distributed KV. SR17 Add multi-region active-active. SR18 Retry a degraded dependency. SR19 Backfill billions of rows. SR20 End an interview design. Starter deck back keys ID Back key SR1 Persist scoped idempotency key/request hash/result atomically; retry returns same result; watch conflicts and unknown age. SR2 Cache/replica is allowed; define invalidation/lag and origin protection; switch if freshness tightens. SR3 Measure serialized resource; split ownership or serialize intentionally; more ordinary shards do not split one key. SR4 Durable acceptance plus async state machine; bound queue and expose age; direct sync remains simpler below budget. SR5 Mark unknown and reconcile; use provider idempotency where supported; do not blind retry. SR6 Survivors exceed capacity; add headroom or defined shedding before claiming zone tolerance. SR7 Search is stale projection; checkout checks canonical inventory; expose freshness. SR8 Prefer local transaction plus outbox and compensatable state machine; distributed transaction only with supported boundaries. SR9 Investigate dependency latency, partitions, poison work, locks, and caps; CPU scaling may not help. SR10 Additive schema, tolerant readers first, dual emit/read window, replay validation, deprecation gate. SR11 Set RTO/RPO, prove replication lag, fence old writer, promote, route, reconcile; define failback. SR12 Prevent origin stampede with admission, request coalescing, stale serve where safe, and gradual refill. SR13 Tenant-aware quotas, weighted fairness, partition isolation, reserved policy if needed; measure per-tenant age. SR14 Define effect and boundary; combine atomic commit, idempotency, dedupe, and reconciliation; state residual ambiguity. SR15 Durable deletion workflow/tombstone, scoped inventory, retries, proof, backup/restore policy, audit separation. SR16 Start from invariants, access paths, transactions, and scale; choose simplest that meets them and name migration trigger. SR17 Require a business driver; define ownership/conflicts/residency; prefer simpler single authority if SLO permits. SR18 Deadline, exponential backoff with jitter, retry budget, circuit/admission; retries consume scarce capacity. SR19 Stable cursor/checkpoint, idempotent writes, rate limit, shadow/reconcile, pause/rollback, source-of-truth rule. SR20 Restate contract, core flow, strongest decision, failure behavior, top risk, and metric-triggered next step.

docs.title: Schedule
docs.text:
Rating Next interval Again 10 minutes, then next day Hard 1 day; if already mature, halve prior interval Good 3, 7, 16, 35, then 70 days Easy 7, 21, 45, then 90 days

If a card fails twice, do not repeat wording. Complete one related drill or lab, then rewrite the front with a different domain and numbers. Retire a card after three Easy ratings at least 21 days apart; sample retired cards monthly.

docs.title: Daily protocol
docs.text:
1. Answer all due cards aloud before viewing keys.
  2. Require a decision, reason, failure, and trigger in under 90 seconds.
  3. Record rating and next date in a plain table or paper ledger.
  4. Add at most two cards from the day's real misses.
  5. Convert repeated misses into a failure lab or migration lab.

docs.title: Weekly transfer test
docs.text: Draw four unrelated cards and apply them to one case study. Score whether the decisions remain mutually consistent. Passing isolated cards but producing a contradictory architecture is not mastery.

docs.title: Distributed Job Scheduler Practice Pack
docs.text: Design a multi-tenant scheduler for one-time, recurring, and dependency-driven work. This is a blind-first L5/L6 exercise: attempt the prompt before opening the reference design, hints, or exemplars.

docs.title: Recommended order
docs.text:
1. Choose a timed mode in the prompt.
  2. Record decisions in the workbook.
  3. If blocked, freeze the blind artifact before using the hint ladder; label the continuation assisted.
  4. Score the result with the evidence rubric.
  5. Compare against five annotated exemplar levels.
  6. Run the hidden-defect design review.
  7. Diagnose the failure lab.
  8. Plan the cron and DB polling migration.
  9. Use the branching interviewer packet for a mock interview.
  10. Only then read the existing scheduler design.

docs.title: Blind-first boundary
docs.text: Do not open the hints, rubric, exemplars, design review, failure lab, migration, interviewer packet, or reference design until your selected timer says to do so. The prompt and workbook intentionally omit solution architecture.

docs.title: Skills under test
docs.text: Open after the first attempt: L5/L6 skill map Area L5 signal L6 signal Correctness Durable state, explicit transitions, retries, cancellation Invariants across leases, fencing, clocks, and regional epochs Scale Partitioned due-work and dispatch paths Skew control, repair capacity, overload policy, and cost Execution Compatible workers and bounded retries At-least-once effects, stale workers, and capability evolution Multi-tenancy Rate and concurrency quotas Hierarchical fairness, reserves, borrowing, and blast-radius control Operations Metrics, alerts, and recovery Evidence-led diagnosis, regional promotion, and migration safety
