docs.title: Practice rules
docs.text:
• State assumptions before adding components.
  • Define guarantees, boundaries, overload behavior, and unresolved risks in your own terms.
  • Record alternatives and the evidence that would change a decision.

Previous: Course home | Next: Prompt

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Read the proposal once. In 15 minutes, list defects by severity. For each, identify the violated invariant, a concrete failure sequence, and the smallest safe correction. Do not optimize style.

docs.title: Proposal under review
docs.text:
The Scheduler API writes each job to a globally replicated database and immediately publishes it to a queue. A successful database write returns acceptance even if publishing fails. Every region scans all schedules whose next_fire_at <= local_now, and a distributed lock on schedule_id prevents duplicate cron runs. The scanner updates next_fire_at after publish.

Workers consume from one priority queue. A worker takes the message if its labels match; otherwise it returns the message. Premium tenants use higher priority. Each worker creates a 60-second Redis lease and renews every 30 seconds. If the lease expires, the message is retried. Completion always updates the execution row because the execution ID is unique. Handlers do not need idempotency because only one worker owns the lease.

Retries occur immediately up to ten times. Cancellation sets cancelled=true and deletes queued messages. Running workers check the flag every minute. A DAG child stores remaining_parents; every parent completion decrements it. When it reaches zero, the child is published. A transaction is unnecessary because queue delivery is durable.

Each tenant has a daily submission quota. Queue priority ensures important jobs start first. Autoscaling uses total queue depth. Worker capability labels can contain arbitrary key/value pairs, and the dispatcher creates one queue per unique label set.

Cron expressions use the API server's local timezone. During downtime, scanners replay all missed occurrences. Regional failover occurs when the standby has not heard from the primary for 30 seconds; it starts scanning and dispatching. Replication is asynchronous. Operators consider recovery complete when queue depth returns to normal.

docs.title: Review worksheet
docs.text: Severity Defect Failure sequence Violated invariant Minimal correction Evidence of repair

docs.title: Stop line
docs.text:
Do not read below until your review is complete.

Reviewer key

Previous: Exemplars | Next: Failure lab

docs.title: Critical defects
docs.text:
1. No durable publish coupling or repair. A crash after DB commit strands accepted work. Use a transactional outbox plus sweeper; measure outbox lag and oldest canonical ready age.
  2. All regions actively scan the same schedules. A lock timeout does not establish regional ownership. Assign a home region and require a monotonically higher regional epoch for promotion.
  3. Lease mistaken for process exclusion. A paused worker can resume after expiry. Fence every scheduler mutation by attempt epoch and require effect idempotency.
  4. Stale completion is accepted. Updating by execution ID alone lets attempt N overwrite attempt N+1 or a cancellation. Require expected state, attempt ID, and lease epoch in the conditional transition.
  5. Unsafe recurring materialization order. Publish-before-advance can duplicate; advance-before-publish can lose. Transactionally insert a uniquely keyed occurrence, advance schedule state, and write an outbox record.

docs.title: High defects
docs.text:
1. Queue durability is treated as a transaction. Parent-counter update and child publication can split. Deduplicate edge contributions, transition child eligibility atomically, and publish through an outbox.
  2. Cancellation relies on message deletion. Messages can be in flight or duplicated. Canonical cancellation must prevent future claims; running work needs cooperative stop and stale completion rejection.
  3. Immediate retries create storms. Add retry classes, exponential backoff with jitter, deadline and attempt bounds, tenant retry budgets, and dead letters.
  4. Single strict-priority queue starves lower classes and tenants. Use hierarchical fair selection with rate/concurrency quotas and bounded reserved capacity.
  5. Arbitrary capability queues explode cardinality. Use coarse pools and final-fit matching; index scarce capabilities and track no-fit age.
  6. Local clocks define cron. API server placement changes semantics. Persist timezone and recurrence mode, use authoritative server/database time, and define DST/missed-run policy.
  7. Unbounded catch-up amplifies outages. Support skip/latest/bounded catch-up and admission caps.
  8. Timeout-only regional promotion allows split brain. A partitioned primary may remain live. Promotion needs an external quorum/lease authority that grants a higher epoch and fences old work.

docs.title: Medium defects
docs.text:
1. Daily admission quota is not runtime isolation. Add start-rate tokens, concurrent-execution limits, resource budgets, and DAG fan-out caps.
  2. Queue depth is a weak scaling signal. Track oldest compatible eligible age, arrival/start rate, worker saturation, capability deficit, and tenant denial time.
  3. One lease profile ignores runtime range. Separate short offers from renewable running leases; use jitter and workload-aware bounds.
  4. One-minute cancellation polling may violate expectations. Define cancellation SLO, use push plus polling fallback, and expose cancellation_requested separately from terminal CANCELLED.
  5. DAG decrement lacks a deduplication key. Duplicate parent events can release a child early. Persist one contribution per parent-child-parent outcome identity.
  6. Recovery is defined by depth only. Verify p99 schedule delay, oldest ready age, repair backlog, duplicate/stale rejection, and tenant fairness.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Select three fixes and name the owning team, rollout gate, rollback trigger, and new operational cost. A sound correction without ownership and evidence is not yet a production plan.

docs.title: Five Annotated Exemplar Levels
docs.text: These compressed responses show progression, not scripts to memorize. Annotations explain why evidence gains or loses credit under the rubric.

docs.title: Level 1: Component inventory
docs.text:
Put jobs in a database. A scheduler sends due jobs to Kafka, and workers consume them. Redis locks prevent duplicates. Failed jobs retry three times. Deploy everything in three regions.

What works: identifies durable storage, asynchronous dispatch, and retries.

Why it falls short: no acceptance contract, state model, partitioning, clock policy, fairness, capability matching, or regional owner. A Redis lock cannot stop a paused worker or guarantee exactly-once effects. "Three regions" increases split-brain risk without a fence.

Calibration: component inventory; no defensible exact total from this fragment.

docs.title: Level 2: Coherent happy path
docs.text:
Store schedules and executions separately. Poll an index on next_fire_at, enqueue due execution IDs, and let workers heartbeat while running. Use exponential backoff, statuses, tenant queues, and a dead-letter queue. DAG children run when all parents finish.

What works: separates definitions from occurrences and sketches a usable lifecycle.

Missing evidence: duplicate materialization, lease races, queue loss, dependency-event deduplication, recurring clock semantics, cancellation, estimates, and hot-tenant behavior. Per-tenant queues may be operationally unbounded.

Calibration: coherent pieces, not evidence of all ten dimensions.

docs.title: Level 3: Borderline L5
docs.text:
Acceptance commits a canonical execution row before success. Queue entries are replaceable hints published through an outbox; a sweeper re-enqueues stranded READY rows. Schedules and executions partition by tenant plus ID, while due scans use hashed schedule shards and time buckets. A unique (schedule_id, scheduled_for, definition_version) key makes materialization idempotent within one definition. Edits also need an effective-time ownership boundary, checked atomically with materialization, so old and new definitions cannot both own the same intended occurrence.

Dispatchers select a worker pool, enforce tenant token and concurrency limits, and conditionally move READY to LEASED. Each attempt has a lease epoch. Expiry returns work to READY; a late completion with an old epoch is rejected. Since the old process may still call an external service, all attempts carry one business idempotency key. Retryable failures use jittered exponential backoff bounded by attempts and deadline. Cancellation conditionally blocks new claims and sends a cooperative stop to current workers.

DAG parent events decrement child dependency state once, and a repair scan catches missed events. Workers advertise runtime, version, resources, and drain state. I track p99 scheduling delay, oldest eligible age, lease expirations, quota denials, worker saturation, and reconciliation repairs.

Why it approaches the bar: gives authority, state transitions, duplicate handling, stale-worker fencing, bounded retry, cancellation, DAG repair, worker fit, fairness controls, and operable metrics.

What keeps it from L6: no quantified heartbeat/storage design, DST policy, giant fan-out control, fairness algorithm, or safe regional promotion.

Calibration: borderline-style discussion; capacity, recurrence, and regional recovery evidence remain incomplete.

docs.title: Level 4: Strong L5 / emerging L6
docs.text:
At 50,000 starts/s, three canonical transitions imply about 150,000 writes/s before results and retries. One million jobs heartbeating every 15 seconds add about 67,000 updates/s, so heartbeats use a lease store or batched renewals rather than history rows. I reserve recovery headroom and alert on oldest compatible ready age and capacity deficit, not depth alone.

Recurring schedules declare wall-clock timezone or fixed interval. Wall-clock schedules define DST gap/overlap behavior and skip, latest-once, or bounded catch-up. Fenced scanners use database time for due comparisons. Definition updates affect future occurrences; generated executions keep an immutable version.

Ready queues are coarse worker pools. Within a pool, weighted deficit round robin selects a tenant with start tokens and concurrency room, then highest-priority fitting work. Reserved critical capacity can be borrowed under an explicit revocation policy. Million-node DAG fan-out is paged, deduplicated per edge contribution, and protected by node/depth/admission caps.

Each schedule has a home region. A standby may dispatch only after acquiring a higher regional epoch from a quorum-backed authority. Database failover pauses claims from stale replicas. Promotion includes queue rebuild and expired-lease reconciliation.

Why it is strong: quantifies write pressure, defines clock semantics, addresses skew and capability fit, bounds DAG fan-out, and supplies a regional fence.

Remaining gap: migration and operational decision thresholds are thin; regional RTO and stale-region containment assumptions need proof.

Calibration: strong extension only when supported by the earlier complete design. This paragraph alone omits core APIs, retry, and cancellation details.

docs.title: Level 5: Meets the L6 bar
docs.text:
I would launch the smallest correct control/data-plane split, but make every derived path rebuildable. The transactional store owns versioned schedules, executions, terminal monotonicity, and regional epoch. Outbox relays, queues, search indexes, and lease caches are accelerators. Every accelerator has a bounded reconciliation owner, scan budget, repair metric, and overload policy.

Fairness is a product policy: weighted tenant shares, rate and concurrency ceilings, optional reserves, and bounded borrowing. We measure attained share only among tenants with compatible eligible work, because scarce GPU or regional capability can otherwise look like scheduler unfairness. Admission delays catch-up and DAG expansion before interactive critical jobs. Queue partitions remain coarse enough to avoid capability-combination explosion; dispatch applies final fit and records no-fit reasons.

Regional recovery targets define the mechanism. Home-region writes stop or fail over through a quorum-granted epoch; a region unable to reach the authority cannot self-promote. The standby validates replication freshness against the accepted RPO, acquires epoch N+1, rebuilds hints, fences old completions, and reconciles ambiguous attempts. A nonzero RPO can lose acknowledged intents or their effect keys; promotion must recover that evidence or explicitly declare the contract breach and hold affected work, rather than recreate ambiguous effects under new keys. We communicate that external effects may overlap and certify critical handlers for idempotency.

Migration from cron plus DB polling uses shadow materialization, dual-read comparison, tenant cohorts, and per-schedule ownership fencing. Rollback returns ownership only after the new dispatcher drains or invalidates leases. Gates include duplicate occurrence rate, p99 schedule delay, stale completion rejection, fairness deviation, and repair backlog. Fake-clock, crash-window, skew, fan-out, and region-isolation tests run before expansion.

Why it meets L6: turns correctness into owned mechanisms, integrates policy with overload, makes regional assumptions explicit, and includes measurable migration and rollback. It treats repair capacity as part of production capacity.

Calibration: L6-style operating model, conditional on actual proof of quorum enforcement, capacity, and the omitted baseline. A region acquiring N+1 must make stale N unable to claim or commit, not merely write a token the old region never checks.

docs.title: Exact score breakdown
docs.text:
An exact total requires a complete candidate artifact. The former arithmetic totals concealed unsupported per-dimension credit; do not fill omitted evidence from the exemplar heading or assume later fragments include earlier ones.

Fragment Visible evidence Probe before full scoring Level 1 Storage, queue, retries Lease versus effect, authority, time, tenant isolation Level 2 Separate schedule and execution, polling, heartbeats Parent success predicate, occurrence uniqueness, cancellation, regions Level 3 Canonical state, epochs, bounded retries, repair Worked capacity, DST/update ownership, regional fail-closed behavior Level 4 150K transition writes/s, 66,667 heartbeats/s, pool fairness Earlier baseline, RTO/RPO proof, migration thresholds Level 5 Repair ownership, fairness policy, staged migration Actual estimates, API semantics, recurrence, cancellation, enforcement of old-region rejection

Use the rubric's raw score plus lowest cap on the actual attempt. Headings describe the style to practice, not an awarded readiness level.

docs.title: Comparison prompt
docs.text:
After reading, identify one sentence from your answer that belongs at each level. Rewrite the weakest sentence so it contains a mechanism, failure boundary, and observable proof.

docs.title: Failure Lab: Stale Workers and Queue Backlog
Scenario
docs.text:
At 00:00 UTC, tenant catalog releases a large recurring batch. At 00:03, a network policy rollout drops worker heartbeats from one availability zone but does not stop worker processes or their outbound calls. Leases expire and retries begin elsewhere. At 00:07, a queue partition becomes leader and replay pressure rises. By 00:12, critical one-time jobs miss the 5-second SLO.

Your task is to diagnose, contain, recover, and prevent recurrence without assuming that expired workers stopped.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. What are the primary fault, secondary amplification, and customer-visible symptom?
  2. Which metrics prove workers are alive but scheduler ownership is stale?
  3. Did fencing preserve scheduler correctness? Did it preserve external effect correctness?
  4. Why did critical work starve despite reserved capacity?
  5. Is the queue leader change a root cause, amplifier, or coincidence?
  6. Which actions are safe in the first 10 minutes?
  7. What evidence declares recovery complete?

docs.text: Phase Decision Expected metric movement Risk/abort condition Detect Contain Stabilize Drain Validate

docs.title: Stop line
docs.text:
Complete the worksheet before reading the runbook.

Facilitator diagnosis and recovery runbook

Previous: Design review | Next: Migration

docs.title: Expected diagnosis
docs.text:
• The primary fault is heartbeat-path isolation for zone z2, not worker death.
  • Lease expiry creates overlapping attempts. Epoch rejection protects scheduler state, as shown by stale completion rejects, but the HTTP 200 shows an old worker still reached a successful external response. Confirm the actual effect and duplicate status in the downstream ledger; the status alone does not prove a new effect occurred.
  • Queue replay amplifies load through duplicates and claim conflicts. Rising outbox lag then delays fresh notifications.
  • The fairness policy incorrectly lends the critical reserve during a backlog, allowing catalog to dominate starts. Strict priority alone is not restoring it.
  • GPU no-fit work is a separate capability-capacity problem and should not drive CPU scaling.

docs.title: 0-5 minutes: contain
docs.text:
1. Halt the network policy rollout and isolate the affected change.
  2. Stop new catalog catch-up materialization and DAG expansion; do not delete canonical executions.
  3. Revoke reserve borrowing and enforce critical CPU capacity.
  4. Reduce retry admission for infrastructure-expired attempts using per-tenant retry budgets.
  5. Confirm stale epochs are rejected on start, heartbeat, and completion paths.

docs.title: 5-15 minutes: stabilize
docs.text:
1. Restore heartbeat connectivity or drain z2 workers at the scheduler and execution-sandbox layers.
  2. If external calls cannot be blocked, rotate or revoke short-lived attempt credentials for stale epochs where supported.
  3. Rate-limit queue replay and prioritize outbox records for critical work without reordering canonical state.
  4. Scale dispatch and workers only after checking database conditional-write headroom.
  5. Sample duplicate external effects by business idempotency key and notify effect owners if deduplication fails.

docs.title: Drain and validate
docs.text:
1. Drain by hierarchical tenant fairness, not FIFO backlog order.
  2. Reconcile READY rows against enqueue evidence and expired attempts against current epochs.
  3. Resume bounded catalog catch-up only when critical oldest age is below SLO and spare capacity is stable.
  4. Keep incident mode until outbox lag, claim conflicts, and stale rejects return to baseline.

docs.title: Recovery gates
docs.text:
• Critical p99 scheduling delay is below 5 seconds for 15 minutes.
  • Oldest compatible ready age trends down over agreed windows in every admitted CPU class; individual samples may rise when an older stranded row is rediscovered. Reconcile canonical ready work as well as queue observations.
  • Outbox lag is below 5 seconds and queue replay is below dispatch capacity.
  • Lease expiry rate and stale completion rejection return near baseline.
  • Critical reserved share is delivered while demand exists.
  • No unexplained terminal-state regressions occur.
  • Duplicate external-effect rate is measured and assigned, not inferred from scheduler success.

docs.title: Prevention actions
docs.text: Action Verification Make reserve borrowing revocable on critical backlog Fairness load test with a large midnight tenant Separate infrastructure retry budget Zone heartbeat partition game day Bind short-lived credentials to attempt where feasible Stale-worker effect test Rate-limit replay and duplicate claims Queue failover benchmark Alert on heartbeat/process-health divergence Synthetic network-policy canary Certify critical handlers for idempotency Duplicate-attempt conformance suite Scale on oldest compatible age and deficit Capacity-controller replay test

docs.title: Hint Ladder
docs.text:
Open one rung at a time. After each rung, return to the workbook for at least five minutes.

Rung 1: Frame the promise

Separate these claims:

  1. The service durably accepted an execution intent.
  2. An eligible execution receives at-least-once attempt delivery.
  3. Scheduler state accepts completion from only the current attempt epoch.
  4. An arbitrary external side effect happens exactly once.

The first three can be designed inside the platform. The fourth generally needs handler idempotency or a transactional effect pattern.

Rung 2: Choose authority

Ask which record survives if every queue message disappears. A durable execution row can be canonical while a queue message is only a wake-up hint. Once that is explicit, queue duplication and loss become repair problems rather than correctness contradictions.

Rung 3: Split intent, occurrence, and attempt

A recurring schedule is not a running job. Consider separate records for:

  • the versioned schedule definition;
  • each logical execution occurrence;
  • each physical attempt and its lease epoch.

A uniqueness key based on schedule, intended fire time, and definition version can suppress duplicate materialization.

Versioned uniqueness alone permits the old and new definitions to generate the same intended time. Choose an effective-time ownership boundary and condition scanner writes on the current definition/owner version in the materialization transaction. Decide explicitly whether an edit replaces or adds an occurrence, including already materialized work.

Rung 4: Make time policy explicit

Do not say only "use cron." Decide:

  • wall-clock timezone or elapsed fixed interval;
  • what happens in DST gaps and overlaps;
  • skip, latest-once, or bounded catch-up after downtime;
  • whether deadlines use server time and where that time is read;
  • how scanners tolerate bounded skew without double materialization.

Fake clocks should test the policy.

Rung 5: Design the hot path

Partition the due-time index so one advancing timestamp edge does not overload a single shard. Fenced scanners materialize executions idempotently. Dispatchers combine ready hints, tenant policy, worker capacity, and a conditional state transition.

Keep heartbeats out of immutable history writes when one million jobs report frequently.

Rung 6: Reason about stale workers

A lease expiry means the scheduler may assign a retry. It does not stop the old process. Give each claim a monotonically increasing epoch. Reject stale state mutations, but assume external effects can overlap. Carry a stable business idempotency key across attempts.

Rung 7: Bound retries and cancellation

Retryable classes, exponential backoff with jitter, maximum attempts, and an absolute deadline prevent infinite work. Decide whether infrastructure loss consumes an application attempt. Cancellation must block future claims after its canonical commit; already-running code needs cooperative stop and may still finish an external effect.

Rung 8: Make DAG progress repairable

Parent completion events can duplicate or vanish. Deduplicate each parent-to-child contribution, update dependency state atomically, and periodically reconcile edges against terminal parents. Page million-node fan-out instead of updating every child in one transaction.

Rung 9: Match workers without starving tenants

Partition ready work by coarse compatible pool, not every capability combination. Workers advertise version, resources, locality, and capacity. Within a pool, choose a tenant through weighted fair scheduling, enforce start-rate and concurrency budgets, then choose the highest-priority fitting job. Track oldest compatible ready age, not queue depth alone.

Rung 10: Fence a region

Home-region ownership avoids two active schedulers for one schedule. Promotion requires a higher regional epoch from an authority the isolated old region cannot also obtain. Old lease owners may still perform external effects, so regional fencing complements rather than replaces idempotency.

docs.title: Final synthesis check
docs.text:
Can your design explain all five?

  • A queue outage lasting 20 minutes.
  • A worker resuming after two lease periods.
  • A tenant releasing 10 million midnight jobs.
  • A DST overlap producing the same local wall time twice.
  • A region that is isolated but not powered off.

If not, revisit the rung that names the missing boundary.

docs.title: Branching Interviewer Packet
docs.text: Use with the candidate-facing prompt. Do not reveal this file before the exercise.

docs.title: Interview goals
docs.text: Assess whether the candidate can turn ambiguous scheduling language into explicit guarantees, model state and time, design for stale workers and repair, isolate tenants, and connect regional recovery to a real fence.

docs.title: Suggested formats
docs.text: Format Flow 35-minute L5 Framing 5, architecture 12, leases/retries 8, scale/failure 7, close 3 50-minute standard Framing 7, baseline 15, two branches 20, close 8 70-minute L6 Framing 10, baseline 18, three branches 30, migration/close 12 20-minute drill One branch, one failure injection, one summary

docs.title: Opening script
docs.text:
Design a multi-tenant distributed job scheduler for one-time, recurring, and DAG work. It must start 50,000 jobs per second at peak, support one million concurrent executions, and target p99 eligible-to-start latency under five seconds when compatible capacity exists. Explain guarantees, state, dispatch, failures, and regional recovery.

If the candidate asks what exactly-once means, say: "The platform promises at-least-once attempts. Worker code can call arbitrary external systems. Define the remaining contract."

docs.title: Baseline checkpoints
docs.text:
Before branching, look for:

  • separation of schedule, execution, and attempt;
  • durable acceptance and canonical execution state;
  • due-time discovery plus a dispatch path;
  • worker leases/heartbeats and retry bounds;
  • at least one partitioning and tenant-isolation decision.

If three are absent after 15 minutes, use the recovery branch. If four or five are present, choose a deep branch.

flowchart TD
  Start[Baseline design] --> Check{Core state and authority clear?}
  Check -->|No| Recovery[Recovery branch]
  Check -->|Yes| Claim{Claims exactly-once effects?}
  Claim -->|Yes| Stale[Stale-worker branch]
  Claim -->|No| Depth{Strongest dimension?}
  Depth -->|Time| Clock[Clock branch]
  Depth -->|Scale| Fair[Fairness and DAG branch]
  Depth -->|Reliability| Region[Regional branch]
  Recovery --> Close[Summary and score]
  Stale --> Close
  Clock --> Close
  Fair --> Close
  Region --> Close

docs.title: Branch A: recovery for a stalled candidate
docs.text:
Ask in order:

  1. "What record proves we accepted a job?"
  2. "If every queue message vanishes, how do we find that job?"
  3. "What states can one execution enter?"
  4. "How does a worker prove it still owns an attempt?"
  5. "Which key prevents a client retry from creating a second intent?"

Positive evidence: candidate makes storage canonical, queue repairable, and claims conditional.

Stop condition: if answers remain component-only, move to one simple failure and preserve time for a summary.

docs.title: Branch B: stale worker and effect semantics
docs.text:
Inject:

A worker pauses for 90 seconds. Its 60-second lease expires, a retry starts, and then the old worker resumes. Both can reach the payment API.

Ask:

  • What may overlap?
  • What does a fencing epoch reject?
  • Why can it not retract an HTTP side effect?
  • Does cancellation change the answer?
  • Where does the business idempotency key originate and persist?

L5 signal: conditional completion and handler idempotency.

L6 follow-up: distinguish attempt ID, lease epoch, execution ID, and business effect key; discuss scoped credential revocation and infrastructure retry budgets.

Red flag: "Redis lock means only one worker can run."

docs.title: Branch C: clocks and recurring work
docs.text:
Inject:

A schedule says 01:30 every day in America/New_York. The next DST transition repeats 01:30. The scheduler was also unavailable for three hours.

Ask:

  • Run once, twice, or skip during overlap?
  • How does fixed interval differ from wall-clock recurrence?
  • Who supplies now to scanners and deadlines?
  • How are duplicate occurrences prevented across scanner failover?
  • How does a schedule edit affect already materialized work?

L5 signal: persists timezone and defines missed-run behavior.

L6 follow-up: unique occurrence key, definition version, fenced scanner shard, bounded catch-up, fake-clock cases for gaps, overlaps, leap days, and skew.

docs.title: Branch D: fairness, capabilities, and DAG scale
docs.text:
Inject:

One tenant releases 10 million CPU jobs at midnight. Another has 500 critical jobs. Some work needs GPU model v3. A DAG parent has one million children.

Ask:

  • How do jobs and workers find a compatible pool?
  • Why not create one queue per capability set?
  • What is selected first: priority, tenant, or job?
  • How do rate and concurrency limits differ?
  • How is fan-out processed without a million-row transaction?
  • Which metric distinguishes shortage from unfairness?

L5 signal: coarse pools, quotas, and paged fan-out.

L6 follow-up: weighted deficit round robin, reserves/borrowing, no-fit age, capability deficit, edge-event deduplication, dynamic DAG bounds, and reconciliation.

Red flag: one strict global priority queue.

docs.title: Branch E: queue loss and backlog
docs.text:
Inject:

The ready queue loses a partition for 20 minutes. The database remains available. On recovery, replay traffic is twice dispatch capacity.

Ask:

  • Which accepted jobs remain discoverable?
  • How are missing and duplicate notifications repaired?
  • How do you prevent replay from starving fresh critical work?
  • What determines safe drain rate?
  • When is recovery complete?

L5 signal: outbox or equivalent plus a sweeper and bounded replay.

L6 follow-up: repair budget, database headroom, hierarchical drain, admission shedding, oldest eligible age, and claim-conflict telemetry.

docs.title: Branch F: regional isolation
docs.text:
Inject:

Region A cannot contact region B but still serves workers and its local database. Region B sees no heartbeat for 30 seconds. Product wants automatic failover.

Ask:

  • Can B promote on timeout alone?
  • Which authority grants a higher epoch?
  • What must an isolated A be unable to do?
  • How do RPO and replication freshness affect promotion?
  • What happens to in-flight external effects?

L5 signal: home-region ownership and explicit failover.

L6 follow-up: quorum-reachable promotion authority, fail-closed claims, epoch propagation, queue rebuild, ambiguous-attempt reconciliation, and game-day proof.

Red flag: active-active scanning of the same schedule without consensus or disjoint ownership.

docs.title: Cancellation probe
docs.text:
Use in any branch:

Cancellation commits while an offer is in flight, and the worker reports success one millisecond later.

Expect a conditional state transition policy. Strong candidates distinguish cancellation requested, future-assignment prevention, cooperative worker stop, terminal conflict resolution, and irreversible external effects.

docs.title: Evidence capture
docs.text:
Use the rubric. Record exact candidate claims, not impressions.

Moment Claim or diagram evidence Follow-up Result Contract Authority Race Overload Region

docs.title: Adaptive closing questions
docs.text:
Choose one based on performance:

  • Below bar: "Which single invariant would you add first, and what mechanism enforces it?"
  • L5 borderline: "What breaks when queue notifications are lost after database commit?"
  • Meets L5: "Name the three highest-risk races and the conditional writes that contain them."
  • Strong L5: "How do fairness policy and capability scarcity interact in your metrics?"
  • L6: "Which parts are authoritative, which are rebuildable, who owns repair capacity, and what rollout evidence permits regional automation?"

Then ask for a summary containing contract, canonical state, hot path, duplicate boundary, overload policy, and regional fence. Use the selected mode's closing allocation: three minutes in the 35-minute screen; up to five in longer loops. Do not add five unbudgeted minutes.

docs.title: Debrief guide
docs.text:
• Award L5 for a complete and defensible design, not exhaustive feature coverage.
  • Award L6 only when policy, hidden races, repair, migration, and regional assumptions form one operating model.
  • Do not reward unexplained product names.
  • Apply critical caps from the rubric.
  • Use the exemplars to calibrate response depth, not wording.
  • For an operational extension, use the failure lab.
  • For an evolution extension, use the migration exercise.

Previous: Migration | Next: Reference design

docs.title: Migration: Cron and DB Polling to a Partitioned Scheduler
Starting point
docs.text: Teams own cron entries or poll application tables for rows such as status=PENDING AND run_at<=now. Each worker claims rows with local conventions. Timezones, retries, cancellation, and history differ by service. Some jobs perform side effects before their claim transaction commits. There is no global quota, capability registry, or regional ownership model.

docs.title: Candidate task
docs.text:
Create a compatibility and rollout plan that preserves one owner per occurrence while legacy cron, database pollers, and the new scheduler coexist.

Complete before opening the facilitator material:

Phase Scheduling authority Compatibility or shadow evidence Promotion gate Rollback and in-flight rule Inventory and contract Identity and observation Shadow materialization First execution cohort Fairness and partitioning DAG and regional workloads Legacy retirement

State how identity, recurrence semantics, leases, external-effect keys, and regional ownership survive both promotion and rollback.

docs.title: Stop line
docs.text:
Do not open the facilitator material until the worksheet is complete.

Facilitator target and reference migration

Previous: Failure lab | Next: Interviewer packet

docs.title: Target
docs.text:
Move execution intent to versioned schedules and canonical execution rows. Fenced time scanners materialize due occurrences. An outbox publishes replaceable ready hints to partitioned worker pools. Dispatch enforces compatible capacity, tenant fairness, leases, fencing, retries, and cancellation. Reconciliation repairs missing ready hints and stale state.

flowchart LR
  Legacy[Cron and DB pollers] --> Shadow[Shadow materialization]
  Shadow --> Cohort[Single-owner tenant cohorts]
  Cohort --> Scale[Partitioned scheduler]
  Scale --> Retire[Retire legacy claims]

docs.title: Non-negotiable migration invariants
docs.text:
1. One logical occurrence has at most one active scheduling owner.
  2. Every accepted intent remains discoverable from durable state.
  3. Rollback cannot revive an old owner until new leases are expired or fenced.
  4. Business idempotency keys remain stable across legacy and new attempts.
  5. Recurrence timezone, missed-run, retry, and cancellation semantics are recorded before cutover.
  6. No phase depends on queue history as the source of truth.

docs.title: Phase 0: inventory and contract
docs.text:
Classify every workload by:

  • owner, business criticality, frequency, timezone, and runtime;
  • one-time, recurring, or DAG shape;
  • current claim transaction and side-effect order;
  • idempotency support and external credentials;
  • retry, timeout, missed-run, and cancellation policy;
  • resource, runtime version, locality, and network capability;
  • peak synchronized load and regional/data-residency constraint.

Block migration for jobs whose business effect has neither idempotency nor an accepted duplicate-risk policy.

docs.title: Phase 1: establish identity and observability
docs.text:
• Assign stable schedule_id, execution_id, and business idempotency keys.
  • Normalize states and failure classes without changing ownership.
  • Emit scheduling delay, claim age, runtime, retries, duplicate-key outcomes, and terminal state.
  • Measure database polling load and synchronized cron peaks.
  • Define SLOs and rollback gates per workload class.

Exit gate: 14 days of comparable telemetry and no unclassified critical jobs.

docs.title: Phase 2: shadow materialization
docs.text:
Import definitions as inactive versioned schedules. New scanners compute occurrences but write them to a shadow namespace and never dispatch. Compare legacy starts with shadow occurrences by logical key.

Check:

  • missing and duplicate occurrences;
  • DST gaps/overlaps and timezone conversion;
  • schedule edits during a due window;
  • downtime catch-up policy;
  • partition skew and scan delay;
  • projected quota and capability fit.

Exit gate: agreed mismatch threshold is sustained through at least one recurrence boundary and one failure drill.

docs.title: Phase 3: dual publish, single claim
docs.text:
Publish new ready hints for canary workloads, but place an ownership fence in the canonical migration registry:

WorkloadOwner(workload_id, owner=LEGACY|NEW, owner_epoch, effective_at, version)

Both paths must condition claims on owner and owner_epoch. The ownership check and claim must share a transaction or an equivalent authority-enforced fence; reading a registry and later writing an unrelated database leaves a cutover race. Before granting NEW, close legacy admission, enter a higher-epoch DRAINING state, and drain or contain old attempts with stable effect keys. The non-owner can observe but cannot execute. Start with idempotent, low-criticality, short-running jobs.

Rollback: first close cohort admission and mark ownership DRAINING under a higher epoch so neither path can claim. Fence new state writes, drain or contain in-flight attempts, and reconcile ambiguous effects. Only then grant LEGACY another higher epoch and enable its claims. Publishing owner=LEGACY first would immediately authorize live legacy pollers before draining. Lease expiry alone does not stop old external calls; preserve effect keys and enforce downstream fencing where supported.

docs.title: Phase 4: tenant and workload cohorts
docs.text:
Expand in this order:

  1. one-time idempotent jobs;
  2. fixed-interval recurring jobs;
  3. wall-clock cron with explicit DST/missed-run policy;
  4. long-running and scarce-capability jobs;
  5. DAGs with bounded fan-out;
  6. critical external-effect jobs after handler certification.

For each cohort, canary one partition, then one tenant slice, then one region. Hold long enough to cross retries, cancellation, and a recurrence boundary.

docs.title: Phase 5: activate fairness and partitioning
docs.text:
• Map legacy workers into coarse pools and register capabilities.
  • Enforce start-rate and concurrency limits in observe-only mode first.
  • Compare intended and attained tenant shares under compatible demand.
  • Enable hierarchical fairness and reserved capacity with explicit borrowing rules.
  • Repartition by tenant plus execution ID and hashed due-time shards before peak load.
  • Validate that shard movement uses epochs and does not duplicate scans.

docs.title: Phase 6: DAG and regional cutover
docs.text:
• Import immutable DAG definitions, cycle-check them, and cap nodes, depth, and dynamic expansion.
  • Shadow dependency counters and compare terminal outcomes before dispatch.
  • Assign each schedule a home region and replicate metadata to standby.
  • Rehearse promotion: verify freshness, acquire epoch N+1, rebuild notifications, fence stale completions, and reconcile.
  • Keep regional automatic failover disabled until isolation game days pass.

docs.title: Phase 7: retire legacy polling
docs.text:
Remove legacy write permission only after all of these hold:

  • no active legacy-owned workloads;
  • no legacy claims during two maximum lease periods;
  • no unmatched shadow/actual occurrence;
  • rollback artifacts and audit history are retained;
  • polling query load reaches zero;
  • ownership alerts detect any old binary attempting a claim.

Archive cron definitions only after the target schedule version and policy are independently recoverable.

docs.title: Rollout scorecard
docs.text: Gate Pass condition Rollback trigger Correct occurrences Missing/duplicate rate within approved bound Any critical duplicate without containment Scheduling SLO p99 within cohort objective Sustained breach over two windows Lease safety Stale transitions rejected Stale terminal overwrite Effect safety Idempotency outcome measured Unbounded duplicate effect Fairness Attained share tracks policy Critical reserve not delivered Repair Reconciliation backlog drains within budget Repair debt grows across windows Region Single valid epoch and tested promotion Concurrent regional ownership

docs.title: L6 decision questions
docs.text:
• Who owns policy translation when legacy semantics are ambiguous?
  • How much spare capacity is reserved for migration replay and repair?
  • Which jobs must remain region-pinned for data or credentials?
  • Can rollback preserve recurrence version and intended fire time?
  • What evidence permits automatic regional failover rather than manual promotion?
  • When can a legacy exception expire, and who approves it?

docs.title: Prompt: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler
Candidate brief
docs.text:
Design a multi-tenant platform that accepts background work and starts eligible executions on compatible workers. It must support:

  • one-time jobs scheduled now or in the future;
  • recurring schedules with timezones and explicit missed-run behavior;
  • DAGs whose nodes become eligible from dependency predicates;
  • priorities, deadlines, cancellation, timeouts, bounded retries, and dead letters;
  • worker pools with capabilities, versions, resources, and graceful draining;
  • tenant rate limits, concurrency quotas, and fairness;
  • regional failure without silently scheduling the same intent in two regions.

The service promises at-least-once execution after acceptance. Arbitrary worker code can call external systems. You must define what the platform can and cannot guarantee about those effects.

docs.title: Initial scale
docs.text:
Use these figures unless you replace them with stated assumptions:

Dimension Value Stored schedules 100 million New execution intents 20 million/day Peak starts 50,000/s Concurrent executions 1 million Eligible-to-start SLO p99 under 5 seconds when compatible capacity exists Metadata retention 30 days Regions 3, with one home region per schedule Tenant skew Largest tenant can create 35% of ready work DAG size Typical 20 nodes; maximum 1 million nodes Runtime 10 ms to 12 hours

docs.title: What to deliver
docs.text:
1. Clarify requirements, non-goals, and SLO semantics.
  2. Estimate hot-path load and identify the dominant bottlenecks.
  3. Define APIs, entities, and execution state transitions.
  4. Draw the end-to-end architecture.
  5. Explain due-time discovery for one-time and recurring work.
  6. Explain DAG eligibility and large fan-out.
  7. Define queue, lease, heartbeat, fencing, retry, and cancellation behavior.
  8. Match work to worker capabilities without head-of-line blocking.
  9. Enforce quotas and fairness under tenant skew.
  10. Handle wall clocks, clock skew, DST, missed runs, and deadlines.
  11. Recover from process, queue, database, worker, zone, and regional failures.
  12. Define observability, reconciliation, tests, and a safe evolution path.

docs.title: 35-minute L5 screen
docs.text: Time Focus 0-4 min Clarify scope, guarantees, and SLO 4-8 min Estimate starts, state writes, and worker heartbeats 8-18 min APIs, state model, and high-level architecture 18-27 min Due-work indexing, dispatch, leases, retries, cancellation 27-32 min Partitioning, fairness, and failures 32-35 min Metrics, tradeoffs, three-minute summary

docs.title: 50-minute full loop
docs.text: Use the L5 flow, then spend 15 minutes on recurring time semantics, DAG fan-out, capability matching, queue loss, and one regional failure.

docs.title: 70-minute L6 deep dive
docs.text: Time Focus 0-10 min Product contract, invariants, failure budget, estimates 10-25 min Baseline design and canonical data model 25-40 min Leases, fencing, idempotent effects, cancellation races 40-52 min Fair dispatch, overload, DAGs, and heterogeneous workers 52-62 min Clock policy and regional ownership/failover 62-70 min Migration, observability, validation, executive summary

docs.title: 20-minute drill
docs.text: Pick one: lease expiry, recurring time semantics, million-node fan-out, noisy-tenant fairness, or regional fencing. State one invariant, one race, one metric, one recovery action, and one rejected alternative.

docs.title: Interviewer-provided clarifications
docs.text:
Reveal only when the candidate asks:

Interviewer only; solo learners reveal after writing their clarification questions
  • Schedule creation must be idempotent across client retries.
  • Payloads over 64 KB may be stored outside the scheduler.
  • Workers may disappear without a final message.
  • A worker paused by a long GC cycle may resume after its lease expires.
  • Cancellation cannot undo an external side effect that already occurred.
  • Recurring users need wall-clock timezone semantics and a fixed-interval option.
  • Queue messages may be delayed, duplicated, reordered, or lost.
  • A region can be partitioned from peers while still serving local traffic.

docs.title: Finish condition
docs.text:
Your answer is complete when another engineer can state: what is durable, what may duplicate, who owns each transition, how overload degrades, and how operators repair stranded work.

docs.title: Evidence Rubric
docs.text: Score only demonstrated reasoning. Component names without a mechanism, invariant, number, or failure response earn no evidence credit.

docs.title: Scoring method
docs.text:
Each dimension receives 0-4 points:

Score Evidence standard 0 Missing or materially incorrect 1 Names the topic but gives no workable mechanism 2 Coherent happy path with important gaps 3 Correct mechanism, tradeoff, and primary failure behavior 4 Quantified, testable, repairable design with explicit boundaries

Ten dimensions yield 40 points.

docs.title: 1. Contract and invariants
docs.text:
• Durable acceptance and at-least-once attempts are explicit.
  • Exactly-once external effects are rejected or narrowly proven.
  • Terminal monotonicity, DAG eligibility, and cancellation boundaries are stated.

L6 evidence: connects each invariant to its authority and repair mechanism.

docs.title: 2. Capacity and partitioning
docs.text:
• Estimates peak starts, transition writes, heartbeat load, storage, and recovery capacity.
  • Partitions schedules/executions and due-time scans while addressing skew.

L6 evidence: budgets spare capacity and quantifies backlog drain or hot-tenant isolation.

docs.title: 3. Data model and APIs
docs.text:
• Separates schedule, execution, attempt, dependency, and worker.
  • Uses idempotency keys, definition versions, conditional updates, and stable pagination.

L6 evidence: distinguishes canonical rows, event history, ephemeral leases, and derived indexes.

docs.title: 4. Time and recurrence
docs.text:
• Prevents duplicate occurrence generation.
  • Defines timezone, DST, missed-run, update, deadline, and clock-skew behavior.

L6 evidence: names authoritative clocks and fake-clock test cases.

docs.title: 5. Dispatch, leases, and effects
docs.text:
• Uses bounded offer/running leases and heartbeats.
  • Fences stale state mutations and preserves a business idempotency key across attempts.

L6 evidence: analyzes pause-after-expiry and completion/cancellation races without claiming leases stop effects.

docs.title: 6. Retries and cancellation
docs.text:
• Classifies retryability and applies bounded backoff, jitter, deadlines, and dead letters.
  • Blocks future assignment after cancellation commit and supports cooperative stop.

L6 evidence: separates infrastructure attempts from application retry budget and preserves audit links on replay.

docs.title: 7. DAG correctness and scale
docs.text:
• Makes child eligibility depend on durable predicates.
  • Deduplicates dependency events and handles failure propagation.

L6 evidence: pages fan-out, bounds dynamic expansion, detects cycles, and reconciles counters.

docs.title: 8. Capabilities, quotas, and fairness
docs.text:
• Matches work to compatible workers and supports draining.
  • Enforces tenant start-rate and concurrency controls.

L6 evidence: uses hierarchical fairness, prevents head-of-line blocking, defines reserve borrowing, and measures fairness by eligible age/share.

docs.title: 9. Failure recovery and regions
docs.text:
• Covers scanner, queue, dispatcher, worker, database, and retry-storm failures.
  • Uses home-region ownership and a promotion fence.

L6 evidence: states split-brain assumptions, RTO/RPO consequences, fail-closed points, and post-promotion reconciliation.

docs.title: 10. Observability, testing, and communication
docs.text:
• Uses scheduling delay, oldest ready age, lease expiry, retries, saturation, quota denial, and repair metrics.
  • Proposes state-machine, fake-clock, fault, load, and failover tests.

L6 evidence: ties alerts to operator actions and communicates rejected alternatives and residual risks.

docs.title: Critical caps
docs.text:
Apply these caps even if the arithmetic score is higher:

Apply the hint policy before summing. For 35 minutes score dimensions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, and 10 out of 28; normalize with round(subtotal / 28 * 40), then apply the lowest relevant cap. For 50 or 70 minutes score all ten out of 40. Record raw, normalized, and capped results. In a 20-minute drill report tested dimensions and their subtotal only, without a full L5/L6 label. Do not apply an omission cap to an unassessed short-mode dimension; explicitly unsafe claims still trigger caps. Scenario-local bands are not the general competency model's repeated-domain readiness result, and screen normalization does not establish L6 coverage.

Defect Maximum result Claims leases or a queue guarantee exactly-once external effects 23/40; below L5 Has no durable canonical execution state 23/40; below L5 Cannot prevent stale completion from overwriting a newer attempt 29/40; L5 borderline Omits tenant isolation at the stated skew 29/40; L5 borderline Runs both regions after timeout without a shared promotion fence 23/40; below L5 Omits clock/DST policy for recurring work 29/40; L5 borderline

docs.text: Total Interpretation 0-15 Fragmented; core correctness is absent 16-23 Developing; coherent pieces but not an operable system 24-29 L5 borderline; baseline works, major edge remains 30-34 Meets L5; owns an end-to-end design and its main failures 35-37 Strong L5 / emerging L6; exposes most hidden boundaries 38-40 Meets L6; shapes policy, migration, repair, and regional safety
