docs.title: Facilitator diagnosis
docs.text:
Open after the exercise

The provider latency increase is the trigger. The deployment amplifies it through a tenfold concurrency increase, fixed rapid retries, and fewer shards. Query throttling prevents resolution and pod restarts create repeated claims. Half the suffix space lacks healthy lease renewal. Verify the assignment-to-suffix map before attributing the 0 through 7 concentration to those four unhealthy assignments; the counts alone do not identify which half is missing.

The latent correctness defect is that a callback losing an optimistic-version race is acknowledged but not placed on a durable reapply path. Low consumer lag therefore does not mean every verified fact was applied. Normal outbox age is consistent with a pre-commit apply failure: there may be no event to relay. It does not prove publication completeness, correct payloads, or merchant delivery. The selected missing posting and version conflict support unapplied verified captures as the leading explanation; verify per-operation evidence before excluding an additional ledger or publication defect.

Immediate action: roll back resolver policy, enforce provider-specific concurrency and jittered budgets, restore all shard leases, and persist callback transition conflicts for retry. Preserve new operations and identities. Do not reroute ambiguous calls or mass-mark them failed. If provider capacity remains unsafe, shed or pause new confirms before starving resolvers.

Repair: for each unresolved operation, claim it durably; obtain authenticated provider status or reconciliation evidence; conditionally apply the allowed intent transition; in the same transaction insert balanced ledger rows under unique reference provider_capture:<operation_id> and an outbox event. Treat an existing reference as an idempotent success only after verifying provider scope, payment, amount, currency, and posting type; quarantine a conflicting payload. Replay conflicted callbacks. Reconcile counts and value, not just rows.

For a recovery sizing example, assume an independently measured spare budget resolves 200 old records/s after serving new unknowns and retries. Clearing 18,400 takes at least 18,400 / 200 = 92 s; raw status-query QPS is not net successful repair throughput. If new unknowns consume the entire budget, the backlog will not drain. Keep this distinction in the exit criteria.

docs.title: Prevention review
docs.text:
• Load-test the resolver against provider quotas and 429 behavior.
  • Require deployment guards on concurrency multiplied by replicas.
  • Alert on oldest unknown and suffix-bucket coverage, not only queue lag.
  • Make every conditional-apply conflict durable retry work.
  • Reserve provider capacity for resolution traffic.
  • Run periodic provider-to-ledger value reconciliation.
  • Fault-test callback/resolver races and repeated repair execution.

Continue to the migration exercise.

docs.title: Progressive Hints
docs.text:
Practice home | Prompt | Workbook

Open one level at a time. Each level spends interview signal.

Hint 1: Find the irreversible boundary

List all statements that can cause an external financial effect. A network timeout does not tell you whether that effect happened. Your state model needs a non-terminal state for unresolved evidence.

Checkpoint: Can your API distinguish a proven decline from an unknown result?

Hint 2: Separate business identity from transport attempts

Use different identifiers for the merchant operation, internal attempt, provider operation, callback event, ledger posting, and webhook delivery. Decide which remain stable when a transport attempt repeats.

Checkpoint: Can a retry create a new provider operation ID after the old call may have succeeded?

Hint 3: Persist before crossing the trust boundary

Before calling a provider, persist enough information for another worker to discover what was attempted and to query or safely retry it. Sticky routing matters after an operation may have reached one provider.

A stable reference is not itself a deduplication guarantee. Verify provider scope, request-hash matching, retention, and status visibility. A not-found query may race a delayed original request; retry only within guaranteed same-key semantics or after definitive no-effect termination. For a concrete provider-specific limit, Stripe documents pruning keys after at least 24 hours; this is not a universal provider contract or a seven-year dedupe guarantee.

Checkpoint: After a process crash, can a resolver recover without relying on memory or logs?

Hint 4: State and money are related but not identical

A payment lifecycle explains what the customer can do next. A ledger records immutable economic facts. Authorization is not capture. A provider callback is evidence to validate, not a ledger entry by itself.

Checkpoint: Which verified transition creates financial entries, and can observers see success without them?

Hint 5: Close the database-to-message gap

Writing a database row and publishing an event are two writes. Put an event record in the same local transaction as the authoritative state change, then relay it with at-least-once delivery. Consumers need stable event identity.

Checkpoint: What happens if the process crashes immediately after commit and before publish?

Hint 6: Serialize competing financial commands

Refunds, capture completion, callback application, cancellation, and timeout resolution can race. Use an intent version, row lock, or equivalent conditional transition. Reserve amount capacity before an external refund or capture call.

Checkpoint: Can two valid-looking partial refunds exceed the captured amount?

Hint 7: Use independent evidence

Provider callbacks and synchronous responses may share the same failure modes. Reconciliation should ingest signed settlement files or independent provider query results, retain raw evidence, match multiple identifiers, and classify breaks.

Checkpoint: Which disagreements can software repair, and which require controlled financial adjustment?

Hint 8: Start with one strong boundary

At the stated scale, a partitioned relational system may be a safer starting point than several independently committed financial services. If you split the ledger later, introduce an explicit pending-ledger state and an idempotent posting command. Do not call a payment successful before required posting is durable.

Checkpoint: Is service separation solving measured capacity or creating a distributed transaction?

Hint 9: Availability has a safety ceiling

When the authoritative store is unavailable, accepting a financial command into an uncoordinated queue may violate idempotency or amount limits. It can be correct to reject or return unavailable. When a provider is slow, persist first, bound concurrency, and avoid retry storms.

Checkpoint: Which dependency failures degrade reads, notifications, or financial writes differently?

Hint 10: L6 evidence

Name evolution triggers, ownership, alarms, repair loops, overload policy, regional fencing, rollout gates, and rollback conditions. Explain a rejected design and the evidence that would reverse your choice.

Checkpoint: Could another team operate and evolve the system using only your design decisions?

After scoring your first pass, continue to the rubric.

docs.title: Interviewer Packet
docs.text:
Practice home | Rubric | Exemplars

This file contains disclosures, probes, and calibration material. Keep it closed to candidates until the first design pass is complete.

docs.title: Interview objective
docs.text: Assess whether the candidate can make irreversible external effects safe, establish financial authority, recover ambiguous outcomes, and evolve the design with operational and organizational judgment. Reward depth on a coherent path over breadth across payment features.

docs.title: Mode selection
docs.text: Mode Use when Required evidence Optional extension 15 minutes Screening or warm-up Scope, invariants, API, confirm trace, timeout One refund race 30 minutes Standard L5 loop Safe core, lifecycle, data, ledger, outbox, telemetry Reconciliation 45 minutes Deep L5 or L6 signal Full core plus scaling, repair, tradeoffs Multi-region 60 minutes Dedicated L6 exercise Full design, failure response, migration, leadership Adversarial review

docs.title: Opening script
docs.text:
Design a payment orchestration platform for merchants. Providers may respond synchronously, asynchronously, or ambiguously. Start by clarifying scope and stating correctness invariants. I will provide assumptions when you ask. Please narrate authority, transaction boundaries, retry identity, and failure behavior as you draw.

Do not steer the candidate toward intent, ledger, or outbox terminology. The prompt already requires those capabilities; let the candidate define their boundaries.

docs.title: Assumptions available on request
docs.text:
Disclose only when asked or when the selected mode requires forward progress.

Candidate asks about Interviewer disclosure Signal to observe Payment methods Start with tokenized cards and two providers. Provider calls support a merchant-supplied operation reference. Narrows scope without designing rails Authorization/capture Automatic capture is required. Manual and partial capture may be discussed as an extension. Distinguishes authorization from money movement Currency Multiple currencies; no conversion inside one payment. Amounts use integer minor units. Names per-currency invariants Balances The platform tracks merchant payable balances; settlement is downstream. Introduces ledger without making it a bank Refunds Partial refunds are required and may race. Total successful plus reserved refunds cannot exceed captured amount. Looks for atomic reservation Provider behavior Calls can time out after acceptance. Callbacks can duplicate, reorder, or be delayed. Status query exists but is rate-limited. A merchant-supplied reference alone does not promise deduplication: ask the candidate to specify provider key scope, retention, and lookup visibility, then record the agreed exercise assumptions. Models unknown, retention expiry, and resolution budget Idempotency Merchants retry for days and may accidentally reuse a key with changed payload. Uses durable key plus request hash Webhooks Merchant endpoints can be slow or unavailable for hours. Global ordering is not required. Isolates endpoints and supports replay Ledger Auditors require immutable history and balanced entries per currency. Names posting authority and corrections Scale Use the prompt numbers; one merchant can be 20% of traffic. Quantifies amplification and skew Regions Each merchant may have a home region. A short write outage is preferable to duplicate money movement. Chooses ownership and fencing Compliance General services receive tokens, not raw card numbers or security codes. Maintains trust boundary and redaction Existing system For migration, use the synchronous legacy processor in migration.md. Preserves authority during evolution

docs.title: Minute 5
docs.text:
Look for scope, an authority question, and money invariants. If absent, ask:

Which facts must never become contradictory, even during retry?

docs.title: Minute 15
docs.text:
Look for durable operation identity before the provider call and an unknown outcome. If absent, ask:

The provider captures but the response is lost. The merchant retries. Trace every identity and state transition.

docs.title: Minute 30
docs.text:
Look for ledger timing, outbox, callback races, and repair. If absent, ask:

Which single commit makes a successful result valid, and how does a merchant event leave that commit?

docs.title: Minute 45
docs.text:
Look for quantified backlogs, skew, regional ownership, and evolution triggers. Ask:

What measurement would make you split the ledger, and what new failure state would that create?

docs.title: Minute 55
docs.text:
Look for migration gates and operational ownership. Ask:

A canary posts correct entries but its projection lags for 20 minutes. Do you promote, pause, or roll back? Who decides?

docs.title: Branching follow-ups
docs.text: Choose one branch based on the candidate's current strength. Do not ask every question.

docs.title: Branch A: Candidate relies on exactly once
docs.text:
1. Which boundary provides exactly once: client/API, provider, queue, database, or webhook?
  2. A consumer commits its database work and crashes before acknowledging the message. What repeats?
  3. What stable business key makes the repeat harmless?
  4. How do you detect a missing effect rather than only a duplicate?

Strong evidence: replaces the claim with durable identity, idempotent transitions, inbox/outbox, and reconciliation.

docs.title: Branch B: Candidate handles provider timeout well
docs.text:
1. The provider status endpoint is throttled for an hour. How do you allocate query capacity?
  2. A callback and resolver observe capture simultaneously. Which write wins and what happens to the loser?
  3. The provider cannot find the operation. When may you retry the financial request?
  4. How does unknown age affect merchant UX and operations escalation?

Strong evidence: sticky operation, conditional transition, durable loser replay, bounded retry budgets, quarantine when evidence remains insufficient.

docs.title: Branch C: Candidate separates the ledger immediately
docs.text:
1. What customer status exists after provider capture but before ledger acknowledgement?
  2. Can settlement consume that payment?
  3. What is the posting idempotency reference?
  4. What measured constraint justifies accepting this distributed workflow now?

Strong evidence: explicit pending-ledger state, durable posting command, blocked finality/settlement, reconciliation, and willingness to begin colocated.

docs.title: Branch D: Candidate keeps one database
docs.text:
1. Which rows commit together?
  2. How do you partition without creating cross-shard ledger transactions?
  3. At what sustained saturation or ownership threshold do you split?
  4. How will the state model change after the split?

Strong evidence: sees colocation as a deliberate safe baseline, not an inability to scale.

docs.title: Branch E: Candidate proposes active-active writes
docs.text:
1. Region A accepts a $70 refund while Region B accepts a $50 refund against $100. What merge is valid?
  2. How are stale writers fenced after failover?
  3. Which operations truly require global writes rather than local reads?

Strong evidence: converges on single home ownership, epochs, recovery pause, and globally available replicas.

docs.title: Branch F: Candidate is operationally strong
docs.text:
1. Which metric pages a finance on-call rather than an SRE?
  2. How do you express value at risk without high-cardinality merchant labels?
  3. What automated repair is safe for a captured-at-provider/missing-local break?
  4. Which chaos test could accidentally move real money, and how do you isolate it?

Strong evidence: separates technical and financial SLIs, defines approval boundaries, and uses provider sandboxes or simulators for destructive tests.

docs.title: Branch G: Candidate is migration strong
docs.text:
1. A retry arrives after its merchant cohort flag changed. Which implementation owns it?
  2. Shadow ledger totals match globally but not per merchant. Can you promote?
  3. What does rollback mean after valid ledger entries exist?
  4. When can legacy mutable columns be deleted?

Strong evidence: recorded generation, per-entity/value comparison, immutable rollback, and consumer inventory.

docs.title: Evidence notes
docs.text:
Capture candidate statements, not interviewer interpretations.

Topic Positive evidence Risk evidence Authority Unknown outcome Idempotency Transaction boundary Ledger Concurrency Reconciliation Operations Scale/regions Evolution/leadership

docs.title: Weak L5
docs.text: Component-oriented answer with shallow failure or operations evidence but no confirmed 17/40 safety-cap defect. If retries can duplicate money or unknown outcomes are guessed, classify below L5 according to the rubric, not weak L5. Record any interviewer-supplied repair separately from independently demonstrated evidence.

docs.title: Borderline L5
docs.text: Safe direction and coherent lifecycle, but one important atomicity, race, or repair gap remains after probing. Can implement a bounded component but needs review on financial workflows.

docs.title: Strong L5
docs.text: Independently produces safe end-to-end flow, explicit transaction boundaries, ambiguity resolution, reconciliation, and actionable operations. Tradeoffs are appropriate to current scale.

docs.title: Borderline L6
docs.text: Adds platform evolution, regional posture, quantified risk, and cross-team interfaces, but rollout ownership or decision gates are incomplete.

docs.title: Strong L6
docs.text:
Shapes ambiguous requirements, protects business invariants across teams, manages migration and incident risk, defines reversible decisions, and gives other teams an operable contract.

Use annotated exemplars and the evidence rubric to resolve close calls.

docs.title: Calibrated debrief
docs.text:
Deliver a four-part debrief in under three minutes.

  1. Demonstrated strength: cite one exact decision and why it reduces risk.
  2. Highest-risk gap: describe one concrete failure sequence, not a missing buzzword.
  3. Level evidence: name the rubric dimension and what was independently demonstrated versus prompted.
  4. Next-level action: give one design artifact or exercise that would close the gap.

docs.title: Debrief examples
docs.text:
Strong L5:

You made the provider operation durable before the call and kept timeout as unknown, which protected the core money boundary. The main gap was regional recovery: failover had replicas but no stale-writer fencing. This is strong L5 evidence because the single-region implementation and repair loops were independently complete. To reach L6, write the ownership epoch, promotion gate, and in-flight migration protocol.

Borderline L6:

You connected the ledger split to measured database saturation and introduced a pending-ledger protocol. The remaining risk was rollout ownership: the plan had shadow comparison but no value-at-risk threshold or authority to pause promotion. That supports borderline L6 rather than strong L6. Add cohort gates, immutable rollback behavior, and accountable finance and SRE owners.

docs.title: Interviewer anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Do not award points for naming Kafka, SQL, or Redis without semantics.
  • Do not force the candidate to reproduce one architecture.
  • Do not penalize a safe single-database baseline merely for lacking microservices.
  • Do not reveal the expected state names before the candidate models ambiguity.
  • Do not average a duplicate-money defect into a passing total.
  • Do not treat omitted optional features as a failure when the selected timed mode excludes them.
  • Do not open the reference case study during the interview.

docs.title: Post-session reading
docs.text: After scoring and debrief, invite the candidate to compare their design with Design a Payment System. Ask them to write three deltas: one correctness improvement, one unnecessary complexity they would remove, and one operational decision they would add.

docs.title: Migration Exercise: Legacy Processor to Intent, Ledger, and Outbox
docs.text: Practice home | Failure lab | Interviewer packet

docs.title: Legacy system
docs.text:
The current endpoint validates a request, calls one provider synchronously, writes a mutable payments row, and sends a merchant webhook inline.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant M as Merchant
    participant L as Legacy processor
    participant P as Provider
    participant D as Payments table
    participant H as Merchant webhook
    M->>L: POST charge
    L->>P: Charge
    P-->>L: Result or timeout
    L->>D: Insert or update row
    L->>H: Notify inline
    L-->>M: Response

Known constraints:

  • Merchant retries can create duplicate rows.
  • Provider operation IDs are generated inside the adapter and are not always retained.
  • A timeout is recorded as FAILED.
  • Fees and merchant balances are mutable columns maintained by a nightly job.
  • Webhook failure can delay the API response and has no replay record.
  • Operations repairs rows with SQL scripts.
  • The endpoint processes 2,000 peak requests/s today and cannot stop for a big-bang cutover.
  • Historical provider reports are available for 18 months.

docs.title: Target capability
docs.text:
Evolve toward durable payment intents, attempts with stable provider operation IDs, an immutable balanced ledger, and a transactional outbox. Preserve service during migration. Do not dual-write financial truth from application code.

The target label is not the plan. Your answer must define intermediate authority, in-flight ownership, verification, rollback, and deletion rules.

docs.title: Candidate tasks
docs.text:
1. Identify the first three legacy risks to remove and justify the order.
  2. Define the schema additions and compatibility contract.
  3. Produce migration stages with entry, observation, promotion, and rollback gates.
  4. Explain how old and new requests remain idempotent during mixed operation.
  5. Backfill historical ledger entries without pretending reconstructed data is original real-time truth.
  6. Move financial authority exactly once and preserve an audit trail.
  7. Remove legacy fields and jobs only after proving no reader or repair path depends on them.

docs.title: Required control plane
docs.text: Every payment records an immutable processing generation such as LEGACY_WRAPPED, INTENT_V1, or LEDGER_V1. Retries and callbacks follow the recorded generation, not the current feature flag. Cohort assignment is stable by merchant and environment. Operators can pause promotion but cannot rewrite an in-flight generation.

docs.title: Migration worksheet
docs.text:
Stage Authority Writes enabled Shadow or comparison Promotion gate Rollback behavior 0. Baseline and observe 1. Durable identity wrapper 2. Intent state machine 3. Transactional outbox 4. Shadow ledger 5. Ledger authority 6. Retire legacy paths Open after drafting: reference migration and facilitator notes

After completing the exercise, interviewers can use the branching follow-ups.

docs.title: Reference migration shape
docs.text: Use this after drafting your own plan.

docs.title: Stage 0: Baseline and evidence
docs.text:
Instrument the legacy path before changing authority. Generate a correlation ID at ingress. Measure provider requests by merchant request, timeout outcomes, duplicate order references, webhook latency, mutable-balance drift, and provider-to-local reconciliation value. Retain signed or authenticated provider evidence. Create runbooks and assign financial-break ownership.

Gate: baseline covers at least normal peaks and one provider incident window; reconciliation can quantify known disagreement.

docs.title: Stage 1: Durable identity wrapper
docs.text:
Place an adapter around the legacy endpoint. In SQL, reserve (merchant_id, operation, idempotency_key) with request hash, stable internal payment ID, processing generation, and original response. Persist a provider operation ID before invocation and change the provider adapter to use that exact ID on the wire; retaining an unrelated wrapper ID while the adapter generates a new one does not close the crash window. Verify provider deduplication scope and retention. Retries return the existing operation or result. Stop translating timeout into failure; expose processing while a resolver gathers evidence.

Authority: the legacy payment row still serves final business state. The new identity record owns request deduplication and operation recovery.

Rollback: pause new cohort enrollment and keep the durable identity wrapper for all already enrolled traffic. Roll back implementation changes behind that wrapper without restoring unsafe provider identity generation or timeout-as-failure behavior. Existing wrapped operations continue under LEGACY_WRAPPED; never create a second provider identity.

docs.title: Stage 2: Introduce payment intents
docs.text:
Create versioned intents and attempts. For wrapped cohorts, write the intent before the call and mirror verified legacy outcomes through conditional transitions. Callbacks map by provider and stable operation reference, not merchant order alone. Run read comparisons between intent projection and legacy status. API reads remain on legacy authority until mismatch classes are understood.

Gate: no unexplained terminal-state mismatch, duplicate provider operation, or over-refund in the canary window. Unknown-age SLO and resolver capacity pass fault tests.

docs.title: Stage 3: Introduce the transactional outbox
docs.text:
When an authoritative transition commits, insert an immutable outbox event in the same database transaction. Relay at least once. Build webhook delivery records with stable event IDs, endpoint isolation, retries, and replay. Initially shadow inline webhook delivery, then move cohort by cohort. Duplicates are acceptable only when merchants can deduplicate the same business event ID.

Gate: no committed transition lacks an outbox row; oldest outbox and webhook delivery age stay within budget during a simulated broker outage.

Rollback: pause the relay or route notification reads back, but do not delete outbox rows or regenerate business event identities.

docs.title: Stage 4: Build a shadow ledger
docs.text:
Define posting templates and unique business references. Backfill historical captures, refunds, fees, and settlements from retained provider evidence and legacy records into a separately labeled migration journal. Record source, source timestamp, reconstruction timestamp, and confidence. Post corrections as new linked transactions.

Only 18 months of provider reports are supplied, whereas the main prompt requires seven-year availability of financial records. Preserve older legacy evidence and explicitly inventory gaps; do not fabricate transaction history to make the new ledger appear complete. Finance must approve any opening-balance migration and document what cannot be independently reconciled before authority moves.

For live shadow traffic, derive proposed postings from verified intent transitions. Compare per-payment references, per-currency zero sums, merchant payable deltas, and provider receivable totals. The legacy balance remains serving authority during shadowing.

Gate: all transactions balance; duplicate references are zero; unexplained provider-to-ledger and legacy-to-ledger value differences remain below an approved threshold and age budget for multiple close cycles.

docs.title: Stage 5: Move ledger authority
docs.text:
For a small merchant cohort, make verified capture, balanced ledger rows, and outbox commit in one local transaction. Serve balances from ledger-backed projections with an authoritative fallback. Freeze legacy balance mutations for migrated payments; mirror ledger results into legacy columns only for compatibility and label them derived.

If ledger ownership is already a separate service, use a durable CAPTURED_PENDING_LEDGER state and idempotent posting command. Do not expose final success or permit settlement until acknowledgement. Bound the pending queue by value and age.

Promotion gates: zero invariant breaches, no unexplained value breaks, posting p99 within budget, projection lag visible, rollback rehearsed, operations sign-off, and finance sign-off.

Rollback: stop assigning new cohort traffic. Finish in-flight operations under their generation. Keep committed ledger entries authoritative and immutable; route reads through a compatibility projection. Never reverse valid entries merely to make the old schema look primary.

docs.title: Stage 6: Retire legacy paths
docs.text:
Inventory every reader, SQL repair script, report, and job. Replace mutable repair with audited commands and ledger adjustments. Compare legacy and new reads through the agreed compatibility window and enough financial-close cycles to exercise reconciliation. Test archived reads across the full retained history; keeping seven years of evidence does not require keeping obsolete online writers running for seven years. Then remove inline webhook calls, mutable-balance jobs, legacy writes, and finally obsolete columns in separate releases.

Exit: no production access for legacy mutation, no unknown consumers, archived reconciliation evidence remains queryable, and disaster-recovery restore includes intent, idempotency, ledger, and outbox state.

docs.title: Authority map
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Legacy mutable row] --> B[Durable identity wrapper]
    B --> C[Versioned payment intent]
    C --> D[Intent plus transactional outbox]
    D --> E[Shadow immutable ledger]
    E --> F[Intent plus ledger plus outbox authority]
    F --> G[Legacy path retired]

docs.title: Migration traps
docs.text:
• Application dual writes to legacy and ledger databases without one authority.
  • Feature flags that reroute retries instead of honoring recorded generation.
  • Backfills that use current mutable balances as if they were historical entries.
  • Rollback that deletes postings or replays a provider call with a new operation ID.
  • Aggregate-only comparison that hides offsetting per-payment breaks.
  • Promoting on row parity while value, currency, and age distributions disagree.
  • Removing legacy columns before unknown reports and manual scripts are inventoried.

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text: Assign accountable owners for API compatibility, provider adapters, ledger templates, reconciliation, SRE capacity, finance controls, merchant communication, and decommissioning. State which owner can pause a cohort, which requires dual approval to post an adjustment, and who accepts residual break thresholds.

docs.title: Candidate Prompt: Payment Orchestration
docs.text: Practice home | Workbook | Hints

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Design a payment orchestration platform for online merchants. A merchant creates a payment, confirms it with a tokenized payment method, checks its status, and may issue a refund. The platform chooses among external payment providers. Providers can reply immediately, send a later callback, or time out after processing the request.

The platform must present one stable business result even when clients, queues, and providers retry. It must maintain auditable money records and notify merchants of changes.

Do not design card networks, a token vault, fraud models, merchant settlement, or a general-purpose bank. Define interfaces to those systems where they affect correctness.

docs.title: Starting scale
docs.text:
• 10,000 peak confirmation requests per second.
  • 50,000 peak status reads per second.
  • 50 million payments per day.
  • A small number of merchants and providers can dominate traffic.
  • Query availability target: 99.99%.
  • Confirmation availability target: 99.95%.
  • When a provider responds, confirmation should complete within 2 seconds at p99.
  • Financial and audit records must remain available for seven years, with a shorter hot-storage window.

You may challenge any number. Explain what changes if your assumption differs.

docs.title: Functional requirements
docs.text:
1. Create and confirm a payment.
  2. Read canonical payment status.
  3. Route an operation to one provider.
  4. Accept authenticated provider callbacks.
  5. Refund all or part of a successful payment.
  6. Record financial effects in an immutable ledger.
  7. Deliver retryable merchant webhooks.
  8. Reconcile local records against independent provider evidence.

docs.title: Questions your design must answer
docs.text:
• What are the correctness invariants?
  • Which object owns the customer-visible lifecycle?
  • What does an idempotency key cover, and what happens when its payload changes?
  • What is persisted before an external provider call?
  • What state is returned after an ambiguous timeout?
  • When does a successful payment create ledger entries?
  • How do callbacks, pollers, refunds, and client retries race safely?
  • How are database state and events published without a dual-write gap?
  • Which reads may be stale, and how is staleness communicated?
  • How do operators find and repair disagreements without inventing money?
  • How does the system degrade during provider, stream, or database failure?
  • What is the initial deployment shape, and which measurements justify splitting it?

docs.title: 15-minute mode
docs.text:
By minute 3, state scope and at least three invariants. By minute 7, define the API and lifecycle. By minute 12, draw the confirm path. Use the final 3 minutes for one ambiguous timeout and one tradeoff.

Expected artifact: one page or board containing assumptions, invariants, a compact architecture, and a timeout trace.

docs.title: 30-minute mode
docs.text:
Complete the 15-minute artifact, then add:

  • intent, attempt, idempotency, provider event, ledger, and outbox records;
  • allowed state transitions;
  • refund-capacity protection;
  • webhook delivery semantics;
  • top operational signals.

Use the final 4 minutes to summarize authority, consistency, and recovery.

docs.title: 45-minute mode
docs.text:
Complete the 30-minute artifact, then add:

  • a clear local transaction boundary;
  • outbox relay and idempotent consumer behavior;
  • provider routing and retry restrictions;
  • reconciliation inputs and break categories;
  • partitioning and hot-merchant controls;
  • one evolution trigger that would justify separating the ledger.

Use the final 5 minutes for adversarial review.

docs.title: 60-minute mode
docs.text:
Complete the 45-minute artifact, then add:

  • multi-region ownership and fencing;
  • backlog and overload behavior;
  • a phased migration from a synchronous legacy processor;
  • rollback gates and financial controls;
  • two rejected alternatives with reversal conditions.

Use the final 8 minutes for interviewer follow-ups and executive summary.

docs.title: Deliverable format
docs.text:
Present in this order:

  1. scope and assumptions;
  2. invariants and SLOs;
  3. API and state model;
  4. architecture and authoritative stores;
  5. confirm and refund traces;
  6. failure handling and reconciliation;
  7. scaling, security, and operations;
  8. tradeoffs and evolution.

Diagrams may omit routine gateways and load balancers. Every arrow that can move money or change financial state must identify its retry and deduplication behavior.

docs.title: Candidate stop point
docs.text: Do not read the exemplars, design review, failure lab, migration exercise, or interviewer packet until your first pass is complete.

docs.title: Evidence Rubric
docs.text:
Practice home | Exemplars | Interviewer packet

Score demonstrated evidence, not vocabulary. A component name earns no credit without its responsibility, authority, and failure behavior.

docs.title: Scoring model
docs.text:
Each dimension receives 0 to 4 points.

Score Evidence standard 0 Missing, contradictory, or unsafe 1 Names a concern but gives no enforceable mechanism 2 Coherent happy path with material gaps under retries or failure 3 Correct mechanism, boundary, and important failure behavior 4 Level 3 plus quantified tradeoff, operational proof, or evolution judgment

Safety caps override totals.

docs.title: A. Framing and requirement control
docs.text:
• Separates orchestration, provider rails, ledger, settlement, disputes, risk, and tokenization.
  • Clarifies authorization versus capture, refunds, currencies, and whether balances are held.
  • Prioritizes money correctness before broad availability.

docs.title: B. Invariants and authority
docs.text:
• States once-only business effects, valid transitions, refund/capture limits, balanced immutable entries, and evidence requirements.
  • Names the authoritative payment and money records.
  • Connects each invariant to a transaction, uniqueness constraint, conditional update, or reconciliation proof.

docs.title: C. API and lifecycle semantics
docs.text:
• Defines idempotency scope, request hash conflict, canonical retry response, processing result, and invalid-transition conflict.
  • Models unresolved provider outcomes without guessing.
  • Supports query and safe partial refund behavior.

docs.title: D. Data and transaction boundaries
docs.text:
• Defines intent, attempt, provider event, refund, ledger, idempotency, and outbox identity.
  • Persists a stable provider operation before the external call.
  • Makes verified success, required ledger posting, and outbox atomic in the initial design, or models an explicit pending-ledger protocol after separation.

docs.title: E. External calls, retries, and concurrency
docs.text:
• Keeps a provider operation stable and routing sticky after possible submission.
  • Distinguishes transient retry from terminal decline and forbids unsafe write hedging.
  • Serializes callback, resolver, cancel, capture, and refund races; reserves amount capacity.

docs.title: F. Ledger and financial controls
docs.text:
• Uses integer minor units, currency-scoped balanced postings, immutable corrections, and unique business references.
  • Distinguishes authorization from captured money.
  • Includes balance verification, adjustment controls, and auditability.

docs.title: G. Events, webhooks, and reconciliation
docs.text:
• Closes dual writes with an outbox and treats queues as at least once.
  • Gives consumers and merchants deduplication keys and bounded ordering.
  • Uses independent provider evidence, break classification, aging, and controlled repair.

docs.title: H. Scale, availability, and multi-region
docs.text:
• Quantifies write amplification and backlog, not only API QPS.
  • Handles provider and merchant skew with quotas, isolation, and backpressure.
  • Defines strong versus eventual reads, safe dependency degradation, home-region ownership, and fenced failover.

docs.title: I. Security and abuse boundaries
docs.text:
• Keeps sensitive instrument data outside general services and logs.
  • Authenticates callbacks and merchants; protects provider credentials.
  • Addresses replay, refund privilege, webhook egress risk, audit, and key rotation.

docs.title: J. Operability and evolution
docs.text:
• Uses IDs across traces, actionable SLIs, unknown-age and reconciliation alarms, outbox and webhook backlog, and financial integrity checks.
  • Names owners, runbooks, and repair paths.
  • Starts with the simplest safe transaction boundary and gives measured split or migration triggers, rollout gates, and rollback.

Maximum: 40 points.

docs.title: Safety caps
docs.text:
Apply the lowest relevant cap.

Apply the hint policy to supplied evidence before summing and normalizing. Keep raw, normalized, lowest cap, and final result visible. An unresolved universal critical gate still blocks general readiness, even if this scenario-local band is named weak L5.

Defect Maximum outcome Retries provider writes with a new identity after timeout 17/40; below L5 Converts timeout to failure or success without evidence 17/40; below L5 Allows successful payment state without required durable money record or pending protocol 17/40; below L5 Uses mutable ledger history or permits unbalanced postings 17/40; below L5 Claims exactly-once delivery as the primary correctness mechanism 23/40; weak L5 Has no reconciliation path for external money 23/40; weak L5 Strong single-region design but no credible operations or evolution at 60 minutes 32/40; strong L5 Multi-region active-active financial writes without ownership, fencing, or another demonstrated invariant-preserving protocol 17/40; below L5

docs.title: Level calibration
docs.text:
Outcome Typical total Required pattern Weak L5 18-23 Coherent happy path, but at least two significant retry, ledger, or operations gaps Borderline L5 24-27 Mostly safe core with shallow failure handling or inconsistent boundaries Strong L5 28-32 End-to-end safe design, clear tradeoffs, credible recovery and operations Borderline L6 33-35 Strong L5 plus cross-team and evolution judgment, with one material leadership gap Strong L6 36-40 Shapes requirements, quantifies risk, designs repair and migration, and makes reversible organizational decisions

A total below 18 is below the target band. Totals do not override a safety cap.

docs.text:

docs.title: Mode adjustment
docs.text:
Score only the dimensions listed for the selected mode, then normalize the subtotal to 40 with normalized = subtotal / available points * 40. Round to the nearest whole point and apply safety caps afterward.

Mode Scored dimensions Available points Required evidence outside those dimensions 15 minutes A-E 20 One failure trace; omitted migration and multi-region detail is not penalized 30 minutes A-G and J 32 Operational signals score under J 45 minutes A-J 40 Evolution triggers are required; detailed migration execution is not 60 minutes A-J 40 Strong L6 requires migration and organizational judgment

Record both values as subtotal/available -> normalized/40 so attempts from different modes are not confused with equal-depth artifacts. Normalization permits comparison but does not create evidence for omitted dimensions; use the mode label whenever reporting a level.

A 15-minute subtotal cannot establish L6 operations or migration competence, even when normalization yields 40. Report the demonstrated mode-scoped result and leave untested competencies unassessed. Short mode is not a waiver for an unsafe mechanism the candidate explicitly proposes.

docs.title: Debrief rule
docs.text: Give feedback in this order: one demonstrated strength, one highest-risk gap, the evidence needed to close it, and one stretch question. Avoid averaging away a money-safety defect.

Post-attempt workload calibration
