docs.title: L5/L6 Chapter Checklist
docs.text: Use this checklist while practicing any design.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• Identify three core functional requirements.
  • Name important exclusions.
  • Clarify users, geography, traffic shape, and data lifetime.
  • State which failures are unacceptable.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Estimate average and peak read/write QPS.
  • Estimate storage and bandwidth.
  • Identify skew, fan-out, and hot-key multipliers.
  • Use the estimates to justify design choices.

docs.title: Interface and Data
docs.text:
• Define request, response, pagination, and idempotency behavior.
  • Model canonical entities and state machines.
  • Add constraints for domain invariants.
  • Align indexes and partitions with access patterns.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Satisfy each requirement end to end.
  • Identify sources of truth, projections, caches, and event streams.
  • Explain synchronous and asynchronous boundaries.
  • Show overload, retry, and backpressure behavior.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Handle dependency, region, and partial-workflow failures.
  • Define reconciliation and rebuild paths.
  • Specify meaningful SLIs and alerts.
  • Discuss security, abuse, privacy, and cost.

docs.title: Seniority
docs.text:
• L5: coherent design, key tradeoffs, primary bottlenecks, and correctness.
  • L6: hidden invariants, evolution, migrations, policy, failure isolation, and organizational boundaries.

docs.title: Content Depth Tiers
docs.text: Use tiers to set a truthful depth promise before writing. Tier measures the decisions a reader can practice, not word count.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Core content builds a reusable foundation.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• State the reader outcome, scope, prerequisites, and important exclusions.
  • Define the mental model and vocabulary before product names.
  • Present the smallest correct design and its primary invariant.
  • Explain one important alternative and why it loses under the stated constraints.
  • Walk through one concrete example and one failure path.
  • End with a recall or application prompt.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text: For a caching chapter, define cache-aside, canonical storage, key and value shape, TTL ownership, and the stale-read boundary. Walk through one hit, one miss, and a database write followed by invalidation failure. Compare cache-aside with write-through for the stated workload. Include a request timeline a reader can annotate. Do not add distributed invalidation, leases, or multi-region replication unless a requirement demands them.

docs.title: Acceptance check
docs.text:
• Can a reader explain the invariant without naming a vendor?
  • Does the example expose both the normal path and one failure?
  • Is every component justified by a requirement?
  • Is there at least one worked artifact?

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text: Advanced content teaches design defense under changing constraints. It includes every Core requirement.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Quantify throughput, data size, latency, skew, and a relevant sensitivity case.
  • Define consistency, idempotency, ordering, pagination, and backpressure where applicable.
  • Compare at least two viable alternatives using explicit decision criteria.
  • Cover overload, dependency failure, recovery, and observable symptoms.
  • Explain an evolution or migration path and rollback boundary.
  • Include at least two practical artifact types and a test strategy.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text: An advanced caching chapter estimates peak QPS, working-set bytes, hot-key amplification, and database fallback capacity. It compares cache-aside, read-through, and write-through by staleness, write amplification, and failure coupling. A failure table covers cache loss, stampede, stale invalidation, and database saturation. A rollout plan starts with bounded TTL and request coalescing, measures hit rate and fallback load, then adds event invalidation only if staleness evidence requires it. Artifacts include the capacity calculation and failure table.

docs.title: Acceptance check
docs.text:
• Do numbers change a design choice rather than decorate the text?
  • Are overload and recovery behavior explicit?
  • Can the reader identify the authoritative state at every step?
  • Are rollout and rollback observable and bounded?

docs.title: Flagship
docs.text: Flagship content is an interview-ready, production-informed scenario. It includes every Core and Advanced requirement.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Satisfy the full scenario package contract.
  • Include at least three problem-specific deep dives with alternatives and measurable decision criteria.
  • Separate control and data planes when that distinction changes failure or scaling behavior.
  • Cover cost, security, privacy or abuse, multi-region policy, organizational ownership, and long-term evolution where relevant.
  • Attribute benchmark, vendor, and production claims using the source standard.
  • Include capacity math, interface or data, failure, operations, test, and decision artifacts.
  • State L5 and L6 expectations and provide a five-minute compressed answer.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text: A flagship payment design defines authorization, capture, refund, and reconciliation invariants; calculates peak attempts and ledger growth; and supplies versioned APIs, idempotency keys, ledger schema, state transitions, and three end-to-end sequences. Deep dives cover duplicate effects, external-provider uncertainty, and regional ownership. It includes a failure matrix, SLIs, reconciliation runbook, migration and rollback plan, threat analysis, cost drivers, and adversarial tests. Claims about provider behavior are dated and attributed. The final section distinguishes an L5 coherent design from L6 policy, operations, and evolution leadership.

docs.title: Acceptance check
docs.text:
• Could an interviewer pivot to failure, scale, cost, migration, or policy and find a defended answer?
  • Do deep dives solve scenario-specific risks rather than repeat generic patterns?
  • Can an operator detect, contain, recover, reconcile, and roll back?
  • Are evidence labels and dates present where claims can age?
  • Does the five-minute summary preserve the key invariants and tradeoffs?

docs.title: Tier Selection Worksheet
docs.text:
Question Core Advanced Flagship Reader goal Explain and apply Defend under pivots Lead an ambiguous design Quantification One useful worked example Limits and sensitivity End-to-end capacity and cost model Failures One representative path Overload and recovery set Operational containment and reconciliation Alternatives One comparison Decision matrix Decisions revisited across evolution Practical artifacts One Two types Six required types Evidence Cite material borrowed claims Date changing claims Full evidence labels and production context

Choose the lowest tier that meets the learning objective. A narrow, complete Core chapter is better than a nominal flagship chapter with missing contracts.

docs.title: System Design Glossary
docs.text: Concise definitions for interview use. A strong answer explains what a term changes in the design rather than merely naming it.

docs.title: A–C
docs.text:
Availability The proportion of valid requests the system can serve successfully. Define it for a specific operation and time window.

Backpressure A mechanism that slows or rejects producers when downstream capacity is exhausted, preventing unbounded queues and cascading failure.

Cache stampede Many callers recompute or reload the same expired hot value simultaneously. Common controls include request coalescing, jitter, and stale-while-revalidate.

CAP theorem For a replicated read/write object subject to network partitions, linearizability and completion of every request at every non-failing node cannot both be guaranteed. This formal availability differs from the operational success ratio above. It is not a global database label or a claim that every invariant needs coordination. See the CAP model and examples.

Canonical state The authoritative durable representation from which caches, indexes, and projections can be rebuilt.

Change data capture (CDC) Publishing database mutations from a transaction log so downstream systems can build projections or integrations.

Control plane The path that configures placement, policy, metadata, or orchestration; usually lower-volume than the request-serving data plane.

docs.title: D–I
docs.text:
Data plane The path carrying user requests, records, messages, or bytes during normal service operation.

Exactly-once effect A business outcome applied once despite retries or duplicate delivery within a stated boundary and retention horizon. Durable deduplication prevents repeats; durable intent, delivery, and recovery are also needed to avoid missing effects. Local deduplication alone does not guarantee a remote provider effect. See distributed transactions.

Fan-out One action producing work for many destinations. Fan-out-on-write shifts cost to writes; fan-out-on-read assembles results at query time.

Hot key A key or partition receiving disproportionate traffic, making average load misleading and often requiring splitting, replication, or admission control.

Idempotency The property that repeating an operation with the same identity does not change the result beyond the first successful application.

Invariant A condition that must remain true, such as “available inventory never drops below zero” or “ledger entries balance.”

docs.title: L–R
docs.text:
Lease A time-bounded grant of authority. Leases reduce permanent lock ownership but require careful handling of clocks, expiry, and fencing.

Linearizability A consistency model where each operation appears to occur atomically between invocation and response, respecting real-time order.

Outbox pattern Writing domain state and an event record in one local transaction, then asynchronously publishing the event to avoid dual-write gaps.

Partition key The value determining data placement. Its choice controls locality, distribution, hot spots, and query fan-out.

Projection A derived, query-optimized view built from canonical state or an event stream and designed to be rebuildable.

Quorum A required subset of replicas participating in an operation. Quorum overlap can provide consistency under specified failure assumptions.

Reconciliation A background process that detects and repairs divergence between intended, canonical, and derived state.

Recovery point objective (RPO) The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time.

Recovery time objective (RTO) The target maximum time to restore service after disruption.

docs.title: S–Z
docs.text:
Saga A sequence of local transactions coordinated through events or commands, with compensating actions for incomplete workflows.

Service-level indicator (SLI) A measured property of service behavior, such as successful checkout latency or fresh-feed availability.

Service-level objective (SLO) A target range for an SLI over a defined window, used to guide engineering and reliability decisions.

Split brain Multiple nodes or regions simultaneously believe they have authority, risking conflicting writes. Quorums, leases, and fencing limit it.

Tail latency Latency at a high percentile such as p99. Fan-out can amplify tail latency because a request waits for its slowest dependency.

Write amplification The extra writes caused by one logical mutation, including indexes, replicas, feed entries, or storage compaction.

docs.title: Interview reminder
docs.text: If a term does not alter an API guarantee, data model, component boundary, scaling choice, or failure behavior, it probably does not yet add value to the answer.

docs.title: Interview Scorecard
docs.text: Use this after a timed attempt, not during it. Score observable decisions rather than diagram polish.

docs.title: Scoring scale
docs.text: Score Meaning 0 Missing or materially incorrect 1 Mentioned but vague, reactive, or disconnected 2 Correct and connected to requirements 3 Proactive, quantified, and defended with tradeoffs

docs.title: Core scorecard
docs.text:
Dimension What strong evidence looks like Score Framing and scope Users, core requirements, exclusions, assumptions, and priorities are explicit /3 Invariants and SLOs Correctness conditions and measurable reliability/latency targets precede architecture /3 Estimation Peak QPS, storage, bandwidth, skew, and fan-out influence concrete choices /3 API and data model Contracts, identifiers, state transitions, pagination, and access patterns align /3 Baseline architecture A simple end-to-end path satisfies each core requirement /3 Scaling and partitioning Bottlenecks, keys, replication, hot spots, and growth triggers are reasoned through /3 Consistency and idempotency Guarantees are operation-specific; retries and duplicate effects are safe /3 Reliability and recovery Timeouts, overload, dependency failures, reconciliation, and rebuild paths are credible /3 Security and abuse Authentication, authorization, privacy, abuse, and domain threats are addressed /3 Observability and operations SLIs, alerts, capacity signals, rollout, and incident recovery are actionable /3 Tradeoff communication Alternatives are compared against requirements; complexity is justified /3 Delivery The narrative is structured, collaborative, and responsive to interviewer signals /3

Core total: /36

docs.title: L6 extension
docs.text:
Score these dimensions when targeting staff-level performance.

Dimension What strong evidence looks like Score Hidden constraints Identifies policy, compliance, tenant, or product interactions not stated directly /3 Evolution and migration Provides safe rollout, compatibility, backfill, rollback, and decommission paths /3 Control and data planes Separates configuration/orchestration from serving and defines failure boundaries /3 Regional and overload strategy Quantifies degradation, isolation, failover, and consistency consequences /3 Cost and ownership Connects design to cost drivers, team boundaries, and operational responsibility /3

L6 extension: /15 · Combined total: /51

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Core result Interpretation Next action 0–16 Foundations are inconsistent Return to the delivery framework and practice one dimension at a time 17–24 Coherent but important gaps remain Repeat the same case with two targeted deep dives 25–30 Strong L5 trajectory Increase domain variety and interviewer-led pivots 31–36 Consistently strong L5 execution Focus on compression, nuance, and L6 extensions

For L6 practice, a high core score is necessary but not sufficient. Look for 11+ out of 15 on the extension with no zero in migration or failure isolation.

docs.title: Post-practice notes
docs.text:
Record only the highest-leverage observations:

  1. Best decision: What did I identify early that shaped the design?
  2. Largest gap: What requirement, invariant, or failure did I miss?
  3. Unjustified complexity: What component could I remove?
  4. Weakest defense: Which tradeoff became hand-waving under questioning?
  5. Next retry: What will I deliberately improve within 48 hours?

Do not game the total

A design with a broken money, inventory, privacy, or durability invariant is not strong because it accumulated points elsewhere. Treat critical correctness failures as interview-level risks.

docs.title: Read a diagram as a protocol
docs.text: A useful diagram helps you predict an observable outcome. Before naming technologies, locate the state that decides whether an operation succeeded. Then follow one request to that state and back to the caller.

docs.title: Three views, three questions
docs.text:
View Question it answers What it cannot prove Architecture map Which component owns a responsibility or state? Whether two writes happen atomically Numbered sequence Which message or commit precedes the next action? That a timeout cancels remote work State model Which transitions are allowed, and under what conditions? That every writer enforces those conditions

Sequence numbers are reading aids. Concurrent branches may execute in a different interleaving. A drawn arrow does not imply durable delivery, authorization, or a transaction. Read its label and the surrounding contract.

docs.title: Follow acceptance through a crash
docs.text:
Illustrative design: A reservation service stores a command key, the reservation, and an outbox event in one database transaction. A separate relay publishes committed events. This is a proposed protocol, not a description of a named company's internals.

flowchart LR
    Client["Client<br/>Retry with command K"] -->|request| API["Reservation service"]
    subgraph TX["One atomic transaction"]
        Result["Command K and saved result"]
        Hold["Seat hold"]
        Event["Outbox event E"]
    end
    API -->|commit together| TX
    TX -->|commit acknowledged| API
    API -->|accepted hold| Client
    Event -.->|relay may publish again| Consumer["Idempotent projection consumer"]

The solid arrows show the request and commit path. The dashed arrow marks asynchronous publication. Shape and explicit labels carry the meaning; color is not a correctness guarantee. The transaction boundary includes all three records. It does not include the consumer.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Reservation API
    participant D as Database
    participant R as Outbox relay
    C->>A: reserve(command K, request hash)
    A->>D: atomically claim K, hold seat, append E
    D-->>A: commit acknowledged
    A--xC: response lost
    C->>A: retry identical K
    A->>D: read recorded outcome for K
    D-->>A: same hold
    A-->>C: same accepted result
    R->>D: read committed outbox E
    R->>R: publish E and retry if outcome unknown

At step 4 the client is uncertain, but the reservation already exists. Retrying with a new key would create a new command. Retrying with the same key requires an atomic uniqueness rule and a stored request hash: the server must reject reuse of K with different parameters. The relay can publish E more than once; each consumer needs its own effect and deduplication boundary.

docs.title: Test the boundary yourself
docs.text:
Before revealing the answer, decide what happens if the relay publishes E and crashes before marking it sent.

Reason through the replay

The relay reads E again and may publish it twice. Marking it sent before publishing instead risks losing E. The correct response is to tolerate replay: the consumer applies its local effect and records E in the same transaction where possible. An external effect, such as charging a provider, additionally needs the provider's idempotency contract and reconciliation for uncertain outcomes. A local inbox alone cannot make a remote charge atomic.

docs.title: Diagram controls
docs.text:
• Read restores a readable scale. Scroll inside the canvas to follow a wide flow.
  • Fit shows the whole width, useful for an overview. Small labels are expected in that mode.
  • Expand opens a larger canvas. Escape closes it and returns keyboard focus.
  • Text diagram exposes the underlying named participants, messages, and branches.

On a narrow screen, swipe or keyboard-scroll the focused canvas. The page itself should remain within the viewport. A pale canvas keeps contrast stable across the course's light and dark reading modes.

docs.title: Before trusting an architecture sketch
docs.text:
1. Locate the authoritative state, derived copies, and trust boundaries.
  2. Identify which acknowledgment means durable acceptance.
  3. Distinguish message order from commit order and apply order.
  4. Stop the protocol after each arrow and predict recovery.
  5. Name the key, epoch, or version that rejects duplicates or stale actors.
  6. Check that the prose, API responses, and final diagram promise the same outcome.

Continue with the delivery framework, distributed transactions, and outbox/inbox fault lab.

docs.title: Scenario Package Contract
docs.text: A flagship case study is a package of decisions and artifacts that supports a full interview loop. The contract is semantic: authors may combine, split, rename, or reorder sections when the responsibilities remain easy to find.

docs.title: Frame the problem
docs.text:
• Interview roadmap and product framing.
  • Users, use cases, exclusions, functional requirements, SLOs, and non-functional requirements.
  • Correctness, safety, privacy, and business invariants stated before technology choices.

Accepted heading examples include "Product framing," "Scope and requirements," "Requirements, SLOs, and invariants," and "What must be true." Exact wording is not required.

docs.title: Quantify the workload
docs.text:
• Labeled assumptions with units and dates when context can age.
  • Average and peak traffic, storage, bandwidth, fan-out, skew, and retention as relevant.
  • At least one sensitivity case and an explicit design consequence.

Accepted heading examples include "Capacity estimates," "Sizing the workload," "Back-of-the-envelope model," and "Traffic and storage assumptions."

docs.title: Define contracts and state
docs.text:
• Concrete APIs, commands, events, callbacks, pagination, errors, retries, and idempotency behavior as applicable.
  • Canonical entities, keys, constraints, indexes, state transitions, retention, and deletion.
  • Clear separation of authority, caches, projections, and replayable evidence.

"APIs and model" may satisfy both interface and data-model coverage. A diagram alone does not.

docs.title: Build and trace the design
docs.text:
• High-level architecture with control, data, and administrative boundaries where relevant.
  • End-to-end normal flows for every core requirement.
  • At least three scenario-specific deep dives that expose algorithms, state changes, bottlenecks, and alternatives.
  • At least three valid Mermaid diagrams that clarify different concerns.

docs.title: Defend correctness and scale
docs.text:
• Partition keys, hot-key and skew behavior, consistency boundaries, ordering, deduplication, and backpressure.
  • Dependency, host, zone, region, data-corruption, retry-storm, and overload behavior as applicable.
  • Detection, containment, recovery, reconciliation, rebuild, RPO/RTO, and degraded modes.
  • Multi-region ownership and conflict policy, or an explicit explanation of why multi-region is out of scope.

Combined headings such as "Partitioning, consistency, failures, and regions" are valid semantic coverage.

docs.title: Make it operable and safe
docs.text:
• Authentication, authorization, secrets, encryption, abuse, privacy, retention, and audit concerns relevant to the domain.
  • SLIs, SLOs, alerts, dashboards, traces, and operator actions.
  • Deterministic, load, fault-injection, compatibility, and reconciliation tests as applicable.
  • Cost drivers, ownership boundaries, rollout, rollback, migration, and version evolution.

docs.title: Close the interview
docs.text:
• Important tradeoffs and why alternatives lose under the selected constraints.
  • Final architecture after the deep dives, not merely a repeated opening diagram.
  • Interviewer deep-dive questions, explicit L5/L6 expectations, and a five-minute summary.

docs.title: Required Practical Artifacts
docs.text: Artifact Minimum complete form Capacity Inputs, units, equation, result, sensitivity, design consequence Interface or data Concrete payload/schema/state transition plus errors and idempotency Failure Trigger, detection, user behavior, data impact, containment, recovery Operations SLI or alert, threshold/window, owner action, rollback or reconciliation Test Invariant or risk, setup, perturbation, expected observation, pass condition Decision Viable options, criteria, selected option, losing conditions, revisit trigger

docs.title: Complete Heading Example
docs.text:
The following outline satisfies the semantic contract without copying the canonical labels:

# Design a Regional Ticket Marketplace
## Interview map and product boundaries
## Requirements, SLOs, and safety properties
## Sizing sale-day demand
## Resources, state transitions, and public APIs
## System shape and purchase flow
## Seat ownership under contention
## Waiting-room admission and overload
## Payment uncertainty and reconciliation
## Partitioning, consistency, failures, and regions
## Security, abuse, observability, and verification
## Migration, cost, and operating model
## Decisions and final system
## Interview probes and L5/L6 bar
## Five-minute recap

"Resources, state transitions, and public APIs" covers both model and interface. "Security, abuse, observability, and verification" covers several responsibilities. The three domain headings are deep dives even though none says "deep dive."

docs.title: Author Review Checklist
docs.text:
• Can every requirement be traced through an API, state transition, component path, and failure outcome?
  • Are invariants visible before the mechanisms chosen to enforce them?
  • Do estimates use labeled inputs and produce design consequences?
  • Are deep dives specific to this scenario rather than reusable filler?
  • Is every asynchronous boundary explicit about ordering, retries, deduplication, and backpressure?
  • Are authority, projection, cache, and replay boundaries unambiguous?
  • Can operators detect, contain, recover, reconcile, and roll back each critical failure?
  • Are dated evidence labels used for claims that can age?
  • Do practical artifacts have enough detail to reproduce or challenge the decision?
  • Does the final summary preserve the core invariants, numbers, architecture, and tradeoffs?

docs.title: Automated Validation Boundary
docs.text: npm run validate:content recognizes semantic heading aliases for major contract areas. It catches missing coverage signals, not weak reasoning. Reviewers must still inspect depth, traceability, evidence quality, practical artifacts, and whether combined sections genuinely cover every responsibility.

docs.title: Source and Evidence Standard
docs.text: Sources make the boundary between durable reasoning, design input, measurement, and product behavior visible. Add evidence where it affects a decision; do not turn a chapter into a bibliography.

docs.title: Principle
docs.text:
A principle follows from stated system properties and remains useful across products.

Principle: A checkpoint over a contiguous source prefix advances only after every required record in that prefix has been durably published. A crash may cause replay, but this ordering does not skip a record in that prefix. Completing offset 102 before 101 is not permission to checkpoint 102.

Cite a source when the principle is borrowed, disputed, or depends on a formal result. Explain the derivation when it is not obvious.

docs.title: Assumption
docs.text:
An assumption is selected for the exercise and must be easy to replace in sensitivity analysis.

Assumption (2026-09): Peak checkout traffic is 10 times daily-average traffic, and one checkout creates six durable writes.

Give units, scope, and date when the scenario is time-bound. Say "illustrative" if the value does not describe a real deployment.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
A benchmark is a measurement, not a product guarantee.

Benchmark (2026-08-15): In the linked test, configuration X sustained N requests/s at p99 latency Y on hardware Z with dataset D and concurrency C. Method and results

Record workload, dataset, hardware or service class, software versions, concurrency, warm-up, duration, metric definition, result, source, and measurement date. Do not generalize beyond that envelope.

docs.title: Vendor
docs.text:
A vendor claim describes documented product behavior or a limit.

Vendor (Product 4.2, accessed 2026-09-06): The service documents a maximum item size of N bytes. Limit documentation

Name product, edition or service, relevant version or region, access date, exact behavior, and primary documentation. Treat defaults as configuration, not invariants. Prefer official versioned documentation over search snippets.

docs.title: Production Report
docs.text:
A production report is an attributed account from a real system. It is evidence of one context, not a universal recipe.

Production report (published 2025-11-03): Team A reports moving from design X to Y after workload condition Z; their stated outcome was M. Engineering report

Name the organization, publication date, workload context, original claim, outcome, and source. Preserve caveats and distinguish reported causation from correlation.

docs.title: Version-Sensitive Claims
docs.text:
Date any claim that can change without invalidating the underlying design:

  • product features, defaults, quotas, limits, prices, regions, and service availability;
  • API, language, database, protocol, or framework behavior tied to a version;
  • benchmarks, market or traffic statistics, hardware performance, and cost comparisons;
  • production architecture descriptions and statements using "currently," "now," or "as of."

Use YYYY-MM-DD for access, measurement, and publication dates. YYYY-MM is acceptable only when the source has no exact day. Include timezone for observations where a boundary matters. A version alone does not replace a date, and a date does not replace a version.

docs.title: Placement and Citation
docs.text:
Put the label and source next to the claim. Link to the primary source, stable report, paper, specification, or reproducible repository. Quote only language whose wording matters; otherwise paraphrase and retain the original meaning. If a source is inaccessible, say so and do not use it as sole support for a critical decision.

For repeated use, define a short source once and link back by descriptive name. Avoid bare numeric footnotes that force the reader to hunt for context. Never cite a vendor page as proof that one architecture is universally best.

docs.title: Claim Review Checklist
docs.text:
• Is this a principle, assumption, benchmark, vendor claim, or production report?
  • Would a reasonable reader mistake an illustrative value for measured reality?
  • Does a changing claim include both date and relevant version or environment?
  • Does a benchmark state workload, setup, metric, and limits of generalization?
  • Does a production report preserve organization, context, outcome, and caveats?
  • Is the primary source linked beside the claim?
  • Do calculations show units and derive from labeled inputs?
  • Are conflicting sources or uncertainty material to the decision disclosed?
  • Can the design argument survive if the source value changes?

docs.title: Complete Claim Block
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): A regional peak reaches 120,000 requests/s, with 2 KiB average payloads and 30% failover headroom.

Calculation: 120,000 * 2 KiB = 240,000 KiB/s, approximately 234 MiB/s before protocol and replication overhead. If 30% headroom means keeping 30% of provisioned capacity unused, payload capacity must be at least 234.375 / 0.70 = 334.82 MiB/s, not 234.375 * 1.30. Define the denominator: 30% extra load and 30% unused capacity are different assumptions. Serialization, TLS, retries, and replication add further work.

Vendor (Product 4.2, accessed 2026-09-06): Official documentation states the selected service class has limit L in region R. Primary documentation

Decision: Keep admission control below the measured safe envelope and load-test the actual payload and replication factor. The vendor limit is an outer bound, not expected throughput.

This block demonstrates the metadata shape: the inputs are labeled, units are visible, changing product behavior is versioned and dated, and the decision does not confuse a limit with a benchmark. Product 4.2, L, and the example.com links throughout this page are placeholders, not verified measurements or vendor evidence. Replace them with an actual checked primary source before using the template to support a design decision.

docs.title: Specialist System Design Electives
docs.text:
These electives begin where a strong generalist answer stops. Each chapter assumes that you can already define APIs, estimate load, partition state, use queues and caches, set SLOs, and explain retries, idempotency, observability, and multi-region tradeoffs.

The goal is not to memorize another architecture. It is to recognize domain-specific invariants, control planes, evidence, and economics that change the design.

docs.title: Choose an elective
docs.text: Elective Specialist question Generalist boundary Production AI Lifecycle Can a model change safely after launch? Generic deployment and A/B testing do not establish data lineage, evaluation validity, drift policy, or human-review safety. RAG and Agent Security Can untrusted context influence a privileged action? Ordinary API authorization does not contain prompt injection, provenance loss, tool escalation, or nondeterministic replay. GPU Inference Platforms How should scarce accelerators schedule token workloads? CPU autoscaling intuition misses prefill/decode asymmetry, KV-cache pressure, dynamic batching, and model residency. Local-First Systems and CRDTs How can replicas remain useful offline and converge later? Last-write-wins plus sync is insufficient for concurrent edits, tombstones, undo, permissions, and metadata growth. Edge and IoT Fleets How can a remote fleet change without violating local safety? Standard service deployment assumes reliable links, reversible hosts, and a reachable control plane. Devices often have none. Data Contracts and Governance What must remain compatible when data crosses teams? Schema registries alone do not protect semantics, lineage, quality SLOs, ownership, or downstream decision use. Regulated Evidence Systems Can the organization reproduce and defend a decision? Logging and backups do not provide traceability, evidence integrity, reproducibility, retention, or legal holds. Practical Formal Methods Which design claims can be checked over all small executions? Tests sample runs. Formal models expose safety and liveness failures across interleavings before code exists.

docs.title: How to use this track
docs.text:
1. State the general system design first.
  2. Name the specialist boundary that changes its correctness model.
  3. Write domain invariants before adding infrastructure.
  4. Quantify the scarce resource: labels, context tokens, GPU memory, offline log, bandwidth, data quality budget, evidence, or state space.
  5. Design rollout and rollback as part of the control plane.
  6. Close with the evidence that would justify launch and operation.
flowchart LR
    G[Generalist baseline] --> B[Find specialist boundary]
    B --> I[State domain invariants]
    I --> Q[Quantify scarce resource]
    Q --> C[Design control plane]
    C --> E[Define launch evidence]
    E --> O[Operate and evolve]

docs.title: Interview standard
docs.text:
A strong specialist answer does not replace ordinary distributed-systems reasoning. It layers domain-specific correctness over it. Staff-level candidates make hidden policies explicit, separate control and data planes, define measurable release gates, and explain how the organization can reverse or defend a decision months later.

Before opening a worked answer, record one failure trace and one resource bound for the chosen elective. Afterward, mark which claims are derived arithmetic, primary-source contracts, proposed mechanisms, or executed evidence. For example, Orca's iteration-level scheduling motivates a scheduling mechanism, but its published benchmark does not size a different model or GPU. This distinction is part of the elective assessment, not optional citation formatting (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Data Contracts and Governance
docs.text: A data contract is a versioned agreement between producers and consumers about structure, meaning, quality, ownership, and change. It turns an implicit cross-team dependency into reviewable system state. A schema is necessary but cannot say what "revenue," "active," or "event time" means.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can design a warehouse, event bus, schema registry, and ETL pipeline. Specialist depth begins with semantic compatibility, field-level lineage, quality SLOs, ownership and escalation, policy propagation, backfills, and coordinated change across unknown consumers. If one team owns both ends and can deploy atomically, a lighter interface specification may suffice.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design contract governance for a commerce organization with 400 producers, 3,000 datasets and streams, and analytical, operational, and ML consumers.

  • Every governed asset has an accountable owner, purpose, classification, and support channel.
  • A published version defines physical schema and business semantics.
  • Compatibility is checked against declared consumers and use, not syntax alone.
  • Event time, units, null meaning, identifiers, and update/delete behavior are explicit.
  • Quality is measured at the contract boundary with freshness and completeness SLOs.
  • Lineage connects source fields through transformations to material decisions.
  • Breaking changes use migration or versioning; a producer cannot redefine a field in place.
  • Access, retention, and deletion obligations follow derived data where policy requires.

docs.title: Architecture and state
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Producer CI] --> C[Contract registry]
    C --> K[Compatibility and policy checks]
    K --> D[Deploy gate]
    P --> R[Runtime boundary]
    R --> B[(Streams and tables)]
    B --> Q[Quality monitors]
    B --> L[Lineage collectors]
    C --> Q
    L --> G[(Governance graph)]
    Q --> S[SLO and incident service]
    U[Consumer declarations] --> C
    G --> I[Impact analysis]
    C --> I
Asset(id, owner, domain, purpose, classification, retention, lifecycle)
Contract(asset_id, version, schema, semantics, keys, time_model, change_policy)
Field(name, type, nullable, unit, definition, classification, constraints)
Consumer(asset_id, consumer_id, owner, fields, use, criticality, version_range)
QualitySLO(asset_id, dimension, target, window, measurement, response)
LineageEdge(input_field, output_field, transform_id, code_version, observed_at)
Change(id, old_version, new_version, compatibility, migration, approvals, status)

Keep authored lineage from transformation code separate from observed runtime lineage. Authored lineage explains intent; observed lineage catches ad hoc queries and actual use. Both can be incomplete, so display confidence and last observation rather than claiming omniscience. Where deletion rights apply, do not use lineage as the sole discovery mechanism: require policy tags, durable subject-to-record indexes or equivalent sink-native lookup, registered sink obligations, and deletion acknowledgements reconciled against the expected sink inventory.

Model a transformation run as an activity, its input/output snapshots as entities, and its responsible service/team as an agent, following the W3C PROV overview. For net_amount = gross_amount - discount_amount, retain edges from both fields and the transform version; a table-level edge cannot identify which consumers depend on discount semantics. PROV standardizes representation and interchange, not automatic completeness or policy enforcement (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Schema and semantic compatibility
docs.text:
Schema rules depend on encoding and reader/writer behavior. Adding an optional field may be backward compatible for Avro-like readers, yet break a CSV positional consumer or a strict deserializer. Removing an enum value may break a consumer even when no current row uses it. Test serialized fixtures against supported consumer versions.

Semantic compatibility asks harder questions:

Change Schema view Semantic risk cents to dollars, same numeric type compatible 100x monetary error UTC timestamp to local time string possibly accepted ordering and window corruption null changes from unknown to not applicable compatible wrong imputation or counts customer ID changes merge rules same string joins and deduplication change order event becomes latest-state upsert same fields replay and counting break

Define keys, grain, event-time source, time zone, currency or unit, null taxonomy, mutability, deduplication key, late-arrival policy, delete/tombstone behavior, and known exclusions. For a derived metric, include formula, eligible population, attribution window, and revision policy.

Compatibility policy should support compatible, conditionally compatible, and breaking. A condition may require that no declared consumer uses a field, or that all critical consumers have moved to version 2. Human review owns semantics; automation checks mechanical rules, fixtures, lineage impact, and migration evidence.

docs.title: Quality SLOs, lineage, and ownership
docs.text:
Quality dimensions need executable definitions. "Fresh" might mean p99 source-event age under 15 minutes at the curated table. "Complete" might mean received distinct order IDs divided by authoritative created orders, excluding declared cancellations. Specify measurement location, window, denominator, tolerance, and incident action.

Not every quality check pages. Use severity based on consumer criticality and error budget. A dashboard dataset may tolerate delayed freshness; a fraud feature might fail closed when freshness exceeds five minutes. Producers own correctness at the boundary, platform teams own the measuring mechanism, and consumers own use-specific validation.

Lineage enables impact analysis, but it does not transfer accountability automatically. Each asset has one accountable owning group even if many teams contribute. The registry should expose on-call route, expected response, deprecation date, and consumer acknowledgements. Orphaned assets cannot remain tier 1.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Suppose a stream emits 20,000 events/s and a completeness SLO allows 0.01% loss per day:

events/day = 20,000 * 86,400 = 1.728 billion
allowed missing events/day = 1.728 billion * 0.0001 = 172,800

That percentage sounds strict but permits many missing orders. For financially material data, add an absolute loss cap and amount-weighted invariant.

If freshness SLO is 99.9% of five-minute windows per 30 days, there are 8,640 windows. The continuous error-budget approximation is 8.64 windows or 43.2 minutes, but windows fail discretely: eight bad windows, or 40 minutes, still achieve about 99.907%; nine fall to about 99.896% and miss the target. Correlated pipeline failures consume the budget quickly; alert on burn rate rather than every late row.

For 3,000 assets with 50 fields each, naive all-pairs field impact is not useful. If observed lineage averages 8 outgoing edges per field, the graph has about 1.2 million edges. Precompute bounded downstream closures for critical assets, but cap traversal by domain, depth, and freshness to keep change review interpretable.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure Control producer bypasses registry runtime schema identity and quarantine lane compatible schema changes meaning semantic review, fixtures, consumer declaration quality monitor depends on broken source independent control totals and monitor health lineage goes stale code and runtime collectors with freshness indicator backfill floods consumers separate versioned path, rate plan, replay declaration PII copied into derived table field classification propagation and sink policy owner leaves team ownership tied to group, periodic attestation deletion misses derivative expected sink inventory, policy tags, subject lookup, sink acknowledgement, and reconciliation; lineage aids discovery but is not proof of completeness

Monitor unknown schema IDs, contract-check bypasses, undeclared consumers, quality SLO burn, monitor coverage, lineage freshness and cycles, owner attestation, deprecation age, policy violations, quarantined volume, and migration progress. Preserve representative rejected records in access-controlled storage, not unrestricted logs.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Inventory critical assets and consumers first. Add owners, schemas, semantics, and a visible quality baseline without blocking releases. Introduce warnings for incompatible changes, then gates for tier-1 assets after false positives are reduced. Require consumer declarations and migration plans before enforcing deprecation.

For a breaking change, publish version 2 alongside version 1, dual-produce or derive it, provide test fixtures, compare control totals, and migrate declared consumers. Observe unknown use through query and job telemetry. Stop version 1 writes only after acknowledgements and a defined quiet period; retain or delete old data by policy. Version the contract format itself and support old agents during rollout.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
The orders event feeds fulfillment, finance, growth analytics, and fraud models. The producer wants to redefine order_total from pre-discount cents to post-discount decimal currency and remove cancelled orders. Design the change process and platform controls.

Clarify event grain, authoritative ledger, currencies, consumer criticality, late cancellations, replay behavior, retention, unknown consumers, and whether finance needs immutable facts or current state.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Reject an in-place change because type compatibility hides changes to units, discount treatment, and the included order population. Publish orders.v2 with explicit gross_amount_minor, discount_amount_minor, net_amount_minor, currency, and order_state. Keep immutable order-created facts and represent cancellation as a versioned event or tombstone according to each stream contract; do not silently omit history.

Register fulfillment, finance, analytics, and fraud uses with field-level dependencies. Provide golden serialized fixtures and a historical backfill with a source cutoff and code version. Dual-publish from the transactional outbox, reconcile counts and amount totals against the ledger, and measure freshness and completeness separately. Finance receives an amount-weighted zero-unexplained-difference invariant; analytics receives documented revision behavior.

Lineage impact creates migration tasks and owners. Consumers validate v2 in shadow, then acknowledge cutover. Unknown consumers are detected from broker and query telemetry and contacted or accepted as risk by an accountable owner. Deprecation ends v1 only after critical acknowledgements, a quiet window, and rollback retention. The registry retains both definitions according to its record schedule, with sensitive examples and payloads excluded or separately governed.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Separates physical compatibility from semantic compatibility.
  • Defines grain, units, time, nulls, keys, and mutation behavior.
  • Gives quality SLOs exact denominators and operational responses.
  • Treats lineage as evidence with confidence, not perfect truth.
  • Names producer, platform, consumer, and accountable-owner duties.
  • Designs backfill, dual publication, impact analysis, and deprecation.
  • Connects classification and deletion to derived data.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Apache Avro Specification, Schema Resolution
  • Protocol Buffers, Updating a Message Type
  • OpenLineage Specification
  • W3C PROV-O
  • ISO/IEC 25012:2008, Data Quality Model

docs.title: Edge and IoT Fleets
docs.text: An edge fleet is a distributed system whose nodes may be physically exposed, intermittently connected, power constrained, heterogeneous, and responsible for real-world safety. The cloud expresses intent; each device must decide whether, when, and how that intent can be applied locally.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can design device registration, telemetry ingestion, queues, and a deployment API. Specialist depth begins with hardware roots of trust, signed desired state, unreliable links, constrained flash and power, staged firmware, anti-rollback, local control loops, and physical failure. If a gateway can safely abstract simple sensors, avoid putting cloud-style orchestration on every endpoint.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design a platform for 2 million refrigerated-display controllers in stores. Devices report temperature, run local safety rules, and receive configuration and firmware. Some are offline for a week.

  • Loss of cloud connectivity never disables the local safety loop.
  • A device applies only authentic, authorized, compatible, non-rollback desired state.
  • Reported state is distinct from desired state and includes the applied generation.
  • Firmware update is power-loss safe and has a verified recovery path.
  • Commands are idempotent or carry explicit one-shot semantics and expiry.
  • Telemetry buffering is bounded; safety events outlive routine samples.
  • Fleet rollout stops automatically when health exceeds a defined risk threshold.
  • Device identity can be rotated or revoked without trusting mutable application storage alone.

docs.title: Architecture and state
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    O[Operator] --> C[Fleet control plane]
    C --> S[Signer and transparency log]
    S --> M[Independent log monitors]
    S --> B[Regional brokers and artifact CDN]
    B <--> G[Store gateway]
    G <--> D[Device agent]
    D --> V[Signature and compatibility gate]
    V --> A[A/B updater]
    D --> L[Local safety controller]
    D --> Q[(Priority telemetry spool)]
    Q --> G
    G --> T[Telemetry ingestion]
    T --> C
    subgraph DeviceLane[Device execution and safety]
      D
      V
      A
      L
      Q
    end
    subgraph FleetLane[Fleet control]
      O
      C
      S
      M
    end
Device(id, hardware_rev, trust_key, cohort, status, last_seen)
Desired(device_or_group, generation, config_digest, firmware_digest, constraints, expiry)
Reported(device_id, boot_id, desired_generation, software_slot, health, safety_state)
Artifact(digest, size, compatibility, signature, minimum_security_version)
Rollout(id, artifact_digest, cohorts, gates, state, pause_reason)
Telemetry(device_id, boot_id, seq, class, event_time, payload)

Desired state is declarative: "run artifact digest X with config generation Y," not a brittle sequence of shell commands. The device reconciler validates signature, target hardware, dependencies, expiry, minimum security version, disk, battery or line power, and local safety conditions before applying. It reports outcome separately.

docs.title: Signed desired state and device trust
docs.text:
Provision each device with a unique identity anchored in a secure element or protected boot key where hardware permits. Authenticate mutually, rotate operational certificates, and keep signing keys offline or in tightly controlled hardware-backed services. Separate artifact signing from fleet authorization so compromise of a deployment account cannot mint arbitrary firmware.

The signed manifest includes artifact digest, target hardware and bootloader range, configuration schema, minimum security counter, rollout channel, creation and expiry, and key ID. Secure boot verifies the chain from immutable root through bootloader and application. Anti-rollback counters prevent installation below an administratively advanced security floor. Do not irreversibly advance that floor before a trial image passes boot and application health checks. If policy forbids returning to the old image immediately, the recovery slot must already meet the new floor; emergency recovery uses an authorized higher-or-equal transition rather than clearing the counter.

A transparency log is useful only with an enforcement contract. The signer submits each authorized manifest, devices or gateways require a fresh inclusion proof under a signed tree head, and separately administered monitors verify append-only consistency and alert on equivocation or an excessive merge delay. If constrained devices cannot verify proofs, state that the log is an operator audit control rather than claiming it prevents targeted releases.

One-time commands are difficult across reconnects. Give each command an ID, target generation, expiry, precondition, and acknowledgement state. A command such as "unlock" should usually remain a locally authorized action with a short lease, not a durable desired state that might execute days later. Enforcing expiry requires a trusted time bound: after clock loss, reject remote actuation until time is re-established while keeping local safety control operational. Persist command identity across restart, but do not assume this makes the physical effect atomic with the acknowledgement. If power fails between actuation and recording completion, reconcile observed hardware state or require local intervention before retrying.

docs.title: Intermittent links and local safety
docs.text:
Use store-and-forward with independent lanes: critical alarms, security events, control acknowledgements, and routine telemetry. Reserve space for high-priority records. Sequence by (device_id, boot_id, seq) and accept duplicates. Event time and receive time are separate because device clocks drift. Gateways batch, compress, and acknowledge durable receipt.

The local controller uses sensor input and locally stored limits to keep temperature safe. Cloud optimization can suggest set points, but a validated envelope clamps them. A watchdog and fail-safe hardware state protect against application deadlock. Define behavior for sensor disagreement, clock loss, storage-full, repeated reboot, and stale desired state. The cloud cannot be in a millisecond control loop over an intermittent network.

docs.title: Calculations and staged firmware
docs.text:
Use A/B partitions or a recovery image. Download to the inactive slot, verify digest, signature, transparency proof where enforced, and security version, then install and trial-boot it. Run boot and application health checks before marking the slot good and committing any irreversible security-counter increase. If the boot-success deadline expires, the bootloader returns to a previous slot that still satisfies the current security floor. Database migrations must remain backward compatible across rollback or use dual-format storage.

At 2 million devices, a 180 MB image is:

2,000,000 * 180 MB = 360 TB of payload

With 20% protocol, retry, and CDN overhead, budget about 432 TB. A 1% global canary is still 20,000 devices, too large for the first exposure. Start with lab and employee fleets, then perhaps 50 representative devices, 500, 5,000, 1%, 10%, and broader cohorts.

If a store link provides 10 Mbit/s for 200 devices, simultaneous full downloads would offer only 50 Kbit/s/device and take roughly eight hours before overhead. A gateway should download each hardware artifact once, verify it, and serve peers locally with rate limits and randomized device schedules.

For telemetry, 2 million devices sending 300-byte samples each minute produce about 33,333 messages/s and 10 MB/s raw:

messages/s = 2,000,000 / 60 = 33,333
raw bytes/s = 2,000,000 * 300 / 60 = 10,000,000 bytes/s
seven-day backlog = 10,000,000 * 604,800 = 6.048 TB

A synchronized reconnect could therefore release about 6.05 TB if every sample is retained. Devices should downsample routine history, preserve min/max/average and alarms, and add randomized catch-up limits to avoid a reconnect storm.

Per-device raw seven-day storage is 300 * 10,080 = 3.024 MB, before envelope, flash alignment, and wear overhead. If fleet catch-up capacity is 30 MB/s while live input remains 10 MB/s, net drain is 20 MB/s and 6.048 TB takes 302,400 seconds, or 3.5 days. Reserve alarm/control lanes throughout recovery; a spool that fits does not imply a short recovery time. NIST SP 800-193 distinguishes protection, detection, and secure recovery; these numbers are a designed fleet budget, not a hardware certification (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure or attack Control corrupted or partial download content digest, resumable chunks, inactive slot signing-key compromise key hierarchy, revocation, threshold process, verified log inclusion and independent consistency monitoring power loss during update atomic boot metadata and A/B rollback bad release passes lab representative cohorts, sequential gates, automatic pause broker outage local operation, bounded spool, backoff and jitter cloned identity hardware-bound key, attestation where justified, anomaly detection device capture least privilege, no fleet-wide secret, encrypted sensitive storage telemetry replay boot ID, monotonic sequence, server dedupe, freshness policy unsafe cloud config signed schema, local envelope and invariant checks

Monitor fleet last-seen distribution, desired-to-reported convergence, update download/install/boot success by hardware and cohort, rollback rate, crash loops, safety-envelope activations, sensor faults, spool occupancy and drops by priority, certificate expiry, signature failures, gateway saturation, and reconnect backlog. Never report only the success percentage; missing devices are a separate denominator.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Inventory hardware, bootloader, storage, and connectivity before adding remote update. Establish unique identity and signed manifests. Add reported generation and read-only telemetry. Introduce configuration rollout with no safety impact, then A/B firmware in a lab, destructive power-loss tests, and small diverse cohorts.

Advance cohorts on minimum sample size and observation time, not a fixed clock alone. Hold long enough to include reboot and duty cycles. Pause automatically on rollback, safety, crash, battery, or connectivity regression. Keep old server protocols through the maximum offline interval and version desired-state schemas. Decommissioning revokes identity, wipes secrets when reachable, records final state, and does not assume an offline device received the command.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design firmware and configuration management for 500,000 smart electrical breakers. Devices may be offline, and an incorrect action can disconnect critical equipment. A security patch must reach 95% of reachable devices in 72 hours.

Clarify the safety authority, hardware root, local manual override, definition of reachable, connectivity distribution, breaker command semantics, firmware size, power-loss behavior, rollback limits, regulatory evidence, and incident kill switches.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Keep trip protection and manual control in an independently validated local path. The cloud publishes signed declarative manifests; the device verifies hardware compatibility, signature chain, required transparency inclusion proof, security counter, expiry, power, and local safe state. Independent monitors verify log consistency and merge delay. Breaker actuation is not modeled as durable desired state: it requires a short-lived, scoped, dual-authorized command and local preconditions.

Firmware uses an inactive slot and recovery bootloader. A new image trial-boots and passes health checks before the device commits an irreversible security-counter increase; every fallback slot must satisfy the committed floor. Rollout progresses through lab, employee, hardware-revision cohorts, then regional percentages. Gates use boot success, rollback, trip anomalies, watchdog resets, and at least one duty cycle. Store gateways cache content once and stagger devices. Offline devices keep operating and install only when they reconnect before manifest expiry; the 95% objective is measured against devices observed reachable in the window.

Every reported state names the applied generation, slot, boot ID, and health. Critical events occupy a reserved spool. A compromised deployment account cannot sign firmware; signing and rollout authorization are separate. The emergency response can pause manifests, revoke a signing chain, and ship a higher security-counter recovery release without allowing arbitrary downgrade.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Keeps safety local and independent from cloud availability.
  • Separates signed artifacts, deployment authorization, desired state, and reported state.
  • Designs power-loss-safe update and rollback-compatible local data.
  • Uses representative cohorts and denominator-aware rollout gates.
  • Quantifies image distribution and reconnect storms.
  • Distinguishes durable configuration from expiring physical commands.
  • States the limits of remote revocation and decommissioning.

docs.title: Practical Formal Methods
docs.text: Formal methods describe systems with mathematical precision and check whether stated properties hold. In system design, their highest leverage often comes before production code: model the small protocol that carries the largest correctness risk, explore all bounded interleavings, and turn counterexamples into design changes and tests.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can reason about consistency, write state machines, run tests, and inject failures. Specialist depth begins with explicit transition systems, safety and liveness properties, fairness assumptions, refinement boundaries, model checking, and proof obligations. Formal methods do not replace load tests, observability, code review, or security analysis. They are most valuable where rare interleavings have severe consequences and the core protocol is small enough to model.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design and validate a lease-based leader that issues fencing tokens to storage writers.

  • At most one unexpired authority is recognized for a resource under the model's clock assumptions.
  • Fencing tokens accepted by storage increase monotonically.
  • A writer with an old token can never overwrite state written under a newer token.
  • If failures stop, a quorum is available, and scheduling is fair, some contender eventually obtains authority.
  • Message loss, duplication, delay, process crash, and retry are modeled explicitly.
  • The specification states what clocks can do and whether leases depend on bounded drift.
  • Model results, tool version, parameters, and checked properties are reproducible.
  • Tests connect implementation behavior to modeled actions and invariants.

docs.title: Architecture, state, and specification workflow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R[Risk and requirement] --> S[Small state-machine spec]
    S --> P[Safety and liveness properties]
    P --> M[Model checker]
    M --> X[Counterexample trace]
    X --> D[Protocol correction]
    D --> S
    M --> T[Trace and model-based tests]
    T --> I[Implementation]
    I --> O[Runtime monitors]

Separate the modeled protocol from infrastructure detail. A useful model might contain three clients, three lease replicas, one storage object, bounded token values, and nondeterministic messages. It need not model TCP packets, JSON, or threads unless those details affect the property.

VARIABLES
  leaseOwner, leaseExpiry, nextToken,
  clientToken, storageToken, storageValue,
  now, messages, alive

ACTIONS
  RequestLease(c), GrantLease(c), Renew(c), Expire,
  SendWrite(c), DeliverWrite(m), Crash(c), Recover(c), Tick

The state is all variables. Init defines legal initial states. Next is the disjunction of legal actions. The behavior formula is conceptually Init AND always [Next]_vars, plus explicit fairness when checking progress.

docs.title: Safety, liveness, and assumptions
docs.text:
Safety says that nothing bad happens and is violated by a finite trace. Examples: no double spend, no stale fenced write, no two committed values for one consensus slot. Liveness says something good eventually happens. Examples: a queued job eventually runs or a request eventually receives a terminal result.

Illustrative TLA+/PlusCal-style pseudomodel, not an executable or verified specification:

--algorithm FencedLease
variables nextToken = 0,
          granted = [c \in Clients |-> 0],
          storageToken = 0;

process Client \in Clients
variables mine = 0;
begin
Acquire:
  await CanObtainLease(self);
  nextToken := nextToken + 1;
  mine := nextToken;
  granted[self] := mine;
Write:
  if mine >= storageToken then
    storageToken := mine;
  end if;
  goto Acquire;
end process;
end algorithm

This sketch is intentionally incomplete: nextToken := nextToken + 1 must be atomic or implemented by consensus/transactional storage, lease expiry is absent, and >= may allow duplicate-token writes. The model should refine these ambiguities rather than hide them behind a box named "lock service." No property in this sketch has been checked or proved.

Candidate safety properties:

TypeOK == variables remain in declared domains
MonotonicFence == storageToken never decreases
NoStaleWrite == accepted write token >= token already stored
UniqueToken == distinct successful grants have distinct tokens

Liveness requires assumptions. An asynchronous network can delay a message forever; no algorithm can guarantee progress without some delivery or timing condition. Write assumptions such as weak fairness for enabled delivery actions, eventual quorum availability, and bounded clock drift. Never smuggle these into prose after the checker reports a failure.

Weak fairness requires progress for an action that remains continuously enabled; strong fairness addresses an action enabled infinitely often but repeatedly disabled. Neither means every queued message is delivered if the fairness condition is only on "deliver some message." Name the per-request action or an explicit network progress assumption. For grant renewal, include a trace where competitors keep disabling a contender and ask which fairness property the claimed liveness needs. Specifying Systems separates Liveness and Fairness (chapter 8), Real Time (9), and the TLC checker (14); the sketch here remains illustrative, not a checked spec.

To claim demonstrated behavior, publish an executable specification and checker configuration with tool version, constants and bounds, invariants, temporal properties, fairness assumptions, state constraints, symmetry settings, exit status, explored and distinct states, and any counterexample traces. Until those artifacts exist and run successfully, describe the protocol and properties as designed or illustrated, not validated.

docs.title: Calculations and state-space reduction
docs.text:
Suppose a simplified model has 3 clients, 4 local states each, 3 nodes that are up/down, 5 possible lease owners including none/expired, 6 token values, and 8 abstract network states:

rough product = 4^3 * 2^3 * 5 * 6 * 8
              = 122,880 states

Adding one client multiplies the local-state factor by 4 before changes to owner choices and new message combinations. A queue of exactly 6 messages chosen from 10 kinds has 10^6 ordered possibilities; allowing lengths 0 through 6 yields sum(10^k, k=0..6) = 1,111,111. These are raw product estimates, not counts of reachable states. State explosion is the central operational constraint.

Reduce safely by using small finite constants, symmetry among identical clients, sets instead of irrelevant queue order, abstract values, bounded histories, and decomposition. Do not remove the distinction that causes the bug. For example, collapsing every message into "request" erases stale grant and retry behavior.

Check the smallest configuration capable of the failure. Two clients may expose mutual exclusion; three replicas expose quorum overlap; wraparound needs a deliberately tiny token domain. Choose bounds from the topology and bug class being examined, then increase them to probe additional behaviors and publish resource limits. A plateau in state or action coverage is not evidence that larger configurations are correct. Record states generated, distinct states, depth, seed, workers, and model parameters.

docs.title: Model-based testing and refinement
docs.text:
A specification can generate action sequences and expected abstract states. An adapter maps actions such as CrashLeader, Acquire, and Write(token) to a real test cluster. After each step, observe and map implementation state back to the model. This finds mismatches in retry, timeout, and recovery code that unit tests rarely compose.

Three useful connections are:

  1. Turn each model-checker counterexample into a deterministic regression trace.
  2. Generate randomized valid command sequences from the model and compare an implementation to a reference state machine.
  3. Export runtime assertions for cheap safety properties, such as monotonically increasing accepted fence tokens.

Refinement asks whether lower-level behavior implements the abstract spec after hiding internal steps. Full refinement proofs are expensive, but a practical project can maintain a mapping table from modeled actions and state to code APIs, durable fields, and tests. Review the mapping whenever implementation semantics change.

docs.title: Where formal methods pay
docs.text:
High-value targets include consensus and membership changes, distributed locks and fencing, payment or inventory state machines, exactly-once claims, idempotency protocols, failover ownership, access-control policy, cryptographic protocols, database isolation algorithms, and safety interlocks.

Lower-value targets include conventional stateless CRUD, presentation logic, rapidly changing product flows with low consequence, performance tuning without a correctness model, and systems whose dominant risk is an unknown requirement rather than concurrency. Use a decision test: severe failure, subtle concurrency, compact state, stable invariant, and repeated implementation. The more boxes it checks, the better the return.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure in formal work Control spec proves the wrong requirement review invariants with domain owners and concrete examples environment assumption is false list and monitor timing, quorum, and failure assumptions model omits retry or crash state threat/failure inventory and counterexample review bounded check creates false confidence publish bounds and complement with proof or testing liveness check hangs inspect fairness and unbounded state; separate safety runs implementation drifts from model action-to-code mapping and model-based conformance tests secrets enter traces synthetic identifiers and controlled artifact retention toolchain becomes tribal knowledge pinned version, one-command CI, reviewed documentation

Operate the specification like code. Version it beside the protocol, run fast bounded checks on each change and deeper checks on schedule, retain counterexample traces, review warnings, and assign ownership. Metrics include check duration, explored and distinct states, depth, coverage of actions, invariant count, liveness configurations, counterexamples by cause, flaky nondeterminism in test adapters, and implementation changes without spec review.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Start with one costly incident or unresolved design argument. Write five to ten state variables, actions, and one safety invariant. Model normal behavior first, then duplicate, delay, crash, and recovery. Keep the first configuration small enough to check in seconds. Socialize counterexample traces as ordinary engineering artifacts.

Add CI after the model has found or ruled out useful bugs. Convert traces to implementation tests and add a spec-to-code map. Before protocol evolution, update the abstract state and properties, check mixed-version actions, then roll code through a canary. Preserve old-format states in the model until the production migration can no longer encounter them.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design a multi-region payment idempotency service. A client retries the same key across regions after timeouts. The service must never execute two charges but should recover when a reservation owner crashes.

Clarify charge reversibility, idempotency scope and expiry, regional consistency, external processor behavior, owner lease assumptions, terminal-state durability, and what "eventually" requires from the network and processor.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Model each key as ABSENT, RESERVED(owner, epoch), SUCCEEDED(result), or FAILED(final_reason). Acquisition is a conditional durable transition that issues a monotonically increasing epoch. A worker calls the processor with a derived stable processor idempotency key. Completion is accepted only from the current epoch, but a late processor success cannot be discarded: reconciliation queries by the stable key before a new owner attempts execution.

Safety properties state that a key has at most one successful processor identity, terminal success never changes, and an older epoch cannot commit over a newer one. Actions include cross-region retry, duplicate request, delayed processor response, owner crash, reservation expiry, failover, reconcile, and completion. Liveness is conditional on eventual home-region or quorum availability, fair scheduling, and a processor that eventually returns or supports lookup.

Build and run an executable small model with two regions, two workers, bounded epochs, duplicate messages, and nondeterministic timeouts. Before checker artifacts exist, the following is an illustrative failure trace rather than a verified counterexample: worker A charges, its response is lost, the lease expires, and worker B charges again. The correction is not a longer lease; it is stable downstream idempotency plus reconciliation before re-execution. Once the checker produces that trace, retain its configuration and output, convert the trace into a fault-injection test, and assert accepted epochs monotonically at runtime.

Add provider receipt expiry and delayed lookup visibility to that model. Otherwise the provider may be modeled as an eternal deduplicator when the real contract is weaker. Vendor (accessed 2026-09-08): Stripe's idempotency contract permits key pruning after at least 24 hours and creates a new request on reuse after pruning. Safety after that horizon may require retaining the unknown state and manual reconciliation rather than re-execution; liveness must not silently assume that every unresolved charge can be retried safely.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Writes state and transitions before naming a formal tool.
  • Separates safety from liveness and names fairness assumptions.
  • Models retries, crashes, stale messages, and recovery paths.
  • Understands bounded checking and state explosion without claiming proof.
  • Turns counterexamples into protocol changes and implementation tests.
  • Maintains an explicit abstraction/refinement boundary.
  • Chooses formal methods where consequence and concurrency justify cost.
