docs.title: GPU Inference Platforms
docs.text: An inference platform turns accelerator memory and compute into latency-bounded tokens. The workload is unusual: prompt processing and token generation stress different resources, each active sequence retains a growing KV cache, and batching improves throughput while adding queue delay.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can build an API gateway, autoscaler, queue, and service mesh. Specialist depth begins with model placement, tensor or pipeline parallelism, prefill/decode scheduling, KV-cache accounting, continuous batching, admission based on token work, and fairness across requests with very different lengths. For low-rate or small models, a managed endpoint or CPU may be simpler.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design a multi-tenant platform for chat and batch summarization. Interactive requests target 500 ms time to first token (TTFT) p95 and 60 ms inter-token latency p95. Batch jobs target completion within one hour.

  • Admit against bounded prompt tokens, output tokens, KV memory, and deadline, not request count alone.
  • No tenant can monopolize all model replicas with long contexts or outputs.
  • A replica loads only verified model and tokenizer artifacts with compatible runtime versions.
  • Cancellation releases scheduler state and KV blocks promptly.
  • Streaming retries never silently duplicate user-visible prefixes or side effects.
  • Batch traffic yields capacity before interactive SLOs fail.
  • Cost, latency, and quality are reported by model and serving configuration.

docs.title: Architecture and state
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Clients] --> G[Auth and token limits]
    G --> A[Admission controller]
    A --> Q[Deadline and fair queues]
    Q --> R[Model router]
    R --> P[Prefill workers]
    P --> K[(KV block pool)]
    K --> D[Decode scheduler]
    D --> S[Streaming gateway]
    S --> C
    M[Placement controller] --> P
    M --> D
    M --> W[(Model registry)]
    O[Telemetry and cost] --> A
    P --> O
    D --> O

Some runtimes colocate prefill and decode; disaggregation is useful only when KV transfer cost and operational complexity are justified. A disaggregated design must specify KV format compatibility, ownership, transfer admission and backpressure, timeout behavior, and whether a failed transfer is retried, recomputed, or abandoned. The control plane tracks accelerator type, memory, topology, runtime, model shards, health, fabric capacity, and warm capacity. The data plane schedules token and KV-transfer work.

ModelRevision(id, weights_digest, tokenizer_digest, dtype, parallelism, max_context)
Replica(id, model_revision, gpu_set, runtime_version, state, loaded_bytes)
Request(id, tenant, class, prompt_tokens, max_new_tokens, deadline, state)
Sequence(id, request_id, generated_tokens, kv_blocks, worker, last_progress)
Quota(tenant, prompt_rate, output_rate, concurrent_kv_bytes, priority)

docs.title: Prefill, decode, batching, and KV cache
docs.text:
Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel and often uses large matrix operations with high compute utilization. Decode generates one token per active sequence per iteration and repeatedly reads model weights plus KV state, so it is commonly memory-bandwidth sensitive. A 20,000-token prompt and a 100-token answer is prefill-heavy; a short prompt with a 4,000-token answer holds cache and decode slots for much longer.

Static batching waits for equal-shaped work and wastes capacity when sequences finish at different times. Continuous batching inserts new sequences and removes completed ones between decode iterations. Larger batches amortize weight reads, but excessive batching raises time between tokens. A single batch-token count is insufficient: the scheduler separately bounds prefill tokens, active decode sequences, context-dependent KV bytes, and a benchmark-derived per-iteration work estimate.

Paged KV allocation uses fixed-size blocks so sequences can grow without reserving their maximum context contiguously. It reduces fragmentation and enables prefix sharing, but block tables, copy-on-write, eviction, and cache-aware routing become correctness concerns. Never share prefix cache entries across security domains unless the key includes all relevant model, adapter, tokenizer, prompt, and tenant isolation dimensions.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
For a transformer with 32 layers, hidden size 4,096, key and value tensors, and 2-byte elements, approximate KV bytes per token are:

2 * layers * hidden_size * bytes
= 2 * 32 * 4,096 * 2
= 524,288 bytes, or 512 KiB per token

This simplified formula assumes full multi-head KV. Grouped-query or multi-query attention stores fewer KV heads and can reduce the result. At 8,000 cached tokens, one sequence would use about 4 GiB under the simple assumption. On an 80 GiB GPU with 60 GiB available after weights and runtime, only about 120,000 such KV tokens fit, before fragmentation and safety headroom.

The general form is 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dimension * bytes_per_element per token. With 8 KV heads and head dimension 128, the same 32-layer, 2-byte model needs 128 KiB/token, one quarter of the full-MHA example. At block size 16, reserve ceil(sequence_tokens / 16) * 16 * bytes_per_token; actual residency also depends on tensor-parallel sharding or replication. PagedAttention addresses fragmentation and sharing, while Orca schedules at iteration granularity; neither establishes a universal GPU throughput number (primary abstracts accessed 2026-09-08).

Disaggregation must also budget moving that cache. Transferring 4 GiB over a measured 25 GiB/s effective path takes at least about 160 ms before queueing, serialization, and synchronization. Prefix reuse, GQA, and faster fabrics can lower this, but a transfer near that size already consumes a material part of a 500 ms TTFT target. Capacity tests must measure concurrent transfer throughput rather than quote link line rate.

If a replica sustains 4,800 decode tokens/s and average output is 240 tokens, the throughput ceiling is roughly 20 completed requests/s, but only if prefill, queueing, and length skew do not dominate. At 60% target utilization, plan for 12 requests/s. A peak of 1,200 requests/s needs about 100 replicas at that conservative capacity.

Cost per million output tokens for a $4/hour replica producing 4,800 tokens/s at 60% useful utilization is:

useful tokens/hour = 4,800 * 3,600 * 0.60 = 10.37 million
cost per million output tokens = 4 / 10.37 = $0.386

Include prompt work, idle warm capacity, failed requests, networking, control plane, and reserved-capacity terms. Compare configurations at the same quality and SLO, not raw token rate.

docs.title: Admission, fairness, and cost control
docs.text:
Estimate service demand from prompt length, requested output cap, current context, model revision, and class. Reject unsupported context before queueing. Reserve KV headroom and use earliest-deadline-first within weighted tenant queues, with aging to prevent starvation. Charge prompt and generated tokens separately. A request that reaches its output or spend cap terminates with an explicit reason. For disaggregated workers, admission reserves transfer bytes and fabric time as well as accelerator work.

Use chunked prefill to prevent one giant prompt from blocking decode progress. Batch jobs enter a preemptible queue and checkpoint source progress outside GPU memory. When interactive load rises, stop admitting new batch sequences, then drain or preempt at safe boundaries. Avoid GPU memory oversubscription that converts predictable rejection into process-wide out-of-memory failure.

Route to a warm compatible replica. Cache affinity may reduce prefill, but it must not defeat load balancing or tenant isolation. Cold loading a 140 GB sharded model over 20 GB/s effective storage bandwidth takes at least seven seconds before initialization, so reactive autoscaling alone cannot satisfy a subsecond spike.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure Control GPU out of memory reservation-based admission, block watermarks, bounded context stalled collective watchdog, fail replica group, topology-aware replacement KV transfer stalls or arrives after ownership changes transfer deadline, generation-bound ownership, backpressure, recompute-or-fail policy one GPU in a tensor-parallel set fails fail the whole replica and requeue only safe requests streaming disconnect cancel or retain briefly by policy; resume with sequence token if supported tokenizer mismatch artifact compatibility digest and golden-token tests noisy tenant weighted quotas for tokens, KV bytes, and concurrency malicious long prompt authenticated limits, pre-tokenization cap, budget admission model artifact tampering signed registry, digest verification, restricted loader prefix-cache leak security-domain cache keys or disabled sharing

Monitor TTFT, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency, queue age by class, prompt and output token rates, prefill/decode utilization, active sequences, KV occupancy and fragmentation, KV transfer bytes, queueing, bandwidth and failures, batch size, cancellations, admission rejection, output truncation, GPU memory and power, collective errors, cold-load time, and cost per successful million tokens. Autoscaling should react to admitted workload and queue delay while respecting model load and KV-transfer capacity.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Benchmark each tuple of model, quantization, accelerator, runtime, parallelism, and scheduler settings. Validate output quality and numerical stability, then replay representative length distributions. Shadow only if duplicate computation is affordable. Canary by stable request class, compare latency distributions and output-quality gates, and retain old warm replicas for rollback.

Drain a replica by refusing new sequences and allowing bounded completion; terminate leftovers at a declared deadline. Roll out control-plane and runtime changes separately. Evolve from dedicated model pools to shared pools only after quota, accounting, and failure isolation are proven. Quantization or speculative decoding is a model-quality release, not just an infrastructure optimization.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design inference for a 70-billion-parameter coding model. Peak traffic is 600 interactive requests/s with 3,000-token average prompts and 500-token outputs. A nightly batch workload can consume unused capacity. Product needs streaming and enterprise tenant isolation.

Clarify quality-preserving precisions, accelerator memory and topology, prompt/output percentiles, TTFT and inter-token SLOs, allowed truncation, regional demand, prefix reuse, tenant quotas, cost target, and provider capacity.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Create signed model revisions that pin tokenizer, quantization, runtime, and parallelism. Use topology-aware multi-GPU replicas and maintain a measured warm pool because load time exceeds the TTFT target. The gateway tokenizes within limits, authenticates tenant quotas, and sends estimated prefill, decode, KV, and deadline demand to admission.

Use weighted per-tenant interactive queues, chunked prefill, and continuous decode batching under separate prefill-token, decode-sequence, context/KV, and measured iteration-work budgets. Allocate paged KV blocks with hard high-water rejection rather than risking OOM. If prefill and decode are disaggregated, reserve measured fabric capacity and bind each transfer to a sequence ownership generation. Enterprise security domains do not share prefix cache entries. Batch requests use a preemptible pool and yield as queue-age burn approaches the interactive SLO.

Capacity comes from benchmarked prompt and decode curves, not parameter count alone. Provision for p95 length mix and one replica-group failure per zone. Stream sequence IDs and explicit completion reasons; cancellation frees KV. Canary runtime changes on stable tenant hashes, compare quality, TTFT, inter-token latency, OOM, and cost, then drain old replicas. A write-capable coding agent would require a separate security design; this platform only serves model tokens.

For the case, offered work is 600 * 3,000 = 1.8M prompt tokens/s and 600 * 500 = 300K output tokens/s. A hypothetical 4,800-output-token/s replica at 60% useful utilization implies ceil(300,000 / 2,880) = 105 replicas on the decode constraint alone. Do not transplant that small-model benchmark to a 70B model: separately measure its prefill, KV, collective, and latency limits. Test the full tail up to enforced context/output caps, not merely p95 lengths.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Distinguishes prefill, decode, TTFT, and inter-token latency.
  • Capacity-plans KV bytes and token work rather than request count.
  • Explains continuous batching and its latency tradeoff.
  • Uses reservation admission and fair queues before autoscaling.
  • Includes topology, cold-load time, and whole-replica failure.
  • Treats quantization and runtime changes as quality-bearing releases.
  • Reports cost at a fixed SLO and output quality.

For the full product path around this runtime - workload contracts, gateways, evaluation, observability, reliability, and platform governance - use the Applied AI Systems track.

docs.title: Local-First Systems and CRDTs
docs.text: Local-first software treats a local replica as the primary interaction surface and synchronizes replicas when networks permit. Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) can make selected concurrent operations converge without central serialization, but they do not choose product intent, authorization, retention, or a usable undo model.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can design offline caching, optimistic updates, and server reconciliation. Specialist depth begins when multiple replicas accept writes while disconnected, operation order differs, deletes must dominate late updates, metadata must be compacted, and users expect undo to preserve other people's work. If edits always require connectivity or one server can serialize all writes, a simpler version check may be better.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design a collaborative field notebook used offline for days on phones and laptops. Notes contain text, checklists, tags, and attachments. Teams can revoke access.

  • Local accepted operations survive process and device restart before the UI confirms them.
  • Applying the same operation more than once has no additional effect.
  • Replicas that receive the same authorized operations converge.
  • Conflict behavior is defined per field; no generic merge silently discards intent.
  • Delete, restore, retention, and garbage-collection semantics are explicit.
  • Undo creates a new operation and never rewinds another replica's history.
  • Revocation blocks future server-mediated access but does not claim to erase plaintext already obtained offline.
  • Sync works incrementally and can recover from lost cursors and compacted history.

docs.title: Architecture and state
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[Local UI] --> O[(Durable operation log)]
    O --> L[(Local materialized state)]
    O --> S[Sync client]
    S <--> G[Sync gateway]
    G --> A[Authorization and epoch check]
    A --> J[(Team operation journal)]
    J --> M[Snapshot materializer]
    M --> P[(Compacted snapshots)]
    J --> N[Other device sync]
    P --> N
Replica(replica_id, user_id, team_id, membership_epoch, counter)
Operation(op_id, replica_id, counter, object_id, causal_context, type, payload)
Journal(team_id, server_seq, op_id, auth_epoch, accepted_at)
SyncCursor(replica_id, team_id, last_server_seq, snapshot_generation)
Snapshot(object_id, generation, state, causal_summary, digest)
Tombstone(object_id, delete_dot, causal_context, retain_until)

Use a unique operation ID such as (replica_id, counter). The client appends locally before materializing. The server deduplicates, authorizes against a membership epoch, assigns a journal sequence for transport, and returns missing operations. Journal sequence is not the semantic conflict order.

docs.title: Conflict models and CRDT tradeoffs
docs.text:
Choose a type that matches user intent:

Data Candidate Tradeoff membership/tag set observed-remove set remove carries observed add identities; metadata grows counter grow-only or PN-counter converges, but per-replica components require retirement one selected value multi-value or LWW register multi-value exposes conflict; LWW can lose intent and trusts ordering ordered text/list sequence CRDT concurrent insertion converges; identifiers and indexing cost grow object map map of nested CRDTs deletion versus nested update needs an explicit rule

State-based CRDTs merge join-semilattice states and tolerate message loss, but naive transfer is large; delta-state forms reduce it. Operation-based CRDTs send compact operations but require reliable causal delivery or additional metadata. A central sync journal often makes op-based transport practical while clients remain offline-capable.

For an observed-remove tag set, A adds urgent with dot A:1. B observes A:1 and removes that dot while disconnected A adds a new dot A:2. Merge retains A:2, so urgent remains: remove means "remove observed additions," not "ban every future or concurrent addition." Duplicate delivery of A:2 must not create another tag. The Delta-state CRDT paper explicitly separates joinable delta dissemination from operation-based delivery assumptions (primary abstract accessed 2026-09-08).

Lamport timestamps order events consistently but do not identify concurrency. Vector clocks identify causal relationships but have one component per replica unless compressed. Dotted version vectors represent a new event plus summarized causal history. Hybrid logical clocks aid observability and LWW ordering, but clock order still does not equal user intent.

For text, index-based patches are unsafe: concurrent inserts shift positions. Sequence CRDTs assign stable position identifiers. Interleaving surprises remain possible, and metadata or identifier length can grow. Operational transformation is a valid alternative when a server orders operations and transforms them; it has different offline and correctness assumptions.

docs.title: Tombstones, compaction, undo, and permissions
docs.text:
A remove must remember enough causal information to reject or distinguish delayed adds. Garbage-collect a tombstone only when every relevant replica has acknowledged a causal frontier, or after the system intentionally expires old replicas and forces them to resync from a fresh snapshot. Time-based deletion alone can resurrect state from a device offline longer than the retention window.

Compaction writes a snapshot plus causal summary, then retains post-snapshot operations. A returning client with an old generation receives the snapshot and rebases or replays still-valid local operations. If its replica identity has expired, reject raw pre-expiry operations: preserve a private export and let an authorized user re-express intended edits as new operations against the current snapshot. Copying old dots into the new generation can resurrect deleted data. Test this path; it is the common path for devices offline for months.

Undo emits a semantic inverse tied to the original operation. Undoing "add tag" removes the observed add dot, not all concurrent adds of the same tag. Undoing a text insertion deletes the elements created by that insertion. Some actions, such as accepting another user's conflict resolution, may need a new forward edit rather than a mechanical inverse.

Authorization is not monotonic. A user may create valid operations offline after an administrator has revoked access. The server must reject operations from stale membership epochs. Product policy decides whether the client exports those changes privately, discards them, or asks an authorized owner to import them. End-to-end encryption further limits server-side validation and deletion guarantees.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Suppose 100,000 active users produce 300 operations/day at 220 bytes each:

operations/day = 30 million
raw log/day = 30,000,000 * 220 = 6.6 GB

Using an explicit planning assumption of three replicas and 3x per-replica storage amplification for indexes plus envelopes:

physical log/day = 6.6 GB * 3 replicas * 3 storage amplification
                 = 59.4 GB/day

The multipliers must be replaced with measured encoding, compression, and index ratios before capacity approval. Under this illustrative assumption, a 30-day uncompacted hot journal is roughly 1.8 TB. Partition by team and server sequence; one large team needs subpartitions or object routing without losing a resumable team feed.

If a sequence element ID averages 24 bytes and a 1 MB document has 500,000 characters, IDs alone consume about 12 MB before payload and indexes. Character-level CRDTs can dominate document size. Chunked runs reduce metadata but make split, merge, and concurrent edit logic harder.

A reconnecting device with 200,000 pending operations over a 256 Kbit/s link cannot upload a 44 MB raw log in less than about 23 minutes. Compress, exchange causal summaries first, batch operations, prioritize visible objects, and resume by acknowledged batch.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure Control duplicate or reordered sync idempotent op IDs and causal merge ancient device resurrects delete tombstone frontier or forced snapshot resync corrupted local log checksummed records, atomic append, last-good recovery replica counter rollback persist counter transactionally or rotate replica ID compromised device floods ops per-device revocation, quotas, signed session, server validation rejected offline edits after revocation explicit export/recovery product flow metadata explosion snapshots, replica retirement, measured compaction attachment referenced before upload content hash, pending state, retryable blob transfer

Monitor local append failures, unsynced operation age and count, sync bytes and duration, deduplication, authorization rejection by epoch, merge failures, snapshot fallback, tombstone age, metadata-to-payload ratio, active replica cardinality, and convergence probes. For state-based CRDTs, property-test merge commutativity, associativity, and idempotence. For operation-based CRDTs, test duplicate delivery and permutations of concurrent operations while preserving required causal-delivery preconditions; do not require arbitrary operations to commute. Fuzz reorder only where the algorithm's metadata or transport contract permits it, plus partition, crash, delete/update, and stale-snapshot cases.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Begin with one offline writer per object and explicit conflict copies. Add durable local logs and resumable sync. Introduce CRDTs field by field where concurrent intent is understood, starting with sets or counters before rich text. Dual-materialize old and new representations, replay recorded traces, and compare visible state.

Version operation schemas and keep old decoders through the maximum offline period. A migration must define how stale clients submit old operations. Roll out compaction only after frontier accounting is observable. Retire replicas through an explicit epoch transition and require old devices to bootstrap from a snapshot. Preserve export before destructive migrations.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design an offline-first incident notebook. Up to 50 responders edit during network partitions. Notes, task status, and timeline events must converge. Access may be revoked during an incident, and the final record is exported for audit.

Clarify offline duration, object sizes, ordering needs, whether edits may be rewritten, conflict visibility, device trust, encryption, membership changes, retention, attachment handling, and audit expectations.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Store a checksummed local operation log and materialized view on every device. Use append-only timeline events, an observed-remove set for assignees/tags, a register with explicit conflict display for task status, and a sequence CRDT for note text. Each operation has a replica counter, causal context, incident membership epoch, and actor signature where device identity is required.

The server authorizes the operation epoch, deduplicates it, and appends it to an incident journal. Devices sync causal summaries and journal cursors, then exchange missing batches. Snapshots contain CRDT state plus a causal frontier. Tombstones remain until all active replicas pass the frontier; expired replicas must bootstrap and cannot replay pre-expiry state. Revoked users' later offline operations are rejected and offered as a private export, not merged automatically.

Undo emits inverse operations scoped to the original dots or sequence elements. The audit export contains canonical operations, actors, wall-clock observations, and final materialized state, while acknowledging that causal order is stronger than device clock order. Rollout starts with timeline and tasks before collaborative text because sequence metadata and UX need separate validation.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Defines convergence separately from user-intent preservation.
  • Selects conflict semantics per field instead of saying "use a CRDT."
  • Explains causal metadata, tombstone safety, and stale-replica expiry.
  • Treats undo as a new operation and permissions as non-monotonic state.
  • Quantifies metadata and reconnect bandwidth, not only document payload.
  • Includes operation-version evolution and forced snapshot bootstrap.
  • States honest limits of revocation and offline plaintext.

docs.title: Production AI Lifecycle
docs.text: Production AI is a change-management system around statistical behavior. The serving endpoint is only one component. The specialist problem is proving which data, code, model, policy, and evaluation produced a decision, then detecting when that evidence no longer predicts production behavior.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can design a highly available prediction API, artifact store, stream, and deployment pipeline. Specialist depth begins when labels arrive late, evaluation sets leak into training, subgroup quality differs, model output is nondeterministic, drift has several meanings, and rollback cannot undo decisions already made. If deterministic business rules can meet the requirement, prefer them.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design a lifecycle for a fraud model serving 8,000 predictions/s at peak with 100 ms p99 model latency. Labels arrive from chargebacks after 1 to 60 days. High-value declines require human review.

  • Every prediction records immutable model, feature-view, code, policy, and request-schema versions.
  • Training data is reproducible from a snapshot manifest, not a mutable query.
  • Offline evaluation uses point-in-time-correct data and an explicitly justified split strategy. Use entity-held-out splits when identity leakage or new-entity generalization matters, and future-period splits when production repeatedly scores existing entities.
  • A model cannot become active without signed evaluation results and release approval.
  • Shadow output cannot affect users, counters used for policy, or downstream learning labels.
  • Fallback behavior is bounded, observable, and tested before an incident.
  • Human overrides preserve the machine recommendation, reviewer identity, reason, and final outcome.
  • Deletion and retention rules apply to lineage artifacts as well as raw features.

docs.title: Architecture and state
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Versioned sources] --> V[Feature and label snapshots]
    V --> T[Training pipeline]
    T --> R[(Model registry)]
    T --> E[Evaluation service]
    E --> G[Release gate]
    R --> G
    G --> D[Deployment controller]
    D --> P[Primary serving]
    D --> H[Shadow serving]
    P --> L[(Prediction ledger)]
    H --> L
    L --> M[Drift and quality monitor]
    Q[Delayed outcomes] --> M
    P --> U[Policy and human review]
    U --> L

Core state:

DatasetSnapshot(id, source_versions, query_hash, cutoff_time, row_count, digest)
TrainingRun(id, code_sha, config, seed, dataset_ids, environment_digest)
ModelArtifact(id, run_id, digest, signature, interface, status)
Evaluation(id, model_id, suite_version, slice_metrics, confidence, decision)
Deployment(id, endpoint, model_id, policy_id, traffic, phase, approver)
Prediction(id, model_id, feature_view, policy_id, score, action, shadow, time)
Outcome(prediction_id, label, label_time, label_source, correction_version)
Review(prediction_id, recommendation, final_action, actor, reason, time)

The model registry is a state machine, not a folder. Suggested transitions are CANDIDATE -> EVALUATED -> APPROVED -> SHADOW -> CANARY -> ACTIVE -> RETIRED, with explicit rejection and rollback edges. Store content digests and signatures so a tag cannot be repointed to different bytes.

docs.title: Evaluation, drift, and decision policy
docs.text:
Offline metrics must match the decision. Ranking may use precision-recall and recall at a review-capacity threshold; calibrated risk decisions need reliability curves and expected cost. Report slices selected before evaluation, plus uncertainty. A single aggregate score can conceal harm to a small but important population.

Separate drift signals:

Signal Meaning Response feature drift input distribution changed validate pipeline and affected slices prediction drift score/action distribution changed inspect model, policy, and traffic mix concept drift relation between inputs and outcomes changed wait for labels, retrain or change policy performance drift decision metric worsened on mature labels constrain traffic or roll back data-quality drift missingness, range, or freshness violated fail closed or use tested fallback

Use population stability index, divergence, or two-sample tests as alarms, not proof of harm. Multiple correlated features generate noisy pages. Route alerts through a model-specific policy that considers sample size, business impact, persistence, and label maturity.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
At 8,000 predictions/s, a 14-day prediction ledger contains:

8,000 * 86,400 * 14 = 9.68 billion predictions

At 600 bytes per compressed record, that is about 5.8 TB before replication and indexes. Keep a hot aggregate path for monitoring and a partitioned immutable detail path for audits. Preserve the minimum audit tuple for every decision so delayed labels, deletion requests, incidents, and slices can be joined later. Sampling may apply only to optional high-volume feature payloads or debugging traces under a declared policy; preserve those richer records for every high-risk or human-reviewed decision.

The calculation assumes the 8,000/s peak is sustained, so it is an upper planning scenario rather than an average forecast. Fourteen days of hot storage cannot support 60-day label joins alone: retain minimal joinable decision evidence in a governed colder tier beyond label maturity plus correction delay. Log actual feature values or immutable versions where reproduction requires them; a feature-view definition does not identify the values it returned. Google's Rules of ML, rules 29-33 addresses serving-time feature capture, mutable joins, and future-period evaluation (accessed 2026-09-08).

Suppose fraud prevalence is 0.8%, the review team can inspect 20,000 cases/day, and traffic is 50 million/day. The maximum review rate is 0.04%. A threshold chosen for generic F1 may overwhelm reviewers. Evaluate precision and prevented-loss recall at the 20,000-case capacity constraint.

For a canary receiving 5% of 8,000/s, one hour yields 1.44 million predictions, but almost no mature 60-day labels. Launch gates therefore combine immediate operational metrics, proxy metrics validated in advance, shadow comparisons, and later outcome checkpoints. Volume cannot fix label delay.

docs.title: Shadow, canary, fallback, and human review
docs.text:
Shadow requests must use the same sanitized input envelope and record both outputs with a pairing ID. They must not write customer-visible state or publish features that contaminate later labels. Compare score distribution, disagreement by slice, latency, resource cost, and policy simulation.

Canary by stable entity hash so repeated decisions for an account do not alternate models. Separate the model score from policy action: a policy can cap decline rates, route uncertain cases to review, or require a deterministic rule for irreversible action.

Fallback order should be explicit:

  1. previous healthy model with compatible features;
  2. degraded model using a smaller stable feature set;
  3. deterministic policy with conservative limits;
  4. queue for human review where delay is safe;
  5. fail closed only when the risk policy justifies denial.

Human review is a limited queue. Prioritize by expected value and deadline, hide protected attributes unless needed and lawful, randomize quality-audit samples, measure reviewer disagreement, and prevent overrides from becoming unexamined training labels.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure Control training-serving skew shared feature definitions, interface contract, online/offline parity tests label leakage event-time cutoffs, entity-aware splits, snapshot review bad feature backfill versioned feature view, point-in-time joins, quarantine registry compromise artifact signatures, separate approval role, append-only audit silent model timeout deadline propagation, fallback counter, circuit breaker runaway review queue admission threshold, age SLO, conservative policy feedback loop exploration holdout, causal review, delayed-label analysis poisoned training data source authorization, anomaly checks, snapshot provenance

Monitor latency, error and fallback rates by model version; feature freshness and missingness; score, action, and override distributions; slice quality on mature labels; shadow disagreement; calibration; review backlog and age; data and code lineage completeness; and artifact verification failures. A drift alert must link to the affected model, feature versions, deployment, slices, and runbook.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Start with a deterministic baseline and a prediction ledger. Add reproducible snapshots and registry gates before automated retraining. Introduce shadow traffic, then a stable-entity canary with operational and policy limits. Expand only after predefined windows pass. Keep the prior model and feature path warm through the rollback window.

Automated retraining should create candidates, not self-approve. As maturity grows, encode release policy as machine-checkable gates while retaining separation of duties for high-impact models. Changing a feature definition, decision threshold, or human-review policy is a release even when model bytes do not change.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design a lending risk-model lifecycle. Applications need a decision in two seconds. Defaults are known 90 days later. Regulators and support teams must reconstruct any adverse decision for seven years. A new model claims 8% higher approval at equal default risk.

Ask about decision reversibility, explanation requirements, prohibited attributes, label definition, appeal flow, reviewer capacity, regional policy, retention, traffic, latency, and how the 8% claim was measured.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Use a versioned application schema and point-in-time feature service. Persist a signed decision bundle containing input references, transformed feature version, model digest, score, policy version, reason codes, action, and correlation ID. Train from immutable snapshot manifests with future-period evaluation and separate entity-held-out slices where new-applicant generalization requires them. Gate candidates on calibration, equal-risk approval metrics, required slices, latency, and reproducibility.

Replay the candidate on historical frozen inputs, then shadow live applications without influencing actions. Compare disagreement and policy simulation. Canary by applicant hash at 1%, with approval-rate and risk-proxy bounds; route borderline disagreements to a capacity-limited blinded review queue. Increase traffic in stages. Because default labels lag 90 days, retain a randomized control slice and schedule outcome gates at maturity. On operational or proxy regression, atomically restore a compatible prior model and decision-policy bundle after validating it against current mandatory rules. Keep current authorization, revocation, and legally required restrictions in a separately enforced layer; rollback cannot restore superseded permissions or prohibited decision rules. Preserve both recommendations on appeal and never overwrite the original evidence bundle.

The design does not promise that an offline uplift proves future default parity. It names the delayed-evidence gap and controls exposure while evidence matures.

Defaults are observed mainly for approved loans. Rejected applicants do not become negative labels merely because no default is observed. Compare mature, equally defined exposure cohorts and retain decision propensities where justified; any exploration of previously rejected applicants needs risk and legal approval with a loss cap. An 8% approval uplift must also say relative percent or percentage points, and whether default risk is per approved loan or per application.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Separates model, feature, policy, and deployment versions.
  • Treats lineage and evaluation artifacts as immutable product state.
  • Distinguishes covariate, concept, performance, and data-quality drift.
  • Designs around delayed labels and constrained human review.
  • Prevents shadow systems and overrides from corrupting feedback.
  • Defines fallback semantics before discussing autoscaling.
  • Makes release evidence, ownership, and rollback windows explicit.

For the complete 18-chapter treatment of pipelines, serving, retrieval, agents, evaluation, security, operations, adaptation, and platform governance, use the Applied AI Systems track.

docs.title: RAG and Agent Security
docs.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives a model selected external context. An agent adds tools that can read or change systems. Both create a confused-deputy risk: content controlled by an attacker may be interpreted as instructions while the runtime holds a user's authority.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can design document ingestion, vector search, chat storage, and API authorization. Specialist depth begins when retrieved text is untrusted executable influence, provenance can be lost through chunking and synthesis, tool arguments are model-generated, and a request may consume variable money or cause an irreversible side effect. Do not use an agent when a deterministic workflow or search UI meets the need.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design an internal support agent over policy documents and ticket history. It may draft replies, look up orders, and issue refunds up to a policy limit.

  • Retrieved content is data, never authority.
  • The caller, not the model, determines tool permissions and tenant scope.
  • Every factual response can expose document and span provenance.
  • Side effects require typed validation, idempotency, and policy checks outside the model.
  • High-impact or ambiguous actions require explicit human approval over exact arguments.
  • Each run has bounded tokens, retrievals, tool calls, wall time, and spend.
  • A replay preserves inputs, versions, retrieved evidence, tool results, decisions, and approvals.
  • Operational credentials and raw secrets never enter prompts. The model receives opaque references; the tool gateway resolves short-lived credentials for an exact authorized call. Cross-tenant data enters context only under an explicit, independently enforced purpose and authorization policy.

docs.title: Architecture and state
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[User] --> A[Agent gateway]
    A --> P[Identity and policy]
    A --> R[Retrieval broker]
    R --> X[(Tenant indexes)]
    R --> C[Provenance packer]
    C --> M[Model runtime]
    M --> O[Plan and typed action]
    O --> T[Tool policy gateway]
    P --> T
    T --> H[Approval service]
    H --> S[Scoped tools]
    S --> T
    A --> L[(Replay ledger)]
    R --> L
    T --> L
Chunk(id, tenant, source_id, source_version, offsets, acl, digest, embedding_version)
Run(id, principal, purpose, model_version, prompt_version, budget, status)
Retrieval(run_id, query, filters, chunk_ids, ranks, scores, index_version)
ToolIntent(id, run_id, tool, typed_args, risk, policy_decision, idempotency_key)
Approval(intent_id, approver, displayed_args_digest, decision, expires_at)
ToolResult(intent_id, status, response_digest, redacted_payload)
Answer(run_id, text, citation_spans, completion_reason)

Index ACL fields and enforce them before candidate material enters the context. Post-filtering a global ANN result can leak existence through counts or timing and may produce poor recall. Prefer tenant or security-domain partitioning, then apply row-level policy again during hydration.

docs.title: Retrieval quality and provenance
docs.text:
Evaluate retrieval independently from generation. Build a versioned set of questions with relevant source spans and unanswerable cases.

Metric Question recall at K did the candidate set contain required evidence? precision at K how much retrieved context was relevant? MRR how early did the first relevant item appear? NDCG at K were graded-relevance items ordered well? citation precision does each citation support its attached claim? citation recall are material factual claims cited? abstention accuracy does the system refuse when evidence is absent?

Chunk provenance must survive parsing, deduplication, embedding, reranking, and prompt packing. Store source version, byte or character offsets, ACL, and digest. The answer layer maps claims to chunk IDs; the UI resolves citations against the same immutable version. If a source changes, do not silently render the old citation against new text.

Treat generated search queries as untrusted. Constrain filters to authorized fields, cap query fan-out, and prevent the model from weakening ACL predicates. Separate authoritative policy sources from low-trust tickets or web content and label trust in the context envelope.

docs.title: Prompt injection and scoped tools
docs.text:
Prompt injection cannot be solved by telling the model to ignore malicious instructions. Use layered containment:

  1. Mark origin and trust level for every context segment.
  2. Keep secrets out of the context and model-visible tool metadata.
  3. Give tools narrow schemas and short-lived capabilities bound to principal, tenant, action, and resource.
  4. Reauthorize each tool call outside the model.
  5. Validate typed arguments, business preconditions, rate limits, and idempotency.
  6. Require approval for risk classes, showing exact action, target, amount, and evidence.
  7. Return allowlisted typed fields where possible; bound and label unavoidable free text as untrusted data before it returns to the model.
  8. Detect loops and stop proposing new work at the budget boundary. Persist unresolved write outcomes for a separate bounded reconciliation path; stopping a run does not undo a dispatched effect.

An approval is not a generic "continue" button. Bind it to a digest of the displayed tool and normalized arguments. Any change invalidates approval. Separate read tools from write tools and use a two-phase flow: prepare a side effect, review it, then commit with an expiring token. At commit, reauthorize the principal and revalidate policy, limits, and business preconditions; bind the prepared intent to relevant resource versions so changed state fails closed instead of reusing stale approval.

There is no general sanitizer that makes attacker-controlled natural language safe to follow. Labels, delimiters, and injection detectors are defense-in-depth signals, not authorization controls. Tools that fetch URLs or process attachments run behind destination allowlists, redirect and DNS revalidation, response-size limits, content-type checks, egress policy, and audit so the agent cannot become an SSRF or data-exfiltration proxy.

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Suppose a request retrieves 40 chunks of 700 tokens, reranks to 8, and uses a 4,000-token conversation plus 1,000 output tokens:

candidate tokens handled by reranker = 40 * 700 = 28,000
model input = 8 * 700 + 4,000 = 9,600 tokens
total model tokens = 9,600 + 1,000 = 10,600

At $3 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens, model cost is about $0.0408 before retrieval, reranking, retries, and tools. At 2 million runs/month, that is about $81,600/month. A three-attempt retry policy can almost triple tail cost during provider failure, so retries consume the same per-run budget rather than reset it.

For retrieval evaluation, if 160 of 200 questions have at least one relevant chunk in top 10, hit-rate-at-10 (question coverage) is 80%. This is not document recall@10 unless each question has exactly one relevant item; recall is retrieved relevant items divided by all judged relevant items. If generation answers 150, but only 120 are supported, answer rate is 75%, supported-answer rate over all questions is 60%, and support precision among answered questions is 80%. Optimize support and correct abstention, not fluency.

Set budgets as a vector, for example: 20,000 input tokens, 2,000 output tokens, 4 retrievals, 6 read tools, 1 write tool, 30 seconds, and $0.10. Admission can lower budgets or reject low-priority runs under provider or tool saturation.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure or attack Control injected document says to reveal secrets no model-visible secrets; context has no authority poisoned high-rank chunk source trust tiers, anomaly review, provenance; signatures prove origin and integrity, not truth cross-tenant retrieval partitioned index, hydration authorization, isolation tests model invents tool parameters strict schema, policy validation, approval binding repeated side effect after timeout stable scoped idempotency key, provider retention bound, and authoritative reconciliation; unknown or not-found is not automatically safe to retry tool output injects a new plan typed allowlisted fields where possible; treat free text as untrusted; tool gateway remains authoritative URL or attachment tool exfiltrates data destination allowlist, redirect and DNS revalidation, egress policy, size and type limits agent loop step, time, token, and spend budgets provider outage bounded retry, alternate model by policy, read-only fallback replay exposes personal data encrypted ledger, field redaction, retention and access audit

Red-team indirect injection and exfiltration through documents, images converted to text, URLs, redirects, DNS changes, tool results, and quoted email.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Launch read-only question answering with citations and abstention. Add draft generation, then low-risk read tools. Shadow proposed write actions without executing them. Introduce approval-bound writes for a small operator group and low limits. Expand tool scope one capability at a time, with per-tool kill switches and immutable policy versions.

Changing the embedding model, chunking, reranker, prompt, base model, or tool description can change behavior. Version each independently, replay a fixed suite, shadow production runs where permitted, and compare retrieval, safety, latency, and cost. Preserve an emergency mode that disables all writes while leaving cited search available.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design a procurement agent that reads contracts and email, compares vendor quotes, drafts purchase orders, and can submit orders under $10,000. Documents may be supplied by vendors.

Clarify tenants, authoritative sources, approval thresholds, separation of duties, quote freshness, contract confidentiality, allowed tools, order idempotency, budget, retention, and whether email content can ever authorize spending.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
Ingest each source into a security-domain index with immutable source versions, offsets, ACLs, and trust labels. Retrieval first applies the employee and project scope, performs hybrid candidate search, and reauthorizes current source versions during hydration before any external reranker or model sees the text. The answer cites exact contract spans and abstains when price, term, or currency evidence conflicts.

The model can call read-only catalog and budget tools through principal-bound capabilities; credentials remain inside the gateway. It emits a typed PreparePurchaseOrder intent, but a deterministic service validates vendor, SKU, contract ceiling, tax, cost center, and duplicate quote. Vendor-controlled text cannot modify those checks. Orders below $10,000 still require an authorized buyer to approve the exact normalized order digest; higher orders require the existing multi-approver workflow. Commit uses an expiring token and idempotency key, reauthorizes the buyer, and atomically checks the prepared quote, budget, and policy versions before execution.

Each run records model and prompt versions, retrieved chunks, tool inputs and redacted outputs, policy decisions, approval digest, and final order ID. Budgets cap search iterations and spend. Rollout begins with cited comparison, then drafts, then shadow intents, and finally limited approved execution. A global kill switch removes write capabilities without changing retrieval.

Also guard cumulative authority: several separately approved $9,999 orders must not evade a $10,000 aggregate limit for one quote, project, or time window. Atomically reserve the applicable budget with the normalized intent and release it only after a definite rejection or compensating resolution. OWASP's agent-specific defenses require permission and parameter checks outside the model; content screening is not that enforcement boundary (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• States that retrieved content is untrusted even when it is internal.
  • Measures retrieval and citation quality separately from answer style.
  • Binds authority to the principal and exact action, never to the model.
  • Uses typed, idempotent, policy-checked tools with risk-based approvals.
  • Treats tokens, steps, time, and money as admission-controlled resources.
  • Designs replay without turning the ledger into an unrestricted data lake.
  • Evolves each model, prompt, index, and tool version independently.

For the complete knowledge, workflow, tool, evaluation, observability, reliability, and practice path, use the Applied AI Systems track.

docs.title: Regulated Evidence Systems
docs.text: A regulated evidence system must show what happened, why it happened, which rules and inputs applied, who acted, and whether the record remained intact. It must reproduce a historical decision under controlled conditions while obeying retention, privacy, and legal-hold obligations. Technical integrity controls support, but do not by themselves establish, legal admissibility or evidentiary weight.

docs.title: Generalist boundary
docs.text: A generalist can design audit logs, immutable storage, backups, and role-based access. Specialist depth begins with end-to-end traceability, controls that support jurisdiction-specific admissibility, evidence integrity, validated reproducibility, separation of duties, record schedules, legal holds, controlled redaction, and proof of operating effectiveness. "We log everything" is neither a data model nor a compliance strategy.

docs.title: Requirements and invariants
docs.text:
Design evidence for a medical claims adjudication platform. A reviewer must reconstruct any claim decision for ten years. Rules and reference data change daily. Litigation can place selected claims on hold.

  • A finalized decision references immutable input, rule, code, model, and reference-data versions.
  • Evidence is append-only; corrections preserve the superseded record and reason.
  • Every object has provenance, classification, retention basis, and integrity digest.
  • Access and export are authorized, minimized, and audited.
  • A legal hold prevents eligible deletion across primary, archive, and derived evidence.
  • Reproduction runs are isolated and cannot mutate production or external systems.
  • Time comes from a documented trusted source and uncertainty is represented where relevant.
  • The system can prove both artifact integrity and completeness of the expected evidence set.

docs.title: Architecture, state, and evidence model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    T[Transactional decision] --> O[(Atomic outbox)]
    O --> E[Evidence assembler]
    E --> M[Manifest and digest]
    M --> W[(WORM evidence store)]
    M --> C[(Evidence catalog)]
    H[Hold service] --> C
    H --> W
    R[Reproduction workspace] --> C
    C --> R
    W --> R
    X[Authorized export] --> C
    C --> X
    X --> A[(Export audit)]
Case(case_id, subject_ref, jurisdiction, opened_at, status)
Decision(id, case_id, outcome, effective_time, actor_or_service, correlation_id)
Artifact(id, type, content_digest, storage_uri, schema_version, classification)
EvidenceLink(decision_id, artifact_id, role, source, captured_at)
Manifest(decision_id, required_roles, artifact_digests, root_digest, signature)
RuleBundle(id, digest, effective_interval, approval, runtime_digest)
Hold(id, authority, scope_query, issued_at, released_at, custodian)
Retention(artifact_id, schedule, trigger, due_at, hold_count, disposition)
Reproduction(id, decision_id, environment_digest, result_digest, variance, approver)

Commit the business decision and an evidence envelope atomically. The envelope contains immutable artifact IDs or captured values plus the exact rule, code, model, schema, configuration, and reference-data versions needed for assembly; it must not ask the asynchronous assembler to rediscover mutable current state. The decision remains PENDING_EVIDENCE until policy-required artifacts and the outbox record are durable. The evidence assembler resolves only those immutable references and produces a manifest. Store large artifacts by content digest and protect them with retention lock or equivalent write-once controls. The catalog supports discovery; it is not the only integrity anchor.

Hash chains or Merkle trees make deletion or modification detectable within a committed set, but they do not prove that an event was never omitted. Completeness needs expected-artifact rules, source sequence reconciliation, control totals, and gap alerts. Periodically anchor signed roots through a separately administered, independently monitored service. Where proof of time matters, use an approved timestamping authority or equivalent protocol and retain its validation material; a locally recorded timestamp or signed root alone does not prove when the evidence existed.

Admissibility is a legal and procedural determination, not a hash algorithm. Define chain-of-custody events for capture, transfer, access, transformation, reproduction, and export; validate collection and export tooling; retain operator and custodian attestations where required; and have counsel map these controls to each jurisdiction. Periodic control tests must demonstrate that the process operated throughout the record's life, not merely that stored bytes verify today.

docs.title: Traceability and reproducibility
docs.text:
Traceability links requirement or policy to approved rule, deployed bundle, decision, evidence, review, and outcome. Use stable identities and effective intervals. A human-readable reason should refer to machine-executed rule IDs, not a free-text explanation generated later.

Reproducibility has levels:

  1. Evidence replay: show the original inputs and outputs.
  2. Logical reproduction: run equivalent logic and obtain the same material decision.
  3. Bitwise reproduction: produce identical bytes.

Bitwise reproduction may be impractical with nondeterministic libraries, floating-point hardware, or external services. State the required level. Pin code, dependencies, container or VM image, configuration, locale, clock inputs, seeds, rule bundles, schemas, and reference snapshots. Replace external calls with captured responses in an isolated workspace.

A reproduction mismatch is evidence, not something to hide. Record the original output, reproduced output, environment, difference classification, and reviewer decision.

docs.title: Retention and legal holds
docs.text:
Retention is a lifecycle state machine. A schedule has a legal or business basis, trigger, duration, jurisdiction, and disposition action. A hold adds a barrier to disposition; it does not necessarily change the ordinary retention date. When the hold is released, recompute eligibility rather than resetting retention blindly.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active
    Active --> Eligible: retention date reached
    Active --> Held: hold matches
    Eligible --> Held: hold matches
    Held --> Eligible: hold released and due
    Held --> Active: hold released and not due
    Eligible --> DispositionReview
    DispositionReview --> Held: hold wins disposition race
    DispositionReview --> Deleted: atomic no-hold check and approval
    DispositionReview --> Active: exception

Hold scope may name subjects, custodians, dates, products, or keywords. Materialize scope matches, record query version and reviewer, and rescan new evidence while the hold remains active. Propagate holds to archives, exports under organizational control, and derived evidence as policy requires. Deletion uses a two-person or policy-controlled workflow and produces a disposition certificate without preserving the deleted sensitive payload.

Serialize hold registration with disposition authority. A scan that has not yet reached an artifact must still block its purge through an active-scope barrier. The final delete authorization checks that barrier and the current hold version atomically; if a remote delete is already in flight, hold activation cannot truthfully claim to have recalled it. Report such uncertainty and coordinate with custodians. Use W3C PROV to record the hold/disposition activities, artifact versions, and responsible agents, without confusing provenance with an atomic storage control (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Suppose 25 million claims/year each create a 400 KB evidence bundle:

annual logical evidence = 25,000,000 * 400 KB = 10 TB
ten-year logical evidence = 100 TB

With 3 copies, index/catalog overhead of 15%, and 20% retained beyond schedule because of holds and operational lag:

100 TB * 3 * 1.15 * 1.20 = 414 TB

Deduplication can reduce repeated rule bundles and reference snapshots, but do not count on deduplicating claim-specific inputs. Capacity-plan restore and scan, not only storage.

If 0.5% of one annual cohort of 25 million claims are held and each claim references 30 artifacts, the initial hold touches 3.75 million artifact links. At 2,000 evaluated links/s, one full evaluation takes about 31 minutes before catalog contention. Large keyword holds may require distributed scans and a conservative ingestion-time hold rule while backfill catches up.

For daily control, if source transactions report 1,000,000 finalized decisions but manifests exist for 999,970, the 30-item gap is a completeness incident even if every stored manifest has a valid signature.

docs.title: Failure, security, and operations
docs.text:
Failure or threat Control outbox backlog decision remains pending unless the applicable policy explicitly permits finality; page on completeness and block regulated use or export artifact overwritten content-addressing, retention lock, digest verification privileged administrator alters catalog signed manifests and separately anchored roots incomplete evidence required-role validation, sequence and control-total reconciliation hold misses new records hold evaluated at ingest plus periodic rescan reproduction calls live provider isolated network and captured dependency responses export leaks unrelated records case-scoped authorization, minimization, dual review encryption key loss tested escrow and rotation aligned to retention malicious insider separation of duties, immutable access audit, anomaly detection

Monitor outbox and assembly age, missing evidence roles, source-to-manifest count gaps, digest-verification failures, anchor lag, hold evaluation backlog, disposition queue, expired-but-held volume, unauthorized access, export volume, reproduction success and variance, restore test results, and key-expiry horizon. Periodically sample cases from source records and prove the entire chain, rather than sampling only records already present in the catalog.

docs.title: Rollout and evolution
docs.text:
Define the evidence matrix first: decision type, required artifacts, owner, retention basis, reproduction level, finality rule, jurisdictional chain-of-custody requirements, and export authority. Instrument one high-risk decision flow end to end. Run completeness reconciliation in report-only mode, then block policy-defined finality, regulated use, export, or closure when manifests are incomplete. Add immutable retention only after hold and correction workflows are tested; immutability without lifecycle design can preserve mistakes and unnecessary personal data forever.

Version evidence schemas with readers that remain supported for the retention period. Migrate by writing new catalog projections while preserving original artifacts and manifests. Test restore, reproduction, hold, release, and disposition in non-production with synthetic records. Any change to rule execution, time handling, or reference data must update reproduction fixtures and evidence requirements.

docs.title: Interview case
docs.text:
Design an evidence platform for automated insurance underwriting. A regulator may ask five years later why a policy was declined. Pricing models, third-party reports, and regulations change over time. A lawsuit may freeze records for a class of applicants.

Clarify jurisdictions, required explanation, model determinism, third-party data rights, record schedule, hold authority and scope, acceptable reproduction level, export format, privacy rights, and who may approve deletion.

docs.title: Worked answer
docs.text:
At decision commit, write the outcome and an evidence envelope together. The envelope pins normalized application input or its immutable reference, third-party response digest and licensed archive reference, model and feature versions, approved rule bundle, reference-table snapshots, policy reason IDs, runtime image, actor, and trusted timestamp evidence. Keep the decision pending until the required envelope and outbox are durable, then assemble and sign the manifest without consulting mutable current state. Store artifacts by digest in retention-locked storage and catalog links by case and classification.

Reconciliation compares finalized underwriting sequences and control totals to manifests; missing evidence blocks policy-defined finality or regulated use as well as regulatory export and pages the owning service. A reproduction workspace has no production write credentials or Internet access. It restores pinned artifacts and captured provider responses, runs the historical image, and records exact or explained variance. Chain-of-custody records cover capture through export, and validated export tooling produces the jurisdiction-required certification without claiming that signatures alone establish admissibility.

The hold service compiles approved class criteria into versioned scope, marks existing matches, intercepts new matching evidence, and rescans. Disposition requires no active hold, elapsed schedule, dependency confirmation, and authorized approval. The certificate keeps IDs, schedule, hold check, digest reference, actor, and time, but not the deleted application. Separate teams control decision rules, evidence administration, and signing roots.

docs.title: Staff-level signals
docs.text:
• Distinguishes integrity from completeness.
  • Models evidence, manifest, retention, hold, and reproduction explicitly.
  • Names the required reproducibility level and nondeterminism limits.
  • Uses atomic decision-to-evidence handoff and control-total reconciliation.
  • Treats hold as a continuing process, not a flag set once.
  • Balances immutability against minimization and lawful deletion.
  • Tests restore and proof of operating effectiveness, not only write success.

docs.text:
For mechanism-to-lifecycle evidence alongside this curriculum, use Engineering Foundations and Practice, its eight-week L6 route, and the Atlas capstone. The new concept registry identifies prerequisite and executable-evidence gaps rather than claiming complete staff-level coverage.

Staff engineers design changes to systems, organizations, and operating models. This track extends the foundations and interview scorecard from a greenfield design to a defensible path through risk, migration, ownership, and economics.

docs.text:

docs.title: How to use the track
docs.text:
For each case, write the invariants and decision record before reading the worked solution. Then draw the intermediate migration states, name the rollback boundary, and assign every control to an owner. A staff answer is not a larger component diagram. It connects local mechanisms to fleet-wide failure, delivery sequence, evidence, and business constraints.

Use this review loop:

  1. State the irreversible loss to prevent.
  2. Quantify steady state, peak, skew, and failure load.
  3. Compare at least three options against explicit criteria.
  4. Describe mixed-version and mixed-data states.
  5. Set promotion and rollback gates from observable evidence.
  6. Assign operational ownership and escalation authority.
  7. Explain how the design is retired or simplified later.

docs.title: Completion standard
docs.text:
A completed chapter exercise includes an invariant ledger, capacity calculation, decision matrix, staged migration, rollback test, failure table, operating artifact, and concise interview narrative. Evaluate it with the L6 extension.

Keep a blind first attempt before the worked solution and distinguish designed gates from executed evidence. One useful transfer test is to remove a region, invalidate a placement cache, and ask which acknowledged writes remain recoverable before any new ones can be accepted. Score both the technical protocol and the owner authorized to stop it; a source such as the SRE Workbook's alerting chapter supports the operating mechanism, not a claim that a fictional case passed production testing (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Capacity and Economics
docs.text: Capacity architecture converts demand, failure objectives, and unit economics into resource commitments. Staff engineers expose where resilience spends money, where utilization creates risk, and which degradation preserves the business.

docs.title: 1. Model demand as a resource vector
docs.text:
Average QPS is insufficient. Model peak arrival rate, concurrency, CPU time, memory, storage growth, IOPS, network, queue age, tenant skew, and downstream quotas.

concurrency = arrival_rate * mean_service_time
required instances = ceil(peak_rate / tested_sustainable_rate_at_target)
required instances = ceil(peak_rate / (max_measured_rate_per_instance * target_utilization))
monthly unit cost = (compute + storage + network + licenses + operations) / outcomes

At 18,000 req/s, 120 ms mean service time implies 2,160 requests in flight before retries and fan-out. If one instance sustains 300 req/s while already operating at the tested 60% utilization target, capacity is 18,000 / 300 = 60 instances; do not apply the 60% factor a second time. Add failure reserve explicitly rather than hiding it by raising utilization.

flowchart LR
    D[Demand forecast and skew] --> M[Resource model]
    S[SLO, RTO, RPO] --> M
    M --> P[Provision and reserve]
    P --> A[Admission and degradation]
    A --> O[Observed unit cost and saturation]
    O -. recalibrate .-> M

docs.title: 2. Resilience has an economics frontier
docs.text:
Topology Failure capacity Cost shape Risk N+1 instances one instance low increment correlated zone loss Three zones, each 50% peak one zone at peak 1.5x regional compute dependency quotas Two regions, each 100% warm full region near 2x plus replication high idle cost 60% warm plus burst partial immediate lower steady cost burst delay/quota risk Backup/restore no serving reserve lowest high RTO and uncertain restore

Choose from business loss curves. If one hour of outage costs $2M and warm reserve costs $120K/month, reserve may dominate. Include probability and correlated failure uncertainty; expected value alone can underweight existential or contractual loss.

docs.title: Forecast bands
docs.text: Use base, high, and event scenarios rather than one number. Record model error and procurement lead time. If weekly peak grows 4% and hardware lead time is eight weeks, expected multiplier is 1.04^8 = 1.37; add forecast error and failure reserve separately.

docs.title: 3. Decision/review matrix
docs.text:
Criterion Weight Warm 100% Warm 60% + burst Restore RTO confidence 5 5 3 1 RPO confidence 5 4 4 2 Monthly cost 4 1 4 5 Testability 3 5 3 2 Dependency readiness 4 4 2 1 Operational complexity 3 3 2 3

Multiply and document actual dollars. Apply hard constraints before scoring. A cheap option that cannot meet contractual RTO is not a candidate.

Review demand source, seasonality, retry amplification, queue limits, hot keys, failover load, autoscaling lag, quota lead time, storage rebuild bandwidth, network egress, license steps, and owner toil. Cost per successful business outcome prevents a failing, retrying system from looking efficient.

docs.title: 4. Capacity migration and rollback
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Baseline
    Baseline --> ShadowCapacity
    ShadowCapacity --> OnePercent
    OnePercent --> RegionalCohort
    RegionalCohort --> NewBaseline
    OnePercent --> Baseline: routing rollback
    RegionalCohort --> Baseline: reserve retained
    NewBaseline --> RetiredReserve: evacuation proven

When changing instance type, autoscaler, cloud, or region, keep old reserve until the new path passes peak and failure tests. Intermediate states can cost more; budget migration overlap. Rollback requires quotas, images, data replication, and credentials still valid, not merely old infrastructure code.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and ownership
docs.text:
Failure Economic/technical effect Control Owner Forecast misses event skew hot shard fails with idle fleet skew scenarios and admission Product plus capacity Autoscale follows bad latency runaway cost and retries causal metrics and max bounds Runtime platform Region evacuation doubles egress quota/cost shock pre-negotiated limits Cloud economics Spot interruption is correlated sudden capacity cliff diversified pools/base reserve Compute platform Storage rebuild consumes serving IOPS cascading latency rebuild budget and priority Storage owner Cost allocation rewards local savings downstream bill rises end-to-end unit metric Finance and architecture

Product owns demand events and degradation order. Service teams own tested resource curves. Platform owns provisioning and quotas. Finance provides rates and allocation. Incident command may exceed budget during recovery; a post-incident owner returns temporary capacity.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: cost-constrained regional evacuation
docs.text: Prompt. A two-region marketplace serves 30,000 req/s peak, 70% in region A and 30% in B. Each region currently has 40,000 req/s capacity. Finance requires a 25% compute-cost reduction. The checkout RTO is 10 minutes, acknowledged orders have RPO zero, and browse may degrade. Design savings without making region loss fictional.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Classify traffic and durability. Peak is 21,000 req/s in A and 9,000 in B. Split 8,000 req/s checkout/status (critical) and 22,000 browse/recommendation (degradable). Require each acknowledged order to be durably stored in at least two independent data regions. A metadata-only witness can decide leadership but cannot replace a data copy: with only A and B holding data, loss of either stops new acknowledgements until a replacement remote copy is ready. To retain critical writes during that loss while preserving regional RPO zero, provision a third data-bearing region and an appropriate consensus/commit protocol. Count that storage and WAN cost before accepting the savings plan. Fence stale writers and reconcile stable command IDs across failover.
  2. Set failure contract. On one-region loss, establish the surviving writer through quorum and fencing, admit all critical traffic, retain basic browse, disable recommendations, reduce expensive search facets, and reject excess browse with retry guidance. Keep at least 24,000 req/s immediately available in either region and burst to 30,000 within the 10-minute RTO.
  3. Choose capacity. Keep 24,000 req/s warm in each region, enough for A's 21,000 normal peak with modest measured headroom, and reserve quota, images, and dependency capacity for 6,000 req/s burst per region. Total warm falls from 80,000 to 48,000 req/s, a 40% raw reduction. Whether billed dollars fall 25% must include burst reservation and execution, synchronous replication, the third data-bearing region, any separate witness, and evacuation egress.
  4. Check timing. At 500 req/s per instance, a surviving region needs 12 burst instances. Starting four concurrently per 90-second wave takes three waves, or about 4.5 minutes, plus routing. Pre-pull images and keep dependencies warm to fit 10 minutes. Test quota allocation and the complete data path; an API promise is not capacity.
  5. Prevent overload. Regional ingress reserves critical tokens. On evacuation, cap retries at 5%, shed recommendations immediately, then facets, then browse. Queue critical work within deadlines; do not mix it with browse workers or database pools.
  6. Migrate. First classify and enforce priorities with existing 40k/region. Add burst pools dark, run weekly synthetic starts, canary 1% traffic, then lower warm capacity in 5k steps. Hold old instances for one peak cycle after each step.
  7. Rollback. Before deallocating old reservations, restore routing. After warm reduction, rollback scales from retained templates/quotas and reverses the last 5k step. Stop further reductions if 10-minute evacuation, dependency saturation, or unit-cost gates fail. Keep data topology unchanged during compute migration to avoid coupled risk.
  8. Exercise. At peak replay, isolate A, fence its order writer, promote B only after durable-boundary verification, shift critical traffic, activate degradation, burst compute, and measure dependency quotas, cache miss load, queue age, and reconciliation.
  9. Account. Track monthly compute, reservations, inter-region replication, evacuation egress, and cost per successful order. Capacity owner reviews forecast monthly; product approves degradation; finance validates realized savings; SRE owns evacuation evidence.

docs.title: Worked cost artifact
docs.text:
Assume one 500 req/s unit costs $900/month and reserving burst capacity costs 30% of full price, before actual burst execution charges:

old: 80,000 / 500 * $900                         = $144,000/month
new warm: 48,000 / 500 * $900                    =  $86,400/month
burst option: 12,000 / 500 * $900 * 0.30         =   $6,480/month
new subtotal                                     =  $92,880/month
compute reduction                                = 35.5%

The 25% savings target permits a new total of $144,000 * 0.75 = $108,000/month, leaving $15,120/month for burst execution, witness capacity, replication, egress, tests, or underestimated rates. If those costs exceed $15,120, this topology misses the savings requirement and must be revised. Validate with billed cost, not list price.

In particular, include the third data-bearing region if checkout must continue acknowledging during a data-region outage. Leadership quorum and durability are separate constraints. FinOps Unit Economics calls for documented cost inclusions and business outcomes; the $92,880 compute subtotal is not evidence that the complete resilient design meets the budget (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 7. Interview prompts and signals
docs.text:
• What load remains after one region fails, including retries and cache coldness?
  • Which capacity is guaranteed versus hoped-for burst?
  • What user work is sacrificed first, and who approved it?
  • How do you prove savings without shifting cost downstream?
