docs.title: Control Planes
docs.text: A control plane turns intent into versioned configuration; a data plane serves traffic from validated local state. Separating them limits orchestration failures, but only if serving does not synchronously depend on control availability.

docs.title: 1. Control loop anatomy
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I[Declared intent] --> V[Validate and authorize]
    V --> L[(Versioned desired state)]
    L --> R[Reconcilers]
    R --> A[Agents]
    A --> D[Data-plane snapshot]
    A --> S[Observed status]
    S --> R
    D --> Q[Serve requests locally]

Intent is durable and auditable. Reconcilers are level-triggered: they compare desired and observed state and repeatedly attempt convergence, conditional on reachable dependencies and a feasible desired state. The Kubernetes controller pattern describes this desired/current-state loop (accessed 2026-09-08), not a bounded convergence guarantee. Agents verify signature, schema, scope, safety constraints, and a monotonic activation epoch before atomic local activation. Policy revision IDs identify immutable content but need not increase during rollback: a newer activation epoch may point to an older known-good revision. Serving uses the last-known-good (LKG) snapshot.

Distinguish:

  • Desired state: operator goal, such as policy revision 42 on 5% of fleet.
  • Observed state: agent report, possibly stale.
  • Effective state: locally active version used for decisions.
  • Status: evidence, never authority for reconstructing intent.

docs.title: 2. Freshness and safety budgets
docs.text:
Assumption (2026-09, illustrative): Policy propagation SLO is 99.9% of healthy hosts within 120 seconds. With 60,000 hosts polling every 30 seconds:

average polls/s = 60,000 / 30 = 2,000
with an assumed 2x burst and 3 balanced replicas = about 1,334 requests/s per replica
5 KB response worst case = 10 MB/s fleet egress average

Use content hashes and conditional fetches. Push notification may reduce latency, but hosts must poll to repair missed pushes. A policy's staleness tolerance determines behavior: availability routing may use LKG for hours; a revoked credential or emergency deny rule needs a short lease and fail-closed semantics.

Jitter reduces synchronization; it does not establish a 2x upper bound. At the assumed 4,000 polls/s burst, losing one of three replicas leaves 2,000 requests/s per survivor before retry overhead. Test that failover envelope and count excluded/unreachable hosts separately from the healthy-host propagation SLO, so its denominator cannot hide a regional outage.

docs.title: 3. Policy decision matrix
docs.text:
These expiry values are illustrative policy choices, not vendor defaults. The worked exercise below explicitly chooses a six-hour LKG allowance for ordinary route and limit policies instead.

Policy class During control outage Expiry Rollback method Rationale Request routing weights LKG 24 h activate prior version continuity favored Feature enablement LKG, default off if unseen 24 h prior immutable revision bounded product risk Credential revocation deny after lease 5 min new signed grant security favored Rate limit local conservative floor 1 h prior budget protects fleet Schema compatibility reject unknown writer no implicit expiry deploy compatible readers protects data

Review scope, default, expiry, signature/key rotation, precedence, monotonicity, partial rollout, agent resource cost, and emergency override. Avoid one generic failure policy.

docs.title: 4. Rollout and rollback state machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft
    Draft --> Validated
    Validated --> Ring0
    Ring0 --> Ring1: health gate passes
    Ring1 --> Fleet: SLO and convergence pass
    Fleet --> Superseded
    Fleet --> Reverted: fleet health gate fails
    Ring0 --> Reverted: gate fails
    Ring1 --> Reverted: gate fails
    Reverted --> Validated: corrected revision

Immutable revisions make rollback a new activation of a known artifact, not an edit. Ring membership must be stable enough for comparison and diverse enough to reveal topology-specific faults. Separate distribution success from policy success: 100% delivery of a destructive rule is not health. A route rollback must not restore revoked credentials or erase emergency denies. Keep those controls in a separately ordered security state, or validate the old route revision against current denies before activating it. If the combination is unsafe, use a prevalidated deny posture instead of blindly selecting the parent.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and ownership
docs.text:
Failure Design response Signal Owner Bad policy validates syntactically semantic simulator and blast-radius limit canary outcome delta Policy domain team Reconciler storm jitter, work queue, per-key coalescing queue age and API saturation Control platform Split control leaders consensus revision and compare-and-set conflicting leader term State-store owner Compromised signing key offline root, rotation, revocation bundle invalid/unexpected signer Security Agent disk corruption checksummed dual slots activation failure Runtime platform Status lies due to partitions age all observations stale fraction Fleet operations

The policy owner defines semantics and safe defaults. The control platform owns storage, reconciliation, distribution, and audit. Runtime owners integrate LKG activation. Incident command controls emergency fleet changes. No single operator should author, approve, and globally activate high-blast-radius policy.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: fleet policy control
docs.text: Prompt. Design a policy service for 60,000 edge proxies in 12 regions. It controls routes, rate limits, and emergency denies. Normal changes must reach 99.9% of healthy proxies in two minutes. A control-plane region may be unavailable for six hours, and one bad policy must not take down the fleet.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Model. Store immutable PolicyRevision(id, parent, scope, payload_hash, signer, created_at) and separate Activation(scope, revision, rollout, epoch). Validate route reachability, rate-limit bounds, referenced services, and conflicting rules.
  2. Distribute. Replicate desired state to regional read endpoints. Agents receive push hints, poll with jitter every 30 seconds, fetch by hash, verify signatures, compile in a sandbox, write an inactive slot, then atomically swap.
  3. Serve independently. Proxies evaluate local snapshots. Routes and ordinary limits use LKG for six hours. Emergency deny bundles carry a five-minute lease and are redundantly distributed; expiration uses a domain-approved deny posture for specifically classified resources.
  4. Roll out. Ring 0 contains 60 representative hosts, ring 1 has 600, then 10%, 50%, 100%. Gates compare proxy crash rate, request success by route, policy evaluation latency, and backend overload against matched controls.
  5. Contain. Enforce maximum affected scope per activation. Global changes require two-person approval. If error budget burn exceeds 2x for five minutes, activate the parent revision automatically and freeze further promotion.
  6. Recover. During control outage, regional agents continue LKG and retain two prior revisions. Operators cannot bypass the audit path; a separately secured emergency channel can activate only predeclared safe actions with short expiry.
  7. Rollback intermediate states. Before any activation, discard draft. In rings, activate parent for exposed rings only. During partial fleet rollout, publish a higher activation epoch pointing all scopes to parent; agents never accept lower epochs. If the new revision changed an external dependency, rollback also drains any created state before route reversal.
  8. Operate. Dashboard desired/effective version matrix by region, p50/p99 convergence, stale and rejected hosts, signer distribution, and policy-attributed data-plane SLO. Quarterly exercises sever control connectivity and revoke a signing intermediate.

docs.title: Review matrix
docs.text: Candidate Availability Safety Convergence Auditability Synchronous control lookup per request Low Medium Immediate High Push-only mutable config Medium Low Fast when healthy Low Immutable revisions, push plus repair poll, LKG High High SLO-bound when reachable High

docs.title: 7. Interview prompts and signals
docs.text:
• Which policies expire, and what happens at expiry?
  • How do you distinguish desired, observed, and effective state?
  • Can rollback itself overload the control plane?
  • How does a data-plane host prove what policy decided a request?
L5 signal L6 signal Separates control and data planes Defines degraded semantics per policy class Adds retries and caching Uses level-triggered reconciliation, jitter, LKG, and monotonic activation epochs Uses a canary Designs representative rings, matched evidence, and blast-radius limits Says revert config Treats rollback as immutable activation with state cleanup

docs.title: Distributed Systems Testing
docs.text:
Executable companion: Correctness and fault methods and eight offline fixtures supply input-derived or hand-specified oracles, seeded counterexamples, mutation checks, and explicit physical-model limits. Use their traces as evidence for the test strategy below.

Distributed testing builds evidence about histories, not confidence from test counts. The central question is whether every observed execution satisfies the promised model under concurrency, retries, delay, crash, partition, and recovery.

docs.title: 1. Turn promises into executable properties
docs.text:
Write a hierarchy:

  1. Local invariants: a journal transaction balances per asset.
  2. State-machine rules: only allowed transitions occur.
  3. History properties: acknowledged operations are linearizable where promised.
  4. Convergence: replicas reach equivalent state after communication resumes.
  5. Metamorphic relations: equivalent input transformations preserve expected results.
flowchart LR
    M[Formal model] --> G[Operation generator]
    G --> S[System under test]
    F[Fault schedule] --> S
    S --> H[Timestamped history]
    H --> C[Model checker or oracle]
    C --> X[Shrink failing case]
    X --> R[Regression corpus]

An oracle must not repeat the implementation's mistake. For a ledger, independently sum immutable postings by account and asset. For linearizability, record invocation and completion intervals and verify that a legal sequential ordering exists. Wall-clock ordering alone is invalid for overlapping calls.

Keep timed-out operations in the history as pending/unknown: a checker may need to include them as committed or omit them, but must not assume failure. etcd's operation contract allows an uncertain client outcome after timeout even for strict-serializable KV operations. Record intervals on a trustworthy harness time base; distributed wall clocks without error bounds cannot prove real-time precedence (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 2. Layer the evidence
docs.text:
Layer Finds Technique Limit Static/model protocol design errors state exploration, invariants abstraction gaps Unit/property arithmetic and transitions generated inputs, shrinking concurrency only if explicitly modeled or exercised Component persistence/retry behavior real database and broker narrow topology History concurrency anomalies nemesis plus checker oracle cost Load/soak queues, leaks, tail latency production-like skew weak correctness alone Production unknown interactions shadow, canary, reconciliation must limit blast radius

Use deterministic simulation when time, scheduling, and network are injectable. Use real fault testing to validate assumptions the simulator omits. Chaos without a stated property is theater.

docs.title: Test-volume calculation
docs.text: Settlement closes 2 million batches/day with a defect target below 1 in 10 million batches. Observing zero failures in 10 million independent trials gives an approximate 95% upper bound of 3/N = 3e-7, still three times the target. Testing alone cannot prove rarity; combine preventive invariants, exhaustive checks over smaller models, runtime reconciliation, and fault containment.

docs.title: 3. Consistency review matrix
docs.text:
Operation Required model Generator Oracle Faults Create settlement exactly one semantic batch duplicate/reordered commands unique key plus payload timeout at commit Append posting atomic balanced set concurrent postings per-asset zero sum leader crash Read status monotonic per session roaming readers version never regresses replica lag Claim batch single active owner competing workers fencing epoch partition/lease expiry Export file deterministic prefix retries and restarts content hash at cutoff object-store timeout

State assumptions explicitly: exactly-once delivery is not required if effects are idempotent; a linearizable claim does not make a downstream bank transfer exactly once.

docs.title: 4. Migration and rollback of test infrastructure
docs.text:
Introduce new correctness checks in shadow mode, measure false positives, then make them release-blocking. Version event histories and fault schedules. If a checker changes semantics, run old and new checkers over the same corpus before retiring the old one.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ObserveOnly
    ObserveOnly --> Warn: oracle stable
    Warn --> BlockCanary: false positives bounded
    BlockCanary --> BlockFleet
    BlockFleet --> RetiredOldChecker
    BlockCanary --> Warn: checker regression
    BlockFleet --> Warn: emergency rollback

Rollback disables the gate, not the evidence. Preserve histories that failed either checker and reconcile production state before resuming release.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and ownership
docs.text:
Failure in testing Consequence Control Owner Shared implementation/oracle code common-mode false pass independent model Domain correctness Fault injected before system is ready meaningless pass readiness barriers Test platform Client drops uncertain outcome hidden duplicate/loss record invocation before send Harness owner Clock-based assertion flaky/incorrect order logical versions and intervals Protocol owner Clean shutdown only misses torn recovery process kill and disk/network fault Storage team Nonreproducible random case slow diagnosis seed, schedule, binary artifacts Test platform

Domain teams own properties. Platform teams own deterministic harnesses and fault mechanisms. Release owners own gate policy. Production on-call owns abort authority; experiments must have steady-state hypothesis, blast-radius cap, stop conditions, and cleanup verification.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: settlement correctness testing
docs.text: Prompt. A settlement service groups ledger entries, claims a batch, writes a bank file, submits it, and records acknowledgment. Workers retry after crashes. Design a test program that supports the claim: no entry is settled twice, every eligible entry is eventually resolved, and every file matches an immutable ledger cutoff.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Model. Represent entry states ELIGIBLE -> CLAIMED(epoch) -> FILED(hash, cutoff) -> SUBMITTED(provider_key) -> ACKED, with FAILED_RETRYABLE edges that preserve identity. Persist immutable file membership before submission. Once an entry belongs to any submitted or provider-accepted file, it may not enter another batch, even if the local outcome is unknown or an operator later cancels local work. File contents equal the batch's immutable eligible-entry set at the signed cutoff.
  2. Generate. Vary batch size, duplicated commands, worker races, account skew, late entries, reversals, and provider responses. Generate amounts near integer boundaries and multiple assets; never net across assets.
  3. Inject. Kill the leader before/after claim commit, truncate connections after file upload, delay replica reads, partition workers from the lease service, duplicate broker delivery, return provider timeout after acceptance, and restart from every durable step.
  4. Observe. Record invocation/completion, idempotency key, batch ID, fencing epoch, ledger cutoff, file hash, provider key, and durable transitions. Capture the provider simulator's independent accepted-key log.
  5. Check safety. Verify unique claim ownership, monotonic fencing epochs, balanced source entries, deterministic file hash, and no ACK without a matching accepted file. Independently join every entry ID across all submitted and provider-accepted file manifests and assert at most one provider effect per entry, not merely one effect per provider key. Unknown submissions retain their original provider key and block rebatching until provider lookup or reconciliation resolves them. Run a linearizability checker for claims.
  6. Check liveness. After faults stop and dependencies recover, every eligible entry reaches ACKED or an owned terminal exception within 30 minutes. Bound retries and assert queues drain. This 30-minute bound is an operational recovery requirement stronger than unbounded eventual liveness; state assumptions about restored capacity, finite arrivals, and fair scheduling.
  7. Scale evidence. Exhaustively explore a small model of three workers/five entries, run property tests in CI, nightly real-dependency fault histories, weekly 10x skew soak, and production shadow reconciliation by cutoff.
  8. Migration. Deploy new epoch-aware workers as readers first. Mixed workers may claim only protocol-v1 batches. Create v2 batches after all readers understand epochs; canary v2 claims; then retire v1 creation. Keep v1 recovery code through maximum batch age.
  9. Rollback. Stop new v2 batches, let committed v2 batches finish under epoch rules, route new work to v1, and retain dual readers. Never downgrade an in-flight batch by rewriting its state.

docs.title: Acceptance artifact
docs.text: Suite Gate Failure action Model exploration zero invariant counterexample redesign protocol Property CI 100,000 generated histories/commit shrink and block merge Nightly faults zero safety failure; liveness under 30 min block release Production reconcile zero unexplained amount/entry delta stop submission, page integrity

docs.title: 7. Interview prompts and signals
docs.text:
• Which claims are safety and which are liveness?
  • What independent evidence proves a provider effect occurred once?
  • How would you shrink a failing concurrent history?
  • What mixed-version state exists during an epoch migration?
L5 signal L6 signal Lists unit, integration, load tests Connects formal properties to generators, histories, and independent oracles Injects crashes Targets ambiguity around durable boundaries and validates recovery Says chaos testing Defines hypothesis, schedule, checker, blast radius, and cleanup Tests new version Models mixed protocols and rollback of in-flight state

docs.title: Evolutionary Architecture
docs.text: Evolutionary architecture makes consequential change through reversible, observable steps. The unit of design is not the target diagram; it is the sequence of valid states between today and the target.

docs.title: 1. Frame change as invariants and evidence
docs.text:
Separate four concerns:

  • Invariant: must remain true, such as every accepted ledger transaction balances per asset.
  • Compatibility envelope: versions and schemas that may coexist.
  • Fitness function: automated evidence that architecture remains within bounds.
  • Commit point: the last state from which rollback does not require semantic repair.

For a migration, maintain an invariant ledger:

ID Claim Enforcement Detection Recovery owner L1 Debit plus credit equals zero atomic write validation journal audit Ledger team L2 One effect per idempotency key unique key and request hash duplicate scan API owner L3 Read balance matches journal prefix sequenced projection shadow reconciliation Data integrity on-call L4 No acknowledged write is lost durable commit before ACK source/target high-water marks Storage on-call

Fitness functions should run continuously: schema compatibility in CI, sampled dual-read comparison, full financial reconciliation, dependency latency budgets, and a ban on writes from stale fencing epochs.

docs.title: 2. Design the transition, not only the destination
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SourceOnly
    SourceOnly --> ShadowCopy: backfill plus CDC
    ShadowCopy --> DualRead: target caught up
    DualRead --> TargetCanary: fence source cohort and verify final prefix
    TargetCanary --> TargetPrimary: transfer further disjoint cohorts
    TargetPrimary --> SourceRetained: all source cohorts fenced
    SourceRetained --> Decommissioned: retention expires
    TargetCanary --> DualRead: fence target and reverse replay writes
    TargetPrimary --> DualRead: reconcile reverse replay and fresh epoch

Each state needs entry criteria, permitted writers, source of truth, observability, exit criteria, and rollback action. Dual write by application code is dangerous: timeouts leave ambiguous partial success. Prefer one authoritative commit plus change-data capture (CDC), or a transactional outbox. If dual write is unavoidable, define a reconciliation state machine rather than claiming atomicity across stores.

docs.title: Backfill arithmetic
docs.text:
A 180 TB journal must copy in 14 days. Reserving 30% for retries and scans:

required payload rate = 180 TB / (14 * 86,400 s) = 149 MB/s
provisioned rate      = 149 / 0.70 = 213 MB/s
at 4 KB/row           = about 53,000 rows/s

The logical historical copy is about 37,200 rows/s; the provisioned 53,000 row-equivalents/s includes retry/scan allowance. If production creates 8,000 rows/s, provision the shared ingest path for about 61,000 row-equivalents/s when the full allowance is exercised. CDC alone needs sustained apply above the 8,000 live rows/s plus recovery margin. Do not label historical copies and retries as new CDC rows. Throttle on source replica lag, target compaction debt, and online p99, not a fixed sleep.

docs.title: 3. Decision and review matrix
docs.text:
Score 1 (weak) to 5 (strong); multiply by weight.

Option Correctness 5 Rollback 4 Delivery 3 Operability 3 Total / 75 Flag-day export/import 3 1 2 2 31 App dual write 2 2 3 2 33 Source authority plus CDC 4 5 4 4 64 Log-first rebuild 5 4 2 4 59

The table records assumptions, not truth. Reject an option if it violates L1-L4 regardless of score. Review mixed-version behavior, replay determinism, schema downgrade, clock use, key remapping, and the decommission test.

docs.title: 4. Failure modes and controls
docs.text:
Failure Signal Containment Repair CDC reorders updates sequence gap/version regression stop target promotion replay partition from checkpoint Backfill overwrites newer row target version decreases conditional upsert by source sequence rescan affected range Comparator hides rounding drift amount delta by asset fail canary gate canonical integer representation Target accepts writes after rollback stale-writer probe succeeds fence target epoch reconcile then rotate epoch Old code cannot read expanded schema decode errors in old cohort halt writer rollout restore compatible writer

Rollback is a designed write path. Before target-authoritative writes, route reads back and keep target writes fenced. After the first target-authoritative write for a cohort, rollback requires reverse synchronization and reconciliation; call this a recovery protocol, not an instant routing rollback.

The boundary is the first target-authoritative write for each cohort, not the later shutdown of source writes for all tenants. PostgreSQL logical decoding documents snapshot alignment, duplicate replay after crashes, and stale-primary subscription hazards. Preserve transaction identity and tombstones in both directions; a routing flag cannot recreate missing target-only history (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 5. Operational ownership artifact
docs.text:
Control Directly responsible Approver Page condition Backfill controller Data migration team Ledger principal source lag over 30 s Reconciliation Ledger integrity Finance controller nonzero unexplained delta Traffic promotion Service owner Incident commander error budget burn over 2x Fencing epochs Storage platform Ledger principal two writable authorities Decommission Service owner Compliance and finance evidence package incomplete

Store each gate result, query version, sample scope, and approver in an immutable migration record. Dashboards without decision history do not prove safe execution.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: live ledger migration
docs.text: Prompt. Move a 180 TB, 40,000 transaction/s ledger from a shared relational cluster to tenant-sharded storage and complete the initial copy within 14 days. Each transaction produces an average of two immutable 4 KB journal rows. Posting p99 is 80 ms, downtime budget is 30 seconds, and acknowledged transactions may not be lost or duplicated. Historical reads must remain reproducible. Produce architecture, calculations, stages, rollback, and ownership.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Preserve authority. Keep the old ledger authoritative. Add immutable global txn_id, tenant routing key, source sequence, request hash, and outbox in the existing atomic transaction. Reject unbalanced entries and conflicting idempotency reuse at source.
  2. Prepare target. Create shard map version 1 and target schema with conditional source_sequence upserts. Deploy readers that understand both stores before any data movement.
  3. Backfill. The base copy requires 180 TB / (14 * 86,400) = 149 MB/s; reserving 30% for retries and scans requires 149 / 0.70 = 213 MB/s, about 53,000 4 KB rows/s. Live CDC contributes 40,000 * 2 = 80,000 rows/s, so the target migration path must sustain more than 133,000 rows/s plus write amplification while foreground reads meet their SLO. Copy by stable primary-key ranges and apply outbox events concurrently. A range becomes caught up only when its backfill watermark and CDC partition watermark cover the same source snapshot.
  4. Shadow. Recompute balances from target journals. Require zero transaction-count and signed-sum difference per tenant/asset, zero missing IDs, and sampled historical query equivalence for seven days.
  5. Canary reads. Route 1%, 10%, then 50% of eligible read traffic to target, with source fallback. Roll back routing automatically when the agreed historical-read latency gate fails, mismatch above zero for money fields, or CDC lag over 10 seconds.
  6. Canary writes. For selected tenants, source still commits first; a routing epoch marks target-ready ownership. At cutover, briefly drain those tenant writes, verify the final sequence, grant target epoch 2, then route. The store rejects stale epochs. Install and prove the source write fence before granting the target; changing a router epoch alone cannot revoke an isolated writer. Keep source immutable for migrated tenants, and gate posting at the stated 80 ms p99 independently of read-query latency.
  7. Expand. Promote tenant cohorts by risk and size. Never move two largest tenants together. Reconciliation signs each cohort's source and target cutoffs.
  8. Rollback. Before target writes, switch reads to source. After a tenant receives target writes, use reverse CDC into a separate source recovery table, reconcile, drain, fence epoch 2, import missing target transactions, then grant source epoch 3. This is tested before the first write canary.
  9. Finish. After statutory and rollback retention, remove source credentials, prove stale writes fail, archive manifests, and delete obsolete paths.

The online target peak is at least 40,000 * 1.5 failover factor * 1.2 retry allowance = 72,000 txn/s, before tenant-skew testing. During backfill it must additionally absorb the measured 53,000 historical rows/s and 80,000 live CDC rows/s; transaction rate and row-ingest rate are separate capacity dimensions. The largest tenant must fit one shard or have an explicit sub-sharding plan.

docs.title: 7. Interview prompts and signals
docs.text:
• Where is the point of no return, and how do you move it later?
  • How do backfill and CDC avoid lost updates?
  • What evidence permits source decommissioning?
  • What happens if old and new writers are isolated from each other?
L5 signal L6 signal Describes dual write and cutover Models every intermediate authority state and fences writers Mentions checksums Defines invariant-specific reconciliation and promotion evidence Says rollback via feature flag Distinguishes rollback from forward recovery after the commit point Estimates steady-state QPS Includes migration amplification, skew, retries, and owner capacity

docs.text:

  • AWS Database Migration Service Best Practices, AWS.

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Isolation
docs.text: Multi-tenancy shares resources while preserving explicit boundaries for data, performance, security, failure, and operations. Isolation is not binary. A staff design chooses a level per resource and a path for exceptional tenants.

docs.title: 1. Build an isolation model
docs.text:
Define the blast-radius unit: the maximum tenant set one overload, bad deploy, credential, or operator action can affect. Common models are pooled, namespace-isolated, cell-based, and dedicated.

Dimension Pooled control Stronger boundary Proof Identity tenant context in every request tenant-scoped credentials negative authorization tests Data row key and policy database/account per cell cross-tenant query audit Compute fair queue cell or dedicated workers noisy-neighbor load test Network service authorization per-cell network policy reachability test Operations scoped tooling two-person break-glass immutable access log Encryption shared service key tenant/cell envelope key key-use audit

Never trust a client-provided tenant ID. Derive tenant context from authenticated identity, bind it to resource names and queries, and propagate it through jobs, events, caches, metrics, and support tools.

flowchart TD
    R[Authenticated request] --> D[Tenant directory]
    D --> C{Assigned cell and epoch}
    C --> A[Cell A ingress]
    C --> B[Cell B ingress]
    A --> QA[Fair queue A]
    B --> QB[Fair queue B]
    QA --> DA[(Cell A data)]
    QB --> DB[(Cell B data)]
    P[Global control plane] -. signed placement .-> D

docs.title: 2. Capacity and fairness
docs.text:
For weighted fair sharing, allocate tenant concurrency c_i and enforce both rate and in-flight limits. Rate limits alone do not contain slow requests.

cell effective capacity = 12,000 req/s
safe utilization target = 65% = 7,800 req/s
largest tenant peak     = 1,900 req/s
failure reserve         = 1,500 req/s
admissible normal load  = 7,800 - 1,500 = 6,300 req/s

Place tenants so modeled p99 cell load stays below 6,300 req/s and no two largest tenants share a cell. Include worker time, database IOPS, cache bytes, queue backlog age, and outbound quotas; QPS alone misses noisy neighbors.

docs.title: 3. Placement decision matrix
docs.text:
Model Unit cost Blast radius Custom policy Migration complexity Best use Shared tables Lowest Fleet Low Low initially small homogeneous tenants Schema/database per tenant Medium-high tenant/data service Medium high at scale regulated moderate fleet Cells with pooled tenants Medium bounded cohort High medium broad SaaS default Dedicated stack Highest tenant Highest high contractual or extreme tenants

Review placement using peak resource vector, jurisdiction, encryption boundary, availability tier, maintenance window, and concentration risk. Revenue is not a capacity metric.

docs.title: 4. Tenant move protocol
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HomeA
    HomeA --> Copying: snapshot at S
    Copying --> CatchingUp: replay changes after S
    CatchingUp --> ReadShadow: lag within gate
    ReadShadow --> Draining: comparisons pass
    Draining --> HomeB: fence A, grant B epoch
    HomeB --> AQuarantined: rollback window
    ReadShadow --> HomeA: discard target
    HomeB --> RecoveringA: reverse replay if rollback

The directory record is (tenant, cell, placement_epoch). Every write carries the epoch; stores reject stale epochs. During drain, stop new writes, finish or abort in-flight work, capture final source sequence, verify target replay, then atomically publish the new placement. Cached directories have bounded validity and must fail closed for writes after expiry.

Directory unavailability must not require a fresh lookup on every request: cache signed placement locally and honor its expiry at the actual write boundary. Separate the placement service's CAS from each cell's installed write guard. A cell isolated before transfer cannot learn a new epoch merely because the directory committed it; prove its old lease has safely expired or externally fence it before enabling the successor. This applies the controller desired/current-state distinction, not an assumption of instantaneous propagation (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and ownership
docs.text:
Failure Containment Recovery Owner Hot tenant saturates DB per-tenant queue and DB budget throttle or move tenant Cell service Directory unavailable cached signed placement for reads restore quorum; writes honor lease Placement platform Cross-tenant cache key include tenant and policy version purge namespace, investigate access Service and security Partial tenant move single writer epoch replay and reconcile Migration controller Cell loss admission plus spare capacity restore/move by availability tier Regional on-call Operator bulk action scoped plan and approval halt job, replay audit Support platform

Operational dashboards must expose cell saturation and tenant contribution without leaking tenant data. Page on user impact and exhausted isolation budgets, not merely a busy tenant. The platform owns placement and fencing; service teams own tenant-safe keys and resource attribution; security owns boundary controls and incident classification.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: SaaS cell migration
docs.text: Prompt. A pooled project-management SaaS has 24,000 tenants, 18,000 req/s peak, one database, and a 4x traffic-skew tenant. Move to four cells without more than 60 seconds of write unavailability. Premium tenants require a 99.99% SLO and EU residency.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Classify and place. Inventory canonical rows, blobs, search documents, events, caches, audit logs, keys, and jobs by tenant. Operate at least two independent EU cells for EU premium tenants; their data, backups, keys, telemetry containing tenant data, and failover routes remain in the approved EU boundary. Non-EU tenants use a separate cell pool. Add a server-derived tenant context and test every access path.
  2. Size by residency pool. With 2x projected growth, global peak is 36,000 req/s. Four cells at 15,000 req/s raw and 65% target provide 39,000 req/s safe capacity, but evacuation of one leaves 29,250 req/s. Surviving three cells need 36,000 / 3 = 12,000 req/s safe each, or 12,000 / 0.65 = 18,462 req/s raw each, about a 23.1% uplift; provision at least 18,500 raw per cell or define explicit standard-tenant shedding. Repeat this calculation independently for the EU pair because global spare capacity outside the EU cannot evacuate EU tenants. Premium replicas, dependency quotas, and keys must be ready in the second EU cell before claiming 99.99% continuity.
  3. Introduce routing. Deploy directory reads and placement epochs while all records still point to legacy cell A. This is behavior-preserving and independently reversible.
  4. Seed cells. Snapshot tenant-consistent data, copy blobs, build search indexes from canonical data, and replay an outbox from snapshot sequence. Jobs remain disabled in targets to prevent duplicate effects.
  5. Shadow. Compare counts, canonical hashes, authorization outcomes, and business aggregates. Read shadow traffic does not answer users. Promotion requires zero security mismatches, zero missing canonical records, and lag below 5 seconds for 24 hours.
  6. Move cohorts. Start with internal tenants, then small standard tenants, then premium. Drain one tenant, fence A epoch 7, verify B through final sequence, publish epoch 8, enable B jobs, and release writes. The hard migration gate is no more than 60 seconds of write unavailability. For a 99.99% monthly SLO, 60 seconds consumes about 23.1% of the 4.32-minute monthly budget, so premium moves must be infrequent, budgeted, and measured separately from ordinary incidents.
  7. Rollback. Before B writes, repoint to A. After B writes, keep A immutable, reverse-replay B into a recovery namespace, reconcile, drain B, grant A epoch 9, then route. Never make both writable.
  8. Contain. Set per-tenant concurrency, worker, storage, and outbound budgets. Place the 4x tenant alone or split its workload only if data invariants permit. Reserve premium evacuation capacity within the same residency boundary and test EU-cell loss, writer fencing, dependency quotas, and RPO/RTO quarterly.
  9. Retire. After the rollback window, delete old tenant copies through the lifecycle workflow, revoke the migrated tenant's old-cell credentials and key grants, and retain signed migration evidence. Revoke shared cell keys only after every remaining tenant and retained artifact has been migrated or retired.

docs.title: Review artifact
docs.text: Gate Threshold Rollback trigger Authority Copy complete all manifests and blob hashes present any canonical gap Migration lead Shadow 24 h, zero auth/data mismatch first boundary mismatch Security incident lead Canary p99 under 250 ms, burn under 1x 2x burn for 10 min Service on-call Cohort target below 65% resource vector any hard resource over 80% Capacity owner

docs.title: 7. Interview prompts and signals
docs.text:
• What exactly is isolated, and which resources remain shared?
  • How do you prevent a stale router from writing to the old cell?
  • How do global operations respect residency and tenant authorization?
  • When does a dedicated tenant become cheaper than pooled complexity?
L5 signal L6 signal Adds tenant_id and rate limits Defines identity, data, compute, operator, and failure boundaries Proposes cells Quantifies placement, concentration, and evacuation reserve Mentions migration Specifies authority epochs, intermediate states, and post-write rollback Monitors cell CPU Attributes multidimensional saturation to tenants and assigns owners

docs.title: Operational Readiness
docs.text: Operational readiness is evidence that a service can enter production, fail predictably, and recover under named ownership. A checklist is useful only when every item has a measurable gate and an authority who can block launch.

docs.title: 1. Turn risk into operating contracts
docs.text:
Start with critical user journeys and loss modes. Define service-level indicators (SLIs), objectives (SLOs), dependencies, overload policy, recovery objectives, and irreversible invariants. See Reliability for the baseline vocabulary.

flowchart TD
    J[Critical journey] --> I[Invariant and SLI]
    I --> B[Error and capacity budgets]
    B --> C[Containment controls]
    C --> T[Load and failure evidence]
    T --> G{Launch gate}
    G -->|pass| R[Progressive release]
    G -->|fail| F[Reduce scope or delay]
    R --> O[Operate, learn, revise]

docs.title: Error-budget arithmetic
docs.text:
A 99.95% monthly availability SLO allows:

30-day bad minutes = 30 * 24 * 60 * 0.0005 = 21.6 minutes
5-minute incident  = 23.1% of monthly budget
14x burn for 30 minutes = 14 * 30 / 43,200 = 0.972% of budget

Page on multi-window burn rate to catch fast disasters and slow leaks. Availability must measure valid user outcomes; HTTP 200 with an empty checkout is not success.

docs.title: 2. Readiness review matrix
docs.text:
Dimension Required artifact Blocking evidence Correctness invariant and reconciliation spec injected duplicate/timeout passes Reliability SLO and dependency budget load plus failure test at peak Capacity resource model and scaling limit 2x forecast or explicit admission plan Recovery RTO/RPO runbook timed restore/failover exercise Observability journey SLIs and change correlation synthetic fault pages correct owner Security/privacy threat and data-flow review least privilege and deletion tested Operations on-call, escalation, rollback game day with unfamiliar responder Change safety canary and stop conditions automatic rollback tested

Risk acceptance records impact, probability, compensating control, expiry, and accountable executive. It is not a permanent waiver.

docs.title: 3. Contain overload before scaling
docs.text:
Use admission control at the earliest trusted boundary, separate priority queues, finite concurrency, bounded retries with jitter, deadlines, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation. Reserve capacity for recovery and control traffic.

If 50,000 checkout requests/s each call inventory, pricing, and payment once, baseline traffic is 150,000 dependency calls/s. Two additional retries per dependency call raise the worst case to 50,000 * 3 * 3 = 450,000 attempts/s. A 10% retry budget relative to baseline dependency calls permits 15,000 additional calls/s fleet-wide, or 5,000 per dependency with equal allocation. State that denominator explicitly; a budget relative to user requests is a different policy.

Google's SLO alerting guidance separates error ratios, budget consumption, and multiwindow gates. The bad-minute conversions above assume a time-based objective or uniform request traffic; sale-hour failures can consume a much larger fraction of a request-based budget (accessed 2026-09-08).

Work Priority During overload Correctness Confirm paid order Critical durably admit only within reserved queue/capacity deduplicate; bounded completion or owned reconciliation New checkout High token admission explicit rejection Cart recommendation Low omit best effort Analytics export Background pause replay later

docs.title: 4. Release and rollback states
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Dark
    Dark --> Internal
    Internal --> OnePercent
    OnePercent --> TenPercent
    TenPercent --> FiftyPercent
    FiftyPercent --> Full
    OnePercent --> RolledBack
    TenPercent --> RolledBack
    FiftyPercent --> RolledBack
    Full --> Mitigated: feature disable or forward fix

Schema and state changes use expand-contract. Rollback before new persistent state can route to the prior binary. After incompatible effects or external side effects, stop exposure, preserve evidence, compensate idempotently, and forward-fix. State this boundary in the launch plan.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and ownership
docs.text: Failure Containment Detection Decision owner Retry storm retry budget and deadline attempts/request, queue age Service on-call Autoscaler lags burst prewarm and admission saturation before latency Capacity owner Dependency returns plausible bad data semantic validation business invariant SLI Domain owner Dashboard/control path fails independent probes and static runbook telemetry heartbeat Incident commander Rollback cannot read new schema compatibility gate old-reader canary Release owner On-call overload bounded alerts and incident roles page volume/ack time Engineering manager

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: sale failure containment
docs.text: Prompt. Launch a two-hour sale expected to peak at 250,000 browse requests/s and 40,000 checkout attempts/s. Inventory is finite, payment capacity is 12,000 requests/s, normal checkout is 6,000/s, and marketing cannot postpone. Prevent oversell, payment collapse, and fleet-wide failure.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Define invariants. Confirmed units never exceed allocated stock; a payment result has one order effect; accepted checkout receives a terminal result; browse loss cannot starve paid-order confirmation.
  2. Budget. Payment leaves 12,000 - 6,000 = 6,000/s incremental capacity before uncertainty. Keep a measured reserve for latency, confirmations, retries, and normal-traffic variance; if that reserve is 1,000/s, admit at most 5,000 sale checkouts/s. Queueing all 40,000 attempts/s would create hours of stale demand. Issue short-lived admission tokens and reject excess explicitly.
  3. Partition failure. Put browse, checkout admission, inventory reservation, payment initiation, and confirmation in separate pools and queues. Cache static sale pages. Reserve 20% checkout compute and queue throughput for confirmations, expiries, and reconciliation.
  4. Protect stock. Allocate inventory rights by shard. Reservation is atomic and expires; capture and expiry race on a version. Do not use a stale cache as stock authority. Stable idempotency keys cover client retries and provider callbacks. An unknown payment does not prove that reserved stock is safe to release. Keep a separately owned pending-payment state, or define a late-success path that reacquires stock or issues an authorized refund; never confirm an order after expiry without proving available rights.
  5. Shape retries. Allow at most one retry within the original deadline and only under the provider's safe-retry contract, preserving the same key and payload. An unknown payment outcome requires reconciliation; same-key retry is safe only if the receiver deduplicates concurrent attempts within the retained-key window. A stale negative lookup is insufficient. Cap aggregate retries at 10% of admitted traffic. Open payment circuits by provider/operation, not globally.
  6. Rehearse. Load 1.5x forecast: 375,000 browse/s and 60,000 checkout/s. Inject payment latency, cache loss, one inventory shard loss, queue slowdown, and telemetry failure. Pass only if invariants hold and critical queues remain bounded.
  7. Release. Dark launch metrics, employee event, 1% geography, then full sale. Because demand is time-bound, gates use both SLO and saturation. Freeze unrelated deploys and name incident command before launch.
  8. Rollback/degrade. Before reservations, disable sale admission instantly. With reservations active, stop new tokens, continue confirmations and expiries, and reconcile unknown payments. Never roll back by deleting reservations. If payment capacity halves, lower token issuance to measured capacity and preserve status reads.
  9. Own. Commerce owns admission and customer status; inventory owns rights and oversell invariant; payments owns provider budget and reconciliation; platform owns cell capacity; incident command alone changes global limits.

docs.text: Gate Pass Stop/rollback Peak load p99 under 800 ms at 1.5x critical pool over 70% sustained Correctness zero oversell/duplicate effects first invariant breach Dependency loss confirmations drain within 10 min unbounded queue age Recovery state reconciles to zero unknowns unexplained payment after 30 min

docs.title: Organizational Architecture
docs.text: Architecture defines how teams coordinate as much as how services call one another. A staff engineer reduces the cognitive load and change coupling of the organization without turning every reporting line into a network boundary.

docs.title: 1. Measure boundaries by change
docs.text:
Conway's law predicts that system communication reflects organizational communication. Use it diagnostically: inspect which changes require synchronized releases, shared database edits, cross-team approvals, and incident handoffs.

flowchart LR
    P[Product outcomes] --> C[Business capabilities]
    C --> T[Team ownership]
    T --> A[APIs and event contracts]
    A --> D[Data authority]
    D --> O[On-call and SLO]
    O -. operational learning .-> C

A good boundary has cohesive change, one authoritative data owner, explicit contracts, independent deployability where valuable, and end-to-end operational responsibility. A service with shared tables and mandatory lockstep deployment is not autonomous.

docs.title: 2. Quantify coordination and load
docs.text:
Track:

  • change coupling: fraction of changes needing another team;
  • lead time and blocked time;
  • cross-team incident handoffs;
  • API/schema breaking-change rate;
  • cognitive load: domains, runbooks, and technologies a team must master.

If 120 monthly changes each involve an average 2.4 teams, there are 120 * (2.4 - 1) = 168 extra team-change involvements. Reducing average involvement to 1.5 removes 108 such involvements/month. This does not count meetings or pairwise communication: one involvement can generate many coordination events. This is directional: weight security reviews and routine automated dependencies differently.

docs.title: 3. Boundary decision matrix
docs.text:
Score candidate capability boundaries before extracting services.

Criterion Weight Evidence Change cohesion 5 files/issues usually change together inside boundary Data authority 5 one team can own writes and invariants Runtime isolation need 3 distinct scale, availability, or security profile Contract stability 4 semantics can be stated and versioned Team cognitive fit 4 domain fits durable team mission Migration reversibility 3 seam can be introduced before network split

Prefer a modular monolith when boundaries remain uncertain or transactions dominate. Extract when independent evolution, isolation, or scaling value exceeds distributed coordination cost.

Structure Strength Failure mode Component team deep technical leverage queues and handoffs by layer Stream-aligned team owns user outcome duplicated platform work Platform team lowers cognitive load as a product mandatory ticket-driven gatekeeper Enabling team accelerates adoption temporarily permanent dependency

The Team Topologies authors also identify complicated-subsystem teams for concentrated specialist expertise. Pair team type with an interaction mode: time-boxed collaboration to discover a seam, facilitation to transfer skills, or X-as-a-Service once the contract stabilizes. For the catalog extraction, write a six-week collaboration exit gate: independent deployment plus a self-service contract test, not a permanent weekly approval meeting (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: 4. Safe decomposition migration
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SharedMonolith
    SharedMonolith --> ModularBoundary
    ModularBoundary --> InternalContract
    InternalContract --> ShadowService
    ShadowService --> RoutedCohort
    RoutedCohort --> IndependentService
    ShadowService --> InternalContract: discard extraction
    RoutedCohort --> InternalContract: compatible data and writer fenced

First assign ownership and enforce module APIs inside the process. Separate tables logically and stop cross-boundary writes. Add an outbox and contract tests. Only then introduce a network. This creates an early rollback: route back to the in-process implementation while both consume compatible data.

After the new service becomes sole writer, rollback requires reverse synchronization or forward repair. Keep old code read-compatible through the rollback window. Avoid a permanent bidirectional database bridge; it obscures authority.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and operating model
docs.text:
Failure Symptom Structural response Owner Distributed monolith lockstep releases versioned contracts and independent tests Domain leads Shared-data ownership unauthorized schema writes one write API/owner Data owner Platform bottleneck ticket queues self-service paved road and SLO Platform product lead Orphan service pages bounce teams catalog owner and escalation Engineering leadership Boundary too fine chatty synchronous graph merge capability or localize workflow Architecture group Boundary too broad team cognitive overload split by change/data authority Team manager

Every capability needs one accountable owner for roadmap, contract, data, SLO, cost, security, and decommissioning. Shared stewardship usually means no one can make a time-critical decision. Architecture forums set principles and resolve cross-cutting risks; they should not approve routine implementation.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: monolith and team split
docs.text: Prompt. A 70-engineer commerce organization has one monolith and shared database. Catalog, checkout, order, payment, and fulfillment changes collide. Releases occur weekly; 45% require three or more teams, and incidents average four handoffs. Reorganize and evolve the architecture without pausing roadmap delivery.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Map work. Use six months of commits, incidents, and product plans to map change coupling and business invariants. Identify catalog, checkout orchestration, order lifecycle, payment, and fulfillment as candidate capabilities, but keep checkout/order together initially if their transaction boundary changes weekly.
  2. Assign teams. Create durable stream-aligned teams around outcomes. A platform team owns build/deploy, observability, service identity, and event tooling as self-service products. A temporary enabling team helps module and contract adoption.
  3. Create internal seams. Add module ownership rules, typed interfaces, and architecture tests. Only the payment module writes payment tables; other modules call it. Introduce stable IDs, idempotency, and an outbox. This stage delivers value without network failure modes.
  4. Choose first extraction. Extract catalog reads because they scale differently and tolerate staleness. Payment may have high isolation value but demands a stronger correctness migration; do it after the extraction path is proven.
  5. Migrate catalog. Backfill catalog service, replay outbox, shadow compare, canary reads, then make it authoritative for writes using an ownership epoch. Intermediate state retains monolith read fallback. Once new writes begin, rollback drains, reverse-replays, fences, and routes to the old module.
  6. Change contracts. Version APIs/events, publish compatibility windows, consumer-driven tests, and deprecation telemetry. Avoid shared client releases that recreate lockstep coupling.
  7. Own operations. Each stream team owns on-call and SLO for its path. The checkout journey has a cross-service SLO with one incident commander; component owners remain responsible for diagnosis and repair. Platform publishes adoption and ticket-deflection metrics.
  8. Measure. Quarterly targets: changes involving 3+ teams from 45% to below 20%, median incident handoffs from four to two, and release frequency from weekly to daily per capability, without worsening checkout SLO or cost per order.
  9. Rollback organization changes. Do not move people weekly. If a boundary fails, merge ownership missions deliberately while preserving contract/data evidence. A reporting rollback does not automatically justify recombining runtime services.

docs.title: Review artifact
docs.text: Decision Evidence after 90 days Adaptation trigger Catalog extraction independent deploys, lower monolith read load cross-service changes exceed 30% Platform team self-service adoption, ticket lead time down tickets rise for two quarters Checkout/order joint ownership fewer handoffs, stable invariant missions/cognitive load exceed team capacity Payment next incident and compliance isolation benefit protocol/ownership not yet stable

docs.text:
• Which data has one writer during and after the split?
  • What should remain a module rather than a service?
  • How do you know the organization improved rather than moved queues?
  • Who owns a cross-service user journey during an incident?

docs.title: Privacy and Data Lifecycle
docs.text: Privacy architecture governs data from collection through deletion and restored backups. The staff problem is to make policy executable across canonical stores, derivatives, logs, models, vendors, exports, and disaster recovery.

docs.title: 1. Establish data authority and purpose
docs.text:
Maintain a data inventory whose unit is a typed field or dataset, not merely a database.

Attribute Required decision Subject and tenant whose data and authorization scope Purpose permitted use and prohibited secondary use Authority canonical source and lawful/contractual basis Classification sensitivity and residency Propagation topics, replicas, caches, indexes, vendors Retention trigger, period, hold exceptions Deletion erase, anonymize, retain, or suppress Evidence manifest, completion, exception approval

Data minimization reduces both risk and deletion fan-out. Pseudonymization lowers direct identifiability but is not deletion if re-linking remains possible.

flowchart TD
    C[Collection with purpose] --> A[(Canonical record)]
    A --> E[Events]
    E --> I[Indexes and caches]
    E --> N[Analytics]
    A --> B[Backups]
    A --> V[Approved vendor]
    D[Deletion authority] --> W[Erasure workflow]
    W --> A
    W --> I
    W --> N
    W --> V
    W --> T[(Tombstone log)]
    T --> RB[Quarantined restore gate]
    B --> RB
    RB -->|absence checks pass| REST[Restored serving state]
    subgraph ProjectionLane[Derived data]
      E
      I
      N
    end
    subgraph RestoreLane[Restore protection]
      B
      T
      RB
      REST
    end

docs.title: 2. Deletion is a distributed workflow
docs.text:
Assign a stable, opaque subject_key that reveals no direct identifier. It remains linkable pseudonymous data, so classify, access-control, retain, and delete it accordingly. A deletion command contains request ID, verified scope, policy version, effective time, and exceptions. Each processor is idempotent and reports an authenticated outcome. The coordinator tracks obligations, not a best-effort fan-out.

Backups are usually immutable. Rather than rewriting every backup, deny normal access, delete active copies, retain a tombstone ledger at least as long as the oldest backup, and reapply tombstones during any restore before serving. Crypto-erasure can help when data has a unique, destroyable encryption key, but shared keys or residual plaintext invalidate the claim.

Deleting the current KEK is insufficient if an older wrapped DEK and a usable old KEK survive in backups or escrow. Inventory the whole key recovery chain and verify destruction or inaccessible retention at every copy. NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2, published September 2025, supersedes Rev. 1 and frames sanitization as making access infeasible at a stated effort level; it does not certify an application's subject-deletion workflow (accessed 2026-09-08).

docs.title: Throughput calculation
docs.text:
For 50 million subjects and a policy-triggered deletion wave of 2% in 24 hours:

requests = 50,000,000 * 0.02 = 1,000,000
average  = 1,000,000 / 86,400 = 11.6 subjects/s
30 sink obligations per subject             = 30,000,000 / 86,400 ~= 347.22 operations/s
up to 3 retries means 4 attempts/obligation  ~= 1,388.89 attempts/s
design peak at 5x average                    ~= 6,944.45 attempts/s

Capacity must include slow vendors and reindexing. Bound per-destination concurrency so deletion does not take production down.

docs.title: 3. Policy decision matrix
docs.text:
Data class Active-store action Backup action Proof Exception Profile PII hard delete tombstone on restore absence query plus manifest legal hold Financial journal retain required facts, remove optional PII retain protected field-level policy result statutory retention Search index delete document rebuild from cleansed source index generation check none Aggregate metric retain if no reasonable link unchanged re-identification review suppress small cohorts Support export revoke and delete object no unmanaged backup access/object audit active case hold

Legal counsel determines obligations; architecture enforces the resulting policy. Do not present a technical pattern as universal legal advice.

docs.title: 4. Migration and rollback
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> InventoryOnly
    InventoryOnly --> ShadowDelete
    ShadowDelete --> DualEvidence
    DualEvidence --> Enforced
    Enforced --> LegacyRetired
    ShadowDelete --> InventoryOnly: false scope
    DualEvidence --> ShadowDelete: processor defect

In shadow mode, compute obligations without erasing and compare with legacy policy. In dual-evidence mode, the old process remains authoritative while the new workflow executes approved test subjects and records manifests. Once destructive deletion begins, rollback means stop new work and restore only records deleted in error from a quarantined, access-controlled recovery copy when policy permits. Never silently resurrect data; require privacy and security approval, notify downstream processors, and issue a new lifecycle event.

Use expand-contract for identifiers: emit old and new subject keys, teach all processors both, backfill mappings, switch deletion authority, then retire old keys only after maximum event and backup age.

docs.title: 5. Failure modes and ownership
docs.text:
Failure Control Evidence Owner Unknown derivative lineage registration blocks new sink inventory coverage Data governance Recreated cache/index entry deletion tombstone dominates updates resurrection probe Dataset owner Vendor misses request contract, retry, escalation vendor receipt Vendor owner Legal hold ignored policy engine excludes scoped records hold decision audit Legal/privacy Backup restore resurrects data mandatory tombstone replay gate restore manifest Backup platform Logs contain raw identifier structured redaction at source sampled scanner Service owner

The privacy platform owns workflow and evidence schema. Dataset owners implement processors and SLOs. Security owns access and key destruction. Privacy/legal owns policy interpretation and exceptions. Incident command can pause deletion but cannot waive obligations.

docs.title: 6. Complete case exercise: global deletion
docs.text: Prompt. A global collaboration product stores account data in US and EU databases, object storage, search, analytics, logs, backups, and three vendors. It must fulfill verified deletion within 30 days while retaining legally required invoices. Design the end-to-end mechanism, migration, rollback, and proof.

docs.title: Worked solution
docs.text:
1. Scope. Verify requester and tenant authority. Resolve account to regional subject_key; never route from an untrusted region header. Freeze new purpose-based processing and revoke sessions immediately.
  2. Plan. A policy engine expands obligations by jurisdiction, dataset version, retention, and legal hold. Invoice facts retain amount, tax, legal entity, and dates; remove optional profile fields and sever the account lookup according to approved policy.
  3. Execute. Persist the command in the subject's home region. Regional workers delete canonical PII and objects, emit tombstones, purge caches/search, suppress or delete linkable analytics, and call vendors with stable request IDs. Global status contains only approved minimal metadata. Opaque subject or request IDs can still be linkable personal data; regional policy must permit each exported field rather than treating all metadata as automatically safe.
  4. Order safely. Tombstone first, then derivatives, then canonical record. This prevents delayed CDC from recreating derivatives. Writers reject updates dominated by a later lifecycle epoch.
  5. Backups. Keep tombstones for backup retention plus restore margin. Every restore enters quarantine, replays the full tombstone range and policy transforms, runs absence checks, then receives serving credentials.
  6. Prove. Produce a manifest listing processor, dataset generation, policy revision, result hash, completion time, and exception. Sample absence queries use one-way test tokens. Vendor receipts and approved invoice-retention decisions attach to the case.
  7. Migrate. Inventory first; deploy subject keys and tombstone-aware consumers; shadow plans for 30 days; test synthetic subjects; dual-run evidence; then make the new coordinator authoritative. New sinks cannot launch without a lifecycle processor.
  8. Rollback. Before destructive execution, cancel the plan. After execution, stop remaining processors. If deletion was unauthorized and restoration is legally permitted, restore to quarantine, reauthorize purpose, issue a higher lifecycle epoch, repopulate only approved stores, and audit every access. Otherwise deletion is intentionally irreversible.
  9. Operate. SLOs: 99% processor completion in 7 days, all deletion obligations complete by day 30, and zero post-tombstone resurrection. Only a policy-authorized legal hold or statutory-retention decision may exempt specific data; an owned operational failure remains a deadline breach and cannot be relabeled an exception. Forecast deadline risk continuously and page early enough to preserve remediation time, with a mandatory escalation no later than day 7 for any request projected to miss day 30.
